If you can build protobuf's unit tests, you can follow its configuration to configure your own projects. Also make sure you are using the latest releases and following instructions in the README.md file correctly.

title: C# handling of wrapper types with explicit default values
body:
Very much a corner case, but merging a message stream which contains (say) an Int32Value with an explicit value=0 into a message which has an Int32Value field with a non-zero value will behave differently in C# code to code on other platforms.

We have a test for this (demonstrating the wrong behaviour) at the moment in WrappersTest, but we should fix it when we can.

nodes.body: I've had a closer look at this, and I believe that fixing it would do more harm than good. This would be an _incredibly_ obscure corner case (even just merging a stream "into" an existing object is pretty rare, IME, and you'd basically only see this if it were deliberately constructed). The fix would probably require using a special new FieldCodec-like type with more abilities, making the code either more complicated, slower or both.

title: C# Custom JSON formatting and parsing for FieldMask well known type
body:
FieldMask uses a custom JSON format.

https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto#L131

nodes.body: we probably don't need this for the initial release.
I think it's probably worth covering as many of the WKT as possible for JSON formatting, at least where it's simple - and this one sounds pretty trivial :)
The formatting is now implemented. Parsing of FieldMask will be done as part of a bigger parsing effort.

title: Mention C# in protobuf docs at developers.google.com
body:
Once C# is released, it should be mentioned here:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3

nodes.body: And appropriately documented, of course. Before the final release we'll want to include generated documentation too, like https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java/index. We should probably start investigating which tool we want to use for that.

I don't have experience with Sandcastle which you originally mentioned as one of our possible choices. For gRPC, I might just use Doxygen, because gRPC is a multi-language project and we will definitely use Doxygen for (at least some) other languages, it might outweigh the fact that doxygen is perhaps less .NET oriented than some other solutions.

The google-api-dotnet-client (Apiary client library) uses Doxygen.
Okay - will certainly give that a try as one option.
We have tech writer who can help with the document. Have send both of you the email
This is now done, in terms of the "generated code guide" and the tutorial. We still need to publish the runtime API (javadoc equivalent) but that is in progress. Closing this issue.

title: C# Custom JSON formatting and parsing for struct well known type
body: even though struct.proto fails to mention that, I think https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/struct.proto should use a custom JSON format.

nodes.body: Other than Any support (which is a separate feature on its own, really) I think all the WKTs now format appropriately. We don't have any JSON parsing support at all yet. Closing this issue for now.

title: Move Coded*Stream.CreateInstance(Stream) to constructors
body: (Unless there's some good reason not to.)

title: Validate that C# code doesn't depend unnecessarily on field ordering
body:
I have a nagging suspicion that we may sometimes be assuming field _number_ order when we've actually got field _declaration_ order instead.

Places where this is relevant:
- Tying generated types to MessageDescriptors (messages rather than fields, so may not be a problem)
- Serialization
- JSON formatting

There may be no changes required, but we should validate that.

nodes.body:
JSON formatting is now fixed (including oneofs) in 4fed0b515fb18b0ffc6f5d382f38e2a1b39912dd.
Tying generated types to message descriptors has been overhauled.
Serialization explicitly uses field number ordering already. Closing.

title: ctype=CORD is broken in open source release
body: DynamicMessageTest.Oneof triggers a heap-use-after-free AddressSanitizer failure because ctype=CORD is half-implemented in DynamicMessage. Commenting out all of the uses of bar_cord in src/google/protobuf/test_util.cc fixes the issue in the tests. According to discussion at https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/protobuf/ICjZgOSMVJA, It sounds like the correct solution is for the compiler to ignore ctype=CORD.

title: Invalid Unicode characters possible with \U escape
body: When parsing \U escape, the fifth symbol is not properly checked, allowing for sequences like \U001FFFFF to be parsed and then converted into UTF-8. According to wiki, these values are not considered valid in UTF-8 even though they can be encoded.

nodes.body: Which language are you using?

I'm using protoc built from master branch. Looking at source code, it seems to me that this is also the case in csharp-experimental and protoc-alpha-3.1 branches.
The resulting invalid strings can be passed into package/namespace names in target language, they are stored for custom option values and could in theory resurface somewhere deep in the user code that reads these options.
Can you give an example of what you mean by "when parsing \U escape"? Do you mean when converting from JSON to protobuf? The context isn't clear at the moment.

Can you elaborate on why you think `\U001FFFFF` should be rejected?

`U+1FFFFF` appears to be a currently unallocated code point. But I don't see anything about it saying it is invalid or should be rejected by tools.

Checking for surrogate pair values probably makes sense though.

title: Investigate support for Unity
body:
quoting @jskeet:
"There's suspicion the current version of C# protobufs won't work with Unity, but we can add another build target for that later when we find a need - we can create a new minor version of the NuGet package for that with no problems. 

My experience with the "old" protobuf-csharp-port is that Unity on iOS has various issues, so I think we'll want to investigate them pretty thoroughly before trying to support it anyway - and we may need to conditionally compile out some features. We'll see... but I'd like to avoid having Unity support block a dotnetcore release."

also see #638

nodes.body: Three +1s in the space of a few minutes suggests this is being linked to from somewhere - it would be nice if someone could provide the context. It would be even nicer if someone with Unity support could try this and inform us where there are problems :)

I can only speak for myself, but in my case we are developing a mobile game with Unity and a Java backend. In order to keep our client compatible with iOS, we are using protobuf-net. Unfortunately, protobuf-net has some known bugs and does not support the latest Protobuf versions, so an official solution from Google would be very interesting for us.

@jayallanjethwa: But how did you happen to reach this issue? It seems unlikely that three people would find an issue raised nearly two months ago entirely independently but within the same 5 minute window. I'm only asking so that I can try to get more context that might help resolve the issue. (I'd love to be able to support Unity - but I foresee some tricky issues, based on previous experience of bug reports.)

@asuuma: Right. Supporting both .NET 3.5 and modern PCLs is painful. I'm hoping that it won't be _too_ long before Unity moves on in terms of runtime - after all, .NET 4.0 was released a _long_ time ago. Could you give the details of the stack trace around `Reflection.Emit`? I suspect the problem is the use of expression trees, which would be feasible to fix, though annoying.

(I'm going to need to balance the importance of supporting a wide variety of platforms with the additional code maintenance headaches and possible performance degredations of doing so. The more I know before making this judgement call, the better...)

@jskeet Yeah, everyone are hoping to move on newer runtime in near future... They opened [roadmap](http://unity3d.com/jp/unity/roadmap) of Unity and it says they are researching about upgrading .NET profile.
Here is the stack trace.

```

Right, thanks - so that is expression tree compilation. It's definitely _feasible_ to write a workaround for that particular one.
@asuuma Could you elaborate on what you did to workaround the .NET version mismatch?

I've applied this patch (without the commented out code) and can confirm this work in unity3d 5.2.2f
This also keeps working when used in a WebGL export. Although i am not using any fancy protobuf features (only string, int, etc and repeated)
Note that with this patch, it won't work with CoreCLR, which is a more important initial target for us. I don't think it's feasible to support both platforms with a single binary.

Agreed, but it would be nice if unity could be supported somehow untill they finally decide to move away from their ancient mono version.
Even a simple readme note for unity users revering to this issue ticket would be enough.

I wouldn't feel comfortable claiming something was "supported" via just a patch with consumers building the code themselves afterwards. This patch is a good starting point for fuller support, but I'd rather get the first version publicly released with just CoreCLR (and therefore normal desktop .NET) support to start with, then revisit.

+1

I've also applied the patch, and have protobuf v3.0.0-beta-2 working in my mod for Kerbal Space Program (running in Unity). I also ran the nunit tests which all passed (although I removed Google.Protobuf.Test.Compatibility)
@jskeet Thanks for your statement. Do you have a rough idea of how the timeline for this could look like?

I don't have any plans at the moment... I'd be very surprised to see it before protobuf 3.0 goes GA. We can look at it again after that.

It's not just a matter of fixing the code itself - it's making sure we can test and maintain it appropriately.

(Any sign of Unity moving off the ancient CLR they use yet? I'd hope that they're looking into CoreCLR now it's nearing release...)

I think it is unlikely that Unity moves off their CLR. They have their own Mono fork and it contains a bug which is already fixed in original Mono repo 5 years ago. I guess merging branches forked at least 5 years ago would be a heavy toll. Plus they have to make their il2cpp work after the update.

But still, I wish that would happen. I'd love to use protobuf and google.apis.v3 in Unity.
You are able to use Protobuf just fine in unity3d though? I'm currently using it for serializing my network packages.

@zeroZshadow: My guess is that you're using protobuf-csharp-port, the old proto2 implementation... which apparently worked on Unity _if you were lucky_. We repeatedly ran into issues to do with JIT or AOT compilation, suspecting them to be bugs with the very old version of Mono being used.
@jskeet I'm using whatever is here https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf together with proto3
@zeroZshadow: So _how_ are you using that? I wouldn't have expected you to be able to install the NuGet package, for example - it targets CLRv4. Which version of Unity3D are you using?

@jskeet  I've copied that entire folder to Assets/Plugins, then applied the fix that is  posted by asuuma.
I'm using Unity 5.3.2, but earlyer versions also had no issues.

Okay - that makes a bit more sense. You should be aware that this isn't an officially-supported scenario at the moment. I make no guarantees about it - you may well find it works in simply situations, but that some more advanced features break :( Obviously we'd _like_ to support Unity eventually - but the nature of the platform does make it hard to support properly, and we want to get the support for more modern platforms rock-solid first.

I've tried copying the folder to Assets/Plugins and applying the posted fix, but I get numerous other errors with Unity 5.3.2, many around string interpolation (i.e. $"...{...}..."), some around defaulted properties, some others sprinkled in as well.  Since the above comments are ~10 days old, it seems unlikely (though possible) that these additional errors were all introduced recently.  Is there something else I need to do to make this work?  I understand this isn't a supported scenario, but I'm hoping that some of the people here can offer advice.

@dmuir: Yes, you need C# 6 support to build the Google.Protobuf library, but not to build generated code. Basically you'd need to build the library with VS2015, and then add it as a reference within Unity. But as you say, it's not supported right now..

FWIW we're successfully using protobuf-csharp-port in our Unity project. The app is live on the store for Android and iOS. We've added Google.ProtocolBuffersLite.dll and Google.ProtocolBuffersLite.Serialization.dll to Plugins, and compiling all messages to C# with the "lite" option.

@zakyg: If that's working for you and you can keep using proto2, then I suggest you stick with that for the moment. But as I say, I've seen issues related to Unity in protobuf-csharp-port and when I was doing that just in my free time, it was hard to provide the level of support I wanted.

@jskeet yes we're not planning on upgrading for now, the comment was to help anyone who looks for a way to integrate some version of Protocol Buffers into their Unity project. The OP mentioned they assumed they would run into issues with iOS, but the problematic Emit call was not included in the C# Proto classes compiled with the lite option. We're using protobuf-csharp-port for all our client-server communication and for persisting data as well. Runs good on production on both iOS & Android.

Hi - 
The simplistic patch above does not fully work (it may be incomplete).
In particular, unit tests (packing) fails.
I have a more extensive patch in which all unit tests pass. All changes are straightforward (if tedious):
- cloned csproj and removed nuspec, etc. set framework to 3.5.
- removed all extension methods (replace with fully qualified static methods)
- removed all GetTypeInfo calls (not supported in 3.5)
- replaced ReadOnlyDictionary with IDictionary (former not supported in 3.5)

Per your comment above, I don't think it makes sense to try and have a single binary for all platforms. But it would be great if this could be rolled into mainline (in some form) to at least have nominal support for Unity. I don't think Unity will upgrade their framework anytime soon. 

I can submit a patch or pull request... please let me know how I can help.

Hi,

we made a Unity compatible version of the C# Protocol Buffers runtime library.
It is available here (https://github.com/bitcraftCoLtd/protobuf3-for-unity) and based on the tag v3.0.0-beta-2.
We fixed the compiler errors to support the runtime 3.5, and all the unit test pass.
Once a new beta version or the final version of the library will be out, we plan to update our repository if Unity is not yet support as this time.
@jskeet +1 for Unity support, even though the mono they use is not modern, Unity is a modern platform. It would be awesome to support it! I'm using @hobein's for now - thanks for making it available!
@hobein Thanks for your work ! Works fine for me :) !
@hobein hi - do you have your unity lib available as a nuget package?

Hi @cperras, no we do not provide NuGet packages, sorry about that. This is because Unity sadly does not make it easy to use NuGet packages. However, we provide prebuilt versions of the DLL here: https://github.com/bitcraftCoLtd/protobuf3-for-unity/releases

I hope this help.

@zhangzhibin Just mentioning the reply to the issue you opened on our repo:
https://github.com/bitcraftCoLtd/protobuf3-for-unity/issues/4#issuecomment-243036556

So basically, it'd be great if this could land in https://github.com/google/protobuf so we are certain that these changes do not impact the rest of the userbase (wondering if the original syntax was a conscious choice)
Unity on iOS is a bit of a complex topic due to the pipeline:
C# -> IL -> cpp
which is why reflection is a bit of a sensitive matter.
From what we gathered so far, it appears that the contributors of this repo do not wish to prioritize Unity-related limitations, so this change will only be accepted here if it makes sense beyond the Unity scope.
If your changes are not accepted here, then we will update the protobuf3-for-unity repo, so please keep us updated.

Note that using reflection-based invocation will be considerably slower than using compiled expression trees. The alternative would be to use `Delegate.CreateDelegate`, but it's more fiddly than the expression tree version.

@TanukiSharp: No, no dictionary would be required. These are already being cached, not in a dictionary but in the descriptor. (Compiling the expression tree each time would also be expensive.) So this could be done, but it would be uglier code - I'd rather not do that at the moment.

@jskeet Sorry I'm not in charge of that project at bitcraft, just a kind of .NET advisory for the team, so I don't know that much about the protobuf code base.

So do you mean the 4 methods `ReflectionUtil.Create*IMessage*()` are guaranteed to be called only once per `MethodInfo` ?

Because the `method` argument would need to be compiled to delegate **outside** of the lambda, and so only the delegate would need to be closured in the lambda, since lambda will be evaluated each time it is called.

Actually we may implement this in our fork anyway, because at some point we will need to support iOS, no matter what.

@TanukiSharp: The usage of ReflectionUtil is (at least currently) in creating descriptors, which are created once per message type basically. I didn't follow your discussion of the delegate being "closured in the lambda" - I was proposing not needing a lambda expression at all within ReflectionUtil, if possible. It's possible that one level of indirection would be required anyway, basically to do the casting... but that would have minimal performance impact.

@jskeet OK I'm interested in your solution to avoid using code emission at runtime.
Actually I think `CreateDelegate` will not work, because we would have to know the type of delegate at compile time, since produced `Delegate` can't be cast to `Func<X, Y>`.

Anyway, if you have a solution to simply and efficiently avoid code emission, that would be much appreciated.

Thanks.

@TanukiSharp: I don't have time to do this now, I'm afraid. But you can absolutely create a delegate of the right type with `Delegate.CreateDelegate` and cast it. We know the target type using the generic type parameter.

To make sure that the project owners don't underestimate the importance of Unity support, I'd add my 5 cents. According to the Unity website, it has been downloaded by 5.5M users. 280K Unity-based games have been released so far. It's a big market. And what is really important, most of the games do sophisticated client-server communication. Protobuffers solve the serialization problem just perfectly, providing support for protocol backward compatibility, which is vital for mobile and online games, and in general making cross-platform interaction a breeze. Please don't drop Unity support on the floor.

title: Status of Python 3 (3.4+) support?
body:
There is a number of open PR regarding adding support for Python 3 (including my own). None of them are merged.

What's the current status? Which of PR's has most chances to be merged anytime soon? I would like to invest some time into this, but really don't want to waste doing work noone will merge.

nodes.body:
I am extremely interested in merging PRs to fully support Python 3.

I commented on https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/166 that I am interested in merging it, but @tseaver said he didn't have time to update it.

I wasn't sure the status of your PR https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/66. As @tamird mentioned we no longer need to support Python 2.5, and I'm interested in making a cleaner code-base that drops 2.5 support.

Here is what I am especially interested in:
1. a code-base that works with 2.6, 2.7, and 3.4 without requiring 2to3.
2. a build process that can test all of these different versions with `tox` (including both pure-Python and Python/C++ implementations).
3. a way of running the conformance tests against all versions also.

I have been working on (2) but my progress is slow since I am not an expert in the Python tool ecosystem. I would greatly appreciate any help with this.

To run tests under multiple versions one would just set up virtualenv for each version and run tests under them.

What kind of build process are you looking for? How are you going to run it?
@Kentzo `tox` is a tool that automates that process.

I want a `tox` setup that works, basically. As @tseaver mentioned, `tox` is designed to automate the process of testing with multiple virtualenvs. But `tox` won't work with our current setup. It throws errors given our current setup.py. And we have to figure out what command `tox` should run to do this actual testing (this is configurable).
Ideally the `tox` setup would also install the actual package into the virtualenv, to verify that the packaging/install step is correct.
At the very least, the documentation should be updated (changelog for v2.6.0) to remove claims that Python 3 is supported. This is misleading at best.

@Kentzo I would be more than happy to assist you with this. If you don't plan on working on this yourself, could you list out the steps we could take to get to 2.7/3.x support? I'm not a python expert, but I've been somewhat successful improving protobuf's python support.

I've taken the work @tseaver started and merged in the latest code from upstream here: https://github.com/dano/protobuf/tree/py2_py3_straddle. tox runs just fine, but a bunch of new tests that have been added are now failing on Python 3, along with a couple of regressions on Python 2.7. If I get some more free time I'll start trying to fix the issues, but it at least gets us closer...
@dano Thanks for rescuing that work!

Ok, I've fixed a couple of long/int compatibility issues on the Python 2 side. There are two Python 2 tests that still fail, but the reason for the regression is a symptom of a fairly large problem on the Python 3 side.

`text_format.py` has a `MethodToString` function that converts a protobuf to text. It's got an `as_utf8` parameter, which determines if the output is utf-8 formatted or not. So far, so good. To collect the output from the protobuf, the Python 2-only version uses a `cStringIO.cStringIO` object, and passes that around the module.  The Python 2/3 compatible version of this is `io.StringIO` - however, those two classes aren't quite the same. The `StringIO` module has this note in it's documentation:

> The StringIO object can accept either Unicode or 8-bit strings, but mixing the two may take some care.

`io.StringIO` doesn't have this leniency - everything you pass to it must be Unicode. If you want to pass 8-bit strings, you need `io.BytesIO`. Unfortunately, the current code is _badly_ abusing the ability to pass both Unicode and byte strings to `cStringIO.cStringIO`. Everywhere it's writing string literals, it's using `out.write('string')`, which are bytes strings, not unicode. It's also writing the same kind of literal, regardless of the value of the `as_utf8` parameter. It should be choosing `b'string'` if `as_utf8 == True` and `u''` if not. It should also decide whether or not to encode fields from the protobuf itself depending on the `as_utf8` value, currently, it just uses the fields returned unconditionally, regardless of the type of string and the value of `as_utf8`

So, there's a whole bunch of work here to fix every single call to `out.write(...)` in text_format.py, to make sure it does the right thing depending on the value of `as_utf8` and the type of string it's trying to write. The good news is it looks like that's the only thing still causing failures on Python 3, so hopefully this is the last big hurdle (aside from making sure things still work on Python 2.6 - I don't have it installed on my machine right now, so I haven't had a chance to test that yet. It should be a fairly simple exercise to get it working in any case).

It's unclear whether the Unix epoch (for example) should be formatted as `1970-01-01T00:00:00Z` or `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`. Looking at the C++ code, it seems like it's the former - but that should be clarified in the documentation.

title: Decide what to do about groups within C# code
body: Currently we do "half a job" at handling groups. Generated code checks for "EndGroupTag" when parsing for example - but we don't support groups in any other way. We may want to throw an exception if we ever encounter a tag using start/end group...

nodes.body:
Feedback: we shouldn't just throw an exception when we see group tags. It's entirely feasible that code will be presented with data which was serialized when a message _did_ have a group and was proto2, but the proto has now been converted to proto3.

It's unclear whether we should try to support legacy group-written messages by parsing them using the different wire format - which would then change when they were re-serialized, of course - or skip the group part. Parsing them as if they were embedded messages simply in a different wire format is somewhat tricky, as it means whenever we have a field with an embedded message we'd need to add a case in the generated switch statement for "yes, a message - but actually as a group" which feels like a lot of extra code to generate for an incredibly rare situation.

Will see what Java does...

Looking at the Java code, if it encounters a tag with a wire format of START_GROUP, it won't match any of the cases - so it will skip the field. That means then generated code should never see an END_GROUP tag when it calls ReadTag - we _could_ make it throw on such a message, or we could just allow it to silently skip that tag.

Currently the Java code, if it sees a "rogue" END_GROUP tag, will treat that as the end of the message - which is "unpicky" in a different way.

For a first pass, I'll implement the "skipping" behaviour including skipping embedded groups, as at least most of that is required anyway. Assigned to Jisi for more consideration of the nuances here - I don't know to what extent all implementations need to handle oddly-mangled message data the same way.

PR #694 changed the behaviour to simply skip unexpected end-group tags; start-group tags cause the whole group to be skipped. We can evaluate whether or not that's what we want.

(It's possible that if we make SkipLastField on an end-group tag simply throw, that would work - we'd normally consume it when reading a tag in SkipGroup... we'd need to change SkipGroup slightly too, in order to avoid it calling SkipLastField when it's read the end group that terminates the loop.)

title: MSAN failure in StatusOr
body:
I built the protobuf compiler and test suites today with the MemorySanitizer in Clang, and ran into an issue with uninitialized variables in protobuf/src/google/protobuf/stubs/statusor_test.cc.

Both StatusOr.TestPointerCopyCtorStatusNotOkConverting and StatusOr.TestPointerAssignmentStatusNotOkConverting are failing.  It looks like they are failing because value_ isn't initialized in the first StatusOr<>.  When you convert a Derived\* to a Base2*, it then triggers the compiler to modify the pointer and that looks like it triggers the failure.

I don't think this is a real issue, but I'm not sure.  Any advice?

nodes.body: value_ is not intialized if the status is not ok. That seems fine to me. Is there any annotation we can add to protobuf code to suppress such errors?
@brian-peloton  Would that work?

I think it might be undefined behavior, which means suppressing the warning isn't the right thing to do. Looking around online didn't yield anything definitive, but it doesn't seem like a good thing to be doing.

The problem seems to be that the compiler has to insert a branch based on whether the pointer is NULL or not (to avoid changing NULL to not-NULL). An uninitialized pointer could change from not-NULL to NULL, which is kind of weird but seems unlikely to be an issue. However, accidentally wrapping a pointer value could definitely have actual effects on the behavior of the code, which seems to me like enough reason to fix this. Optimizers like making assumptions about arithmetic not overflowing to avoid inserting mask operations, which this issue violates.

I just submitted a pull request (#1162) I've been meaning to send for a while which fixes this by not copying the pointer if !ok(). It shouldn't have any detectable effect on performance and completely fixes this issue.

title: PyPI installation lacks __init__.py in top-level google directory
body:
This is a weird one, but I couldn't import google.protobuf for a while because the PyPI installation didn't include an **init**.py file in the top-level google directory. Doing a reinstall produced the same results; the top-level google directory still lacked an **init**.py file.

By looking at this repo, I would expect to see it there. Perhaps you're doing something in the setup.py that is stripping it out unintentionally?

nodes.body: setup.py installs the "google" package as a setuptools [namespace package](https://pythonhosted.org/setuptools/setuptools.html#namespace-packages), which means it gets installed without an `__init__.py`.

+1 on getting this fixed. It's a common enough problem that there is a stack overflow answer:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/13862562/google-protocol-buffers-not-found-when-trying-to-freeze-python-app

And I've had to work around this in three different build scripts, e.g:
https://github.com/google/grr/blob/master/vagrant/install_linux.sh#L166
A PR would be most welcome! None of us are Python packaging experts, so fixing this ourselves often requires a fair amount of background research first. If anyone has a simple fix, I'm all ears.
Seems related to: https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1153

So adding the bits I know:
- The namespace packages PEP suggests using the [variant form](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0420/#namespace-packages-today) via `pkgutil`. 
- I suspect that we should also make a related change to switch from a namespace package to regular package, i.e. switch from `namespace_packages` to an explicit `packages` list or [just use `setuptools.find_packages()`](https://python-packaging-user-guide.readthedocs.org/en/latest/distributing/#packages). 

Now, the real question is this: what happens as we switch? If someone has one of the current versions installed, and we switch over, will everything _just work_? (Does that ever happen?)
Closing in favor of https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1296

title: C++ code generator bug: unused parameter in generated files

nodes.body: This bug is breaking my -Werror build :(
It seems that implementing a virtual function with a no-op should not generate a compiler warning

@gerben-s Even if it would, it is still a hack and not a fix to this issue. The issue is pretty clear:

In terms of C++ compliance having a named argument that's unused is wrong, no matter what.

Why don't you just fix the generator to generate valid code?

 After a year and a half, that's what I call a solution - dismissing the issue... Very disappointing :(
Please cite chapter and verse in the c++11 standard that outlaws unused named arguments as valid c++

Well, if it would be the standard forbidding it, it wouldn't be a warning by definition.

I meant compliance with compilers. Compilers produce a warning and for those who take them seriously with -Werror - it breaks their builds. Isn't that a good enough reason? Especially for a library or a tool generating code.

Re-factor your build such that the protos are organized in a separate lib and compile them without warnings. Compiler warnings are meant to improve and assist human written code. Generated code could just as well be compiled with warnings completely disabled. 

Warning in the headers files would be a completely different story.
I believe protobuf team changed their opinion regarding warnings in the generated code. Please continue at https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4628#issuecomment-470446302.

(master)$ tree

└── README.md
```

Now I change to a different include path, and the output files move again.

```
(master)$ protoc -I=protofiles --cpp_out=. protofiles/CategoryA/MessageA1.proto 
(master)$ tree
.
├── CategoryA                           <------------ ???
│   ├── MessageA1.pb.cc          <------------ ???
│   └── MessageA1.pb.h            <------------ ???
├── Makefile
├── protofiles
│   ├── Base
│   │   └── Base.proto
│   ├── CategoryA
│   │   └── MessageA1.proto
│   ├── CategoryB
│   │   └── MessageB1.proto
│   └── CategoryC
│       └── MessageC1.proto
└── README.md
```

I didn't expect this interactivity btw -I and --cpp_out.  Is this expected behavior?

nodes.body:
Try:

```
(master)$ protoc -I=protofiles --cpp_out=protofiles protofiles/CategoryA/MessageA1.proto 
```

and in your proto files, import the other protos like this:

```
syntax = "proto3";
import "Base/Base.proto";
....
```

This should work for all your proto files.

This is the expected behavior. Let me try to explain.

Quite different from C++, in protobuf, a .proto file must be imported using exactly the same name from all proto files, or the generated code will not compile (likely link error if you manage to prevent protoc from complaining about "file not found"). Let's call this name a .proto file's canonical name. The "-I" flag does more than just specifying an import path: it also defines a mapping from a file's disk path to its canonical name. For example, if you specify "-I=protofiles", you are telling the compiler that a disk file "protofiles/Base/Base.proto" has the canonical name "Base/Base.proto" and should be imported with such a name. When the compiler generates C++ code for the proto file, it will also use the canonical name to determine the output files' layout. For example:

```
(1) $ protoc --cpp_out=. protofiles/CategoryA/MessageA1.proto
(2) $ protoc -I=protofiles --cpp_out=. protofiles/CategoryA/MessageA1.proto
```

In example (1), the canonical name of the file is "protofiles/CategoryA/MessageA1.proto" so you need to import it as "protofiles/CategoryA/MessageA1.proto" from other files and the compiler will generate protofiles/CategoryA/MessageA1.pb.h. In example (2), the canonical path of the file is "CategoryA/MessageA1.proto", so you need to import it as "CategoryA/MessageA1.proto" and the compiler generates CateogryA/MessageA1.pb.h

If you run protoc on each of your proto files separately, it's important to specify the "-I" flag consistently. For example:

```
(3) $ protoc --cpp_out=. protofiles/Base/Base.proto
(4) $ protoc --cpp_out=. protofiles/CategoryA/MessageA1.proto
(5) $ protoc -I=protofiles --cpp_out=protofiles protofiles/CategoryB/MessageB1.proto
```

If both A1.proto and B1.proto import Base.proto, you will never get the generated code compiled because A1.proto assumes the canonical name of Base.proto to be "protofiles/Base/Base.proto" while B1.proto assumes it's "Base/Base.proto". The generated code will reference the same symbol using different names and only one of them can possibly compile.

This is not easy to get right. For most users, I think it's better to just not use this flag and put all proto files in a single directory tree and compile all of them with a single protoc invocation. Use "-I" only when you need to import proto files from another project.
Thanks! I appreciate the helpful explanation.

title: Proto binary to JSON modifies keys
body:
The JSON output serialized from proto binaries (using `google::protobuf::util::BinaryToJsonString`) has different casing for its keys, making it unusable for us. E.g. I deserialize

``` json
{"People": [{"FirstName": "Tommy"}]}
```

and the objects look fine until I serialize them again

``` json
{"people": [{"firstName": "Tommy"}]}
```

nodes.body: In JSON, field names are turned into camelCase (starting with a lower case letter). The serialization result seems correct to me and I think the parsing part should report an error.

According the proto3 JSON spec, JSON names should be the camelCase version of the proto field name. For "FirstName", its JSON name should be "firstName". We haven't decided whether to allow or reject "FirstName" in this case though (or whether to reject first_name if the proto field is named as such). We will publish a more detailed JSON spec. For the time being, it's better to avoid "FirstName" or "first_name" in JSON.
Unfortunately, our JSON schema has been in production for quite some time. Changing it now will break a lot of things for us.

Some update on the json name: we discussed it this week and think it's reasonable to add an option to support that.

Another feature request for this: https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/795
@xfxyjwf  How do you activate this feature in protoc (on the command line, I mean)?

@reece You don't need to do anything with protoc to activate it. It's on by default. Just compile the proto file normally and our JsonFormat libraries should respect the json_name option specified in the .proto file.

I misunderstood. I thought https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/731#issuecomment-173423707 was that there were two features: 1) an "option" to preserve field names and 2) "also" the ability to specify json_name in a field.  Is there a way to disable field renaming?

FWIW, I would much prefer that protoc not modify symbols, ever. Implicit and assumed behaviors create more problems than they solve. (The same functionality with a feature switch would be great!)
I think you were correct. There are indeed two features. Neither of them require anything to turn on.

Thanks. I was way off base... my python models were generating json with camelCase, which incorrectly thought was because protoc had generated that. Instead, I just needed to pass preserving_proto_field_name=True to MessageToJson. Thanks for your replies.

In Python:

```
from google.protobuf.json_format import MessageToJson
json_obj = MessageToJson(msg, preserving_proto_field_name=True)
```

For anyone else that finds this issue the way I did, there's a way you can decode the JSON back into the object representation with the different key format:

```ruby
MyMessage.decode_json(json_string)
```

So even if you have `startedAt` in the JSON but your proto declares it as `started_at`, the `decode_json` method will convert it correctly for you.

Inversely, there is a `encode_json` method on the message class, but I find using `to_json` on the object does the same thing.

> We have added a JsonFormat.Printer option to preserve the field name declared in the .proto file:
> https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L152
> 
> We also added a field option which can be used to customize the JSON name per field:
> 
> ```protobuf
> message Foo {
>   int32 value = 1 [json_name = "some_other_name"];
> }
> ```
> 
> The two cannot be used at the same time though.

Is this only for Java? Is there support for javscript?

title: CVE-2015-5237: Integer overflow in serialization
body:
`int` is used to express the size of serialized messages.  If the size exceeds 4 GiB, the application may allocate a buffer which is too small, or protobuf itself does this, in `google::protobuf::MessageLite::SerializeToString`. This lead to a heap buffer overflow, which may be exploitable for code execution in some cases.

It has been suggested that serialization of messages larger than 2 GiB is unsupported. But there is no good way for an application to ensure that the limit is not exceeded accidentally, without imposing rather draconian limits. To some degree, this is an `gets`-style interface.

Right now, this is more or less harmless because the message sizes involved are substantial. But this will change over time. My worry is that it will be difficult to fix this because some of the overflowing computations end up in generated `*.pb.cc` files, so the eventual fix will not be a simple library update.

nodes.body:
The recommendation has been keeping the protobuf message relatively small (several MBs). There is code checking for sizes when parsing:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h#L612

If you have a message that large (> 4GB), you might already be aware of this limit in parsing and have overridden the default limit. That's a chance to reconsider your design to avoid large messages.
@xfxyjwf, this issue is about serialization, not parsing. There is no default limit for serialization.
Do you mean the data is only serialized but never parsed back? I think parsing/serialization is always paired.

I'm not sure why you are asking this question.  There is no serialized data to parse because the process crashes before in-memory serialization completes, due to the heap buffer overflow. In other words, this crash/security problem resides on the sending side, while constructing a protobuf message.

I was thinking in a more realistic case where the message is gradually grown to exceed 2G when the software evolves (i.e., you add more and more fields and data into the message). If you start straight out with a message larger 4G, it will fail lousily and I don't think anyone ship such software. A more likely case is that you ship a software which serializes/parses data close to 2G and some unusual user input pushes it to exceed protobuf limit. What I was saying is that in such cases, the developer should already be aware of the limit because protobuf parsing fails on a much smaller limit than 2G.

Anyway, for this issue, we can improve the documentation to make it explicit that protobuf does not support messages larger than 2G. We can probably also guard against >2G messages with CHECK errors in some cases, but that may not apply to all cases (e.g., >4G). Making protobuf to support >4G message is a non-goal.
@xfxyjwf: What was the resolution on this issue? Is there some limit in more recent versions of protobuf?
@anderius We now have a MessageLite::ByteSizeLong() method that will return the size in size_t instead of int and the serialization method is guaranteed to fail when ByteSizeLong() >= 2G.
In which release was this issue resolved?

@stephfonder It was first introduced in v3.4.0 release:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/releases/tag/v3.4.0

> @anderius We now have a MessageLite::ByteSizeLong() method that will return the size in size_t instead of int and the serialization method is guaranteed to fail when ByteSizeLong() >= 2G.

Hi I know this is and old issue, but i was hoping that you would clarify that i am right in thinking that this issue has been fixed by the two following things as quoted above,

title: There are other operating systems running on sparc machines
body:
In stubs/platform_macros.h a sparc cpu is always associated with the Solaris operating system (and especially its default non-64bit userland). This causes GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ARCH_64_BIT to not be set despite **LP64** being defined (and building for 64bit). The usage of GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ARCH_64_BIT vs. **LP64** is not always consistent, so this leads to compilation errors.

Easiest fix is to just align the defines, or only special case Solaris.

Like this:

```
--- stubs/platform_macros.h.orig        2015-08-24 23:53:18.000000000 +0200
+++ stubs/platform_macros.h     2015-08-26 21:41:27.000000000 +0200
@@ -67,7 +67,7 @@
 #define GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ARCH_32_BIT 1
 #elif defined(sparc)
 #define GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ARCH_SPARC 1
-#ifdef SOLARIS_64BIT_ENABLED
+#if (defined(sun) && defined(SOLARIS_64BIT_ENABLED)) || __LP64__
 #define GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ARCH_64_BIT 1
 #else
 #define GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ARCH_32_BIT 1
```

Or, if someone can test on Solaris: just get rid of SOLARIS_64BIT_ENABLED and only test for **LP64**?

nodes.body: Feel free to send a PR. We don't have Solaris to test the change though. Better to take the approach that's less likely to break Solaris users.
PR https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/780 seems to indicate that this problem has already been solved. Please re-open if there is still a problem.

title: Consider populating a directory hierarchy for C# based on namespace
body:
Currently we don't do this because in .NET projects there tends to be a "base" namespace, but I think we'll want to address this with another flag, based on a bit of experience of trying to use the current approach.

Proposal:
- Add a new flag of `csharp_base_package`
- When working out where to generate code, generate a directory name based on the namespace from the base package onwards. For example, if the base package is `a.b` and the declared package for the .proto file is `a.b.c.d`, create a directory of `C.D` and put the code in there, in a namespace of A.B.C.D
- If `csharp_base_package` isn't specified, treat it as empty (e.g. create a directory of `A.B.C.D` in the above example)
- If `csharp_base_package` is specified but the .proto package doesn't start with that, fail

Alternatives to consider:
- Specify the base namespace instead of base package (e.g. `A.B` instead of `a.b`)
- Have yet another flag to allow the existing behaviour of not creating directories

The GRPC plugin should do the same thing.

Thoughts?

@anandolee @jtattermusch

nodes.body:
All other languages do not have language_base_package flag, some have language_package flag.

No more flags will be great. If we  have to add, I prefer csharp_package instead of csharp_base_package.

Which other languages have anything like this? I can't see any using protoc --help. I don't think csharp_package would make sense, as it's not specifying a package/namespace that anything should be in - it's specifying the package/namespace that should be used as a relative base for creating directories.

Having thought about it more, I think it should actually be csharp_base_namespace rather than csharp_base_package, as the namespace can be specified in the .proto file... the directory should be generated based on namespace rather than package, so it makes sense for this flag to be in terms of namespaces.

I'll start writing the code to implement it, and we can then work out what to call the flag. I think we _do_ need a new flag, unless we use csharp_out to include both pieces of information, e.g. `--csharp_out=src=Foo.Bar`, which would be equivalent to `--csharp_out=src --csharp_base_namespace=Foo.Bar`... but I'd rather keep them separate.
@pherl Is it OK to add one more flag to FileOptions in descriptor.proto?
This isn't a file option, and shouldn't be - it's a command line flag, which is appropriate given what it controls.

Hmm, this flag seems to make the generated files indeterministic. When will
the base flag be used? What's the default value for google owned protos,
e.g. one platform protos?

On Tue, Sep 1, 2015 at 10:50 AM Jon Skeet notifications@github.com wrote:

> This isn't a file option, and shouldn't be - it's a command line flag,
> which is appropriate given what it controls.
> 
> —
> Reply to this email directly or view it on GitHub
> https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/773#issuecomment-136810705.

It entirely depends on where you want them to go. It's no more indeterministic than --csharp_out being a command line option. It doesn't change the _content_ of the files - it only changes where they're written out to.

Basically it's up to the user to put them into their project however they wish. Different users may want to lay their projects out slightly differently (e.g. one using Google as a base namespace if they have multiple APIs in the same project, and one using Google.Pubsub.V1 as a base namespace if they're only using that API). It doesn't change the compiled code (the IL) at all.

hmm, if I understand this correctly, it's the same as appending the base
directory to the --csharp_out flag? Why the csharp_out cannot be used in
this case then?

On Tue, Sep 1, 2015, 11:07 AM Jon Skeet notifications@github.com wrote:

> It entirely depends on where you want them to go. It's no more
> indeterministic than --csharp_out being a command line option. It doesn't
> change the _content_ of the files - it only changes where they're written
> out to.

No, it's not - it's the _opposite_ of appending the base directory to the csharp_out flag, effectively... it's _removing_ directories from the generated hierarchy... but those directories may not exist.

This is very normal in a C# project layout - you have a root source directory which is effectively some default namespace... like the Google.Protobuf directory represents the Google.Protobuf namespace. There's no "Google" directory and no "Protobuf" directory... just "Google.Protobuf" (which could just be "MainLibrary" or something similar) but code in the Google.Protobuf namespace goes into that directory, and code in the Google.Protobuf.Reflection goes in a Reflection subdirectory, etc.

Now it's true that you can put files into whatever directory you like with csharp_out - but only for one output directory at a time. That's a pain in the neck if you have multiple protos in multiple namespaces, all of which _can_ have their location determined by basically saying "the csharp_out directory is the location of the namespace Foo". For an example of that, look at the changes to generate_protos.sh - we no longer need one call to protoc for descriptor.proto and one for the well-known types.

Ah, I see. It makes sense to introduce a generator flag for this.

C.f. the following output:

```
$ protoc --grpc_out=/tmp --plugin=protoc-gen-grpc=grpc_cpp_plugin something.proto
grpc_cpp_plugin: program not found or is not executable
--grpc_out: protoc-gen-grpc: Plugin failed with status code 1.

/usr/bin/grpc_cpp_plugin

$ echo $?

true: program not found or is not executable

$ echo $?
0
```

nodes.body:
any idea?
update the following is working

```
"plugin=protoc-gen-grpc=/usr/local/bin/grpc_python_plugin
```

Hi,

I think the documentation may be a little misleading here. What the doc meant to say is, if you don't specify the --plugin flag, protocol compiler will try to find the plugin in $PATH with the given output name.

For example:

``` bash
$ protoc --grpc_out=/tmp foo.proto
```

With the above command, protocol compiler will try to find protoc-gen-grpc in $PATH. However, if you do:

``` bash
$ protoc --grpc_out=/tmp --plugin=protoc-gen-grpc=grpc_cpp_plugin foo.proto
```

Protocol compiler will treat grpc_cpp_plugin as a relative file path.

Could you guys point me to the documentation you are looking at?
If you can point us to some documentation that is misleading about this, please re-open and we'll fix it to be more clear.

I also got error in Windows 10:
--grpc_out: protoc-gen-grpc: Не удается найти указанный файл. (program not found or is not executable)

fullpath of grpc_cpp_plugin helps me:
`protoc.exe --plugin="protoc-gen-grpc=D://grpc_cpp_plugin.exe" --grpc_out=src helloworld.proto`

@haberman
This is still a problem.  The error message suggests the plugin binary can exist in PATH, but it does not appear to check for it.  [This (windows) issue](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4867) also appears to be related.

The snip below (from OSX) shows that grpc_php_plugin can be found in PATH, but also that protoc exits non-zero stating the plugin cannot be found.

```
$ command -V grpc_php_plugin
grpc_php_plugin is /usr/local/bin/grpc_php_plugin

$ protoc -I ./tmp_proto -I $GOPATH/src --proto_path=tmp_proto --php_out=src --grpc_out=src --plugin=protoc-gen-grpc=grpc_php_plugin ./tmp_proto/assemble/*.proto
grpc_php_plugin: program not found or is not executable
Please specify a program using absolute path or make sure the program is available in your PATH system variable
--grpc_out: protoc-gen-grpc: Plugin failed with status code 1.
```

Specifying the full path to the plugin does work.

If you want to clean up the documentation I'd suggest removing the suggestion that binaries will be found in PATH, but it would be nicer if it was supported.

Hope this helps.

EDIT: For reference, the issue probably stems from [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc#L2066). I'm happy to make a PR, but i'd like to discuss the desired behaviour first.

I think I understand the confusion.  The error message is saying: "Please either specify an absolute path or *don't specify a program name at all* and make sure the `protoc-gen-grpc` program is in your PATH".

I agree the error message you mentioned could be more clear.

Yes, it does seem possible to allow `grpc_php_plugin` to be searched from `$PATH` also. I'm not sure what the rationale was for not doing this.

I'm guessing the intention was that the plugin would be always be named `protoc-gen-grpc`, and that you wouldn't need to specify a filename unless the program was in a different directory.

I wonder why the gRPC plugin is not just called `protoc-gen-grpc_php`. That would be a better experience all around, because then you wouldn't need to specify `--plugin` at all.

title: in C++ int64 == long long int
body: I've noticed that int64 types are now represented as long long ints in C++. Why the change? Is this because we're only guaranteed that long's are "at least" 32 bits wide? In practice, this seems to mean that long ints are 64 bits wide, but maybe this isn't true for all implementations?

nodes.body:
On Visual Studio, long is always 4 bytes (i.e., 32 bits) no matter whether it's x86 or x64 that your binary is built for.

Any issues for int64 being "long long"?

It's not a fundamental problem, although it adds a bit of a roadbump to development in. Although `sizeof(int64_t) == sizeof(long) == sizeof(long long)` on 64-bit linux systems, we've tended to use `long`/`int64_t` for storing ids. These aren't recognized by compilers as compatible types with `long long` despite the fact that they are the same size, so upgrading to match this change will require a nice bit of finding and replacing. It sounds like it's preferable to have it as you've changed it though.

I'd like to ask to reconsider making `int64` to be `int64_t`, as opposed to being long long. `int64_t` is specifically designed to be just what `int64` is meant to be, and is future-proof -- we might live to see long long to be 128 bit on future platforms. Even though long long is freely convertible to `int64_t` right now, these are not the same types usually, and it really shows when e.g. one wants to declare a variable with type `RepeatedPtrField<int64_t>` (must use `RepeatedPtrField<::google::protobuf::int64>`), or implement their own `ZeroCopyOutputStream` (`int64_t ByteCount()` doesn't work, must be `::google::protobuf::int64 ByteCount()`).

I agree! We should make it future proof and set it to be int64_t.

title: Consider returning null instead of throwing an exception in MessageDescriptor.FieldCollection indexers
body:
Currently it's a bit of a pain to conditionally request a field from a FieldCollection, because the indexers will throw a KeyNotFoundException. This is what `IDictionary<,>` does, but that may be partly because the dictionaries values could be of a value type - whereas here we know it will be a FieldDescriptor.

This is a trivial change to implement - it's a matter of whether or not we _want_ to implement it....

/cc: @jtattermusch

nodes.body:
I've always thought of indexer [] throwing KeyNotFoundException as a rule of thumb. An alternative would be to just add TryGet method.
https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/bb347013(v=vs.110).aspx

I'm not sure it's a rule of thumb so much as what makes sense for `Dictionary<,>` - a lookup returns an empty sequence, for example. We _could_ add `TryGet`, but it feels somewhat unnecessary when `null` is available. Hmm. Will keep pondering.

I'd be probably fine with returning null. Are you convinced getting a field conditionally will have its use?
I imagine two common scenarios:
1. I know what message type I am dealing with, so I only touch fields that actually exist. KeyNotFound Exception probably makes sense here.
2. I don't know what messages type I am dealing with, so I iterate over the fields in fieldcollection. At later point, whenever I decide to use indexer, I know the field should be there. KeyNotFound Exception makes sense again.

I thought about this mostly when I was spiking JSON parsing (which won't actually use the indexers, but...) In that case, I want to detect a field being absent, but throw a _different_ exception. I could catch KeyNotFoundException and rethrow a wrapped one, but it's a bit ugly. Definitely a good idea to think about use cases for this though...
In JSON parsing we're exposing a dictionary anyway. Callers could always create their own dictionary if necessary. Closing this.

title: Consider exposing a Parser property in MessageDescriptor
body:
Generated code knows about a parser for the message type - so when we're parsing JSON, it would make sense to use that, but we only have a descriptor.

If we exposed a `Parser` property (of some new _non-generic_ interface type, implemented explicitly by `MessageParser<T>`) we could avoid reflection in JSON parsing.

Note that this would be a codegen and runtime change, so would break existing generated code - we would want to get it in before 1.0.

@jtattermusch @xfxyjwf @anandolee for comment. I can create a prototype PR if that would help visualize things.

nodes.body: How much does this affect the generated code size? Does it share the same parsing code used to parse binary data?

> How much does this affect the generated code size?

Hardly at all. Passing one more argument to the method to create a `Descriptor`.

> Does it share the same parsing code used to parse binary data?

Yes - it's not changing anything about how parsing's done, it just makes a parser accessible via the `Descriptor`.

How does this work with pure dynamic messages? I.e., a descriptor may not be associated with a generated type.

In C++ and Java, there isn't a one-to-one mapping from descriptor to message type. You can create both generated message type and dynamic message type from the same descriptor and giving only the descriptor, there is no way to map that to a concrete message type. Is the MessageDescriptor in C# different from the descriptor in C++ and Java?

We don't currently have dynamic message types, but when we do we could still return a suitable parser from the descriptor - which would return a `DynamicMessage`, which still implements `IMessage`. Our `MessageDescriptor` has a `GeneratedType` property, but the intention is that that will return `null` if there isn't a generated type associated with it.

Can a MessageDescriptor already associated with a GeneratedType be used to create DynamicMessage? Or users will need to create new MessageDescriptors in order to create DynamicMessage? And is the dynamic message support planed to be included in 1.0?

(sorry, seems I have too many questions to ask here...)

Hmm... hadn't considered that situation, as I'd normally envisaged the descriptor just being loaded from a byte array. We should definitely allow dynamic messages to be generated from message descriptors though... not sure whether that would involve cloning the descriptor objects, or just remembering the context when we parse into such a message.

(Meant to say this before.) As for dynamic message support for 1.0 - unsure. We definitely want to get all the proto3 features in first, most importantly JSON parsing including handling well-known types - Any being the obviously-tricky one.

I would rather not get dynamic message support at all than get the _wrong_ support - but let's see what we can work out. If we have a good set of known use cases for dynamic messages, that would be useful for API checking.

What is the GeneratedType property used for? In Java,  a Descriptor does not have any field that refers to the concrete message type, and the same Descriptor object can be shared by generated message types and dynamic message types. It seems C#'s MessageDescriptor is bound to a concrete type (a generated type or a dynamic message type). This is a different design from Java/C++ and I guess we should think it through before committed to it (especially on how dynamic message can be supported).

Some related questions:

A MessageDescriptor may be associated with a dynamic message so maybe we should name the property as MessageType rather than GeneratedType?

In Java we can compare two messages' descriptors by identity to determine whether they are of the same proto type (a generated message and a dynamic message can be of the same proto type if they are constructed on the same descriptor). Some reflection based methods (like copyFrom) will use this to determine it should proceed or complain about type mismatch. These methods will work seamlessly for both generated type and dynamic type. How would this work with C#'s MessageDescriptor?

About the use case for dynamic message:

The most popular use case I can see in our internal code base involves proto dbs. Basically you get a proto db (either a global db containing all message types, or a local db that comes with the data file you are parsing), retrieve descriptors from the db, construct DynamicMessages to parse the data and do queries/modifications on the dynamic message. For example, a comand-line tool that accepts sql like queries to analyze data files containing protos. Another good example is a grpc client tool that can get descriptor info from any grpc server and do queries (the equivalence of our stubby command line tool). Though arguably these tools are probably better off to use C++ rather than other languages. Supporting dynamic message is something good to have but not a must in other languages in my opinion.

The `GeneratedType` is helpful for creating accessors via reflection. It doesn't _have_ to be exposed, but it's helpful at the moment. I can see how having a "message-type-unaware" descriptor could be useful in some ways, but there are distinct benefits in it "knowing" the relevant generated types as well.

The point about comparing message descriptors by identity only works if the `DynamicMessage` _has_ been created with an existing descriptor - it wouldn't help if the descriptor for the dynamic message had been loaded from a global db, for example, because then it wouldn't be the same object as the generated type's descriptor.

The use case you describe for dynamic messages is exactly the one I was thinking of - and it's one where you wouldn't have the generated types available to create the dynamic messages from to start with. That use case can definitely be served by my current design, with an appropriate `DynamicMessage` type which is given descriptors just as raw data (including dependencies, of course).

So basically, I agree that the design isn't the same as the Java and C++ APIs, but I think it'll make life simpler in a bunch of real use cases, without harming the dynamic message use case we _really_ care about. I would like to get that use case of `DynamicMessage` implemented by 1.0, but probably won't go into more obscure ones.

I've weighed up the pros and cons of this, and looking at the "any" case, I think it's going to be significantly simpler if we go ahead and add the `Parser` property. This will also require a non-generic MessageParser base class for `MessageParser<T>`, but that's okay.
This is now implemented.

title: template method may cause malloc/free mismatch
body:
# Problem description:

My Windows app (VC++ 2008 SP1) uses libprotobuf-lite. When I used the release version libprotobuf-lite for debug mode app development, it reported heap corruption when calling RepeatedPtrFieldBase::Destroy(). But everything was OK when I linked to the debug version libprotobuf-lite.
# Root cause analysis:
1. When building the release version libprotobuf-lite, it uses release version VC library:

``` javascript
void** RepeatedPtrFieldBase::InternalExtend(int extend_amount) {
...
    rep_ = reinterpret_cast<Rep*>(
        new char[kRepHeaderSize + sizeof(old_rep->elements[0]) * new_size]);
```

The above code in repeated_field.cc is a usual member function. The "new" and its underneath "malloc" use the release version VC library.
2. When building the debug version application, its uses debug version VC library:

``` javascript
template <typename TypeHandler>
void RepeatedPtrFieldBase::Destroy() {
...
      delete [] reinterpret_cast<char*>(rep_);
```

This template method needs a template parameter to generate the object target (as an .obj file), thus the code generation has to be postponed until building the application.
Hence the "delete" and its underneath "free" use the debug version VC library.
The mismatch of malloc and free version caused the heap corruption.
# Conclusion:

I suggest to modify such template methods which handle new/delete, so that both new and delete should be in template methods, or neither of them.

nodes.body:
I don't think we can guarantee that (put all new/delete in template methods or none of them). I suggest you use debug lib with a debug app and the release lib with a release app.

Or this should be filed as a bug to VC if mixing release lib with debug apps is a supported use case. Their malloc/free functions must behave consistently in both builds.

title: Objective-C: Conflicting nullability specifier caused by setValue:forKey:
body:
Hi, I'm getting the following error when compiling on Xcode 7.0:

```
Conflicting nullability specifier on parameter types, 'nonnull' conflicts with existing specifier 'nullable'
```

This error occurs for each instance of `setValue:forKey:`:

```
- (void)setValue:(id)value forKey:(BOOL)key;
```

since the superclass (`NSObject`) implementation defines it as:

```
- (void)setValue:(nullable id)value forKey:(NSString *)key;
```

A potential easy fix is to just change the nullability annotations on the `setValue:forKey:` methods to use the `nullable` attribute for the value. Alternatively, I believe these declarations could be deleted because the `setValue:forKey:` method is already present on their superclass.

nodes.body: If possible it would be nice to have an `objective-c` label for this issue.
https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/841 should handle this.

title: Crash on map fields if protobuf library is built without C++11 but used in an app built with C++11.
body:
To reproduce:
1. Build and install protobuf following instructions in README.md.
2. Add the following code snippet to examples/add_person.cc (in main):
   
   ``` cpp
   google::protobuf::Struct st;
   google::protobuf::Value value;
   (*st.mutable_fields())["LogMessage"] = value;
   ```
3. Build add_person_cpp with -std=c++11:
4. Run ./add_person_cpp

It will crash with Floating point exception. Stack trace: [stack_trace.txt](https://github.com/google/protobuf/files/4825/stack_trace.txt)

Compiling without -std=c++11 works fine.

nodes.body:
I'm not sure this is a bug. C++98 and C++11 have incompatible ABIs when it comes to libstdc++. I think that people who are using C++11 need to compile protobuf as C++11 also, if I'm understanding correctly.

For more info see: https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/Cxx11AbiCompatibility

It seems pretty easy to make this mistake if protobuf and the user's application are built separately (e.g., users install protobuf via "apt-get install protobuf" and then use the installed lib to build their code). If there is a way to work-around it, we probably should do. If it's hard to work-around, I guess we should at least try to produce some more meaningful error message.

I don't think there's anything we can do about this case. People who are using C++11 will need to make sure protobuf is built as C++11, and we can't really work around this or usefully warn about this case.

title: setup.py sdist doesn't include enough files to build with --cpp_implementation
body:
A Python source package built with `setup.py sdist` (i.e. what's uploaded to PyPI) doesn't contain the C++ header files necessary to build the accelerated extension using `--cpp_implementation`.

It would really gel better with the Python ecosystem if `pip install protobuf  --install-option="--cpp_implementation"` just works. This would let projects include protobuf in their `requirements.txt`, and still seamlessly benefit from the C++ acceleration. We build and deploy server-side applications, and part of our pipeline includes quickly constructing the virtualenv from scratch using binary wheels, without Internet access and without invoking compilers.

Are there existing ideas on how to reach such a goal?
1. Including all the header files in `python/../src` and `python/google/protobuf` into the final sdist tarball is a good start. And `pip install` can rely on `libprotobuf.so` being already pre-installed somewhere.
2. Of course the most standalone way would involve including all the files to build `libprotobuf.so`. This would bloat the sdist tarball significantly, but many projects already involve such complex build steps, e.g. numpy and friends.

title: Use pkgutil to allow successfully work with python packages that contain google or google/protobuf
body:
google/protobuf is a key dependency of python grpc.

Shortly, gRPC-based  will be published that contain either a top-level 'google' package, and in some cases other modules in the google/protobuf package.

At the moment using, any of these other packages will generally fail  because the protobuf package is installed
- the other google package will contain modules with the google package (sometimes in google/protobuf)
- when the protobuf package is installed, both google and google/protobuf end up being resolved to the protobuf package
- other paths on the sys.path are not searched

The result is importing modules from the other packages ends with 'No module named logging.v1'  for snippets like:

``` python

from google.logging.v1 import ....

```

There is well-known way to resolve this using [pkgutil](https://docs.python.org/2/library/pkgutil.html)
- Use pkgutil.extend_path inside the **init**.py of the google and google/protobuf packages
  E.g,

``` python
import pkgutil
__path__ = pkgutil.extend_path(__path__, __name__)
```

A good online resource explaining this use of pkgutil is available at [pymotw:pkgutil](https://pymotw.com/2/pkgutil/)

title: Static linking to executable and dll (shared object)
body:
I have a project which compiles c++ generated protobuf serializers into a static library. An executable links against this library, and an .so (.dll) does too. The executable later loads the .so file. When that happens, I get:

[libprotobuf ERROR /home/csnelson/meps/projects/mf-toolchain/src/protobuf-3.0.0-beta-1/src/google/protobuf/descriptor_database.cc:57] File already exists in database: mri.proto
[libprotobuf FATAL /home/csnelson/meps/projects/mf-toolchain/src/protobuf-3.0.0-beta-1/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc:1128] CHECK failed: generated_database_->Add(encoded_file_descriptor, size): 
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'google::protobuf::FatalException'
  what():  CHECK failed: generated_database_->Add(encoded_file_descriptor, size): 
Aborted (core dumped)

This didn't happen with 2.6.1, but is now happening with 3.0 beta-1. This is quite a problem since both the .so and the executable need to have a copy of the serializer/deserializer.

I looked at similar errors, but I'm quite sure that I'm only linking against the library, not recompiling the source. As far as I can tell, this should mean that the compiled-in data is the same.

Also note: this problem _only_ happens on Linux. This works fine on Windows and OS X.

Any suggestions to fix this are appreciated.

nodes.body:
Hi,

I had the same issue when my libraries were linked to the dynamic protobuf library, but the issue gone after I changed it to the static one. Also I had to recompile the static protobuf library with the `-fPIC` flag.

However I'm not sure whether this is an issue or a feature. I there is no such issue with 2.6.1, it would be great to have the same behaviour in 3.0 too.

I believe the cause for this is the same as in the issue talked about in https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/194 and that affects protobuf 2.6.1.

I recently ran into this issue and I believe the problem has to do with the existence of non-plain old data static const class members in the source. One example being the variable kEmpty in descriptor.cc. The easiest way to duplicate this bug as mentioned in the initial post is to have a binary and a shared object. Both of which statically link against libprotobuf. Have the binary dlopen the shared object. That will create a memory leak since the static const variable is effectively a global and the symbol table will not resolve them as different since they are both in the global scope. Valgrind will report definitely lost memory showing as much. Upon dlclosing the shared object, the destructor for the static const will be called. When the program ends, the destructor for the static const will be called again, creating a double delete. Also, this practice is against google coding standards as per https://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html#Static_and_Global_Variables.

One possible solution is to replace the static const non-pod type with a getter function that returns a const reference. Inside that function, it is safe to define a static const non-pod variable.

Another solution is to limit the scoping of the symbol table. Have some variables that need to be exported in global scope and others in local scope.

The coding standards link suggests letting the leak happen and dynamically allocating memory for the object on startup, but never freeing.
@nadiasvertex I sent the pull request to fix this problem and it was merged.

title: ObjC: Don't mangle filenames

nodes.body: I believe a few other languages do this also (java?  C#?).  Since this would be a break change for folks, I don't think we're likely to change the behavior at this point.

How do you compile your Obj-C programs?  If you're using Xcode, I'd love to see the Xcode build rules you're using to recompile your protos.  Personally, I would like to use something similar to this with make:

%.objc.h %.objc.m: %.proto
   protoc ...

But that requires that the base filenames match.

Since a proto can reference another proto, you end up needing to also have the dependency change exposes to trigger rebuilds (just like source files).  So Xcode's build rule model already can't capture that.  I've seen script do it to deal with the dependency chain problem, but none of them are pretty.  Google uses http://bazel.io which knows about protos, so we don't directly have this issue.  We've talked about doing an Xcode plugin to make the build/rebuild process better, but haven't really put time into it.
fyi - You might also want to look at the --dependency_out option.  You might be able to use that to help pick off the name transform and dependency info.
