title: FR: Text proto format could support multi-line strings
body:
In a text proto file like:

```
something: <
  description: "this\nwould\n naturally be a\n multiline string"
  ...
>
```

It would be awesome if we could e.g.:

```
something: <
  description: `
this
would
naturally be a
 multiline string
`
  ...
>
```

This could be used for e.g. attaching markdown documentation to configuration entries which could then be displayed nicely. I'm not 100% on backticks (implies quoting in the parser)... Other things like a bash style `<<EOM .... EOM` demarcation could also work and would be easier to parse.

Thoughts?

nodes.body: +1 this idea (whatever syntax it takes). Having the ability to write free-flowing text in the text protobuf is great for people who want to use protobufs but still have it be human readable when you have multiline text.

FWIW, we did actually implement this as a crappy pre-processor over text proto (using the `<<EOM ... EOM` syntax). The tests ("examples") are here: https://github.com/luci/luci-go/blob/master/common/proto/multiline_test.go

It also will do a python-style `textwrap.dedent` on it, so you can do:

``` proto
something: <
  description: <<EOM
    this
    would
    naturally be a
      multiline string
  EOM
  ...
>
```

Which would be the equivalent of:

``` proto
something: <
  description: "this\nwould\nnaturally be a\n  multiline string"
  ...
>
```

(note the _beautiful_ indentation and lack of weird prefix spaces in the translated version :wink:)

Hmm...it does appear to be [an option](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/d5fb408ddc281ffcadeb08699e65bb694656d0bd/src/google/protobuf/io/tokenizer.h#L239), but it's discouraged. I don't know the reasoning for it.

This would be a great feature, we're looking at needing to do large blocks of text in a proto for api documentation, and it would be great to do this! In lieu of this we'll probably make a preprocessor as @riannucci is using, but that is much less elegant. Thanks!
+1 for this.
+1 again.
So, what's the process to getting this implemented?  Does someone simply submit a PR?
I'm going to take a stab at this.  I'm going to use backticks.  Not sure when, or if, I'll get this done.  Feel free to ping me.

So, using backticks was a breeze to implement, but I realized it’s a huge pain for people who want to embed multi-line markdown strings. The current tokenizer only looks ahead one character; I suspect that this is why there's been no movement on this feature request.  I’m extending it to look ahead three characters to accommodate triple single and double quotes.

Multi-line string value is already supported as far as I can tell, see:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/ed4321d1cb33199984118d801956822842771e7e/src/google/protobuf/text_format_unittest.cc#L748

You will need to format it like this:
```
something: <
  description:
    "this\n"
    "would\n"
    " naturally be a\n"
    " multiline string"
  ...
>
```

Probably not as convenient as the proposed ones, but it's also less magical (i.e., don't magically remove indentation and line wraps here and there).

@maguro Before you put more work into it, please make sure someone on protobuf-team is supportive of this feature (+a few other team members @acozzette @liujisi ).

The unit test `TEST_F(TextFormatTest, ParseConcatenatedString)` ensures that multi-part strings concatenate correctly.  I don't think that it has anything to do with multi-line strings.

I understand that that one can use a list of multi-part strings with each part suffixed with `\n`.  It's not  just inconvenient, it's brittle and makes things pretty illegible.  Looking at the comments and emoticons posted on this issue, it seems that the wider community has a very poor opinion on that workaround as well.

My proposal is not to remove indentation, etc.  Whatever is in the string is what you get; any formatting can and should be done after compilation.  It also is backward compatible.

I posted my comments are several weeks ago and the ticket is **_several years old_**.  How can we proceed in a more timely manner?

For changes that will affect multiple languages, there needs to be a formal proposal and it needs to be approved before proceeding. There is no fast path and the process is Google internal only. This change unfortunately falls into this category and has to be carried through by a Google engineer. It doesn't need to be a protobuf team member though. If you are a Google engineer and is motivated enough to push this feature through all the proto text parsers in Google, feel free to send us a proposal doc. When the proposal is approved, we will accept code changes (from anyone, internally or on github). For external contributors, your best bet is probably to convince someone in Google to go through the process on your behalf.

My personal take on this proposal is that it doesn't provide enough benefit to justify the effort. To me multi-line strings aren't so different from multi-part strings, and there are a lot of text proto parsers we need to update if we are to support it.
What are "text proto parsers"?

@maguro Protobuf implementations that support text format apparently have implemented such parsers. Some implementations are opensourced (as in this github repository), but many of them are not and only exist inside Google. Also protobuf implementations are not the only text proto parsers. We have tools that process/convert/format text protos. For example, if you check-in a text proto file in our internal code base, a tool will parse and format the file according to a formatting guideline, which by the way has specific rules about how to format multi-part strings.
So, these tools parse **_raw_** proto source files?  If that is the case, then if a proto file did not use the new multi-line string, then they should be fine, correct?
@maguro If nobody uses the new multi-line string, they will be fine.

So, there doesn't seem to be a problem on that front then; if there is then one could add a flag to turn it off.  I'll try to find a Google engineer to shepherd this on your side.

FWIW, I really don't how one would prefer

    string scope = 2 [(niantic.cfg.fld) = {
          description: "To get an ID Token to authenticate a user, you are required to specify\n"
                       "the scope identifier `openid`. For example: `scope=openid`.\n"
                       "\n"
                       "Additionally, to access private user data from the Yahoo APIs, include\n"
                       "the relevant [API scope\n"
                       "identifiers](https://developer.yahoo.com/oauth2/guide/yahoo_scopes/index.html#scope-identifiers).\n"
                       "The scopes can be delimited by a\n"
                       "space or comma. In the example below, the scope identifier is specified\n"
                       "for requesting the ID Token and an Access Token that provides read\n"
                       "access to the Yahoo Mail API:\n"
                       "\n"
                       "* `scope=openid mail-r`\n"
                       "* `scope=openid,mail-r`"
      }];
  
over the much cleaner

    string scope = 2 [(niantic.cfg.fld) = {
          description: """
                       To get an ID Token to authenticate a user, you are required to specify
                       the scope identifier `openid`. For example: `scope=openid`.
  
                       Additionally, to access private user data from the Yahoo APIs, include
                       the relevant [API scope
                       identifiers](https://developer.yahoo.com/oauth2/guide/yahoo_scopes/index.html#scope-identifiers).
                       The scopes can be delimited by a
                       space or comma. In the example below, the scope identifier is specified
                       for requesting the ID Token and an Access Token that provides read
                       access to the Yahoo Mail API:
  
                       * `scope=openid mail-r`
                       * `scope=openid,mail-r`
                       """
      }];
Good news.  I got a Google manager to shepherd this.  I was also able to maintain the zero-copy stream semantics.  I'll try to get the patch submitted later this week, more likely the weekend.

@maguro 
> over the much cleaner [...]

From your example, what would this become?
```
string scope = 2 [(niantic.cfg.fld) = {
      description: """
                   foo
                   """
```

Would the description be: `foo` or `\n\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\sfoo\n\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s\s`

And what about this?
```
string scope = 2 [(niantic.cfg.fld) = {
      description: """
                   foo
      bar
                   """
```
It would be the latter.  The compiler should not make any asssumptions about the intentions of the author.
What is the conclusion on this? Does this feature get implemented?
Yeah, let me dust this off and chat w/ our lawyers.
Looking good:

The plugin is aware of two kinds of strings, ones that are for string values and ones that are for string names, e.g. import paths: When a string value is used somewhere a string name is required, the proper error occurs:
Ok, as you can see above, it supports **both** backtick and triple-double-quotes to delimit multiline strings.  I'm just making that clear.

Coming from a Python background, I was surprised by the backtick syntax. Then I read about the JavaScript Template Strings. But wouldn't it be confusing for users, since this is not really a template?

> Coming from a Python background, I was surprised by the backtick syntax. Then I read about the JavaScript Template Strings. But wouldn't it be confusing for users, since this is not really a template?

One is free to use `"""` if happens to be stuck in a JavaScript universe and gets confused as to when they are editing a proto file vs a JavaScript file.  :)

Seriously though, I'm not married to backticks and I'm happy to remove them if that's the consensus here.

Interested in this. @maguro was this agreed on internally inside of google in the end?

For others, more info here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1297#issuecomment-390825524

The decision from the Go guys in https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/156 is to keep the current behavior.

title: Why is the map reflection interface private?
body:
If I want to perform operations on messages that have maps, I have no easy way of handling the map internals without manually circumventing the public reflection API.

The MapReflectionTester does perfectly reasonable things but can only do so because it is a friend class of the reflection class.

nodes.body: It's private because we are not sure that's the right public API for users. Currently you can access map fields as repeated message fields in the reflection API. For example, Reflection::GetRepeatedMessage() can return a map entry message. Is that sufficient for your use case?
That should be fine. Is there documentation describing what the field descriptor for those repeated messages is?

The main issue with the repeated message field API that I can see is the following:
1. The internal representation of the fields isn't standardized in any way. Field names are internal as are field numbers, so any implementation that relies on them won't be reliable in the future.
2. The act of finding a key in a map through the reflection interface can't leverage the existing map implementation.

Any effort to make the map reflection API public would be appreciated. I'm considering forking the project just to move the API to the public scope...

Also, the other things you have to juggle yourself if you use the raw repeated field reflection representation are the types of the keys and values. It's a very cumbersome interface and I'm finding myself re-writing maps while doing it!

This API is currently experimental, and we want to get a little more feedback before committing to it. If you did want to try it out and offered feedback, it would help move us closer towards making the API public.
Closing as I believe we answered the original question.

Hi,

Does the map reflection interface has any progress? It seem that these interfaces are still private with the latest release: 3.8.0.

Regards

Good question. The interface hasn't run into many problems, but we also haven't gotten much feedback about it yet. Also the maps code is a mess internally and needs to be cleaned up. I'd feel more comfortable committing to this interface once that cleanup has happened.

Hi @haberman ,

I wrote a Redis Module: [redis-protobuf](https://github.com/sewenew/redis-protobuf), which uses Protobuf Reflection to read and write Protobuf messages with Redis. I was trying to use the map reflection interface by making the corresponding methods public, and recompiling the code. And I'd like to give you some feedback on the map reflection interface.

By now, I can only use the following method to get the map value of a given key:

```
bool Reflection::InsertOrLookupMapValue(Message* message, const FieldDescriptor* field, const MapKey& key, MapValueRef* val) const
```

This is fine if the Protobuf message is mutable. However, if the message is const, and I only want to get the map value without modifying the map, I cannot use that method.

```
const Message *msg = get_a_const_msg();
// CANNOT work, since msg is const.
msg->GetReflection()->InsertOrLookupMapValue(msg, field, key, val);
```

**My suggestion is that you can define another method which does a readonly lookup of the map value**:

```
bool Reflection::LookupMapValue(const Message &message, const FieldDescriptor *field, const MapKey &key, MapValueRef *val) const
```

If key is in map field, saves the value pointer to val and returns true. Otherwise, returns false, and leave the val untouched.

There're similar problems with the `MapBegin` and `MapEnd` methods:

```
MapIterator MapBegin(Message* message, const FieldDescriptor* field) const;

MapIterator MapEnd(Message* message, const FieldDescriptor* field) const;
```

These two methods return `MapIterator`, and I can only create begin and end iterators for mutable message.

**You should also provide methods that return `ConstMapIterator`, so that I can iterate the map values of const message:**

```
ConstMapIterator MapBegin(const Message &message, const FieldDescriptor* field) const;

ConstMapIterator MapEnd(const Message &message, const FieldDescriptor* field) const;
```

Hope this helps :)

Regards

Here is some possible feedback based on what I'm seeing in some heapz profiles from some of my Envoy memory loadtests:
The utility function that Envoy implemented to detect deprecated fields based on proto reflection uses the repeated message API to iterate the contents of a map field.  The iteration of the map field seems to result in some memory allocations as the repeated field representation of the map is populated.  Having a direct const iterator interface to the values of the map would reduce memory usage.

Relevant envoy code link: https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/6858df7eef5867b3ae91c4eab6798ccd4490cf11/source/common/protobuf/utility.cc#L215
Any updates on this? I still don't know any possible way of updating a map field using the reflection API. I got it down for every other types.

title: Missing Conformance case
body:
In working through the JSON coding details, I've run across a case that isn't clear (to me) and doesn't seem to be covered by the current conformance suite:

The case is as follows:

JSON input:  "{\"optionalStruct\": null}")

When this is decoded and then recoded to JSON, what should the result be?  All three of the following seem reasonable to me:

  "{\"optionalStruct\”:null}"  -- Rationale:  output should match input, null should be preserved.  This also matches the behavior of Value.

 "{\"optionalStruct\":{}}"  -- In other places, null decodes to the "default value", which for Struct would seem to be "{}"

 "{}"  -- This would match the behavior of non-magical message fields, where a null input indicates the field is treated as not set.

Adding this case to the conformance test would be a great help.  Thanks!

nodes.body: The result should be "{}". Except for the special well-known type google.protobuf.Value/NullValue, "null" always indicates the field is not present.

The comformance test should have covered this case: 
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/conformance/conformance_test.cc#L1838

title: .proto convention for enum value names conflicts with C# convention
body:
C# convention is to use pascal case while .proto convention is to use upper case with underscores.  If you then mix your protoc-generated code with other conventional code, it is inconsistent and can also trips up style checkers.

Note: this is only about case - there's a separate issue for scope, #1079, for which a PR has already been submitted.

I propose a file level `option csharp_enum_value_case = true` to enable automatic conversion from UPPER_CASE_WITH_UNDERSCORES to PascalCase.  (In fact, I suggest it also convert from camelCase or lower_case_with_underscores also).

I am happy to submit a PR for this, but would be interested in any feedback.  Is this better implemented as an argument to protoc, or an enum-level option?

nodes.body:
+1 to the suggestion.

I think it may be a good idea to generalize this to support for all languages.

```
option enum_field_name_conversion = true
```
1. Java: All caps with underscores
2. Objective C: Pascal naming prefixed with enum-type-name (can be a secondary option `objectivec_enum_field_name_prefix=true` or something to that effect)
3. C-Sharp: Pascal naming

What do you think?

There are definite problems with this, in terms of the possibilities of collisions - values FooBar and FOO_BAR would collide, for example. That exists for fields too, of course...

I'm not entirely against the proposal, but I certainly wouldn't want C# to be the _only_ platform to do this.

As an implementation note, I'd need to check anywhere that we use `Enum.ToString`, e.g. for JSON serialization - it would need to fetch the original name instead.

Will ask internally whether there are other examples...

(It's also very late in the release cycle to be making this change, which would break everyone's code unless we made it optional with a default of "as it was"... and at that point, you could easily end up with massive inconsistency between protos depending on how the author decided to specify them.)

@warrenfalk I definitely agree that it's only widening the existing set of possible collisions. Not something I would like to do lightly, but it's not a total blocker for me.

The compatibility issue is a bigger one for me at the moment - it's very hard to know how many C# developers are currently using 3.0.0-beta2, how many enums they have, and whether they'd prefer a bit of breakage now or permanent non-ideal enum values.

I'm not trying to be coy here - I really don't know what the best course of action would be.

If it's any consolation at all, I'm kicking myself for not thinking of it before. (Somehow I managed to go through the proto2 version without ever considering this a big problem, too...)

@jskeet no problem, I totally understand both hesitations.

If opt-out can't be risked, does that mean opt-in behavior still could (possibly as an argument to protoc)?

Let me just throw out this thought on backward-compatibility: when git changed default behavior, their strategy was to employ a warning when the option was left unconfigured. Perhaps there is an analogous temporary solution to protoc, something like the following (only when affected languages are specified):

```
$ protoc --csharp_out=. test.proto
Warning: enum value blah blah is off by default but will be on by default in the future.
  Use --enum_option_here=false to disable this warning and use old behavior.
  Or --enum_option_here=true to use the new behavior
```
This has now been implemented in #1401. There is a flag to enable the old behaviour for the moment (`legacy_enum_values`) for the moment, but that will be removed in the final release.

title: Cross module proto dependencies (Python)
body:
I have two python modules x, y, both of which define protos. 

Using --proto_path x.proto includes defs from y.proto (i.e., import "y.proto")

x/
  src/proto/x.proto
  src/python/x_pb2.py

y/
  src/proto/y.proto
  src/python/y_pb2.py

The generated file x_pb.y has:

```
import y_pb2 as y__pb2
```

But y_pb2 is not in this directory.

Is it specified how cross module dependencies can be managed? It would be required that x specify the package where y is included (which is part of it's pip requirements, for example).

nodes.body:
I have a similar problem with you.I split the .proto files into different packages.
b.proto includes defs from a.proto
eg:
model/a.proto
view/b.proto    (import "model/a.proto";)

after generated :
python/model/a_pb2.py
python/view/b_pb2.py

the generated file b_pb2.py has:

from model import a_pb2 as model_dot_a__pb2

but start up have this Error

ImportError: No module named model

I think I understand the model now: the python package name is taken from the directory hierarchy where the proto files are saved.

@zhongql I think your solution is to either put the protos in the same file hierarchy, e.g.,

```
src/
  proto/
    model.proto
    view.proto
  python/
    view.py
```

OR define separate python packages:

```
model/
  src/
    proto/
      model/
        model.proto
    python/
      model.py
      setup.py
```

Here, you can create "model" as a separate package that can be installed by your "view" module.

For your use case I recommend the first approach since model and view seem to be quite directly related. In my case I have completely separate python modules, so I am using the second approach.

title: JsonFormat.Printer support minified JSON
body:
It looks like JSON generated by the `JsonFormat.Printer` always has indents. 
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L378
This is good for readability but the serialization size explodes if you want to use the generated JSON to write to wire.

title: SerializeToArray return true when required field not initialized

nodes.body: The `IsInitialized()` check only happens when debug mode is enabled ([it's a DCHECK](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/message_lite.cc#L318)). The assumption is that your app will ensure all required field are set. If you want to check this manually, call `IsInitialized()` yourself prior to serializing.

title: Add support for generating closure extern file
body: I'm working on an java/angularjs app that compiles using closure. I've tested out the javascript support, and have been able to send messages back and forth between the server and client using a json format. It seems to work very well - the message objects do have closure-compatible jsdoc tags, but don't work well with the angular databindings. Since I'm just using json as a wire format, I'd like to just use protobuf for marshaling/unmarshaling on the server, and use `struct` declarations in closure extern files for the client-side javascript objects. How hard would it be to generate closure externs that match the json representation of the messages?

nodes.body:
The JS code protobuf generates has type annotations, e.g. `@param`. So it wouldn't make sense to generate externs files, which are meant for third party libraries that have no formal typing.

It seems like what you want are externs that describe the structure of the raw JSON that the generated proto API operates on. I'm not a proto expert, but I'm pretty sure that this data is an undocumented implementation detail and should not be accessed directly by the user. The protobuf authors might change its structure in the future, without breaking the API.

So I'm predicting that the protobuf authors wouldn't consider this sort of feature. Protobuf messages should be accessed through the generated API.

**Edit:** I rescind this comment, considering Wolfgang's link below.
I believe it is documented here: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json

Ah, I think I understand what you are asking. Your server is serializing as proto3 JSON (ie. using a protobuf library), but on the client you want to use this JSON raw -- ie. without a protobuf library.

I don't think this would be too hard. You would want to write your own protobuf compiler plugin. You can get the "json name" and the type for every field, which would let you generate the client-side structs you want.
Awesome. I looked at the javascript compiler plugin, and it seemed straightforward. Maybe if I can find time I'll contribute a plugin.
Closing it as a compiler plugin can solve the problem.

title: Filename Options for C++ and ObjC
body:
Right now, [C++](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_generator.cc#L117) and [ObjC](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/objectivec_generator.cc#L82) compilers have the filenames hardcoded with no flexibility during code generation.

Provide an option to for the filename infix.

Example:
- [ ] `option objc_filename_infix = ".pb"`
  - Will generate `a.pb.h` and `a.pb.m` for `a.proto`.
- [ ] `option cpp_filename_infix = ".pb"`
  - Will generate `a.pb.h` and `a.pb.cc` for `a.proto`.

Thoughts?

nodes.body: This is not easy to implement because we have build tools (probably all build tools that invoke protoc) hardcoding the file name mappings in their code. If protoc suddenly generates a different file, all those build tools will be broken. Since this option also provides very little value (it seems), I'm inclining to say no for this change.

@xfxyjwf It's about providing an option.

The default value can always be the current value so that this change is 100% backward compatible.

It shouldn't break any of the current stuff. I can provide the PR coz I already have it (almost) ready... and yes, it doesn't (read: shouldn't) break any existing thing.
Feel free to run build tools and verify.
Wouldn't it break if the option is used by a .proto file? I believe the option will causes more problems than the value it can add to protobuf (I actually don't see the value of it).

Here's my take:
- It will not break any tools if this option is not used.
- For those who still want to always use `pbobjc` file extension can override using CLI option (one parameter change in config).
- And, I would argue if [C# generator](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/csharp/csharp_generator.cc#L74) can have the option, why not C++ or ObjC. :-)
  - Question: How would the tools be configured for C# code generation?

Usefulness:
1. For those using [`objc` plugin on 2.x](http://github.com/alexeyxo/protobuf-objc), it will allow drop-in replacement for the generated code and _not require making intrusive changes_ for all `#include` statements. This plugin generates `.pb.{h,m}` files.
   - So, that's a +1 for developers in adoption and faster migration to `protoc v3`.
2. It helps filtering generated code by extension.
   - Not too big an issue 

I'm being selfish here from the adoption and seamless migration standpoint.

If we're looking for a tool to be (preferably) used as de-facto choice, let's make life of its users easy.

Thoughts?

To add to `usefulness` above:
1. Filter by extension --> Build tools, automation etc.
   - In fact, as people switch from `objc` plugin to `protoc`, the existing build tools may break.

So you are talking about a code generator flag rather than an .proto file option. That's less of concern to me, though I still see no reason to add it for C++. For objective-c, you mentioned it could ease the migration from old objc plugin to the new version. title: -lpthread in BUILD breaks Android projects that depend on protobuf
body:
Hi,
Android supports pthreads, but does not provide a libpthread.so library to link against. The functionality is provided in other system libraries.

Since protobuf/BUILD specifies "-lpthread", I've had to add some hacks to get around this to get the Android Tensorflow demo working by creating a dummy pthread library, which is "linked" against and bundled in the APK: https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/tensorflow/examples/android/BUILD

Now that I'm trying to make a standalone Android executable it's becoming even more problematic as the binary expects to find the fake libpthread.so lib somewhere on its library path.

Is there a better way to build protobuf for Android? Or can the -lpthread flag be made selective on build platform, so that these workarounds are not necessary?

thanks!

nodes.body:
You should be able to use bazel selectors to selectively include "-lpthread" on non android platforms. See an example of the selector:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/BUILD#L588

You probably need to contact the bazel guys about how to select on android though.

The problem isn't how to include "-lpthread" for non-Android -- we don't need to do anything for this.

The question is how can we negate the "-lpthread" in [protobuf/BUILD](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/BUILD#L19)? It seems like this requires an edit to the protobuf source. I am not aware of any way to do this in the dependent project unfortunately.

Are there any examples of other Android projects that build with Bazel and use protobuf that you know of?

The comment there says "Bazel should provide portable link_opts for pthread". It's not clear to me if this is a TODO, or a note to users about how to build for mobile. Googling "bazel portable link_opts" just takes me back to that file.

What I am proposing is:

```
    linkopts = select({
        "//conditions:default": ["-pthread"],
        "<android>": [],
    }),
```

though I don't know how to select android in bazel.

Ah, gotcha (I'd thought you were talking about modifying Tensorflow somehow).

We select for Android in Tensorflow [like this](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/tensorflow/core/BUILD#L662). //tensorflow:android is defined [here](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/master/tensorflow/BUILD#L17).

There may be a better way to do it, but if nothing else we could just copy that config_setting into protobuf/BUILD and select against it when defining LINK_OPTS. Happy to do this myself if it sounds good with you.
Fixed by https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/1386

title: iOS ARC Support
body:
It's more of a question to which I've not been able to find an answer to:
- Why does the `objectivec` compiler not generate ARC code?
  - Are there any limitations enforced by a dependency or otherwise low-level code?

I couldn't find a real need for non-ARC code unless the idea is to support very old versions of ObjC / Xcode.

nodes.body: //cc: @thomasvl (on objc team)

So ARC inserts a lot of retain/release calls, and can slow some things down.  In our profiling, it did slow down some things like parsing/serialization.  So the support sources wouldn't want to go to ARC for that reason.

The generated sources are mostly just static data, with a bunch of __unsafe_unretained, we might be able to make them compile cleanly as ARC without any real hits, because there isn't real code there, but I'd have to double check to confirm.

@thomasvl Thnx. Let me know when you have an update.

In addition, do you have perf comparision numbers with and without ARC? Would be keen to see how do they compare...

No real numbers I can publish.  It comes down to picking some proto(s), and running their numbers on some sample data.  Exactly what the the combination of nested messages and field types are can have some larger swings in the numbers.  The more non object types, the less ARC moves the numbers, the more object types, the more they change.

BTW - your question sorta implies you see ARC as only for support old OS versions.  That's not the case, nothing says ObjC code has to be ARC.  ARC can some things simpler for developers because they don't have to do retains/releases/autoreleases them selves, but you still have to pay attention to the memory model because of retain cycles, etc.  Protos is one of those cases, where ARC doesn't really seem to gain much, and since folks like want parsing/serialization to be fast, ARC can be a penalty.

Took a quick look.  __unsafe_unretained is a good chunk of it, but there are some places with direct memory management calls that would then get changed without ARC.  So it wouldn't currently be transparent to switch over (if someone regenerated and left their project as it, they could have issues since the code would assume ARC, but their compile setup would still have ARC disabled for the sources).

@thomasvl Good points (on NFS for `protoc` and not using ARC).

Let me find some time to run some numbers - again, not for publishing but more for comparision to see the benefits.

When and how, if at all, do we change to ARC can be decided later - based on efforts required. But, if we do decide on ARC, it'd be a breaking change then - what do you think?

Regarding `__unsafe_unretained`. Yes, there are ~100 references in `*_PackagePrivate.h` header files. :-)

Yea, it could be a breaking change.  The trick will be if we can tweak the generated code into a form where it is "right" with or without ARC, so we don't cause problems for existing projects.

`__unsafe_unretained` usage in all those was needed to allow the consumers of protos to be ARC if they wanted.  That's sorta different problem space, that's something we have to support and have some basic tests to ensure thing can always build/work that way.

title: Why is JSON parser strict about missing fields
body:
With google/protobuf/json_format.py, if you add new fields to the protobuf, it triggers errors like: `ParseError: Failed to parse message field: Message type "Foo" has no field named "fooId".`

This seems like an odd choice, b/c neither JSON nor pure protobufs are strict in this way (and for good reason). It kind of renders json_format.Parse useless.

I don't see a way to disable this strict field checking. What's going on here?

nodes.body:
Some differences between JSON and protobuf binary format:
1. There is a way to preserve unknown fields when parsing protobuf binary format, but we can only discard unknown fields when parsing from JSON to protobuf message.
2. JSON input may be manually constructed. Ignoring unknown fields may hide real errors (like a mistyped field name).
For these reasons we think the default should be strict. There should be an option to ignore/discard unknown fields though. It's just not implemented yet. Feel free to send us a pull request if you would like to help implement this option.

I see.  1 & 2 are reasonable points, but I think if you're working with JSON, you've already decided to make this tradeoff in the favor of flexibility over strictness.

In any event, making this behavior an option seems like the right next step. I'll look into it...

I happened to start with a go pr instead of python and you can see @dsymonds [response](https://github.com/golang/protobuf/pull/165)...

Any chance of adding it to the spec?

BTW JSON Schema covers this here: http://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-fge-json-schema-validation-00#page-13, and the default behavior is to ignore unknown fields (additionalProperties defaults to empty schema, and if its value is a schema, validation always succeeds).

Developer guide updated:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json_options

> Developer guide updated: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json_options

For the reference, updated link: https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/#json-options

Example for Python API: https://googleapis.dev/python/protobuf/latest/google/protobuf/json_format.html

```
google.protobuf.json_format.Parse(text, message, ignore_unknown_fields=False, descriptor_pool=None, max_recursion_depth=100)

    Parses a JSON representation of a protocol message into a message.

    Parameters:
            text – Message JSON representation.
            message – A protocol buffer message to merge into.
            ignore_unknown_fields – If True, do not raise errors for unknown fields.
            descriptor_pool – A Descriptor Pool for resolving types. If None use the default.
            max_recursion_depth – max recursion depth of JSON message to be deserialized. JSON messages over this depth will fail to be deserialized. Default value is 100.
```

title: Consider dropping support for "generate all in one directory" for C#
body:
Currently if you specify a C#-specific option of "base_namespace" the C# codegen will generate directories relative to that "base" (e.g. with a base namespace of Foo.Bar and a generated class namespace of Foo.Bar.Baz.Qux, we'd create a Baz/Qux directory and put the .cs file in there.) If you don't specify a base namespace at all, we put all the generated files in the directory specified by the --csharp_out option, without creating any directories.

This was raised as a concern by @haberman on #1390. I think we'd have to default to a base-namespace of "", i.e. generate directories assuming the csharp_out directory is a "root".

Pros:
- Avoids the problem where two proto files have the same name, so the latter would just "win"

Cons:
- I suspect this would be surprising behaviour for most C# developers, and it almost never causes an issue in practice. Where it does, it can be fixed by the dev _consuming_ the protos - it doesn't require a change to the proto file itself.

Other options:
- Notice the issue (if all the files are being generated in one go) and warn/error

// cc @jtattermusch, @chrisdunelm

nodes.body:
There are 3 general options for folder names:
1. All in `csharp_out` folder. Has risks.
2. In corresponding `csharp_out/{namespace}/{subnamespace}` folders (see [corefx](https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/tree/master/src) [sub-projects](https://github.com/dotnet/corefx/tree/master/src/System.Collections/src) for example) - currently possible using `base_namespace` option
3. In corresponding `csharp_out/{namespace}.{subnamespace}` folders (see [mono](https://github.com/mono/mono/tree/master/mcs/class/System.Web)) for example)

Any thoughts on the 3rd option?

@gvaish: Isn't the third option really separated by assembly/project rather than namespace? That's why each directory has a Makefile. This is basically option 2, but with no subspace because everything in the assembly is in the same namespace.

@jskeet Look at the folders within https://github.com/mono/mono/tree/master/mcs/class/System.Web
- [`mcs/class/System.Web`](https://github.com/mono/mono/tree/master/mcs/class/System.Web) is assembly
- [`mcs/class/System.Web/System.Web.UI.WebControls`](https://github.com/mono/mono/tree/master/mcs/class/System.Web/System.Web.UI.WebControls) is a namespace in the assembly.
- [`mcs/class/System.Web/System.Web.Caching`](https://github.com/mono/mono/tree/master/mcs/class/System.Web/System.Web.Caching) is another namespace in the assembly.

I've lost touch with active C# development lately but I always preferred this option for two reasons:
1. Not too deep folder hierarchy - that created problems on Windows at times (long path with nested projects and deeper namespaces).
2. Still allowed grouping related files together (in the namespace).

Ah - I must have stumbled on some subdirectories with makefiles. Sorry about that.

Unless we have evidence of this being more pervasive than just in Mono, I'd rather not support it - it's the first time I've ever seen it, and I don't think it's often going to be useful... I don't see why it's particularly handy to have the directory for System.Web.UI _not_ a parent of the directory for System.Web.UI.WebControls, for example.
Not a problem. I just wanted to let you know :)
@jskeet @gvaish realistically is this likely to be changed at this point? If not I can just close the issue.

@anandolee is probably the decider here, but I would suggest leaving it as it is at this point to avoid breaking people's builds.

Maybe we should close this but create a new issue to warn/error if multiple protos end up writing out the same file?
@jskeet Is this on the radar?
@gvaish: I very rarely have the time to contribute in this repository any more; @anandolee is the person to ask. But I doubt that anyone has been working on this.
not likely to be changed at this point

title: Unable to install from npm
body:
The [instructions](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/js/README.md) tell me to do `npm install google-protobuf`, but it's just a [dummy package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/google-protobuf).

Although I think you should take over [protobuf](https://www.npmjs.com/package/protobuf) instead, since it's unmaintained and doesn't work on any version of Node.js that's less than a year old.

nodes.body: It could be nice to have a way to install/use protobuf/nanobuf on node 4+

Thanks for the report. I've messaged the npm maintainers about taking the `google-protobuf` package back. I'll also message the maintainer of `protobuf` to see if he's interested in giving us the name. Wouldn't that break lots of users who might depend on the package already though? Maybe if it doesn't work with recent node then they are broken already.

> Wouldn't that break lots of users who might depend on the package already though?

Only if they haven't specified the maximum version (e.g. `"protobuf": "*"`). If they have specified at least the major version (which people do if they don't want things to break), then they will be fine, since the current `protobuf` version is `0.11.0`, but Google's protobuf is `3.0.0-alpha.5`.

That's of course assuming Google is fine with keeping the old `protobuf` versions on npm after taking over the name.
I've gotten `google-protobuf` back and published the correct code there, so this bug should be fixed.

title: Spelling error in protocol buffer basic c++ documentation on google developers
body:
I've read the protocol buffer basic c++ documentation on [google developers protobuf basic c++ tutorial](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial#the-protocol-buffer-api).

  The first paragraph of "The Protocol Buffer API" chapter says "If you look in `tutorial.pb.h`, you can see that you have a class for each message you specified in `tutorial.proto`". In fact, the name should be `addressbook.pb.h` and `addressbook.proto`. I searched the page and did not get the way to modify the content. To make the people who's willing to read the documentation not be confused, I'm here creating a github issue.

nodes.body: Fixed

title: Statically initialized objects in Status class
body:
The Status class has some statically initialized members for convenience (Status::OK, Status::UNKNOWN, and Status::CANCELLED). It is a good practice to avoid these, so I created a pull request that I thought would transparently remove them (https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/1367). It turned out not to be as compatible with existing code as I though, so I'd like to step back and reconsider the situation.

It seems to me that if we want to remove static initializers, and Status has some statically initialized members, there's really no way other than removing those members or replacing them with something that can be e.g. linker-initialized. In any case, it involves changing the API.

The question is: is protobuf project open to such change? If so, we could start brainstorming on what would be the best and most convenient solution.

nodes.body:
A few notes:
- The desire to remove static initializers is coming from Chromium, where we have a strict policy against such.  However, I believe static instances of non-POD types are also banned by the Google style guide, and thus a change to remove these would be something libprotobuf maintainers should find desirable.
- Here are some ways of removing these static initializers beyond the pull request linked above:

(1) Replace caller instances of "status == Status::OK" with something like "status.ok()".  This requires ensuring sufficient functions similar to "ok()" exist to replace all static objects.
(2) Replace caller instances of "status == Status::OK" with something like "status == Status(error::OK)".  This requires adding an explicit Status(error::Code code) constructor.
(3) Replace caller instances of "status == Status::OK" with something like "status == Status::OK()".  This requires changing the static objects into static methods which return the relevant Status objects.

These are ordered by what I'd personally perceive as decreasing desirability in terms of how "hacky" they feel.

Oh, also, it would be nice to get some sort of indication what the best to go is soon, so we can proceed with doing this locally in Chromium in parallel to trying to upstream that solution here.  This will unblock landing a long-delayed upgrade to our copy of libprotobuf.

@xyzzyz Could you take a look at the implementation of Google-internal util/task/status.h and mimic its implementation in protobuf's fork? I would like to avoid any API difference between the protobuf version and the Google-internal version.

The internal version is pretty hacky, in that it depends on a) compiler generating the same memory layout for two different classes with the same fields in the order (which I'm not sure is guaranteed by the standard) b) making sure one doesn't update fields in Status without also updating ones in Status::Rep (as it will break terribly in runtime).

I could write a pull-request that would mimic the internal solution, but I wouldn't bet that it won't break across different compilers or platforms.

Peter, as for your proposition (1), method .ok() already exists, think of rather things like "return Status::OK" which are quite popular throughout the codebase, so fixing cases like in (1) will not suffice.

Yeah, if you want "return Status::OK" you'd need ideas 2 or 3.

I consulted some other people about the method used by the internal code and it seems like while it is likely to work in practice, it probably violates the C++ strict aliasing rules and thus is technically undefined behavior.  (You can cast from a Rep\* to a containing Status or Status::Pod, but you can't go the other way, or cast across from one of the latter to the other.)  For more info see http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/reinterpret_cast#Type_aliasing .

Unfortunately, given how widely referenced this is internally, it is probably infeasible to change the internal implementation.  Given this, I would reluctantly suggest copying the internal implementation and crossing fingers.  Luckily, the Status::Pod type is never used except in the block that does the static initialization here, so there are no places in which an optimization that assumes strict aliasing rules would introduce incorrect code.  Given this, the chance of something bad actually happening seems fairly remote.
So it seems Status is not really used in protobuf, only by some util code. We should kick that util code out of our lib.
I would like to move json out of core proto and depend on absl for status.
@Josh this bug is related to the discussion around moving to absl::Status.

Ok, there are a couple issues in play here:

1. Internally these constants (OK, CANCELLED, etc) have already been removed from `Status`. So our Status object is already incompatible with `absl::Status`.
2. Ultimately we may not be able to migrate to `absl::Status` anyway, because we expose `Status` in our public API. At the moment we have decided not to expose ABSL types directly in our public API. So our decision for now is to keep our own copy/port of `Status` indefinitely.
3. That still leaves us with the question of how to deal with these global constructors. I wonder if constexpr could help us create linker-initialized globals here.
Protobuf is now using `absl::Status` and the local copy does not exist anymore at head.

title: Generated javadoc on proto3 Java classes has incorrect first line
body:
For example, the javadoc for pubsub's Topic.getName(): 
  /**                                                                                                                                                                                                              
   * optional string name = 1;                                                                                                                                                                        
   *                                                                                                                                                                                                               
   * <pre>                                                                                                                                                                                                         
   * The name of the topic. It must have the format                                                                                                                                                                
   * `"projects/{project}/topics/{topic}"`. `{topic}` must start with a letter,                                                                                                                                    
   * and contain only letters (`[A-Za-z]`), numbers (`[0-9]`), dashes (`-`),                                                                                                                                       
   * underscores (`_`), periods (`.`), tildes (`~`), plus (`+`) or percent                                                                                                                                         
   * signs (`%`). It must be between 3 and 255 characters in length, and it                                                                                                                                        
   * must not start with `"goog"`.                                                                                                                                                                                 
   * </pre>                                                                                                                                                                                                        
   */
Since the first line is the proto declaration ("optional string name = 1;"), that is what shows up in short descriptions of the attribute, which makes the generated javadoc html not very usable.

title: what complex Data Structure are Support by protobuf?( C++  C#)
body:

nodes.body: You can convert your dictionary to a List of key value pairs. This can be easily handled using protobuf. Then you can convert it back to a Dictionary later.
We also have [support for maps](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#maps) so that may be a good fit for your dictionary.

That should work. In fact the wire format of map fields is equivalent to your repeated MapStruct field (see [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#backwards-compatibility)), so you can use your approach and later replace it with a map in a backward-compatible way if you ever upgrade to a newer version of protocol buffers with map support.

title: Don't use null_resettable for field declarations in ObjC
body:
In proto3 all fields are optional, so they should also be optional in the generated code. Currently all the fields are generated as null_resettable which means they are imported to Swift as implicitly unwrapped optionals, so they are not optional, but the code crashes if they are accessed and not set.
My proposal is to generate these fields as nullable, so they are really optional to set.

nodes.body: We're trying to keep proto2 and proto3 generated messages acting the same (they can be mixed, so developers don't always know which one they are getting).  You shouldn't crash as nil should never be returned from a fetch, the default value should be returned (a message with nothing set, or the empty string, etc.).  Do you have an example where that isn't happening?
If anyone else comes across this issue, please see some of the discussion on https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/1431 (sorry, it happened there instead of on the issue itself)

title: undefined behaviour when emulating offsetof
body:
(context: https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=605933)

The UBSan detects undefined behaviours in protobuf code which are using reinterpret_cast on invalid pointers to emulate offsetof() macro. These are: 

1) GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_GENERATED_MESSAGE_FIELD_OFFSET macro that tries to emulate __builtin_offsetof and makes are reinterpret_casts on an invalid pointer (16):
https://code.google.com/p/chromium/codesearch#chromium/src/third_party/protobuf/src/google/protobuf/generated_message_reflection.h&q=GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_GENERATED_MESSAGE_FIELD_OFFSET&sq=package:chromium&type=cs&l=590

2) ZR_HELPER that appears in the generated files:
# define ZR_HELPER_(f) reinterpret_cast<char*>(\

  &reinterpret_cast<BaseLayerProperties*>(16)->f)

Some issue: invalid reinterpret_cast.

The first issue might be fixed by defining GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_GENERATED_MESSAGE_FIELD_OFFSET as __builtin_offsetof and suppressing -Winvalid-offsetof.

For the second, the for the generated code should be in third_party/protobuf/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_message.cc:

The following macro needs to be changed:
-  const char\* macros =
-      "#define ZR_HELPER_(f) __builtin_offsetof($classname$, f)\n\n"
-      "#define ZR_(first, last) do {\\n"
-      "  ::memset(&first, 0,\\n"
-      "           ZR_HELPER_(last) - ZR_HELPER_(first) + sizeof(last));\\n"
-      "} while (0)\n\n";

Note that using __builtiin_offsetof() on non-POD types is still undefined behaviour, but seems like it is better suited for the job, and less likely to break due to compiler optimizing it out.

nodes.body:
To clarify:

-- Using __builtin_offsetof() on non-POD types is undefined behavior, but it's equivalent to the reinterpret_cast scheme used in the macros above. So, using __builtin_offsetof() is not worse than the current state of things.

-- Making reinterpret_cast on naked invalid pointers prevents dynamic tools, like UBSan vptr ([1]) or LLVM CFI ([2]) to work correctly. In Chrome, we aim to enable LLVM CFI for the official Chrome binaries (on Linux first), which should have a measurable positive effect on the overall Chrome security.
1. http://clang.llvm.org/docs/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer.html#availablle-checks
2. http://clang.llvm.org/docs/ControlFlowIntegrity.html
3. https://www.chromium.org/developers/testing/control-flow-integrity

My proposal would be to use __builtin_offsetof() for the compilers which support it (like, Clang or GCC) , and suppress the corresponding warning  (-Winvalid-offsetof) with a pragma. It's probably okay to keep the current scheme for the compilers we don't know much about, just in case if they implement things significantly different and also to ensure that the code would compile without warnings.

Am I right that we don't have a way to fix the undefined behavior and the solution is just to suppress warnings/errors in the compiler/build tool? If so, instead of using __builtin_offsetof which will trigger a compiler warning, can we add something specific for UBSan or LLVM CFI to let them not complain?

Well, the current scheme has two undefined behaviors:
1. It relies on the specific layout of the fields within a non-POD type (just like __builtin_offsetof)
2. It makes a reinterpret_cast on a naked pointer 0x10

So, we can get rid of at least of one of them and keep only the necessary evil in the code.

At least in Clang, the following works:

```
#define GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_GENERATED_MESSAGE_FIELD_OFFSET(TYPE, FIELD)    \
  _Pragma("clang diagnostic push")                                     \
  _Pragma("clang diagnostic ignored \"-Winvalid-offsetof\"")           \
  __builtin_offsetof(TYPE, FIELD)                                      \
  _Pragma("clang diagnostic pop")
#else
```

It turns off the warning, but only for a single line. That should work for GCC too, I believe.

Sorry, missed this message:

> Am I right that we don't have a way to fix the undefined behavior and the solution is just to suppress warnings/errors in the compiler/build tool? If so, instead of using __builtin_offsetof which will trigger a compiler warning, can we add something specific for UBSan or LLVM CFI to let them not complain?

Both UBSan and LLVM CFI rely on reading the vtable pointers to determine if the cast is vaild. In case of UBSan, it should be not hard to just suppress a report for reinterpret_cast(0x10). It's imperfect, as it would make it harder to find bugs in other programs, but it's doable.

For CFI, it's a harder sell, as it's not a bug-finding tool, it's a security hardening approach and invalid reinterpret_cast would defeat the defense. If we allow the cast, we'll also need to prove that the value is not then used to call virtual functions, and running such escape analysis is prohibitively complex in both the time to implement and time to run. It will never be perfect too.
Yes, maybe. Let me take a look / ask around.

@xfxyjwf either of those approaches would work, but I would slightly prefer the approach of using offsetof(), as the suppression would be more localised. You can suppress the warning by using pragmas as Ivan mentioned.

If you do decide to go with the first approach, you can use the no_sanitize http://clang.llvm.org/docs/AttributeReference.html#no-sanitize-clang-no-sanitize attribute on each function that uses the macro.

@pcc no sanitize attribute for each function that uses a macro seems unpractical to me (based on the exploration of proto3 code). It's also unnecessary coarse compared to the use of __builtin_offsetof and enabling / disabling pragmas like I do above, where a single line is excluded from the compiler diagnostics.

title: Building iOS Framework with custom public protobuf message classes
body:
I would like to build an iOS framework with protobuf message classes accessible through public headers. I ran into the following problem.

Headers imported like `#import "google/protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h"` in the protobuf runtime cannot be accessed when added to a framework's public headers as public headers are just copied to the framework Headers directory without keeping the directory structure. These headers are included by the `#import "GPBProtocolBuffers.h"` directive in the generated Objective-C file.

One could use a Copy Files build phase to copy these headers into the Headers directory of the framework but then the files imported into these files like `#import "GPBProtocolBuffers.h"` will not be found.

I suggest changing header imports from:
`#import "google/protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h"`
to:
`#import "Any.pbobjc.h"`
which still works in the xcode project but also makes building frameworks possible.

nodes.body: So there's a secondary problem, and that is the generated code also needing to import the WellKnownTypes or even the base headers themselves.  We're trying to figure out how to full support this.  Doing imports of just the name can lead to header collisions if some two things end up wanting to use the same file name (which we've see with larger proto trees where things are otherwise grouped in directories to avoid it).

Could the well known types file names could also be prefixed with GPB like all others?
Like: `#import "GPBAny.pbobjc.h"`
For those, yea, that could be an option, but the problem can have in protos needed from other places.  Two services should end up with a "user.proto" (or something like that).

I think that is a more general problem and is out of this problem's scope. Services should prefix their classes in general as it is expected in Objective-C. There is a protobuf option for this:
`option objc_class_prefix = "PREFIX";`
The generated Objective-C files should also be prefixed.

That options is documented as only prefixing the symbols and not the files themselves.

If you aren't using CocoaPods/Frameworks, the directory structure that would exist on disk for those duplicate names also works for the includes.  It's just when frameworks are used that things start to fail.  :(

The limited mangling we already do of the filenames (underscores to camelcase), also causes problems for some folks: https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/864.  So for those build systems, having the output files depend on the content of the file would make that even harder to integrate.
Early snapshot (not fully tested), for protobufs being in a framework is in https://github.com/thomasvl/protobuf/tree/framework_includes.
Is there a suggested workaround for this one in the meantime?

@thomasvl the generated code for some of my .protos does not include the `#if #else #endif` style import headers only the Protobuf ones do.

Is there a file option that was added to trigger this output for frameworks? Yes, I am using the pre-released version from HEAD master.

You should only need the conditional imports when importing the headers that are from the core library, imports between your own protos should be fine since they aren't in the Protobuf framework created by the pods.   Can you post a snippet of what isn't working for you?

Sure here it is:

``` objc

// source: redacted/common/validation.proto

// This CPP symbol can be defined to use imports that match up to the framework
// imports needed when using CocoaPods.

#endif

#else

#endif

etc...
```

My podspec:

``` ruby
Pod::Spec.new do |s|
```

I had to remove some stuff but can get the idea. You can replace "redacted" with just another folder name, nothing changes semantically. 

Also the `.proto` definition contains `package redacted.validation;`

Makes sense, I think a file option would help here as you mentioned perhaps something like:

`option objc_framework_import_name = "ValidationProtos_objc"`

Thanks for re-opening this.

re option - the problem is it is data recorded in the proto file that might not be correct for all developers.  i.e. - you might want to package it differently from another developer.  So one of you two has to edit the file.  If the file is part of something like a grpc api, then you both end up editing it to meet your needs, and keeping it up to date as that grpc api updates becomes a pain.

You'll have less frameworks than .proto files, so let's invert that map for the sake of people's fingers:

```
my_framework -> file1.proto, file2.proto
another_framework -> file3.proto, file4.proto
```

There's also `man 3 regex`, but I'm not sure I want to deal with hoping that exists for protoc on all platforms (especially Windows).

I should add, I was only pondering regex because I was trying to think of a way to say something like _All the protos in this directory are this framework_.  They do come with their own complexity, so it isn't a great option.
What about globbing instead of letting people use regex? Every system _should_ have a way to expand programmatically the files that match `dir/*.proto`.

My initial thought/fear with Windows and the whole \ vs / problem.  But I might end up facing that no matter what, I'll have to see.  Maybe `fnmatch()` would work; but I don't know that it really has a way to do things really recursively down directories.

title: Custom options with proto3

body: `Parser.merge(String, Message.Builder)` catches exceptions appropriately, but `Parser.merge(Reader, Message.Builder)` [runs `jsonParser.parse(reader)` without a try-catch](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/0de06f5/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L979). title: Can't use unbundled python protobuf on Linux if python-protobuf package is installed
body:
Here's the problem. On Ubuntu Linux Trusty, I have the python-protobuf package installed from apt.
Now, I am trying to use the python protobuf library from the sources (specifically form a chromium tree, but this is irrelevant) by prepending in the path. The problem is that the dist-package version of google.protobuf gets always picked first.
Repro:

> > > import sys
> > > sys.path.insert(0, '/s/chrome/src/third_party/protobuf/python')
> > > import google.protobuf
> > > google.protobuf
> > > <module 'google.protobuf' from '/usr/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/google/protobuf/**init**.pyc

I investigated a bit with a colleague and this seems to be due to the google/**init**.py
In v3.0.0-beta-2 it does:
_import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(**name**)

the problem seems to be that the corresponding debian site-package is a conventional module w/o namespace (i.e. /usr/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/google/protobuf/**init**.py is just empty)

Later 786f80fe6632902be74f90a577d75e8641494abd  changed that to 
try:
  **import**('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(**name**)
except ImportError:
  **path** = **import**('pkgutil').extend_path(**path**, **name**)

which does not really solve the problem.
The right resolution seems to follow what PEP420 suggests, namely:

> Namespace packages today
> Python currently provides pkgutil.extend_path to denote a package as a namespace package. The recommended way of using it is to put:
> from pkgutil import extend_path
> **path** = extend_path(**path**, **name**)

I confirm that this fixes the issue and makes protobuf sources usable as a module even in presence of the python-protobuf system package.

nodes.body:
@silviulica @craigcitro 
What is the rationale of the try / pkg_resources / except / pkgutil?
I'd go for https://github.com/primiano/protobuf/commit/ed07ef2fc2d55e192e4879c1d062b3886bfc6d5e
but I have no idea if I am breaking something and how to test it

setup.py is failing regardless for me on master:

```
$ python setup.py build
running build
running build_py
Generating google/protobuf/descriptor_pb2.py...
google/protobuf/descriptor.proto:386:3: Expected "required", "optional", or "repeated".
google/protobuf/descriptor.proto:386:12: Expected field name.

```

@primiano We had originally wanted to go with just `pkgutil`, but had heard that trying `pkg_resources` first was the preferred approach. This is one where I know I'm in over my head -- @jonparrott, is there a reason to prefer `pkg_resources` over `pkgutil`?

`pkg_resources` is from `setuptools` which does things better than `pkgutil`. Notably:
- it supports PEP 302, Import hooks.
- If an existing non-namespace package is in `sys.path` and different package is installed that says the first package is indeed a namespace package, then it'll fix the module's `__path__` correctly.
- Other black magic.

The real issue here is that no matter what you can not do a in-place upgrade of a package that once was not namespaced with a version that is now namespaced. The workaround is to have `setup.py` check for this situation and tell the user to uninstall the package first. Prior art [here](https://github.com/google/google-api-python-client/blob/master/setup.py#L51).

So stepping back a little, this is my concrete problem:
In the chrome codebase we have protobuf v3.0.0 ($CHROME/src/third_party/protobuf).
As part of the build I generate a python stub by doing protoc file.proto --python_out=somewhere, where protoc is built from $CHROME/src/third_party/protobuf. So far so good.

Now I would like to consume the generated file_pb2.py as part of the build process itself (i.e. run a python script which does "import file_pb2"). Clearly I want python to pick the protobuf python libs in $CHROME/src/third_party/protobuf/python, as the generated stub must match the runtime library (and concretely it fails if I don't, which is WAI).

Now, my problem is that if the developer has installed the python-protobuf package, I don't know any way to force python to pick $CHROME/src/third_party/protobuf/python instead of the dist-package. Which is bad++. How do I achieve this? I cannot ask chrome devs to uninstall system packages to build, that is unprecedented.

In general feels very weird to me that this python library cannot be imported without installing / uninstalling other stuff.
In this specific case If I prepend  $CHROME/src/third_party/protobuf/python as first element of the sys.path I do expect that library to be picked first. Instead, the dist-package is picked, inverting the order of what I requested.

I admit that I am ignorant about pkgutil vs pkg_resources. The only things that I can see is that:
- pkgutil does the right thing (w.r.t. properly setting up paths in presence of a dist google module)
- PEP420 reccomends pkgutil.
  So my, perhaps naive, question here is: what is the disadvantage of pkgutil vs pkg_resources?

@jonparrott 

> The real issue here is that no matter what you can not do a in-place upgrade of a package that once was not namespaced with a version that is now namespaced.

No my real issue here is not about install. I am not trying to install anything. I just want to use the local protobuf library (which feels to me a reasonable requirement) and I don't see any way to achieve this.

> The workaround is to have setup.py check for this situation and tell the user to uninstall the package first.

I am not interested into running any setup.py here.

> PEP420 recomends pkgutil. So my, perhaps naive, question here is: what is the disadvantage of pkgutil vs pkg_resources?

`pkgutil` is preferred if you need to support `.pkg` files, `pkg_resources` works better for all other cases.

> In this specific case If I prepend $CHROME/src/third_party/protobuf/python as first element of the sys.path I do expect that library to be picked first. Instead, the dist-package is picked, inverting the order of what I requested.

Manipulating `sys.path` is **bad**. People say it's bad and tell you not to do it for a reason. Python's import lookup system isn't as simple as checking directories. For protobuf, this is a "non-trivial" package that requires namespace packages to be setup - this happens as part of the site-packages initialization logic. There's ways to do this after interpreter startup (see darth-vendor which eventually made its way into appengine), but they aren't pretty and you shouldn't do them.

> No my real issue here is not about install. I am not trying to install anything. I just want to use the local protobuf library (which feels to me a reasonable requirement) and I don't see any way to achieve this.

Unfortunately, this isn't a reasonable request. This is a python library and it's designed to be installed to work. Even the tests install it first. This is how it works. Libraries only work without having their `setup.py` run in certain cases. You could try doing some wheel magic, but even that it too much black magic for this.

It seems like what you want to do is setup a virtualenv and install your custom version of protobuf into that, then use it.

```
$ virtualenv env
$ source env/bin/activate
$ pip install src/third_party/protobuf/python
```

closing the loop, in case somebody encounters this in future.
I found this hack that seems to make things work without requiring folks to install virtualenv.

```
import os
_PROTOBUF_DIR = os.path.join(_CHROME_SRC, 'third_party', 'protobuf', 'python')
import pkg_resources
pkg_resources.declare_namespace('google')
pkg_resources.fixup_namespace_packages(_PROTOBUF_DIR)
import google
assert _PROTOBUF_DIR in google.__path__[0]
import google.protobuf
assert _PROTOBUF_DIR in google.protobuf.__path__[0]
import google.protobuf.descriptor
...

```
Let me go ahead and close this since it sounds like the problem is more-or-less resolved.

Wouldn't relative imports break the case that you are importing protos from a different pip package?

@haberman This bug has to do with protos importing protos in the same package, even in the same directory. The compiler converts this into relative imports with defective syntax under Python 3, so the generated code cannot execute at all.
