title: Update project to be compatible with Xcode 8
[C#] Messages with repeated fields can't use object initializers effectively
body:
It is impossible to use object initializers on messages with `repeated` fields in some of the most useful cases.  Any attempt to use it with anything other than just a literal collection initializer will fail with `Property cannot be assigned to -- it is read-only`

This makes mapping from one type to another of the sort that you would do in a LINQ construct (or any functional-like construct) impossible.

So for example, the following assignment is not allowed, even if request.Numbers is another RepeatedField of the same type.

``` csharp
var m = new Person {
    Numbers = request.Numbers, // <- Error: Person.Numbers cannot be assigned to -- it is read-only
};
```

This design appears intentional so that 1) there is always a `RepeatedField<T>` instance, which you can't remove, but you can add to or remove from, and 2) assignment of a reference to a mutable collection can lead to unintuitive behavior (e.g. if the above example were allowed and I were to later modify `request.Numbers`, it would feel wrong and would be surprising if `m.Numbers` also reflected that later change.)

On the other hand, if assignment were just implemented as a copy, would there be any problem?

Furthermore it would make it possible to implement an extension (for use in something like LINQ) of this sort:

``` csharp
public static RepeatedField<T> ToRepeatedField<T>(this IEnumerable<T> e) { ... }
```

This would make code like this possible:

``` csharp
var m  = new Person {
   Numbers = request.Numbers.Where(n => IsValid(n)).ToRepeatedField(), // <- Yay!
}
```

And then even further, RepeatedField<T>, could be modified possibly with an optional copy-on-write flag internally allowing more efficient implementation of the assignment and extension examples above.

What are the reasons not to do this?

nodes.body:
I propose a two part solution.  I'm looking for comments on this as I'm planning to submit a PR for it.
1. Add a setter to the generated C# messages which takes the form `set { myField_ = value.Snapshot(); }`
2. Implement `Snapshot()` on `RepeatedField` which sets a flag on the field to force a copy of the underlying array before any future mutation (add/remove/update) and return a new instance that shares the underlying array and also has this flag set.

The cost of a snapshot when no modifications follow is insignificant.  If modifications follow on either the original or the snapshot, the cost is no different from doing a copy first and then modification.  However if modifications follow on _both_ the snapshot and the original, one additional copy operation is necessary, which is the reason for calling this `Snapshot()` to keep it separate from a possible later shallow copy function.

The benefit of this design is that it allows construction of functions that return a `RepeatedField` instance and allows using those functions within message initializers.

So for example, this allows creation of a `ToRepeatedField<T>` extension as mentioned above which materializes the `IEnumerable<T>` to a `RepeatedField<T>` (much like `ToArray<T>()` does for arrays).  This could then be assigned to a `RepeatedField<T>` field with practically no additional overhead than if `Add(IEnumerable<T>)` had been called directly on an empty field.

The cost of this is
1. the extra boolean field on RepeatedField,
2. the fetch of that field in the mutators,
3. the branch on that value (which should be predictable in bulk operations), and
4. removal of the `readonly` modifier on the underlying fields in the message.

title: If I generate CommonJS code from a proto file that depends on a well known proto file, the generated code has incorrect imports

nodes.body:
Note: two changes are probably required to make this work:
1. The `google-protobuf` node module should include generated code for well known types.
2. The code generator should generate code that refers to those files.
CC @xfxyjwf @pherl
Also CC @haberman
@haberman this bug is the blocking issue for a grpc JS release (planned this week). Could you take a look?
Looking at this now.

After talking this over with @murgatroid99, I think we may need a new file-level option for this. Unlike other languages, Node.js does not seem to have a way to generate `require(x)` statements that will work the same regardless of whether `x` is in the same package or a different package.
1. for files in the same package, we need to require them as `require('./google/protobuf/any_pb.js')`.
2. for files in a different package, we need to require them as `require('google-protobuf/google/protobuf/any_pb.js')`.

To support this, we propose adding a new file-level option: `npm_package`.

When we generate `require()` statements, we will see if the `npm_package` option between the includer and the includee match. If so, we will generate a require like (1). If not, we will generate a require like (2).

Does this sound good to you @pherl?
We should probably special well known types imports (we did this in C++ as well); and then revisit the issue if cross package imports is a common use case.
PR is out: https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/1696
PR is merged, closing this issue.

title: [C#] Project file uses relative path to packages; cannot be added to other solutions
body:
The csproj file references the nuget packages directory using a relative path `..\packages` instead of a more precise `$(SolutionDir)\packages`.  This causes the project to be non-buildable if you add it to any solution outside the git tree.

The error you get is:

```
error : This project references NuGet package(s) that are missing on this computer. Use NuGet Package Restore to download them.  For more information, see http://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkID=322105. The missing file is ..\packages\NuSpec.ReferenceGenerator.1.4.1\build\portable-net45+win+wpa81+wp80+MonoAndroid10+xamarinios10+MonoTouch10\NuSpec.ReferenceGenerator.targets.
```

nodes.body: Note: that this actually occurs due to a bug in NuGet (see https://github.com/NuGet/Home/issues/2368).  The final solution is to switch to package.json instead of package.config, but that feature isn't ready yet.  The temporary solution is to manually correct the paths from `..\packages` to `$(SolutionDir)\packages`.

As it happens, PR #1721 already switches to use `project.json` instead of `packages.config`, but I'm trying to work out how we're going to build and test on Mono at the moment.

I'd rather not manually tinker with the project file at the moment.
#1727 switches to project.json

title: javascript code generator generates unused require of import weak
body:
In our protos, we `import weak "gogoproto/gogo.proto";` and use it for Golang-specific options. Using this proto with `--js_out`, an unused `var gogoproto_gogo_pb = require('../../../gogoproto/gogo_pb.js');` is generated. I believe `import weak` should not result in a generated `require`.

cc @haberman

nodes.body: What do you use "import weak" for? I don't think that's a supported feature in opensource protobuf and should be flagged as a compile error when you invoke protoc.

Well, we've been using it for importing protos that are needed only for various field or message options (and not for any messages).

In other words, we need this proto during code generation of our other protos, but we don't want to have to codegen and compile it into the application.

I have this similar problem. I import the github.com/gogo/protobuf/gogoproto/gogo.proto and use it for Golang-specific options. but the generated cpp file has generated line #include "github.com/gogo/protobuf/gogoproto/gogo.pb.h"

Regarding the imports/includes/requires, protoc is working as intended here. In JS/C++ or even Go, protoc should generate imports/includes/requires for the imported gogo.proto file. This is necessary for the custom options to be correctly interpreted at runtime for every language. Protoc has to assume the .proto file will be used at runtime for every language because it has no way to tell whether an import is used for a specific language, nor it can tell whether the imported .proto file is used at compile time only or both compile time and runtime.

We can probably add a new syntax to support language-specific compile-time custom options, but "import weak" is certainly not the right one. Also can you describe what problem does the additional include/require cause for you? Adding a new syntax is a big change and we need more supporting data for it.

The main downside of additional imports is that we have to compile the
aforementioned file, which in the case of `gogo` is located out-of-tree.
Remember, we have to compile this thing even in JS, so now our JS tooling
needs to know about GOPATH.

title: javascript code generator emiting lists instead of maps
body:
I'm using grpc-tools 0.14.1 off of npm which has protoc 3 bundled.  It looks like it's emitting a list instead of a map for fields defined as maps with syntax="proto3" at the top of the file.  I also noticed the tests in js for proto3 don't actually have a map in the test either. ( https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/3.0.0-beta-3/js/proto3_test.proto )

From my spelunking through the compiler, it appears the offending code is here https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/3.0.0-beta-3/src/google/protobuf/compiler/js/js_generator.cc#L1938 where it checks for is_repeated, but isn't checking is_map first to call toMap instead of toObjectList.  The JSGetterName also needs some minor tweaks to emit a "Map" suffix instead of "List".  If this is the right approach, I'm happy to submit a pull request to get this patched up.

nodes.body: I remember maps support is added in our internal code base. It probably hasn't propagated to the opensource repo yet.

Any idea when that will make it public?  Our team has been pretty actively contributing to grpc-java and working with the gRPC teams, and are expanding to NodeJS and other areas where the protobuf generation is a bit less mature than Java.  We'd like to be able to contribute here as well when needed, and know our efforts to track down the problems(like here) isn't a waste because it's already been patched somewhere we can't see.  I'm looking forward to hear how we can more effectively contribute.  Thanks!
Hi there and thanks for the report. This was indeed committed internally recently. I believe we are working right now on getting these changes to open-source. @acozzette can say more.
Yes, I am working on merging and publishing our internal changes and will try to get that done as soon as possible, hopefully by tomorrow.
Sorry for the delay but our internal changes have now been merged to the master branch and this includes the new maps support for JSPB.
Thanks!  When should we expect a release to npm?

We usually do a protobuf release once a quarter; the last one was around mid-May so a rough guess for the next one would be some time around mid-August. Does that sound reasonable or do you need this feature sooner?

We'd certainly like this sooner since it's a pretty significant gap in the proto3 support, but I understand if that isn't part of the normal release cadence.  The large driver here is that gRPC is moving towards 1.0, and we're starting to consume our Java services in languages like NodeJS.  There's an obvious workaround for now which is simply to convert the array into a map, but it's quite surprising for developers the first time it is encountered, and took me a fair bit to realize what was happening.  I'm also worried about ending up with a significant amount of code working around the list limitation having to be re-written, though there are workarounds there too.

I also just looked at the changes on master to the files I had linked above.  They don't appear to have a test for map, nor do they use the toMap method anywhere in the compiler plugin.  The runtime library has support for maps, but it appears they aren't generating them still.  Am I looking in the wrong place?  I'm also happy to contribute a fix still if it turns out that the fix isn't made yet after all.

I'll check with the rest of the team and see if there's a way we can do a release sooner or at least push the JS changes to npm without a full release for all languages.

About the map changes, I think you're right that something's missing--it looks to me like a file or two didn't make it to master. I'm working on fixing this right now.

title: Add version (v3) to package name in Java
body:
TL;DR I would like to propose that package `com.google.protobuf` becomes `com.google.protobuf.v3` in Java. It is conceivable that one wants/needs to use both library versions simultaneously.

`proto3` is not backwards compatible with `proto2`, at least in Java. I noticed that when I tried to use `proto3` to serialise data to be put into HBase. The thing is that HBase at version `1.2.1` (latest) internally uses version `2.5.0`of the library and one of messages it defines overrides `writeTo` method - which is marked `final` as of `3.0.0-beta`.

Regardless of the reasoning behind modifying autogenerated code this essentially means that I can't use `proto3` with HBase which for me is a major bummer since I want to be able to use gRPC as well as serve the Ruby client which does not support `proto2` 😱.

One way or another, instead of trying to provide backwards compatibility which is a hard target to hit I would like to suggest that `proto3` is explicitly namespaced as to allow both versions to coexist in one app.

nodes.body:
This is a known issue (reported quite frequently by hadoop/hbase users). We discussed and decided to work on fixing up v3.0.0 to make it compatible with 2.5.0 generated code for ease of migration. We are still working on it and will probably soon publish a Java specific version that can be used as a bridge version between 2.5.0 and 3.0.0.

title: Make StringPiece interface match std::string_view
body: C++17 will include std::string_view, which is essentially just a standardized replacement for StringPiece. To plan ahead for this, we should consider updating the StringPiece API so that it exactly matches std::string_view. Then a few years from now when C++17 is widespread we can make StringPiece just a type alias for std::string_view. I believe StringPiece is just used within protobuf internals at the moment and so we can safely change its API without breaking any user code.

title: [ubsan] signed integer overflow in protobuf/stubs/strutil.cc
body:
../../third_party/protobuf/src/google/protobuf/stubs/strutil.cc:984:17: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 42 \* 100000000 cannot be represented in type 'int'

The line:

```
sublt100_000_000:
    u -= digits * 100000000;  // 100,000,000
```

Will overflow if digits is large (e.g. 42) since digits is an int and the constant is an int.

This can be fixed by changing the constant to uint

```
sublt100_000_000:
    u -= digits * 100000000u;  // 100,000,000
```

It also turns out that in the generation for the --.pb.cc it also is following the convention for the location of where the original --.proto is located for it's various includes to the --.pb.h location.

Instead of getting : #include "../src/ProtocolBuffers/Subfolder/Subfolder1/Subfolder2/--.pb.h"
It generates as : #include "../ProtocolBuffers/Subfolder/Subfolder1/Subfolder2/--.pb.h"

I think you should call:
protoc.exe --cpp_out=src/ProtocolBuffers -IProtocolBuffers ProtocolBuffers/Subfolder/Subfolder1/Subfolder2/testMessage.proto

Could someone explain this:

```
[mrozowsk@cnu420dqzs test_case]$ tree top/
top/
└── dir
    └── sub
        └── file.proto

2 directories, 1 file
[mrozowsk@cnu420dqzs test_case]$ protoc --cpp_out=out -Itop/dir/sub -Itop/dir top/dir/sub/file.proto
[mrozowsk@cnu420dqzs test_case]$ tree out/
out/
├── file.pb.cc
└── file.pb.h

0 directories, 2 files
[mrozowsk@cnu420dqzs test_case]$ rm -fr out/*
[mrozowsk@cnu420dqzs test_case]$ protoc --cpp_out=out -Itop/dir -Itop/dir/sub top/dir/sub/file.proto
[mrozowsk@cnu420dqzs test_case]$ tree out/
out/
└── sub
    ├── file.pb.cc
    └── file.pb.h

1 directory, 2 files
```

The output directory layout depends on proto file lookup paths...

Yes, basically `protoc` tries to canonicalize every file path. If you use `-Ia/b` then `protoc` assumes that `a/b` is the root of a tree of .proto files. So then if it comes across `a/b/c/d.proto`, it assumes that `c/d.proto` is the canonical name for that proto. All of the output files will be generated to match the canonical path of the input .proto file.

I really do not recommend doing something like `-Itop/dir -Itop/dir/sub`.

This behaviour is quite annoying, I'm trying to use `protoc` from `meson` (http://mesonbuild.com/) within a subproject.

I have integrated ( https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/mesonbuild/sOus_Wog5_E )  `protoc` like this:

```
gen = generator(protoc, \
  output    : ['@BASENAME@.pb.cc', '@BASENAME@.pb.h'],
  arguments : ['--proto_path=@SOURCE_DIR@', '--cpp_out=@BUILD_DIR@', '@INPUT@'])
```

The `@INPUT@` in my situation is filled with a relative path to the subproject. This leads to a `protoc` command like this:

 '/usr/bin/protoc' '--proto_path=..' '--cpp_out=subprojects/libyami-proto/yami-proto@sha' '../subprojects/libyami-proto/Mumble.proto'

What meson expects is that the generated protobuf files will be placed in 

```
subprojects/libyami-proto/yami-proto@sha/Mumble.pb.c
subprojects/libyami-proto/yami-proto@sha/Mumble.pb.h
```

What happens instead is that `protoc` generates these files:

```
subprojects/libyami-proto/yami-proto@sha/subprojects/libyami-proto/Mumble.pb.c
subprojects/libyami-proto/yami-proto@sha/subprojects/libyami-proto/Mumble.pb.h
```

I don't know how I can work around this.

Using `--proto_path=@CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR@` works using current meson git :).

See also: https://github.com/mesonbuild/meson/issues/1622

The CHANGES.txt and the https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#reserved page explain how to use the "reserved" keyword to forbid using a set of fields. Unfortunately it seems that the latest proto2 compiler (ie. 2.6.1) doesn't recognize it.

src/main/protobuf/metadata_proto.proto:97:3: Expected "required", "optional", or "repeated".

nodes.body: The keyword is supported in proto2 syntax, but you need to use protobuf-3.0.0-beta-3 to use it. Note that protobuf-3.0.0 doesn't correspond to proto3. Protobuf-3.0.0 supports both proto2 and proto3 syntax and some proto2 features (like reserved, map fields) are only supported in protobuf-3.0.0.
Thank you, I wasn't aware of this release process :)

The above should state that you need protobuf-**compiler** (protoc) version 3+ to use those features. They were backported to proto2 syntax precisely because they are things only the protobuf compiler needs to be concerned with ("reserved" being a protobuf compile-time check and "map" being shorthand for previously existing syntax).

title: Python, Protobuf 3: `ListFields` method doesn't return field if it has value equaled default value
body:
In protobuf 3 I can't get the fields in the message which are not empty. ListFields method doesn't work like it is described in the documentation. This problem appears when value in field equals default value. So, for example, I can't get boolean field through ListFields method if the value of field is False or integer field is 0 and so on. In protobuf 2 ListFields method works correct. Following example illustrates problem:

Protofile:

```
syntax = "proto3";

message TestMethodResponse{
    int32 integer = 1;
    string string = 2;
    bool boolean = 3;
    string empty = 4;
    string nonempty = 5;    
}
```

Python example:

```
import testservice_pb2

req = testservice_pb2.TestMethodResponse(
    integer=1,
    string='string',
    boolean=True,
    nonempty='nonempty'
)

print 'All is well:'
print [f[0].name for f in req.ListFields()]

req = testservice_pb2.TestMethodResponse(
    integer=0,
    string='',
    boolean=False,
    nonempty='nonempty'
)

print "Something's wrong:"
print [f[0].name for f in req.ListFields()]
```

Output:

```
>>> All is well:
>>> ['integer', 'string', 'boolean', 'nonempty']
>>> Something's wrong:
>>> ['nonempty']
```

nodes.body: This is working as intended. In proto3, a field with default value is equivalent to an unset field. That's why ListFields() doesn't include fields whose value is set to default.

Thank you for your reply. It is very strange behavior in proto3. Because It has no opportunity to distinguish between a field which are not set and a field whose value is set to default. In this case I think that the description of `HasField` and `ListFields` is not fully correct for proto3. The behavior of these methods is important for me and I will use  proto2 for my aim. Thanks.

title: Required lowerCamelCasing in Proto3 JSON standard
body:
In the Proto3 reference it is [mentioned that JSON exported from Protobuf must be in `lowerCamelCase` format](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json). Why is this part of the standard, and why can't casing of the key values be an option left to the user? 

At my company, and I imagine a handful of others, we prefer to `underscore_our_vars` since we're primarily developing Python where this is the standard. We also do this in the `.proto` definition files, as does Google in its sample `.proto` examples. While primarily a nuisance, this does cause extra work for us in maintaining proto-generated JSON alongside other types of JSON data in our infrastructure. 

If the maintainers are open to making this an option in the JSON formatting routines for the various languages, I would be happy to make those updates.

nodes.body:
The option already exists in some implementations. For example, in Java:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L161

The option will allow you to use whatever field name you declare in the .proto file as the JSON field name.

What language are you particularly interested in?

@xfxyjwf Thanks for your response -- I'm happy to see that the option exists in Java. I'm most interested in the [Python `json_format.py` file](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/json_format.py), which I don't believe offers this option.

If the Java version already supports this option, I assume it would be ok to submit a patch adding this functionality for Python?
Yes, feel free to send us a pull request.  :)
The same option is available in Python also so I'm closing this issue.

title: How to get custom field option? [objc]
body: Is it possible to access all custom options for a field with the current API? We have a few custom field options that we want to access at runtime.

nodes.body: Seems like an equivalent `toProto()` from java does not exist for ObjC is this true? Given a `GPBFieldDescriptor` to get a `GPBFieldDescriptorProto`.

Yea, so the GPB*Descriptor classes aren't the same as they are for some of the languages where the full descriptor is captured.  Most of the mobile spaces, you don't want the full descriptor because it is just binary bloat.  So the ObjC GPB*Descriptor classes really only exist to feed the minimal information the runtime needs to function.  So it intentionally doesn't try to carry all that data (including options) along.

Making it a generation option also becomes a problem as someone ends up with two dependencies that share a comment proto dependency, but one wants an option and the other doesn't.  I've seen that happen before with C++ between "lite" and "full" runtimes there.

@thomasvl thank you for the response. This confirms my suspicion.

We already have a tiny fork so we will be able to manage it on our side for our objc needs.

nodes.body:
It sounds like you are using `import_style=closure` (the default) without `library=`. It is true that this mode of operation can't handle circular dependencies like this.

You have two options for fixing the problem:
1. use `import_style=commonjs` to have CommonJS imports instead.
2. use `library=myprotos_lib.js` so that all of the protoc output is placed into a single output file.

For more info see the readme: https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/master/js

nodes.body:
`unittest.pb.cc` is affected as well.

This is a serious problem as it causes FTBFS on all architectures in Debian. Here is [build log](https://buildd.debian.org/status/fetch.php?pkg=protobuf&arch=i386&ver=3.0.0-1&stamp=1471906844).

Seen on Fedora Rawhide too:

```
google/protobuf/unittest_lite.pb.cc: In member function 'virtual bool protobuf_unittest::TestAllExtensionsLite::IsInitialized() const':
google/protobuf/unittest_lite.pb.cc:8544:3: error: this 'if' clause does not guard... [-Werror=misleading-indentation]
   if (!_extensions_.IsInitialized()) return false;  return true;
   ^~
google/protobuf/unittest_lite.pb.cc:8544:53: note: ...this statement, but the latter is misleadingly indented as if it is guarded by the 'if'
```

Note that the `return false;  return true;` lines in `descriptor.pb.cc` seem to be independent of the fix proposed in #1698.  The `descriptor.pb.cc` file is already in the source and is not generated by `cpp_message.cc` at build time.  Patching `cpp_message.cc` should fix the FTBFS, but `descriptor.pb.cc` will still continue to give (non-fatal) warnings.  It will need to be fixed independently.
This may have been fixed by 98835fb in v3.1.0.

title: proto2 float getting truncated?

nodes.body: What RPC implementation are you using?
I'm using nanomsg.

A little more info. I dump the buffers on both sides trying to send over a .25f value.  According to an IEEE 754 converter I should see .25 as 0x3e800000.  So the data looks ok as long as endianness is handled for me.  Thoughts? 

Windows buf. 
0d00 0080 3ecd cdcd cd

Linux buf. 
000d 8000 cd3e cdcd 00cd
Why is the linux buf dumped in a reverse order for every two bytes? And why are there padding "cd"s?

I'm looking into this now with the transport layer (nanomsg). I assumed it
was just flipping the endianness after going over the network. I'm not sure
why that is happening and I read that protobufs would handle endianness for
me. What is odd to me is that floats like .2551 will work and < 1 will not.

On Tue, Jul 19, 2016, 3:13 PM Feng Xiao notifications@github.com wrote:

> Why is the linux buf dumped in a reverse order for every two bytes? And
> why are there padding "cd"s?
> 
> —
> You are receiving this because you authored the thread.

title: How to make scalar message field which has a default value be serialized on the wire?
body: As we know, in proto3, if a scalar message field is set to its default value, this field will not be serialized on the wire. This feature may result a high transmission speed, but it also bring me a bug sometimes, when a zero value is valid for me but is omitted. How to change this feature, is there any option?

nodes.body: If a field is missing on the wire, you're supposed to interpret it as if it was set to its default value. That's how all implementations I know work.

@seishun thanks a lot for your kindly reply. Imaging such scenario, my proto3 C# client sent a msg to a proto2 C++ server, does what you said also work? As you know, proto2 has a bit to indicate whether a field exists but proto3 has not. In this scenario, can C++ server deserialize the data package correctly?
Not sure what you mean by a "proto2 server". Messages should be serialized and deserialized using the same definitions, and that includes syntax (proto2 or proto3).

There isn't an option to change this. Though you can use the wrapper types:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/wrappers.proto#L84

@xfxyjwf
One more question. Is there a probability that Protocol Buffers will support C language in the future?

@csmatrix We don't have any plans to support a C API in the main project, but there are a handful of third-party C implementations listed [here](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/docs/third_party.md) that you could try.

I got similar issue where proto objects were missing default values for primitive type properties when JsonFormat.printer().print() was used. 

If someone has that issue, JsonFormat.printer().includingDefaultValueFields().print() fixes it.

title: Issues with the objc `named_framework_to_proto_path_mappings_path` parameter

nodes.body: There appears to be another problem with framework support. In the imports that are generated for source files, the headers from within the same module need to be imported using quoted strings and relative paths rather than as framework imports. I'm working on a fix for this now.

One thing you can do is add the path to the mappings file, as so:

```
Path/To/My/Framework:my_proto.proto,other_proto.proto
```

Does this solve your use case?

I don't think it does fully solve the issue. I could set it up as:

Framework/path/to:my_proto.proto
Framework/other/path/to:other_proto.proto

That part is totally feasible. The problem is it doesn't differentiate between headers in the current framework and headers pulled in from other frameworks. Headers pulled in for the current framework need to use "" relative imports, while pulling in headers from other frameworks need to use <> absolute framework imports. 

Cocoapods already handles retaining the directory structure when using the `header_mappings_dir` for Frameworks. This is necessary when we have protos with the same name under different namespaces. For example, we may have "service1/api.proto" and "service2/api.proto". Otherwise, we'd end up with collisions when the folder structure is flattened and have to Api.pbobjc.[hm] files.

so what you're saying is basically:

```
FrameworkA:a.proto,b.proto
FrameworkB:c.proto,d.proto
```

which would generate:

```
// A.pbobjc.m
#import "path/to/A.pbobjc.h"
#import "path/to/B.pbobjc.h"
#import <FrameworkB/C.pbobjc.h>
#import <FrameworkB/D.pbobjc.h>
```

...

```
// C.pbobjc.m
#import <FrameworkA/A.pbobjc.h>
#import <FrameworkA/B.pbobjc.h>
#import "path/to/C.pbobjc.h"
#import "path/to/D.pbobjc.h"
```

?

Close:

```
FrameworkA:path1/a.proto,path2/b.proto
FrameworkB:c.proto,d.proto
```

would generate:

```
// A.pbobjc.m
#import <FrameworkB/C.pbobjc.h>
#import <FrameworkB/D.pbobjc.h>
#import "A.pbobjc.h"
#import "../B.pbobjc.h"
```

The difference is that quoted paths are relative from the current source file. At least, this is what is working for us internally with latest Protobuf w/ `named_framework_to_proto_path_mappings_path` & Cocoapods w/ `use_frameworks!`. I think this should generically work for everyone though. I'll push a branch with my changes for inspection.
actually, would it be possible for you to upload a sample project that mimics your setup? including cocoapods and how you generate the protos?

Here is the change itself that we're using at the moment:
https://github.com/justinseanmartin/protobuf/commit/0f6ae48fe3e0836675b747e00617965d766f5525

Our protobuf generation is decoupled from the app build process and wouldn't be easy to create a sample. I can probably do it, but it might take some time.
Is renaming the proto files possible? Would that be a sensible workaround?

You mean renaming proto files to ensure there is no naming conflict when the protos are flattened? We are doing something similar to ensure unique class names (adding an objc prefix dynamically based on the folder structure).

That said, I don't know if flattening the folder structure would help with this problem or not. We'd still end up with referencing the headers for the current library as `<FrameworkA/a.pbobjc.h>` from `a.pbobjc.m`, which I think is generally considered incorrect.

The changes in my branch seem like something that should be supported by the protoc compiler to enable this. It works for us when integrated as both framework and static library targets, so I'd assume the same for other project configurations as well.

For the class name collision, you could use the expected_prefixes_path option to pass a list of proto packages and their required prefix, instead of dynamically adding a prefix based on path. See the next link for information on how to use it...

https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/objectivec_generator.cc#L65

(we might also have been just hitting issues because the protobuf projects uses "src/" and we don't really want that in the framework hierarchy also (for the Protobuf's pod).

title: Parsing JSON for Any is order sensitive
body:
Parsing `Any` types from JSON relies on the `@type` being the first element. E.g., parsing a boolean value into `Any` works fine for this input:

``` json
{
  "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.BoolValue",
  "value": false
}
```

However, it fails to parse if `value` and `@type` are reordered:

``` json
{
  "value": false,
  "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.BoolValue"
}
```

nodes.body: Are you using the C++ implementation?. Right now you will need to put "@type" as the first entry to work around this problem (all protobuf JSON serializers should already be doing this).

Yes, the C++ implementation. Protobuf serializers generate the JSON in the "correct" order, but then if the payload goes through a different parser/serializer (in our case [JSON::PP](http://search.cpan.org/~makamaka/JSON-PP-2.27400/lib/JSON/PP.pm)) the order may change.
This should already be fixed in 3.2.0.

title: Add Swift options to descriptor.proto
body:
I would like to see the following two options added to descriptor.proto to support Swift code generation:
# File-level option: `swift_prefix`

```
option swift_prefix = "string";
```

When set, all generated top-level Swift types would be prefixed with this string.  If not set, a default prefix is generated from the package name.  If neither this nor a package name is provided, then the generated types are not prefixed.

The behavior here is slightly different than that in the recent Swift design proposal:  That document suggests that swift_prefix should cause type aliases to be emitted.  However, one common use of this is to avoid name clashes which cannot be fixed with a type alias.

I suggest this be added with ID 39.
# Message-level option: `swift_additional_protocols`
## This suggestion is withdrawn; it is not needed.

```
option swift_additional_protocols = "string";
```

Generated Swift code can be customized in many ways by Swift extensions without requiring special code generation options.  The only exception (in Swift 3) is that a Swift extension cannot add protocol conformances.  The text of this option is added to the protocol conformances for the generated message type with a preceding comma (`,`) added if necessary to separate it from other generated conformances.  For example, google.protobuf.Duration might include

```
option swift_additional_protocols = "FloatLiteralConvertible";
```

Note that the implementation of such a conformance can be added in a Swift extension, so there is no need for the code generator to have any special knowledge of these conformances.

I suggest this be added with ID 8.

nodes.body: @pherl @thomasvl
@dmaclach

On a side note, however, I would argue that providing an implicit creation of a `Duration` from a `Float` literal feels unSwifty; aside from Swift's eschewing of most implicit conversions in general, it seems important to the reader that a `Duration` is a structured protobuf message with its own fields and methods and seeing `let x: Duration = 5.0` in code, or worse, passing 5.0 to a method that takes a `Duration` as a parameter, has the potential to add confusion.

> ... the second option you're proposing shouldn't be necessary; extensions for well-known types can be added whether or not they add protocol conformances.

You seem to be right about this.  I withdraw the second option suggested.

Cycling back to this - Looks like we're down to just the file level option for a prefix.  There is a question about if it should generate a type alias or should change the generated type names.

Changing the types names generated:
- One of the arguments seemed to be to work around cases where two proto files use the same package/type naming (and would other wise conflict).  Personally, I'm not sure how valid that is, as those protos files won't work in most other languages because of the conflict (protoc won't even allow you to generate them together because of this).  It also seems to be purely from trying to use some of the unittesting protos in a single binary when they were authored to be unique to each of the test binaries they are used in instead of shared across binaries.
- This would shrink binaries some since the symbol names likely will be shorter due the the prefixes.

Just generating prefixes:
- Editors may or may not pick up the alias to complete.

Any other advantages/disadvantages to these?

If we just generate convenience typealiases but leave all the other references to the types the same, that could be a source of confusion because autocomplete would still show the full names everywhere. For example,

```swift
struct Foo_Bar_Baz {
  var quux: Foo_Bar_Quux
}
struct Foo_Bar_Quux { ... }

typealias FBBaz = Foo_Bar_Baz
typealias FBQuux = Foo_Bar_Quux
```

Someone typing `myBaz.quux = ...` is going to see `Foo_Bar_Quux` but think "Hmm, I was expecting to see `FBQuux`, why is this different?" If we solved that by using the typealiases *there* as well, then there's really no reason to not just have that *be* the name in the first place.

Since they would only exist to save a little typing at the point of usage, it's hard to rationalize adding them. Let's just say that the prefix replaces the package portion of the name and drop what we were thinking about typealiases.

title: Java - Decouple protoc generated artifacts from runtime version
body:
@xfxyjwf 

Currently a protoc 2.4 / 2.5 / 2.6 generated classes cannot be used with the proto3 runtime. Similarly a protoc 3.0 generated artifact cannot be used with non proto3 runtimes. This has created upgrade hell for users of libraries that themselves use protobuf (e.g. HBase, Hadoop, ...)

We need to find a way to:
- Migrate all existing protoc 2.4 / 2.5 / 2.6 generated artifacts onto the proto3 runtime
- For future runtime releases allow them to be drop in replacements for prior runtime versions without requiring code regeneration for:
  -  some number of trailing releases (e.g. 2)
  -  some reasonable upgrade window (12 - 24 months)

nodes.body:
Current plan for Java:
- Starting from 3.0.0 release, minor version changes will be backwards compatible (e.g., protoc 3.0.0 generated code can be compiled/ran against protobuf runtime 3.1.0).
- 3.x runtime will not be compatible with 2.x generated code, but we are working on a Java 2.7 release that can be used as a bridge version between 2.x and 3.0:
  - 2.7 runtime will be compatible with 2.5/2.6 protoc generated code.
  - 3.0 runtime will be compatible with 2.7 protoc genreated code.
- 2.x users can migrate to 2.7 first and after there are no 2.5/2.6 dependencies, they can move to 3.x.
- 2.7 will be forked from 3.0.0-beta-4. It will include all new features in 3.x releases and we will keep updating it until most users are at 3.x.

title: [CSharp][3.0.0-beta4] CodedInputStream.ReadBytes throws when backed by IO.Stream

nodes.body:
It's not clear why you're calling `ReadBytes` here. How did you write the file?

If you're just trying to read the whole of the file as a `byte[]`, that's not something protobuf would normally get involved in. `CodedInputStream.ReadBytes` expects the stream to be positioned at the start of a `bytes` value written out with a length prefix.

It's not clear how this relates to your suggestion, either. Please provide more detail about what you're actually trying to achieve, as it doesn't sound like your file actually contains a protobuf message...

Hi jskeet, 

I have a protobuf message with a bytes field (and other fields). 

`message SomeMessage {
    bytes rawImg;
}`

The intent is to send raw bytes as part of this message. (a small image in my case) 

bytes gets translated to ByteString in C#, thus I need to go from System.IO.Stream to a ByteString in order to be able to construct the message. 
Wrapping my image stream in a CodedInputStream was a workaround I tried in order to create a ByteString from a System.IO.Stream without copying the data twice (Stream -> byte[] then byte[] -> ByteString). 

The exception is probably expected as the stream contains an arbitrary byte sequence. Should I create a new Issue for requesting the ability to create ByteString from a System.IO.Stream ? There is already a WriteTo(Stream outputStream), it would be nice to have ReadFrom(Stream inputStream).

Regards,
Amine.

It's unlikely that a `ByteString.ReadBytes` would be able to read from a stream without multiple copies either - given that the length of the stream isn't generally known beforehand, we don't know how big to create the byte array. It would save one final copy, but that's all.

Personally I don't think this is a sufficiently common use-case (or significant benefit) to make it worth adding to the API, but maybe it would be worth filing the issue and seeing whether others think. (And then probably closing this issue, as the exception you're getting in the original code is expected.)

(As one point in your favour, this _does_ exist in Java already, suggesting that others have found it useful there.)

title: Allow for an ordered variant of `map<K,V>`
body: There is a use case for having an ordered map, as maps are expressed as repeated key value pairs, is there any pain in adding a flag or option to enforce ordering on the map structure.

nodes.body: From what I know, there isn't a plan to add support for ordered map types. We are adding a deterministic serialization API that will serialize map fields ordered by key though.
What's your use case of ordered maps?

Cryptographic signatures and hashes of identical messages. Realistically I would want insertion order which shouldn't be hard to expose from what I understand. It could just be an extended kvp type with an order number. Then if an order number is there use say LinkedHashMap
@xfxyjwf Any ideas?

We are discussing whether to support ordered maps internally inside Google. There isn't a consensus on it though. I believe it's unlikely to be supported in the near future. As to LinkedHashMap, it's language specific and we are actually trying to go the opposite side: randomize hash keys to ensure user are not relying on a specific map ordering.

This seems counter intuitive considering `repeated` is ordered, along with fields. This means that nearly all of protobuf is easily hashable and signable except for map fields. Is there really no way that an ordering field could be added without disrupting the existing API?

We are adding a deterministic serialization API that will serialize map fields ordered. I think you can   hash the deterministic serialization output rather than iterating over map fields yourself. Does that sound like a workable solution to you?

Yes, that is a perfect solution so long as there is some control over the ordering itself. Either by some key ordering, or by insertion order. (We prefer to have insertion order specifically), does this mean the serialised format is guaranteed on the wire and the format is good?

How long on the road map is this feature? This is critical for our product.

We don't care about iteration order as much. But we need to maintain insertion order.

It's guaranteed to serialize map fields ordered.

The API is already available in C++:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h#L840

and @pherl is working on adding it to Java.

https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h#L831

Does this mean numerical provides insertion order?

Our map looks as following 

```
"1JxgSknwdUvrZgASNi6197f6JpAtZcdHX8" : google.protobuf.Any
```
The deterministic serialization only guarantees that the order is stable in multiple instance of the same binary. If you need customized ordering, I'd suggest have a custom sorter instead.

I want to understand the error better so I can know the best way to fix it. I am wondering why the unit tests (which use maps with CommonJS imports) don't trigger the problem.

title: protobuf-lite does not include well-known protos
body:
It does not include generated code nor .proto files. Users need to compile these themselves, which works okay short-term but also means they can't be used from libraries. We can either include the generated code in the protobuf-lite artifact, or create a new artifact to hold them.

The reasoning behind a new artifact is that, until recently, protobuf-lite was a subset of protobuf, which would no longer be possible if it included lite-generated code for wellknown protos. However, if lite isn't going to be a subset of protobuf again, then putting the generated classes in the same artifact would become easier for everyone.

nodes.body: This is not only relevant to java but other languages too such as C++. There is also a huge _problem_ when you compile the well-known protos for lite with type compatibility to full runtime (that is same typename in specification, meaning they reside in similar directory structure), that protobuf ships with pre-generated include files for _full_ runtime in system path, and you can't simply workaround this by include path ordering as some compilers such as Xcode don't seem to respect that fully. So basically the runtime specific files provided in system path should be moved to own directory, and tell developers to add that to their include path if they decide to use full runtime (you could also now provide similar directory for lite, if you want to ship pre-generated well-known types).
The generator also seems to generate PackFrom to UnpackTo methods which depend on symbol only included in full runtime.
I am still seeing this issue, are other folks experiencing this still?
Right now well-known types doesn't work with lite runtime.

For people experiencing this, there is an okay short-term workaround for applications (sorry, no good for libraries) which I alluded to it in my original comment. If using Gradle, you just add a "protobuf" dependency to your build. The normal protobuf jar includes the .protos, so this will extract those to let import work and will generate the code for them.

```
dependencies {
  protobuf 'com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.0.2'
}
```

I think it is harder in Maven, but still possible to some degree. I've not tried it though. The above Gradle snippet appears to work in #2321.

@kamalmarhubi, can you explain what you mean by that?
I will create an artifact for the Java lite version of well-known types in the next Java lite release.
Any updates?
I'll make a Java lite release this quarter (Q3), and for well-known types I plan to create a separate Java artifact.

@kamalmarhubi I'd be interested in hearing more about this as well.

@xfxyjwf Is there still a plan for creating a separate well-known types artifact?

Any updates on this? Would prefer not to shade the dependencies unless we absolutely have to.

@xfxyjwf @BSBandme an update on this? An official javalite artifact would be great, and seems like not too much effort. Fellow googlers over in Firebase land [are already doing this](https://github.com/firebase/firebase-android-sdk/tree/master/protolite-well-known-types). :-)
Any updates on this?

I just tested with 3.10.0 and this seems fixed. The `protobuf-javalite` artifact contains Any.class and Duration.class.  It also includes _some_ of the .protos themselves. It's not clear why duration.proto is missing, for example. But the generated code is there, so closing.

> I just tested with 3.10.0 and this seems fixed. The `protobuf-javalite` artifact contains Any.class and Duration.class. It also includes _some_ of the .protos themselves. It's not clear why duration.proto is missing, for example. But the generated code is there, so closing.

com.google.protobuf.Any class don't have unpack method. when this problem will be solved?

I think closing this might have been premature. For example, the inclusion of `Duration.class` without the proto doesn't (obviously, at least to me) help protobuf-javalite users, since if their proto depends on `duration.proto`, they will also need the proto file itself. But blindly copy-and-pasting `duration.proto` into the local codebase then results in duplicate class errors, as you end up with the Duration.class generated from the copied proto file and the same class included with the artifact.

@ericgribkoff, we can discuss some on Wednesday when it can be in-person, but I don't think it should work like that (you can also discuss with @voidzyc). Android users use Gradle and should use the Protobuf Gradle Plugin. The plugin allows you to include a dependency on a .jar file that contains generated code as well as the `.proto` files themselves. When you do so, the .proto files are extracted and used with `-I` to protoc which makes them available for import but it won't regenerate code for them. Basically, it all "just works" and no copy/pasting is necessary.

There are some details where things do break down, like I don't remember if the .proto files are included in the lite jar, you don't actually want the .proto files to be shipped in your app, and a few similar issues. But I do think this is a step in the right direction and there can be some ways to resolve the other issues.

Here's a great workaround for those who can't wait for an official fix:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7094#issuecomment-586532060

I think the generated code is now missing protobuf.Any.pack() and unpack(). Could not see an issue reported about this yet and this issue in general fits the symptoms.

I get runtime exceptions when unmarshalling grpc responses that include `DateTime`, for example.

I can fix that with `protobuf-gradle-plugin` + `protobuf("com.google.api.grpc:proto-google-common-protos:x.y.z")` in the `app/build.gradle` of the applications that we own. But, I can't ask clients to do that in their apps.

And, I don't want to ship a library that includes a `com.google.type.DateTime`, because it'll cause `DuplicateClassException`.

From my naive perspective, I don't understand the lack of a `proto-google-common-protos-lite` artifact.

datetime.proto is not a "well-known proto." That is part of the googleapis project, not protobuf.

There's no `proto-google-common-protos-lite` because there is no API/ABI stability guarantees for lite codegen. You need to generate all lite protos with the same version of the generator, so pre-built libraries doesn't make much sense. You can't ship a library that has pre-built lite protos, unless you can control the version of protobuf the app uses (which could be the case within a single company, but not for anything that goes on Maven Central). If you use protobuf only internally to your library, you can shade protobuf, but obviously that bloats its size so isn't really much of a help.

title: Opensource C++ zero-copy API
body:
Protobuf has zero-copy support to avoid copying string/bytes fields when parsing protobuf messages and it's used pretty much everywhere inside Google, but the feature has never made its way into the opensource repo. Now protobuf 3.0.0 is released and we will probably have more time to look into incremental improvements. The zero-copy API is a good candidate to be included in the next 3.x release.

Opensourcing the zero-copy API will involve:
1. opensource related string/buffer classes (Cord and its dependencies).
2. un-exclude zero-copy APIs from the message interface (such as ParseFromStringWithAliasing).
3. un-exclude the support for ctype = STRING_PIECE and ctype = CORD.

(1) is probably the most difficult part as that's a large chunk of code and it may not be portable.

nodes.body: Any updates on this feature?

@jjyao This unfortunately hasn't made into our agenda yet. If this feature is useful to you, can you post here your use case and estimate how much it can help? More concrete use case example can help us prioritize it.

I'm also quite interested in this feature.

> More concrete use case example can help us prioritize it.

@xfxyjwf I'm writing an application-specific database server with gRPC and RocksDB. I want to:

- Accept serialized protos from clients through gRPC and store them in RocksDB verbatim, without parsing and constructing a full object in memory.
- Retrieve serialized protos from RocksDB and send them back to clients without parsing and reserializing them, ideally as part of another proto, which would serialize only what's necessary.

I want this because parsing and serialization currently take ~30% of my total response time and I don't really need them.

[Here's a flame graph profile that shows what I'm seeing](http://svgshare.com/i/22m.svg).
Is this the thing that cap'n proto does that makes it fast than protobuf?

@stellanhaglund No, it's not the main cause of the performance difference. cap'n proto is very similar to FlatBuffer and what I described in https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3296 can be said to cap'n proto as well.

I am very interested in this feature. I have been suggesting at my work that we adopt something like protobuf for a long time. One of the major push backs has been the ability to zero copy large binary/string values. This is because we have many applications where an extra copy or two of the data means the processors/memory bus is now saturated.

Our usual process stream for data look a lot like:
 * DMA from network interface to shared memory
 * pass off the shared memory reference to the process(es) to do calculations
 * calculations done from shared memory to shared memory
 * pass shared memory reference to further process(es)
 * DMA out of the machine

Control message and meta data are small enough that copying is no problem (and in fact encoding as json etc. is usually good enough). Typical data is large matrices (think 16+MB) of complex integer (often 16 bit), complex IEEE binary16 (half) or complex IEEE binary32 (float). While meta data may be 64 bytes in total encoded as a struct. Note we often also have the requirement that the data be machine vector aligned (typically 32 byte align). A "slow" data rate is 3-5 Gigabit/s.

It'd be great if we could encode such data as something like protobuf and not have to manually maintain readers and writers and representations in multiple languages. We are already making an effort to use protobuf for control data, which IMO it already excels at.

Perhaps Cord will / could be open sourced as part of the [Abseil library](https://abseil.io/). The initial release doesn't include it, although there is a [passing mention in `malloc_extension.h`](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/cf6ab6bb2b800fae859ccc735f398d22a7336a00/absl/base/internal/malloc_extension.h#L382).
@arthur-tacca Yep. The Cord type will be included as part of Abseil. And after we migrate to use Abseil, supporting zero-copy ctypes should be straightforward.

Hello, I ran into some performance problems at my previous HFT job an thought it be nice to have a zero-copy, heap free, protobuf parser.

If I were going to hand write code that parsed a specific protobuf schema, I'd typically do all my processing on the stack and consume all data in one pass.

I could see writing a C++ functional template heavy low level decoder giving me the same performance.  I would best describe it as X(name proposals welcome) is to SAX as regular protobuf bindings are to DOM.  
* instead of heaping a std::string, you get a std::string_view.
* if you don't care about a field you should be able to say so at compile time
* if you don't want to parse a subobject you should be able to skip it or even break out of parsing

On the generation side I could see doing something something similar.
* it should be possible for a message routing app to pass payloads without decoding them

Is there interest for this kind of thing?  My fear is that C++ guys that really care about performance would avoid protobuf anyway.  I guess my target audience are skilled C++ devs worried about performance forced to speak protobuf for historical reasons or a contract with outside components.

Does anyone have a spiffy name?

Has anyone seen something like this?  I found lots of alternative wire formats with language bindings: SBE, CapNProto, etc.

I don't think we would switch to using a SAX-like parser except maybe in some very specific circumstances in our project. For us, the overhead of most PBs is negligible (and I expect to be even lower when we switch to using arenas). The main exception is the std::string allocation of lots of tiny strings -- we're stuck on the pre-C++11 ABI, so every string ends up being a heap allocation/free pair.

I can't use this library without that feature at all!

I use an arena, because I store sensitive key material in my protobuf messages and I provided an allocator with safe memory to the arena ([sodium_malloc](https://download.libsodium.org/doc/helpers/memory_management.html), not swapped out, zeroed out on free, guard pages etc.).

Given that the key material is stored in `bytes` fields, protobuf allocates them on the heap in `std::string` and completely bypasses the safe memory that I want the keys to reside in.

I already halfway ported my code from protobuf-c to protobuf, only now finding out that all my key material completely bypasses the arena. So now it seems like I have to throw that away and stick with protobuf-c (which makes me really unhappy).
Any updates on this feature?

I think string_view should be a solid contender to be fully released soon. 

Cord's are a thoroughly more heavy weight type. Integrating ZCIS with Cord's ties our most basic library directly into ABSL. We thread a little more carefully here.

@gerben-s 
Could you please elaborate what ZCIS/Cord and StringView are with respect to zero-copy?

Zero copy parsing of strings can be achieved by aliasing string_view's or Cord's with the underlying buffer. Cord is a heavy weight type from the absl lib, which needs to be directly supported by our ZeroCopyInputStream (ZCIS) abstraction.

> We are thinking about how to expose aliasing but we want to be careful and expose the right API.

That makes sense, especially without `std::string_view`/`std::span`
The only way to go for Google would probably be abseil, but that doesn't go well with semantic versioning.

My project, https://github.com/google/nucleus, would very much like this feature.

Nucleus is a package for reading and writing genomics data.  It relies on another package called htslib to parse some of the more complicated formats like VCF.  Unfortunately, htslib insists on putting the parsed data into memory structures it allocates itself, which leaves us the task of copying that data into protocol buffers.

On benchmarks reading a 100M gz-compressed VCF file, this extra copying causes our C++ reader to be almost twice as slow (20 seconds vs. 11 seconds) as another open-source package for reading VCF files (that doesn't rely on protocol buffers and can thus use the htslib allocated memory directly).

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/abseil-io/JzrwSIE_ZSo

With Cord coming soon hopefully this can be unblocked.

Any update on addition of std::string_view/zero-copy support? That would be really useful. I have a client sending data-buffers to a server via gRPC, and right now i can send data only as string/byte fields in protobufs. The client keeps the data-buffers around, until the rpc is successfully completed implying server has received the data-buffer. It will be great to have 'string_view' support in protobufs, so that client doesn't have to make 'string-copies' of these buffers. The buffers are atleast few MBs, data-transfer throughput has to be reduced to take into account memory-overhead of this copy.
@msn-tldr If you use the gRPC async API on the client side then you don't need to keep the request object in memory while the call is in process.

@msn-tldr Regarding freeing the request object: That is correct. Indeed I asked for an almost identical issue to be clarified in the docs in grpc/grpc.github.io#774

Regarding copying to a buffer: That is correct, and is the nature of protocol buffers. When you want to serialise them, they are serialised to a buffer that includes a complete copy of any bytes objects contained within them.

Another important point: If you have a `std::string` object and you want to set a member of a protocol buffer object to it, you can use move semantics to avoid a copy i.e. `my_protobuf.set_myfield(std::move(my_string_obj))`. Of course if you want to set the field to a *substring* of an existing buffer then this won't help.

(More detail than you probably need/want: technically it is possible to serialise a protocol buffer object to a stream, which means its members are not necessarily copied into a single buffer all at once, but eventually every individual byte will still be copied. Besides, I imagine the synchronous gRPC API probably serialises to a single buffer at once, and the async gRPC API almost certainly does. If allocating such big buffers is a problem, the usual recommendation with gRPC is to break the bytes objects into chunks and using a streaming request to send them. You could use [FlatBuffers with gRPC](https://grpc.io/blog/flatbuffers/) which would get you zero-copy when *reading* (the main subject of this issue), but there would still be some copying e.g. when gRPC makes the system calls that send/receive data. TensorFlow uses gRPC but does some other special tricks to avoid copying tensor data around too much, but I don't believe they are available for use outside that library.)

title: Add 'multimap' as a keyword
body:
It would be great to have:

```
multimap<A, B>
```

So that when we use the inbuilt merge functions we have a map implementation that concatenates the entries instead of picking one or the other.

nodes.body: Multimap isn't a built-in data type in many languages. Unfortunately I don't think we will be able to support this in the foreseeable future.

> Multimap isn't a built-in data type in many languages. Unfortunately I don't think we will be able to support this in the foreseeable future.

This does not sound quite right. I hope that most languages have a concept of a Map that contains a List. However, let's run through the languages that Protobuf supports and find out:

 * C++: https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/multimap
 * C#: `Dictionary<Key, IList<Value>>` in the simple case. More examples here: https://stackoverflow.com/q/380595/83446
 * DART: You can get this from the quiver library: https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/quiver.collection/Multimap-class.html
 * GO: Maybe this is the language that you have in mind? It does not seem to support multimaps natively and has poor library support. See https://stackoverflow.com/q/30529970/83446 and https://github.com/jwangsadinata/go-multimap
 * JAVA: This has support. Either via [Guava](https://google.github.io/guava/releases/19.0/api/docs/com/google/common/collect/Multimap.html) or using a `Map<K, List<V>>`
 * PYTHON: Could use defaultDict: https://stackoverflow.com/a/1731989/83446

It seems like this should be possible and would be a powerful addition to Google Protocol buffers. It would indeed be unfortunate to see this marked as closed forever.

Problem with using anything that is not part of the language built-in is that some day, when the language does offer built-in support for them, then we will need to introduce breaking API changes to use that built-in one, which is something that we try very hard to avoid. Or we will need to live with our custom multimap being different from the built-in ones, which is also not ideal.

In may cases above, you can achieve similar results with `map<K, Message>` where Message contains a repeated field. It is slightly more verbose, but achieves almost the same result as `Dictionary<Key, IList<Value>>` or `Map<K, List<V>>`

Maybe some day all languages will have the multimap support built-in. Then maybe we can revisit this.

> In may cases above, you can achieve similar results with map<K, Message> where Message contains a repeated field. It is slightly more verbose, but achieves almost the same result as Dictionary<Key, IList<Value>> or Map<K, List<V>>

That's actually an excellent workaround. Thanks for suggesting it!

title: Using find_package(Protobuf) with 3.0.0
body:
Hi,

I asked this on Google Groups and was advised to ask here and grab the attention of @podsvirov and @yeswalrus . 

As of 3.0.0 the CMake module requires us to set `protobuf_MODULE_COMPATIBLE` in order to get the benefits of the module code such as `protobuf_generate_cpp()`. The example seems to refer to this as "legacy compatibility mode" but the commit message says it is "improved". I must admit I am a CMake newbie to begin with, but in any case I don't quite understand the intention: Am I supposed to set this variable? Am I supposed to not set it unless I have to?

Thanks,
Øsse

nodes.body:
Hello @Osse,
you can use `protobuf_MODULE_COMPATIBLE` variable, and can not use.
Please look at the [examples/CMakeLists.txt](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/examples/CMakeLists.txt) file to see both versions use.

I think I got a conception of what all this is about. The config mode was the original mode with CMake and remained so for some time. That was how all third-party packages, protobuf included, advertised their targets and variables and allowed for their discoverability. Then later on came the module mode as the modern way to discover packages and get information about them, rendering the config mode somewhat obsolete(albeit still supported).

protobuf originally introduced the function `protobuf_generate` in the config mode. The function remained also available in the module mode when it got introduced to protobuf. The module mode however introduced 2 other new functions: `protobuf_generate_cpp` and `protobuf_generate_python`, which are convenience wrappers around the original `protobuf_generate` for some common use cases, as `protobuf_generate` was so versatile and could satisfy many use cases(albeit with complex parameters). Looks like these 2 new functions were intended exclusively for the module mode, but not the config mode; I don't know exactly really. The point is that these 2 functions are readily available for use in the module mode without any special arrangements. Those 2 functions are normally unavailable in the config mode(when `protobuf_MODULE_COMPATIBLE` is left to its default value of `FALSE`), but they can be requested explicitly by setting `protobuf_MODULE_COMPATIBLE` to `TRUE`. This explains a bit its naming denotation; it requests the config mode to be compatible with the module mode by making available the new functions the latter provides. It also explains the comments in the examples when this flag is set to `TRUE`, which means that we're using the legacy config mode with the new functions back-ported to it(upon our explicit request).

> Then later on came the module mode as the modern way to discover packages and get information about them, rendering the config mode somewhat obsolete(albeit still supported).

title: Parsing GPBMessages with an extensionRegistry by default in ObjC
body:
We're converting from using generated C++ protos to the native ObjC output. In the process of conversion, we got bit by not passing a extensionRegistry on deserialization from data. When we went to access the property using `-[GPBMessage getExtension:]` we are returned the default value and `-[GPBMessage hasExtension:]` returns NO.

Doesn't the protoc compiler create a default extensionRegistry for every generated file by default? Couldn't it use that to parse by default if none is specified? Is there a downside to doing this? 

CC: @thomasvl

nodes.body:
The registry in exposed off the message classes are just the ones defined on that message.  The registry exposed off the Root for a given file are all extensions defined in the file (file level and messages within the file).  So it will only get those extension parsed.  Extensions could be declared in other files for that message class, so you need to use a registry from that other file or make one merging the files you need.  So while that might work for some it isn't complete.

I believe C++ avoids some of this because it has a bunch of static initializer that have to run at startup to make master registry.  While useful, it works best for servers, for clients, it means your app startup is delayed while everything is constructed.

The registry exposed off the Root contains extensions for the given file and any imported protos. But your point is still valid that it might still be incomplete.

This is a potential hazard in the ObjC proto compiler that doesn't exist in the C++ version. I think there would be a general solution that'd work and still not require an excessive amount of work at startup. I don't know enough of codebase to say what it is, but I can do some exploration.

Do you see this as being an issue? If so, any thoughts on what an acceptable solution might look like to you? Thanks in advance.
I believe Java also requires passing an extension registry.  Swift will also.  So it is just something that will be different with some languages.

Sorry, meant to add, my one concern with trying to provide a default that is only partial, is that it could end up more confusing to folks as instead of no extensions being handled without a registry, some are.
My thought was to not pass a default that is only partial, but rather to pass a full registry. Do you not think that is feasible? Or not worth the tradeoffs?
To do it it means a hit at startup or the first parse to build that registry.  So I don't think it would be acceptable.

Ok, I'll close this issue then for tracking. We may implement something like this in our own codebase as I believe the risk of not doing this correctly is worse than the hit to startup time for enumerating the extensions. Thanks for the input!

title: Excess copies in CodedInputStream
body:
While running some benchmarks that involve deserializing large protobuf messages.  I noticed a large amount of garbage created by CodedInputStream as well as CPU time spent in it.  Specifically, when data is coming from a ByteBuffer that is known to be immutable,  CodedInputStream still makes a copy.  

For my benchmarks, I am using a simple proto with a single bytes field, set to a size of one megabyte, and sent over the network repeatedly.  The other endpoint reads the entire message off the wire before passing it to CIS.  The two available constructors are newInstance(ByteBuffer), and newInstance(InputStream)  Because I read the data off the network in chunks, I currently have a collection of ByteBuffers that need to be passed in to CIS, The only way currently to do this is to make an InputStream that composites these buffers together.   Sadly, this makes CIS use a code path called `readRawBytesSlowPath`, which makes a lot of defensive copies I don't need.  This is a major source of garbage and slowness.

An alternative approach is for myself to copy all the ByteBuffers into a single ByteBuffer, and pass that into CIS.newInstance.  This factory method _also_ makes a full copy of the buffer before parsing it.  

Going even further down the danger path is class called UnsafeByteOperations, which seems to be able to call the package-private constructors of CIS, but to use it, I have to collapse all my buffers into one before using it.  Even if there is only a single buffer, the buffers I get from the network are direct byte buffers, so to parse them it always incurs a copy.

What would be ideal is if there was a constructor that accepted a List / array of ByteBuffers.  My own benchmarking shows about 50% speed up (320MB/s to 480 MB/s)  in parsing using the Unsafe approach.  I believe it could be faster with even fewer copies.

Ideally, there needs to be a CodedInputStream that doesn't do its own buffering.  I believe it to be common case that Protos are used primarily across the network, which means that the networking libraries already have the data in a collection of ByteBuffers.

title: Make it possible to have lowercase enums in Ruby

nodes.body: Just to check if my understanding is correct: that example proto file can't be used in Ruby, but the .proto file is already used in other languages so you can't easily change the enum values to use UPPERCASE?
I have the corresponding .rb of that .proto that, yes, is used in other languages so the change for uppercase would be a little bit difficult
I assume this is a `WontChange`?

Although the proto file is not conforming to proto style guide, as long as the protocol compiler doesn't fail on such proto files, the generated ruby code should work rather than failing at runtime. This needs to be fixed in the ruby runtime or ruby code generator.

I'd like to request this be re-opened. Using all-lowercase symbols is a common convention in Ruby, and the natural way to map a fixed set of symbols to Proto seems to be as an enum. In my use case, it's not feasible to simply rename the enum values, because they've already been serialized in a number of places. Enforcing a style guide seems like something a linter should do, not a compiler.

If this is as simple as removing an assertion, I'm happy to submit a PR.
@haberman @TeBoring Can you comment on this issue? It seems to me a bug in ruby code generator.
ping @haberman @TeBoring?

FWIW - it's not just a question of removing an assertion, because we declare Ruby constants with the names of the enum values, and Ruby doesn't allow declaring constants with an initial lowercase letter. This still seems to me like a bug in the Ruby generator, but one that might require breaking API changes to fix. (Alternatively, maybe there's a way to just warn + avoid declaring the constants in the case where lowercase names were used.)
Can we add a ```PB``` prefix to fix that?

Hi team, I understand this issue has been hanging for a while, but wondering is there a solution to it? I can see [ruby-protobuf](https://github.com/ruby-protobuf/protobuf/blob/4f45a8a44cb864a561fc7988994c4886bf22453b/lib/protobuf/generators/enum_generator.rb#L32) gem introduced a env var to upcase enum name, is it an option to do something similar? cheers

+1 to add an option automatic capitalize enum name.

I try to write a monkey patch to handle this case https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/10454.

You're welcome to comment and show me how to make it solid or introduce any option.
Another manifestation of #10491
could someone make it clear what's the new bug in this issue. I am not very clear if this issue has been solved...

```
YourEnumType.resolve(:lowerCaseEnums)
```

to get the int number. So I may prefer to close this as having a workaround.

Auto capitalize can break existing code making use of JSON codec or the method above already.
