title: google.protobuf.Any and lite runtime
body:
Hi.
I have some issue with Any type and lite runtime in protobuf3.
First, is there support for Any type in lite runtime for cpp? Any cpp class inherits Message, which i cannot use with lite runtime library.

Thanks a lot!

nodes.body: Another issue is when I compile some proto files which use Any with :lite option, the methods PackFrom and UnpackTo has Message parameter (not MessageLite)
The pack and unpack method has to take a Message parameter because currently it requires descriptors to work. I think we should exclude them for lite runtime.

Hello. Thank you a lot for the reply!
But you can implement another logic for lite runtime. Any only contains bytes and some type identifier (encoded into string), so instead of descriptors you could use type-string comparison for lite runtime. "Any" type is very useful in many cases (on mobile devices too), and just exclude it from lite runtime library is not the best solution.
Yeah, I think your suggestion is a good alternative actually.

@xfxyjwf Hi! What happened in response to this issue? It's already 2 years old. Is there a `any` implementation for lite planned? We tried to use it and failed because `pack` wasn't found. Are there any reasons that the proposal of @ddovod was not implemented?

We also did not wait for a solution, so we just dropped lite runtime and started use of full protobuf3 (mobile application, works fine, overhead is not noticeable at all). But for integrity reasons it makes sense to fix this "Any" issue ofc.

@ddovod thanks for sharing your solution! I am building with bazel now and the bazel scripts for grpc use lite automatically. So no way for me to use the full proto if I don't switch the build system. :sweat:

The work around I use in my code is basically to roll my own version of Any. Make a copy of the original Any.proto, then implement the pack functions for your new Any type (which is not that hard).

Then, when you want to use the lite runtime, use your custom Any in your .proto files, and when you want to use the full runtime, use the original Any in your .proto files.

Because the custom Any has the same .proto definition as the original, it’ll have the exact same layout when encoded in the wire format, so your custom Any will be compatible with the original.
@aiusepsi Thanks for sharing that! I had the same idea but hesitated implementing it in search of a default solution. But knowing that this works for you helps!

The concern about supporting Any in lite is that Any will leak message names which the author of the proto may not want to. This may or may not be a concern to different use cases but we need to sort this out before introducing the feature.
Any update on this?

There is now support for building `Any` in lite mode for C++. You can do this by invoking `protoc` and passing the `lite` flag to the C++ generator, e.g `--cpp_out=lite:...` Ideally we should have better build system support for this, but at least for now you can make it work by directly invoking `protoc` on `any.proto`.

@acozzette Could you elaborate a bit on this topic?
I understood Any is supported in lite. Since which version?
I checked the release notes but did not find something related.

The problem I am facing is when using the lite lib, e.g. the constructor and destructor of `Any` are missing in the lite-library.
So according to your comment I assumed I need to manually run `protoc` on `any.proto` with the `--cpp_out=lite:` flag specified.
This obviously then results in redefinition errors, as it includes the `any.pb.h` shipped along / installed with protobuf and the `any.pb.h` generated by `protoc`.
For sure I can just remove / ignore the shipped / installed file, but is this intended?

What would be the intended workflow?

@tiolan I can't remember offhand what release introduced this, but I believe it's been around for at least a couple years or so, so any recent version will include it.

You are right that this workflow does not mesh well alongside the installed protobuf headers. There is not really a well-lit path for lite Any, and instead it requires you to make some tweaks to your own build system. It's up to you how to set it up, but the important thing is to avoid mixing lite and full Any in the same binary.

title: [feature request] Support options in the Objective C Descriptor API
body:
Several of the protocol buffer Descriptor APIs expose options, e.g. in Java:

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java/com/google/protobuf/Descriptors.FieldDescriptor#getOptions()

It would be extremely useful if a similar method were present in the Objective C descriptor API in GPBDescriptor, GPBMessageDescriptor, etc.

nodes.body: This came up before in https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1779.  ObjC doesn't have the full descriptor, and most consumers don't need them, so capturing the data would end up just bloating the binary.  Given ObjC is mostly used for mobile, larger binaries is something we try to avoid.

title: [C#] Allow reuse of CodedInputStream and CodedOutputStream
body:
`CodedOutputStream` can take use flat array as the output. This is a great to just convert between object and bytes. Problem is an instance of `CodedOutputStream` can only be used once. 

Adding a Reset method allows you to reuse the same `CodedOutputStream` to serialize different objects.

Same is true for `CodedInputStream`.

See https://github.com/yufeih/protobuf/commit/d6ffc2f37cad8e85cbd71b1d144093250894aeb8

nodes.body: Any reason why this was closed? We use protobuf for serialisation in our game's networking and CodedOutputStreams are generating a lot of garbage. It would be great if it could be reused.
Same issue here. #4742

Any plan to implement it?
This issue is open for more than 7 years.

I also see a huge garbage collector pressure because CodedInputStream and CodedOutputStream are not reusable.  I have managed to reuse everything else that comes in the way.

title: Is the Any networking behavior really needed?

nodes.body: PS - it is probably too late, but given the host isn't really needed, and likely shouldn't be fetched, it means we're burning bytes in any proto that uses any to include a host that isn't needed.  Is it worth updating helpers and making the host optional so it can be left off?

We probably should just remove that sentence. It's a requirement/recommendation for an Any type service, not for Any proto itself, and we don't currently have any type service setup or any runtime library support to build or use such type services.

@pherl

Thinking about this some more, with the global registry in some of the proto runtimes and/or the symbol collision it would cause; could we even support a package.Message duplicated from two different hosts?  Don't they really have to be global unique if they are built into a single binary?

Maybe we could trip this down to just "/[full_name]" and save those host on the wire?

You are right. "package.Message" must be globally unique, or otherwise protoc will complain about it at compile time or protobuf runtime will complain about it at runtime. The URL prefix  doesn't help identify a message uniquely. Instead it only points to a place where the type info is available. In existing use case where type info all comes from the local binary, the type URL prefix is useless, but if we build tools that will actually query remote type services to interpret an Any type, the prefix will be needed. I agree that "/[full_name]" as the default makes more sense, but it's not easy to change the behavior now because tons of existing code is already baked with hard-coded string comparison code against "type.googleapis.com".

For users who do want to avoid this additional type URL prefix cost, the generated Any API actually has a PackFrom(prefix, message) method where the user can simply pass an empty URL prefix. It is available in C++/Java and Python.
If the user specifies an empty prefix, does that result in "/[full_name]" as the stored type?

For C++, it appears to: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/any.cc#L63

Not sure if that is expected for all languages or not.

Is there any information about type repo or fetching type information by URL? It seems to be quite useful. Not just for Any type, but as well for code generation. May be even importing types by URL rather than fetching them manually and then placing into proper folders and so on.

I found this issue after intending to file one, after an [exchange on the protobuf Google Group](https://groups.google.com/d/topic/protobuf/ekLpBKo2kPA/discussion).

*Please* update the docs if there is no intent to provide dynamic type resolution (like via the HTTP service described in the docs for the Any type). Also, if that is the fate of this, I agree with the above suggestions to ditch the hostname: the field should simply be a fully-qualified message name, not a URL.

The Any documentation has been updated to call out the networking behavior as optional:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blame/master/src/google/protobuf/any.proto#L129-L132

> In practice, teams usually precompile into the binary all types that they
> expect it to use in the context of Any. However, for URLs which use the
> scheme `http`, `https`, or no scheme, one can optionally set up a type
> server that maps type URLs to message definitions as follows:

nodes.body:
I've added the following patch to work around this issue
(`sysconf` is the proper solution, see: [GNU/Hurd porting guidelines](https://www.gnu.org/software/hurd/hurd/porting/guidelines.html#PATH_MAX_tt_MAX_PATH_tt_MAXPATHL)):

``` patch
Description: Add support for GNU/Hurd which doesn't define PATH_MAX.
Author: Bas Couwenberg <sebastic@debian.org>

--- a/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc
+++ b/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc
@@ -51,6 +51,9 @@
 #include <ctype.h>

 #include <limits.h> //For PATH_MAX
+#if defined(__GNU__)
+#define PATH_MAX 4096
+#endif

 #include <memory>
 #ifndef _SHARED_PTR_H
```

title: Ruby assert can sometime trigger, depending on garbage collector.
body:
Basically, we were investigating this: https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/7661

Our investigation led to realize that this assert in the protobuf code is being triggered, but only if the garbage collector has been exercised enough: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/map.c#L74

If the garbage collector is really under heavy stress, we can even produce a VM crash: http://pastebin.com/hzgHPJGq

I have included a zip file with our current reproduction case: [ruby-repro.zip](https://github.com/google/protobuf/files/434152/ruby-repro.zip). Right now, this can crash any of the versions of Ruby I've been able to try this with. The reproduction steps are as follow:

```
$ bundle install
$ bundle exec gem repro.rb
```

The idea of the repro is to load a baked binary protobuf from the disk, and deserialize it enough times in memory to eventually cause a failure. The failure is evidently due to some corruption that happens in the Ruby VM. We have checked that the actual raw memory itself hasn't been altered - and even though it would've been, the internal assert being triggered shouldn't have happened in the first place.

When using a vanilla version of Ruby, the crash will not be deterministic. However, compiling a custom Ruby library with the timer_thread disabled causes the crash to become fully deterministic. Changing the value of the number of times we try to deserialize the object while the garbage collector is disabled will alter the behavior of the problem.

It would also be reasonable to suspect that there is an actual bug in the Ruby VM. I have cross-filed a bug there too: https://bugs.ruby-lang.org/issues/12699

nodes.body: If this problem is caused by a bug in protobuf code, it could be caused by a Ruby object that is temporarily not visible to the garbage collector. This means that it is not on the stack, and no other Ruby object holds a reference to it. That could happen if at some point the only reference to a Ruby object is in a C struct on the heap.

title: Java JsonFormat.printer().preservingProtoFieldNames() incompatible with Python google.protobuf.json_format.Parse()
body:
Yo!

Using `JsonFormat.printer().preservingProtoFieldNames()` to serialize Protobuf to JSON in Java can make the result incompatible with Python's `google.protobuf.json_format.Parse()`.

Example:

``` protobuf
// test.proto
syntax = "proto2";
message Test {
  optional int32 under_score = 1;
}
```

``` python
# test.py
import test_pb2
import google.protobuf.json_format
google.protobuf.json_format.Parse('{"under_score":1}', test_pb2.Test())
```

The Java code will generate the following JSON:

``` json
{
    "under_score": 1
}
```

while the Python parser expects the following JSON:

``` json
{
    "underScore": 1
}
```

which results in the following error:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test.py", line 3, in <module>
    google.protobuf.json_format.Parse('{"under_score":1}', test_pb2.Test())
  File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/site-packages/google/protobuf/json_format.py", line 332, in Parse
    parser.ConvertMessage(js, message)
  File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/site-packages/google/protobuf/json_format.py", line 363, in ConvertMessage
    self._ConvertFieldValuePair(value, message)
  File "/usr/local/lib/python2.7/site-packages/google/protobuf/json_format.py", line 441, in _ConvertFieldValuePair
    raise ParseError(str(e))
google.protobuf.json_format.ParseError: Message type "Test" has no field named "under_score".
```

title: Ruby `hash` broken for Messages with repeated fields.
body:
## Expected

All Ruby Message objects return a `hash`.
## Actual

Calling `hash` on a Message with a repeated field will occasionally raise the following error:

``` ruby
RangeError: bignum too big to convert into `long'
```
### Test Case

I have written a [gist with tests](https://gist.github.com/abscondment/d8254d4482c024ad06a7e683c690ff98) demonstrating the behavior.
### Details

This is because of a bug in [`repeated_field.c`](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/repeated_field.c#L448), wherein the hash function occasionally returns a `Bignum` instead of a `Fixnum`. `RepeatedField_hash` can return a Bignum because of the algorithm it uses for combining hashes: bitwise shift left, then xor. If the original hash is large enough, the `<<` will cause Ruby to automagically promote the value from a `Fixnum` to a `Bignum`.

Ruby indicates that [`hash` should return a Fixnum](https://ruby-doc.org/core-2.3.1/Object.html#method-i-hash), so this behavior is not correct.

Up the stack, `storage.c` [attempts to convert this Bignum](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/storage.c#L863) to a long, which produces the `RangeError`.
## Proposal

I _think_ the correct behavior is to use `rb_hash_start` -> `rb_hash_uint` -> `rb_hash_end` -> `INT2FIX` as `storage.c` does. ~~I'd be happy to provide a patch for this if that sounds correct.~~ I've provided a PR.

title: MergeFrom unexpected result in python cpp implementation
body:
About python protobuf-3.0.0 (build from source).

I believe there is a difference in behaviour of `MergeFrom` between cpp_implementation and python implementation (joining simple code to demonstrate what I believe is an issue in cpp_implementation).
In short, **with cpp_implementation**, if a Message has sub-message, the `MergeFrom` method do different things depending if a sub-message is initialized or left to default in original message.

If the sub-message is left to default as construction time, after merge, accessing the sub-message field will always return the default (note that making of copy of the merged message give back a valid message returning correct values).

This is all easier to show with code, see below. The first test works as expected (see the sub-message is initialized). The second test fail on last line (note that the copied message behave correctly). By the way, both tests pass when using protobuf python (not cpp_impl).

(tested for both python 2.7 and 3.4, built with standard gcc compiler on fedora core 23)

```
# Using protobuf-v3.0.0
# Tested with python2.7.10 and python 3.4

import unittest

import mergetest_pb2 as mpb

# Content of mergetest.proto
"""
message MySubMsg {
    optional uint64 i = 1;
}

message MyMsg {
    optional uint64   singular = 1;
    optional MySubMsg sub = 2;
}
"""

class PbTest(unittest.TestCase):

    def test_merge_ok(self):
        m = mpb.MyMsg(
            singular=1,
            sub=mpb.MySubMsg(),  # Note: sub-message is defined
        )
        assert m.sub.i == 0

        m2 = mpb.MyMsg(
            singular=2,
            sub=mpb.MySubMsg(i=1),
        )
        assert m2.sub.i == 1

        m.MergeFrom(m2)
        assert m.singular == 2
        assert m.sub.i == 1

    def test_merge_bad(self):
        m = mpb.MyMsg(
            singular=1,
            # Note: sub-message is not defined (default)
        )
        assert m.sub.i == 0

        m2 = mpb.MyMsg(
            singular=2,
            sub=mpb.MySubMsg(i=1),
        )
        assert m2.sub.i == 1

        m.MergeFrom(m2)

        # The merge is ok, underlying data struct has correct value.
        # If we copy the message, we obtain a valid message back.
        mcopy = mpb.MyMsg()
        mcopy.CopyFrom(m)
        assert mcopy.singular == 2
        assert mcopy.sub.i == 1

        # However some of original message accessor return wrong result.
        # Singular field are ok
        assert m.singular == 2
        # Sub-message are NOT ok
        assert m.sub.i == 1  # <-- This raises! We expect this to works, right?
```

nodes.body: For info, just noted that calling `m.Clear()` before `m.mergeFrom(m2)` make the test pass (obviously it doesn't fix merging, but just for info).
Forcing `MergeFrom` on sub-message also wroks. Could be related to the recursive behaviour of `MergeFrom` wrt default value.
It is fixed in internal code by adding a "struct FixupMessageAfterMerge : public FixupMessageReference". Expect to see the fix in next release

title: Support IReadOnly* in C# collections
body:
Our RepeatedField and MapField classes implement everything required for `IReadOnlyList<T>` (and implicitly `IReadOnlyCollection<T>`) and `IReadOnlyDictionary<T>` respectively, but don't implement those interfaces themselves, which can be annoying. We should implement them.

(Note that IReadOnly\* doesn't actually mean it's read-only; it just means the interface is read-only. A bit confusing...)

title: [proto3] Deprecated method `valueOf()` called in generated code

nodes.body:
Would appreciate if this issue is fixed soon.
Our application is built with `-Werror` flag and this is blocking us from upgrading to Grpc 1.0.
+10 - proto2 also generates valueOf() calls - creating warnings - for us also prevent build

It looks like we need to have the generated code continue to call `valueOf()`, because we need to remain compatible with older generated code that does not yet have the recommended `forNumber()` method. So it seems to me like the right solution is to update the compiler to stop putting a deprecation annotation on `valueOf`. That should happen in these two places:
- https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_enum.cc#L186
- https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_enum_lite.cc#L150

Would anyone be interested in sending out a pull request to make this change?

... I used c last time a decade ago .. so my temp solution was

```
sed -i '' 's/@java.lang.Deprecated//g' *.java
sed -i '' 's/ @deprecated/ deprecated/g' *.java
```

Actually, I think you should not remove the deprecate but change the call to `forNumber()` as if you update the server library, you should also update the client library.  And that is just using the new version in the build - not code changes.

Unfortunately I don't think it's practical to update all generated code at the same time in many cases. This works well if you control your entire codebase and its dependencies, but it becomes a problem if you're using something like Maven and depending on multiple open source projects that all use protobuf. Projects sometimes publish their protobuf generated code through Maven because that's often easier than having to run `protoc` during your build. So let's say you depend on three open source projects that all include generated code. If we introduced a breaking change then you would have to simultaneously update all three projects and of course also simultaneously update any generated code of your own. We actually used to require the generated code to match the library version but we're now intentionally supporting older generated code so that we don't run into these problems.

@blendmaster Your script would work but the regex too wide. It will match any deprecated notation, not only those on `valueOf` methods... Can't you make the multi-line regex that would find only `@java.lang.Deprecated` above `valueOf` method?

looks like if you set `byline: false` then yeah, you could try to scope this to `valueOf` methods.

https://ant.apache.org/manual/Tasks/replaceregexp.html

I don't have any other deprecated methods to test against though. If you can figure out the right regex @vgarmash, I'll update my comment.
As well as valueOf, can you also fix usages of PARSER instead of parser() as mentioned on #1596
So you prefer to use deprecated code which could be eventually removed from JDK and just hide the warning?

What's the concern moving to forNumber() ?? 
For outdated JDK support, one could check the JDK version when generating the code and then generate either valueOf() or forNumber().
Not sure about this.
This should be fixed now with pull request #4046.

title: Use java boxed types when setting well known types
body:
I would like the functionality that using things like Int32Value, Int64Value, StringValue, BoolValue, etc would allow for using setters of the form setFoo(Integer), setFoo(Long), setFoo(String), setFoo(Boolean) where a passed null will essentially no-op, but a value would call the XYZValue.newBuilder.setValue(arg), but that on the getter side of things the interactions still have hasFoo() and getFoo().getValue() to access the data.  Given that the return type can't be type parameterized easily in Java, this seems like a good place to start, possibly with discussion as to whether there should be getters of the form getNullableFoo() or getOptionalFoo that gets generated.

If this is something that would be helpful to others(I think it would) I'd be happy to contribute a pull request that at least makes these changes to the setter side of things with further discussion for proper use on the getter side.

I will write that up!  Do you have a template I should follow?

We did a Java API review for this and a new wrapper types API was added to improve the usability. You can now do:

title: javascript: maps are converted to arrays of arrays
body:
I'm using gRPC 1.0.0 with a google-protobuf.js build from master (to fix the valueWriterFn_ bug in the 3.0.0 release). Calling toObject() on a result that includes a map will express the map as an array of arrays. I would expect it to produce a javascript object.

proto definition: `map<string,string> definedscopes = 1;`

client code: `result.toObject();`

result: `{ definedscopesMap: [ [ "key1", "value1" ], [ "key2", "value2" ] ] }`

desired result: `{ definedscopesMap: { "key1": "value1", "key2", "value2" } }`

Using the same proto definition with the grpc.load() dynamic generation method produces a normal javascript object.

nodes.body: @haberman Is the plan to make toObject() produce valid proto3 JSON?

Per https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1591 I don't think proto3 JSON support is implemented for JavaScript (even internally at Google). My understanding is that `toObject()` does not / is not intended to return proto3 JSON.

https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1904 states it even more clearly:

"""
Yes, to be clear, toObject() is not proto3 JSON, it is a pre-existing JSON mapping that does not conform to proto3 JSON.
"""
I believe toObject() is not intended for public use. Closing this issue for now.

title: Support proto2 syntax with both v2.x and v3.x
body:
Without the `syntax = "proto2"` statement, v2.x builds fine, v3.x emits warnings
With the `syntax = "proto2"` statement, v2.x builds fail, v3.x has no warnings

As per the release note -

> If omitted, the protocol buffer compiler generates a warning and "proto2" is
> used as the default. This warning will be turned into an error in a future
> release.

Is there a way for .proto files using proto2 syntax to be compatible with both v2.x and v3.x without any warnings? Since v3.x non-beta just got released recently, as a proto2 user, I would like to support both proto v2.x and v3.x for some time before making pre-requisite as v3.x+

nodes.body: Since v2.x doesn't accept the "syntax" statement at all, I think your only option is to live with the warnings in v3.x.
@xfxyjwf In that case, can we make sure that the missing syntax warnings don't get converted to error any time soon? Is there a tentative date/release when this is likely to happen?

I think we should probably follow the same deprecation timeline in Java (see: [java compatibility notice](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/java/README.md#compatibility-notice) that a deprecated API will be removed two years after it's first marked as deprecated. So in this case, the warning should be turned into an error two years after it's first marked as a warning.

2 years sounds good to me.

I'm closing this issue now. Thanks!

title: Request to expand MessageDereferencer implementation with hash computation of the message

nodes.body: It's not a very good idea to use proto message as keys because they are not true value types. With the presence of unknown fields, two equal messages in one binary might be treated as different by another, and therefore two different binaries might get two different unordered_map<> even given the exactly same input data (if the hash function is implemented using MessageDifferencer). It's probably better to write your own hash function that has your desired behavior rather than replying on a generic one.

@slavanap Thanks for the detailed explanation. If the proto message is simple enough (doesn't involve unknown fields etc), a generic hash function should work fine.

If you would like to contribute an implementation, can you first create one with only the public interface? We can start there and once we agree upon the public interface of this feature you can add the actual implementation.
@xfxyjwf I don't mind to implement this feature by myself, but my pull request code will need a review.

title: generate_descriptor_proto.sh: Syntax error: "(" unexpected
body:
When using script to regenerate descriptors on Ubuntu, it fails with following error:

```
$ ./generate_descriptor_proto.sh
./generate_descriptor_proto.sh: 31: ./generate_descriptor_proto.sh: Syntax error: "(" unexpected
```

Because on Ubuntu, by default /bin/sh is dash, so if user executes this script directly, it will fail with this error.

There are 2 ways to fix it:
1. Change the first line of `generate_descriptor_proto.sh` to `#!/usr/bin/env bash`
2. Prompt user to use: `bash generate_descriptor_proto.sh`

title: Should the conformance checks be checking for NaN float values?
body:
Example: [ProtobufInput.FloatFieldNormalizeSignalingNan.JsonOutput](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/80f65d2df82cc23eb92ef5355d638b9102074190/conformance/conformance_test.cc#L1147)

I'm writing conformance tests for Go in https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/2084, and I noticed that the Go encoder fails with an error for the following conformance tests:

```
ProtobufInput.FloatFieldNormalizeQuietNan.JsonOutput
ProtobufInput.FloatFieldNormalizeSignalingNan.JsonOutput
ProtobufInput.DoubleFieldNormalizeQuietNan.JsonOutput
ProtobufInput.DoubleFieldNormalizeSignalingNan.JsonOutput
JsonInput.ValueAcceptNull.JsonOutput
```

For all but the last one, these are conformance tests where there is a NaN value in JSON input or output. I believe this is caused by the underlying issue in the Go JSON encoding package: https://github.com/golang/go/issues/3480

The Go issue links to https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4627#section-2.4

>  Numeric values that cannot be represented as sequences of digits
>    (such as Infinity and NaN) are not permitted.

If the spec doesn't allow such values, shouldn't we not be expecting them in JSON input/output? It would mean, unfortunately, that round trip between Protobuf and JSON could get lossy when dealing with floats, though.

nodes.body: Cool. The conformance tests are probably correct, then. I've filed https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/231 to track this encoding for the Go encoder.

title: [C#] Provide a way to construct a ByteString from a stream
body:
Hi, 

The C# implementation of ByteString does not provide a way to construct the object directly from a System.IO.Stream. 
In scenarios where the message contains bytes for binary data (such as images from the file system), we need to copy the data twice (Stream -> byte[] -> ByteString).

Although the Stream length is not always known, there are still many cases where it is known (such as files, request body in .net MVC applications, MemoryStream ...). 
A method like `ByteString.ReadFrom(System.IO.Stream input)` would solve this problem.

Please note that the Java implementation does have a `static readFrom(InputStream streamToDrain)` method to construct a ByteString. 

Regards,
Amine.

nodes.body:
Yes, aside from anything else this would be _convenient_.
(I thought I'd seen a similar request before, but I can't find it now.)

title: Export functions to convert between C/Python protos to Python extensions.
body:
Currently, a python extension that wishes to return protos to python code must serialize them, and de-serialize using python methods. It would be convenient to expose the underlying Message objects to C-language extensions.

There appears to be a start to this functionality in pyext/python_protobuf.h, but the corresponding .cc file was deleted at some point (by mistake?), and it was never exported in a capsule.

nodes.body: It was deleted by mistake. Will add this back
Added in internal. python_protobuf.cc should be there in next release.

It smells bad to me to expose this in public API. How the Python protos are implemented is an implementation detail. It's especially so regarding to how the internal C++ objects are managed. Exposing these C++ objects for public use will make it significantly harder to change/optimize the python C++ implementation later and the exposed API itself will also be very hard to use correctly because of the very complicated ownership management in Python C++ wrapper.

title: Java lite does not generate hasField methods and does not serialize zero values
body: This was a big design issue in nano and I was under the impression that it was fixed in lite, but apparently not. nodes.body:
You are probably using proto3 syntax and has-bits has been explicitly removed from proto3.

If you declare your .proto files with 'syntax = "proto2";', you should be able to get the hasField() methods back.

I am using proto3 and hasField() methods are still generated for submessages, but not for scalar fields. It makes no sense to generate them for one field type, but not another. Scalar fields need to be represented with autoboxed types where `null` means missing for both encoding and decoding. That's the only sensible design. There must be a way to transmit the value `false` or `0` and have the receiver distinguish that from a missing field.
You might find this relevant: https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/249

Fair enough. Until I can redesign my messages, I've switched to [square/wire](/square/wire) to interact with [nanopb](/nanopb/nanopb) on the other side. Both provide field presence information. Personally, I think this change is more likely to result in ugly designs with many single-field messages or bools represented by enums to have three separate values for unset, true, and false.

title: Excessive copying leads to slow serialization
body:
I'm working on a project which is consist of 1) producer 2) message broker 3) consumer. The project uses protobuf as a serialization protocol both for the producers and for the consumers. The project is settled a long ago and the beans are widely used along company so I'm not allowed to change anything easily.

I'm trying to get highest possible throughput with this bean library and it happens that it's protobuf that limits me - not the message broker nor anything else.

The problem is that some beans are quite huge and linear. Such a bean can contain ~300 fields in root object. Some fields are of primitive types and some fields are nested objects. I found out that due to nature of protobuf the only way to serialize object in producer is to make a immutable object from a builder. For huge bean this operation takes too long. It could be disputable question about immutable vs non-immutable - but I don't need both on producer side. All I need is to set some fields and serialize these to byte array.

I've wrote a simple test which describes the problem: https://github.com/mazurkin/protobuf-test
A monster bean: https://github.com/mazurkin/protobuf-test/blob/master/src/main/config/proto/Monster.proto
A test: https://github.com/mazurkin/protobuf-test/blob/master/src/test/java/org/test/MonsterTest.java

Test shows that build() for a simple object takes 20-30 microseconds that too much for a 'fast' protocol.

All I need is to serialize builder without excessive copying. I see that writeTo() could be implemented write in builder object. A builder has all the fields, all the mask and references child objects/builders.

nodes.body:
I have manually fixed build() method and now performance is comparable to 'nano' mode of protoc v3 

As I see just some GenerateBuildingCode(io::Printer\* printer) should be fixed in protoc compiler
Do you mind send us a pull request to fix that?
I've created pull request: https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/2121
Let's continue on the PR

nodes.body: @haberman @acozzette

Thanks for the detailed report, Priyatham. We expected there to be some performance hit from syncMapFields_ but it's surprising that it would be so big. I will look into this some more tomorrow and see if I can find a way to fix the regression. nodes.body: See https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/master/objectivec#building, you shouldn't be compile the generated source with ARC enabled.  You can use ARC in all your code, but compile the library and generated `.m` files without ARC.

Or just add use a static library target with ARC turned off.  i.e. - your rule could still work, just add the .proto files to the target that doesn't have ARC enabled.

Help please. I'm not using CocoaPods, or any other dependency injection system. The GitHub "last release" for MacOS/iOS contains only the `protoc` compiler binary, plus an "include" directory with some base `.protoc` files. When I use them (via Xcode 10 build-rules) my generated sources fail to build because they're looking for nonexistent  ` #import "GPBProtocolBuffers_RuntimeSupport.h"`. I understand from the above, that there must be some extra protobuf "library" or "framework" or some other "runtime support" that must be built/obtained for this. BUT I CANT FIND WHERE. Nor the instructions on building it, or what repo should I download, or how to go about it. I've been googling around for 2 days now, without any answer. Please help. This question seems to be related to my issue.

@Motti-Shneor did you look at the directions mentioned in the [previous comment](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2127#issuecomment-247651294)?  That talks about how to build by directly adding the sources.

Yes, I read it, and also finally worked this out, and it kind'a works - although I'm not happy with These non-arc sources. What bothers me, is that google's famous "protobuf" used in no less than 300000 projects - has such a poor support for ObjC - that actually no official documentation states HOW to build the needed components, the existing documentation and pre-built downloads fool you to believe you only need the protoc compiler + some accompanying .proto files to include in your own - and there is absolutely no description or even discussion of the limitations performance envelope or actually any technical aspect of the Obj-C support - let alone not being compatible with Apple's ARC which is here over a decade and is Xcode's default and standard for the last 5 years at least. This neglect is very frustrating  - an not really encouraging when selecting a technology to use.

There is a small section on the ObjC pages, but we've avoid duplicating the main pages documentation for building protoc since that has changed with time, and having two places vs. one for something can lead to confusion when one gets updated and the other doesn't.  I'm happy to take suggestions for improving the setup docs. Docs can be harder to write/validate the more familiar one is with something, so "fresh eyes" often are better at pointing out the stumbling blocks.

As far as ARC goes, ObjC code doesn't have to use ARC, and in the case of protocol buffers, a lot of developers want them to be as performant as possible, so by not using ARC and manually doing the retains/releases (MRR) within the generated code/runtime library we actually get better performance (and are still completely retain count safe) compared to the the compiler will insert with ARC.

ps - The newer runtimes have helped close the performance gap (ARC vs. MRR), but revisiting/changing the ARC usage at this point would also break existing project setups, so we always haven't looked at revisiting the decision because of that cost for developers.

title: Parser erroneously allows whitespace in package declaration.
body:
We had a case where `protoc` allowed a `package` declaration that had newlines in it but other tooling based on the spec failed to parse the file. I believe this should have failed to parse inside `protoc` as well.

Relevant parts of the spec:

```
package = "package" fullIdent ";"
fullIdent = ident { "." ident }
ident = letter { letter | decimalDigit | "_" }
letter = "A" … "Z" | "a" … "z"
decimalDigit = "0" … "9"
```

Example showing `protoc` allowing newlines:

```
$ echo "package example.

foo

;

message Foo {}" > test.proto

$ protoc --version
libprotoc 3.0.0

$ protoc --java_out=. test.proto
[libprotobuf WARNING google/protobuf/compiler/parser.cc:547] No syntax specified for the proto file: test.proto. Please use 'syntax = "proto2";' or 'syntax = "proto3";' to specify a syntax version. (Defaulted to proto2 syntax.)

$ tree
.
├── example
│   └── foo
│       └── Test.java
└── test.proto
```

nodes.body: Yes this seems like a bug.
@xfxyjwf Is the syntax spec checked in anywhere? What actually needs to be fixed here?

The syntax spec here:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto2-spec

The spec needs to specify where spaces are allowed and where not.
I suspect this is still a bug...

There is definitely code in the wild that expects qualified names (dot-separated sequence of identifiers, such as in type names, extension names in message literals and custom options) to _allow_ whitespace, including newlines, in between name components. (Admittedly, this might be less likely in package declarations.) But either way, this would not be a backwards compatible change.

There is definitely an issue with the clarity in the spec (or lack thereof). Which productions are lexical elements (where whitespace is generally disallowed between adjacent rule references)? Which are syntax elements (where whitespaces are not only allowed but sometimes required between adjacent rule references)? The whole dichotomy of tokenization vs. parsing is not mentioned at all, and there is nothing in the spec about whitespace or comments.

We triage inactive PRs and issues in order to make it easier to find active work. If this issue should remain active or becomes active again, please add a comment.

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago.

AFAIK, this hasn't been fixed and should remain open. 

That said, I'm not sure that this is solely a documentation issue. In the original description, @JakeWharton points out that "`protoc` allowed a `package` declaration that had newlines in it but other tooling based on the spec failed to parse the file." That's seems to point to a functionality issue along with the documentation issues.

If we do want to update the spec to reflect the ability to have whitespace characters between the package name elements, I'll need some direction on how to show that. I'm not EBNF proficient.

We triage inactive PRs and issues in order to make it easier to find active work. If this issue should remain active or becomes active again, please add a comment.

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago. This issue will be closed and archived after 14 additional days without activity.
That's not how bugs work. Bad bot.

We triage inactive PRs and issues in order to make it easier to find active work. If this issue should remain active or becomes active again, please add a comment.

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago. This issue will be closed and archived after 14 additional days without activity.
That's not how bugs work. Bad bot.

So I've started updating the spec, and it's starting to look somewhat comical. Here is a snippet:

```
WS = any combination of spaces, tabs, and newlines

mapField = "map" [WS] "<" [WS] keyType [WS] "," [WS] type [WS] ">" [WS] mapName [WS] "=" [WS] fieldNumber [WS] [ "[" fieldOptions "]" ] [WS] ";"
```

I've tested this definition with line breaks in each spot, and it still compiles. Is this what you'd expect to see in the spec? I'm open to suggestions for a different way to handle this.

The way this is handled in the [Go](https://go.dev/ref/spec#Lexical_elements) and [Java](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se23/html/jls-2.html#jls-2.2) language specs, for example, is that they separate lexical analysis from semantic analysis and then indicate that whitespace and comments are effectively ignored/discarded during lexical analysis but serve to separate adjacent lexical elements.

title: Support custom options in C#
body: Currently there's no way of accessing options metadata in the C# API.

nodes.body:
as some others, we'd also need this feature. Removing the support for custom default values left a little gap that custom extensions could solve.

@jskeet: We're thinking about providing a Pull Request for the custom extension feature in C#. To assess the situation, could you please outline a possible implementation?

I'll see what I can do in the next few days, but it won't be much sooner than that - I'm very busy at the moment on other projects.

@pherl may be able to help out too...

I've been looking at this today, and trying to work out how we can support it reasonably simply without adding too much to the API surface area. One issue is that options can be of any of the various types available - messages, strings, scalars etc.

If FieldDescriptor, MethodDescriptor, MessageDescriptor etc were to have a method such as:

``` csharp
IList<ByteString> GetOptions(int fieldNumber)
```

would that be enough to start with? I'd need to also provide a `CodedInputStream` constructor accepting a `ByteString`, but basically the idea would be:
- For messages, you'd just call `YourMessage.Parser.Parse(value)`
- For strings, you'd call `value.ToStringUtf8`
- For byte strings, you'd already have the value
- For scalars, you'd create a `CodedInputStream` and read the value from that

You'd need to know the option's field number, which I wouldn't _initially_ be generating any support for. In future, we could potentially generate a helper class for each option, which would know the right type, the field number etc - but that would take quite a bit more work. This "halfway house" would at least unblock users.

Thoughts?

Full support for what, exactly? Custom options, yes. Default values? No.

I'm putting together a pull request, which you could then look at and try for yourself.

I meant custom options... Default values won't be re-introduced as I understood.

Thanks, I'll give feedback...

I've created #2317 for this - more testing is needed, but it's a start. In particular, it shows how crude and low-level the code is to retrieve the custom options.

I'd suggest encapsulating that in your own hand-written types to start with - and we can eventually autogenerate them.

I've currently allowed multiple values per option - I need to check whether that's actually reasonable, or whether I should just make the method return a single `ByteString` (or null if it's not found). Repeated options would be "interesting" at that point...

Thanks for your fast reply! Protobuf low-level code is :flushed:.

One of my colleagues is currently porting over our current custom message option solution from C++ to C#. I'll give you feedback, once we have a testcase running..

One thought on the multiple values per option solution: although I'm probably not deep enough into protobuf architecture, i see a problem when multiple options have different types. How do you distinguish them before parsing?

@gabm: You'd need to know which option had which type. As I say, eventually we'd be able to generate a class which knows the names, field numbers, wire formats etc... this is a temporary measure which unblocks things for now, without causing problems down the line. Code using it before we make it cleaner should definitely isolate their usage into a single place, of course... keep all the ugliness away from everything else.

I still haven't checked what the deal is in terms of repeated fields etc. Will need to investigate that before going for proper PR review.

Aah misunderstood the "repeated options" thing. Somehow thought that `List<ByteString>` could actually contain multiple values of _different_ types - nevermind... for sure, we'll encapsulate everything... But in our usecase thats not too limiting since we'd only use one single option for now...

We tested your code by retreiving a custom MessageOption from our messages. Everything works as expected, thank you!

For reference, how we retreive the message option on `ProtobufType`, ID field number `1000`:

```
ProtobufType.Descriptor.GetOptions(WireFormat.MakeTag(1000, WireFormat.WireType.Varint)).Single().CreateCodedInput().ReadInt64();
```

Python generated API is documented here:

In Google we have some really big binaries half of which is just the proto generated code and we have to spend time on shrinking the size or otherwise some binaries can not be compiled any more... 2. the interface between generated code and the protobuf runtime is minimum and that makes it far more easier to remain binary backwards compatible when we make changes to protobuf (i.e,. if the generated code doesn't change at all, a program compiled using an older version of protobuf can switch to depend on a newer version protobuf without needing any change).

currently C# `protoc` will gen :

nodes.body:
You can already write

``` csharp
public partial class TestMessage : CacheableObject
```

It being sealed doesn't stop you from specifying a base class.

@jskeet ah yes right you are - but what if you're attempting to translate a set of types with hierarchical inheritance ( as expressed in xml , for example ) to proto3 + generated-classes ?  

Are there reasons why protoc generates C# class as sealed ?  ( or I suppose Java class as final )

> but what if you're attempting to translate a set of types with hierarchical inheritance ( as expressed in xml , for example ) to proto3 + generated-classes ?

Then you need to think of an alternative approach, because proto simply doesn't "do" inheritance, only composition. I would strongly urge you to just go with that instead of fighting it - you'll end up with a much simpler experience.

> Are there reasons why protoc generates C# class as sealed ? ( or I suppose Java class as final )

In Java it's vital as proto messages are immutable. In C#, messages are mutable, so we _could_ unseal the classes - but there are all kinds of extra difficulties introduced by that. How do you parse to a derived type, for example? It's all much simpler without inheritance, and as protos don't model inheritance anyway, I felt it best to enforce that in the .NET type system too.

> we could unseal the classes - but there are all kinds of extra difficulties introduced by that. How do you parse to a derived type, for example?

@jskeet - You all really should unseal them in this situation and probably for any future codegen tools. I think that the problems with derived types would not be the problems of the generation tool author to solve. This is primarily because the the generated code does not belong to the tool author in the first place. A code generation tool using protections like this is just like forcing DRM on users.
At least they could make it optional on generation.

> At least they could make it optional on generation.

Totally agree. I have a couple of CG scenarios in which it would make sense to unseal them so that I can wrap some message parameters for bridging, adptation purposes.

title: Python implementation does not support json_name on descriptors
body:
The python implementation doesn't have awareness of a descriptor's `json_name`, which means that serialization (to JSON) and parsing (from JSON) behave incorrectly when a custom JSON field name has been defined.

It would be good to test the Python implementation against definitions that include custom JSON field names — e.g. `./src/google/protobuf/util/internal/testdata/books.proto`).

---

Example:

``` protobuf
message Person {
  string id = 1 [json_name = "@id"];
}
```

An instance should serialize to `{"@id": "my-id"}`, but instead serializes to  `{"id": "my-id"}`:

``` python
p = Person()
p.id = "my-id"
json_format.MessageToJson(p)
```

title: ByteSize/ByteSizeLong/GetCachedSize idempotent accesses present as data race in open-source TSAN
body: The ByteSize function generated in C++ triggers a data race in open-source TSAN on `cached_size_` . This is marked as an idempotent and benign data race, but the annotation has no effect. That said, I don't think that C++ supports anything other than catch-fire semantics on any data race, including idempotent writes, so I'm not sure that an annotation is really effective as a matter of course.

nodes.body: We have seen this issue in grpc/grpc#8174 and are working around it with grpc/grpc#8188

The annotation's sole purpose is to suppress TSAN warnings. If it doesn't have effect, we are either using the wrong annotation for opensource, or there is some problem in TSAN to recognize the annotations.

I agree with your assessment that the current situation is a data race per the standard. However I think it would be very difficult to change this to not have the idempotent write. I think annotations are the way to go for the foreseeable future.
We actually can use atomicops to avoid this race, but it's considered not worthwhile to change.
This did not trigger a warning for us until very recently. I am not sure if it is because we have just improved our tests, or if it is because thread sanitizer is stricter than it was before.

Mind if I try sending that as a PR? I want to make sure that it won't hurt
our portability with gcc4.4+

Or if you already have it as a PR, I can test it out on our portability
suite.

We can't use C++11 atomics, and the [atomicops support in protobuf](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/stubs/atomicops.h) is far from a standard. For now I think I would prefer figuring out why the annotations is not working and fixing that.

And how does this hurt portability?
It looks like there will be no portability issue. gcc4.4+ supports atomic and memory_order_relaxed; but it sounds like that's a moot issue if you can't use C++11 atomics for other reasons.
For the moment we are trying to support C++98 compiles.

title: Proposal for a 128 bit type
body:
These days people communicating uuids and ipv6 addresses between processes is quite common.  These can both be addressed with a 128 bit type.

Just to give an idea of how many users already want this and hack around this.
I have protobuf code generator for go (gogoprotobuf) and I have added a feature called customtype.  This allows you to change a bytes type to a type of your choice, but still transfer it as bytes.  This allows for quite a large variety of applications, but what people use it for is very constraint.   Most users just want some 128bit type.

nodes.body: Transferring this type as bytes (i.e. with the length-delimited wire type) sounds like a good idea. That way we would have the option of implementing it first just for one or two languages, and other languages without support for it could at least handle the data gracefully (e.g. by treating it as an unknown field or just a bytes field). I wonder what the API would look like since as far as I know most languages don't have a standard 128-bit type--maybe just the raw array of 16 bytes?
perfect :)

For Go you can do this nicely with a [16]byte into the struct so no extra malloc. Same goes for C when you expose the length as a constant.
How would one do that for Java? Two (signed) long? :-( Just a byte array couses marshalling errors on size mismatch. A generated class with fields byte0 to byte15?
@gerben-s @jtattermusch why is this closed?
+1 to this feature request -- we could make a good use of it in [YugaByte DB](https://github.com/yugabyte/yugabyte-db) as well, for UUIDs, IPv6 addresses, MVCC timestamps, etc.
Any progress?
I'm trying to get this one right at pascaldekloe/colfer#36. Feedback wanted.
u128 is pervasive in blockchains. bytes is not good as cannot 7bit compress small amounts of assets which usually start from trillions.
The need is clear. No need for more use-cases here please. Same with the status requests. Unless you have something to contribute, this feature is pending on some serious work.

For those who can reproduce it, have you tried using the replacement that the deprecation warning suggests (`std::atomic_compare_exchange_strong_explicit(std::memory_order_relaxed)`)? I'm not sure if this will work because we don't compile for C++11 by default and I believe the atomics are new in C++11. The other thing we could try is to disable the warning with `-Wno-deprecated-declarations`, but that's not ideal because it might have to be changed in the build setups not in protobuf itself but in the projects that depend on it (e.g. Mesos).

I think the right solution is to add another atomicops_internals_cxx11.h header file using C++11 atomics for the implementation, then add a #ifdef/#else/#endif in atomicops.h to select atomicops_internals_cxx11.h instead of atomicops_internals_macosx.h when the macos version is high enough:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/stubs/atomicops.h#L199

Can someone having access to Mac Sierra help contribute a pull request?

btw: If you're here because  https://github.com/grpc/grpc fails to build, note that the gRPC Makefile passes its own `CPPFLAGS` to the protobuf make invocation: https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/Makefile#L1190

In that case, removing `-Werror` from the protobuf Makefile won't be enough because it still gets passed as `CPPFLAGS` from the gRPC Makefile.

The easiest work-around for us was to run the **gRPC** `make` with the environment variable `CPPFLAGS="-Wno-deprecated-declarations"` set.

From license terms

```
//     * Redistributions of source code must retain the above copyright
```

> In all source files, we have included the text.

title: Redefined specialization in type_traits.h using MSVC (Protobuf 3.1.0)
body:
This commit added [explicit specializations](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blame/b9bad65bf32cebc6210b4da9251919503d479dbd/src/google/protobuf/stubs/type_traits.h#L146) for `is_integral<__int64>` and `is_integral<unsigned __int64` when compiling with Visual C++: https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/3c88e1b53de832547e04f2e1c075bb1aae0ca0b4

It seems that by default `HAVE_LONG_LONG` is not defined on this platform, so these specializations do not collide with the specializations for `is_integral<long long>` and `is_integral<unsigned long long>` [immediately above](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blame/b9bad65bf32cebc6210b4da9251919503d479dbd/src/google/protobuf/stubs/type_traits.h#L142) them.

However, other projects use `HAVE_LONG_LONG` on Windows, which leads to an error about the specialization already being defined. In particular, when I include `<Python.h>` from Anaconda for Windows before a header that includes some protobuf headers, I get the following compilation error:

```
[...]google/protobuf/stubs/type_traits.h(151): error C2766: explicit specialization; 'google::protobuf::internal::is_integral<__int64>' has already been defined
[...]google/protobuf/stubs/type_traits.h(143): note: see previous definition of 'is_integral<__int64>'
[...]google/protobuf/stubs/type_traits.h(152): error C2766: explicit specialization; 'google::protobuf::internal::is_integral<unsigned __int64>' has already been defined
[...]google/protobuf/stubs/type_traits.h(144): note: see previous definition of 'is_integral<unsigned __int64>'
```

Here's a simple repro, `test.cc`:

``` c++
//#include <Python.h>  // The following #define has the same effect.
#define HAVE_LONG_LONG
#include "google/protobuf/stubs/type_traits.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  return 0;
}
```

Reproduced using the following command line with Visual Studio 2015 Update 1:

```
C:\temp> cl.exe test.cc /I<path\to\protobuf\src\>
```

Could the conditional compilation be refactored to avoid this problem? @xfxyjwf, since you made the commit, any ideas?

nodes.body:
When reading https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/29dh1w7z.aspx, it says:

```
The __int64 type has no ANSI equivalent.
```

That made me think __int64 is different from long long on MSVC. Apparently it's either my reading is wrong or the MSVC doc is lying.

I guess we can change it to:

``` cpp
#if defined(HAVE_LONG_LONG) || defined(_MSC_VER)
template<> struct is_integral<long long> : true_type { };
template<> struct is_integral<unsigned long long> : true_type { };
#endif
```

Or maybe just drop the #ifdef/#endif entirely as compilers that don't support "long long" are probably too old to compile protobuf code any way.

Can you help send a pull request to fix that?
Thanks for the quick response! Yes, I'll send a quick Pull Request with your first suggested change (after testing it with the code I'm building).

title: Java: New Runtime Proposal
body:
Today's generated code does all the heavy lifting (serialization/deserialization, merging, etc.). Every field adds baggage to nearly every method. This leads to problems (many of which are described in #1852):
- Broad ABI between the generated code and the runtime
  - Refactoring the runtime is incredibly difficult
  - Generated code may require certain versions of the runtime
- Generates a ton of boilerplate code
  - This is a big problem on Android
  - Can’t fix bugs or improve performance without regenerating code

The attempt here is to begin discussion for a new runtime that will address (or eliminate) these issues.

For experimentation, I've created the [java_experimental](https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/java_experimental) branch. PR #2216 is an initial attempt that moves functionality into the runtime. It makes use of "schemas", which are dynamically generated runtime components that implement various capabilities (e.g. serialization) on behalf of the message.
# Schema Creation

Before we can create a [Schema](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/java_experimental/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/Schema.java), we need to reflect on a given protobuf message to generate a [MessageInfo](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/java_experimental/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/MessageInfo.java).  This is currently done in one of two ways:
1. For standard proto, we just transform Descriptor -> MessageInfo
2. For android (proto lite), we use annotations on the fields of the message and manually parse the Dex. _The code for this is not currently in github._
# Schema Types

There are currently two types of schema implementations:
1. Table-based
   - Information for all fields of a given message is stored in a `ByteBuffer` (e.g. [Proto2Manifest](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/java_experimental/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/Proto2Manifest.java#L70))
   - The same class will work for any message
   - Code size stays constant as # messages increases
   - Only schema supported on Android
2. Bytecode generation (via ASM)
   - Slower to create
   - Faster at runtime
   - Additional bytecode is generated for each message type
   - _The code for this is not currently on github_
# Runtime API

The new [runtime API](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/java_experimental/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/Protobuf.java) will provide the capabilities to the application.  Ideally, this will lead to generated code becoming little more than POJOs where the application will interact with the runtime directly.  However, for existing code we can have an intermediate step where we still generate all of the methods, but they simply delegate to the runtime.
# Bechmarks

Initial Benchmarks (the code is not yet on github ... stay tuned!) show overall performance wins for the new code.
## Serialization

```
(schemaType)                  Score      Error  Units
PROTO2                        27193.351 ±  542.185  ops/s
PROTO3                        27910.265 ±  447.149  ops/s
GENERIC_PROTO2_TABLE          46455.018 ± 3189.952  ops/s
GENERIC_PROTO2_LOOKUP         48501.404 ±  572.482  ops/s
GENERIC_PROTO3_TABLE          48214.251 ±  677.677  ops/s
GENERIC_PROTO3_LOOKUP         44418.246 ± 4995.708  ops/s
ASM_PROTO3                    58715.064 ±  731.199  ops/s
```

To be fair, the new runtime uses a reverse-writing serializer which avoids the size calculation cost.
Adding reverse writing to current proto implementation has been determined infeasible due to the extra code bloat required.
## Deserialization

```
(schemaType)                   Score     Error  Units
PROTO2                         15099.911 ±  93.873  ops/s
PROTO3                         14573.616 ± 177.748  ops/s
GENERIC_PROTO2_TABLE           20058.241 ± 440.657  ops/s
GENERIC_PROTO2_LOOKUP          20092.639 ± 110.975  ops/s
GENERIC_PROTO3_TABLE           20402.281 ± 447.267  ops/s
GENERIC_PROTO3_LOOKUP          19582.969 ± 733.465  ops/s
ASM_PROTO3                     22213.371 ± 494.667  ops/s
```

Again to be fair, the new code is able to leverage some optimizations:
- Switches on field number (rather than tag). Higher chance of tableswitch (O(1)) rather than lookup switch (O(logn)).
- Lists are read all at once rather than field by field
  - Reduces overhead introduced by virtual method calls on the Reader

title: iOS Cocoapod Errors
body:
Using Cocoapods 1.0.1

**Podspec**

```
s.dependency 'Protobuf', '3.0.2'
s.pod_target_xcconfig = { 'GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS' => '$(inherited) GPB_USE_PROTOBUF_FRAMEWORK_IMPORTS=1' }
```

**Steps**
- Build .proto file
- Include .pbobjc.h / .m into xcode project (development pod folder) with `-fno-arc-objc`
- `pod install`

**Outcome**
- `GPB_DEBUG_CHECK_RUNTIME_VERSIONS();` implicit declaration invalid in C99
- `GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_OBJC_VERSION` is < 30002
- `GPBDescriptorInitializationFlag_None` not found. XCode's Suggested replacement `GPBDescriptorInitializationFlag_WireFormat`

**Workaround**
- Comment out `GPB_DEBUG_CHECK_RUNTIME_VERSIONS();`
- Comment out `GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_OBJC_VERSION` check
- Updated podspec to: `s.pod_target_xcconfig = { 'GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS' => '$(inherited) GPB_USE_PROTOBUF_FRAMEWORK_IMPORTS=1 GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_OBJC_VERSION=30002'`
- Changed `GPBDescriptorInitializationFlag_None` to 0

**Question**
Is this a protobuf ios sdk bug when using protobuf 3.0.2 as a cocoapod dependancy?
