As a matter of fact, the **CdmAdapterTest.Initialize** Chromium test :
- reports leaks using https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/337a028bb65ccca4dda768695950b5aba53ae2c9 without **GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_NO_STATIC_INITIALIZER** define
- doesn't report leaks using https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/337a028bb65ccca4dda768695950b5aba53ae2c9 with **GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_NO_STATIC_INITIALIZER** define
- reports leaks using https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/cc8ca5b6a5478b40546d4206392eb1471454460d with **GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_NO_STATIC_INITIALIZER** define
- doesn't report leaks using https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/cc8ca5b6a5478b40546d4206392eb1471454460d without **GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_NO_STATIC_INITIALIZER** define

So the leak wouldn't be a leak per say, but just a detection of statically initialized objects that are not freed (as we could expect).

I'll try to work on a fix on monday

title: PHP: Only variables should be passed by reference

nodes.body: Could you be more specific about the problem?

The "setFile" method expects its parameter to be a reference, and you cannot reference something that is not a variable.

http://php.net/manual/en/language.references.pass.php

"No other expressions should be passed by reference, as the result is undefined."

```
$this->setField(new RepeatedField....
```
But setFile expect to take a message instance, which should be a variable. Isn't it?

Hmm, I must be running an old version. My bad.

New version (v3.1.0-alpha-1)
```
$repeated_field = new RepeatedField(
                            $field->getType(),
                            $field->getMessageType()->getClass());
                        $this->$setter($repeated_field);
```

Old version
```
 $this->$setter(
                            new RepeatedField(
                                $field->getType(),
                                $field->getMessageType()->getClass()));
```

Sorry, I still don't get what's wrong here.
According to the manual, following can be passed by reference:

1. Variables, i.e. foo($a)
2. New statements, i.e. foo(new foobar())
3. References returned from functions, i.e.

The example you've shown here is case 2.

This issue has been resolved as of https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/9372292b2940bba4e69904744eee358f0bcfc436

Example demonstrating the old issue. 
The execution will result in a error notice. "Notice: Only variables should be passed by reference"

```
class Example {}

function method(&$arg1) {}

method(new Example()); <-- Notice: Only variables should be passed by reference
```

@vext01 I think if you look carefully the bytes fields actually are different. You're right that there is a small formatting difference between the "Expected:" and "Which is:" lines, but that is just because the former shows the literal text from the source file while the latter represents the string evaluated from that. The "Actual:" line is substantially different from the other two.

The actual value for the bytes_value field was `GEgc2V0YiB0ZXR5diBzdWxhZXU=` while the expected value for that is `aSBhbSBhIHRlc3QgYnl0ZXMgdmFsdWU`. These are both supposed to be the base64 encoding of the string `i am a test bytes value`. But if you base64-decode the actual output you get `ma  a setb tetyv sulaeu`. This is almost an anagram of the original text, so it seems as if the base64 encoding step is somehow getting jumbled up in your environment.

@xfxyjwf  so indeed it's endianess and i managed to fix it. from what i see noone cares setting PROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN . and i'm wondering why on other little endian platforms it works.
does the following configure.ac patch look reasonable to you?
```
diff --git a/configure.ac b/configure.ac
index 896f347..c3ae08b 100644
--- a/configure.ac
+++ b/configure.ac
@@ -101,6 +101,15 @@ AC_FUNC_MEMCMP
 AC_FUNC_STRTOD
 AC_CHECK_FUNCS([ftruncate memset mkdir strchr strerror strtol])

+#endianess
+AC_CHECK_HEADERS([endian.h],
+ AC_TRY_COMPILE([#include ], [switch (1) { case __LITTLE_ENDIAN: break; case __BYTE_ORDER: break; } ],[is_little_endian=0], [is_little_endian=1]),
+ AC_MSG_RESULT([Can't Determine Endianess])
+)
+if test $is_little_endian = 1 ; then
+  CXXFLAGS="$CXXFLAGS -DPROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN"
+fi
+
 # Check for zlib.
 HAVE_ZLIB=0
 AS_IF([test "$with_zlib" != no], [
```

@xfxyjwf actually sorry but this as is won't work cause in the beginning of the file there is an
```
#undef PROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN
```
what do you think is the correct way to proceed here? should we create another name (like HOST_LITTLE_ENDIAN ?) that is passed from the configure? 
it seems that some comments are hinting towards something like that cause PROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN is also used in coded_stream.

@ramrunner Thanks for helping. I would prefer a fix that applies to the source code instead of the build configure though. That's because we build protobuf code with different build tools (such as cmake/bazel) and updating configure.ac does not fix the problem with other build tools.

In the code we are detecting the endian with this:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/fd046f6263fb17383cafdbb25c361e3451c31105/src/google/protobuf/stubs/port.h#L63

Probably we are missing some macros for OpenBSD?

@xfxyjwf ok finally got it. 
BSD sys/param.h does not deal with endianess. cause it actually shouldn't
there is endian.h for that. and actually endian.h is considered POSIX since 2011
http://www.opengroup.org/austin/docs/austin_514.txt
so if on that line we also include endian.h the BYTE_ORDER macro will be defined and it will equal to the appropriate machine {LITTLE,BIG}_ENDIAN
anyway i am sending a PR in a bit that will include endian.h if __OpenBSD__ defined. i understand that the android SDK might not have it although it would be nice to. :)

edit: PR is #2445
Thanks @ramrunner!
Closing as the fix https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/2445 is in.

title: g++ error with -Wextra when compiling protobuf
body:
When turning on extra warnings (-Wextra) and enabling warnings as errors (-Werror) protobuf3 map implementation hits a G++ (version 5.2.0, on Linux) error on the following line 

include/google/protobuf/map.h|677 col 31| error: type qualifiers ignored on function return type [-Werror=ignored-qualifiers]
||      value_type* const value() const { return v_; }
||                                ^
|| cc1plus: all warnings being treated as errors

The problem with that line is that it's making the pointer itself const, not the value pointed to.
That's what G++ complains about.

Example to reproduce:

#include <include/protobuf/map.h>
int main () { return 0; }

And compile with
g++ -Wextra -Werror file.cpp

The fix should be to either remove that 'const' keyword, as it does nothing, or if const-ness of the pointed value is desired, change it to:

const value_type * value() const { return v_; }

title: Features needed in Bazel
body:
As discussed offline with @xfxyjwf, here's the list of features Bazel needs for its native proto-library rules:

- `--direct_dependencies`
- `--direct_dependencies_violation_msg `
- A yet-to-be-implemented flag to make direct-dep violations a warning instead of an error.

The motivation for the 3rd flag is similar to that of the strict-deps warning mode of Bazel's JavaBuilder. It allows developers to more quickly work on their code, without being interrupted by strict-deps errors.

nodes.body: I would prefer not adding any more flags. For (3) the argument of allowing developers to ignore errors for fast development is weak and actually against common practice as far as I can see.

1. I'm not proposing we ignore the errors (we don't need the flag for this). I'm proposing that we let developers keep testing their code in a loop (or whatever) without stopping everything because of something that's very easy to fix and is non-consequential in the short term.
2. Why is it against common practice?

The common practice is to treat warnings as errors, i.e., be strict when you build code. In Google we even report style issues as build errors and stop compiling. What you suggested is apparently the opposite and I'm not convinced that's beneficial.

That's the common practice when submitting code, but while developing there's no reason to make people's lives harder. 

1. Bazel's strict deps implementation takes this approach.
2. In Go, there are highly upvoted StackOverflow questions about turning off the unused import error ([1](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/19560334/how-to-disable-golang-unused-import-error), [2](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/21743841/how-to-avoid-annoying-error-declared-and-not-used-from-golang)) and an [FAQ on Go's site](https://golang.org/doc/faq#unused_variables_and_imports).

In these cases, the intention is to be forgiving when developing, and only making this an error before submitting. The rationale is that there are almost no short-term disadvantages to wrong imports, so there's no reason to disallow wrong imports in the short term.

There is no such difference between submitting code and developing code. We enforce build rules upon building the code, regardless whether you are trying to submitting the code or experimenting a dirty hack temporarily. Your argument is still "ignore errors for fast development", which I believe is the opposite of the common practice we are following, and I do not want to add a protoc flag for that. I don't know about bazel, but the Go team apparently decided to not provide compiler options to turn off unused import/variable errors as well.

Ok, fair enough.

Regarding the 2 other flags - any chance of getting them released in the near future?
The current Bazel canary already contains the direct-deps feature in `proto_library`.
The next protobuf release would be 3.2.0 with a stable php API. It's targeted the end of Dec. @Teboring for more status updates.
Any chance of doing another release before that? A month is a long time to block this feature in Bazel :)

@cgrushko An earlier release is not possible. The way protobuf release process is setup makes it very cumbersome to do one single release. No matter whether it's a patch release 3.1.1, or a minor release 3.2.0, at least two weeks are needed to finish the integration/testing/packaging process. The end of Dec. is likely the best we can do.

@xfxyjwf Is it possible to sync protobuf's github repo with the internal one? `--direct_dependencies_violation_msg` isn't in the repo yet, so the native Bazel rules can't be used even if one builds from HEAD.

CC @nicolasnoble 
As grpc is moving to bazel based build system this bug has become important. @xfxyjwf is there a timeline for fixing this issue?
This feature is already available as of protobuf 3.2.0 release.

title: Add proto_lang_toolchain() rules to root BUILD file
body:
Bazel's upcoming proto support rules look for toolchains in the external repository `@com_google_protobuf_xxx//:xx_toolchain` for language/flavor `xxx`.

For example, in order to use `cc_proto_library`, one should place the following in their protobuf's distro's root `BUILD` file:

```
proto_lang_toolchain(
  name = "cc_toolchain",
  runtime = ":protobuf",
  command_line = "--cpp_out=$(OUT)",
  visibility = ["//visibility:public"],
)
```

And the following in their own project's `WORKSPACE` file:

```
local_repository(
  name = "com_google_protobuf_cc",
  path = "/path/to/protobuf-3.1.0/"
)
```

This feature-request is about adding these toolchains to protobuf's distributions.

nodes.body: Could you help send a pull request to add these rules?

2. Where would Java and JavaLite toolchains go?

Your change only adds cc_toolchain so that would only covers C++. The binary release is not related to bazel. For other languages, the toolchain rule should live where the runtime rule is defined. For Java/Python, they should live with the C++ rule. JavaLite toolchain will need to go into the javalite branch.

I now have explored the PHP library of protobuf a good bit and even though I realize it is still in Beta state I would like to make two suggestions that could improve the library.

title: keep unknown data after deserialization to from json
body:
Recently support to ignore unknown fields when deserializing json encoded proto message was added. But the other important feature is still missing which is retaining the unknown data.

So in binary protobuf, if you are on v1.0 of some proto message and you deserialize v1.1 not only you dont break the api but you also keep the unknown fields intact, so that if you serialize the same message from 1.0 version app and send it to different client who is on v1.1, this client will be able to use that data...

native protobuf 1.1 -> 1.0 -> 1.1 works
json protobuf 1.1 -> 1.0 -> 1.1 loses information on deserialization to 1.0

nodes.body: Keeping unknown fields in JSON convention isn't possible because the data structure used to store unknown fields is specifically designed for protobuf binary format and isn't capable of storing JSON data.
oh i see, you cannot properly represent remaining unknown json in protobuf binary...

Note that right now in proto3 unknown fields are discarded when parsing binary just like JSON. To retain unknown data you need to stick with proto2 syntax.

The discussion about the drop of unknown fields in proto3 is tracked here: https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/272
Oh i didn't know that, didn't use proto3 though. Thanks

title: Inconsistency when parsing -0/"-0" in JSON in C++

nodes.body: -0 should be accepted because it's a valid JSON numeric value and is equivalent to 0. For the "-0" case, the current C++ behavior kind of makes sense to me. When parsing integers, the parser is more lenient on numeric values. For example, 1.234e3 will be accepted as equal to 1234. That's because they are equivalent JSON values (e.g., you can't distinguish between the two in Javascript). However, when the value is a double-quoted string, whether it's equivalent or whether it's valid at all is entirely up to protobuf JSON parser to interpret. And in that case being strict on what it accepts depending on the field type doesn't seem a bad idea. In this sense the current behavior looks reasonable to me.

title: Support for MonetaryAmount
body:
Hi,

I would love to see support for MonetaryAmount in a similar way that exist with the JSR354 to solve the question of how to we serialize over the wire a monetary amount in a language neutral way and been able to have different languages working with the same concept of money. 
At the basics we I now that a monetary amount has a currency and an amount value, but how do we serialize the amount is it a double or a BigDecimal ? 
This seems to be such a common use case the that maybe would be support out of the box the same way that the is support for Timestamp.

Thank you, kindly
 Luis Oscar Trigueiros

nodes.body:
I can see how this would be convenient. However I think it is (currently) outside the scope of protobuf.

Almost every language has a time type, so Timestamp lets us convert back and forth easily between protos and language-native types. Money is much more complicated, and there are far fewer language-native types for it.

I think it would make a lot of sense to create a `money.proto` file that could serialize the types defined in JSR354. You could put this in its own GitHub project and provide convenient conversion to/from the JSR354 types. If other languages also started creating money types, you could provide conversion to those types also.

If this `money.proto` became popular across many languages, we could consider putting it (or something like it) in the main protobuf repository. I think this would be the best approach towards getting money into protobuf.
For those visiting this issue, money.proto exists as part of googleapis: https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/money.proto
But how to use money.proto? How to convert decimals to nanos and nanos to decimals? Too little information to use it. That's the only thing putting me off from using protobuf

title: why messge type  remove 'required,optional'?
body: The 'required,optional' types are useful for client to know which param is required and which is optional.

nodes.body: You mean in proto3? Because proto3 doesn't have a notion of presence anymore, so optional and required doesn't make sense.

We dropped required fields in proto3 because required fields are generally considered harmful and violating protobuf's compatibility semantics. The whole idea of using protobuf is that it allows you to add/remove fields from your protocol definition while still being fully forward/backward compatible with newer/older binaries. Required fields break this though. You can never safely add a required field to a .proto definition, nor can you safely remove an existing required field because both of these actions break wire compatibility. For example, if you add a required field to a .proto definition, binaries built with the new definition won't be able to parse data serialized using the old definition because the required field is not present in old data. In a complex system where .proto definitions are shared widely across many different components of the system, adding/removing required fields could easily bring down multiple parts of the system. We have seen production issues caused by this multiple times and it's pretty much banned everywhere inside Google for anyone to add/remove required fields. For this reason we completely removed required fields in proto3.

After the removal of "required", "optional" is just redundant so we removed "optional" as well.

> After the removal of "required", "optional" is just redundant so we removed "optional" as well.

Note that removing optional does not mean that the "optionality" concept is gone.
The flaw of removing completely the optionality concept is more debatable, as often people want to have the old "has_<field>()" API for testing user intention.

title: Generated Java source should be annotated with @Generated
body:
Generated Java source code should be annotated with [`@Generated`](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/javax/annotation/Generated.html) to aid static analysis and tooling. For example [Error-Prone will ignore errors in `@Generated` code](https://github.com/google/error-prone/issues/329).

As a workaround presently I have a pre-compilation step that adds the annotation manually, but ideally the protoc compiler would do this for me.

    <!-- based on http://stackoverflow.com/a/5941279/113632 -->
    <replaceregexp match="public(.*) class" replace="@javax.annotation.Generated("protoc") \0">
      <fileset dir="${proto.src}" includes="**/*.java" />
    </replaceregexp>

title: generated c++ include guards are not unique for different message types

nodes.body: If you pass a/query.proto when invoking protoc, I believe the "A" should end up in the include guard also.

Thanks for the hint @thomasvl 
It is true what you write, but for me in best case a workaround and sometimes not even practicable
for example, if the proto files are processed and generated via CMake or come with a 3rd party library

would the include guard be generated  like that  
namespace_namespace_typename
than everything would just work. And the namespace names are also generated and not thrown away.

I think a place in the file location that defined the include guard is not the best solution , this means, depending on the location of the file, generated output looks different and might one time work, an other time, as described above, not.

I just ran into this problem myself. I had to rename some messages to get everything to compile again. Since I work with CMake the tip posted by @thomasvl doesn't work either (the messages all have to be in the same folder for CMake to process them correctly).

This should be easily fixable. I'd send in a pull request but that is impossible to do for google because I don't have the google account linked to my github email address so that'd be a waste of time.
do you need a google account for submitting a pull request here on github @martijnotto ?
Yes. If you don't they won't even look at it.

aha, I have a google account, could it work if I fork this, you fork my fork, I pull you changes and sent them here?
edit:
just checked, the fix is indeed not difficult, I can do this but it has to wait until since it is summer now

@xfxyjwf of course changing the include path that gets written would solve the problem, 
if this would effect anything else and you use 'unique ids' that special, the bug is actually much more serious. (imaging a unbelievable head shaking from me ;-)

@xfxyjwf Signing the CLA only works if the email address for the commits is the same as that of the google account used. Since I use unique addresses for services I have no google account linked to my github address and thus it doesn't work. I have tried in the past and gave up.

Anyways, to fix this the unique identifier should be changed so that it is a combination of the filename and the package it uses. It makes no sense to only use the filename as the include guard. An even easier solution would be to just use #pragma once, it seems all common compilers now support this. Is there any rule prohibiting you from simply doing that?

About CMake, the usual way to do this is to use 'protobuf_generate_cpp', of which the documentation says the following:

"NOTE: The PROTOBUF_GENERATE_CPP macro & add_executable() or add_library() calls only work properly within the same directory."

It's by design that different proto files must use a different import path. Imagining someone tries to import your query.proto:
```proto
syntax = "proto2";
import "query.proto";
```
Protoc has to know which query.proto you are trying to import. If you make two query.proto appear exactly the same to protoc, protoc won't be able to tell which one is the correct one.

This semantics is built into the proto langauge and implementation. Changing the include path to avoid the immediate symbol conflict only leads to more serious problems down the path (where you will find it's impossible to reuse these protos or simply can't build anything in a different language).

For CMake, @martijnotto Have you tried this:
```
protobuf_generate_cpp(PROTO_A_SRCS PROTO_A_HDRS a/query.proto)
protobuf_generate_cpp(PROTO_B_SRCS PROTO_B_HDRS b/query.proto)
```

Thanks for explaining the reasons @xfxyjwf , however, imho these are total different problems.
One is not generating include guards respecting the package name specified withing the proto file itself, let us see this in isolation.

The other problem, you describe, is a different issue and I can see no relation, we should not talk about this here, but just to show why I think it is something different:
what if you `#include foo.h` in your code and you have multiple include paths where each contain a foo.h, how can the compiler find the right one? This is not an issue. On the compiler it is `-I`, for protoc it is `-IPATH, --proto_path=PATH`. 
Referring to your example protoc should pic up the first "query.proto" it finds. 
Of course the user has to do/specify it correct, either by using the correct search path or by fully qualifying the import path.

However, what is the relation to  generated include guards  that contain the specified packages form within the proto file itself ? There is none!
That
```
package PackageName;
message Query {;  
  string what = 1;
}
```
should generate `#ifndef PROTOBUF_PackageName_query_2eproto__INCLUDED` , because that is  what is specified within the protofile,  there is no relation to what you describe. 
I can see no breaking change in simply adding the user specified package name into the include guard.

Referring your question to cmake, @martijnotto has given you the information form the cmake hellp
https://cmake.org/cmake/help/v3.1/module/FindProtobuf.html

>  **Note** The PROTOBUF_GENERATE_CPP macro and add_executable() or add_library() calls only work properly within the same directory.

1. Using the same import path for multiple .proto files is an unsupported use case.
2. You tried to use .protos in this unsupported way and ran into macro conflicts.
3. You are proposing a change to workaround the macro conflicts so you can use .protos in an unsupported way.
4. We do not intend to allow using identical import path for multiple .proto files. Therefore we will not accept any change that makes protobuf more permissive on this.

Thanks, understood that its  easier to change the  cmake  find protobuf than you to accept  `namespace_class` include guard instead of just `class` include guard as all sane code  does it. Except protoc generated code but this is of course a feature, not a bug ;-)

I believe this needs to be revisited. Other than the fact that such generic include guard can be really limiting it is not possible to apply the workaround that @thomasvl mentioned in multi-dependent proto structures.

The situation is that the proto definitions are externally defined, as is often the case in real-world applications, and it is not possible (or desirable) to alter any names, to properly and hack-free integrate and allow proper updates as submodules.
In case we have multiple proto files with many inter-dependecies, our include path will point to the parent directory of protos, in which case supplying relative paths to the compiler (a/query.proto on thomas' example) will indeed force the include guard to contain _a_ prefix.

However, in my tests the complier will create the descriptor_table_deps disregarding the actual generated name of the "dependee" file based on the relative path. My guess is that it still looks at the import statement of the dependent file. Let me give an example.

─ main
│── main/proto
│─│─ main/proto/Dependent.proto
│─│─ main/proto/Dependee.proto

In order to come around the include guard collision, we are forced to compile the above structure with a relative path like: 

`protoc -I=./main -I=./main/proto proto/Dependent.proto`

This will indeed create a guard `GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_INCLUDED_proto_2fDependent_2eproto`, which solves the initial issue of having the same guard definition as another file called Dependent.proto elsewhere in the code.
When Dependent.proto imports Dependee.proto, the generated Dependent.pb.cc will have a section: 
```
static const ::_pbi::DescriptorTable* const descriptor_table_proto_2fDependent_2eproto_deps[1] = {
  &::_descriptor_table_Dependee_2eproto_,
};
```
while it should have been `descriptor_table_proto_2fDependee_2eproto`. If someone can share insight on how to address this issue will be much appreciated.

I suppose if the include guard by default incorporated the namespace, as proposed in this story, will very much simplify compilation and solve collisions. 
I do not understand why while in java the java_package is used to define and identify generated classes, the equivalent component here (simply package) is only used partially.

title: [objectivec]what's the reason KeyedSubscript are not in the interface

nodes.body: Can you provide a code snippet for what's failing?  The keyedSubscript support is just in GPBAutocreatedDictionary to help bridge things over when it the field is would be an NSMutableDictionary.  NSArray shouldn't used keyedSubscript, it would be indexedSubscript, but I believe the default implementations will call through to the other methods that NSArray subclasses have to implement.

Finally got some time post holidays to circle back to this.

Re `GPBDictionary` - There are actually several classes defined there, the one you are looking at is an internal detail for the autocreator behavior \(more info in the [objectivec/README.md](https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/master/objectivec#usage)\).  The overrides are just there for a minor performance improvement, things would work without it.  As far as why they aren't in the header, that class isn't in the header in general since it is an internal implementation detail.  Even if it was public, the methods don't need to be in the `@interface` block as the class is a subclass of `NSMutableDictionary` and thus the methods have already be declared there.

Re `GPBArray` - This also is a few specific classes for the different datatypes.  There also is a custom `NSMutableArray` subclass for autocreators, assuming that is the one you are asking about for indexedSubscript; those methods work without custom overrides because `NSArray`/`NSMutableArray` will channel the subscripting methods through to the methods subclasses have to implement, so there is no need to override anything.

title: support native C++ UWP applications
body:
_edit 02/26/2017: [(working build on the HoloLens)](https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/2549#issuecomment-282590160)_

Updated path towards supporting UWP:
- CMake flag to append UWP projects for `libprotobuf` and `libprotobuf-lite` to usual set of Win32 projects
- `gmock` support for UWP build target _(HARD)_
- unit tests support for UWP build target (primarily the alternate filesystem API) _(HARD)_

----

Straightforward support for native C++ UWP applications will require the following fixes:

- CMake generation of minimal project set (`libprotobuf` and `libprotobuf-lite` for now)
- compilation warnings related to missing inline function definitions
- compilation warnings related to missing template function definitions
- `gmock` support for UWP build target
- unit tests support for UWP build target (primarily the alternate filesystem API)

Detailed reports to follow. I'll edit this to include additional requirements as they're discovered.

(aside: primary motivation is for use on the MS HoloLens, which only supports UWP applications)

nodes.body:
I've been exploring the compilation of `libprotobuf 3.0.2` for use in native UWP applications.  Here are some progress notes and findings.

**CMake Invocation**
To generate the appropriate VS2015 solution, use the following CMake invocation:
```
cmake -G "Visual Studio 14 2015" ^
-DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=WindowsStore ^
-DCMAKE_SYSTEM_VERSION=10.0 ^
-Dprotobuf_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON ^
-Dprotobuf_BUILD_TESTS=OFF ^
../..
```

**Extraneous Projects**
I'm not an expert in CMake configuration, so I'll simply point out that all of the generated projects except `libprotobuf` and `libprotobuf-lite` are incompatible with the UWP build target.  In particular, it appeared that `gmock` and `libprotoc` use pipes and other features unavailable to a UWP application.  The `INSTALL` and `protoc` projects don't really make sense in the context of a UWP application.

Ideally only `libprotobuf` and `libprotobuf-lite` would be generated when a UWP build target is specified, at least until the test infrastructure can be adapted.  I'm not sure that compilation infrastructure can or should be adapted.

In the meantime, one can simply delete all the extraneous projects.

**`libprotobuf` Compilation Errors**
When building `libprotobuf` for both debug and release targets, I encountered symptoms similar to #240 in the form of dozens of `C4506` compilation warnings:
`warning C4506: no definition for inline function <inline function declaration>`

These were fixed by editing properties for `message.cc`, `arena.cc`, `generated_message_reflection.cc`, and `repeated_field.cc` such that `C/C++ > Optimization > Inline Function Expansion` is set to `Disabled (\Ob0)`.

Circling back around to this - I've successfully compiled and linked `protobuf/master` with a test UWP application that runs on the HoloLens.  Brief instructions:

1. Configure the VS solution to produce a static library _with the dynamic MSVC runtime_.
```
cmake -G "Visual Studio 14 2015" ^
-DCMAKE_SYSTEM_NAME=WindowsStore ^
-DCMAKE_SYSTEM_VERSION=10.0 ^
-Dprotobuf_BUILD_TESTS=OFF ^
-Dprotobuf_MSVC_STATIC_RUNTIME=OFF ^
../protobuf/cmake
```

2. Open the solution and delete projects for `INSTALL`, `libprotoc`, and `protoc`.
_NB: neither `INSTALL` nor `protoc` make sense in the context of UWP, and `libprotoc` would require significant effort to port._

3. Build, copy, and link static libraries from your UWP HoloLens solution!

4. Configure and build a separate, normal Win32 solution, so that `protoc` is available.
_NB: I found it useful to create a separate project within my HoloLens solution which built the generated cpp data structures as a static library (linked with the application alongside `libprotobuf`).  This project was configured without precompiled headers, which can't easily be inserted into the generated cpp files._


Moving forward, I think the best option for semi-official support of C++ UWP is to add a CMake flag which appends UWP projects for `libprotobuf` and `libprotobuf-lite` to the usual set of Win32 projects.  Anyone consuming the UWP libraries will need to build `protoc.exe` anyways, and `INSTALL` can put the UWP `.lib`s into an appropriate location alongside the Win32 products.

I'm not sure there's any good path for `gmock` to support UWP, which may preclude truly official support for UWP.

...fixes/hides the issue.

title: Enable support for java.util.Optional<T> in Java codegen

nodes.body:
Since java.util.Optional is a Java 8 feature, we won't be able to support it until we can require all protobuf users to have Java 8+. That might take quite a while.

Also note this is proto2 specific as in proto3 field presence is not supported any more (i.e., no way to distinguish a field having the default value vs. a field not present). We might not want to extend a feature that we have knowingly dropped in proto3.

This is a feature I've been missing too, and it has nothing to do with wire format. All non primitive fields should return Optional<T>. This is also how the Scala protobuf compiler works, and it generates getter methods that take a default value that's returned if the field is not present.

> Since java.util.Optional is a Java 8 feature, we won't be able to support it until we can require all protobuf users to have Java 8+. That might take quite a while.

Hi.
I don't think there will be any more non-java8+ users in 2023, but you don't want to deal with it?
The optional is now available in protobuf3, but it is very uncomfortable to use.

title: Feature request: support field masks in the JsonFormat util
body:
Use case:

I am using the `JsonFormat.Printer` to print messages destined for a JSON database (Elasticsearch). The database supports [partial document updates](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/docs-update.html#_updates_with_a_partial_document). It would be nice to take advantage of this and send only fields that need to be updated.

However, with proto3 and optional fields all fields have default values. So when serializing a message to JSON, there's no way to specify whether a string has been set to empty or has not been set on the message at all. For example, suppose I have:

```
message Post {
  string title
  string body
}
```

Then the user updates the body and sets it to empty. I would like to send a partial update of the message to the database with `body` set to `""`:

```
{
  "body": ""
}
```

Using the current version of `JsonFormat.Printer`, there's no way to print a `Post` message and get this result. With `includingDefaultValueFields` enabled, you get:

```
{
  "title": ""
  "body": ""
}
```

Sending this to the database would result in emptying the `title` field too. And without `includingDefaultValueFields` you get:

```
{}
```

which leads to a no-op update. 

My solution right now is just to send full document updates. Which is fine, but obviously not optimal. So, **it would be great if one could specify `FieldMask`s when configuring the `JsonFormat.Printer`**. I am envisioning the a registry of `FieldMask`s like the `TypeRegistry`. As a message is printed, the field mask registry is consulted. If a field mask exists for the current type, it is used to determine which fields are printed. Otherwise, all fields are printed. I don't think this functionality is needed for the parser—just the printer.

nodes.body:
Ah, that's interesting @xfxyjwf. Thank you for the suggestion! Yes, that would work with `JsonFormat.Printer` because then `Message#hasField()` will distinguish set vs unset fields. 

However, doesn't it seem strange to deviate from the core protobuf paradigm just to accommodate the JSON printer? At this point, I think I would rather keep my messages the way they are and just send full updates, at least until I see a performance-based reason to change.

>  at least until I see a performance-based reason to change.

at which point I would PR this utility. Would this be a feature you're okay with?

@dminkovsky This new API will need to go through an API review process which is unfortunately Google internal only at the moment. I can help make a proposal for it to the review committee but I cannot accept your PR until the proposal is approved.
Makes sense. And otherwise, I am guessing this will not be implemented internally? If not, what is needed for the proposal? A patch and tests?
It looks like what you want can now be achieved with https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L221

title: JS compiler with one_output_file_per_input_file option

nodes.body:
That conditional is intentional--the idea is just that some options are of the form `option=value` and others are just of the form `option`. That particular option doesn't take a value a so it would be invalid to try to say something like `one_output_file_per_input_file=whatever`.

I believe the `library` option [here](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/2deb139bc952fcc313803c4520e802dc1f6da9be/src/google/protobuf/compiler/js/js_generator.h#L112) should do what you want by allowing you to compile everything into a single .js file.
@acozzette I see. Well, those two options, `library` and `one_output_file_per_input_file`, are kinda confused. Anyway, I just want to know if it is on purpose.

@petehouston You're right, those two options are a bit confusing. Part of the reason for that is that at one time we had multiple JS implementations that had different ways of organizing their output and then we eventually unified them but had to keep both options around to preserve compatibility with the different implementations' quirks.

title: JS Protobuf Compiler Assumes Packed Arrays

nodes.body:
Hi,
I am having a related issue. After .toObject(), the repeated field in the message will be displayed as an array with an object in it. For example, the message will show: 
{ field1: 0,
  field2: 1,
  repeated_field: [Object]}

@jsievenpiper Are you using proto3? In proto3 primitive fields are packed by default, so that might explain the behavior you're seeing. I think this is a duplicate of https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1701.

nodes.body:

What I also noted is that the generated file has the following property declaration while the [documentation ](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/csharp-generated#wrapper_types) says that the well-known types should be generated as Nullable<T> types in C#. 

` private global::Google.Protobuf.WellKnownTypes.UInt32Value testUintProperty_;`



Would you mind sharing the class file that got generated for you? I am attaching mine 
[Test.cs.txt](https://github.com/google/protobuf/files/696330/Test.cs.txt)

Right, this is definitely the problem then. Just use `-I path/to/Google.Protobuf.Tools/3.1.0/tools` and import `google/protobuf/wrappers.proto`. Basically, the way you're compiling isn't treating them as well-known types. I've attached my generated code.


[Test.cs.txt](https://github.com/google/protobuf/files/696357/Test.cs.txt)

Yes, that was the problem. Got it to working now. .
Though I am still curious about why having all the proto files & protoc compiler under one folder wasn't working as the protoc help definitely mentions that not specifying the proto-path mean the current folder is used. I hope this can be fixed some point of time in future.

Sorry, I don't fully understand how you compiled before - you've described bits of it, but not everything. 

protoc (for C#) definitely [checks for the file being `google/protobuf/wrappers.proto`](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/c44ca26fe89ed8a81d3ee475a2ccc1797141dbce/src/google/protobuf/compiler/csharp/csharp_helpers.h#L125).

This isn't a matter of the options to pick up the proto path, but just where the wrappers.proto file is expected to be found, based on its package.

Even if things are changed, I'd *strongly* discourage you from either mixing the "built-in" proto files with your own ones.
We could potentially change that check to see whether the package name is `google.protobuf` instead, admittedly. I think we do this in a few places - I can check later on.
I'm going to close this issue as it's not really a JSON parser issue, but I've opened #2575 to log the possibility of a related change.

title: Reconsider how C# code detects well-known type files
body:
Currently (in both protoc and the support library, I believe) we use the filename (e.g. "google/protobuf/wrappers.proto") to detect that a proto is a well-known type. We could potentially use the final part of the name and the package name to be slightly more forgiving for users who copy the original proto files around.

See #2574 for more context.

title: Protoc on windows is highly confusing

When using Protoc.exe on windows, it's somewhat a battle of trial and error in order to get import paths working correctly.

Which works fine on *nix.

Trying to do the same on Windows, one would assume that we could simply swap out the GOPATH to match windows env vars like so:

```
protoc --gogoslick_out=Mgoogle/protobuf/any.proto=github.com/gogo/protobuf/types,plugins=grpc:. --proto_path=. --proto_path=%GOPATH%/src protos.proto
```

This however results in `google/protobuf/any.proto not found`.
And I have verified that it does indeed exist at the github.com/gogo/protobuf/types folder.

Should we be able to use the same paths on windows as in nix or do we have to deal with different `/` vs `\`

Better error messages explaining in what folders it has tried to find the files would help _alot_

Currently, I have solved it using a hack, placing a "google/protobuf" folder with the relevant protos in `%GOPATH%/src`.
this makes it all work.

So the problem seems to be a mapping issue

nodes.body: What is --gogoslick_out? It seems it's actually that gogoslick plugin who is responsible for the resolution of google/protobuf/any.proto=github.com/gogo/protobuf/types and it doesn't work on windows. Protoc itself doesn't fetch anything from remote services so you have to put the any.proto in some local path for protoc to work.

`gogoslick_out` is an alternative Golang generator.
So the plugins are responsible for resolving imports? I'll crosspost this in their repo in that case.
Thanks

Do you have the same problem when generating `protoc` outputs for other languages?  That would help narrow it down to `protoc` or `protoc-gen-go`.  (It's certainly possible that we're using `path` somewhere we ought to be using `filepath` or vice-versa.)

title: JavaScript Message.deserializeBinary failing to handle empty Map fields
repeated oneof support?

nodes.body:
Is it impossible?
"You then add your oneof fields to the oneof definition. You can add fields of any type, but cannot use repeated fields." (https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#oneof)
On the outside "repeated" should be legal.

From a wire-encoding point of view, there is no reason not to allow it. "repeated" already sets the semantics that additional fields need to be collected (instead of overwriting prior values). 

Note: your code will not work because "page" and "user" are part of "from" and "to". But "oneof" members are in the namespace of the message! Here you have two "page" elements and two "user" elements in the namespace of "Post".

Repeated oneof was in the initial proposal but as we later found out, there were lots many complicated corner cases in wire and API. We decided not to add repeated for oneof.

You can always define a message which wraps a oneof and have a repeated field of that message instead.

I wasn't around for the initial design of the oneof feature, but my guess would be that the repeated-inside-oneof capability was left out just because the extra complexity was not considered worth it given that you can just use a wrapper message to accomplish roughly the same thing (even if it's a little more verbose).

I understand that it may make the implementation more complex, but what it's done is create a whole class of message-shapes that cannot be expressed in protobuffer.

For instance, one of the huge use cases I see for protobuffer is to take an existing *implicit* schema that has already been in use for some time in a large system and define an *explicit* schema that can validate all of these messages flying around and bring some order to this madness. I feel this is a pretty common concern that leads people to a schema language like this.

So then the important question becomes: given any arbitrary pre-existing message shape, can I write a protobuffer schema that expresses it? It turns out that having arrays live under keys is an extremely common scenario that comes up... all the time. Not being able to put an array under a key at the top level rules out what may be one of the most common patterns found in the wild. So do you tell these people that they have to start nesting their lists under yet-another-key? And that they have to change all of this code, existing in many different places (some in scary legacy places that no one wants to touch), and go through the long debugging process of things that settled long ago and we don't want to mess with? 

It seems to me this limits the applicability of protobuffer to an unreasonable degree. I can understand if you are just generating schemas from scratch, then you have no concern for nesting things however you want. If you have the luxury of creating something without regard for pre-existing conditions, maybe life is okay. But in the vast world of software persisting far beyond when it should be reasonably put down and forgotten, I feel the greatest value and potential of protobuffer is currently lost.

It seems a goal of protobuffer would be the ability to express the range of possible message shapes, but I guess that is not the case?

Thanks @acozzette for the response!
Thanks @alexagriffith, fixed!
@isc30 @Xopherus @VolkerKamin @liujisi @acozzette @alexagriffith I think the problem is not fully resolved, and could you have a look at this relevant issue #8628?

As noted by @prismofeverything in 2017, support for repeated fields in oneof would be a tremendous design tool. The engineering effort to support this would be well worth the effort.

Still worth reconsidering.
@liujisi - What's just one of the complicated corner cases ?

Something to keep in mind is that protobuf is a wire protocol. Not only does that speak to a panoply of corner cases when you think about the wire format, but protobuf isn't a "schema language". I think of things like AVRO in those circumstances if you need a non-NP-complete schema shape ;), or just JSONSchema if you need some flexibility. Fast and flexible rarely go hand in hand.

title: What are the common patterns for including the intermediate .proto files?
body:
Hi folks,

I've been working with `grpc-gateway` and stumbled upon the following behavior of Protocol Buffers.

Say, we have a file `server.proto` that also imports a file `some/location/http.proto`. Then, in order to make, say, a generated file `server_pb.py` work, we need to make sure that a Python module `some.location.http_pb.py` actually exists and is accessible. Same applies to most other languages, I guess.

This may be a problem, for example if a package with the same name already exists, plus it makes the automation a bit harder. My real-life case with this is described in a bit more detail at https://github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway/issues/298.

An alternative could have been, that we go through the entire dependency tree, resolve it and build into a single file, and then compile that file into one module. But, my guess is, there has been some certain idea behind the current behavior (more explicit dependency updating, perhaps?)

So, my question is: what's the common practice of importing `.proto` files from some external sources and making sure their compiled counterparts are also accessible? In my example with Python, I could only come up with a workaround: https://github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway/issues/298#issuecomment-272992936.

Sorry if my explanation is too vague, I can try to provide a more concrete explanation of the problem, with code examples, if needed.

Thanks!

nodes.body:
I think the usual practice is to express the dependencies in your build system so that it can keep the generated code up to date, by rerunning `protoc` when a `.proto` file changes, for example. If you prefer you can also check in the generated code and have a script for updating it; this is a bit clunky but might be simpler depending on the situation.

For depending on `.proto` files in external repos, this varies a bit with each language and the language-specific packaging mechanism, but usually the easiest way to do it would be to just publish the generated code as part of the project artifact. This way if you depend on some package that uses protos, the package comes with the generated code and you don't have to run protoc yourself. The one exception would be C++, since it doesn't seem to have a dominant packaging mechanism and for C++ we don't attempt to keep the generated code compatible with different versions of the runtime library.

title: Well-known protos are in src/google/protobuf/, but are imported from google/protobuf/
body:
For example, `api.proto` contains

```
import "google/protobuf/source_context.proto";
import "google/protobuf/type.proto";
```

Bazel's `proto_library` expects to find these files relative to the `WORKSPACE` file, but they're in the `src/` subdirectory.

In practice, this makes it impossible for a user to import `google/protobuf/type.proto` and satisfy this dependency with `@com_google_protobuf//:well_known_protos` (where `com_google_protobuf` is the name of the remote repository the user gave the protobuf repo).

The reason is that `proto_library` will pass `-Isrc/google/protobuf/type.proto=src/google/protobuf/type.proto` to the proto-compiler.

**tl;dr**, is it possible to move the well-known protos one leve up in the repo?

If a `.proto` imports e.g., `google/protobuf/Any.proto`, that file must be in the `google/protobuf` directory relative to the workspace root.

Can do a genrule instead? Or we can change the filegroup to copy the files if that's easier. However, I'm not sure if there are any other projects using the filegroup already. It could be breaking for those projects.

1) the directory structure becomes confusing and less readable.
2) we have other build tools that rely on the path of those files. Moving them creates lots other issues.
3) there will be external projects depending on the path of the files as well.
4) it doesn't seem right to me to move the code just to make one build system happy.

title: BSON <=> google::protobuf::Message
body:
Is there any plan on extending https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1690 (Serialize and Parse directly to and from JSON using google::protobuf::Message) to support directly `BSON <=> google::protobuf::Message` ?

Benefits:
* speed (`proto <=> bson` instead of `proto <=> json <=> bson`) especially for binary data which would need to be encoded/decoded when passing through the json layer (eg base64)
* avoid loss of information when converting to/from json: quoting from http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6355497/performant-entity-serialization-bson-vs-messagepack-vs-json/6357042#6357042: 
> BSON has special types like "ObjectId", "Min key", "UUID" or "MD5" (I think these types are required by MongoDB). These types are not compatible with JSON. It means some type information are lost when you convert objects from BSON to JSON. It can be disadvantage to use both JSON and BSON in single service.

nodes.body:
> speed (proto <=> json <=> bson instead of proto <=> json <=> bson)

Did you mean to say?

> speed (proto <=> bson instead of proto <=> json <=> bson)
yes, thanks; just corrected in the text above

We don't have such plans at the moment. Code size and complexity is one concern for us. We'd like to make the library lite-weight. If BSON was supported for one language then we have to extend the support for all the other languages as well.

However, you can always implement a proto <=> bson conversion yourself if performance is a concern.

title: Well known types for sint32 and sint64?
body:
Hi,
The `wrappers.proto `contain well-known types for few primitive types but the ones for `sint `are missing. Given that the sint provides more efficient encoding for small numbers [https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding#signed-integers](url), I am wondering why the wrappers are not defined for them? 
 As per Issue#2575 [https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/2575](url), google/Protobuf path need to be maintained for importing well-known types. Can we define wrapper types for `sint32 `and `sint64 `following the same convention & keep them under google/protobuf?

nodes.body: One drawback of the wrappers is that they add at least two bytes of overhead on the wire, since they wrap the primitive field inside a submessage. So I think if you're concerned enough about wire size that you're using `sint32` or `sint64`, you would probably want to avoid using a wrapper in that case anyway. One thing you can do is have a `oneof` containing just a single primitive element; this makes the syntax slightly more awkward but will let you have a nullable `sint32` or `sint64` without the overhead of a wrapper.

Think this is a bit of an oversight as the work required to add a new well-known-type is minimal and if a field requires nullability and is likely (or in our use case, guaranteed) to be a small negative number then SInt32Value can save you 9 bytes over Int32Value. The issue of an Option type is separate and doesn't prevent this from being implemented. But not adding SInt32Value does prevent libraries from providing special handling like they do for some other well known types.
Why was this issue closed?  If the whole point of wrappers.proto is to wrap the basic scalar types, then shouldn't it have wrappers for all the basic scalar types???
I petition we remove all wrappers and only leave the `BytesValue` wrapper since you can place anything into the BytesValue wrapper, why support all the scalar types 😄

    var value = getExtensionFn.call(proto, fieldInfo);

title: The new 'Any' type and JavaScript
body:
Hi, 

I recently started using protobuf for JavaScript. I have been using protobuf for the past few years but mostly with C#/C++.
Everything seems to go well, except I was not able to find a way to work with the new 'Any' type (defined in protobuf3). I am using the binary encoding which according to the doc, should be supported in JavaScript.

I have used protoc to define the JavaScript equivalent of my proto files. I can make instances of all my types, set properties, encode them (binary), etc. 

Basically, I do not seem to be able to access (see them) the Pack/Unpack functions.

Would anyone know how to do that? Any examples?

PS: I should add that my JavaScript expertise is very basic so the solution may be something obvious :)

Thanks!

nodes.body: @haberman
JavaScript does have `pack` and `unpack` -- see: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/js/well_known_types/any.js

Thanks @haberman, 

I think that there may be an issue with my generated code since it does not contain the pack and unpack functions. It does have the other ones though (set/getType and set/getValue).

From the source code that you linked I see that the implementation is very similar to my workaround.

I tried calling pack on one of my Any instances and I got:
"0x800a01b6 - JavaScript runtime error: Object doesn't support property or method 'pack' occurred"


Thank you

Also, note that when generating the code, I have followed the instructions documented here for CommonJS:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/master/js

$ protoc --js_out=import_style=commonjs,binary:. messages.proto base.proto

After that I browserify it (since the current protoc does not support generating browser targeted files -- well it does define support for browsers but it does not implement it -- see https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/2556)

The resulting file does not seem to contain the pack/unpack functions...(unless I am doing something wrong). If I am right (and there is a good chance that I am doing something wrong), there may be an issue with the code generator.
I should have mentioned that the well-known type support is not currently released (it's only on GitHub) but will be part of the upcoming 3.2 release.

Aha! :)

OK, thank you for your time! I will use my workaround until then.
This was released as part of 3.2! Resolving this issue.

title: Support for disambiguating nested protos versus other length-delimited types
body:
I am attempting to apply @benlaurie's objecthash idea to protos:

https://github.com/benlaurie/objecthash

I would like to use Merkle-ish hash trees to compute unique digests for every proto in a nested object graph. This allows protos to be authenticated without canonicalization, while also allowing portions of them to be authenticated in Merkle inclusion proofs e.g. by choosing a child object in an object tree and providing the necessary digests of the other objects in the tree to get back to the root hash of the object graph. This is described as "redaction" in objecthash.

Unfortunately, there's a pretty big snag to actually pulling this off in practice: extension fields. Without knowledge of the schema, older clients can't compute the objecthash of fields they don't understand, since they need to be able to see into the nested structure of the protos to compute the ultimate hash. One option is for older clients to ask for a proto containing only the fields they understand, but that only works in scenarios where they're consuming protos from an interactive service, and not if they were pulling them from e.g. a stream processing system like Kafka.

The rather unfortunate thing is we could *almost* compute objecthash for a proto in absence of the schema, save for one small annoying thing: it's not possible to tell, in absence of the schema, whether a given field contains a nested proto, or whether it's any other type of length-delimited data. They all use wire type 2:

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding#structure

If there were a different wire type for telling "nested proto" versus "any other type of length-delimited data" this would be possible.

Has this been considered before?

nodes.body:
(@tarcieri is a friend of mine and asked me for an opinion on this, so here I am.)

I think your goal here should definitely be to design the algorithm such that it doesn't need the schema. As you noted, the main issue with this is distinguishing between sub-messages vs. arbitrary bytes.

One possible solution: Make a rule that if a length-delimited field's contents parses successfully as a protobuf -- and matches the canonical form of that message -- then it should be hashed as a protobuf. Otherwise, hash it as a byte blob. Usually, an arbitrary byte blob or string won't parse successfully as a protobuf, but if one coincidentally does, that's fine.

This present a new problem, though: You must require that protobufs being hashed this way are encoded "canonically" (fields appear in numeric order, varints use only as many bytes as necessary, etc.). Most protobuf encoders will produce canonical output _if_ all fields are defined in the schema. However, when unknown fields are present (and being retained), many encoders will push them to the end as an optimization. That said, as I understand it, unknown field retention has been removed in proto3, which would make this problem moot.

Of course, the other problem is that checking every string to see if it's a canonically-encoded message may be slow. I'm not sure what your performance requirements are like.

Another option entirely could be to simply transmit the schemas along with the messages or hashes, and then use a schema-aware algorithm. Protobuf has good support for dynamically loading schemas. But this would be kind of sad in that you'd have to transmit a lot of extra data, and dynamic schema loading can be slow.

I'm curious if there are any plans to to use wiretype 6 any time soon. It seems to presently be unused, and it doesn't look like wiretypes change that much:

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding#structure

6 has the nice property that going from 2 -> 6 involves flipping a single bit: `010` -> `110`

Since the objecthash validator has to do a first-pass traversal of the proto anyway, it could easily flip the `110` -> `010` bit back before feeding it through to a standard proto parser (provided it validates in the first place).

The serializer would, of course, have to know the schema and set the appropriate bit on fields containing nested messages.

If wiretype 6 were ever used for something else, I guess you'd have to convert all the actual-6 fields to 7, and if 7 were ever used I guess you're out of luck. But it looks like the wiretypes are pretty settled at this point, so I think it could actually work.

While it's obviously not my decision, I would be very surprised if wiretypes 6 and 7 ever end up being used. The other wire types have been in place for well over a decade with no serious proposals for new ones AFAIK. More importantly, if a new wiretype were introduced, then any message using it would be completely unparseable using old implementations -- they wouldn't even know how to skip the field, they'd just error out. Hence it makes a lot more sense, when introducing new protobuf features, to shoehorn them into the existing wire types.

That said it's not clear to me how this solves your problem. You still need to know the schema in order to know which tags' wire types to tweak, or you somehow need to convince everyone encoding a part of the message to use the alternate wire type (leading to similar compatibility problems).

(Terminology nitpick: When you say "extension fields", are you actually talking about protobuf extensions (a specific feature which not many people use) or are you talking about new regular fields that have been added in a newer version of the protocol? I suggest calling the latter "unknown fields" (in the context of an older binary that doesn't understand them), or I guess otherwise "new fields".)

The latter: "unknown fields" / "new fields"

The main problem being: these fields may contain nested messages, and if so you need to recurse through them to compute a nested/tree hash of them.

Map fields would also be an issue; these are semantically unordered and represented on the wire like a repeated field of messages, each containing a key at field 1 and value at field 2. If you come across an unknown map field then you won't be able to tell for sure whether it's a map or just a repeated field. And if it's a map then you'll need to sort it before hashing, whereas if it's a repeated field you must not sort it. To get around this I think you would either have to choose not to support map fields or choose to treat repeated field ordering as insignificant.

Another issue to watch out for is that if you do a schema-less hash (which I think you must do if you want to handle unknown fields), then you're verifying the hash of a sort of abstract serialized proto that might not match the way your program actually interprets the data. For example, let's say you successfully verify a repeated field of two elements but then your code actually expects a singular field there, and so you see [42] when the sender of that message actually meant [11, 42]; an attacker could trick you into misinterpreting a proto with a valid hash (see [Horton Principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horton_Principle)).

@acozzette those are all very good points. I think it may be possible to support maps by defining yet another wiretype (7 being the only one remaining) to identify map keys. I think if you have that, you should be able to treat protobuf maps as objecthash dicts (sorting them as you suggested), and use wiretypes 2 vs 6 to determine whether the corresponding values contain nested messages.

I'm not sure what to think about the sharp edge you mention regarding repeated fields. I think in some cases you may actually *want* to upgrade a singular field to a repeated one, in which case the old clients will need to verify the repeated fields with objecthash but still interpret them as singular.
I'm cleaning up some old issues. Let me go ahead and close this one because while it's an interesting idea, I don't think we will be able to support this kind of feature.

raise "Asked to both add and remove test: " + line

title: [python] Add type hints for generated classes
body:
It would be great to generate type hints ([PEP484](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0484/)/[PEP526](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0526/)) for the python generated class so we have IDE completion and type incompatibility warnings.

Eg for :
```java
message Foo {
  string bar = 1;
}
```
generate
```python
@overload
class Foo:
  bar = None  # type: str

  def __init__(self, bar=None):  # type: (str) -> None
    pass

Foo = _reflection.GeneratedProtocolMessageType('Foo', (_message.Message,), dict(
```

Note: this way of writing types works with both python 2 and 3. With python >= 3.6, the Foo class could be documented more nicely.
The type annotations are well handled at least by pycharm.

title: Javascript: negative int32 values were decoded incorrectly

nodes.body: @murgatroid99 @TeBoring FYI

FYI, I tried out parsing the varint32 representation of -746188906, i.e. [0x96, 0x9f, 0x98, 0x9c, 0xfd, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0xff, 0x01], using [jspb.BinaryDecoder.prototype.readSignedVarint32](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/js/binary/decoder.js#L617), and got -746188906 back with no problem.
[Reader.readInt32](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/3.2.x/js/binary/reader.js#L608) calls decoder.readSignedVarint32

Per the [spec](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding), negative int32 or int64 is always ten bytes long. So seems that PHP encoding is buggy, as it serializes int32 value -746188906 as [96 9f 98 9c 0d], which is only 5 bytes long.

Now I am back to believing that there may be a problem with PHP encoding.

So first I modified my PHP program to print the binary encoding to stdout
```
$b = $p->encode();
print($b);
```

So here's the hex representation of the PHP output:
```
$ php test.php | xxd -l 16 -p
089aa68cc30110969f989c0d
```

Here's the text representation of that
```
$ php test.php | protoc --decode=math.Point test.proto
latitude: 409146138
longitude: -746188906
```

Now I try to encode that text representation again, and convert it to hex, I got something different
```
$ php test.php | protoc --decode=math.Point test.proto | protoc --encode=math.Point test.proto | xxd -l 16 -p
089aa68cc30110969f989cfdffffffff
```

When encoding negative int32, php encoder doesn't padded it to make it compatible with int64. Working on the fix now.
However, js decoder should be compatible enough to recognize unpadded negative int32 value.

Yeah, make sense. I will fix the JS side.

Can you please add me to assignee?
Fixed in #2660

title: Support for setters and getters insertion points
body:
Adding insertion points in various field modifier could help extending generated classes with additional logic in those.

I think about implementing nullable support by using these insertion points the following way:

I will create a protobuf plugin that does the following:
- when a specific option is present on a message (say 'allowNullableFields') then the plugin looks for a map[int]->bool map.
- If the map exists then insert code that set value to true for the corresponding field ID in the map in various setters scopes.
- If the map does not exists then the protobuf plugin fail compiling the corresponding schema.
- Also the plugin will generate a hasXXX method for each of the field that will simply look for the field id in the map an return true if the corresponding value is set to true.

Sounds like a less intrusive approach to solve issue #1606 but still requires additional insertion points.

title: Build fails on Cygwin - need to be using -std=gnu++11, not -std=c++11
body:
Not sure how autoconf chooses c++11 over gnu++11, but the latter needs to be used in order to compile successfully on Cygwin (64 bit).

For example, `src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc` uses `readlink()` which is only available through the GNU extensions.

nodes.body: You can overried it in compiler flag: ./configure CXXFLAGS=-std=gnu+11

The user should not have to be concerned with what compiler variant they have to use - not everyone knows that readlink() is only available under GNU extensions.

If you use GNU, the configure script should select the correct GNU compiler flags.

title: Installation instructions lacking key point
body:
I just spent 3 hours debugging my protobuf installation only to realize that the instructions in the readme are incomplete.  They say:

`To install, simply place this binary somewhere in your PATH.`

So, I did that.  Here's what I did:  

unzip the zip file to a random directory.
sudo mv protoc /usr/local/bin/

However, when I ran protoc I would get weird errors like this:

```
google/protobuf/timestamp.proto: File not found.
event.proto: Import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto" was not found or had errors.
```

This might be obvious to people who have used protobuffers a lot, but to a newbie, that is a mysterious error. My colleagues could run this line just fine, why couldn't I?

The readme needs to also say that you need to put the include directory near protoc.  I don't actually know the heuristics, but extracting to a directory and then symlinking from /usr/local/bin to that directory/bin/protoc seems to work.

But that's incredibly non-obvious.  Generally, binaries don't care where they are located.

Also, it would be nice if protoc had better error handling, so that it could tell that it doesn't have the include directory next to it, and could make complain that you've probably installed incorrectly.

nodes.body:
Thanks for the report. Do you mind creating a pull request to help improve the documentation?
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/protoc-artifacts/build-zip.sh#L74

We found that this seemed to work for most people:

Move the contents of the `include` directory to your `%GOPATH%\src` directory to ensure wellknown types work.

This would require that when the `readme.txt` file is generated, that it places different instructions for the `windows` package.

title: Typos in the C++ Tutorial
body:
I was reading https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial and I think I found a few typos in the code examples.

1. In https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial#writing-a-message the code reads

    ```C++
    tutorial::Person::PhoneNumber* phone_number = person->add_phone();
    ```

    but it should read

    ```C++
    tutorial::Person::PhoneNumber* phone_number = person->add_phones();
    ```

    and

    ```C++
    PromptForAddress(address_book.add_person());
    ```

    should be

    ```C++
    PromptForAddress(address_book.add_people());
    ```

2. In https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial#reading-a-message the code reads

    ```C++
    for (int i = 0; i < address_book.person_size(); i++) {
    ```

    but it should read

    ```C++
    for (int i = 0; i < address_book.people_size(); i++) {
    ```

    and

    ```C++
    const tutorial::Person& person = address_book.person(i);
    ```

    should be

    ```C++
    const tutorial::Person& person = address_book.people(i);
    ```

3. Finally, I would consider adding
    ```C++
    syntax = "proto2"
    ```
    to the top of https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial#defining-your-protocol-format, so that no scary warning is printed if one installs a recent version of protobuf.


I would have submitted these changes as a PR, but the repo that generates the documentation at https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/ is not public. Feng Xiao in https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/protobuf/T1lRnPZoTK8 suggested to submit this as an issue, so here we are.

NB: the code in https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/ef927cc428db7bf41d3a593a16a8f1a0fe6306c5/examples is correct, the documentation isn't.

title: Update/correct docs on FieldDescriptorProto's type_name and extendee
body: [FieldDescriptorProto type_name](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/7f3e23707122f31ebfa58b7280bd56cbe77cb44e/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L174-L179) says the name can be fully qualified or partial. [FieldDescriptorProto extendee](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/7f3e23707122f31ebfa58b7280bd56cbe77cb44e/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L181-L183) says the same thing.  But they actually seem to always be complete.  As this the the wire data between `protoc` and a plugin, it they will always be complete, it would seem to be better to document it as such otherwise, a plugin could be broken as they likely don't have a good way to test their support for the partial form.

nodes.body:
Depending on where you get the FieldDescriptorProto, type_name is not always fully qualified. For example, a FileDescriptorProto produced by [the Parser class](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/parser.h#L72) does not have fully qualified name in the type_name field. Such a FileDescriptorProto is still valid and should be accepted by a DescriptorPool.

Though in the specific protoc + plugin case, it's safe to assume FileDescriptorProto sent by protoc to the plugins always contain fully-qualified names. I guess we can add additional comments in descriptor.proto to make that a documented behavior.
I added some comments in the plugin.proto instead internally. Closing this for now.

title: java: ErrorProne generates warnings for codegen
body:
protoc 3.2.0 generates code that fails ErrorProne's MissingOverride, ReferenceEquality, and FunctionalInterfaceClash checks. It's not obvious that the protobuf project has any legitimate problems to fix based on those warnings, but their presence makes it hard to use ErrorProne to check non-generated code.

Maybe the best option is just to add `@SuppressWarnings` for each of those warnings at the top of the generated class.

nodes.body: Protobuf code base should now pass the default ErrorProne settings. Do you have a list of patterns that you'd like to also cover? I guess maven only reports Error patterns, and didn't output anything for Warning patterns. I'd have to manually enable them.

Oh, sweet! We use `-Werror` in our CI to prevent drowning in warnings, so resolving warnings would be good. We do use the default set of options though. The only ones I noticed failing were those I listed initially: MissingOverride, ReferenceEquality, and FunctionalInterfaceClash.
It seems like SuppressWarnings doesn't work for those ErrorProne specific warnings -- I tested @SuppressWarnings("FunctionalInterfaceClash"). Could you blacklist those patterns in grpc instead?

Huh. That's strange. Did you apply it to the class or the method? I think that one is necessary to suppress at the class level. I just tested and SuppressWarnings worked for me and it [is documented](http://errorprone.info/bugpattern/FunctionalInterfaceClash#suppression).

We are using `-Xep:FunctionalInterfaceClash:OFF` now in order to build. But that also means the check is ignored for our own code, not just the generated code. I do agree that it doesn't seem quite protobuf's fault to fix. It's a combination of how generated code, errorprone, gradle, and the gradle-protobuf plugin interact. At this point I think I the individual decisions make sense, but overall we're left with an issue and nowhere obvious to fix it.

Could you annotate the generated protobuf with the `javax.annotation.Generated` annotation? Then downstream projects that use protobuf just need to add `-XepDisableWarningsInGeneratedCode`, and can still add `-Werror` too!
The idea of adding generated annotations is covered in this issue: https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/42
