title: Add --descriptor_set_in protoc option
body:
Protoc currently supports `--descriptor_set_out`. It would be great if it also supported `--descriptor_set_in`.

Using `--descriptor_set_in`, users could pipe pre-compiled protos directly into the standard code generation pipeline (c++, java, c#, and plugins). 

`--descriptor_set_in` really shines when coupled with the gRPC reflection service. This would allow a gRPC service client to be generated knowing only the host and port of the service. Taken a step further, a developer tool could iterate the contents of a service discovery registry to present the user with a catalog of services. The user could then pick a service and add a generated stub to their project with a single command.

nodes.body:
This FR is also useful for proto support in Bazel: there's considerable complexity around passing the right arguments to proto-compiler, which can be simplified if `proto_library` was the only piece of code responsible for this.

Bazel has a class to create the arguments, but it isn't yet exposed to Skylark, and either way it won't be as elegant as passing descriptor sets.
(note that Bazel needs to pass multiple descriptor sets to protocol-compiler)

@xfxyjwf this becomes more important the more complicated `proto_library` becomes.
For example, right now `proto_library` performs direct-dependency checks, which further complicates the command-line it produces.

As more languages get their implementations for `LANG_proto_library`, it becomes more important to have all of them behave the same. 

I just had a conversation about `swift_proto_library`; if it's written by constructing the command-line directly from the `.proto` sources, there's a good chance it'll miss enforcing direct dependencies.
This means that in a multi-language repo, a commit from a Swift developer could break other language builds.
FYI: It looks like this flag was added in v3.4.0, but hasn't been documented yet.

For protoc command line flags, `protoc --help` is likely the best place of documentation. It has this to say for `--descriptor_set_in` right now:
```
  --descriptor_set_in=FILES   Specifies a delimited list of FILES
                              each containing a FileDescriptorSet (a
                              protocol buffer defined in descriptor.proto).
                              The FileDescriptor for each of the PROTO_FILES
                              provided will be loaded from these
                              FileDescriptorSets. If a FileDescriptor
                              appears multiple times, the first occurrence
                              will be used.
```
If you find it unclear, feel free to ask questions or send us pull requests.
How does this actually work? If I run `protoc --descriptor_set_in={path to descriptor}` with some set of `*_out` options, I get an error complaining that I did not specify a proto file.

You still specify the files you want to generate code for normally. For example:
```bash
$ protoc --descriptor_set_int=/path/to/descriptors --cpp_out=. google/protobuf/descriptor.proto
```

If I have to pass in the text proto definitions to generate code, what does passing the descriptors in actually do? Is there a way to generate code given just the descriptors? (Which would allow me to parse the proto definitions once and then generate code for multiple languages in subsequent invocations of the tool.)

The descriptors are more-or-less just a machine-friendly representation of the human-friendly .proto file. (The descriptors are themselves proto messages and can thus be serialized just like other protos.) You can indeed use the `--descriptor_set_out` and `--descriptor_set_in` options as a way to parse the definitions just once and then invoke `protoc` multiple times on the resulting descriptors.

That's what I expected, but I haven't been able to make this work. If I don't pass in at least one `.proto` file on the command line, I get an error about missing input files. This applies to both `--cpp_out=` and `--encode`. The only workaround I've found is to pass the entire set of `.proto` files in on every invocation.

I believe you just need to give it the name of the .proto file you want to generate code for, and it will look up that name in the descriptor set. It still needs this because otherwise it can't know what .proto file you want to generate code for--in general the descriptor set may contain many files but you wouldn't necessarily want to generate code for all of them at once.

So I've just run into this problem again and hey look I seem to have commented on this before...

I made this work this time! But it's not intuitive. For `--encode` you need to pass in both the name of the message type being encoded, and also the filename of the proto source file. This appears to be looked up in the descriptors. This really surprised me, as surely the message can be found from the type name passed in as the parameter to `--encode`?

This is rather awkward when using compiled protos as (at least in bazel) as once you've generated the proto library, the filenames aren't available in the build system any more. The consumer of the proto library shouldn't need to know about the filenames of the source files inside the proto library, IMO.

I think the tricky thing here is that if we're working with serialized descriptors then we could potentially get away with omitting the file name, but that would not work well in the case where we're reading proto files from the filesystem. In that case we would have to open up every file in the search path that looks like a proto file until we're able to find the right one, and this would get messy. So I think it's probably best to keep the `--encode` behavior consistent whether we're reading proto files or serialized descriptors.

In the case of Bazel we could potentially provide a rule that works around this, though. We actually have an internal rule that does this, but it would be hard to directly open source because it depends on various other internal-only things. It wouldn't be that hard to write a simple binary that takes in a text proto and a descriptor set and transcodes the text to binary, though, along with a Starlark rule that invokes this binary.

title: javascript feature request: generate exports.js for generated code

nodes.body: At the moment I'm not sure of a better way to do it than the way you're currently doing it. Perhaps we could eventually do something fancy where we could have a `protoc` plugin that would take in the `.proto` file and spit out a `.js` file with all the necessary exports. It might also be worth asking on the Closure compiler [mailing list](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/closure-compiler-discuss) if anyone there has any ideas on the best way to do this.

This seems totally doable but probably not something that would be a priority for us. We might be able to accept a contribution for this. It could just be another code generator for generating `exports.js` that is kept in sync with the main code generator. We'd want a test that verifies that this works when compiling with Closure.

Alright, I'll go ahead and leave this open, but we ended up switching to a different Javascript Protobuf implementation that works out of the box so we probably won't be pushing a contribution from our end.
In that case I might just close the bug. Out of curiosity, what implementation did you switch to and does it support generating an `exports.js`?

We went with Protobuf.js: https://github.com/dcodeIO/protobuf.js

It doesn't create an exports.js, it just generates CommonJS code out of the box, so it is much easier to work with when using other tools. We also found that it was 4-5x faster and produced a 75% smaller JS file with only minor configuration.

title: Android Java Guidance - Nano or Lite?
body:
There is some confusion regarding the way forward for using Protobuf on Android with Java. Should one be using JavaNano or Lite? Right till the release of 3.0, the recommended option seemed to be JavaNano and then something suddenly switched.

The only hint is this line
>Since Protobuf 3.0.0, protobuf-lite is the recommended Protobuf library for Android

from https://github.com/google/protobuf-gradle-plugin

On the other hand, https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3 does not seem to suggest nano over lite or vice versa.

It would be great if there is guidance and a set of how-to's (why's if possible) delivered for Android Java. It would greatly benefit the community. There is information present, but is disparate and sometimes not updated, which regularly confuses folks using Protobuf. Case in point #956 which got duped in #2479 .

If there is such information already present, could you please point us to it.

nodes.body: I think we have never officially released nano. So lite is the only thing we support.

@anandolee Could you please reopen this issue? 

@TeBoring I am not sure if I understand the idea behind "officially releasing" nano. I am also not sure if lite is the only thing that is supported. I base this on the following:

The following page is the official documentation for Protocol Buffers v3
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3

Doing a simple search on this page for "nano" should throw up results for JavaNano. In fact, there is this snippet
```
--javanano_out generates JavaNano code in DST_DIR.
The JavaNano code generator has a number of options you can use to customize the generator
output: you can find out more about these in the generator README.
JavaNano generated code reference is coming soon!
```
The README points to https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/master/javanano, which has the following content
```
JavaNano is a special code generator and runtime library designed
specially for resource-restricted systems, like Android. It is very
resource-friendly in both the amount of code and the runtime overhead
```

So, I would appreciate if there is guidance from the Protocol Buffers team with respect to Android Java.
Lite is recommended for Android

We are in general deprecating nano in favor of lite for mobile usages. And we have no plan to further improve nano runtime.

We have just updated the doc in README that "Nano is no longer supported by protobuf team. We recommend Android users to use protobuf lite runtime instead.":
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/javanano/README.md

Danke @anandolee for the helpful context.

Would it be possible to please update https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3 with the Nano deprecation message?

On a side note, it is easier to understand things from the outside when there is communication and guidance in terms of future direction.

I'm out of the loop with Java, but until reading the protobuf docs I'd never heard of JavaLite or JavaNano, and googling for them isn't very elucidating (this issue was one of the top results, though). I agree with Brahmasmi, though, that the docs should be updated to reflect deprecation of nano. They still say "For JavaNano, the compiler output is similar to Java but there are no Builder classes." and this is nearly a year after @anandolee's message. 🤷‍♂️
I'm reopening this issue while I'm getting rid of every mentioning of javanano in our docs.

About the question of nano vs. lite, nano has never been well supported by protobuf-team. Internally we are actually migrating teams from nano to lite. In the opensource world, the lite support is a bit lacking (not so much better than nano), but we do plan to improve opensource lite support in Q2 this year (new releases, better documentation, and tooling support to achieve optimal code size savings).
Closing as references to javanano have been removed from protobuf developer guide.
[This](https://developer.android.com/topic/performance/memory#NanoProto) too requires change? It still says to go for nano in case of Android.
That too is out of date. I will file a bug on the Android docs team.

title: Add option to watch files for changes and recompile
body:
This should make the development easier. `protoc` should have an option (like `--watch`) where it initially compiles all the definitions and then watches them for changes and recompiles them as soon as any changes.

I've searched through open issues and could not find a similar one, my apologies if this is a duplicate

nodes.body:
I think this functionality might make more sense to implement outside of `protoc`. Actually it's fairly straightforward to get something working just using existing tools on the command-line; for example on Linux you can do something like this using inotify to watch for changes:

    while true; do
      # Wait for a .proto file to change
      inotifywait -e modify,move_self $(find . -type f -name '*.proto')
      # Run protoc...
    done

@acozzette while I appreciate the team trying to keep the project focused and minimal, the solution you posted is not the ideal way to go IMHO

The reason I don't like doing a inotifywait or anything similar is because it's heavily platform dependent and the code it requires cannot be reused for something else. For example, babel, typescript, coffee-script and all the other file transformers or compilers I've worked with (not project compilers, individual file compilers like protobuf) support file watching out of the box
This is more of a build system feature rather than protobuf one. Implementing it is out-of-scope of this project.

title: CMake FindProtobuf finds protobuf but not protobuf_include_dir
body:
Hi,

I am trying to compile a C/C++ project for windows that uses protobuf (grpc). The project works well with unix but I am struggling with the windows compilation. I added a third_party directory to the project where I've installed grpc together with protobuf. The protobuf installation directory (bin/lib/include) is in grpc/third_party/install. To add this custom protobuf build to the cmake file of the project I manually set the locations for all the protobuf stuff like this:

```cmake
set(PB_INSTALLATION "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/third_party/grpc/third_party/install")

set(PROTOBUF_LIBRARY "${PB_INSTALLATION}/lib/libprotobuf.lib")
set(PROTOBUF_PROTOC_LIBRARY "${PB_INSTALLATION}/lib/libprotoc.lib")
set(PROTOBUF_INCLUDE_DIR "${PB_INSTALLATION}/include")
set(PROTOBUF_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE "${PB_INSTALLATION}/bin/protoc.exe")
set(PROTOBUF_LITE_LIBRARY "${PB_INSTALLATION}/lib/libprotobuf-lite.lib") 
```

When trying to create the visual studio stuff with cmake generators it finds protobuf but seems to completely ignore the `PROTOBUF_INCLUDE_DIR`:

```
-- Found Protobuf: C:/Users/martinmende/Documents/development/tts-nativeclient/src/c_cpp/third_party/grpc/third_party/install/lib/libprotobuf.lib (found version "3.1.0")
CMake Error at C:/Program Files/CMake/share/cmake-3.7/Modules/FindPackageHandleStandardArgs.cmake:138 (message):
  Could NOT find Protobuf (missing: Protobuf_INCLUDE_DIR)
Call Stack (most recent call first):
  C:/Program Files/CMake/share/cmake-3.7/Modules/FindPackageHandleStandardArgs.cmake:378 (_FPHSA_FAILURE_MESSAGE)
  C:/Program Files/CMake/share/cmake-3.7/Modules/FindProtobuf.cmake:389 (FIND_PACKAGE_HANDLE_STANDARD_ARGS)
  src/CMakeLists.txt:2 (find_package)
```

Is there something wrong with the FindProtobuf.cmake module or am I doing something completely stupid here?
Kind regards

nodes.body: It might not hurt to ask the CMake developers about that module. As far as I know the protobuf team hasn't actually been involved in creating FindProtobuf.cmake and so I don't really know anything about how it works. It could be that you're using it right but that there's a bug in it somewhere.
We are closing open issues. Feel free to send PRs and reopen if you'd like to follow up on the issue.

I had this issue, and I was able to fix is by adding `include(FindProtobuf)` before `find_package(protobuf REQUIRED)`. I'm not sure if I just don't understand the find_package function, but it seems a little strange to me.

title: Pylint and installation from PyPi
body:
I tried using the python module with pip `pip install protobuf`.

This works, however pylint is complaining that it cannot find a submodule:
```
E: 20, 0: No name 'json_format' in module 'google.protobuf' (no-name-in-module)
```

After poking around to see the differences with the manual install, it seems that there are no `__init__.py` in the `/usr/local/lib/python3.5/site-packages/google/` folder when installing with pip which makes the subfolders invisible to pylint.

Would it be possible to add this file please?

nodes.body: So you have installed other google python packages along with protobuf? I remember there were lots of discussions about how to solve this problem but I don't know if we have a good answer for it. @haberman

No I have not installed any other google python package. Is there a small google package that you would recommend adding there? (Note that the protobuf package works fine, only pylint complains about it).

I asked a local Python expert about this and this was the answer:

>I think they just have a really old version of pylint. :)
>
>setuptools and pip intentionally don't install `__init__.py` files for namespace packages, instead, it creates a magical nspth.pkg entry in site-packages that tells the interpreter where the search path is.

So it sounds like the current behavior is correct. I'm closing this for now, but please re-open if you have other information that contradicts this.
For closure (sorry for the latency), it indeed now works properly. I'm not sure what went wrong last year. Sorry about the noise.

Bazel now has built-in rules for building Java and C++ protos (`proto_libarry`, `java_proto_library`, `java_lite_proto_library` and `cc_proto_library`).

For users to import well-known types (e.g., `descriptor.proto`) from their `.proto` files, they must depend on a `proto_library` that `srcs` the former.

This FR is about adding such a `proto_library`.

I have the annotation proto-files in my path when I parse it (google/ dir is at same level as helloworld.proto) so shouldn't it pass it along to stdin of my script? Is there a different `CodeGeneratorRequest` parser I should be using, other than the one generated by protoc (using `--js_out`) or the one generated by protobuffjs (via `pbjs`)?

This sheds some light on the possible reasons behind protobufjs making their own CLI tool (`pbjs`) , rather than a plugin for protoc. I was wondering about that.

@konsumer I think the problem is that the constructor takes a data array which is just the internal representation of the message and an implementation detail. To actually parse the raw binary you have to use `CodeGeneratorRequest.deserializeBinary()`. The other thing is that I wouldn't really recommend using `toObject()`; the `toObject` and `fromObject` methods are a sort of legacy feature that we wish we could remove; they are confusing because their output is pretty similar to proto3 JSON but not actually the same. It's better if you can just use the `CodeGeneratorRequest` directly.

@acozzette I appreciate the help, but I think I'm still not getting it. The tests don't seem to clearly demonstrate "turn this binary buffer into a js object" and "turn this js object into binary buffer" and the README says "For more examples, see the tests.", but maybe I am misunderstanding or missed something.

For illustration, here is my current code (using highland and tou8 to make trying out ideas go faster and be more readable)

```js
const _ = require('highland')
const tou8 = require('buffer-to-uint8array')
const pb = require('./google/protobuf/compiler/plugin_pb')

_(process.stdin)
  .reduce1((a, b) => Buffer.concat([a, b])) // mash all incoming together to avoid partial messages
  .map((req) => tou8(pb.CodeGeneratorRequest.deserializeBinary(req))
  // here I would do processing and conversion back into CodeGeneratorResponse
  // below is just for outputting
  .map((res) => JSON.stringify(res, null, 2))
  .pipe(process.stdout)
```

I added tou8, because I got this error: `AssertionError: Failure: Type not convertible to Uint8Array.` but I still get the error with it.

Here is the full error with tou8:

```
events.js:160
      throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event

I think the problem is probably that `toObject()` does not output data for extensions and the output of `JSON.stringify()` just shows you the internal representation, which isn't very useful. @acozzette In the above example, I am using `deserializeBinary()`, not `toObject()`. It's not that I want to convert it to JSON, I just want to hand something to the protoc plugin-writer that is useful, and I need to see the structure because I can't find any documentation on what the generated parser outputs. Since `stdout` only accepts strings (not JS objects) I am outputting what I can there. title: Add protoc --parse-only to facilitate building linters/auto-formatters
body:
It would be *fantastic* if `protoc` command had a `--parse-only` flag which would output the 
"text-file equivalent", non-imports-dependent output of https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/parser.h#L72 
Right now

This would make it easy to build source-tree layout-independent tooling, basically an ability to get the `FileDescriptor` equivalent of the text of `.proto` files independently without relying on the appropriate imports path.  

This, combined with `--include_source_info` would allow developers to build auto-formatters and linters, which can be run on individual `.proto` files, either from editors or from the command line.

title: Make C++ implementation C++11 only.
body:
C++11 has been out for several years and we are thinking of moving to allow C++11 features from being used in the code base. That means the implementation will not be able to compile if you don't have a C++11 compiler.

We may create a branch that works for C++98. The branch will only accept bug fixes, but not new features, optimization, etc

Please reply in this thread if you think this would be an issue for your project.

nodes.body:
Hello,

Thank you for collecting feedback about this.  My project consists of shared libraries on linux.  Some libraries are built with c++11 and others must be built with c++98 (for compatibility with some other libraries).  We link protobuf dynamically so this may not an issue for us, unless any c++11 language features will be used in header files that our c++98 libraries use.

This would be an issue for our project. We support back to centos5 (gcc 4.1) and a number of platforms in between for which we are not yet able to turn on the c++11 flag. One of the attractive things about protobuf was its impressive backwards support, and would be sad to have older platforms be stuck with less.

(PS. I feel bad saying this since I would _love_ to move to c++11 only for our project too, haha! It is a sad world that we can't use "new" features from 6 years go yet. I'm sure libraries feel this pain more than applications do even. All of which to say, I feel your pain! 😭 )

Hi there, we made a related decision in gRPC - version 1.0 supports older compilers with only limited C++11 support (not as few as protobuf, though), but version 1.1 and beyond only support true C++11 compilers (as of grpc/grpc#8602 ). I understand, though, that protobuf's predicament is greater since it is a package that has been public for much longer, has more users, and has been supporting C++98.

I strongly favor moving to a 4.x C++11 only branch. Users tight to pre-c++11 can continue using the 3.x branch which we support in maintenance mode.

Note that linking pre-c++11 and post-c++11 libraries is already very tricky due to the standard libraries being slightly incompatible (see https://gcc.gnu.org/wiki/Cxx11AbiCompatibility). Hence I think the impact of not being able to link libs depending on pre-c++11 and post-c++11 proto runtime is minor, given you already have dangerous issues lurking around.

Furthermore, for c++ protos, we already have the rule that all proto files in a binary have to be compiled with the exact same version of the compiler and runtime.

We have C++14 enabled at work so this change would be welcome. Protobuf has great compatibility w.r.t. the serialized format, so people who are stuck with old environments can continue using the old libs.

Hello all,

Now I'm using gcc-5.4.0 to compile protobuf.  However it couldn't be built because of C++11 new features.
I tried to modify "Makefile" to add compile options "-std=c++11" into "CXXFLAGS", but it still didn't work. How could I make it?

Solution:

I used command "configure CXXFLAGS=-std=c++11" to config protobuf.
+1 , backporting gcc5.4.x /7.x on old unmaintained distros is straightforward also with proper stripping unneeded language target at configure build flag.

Requiring C++11 will make it basically impossible to support protobuf on some Python versions on Windows. In particular, Python 2.7 support will not be possible and Python 3.5 will need to be a minimum requirement. This is assuming that protobuf continues to need to have compiled portions for these Python versions. The reason being that CPython ties each major minor version of the interpreter to a particular Visual Studio version on Windows. As a result, any extension one builds needs to be built with the same runtime as the interpreter or risk segfaults. A full listing can be found in this [reference]( https://wiki.python.org/moin/WindowsCompilers#Which_Microsoft_Visual_C.2B-.2B-_compiler_to_use_with_a_specific_Python_version_.3F ). Note that Python 2.6 and 2.7 requires Visual Studio 2008 (VC 9), which does not have C++11 support. Also Python 3.4 requires Visual Studio 2010 (VC 10), which also does not have C++11 support. Only Python 3.5 and 3.6, which requires Visual Studio 2015 (VC 14), have C++11 support.

cc @xfxyjwf

With respect to @jakirkham's note, Python does not let people build their recent recent releases with older Visual Studio versions. IMO Protobuf should follow suit. There will be no way to move forward otherwise.

Also note that Visual Studio 2010 has basic C++11 support, see the official [reference](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/hh567368.aspx).
The [googlei18n/libphonenumber](https://github.com/googlei18n/libphonenumber) project which uses protobuf currently doesn't support C++11. See googlei18n/libphonenumber#1594 for the discussion.

Make it a `4.x` and require `C++11`. Should be a clean slate. `C++98` is old now and people should really make up their minds using a newer C++ version. There are so many benefits, it's not even funny.
support,use c++ 11 later

Hi,

we use WindRiver compiler, and there is no support for C++11 there. Unfortunately it is not possible to switch to different compiler for us (company defined compiler...).

If you switch, do you plan to support older releases?
If we go with C++11 only, we will probably maintain a branch and only back port severe bug fixes.

Why don't you just fast forward to C++14?
Lots of goodies!
There are a lot of projects that aren't C++11 compatible.

I notice that move constructors for generated messages has landed in master. Fantastic! But there still aren't move constructors/assignments for the containers `RepeatedField`, `RepeatedPtrFieldBase`, `RepeatedPtrField<T>`. (I mean for the whole object, rather than for the elements they contain.) Any chance of adding these too? I think it would be useful and a very small change.

(I hope it's OK that I cross posted this from #2791; this seems to be the main report.)
According to the plan, 3.5 will start to reserve unknown fields. I hope 3.5 will be C++98 compatible, so old compilers will get this important feature in their final release.

@zzm3145 the next 3.5.0 release will not require C++11. We will likely start to require C++11 when we migrate to use Abseil: Google's C++ common libraries:
https://opensource.googleblog.com/2017/09/introducing-abseil-new-common-libraries.html

I do not know how efficient are the calls guarded by `GoogleInitOnce()` (they happen once per message parameterless constructor invocation), but replacing them with C++11 [singleton guarantee](https://stackoverflow.com/a/11711991/1149924) on the generated fileset's `TableStruct` would certainly remove the efficiency concerns away from the platform (trusting the platform to do that is the best way, in my opinion). 

As implemented, unless doing link-time code generation, it seems to me that  `GoogleInitOnce()` is a real call into the library, with a real call frame setup and prefetch pipeline kaput at the very least.

@kkm000 With C++11 support removing GoogleOnceInit is indeed something we want to do.

However GoogleOnceInit is implemented smart enough that after inlining the function it's a atomic read on a global variable and only a call in the initialization case. However using c++11 support will remove this dependency and allow the compiler to do whatever is best for the platform and is more readable.

@gerben-s: Yup, my bad, I misread the inline piece. It only calls `GoogleOnceInitImpl` (which is out-of-line) only after the inline lock-free flag test. D-oh!

Yes, c++11 and its library removes a lot of low-level stuff, like atomics, mutexes, threads, futures, you name it. Great stuff! `atomicops_internals_x86_msvc.h`? Oh, not any more! :)
Using C++11 would be great. I'm trying to use Protobuf on an embedded ARM target with FreeRTOS and a C++ 11 layer, and it's tricky because of all the PTHREAD stuff.

One of the reasons we like and use protobuf, is that it can easily help us bridge the communication gap between the embedded world and the server world.  Some of the embedded devices we use are not running the latest Linux, nor do they support C++11.  I think it would be a shame if protobuf were to require C++11, for this reason.  If you are only targeting fast, modern devices, the protobuf loses its edge, because faster, more modern "embedded" devices like a Raspberry PI have less of a problem with more bloated protocols and bloated languages.

Is not it striking that @mikejt4 noted how *beneficial* is C++11 for an embedded ARM system, and right in the next comment @kenlars99 has argued that C++11 is *deleterious* for an embedded ARM system? (☉_☉)

I would add that we use a number of major libraries in our embedded system: boost, poco, cppunit, and a number of C-only libraries like sqlite, openldap, openssl... None of these require C++11.  My issue is not with C++11 (I was very disappointed when we could not use it due to some of the target embedded systems we have to support), but with requiring it.

@kenlars99 I see, so the actual problem is those older systems have no support for C++11 at all, like the runtime libraries and such have not been built for them. Fair point. How viable do you think it is to stay on the latest protobuf version that still can cross-compile for these targets? The C++ world is moving on anyway, so if not protobuf, then you would likely hit the same issue with another product. title: Formally document and support python-protobuf-attribute-setting-by-keyword-argument-to-constructor
body:
For years I've favored writing code shaped like
```
my_message = my_module_pb2.MyMessage(my_first_attribute=3, my_second_attribute=4)
```
rather than
```
my_message = my_module_pb2.MyMessage()
my_message.my_first_attribute = 3
my_message.my_second_attribute = 4
```
. Are these construction semantics documented anywhere? Could they be, along with the similar semantics of
```
my_message.repeated_sub_message.add(up='↑', down='↓')
```
rather than
```
my_sub_message = my_message.repeated_sub_message.add()
my_sub_message.up = '↑'
my_sub_message.down = '↓'
```
?

Would [this page](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated) be the right place for such documentation?

nodes.body:
I also find it confusing that the doc indicate this is wrong:
```
foo = Foo()
foo.bar = Bar()  # WRONG!
```
But this seem to be ok:
```
Foo(bar=Bar())
```

I think this is a better place:

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/pythontutorial#the-protocol-buffer-api

`.add()` accepting keyword arguments for the constructor [is documented nowadays:](https://protobuf.dev/reference/python/python-generated/#repeated-message-fields)

```py
# add() also forwards keyword arguments to the concrete class.
# For example, you can do:

foo.bars.add(i=12, j=13)
```
and also in the `.add()` [Sphinx docs](https://googleapis.dev/python/protobuf/latest/google/protobuf/internal/containers.html#google.protobuf.internal.containers.RepeatedCompositeFieldContainer.add).

----
However, the fact that message **constructors** accept keyword arguments appears to remain **undocumented**.

There is a now a mention of message constructor arguments; however, it's buried in the [*Repeated Message Fields*](https://protobuf.dev/reference/python/python-generated/#repeated-message-fields) section, with inadequate explanation:

> ```
> # Initializers forward keyword arguments to a concrete class too.
> # For example:
> 
> foo = Foo(             # Creates Foo
>   bars=[               # with its field bars set to a list
>     Bar(i=15, j=17),   # where each list member is also initialized during creation.
>     Bar(i=32),
>     Bar(i=47, j=77),
>   ]
> )
> ```

An explanation of constructor arguments ought to be added to the [Message section](https://protobuf.dev/reference/python/python-generated/#message).

title: Need C++11 move semantics in the generated code
body:
It is 2017 and the protobuf-generated code needs the following C++11 features:
* Move constructor for every generated message
* Move assignment

The patch is trivial, see PR #2778. Yet this thing seems to be stuck due to political reasons... Opening an issue to track the progress.

nodes.body:
We are currently experimenting with this inside Google and evaluating the effects on binary size, compile times, runtime performance, etc.  This isn't political so much as technical; we need to ensure that this doesn't have adverse effects when deployed at scale across our large code base.

If these experiments go well, this change should show up in one of our merges from our internal code-base.

Perhaps stating the obvious:
* my request is about *generating* C++ code and that has nothing to do with how `protoc` is written
* so you could just add  `--with-c++11` option to `protoc` and a corresponding option to `configure` which makes that default for the given installation

This will appease both camps - the ones who use the modern compiles as well as the rest, that are stuck with old distros.

The plan is to have protoc generate movable constructors by default (guarded by #ifdef CXX11). We are already experimenting this inside Google and I would rather not take a detour here.

For options, we are generally against them because they complicate our code base, build scripts and more importantly complicate user API/interface. Options also tend to cause interoperability problems. For example, what if an user uses a protoc built with --with-c++11 but depends on a protobuf library built without this --with-c++11 flag? It really doesn't worth the trouble to add options for a feature that we will soon have anyway.

BTW, in addition to what I initially did in #2778, the generated code needs the following:
* move assignment for the generated message classes
* move-aware setter functions for the string fields

I notice [this has landed](https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/09354db1434859a31a3c81abebcc4018d42f2715) in the 3.4 branch. Thanks! 

I noticed a little problem though: there are move constructors for generated messages, but not for message containers (`RepeatedField`, `RepeatedPtrFieldBase`, `RepeatedPtrField<T>`). It would be useful to have these too. 

With the original proposal there was concern about code bloat because there's a move constructor and assignment for every generated message type, which there can be many of in an application. This worry doesn't apply to the containers, because we're just talking about four non-templated functions (move constructor and move assignment for the two classes), possibly inlined, plus two templated functions that are only instantiated if they're used.

I've realised another problem: The move constructor is not declared `noexcept`. I believe this means that `std::vector` will copy items rather than move them when resizing (including due to `push_back` etc.). It would also be sensible to declare move assignment operators as `noexcept`, although I don't know of any consequences of not doing that.

Of course the workarounds for this are the same as before move constructors were introduced: replace `std::vector<MyMsgType>` with `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<MyMsgType>>` or `google::protobuf::RepeatedPtrField<MyMsgType>`.
What about such C++11 feature as 'enum class' ?
@arthur-tacca @denisiussion  Can you create separate issues for RepeatedField/noexcept/enum class?
@xfxyjwf Apologies that I never made an issue for move constructors/assignment for RepeatedField and co. I notice someone has added them anyway, so many thanks for that. 👍

title: parse pb in python, member is empty if its' value is zero.

nodes.body:
This behavior is actually to be expected, because proto3 does not make a distinction between a primitive field being empty and being set to its default value (which in this case is the 0 value, `NOT_FRIEND`). In other words, there is no way to distinguish whether `error_code` was set to `NOT_FRIEND` or was not set at all. See here for more about proto3 enums: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#enum

title: How to decode Bytes field to binary String instead of Base64 String in the Ruby parser?
body: When I call to_json on a message in Ruby, the Bytes fields in the message is converted to a Base64 String, which I have to manually convert back to a binary string.

nodes.body: This behavior is actually to be expected, because `bytes` fields (unlike `string` fields) can contain non-UTF8 binary data, and since that cannot be directly represented in JSON, we have to base64-encode it.

Hi there,

Sorry to reopen the subject but I still don't understand this base64 encoding story. Whether it is in JS or another language, bytes must be represented in an array of uint8. Now, going back to normal behavior would break the ABI, it's a shame. It would be useful to have at least one option to change the management of bytes in an array. 
  
All the best
Michael

@mykiimike I don't think we really have much of a choice here, because we're constrained by the fact that JSON strings must be UTF-8. As a result we can't put a raw `bytes` field directly in a JSON string without encoding it in base64 or similar. That would result in invalid JSON (unless the bytes coincidentally happen to be valid UTF-8).
Unfortunately JSPB does not support the proto3 JSON format. The `toObject()` method returns something which looks similar to proto3 JSON but is not quite the same thing.

Yes, I understood that you can't change that without affecting compatibility. Maybe in proto4 then :) 

On the other hand I can assure you that in a future version it would be possible without B64 encoding ,)

I think I see what you mean now; if we were to use an array of ints then that would work and would remove the need for base64. Base64 might still have some advantages--smaller wire size and perhaps faster to decode, but you are right that in any case we can't change it now since we have to maintain compatibility.

> Base64 might still have some advantages--smaller wire size

I agree but that's not the purpose because the JSON memory is (generally) transitional in PB, we shouldn't have to store it in this state.

> perhaps faster to decode

I'm less sure because B64 requires some rotation & branching in addition to parsing. To tell the truth, I think the performance benefit would be quite significant without B64. We can measure it :)

I'd have to think about it some more but intuitively it seems to me like base64 would be easier to parse efficiently. It should be more predictable because four bytes of input leads to exactly three bytes of output, whereas if you're parsing decimal ints then each byte of output corresponds to a variable-sized input (between one and three bytes). I would expect it to be harder for the CPU to speculatively scan ahead because you can't know in advance where the next element begins.

title: Deterministic serialization
body:
Hi,

I am trying to determine what (if any) programming languages serialize protobuf models deterministically?

Based on my understanding of the protobuf format all `map` types must be sorted lexically bytewise using the `key` value for serialization, if a model to be serialized deterministically.

I have had a look at some source code, it appears that the [javascript implementation](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/7f3e23707122f31ebfa58b7280bd56cbe77cb44e/js/map.js#L426) is serialized deterministically, is this correct?

#1937  would suggest that the Java implementation does not currently serialize deterministically.

I couldn't find any documentation on this, does a document exist that indicates what languages serialize deterministically?

Thanks, Adam.

nodes.body:
The way this works is that map fields are ordinarily serialized in an arbitrary order, but for C++ and Java we have APIs to provide deterministic serialization (and thus sorting of maps) if you need that feature:
- C++: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/a1bb147e96b6f74db6cdf3c3fcb00492472dbbfa/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h#L834
- Java: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/a1bb147e96b6f74db6cdf3c3fcb00492472dbbfa/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/CodedOutputStream.java#L159

One thing to note is that these APIs give you serialization that is deterministic for a single executable, but not necessarily stable across multiple builds. So if you need some kind of identifier that will be stable for a long time, it's best to create your own format rather than trying to rely on deterministic proto serialization.

That's interesting that you point out that the JavaScript implementation always sorts its maps. I think this is actually a bug we should fix, because it's confusing that it does something different from the other implementations, and on top of that we would probably get better performance by skipping the unnecessary sorting. I'll try and see if it's feasible to remove the sorting there.

Thanks for the info @acozzette.

I do require an identifier that will remain stable across builds and multiple programming languages. To ensure I correctly understand how to achieve this, can you confirm first that a message without any map fields will always be serialized deterministically across all programming languages?

Can you elaborate on what has/may change between builds that prevents the deterministic serialization of fields from being stable? And does this relate only to map fields, or can this apply to other fields also (assuming the same proto version across builds)? How does this impact serialization/deserialization between different programming languages?

Sorry for all the questions, just need to ensure I can create a stable identifier thats reliable and correct.

Thanks again, Adam.

Even without map fields, at the moment you might technically be able to get the same serialized bytes for the same proto across builds and languages, but it would probably not be a good idea to rely on this. The main reason is that we want to have the option of evolving the format over time, and if code starts relying on the serialized bytes remaining 100% identical then we can no longer do that. For example, our serializers generally produce their output sorted by field number, but this is not a requirement and parsers have no problem parsing unsorted input. We could potentially find a good reason to stop serializing in sorted order and if that ever happens then code that uses the serialized bytes as an identifier would break.

The other issue is unknown fields. You can canonicalize map fields by sorting their entries, but only if you know where the map fields are; if you have an unknown field that contains map data then there's no way to canonicalize the maps. So this is one reason the serialized output can change from one build to the next. One build might see an unknown field and leave it alone, while the next build has an updated schema and changes the output because it knows that this field contains a map.

None of this affects compatibility between languages; you can always serialize a message in one language and parse it back from another.

I hope that makes sense, let me know if you have any other questions.
Thanks for the details response, that answers all my questions :)

title: JsonParser will not ignore unknown field when parsing - C#

nodes.body:
Thanks for all of your hard work on protobuf.

Hi, has this bug been looked at by Google?  This is a show stopping bug for us.  We are sending proto3 messages encoded as JSON via pubnub and then deserializing the JSON using the proto3 autogenerated json parsing.  Is it really the case that proto3 can encode a message as json with a new field but proto3 cannot successfully parse a message with that new field from json using an older definition of the containing message?  The new field was added with a higher flag and we followed all the rules, so why can't Google's own C# proto3 JSON demarshaller handle the field that was added by its json marshaller?  :-(
I hadn't seen it before a few days ago. I'm no longer working on the Protobuf team beyond a 20% capacity, but I'll try to have a look this week.

I'm having a heck of a time making this work with version 3.8.0

`MessageParser<T>.WithDiscardUnknownFields(true).ParseJson` will always throw an exception about unknown fields

> I'm having a heck of a time making this work with version 3.8.0
> 
> `MessageParser<T>.WithDiscardUnknownFields(true).ParseJson` will always throw an exception about unknown fields

Seems to only work by instantiating a new `JsonParser`.  The static parser property available for each message doesn't appear to respect the json parsing settings.

So this works:
`new JsonParser(JsonParser.Settings.Default.WithIgnoreUnknownFields(true)).Parse<T>(json);`

@aaronhudon-ts: Are you sure you weren't just confusing `WithDiscardUnknownFields` (used when parsing and then serializing protos in binary form) and `WithIgnoreUnknownFields` (used when parsing JSON)? I do appreciate that they're not the clearest names in the world.

The `MessageParser<T>` doesn't include JSON settings, so yes, constructing a new JSON parser is the right way to go here. It's fine to construct a single instance and keep it around though.

> @aaronhudon-ts: Are you sure you weren't just confusing `WithDiscardUnknownFields` (used when parsing and then serializing protos in binary form) and `WithIgnoreUnknownFields` (used when parsing JSON)? I do appreciate that they're not the clearest names in the world.
> 
> The `MessageParser<T>` doesn't include JSON settings, so yes, constructing a new JSON parser is the right way to go here. It's fine to construct a single instance and keep it around though.

Hey @jskeet I was originally using the `Parser` property that comes for free in the auto-generated message classes.
E.g. `MyMessage.Parser.WithDiscardUnknownFields(true).ParseJson(...)`

Too bad this doesn't work - as it seems relatively natural in the syntax (once you find the extension method).

Looking back, I don't know whether we'd want to make that work or not, if we'd thought about it from the start. There's a subtle difference between the JSON and pb parsing here - if you preserve unknown fields in the pb parser, it retains them and then emits them later if you write out the proto. The JSON parser doesn't do that (and can't, really) - it just throws if you have any unknown fields.

That said, I can see how the parser retaining JSON settings could be useful.

title: Segmentation fault when using arena allocation with gcc 4.8
body:
Hello, 

The line
`ptr_ = new ::std::string(*initial_value);`
in `CreateInstance` (arenastring.h) causes a segmentation fault when compiled with gcc 4.8.4.
This method is called  eventually when calling `mutable_<string-field>`.

There the method `::google::protobuf::internal::GetEmptyStringAlreadyInited()` is called which uses a reinterpret_cast to cast a `char[sizeof(std::string)` to `std::string*` (btw isn’t  that undefined behavior?). This works fine on newer versions of gcc when the cxx11-abi version of std::string is used (sizeof(T) = 32).  gcc 4.8.4 however uses the pre cxx11-abi version std::string (sizeof(T) = 8) in which the cast fails and causes a segmentation fault when accessing the the reinterpret_cast result.

When stripped down to the the relevant parts you get this code (to try it on different compilers):
```
    char arr[sizeof(std::string)] = {0};
    const std::string* str = reinterpret_cast<const std::string*>(&arr);
    string* s = new std::string(*str);
```
This doesn’t work on gcc 4.8.4 but works fine on gcc 5.4 and newer (if not compiled if flags that disable the use of the newer abi)

nodes.body:
I believe that reinterpret_cast is OK and is defined behavior, because we do initialize the char array with placement-new [here](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/a69bc9de75fe08f5fe7ad6e2339dfc5b0da5d8ef/src/google/protobuf/generated_message_util.h#L90), like this: `new (&union_) T();`

It sounds to me like this must be some ABI issue then. This page seems to describe the GCC ABI change for std::string: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/libstdc++/manual/using_dual_abi.html Based on that it sounds like all object files linked together must use the same ABI; would that possibly explain the problem? I have been using g++ 4.8.4 without any problems, but perhaps in your setup you are linking the protobuf library against code compiled against a newer ABI.

this is carefully designed to be c++14 conforming. It's basically a reimplementation of the c++14 http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/types/aligned_storage so it works with pre-c++14. It's based on an exception that a char/byte array is allowed as a backing buffer for other types.

Your segfault seems like an ABI linking incompatibility of libs compiled with different versions.

Thank you for your answers!

Sorry I missed the `new (&union_) T();`

I don't think it's an abi issue because the installed libstdc++ doesn't even support cxx11 abi std::strings. (_GLIBCXX_USE_DUAL_ABI 0 and _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI 0 are set).

After some hasty investigation it looks like an initialization issue. `DefaultConstruct()` is never called or so it seems since `init_` is always false. If i add `fixed_address_empty_string.DefaultConstruct();` to `GetEmptyStringAlreadyInited()` it works fine - no segmentation fault. Is a special step necessary to make sure everything necessary is initialized? Anyways I'll look further into it.

I will provide a minimal example project at a later time. Thank you!

Unfortunately Git does not store file read and write permissions (only execute permission) and so the read/write permissions just end up determined by the `umask` that you happen to have when Git creates those files. I guess we could manually do something like `chmod 644 $(find . -type f -name '*.[ch]')` but that seems a bit tedious. Do you happen to know if there is some recommended best practice for this issue? title: JsonPrintOptions : option to always print optional fields that are set (regardless of value)
body:
JsonPrintOptions has always_print_primitive_fields which, when false, will skip fields set to default value (even if these fields are optional and set to the default value).

Could we have another option in JsonPrintOptions:`print_optional_fields_when_set` which will only print optional fields when they're set (regarless what value they're set to)

This would be most useful to have a closer 1:1 relationship between what's in json and what's in the protobuf.


FYI @mojoBrendan  since you've implemented https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/2867

implementation: I would imagine this would use proto reflection, eg: `HasField` in https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp/google.protobuf.message

NOTE: always_print_primitive_fields is different from print_optional_fields_when_set, see:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/9168052/how-do-has-field-methods-relate-to-default-values-in-protobuf

nodes.body: Are you using proto2 or proto3 syntax? If proto3, what you observed is the correct behavior because proto3 doesn't keep field presence and can't distinguish between unset fields and fields set to default value. However, if you are using proto2, the JSON conversion library should already do what you suggested, i.e., print fields that are set (even it's set to the default value). If that's not the case, I think we have a bug to fix in protobuf library.

The doc about always_print_primitive_fields is for proto3 specifically (and it should be fixed/updated for proto2). Actually the whole JSON conversion library is designed for proto3, but it should also work reasonably for proto2 types. You should not need to set any option to get the behavior you want. Please give it a try and report back if it doesn't work as I suggested here.

I have added a [currently failing on my machine] test (PR https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/2887) that tries to search for an extension via its full name. 

I also base this on the assumption that *Symbol* includes extension names, as nowhere in the documentation it is explicitly mentioned otherwise.
@anandolee to take a look

Only top level extensions are included in Symbol. You test "python.internal.Factory2Message.one_more_field" is not a top level extension. Is grpc also this case?
Test can pass if you try "python.internal.another_field".

I see. It would be great if that restriction was [documented in the API](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/259dd7e842dd3a848a1094a42c05610e8a31dcbb/python/google/protobuf/descriptor_pool.py#L275). Is there a supported way to get the file descriptor representing any extension? We need such API to implement the [reflection service for gRPC](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/2565). 

By the way, it is interesting that the exact same test would pass on a clean Ubuntu 16.04 LTS environment on GCE) with just  `sudo apt install unzip python-dev python-pip python-virtualenv` when you extract the zip file and run the `./repro.sh` file.
Make sense to fix FindFileContainingSymbol be able to find none top extensions. Just want to confirm with you that if this can fix grpc's issue.

Right. Yes, we basically need a mechanism to map a type name and extension number to the file descriptor—as seen in this short function linked below, we are trying to use `FindFileContainingSymbol` now: https://github.com/mehrdada/grpc/blob/python-service-reflection/src/python/grpcio_reflection/grpc_reflection/v1alpha/reflection.py#L88

I have dug further into the problem and realized why the behavior is platform dependent. It seems the root cause for the particular repro instructions I have attached above in my *original post* (which is similar to how we use it in gRPC reflection) is correlated with that the python wheels on PyPI having the C extension compiled in them.

On Mac, `pip` tries to fetch `protobuf-3.2.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl` and it doesn't have any `.so` files within itself. Likewise, on a default Goobuntu instance with an old `pip` version, the same file will be downloaded and it fails to work. **Update**: I just realized there are two distinct implementations of protobuf python. The inconsistency seems to have arisen from a behavioral discrepancy in the pure python implementation vs the C++ implementation.  Is there a way for us to specifically depend on the Python+C++ implementation from our python package?
See also b/36569071

title: Cpp: Characteristic of IsInitialized() doesn't match with documentation

nodes.body: It looks like this is working as intended, because `IsInitialized()` only checks required fields. Required fields are actually largely discouraged and do not even exist in proto3. If you want to check that every field (include ones that are not required) is set, there is no simple way to do that, though with a little bit of work you could probably use the reflection API to do this. Let me close this issue but feel free to reopen it if you have any more questions.

title: Why implement GetCurrentTime with nanos always 0?

nodes.body:
The `nanos` field is part of the `Timestamp` [message](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/fd046f6263fb17383cafdbb25c361e3451c31105/src/google/protobuf/timestamp.proto#L107) because it may be handy for implementations of that proto to provide that level of accuracy.

The `time` function [typically returns an integral number of seconds](http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/chrono/c/time) so it's most accurate to use 0 for `nanos` if `time()` is your clock.

If you have a higher-resolution clock you can just avoid using this helper method and set `seconds`/`nanos` directly.

title: Python generated file compiled with Cython causes error with protobuf 3.2.0
body:
When a _pb2 is compiled with Cython, and the C++ backend of the Python library is turned on (as it now is on Linux for the PyPI deployed protobuf, as of 3.2.0), instantiating any message object gives an error. I am using Python 3.5. Here's an example of the error:

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "bug.py", line 1, in <module>
    from addressbook_pb2 import Person
  File "addressbook_pb2.py", line 34, in init addressbook_pb2 (addressbook_pb2.c:1997)
    _descriptor.EnumValueDescriptor(
  File "/home/arthur/envs/default/lib/python3.5/site-packages/google/protobuf/descriptor.py", line 649, in __new__
    _message.Message._CheckCalledFromGeneratedFile()
TypeError: Descriptors should not be created directly, but only retrieved from their parent.
```

The immediate cause of the error is [`_CheckCalledFromGeneratedFile` in `google/protobuf/pyext/message.cc`](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/v3.2.0/python/google/protobuf/pyext/message.cc#L2564), which calls [`_CalledFromGeneratedFile` in `google/protobuf/pyext/descriptor.cc`](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/v3.2.0/python/google/protobuf/pyext/descriptor.cc#L95). I haven't looked any further than this, but my suspicion is raised by the `strcmp` against `"_pb2.py"` at the end of this function.  I think that for Cython the filename would end with `"_pb2.c"`, but I'm not sure.

Just to be completely explicit, here are steps to reproduce:

1. Create a new Python virtual environment with the relevant packages (I am just using grpio-tools for easy access to protoc):

```
pip install grpcio-tools==1.1.0 protobuf==3.2.0 Cython==0.25.2
```

2. Generate a pb2:

```
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google/protobuf/master/examples/addressbook.proto
python -m grpc_tools.protoc -I. addressbook.proto --python_out=.
```

3. Cythonise and compile this file. The easiest way to do this is with a little setup.py:

```
from distutils.core import setup
from Cython.Build import cythonize
setup(name="bug", ext_modules = cythonize("addressbook_pb2.py"))
```

Then run: `python setup.py build_ext --inplace`

4. Try to instantiate a message:

```
python -c 'from addressbook_pb2 import Person; p = Person()'
```

  0: filename: <frozen importlib._bootstrap>
  1: filename: <frozen importlib._bootstrap_external>
  2: filename: <frozen importlib._bootstrap>
  3: filename: <frozen importlib._bootstrap>
  4: filename: <frozen importlib._bootstrap>
  5: filename: <frozen importlib._bootstrap>
  6: filename: bug.py
  7: frame is NULL
```
I also forced `_CalledFromGeneratedFile` to return `true` and did a basic test of functionality: I made a `Person` and added some phone numbers, serialized to bytes, then deserialized to a new object. This all worked fine. 

One option of course is to turn off this check, as is already done for PyPy. An argument in favor of this is that the [docs for `PyFrameObject`](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/veryhigh.html#c.PyFrameObject) say that "the fields of this type are subject to change at any time", but this function reaches into them gratuitously. A compromise might be to look at the module filename, and if it ends with ".py" check further that it ends in "_pb2.py", but if not just pass the check.

If this check can't be implemented with Cython, feel free to disable it for that environment.

I'm not aware of anyone using protobuf with Cython! Will be interested to hear more about how well it works (or doesn't) on this issue.

I'm not Cythoning the protobuf library, only the generated user _pb2.py files. This means there can't be a static check (something like `#ifdef CYTHON`) because it's impossible to tell when the protobuf library is built whether it's going to be used with Cythoned generated files. The closest I can think of to a run time check is the compromise I mentioned at the end of my second comment. I can't do that (maintainably) on my end because it requires changing the protobuf library and recompiling, whereas I'd prefer everyone to keep installing it just by using pip.

The pure-Python versions of Protobuf seem to work fine with Cython, and as I mentioned in my second comment a brief check suggests the C++-based version works fine too. I can't tell you if it works any *better* i.e. faster because we're not really Cythoning it for that... We just have some _pb2 files as part of larger packages where other modules definitely *do* benefit from Cython, and it would be a huge administrative pain to run Cython on some modules and not others (essentially I think we'd have to separate them out in to separate packages). I expect the fancy descriptor stuff that generated pb2s use are quite opaque to Cython, and even if they used normal Python methods instead they'd probably also need some static type hints (i.e. cdefs) to get much benefit.
Just for reference, the issue where Linux wheels were enabled is #2623 (but don't get me wrong, it's great that they are).

Pure python does not do the check because it "is somewhat difficult to implement correctly in PyPy". I don't think we have enough reasons to disable it in cpp implementation only for Cython.

nodes.body: Can you try if you can refer to other modules under google.protobuf? This is usually caused conflicts with a previous installed version. Can you use virtualenv and have a clean protobuf python install?

This is because that original code snippet *shouldn't* work. But presumably you filed the bug because it did seem to work at some point in the past. Just for future reference, this is how this error can arise.

I believe that the root cause is that in the past you were (unwittingly) using some dependency that had been importing `google.protobuf.text_format`. So long as that other library is imported before you import `google.protobuf`, your code will work by accident:

    # in some_other_library:
    from google.protobuf import text_format  # Imported the proper way
    # import google.protobuf.text_format would also work fine
    
    # in your code:
    import some_other_library
    import google.protobuf     # Doesn't mention text_format!
    t = google.protobuf.text_format  # works by accident

But if the other library removes its import, or you move the import of that library after your import of `google.protbuf`, then your code will break:

    # in some_other_library:
    from google.protobuf import json_format  # Switched to using JSON
    
    # in your code:
    import some_other_library
    import google.protobuf     # Doesn't mention text_format!
    t = google.protobuf.text_format  # throws AttributeError

title: ambiguous unqualified symbols from std namespace
body:
Issue #1136 has been closed without resolution with the offer to reopen. Since I cannot reopen, here is the duplicate.

[Protobuf 3.2.0, MSVC 2015.3]

Unqualified "string" usage in header files causes conflicts with string classes from other, unrelated, namespaces (line numbers are from Protobuf 3.0.0-beta-2, they may be different now):

> ...\protobuf\src\google\protobuf\map_entry_lite.h(123): error C2872: 'string': ambiguous symbol
> ...\protobuf\src\google\protobuf\map_type_handler.h(625): error C2872: 'string': ambiguous symbol

Changing "string" to "::std::string" in relevant locations fixed that particular compilation issue, although there appear to be more similar "string" usage instances.

nodes.body: We can't change string to std::string because our google internal code base cannot use std::string. If you have the issue, it's likely you have some code somewhere importing a different string into the global namespace. Please fix that code instead (just don't import a string class into global namespace).

@xfxyjwf Please clarify: does this mean that that "string" is supposed to refer to std::string for external users and to something very different when used in your internal code base? Shouldn't this be properly handled by an appropriate #if + typedef or something similar, then?

Also, for the record, as mentioned in the original issue, the code in question imported a namespace containing a string class in a certain translation unit. Not a string class, but a namespace containing it; so trying to change it to individually importing everything except "string" would be a highly inconvenient solution. Especially since importing namespaces is a perfectly valid language feature, therefore your proposed solution is not a fix, but a workaround for the issue caused by protobuf.

@ardatur Yes, you are right. "string" refers to some other type in our internal code base. There is ongoing effort to make it std::string though. I'm not sure what you mean by "#if + typedef" handling. Note that the string type is not defined by protobuf, but is part of the base library every Google code uses (e.g., #include <string> will include that special string). There is no way we can change it specifically for protobuf.

What you are proposing has a cost: everyone who touches protobuf code must use proto_string rather than the standard string type. I don't see it as a worthwhile investment given how many people touches protobuf code everyday and how few people actually pulling another string type into global namespace.

If you think it's common for users to pull a certain non-standard string type into global namespace, let me know what project defines that string type so we can better understand the tradeoff here. For example, if the other string type is from grpc, we certainly want to fix it one way or another.

> everyone who touches protobuf code must use proto_string rather than the standard string type

Not at all. I am introducing a type alias, not a new type. From the user code's point of view, the actual types will be exactly the same as they are / should be now: your internal strings for the internal codebase, std::string for everyone else. If you are worried about introducing type aliases, just wrap the types in a slightly different fashion:
```
#if THIS_IS_THE_INTERNAL_CODEBASE
#define INTERNAL_OR_EXTERNAL_STRING google::string
#else
#include <string>
#define INTERNAL_OR_EXTERNAL_STRING std::string
#endif
```
and use `INTERNAL_OR_EXTERNAL_STRING` precisely in those places within protobuf that require different types for different codebases.

The point of my proposal isn't the specific implementation, but rather the idea that if we want to employ different types in different usage contexts (internal/external), then we should do just that—explicitly!—instead of hoping that a compiler will be capable of resolving just the "string" the way we want.

> If you think it's common for users to pull a certain non-standard string type into global namespace

I can agree that such pulling is a contentious issue. According to protobuf itself (stubs/common.h):

3.2.0:
```
using namespace std;  // Don't do this at home, kids. 
```
3.5.0:
```
// TODO(acozzette): remove these using statements
...
using std::string; 
```
These snippets are not in the global namespace, but they are clearly considered an issue by protobuf developers. And they are directly related to the problem at hand, aren't they?

> if the other string type is from grpc, we certainly want to fix it one way or another

It is not a Google project, but thank you.

title: Packed repeated fields cannot be read as non-repeated fields in C++

nodes.body:
Singular field is compatible with non-packed repeated field and non-packed repeated field is compatible with packed repeated field, however, just as you have observed, singular field is not compatible with packed repeated field.

We are concerning that fixing this would have a significant impact on the parsing performance of singular fields and for this reason there is no plan to fix it at the moment.
OK, thank you for the clarification. It might be helpful if this was made clear in the docs.

title: use_fast_cpp_protos breaks pythonic reload()
body:
Python's [reload()](http://pydoc-zh.readthedocs.io/en/latest/library/functions.html#reload) is useful for reloading modules that are edited after already being imported into the runtime, to support iterative/experimental working styles.
protobuf's use_fast_cpp_protos breaks this use-case with an error like:
```
TypeError: Couldn't build proto file into descriptor pool! 
Invalid proto descriptor for file "<FILE>.proto": 
<FILE>.proto: A file with this name is already in the pool.
```

It would be great if DescriptorPool knew how to reload().

One twist is that extant messages of the type being reloaded will have a different type to that of new messages created after the reload, but that's something that's true of vanilla python's use of reload() as well.  Hopefully the perfect doesn't have to be the enemy of the good here.

nodes.body: There might be no way to solve this problem, i.e., there is no way to unload registered types in C++ descriptor pool. C++ runtime maintains several globals (descriptor pool, descriptor database, extension registry, etc.). These globals need to be kept in a consistent state (or you will get random crashes) and none of them supports unloading. Only addition is supported at the moment. Although theoretically it's possible to make every component support unloading, in practice it might be too hard to refactor the existing code base to do so.

@xfxyjwf: thanks for the answer and sorry for this slow reply (your answer went to a spam folder :/).
Can we take advantage of the indirection between the Python and C++ layers to lie to the C++ side about the identity of a reloaded type on the python side?  In other words pass it a generated, unique, name and maintain the mapping between python and C++ names in the python side.
Have added warnings for duplicate register a few month ago. We can't reject duplicated register which will break a lot current projects. Thus we choose to raise warnings
I don't think this has been changed yet. I just ran into this issue today, with the same original error @fischman reported.

nodes.body: @oflebbe Thank you for reporting this, but I believe this is actually working as intended. title: Serialized Binary string generated using C++ can't be deserialized in Javascript
body:
I'm using google protobuf 3.2.0 and have a proto-file for which I generated C++ and Javascript code. 

A binary string is created using the generated C++ SerializeToString member function 
`bool SerializeToString(string* output) const; // serializes the message and stores the bytes in the given string. Note that the bytes are binary, not text; we only use the string class as a convenient container. `
and sent over HTTP in binary form as "application/octet-stream".
On Javascript side we receive the string and deserialized using the generated javascript function deserializeBinary. Here we get the error message:
"Unknown base64 encoding at char"

This is the complete callstack:
[2]</</goog.crypt.base64.decodeStringInternal_ http://localhost:34568/phoenix/configuration/RESTFulPhoenix_bundle.js:1208:312
	[2]</</goog.crypt.base64.decodeStringToUint8Array http://localhost:34568/phoenix/configuration/RESTFulPhoenix_bundle.js:1207:367
	[2]</</jspb.utils.byteSourceToUint8Array http://localhost:34568/phoenix/configuration/RESTFulPhoenix_bundle.js:1278:198
	[2]</</jspb.BinaryDecoder.prototype.setBlock http://localhost:34568/phoenix/configuration/RESTFulPhoenix_bundle.js:1283:253
	[2]</</jspb.BinaryDecoder http://localhost:34568/phoenix/configuration/RESTFulPhoenix_bundle.js:1281:481

The jspb.utils.byteSourceToUint8Array function assumes that the binary stream is encoded as base64 which seems an erroneous assumption to me...

nodes.body:
@rodiers I'm not a Javascript expert, but I think this is working as intended since as I understand, Javascript strings are not intended for storing arbitrary binary data. Serialized protocol buffers are not safe to store in Javascript strings since in general they contain binary data that has no meaning as a Unicode string.

For your problem, I think the right solution is to either switch to using `ArrayBuffer`/`Uint8Array`, or else keep using a string but base-64 encode it.

title: Update Protobuf Lite on mavenCentral
body: Hi, Protobuf 3.2.0 has been released, but I don't see the protobuf lite 3.2.0 version on Maven Central here : https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/com.google.protobuf/protobuf-lite

nodes.body:
@LouisCAD The reason we are not regularly updating protobuf-lite on Maven Central is that we have been making a number of major changes to the Java lite implementation that break compatibility with existing generated code. So if we published a new version and you updated your project to use it, it would break unless you simultaneously updated all your protobuf generated code, including generated code in dependencies. We are recommending that if you want to use lite with Maven, just stick with 3.0.1 for now.

(Let me close this issue for now, but feel free to reopen it if you have any other questions.)

@LouisCAD The breaking changes we are making are mostly not public API changes, but "internal" changes to the interface between protobuf runtime and protobuf generated code. Although this interface is usually not visible to users, changes to the interface do break users who want to upgrade protobuf runtime from one version to another, and as such we don't want to deploy multiple versions that aren't compatible with each other to maven.

I would suggest you use 3.0.1 for now. Protobuf public API is fairly stable and we almost never remove public APIs. All public APIs documented in our developer guide can be relied on. There is no worry about the need to refactor your code for new versions.

title: Java: Maps with enum value type should allow putting unknown values
body: Currently, the singular ```put*Value``` method of a map with enum value type does not accept values that are not valid enums. This seems to literally be the only place in generated code that checks the validity of an enum value when using the ```*Value variants``` of the methods (e.g. singular, repeated fields). Even the ```putAll*Value``` variant that takes a ```Map<Key, Integer>``` parameter allows unknown values. I think the ```*Value``` variants were added to allow working with unknown values, for backwards compatibility situations, and in particular, just having the check in one location seems highly inconsistent.

1. The main binary doesn't link with protobuf; the .dylib static linked with libprotobuf.a.
2. The main binary doesn't link with protobuf; the .dylib is dynamically linked with libprotobuf.a.
3. The main binary is dynamically linked with protobuf; the .dylib is also dynamically linked with protobuf

3. The main binary is dynamically linked with protobuf; the .dylib is static linked with libprotobuf.a

title: google.protobuf.json_format.MessageToJson skips serialization of zero index enums

nodes.body:
This is working as intended. In proto3, a field set to default value  (0 for primitives) is indistinguishable from an unset field so the JSON formater will not print any field that's set to default unless you set the including_default_value_fields flag = true on MessageToJson:
