title: MessageToJson outputs the wrong type for uint64 and int64 in Python
body:
Here's a very simple proto file:

```
$ cat test.proto
syntax = "proto3";

message Message {
    uint64 foo1 = 1;
    uint32 foo2 = 2;
    float  foo3 = 3;
    double foo4 = 4;
    bool   foo5 = 5;
    int64  foo6 = 6;
    int32  foo7 = 7;
}
```

and I created a protobuf message in Python as follows:
```
In [1]: import test_pb2
In [2]: message = test_pb2.Message()

In [3]: message.foo1 = 11

In [4]: message.foo2 = 22

In [5]: message.foo3 = 33

In [6]: message.foo4 = 44

In [7]: message.foo5 = True

In [8]: message.foo6 = 66

In [9]: message.foo7 = 77

In [11]: message
Out[11]:
foo1: 11
foo2: 22
foo3: 33
foo4: 44
foo5: true
foo6: 66
foo7: 77

In [12]: from google.protobuf.json_format import MessageToJson

In [13]: print(MessageToJson(message))
{
  "foo6": "66",
  "foo4": 44,
  "foo7": 77,
  "foo5": true,
  "foo2": 22,
  "foo1": "11",
  "foo3": 33
}
```

Note that `foo6` and `foo1` should **not** have quotes as they are integers and not strings. Using the `protobuf_to_dict` module does not have this problem

```
In [15]: from protobuf_to_dict import protobuf_to_dict

In [16]: protobuf_to_dict(message)
Out[16]:
{'foo1': 11,
 'foo2': 22,
 'foo3': 33.0,
 'foo4': 44.0,
 'foo5': True,
 'foo6': 66,
 'foo7': 77}

In [17]: import json

In [18]: json.dumps(protobuf_to_dict(message))
Out[18]: '{"foo6": 66, "foo4": 44.0, "foo7": 77, "foo5": true, "foo2": 22, "foo1": 11, "foo3": 33.0}'
```

My `protoc` version is `3.2.0` and python version is `3.5.2`

```
$ protoc --version
libprotoc 3.2.0

$ python --version
Python 3.5.2 :: Anaconda custom (x86_64)
```

nodes.body:
As per proto3 JSON spec, uint64/int64 fields should be printed as decimal strings. See:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json

The reason is that uint64/int64 is not part of JSON spec and many JSON libraries only support double precision. To prevent precision loss our proto3 JSON spec requires serializers to put int64/uint64 values in strings.

I wanted ask the same question for `MessageToDict` here before creating another issue.

I respect `MessageToJson` converting `int64` and `uint64` into string for some reason even though it is hard to understand, why a long / integer value (without precision?) should be translated into string when there is no limit on a JSON integer by the specs.

Regardless to this _unexpected behavior_, I am assuming only by the name `MessageToDict` has nothing to do with JSON specs or whatnot, and all it is expected to do is to take a message object and give back a _Python dictionary_ without touching its data types. Unfortunately, it's behavior is the same with `MessageToJson`, which makes us impossible to use these utility functions who deal with int64 data types.

The question is, should `MessageToDict` return these values in Python dictionary without touching their data types?
Isn't MessageToDict part of the json_format package? It should honor the same proto3 JSON spec as with MessageToJson.

It's all nice that `json_format` package follows the spec but it's laughable that I can't do this:
```python
m = test_pb2.Message.FromString(serialized_proto_bytes)
d = MessageToDict(m)
copy = test_pb2.Message(**d)
```
because of type inconsistency.
I know I'm using wrong package for this but if you went that far to produce Python `dict` which is JSON spec compatible and you allow to create message instances out of unpacked nested `dict` structures then why we have to use another Python package to add the missing link for proper `dict` serialization?

I'll add my vote to @WloHu that the code fragment above should work (ie the process should be reversible), even if we have to specify some optional argument like:
`d = MessageToDict(m, preserve_int64_as_int=True)`
Is something like that open for consideration or is there an existing recommended solution to this?
Even if it is part of the json_format package, it is not formatting to json when calling MessageToDict. So why on earth keep this JSON convention as the default behavior?

nodes.body:
Unfortunately early Google style suggested using `int` for lengths. This is inconsistent with modern C++ practice, so you wind up getting nasty mixed comparison errors.

While I certainly agree with the sentiment, it is not something we have the bandwidth to fix, since it would be a major effort to clean up within Protobuf. I'm going to close this as "not planned", since I'd rather we be clear that we simply do not have the bandwidth to fix this. :(

nodes.body: Same issue here on Fedora 25

Unlike other languages, go is implemented by a compiler plugin. protoc has no idea it's available until you invoke it with "protoc --go_out=..." at which time protoc will look for the go plugin binary.
Can we add `--go_out` into the option list, and remind user that it requires the compiler plugin?

As Feng pointed out, both javascript and go are compiler plugins now and not shipped with protoc by default.  It's not really appropriate for protoc to list external plugins, because the dependency is in the other direction.

title: Convert .proto from "proto2" to "proto3"
body: I just wish to know if there's any tool that converts proto files from "proto2" to proto3". At this point I don't really care about backward compatibility.

nodes.body: I don't know of any tool for this, but in practice it is usually fairly easy to convert a .proto file if you don't care about backward compatibility. You can basically just update the syntax line to say `syntax = "proto3"` and remove all `optional` and `required` keywords. The other main things are that proto3 doesn't support extensions (so you would have to remove those), and it requires every enum definition to have a 0 value as its first element. title: Inconsistent dll linkage when compiling with PROTOBUF_USE_DLLS on Windows
body:
Since https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/b1295eeffbf2ae7da8a5c7d8601c3ace0663fa09 the [compiler/plugin.pb.h](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/plugin.pb.h) file contains lines like this:
`LIBPROTOC_EXPORT extern DescriptorProtoDefaultTypeInternal _DescriptorProto_default_instance_;`
That file also includes [descriptor.pb.h](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.pb.h) which uses `LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT` for the same instances.
(This latter seems to be the correct one as they reside in [descriptor.pb.cc](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.pb.cc))
This emits [inconsistent dll linkage warnings](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/35bhkfb6.aspx).

I think the proper fix would be not to write these lines into plugin.pb.h at all as the included descriptor.pb.h contains them already correctly.

For those like me looking for a way to get around this bug, and who cannot wait until the fix has made it into final releases (and who need this to work in a conda environment), the following is worth trying:

1. create/activate your conda env (no need to have `libprotobuf` or `protobuf` installed), say `protoenv`
2. download suitable release candidate, e.g., `wget https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/download/v3.7.0rc2/protobuf-python-3.7.0-rc-2.tar.gz`
3. extract `tar xzvf protobuf-python-3.7.0-rc-2.tar.gz` and `cd` into `protobuf-3.7.0-rc-2` folder
4. run `./configure --prefix=/path/to/conda/envs/protoenv`
5. subsequently, run `make` and `make install`
6. after successful setup, the command `which protoc` should show the correct path: `/path/to/conda/envs/protoenv/bin/protoc` ; and this `protoc --version` should show `libprotoc 3.7.0`
7. now `cd` into `python` subfolder (i.e., `protobuf-3.7.0-rc-2/python`), and run `python setup.py build`, `python setup.py test` and finally `python setup.py install`
8. start python and try `import google.protobuf as pb` followed by `pb.__version__`, which should show `3.7.0rc2` (if the module is importable)

title: [Java] Generate hasXXX() methods for fields inside a oneof
body:
Currently in Java, one must compare the value of the oneof enum to know which field is contain in a oneof.
This is not very friendly to the end-user especially when you want to use oneof to provide nullability of the field. A generated hasXXX() method would be much more handy.
Also, I use [mapstruct](http://mapstruct.org/) to map the generated protobuf classes to internal POJOs and it is capable of detecting if there is a `hasFoo()` method for a given `foo` field and using it in the mapping code it generates (see http://mapstruct.org/documentation/stable/reference/html/#source-presence-check). So such an enhancement would allow me to remove a lot of boilerplate code.

See also #1606 for the interest when dealing with nullable fields.

nodes.body: Hi there, any comment ?

@cbornet In the past we have talked about this a bit within the protobuf team but I think our conclusion has been that for proto3 we want to avoid hazzer methods for non-message oneof elements. The main reason is just to be consistent with primitive fields outside of oneofs. Another thing is that although oneofs can be useful for providing nullability, that is not really their intended use.

Sorry but I don't get it. Primitive fields outside oneof are always present (they have a default value if not explicitely set) so I understand that a hazzer is not useful there. But in a oneof, the field can be there or not so a hazzer makes perfectly sense for this !
Nullability is just a particular case where the hazzer makes even more sense but it would also be useful for the general case.
That's not nice... A lot of people want this...

I'd love to see this too. It might actually be the reason why we decide against `Oneof` in some cases although it is really convenient to use in powerful languages that support sum types (Swift, Scala, Haskell, Rust...) it becomes a hassle in e.g. Java and C#.

@acozzette "... I think our conclusion has been that for proto3 we want to avoid hazzer methods for non-message oneof elements."

Does this mean we shouldn't rely on the HasField() functionality in generated Python code for oneofs that contain scalar values?

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated#oneof

If you are going to take away this kind of functionality in Python, then that will change how I deal with nullable fields.  

Or is this just a case of Python getting to have a friendlier API than Java for some reason?

I'm not really familiar with the Python API, but I think if it has HasField() methods for oneofs then it should be fine to use them. That seems inconsistent with the other languages, but it would be pretty unlikely that we would make a breaking change to try to remove those accessors.

title: [C#]: Provide a switch so that the C# code generator can just ignore proto2 syntax features, rather than erroring out
body:
Currently, attempting to generate C# from a proto2 file produces the following:

` C# code generation only supports proto3 syntax`

This makes sense - however, it would be tremendously useful to have a mode/switch that will silently ignore the unsupported syntax, and produce code that just doesn't honour the required/optional statements

## Rationale
proto files are frequently shared between multiple languages/tools - and because 'required' is enforced differently by certain libraries/implementations, sometimes it _is_ useful to have this statement in the .proto, even if you don't want it to do anything when using C# codegen

For example, [protobuf-jsonschema](https://www.npmjs.com/package/protobuf-jsonschema) can generate JSON schemas with the necessary 'required' attributes.

### Moving to proto3 
Moving to proto3 syntax and just dropping required and optional is fine - the problem is that other tools/libraries that _are_ doing something useful with the extra attributes cease to do so

The only alternative is to either have multiple copies of the file (which is obviously not helpful) or to preprocess the files ourselves before running protoc

nodes.body: Now that C# supports proto2 features, it seems this issue is obsolete.

title: Ruby decode_json not handling timestamps and int64 per JSON Mapping spec
body:
The Ruby `decode_json` method is not handling the `timestamp` and `int64` types per the [JSON Mapping spec](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json). The spec says:

> Timestamp	string	`"1972-01-01T10:00:20.021Z"`	Uses RFC 3339, where generated output will always be Z-normalized and uses 0, 3, 6 or 9 fractional digits.

and 

> int64, fixed64, uint64	string	`"1", "-10"`	JSON value will be a decimal string. Either numbers or strings are accepted.

However, when trying to decode messages including these types, it raises:

```
Google::Protobuf::ParseError: Error occurred during parsing: String specified for non-string/non-enum field
```

Decoding these same messages in native format works. Also, decoding these messages in JSON format works in Go.

To demonstrate the problem, I created an example [project](https://github.com/ryanbrainard/ruby-pb-example) with a [failing test](https://github.com/ryanbrainard/ruby-pb-example/blob/master/example_rb_test.rb).

title: protoc doesn't find include path
body:
protoc doesn't find a proto file, when it's full path is specified via `-I`.

```
$ cat foo/bar.proto
syntax = "proto2";

$ protoc -Ibar.proto=foo/bar.proto --descriptor_set_out=bar.proto.bin bar.proto
bar.proto: No such file or directory
```

This actually breaks bazel's `proto_library` rules.

nodes.body: The file parameter must be the actual physical path, i.e., regardless of other flags, you have to use foo/bar.proto when specifying the file to generate code for.
Note that that's actually contrary to the internal version of protocol compiler where you have to use the google3 relative path. It has been that way for reasons I don't know of...
Thanks @xfxyjwf . Closing this for now.

title: Parameters set to have certain value but, don't want to send that over wire (GPB: Proto 3)
body:
My comments/questions here are only for Google ProtoBufs, syntax=proto3 (and not proto2)

Upon doing some research online, it looks like unset fields are simply absent from the encoded message. If you have three fields, a, b, and c with tags 1, 2, and 3 respectively, and you encode a message with only "a"set to "100", then the encoded message will contain "field(1) = 42", and nothing else.

Now, I wanted to understand another aspect of GPB using proto3 syntax. Lets say, I have a parameter which has been set to a value (not hardcoded, but say by parsing another file in my source code). And if that parameter is set to certain value and I don't want to send that over wire, is there a way to accomplish this? Or do I need to have a separate flag for this parameter setting it to be true or false based on weather I want to send this particular parameter over wire?

I appreciate your help.

Thank You.

nodes.body: There isn't any option or feature to omit values other than the default.

title: NodeJS: String fields retain Int characteristics

nodes.body:
Sorry but although this seems weird to you, it's the intended behavior. Currently we don't have type check for the string field in JS. 
We're working on making JS protobuf format standard, when the standard is ready to go, we'll make some announcement about that.

title: Non-functional fallthrough annotation macro (macOS, C++)
body:
When compiling the simple protocol buffer shown below, there's an implicit fallthrough warning generated even though the fallthrough is annotated with GOOGLE_FALLTHROUGH_INTENDED. This macro appears to be disabled on Apple platforms in ports.h.

macOS: 10.12.4 (16E195)
Clang: Apple LLVM version 8.1.0 (clang-802.0.42) Target: x86_64-apple-darwin16.5.0
Protobuf: 3.3.0

Minimal repro:

test.proto
```
syntax = "proto3";
message TestMsg {
  map<string, string> test = 1;
}
```

```bash
protoc --cpp_out=. test.proto
clang++ -isysroot /Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer/Platforms/MacOSX.platform/Developer/SDKs/MacOSX10.12.sdk  -I/usr/local/include -std=c++11 -Wimplicit-fallthrough  -c test.pb.cc -o test.pb.o -Werror
```

Output:
```
In file included from test.pb.cc:5:
In file included from ./test.pb.h:32:
In file included from /usr/local/include/google/protobuf/map_field_inl.h:40:
In file included from /usr/local/include/google/protobuf/map_field.h:40:
In file included from /usr/local/include/google/protobuf/map_entry.h:35:
/usr/local/include/google/protobuf/map_entry_lite.h:207:9: error: unannotated fall-through between switch labels [-Werror,-Wimplicit-fallthrough]
        case kValueTag:
        ^
test.pb.cc:140:29: note: in instantiation of member function 'google::protobuf::internal::MapEntryImpl<TestMsg::TestMsg_TestEntry, google::protobuf::Message, std::__1::basic_string<char>,
      std::__1::basic_string<char>, google::protobuf::internal::WireFormatLite::FieldType::TYPE_STRING, google::protobuf::internal::WireFormatLite::FieldType::TYPE_STRING, 0>::MergePartialFromCodedStream'
      requested here
TestMsg::TestMsg_TestEntry::TestMsg_TestEntry() {}
                            ^
/usr/local/include/google/protobuf/map_entry_lite.h:207:9: note: insert '[[clang::fallthrough]];' to silence this warning
        case kValueTag:
        ^
        [[clang::fallthrough]]; 
/usr/local/include/google/protobuf/map_entry_lite.h:207:9: note: insert 'break;' to avoid fall-through
        case kValueTag:
        ^
        break; 
1 error generated.
```

nodes.body: I remember GOOGLE_FALLTHROUGH_INTENDED was explicitly disabled on Apple platforms because the fall through annotation just didn't work. It may be fine to enable it now. Could you help send us a pull request?
Closing since GOOGLE_FALLTHROUGH_INTENDED was removed from the code-base.

nodes.body: How is protobuf installed in your test? Does your test just grab the latest version of protobuf?
right now the protobuf python package I pushed to PyPI is the pure python version, so I'm not sure why it tries to reference libprotobuf.so.13 in your test.
It grabs the latest version that is `>=3.2.0, < 4.0.0dev`. So, it opts in to semver minor or patch bumps, but not major ones.
I removed protobuf-3.3.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl from PyPI. Can you rerun the test and see if it makes a difference?
At the moment, I am getting the same error. It still works in Python 3.
Can you try again? I removed another protobuf-3.3.0-py2.7.egg file.

I intended to deploy a pure python version but it seems "python setup.py bdsit_egg bdist_wheel" will actually include lots of temporary files in my workspace and that happens to add "_message.so" to the package. That's the only reason I can think of. Not sure why it works for python 3.x but not python 2.7 though.
This broke for us too. We downgraded back to 3.2.0 and it fixed itself. It appears that rather than use the pure python version it's looking for the shared library.
Fixed: https://travis-ci.org/googleapis/artman/jobs/228147078

title: protoc order of ipaths results in different directory structure
body:
When using messages defined in sub-directories the protobuf compiler (3.2.0) will generate a  different structure based on the order of ipaths entered. 

Assume the following structure : 

/root_dir/root.proto
/root_dir/foo_dir/foo.proto

1.) 
protoc --cpp_out /dest_dir **-I /root_dir** -I /root_dir/foo_dir/ /root_dir/root.proto
protoc --cpp_out /dest_dir **-I /root_dir** -I /root_dir/foo_dir/ /root_dir/foo_dir/foo_file.proto

results in  : 

/dest_dir/root.pb.[cc|h]
/dest_dir/**foo_dir**/foo_file.bp.[cc|h]

2.) 
protoc --cpp_out <somewhere> -I /root_dir/foo_dir/ **-I /root_dir**  /root_dir/root.proto
protoc --cpp_out <somewhere> -I /root_dir/foo_dir/ **-I /root_dir**  /root_dir/foo_dir/foo_file.proto

results in  : 

/dest_dir/root.pb.[cc|h]
/dest_dir/foo_file.bp.[cc|h]

This causes PROTO_SRC/HDR in protobuf_generate_cpp to be wrong for 1.) Please find attached a quick cmake project illustrating the issue. 

1.) tar -zxf protoc_issue.tgz
2.) cd protoc_issue/build
3.) cmake ..; make
[protoc_issue.zip](https://github.com/google/protobuf/files/972255/protoc_issue.zip)

nodes.body:
This is sort of working as intended. Not only the output file path will be different depending on the "-I" flag, the actual content of the generated file will also be different. It works this way because protoc uses the "-I" flag along with the file path to determine an unique import name for each .proto file. For example,
```bash
protoc -I /root_dir /root_dir/foo_dir/foo_file.proto
```
In the above example, the .proto file has an unique import name as "foo_dir/foo_file.proto".
```bash
protoc -I /root_dir/foo_dir /root_dir/foo_dir/foo_file.proto
```
In this example, the .proto file's import name is "foo_file.proto".

This import name is used by the "import" statement and is also the file name if you are to look up its descriptor in protobuf global descriptor pool. As such, you need to make sure the same file always have the same import name across different protoc invocations.

At the moment, the import name is determined by matching the "-I" import path as a prefix of the .proto file path. As such if you happen to have multiple "-I" import path that are prefixes of the .proto file path, order of these "-I" will matter because the matching process is done in command-line order.

The only fix I can think of is the make the matching process match the longest import path first so in your case, /root_dir/foo_dir/foo_file.proto will always be matched to "-I /root_dir/foo_dir", but that's a behavior change and will likely break some users who rely on the current behavior.

It seems to me that more options would resolve the overloading of the Ipath when it comes to determining the import name? I assume something like -r <root_dir> would allow for deterministic import names across multiple protoc invocations without changing current behavior!? 

At the very least the current behavior this should be documented in --help to limit the confusion!?

title: Python "./setup.py sdist/bdist_egg/bdist_wheel" is hard to use correctly.
body:
Several problems:
1. If "./setup.py build" is not ran before "./setup.py sdist", "./setup.py sdist" will create a broken package missing well-known types.
2. If "./setup.py test --cpp_implementation" is ran, "./setup.py bdist_egg/bdist_wheel" will include "google/protobuf/_message.so" in the resulted package and since the package doesn't contain protobuf C++ runtime, it will cause import errors. See an example in https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3042
3. "./setup.py sdist" includes files under python/compatibility_tests and *.h/*.cc files under python/google/protobuf/pyext, which shouldn't be included for pure python implementation.
4. "./setup.py bdist_egg/bdist_wheel" includes generated code of many unittest protos.

(1) and (2) make it very easy to deploy broken packages to PyPI. You must make sure a clean workspace is used and execute the commands in the right order.

What is the status of this ticket? Is this on any roadmap, or is there any work in progress to implement this? Being able to use custom options in PHP would be huge for my team's use case, however it seems this ticket hasn't seen activity for almost 3 years now.

I think PHP support for custom options should be achievable within the next six months.

upb (the C library underlying PHP's extension) will soon be getting support for extensions, which is the last major hurdle to supporting custom options.
Update: This is now supported in upb. We would need to prioritize creating the glue code to make it work.

@haberman  @esorot 

any update?

Custom options are supported in the "upb" C library that underlies that PECL extension, so all external blockers are removed.

But there are several things that would need to be implemented at the PHP layer to offer this feature.

1. We'd need to implement, both in pure-PHP and the PHP C extension, the code to expose options protos from the `*Descriptor` classes. A good model for this would be the Ruby support for descriptor options, which was added somewhat recently in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/14594.
2. We would need to make a decision how to handle immutability for those options protos. In other languages, the returned options are usually immutable, but PHP doesn't currently have any facility for making messages immutable. We would either need to add support for immutability, or have the accessors for options protos return a new copy of the options (ie. not shared).
3. To expose *custom* options, as opposed to built-in options, we'll also need to support extensions in PHP. PHP currently doesn't support extensions, so this would be a new feature in general for message objects.

We don't have anyone working on this currently.

> We would need to make a decision how to handle immutability for those options protos. In other languages, the returned options are usually immutable, but PHP doesn't currently have any facility for making messages immutable. 

PHP has the `readonly` keyword, which is effective immutability. It makes properties "write-once", and throws an error on any attempt to change the value thereafter. See https://php.watch/versions/8.1/readonly

To use `readonly` I think we'd need to have separate types. For example, given a message `Foo`, we currently generated a PHP class `Foo`. Would we also need to generate a separate class `ReadonlyFoo`? That would be a major change to the generated API.

title: Add bytes_value (and possibly others) to the struct.Value well-known-type proto.
body:
google/protobuf/struct.proto defines the Value message, which can represent only values of type NullValue, double, string, bool, Struct or ListValue. It would be very helpful to have a bytes option as well.

This is especially useful when using the Value message in tandem with the ListValue message, and even more so with the map<> feature.

For example, in the following proto:
```
message MyMessage {
    map<string, struct.ListValue> my_map = 1;  // Map from string to a list of strings.
}
```
The generated python code for this gives a very nice syntax:
```
mm = my_pb2.MyMessage(my_map = {"a": ["1", "2", "3"], "b": ["4", "5", "6"]})
```

This can also be done with lists of numbers (although they'll be always coded as double), and with booleans, but can not be done with bytes.

nodes.body: The types in struct.proto is designed to represent JSON values but "bytes" is not an standard JSON value type so it won't be in struct.proto. You should use a string (base64 encoded maybe) instead.

title: Cant deserialize messages from C++ in Javascript
body: Messages serialized in C++ can not be deserialized in JavaScript but it works the other way around

nodes.body: Can you post the proto definition you are using?
@xfxyjwf do you know how can I deserialize data from c++ in javascript?
anyone?
How does your C++ serialization code and Javascript code looks like? I don't see anything special in your proto so it's likely how you send the data from C++ to Javascript that has caused the issue.
Javascript gets the data as a http POST response from a C++ webserver

Can you check if the length of the data is the same on the C++ server before serialization (use ByteSize()) and on the Javascript side before deserialization (check length of the input)? It happens quite often that people only send data partially to a remote end.
the size before serialization in c++ (ByteSize()) is 60 and 59 in before deseralization javascript (.length)

That explains why the javascript parsing fails. My guess is that some data get trunked/corrupted while sending over http. Something to look out for example:
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1509743/what-is-a-good-way-to-transfer-binary-data-to-a-http-rest-api-service

Closing as the problem doesn't seem to be in protobuf.

I got it fixed, responseType should be set to "arraybuffer" for the XHR, for example:

```
$.ajax({
	responseType: "arraybuffer",
	type: 'POST',
	url: url,
	dataType: 'application/octet-stream',
	contentType: 'application/octet-stream',
	cache: false,
	processData: false,
	data: Message.serializeBinary(),
	crossDomain: true,
	success: function(){}
})
```

> responseType should be set to "arraybuffer" for the XHR,

Hello, i meet the same problem. And i am comfused about your solution. Can you explain it in detail? Thank you very much.

`ArrayBuffer` is used to store binary data in javascript (for example, you would use it to store a video file you want to process in javascript)

protocol buffers uses binary data.

`responseType: "arraybuffer"` is telling it to not "process" the data and read it raw just as it is.... as an example `responseType: "json"` is telling it to create a json object from the data meaning it wouldn't require you to use 'JSON.parse(data)` to access json data sent by the server, while using `responseType: "text"` would require `JSON.parse(data)`.
was `arraybuffer` set on the client side?

title: 16 bit integer / unsigned integer support AND/OR FP16 support

In tensorflow it would be useful to define an FP16 type.  Since many compilers don't support this natively, uint16 is used as an equivalent for storage and transmission.

nodes.body: It's unlikely that we will ever add a new field type to protobuf. The only viable solution is to use the length-delimited field type to mimic other field types but it also doesn't actually save anything compared to uint32.

title: Timestamp TZ offsets
body: The [timestamp.proto](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/timestamp.proto#L106) file documents that only UTC (Z suffix) is supported. The conformance tests [TimestampWithPositiveOffset](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/conformance/conformance_test.cc#L1996) and [TimestampWithNegativeOffset](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/conformance/conformance_test.cc#L2000) require other TZ offsets as well. Please correct one or the other.

nodes.body: The JSON serializer must only use Z suffix, but the parser should accept other timezones. The comment in timestamp.proto needs some more clarification.

title: MergeFrom: add option to replace instead of append repeated fields
body:
could we have an option in MergeFrom to replace instead of append repeated fields? It's a more natural behavior.
It would occur when the 2nd message contains elements of that repeated field.

nodes.body:
What language are you referring to?
On Wed, May 17, 2017 at 14:06 Timothee Cour <notifications@github.com>
wrote:

> could we have an option in MergeFrom to replace instead of append repeated
> fields? It's a more natural behavior.
> It would occur when the 2nd message contains elements of that repeated
> field.
>
> —
> You are receiving this because you are subscribed to this thread.
> Reply to this email directly, view it on GitHub
> <https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3106>, or mute the thread
> <https://github.com/notifications/unsubscribe-auth/AE9H5d6Nj8SYww5Kc55z3ZSTkUX-BXMQks5r62FMgaJpZM4NecEl>
> .
>

@timotheecour We would probably be hesitant to implement this feature, because usually we don't want to take on the maintenance commitment of a new option unless there's a pretty compelling reason for it. What's your use case for this behavior? Note that the current behavior does make sense when you consider that it's consistent with MergeFromCodedStream and MergePartialFromCodedStream--when we're parsing we want new repeated field elements to be appended and so it makes some sense that MergeFrom does the same.

It's unlikely that we will ever introduce such an option to generated MergeFrom API. You can though implement the merging behavior using proto reflection API. You can take a look at FieldMaskUtil which has an example MergeFrom() implementation that allows you to replace repeated fields rather than appending.

A lot of people are using Protobuf to represent arbitrary large data sets (though I know this isn't its original purpose). It is very common to want to change the data with some kind of small delta instead of re-transmitting the entire large data set. For example, using Protobuf for a configuration file that's shared on client or server and wanting to modify the configuration for an A/B test. Or using Protobuf to store a user's data on client and server. In these cases, we take the server version, create a "delta" version of the message, merge the delta into the server version, then send the "delta" to the client and merge that there. We've now modified client and server data without sending the whole data. But in this delta case, the "mergeFrom" appends repeated fields which is far from the desired behavior. Replacing the repeated field works as long as the delta includes the entire repeated array. Ideally, the arrays would smart merge (if the original has elements 1-9 the other 1-7, then 1-7 would be replaced and 8-9 would remain).

Anyway, I understand that this use case is not the original intent of Protobuf, but patterns like this are used a lot which is why people keep requesting it.

Just my 2 cents, I'd also like to have this possibility.
Got a similar use-case as @doom-goober.

Protobuf Java

title: Improper implementation of PHP Autoloader
body:
The [PHP Autoloader](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/composer.json#L20) is including the class files at the start of each request instead of using proper PSR standards. This means if the `protobuf.so` C extension is used in tandem with this library, a fatal error is thrown due to the classes being redeclared.

If the classes are split into files based on their classnames, and `Classmap` or `PSR-0` is used for the autoloading instead of `files`, this will be resolved.

nodes.body:
Here's the error if I load the protobuf via both composer and pecl

```
PHP Fatal error:  Cannot redeclare class Google\Protobuf\Internal\Descriptor in /home/stanleycheung/grpc/examples/php/vendor/google/protobuf/php/src/Google/Protobuf/descriptor.php on line 96
PHP Stack trace:
PHP   1. {main}() /home/stanleycheung/grpc/examples/php/route_guide/route_guide_client.php:0
PHP   2. require() /home/stanleycheung/grpc/examples/php/route_guide/route_guide_client.php:35
PHP   3. ComposerAutoloaderInitdcce3c6391bcbad0cee5c2b1d4bfac07::getLoader() /home/stanleycheung/grpc/examples/php/vendor/autoload.php:7
PHP   4. composerRequiredcce3c6391bcbad0cee5c2b1d4bfac07() /home/stanleycheung/grpc/examples/php/vendor/composer/autoload_real.php:56
PHP   5. require() /home/stanleycheung/grpc/examples/php/vendor/composer/autoload_real.php:66
```

I don't think the php implementation and c extension are supposed to be used together.
What's the use case?

The use case is that, if a user decides to install the protobuf C extension (for better performance), they usually would have "extension=protobuf.so" added to the `php.ini` file. So every time PHP is loaded, the protobuf C classes will be loaded.

Now let's say the user is also using some other composer packages. And thru dependency, the `google/protobuf` composer package is pulled in. That will create the error above.

So it's less about user deliberately using both at the same time. But as a consequence of using composer.

@TeBoring they aren't supposed to be used together, but also they shouldn't throw a PHP fatal error if they are accidentally used together. There's no reason for this, since PHP's autoloader is only activated when a class is missing.

One use case is if you have a user install a library requiring `grpc/grpc`, and they have the `grpc.so` extension installed, the library calls will work out of the box if `google/protobuf` is also required. However, if they'd like to optimize the protobuf layer, they can enable the `protobuf.so` extension at any time and are immediately making calls to the C library. This provides an easy default path and an easy upgrade path, without requiring every user to manage this themselves.
This was resolved in #3123

title: Split PHP directory into sub-repo for composer
body:
As composer has a strict one-package-per-repository rule, the only way to avoid pulling in the entire `protobuf` repository instead of just the files relevant to PHP is to split this out into its own repository.

As a result, the package `google/protobuf` contains `32M` of data and `1912` files. The only files needed are in `php/src`, which contains 110 files which combined are less than a single megabyte. This means we are pulling down more than **30x the data** required when installing this package.

Additionally, platforms like App Engine [limit the number of files](https://cloud.google.com/appengine/quotas) that can be uploaded. Repositories like this consume a sizable chunk of that limit for no reason.

Can we make a subtree-split for php (`google/protobuf-php`)? This could be mirrored and versioned automatically, and is already being done for other composer packages for php (see [google-cloud-php](https://github.com/googlecloudplatform/google-cloud-php) vs [google-cloud-php-bigquery](https://github.com/googlecloudplatform/google-cloud-php-bigquery)). There is also an open ticket to do this for grpc (https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/10489)

nodes.body: We need to verify we can make this change w/o breaking composer compatibility.

Composer respects `.gitattributes`, and anything marked as [`export-ignore`](https://feeding.cloud.geek.nz/posts/excluding-files-from-git-archive/) will not be installed by composer. We use this in [google/cloud](https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-php/blob/master/.gitattributes), and we could use it to ignore the `src` directory. However, this could have unintended effects with other tools using gitattributes. 

`export-ignore` is for exporting the git repository as a tar/zip. So making it only export the PHP directory here would not be semantically correct.
This is a P1!

In our new repo, we have already changed this:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-php/blob/master/composer.json
I think it's composer's work. We cannot do anything.
@wsamoht sorry for the inconvenience, we were under the impression this change would be transparent.
No prob :) Appreciate the response!

title: PHP: Using native types in place of proto types

nodes.body: See https://github.com/googleapis/toolkit/issues/1273
@michaelbausor this issue could (and maybe should be) be solved at the GAPIC layer

This can certainly be solved in the GAPIC layer, as described in the toolkit issue you linked to above, and this may be the best option. (In fact, we already have similar functionality implemented in the google-cloud-php library which is used by logging, pubsub and spanner).

One reason to prefer implementing this in protobuf instead of the GAPIC layer (perhaps in the long term) is that we would implement this functionality in our GAX library (https://github.com/googleapis/gax-php), but if it is a real usability win then it makes sense to make it available to other users of protobuf.

Is Timestamp the only one needs to be taken care of?
For timestamp, I think it's ok to accept DateTime for setter.
We don't need to change the return value for getter, right?

I don't think we should change the return type of the getter. I think Timestamp/DateTime is the only one, @bshaffer are there any others you know of?

The toolkit issue linked above (https://github.com/googleapis/toolkit/issues/1273) describes how the generated GAPIC layer could accept an associative array in place of a protobuf message, with keys matching the fields to be set. This is a change in our surface that can be done independently from protobuf, but if using an associative array is a good feature for users, then we may want to consider supporting it directly in protobuf. This could be one or both of:
- Accepting an associative array in the constructor
- Accepting an associative array in the setter methods for message fields

Maybe this should be split into a separate issue?

I agree that we shouldn't change the return type of the getter.

Is there still a desire for the setter to accept different types like DateTime?
Going to close due to no response. If you still want this, please reopen with more information.

nodes.body:
This has been opened since 2017, and there are many disparate fragments and variations of the proto gmock matchers floating around. It would be great to have an officially maintained version.

Are there any plans to do this?

We triage inactive PRs and issues in order to make it easier to find active work. If this issue should remain active or becomes active again, please add a comment.

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago.
Has there been any progress on this?

We triage inactive PRs and issues in order to make it easier to find active work. If this issue should remain active or becomes active again, please add a comment.

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago. This issue will be closed and archived after 14 additional days without activity.

Hello,

The reason that this hasn't been done after all this time is due to a slightly-weird ownership model. Matchers like `EqualsProto` are not owned by GoogleTest. Internally `EqualsProto` uses MessageDifferencer that actually does the matching, and of course, we own MessageDifferencer.

I think the right way to think about this is that the core GoogleTest shouldn't need to know about protobufs. If anything, Protobuf should depend on GoogleTest, instead of the other way around.

Internally within Google though, GoogleTest folks are the ones supporting matchers like `EqualsProto`, while we support MessageDifferencer. This isn't a big deal if you have a monorepo like Google, but in the open source world every package has a different repo, "lockstep changes" can be harder to make.

Expanding a bit on what I mean by "lockstep changes": imagine there is a single change in GoogleTest that necessitated changes in something like `EqualsProto`. Now in order to export this change, two PRs needs to be sent simultaneously to both GoogleTest and Protobuf, and integration tests for each repo will fail, because they are still running with the old version of protobuf/googletest.

I think this is something we want to open source eventually, because Google is using/starting more and more third party projects -- and not being able have `EqualsProto` etc can be quite a pain. We just need to figure out the support story here first.
This seems related to https://github.com/google/googletest/issues/1761

title: [Proposal] Async version of CSharp protobuf
body:
I would like to implement support for async/await versions of all methods dealing with I/O.

## Rationale
Mixing async and sync code in C# is very inefective thread-wise. It is a good practise to have entire code top-down async, but the worst case-scenario is when synchronous code calls async code like in case of Stream.Read and Stream.Write.

Today the only way to efficiently use protobuf in async code is to copy buffers to the memory and then perform deserialization synchronously. What makes it virtually impossible to use protobuf in streaming scenarios with near-to-constant memory.

## Background
Lately there have been many improvements to the TPL to allow more efficient (allocation-wise) handling of many scenarious especially parser-like where most of methods return synchronously. ValueTask and Task.CompletedTask are the most important of those improvements.

## High-level plan
1. Duplicate all I/O-bound methods in the following manner:
ReturnType MethodName(Arguments) 
to
async ValueTask<ReturnType> MethodNameAsync(Arguments, CancellationToken cancellationToken)

void MethodName(Arguments)
to
async Task MethodNameAsync(Arguments, CancellationToken cancellationToken)

And all references in async methods to those methods with await CalledMethodAsync(..., cancellationToken)

This way we have perfectly correct implementation (but not optimal, especially allocation-wise).

Replace all calls to Stream.Read/Write with proper ReadAsync/WriteAsync

2. After testing this version start optimizations:
a. Remove constructs like async await = where possible
b. Try to use as much of ValueTask<T> and Task.CompletedTask as possible.
c. Try to inline some async calls to avoid generation of separate state-machines

3. Modify code-generator to generate async variants.

I would be happy to create PR for this proposal.

However I believe optimization will be a bit longer process, going far beyond this single PR.

nodes.body:
I would strongly suggest not using `ValueTask` or any C# 7 features that require additional dependencies. Any dependencies we add - or additional requirements for more recent frameworks - will add a toll in terms of maintenance and may reduce the potential audience. Creating regular async methods for parsing is more reasonable, although it's tricky in terms of the *generated* code... if any code needs to be generated with async methods, that would probably need to be specified via an option, as otherwise it could very easily break existing users. (And it seems likely - without having looked at this at all yet in detail - that it really *would* require additions to generated code.

More worryingly, it may require additions to interfaces, which basically can't happen due backwards compatibility. You may well want to look at an `IAsyncMessage` interface or similar.

"ValueTasks should be working without any problems on top of .NET Standard" - not without adding a new dependency. Adding any dependency to a widely-used library is fraught with problems. `ValueTask` isn't in netstandard1.x at all - it's in netcoreapp1.0, and obviously it's not in net45 either. And no, we're not going to just arbitrarily stop supporting net45. (I'm working in the opposite direction, hoping to support .NET 3.5 and Unity in the future.)

My aim wouldn't be nearly as aggressive as yours of removing all heap allocations. If you really want to do that, just do all the *reading* asynchronously into a `MemoryStream` and then just use the synchronous protobuf parsing code. If any of the I/O is asynchronous, you'll end up with the allocations even with `ValueTask` anyway.

I can see a benefit in having *optional* async code generated and async code using just `Task<T>` in the support library - no new dependencies, and by default still only generating the synchronous code to avoid taking a dependency on the C# 5 compiler. But adding dependencies, breaking backwards compatibility for older C# compilers from the generated code, and moving the frameworks we target? They're not a roadmap I'd support.

Of course, the Protobuf team could go ahead with that anyway - I'm just a contributor - but I'd strongly recommend against it.

I see you point. However I am not sure whether Unity isn't going towards .NET Standard as well (but I don't use Unity).

OK. So we basically expect different things from this library. I expect ultra-high performance serialization library where it's worth to use latest developments in .NET CoreFX. And you expect widely supported and widely compatible. But it is impossible to have both of these goals in a single library.

I had many perf ideas including using for example buffers rental (I have seen new byte[1024] in code way too many times :) - I understand now - buffer rental requires System.Buffers... ), adding streaming serialization support, better struct support.

But this is exactly the opposite direction you want this library to go. I am aware that you are the author of the original code, and I definitely don't want to push against you. So I will probably end up creating an unsupported fork.

BTW. How does MemoryStream avoid heap allocations as it is itself allocated on heap (even on LOH)? And with it's reallocation algorithm it is the most useless of doom class in entire .NET Framework responsible for most OutOfMemoryException people have due to LOH fragmentation. But I get your point about pre-buffering (using something better than MemoryStream) the data and using the current synchronous code. I have even mentioned this approach in the Rationale.

What I wanted, is to use as many stack allocations as possible. C# is not Java and you can do a lot of perfwork here.

To sum up: doing async without ValueTask is basically non-sense in this specific case. If you can't accept ValueTasks, I understand. And I will not pursue this PR here.

In terms of MemoryStream and the heap allocations: you'd load the data into a single MemoryStream (which could potentially be pooled and reused) - but then you'd know that everything would be synchronous, so you'd just use the sync code instead of async, so you wouldn't end up with lots of tasks being allocated.

I still don't accept that it's pointless to do async without `ValueTask`, but I wish you well with your private fork. You'll certainly be able to move a lot faster without the limitations that a public, widely used (in a large variety of situations) library has.

If you really think it's not pointless to do async without ValueTask in this specific case, then I can create a PR with the 1st step of my Proposal (except with Task instead of ValueTask), and then I can do performance optimizations in my fork.

We can then do then some benchmarks to see if they are worth and maybe it will be easier to make an informed decision about ValueTasks based on some hard number.

Does this sound reasonable?

I'll see whether I can get time to review the PR later this week. I've been thinking about the parser part, and I wonder whether it may be feasible to do it all with extension methods on the parser instead. But let's get to that later...

It's only feasible as much as some of the synchronous could be moved to an extension class and even if we do it's a terrible moment because I will want to do some perf-work focusing on replacing as many async functions as possible with their synchronous versions (still returning Tasks - don't worry ;) ) (to avoid compiler-generated state-machines and unnecessary allocations).

I've started looking now, mostly at the class/interface hierarchy around messages and parsers.

Are there reasons why we need to have a single parser for both, rather than having an async parser entirely separate from a sync parser? I wouldn't normally be suggesting that, but basically `AsyncMessageParser<T>` really wants to derive from both `AsyncMessageParser` and `MessageParser` at the moment, which makes things weird.

Separating the two would also leave more room for the option of not generating the synchronous code at all - so you could have:

- Sync only: `Parser` property, of type `MessageParser<T>`
- Async only: `AsyncParser` property, of type `AsyncMessageParser<T>`

We'd need to think about JSON parsing for the async case... I wonder whether that could wait for the moment though.

I also feel that the class hierarchy is a bit sloppy... but had no better idea.

To be honest I feel like it would take a considerable amount of time to get before we get async version to be as fast as synchronous version in a synchronous scenario, but this **might** happen eventually (I really hope so). But that's a good future-proof idea.

You very often have synchronous parsing even in full async async scenarios for example sub-message parsing (Any-type).

OK. It was 2 week ago so I don't remember all the details, but I will try to recall most important reasons:
1. We would need to keep both parsers in `FieldCodec`, `GeneratedClrTypeInfo`
2. Single parser is a bit more convenient
3. Memory is not an issue here: because it's like an additional pointer because it would not even save a single field, because for performance reasons event class factory is duplicated...

On the other hand I don't like original class hierarchy as well. For example I don't see a good reason to have `MessageParser<T>` inherit `MessageParser` instead of implementing IMessageParser. actually going this way would allow to save memory on `Func<IMessage>` factory.

So my recommendation would be:
1. make `MessageParser` => `IMessageParser` interface
2. make `AsyncMessageParser` => `IAsyncMessageParser` interface
3. make AsyncMessageParser impelement both interfaces (even if it involves a bit copy-and-paste)

And here we save yet-another-class-factory - with much cleaner hierarchy.

UPDATE:

Fun fact: https://github.com/aspnet/Announcements/issues/252

Regarding codegen order: not sure if this is a case here, but It's very important to have proper order of nested class declarations and descriptor declarations as it causes static constructors to fail due to undefined static fields.

Current order was made to what I've felt was a good compromise of: correctness (aforementioned descriptor/nested order), not complicating codegen code too much and having a reasonable layout. I am not going to push on a specific order or partial classes.

I don't see many potential benefits here and it can be easily changed without affecting the generated binaries.

BTW. Regarding class hierarchy: what would be your opinion on:
1. Introducing IMessageParser interface
2. deprecating MessageParser with a suggestion to use IMessageParser? 

I fully understand we cannot remove MessageParser class in a minor version.

First comment: Okay, I'm fine with it as it is.

Second comment: I'd rather not deprecate MessageParser when we don't really need to. I don't think it would provide any *concrete* benefits, to be honest.

I'd like to come back to async this quarter. I think we could use `ValueTask` within Google.Protobuf, but just `Task` within the generated code. @mkosieradzki: what's your current thinking around your PR? Any changes you want to make to it, given the time that's elapsed?

@jskeet 
ValueTasks (AFAIK) and other .NET Standard features did finally make into the full .NET Framework (4.7.1). However the corefx team did some mistakes in the way they designed in-boxing of the .NET Standard added-on features into the core .NET Framework. IMO it would be worth monitoring whether we are or we are not affected here.

After this incident: dotnet/corefx#24653 . I can say you were right being skeptical toward using nuget package bundled new framework features (despite ValueTask specifically was not affected AFAIK). However before incorporating ValueTasks I would be very careful to see how they handle this specific case.

Also: I have second thoughts in the area of `Span<T>` - because I definitely think it's a good idea to use `Span<T>` / `Memory<T>` instead of `byte[]` but there are also many unknown variables here. And `Span<T>` has additional implications because it's an ultra-fast stack-only type (ref struct) what means it will require significant changes to the way CodedInputStream is implemented, but also *might* be incompatible with async (obviously stack works differently in async).

So there are serious considerations here in terms of the API re-design and it would be a good idea to avoid changes in future.

This is all no ultra-serious, however just pointing out some risks and opportunities - I have learned since our last pass here.

And yes: `Task` in the generated code and ValueTask in the hot-path. Avoid async-generated in the hot-path.

I'd definitely like to separate out the span part from the async part, unless there's some reason we need to tackle them together.

Thanks for the heads-up on the `ValueTask` issue - we definitely want careful testing of this in multiple environments.

I agree. The only reason to tackle them together is that both require significant API redesign and both redesigns might be affecting each other. However IMO it's way to early to tackle `Span<T>`. I think that the proper moment would be after JIT and compiler optimizations are in place and we will be able to collect meaningful perf data.

So let's focus on async only.

Just to be sure (those names are very similar ;) ) this specific issue is for `ValueTuple` not `ValueTask` but the other one might be affected as well. Unfortunately `System.Buffers` is affected too - and I wanted to replace all the local buffer allocations with buffer rentals: dotnet/corefx#24716 .

I think it's definitely worth trying to work out an endpoint in terms of all the possible options, then consider how we want to get there - it would be a real shame to make a change in one direction that then limited us for another option.

I'll be learning a lot more about `Span<T>` this month, so will have a more informed viewpoint soon...

I had some spare time to implement and run tens of experiments in area of parsing using `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySequence<T>`, `Pipe` and I have made following observations:

1. Parser on Spans is more roughly 10% percent more efficient than existing parser on .NET Core 2.1 preview 2. It also does zero allocations and is able to work using only single externally provided span.
2. Asynchronous parser using non-contiguous memory from `Pipe` is roughly 3x slower than the original parser. It is also zero alloc.
3. Parser from point 2 with additional heuristic - trying to get contiguous span buffer and then use parser from 1 otherwise 2 is comparable performance-wise to 1. Worst case ~1.7 times slower. It can be also optimized to use have more contiguous memory “hits” by either increasing min buffer size in pipe from 2048 to something larger or by using stackallocated Span. Both are still zero GC alloc as they are using either stack memory or slab allocator from Pipe.
4. I have also tried to measure alternative parser generated abstraction using interface (virtual calls), but their performance impact is huge so a more generic code gen is probably irrelevant.

Conclusions:
According to my reasearch we need to generate three additional methods:
```
ValueTask SlowMergeFromAsync(CodedInputReader, CancellationToken)
ValueTask MergeFromAsync(CodedInputReader, CancellationToken)
void MergeFrom(ReadOnlySpan<T>)
```

`MergeFromAsync` will attempt to acquire a contiguous buffer and pass it to `MergeFrom`, otherwise fallback to `SlowMergeFromAsync`.

`MergeFrom` will be an optimal span-based parser.
`SlowMergeFromAsync` will be a generated-state machine (`async`) for asynchronous parsing of huge messages either not fitting a single buffer or streamed too slowly...

I will try to start implementing a proper PR soon, unless you see some downsides to this approach. I think we can also improve in future `CodedInputStream` implementation to use a Span-based parser where buffer is large enough.
I forgot describe what a `CodedInputReader` is: https://github.com/mkosieradzki/protobuf/blob/spans/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf.Pipelines/CodedInputReader.cs

I think its fine to add support for Async as long as it doesn't replace the existing synchronous APIs. The code I write normally has custom threading implementations and I don't want to rely on the thread pool used by Async.

Now that Dotnet 5 and 6 are out and there is consensus about where the language is moving, many of the concerns raised early on in this issue may be resolved.

Definitely would love to see this implemented.

title: Should message descriptors should link to message classes?
body: In generated Python code there are [message descriptors](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python/google.protobuf.descriptor.Descriptor-class) (reachable by way of the module-level `my_generated_module_pb2.DESCRIPTOR` and possibly also the global descriptor pool) and generated message classes (available as module-scope code elements). The generated message classes link to their respective descriptors (`my_generated_module_pb2.MyGeneratedClass.DESCRIPTOR`), but the descriptors don't seem to link to the classes. Should they? Why not?

nodes.body:
The descriptor describes a type whereas the generated class is one implementation of the type. Usually multiple implementations exist for the same type, so the descriptor can not be tied to a specific implementation. For example, in C++/Java, we have a DynamicMessage class which can use the same descriptor used by generated classes. In google3 where proto1 is still a thing, we even have multiple generated classes with the same descriptor.

Although there is no direct link from descriptor to the generated class, there is usually a factory class to provide such mapping. In python I believe the MessageFactory class does that.

title: Cardinality (streaming versus non-streaming, and in each direction) information available from descriptors?

nodes.body: I guess it's just not implemented in python protobuf yet. The MethodDescriptor in python should have a client_streaming and a server_streaming attribute just like in C++.

Neither CPP, Java or Python mention these at all: 
  - https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_service.cc
  - https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_service.cc
  - https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/python/python_generator.cc

On the other hand, the grpc implementations use them.
  - https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/src/compiler/protobuf_plugin.h

Question is: is there a plan on implementing these?

title: Bug Report: The output file location of `protoc` is not expected under certain circumstances.
body:
protobuf version: 3.2
System: Ubuntu 16.04

When `--proto-path` is specified twice with certain setup, the `--cpp_out` will not be the direct output directory. 

Set up 
* .proto file: `~/project/proto/main.proto`
* another .proto file: `~/project/proto/shared.proto`

Process
1. change directory to `~/project/build/`
2. run 
    `/usr/local/bin/protoc --cpp_out ~/project/build/ -I ~/project/ -I ~/project/proto/ ~/project/proto/hello.proto `

Result
Output files are under `~/project/build/proto/` but not `~/project/build/`, which is unexpected.

3. Remove first ipath:
  `/usr/local/bin/protoc --cpp_out ~/project/build/  -I ~/project/proto/ ~/project/proto/hello.proto `

Result
Output files are under `~/project/build/`, which is expected.

nodes.body: The correct command line parameter for --cpp_out is: protoc --cpp_out=~/project/build/

@adhesiveNOR  both forms are valid.

Part of the mechanism is explained in :
https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3044

Seems like searching in ipath is recursive. It goes deep down to the every leaf of directory tree. Multiple ipath are assigned priorities.

The directory layout of generated files is determined by their import name (the name you use in the 'import "path/to/other.proto";' statement to import that .proto file) and the import name as I explained in https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3044 is determined by matching the .proto file path against the --proto_path flags in order.

For
```bash
/usr/local/bin/protoc --cpp_out ~/project/build/ -I ~/project/ -I ~/project/proto/ ~/project/proto/hello.proto
```
The import name is "proto/hello.proto" because ~/project/proto/hello.proto matches the first "-I ~/project", and as such protoc will generate ~/project/build/proto/hellp.pb.h|cc.

If you instead do
```bash
/usr/local/bin/protoc --cpp_out ~/project/build/ -I ~/project/proto -I ~/project ~/project/proto/hello.proto
```
The import name will be "hello.proto" because "-I ~/project/proto" will be matched first.

Usually it's better to just put all .proto files in a single directory tree and specify the -I flag only once on the command line. More complex setup is usually not necessary and is very easy to get it wrong.

title: JsonFormat int64 converting
body:
Hi. Why int64(long in java) convert to string?
```java
case INT64:       
case SINT64:
case SFIXED64:
          generator.print("\"" + ((Long) value).toString() + "\"");
          break;
```

nodes.body:
It's required by proto3 JSON spec:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json

It's because int64 is not a standard JSON type and many JSON parsers don't support int64 precision. To avoid precision loss for int64, we decided to print int64 as strings in proto3 JSON.

title: why defaut value is not returned

nodes.body: ![qq 20170608155557](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3361705/26918060-030461ae-4c63-11e7-8a03-11ba2eeb59cd.jpg)

Seems like an optimization. To me it appears that serializing the message to text skips outputting any fields that are currently their default value. This saves space since you don't need to explicitly store a field that is the same as its default value. 

De-Serializing the output text back into a message would have the missing '2:0' you point out available, since it doesn't see a value for that field in the text being imported, it will automatically set that field to its default value.

Addendum:
Serializing to text with protobuff is not intended to be used to print out the results for display. The Serialization is intended to minimize needed space to either store or transmit the message, while ensuring that the message can be parsed back in from text with all fields intact. 

When a field is still set to it's default value it can be safely ignored when serializing the message, since the parser doing the de-serialization will automatically fill in the correct default value for that field.

title: Python including_default_value_fields does not work for singular message types
body:
Looks like `google.protobuf.json_format._RegularMessageToJsonObject` intentionally skips over singular message types, which results singular message types and the Struct WKT being omitted in the JSON output even with `including_default_value_fields = True`.

The default values for Struct WKT should serialize to `{}` and singular message types to `null` respectively.

nodes.body:
It is documented "Singular message fields and oneof fields are not affected by this option."
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/39f9b43219bc5718b659ed72a2130a7b2ce66108/python/google/protobuf/json_format.py#L96


It is in Proto3 JSON Specification design doc that all protobuf languages are following this behavior

@anandolee I believe the Proto3 JSON spec does state that the default value for message type as well as the WKT wrapper types can be null. The Python json_format module currently does not seem to conform to the spec.

As an example, the Go protobuf jsonpb module correctly serializes unset message and WKT wrapper types as null when the emit defaults option is set to true.

Proto3 JSON spec states "When parsing, a null value is accepted for all field types." But for serialize, it states "A serializer could provide an option to always serialize fields with default values. This option will affect singular primitive fields, repeated fields and map fields. Singular message fields and oneof fields will not be affected by this option. "

@xfxyjwf who wrote Proto3 JSON spec. Do you think it is a bug for Go?

@anandolee If this helps clarify, at least for the WKT wrappers.proto types: "Wrappers use the same representation in JSON as the wrapped primitive type, except that null is allowed and preserved during data conversion and transfer.", specifically the part about preserving null values during data conversion/transfer.

In this case even w/ including_default_value_fields = True, we currently just omit the fields corresponding to the unset WKT wrapper types (StringValue, DoubleValue, etc...).

@ewang The comment of "null is allowed and preserved during data conversion and transfer" is probably a bit misleading. It doesn't mean "null" will always be printed in proto3 JSON. Actually all implementations I know of by default don't print "null" value in JSON. The comment is supposed to mean "unlike regular primitive types, a null value for wrapper type can be distinguished from 0 (or false), and that state is maintained in proto-to-JSON and proto-to-binary conversion".

As to whether it should print a null value if including_default_value_fields = true, I don't have strong opinion either way. Both should be accepted and treated the same by proto3 JSON parser. What's your use case for a null value of absent singular message fields?

Singular message fields are different from primitive fields. This difference is a special-case in proto3 design in a sense. I don't feel like there is a need to make singular message fields behave more like primitive fields. Right now we don't print fields that support field presence but are unset. That includes singular message fields and oneof fields. The current behavior is actually consistent in that perspective.

In any case, I don't think not printing null values will cause any interoperability issues. If you actually need it to be printed as null for some reason, we can consider that and probably provide a different flag. But otherwise python json_format is working as intended.

@xfxyjwf Would you say the official stance on the default value for message types as well as WKT types such as IntValue, StringValue, DoubleValue, etc is undefined and thus not included in the output when including_default_value_fields is set to True?

@ewang Singular message fields support field presence, so it can be present or not present, and there are APIs to check their presence. If a singular message field is not present, it will not be included in JSON output.

```
$ ls -l ./Pods/Headers/Public/Protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h
lrwxr-xr-x  1 paulbeusterien  eng  57 Mar 27 10:41 ./Pods/Headers/Public/Protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h -> ../../../Protobuf/objectivec/google/protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h
```
That's what I'm seeing as well. Can I resolve this warning by modifying my local setup, or should a change be made to the CocoaPod? If the latter, should this issue be reopened?

So clang is following the symlink and looking at the path the link cocoapods created resolves too?

And just because it happens to have the same name (but different case), clang kicks out this warning?  But if the target directory had a different name, clang would probably go silent?

If that's the case, it sounds more like pushing this over to clang for looking at the resolved path vs. the path the header was found at is the right "solution".

Ah, now I better understand your earlier comments about clang, thanks. I started to put together a sample project for a radar, and noticed I can only repro the issue with:
 1. A Swift project
 1. `Firebase/Firestore`, which depends on `Protobuf`

I could not repro the issue by using `Firebase/Firestore` in your TestApp Obj-C project above, or by using `Protobuf` in my Swift project. This is the project: [TestApp (Swift with Firestore).zip](https://github.com/google/protobuf/files/1854645/TestApp.Swift.with.Firestore.zip)

@thomasvl, does this change your understanding of the problem, or should I go ahead with the radar?

Two other notes:

 - I was able to silence the warnings by making this change: https://github.com/lehrblogger/protobuf/commit/8d7916caf859a5ad174849b5beb090c57f3c6d9f. You can verify by uncommenting the line in the `Podfile` that points to my fork (but you'll need to `rm Podfile.lock` before re-running `pod install`).
 - [This Sack Overflow comment](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/43067017/non-portable-path-to-file-file-h-specified-path-differs-in-case-from-file-na#comment73217482_43067018) suggests relatively-recent changes to clang for APFS might explain why this started happening.

I haven't gotten a chance to look at your example, but answering the other parts:

I'd go ahead and file the radar, point out how the Framework/include is clearly done via the capital 'P' version, but since it points to a symlink under the hood, clang is checking the wrong path.

Your change - yea, it makes sense that that "fixes" it, but just like you couldn't get the warning in other situations with different links/directory structures, I'd expect that change to result in warnings in the other cases where the change would now be wrong compared to the real paths on disk.  i.e. - it works in one condition, but not the other.

Stack Overflow comment - Yea, I sorta figured they added the warning to help developers with the migration from cases insensitive files systems to case sensitive ones.  But they seem to be looking are a symlink resolved path instead of the path clang actually found the file via.  So while trying to help with one filesystem issue, the coded another one.  😮

I also tried a bit to repro in [a smaller example](https://github.com/paulb777/CaseBug) yesterday and failed.

I did verify that moving `Pods/Protobuf/objectivec/google/protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h` to another location and linking `./Pods/Headers/Public/Protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h` eliminated the build warning:

```
mv ./Pods/Protobuf/objectivec/google/protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h ~/backup
rm ./Pods/Headers/Public/Protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h
ln -s ~/backup/Any.pbobjc.h  ./Pods/Headers/Public/Protobuf/Any.pbobjc.h
```

So +1 on the radar, but there is something in addition to the symbolic link to the lower-cased directory that is necessary to trigger the issue that we don't fully understand yet.

Renaming the pod and module would require migration for CocoaPods clients. A better CocoaPods solution is renaming the header directory.  I sent a PR doing this at #6190.
Can confirm renaming the Protobuf directory solved all errors for me.

#6190 doesn't work since while it renames the directory, the directory actually comes from the input paths of the files that are generated, so the next time they regenerate (especially on a case sensitive file system), the lower case names would be recreated.

It seems there is a solution for this.
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/28789807/how-to-rename-a-cocoapod

Publish a new pod and deprecate the current.
https://guides.cocoapods.org/syntax/podspec.html#deprecated_in_favor_of

Yes, that process can work, but if someone depends on the pod via two dependencies, they need them both to update at the same time otherwise they will get two copies of the code (thru the differing names) and that will result is duplicate copies of the code that conflict.

If they directly directly depend on the pod it is pretty easy, it is when they are transitive that is quickly gets hard because they need other things to update.

Would `module_name` solve the issue without a new pod?
https://github.com/CocoaPods/CocoaPods/blob/master/lib/cocoapods/target/pod_target.rb#L244

related: https://github.com/CocoaPods/CocoaPods/issues/6683
@BugsBunnyBR Good idea!  It seems to work in #6464

#6803 got opened which seems to loop back to this original problem, and it seems `module_name` doesn't fully work, from some of the paths there is looks like maybe cocoapods isn't always using the right name for things so we get different cases in different places, and if running on a case sensitive file system, things then choke?

Anyway, for those that were on this issue, you might want to track the other one also, as this could still be a problem in some configurations.

title: Using Library Without Download
body:
I am trying to use the google protobuf library without having to download the whole library and run through ./configure, make, make check, ... I am currently putting the protoc executable in /usr/local/bin and the google folder in /usr/local/include. When I try running my program, I get this error

`/usr/local/bin/protoc: 1: /usr/local/bin/protoc: Syntax error: "(" unexpected`

What am I doing wrong? What can I do to get my program working correctly? My program is somewhat similar to the example code in C++. I have also tested using the example code given and the same problem occurs.

I am obtaining the protoc executable and the google folder from "protoc-3.3.0-linux-x86_32.zip". I am working on a Raspberry Pi 3 Model B.

nodes.body: How did you invoke protoc? And how does your .proto file look like?

I am calling protoc by calling make in the examples folder. My .proto file is also the same one from the examples folder. I am now just trying to get the example working. I am starting with a new machine, copying the "examples" folder over, then putting the protoc executable in /usr/local/bin and the google folder in /usr/local/include.

I wish to just use the examples add_person_cpp and list_people_cpp for now, without having to download and run the whole protobuf library.

Can you try this in the examples directory and report back what you get:
```bash
protoc --cpp_out=. addressbook.proto
```

`bash: /usr/local/bin/protoc: cannot execute binary file: Exec format error`

What could this mean?

It means the protoc binary you downloaded is not the correct format for your system. Try:
```bash
$ file /usr/local/bin/protoc
$ uname -a
```
The above 2 commands should show you the type of the binary you downloaded and the info of your operating system.

It seems you are using C++. I suggest you build the protobuf library from source code. It's actually quite easy. Just download https://github.com/google/protobuf/releases/download/v3.3.0/protobuf-cpp-3.3.0.tar.gz, extract it and run ./configure && make && sudo make install. It should only take a couple of minutes.

On a Raspberry Pi, running make takes at least 45 minutes. I want to be able to distribute it without everyone having to run make. I am currently running armv7l, which is a 32-bit system. I have also downloaded the 32-bit version of protoc. I have tried using the protoc that I created on a previous version by running make on the Raspberry Pi and that also has the same error.

The protoc binary we put up on the release page is for x86/x64 only. For arm you have to build it from source code. I think you can build it once and store/distribute the binary you build for others to use. Cross-compiling may also be an option.

I have used the same protoc and now I get a different error.

`protoc: error while loading shared libraries: libprotobuf.so.13: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory`

libprotobuf.so.13 is a linker to libprotobuf.so.13.0.0, where both files are in /usr/local/lib. Where is it looking for this file?
So you are using the protoc binary and protobuf library you built from source code? Try if "sudo ldconfig" helps.
I have tried that
See: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/25518701/protobuf-cannot-find-shared-libraries

It worked!!! Thank you very much. You have been extremely helpful.

In the end I was copying over "libprotobuf.so.13". This created an error because "sudo ldconfig" is suppose to create this file based off of "libprotobuf.so.13.0.0".

title: HHVM Incompatibility: Can't use function call result as array base in write context
body:
The following line of code produces a fatal error when run with HHVM: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/6f325805c0bc956f927b0e2dbfb4dd8133b4ed69/php/src/Google/Protobuf/descriptor.php#L84

```
$file->getEnumType()[] =
                $file->addEnumType(
                    EnumDescriptor::buildFromProto(
                        $enum_proto,
                        $proto,
                        ""));
