title: Why LABEL_REPEATED for non-repeated maps?

nodes.body: The map field is a syntax sugar for repeated map entry messages, as you posted in the descriptor. This gives language/implementations without maps support being able to parse and serialize map fields.
Also you can not specify "optional/required/repeated" label on map fields, because they will always be translated into repeated MapEntry messages.

Thanks for explaining. I didn't know that maps couldn't be optional/required/repeated, so I was wondering how you would e.g. support **real** map field repetition, if you always use the label with the repeated value. Thanks.
You would have to define a wrapper message which contains one map, then have a repeated field of that message.

title: [CSharp] Consider implementing arena allocation in C#
body:
# Background
Objects deserialized by protocol buffers have very often very similiar life time and can strongly benefit from Arena allocation as in C++ version. (https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/arenas)

C# 7.0 introduces new powerful feature called ref returns and ref locals (https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/ref-returns) practically making structs a first class citizen.

# Benefits
Using arena allocation can strongly decrease pressure on the GC during deserialization (and together with some other perf-works can remove completely GC from the deserialization path).

# Drawbacks
This feature requires dramatic changes to the generated code - it requires to generate an additional struct for every message contract. Structs are required for custom memory management and we do not want to break compatibility and APIs for pre-existing code. Also there should be some conversion possible from structs to classes if user decides to keep his/her struct a bit longer (at least longer than arena lifetime).

# POC
I have created some early POC structs allowing to implement arena allocation for protocol buffers deserialization and they seem to do the job, however as I told I see no even remote possibility to do this on classes.

# Open questions
Are you interested in accepting such a PR?

There is also a decision to be made whether we would like to prefer performance: i.e. refs everywhere, limited safety checks over preventing developer from hurting himself by freeing arena and still trying to use some remaining refs.

nodes.body:
Hi I had some time today and I have created a prototype implementation.

I have implemented VERY basic prototype using Address book contract.

From my very trivial "benchmarks"
~100KB size message
~250KB arena size
10000 repetitions (deserialization) including arena clearing
.NET Core 2.0

I can observe:
10-15% performance gain deserialization takes less time (time-wise) - even in a single threaded test (I can expect much more serious impact in multithreaded environment)
0 (!) Garbage collections

I was using a lot of managed memory. There is still a huge field for optimization. But current results look quite promising.

Data:
Original PB:
Elapsed: 25824ms GC0=1021 GC1=470 GC2=0 PeakMem=21815296
My PB:
Elapsed: 23422ms GC0=0 GC1=0 GC2=0 PeakMem=15925248

You can preview my prototype implementation here: https://github.com/mkosieradzki/protobuf/tree/arena-allocator

This is just a PoC!!!

@jskeet You might be interested in this one ;).
I'm interested, but I have very little time - protobuf is only a very small part of my work these days, I'm afraid. I don't know when I'll have time to take a close look at this.

Quick update: I have run the same test on a different computer in "Release" mode:
Elapsed: 6307ms GC0=989 GC1=459 GC2=0 PeakMem=21917696
Elapsed: 5383ms GC0=0 GC1=0 GC2=0 PeakMem=16003072

With compiler/JIT optimizations the difference is even bigger.

Update: I am simultaneously experimenting with the new language features (and System.Memory package):
https://github.com/mkosieradzki/protobuf/tree/arena-allocator-spans

However I am getting significant performance regressions there (hopefully due to the invalid compiler version). However I have succeeded in implementing version that can possibly enforce safety (and without using unsafe code outside of arena allocator).

@mkosieradzki: It feels to me like this is probably a dead-end - there's *so* much code that assumes that we're using classes, I find it hard to see how this could be anything other than a complete rewrite - in terms of design, generator *and* library. It's something we might consider if we were ever going go to rewrite the whole .NET support from scratch (and almost certainly base it on records) but it seems very unlikely to happen any time soon.

I'll close this issue now, but please feel free to add a comment with a reason for re-opening it if you feel strongly.

title: Update protobuf-java-util gson dep from v2.7 to v2.8.1
body: protobuf-java-util isn't using the latest gson. I had to add a gradle exclude rule. It'd be nice to update to the latest stable version.

nodes.body: Will the 2.8.1 be binary compatible with 2.7? I'm just cautious about whether this will break other users of protobuf.

> Will the 2.8.1 be binary compatible with 2.7?

I'm not sure. Is there a way to tell?
@xfxyjwf
Are you directly depending on a newer version of gson? If so, can't gradle pick the newer version automatically?

I have to do this:

```gradle
androidTestCompile('io.grpc:grpc-protobuf:1.5.0') {
  exclude group: 'com.google.code.gson', module: 'gson'
}
```

It works fine so there's no problem. I was just wondering when these dependencies get updated in `protobuf-java-util` after upstream has made a new stable release?

It's possible that upgrading would break people.
What happens if you don't use "exclude ..."?

> What happens if you don't use "exclude ..."?

This:

> Error:Conflict with dependency 'com.google.code.gson:gson' in project ':app'. Resolved versions for app (2.8.1) and test app (2.7) differ. See http://g.co/androidstudio/app-test-app-conflict for details.

This seems an issue in your configuration. Have you tried the suggestions in the linked android studio doc? Specifically it suggests:
```
If the error is about an indirect dependency (a library you didn't mention
in your build.gradle), just add a dependency for the newer version to the
configuration ("compile" or "androidTestCompile") that needs it.
```

> Have you tried the suggestions in the linked android studio doc? 

The app is setting the required version of gson via an indirect dependency. If I explicitly depend on a version of gson, that will work for now but may break in the future.

Excluding means I'm using the same version of gson as the app, regardless of which version that happens to be. I don't have to update it in the future.

Ideally the dependencies would update over time. If gson ever broke their API then this exclude strategy would stop working. I'm not sure what kind of guarantees they provide around API stability. 

To clarify there are a few options which work:

- Explicitly depend on gson & update version over time
- Exclude gson from grpc-protobuf

I'm mostly interested in why grpc-protobuf depends on gson from 2016. It sounds like there are compatibility concerns around upgrading.

title: PHP protobuf generation and reserved keywords
body:
There are some keywords that are not correctly handled in protobuf generation:
- `DEFAULT` - see here: https://github.com/googleapis/gax-php/blob/master/src/generated/Google/Logging/Type/LogSeverity.php#L30
- `Namespace` - we have an upcoming API that has a protobuf message type called `Namespace`

In the first case, we have resolved the issue with a manual edit. In the second case, it is not possible to rename the class with a manual edit.

It would perhaps be appropriate to also attempt to determine all possible PHP keywords, and handle them correctly, rather than only addressing these cases. I can put together a test protobuf file that uses all of the keywords that require special case handling.

title: C++ TextFormat float rendering inconsistent with Python

nodes.body:
It is float precision difference between C++ and python languages themselves, not protobuf. (It has the same issue if it is not a protobuf message) So both behaviors are correct. 

Note: text-format is intended for communications with humans. For machine communications, use wire format instead.

I am not sure what "precision" difference there could be: a float in protobufs is always four bytes, no matter what language you are in. Perhaps you are saying something like, the default rendering of float in C++ and Python is different, but that's strictly an implementation detail for the implementation of TextFormat.

I'm interested in the text-format being the same because we are using the text-format as "expect files" for various protobuf serialization tests we are doing, where it is important for a human to be able to visually inspect the diff of how a protobuf serialized. Some folks on the internet have claimed that textformat is deterministic.

Yes, I am talking about that Python does not have C-style float, it only has a C-style double. Python's built-in float type has double precision. So the behavior is consistent with Python language.

For now, unlike JSON format we do not have a standard for text-format yet. Different languages might have some difference besides float.

"Some folks on the internet have claimed that textformat is deterministic."  Yes textformat is deterministic, but it is talking about the field order especially the map field. The map was un-ordered  so the serialize result might be different every time. Text format sort the keys for textformat to make it 'deterministic'
Closing the issue as no follow up messages. Free feel to reopen if needed

@anandolee 

Is it possible to output the text-format which is consistent with python?

For example (https://github.com/BVLC/caffe/blob/master/src/caffe/proto/caffe.proto#L50),

title: Allow jspb.Message.GENERATE_FROM_OBJECT to be configured externally
body:
The [`jspb.Message.GENERATE_FROM_OBJECT` flag](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/js/message.js#L189) is used to control the generation of the `fromObject()` method in the JavaScript compiler.  

IMHO the `fromObject()` method provides a friendlier API for JavaScript developers and I would like to be able to enable this in my project; however this feature is gated behind the [`testonly` flag](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/js/js_generator.h#L78).

I would like to change this so `fromObject` generation can be enabled independently of the other features gated behind the `testonly` flag.

Would a PR that enables this functionality be welcome / be considered for landing?

title: [bug] C++ serialized message and Java, JS, Swift serialized messages are different

nodes.body:
The problem is how you print the binary string in hex form. The 2nd char 0xB9 is negative. When casting into an int, it's sign extended to 0xFFFFFFB9. Similar to the 0xFFFFFFBA conversion on the 6th char.

Changing your lamda to:
```c++
[](unsigned char i) { std::cout << std::hex << std::uppercase << (int) i; }
```
should fix the issue

Also, you probably want to preserve leading 0 when hex printing a byte, (e.g. the first byte should be 08 instead of 8) to avoid false positives in equal checks. Otherwise e.g. 101 can be {0x10, 0x1} or {0x1, 0x0, 0x1}
Thank you so much.

title: build fails on macosx/i386
body:
Main fails to build on macosx sierra for i386 arch. It happens because Atomic32 and AtomicWord both typedef to intptr_t so atomicops_internals_x86_gcc.h and atomicops_internals_atomicword_compat.h redefine functions like NoBarrier_Load.

To reproduce issue
export CXX=clang++
export CXXFLAGS="-arch i386" 
./configure && make

To fix
--- src/google/protobuf/stubs/atomicops.h.prev	2017-09-01 11:17:30.000000000 +0300
+++ src/google/protobuf/stubs/atomicops.h	2017-09-01 11:20:07.000000000 +0300
@@ -231,7 +231,7 @@
 
 // On some platforms we need additional declarations to make AtomicWord
 // compatible with our other Atomic* types.
-#if defined(GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_OS_APPLE)
+#if defined(GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_OS_APPLE) && !defined(GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ARCH_32_BIT)
 #include <google/protobuf/stubs/atomicops_internals_atomicword_compat.h>
 #endif

title: C++ tag decoder succeeds on malformed input
body:
The string "88d4c394a303862edd239fd0ec1c" is successfully decoded by protoc & C++ generated code.  However, it starts with an illegal tag.  Instead protoc & C++ both truncate to 32-bits & interpret it from there.  Should decode perhaps fail instead?

Version: 3.3.0

nodes.body:
When I pass that string in binary to `protoc --decode_raw`, I get back this:
```
106044737: 5894
571: 0x1cecd09f
```
I think what is happening is that the parser attempts to read a tag and finds a 6-byte varint. Although that's too big to be a tag, the parser just truncates the value to fit in 32 bits: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/6699f2cf64c656d96f4d6f93fa9563faf02e94b4/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.cc#L340 So the parser ends up treating the field number as 106044737 when the encoded number is actually much larger than that. After that, the remaining encoded bytes are valid and so the parse succeeds.

While this could be considered a bug, I'm not sure if it's worth trying to fix. Fixing it could add complexity to the code and possibly harm performance. Also, the parser generally tends to be lenient and so it's best not to assume that a return value of true means that the serialized data was completely well-formed.

title: C# Support for SQLCLR Host
body:
I'm trying to deploy the Protobuf.dll library, and generated classes for my models into SQL Server using SQLCLR Assembly feature, so that I can decode protobuf-encoded columns as part of a SQL stored proc.

I'd like to refrain from using the UNSAFE permission set, so that this could be deployed to PaaS services such as SQL Azure.

Compatibility is easy to achieve (have it working for myself, including deployment to SQL Server):
1. Make generated `private static pbr::FileDescriptor descriptor` fields readonly
2. Update generated WellKnownTypes, so this is reflected in all generated C# classes within the Protobuf library
3. Replace all occurrences of HashSet<T> with IDictionary<T,bool> (not too many), since HashSet is decorated with `[HostProtectionAttribute(SecurityAction.LinkDemand, MayLeakOnAbort = true)]`. SQLCLR .NET Host does not allow MayLeakOnAbort. `ContainsKey` and `Add`, which are the primary operations being used, have very similar performance characteristics to HashSet, so there is no drawback here.

Happy to submit a Pull Request, but before I put in the effort to figure out the entire build system and how to run tests etc, want to throw this idea out there in case anyone has thoughts / objections.

> @chriscosta: I don't believe the change was ever made. There's certainly still code using `HashSet<T>`.

I was hoping there was! Is there any workaround for this? @tastyeggs , u say that u have implemented it for you! Any chance you could share what you have done?

@chriscosta 

We didn't go all the way with this approach, however verified it as working in a proof-of-concept. I can get you half the way there, where (1) and (2) above are addressed (they're the same problem, where a static variable isn't marked as readonly, something SQLCLR doesn't like). (3) shouldn't be too difficult to do, just find and replace all instances and usages of HashSet<T> with Dictionary<T, bool>.

What we have is a bit kludgy, since we didn't modify the protoc tool.

1. A dotnet msbuild task that adds in "readonly" to `pbr::FileDescriptor` on generated .cs files, something like this. This goes into your project, where the .proto files are compiled to .cs files.
```
<Target Name="GenerateCsForProtoC" Inputs="@(ProtoC)" Outputs="$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)\obj\$(Configuration)\ProtoC-v1\$([System.String]::Copy('%(ProtoC.RelativeDir)').Replace(':','__DRIVE__'))%(ProtoC.Filename).cs" BeforeTargets="BeforeBuild;BeforeCompile">
    <MakeDir Directories="$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)/obj/$(Configuration)/ProtoC-v1/$([System.String]::Copy('%(ProtoC.RelativeDir)').Replace(':','__DRIVE__'))" />
    <ReadLinesFromFile File="$(SolutionDir)/Solution Items/ProtoBuf/ProtoCReplPsCmd.txt">
        <Output TaskParameter="Lines" PropertyName="PsCmd" />
    </ReadLinesFromFile>
    <Exec Command=""$(NuGetPackageRoot)/Google.Protobuf.Tools/3.4.0/tools/windows_x64/protoc.exe" --proto_path="$(SolutionDir)\Libraries\Egg.Grocery.Shared" --proto_path="$(SolutionDir)\Libraries\Egg.Grocery.Shared.Backend"  --proto_path="$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)" --csharp_out="$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)/obj/$(Configuration)/ProtoC-v1/$([System.String]::Copy('%(ProtoC.RelativeDir)').Replace(':','__DRIVE__').TrimEnd('\\'))" "%(ProtoC.FullPath)" 2>&1 | powershell -Command "$(PsCmd)"" IgnoreStandardErrorWarningFormat="false" />
    <PostProcessGeneratedCsFile InputFilename="$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)\obj\$(Configuration)\ProtoC-v1\$([System.String]::Copy('%(ProtoC.RelativeDir)').Replace(':','__DRIVE__'))%(ProtoC.Filename).cs"
        OutputFilename="$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)\obj\$(Configuration)\ProtoC-v1\$([System.String]::Copy('%(ProtoC.RelativeDir)').Replace(':','__DRIVE__'))%(ProtoC.Filename).cs"
        MatchText="private static pbr::FileDescriptor"
        ReplacementText="private static readonly pbr::FileDescriptor" />
    <ItemGroup>
        <Compile Include="$(MSBuildProjectDirectory)\obj\$(Configuration)\ProtoC-v1\$([System.String]::Copy('%(ProtoC.RelativeDir)').Replace(':','__DRIVE__'))%(ProtoC.Filename).cs">
            <DependentUpon>%(ProtoC.FullPath)</DependentUpon>
        </Compile>
    </ItemGroup>
</Target>
```

2.  A change to the Protobuf C# nuget library, so this readonly modifier is added to WellKnownType IMessages:, I pushed our code here: https://github.com/tastyeggs/protobuf/commit/4395ffc1861feff9f3f5be1617fe38504a2c3647.

You can avoid the kludgy the BeforeCompile msbuild task by modifying the protoc compiler, in particular this file: `src\google\protobuf\compiler\csharp\csharp_reflection_class.cc`, and add in the readonly modifier.

title: Feature Request: Field Validation Parity with JSON Schema
body:
In the REST+JSON world you often see protocols defined with JSON schemas as an alternative to Protobufs. These schemas function very similar to protobuf definitions to define your message payloads. They also offer many of the same rules such as oneof, required, repeated (aka arrays), etc.

However, with JSON schema validators you can provide additional business rules on your fields and get the data validation free as part of using the JSON schema. How do developers using gRPC + Protobufs maintain these validation rules across multiple languages in a consistent way, without these type of rules in the proto definitions?

There are a couple main rules that are badly needed, such as pattern matching, checking int values, and checking repeated field item counts. Could look something like this:

```
message Example {
    string message = 1; `pattern: ^[a-zA-Z].*`
    int32 percentage = 2; `minValue: 0, maxValue: 100`
    repeated int32 list = 3; `minItems: 1, maxItems: 10`
}
```

And then have the protoc compiled code for reading/writing the message automatically check these simple rules during the serialization and deserialization of this message and throw an error if the data is not valid.

Wouldn't that be awesome?

nodes.body:
I put together an example to point out how much boilerplate is involved in doing this kind of data validation: https://github.com/jaybennett89/protox-go-example. It implements the `message Example { ... }` from my original post, but with the validation code created manually.

The main issue I have is that I've got no way to automate the generation of the boilerplate validation code (https://github.com/jaybennett89/protox-go-example/blob/master/example/validate.go) when using protobufs without this kind of feature.

I wrote ~150 lines of code and tests just to validate my 5 simple rules, and this scales quite badly as you add new messages that need new rules. It scales even worse if you have multiple languages involved.

What you're talking about would be a lot of work to create, to support every programming language protobuf supports. For example a language like C++ doesn't even have regex pattern matching built-in (well, unless you use C++11 or newer, but protobuf doesn't require C++11).

For now, for your use-case, maybe you could add your rules to the `.proto` file as [Custom Options](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#customoptions), and during `.proto` file compilation either hook into the `protoc` compiler as a plugin to get the custom option info and generate your Go language rule verifiers, or parse the `.proto` files for them in a second stage?

This has been brought up before (inside Google, multiple times) and it was decided that we are not going to include such features in core protobuf library. It can, however, be supported as a separate library using custom options as suggested by @hadrielk above.
https://github.com/lyft/protoc-gen-validate is an OSS project to do this.

title: Lazy parsing for protobuf
body: Marking sub messages lazy in protobuf does not affect deserialization time. Is this feature implemented for java yet , i do see few LazyField.java and test cases , but marking nested fields (mostly maps) lazy , does not change any generated code or the deserialization performance.

nodes.body: I'm not 100% sure for Java, but I believe laziness only works for singular submessage fields, not repeated fields or maps, so that may explain the performance you saw.

ahh i see. yes my message consists a bunch of maps and repeated fields and few singular/scalar fields like string.
Is this something that is available internally and will be a feature in future version ? Or are there some more fundamental issues limiting this behaviour ?
If this is indeed the case , are there any recommended or good practices when writing a proto schema , for example , always wrap my repeated fields or maps or scalar fields within another message and have the outermost message consists only few sub messages in order to achieve lazy decoding ?

We haven't implemented this even internally, and as far as I know we don't have any plans to make laziness work with more field types. I'm not sure if there are any fundamental issues blocking it; it might just be that singular submessages were the most important use case for lazy fields. Using a wrapper message does sound like a reasonable idea if lazy parsing is important for you.

Could you explain some more about why you need to use lazy fields? If it turns out that you don't actually need to access the field at all but you just want to persist it, there are also some techniques you could try to avoid parsing the data but without relying on lazy fields.

My use case is : I have a huge protobuf with hundreds of nested sub messages/repeated fields/maps.  (actually i realized the most heavy weight objects are maps). When i receive these messages (about few hundred million) i want to filter them out based on some identifiers (which are small sub nested messages). So in order to filter quickly i only want to decode only the sub message within this giant protobuf and if that filter predicate evaluates to true i want to pass in and de serialize rest of the huge message. Another use case is I have to join these huge protobuf objects to another proto object , where my join in only based on a small string (or sub message) id field , so to improve the join speed i want to only decode the id sub message instead of the entire proto.

If you do have additional ideas please let me know. Right now the way i am working around this is having my id as a separate duplicated field in my schema  . Also would be good to know how can i just persist the data (that is my use case for the join , i just want to join huge protos and persist in some data storage , dont care about accessing other fields in that job itself )

If you're using proto2, one thing you could try is replacing some of the huge fields that you don't always need to read with [extensions](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#extensions). That way those parts of the message will only be parsed if you pass an extension registry including the extensions you want.

If that's not flexible enough, another thing you could try would be to create a separate schema that is effectively just a subset of your original schema containing only the fields you want to filter on--just make sure the field numbers match exactly. Then you could parse the message as this simpler schema and that would give you enough information to know whether you need to parse the whole thing with the full schema. This approach is kind of hacky but might be justified if you really need the performance.

i use proto3.
About the hacky solution (create another subset schema with same field numbers)  : seems like this will work with the repeated and map fields , is that true ? Not sure how lazy is actually implemented but hacky solution seems to be working in this case as well  ?
The hacky solution should work for repeated and map fields, too, yes. Any fields that are not included in the smaller subset schema would just be treated as unknown fields.

@sclasen I'm guessing that we must have a special case somewhere that is preventing `lazy=true` from taking effect on an `Any` field. Do you really need the `Any` to be lazy, though? It seems to me like `Any` is already inherently lazy since its main payload doesn't get parsed until you explicitly unpack it.

@sclasen Sorry for giving you the wrong answer before--I actually just learned that we disabled lazy fields for Java not too long ago, the one exception being that they're still used with MessageSet. The rationale as I understand is that lazy fields did not work well with hash and equals, and lazy parsing turns out to be bad for mobile since it can unexpectedly tie up the UI thread.

Ah, gotcha, thanks @acozzette .  I suppose using Any could accomplish the same thing.  Do you have any background on why the following statement is in the docs?

"Currently the runtime libraries for working with Any types are under development."

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#any

@sclasen I think that statement is just referring to the fact that for some languages we have not yet finished implementing the helpers for packing and unpacking Any fields. Actually at this point that may be out of date, though; I'm not sure of the current status for all languages.
Close this as we have no plan to implement this for now.

title: Protobuf 3.3.2 missing on maven central
body: Version 3.3.2 is missing on maven central. Even if there is backwards compatibility this contradicts the usual recommendation that versions should match exactly. We have incorporated this into our build systems and these fail now with the missing version in maven.

nodes.body: I believe 3.3.2 was a release we only needed for bug fixes for certain languages, and so we did not push new artifacts for every language with that release (see #3302). That's a fair point that ideally it should be possible to match versions exactly, though. Is your problem that you are using 3.3.2 for some languages but cannot using the matching version for Java?

The problem is that our build system defines the versions of the libraries to use from the version `protoc` prints out using the `--version` flag. And on archlinux, this is currently 3.3.2, so we try to find the matching maven artifact, which fails.

I'd suggest setting the version to the latest version in the same minor version. e.g. for 3.3.2, look for the latest one >=3.3.0 && < 3.4.0. This will make the dependency much stable. We typically have per-language fixes and releasing all other languages will slow down the release and development. Hopefully it would be better when we break down each languages to have their own release schedule.

Before we automate the binary release process, releasing binary artifacts for patch versions is just too much work and as Adam mentioned there are likely no changes made in many languages in a patch release. I would recommend updating your build setup to allow protoc version to be different from runtime version. Our release process will likely stay this way for a while until we get to build an automated release pipeline.

Sure I can do that. But an explicit statement somewhere in the documentation about these assumptions and rules would be very helpful. At the time we looked on how to automate things, there was just the general rule to "use the same version everywhere", which fails here.

title: UnmodifiableLazyStringList is not Serializable
body:
Cont'd from https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/protobuf/7bFAlrtK_SU/lro6ajJJrXMJ, I basically got the same error, but 6 years later.

The idea is of course that I have a `repeated string` field that I get from a serialized protobuf and store in a POJO. That POJO is later elsewhere serialized and sent over the network. Imagine our surprise when a `List<String>` failed to serialize, it's just something that you do not expect to happen at all (even though it's completely valid).

Yes, the workaround, to copy the list out, is simple. But still, the list could simply be serializable itself...

That's a shame, but I understand the decision. Is the rationale that you don't think the feature would pull its weight, or is it a more philosophical problem, e.g. that serializing a lazy list is not well defined?

title: Max float encoded into JSON cannot be decoded back again
body:
Hi, using the protobuf C++ API on a Centos system, encoding a `FLT_MAX` value into JSON yields:

```json
{ "float_value": 3.4028235e+38 }
```
...but when deserializing that back into protobuf, I get the following error:
```
INVALID_ARGUMENT:float_value: invalid value 3.4028235e+38 for type TYPE_FLOAT
```
That's because `3.4028235e+38` is actually a rounded-up value of float's actual maximum, which is something like `3.402823466e+38`.

Internally protobuf decodes it in `util::converter::SafeStrToFloat()` in `utility.cc`, I believe; and in that function it actually decodes it to a `double` first, and then checks if the double is bigger than `std::numeric_limits<float>::max()`. But of course it will be bigger than that max, since it was rounded up from max.

One could argue it should accept that number as a valid `float`, or else serialize `float` with fewer significant digits so that it gets encoded as `3.402823e+38`. It looks like the encoding occurs in `FloatToBuffer()` in `strutil.cc`, which first calls `snprintf()` using `FLT_DIG` for precision, but then checks the encoded value is correct by decoding the encoded string in `safe_strtof()` and checking the decoded value equals the original value. But those will not be equal (and frequently not be equal for other values either). So then it encodes it again using `FLT_DIG+3` precision, which is how this problem arises.

Arguably the whole point of `FLT_DIG` is to be the number of digits that can be safely encoded to string without rounding errors, so the right fix here might be to get rid of that `safe_strtof()` checking and re-encoding with `FLT_DIG+3`.

nodes.body: Assigned to Mike who is looking at moving the underlying conversion routines to Abseil, which shouldn't have this problem.

title: No matching function for call to 'MessageToJsonString'

nodes.body: Looks like you're using `MessageLite` rather than `Message`. The difference between these two classes is that `MessageLite` does not include reflection (i.e. a run time list of field names and types) whereas `Message` does. This information is necessary for the JSON functions to work.

You're passing it `JsonParseOptions`, but `MessageToJsonString()` takes just `JsonOptions` (or `JsonPrintOptions` if you prefer, which is a typedef for the other). It's the deserializer side `JsonStringToMessage()` that takes the `JsonParseOptions`.

title: C++11 enum class
body: It would be great use 'enum class' in the C++11 code generation.

nodes.body: yes it would be awesome, but it sounds like it would be surprisingly hard to achieve: see #1079

So I guess the advantage with that latter case is you'd get to avoid implicit type conversion when it's used in the generated accessor functions? That's good sure. But yeah for me the goal is to use the same enumerator names in different enums in the same namespace/package. 😢

Out of curiosity, is it "flattened" in the sense that the reflection/descriptor stuff can't deal with it being scoped, or do you just mean in the outputted .h/.cc files it's flattened (e.g., in the `const` variables created for each enumerator name and such)

It's the former. When we store enum values internally in descriptors, the names we use in indices are flattened (i.e., both Foo.UNKNOWN and Bar.UNKNOWN are indexed by the name "UNKNOWN"), and this is exposed in public APIs such as FileDescriptor::FindEnumValueByName():
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.h#L1327

If we are to allow two enums to define the same enum value name, all such FindEnumValueByName() APIs will be broken and it will have unpleasant consequences.

It's probably possible to deprecate all such FindEnumValueByName() methods (and all similar enum value name related APIs in every protobuf implementation) and change the behavior after all usage is gone, but that will take time and work. It's hardly worthwhile, I would say.

title: protobuf can't generate add_* member function for "repeated repeated" type
Generated move constructors marked as noexcept, but may throw exceptions

nodes.body:
This is partly a result of our Google C++ Style Guide where exceptions are not allowed:
https://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html#Exceptions

So in Google code base, throwing an exception equals program termination. Therefore marking protobuf move constructors noexcept has no negative consequences even if they may actual throw.

I don't really have a great answer here. The movable operator= can't assume the two message are from the same arena because we do have use cases where they are from different arenas. It seems to me the CopyFrom() call is inevitable. To make code work correctly with the presence of exceptions, the only solution I can think of is to remove the noexcept annotation...

I suggest that for the move *assignment*, it is probably fine to just remove `noexcept`. The main thing I was worried about was message objects in containers, which only use the move constructor. Of course, perhaps I've missed some other situation where move assignment is important.

For the move *constructor*, I think `noexcept` could truthfully be left in place by changing the behaviour when the source object uses an arena. This situation is limited because it only arises if there is an explicit call to `std::move` (or equivalent), because arenas return pointers to objects. Moving from a message with an arena is documented to already have defined behaviour (perform a copy), but I suspect that most code using this, if it exists, is accidental. I can think of two alternatives.

**Option 1: When move constructing a message, force the destination message to use the same arena as the source.** This means the move can be implemented as a simple swap (see note below) even for objects with an arena. This would possibly be quite a big change, in two related respects:

 * It could be a big code change in the library, because messages currently only use an arena for submessages if their own memory was allocated with that arena. It's possible that this assumption is currently used in `Message`, either deliberately or accidentally.
 * It could be argued that it is a big API change to the library. Currently, messages returned by value or allocated on the stack cannot use arenas (for submessages). Developers seeing these variables/return values may be surprised in future if this no longer holds.

**Option 2: Make it undefined behaviour to move from a message with an arena (with `GOOGLE_DCHECK`).** Forcing an `abort()`, is quite drastic. But as I said, I believe anyone who encounters this is more likely to believe they were getting constant-time behaviour, in which case it is better they find out about it during testing than in production. Assuming, that is, that they find it during testing ...

These two options apply equally well to move constructors for `RepeatedField` and `RepeatedPtrField`, if those get added (also see note below).

Note about simple swap: The only worry I can think of here is making sure that the moved-from object still has a reference to the arena. If the arena is in some separately-allocated `Rep` object (as it is in `RepeatedPtrField`) then there may need to an allocation after all.

Protobuffers doesn't throw exceptions. Throwing an exception is equivalent to aborting for us, so if any part (for instance new) throws in the proto library, you should see protos as inconsistent and only aborting is defined. Given this semantics adding noexcept is correct. Furthermore move-semantics is only useful with noexcept otherwise containers will not use move, so we can't remove noexcept.

Arguably noexcept should be added to ALL proto functions so that abortion is guaranteed instead of continuing with a inconsistent proto system which can't even be cleaned up.

nodes.body:
Pure python is using double precision for float. However python cpp implementation calls our c++ code thus float is float precision. This is a known behavior difference that we are currently hard to change.

I guess your linux is using cpp implementation and Mac OS is using pure python?

title: Java Enum Generation
body:
So I was wondering in the Java Enum Compiler why is there an `UNRECOGNIZED` value if `default` for the `forNumber` returns `null` would it not make more sense to `return UNRECOGNIZED`?

https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/80a37e0782d2d702d52234b62dd4b9ec74fd2c95/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_enum.cc
Line 202

nodes.body: @xfxyjwf  java enum behavior question

`forNumber` replaces `valueOf` and since `valueOf` returns `null` on unknown value so must `forNumber`. The `UNRECOGNIZED` value is only generated for proto3 and was introduced after `valueOf`/`forNumber` exists, so it can't really be used there. We also can't make the change now because it's an API breaking change.

title: Handle field access with Python 2 unicode literals
body:
I was a bit perplexed by the following error:

```
from __future__ import unicode_literals
import mything_pb
p = mything_pb.MyProto()
p.ClearField("my_field")
```

This doesn't work on Python 2, it will throw:

```
TypeError: field name must be a string
```

This is because `unicode_literals` turns the string literal into a Unicode literal, but Python protobufs is only doing a native string test to decide if the field name is OK or not. It would be great if it could handle both cases. (This code works on Python 3 because Unicode strings are the "native" string.)

To work around this problem, call `future.utils.bytes_to_native_str` on a binary string literal first.

nodes.body: Hmm, I cannot reproduce it locally. It works fine on my machine (python 2.7.13). The relative code is at: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/fa5a69e73b0dd667ff15062adbc170310d440ee9/python/google/protobuf/internal/python_message.py#L831 The field name map was created during the import. So I guess if you import unicode_literals before the module import, the map key will be a unicode literal? Feel free to send out a PR if there's a simple fix.

I just started running into this with some of my own code today.  The odd thing is that things work fine with the python installed by homebrew on my Mac.  But they fail under various flavors of Linux.

In my unit tests under Linux, everything also works fine when they're run by `fabric` but not with `pytest` or `nose`.

Which Python 2? We do not support python2.6
Python2.7 and above should work fine
This is python 2.7 for me

I can reproduce it in my environment when the protobuf is installed with cpp implementation.
```
>>> from google.protobuf.internal import api_implementation
>>> print(api_implementation._default_implementation_type)
cpp
>>> p.ClearField(u"values")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: field name must be a string
```

There is no error if cpp implementation is not installed.
```
>>> from google.protobuf.internal import api_implementation
>>> print(api_implementation._default_implementation_type)
python
>>> p.ClearField(u"values")
>>> 
```

This error was fixed in internal around Aug, 2018. And also in master by PyUnicode_Check(arg) :
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blame/master/python/google/protobuf/pyext/message.cc#L1810

 Expect to see the fix in 3.7.0 release
Closing it as 3.7.0 is already released

title: 64 bit integer
body:
According to https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number/MAX_SAFE_INTEGER

> The Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER constant represents the maximum safe integer in JavaScript (2^53 - 1).
> 
> The MAX_SAFE_INTEGER constant has a value of 9007199254740991 (9,007,199,254,740,991 or ~9 quadrillion). The reasoning behind that number is that JavaScript uses double-precision floating-point format numbers as specified in IEEE 754 and can only safely represent numbers between -(2^53 - 1) and 253 - 1.

So we have problem with 64 bit integers , When I want to open a `uint64` field that is larger than (2^53 - 1) it is rounded to another number


unofficial protobuffer library , https://github.com/dcodeIO/ProtoBuf.js/ , uses https://github.com/dcodeIO/long.js and solved problem

Please use long.js for 64 bit integer 

> As of ECMA-262 5th Edition, "all the positive and negative integers whose magnitude is no greater than 2^53 are representable in the Number type", which is "representing the doubleprecision 64-bit format IEEE 754 values as specified in the IEEE Standard for Binary Floating-Point Arithmetic". The maximum safe integer in JavaScript is 2^53-1.
> 
> Example: 2^64-1 is 18446744073709551615 but in JavaScript it evaluates to 18446744073709552000.
> 
> Furthermore, bitwise operators in JavaScript "deal only with integers in the range −2^31 through 2^31−1, inclusive, or in the range 0 through 2^32−1, inclusive. These operators accept any value of the Number type but first convert each such value to one of 2^32 integer values."
> 
> In some use cases, however, it is required to be able to reliably work with and perform bitwise operations on the full 64 bits. This is where long.js comes into play.

nodes.body: Any chance of using `BigInt`?

> Any chance of using `BigInt`?

Anyone on this?

I understand adding [jstype = JS_STRING] is an option, however I concern about the performance when I pass millions of bigint through the field `repeated int64 big_values`. With this option, I guess we pay unnecessary serde of these values
- client: it has to convert long[] to string[] to call the REST API (node.js)
- server: it can get int64_t[] due to the proto declaration, but I guess protobuf pays cost to deserialize strings to int64

So the ideal case is, if protobuf can support bigint (long.js or native bigint if supported), then we can completely remove above conversions, and we don't pay the cost any more.

It will be great if this support can be added.

> it has been fixed in 3.4 : https://github.com/google/protobuf/releases
> `message dummy { uint64 bigInt = 1; [jstype = JS_STRING] }`

I wouldn't personally consider this to be a fix. Imho the default unsafe conversion of 64 bit integers to JavaScript `number`s is a problem. Merely giving developers the option to overwrite this (on an individual field basis) doesn't justify the unsafe default behavior of silently loosing precision. It is also inconsistent with protobuf's [JSON mapping](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json) which converts these to strings.

We just get bitten by the same issue. Silently not converting a uint64 to its full precision is a real issue. Our server is in Golang and using 64bits integer is a basic thing. I understand the JS limitation but maybe we should consider using an open source uint64 library until it s part of the language (if it ever will)
Someone has suggested BigInt.
If you dont want to make BigInt the default for retro compatibility reason. Would you consider adding a new `[jstype = JS_BIGINT` ?

title: No such target '//external:six': target 'six' not declared in package 'external'
body:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/c627530946e5d8783c1d9c2bbeb1704e4e868963/BUILD#L756

I'm using Bazel to build a Python project that uses protos. Bazel doesn't yet generate Python language bindings `.proto` files. See https://blog.bazel.build/2017/02/27/protocol-buffers.html. However, the Proto team have defined their own: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/c627530946e5d8783c1d9c2bbeb1704e4e868963/protobuf.bzl#L313

```
def py_proto_library(
        name,
        srcs=[],
        deps=[],
        py_libs=[],
        py_extra_srcs=[],
        include=None,
        default_runtime="//:protobuf_python",
        protoc="//:protoc",
        use_grpc_plugin=False,
        **kargs):
  """Bazel rule to create a Python protobuf library from proto source files
  NOTE: the rule is only an internal workaround to generate protos. The
  interface may change and the rule may be removed when bazel has introduced
  the native rule.
  Args:
    name: the name of the py_proto_library.
    srcs: the .proto files of the py_proto_library.
    deps: a list of dependency labels; must be py_proto_library.
    py_libs: a list of other py_library targets depended by the generated
        py_library.
    py_extra_srcs: extra source files that will be added to the output
        py_library. This attribute is used for internal bootstrapping.
    include: a string indicating the include path of the .proto files.
    default_runtime: the implicitly default runtime which will be depended on by
        the generated py_library target.
    protoc: the label of the protocol compiler to generate the sources.
    use_grpc_plugin: a flag to indicate whether to call the Python C++ plugin
        when processing the proto files.
    **kargs: other keyword arguments that are passed to cc_library.
  """
```

I thought I'd use this to generate Python language bindings by depending on the external repository in my WORKSPACE:

```
http_archive(
    name = "com_google_protobuf",
    urls = ["https://github.com/google/protobuf/archive/v3.4.1.zip"],
    strip_prefix = "protobuf-3.4.1",
)

```
Then in my BUILD file

```
load("@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf.bzl", "py_proto_library")

py_proto_library(
    name = "py",
    visibility = ["//visibility:public"],
    deps = [
        ":my_proto",
        "@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf_python",
    ],
)

# The proto_library rule implicitly depends on @com_google_protobuf//:protoc
proto_library(
    name = "my_proto",
    srcs = ["my.proto"],
)
```

However, the [protobuf_python](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/c627530946e5d8783c1d9c2bbeb1704e4e868963/BUILD#L756) library adds a list of other `py_library` targets (`"//external:six"` and `":python_srcs"`) depended by the generated code.
    
```
py_proto_library(
    name = "protobuf_python",
    srcs = COPIED_WELL_KNOWN_PROTOS,
    include = "python",
    data = select({
        "//conditions:default": [],
        ":use_fast_cpp_protos": [
            ":python/google/protobuf/internal/_api_implementation.so",
            ":python/google/protobuf/pyext/_message.so",
        ],
    }),

    protoc = ":protoc",
    py_libs = [
        ":python_srcs",
```

These dependencies cannot be resolved:

`No such target '//external:six': target 'six' not declared in package 'external'`

title: Is python's google.protobuf.json_format using c++ extension?
body:
I have installed python protobuf with the c++ extensions:

```
>>> from google.protobuf.internal import api_implementation
>>> api_implementation._default_implementation_type
'cpp'

```

but it takes ages to process messages to json. To give an idea, the amount of data is saved as serialized string and read  in about **3 seconds**. Then, to process these messages to json takes about **2 minutes**.

nodes.body: JSON support is implemented using protobuf reflection API and it's known to be 10x to 100x slower than the generated parsing/serialization code. 2 minutes sounds slow but it may well be in the expected range of JSON parsing performance... If you have that much amount of data to process, you might want to stay with protobuf binary format.

The python implementation of JSON format is here:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/json_format.py

Feel free to send us pull requests if you have identified places to improve.

The corresponding C++ implementation is here:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/util/json_util.h#L83

Not sure if it's easy to hook up the C++ implementation to the python one. Also I suspect even after that it's still much slower than the proto binary parsing.

This morning the google-cloud-ruby project had a segfault on the [CircleCI build](https://circleci.com/gh/GoogleCloudPlatform/google-cloud-ruby/2373#tests/containers/3) system used to run tests on Linux.

System details:
 
* gRPC language and version: grpc 1.6.2 (x86_64-linux)
* Protobuf version: google-protobuf 3.4.1.1 (x86_64-linux)
* Operating System: Linux
* Runtime version: ruby 2.1.9p490 (2016-03-30 revision 54437) [x86_64-linux]

<details><summary>segfault details</summary>

title: v
Migrate protobuf to use Abseil: Google C++ common libraries.
body:
For a long time protobuf has been keeping its own fork of Google C++ common libraries under the stubs directory:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/tree/master/src/google/protobuf/stubs

They have to be forked because Google never released these common libraries as an opensource project, util now:
https://opensource.googleblog.com/2017/09/introducing-abseil-new-common-libraries.html

With the release of Abseil, we should be able to deprecate code in the stubs directory and migrate protobuf to use Abseil instead.

nodes.body: This is already fixed in trunk, and will be part of our next major release!

title: GOOGLE_ATTRIBUTE_ALWAYS_INLINE is incorrectly implemented
body:
Currently, in port.h
```
#if defined(__GNUC__) && (__GNUC__ > 3 ||(__GNUC__ == 3 && __GNUC_MINOR__ >= 1))
// For functions we want to force inline.
// Introduced in gcc 3.1.
#define GOOGLE_ATTRIBUTE_ALWAYS_INLINE __attribute__ ((always_inline))
```
which is then used in the wire_format_lite.h as

`#define INL GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ATTRIBUTE_ALWAYS_INLINE`

Note that gcc specifies that just putting always_inline attribute is not enough. It should be preceded by the 'inline' keyword. Based on a combination of things (include order etc.), it showed up as an error on CentOS 6/ gcc 4.8

See the signature from this https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Inline.html 
`inline void foo (const char) __attribute__((always_inline));`
Also, a similar bug in another project - https://github.com/rogerclarkmelbourne/Arduino_STM32/issues/54

nodes.body:
The INL usages are for declaration, the definition will have the inline keyword (in wire_format_lite_inl.h). I think this falls into this category `when a function is first declared without using the inline keyword and then is defined with inline`

Even if the attribute is ignored, it shouldn't be an error. I suspect you miss the include on the wire_format_line_inl.h in which those functions are actually defined.

ah, I have not seen this usage pattern (declaring non-line and defining inline). After I changed my includes from wire_format_lite.h to wire_format_lite_inl.h, the problem went away. 

Thanks.

title: Internal variable name confusion when generating c++ code on windows with relative paths
body:
When you generate c++ files from proto files and there is a path involved in protoc command line, it will use that exact same command line in internal variable names regardless if the path is correct.

Say, we target a file `relative/Parser/error.proto`, if there is a file `relative/parser/error.proto` it will be found and the code will be generated but when you try to link this file with 
`import relative/parser/error.proto`

it will not compile in because name mangling in protobuf internal variables will have `Parser` and not `parser`

This is very confusing to debug and can baffle people for quite some time. Is it possible to use the _actual_ paths/names while generating or throw an error?

title: Building no-warning-test fails with -Og in CXXFLAGS
body:
When building with GCC, inclusion of `-Og` in `CXXFLAGS` causes `make check` to fail with errors such as:

```
In file included from google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_test_bad_identifiers.pb.cc:5:0:
./google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_test_bad_identifiers.pb.h: In member function ‘virtual bool protobuf_unittest::TestConflictingEnumNames::MergePartialFromCodedStream(google::protobuf::io::CodedInputStream*)’:
./google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_test_bad_identifiers.pb.h:3798:21: error: ‘value’ may be used uninitialized in this function [-Werror=maybe-uninitialized]
   conflicting_enum_ = value;
   ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~
google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_test_bad_identifiers.pb.cc:6765:15: note: ‘value’ was declared here
           int value;
               ^~~~~
```

This appears to be related to [Bug 58455 - spurious "may be used uninitialized" warning with -Og](https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=58455) and [Bug 42145 - bogus "may be used uninitialized" (a || b converted to a|b)](https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=42145).  As part of protobuf gets built with `-Werror`, such spurious warnings become fatal.

Tested with protobuf-3.3.0 using GCC-5.4.0 and GCC-6.4.0.

See also [Bug 618150 - dev-libs/protobuf-3.3.0 - error: 'value' may be used uninitialized in this function [-Werror=maybe-uninitialized]](https://bugs.gentoo.org/618150)

title: Message serialization ignores flush errors
body:
Message::SerializeToFileDescriptor and Message::SerializePartialToFileDescriptor both have a local FileOutputStream instance that they write to with other helper function which can leave unwritten content. On destruction, this gets flushed out, however there are no checks on whether that succeeds (and nowhere to report to at that point), so I/O errors on flushing are silently ignored and the caller doesn't have a chance to check on that.

It would be better to have these functions flush explicitly, and propagate the error result if the flush operation fails.

body:
I got an error when parse special gRPC enum value = 0 to json.

```java
public enum Status implements ProtocolMessageEnum {
  ACTIVE(0),
  SUSPENDED(1),
  UNRECOGNIZED(-1);
}
```
I parse to json with default options

```java
String json = JsonFormat.printer().print(message);
```

When `message` enum status was `SUSPENDED`, I got json with status is `SUSPENDED` string
But when `message` enum status was `ACTIVE`, I lost status field in json.

I think that problem is `ACTIVE` has value is `0` and parser was confuse this case.

nodes.body:
In proto3, the default values are not serialized for primitive fields. However, you can set the option to always print default values, like:

```java
String json = JsonFormat.printer().includingDefaultValueFields().print(message);
```
Thank you, It works well in my case.

title: [Java] expose field comments
body:
currently, comments in the .proto definitions like ``` // this is the foo field optional string foo = 1; ``` are included in the generated java class as comments as well: ``` /** * 
       * this is the foo field
       *
* * optional string foo = 1; */ java.lang.String getFoo(); ``` Unfortunately the comment is not exposed in the Java API. I would like to access field comments and expose them in other output objects, e.g. through the FieldDescriptor? Maybe with a new getComment() method? Use cases would be for example exposing this information in a metastore Since the comments are already detected correctly and included in the Java code it shouldn't be too hard.

nodes.body:
Comments are intentionally stripped out from generated descriptors because it adds additional overhead to the generated code while not used in almost all cases.

If you need to make use of comments, consider using a protoc plugin instead.

title: Ruby MessageExts should define to_json with an `options` parameter
body:
The Ruby standard JSON module assumes `to_json` methods have a single positional parameter for propagating serialization options down the call stack. The protobuf `MessageExts` module ([message_exts.rb](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/ruby/lib/google/protobuf/message_exts.rb)) defines `to_json` with no parameters, which causes errors when serializing containers:

```ruby
# $ ruby test_json.rb 
# test_json.rb:3:in `to_json': wrong number of arguments (1 for 0) (ArgumentError)
# 	from test_json.rb:7:in `to_json'
# 	from test_json.rb:7:in `<main>'
require 'json'
class Foo 
  def to_json
    'FOO'
  end 
end
puts [Foo.new].to_json

# $ ruby test_json.rb 
# [FOO]
require 'json'
class Foo
  def to_json(opts)
    'FOO'
  end
end
puts [Foo.new].to_json
```

nodes.body: Was this fixed by #4252?
Yes, that PR looks like it fixes this ticket.

title: C# and message equality - double.NaN values don't compare as equal
body:
I'm not sure what other languages do, but in C# NaN values are handled differently between `==` and `Equals`:

```csharp
double d1 = double.NaN;
double d2 = double.NaN;
Console.WriteLine(d1 == d2); // False
Console.WriteLine(d1.Equals(d2)); // True
```

Currently we use `==` in the autogenerated `Equals` code in messages, which means two messages with `NaN` values in compare as non-equal.

Changing the generated code would arguably be a breaking change - but perhaps a more correct one.
Thoughts? Do we know what other protobuf languages do?

nodes.body:
This bug is made harder to fix by [CoreCLR issue 6237](https://github.com/dotnet/coreclr/issues/6237), where `Equals` and `GetHashCode` are inconsistent in `double`.

There are three options:

- Leave this as it is (would prefer not)
- Fix it using the .NET idea of equality, i.e. message 1 containing a signalling NaN and message 2 containing a quiet NaN are considered equal, even though they serialize to different values. (At that point, we propagate the hash code inconsistency too.)
- Use the Java codegen approach of using the raw 64-bit values for equality. It's then bitwise equality, which is at least easy to understand, but has the odd property of `message1.Value.Equals(message2.Value)` returning true, but `message1.Equals(message2)` returning false

I think I'm most in favour of the third option at this point (and will start implementing that), but value other feedback.

Urgh - it gets nastier, as if we have a repeated field or a map containing doubles, we need to use the right comparison there, too. (By default, we'd get the .NET behaviour.)

Then there's the handling of wrapper types.

```
version: '3.4'
services:
  python:
    image: python
    volumes:
...
  protobuf:
    image: google/protobuf
    volumes:
....
```
@yunspace What if the images are compatible?
@yunspace Sorry, I meant to ask what if the images are not compatible...

@xfxyjwf sorry I'm not sure what you mean. Not compatible with what? 

In the above example you use python to build python and you use protobuf to build protobuf. It's basic composition over inheritance. If the official images aren't sufficient, you can always create your own images, such as `xfxyjwf/protobuf`. I have a full example here: https://github.com/serverlesscloud/musketeers-lambda-go-sls/blob/master/docker-compose.yml

> If user want to use other software together with protobuf, do they write additional docker file based on the proposed protobuf image? Or there is some easy way to combine different docker image? (e.g., if user want to use both python and protobuf, he just combine python official image and protobuf official image)

`protoc` is more or less just a binary (to users). The images would presumably just be the base images (ubuntu:16.04, alpine:3.8, etc.) with the appropriate protoc release added, and possibly the well-known types in `/usr/local/include` or similar.

This actually *would* be really useful. Not only would it be a way to handle running protoc, but for those of us that need to expose a Docker image that somehow uses protoc under the hood, we could reference it in a multi-stage build:

```Dockerfile
COPY --from gcr.io/protobuf/protobuf:3.6.1 /usr/local/bin/protoc /usr/local/bin/protoc
```

...and then you add _only_ the size of the executable to your Docker image.

@lukebakken's proposal makes more sense to me. I think users should base on central repositories (e.g., apt-get or maven) to install protoc. Because Docker can only inherit from one base Dokerfile, if users have different combination of software to use, providing a Dock image for protoc alone doesn't work.

title: Issue with protobuf-java generating TimestampProto$Timestamp class
body:
Hi,

I'm using protobuf-java version 3.3.0 with dozer to do some mapping rules, you can find one repo reproducing the issue: [https://github.com/panes/dozer-protobuf](url)

And I got one issue trying to do so, timestamp.proto specifies TimestampProto as outer class name, so dozer expects to find the Timestamp class in TimestampProto$Timestamp not directly Timestamp. If I generate a class with proto3 from the same proto message like timestamp, everything is fine, because I have TimestampProto$Timestamp, and dozer works well.

Here the link of opened dozer topic: [https://github.com/DozerMapper/dozer/issues/514](url)

Could you explain me why Timestamp class is generated like that in protobuf-java?
And how can I fix it?
Thanks.

Best regards,
Phil

nodes.body:
Protobuf generates com.google.protobuf.Timestamp because of the "java_multiple_files = true" option. It sounds to me dozer doesn't have the right support for this option.
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/timestamp.proto#L40
Ok got it, I'll push it to dozer side then, to see how they can support this option. Thanks for your reply.

title: Truncated Message due to "TypeError: unhashable type: 'bytearray'"
body:
I am receiving these errors on a Raspberry Pis:  "TypeError: unhashable type: 'bytearray'"

The code to reproduce the problem is very simple:

- Python 3.5.3
- Raspbian Stretch 9.1
- The following packages:
   grpcio (1.6.3)
   grpcio-reflection (1.6.3)
   grpcio-tools (1.6.3)

test.proto (very simple):
```
syntax = "proto3";

package bug;

message Foo
{
    string field1 = 1;
}
```

and the Python code:

```python
from test_pb2 import Foo

EXPECTED = bytearray(b'\n\x04AAAA')
foo = Foo()
foo.field1 = 'AAAA'
print(foo)

data = foo.SerializeToString()
print(data)
assert (data == EXPECTED)

foo.ParseFromString(EXPECTED)
assert (foo.field1 == 'AAAA')
```

The deserialization only fails in Raspberry Pi (Ubuntu is fine):
```
field1: "AAAA"

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/pi/.local/lib/python3.5/site-packages/google/protobuf/internal/python_message.py", line 1069, in MergeFromString
    if self._InternalParse(serialized, 0, length) != length:
  File "/home/pi/.local/lib/python3.5/site-packages/google/protobuf/internal/python_message.py", line 1092, in InternalParse
    field_decoder, field_desc = decoders_by_tag.get(tag_bytes, (None, None))
TypeError: unhashable type: 'bytearray'

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test.py", line 13, in <module>
    foo.ParseFromString(REF)
  File "/home/pi/.local/lib/python3.5/site-packages/google/protobuf/message.py", line 185, in ParseFromString
    self.MergeFromString(serialized)
  File "/home/pi/.local/lib/python3.5/site-packages/google/protobuf/internal/python_message.py", line 1075, in MergeFromString
    raise message_mod.DecodeError('Truncated message.')
google.protobuf.message.DecodeError: Truncated message.
```

nodes.body:
I managed to find a workaround for the problem in the Raspberry Pi.

The issue was that when running in the Pi deserialize fails for `bytearray`, however, if the data is passed as `bytes` things work well.

So my current workaround is to do something like:

```python
foo.ParseFromString( bytes(EXPECTED) )
```

I am still not sure why the same problem does not happen in desktops. What I have noticed is that when debugging in desktops, `foo.ParseFromString` is shown as `<built-in method ParseFromString of Foo object at 0x7fedcc0b3fa8>` so I suppose that there is some native optimization in desktops that is not available when running in the Pi.

When I have a little more time I will try to investigate a little more on how protobuf is deployed. Maybe in the meantime someone can share some details.

It seems that this is affecting other users too.
I have submitted a PR to fix this issue https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/3736
PR #3736 has been merged so this issue can be closed

title: kotlin  support request
body: please support convert to kotlin

nodes.body: Right now it is not planned. We recommend using the Java bindings instead given the interoperability, mostly due to the code size bloat when both kotlin and Java are generated in the same app. Will keep this posted when anything changes.
Kotlin support would be so much better than the current Java builders. :)
Don't forget that Kotlin can compile to non-jvm environments, so just saying 'use java' actually doesn't solve the kotlin problem.

If a Kotlin code generator is ever created, it would be great if "oneofs" were turned into sealed classes, rather than having the "*Case" enum.

Also, given how nice null handling is in Kotlin, I wish optional fields could simply be implemented as nullable properties, rather than having the separate "has*" methods.
Btw kotlinx.serialization supports protobuf already without any code generation. Sent with GitHawk

@christophsturm that's interesting, but it doesn't seem like it really addresses the issue.  The problem is that you usually start with a .proto file that you really do want to use for code generation, and it looks like there's only partial support for protobuf anyway - https://github.com/Kotlin/kotlinx.serialization/issues/67.
yes it has a different focus and i would love to see kotlin code generation in protobuf.

I am toying around with implementing this.

The ideal situation would be to generate all the required data classes (yes, that means immutable and sealed hierarchies for oneofs) and abstract the sizing, marshalling, and unmarshalling via multiplatform expect/actual classes and defer to existing protobuf serialization code for the three primary targets (JVM, JS, native). Maybe could have hand written serialization, but the existing language impls are highly optimized, especially in the JVM case. Also, for `protoc-gen-kotlin`, I am bootstrapping with the JVM impl for now but once complete, I am planning on it actually using Kotlin native so it can ship as a single binary (so I'm not using KotlinPoet). I am leaving enumerates open ended as data classes w/ a single int value and the known values as vals on the companion object. I may only support proto3 at first, we'll see. 

I will update if/when complete.

Initial version complete: https://github.com/cretz/pb-and-k. I'll broadcast to Kotlin forum and/or Reddit tomorrow so no need to clutter up this issue discussing. It only has basic features now, but I'll implement more if the project becomes popular.
An another projet looks promising [kroto-plus](https://github.com/marcoferrer/kroto-plus)

This is a project we are (and specifically I am) working on for Google, with an unstable prototype landing in open source sometime in the late Q2-early Q3 range.

Some specifics, just to be clear:

- We're initially focusing on building extensions atop the generated Java APIs.  A major goal of Kotlin is to support incremental migration of existing Java projects without compatibility hassles; we would intend the same approach here.  Down the line, we might investigate generating pure Kotlin, but it would be API compatible with the generated Java APIs.
- Oneofs can't be sealed without breaking on future additions to the oneof, which are supposed to be compatible changes.  I think we'll be generating something that "looks like" the sealed class would, except for the sealed keyword.
- We're still discussing nullable representations of optional fields.
@lowasser interesting! Can we expect data class generation rather Java builders?

Neither.  Data classes as in `data class` have difficult conflicts with ways protos are supposed to be able to evolve forward-compatibly.  (For example, new fields can be inserted "between" old fields.)  We're thinking in terms of DSLs:

```
myMessage {
   field1 = 5
   field2 = "foobar"
}
```

...which is not actually that different, all things considered, from

```
MyMessage(
  field1 = 5, 
  field2 = "foobar"
)
```
I've posted https://github.com/lowasser/protobuf/blob/master/kotlin-design.md , which is a complete description of the design our internal process came up with.

@lowasser it’s really great to see this starting to gain some attention. I author a library that provides dsl generation for proto messages https://github.com/marcoferrer/kroto-plus

I still think it falls short of true first party kotlin support though. 

A couple of notes I wanted to add. One thing we experienced early on was the need to have message types annotated with kotlins DslMarker annotation. This provides compile time safety so that one nested lambda doesn’t mutate the scope of a parent lambda. 

Also I saw that you mentioned that there is a separate discussion for improvements to grpc apis. Is this public yet? The kroto project has been working on refining grpc integration with coroutines and I wouldn’t mind helping contribute

@lowasser I understand the design constraints might be different for google's kotlin generator (for instance with regards to positional args, data classes, or a copy method), but if your team hasn't yet, it might be helpful to take a look at the approach @thesamet took for ScalaPB:

* support for optional scalars from proto2 sources, repeated fields as immutable vectors, and map fields as immutable maps:
https://scalapb.github.io/generated-code.html#messages

* `withX` methods for updating field `X` in a message, an `update` method that takes a list of mutations, and mutations on deeply nested fields:
https://scalapb.github.io/generated-code.html#updating-messages

* all proto objects immutable

* oneofs as sealed types:
https://scalapb.github.io/generated-code.html#oneof-fields

* alternative representation for oneofs:
https://scalapb.github.io/sealed-oneofs.html

* google's well-known wrapper types for proto3 scalars as optionals:
https://scalapb.github.io/customizations.html#primitive-wrappers

* support for wrapping primitives in inline classes:
https://scalapb.github.io/customizations.html#custom-types

* It's a replacement for the protoc java output so your application doesn't have to pay the cost of generated code twice, but there is an option to generate interop code:
https://scalapb.github.io/generated-code.html#java-conversions

Although the target language for ScalaPB is different, some of the ideas would translate fairly well to a Kotlin code generator.

@dsilvasc Point by point:

 * support for optional scalars from proto2 sources, repeated fields as immutable vectors, and map fields as immutable maps:
https://scalapb.github.io/generated-code.html#messages

We already do surface repeated fields as immutable lists and map fields as immutable maps.   (I don't believe there's currently a way to expose the unmodifiable *interface* while keeping the base proto in Java, unless there's an annotation available for that...?) Optional scalars is something we may well do for proto2, though we're mostly focusing on proto3 right now.  (If I didn't list that in the "Open Questions" section, that was an oversight on my part.)

* withX methods for updating field X in a message, an update method that takes a list of mutations, and mutations on deeply nested fields:
https://scalapb.github.io/generated-code.html#updating-messages
I think we're seeing that as all-encompassed by the `copy` method: `myMessage.copy { field = foo }` is about even with `myMessage.withField(foo)`.  Deeply-nested changes aren't too bad either: `myMessage.copy { field = field.copy { subField = foo } }`.

* all proto objects immutable
This is already part of the Java API.

* oneofs as sealed types: https://scalapb.github.io/generated-code.html#oneof-fields
FWIW, the doc discusses this as an idea we specifically considered and decided was *actively* a bad idea, because protos are supposed to support evolution.  It doesn't actually make that much difference, FWIW.

* google's well-known wrapper types for proto3 scalars as optionals:
https://scalapb.github.io/customizations.html#primitive-wrappers
Definitely falls under the category of the "Open Questions" discussion.

* support for wrapping primitives in inline classes:
https://scalapb.github.io/customizations.html#custom-types
Huh.  Interesting.  I feel kind of weird about this, and I'm not sure the implicit type mapping is in scope.

@lowasser - can you clarify why sealing oneofs inhibits proto evolution? In ScalaPB, we generate an `Empty` case, so users can pattern match on `Empty` to handle unexpected future developments. The advantage of sealing is, of course, that you can get a compiler warning if there are unhandled cases. Agree this is not much of a difference, but as author/maintainer of ScalaPB I'd be happy to fully understand the perspective that considers this an actively bad idea.

@thesamet In Kotlin, my understanding is that an unhandled case in a when-expression is an _error_, not a warning.  When expressions are required to be exhaustive.  That makes adding new cases a source-incompatible change.  (Demo: https://pl.kotl.in/yWJloqTKg, for a scenario where code that worked before the addition of `DoubleOneof` stops compiling when it's added.)
(I'm actually a little surprised to hear it's not an error in Scala -- what actually happens when there's an unhandled case in a match expression?)

@lowasser Thanks for clarifying. In Scala you get a warning at compile time and a `MatchError` exception at runtime: https://scastie.scala-lang.org/RWeVMPvoSJypVulnb8DjLw. Some people use a compiler option to promote warnings into errors so they don't miss on cases.

Taking an optional field removal as a potential proto evolution step: this breaks source compatibility for all compiled languages since getters/setters will not be generated.  I personally find it desirable to get a compiler warning/error at the use-site when a case or a field is added or removed so I know everything is being handled. Also is scala, it is easy to fix for future unknown cases by pattern matching on `_` (which is a catch all).

We've never supported optional field removal as a source-compatible change -- do any language proto APIs? -- but supporting adding new fields without breaking existing code's compilation has always been a business-critical use case for us.  As far as I know, all the other officially supported proto APIs have similar support.

It's easy to handle unknown future cases in Kotlin, too -- just have an `else` branch in your `when`, which behaves analogously to how you describe `_`.  Omitting the `sealed` keyword on the class really only means users should match `else` instead of `NotSet`, which seemed like an acceptable balance to guarantee protos can evolve the ways we expect without breaking builds or tests.

Giving users an option to represent oneofs as sealed would be helpful for teams who want their source to break when they update their schemas -- teams who want to be forced to handle new possible cases.

The java code generated for enums already does this and it's helpful that teams can choose on a case-by-case basis whether they want source-breaking exhaustive matches or source-forward-compatible `else`/`_` branches (in addition to the generated Unknown case, which is different from default/NotSet).

An option to make oneofs effectively sealed seems like a reasonable addition, though in some ways I wonder if that should really be a Kotlin-exclusive feature.  Do other languages for protobufs already have such an annotation?  Or was it suggested, and rejected?

I don't think sealed hierarchies are easily expressible in the languages targeted by this repo (Java, C++, Python, ObjC, C#, JS, Ruby).

In languages with sealed types (Scala, Rust, Swift), their protobuf code generators opted for representing oneofs as sealed:

https://github.com/apple/swift-protobuf/blob/master/Documentation/API.md#oneof-fields
https://github.com/danburkert/prost#oneof-fields
https://github.com/stepancheg/rust-protobuf/blob/ad2518b81351399ab8f0e6e3a88367e0b066399c/protobuf-codegen/src/oneof.rs#L196
Sorry, we don't have time to support this in the near future. Close this for now.
Noooo @TeBoring
I think there's just been some confusion -- the work is getting done by the Kotlin team instead of the proto team.  The project is continuing on the timeline I described above.

> I think there's just been some confusion -- the work is getting done by the Kotlin team instead of the proto team. The project is continuing on the timeline I described above.

Yes, it's still happening.  Progress, when it occurs in open-source, will be posted right here.

We've built another Kotlin protobuf compiler: https://github.com/open-toast/protokt. The design was inspired by many of the projects referenced above: pb-and-k (oneofs, enums), scalapb (extensions, enums), kroto+ and the Google design doc (DSL constructor pattern).  

We invite everyone to try it out and give feedback!
The official Kotlin protobuf API is now moving through the open-sourcing process; we hope to have a full announcement soon.

@pratik-brex There isn't explicit support for gRPC in pbandk.
