@lowasser It's been over 7 month since your last update on Protobuf team plans for first-class Kotlin support.
Could you please share current status with community?

I would also want to see an update here. I'd like to use gRPC in my Kotlin application, yet the not at all idiomatic code generated by protoc-java is really deterring me from using it. Google has made great efforts in embracing Kotlin, especially in the Android world, but just saying that Kotlin is the preferred language for this and that is not enough. Kotlin stands out because of its unique and ergonomic language features. Simply translating Java code into Kotlin completely defies the point of using Kotlin instead of Java.

In my opinion, writing and generating Kotlin-idiomatic code instead of Java-like code (as explained in [Koans](https://play.kotlinlang.org/koans/overview)) should be an integral part of promoting Kotlin as, for example, the preferred Android language. This also includes proper Kotlin support in both ProtoBuf and gRPC.

Probably one of the most important features that a hypothetical protoc-kotlin compiler should have is to implement the officially promoted [type-safe builder pattern](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/reference/type-safe-builders.html) instead of a Java-style builder pattern. This has already been addressed in this discussion.

Concerning the discussion about sealed classes, a few points seem to be relevant to add:

1. Since the discussion is quite old by now, things have changed: sealed classes are now not only a thing in Kotlin, but also an experimental feature in Java 15. I think that by now the discussion is almost language-agnostic, since closed polymorphism becomes more and more popular and gets added to more and more languages.
2. Adding an `else` branch in an (exhaustive) `when`-expression is as well possible when working with sealed classes. It is however true that this might issue a warning because it is unnecessary in an exhaustive case.
3. `when`-statements _do not_ have to be exhaustive in any case. As well as `if`-statements, they only have to cover all outcomes **if and only if** the statement is used as an expression (which makes kinda sense). Also, the presence of an `else` branch automatically makes any `when`-expression exhaustive (but then again, it might issue warnings..)

Anyway, I hope that this feature is still being worked on, because I really think it is a necessity as of today. Since the discussion is already 5 months old, I am not sure about the state of third-party Proto/gRPC for Kotlin projects. If anyone can point me towards the currently active projects, that would be very nice.

I think we deserve some kind of update on this feature by now.

The state is that yes, it is still being worked on extremely actively; no, there is not much to show for it publicly yet.

Some things that have happened in the past few months:

* the code generator has been rewritten entirely in C++ as part of the main protobuf compiler, in particular to make it easier for the main protobuf team to own the project long term and make it easier to open source
* the design has been somewhat simplified and thoroughly reviewed, because pretty literally every bit of Google's Kotlin code will use this and backwards-incompatible changes would be extraordinarily painful; the sealed class oneofs are being left off for the moment; the typesafe builder pattern is clearly the best way to do this in Kotlin and that's what we're doing
* the protobuf team has hired a new employee who is working on this as one of their main projects

If you're looking for third-party support, as mentioned above (disclaimer: I'm a developer), https://github.com/open-toast/protokt generates idiomatic Kotlin code and supports ServiceDescriptor and MethodDescriptor generation that is compatible with both grpc-java and grpc-kotlin. It does not interoperate at the Java/Kotlin level with code generated with protobuf-java, which is something the protobuf team is doing. It has the potential for cross-platform functionality but that's not currently in the roadmap. It is used in production at Toast.

If you're looking for a solution that does have interop with protobuf-java's generated code, you might look at https://github.com/marcoferrer/kroto-plus. My guess is that it will be mostly straightforward to migrate from that to an official library when that time comes.

Note also that you can use grpc-kotlin with the Java bindings that exist today and get coroutine support. Later, when an official Kotlin generator is released, you can migrate message building separately.

To add another option, https://github.com/streem/pbandk generates idiomatic Kotlin code and supports Kotlin Mulitplatform (JVM, JS, and Native). Disclaimer: I'm the primary maintainer of the project. We use it in production at Streem in our backend and Android code.

pbandk is pretty similar in spirit to protokt. I'd say the main differences with protokt are that protokt includes built-in support for gRPC (which pbandk lacks), but pbandk includes support for JSON and Kotlin Multiplatform (which protokt lacks). pbandk also focuses on implementing serialization/deserialization in the runtime library, whereas protokt implements it in the generated code. There are of course lots of smaller differences too.

pbandk currently generates Kotlin data classes for each proto message, which are idiomatic Kotlin but run into some backwards-compatibility concerns when the proto message definition evolves (as discussed above). We plan to replace those with Kotlin-style type-safe builders in an upcoming version.
@lowasser Is there any date that is being aimed for? I think many people would like to support the project, but as long as it's not out in the open, no one can.

title: TextFormat specification seems to be undocumented
body:
I'm trying to figure out how to print a protocol buffer in text format that is compatible with the existing implementations of text format. The issue is that I cannot find any specification of TextFormat and only implementations. Given that there are multiple implementations (C++,Java,Go) that are interoperable it seems that there is a spec even if it isn't yet documented.

The binary format and proto file format are all well documented on the developer site:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers.

nodes.body: The textformat isn't intended to be interoperable across languages/implementations, and I believe it already isn't fully portable. I'd recommend using binary format for any use cases that require portability.

I'm implementing support for protocol buffers in a language that doesn't already have support, even if text format isn't fully portable, it is used in many existing systems as a human readable version.

protoc seems to support some version of Text Format for use with the --encode and --decode options. Can that version at least be documented?
@endobson If you are implementing protobuf for a new language, can you support proto3 JSON format instead?
I'll investigate it. That probably is a better choice if protobuf is moving away from the old text format.

FWIW There exists internal documentation available to Googlers. It might make sense to publish it publically   https://b.corp.google.com/issues/173410810 (Googlers only)

https://stackoverflow.com/q/18873924 "what does textproto look like?" is a popular question.

There are over two million textproto files on GitHub https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Apbtxt

> FWIW There exists internal documentation available to Googlers. It might make sense to publish it publically https://b.corp.google.com/issues/173410810 (Googlers only)
> 
> https://stackoverflow.com/q/18873924 "what does textproto look like?" is a popular question

Yes. What's the status on that? I helped write that spec when I was there and would love to see it released.

I, for one, don't love the ergonomics of JSON for human readable and editable applications and would greatly appreciate a documented specification for the text format. For those of us that maintain third party proto implementations and compiler plugins, this would be a useful reference. My use cases are largely human editable config for a single language. Having portability across implementations would be great, but I don't know that it's necessary, at least for the use cases I am thinking of. Also FWIW, it looks like there is now a conformance suite for the text implementation?

I'm also a fan of textproto for human writeable and readable configuration files , since it doesn't have any of JSON downfalls, an actual number type. I and many others would appreciate a OSS Release of the textproto Spec. 

There are currently about 2.3 Million files on Github which implicitly depend on this spec.


AFAIU there's an internal spec available at [go/textproto-spec](https://goto.google.com/textproto-spec), which is under further discussion at [b/173410810](https://b.corp.google.com/issues/173410810) (Googler only)

*Queries*:
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Apbtxt
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Apbtext
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Atxtpb
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Atextproto
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Atextpb
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Aasciipb
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Apbascii
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Aprotoascii
- https://github.com/search?q=extension%3Aprototxt

The Go (golang) implementation seems to know how to marshal to and from the textual format. I presume they must have implemented this to some defined standard?

Old/v1:

- Doc: https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/golang/protobuf@v1.5.2/proto#MarshalText
- https://github.com/golang/protobuf/blob/v1.5.2/proto/text_encode.go
- https://github.com/golang/protobuf/blob/v1.5.2/proto/text_decode.go

Current/v2:

- Doc: https://pkg.go.dev/google.golang.org/protobuf@v1.27.1/encoding/prototext
- https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-go/blob/v1.27.1/encoding/prototext/encode.go
- https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-go/blob/v1.27.1/encoding/prototext/decode.go

The docs above do contain this warning:

>Do not depend on the output being stable. It may change over time across different versions of the program.

The defacto spec is the c++ [implementation](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/text_format.cc). That's what everything else is based on, including the aforementioned internal spec (at least that was the case when I was there 3 years ago). The v2 go implementation was made in conjunction with the reverse-engineered internal spec.

Is there any chance we can get this reopened? It's unclear to me why this was closed.

Some of the C++ gRPC folks might be in the right place to get this moving again (unless there's a dedicated C++ proto team- I don't remember if there was one when I left last year).
There's a newer, open issue at https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8636

title: Bazel workspace name mismatch for @com_google_protobuf_cc causes build warnings
body:
Bazel's native `proto_library` rules have an implicit dependency on `@com_google_protobuf//:protoc`, while `cc_proto_library` rules have one on `@com_google_protobuf_cc//:cc_toolchain`. I believe the normal way of configuring a Bazel project to use these rules is to point both the plain and `_cc` remote repositories at the code in this GitHub repository.

With the recent addition of `workspace(name = "com_google_protobuf")` in the protobuf `WORKSPACE` file, any use of `cc_proto_library` (after pointing it at this code) is now causing the following warning:

`WARNING: /.../external/com_google_protobuf_cc/WORKSPACE:1: Workspace name in /.../external/com_google_protobuf_cc/WORKSPACE (@com_google_protobuf) does not match the name given in the repository's definition (@com_google_protobuf_cc); this will cause a build error in future versions`

There's an analogous issue for `java_proto_library`'s implicit dependency on `@com_google_protobuf_java`, which could also be pointed at the same codebase. (`java_lite_proto_library` manages to avoid this because the `javalite` branch doesn't have the workspace name definition.)

FWIW, I'm not really sure whether this counts as a protobuf issue or a Bazel issue.

I've managed to partially work around the issue by using `build --proto_toolchain_for_cc=@com_google_protobuf//:cc_toolchain` in my project's `bazel.rc`, but that does not work for example for "bazel query", which has no equivalent flag.

nodes.body: Forgot to mention: this was using the latest Bazel release (0.6.1).

@cgrushko The options I can think of to address this warning:
1. Remove `workspace(name = "com_google_protobuf")` from protobuf's WORKSPACE file.
2. Remove the warning from bazel and be tolerant with the workspace name discrepancy. 
3. Make bazel point at com_google_protobuf by default for cc/java_proto_library rules.

Option (3) seems the only reasonable solution.
Seems this is fixed according to https://github.com/cgrushko/proto_library/issues/4

title: Protobuf import error between protobuf 3.1 and 3.2 - Python

nodes.body:
This error message indicates the _pb2.py files are not generated correctly:
```
Invalid proto descriptor for file "third_party/google/api/annotations.proto":
third_party/google/api/annotations.proto: Import "google/api/http.proto" has not been loaded.
google.api.http: "google.api.HttpRule" seems to be defined in "third_party/google/api/http.proto", which is not imported by "third_party/google/api/annotations.proto". To use it here, please add the necessary import.
```
When you run protoc, make sure you are running it in the third_party directory and pass command line flags like this:
```bash
$ protoc --python_out=... google/api/annotations.proto google/api/http.proto
```

Thanks for the reply Feng.  I did a quick test and looks like compiling within the  third_party directory solves this issue.   Was this something that changed from release 3.1 to 3.2?

The current compile that does not cause the above runtime issue in 3.2:
python -m grpc.tools.protoc     -I.    --python_out=.     --grpc_python_out=.     --descriptor_set_out=google/api/annotations.desc     --include_imports     --include_source_info   google/api/http.proto  google/api/annotations.proto

The commands that does not cause the issue in 3.1 (but had the issue in 3.2).  The compile was done in the same directory as third_party:

python -m grpc.tools.protoc \
    -I. \
    -I./third_party \
    --python_out=. \
    --grpc_python_out=. \
    --descriptor_set_out=third_party/google/api/annotations.desc \
    --include_imports \
    --include_source_info \
    third_party/google/api/annotations.proto

python -m grpc.tools.protoc \
    -I. \
    -I./third_party \
    --python_out=. \
    --grpc_python_out=. \
    --descriptor_set_out=third_party/google/api/http.desc \
    --include_imports \
    --include_source_info \
    third_party/google/api/http.proto

@khenaidoo I think you can solve the issue by omitting "-I." in the protoc command line. I.e.,
```bash
$ python -m grpc.tools.protoc -Ithird_party ...
```
The additional "-I." flag is unnecessary and will just confuse protoc.

When invoking protoc, it's better to just invoke it in the "root" directory of the protos you are compiling. In this case the "root" directory for "google/api/http.proto" is "third_party". If you are running protoc in some other directory, you need to make sure the "-I" flags are set correctly and ordered correctly. Most users will likely get it wrong due to protoc's unusual interpretation of the "-I" flags...

Thanks for the explanation Feng.   I tried when removing the extra "-I" but I still get a runtime error.  The only way that seems to work is inside the third_party directory:

python -m grpc.tools.protoc -I. --python_out=. --grpc_python_out=. --descriptor_set_out=google/api/annotations.desc --include_imports --include_source_info google/api/http.proto google/api/annotations.proto

Is it an issue to have a single desc output (annotations.desc) when compiling two files (http.proto, annotations.proto)?  I think it should not but wanted to double check.

Thanks
Khen
Having multiple files with one descriptor_set_out is fine.
Closing this issue as the above recommendations fixed the issue I was having.  Thanks Feng.

title: how to write .proto file?

nodes.body: What problems did you encounter?
@acozzette  how to wirite bit field in proto file?

@dongjiang1989 Protobuf doesn't directly support bitfields. To accomplish this sort of thing you would need to work with the regular integer types and then manually use bit operations to manipulate your data.

title: How can i reduce librarys size?
body:
Hi,
I just want work with c++ and my device storage is too small(128M), so how can i reduce libs size?

Thanks.

nodes.body: I would recommend setting `option optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME;` in your .proto files and linking against `libprotobuf-lite`. This will save size by leaving out support for reflection.
There are also on-going efforts to further reduce the size. Probably will be available in 3.6+ releases.

Thanks for reply.
i used `CXXFLAGS="$(pkg-config --cflags protobuf-lite)" LIBS="$(pkg-config --libs protobuf-lite)" CFLAGS="$(pkg-config --cflags protobuf-lite)" --enable-static=no` for configure flags and the out libs size was reduced.

change to ```tender.getOwner().getFirstName()```?

Feel free to reopen if you still have question.

title: Where to find `protoc`?
body:
I'm attempting to use protobuf and, having carefully followed the docs, I now have a .proto file that is ready to compile.  But I cant find the protobuf compiler: `protoc` anywhere.  The `readme.md` says: 
> In the downloads section of each release, you can find pre-built binaries in zip packages: protoc-$VERSION-$PLATFORM.zip. It contains the protoc binary as well as a set of standard .proto files distributed along with protobuf.

I have downloaded the 3.4.1, 3.4.0 or 3.3.0 releases, but I cant find a "downloads" section in any of them.  Are we supposed to compile from source?  Or are binaries provided?  If so, where?

I've seen another discussion (https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3775) where we told to go to Maven for precompiled versions.  However those `protoc` files are all compiled for windows ("protoc-3.4.0-osx-x86_64.exe").  I bit of cruel irony, I guess.

So what is the preferred method of using `protoc`?  
And, once answered, will someone update the `readme.md` file to match?
Thanks!

nodes.body:
Open this release page:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/releases/tag/v3.4.0

and in the downloads section you can find protoc-3.4.0-osx-x86_64.zip.

The protoc binaries we put up in maven are indeed compiled for multiple platforms. protoc-3.4.0-osx-x86_64.exe is a OSX binary. Don't be fooled by its file name... You can just change it to `protoc` after download (or at the time of download). You probably also need to `chmod +x` on it.

@xfxyjwf Thank you for the help.  I spent several hours and just couldn't "see" the files.  Clearly they were right in front of me in the "Downloads" section at the bottom of the list.  Its so frustrating when one misses stuff like that!  My Bad!  Thanks for the help.

nodes.body:
This is from the unsafe utility that we use in Google to optimize for performance without generating code. We are aware that the unsafe APIs are planned to be deprecated/removed since Java9 - thus this warning. The UnsafeUtil code is opensourced to show the usages of those APIs, and we are still working with the Java9 community to resolve the issue.

That said, your project are not relying on the unsafe access, unless you explicitly call the unsafe APIs. The log is printed only because of the class initialization.

Most major libraries have fixed this, or are working on it, protobuf should do the same:
https://github.com/netty/netty/pull/7650
https://github.com/google/guice/issues/1085

Tolerating warnings in logs is universally considered a bad practice. Java 9 has been GA for four months.
@bartlomiej-dawidow Do you have a suggestion about how to fix the UnsafeUtil code? It's not clear to me whether there is an alternative that works on Java 7+ and doesn't trigger the Java 9 warning.

Based on @pherl 's response the unsafe code is only used for optional optimizations and it is not needed for the library to work:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3781#issuecomment-339794368

So a natural fix would be to move that functionality to a separate Maven module, for example protobuf-java-unsafe. You could probably achieve the same effect with some class loader magic that would delay the problematic class's initialization until it is actually called.
@bartlomiej-dawidow It's not a requirement at the moment, but will likely become one in the future. Separating the code or delay the initialization won't fix the issue.

@xfxyjwf Do a multi-release jar: http://openjdk.java.net/jeps/238 - The main issue is how to wrangle bazel  an acceptable fashion to make one of those, since the Java 9 version of the class will need to have the same name of com.google.protobuf.UnsafeUtils in a dir bazel doesn't natively support.
@shemnon Thanks! That multi-release jar seems exactly what we need to provide support for both Java 9 and pre Java 9. I'll investigate how we can make use of it in protobuf.
Hello! What's the status of work on the multi-release jar mentioned above? Thanks!

It is Java 10 here and I'm still getting warnings! 
Any news?

```
WARNING: An illegal reflective access operation has occurred
WARNING: Illegal reflective access by com.google.protobuf.UnsafeUtil (file:.......) to field java.nio.Buffer.address
WARNING: Please consider reporting this to the maintainers of com.google.protobuf.UnsafeUtil
WARNING: Use --illegal-access=warn to enable warnings of further illegal reflective access operations
WARNING: All illegal access operations will be denied in a future release
```
trying to use Graal and definitely hit issues w/ unsafe usage.
quick ping; java 11 is released.

It's nearly two years since this issue popped up and there are only a few months left (Feb '19) until Java8 runs out of support. Please provide a new version that makes protobuf compatible with current Java versions.

What's the current blocker? Is this waiting on Bazel's ability to create Multi-Release JAR? - https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/5947

In the meantime could we move on using any other build tool like Maven, Gradle, or sbt that can build Multi-Release JAR, please? Also if anyone has created a fork, please let me know.
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/4557 got closed in April, but since the use of Unsafe is guarded by if condition, putting null in there based on `System.getProperty("java.version")` should be slow, but an okay workaround right?
Once Google moves off of Java 8 internally I suspect they will just fix it and say Java 8 (or performant Java 8) is out of scope of this library.

They can be under different versions! it would be simple like that, like v4 for JDK 9/10/11+ and v3 for JDK 7/8, We have 3 versions, and soon 4th version after JDK 8, I understand that Java 8 is mostly used now (since Oct. 2013) and Java 9 from 2017, but still last 3 versions added a lot of things for Java.
@xfxyjwf Any updates on this?

FYI: I tested with `--illegal-access=fail` and protobuf operated correctly and got no warning. Seems it may be a false positive.

I'd be very interested to see a failure caused by the access.

I am continuing to get this error message with `protobuf-java-3.6.1` with Java 9:
WARNING: Illegal reflective access by com.google.protobuf.UnsafeUtil
@cushon, I ran it with `deny` as well :). I ran it and then later mentioned I had done it, and so got mixed up with with flag actually worked.

@cushon, also your code snipped isn't quite equivalent. [The actual code](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/29f27bfd0bd474bc3272fead14917a689c1825db/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/UnsafeUtil.java#L390-L396) will catch the exception and move on. Now there may be a bug, but the code at least attempts to behave well.

It looks like `IterableByteBufferInputStream`, for example, fails to check `hasUnsafeByteBufferOperations()`. But I see lots of other places that do check for availability first.

I started digging into this issue. The warning stems from [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/UnsafeUtil.java#L401). The Field returns by this method is simply used to pass to [Unsafe.objectFieldOffset()](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/UnsafeUtil.java#L418), which seems to work even without `setAccessible(true)`.

I might be missing something, but we may be able to simply remove that call, which will get rid of the warning.
(@haon4 Your second link does not jump to the line)

> (@haon4 Your second link does not jump to the line)

Oops. Missing an L in the URL. Fixed.
The setAccessible is necessary to have later reflective calls of the field work, because the fields are private.
It was pointed out to me that the `field()` method is only used once. So it does actually look like the `setAccessible()` may be unnecessary.

This issue should be fixed at master with https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/624a40a387e1b2da4c6bbde44ad3d0a5efb9879b#diff-6c9e043b78f78efc096211703bb7fa4a, which should be included in our next release.

title: How to use Gzip?
body:
I want to compress protobuf to string by Gzip. Then I write string to db.
Next I read db to string, uncompress string to probobuf struct.
I look for protobuf org doccument, but I don't found example.

nodes.body:

@matthauck We are not aware of any alternative except for disabling the warning and protobuf requires these offsets to function. If you know of better ways, feel free to suggest...

I'm not entirely familiar with `offsetof` and what protobuf depends on them for. It looks like if there was a virtual table or something then `offsetof` doesn't calculate the correct offset for non-POD types perhaps? It just seems that if the compiler is saying the offsets are not valid, then it could be broken. Surmised from here: https://stackoverflow.com/a/1130035

> This will crash when trying to locate the field a inside type B statically, while it works when an instance is available. This is because of the virtual inheritance, where the location of the base class is stored into a lookup table.

I'm happy to leave it as it is though if its working. Just wanted confirmation that protobuf knows what it's doing here and disabling the warning is The Right Thing. :) 

If this is the final resolution, it would be cool to add `#ifdef'd` scoped warning disables for gcc/clang at least so that we don't have to set `-Wno-invalid-offset` for anything that includes a protobuf generated c++ file.

It's also worth noting that whatever protobuf was doing in 3.3.x branch worked just fine for older compilers. It looks like this was introduced in 3.4.x. So maybe the 3.5.x branch could revert back to the previous offset mechanism that seemed to work better with older compilers perhaps?

Here is what we were using before:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/generated_message_util.h#L101-L105
```cpp
#define GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_GENERATED_MESSAGE_FIELD_OFFSET(TYPE, FIELD)  \
  static_cast< ::google::protobuf::uint32>(                           \
      reinterpret_cast<const char*>(                                 \
          &reinterpret_cast<const TYPE*>(16)->FIELD) -               \
      reinterpret_cast<const char*>(16))
#endif
```
It's trying to calculate an offset from addresses of an invalid object... The compiler doesn't produce a warning for it, but really it's more broken than than warned offset usage...

Ah. interesting.

title: Documentation for adding comments only mentions line comments, not block comments
body:
In proto [documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#adding-comments), it is mentioned that only line comments are supported
However, in [descriptor.proto](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L834) block comments are specifically supported. 
I wanted to fix documentation in PR, but apparently it's not coming from a public git repo.
I think documentation should state that block comments are supported.

nodes.body: Thanks for reporting this. I wrote a fix for the documentation and it should be published on the site soon.
The update is now live on the documentation site.

title: Please allow the addition of stubs for the Python protobuf API to typeshed
body:
In https://github.com/python/typeshed we are collecting type-checking stubs for the Python standard library and for popular third party Python packages. These stubs are used by mypy, PyCharm and Google's own pytype.

We'd like to add stubs for protobuf. Our policy is to first request permission from the original package developers, to ensure that we don't do double work or cause additional problems for them. (See https://github.com/python/typeshed#third_party for the policy.)

To give permission, just say so in this issue and we'll do the rest (unless you want to be more involved, that would be great of course).

PS. I know of several projects that automatically generate stubs from protobuf specifications. Such stubs will be more useful if the protobuf base library APIs have stubs.

nodes.body: Sounds great! Will this require some kind of support in protoc for generating stubs? It sounds like you already know of some projects that must be automatically generating stubs from .proto files.

Glad to hear it! At Dropbox we already have *two* utilities that generate stubs from protobuf source code -- one in Go, one in Python! Of course it would be great if we could replace both of these with a new flag to protoc. But in the short term we are now in control of our own destiny.

Not yet; their respective authors want to open-source them but it takes time.

We could really do with using these utilities at work, sorry to bother you but is there any chance of a release sometime soon?

Wrote my own little util for it, but it's not particularly thorough.

@wkiser, @wjh: The stub generating utilities are now available: https://github.com/dropbox/mypy-protobuf/

Also, since we've now got the permission to proceed with including the stubs in typeshed, closing this issue.

title: Enum value with index 0 not shown

nodes.body: This is by design actually: proto3 enums must start with a zero-valued entry, which is used as the default value. Is it possible to get the JSON serializer to write the fields which are set to their default values?

@uldall I think it might depend on which language you're using but at least for some languages there's an option to print primitive fields even if they're set to the default. Here is it for C++ for example: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/23adfeb00327fbdccacc99806acb1a9a073bd8e0/src/google/protobuf/util/json_util.h#L63

title: protoc produces SourceCodeInfo that references uninterpreted options, which are not present
body:
When protoc produces `SourceCodeInfo` for a file descriptor, all details related to options are attributed (according to the `path` field) to uninterpreted options. There is no way, however, for client code to actually map uninterpreted options to the actual options. During linking, protoc updates the options message and then *discards* the uninterpreted versions. So the path refers to absent elements of the descriptor.

This makes it effectively impossible to extract, for example, comments associated with options. Another task that *seems* like it should be possible is to reconstruct a proto source file from a descriptor that includes source code info (with the understanding that certain things, like trailing comments, cannot be preserved in the descriptor). But the way options are handled in source code info further reduces the fidelity that is possible.

Possible approaches to solve:

1. During linking, the source code info could be updated so that the info for options is actually attributed to the options (e.g. references proper option field numbers, or extension numbers for custom options). For options that define values nested deep inside of options that are messages, the path could contain additional elements that pinpoint exactly the field that is being set. This would lose fidelity since the current representation allows attribution of source code location and comments to option names (even name parts, when the option type is itself a message) whereas this could not be preserved with the suggested transformation.

2. During linking, preserve uninterpreted options in the descriptor when source code info is being included. Furthermore, add fields to the uninterpreted option (or maybe just the name part message) that provide the resolved field/extension numbers. This allows client code to discover the link between uninterpreted option source code info and the actual option values in the descriptor.

nodes.body:
In an ideal world, the source code info for aggregate options (where the option is a message and its defined value is an aggregate, like `{ foo: 123, bar: "baz" }`, could also be preserved. It would allow, for example, a source code info that pinpoints the `foo` field in the example above, giving the exact source code location for that part of the option.

However, this seems much more complicated, due to how protoc internally stores the AST (which models the aggregate value as a text blob, instead of as a sub-AST for which sub-portions could be correctly attributed to locations in the source file).

I'm leaning towards (1). When we convert uninterpreted options to interpreted ones we are already losing some information. Doing the same transformation for the source code info accompanying the uninterpreted options seems reasonable and is consistent with what we are already doing.

(2) involves a larger interface change (1 can be considered a bug fix while 2 is adding new behavior and new public API) and I think it's also harder for users to use. I can see very little of its value (can't really think of an use case of the preserved source code info for option names...) and would say it's not a worthwhile change to make.
@jtattermusch was this resolved?
I guess this was closed by mistake. @jhump do you plan to make a pull request for this?

@xfxyjwf, I do hope to eventually. I started working on it, and have a pretty decent grasp of the changes I need to make. (To be honest, I lost a little momentum after I addressed it in my own proto parser that produces source code info, in a Go library named [protoreflect](https://godoc.org/github.com/jhump/protoreflect/desc/protoparse). But I do expect to return to it.)

@xfxyjwf I made a pull request to address this: #4342. When testing, I also discovered that protoc produces invalid source code info for extension range options, and that is also fixed in that same pull request.

Do you mind taking a look? It does not yet have tests. I was hoping to get a pointer or two on best approach and maybe to example similar tests. I was also hoping to go ahead and get some eyes on my C++ code: I have not professionally written C++ in 15 or so years, and it's a little slower to pick back up than riding a bike 😄.  It was a decent challenge just getting my head around the existing code and understanding where different responsibilities lie. And I wanted the change to be fairly surgical and low impact.

Since the package is crosspatform, however, it would probably be a better idea just to define one property for the root tool directory, like
```xml
<GoogleProtoCompilerRoorDir>$([System.IO.Path]::GetFullPath('$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)../tools/'))</GoogleProtoCompilerRoorDir>

The GetFullPath function will take care of proper path separators in the property name; you can give it any mix of `\` and `/`, and it'll straighten them out for the system it runs on.

@ObsidianMinor, @anandolee: #4648 is a very breaking change. Please please do not ship it as is, requires fixing. It blindly relies on MSBuild version 15.3+, and .NET Framework 4.7.1+ or .NET Core. Otherwise, a project adding the package will not even load.

So this works with .NET SDK, but breaks on Windows unless very latest build tools *and* .NET Framework are installed. And on Mono, no support at all.

I would just remove the `<protoc Condition=...` lines. It is well known that there is no universally consistent way to figure out the OS and platform from inside all of living MSBuild species, outside of .NET Core (or its backported functionality in .NET 4.7.1+). Even finding the MSBuild version itself is a tricky task, so even degrading gracefully not to define `protoc` property in a less capable MSBuild  is quite a scripting task! I am resolving tools directory this in Grpc.Tools with a custom build task, and weeks of work went into making tool resolution backwards-compatible with VS2013+ and Mono.

So instead of defining the `protoc` property, I'd just stop at defining the root directory, [as was initially suggested](https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3820#issuecomment-342011424) and leave the rest to the user. 

Also, please add namespace to the first line as `<Project xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/developer/msbuild/2003">`, otherwise it won't be compatible even with MSBuild v14.x!

Edit: PR is #4817

@ObsidianMinor ,

> I never realized their addition was so recent.

if you are interested in this saga (just one of the whole multiplatform MSBuild epics), the discussion is here: https://github.com/Microsoft/msbuild/issues/539.

It's really tough to expand a 20-year old build system used by millions in the wild, and also cloned by an outside project (Mono) without breaking its API and behaviors, and, having read MSBuild code and contributed a couple of small fixes, I can really the great lengths the MSBuild SWE have to go to support backward compatibility. This also implies, naturally, that scripting build snippets that are compatible with all the many dozens of MSBuild version, platform and even vendor variants, which are in the wild today, is a tricky business. While simple conditions like `'$(MSBuildRuntimeType)' == 'Core'` are easily backwards-compatible and correct (the property is not set in non-Core builds), even an innocuously looking API invocation, like `$([System.Version]::Parse($(MSBuildVersion)))` is dangerous, as the function throws if given an empty string as an argument, and even `MSBuildVersion`, which is easy to take for granted, does not exist is older MSBuild versions. And any exception in property evaluation prevents the build from proceeding (and, should it happen in a static property evaluation, causes the project load in Visual Studio to fail, as VS also uses the MSBuild engine to load the project, and even invokes a few manifest targets from it to discover the list of project files and other certain things).

So in the end, *almost all* additions to MSBuild are "recent," given it's long history. It has been expanded greatly due to the multiplatform work. And it's still WIP. The first stage was to make *an* MSBuild for the new .NET Core platform for Linux etc. Now it seems to be in the phase of convergence, when all the API added to .NET Core are being backported to .NET Framework. But this is happening only now, with the Framework version 4.7.1+, and too many field installation still do not have it. Good thing is Windows 10 comes with it, and upgraded automatically with every semiannual release. Bad thing is that even Windows Server editions of the same OS are often not (enterprise admins are conservative), that Windows 7 came with 3.5, the first .NET on the CLR4, and is still supported and used widely, and that people also run all different versions of Mono. The APIs are converging now, but sadly it will take years to pass before anyone can take the new features for granted and just say "oh, just update your build tools, you rig is too ancient to support!"

On the practical side, one can guess the platform OS from different clues, including probing for the existence of well-known runtime .dylib files to tell OSX apart from Linux), but host bitness (64 or 32) can be guessed only by probing for well known files (e. g. /lib64). Tricky and unreliable business (what if the user unwittingly installed a badly scripted deb package that creates /lib64 on a 32-bit system?) without adding a custom MSBuild task or requiring MSBuild 15.3+, which is yet too new.

Sorry about the long-winded comment. I just wanted to share some of the stuff I learned, mostly unwillingly, while solving similar problems when I was writing compatible build scripts for another project.
And thank you @ObsidianMinor again for your contribution and collaboration. This change, even if it does not fully abstract the tool location, makes life a lot easier for the package users!
Closing as this looks resolved to me. If there is still an action item for the protobuf team, feel free to reopen!

nodes.body:
protobuf-java-lite will not have the same version number as protobuf-java/protoc. Instead, protoc-gen-javalite/protobuf-java-lite will be versioned together and independently from protoc/protobuf-java. When using lite, make sure:

1. You have the same version number for protoc-gen-javalite and protobuf-java-lite.
2. The version of protoc doesn't matter for lite and any version should work.
3. Never use protobuf-java with lite because they are incompatible.

title: [JS] proto.google.protobuf.StringValue does not work correctly.

nodes.body: Also, including the StringValue in a message and serializing to binary seems to serialize it as an array of one character

Still, shouldn't the constructor work correctly if at all?

`StringValue` is a message type, and it's constructor accepts an array representation of created message and not the string itself.

The right way to build StringValue message is to create it, and then to invoke `setValue`.

Of course, because you know it's internals you can also use `new StringValue([mystr]);`, it will put first array element inside first message field.
@nvartolomei is correct here, StringValue is a message with a single field. You have to set its value manually, there is no special support for this.

nodes.body: It is a bad idea to call `Py_Finalize` in the exit handler because other things might have been cleaned up before and so anything e.g. STL related might break, which seems to be the issue here. The solution is really to not call `Py_Finalize` in the exit handler but before, e.g. at the end of `main` or in `uwsgi_exit` or whereever you think it is appropriate in your application.

There is a special case in uwsgi for apps that should'nt call Py_Finalize: https://github.com/unbit/uwsgi/blob/master/plugins/python/python_plugin.c#L414
an option is added in another commit : https://github.com/avar/uwsgi/commit/f41da12c546717fefc22c389912543bc05488add

Note that usually you do not want to skip calling `Py_Finalize` at all. Some Python modules really expect to be cleaned up, e.g. to remove some file locks or so. The solution rather is to call `Py_Finalize` earlier and not in the `atexit` handler.

title: Discuss adding an option to preserve file names in C# codegen
body:
This is related to https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/13207. When automating the build process, it is necessary to know the exact names of the files generated by protoc. In the build process I am trying to introduce for .NET Core and Visual Studio, the generated outputs files are considered transient (just like .o files would be for a C++ compilation). The problem is the filenames need to be known ahead to the build process, and they are currently camelized (and, well, deunderscored?..)

What I would like to do is add an option `preserve_filename` for the C# codegen plugins (both proto and gRPC) so that the generated file has the same name as the input, e. g. `one_two.proto` would produce `one_two.cs` (and `one_twoGrpc.cs` in the gRPC codegen). Are there any issues with that? Would such a change be acceptable?

On the same note, the function `GetOutputFile` in `csharp_names.h` would have to change. It is marked `LIBPROTOC_EXPORT` but is not actually used by gRPC codegen. Would it be ok to change it? Un-export and move the declaration to `csharp_helpers.h`? Or keep the existing API for compatibility with something else? I am thinking of passing it a const pointer to `struct Options` instead of the 3 last parameters, as it contains all codegen plugin options already (and will need more).

If the decision is to go ahead with this, unit tests for name generation are on me. There are currently none at all, and I would not start changing anything without them in place first.

/cc @jtattermusch, @jskeet

nodes.body:
I don't have a particular issue with this, but I know the protobuf team generally want to restrict the number of options. This does seem a nicely orthogonal one to everything else though.

/cc @xfxyjwf @anandolee for comment.
Ahem....
@xfxyjwf @anandolee, any opinion on this?

I'm not quite sure what problem you are trying to solve with this new option. Is the build tool unable to convert .proto file name to camel-case names? Or maybe you are just trying to avoid coding a camel-case conversion in the build tool? If it's the later, I would suggest just implement the conversion code in the build tool. The mapping from .proto file name to generated file name is public API. Adding complexity to protobuf public API to save a few lines of code in a specific build tool is hardly a good tradeoff.

If the build tool is unable to do the mapping for some reason, there are some other options we can consider:
1. Make protoc generate files into a zip package. For example, protoc can generate Java files into a source .jar file, and we can do something similar for C#.
2. Make protoc generate a mapping file to be used by the build tool. protoc already has the ability to generate a dependency file between proto imports for make to use. We can also generate something specific for this build tool to use.

I think it would be possible to recreate the mapping, certainly, but that to me looks rather a workaround, which would require maintenance to always match the algorithm. This is very error-prone as well, as an error here will likely result in incorrect dependencies. Or, in a sense, going through self-imposed hoops.

My general target is to make proto files the first class citizen in the .NET land. We got quite a discussion going in https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/13207, and may I please invite you to join into it? There are certain problems with proto toolset packaging in NuGet. Everything [I said there about the Grpc.Tools package](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/13207#discussion_r152106277) applies to Google.Protobuf.Tools as well; in short, the tools as packaged are impossible to discover in the build process, even if the package is added to the project. So, generally speaking, the current packaging is no more useful that a simple .tar.gz or .zip archive with tools and import protos in known subdirectories, if just downloaded and unpacked. And an automatic installation of the NuGet package makes it worse than that.

Also, if you do not mind my asking, what exactly do you see wrong with adding the option? The suggestions that you are providing seem to involve much bigger changes to the codegen that just the single option. I am probably missing something deeper, but why do you deem it preferable to the single option? (And, really stumbling to me, how generating files into a .zip package would not require another option just for that purpose?)

> The mapping from .proto file name to generated file name is public API. Adding complexity to protobuf public API to save a few lines of code in a specific build tool

I think I did not address this one. The public API is C++, if I understand it correctly, and the build tool in question is MsBuild, which is pure .NET. So just to access the API from the build will require supplying 6 precompiled native libraries for every platform and architecture for which Protobuf and gRPC are packaged. This would probably add more problems than it solves.

Another stumbling block in this direction that it will need a kind of cross-package discovery of protoc libraries, so that, even if I am missing it and the .NET protoc (not the compiler) API is exposing the function, using it is still not as simple, as it should be uniformly available and discoverable at the build time. And we have "old" csprojects on Windows, "new" on Windows, Linux and Mac, and mono supporting both styles on Mac and Windows.

It's not that it's not doable; it's just the amount of work does not seem right to end up with just a predictable file name.

I'll see what I can get from the option 2, thanks for this pointer.

> I think I did not address this one. The public API is C++, if I understand it correctly, and the build tool in question is MsBuild, which is pure .NET. So just to access the API from the build will require supplying 6 precompiled native libraries for every platform and architecture for which Protobuf and gRPC are packaged. This would probably add more problems than it solves.

I'm suggesting the mapping algorithm from .proto file name to generated .cs file name is public API, not one particular implementation. We just need to document precisely what s done in the transformation so you can implement the same logic in any other language.

@xfxyjwf: Ah, I see what you mean. Either way, doing that requires writing an MSBuild task (a dynamic .NET library used as a build extension, in case you are not familiar), and if we should go this way, then using the `--dependency_out` is certainly a better source of truth. Except it's not available on the initial build, which makes it an interesting problem to solve.

(And writing the task opens a whole new can of compatibility worms; I am still trying to investigate what kind of thing we are going to step into with this. This is not as exciting to solve, tho :))

There is another interesting thing I noticed:

```
$ protoc --cpp_out=out ptree/proto1.proto ptree/sub1/proto1.proto
$ protoc --csharp_out=out ptree/proto1.proto ptree/sub1/proto1.proto
Proto1.cs: Tried to write the same file twice.
```
`cpp_out` lays output files into a nice directory structure according to their source, but `charp_out` lumps them together into the same flat directory. Is this by design? No problem with the build either way, just have to ask if this is not a bug.
As I said before, I'd personally be okay with this as an option (probably a C#-specific option) but it's really not my call - I'm not in the protobuf team, I just wrote most of the code earlier.

@xfxyjwf: Can you please help with this error?
```
Can only process one input file when using --dependency_out=FILE.
```
Am I using it wrong? Is this a principal limitation, hard to change? I was so gung-ho about this option, but it shoot back at me!  The currently generated dependency file is a conceptually one long line, wrapped with backslashes. Either way would work, ideally 1 line per output, each listing transitive dependencies
```
out/file2.pb.cc: file2.proto  /include/timespamp.proto
out/file1.pb.cc: file1.proto  /include/wrappers.proto /include/timespamp.proto
```
but even 1 line per protoc invocation would also work (although it may introduce false positives), e. g.
```
out/file1.pb.cc out/file2.pb.cc: file1.proto file2.proto /include/wrappers.proto /include/timespamp.proto
```
Invoking protoc on each file separately is far from ideal, and since the dependencies may change, there is not even a shortcut even when the cached dependency file exists.

@kkm000 I'm not sure why we have that restriction. It was added in https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/e2555e235f867f3d7a0378e95a45109c8fd2dfbe by @TeBoring . Bo, do you remember why we restrict the number of input files to be 1 for the `--dependency_out` flag to work?

Extending it to support multiple files seems good to me.

@xfxyjwf, @TeBoring: FWIW, I just disabled the check in command_line_interface.cc, and got an apparently  good dependency output from two source proto files with a gRPC service in each.
```
out/Proto1.cs \
out/Proto1Grpc.cs \
out/ProtoSub1.cs \
out/ProtoSub1Grpc.cs: ptree/sub1/proto_sub1.proto\
 ptree/proto1.proto
```
Explained in #3959.

Why are identifiers transformed by the C# generator at all (file, message oder field names)?
If the proto interface uses snake case, it should be transparently named in the generated code IMO.
If there is no reason, an option to opt-out identifier transformation would be great to get rid of this extra complexity.

If anyone could bump me towards an according document or discussion I would be glad.

> Why are identifiers transformed by the C# generator at all (file, message oder field names)?

Because failing to do so would:

- Make all the C# code look non-idiomatic
- Fail with any C# keywords (I guess we could use `@` everywhere but that would also be ghastly)

The first of these reasons is the primary one. C# code using protos should feel natural - I would really *hate* having a completely inconsistent codebase with properties not following conventions, having to use `@` because someone chose to call a field `private` etc.

It would certainly be technically feasible to add a command-line option to opt out of this (rather than an annotation, given that multiple users may want to generate the same proto in different ways) but I very much doubt that "we" (in Google) would want to do the work for that, and I'm not even convinced we'd want to accept it as a pull request. I can raise it with the rest of the Protobuf team if you like though.

@jskeet
Thanks for taking this serious and this incredibly quick response.

Being with cpp-proto quite a while now and joining csharp recently I'm aware of the fact that using PascalCase is quite popular in C#. Probaly because the initiators and library designers chose so.

Nevertheless, there are arguments for and trends towards alternative styles - which can very well co-exist in the same code base - and my argument would be, that it should be up to the particular dev-team which style to follow and to do so in the proto. And that the tool should, in order to allow future trends, not cement a particular style. Even the compilers, fortunately, allow this.

Having to maintain implementations of the same interface in different languages lets this identifier transformation feel a bit like an obfuscation.

_If the interface calls a thing like this, one would expect, that THE or all implementations call it the same way  - wouldn't one?_

After skimming the code I would dare to give it a try, given that there is a chance of acceptance.

So yes, if it isn't asked too much, I would like to know what the team thinks about this.

in any case, a big Thank You for you and the team for all this effort
gRPC is great

I won't try to argue the case for why I believe this is a bad idea - because I don't have lots of time to commit to this, and my experience of other similar discussions is that no-one actually persuades anyone of anything.
However, I will ask the protobuf team what they think of the proposal for a command-line argument. Of course, you'd *also* have to persuade the gRPC generator maintainers to add a similar command-line argument to the gRPC generator...

@RalfKubis: I've heard back from the protobuf team, and we wouldn't want to accept the change into this repo, I'm afraid. Of course that doesn't stop you from creating your own fork for it and maintaining that; it shouldn't cause any wire format issues. But it's not something we want to pursue. Thanks for the suggestion though.

title: ParseFromIstream() exits unexpectedly when there are tags whose numbers are 3

nodes.body: Besides, after replacing all "=3" to something else like "=77", the mysterious bug is still happening that there are some fields ignored during the deserialization.

Please do what I suggested in https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1932#issuecomment-238648920

If after that you can get the issue, please create another issue.

The code above is just an minimal working example.
However, there are a lot of fields in my original code and the ParseFromIstream() returns before the entire object is loaded, and the number of the last loaded field is 2.
So it can't be the case that the file is simply not created after SerializeToOstream().

With "person3" working it should be clear that the issue lies in file read/write operations rather than protobuf parsing/serialization. The real culprit is that the file is not opened in the correct mode. To store protobuf binary data the file needs to be opened in binary mode and the default mode is unfortunately text.

If you are still not sure how to fix the issue, take a look at our example code here:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/examples/add_person.cc#L77

It's a perfect example showing how to read/write protos from/to file using ParseFromIstream/SerializeToOstream.

Got it. Thanks!

I thought there won't be any problems if the input and output streams were opened in the same mode, which turns out to be wrong (http://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/io/c#Binary_and_text_modes)...
Sorry for the false report.

Then, I couldn't create the above message with keyword arguments and couldn't access these attributes:

```python
# couldn't create message with keyword arguments
msg = xxx_pb2.TestMessage(
    global=True,  # Here raises syntax error
    as=100,
)
# required to pass arguments like
kwargs = {
    'global': True,
    'as': 100,
}
msg= xxx_pb2.TestMessage(**kwargs)

# Also couldn't access these attributes
print(msg.global)  # Here raises syntax error
# required to use getattr() like
print(getattr(msg, 'global'))
```

### Request

[pep8](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0008/#function-and-method-arguments) says "If a function argument's name clashes with a reserved keyword, it is generally better to append a single trailing underscore", so I want to pass arguments appending "_" like:
```python
msg = xxx_pb2.TestMessage(
    global_=True,
    as_=100,
)
```
and also access attribute like:
```python
print(msg.global_)
```

What do think about it? Does anyone know better workaround?

---

The answer of "#65" recommended to rename the field, but ".proto" is defined on the server side (Go implemented and out of our project), so difficult to rename it.

nodes.body:
FWIW, people also hit this problem internally at Google with field names such as "import" or other keywords in an occasional message.  I believe `getattr` and `setattr` on your message instance should work for these field names.

```python
global_, as_ = getattr(msg, 'global'), getattr(msg, 'as')
```

Otherwise, agreed, surfacing them as trailing underscore attribute names seems desirable - though the implications on which names APIs such as `ListFields` returns and `HasField` requires need to not break existing users.

Thanks for your reply!
I don't know the internal implementation though, I just guess it might be able to represent with trailing underscore by using `__getattr__` for example.
e.g., If user tries to access a field with trailing underscore and that name collides the reserved keyword, remove trailing underscore then use it as real-name of the protobuf field.
This approach does not take effect to the APIs such as `ListFields` and `HasField` because this does not changes the "real" field names in the descriptor.
getattr() can work with field that have name conflict with keyword. We are also working on make messages, top level enum, top level extensions also work with getattr() for keyword conflict

title: Add option for a flat directory layout
body:
Currently if you have protobuf files in a hierarchical tree and then compile them with something like:

    protoc -I proto_subdir --cpp_out outdir proto_subdir/dummy_service.proto
    protoc -I proto_subdir --cpp_out outdir proto_subdir/messages/dummy_messages.proto 

this results in files

    outdir/dummy_service.pb.*
    outdir/messages/dummy_messages.pb.*

And inside dummy_service.pb.cc there is this:

    #include "messages/dummy_messages2.pb.h"

Besides looking like Java, this forces a directory layout on generated sources which makes integration difficult.

It would be nice to add a flag to the protoc compiler, say `--flat-layout` which would do the following:

 - output all files to `cpp_out` subdir without any extra directory segments
 - change `#include` statements to not have extra directory segments

nodes.body: If you want dummy_messages.pb.* under outdir/ directly, try -I proto_subdir/messages/

title: WriteDelimitedTo needs to specify format of length field
body:
The C# documentation does not specify the format of the length field that is prepended when using the WriteDelimitedTo function. I poked around a bit in the documentation and for me it was not easy to find. For instance, it would be useful to mention here: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/csharp/class/google/protobuf/message-extensions#class_google_1_1_protobuf_1_1_message_extensions_1a99a4de2ce4de5bc1da1e1f5c367f4c7c

From source, I checked it is a [variable 32 bit int](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/ce0a53273a400369932ba788d17500336a6ecaad/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/MessageExtensions.cs#L157). Which is actually not what I expected.

On a side note it would be useful to offer some way to specify the size of the length field. In my case I have instances where I need to write fixed length fields of 32 or 16 bit int.

nodes.body:
+1 on documenting the format for delimiting. It is useful if you are starting with a byte[] and need to forward it to a recipient expecting it to be delimited.

-1 on adding other delimiting formats. For those cases, it's better to leave the custom size and endianness concerns in the application.

optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME works if you have a matching protobuf-lite
runtime (not the 3.0.0 runtime). The error was triggered by the mismatched
generated code and runtime which we are not able to detect at compile time.
It's unfortunate that 3.0.0 runtime works with 3.4.0 generated code - it is
completely untested. I would use the 3.0.0 compiler instead even if it
seems to work. In the future, we will always throw runtime exceptions for
such version mismatch.

title: Protoc compiler execute from source
body:
in README.md you wrote, that "sudo make install" for

> To build and install the C++ Protocol Buffer runtime and **the Protocol Buffer compiler (protoc)** execute the following:

but protoc dont installing to usr/bin or usr/local/bin

P.S. I know that I can use "apt-get install protobuf-compiler"

nodes.body:
Why you don't install protoc?
Thank you.
`sudo make install` will install the protoc and the runtime in your `--prefix` when you run ./configure, which defaults to /usr/local. Could you paste the log when you run the installation?

I do next steps
```
$ git clone https://github.com/google/protobuf
$ cd protobuf
$ ./autogen.sh
$ ./configure
$ make
$ make check
$ sudo make install
```

Before "make install":
```
grifff@debian:/usr/local$ ls bin
grifff@debian:/usr/local$ ls lib
pkgconfig  python2.7  python3.5
grifff@debian:/usr/local$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/local/games:/usr/games:/home/grifff/dev/buildroot/output/host/usr/bin:/home/grifff/dev/buildroot/output/host/usr/bin
```
after:
```
grifff@debian:/usr/local$ ls lib
libprotobuf.a       libprotobuf-lite.la     libprotobuf-lite.so.14.0.0  libprotobuf.so.14.0.0  libprotoc.so         pkgconfig

title: Issues identified in version 3.4.0 by security scan
body:
Tho following 3 issues were flagged by a security scan where we use Protobuf v3.4.0. Will these be resolved in an upcoming version?
 
1. Unchecked CString Convertion
The element Param at line 273 of /Protobuf/objectivec/GPBCodedOutputStream.m contains a C-String that was converted from a CFString object. The length of Param was not checked after conversion.
Method: (void) writeStringNoTag:(const NSString *) value 
Line: 294
**result = [value getBytes:state_.bytes + state_.position** 
 
2. Unchecked CString Convertion
The element CFStringGetCStringPtr at line 273 of /Protobuf/objectivec/GPBCodedOutputStream.m contains a C-String that was converted from a CFString object. The length of CFStringGetCStringPtr was not checked after conversion.
Method: (void) writeStringNoTag:(const NSString *) value 
Line: 281
**CFStringGetCStringPtr((CFStringRef)value, kCFStringEncodingUTF8);** 
 
3. Improper Resource Shutdown or Release
The application's - method in /Pods/Protobuf/objectivec/GPBCodedOutputStream.m defines and initializes the output object at 173. This object encapsulates a limited computing resource, such as open file streams, database connections, or network streams. This resource is not properly closed and released in all situations.
Method: (instancetype)initWithOutputStream:(NSOutputStream *)output 
Line: 177
**[output open];**

nodes.body:
First up, what tool is this and is there a way we can run this?  I'm wondering if there is some more info in a UI or something that would help use directly to see if there is more info provided to help understand these better?

For 1 - We aren't really sure what the issue is talking about here.  I believe the _C-String_ reference could be to the `quickString` variable in that code, but line 294 doesn't use the variable.  So it isn't really clear what it is saying is an issue.  Was there anything more in the report to help understand it?

For 2 - Again we aren't completely sure what this one is trying to say.  Line 281 does extract the C-String, but where `quickString` is used (lines 290 and 310), we use `length` which was directly collected from the original `NSString` (`value`) with a UTF-8 conversion matching out the C-String was collected.  I guess in theory could could be a mismatch, but at that point you are worrying about about some pretty fundamental bugs in Foundation, and I'm not sure one could be defensive against apis returning wrong values.  Anyway, more info for specifically what it is raising as an issue would help confirm if it is these two later lines or something else.

For 3 - Our guess here is the tools doesn't like the fact that the `-open` was done with the `output` parameter, but the `-close` in `-dealloc` is done with `_state.output` (because it does't realize the assignment into `_state.output` is tracking the same resource.  I've done #3916 to tweak the code so maybe the tool will see that better, but the existing code always did close the stream.
We are closing it for cleaning. Feel free to reopen it if it is still an issue

title: Please upload non-language-specific tarballs for releases
body:
Protobuf releases currently have language-specific tarballs such as "protobuf-cpp-3.5.0.tar.gz" or "protobuf-python-3.5.0.tar.gz", which include subsets of the repository. Tarballs of the full repository are only available via GitHub's automatic tarball endpoints.

This can be frustrating for users of Bazel, who expect tarball SHA checksums to be stable. GitHub does not guarantee that it always returns the exact same bytes for a tarball of a given commit/tag.

As a solution, when cutting a release, please upload a full source tarball. Then users can depend on it and expect a stable SHA.

Changing SHAs have broken Protobuf for Bazel users:

* https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3619
* https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3628
* https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3648

Other projects that have had builds broken by GitHub archive checksum changes include:
* Bazel: https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/3722
* Kubernetes: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/52307
* Homebrew: https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/issues/18044

Done.

title: build[python]: avoid symbols conflicts with other loaded libprotobuf.so (Linux)
body:
There are several libraries/tools that uses protobuf via linking with system-wide libprotobuf.so.
Protobuf version mismatch between system protobuf binary and protobuf Python's extension (from [PyPi](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/protobuf/3.4.0)) usually cause a fatal crashes.

Symbols conflict detection:
- Fedora 26 with protobuf-devel package installed (protobuf version is 3.2.0).
- Python virtualenv with installed protobuf package (`pip install protobuf`, protobuf version is 3.4.0)

> $ python -c 'from ctypes import *; CDLL("/lib64/libprotobuf.so", mode=RTLD_GLOBAL); from google.protobuf import api_pb2'
> Segmentation fault (core dumped)
- `LD_PRELOAD=/lib64/libprotobuf.so` instead of `CDLL` works too

Related SO question: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/7201667/ld-magically-overrides-statically-linked-symbols

Possible solution is to isolate protobuf symbols in Python extension (assume gcc+ld on Linux):
1. link Python extensions with `-Bsymbolic` linker flag
2. don't export protobuf symbols by using `-fvisibility=hidden` compiler flag. But this breaks .so build.
3. don't export symbols from .a files: `-exclude-libs=ALL` linker option

There are many "magic" crashes related to conflicts of different protobuf versions, so lets try to resolve this issue.

Additional information:
- similar problem can be observed on Ubuntu
- Installing the same version of Python extension (`pip install protobuf==3.2.0`) doesn't help (still SIGSEGV)

nodes.body: I think we need a more realistic example that can lead to the crash. From what I can tell, few people load .so directly as shown in the above example and that isn't the use case we want to support either.

title: Names of namespaces clash (C++)
body:
It seems protoc generates namespaces based on the name of the `.proto` file in the pb.h/pb.cc files. In my case there is a file `testcase.proto` and a namespace `protobuf_testcase_2eproto`. Problem is: I have multiple files with the same name in different directories which leads to "duplicate symbol" errors from the linker.

Note that this is not the namespace based on the `package` setting in the `.proto` file, I have different names for those.

This used to work in 3.0 and doesn't work any more with 3.5. I don't know where exactly the problem was introduced.

nodes.body: Thanks for reporting and sorry for the breakage. It will be fixed in the next minor release.

So the descriptor pool already indexes descriptors on the filename. Having multiple files with the same name was already broken. Although it might not have triggered as this happens on calls to reflection.

In a sense this improves things. What used to be a hidden runtime problem, now becomes a static linker error.

title: Any plans to modularize (or add Automatic-Module-Name properties to) protobuf-java?
body:
Hello.

In order to play nicely with programs/libraries that have been modularized, it would be good if `Automatic-Module-Name` properties could be added to the `protobuf-java` jar files. This would give a stable name that can be used in the `requires` directives of modules.

http://blog.joda.org/2017/05/java-se-9-jpms-automatic-modules.html

> Do not release to Maven Central a modular jar file that depends on an automatic module, unless the automatic module has an "Automatic-Module-Name" MANIFEST.MF entry.

I'd submit a PR, but I'm not sure what module names you'd want to use. Presumably something like `com.google.protobuf.core` and `com.google.protobuf.lite`.

nodes.body: This is a very much needed change. Currently google protobuf is the only dependency we use that still has not been modularized.
Thank you!

Adding Automatic-Module-Name is a step in the right direction. Fully modularize protobuf-java would be the next step.
A drastic shift was recently done for C++ when it moved to C++11, why not also shift Java towards Java LTS 11.

title: Allow extendable WellKnownTypeParser and  WellKnownTypePrinter for JsonFormat
body:
In Kubernetes' protos there is an [IntOrString](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/master/pkg/util/intstr/generated.proto) message which is able to be printed/parsed via Golang to an atomic type in JSON messages.

This is very similar to what is provided in [wrappers.proto](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/wrappers.proto) and handled in JsonFormat. However, JSONFormat doesn't allow these Parsers/Printers to be extended by the user.

Can we extend JsonFormat to allow custom additions for formatting so examples such as IntOrString used in the Kubernetes project can be printed/parsed from atomic values?

nodes.body: JsonFormat implements proto3 JSON spec and for better interoperability between languages it is not intended to be customized.

We changed the type check to accept numbers.Real (it was int, long, float in 3.4.0). However, the original 3.4.0 should also reject 'decimal.Decimal'. Can you double check if it can pass on 3.4.0.

Sorry, my bad. Just doublechecked and found the same behaviour in 3.4.0

I realise this is an old and closed issue, but I've just hit something similar while upgrading from Python 3.9 to 3.10. I was using protobuf 3.15.8, which has wheels for 3.9 but not 3.10.
The difference for me seemed to be that on 3.10, which appeared to use the pure-Python implementation I got the error whereas on Python 3.9 my input `decimal.Decimal` was converted to a `float`.

On both Python 3.9 and 3.10 `decimal.Decimal` is not considered a `numbers.Real`, so that's unlikely to be responsible for the difference.

This would appear to suggest there's a difference between the native implementation and the pure-Python implementation.

I note however that following https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/3ab97ce8301183b46a4412b28171512f00f8edb9 the implementation of the pure-Python version has changed substantially so it's possible that the difference is now gone too (certainly it looks to me like the new implementation would allow `Decimal`s).

title: How to get message level comments?
body:
I write a plugin and I want to get message's comments, but I didn't find the interface to get the message comments. Can add this interface, or did I not find out?
ps: I use golang write plugin.

nodes.body:
Comments are included in the SourceCodeInfo message as part of FileDescriptorProto:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L842

If you use C++ to write the plugin, there are some helper APIs for you to retrieve the comments:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.h#L416

It's built on top of the SourceCodeInfo message inside FileDescriptorProto and is more convenient to use than a raw FileDescriptorProto. Such support is available only in C++ and I would recommend using C++ to write the plugin instead.

title: %1 is not a valid Win32 application
body:
I'm trying to get the Lua generator working on Windows (MSYS2/mingw64).
I installed 'protobuf' with luarocks.
It installed also the file /mingw64/lib/luarocks/rocks/protobuf/1.1.1-0/protoc-plugin/protoc-gen-lua, which I can run in a terminal without errors due to missing packages and such.
But if I run the protobuf compiler with this file as a plugin, I get:
```
$ protoc --plugin=protoc-gen-lua=/mingw64/lib/luarocks/rocks/protobuf/1.1.1-0/protoc-plugin/protoc-gen-lua --lua_out=. pubsub.proto
--lua_out: protoc-gen-lua: %1 is not a valid Win32 application.
```

Useful info:
```
$ pip3 show protobuf
Name: protobuf
Version: 3.4.0
Summary: Protocol Buffers
Home-page: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/
Author: protobuf@googlegroups.com
Author-email: protobuf@googlegroups.com
License: 3-Clause BSD License
Location: /usr/lib/python3.6/site-packages
Requires: six, setuptools
```

nodes.body: is this article related? https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/help/812486/event-id-7000-and-1-is-not-a-valid-win32-application-error-message-whe
@fferri Could you attach the protoc-gen-lua binary you are using?

@xfxyjwf you can find protoc-gen-lua here https://github.com/urbanairship/protobuf-lua inside the protoc-plugin directory. it is a python script (it's the same thing you get by installing the luarocks package I mentioned)
@fferri Hmm, a python script? If I remember correctly, the plugin must be either a .exe or a .bat. Could you try to create a .bat wrapper about the python script and try again?

I have verified a .bat file will work. Just create a protoc-gen-lua.bat file with the following content:

```
@<path_to_python.exe> <path_to_protoc-gen-lua>
```

and invoke protoc with:

```
protoc --plugin=protoc-gen-lua=protoc-gen-lua.bat --lua_out=. <proto>
```

title: Go output with grpc plugin in super-directory doesn't work
body:
On Windows 10, `protoc --go_out=plugins=grpc:../output input.proto` doesn't work (even if `../output` directory exists). Error message:

```plugins=grpc;..\output/: No such file or directory```

`protoc --go_out=plugins=grpc:output input.proto` and even `protoc --go_out=plugins=grpc:./output input.proto` do work (with existing `./output` directory of course).

I'm not sure if this issue is correctly placed here, or rather in https://github.com/grpc/grpc or in https://github.com/golang/protobuf.

title: proto3 => json docs don't include a serialized oneof field
body:
It would be nice if there was an example of a proto that had a oneof field being JSON serialized.

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3

nodes.body:
Why specifically ask for oneof field?
Isn't it just the same as an optional field?
Close this for cleanup. Free feel to reopen if this is still needed.
People got confused because there are multiple ways to represent it in json. [ref](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/44069789/what-is-the-expected-json-serialization-of-oneof-protobuf-field)
Can we *please* have this explicitly stated in the spec?  It would help to settle a lot of bike-shedding debates on my team over how JSON should be formatted.
