title: generated enum for oneof fields don't have corresponding EnumCase_Name() function

nodes.body:
What is the "name of the oneof case" you are referring to? Do you want "oneof_name", or "foo_int", "foo_string"? Assuming it's the later, they are protobuf field names so you can get their names by field number:

```cpp
string name = ContainingMessage::descriptor()->FindFieldByNumber(kFooInt)->name();
```

Note that the Foo_Name() methods for enums are simple wrappers around the descriptor API. If we add a OneofNameCase_Name() method, it's likely implemented exactly as I suggested above. Due to binary size concerns we are unlikely to add new generated methods like this though.

Thank you for providing workaround. This will make my CL significantly simpler.

I understand your concern about binary size. However, couldn't we just make the new method be inline? Then, existing binaries that don't use this new feature will not be affected by binary size increase (hopefully the users that care about binary size, like e.g. Chromium, already optimize out unused symbols during linking).

@xyzzyz It's not just the size of the end binary that we care about. Adding new C++ symbols will increase the size of intermediate object files and there are some really big binaries in Google that are sensitive to the size of intermediate object files because the linker can't handle it if they grow any bigger... So even adding inline functions can cause a problem for them (and they are constantly monitoring any size changes).

If the new method is going to be as simple as what you have shown above, it shouldn't increase binary size by more than a few dozens of bytes per oneof field. As internal binaries don't use oneof that often, I'd estimate the binary size increase to be less than 10 KB even for the very large binaries. I would like to test it. Could you ping me internally and give me some candidate binary to test?
@xyzzyz If you are still interested, feel free to send us a CL. We should already have some presubmit checks that checks binary size increase.
Close this for cleanup. If this is still going on, feel free to reopn it.

If the oneof int values are always equal to their corresponding field numbers, you could generate macros instead of methods to avoid adding new symbols. The FOO_CASE_NAME(enum_val) macro could static-cast enum_val to an int, which could then be used as the field_number param needed to obtain the name.

title: Generated implementation for SpaceUsed in C++
body:
As noted in the C++ docs, SpaceUsed is quite slow:

> SpaceUsed() is noticeably slower than ByteSize(), as it is implemented using reflection (rather than the generated code implementation for ByteSize()). Like ByteSize(), its CPU time is linear in the number of fields defined for the proto.

In our application we have a lot of protobufs that end up in various memory-limited caches and assigned to various memory budgets. In some cases the difference between ByteSize and SpaceUsed can be significant enough (eg with many optional fields) and therefore we use SpaceUsed to track the memory consumption of these objects. This is becoming a fairly significant CPU consumer despite our best efforts to only compute it once per PB.

If I were to work on a change to optionally generate a SpaceUsed method rather than use reflection, would it be acceptable to the community?

nodes.body: We likely won't accept changes that add new generated methods in the existing .pb.cc file. However, you can easily implement it as a protoc plugin that generates a standalone static SpaceUsed() method for each proto type. That's the common way to add utility functions for protos (e.g., we have such protoc plugins to generate Equals() and HashCode() functions).
Good idea. I had missed that the existing implementation was virtual and thus could be easily overridden.
Hey! Did either of you figure out a SpaceUsed that could be generated such that it could give you a "pre calculated" SpaceUsed rather than the run time reflection based one?

### Steps to reproduce:

1. Create a simple protobuf message object with just a string as a field
2. Generate the java code
3. Set the value of the string to `𤭢` or `😀` (**_any_** 4-byte unicode character)

I haven't worked on that particular code, but I think what it's saying is essentially that 2 bytes worth of UTF-16 can expand to at most 3 bytes of UTF-8. From what I can tell, this assumption is true and so I can't see how that would be a problem.

I can verify that protobuf Java supports 4-bytes UTF-8 characters correctly. See example code:
https://gist.github.com/xfxyjwf/98ae915d3a076c46586f4af7435e1f46

Adam's explanation is correct. For your given examples, it takes 2 chars to encode each character in UTF-16, and 4 bytes in UTF-8. So the ratio is `4 / 2 = 2` which is smaller than `MAX_BYTES_PER_CHAR = 3`.

title: c++: gRPC service descriptors are missing if the source proto has no messages defined
body:
It seems that if my protobuf file consists of a single service, and I link against the resulting `.pb.h` then the service descriptor is missing from the generated descriptor pool. For context, this is happening in Envoy (https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/master/source/common/upstream/cds_api_impl.cc#L40) using Bazel to generate protobuf files.   

The workaround is to (1) add a dummy message to the service proto; (2) instantiate the dummy message from the resulting `.pb.h` file.  

cc @htuch

nodes.body:
What you observed is most likely due to the linker dropping unused symbols (i.e., the descriptor registering code is not reachable from your application code so they got removed by linker). Besides adding a dummy message and referencing it in C++ code, there are a few other options:
1. Add "option cc_generic_services = true;" to the proto file and reference the generated service code.
2. Use bazel's always_link attribute to prevent linker dropping the proto library.
`always_link` makes the most sense in our situation, since we do not want to use the generated service code. @kyessenov can you confirm this works? Thanks @xfxyjwf.

@TeBoring I use release 3.5.1, but this phenomenon still appears. This phenomenon don't occur when i delete internalAddGeneratedPool this line.

@TeBoring i know, the internalAddGeneratedPool  will do nothing at the second time in the same request, but next request, it will be built again, it will cause cpu become very high, when many request visit server. Can this built action cache in php-fpm process ? Because the proto does not change in the different requests.

@TeBoring what was the use case in mind when having the `DescriptorPool` be rebuilt every request? Is it for long-running PHP servers? 

Rebuilding the `DescriptorPool` every request is having a massively detrimental effect on performance for us because we have a ton of proto classes. Does the C extension have to do the same thing? Would you be amenable to us adding some methods to `DescriptorPool` that allow us to cache it externally?

title: [ruby] UTF-8 issues for :bytes fields
body:
I have the following specification

```ruby
Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_message "api.Mutation" do
    optional :set_json, :bytes, 1
  end
end
Mutation = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("api.Mutation").msgclass
```

When I try to set a UTF-8 string like this `Api::Mutation.new(set_json: 'Möp')` it fails with ``initialize': U+00F6 from UTF-8 to ASCII-8BIT (Encoding::UndefinedConversionError)`.

Is this not supported or is it a bug? From what I have read, UTF-8 and ASCII Input should be fine for bytes.

nodes.body:
Ok, my bad… in ruby you are supposed to call `.b` on a string to return a copied string whose encoding is ASCII-8BIT.

https://ruby-doc.org/core-2.3.0/String.html#method-i-b

title: Clean up warnings flagged by error prone
body:
//CC @cushon

[Gerrit Code Review](https://www.gerritcodereview.com/) depends on [`rules_closure`](https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_closure/), that started to build protobuf from source in their build tool chain [recently](https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_closure/commit/d3e0437b6964db0719d71f075833614df3348fa7). We regularly build gerrit code with patched Bazel version with all [Error Prone (EP)](https://github.com/google/error-prone) warnings activated. Given that Bazel and EP don't offer all EP warnings activation mode out of the box, Bazel must be patched with this CL: [1].

With all EP warnings activated Bazel version the gerrit build is flooded with Protobuf related EP warnings (a short list of protobuf related warnings in gerrit build log) now: [2]. Consider to fix them.

To reproduce, clone [gerrit code review](https://gerrit.googlesource.com/gerrit), patch Bazel with: [1] and run `<path-to-patched-bazel> build gerrit`.

Alternative repro instruction: Patch Bazel with: [1] and run `<path-to-patched-bazel> build :protobuf_java` on protobuf@HEAD (ed14fe423b86b0d9d6e23ada61e649d173bd1350). These warnings are reported by EP: [3].

Related issue filed in `rules_closure` repository: [4].

* [1] https://bazel-review.googlesource.com/7891
* [2] http://paste.openstack.org/show/653548
* [3] http://paste.openstack.org/show/653551
* [4] https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_closure/issues/211

title: Reading .pb files.
body: I know that `.proto` files can be used to generate code. However, can someone tell me how are `.pb` (binary format ) files useful? And how can I generate data structures using `.pb` files?

nodes.body: The binary format is just the stored representation of your data, based on the message schema you define in your .proto file. For any language we support, you can use `protoc` to generate code from your `.proto` file and use that code to read and write your messages in binary format.
@acozzette Suppose I don't have the .proto file, but only the .pb file. Is there a way of generating the data structure (with only the .pb file)?

If you don't have access to the .proto file, you won't be able to determine the exact meaning of the data, but just as a debugging tool you can use `protoc --decode_raw` to print a human-readable view of the general structure of the data.

@acozzette Suppose I want to make a reader for onnx models. Since onnx models contain a model.pb file, how can we generate a data structure from this? Since no .proto file is present here, I'm confused.
@ayush1999 I would talk to the onnx folks about that--I'm not familiar with onnx but if they're indeed storing protocol buffers then they must have a .proto file somewhere.
@ayush1999 Did you find the answer to this question?

title: Ignore unknown fields in Ruby for decode_json
body:
There is a somewhat longstanding [TODO](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/upb.c#L13350-L13351) to allow for decode_json to ignore unknown fields, which currently forces us to upgrade clients in lockstep before any server code can add an additional field. I'd love to help put up a PR to make this configurable if someone can point me in the right direction!

I know the C++ API and the Java API already support this feature: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp/google.protobuf.util.json_util#JsonParseOptions

Also to be clear, I'm not looking for preserved unknown field support, which I know is being worked on, but rather the ability for clients to safely parse messages with new fields (and drop them).

title: Factory methods for non-wrapper types in Java
body:
Protobuf generated code in Java enables a convenient feature for the primitive wrapper types — the message has the `of(<primitive type>)` static method.

According to the [codebase](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_message.cc#L544), the methods are generated only for the [wrapper types](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/07b9238a1c03ef0351bcb4ca57d773eb7b7c5824/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_helpers.h#L381), at least as far as I can see.

My question is: is there another way to generate this kind of method for all the single-field types?
If not, may we expect to see this feature in future?

Also, I'm aware of the possibility to create custom `protoc` plugins and generate factory methods "manually". Though, this seems a bit too complicated for such purpose.

nodes.body:
Generating the 'of' method is only possible if the proto is guaranteed to only ever has one single field. I doubt we will add it for users' protos because we just don't have the same level of guarantee.

You can though propose new proto types into the protobuf library. If it's added to protobuf library, we are not limited to the 'of' method but can actually provide more specialized helpers appropriate for the type (e.g., google.protobuf.Any has pack() and unpack() methods).
Thank you for making it clear, @xfxyjwf.

title: Implicit arena allocation resulting in OOM on Linux

nodes.body: @ekigwana Are you able to figure the root cause of the problem?

Sorry for the delay in replying but I wanted to be sure I had diagnosed the issue correctly.

Turns out it was pure coincidence that protobufs were involved (I use them a lot).

Looked at the OOM issue and found that i needed to adjust the kernel configuration.

Previous option caused task to run out of virtual memory due to glibc's performance tuning that allocates memory per thread:
Enabling Transparent Hugepage always, can increase the
memory footprint of applications without a guaranteed
benefit but it will work automatically for all applications.

New option (which was used in previous kernels. Not sure how it was dropped but was not deliberate in any case:
Enabling Transparent Hugepage madvise, will only provide a
performance improvement benefit to the applications using 
madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) but it won't risk to increase the
memory footprint of applications without a guaranteed 
benefit.

I also set a hard limit on the maximum number of arenas that can be created.
`mallopt(M_ARENA_MAX, 8);`

The combination reduced the virtual memory usage an order of magnitude to Mega instead of Giga for our massively threaded server that uses protobufs everywhere. So uptime went from randomly between 3 hours and 11 hours to now It looks like it should stay up forever.

Not sure I needed to set M_ARENA_MAX but I did since I was up against a deadline so testing is key. I got higher CPU use but I can accept that due to the deadline since I don't time to twiddle.

I saw a lot of JAVA references when looking for a solution so at least when google caches this, it might help someone else.
Thanks for the explanation. Not that I understand much about this kernel option but it's good to know protobuf is not the culprit here.

TL:DR: [documentation](http://www.rubydoc.info/gems/ruby-protocol-buffers/1.0.1/ProtocolBuffers/RepeatedField#replace-instance_method), you will need to use the instance method `#replace` instead of `+=`.

I ran into similar issue recently and was able to solved it by replacing `+=` with the `#replace` method. As such, you will need to do `test.repeated_custom.replace([custom_value])` instead of `test.repeated_custom += [custom_value]` in your code. I hope that help.

title: No way to determine unknown fields in C++-backed Python protocol buffers
body:
If I have a proto message object in C++, I can access its unknown fields using `Reflection::GetUnknownFields`. If I have a proto message object in Python backed by the pure Python message implementation, I can access its unknown fields using `msg._unknown_fields`. However, if I have a proto message object in Python backed by the C++ implementation of messages, there doesn't appear to be a way to access its unknown fields. There is no `_unknown_fields` attribute on such objects.

For completeness, shouldn't the C++-backed Python implementation also expose unknown fields? Probably via an `_unknown_fields` attribute, so it shares the same interface with the Pure Python implementation?

nodes.body: I'm not a protobuf developer but I would venture that `_unknown_fields` is not a supported API anyway: in Python a leading underscore usually indicates a private variable, and `_unknown_fields` is not mentioned in the [docs](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python/google.protobuf.message.Message-class). So maybe the issue should be "No way to determine unknown fields in ~~C++-backed~~ Python protocol buffers"
@arthur-tacca is correct. `_unknown_fields` is supposed to be private and should not be used by users. The problem here is that Python doesn't have a public API for unknown fields.

I understand. Are there plans to introduce a public API for unknown fields in Python?

The scenario we have is that the versions of our proto definitions used by our client and server occasionally fall out of sync with each other, and we need a way for the server to recognise that the client is using a newer version of our proto definitions.  Is there a good way of doing this that doesn't depend on checking unknown fields server-side?
I think it's up to @anandolee to decide whether or not to add this new unknown field API in python.
We do not have any plan for public unknown fields API. But to better support pure python users switch to C++ python, it make sense to implement _unknown_fields attribute in C++ python.
Great, looking forward to it.

Update: we are adding unknown fields APIs in internal code. Will not provide _unknown_fields attribute in C++ python. 
_unknown_fields in pure python will be removed sometime in future.
Update: UnknownFields API has been submitted in internal code. Expect to see it in future release

It is Down-integrate from google internal to master branch:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/6bbe197e9c1b6fc38cbdc45e3bf83fa7ced792a3#diff-23eeeb4347bdd26bfc6b7ee9a3b755dd
How can be used the new UnknownFields API ?

Example usage:

```

def PrintUnknownFields(unknown_fields):
  print(len(unknown_fields))
  for unknown_field in unknown_fields:
    print(unknown_field.wire_type)
    print(unknown_field.field_number)
    if unknown_field.wire_type == 3:  # group, nested unknown fields
      PrintUnknownFields(unknown_field.data)
    else:
      print(unknown_field.data)
PrintUnknownFields(some_message.UnknownFields())
```

Or you can see the tests for example:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/ba8692fbade4ba329cc4531e286ab5a8e0821d97/python/google/protobuf/internal/unknown_fields_test.py#L190

title: Ruby RepeatedField doesn't implement #delete_if correctly
body:
`Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField#delete_if` doesn't appear to be implemented correctly. I think it's defined using the wrong helper method (`define_array_wrapper_method`, instead of `define_array_wrapper_with_result_method`).

Given the following generated Ruby classes:
```ruby
# Generated by the protocol buffer compiler.  DO NOT EDIT!
# source: testing.proto

require 'google/protobuf'

Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_message "Member" do
    optional :id, :string, 1
  end
  add_message "Collection" do
    repeated :collection, :message, 1, "Member"
  end
end

Member = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("Member").msgclass
Collection = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("Collection").msgclass
```

This is the behaviour of `RepeatedField#delete_if`:
```ruby
[7] pry(main)> coll = Collection.new(collection: [{id: "a"}, {id: "b"}])
=> <Collection: collection: [<Member: id: "a">, <Member: id: "b">]>
[8] pry(main)> coll.collection.delete_if { |m| m.id == "a" }
=> #<Enumerator: ...>
[9] pry(main)> coll.collection
=> [<Member: id: "a">, <Member: id: "b">]
```

This is the expected behaviour as demonstrated by `Array#delete_if`:
```ruby
[3] pry(main)> arr = [Member.new(id: "a"), Member.new(id: "b")]
=> [<Member: id: "a">, <Member: id: "b">]
[4] pry(main)> arr.delete_if { |m| m.id == "a" }
=> [<Member: id: "b">]
[5] pry(main)> arr
=> [<Member: id: "b">]
```

nodes.body: (Also affects `#reject!`, since that's aliased to `#delete_if`.)

title: Grammar for strings is incorrect
body:
```
strLit = ( "'" { charValue } "'" ) |  ( '"' { charValue } '"' )
charValue = hexEscape | octEscape | charEscape | /[^\0\n\\]/
hexEscape = '\' ( "x" | "X" ) hexDigit hexDigit
octEscape = '\' octalDigit octalDigit octalDigit
charEscape = '\' ( "a" | "b" | "f" | "n" | "r" | "t" | "v" | '\' | "'" | '"' )
quote = "'" | '"'
```

This allows strings like `"""` or any number of quotation marks really both double and single quotes.  To fix this, you need two variations of `charValue`, one that only allows unescaped double quotes and another one that only allows unescaped single quotes and use them with matching string delimiters.

On top of this, this grammar defines `quote` rule, but it never uses it anywhere.

#2424 is related

nodes.body:
Below is some Prolog code, which, I believe, gives correct grammar for string literals (the best I could understand the intention of the grammar above):

``` prolog
octal_digit(O) --> [X], { O is X - 48, O < 8, O >= 0 }.

quote(39) --> "'".
quote(34) --> "\"".

escaped(92) --> "\\".
escaped(7)  --> "a".
escaped(8)  --> "b".
escaped(12) --> "f".
escaped(10) --> "n".
escaped(13) --> "r".
escaped(9)  --> "t".
escaped(11) --> "v".
escaped(X)  --> ("x" | "X"), xdigit(A), xdigit(B), { X is A * 16 + B }.
escaped(O)  -->
    octal_digit(A),
    octal_digit(B),
    octal_digit(C),
    { O is A * 64 + B * 8 + C }.

string_content([E | T], Q) -->
    "\\", escaped(E), !,
    string_content(T, Q).
string_content([Q | T], Q) -->
    "\\", [Q], !,
    string_content(T, Q).
string_content([H | T], Q) -->
    [H],
    { not(member(H, [Q, 92, 10, 0])) }, !,
    string_content(T, Q).
string_content([], _) --> [].

string_literal(S) -->
    quote(Q),
    string_content(I, Q),
    quote(Q),
    { string_codes(S, I) }.
```

Note that the grammar above disallows strings like `"\'"` (i.e. when escaping is redundant). To allow this, you may modify `string_content//2`, by removing second predicate and adding two more `escaped//1` predicates for single and double quotes.

This allows strings like """  ,  I don't see """ can be allowed in this Grammar.

"this grammar defines quote rule, but it never uses it anywhere." Yes, we used to use
```
strLit = quote { charValue } quote 
```
Which has same issue with #4589. We changed strLit but forgot to remove quote and fix 
```
syntax = "syntax" "=" quote "proto3" quote ";
```

> strLit = quote { charValue } quote 

Please look at the quote above (in my post).  Maybe you have the grammar you are quoting written somewhere, but it is not on the documentation web site: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec , the web site looks exactly as I posted it.

However, the rule you suggest, viz.

```
strLit = quote { charValue } quote 
```

Is even worse because it will recognize `""'` (double quote, double quote, single quote) as a string literal, i.e. you lose the requirement of having balanced quotation marks.

Well, it's easy... translate your rules literally into a grammar and try feeding it the input I suggested.

But, if you need this to be put into words:

1. Second tail of the rule `strLit` matches `"""` because:
2. First rule of second tail of `strLit` matches `"`.
3. `charValue` matches `"` because fourth tail of `charValue` matches `"`.
4. Third rule of second tail of `strLit` matches `"`.

> This allows strings like """ , I don't see """ can be allowed in this Grammar.

```
strLit = ( "'" { charValue } "'" ) |  ( '"' { charValue } '"' )
charValue = hexEscape | octEscape | charEscape | /[^\0\n\\]/
```

`"` is a valid `charValue`. A `strLit` is any number of `charValue`s enclosed by either `"` or by `'`. `"""` is a `charValue` enclosed by `"`. QED.

The same problem noted by @wvxvw does in fact come up with e.g. this definition:

`syntax = "syntax" "=" quote "proto3" quote ";"`

According to this rule, `syntax = 'proto3"` should be accepted. (It isn't.) This at least the only place the `quote` production is used.

There's an additional problem that the syntax-defining syntax `/[^\0\n\\]/` is not actually defined anywhere in the specification. One *assumes* it's meant to be a regular expression. But this is not actually stated anywhere!

title: Extranous code in python protobuf generation

nodes.body:
(Note: I am not a protobuf maintainer, I am just passing by. No warrenties on the contents of this comment.)

There are a few problem with the way you're calling protoc:

 * You're not passing `gogo.proto` to protoc. If you did, it would generate the corresponding `pb2`, so you wouldn't get an import error.
 * You're not using the correct relative path for `gogo.proto`. Perhaps everything will actually work with this incorrect path once you fix the previous point, but you'll find the generated `gogo_pb2.py` is in a surprisingly deep nested directory, and actually it will probably still break because `github.com` is not a valid Python package name.

## Passing `gogo.proto` to protoc

This is pretty easy. Just add it to your command line, including the full path:

    protoc -I=. -I=$GOPATH/src -I=$GOPATH/src/github.com/gogo/protobuf/protobuf --python_out=. etcd.proto $GOPATH/src/github.com/gogo/protobuf/protobuf/gogoproto/gogo.proto


## Fix relative path of `gogo.proto`

Compare the file path against the first `-I` it matches to get the relative path:

    file: $GOPATH/src/github.com/gogo/protobuf/protobuf/gogoproto/gogo.proto
    -I:   $GOPATH/src
    rel:  github.com/gogo/protobuf/protobuf/gogoproto/gogo.proto

But the relative path ought to just be `gogoproto/gogo.proto`. To fix the problem, remove that `-I=$GOPATH/src` option; you don't seem to be using it for anything. Then the path will match against the other import switch:

    file: $GOPATH/src/github.com/gogo/protobuf/protobuf/gogoproto/gogo.proto
    -I:   $GOPATH/src/github.com/gogo/protobuf/protobuf
    rel:  gogoproto/gogo.proto

This is the correct relative import. So your protoc invocation now looks like this:

    protoc -I=. -I=$GOPATH/src/github.com/gogo/protobuf/protobuf --python_out=. etcd.proto $GOPATH/src/github.com/gogo/protobuf/protobuf/gogoproto/gogo.proto

You'll need to change the `import` statement in the `etcd.proto` to reflect this, back to what it originally was. The fact you had to change this before was the hint that something wasn't right in the way you were calling `protoc`. 


## Bonus changes: Package for `etcd_pb2.py`

I would suggest putting etcd.proto in a directory e.g. `etcdserverpb`, but leave the `-I.` (i.e. pointing to its parent directory). This way the generated file is considered to be in a Python package i.e. you would import it with `import etcdserverpb.etcd_pb2`.

title: C#'s ParseDelimitedFrom handles EOF differently from Java's
body:
**Problem**
- Java's `ParseDelimitedFrom` returns null if the input stream is exactly at EOF.
- C#'s `ParseDelimitedFrom` throws `InvalidProtocolBufferException: While parsing a protocol message, the input ended unexpectedly in the middle of a field. This could mean either that the input has been truncated or that an embedded message misreported its own length.`

I believe the Java behaviour is more useful e.g. for reading from sockets. Also the C# error message seems a little misleading.

**Solutions**
If we don't want to break backwards compatibility in C#, we could either add a new function (as requested by #4100) or throw a more specific exception type like `ProtocolBufferEndOfStreamException` that users could catch.

At minimum it would be good if there was a different exception message for immediate EOF.

**Workaround**
I wrapped my stream in a subclass of `Stream` that counts the number of bytes read. If the count doesn't change during `ParseDelimitedFrom` then I know it was an EOF.

title: ODR violation using the Bazel build
body:
As best I can tell, if you use the included Bazel build and attempt to depend on `descriptor.proto` (by way of `@com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_proto`), the build ends up with two copies of `descriptor.proto` and multiple definitions of the C++ symbols contained therein. This triggers ODR violations from ASAN, and we've seen deadlocks inside static initializers that we believe to be related.

I've pushed a minimal reproducer to https://github.com/nelhage/rules_proto_odr

If you build that repository with a newish clang (I'm using a clang 6 nightly), and `bazel run main`, you'll see the ODR violation from ASAN:

```
[nelhage@nelhage5:~/code/proto_odr]$ CC=clang-6.0 bazel run main
INFO: Analysed target //:main (0 packages loaded).
INFO: Found 1 target...
Target //:main up-to-date:
  bazel-bin/main
INFO: Elapsed time: 0.274s, Critical Path: 0.00s
INFO: Build completed successfully, 1 total action

INFO: Running command line: bazel-bin/main
=================================================================
==16003==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: odr-violation (0x7f6baf98b340):
  [1] size=48 'google::protobuf::_FileDescriptorSet_default_instance_' bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/external/com_google_protobuf/google/protobuf/descriptor.pb.cc:28:3
  [2] size=48 'google::protobuf::_FileDescriptorSet_default_instance_' external/com_google_protobuf/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.pb.cc:28:3
These globals were registered at these points:
  [1]:
    #0 0x431fa0 in __asan_register_globals.part.11 (/home/nelhage/.cache/bazel/_bazel_nelhage/59eff58f9c182bc06a3fc860075e892e/execroot/com_github_nelhage_proto_odr/bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/main+0x431fa0)
    #1 0x7f6baf805bfd in asan.module_ctor (/home/nelhage/.cache/bazel/_bazel_nelhage/59eff58f9c182bc06a3fc860075e892e/execroot/com_github_nelhage_proto_odr/bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/_solib_k8/libexternal_Scom_Ugoogle_Uprotobuf_Slibdescriptor_Uproto.so+0x2a7bfd)

  [2]:
    #0 0x431fa0 in __asan_register_globals.part.11 (/home/nelhage/.cache/bazel/_bazel_nelhage/59eff58f9c182bc06a3fc860075e892e/execroot/com_github_nelhage_proto_odr/bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/main+0x431fa0)
    #1 0x7f6bae6c7d2d in asan.module_ctor (/home/nelhage/.cache/bazel/_bazel_nelhage/59eff58f9c182bc06a3fc860075e892e/execroot/com_github_nelhage_proto_odr/bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/_solib_k8/libexternal_Scom_Ugoogle_Uprotobuf_Slibprotobuf.so+0xd02d2d)

==16003==ABORTING
```

nodes.body:
Based on the existence of `internal_bootstrap_hack` in `cc_proto_library` I believe this is a known issue, but the protobuf devs should document it better.

`@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf` has `srcs=[..., "src/google/protobuf/descriptor.pb.cc", ...]` which makes the headers and symbols available to C++ code. `@com_google_protobuf//:cc_wkt_protos` is a `cc_proto_library` that can be depended on, and uses `internal_bootstrap_hack` to avoid actually generating any C++ sources (because they would create duplicate symbols).

Is there any way to cause a warning to be emitted if a user tries to wrap one of the internal protos in their own `cc_proto_library` target? Perhaps by checking if any of the `srcs` labels is a member of `WELL_KNOWN_PROTOS` ?

I may have minimized too far; https://github.com/nelhage/rules_proto_odr/tree/69ecec3d7182499acc2fe7a807f99abf4f58aa5e contains an example that's closer to what triggered this in our real application. We weren't creating a `cc_proto_library` directly out of `@com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_proto`, but out of our own `.proto` which `import`ed `descriptor.proto`, which we accessed by adding `@com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_proto` to its `deps`. Is that unsupported? Is there another way to access `descriptor.proto`?

Agreed that an earlier error here would be nice.

Ooh, I think this is a Bazel bug. Details at https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/4650

---

Building nelhage/rules_proto_odr@69ecec3d7182499acc2fe7a807f99abf4f58aa5e generates these commands:

```
SUBCOMMAND: # //proto:proto_proto [action 'Generating C++ proto_library //proto:proto_proto']
(cd /root/.cache/bazel/_bazel_root/f8087e59fd95af1ae29e8fcb7ff1a3dc/execroot/com_github_nelhage_proto_odr && \
  exec env - \
    PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin \
  bazel-out/host/bin/external/com_google_protobuf/protoc '--cpp_out=bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles' '-Iproto/with_extensions.proto=proto/with_extensions.proto' '-Igoogle/protobuf/descriptor.proto=bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/external/com_google_protobuf/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto' --direct_dependencies google/protobuf/descriptor.proto:proto/with_extensions.proto '--direct_dependencies_violation_msg=%s is imported, but //proto:proto_proto doesn'\''t directly depend on a proto_library that '\''srcs'\'' it.' proto/with_extensions.proto)

SUBCOMMAND: # @com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_proto [action 'Generating C++ proto_library @com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_proto']
(cd /root/.cache/bazel/_bazel_root/f8087e59fd95af1ae29e8fcb7ff1a3dc/execroot/com_github_nelhage_proto_odr && \
  exec env - \
    PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin \
  bazel-out/host/bin/external/com_google_protobuf/protoc '--cpp_out=bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/external/com_google_protobuf' '-Igoogle/protobuf/descriptor.proto=bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/external/com_google_protobuf/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto' --direct_dependencies google/protobuf/descriptor.proto '--direct_dependencies_violation_msg=%s is imported, but @com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_proto doesn'\''t directly depend on a proto_library that '\''srcs'\'' it.' bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/external/com_google_protobuf/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto)

SUBCOMMAND: # //proto:proto_proto [action 'Compiling proto/with_extensions.pb.cc']
(cd /root/.cache/bazel/_bazel_root/f8087e59fd95af1ae29e8fcb7ff1a3dc/execroot/com_github_nelhage_proto_odr && \
  exec env - \
    PWD=/proc/self/cwd \
  /usr/bin/clang-5.0 -U_FORTIFY_SOURCE -fstack-protector -Wall -B/usr/bin -B/usr/bin -fcolor-diagnostics -fno-omit-frame-pointer '-fsanitize=address' '-fsanitize=undefined' '-std=c++0x' '-fsanitize=address' '-fsanitize=undefined' -MD -MF bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/proto/_objs/proto_proto/proto/with_extensions.pb.pic.d '-frandom-seed=bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/proto/_objs/proto_proto/proto/with_extensions.pb.pic.o' -fPIC -iquote . -iquote bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles -iquote external/com_google_protobuf -iquote bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/external/com_google_protobuf -iquote external/bazel_tools -iquote bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/external/bazel_tools -isystem external/com_google_protobuf/src -isystem bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/external/com_google_protobuf/src -isystem external/bazel_tools/tools/cpp/gcc3 -no-canonical-prefixes -Wno-builtin-macro-redefined '-D__DATE__="redacted"' '-D__TIMESTAMP__="redacted"' '-D__TIME__="redacted"' -c bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/genfiles/proto/with_extensions.pb.cc -o bazel-out/k8-fastbuild/bin/proto/_objs/proto_proto/proto/with_extensions.pb.pic.o)
```

There's no `protobuf.bzl` skylark involved here, it's pure Bazel native protobuf rules. The native aspect transits down the `deps` to find all `proto_library` targets, generates C++ code from them, and presumably links it into the final binary.  It ought to be skipping code generation for .proto files that are required by `libprotobuf.a`, but isn't.

I see that you are linking the binary dynamically. Usually ODR violation at runtime will turn up as linker errors if it's linked statically, however, in this case it compiles fine after I change it to `linkstatic = 1`. It seems to me bazel is building the dynamic library for descriptor_proto incorrectly.

The use case here is supported and we have an example doing just that in (it's using timestamp_proto instead of descriptor_proto but they are built the same way):
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/examples/BUILD

Both depending on descriptor_proto in another proto_library and depending on descriptor_proto in your own cc_proto_library should work. Although the later isn't really useful.

And yes, this is more of a bazel issue than a protobuf one.

Yeah, I built dynamically specifically to illustrate the problem, since linking statically succeeds for reasons that I don't fully understand. I'm happy to close this one out and follow up on the bazel issue, if that's your recommendation.
I think we can leave it open until the bazel issue is confirmed/fixed. Right now it's unclear if there is anything needed to be done on the protobuf side.

Hit this for a personal project today, so figured I'd get to the bottom of it. Turns out the C++ proto toolchain defined by this package (not Bazel, surprisingly) is missing a "blacklist protos" setting.

PR https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/4334 fixes the error for me.

nodes.body: Also forgot to mention that this problem is related to the use of: `optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME`. When that option is removed the tests pass without a problem.

`optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME` is not supported by protobuf-java any more. To use lite runtime, use the protoc-gen-java-lite plugin with com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java-lite instead:
https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/com.google.protobuf/protoc-gen-javalite
https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/com.google.protobuf/protobuf-lite

With the plugin in PATH, run protoc with --javalite_out=... instead of --java_out=...

@xfxyjwf sure, but what are we going to do with artifacts that were pushed to maven using non-lite version and because of how dependency management works in Java they pick a transient dependency on a newer protobuf-java and break their application?

If you use non-lite version everywhere, we guarantee the generated code of older protoc will work with newer version of protobuf-java runtime. So no problem there.

However, we no longer support 'optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME' any more with protobuf-java so there is no guarantee of such compatibilities if you have 'optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME' in your proto. And that's the exception you are seeing here.

And yes, I agree that we should start to disallow 'optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME' for Java so you will get a compile failure instead of runtime failure.
I think this issue should become a request to disallow 'optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME' for Java.

It turns out we can't disallow 'optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME' because the option is used by other languages as well. In https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/4504 I updated protoc to print a warning instead.

@xfxyjwf, that puts us in a weird situation. If the option is required for other languages and broken for Java, then how are we supposed to resolve issues? It seems protoc should generate code for full protobuf and ignore the option for Java other than provide the warning.

@ejona86 Yes, we do need to change protoc to ignore 'optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME' instead. Some cleanup needs to be done before we can switch away from the current 'generating broken code with a warning' situation. See b/77980691

title: C# copy ctor inconsistently writes to property rather than backing field for non-repeated messages
body:
For example, in the [copy ctor for the Subscription type in Pubsub.cs](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/google-cloud-dotnet/blob/master/apis/Google.Cloud.PubSub.V1/Google.Cloud.PubSub.V1/Pubsub.cs#L1967); `PushConfig` and `MessageRetentionDuration` write to the property because they refer to non-repeated message types, whereas all other writes are to the backing field ([from pubsub.proto here](https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/pubsub/v1/pubsub.proto#L405)).

Is there a reason these writes are not always consistently to the backing field?

Thanks :)

nodes.body:
non-repeated message field is also write to backing field, please search pushConfig_. Correct me if I misunderstand your question.

I am closing it for clean up. Feel free to reopen if it is still an issue.

This is writing to the property, not the backing field.
```cs
PushConfig = other.pushConfig_ != null ? other.PushConfig.Clone() : null;
```
To be consistent with other field types it should write to the backing field like this:
```cs
pushConfig_ = other.pushConfig_ != null ? other.pushConfig_.Clone() : null;
```

title: Why should we use arena?
body: As far as I know, Arena is not a memory pool which can reuse allocated memory by maintain a freelist, it just cache more and more memory when create message with arena; Isn't google tcmalloc a better and straighter way to improve overall performance? I just want to take the advantage of network transmission with protobuf.

nodes.body:
Right now using arena with opensource protobuf doesn't gain you much, but inside Google, we have seen massive improvement by adopting arena. I think protobuf arena has two advantages that tcmalloc can't offer:

1. The ability to deallocate a entire proto message tree in big chunks. With arena, it's possible to allocate everything in a proto message tree in one or several bulk chunks of memory. When you are done with the message, you just need to deallocate these few large chunks. Without arena, deleting a proto message tree will result in numerous small delete calls for every single small object a proto may hold. Basically we have the ability to skip all the desctructor calls with arena which we can't do otherwise.
2. Better locality. With protobuf arena, objects belong to the same proto message tree are put in adjacent memory whereas tcmalloc doesn't know whether an object is part of a proto message tree and is likely interleave protos with non-protos.

I think the most benefit we saw is from (1). This unfortunately isn't the case with opensource protobuf because all string fields are not allocated in the arena. Internally we have a hack to allocate something that looks like a string in the arena and cast it to a string with accessed, but that isn't portable. We also don't have ctype=STRING_PIECE support in opensource which can help with the issue. I know there are some users using arena with their own patch to implement ctype=STRING_PIECE. I don't think arena will can be widely used until we address the string issue.
I think i got it.

@xfxyjwf 

You mention strings not working great in arenas, but what about `bytes`.  Bytes are pseudo strings, but since they don’t need to marshaled into some object, my assumption would be that arenas would be excellent for receiving bytes. 

Especially if you wanted to receive these bytes directly into some special block of pinned memory, eg. cudaMallocHost memory using ArenaOptions. 

Do arenas make sense for FlatBuffers?  It seems like this might be the mechanism to do zero copy directly in and out of the memory blocks you reserve for messages.

@ryanolson In protobuf C++ API, `string` fields and `bytes` fields are both stored as `std::string` so the same issue applies: neither of them will be stored efficiently in protobuf arena. That can be solved by open-sourcing the zero copy support (see https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1896), which includes StringPiece (basically std::string_view) support and that will allow a `string` or `bytes` field to alias memory in the arena directly.

title: enum values should have `json_name` pseudo-option just like fields
body:
Fields can be renamed, even when using JSON format, by setting `json_name` and ensuring that it never changes. This allows the field's name to change without impacting how it is serialized to/de-serialized from JSON.

Since enum values are also identified by name in the JSON format, they should have an analogous feature: a `json_name` pseudo-option, allowing the enum value's actual name to change while its JSON encoding remains the same.

I call the existing field `json_name` a "pseudo-option" because, though it uses the option syntax in proto source, it does *not* end up in the `google.descriptor.FieldOptions` message. Instead, it is promoted to a field of `google.descriptor.FieldDescriptorProto`. For symmetry, I would expect the enum value option to behave similarly, resulting in a new `json_name` field on `google.descriptor.EnumValueDescriptorProto`.

You can use proto2 syntax instead, then if you explicitly set them to zero (the default) they will still be serialized.  proto2 syntax supports the concept of field presence, so while getting the value will return the default if it isn't set, you can also explicitly set things to the default and the presence will capture it was set to ensure it is serialized.

ps - there are other difference you get when picking proto2 vs. proto3 syntaxes, so make sure you read the docs for some of those details.
You can also use wrappers in well know types: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/wrappers.proto

title: [Java] [Request] Add @Nullable annotations to java code.
body:
The addition of info if a value can be null or not would make working with protobuf in Kotlin way easier. Since Kotlin offers a pretty good [null safety](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/reference/null-safety.html) when using pure Kotlin or just the java standard library.

It also takes into account when there is a @Nullable annotation present so this would be a nice addition and would prevent bugs when using code generated by protoc with Kotlin.

nodes.body: @usbpc I would be willing to own this ! Please advise next steps. How can I assign this project to myself?
@usbpc which of the annotations ( required, optional or repeated ) correspond to @nullable ? Would it be optional ? Thanks.
@usbpc Thanks for clarrifying.
Protobuf Java API never returns null. If a field is absent, the accessor will just return the default value. For this reason I think @nullable isn't useful for protobuf.

I think there might be a bit of confusion here. There are (roughly) two kinds of nullability annotations:

1. value can sometimes be null, aka "nullable"
2. value can never be null, aka "not-null"

If the Protobuf Java API never returns null then it doesn't need to use the former, **but it would still be very helpful if it used the latter**.

Kotlin currently uses "platform types" for values going into or out of protobuf methods. Kotlin doesn't do *any* compile time null checking when dealing with platform types (ie: it behaves just like Java).

However, if the Kotlin compiler sees annotations that say a value "can never be null", then it will use the a more strict type. That means that if the parameters and return types of these methods were annotated one way or the other, then Kotlin could do compile time null checks for code that uses these methods.

More details can be found [here](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/reference/java-interop.html#nullability-annotations).

tl;dr: Since Protobuf Java API never returns null then it should be annotated as never returning null. Likewise, parameters of methods that should never be null (like the parameters to the generated setters) should be annotated as not-null.
@xenomachina As far as I know there is no such not-null annotation in Java 7 and protobuf does not take additional dependencies.

Not even JSR-305 annotations?

I've found a workaround that may be useful to others: place a `package-info.java` in the same package that the proto-compiler is generating into that looks something like this:

``` java
@javax.annotation.ParametersAreNonnullByDefault
package com.example.mypackage;
```
The Kotlin compiler will then behave as though all parameters to methods in that package are annotated as not null, except those that are explicitly annotated otherwise.
What about annotating arguments of setters with @NotNull? It throws NPE when null is passed anyway.
Luckily for us, https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5526 was recently reopened. Let's hope it gets implemented eventually. :pray:
We should be using the javax.annotation.Nullable

FYI: There's another method that can accept and return null values: a [`map` field](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java-generated#map-fields)'s `getFooOrDefault` method. And of course `equals` is an example of a method that accepts a null parameter.

\[edit: And I think protobuf might still generate `valueOf` as a deprecated equivalent to `forNumber`?\]

I don't want to claim with absolute 100% confidence that those are the only other such methods, but we've been getting by pretty well with our temporary Google-internal nullness annotations (which are recognized by our Kotlin and Checker Framework users), and I _think_ those are the only ones in the generated code that I see nullness annotations on.

---

Jerry, if you get to the point that you think the protobuf team may want to investigate this soon, let me know. There have been some past discussions about dependencies (including on javax.annotation specifically), and my team has been working through some similar issues.

I still expect to make this happen eventually. (And it helps that there's been a renewed push toward JSpecify 1.0.)

The actual Protobuf team can step in if they'd like this to be closed, but I'm at least not letting the bot close it :)

title: C++11 features
body:
Hello,

I want to use move semantics for the getter methods. Is that supported? I see all getter methods return const &. I want to move some of the variables like string . Any plans for adding this feature?

nodes.body: The object returned by the getter is still owned by the parent message.  They are not rvalue and cannot be moved. Otherwise the parent message would end up in a corrupted state.

Thanks for the response. 

I understand what you have mentioned is the current implementation which does not support move. However with support for move available in C++ we should make use of it. And it's pretty basic and widely use case we will be supporting - apps receiving data would be able to use move instead of copying the data in their own data structures.

But the getter returned objects are not temp objects. There is no copy happening when you call the get - it returns the address pointing to the original data, which you cannot and should not modify. 

If you need to consume the input message and move the fields in it to another message, you can explicitly call release_foo() to transfer the ownership of the sub message fields to the new message.

I think there is some confusion here about whether you really want to move from a field in your source message, which would modify it. Just to be clear here, imagine this bit of pseudo-code:

    // This is just pseudo-code
    dest_msg.my_str_field = src_msg.my_str_field

Obviously, this should change the value in `dest_msg.my_str_field`. But what do you want to happen to the value in `src_msg.my_str_field`?

1. `src_msg.my_str_field` should be unchanged i.e. retain its original value.
    * In that case it is absolutely necessary to do a copy of the underlying string.
    * That looks like this: `dest_msg.set_my_str_field(src_msg.my_str_field())`
    * As @pherl already said, the current implementation only does one copy, which is the best that can be done:
    * `my_str_field()` does zero copies because it returns a reference to the underlying string.
    * `set_my_str_field()` with a `const std::string&` does a single copy.
2. You don't care about the new value of `src_msg.my_str_field` i.e. it can be changed to anything.
    * If this really is what you want, this is already possible: use the `mutable_*()` accessors.
    * It looks like this: `dest_msg.set_my_str_field(std::move(*src_msg.mutable_str_field()))`
    * `mutable_my_str_field()` returns a `std::string*` which you can dereference and move from.
    * `set_my_str_field()` has an overload that takes a `std::string&&`.
3. `src_msg.my_str_field` should become empty.
    * In this case, you can do a move as suggested in 2, but then you need to clear the source string.
    * The second line looks like this: `src_msg.clear_my_str_field()`.
    * I mention this because a common mistake is to believe that objects should be empty after you move from them, when in fact they are allowed to have *any* value unless explicitly documented.

To reiterate, you can move from a field already but it will change the source value (of course), and it looks like this:

    destination_msg.set_my_str_field(std::move(*source_msg.mutable_my_str_field()));

Or to move into a new string:

    std::string result = std::move(*my_msg.mutable_my_str_field());

There are already rvalue overloads of setters, constructors and assignment operators for strings, singular message fields and all repeated containers. Combined with `mutable_*` methods, this should give you what you want.

As pherl mentioned, you can alternatively use the `release_*` methods, which existed before move semantics were added to protobufs:

    destination_msg.set_allocated_my_str_field(source_msg.release_my_str_field());
    std::unique_ptr<std::string> result(another_msg.release_my_str_field());

These can be a bit more efficient for messages, because they change a single pointer rather than moving each of the fields individually. But I imagine the difference is not noticable unless you have a message with hundreds of fields, and perhaps not even then. Besides, `release_*` does a deallocation whereas a move would preserve the footprint of the message, which may save a later allocation.

For singular messages, yet another alternative is the `Swap()` method.

At a higher level, consider passing the whole protobuf object around rather than moving lots of individual fields. For example, if you have a protobuf `UserData` with 10 fields, and a class you've hand written called `User` with the same 10 fields plus a few more and some methods, consider having `UserData` be stored directly in the `User` class instead. You can use the message's move constructor to make construction of `User` efficient. This idea doesn't work for all applications, but can simplify code a lot when it does.

title: JS: Node Buffer support removed in 3.4.0
body:
After updating to from 3.3.0 to 3.4.0 or 3.5.0, I started getting the error `AssertionError: Failure: Type not convertible to Uint8Array.` from `byteSourceToUint8Array`.

This happens when I set a value with type `optional bytes` to a Buffer, then call `serializeBinary()` on the object.

google-protobuf used to explicitly support Buffers, but this was removed in https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/3043. This seems like a breaking change that should not happen in a minor version.

title: enum reserved ranges allow overlap -- off by one error

nodes.body: BTW, I verified that this off-by-one error does not extend to validating that actual values are not using reserved values. And that works fine. Even though the above message prints ranges `3 to 4` and `4 to 9` (instead of 3 to 5 and 5 to 10), it correctly fails if I try to create an enum value assigned to 10.

This is probably a bug in validation error printer. Note that the values used in reserved statement in the proto file are always inclusive. The protoc converts it to open end range in the descriptor. As enums allow higher value, we changed the descriptor internal to use inclusive ranges for enum reserve. Looks like the error printer logic isn't updated about this change.
I think this should have been fixed in the recent down-integration. Thanks for reporting the issue.
Marking this closed since it sounds like it was fixed.

title: Compact varint
body:
advantages:
1. It generates a unique value for each byte sequence.
2. It allows you to encode larger values in a sequence of bytes of the same size.

### Encoding to compact varint:

https://github.com/ivan386/protobuf-1/blob/b76098a2adb7a080231cf14903ab7f3687667ce6/proto/encode.go#L95-L106
```
func EncodeVarint(x uint64) []byte {
	var buf [maxVarintBytes]byte
	var n int
	for n = 0; x > 127; n++ {
		buf[n] = 0x80 | uint8(x&0x7F)
		x >>= 7
		x -= 1
	}
	buf[n] = uint8(x)
	n++
	return buf[0:n]
}
```

#### Example
300 = `000 0010 010 1100`

1. split first 7 bit
 `010 1100`

2. add MSB to it
 `1 010 1100`

3. decrement next bits
 `(000 0010) - 1 = 000 0001`

5. add MSB to it
 `0 000 0001`

6. concat with first
 `1 010 1100 ++ 0 000 0001 =  1 010 1100 0 000 0001`

### Decoding compact varint:
https://github.com/ivan386/protobuf-1/blob/b76098a2adb7a080231cf14903ab7f3687667ce6/proto/decode.go#L63-L78
```
func DecodeVarint(buf []byte) (x uint64, n int) {
	for shift := uint(0); shift < 64; shift += 7 {
		if n >= len(buf) {
			return 0, 0
		}
		b := uint64(buf[n])
		n++
		x += (b & 0xFF) << shift
		if (b & 0x80) == 0 {
			return x, n
		}
	}

	// The number is too large to represent in a 64-bit value.
	return 0, 0
}
```

#### Example
300 in compact varint format = `1 010 1100 0000 000 1`

1. split
```
1 010 1100
0000 000 1
```

2. extend
 ```
1 010 1100 = 0000 000 1 010 1100
0000 000 1 = 0000 000 1 000 0000
```
3. sum
 ```
0000 000 1 010 1100
+
0000 000 1 000 0000
=
0000 001 0 010 1100 
→  256 + 32 + 8 + 4 = 300
```

### Why it more compact:
#### 2 byte max value
```
a := []byte{255,127} //  1111 1111 0111 1111
```
***New 2 byte compact varint max is:*** 16511
encoded: `1 111 1111 0111 111 1` 

1. split
 ```
1 111 1111
0111 111 1
```
2. extend
 ```
1 111 1111 = 0000 000 1 111 1111
0111 111 1 = 0111 111 1 000 0000
```

2. sum
 ```
0000 000 1 111 1111
+
0111 111 1 000 0000
=
1000 000 0 111 1111 = 16511
```

***Old 2 byte varint max is:*** 16383
encoded: `1 111 1111 0 111 1111` 
1. split
 ```
1 111 1111
0 111 1111
```

2. drop MSB
 ```
111 1111
111 1111
```

3. concat
 ```
111 1111 ++ 111 1111
→ 111 1111 111 1111  = 16383
```

***difference:*** 16511 - 16383 = 128

#### 8 byte max value
```
a := []byte{255,255,255,255,255,255,255,127} // 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 1111 0111 1111
```

```
8 byte compact varint max:  72624976668147839
                            -
old 8 byte varint max:      72057594037927935
                            =
difference:                   567382630219904
```

### difference test code:
```
func DecodeVarintDifference(buf []byte) (difference uint64, newVarint uint64, oldVarint uint64, n int) {
	for shift := uint(0); shift < 64; shift += 7 {
		if n >= len(buf) {
			return 0, 0, 0, 0
		}
		b := uint64(buf[n])
		n++
		newVarint += (b & 0xFF) << shift
		oldVarint |= (b & 0x7F) << shift
		if (b & 0x80) == 0 {
			return newVarint - oldVarint, newVarint, oldVarint, n
		}
	}

	// The number is too large to represent in a 64-bit value.
	return 0, 0, 0, 0
}
```

Thanks for the proposal. However, wireformat is fundamental to compatibility and serialization libraries. Internally we have proposed wireformats that are 50% faster than the current encoding format, but still decided not to proceed as the gain is still not justifiable for a wireformat breakage and its introduced complexity.

I guess the gain of the new wireformat in this proposal won't be able to out-weigh of the cost of introducing incomopatibility. I will keep this in the back log and we could revisit when there is a significant gain to create a new wireformat. We can combine the proposals then.

title: YAML serialization in Ruby does not work
body:
```
syntax = "proto3";
package res_testing;

message OrderCreated {
  string event_id = 1;
  string order_id = 2;
  int32 customer_id = 3;
}
```

```ruby
# Generated by the protocol buffer compiler.  DO NOT EDIT!
# source: events.proto3

require 'google/protobuf'

Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_message "res_testing.OrderCreated" do
    optional :event_id, :string, 1
    optional :order_id, :string, 2
    optional :customer_id, :int32, 3
  end
end

module ResTesting
  OrderCreated = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("res_testing.OrderCreated").msgclass
end
```

```ruby
event = ResTesting::OrderCreated.new(
  event_id: "f90b8848-e478-47fe-9b4a-9f2a1d53622b",
  customer_id: 123,
  order_id: "K3THNX9",
)
YAML.dump(event)
# => "--- !ruby/object:ResTesting::OrderCreated {}\n"
```

As you can see dump YAML version does not contain the attributes and their data.

nodes.body: Why are you using YAML with proto? I don't think that's supported at all. You can use proto binary format instead?

I know this is a strange _issue_. It's just that most ruby objects/data structures are serializable with `YAML` and sometimes as a client of some libraries (ie for asynchronous processing) your object will be internally (inside your app only) serialized as yaml, then deserialized and then you will do something with it. I believe it would be nice to support it.

Here is a proof of concept of how it could work in a non-optimized way:

```ruby
class ResTesting::OrderCreated
  def encode_with(coder)
    coder['protobuf'] = self.class.encode(self)
  end

  def init_with(coder)
    clone = self.class.decode(coder['protobuf'])
    clone.to_hash.keys.map(&:to_s).each do |field|
      self[field] = clone[field]
    end
  end
end
```

It's not ideal because:
* `self.class.decode(coder['protobuf'])` - creates a new object just to be discarded. You know better the internals of the library and perhaps you could deserialize and fill out each field without doing that.
* `to_hash.keys.map(&:to_s).each` - was the only way for me to get a list of all possible fields from Ruby.

Source 1: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/10629209/how-can-i-control-which-fields-to-serialize-with-yaml
Source 2: `Psych::Visitors::ToRuby#deserialize` code:

```ruby
      def deserialize o
        if klass = resolve_class(Psych.load_tags[o.tag])
          instance = klass.allocate

          if instance.respond_to?(:init_with)
            coder = Psych::Coder.new(o.tag)
            coder.scalar = o.value
            instance.init_with coder
          end

          return instance
        end
        # ....
```

Also I could not find an easy way to hook into YAML/Psych engine before the instance is already allocated. If we could then the code could possibly be smaller and doing something similar like `clone = self.class.decode(coder['protobuf'])`
Thank you for assigning @TeBoring :) I wonder what you think about it.
Right now, we haven't seen many request for this feature. Will wait to see.

title: Efficiently filter repeated message fields in python
body:
I have a repeated message field and I would like to remove certain elements based on a predicate. Unfortunately, I cannot find documentation on how to do that and all approaches I can think of either don't work or are not optimal (involve copying memory) and not pythonic. 

I first tried 
```python
message.field[:] = [v for v in message.field if v.keep]
```
But it breaks since repeated message fields have no set items method (as opposed to repeated scalar fields).

I ended up doing
```python
new_fields = [v for v in message.field if v.keep]
del message.field[:]
message.field.extend(new_fields)
```
But this does one memory copy for each element in `new_fields`

title: Protobuf CocoaPod depends upon umbrella header ordering
body:
CocoaPods will fail to build the Protobuf CocoaPod if the explicitly pathed headers are ordered before the wild carded headers in the generated umbrella header file.

This is exposed in the unreleased CocoaPods master branch. CocoaPods may change back to the old behavior, but it would probably be good to make the Protobuf CocoaPod less fragile.

Details and example at https://github.com/CocoaPods/CocoaPods/issues/7518.

nodes.body: Part of the problem seems to be a circular dependency chain between Any.pbobjc.h and GPBWellKnownTypes.h. Other strange things are GPBProtocolBuffers.h being kind of a duplicate umbrella header and header sequencing to test the protoc versioning.

This sounds a little like #4301, is it the same thing?

From a quick look at the linked issue, that seems to say it is an ordering problem, but it isn't clear that protos has and ordering problem vs. something causing the imports to be found via different paths, so the `#import` doesn't collapse into a single definition?

It's similar to #4301, triggered by a different cause, with likely the same solution.

In this case, because the pre-release version of CocoaPods generated the umbrella header with a different order, the Protobuf module failed to be created during the build because of the order requirements. 

The CocoaPods team decided that even though relying upon header order is not technically correct, that it wasn't an acceptable change for a minor CocoaPods release update and decided to maintain the requested order with https://github.com/CocoaPods/CocoaPods/pull/7539 that got in before the first 1.5.0 beta went out.

So there is not a near term CocoaPods risk.

To reproduce :
- install from CocoaPods normally
- open `Pods/Target Support Files/Protobuf/Protobuf-umbrella.h`
- move the "Any.pbobjc.h" through "Wrappers.pbobjc.h" in front of the other headers
- build

> Other strange things are GPBProtocolBuffers.h being kind of a duplicate umbrella header

I'm not sure how to resolve this one.  Cocoapods isn't the only packaging system, we need to provide an umbrella for others (Carthage, direct source usage, etc).

> header sequencing to test the protoc versioning

Not sure I follow this one, this should just mean the defines have to exist before we import other headers, no?
If you create your own module_map with your own umbrella header - https://guides.cocoapods.org/syntax/podspec.html#module_map, then CocoaPods shouldn't generate one.
