title: Decimal Type?
body: It'd be amazing to have a Decimal type as a Well Known Type that can be leveraged across all the languages. I have no preference around the back-end implementation of it, as an end user I just think it'd greatly simplify codebases using Decimals

nodes.body: By "Decimal", I guess you mean something like java.math.BigDecimal in Java that can represent arbitrary precision. I think we should only introduce it if such a decimal type is supported as a built-in type or standard library type by all programming languages that we officially support. That probably won't happen any time soon though.
Yes exactly !

The java implementation could understand how to serialize BigDecimal or BigInteger to/from strings. I think this is a missed opportunity. Without it this causes developers to use floating pointing types instead, and use these type for calculation which may be bad. Leveraging protobuf to promote these types would help to use consistent and safe way to handle precision numbers.

I'm currently struggling with it myself (I'm using C#). I think you can't avoid having to map(convert) to decimal manually everytime you want to use decimal.

Some people pointed to https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/money.proto but there's no information on how to convert from nanos and to nanos. 

And it gives you the same result as just storing it as a string.

I wanted to rewrite my code to use gRPC but the state of things with `decimal` is really putting me off.
Maybe a util method from protobuf's supported type (e.g., string) to the decimal type in the specific language?

@TeBoring  that'd be the easier one. I'd rather have this than Avro's `bytes` method, as it destroys the user experience, but I'm sure their choices would be important to understand https://avro.apache.org/docs/1.8.1/spec.html#Decimal https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/AVRO-1402
@anandolee, this seems to be c# specific. Could you follow on that?
We are also using decimals quite heavily in our application and this is currently an issue for the migration to protobuf. Is there any update on this?

@TeBoring I would say this is not C# specific. We have:
* BigDecimal in Java https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/11/docs/api/java.base/java/math/BigDecimal.html
* decimal in Python https://docs.python.org/3/library/decimal.html
It is really important for all systems handling finance data.
I also think a util function converting from string would be bad from a performance perspective. Better to use something like the money type, without currency, as input to the util function. Or look on Avros Logical type for decimal https://avro.apache.org/docs/1.8.0/spec.html#Decimal. Both ways would be more efficient than string.

https://avro.apache.org/docs/1.8.2/spec.html#Decimal
When we talk about 'Decimal' most of us mean type that can be keep 'precision' and 'scale' value for float values. Avro is good example, they use unify serialisations of decimal to Bytes + keep two additional properties (scale, precision).
Why its important:
All use same serialisations process
Previously some serialised it to string, some to Byte Array with Ascending Order, some With Descending, etc
Now every one use same bytes, with same order, and keep metadata in same fields.
decimal would be very handy, I'm currently converting to a byte array base-256 digit, I guess is the most efficient way

"While suitable for many purposes, binary floating-point arithmetic should not be used for financial, commercial, and user-centric applications"

Yes, Google we need a Decimal type!  This is an example of the issue and probably demonstrates the issue in any language:
bool result = ((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3);  // result is false

The following link provides a detailed explanation and examples to explain the motivation for the "Decimal" data type, which is available in Python, Java and C#.
http://speleotrove.com/decimal/

Update: I'm currently driving internal proposal for the "decimal" type and I published the proposal document externally, so that people can chime in as needed.

See https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7039

There's class BigDecimal in Ruby. So strong +1 to add Decimal to protobuf types 👍 

I'd get rid of workaround for `Google::Protobuf::TypeError: Expected number type for double field (given BigDecimal).`

Decimals are exceptionally popular in C#, especially with database-backed business software. Almost all the "number" types in our application (and there is a lot of them) are decimals, there are only few floats here and there. Since float is not a safe replacement, we would end up mapping decimals to strings which is sort of embarrassing (and unsafe since not every string is a valid decimal).

Since it's a missing fundamental type, it should be in WellKnownTypes (as the suggested FixedDecimal). Alternatively, there should be another source of these "well known types" to avoid everyone copy-pasting the FixedDecimal to their codebases (in different namespaces)
Are there any preview ports of this? Writing a finance app with millions of messages per second, non-native support and casting each time is a non-starter for gRPC currently without this

For those working with decimals, can I confirm that there are two approaches that we are left with while we await movement on #7039 :

1. Use of string marshalling for decimals
2. Use of a custom protobuf message with either units and nanos (ala Google's [Money.proto](https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/money.proto) example) or an coefficient, exponent and sign (ala [big.js](https://mikemcl.github.io/big.js/))

Then hand off the expected marshalling of such messages to internal implementations of each application.

If this is the case, can people chime in with their preferred approach to date?

> For those working with decimals, can I confirm that there are two approaches that we are left with while we await movement on #7039 :
> 
> 1. Use of string marshalling for decimals
> 2. Use of a custom protobuf message with either units and nanos (ala Google's [Money.proto](https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/money.proto) example) or an coefficient, exponent and sign (ala [big.js](https://mikemcl.github.io/big.js/))
> 
> Then hand off the expected marshalling of such messages to internal implementations of each application.
> 
> If this is the case, can people chime in with their preferred approach to date?

Many thanks! Personally, would prefer custom profobuf message (this is what i have been doing to date). If there are any one-time/optimised marshalling that can be implemented as part of the codegen to prevent repeated casting that would be my main concern

There's a reference to this and a workaround here for wcf/recode, but I can't believe this is still an open issue 
https://visualrecode.com/blog/csharp-decimals-in-grpc/

Likewise. Decimal is an absolutely critical type for handling money in C#. Please add this to WellKnownTypes.

Thank you!
Now that Google killed https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7039, what is going to happen with this ticket and/or C# decimal support?
My intention is to leave this ticket open.  The desire is not invalid, it is simply the case that we are not actively pursuing it.
Any update on this? Please add 'Decimal' to WellKnownTypes

The signal is strongly (see @vivainio's comment above) that Google's team has placed any updates to support a decimal type on ice.

In the meantime, projects will need to DIY support for fixed decimal types.

Need support for Decimal128, so new fixed width wire type.

Workaround is to use with additional validation, but would prefer native scalar Decimal128.

Big Decimal can also be represented with bytes, or else string.
Any progress on this?

As noted above, we have no intention of pursuing this in the near term.  The language specific aspects of this make it a very large amount of effort to implement across our entire surface.  I recommend that users use a string field with appropriate parsing in their own code.

> As noted above, we have no intention of pursuing this in the near term. The language specific aspects of this make it a very large amount of effort to implement across our entire surface. I recommend that users use a string field with appropriate parsing in their own code.

The decimal data type is not a language specific type.  It is an IEEE standard -https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_754#Decimal
In particular it is extensively used in SQL storage systems.  The recommendation to use a string misunderstands the problem.  Decimal is a bitwise encoding therefore one cannot transform from a string field to a correctly encoded decimal type.  

Probably what needs to happen is for somebody to create a PR showing Google exactly how to implement a solution, since Google engineers appear to consistently misunderstand this issue.

While you are welcome to create a PR, the odds that it is adopted are low.  As mentioned, any sort of increased precision datatype needs to be handled in the full set of languages supported consistently which makes this a substantially larger amount of effort then most anticipate.  For every primitive datatype in protobuf that type must be reified into some language specific type for each target language.  

Decimal as you have pointed to is a general encoding of a particular format for storing arbitrary precision numbers.  It can in fact be stored as a string field (or rather a bytes field).

> The decimal data type is not a language specific type. It is an IEEE standard

The IEEE standard is one way of representing decimals, but it is unrelated to the arbitrary precision decimals that most contributors to this issue have been asking about (`BigDecimal` in Java, `decimal` in Python, `BigDecimal` in Ruby, and `Decimal` in Avro).

The C# `Decimal` type is more similar to decimal128 from IEEE 754-2008, as it is a fixed-size 128-bit representation. However the C# type does not use the IEEE format, as it appears to predate it by several years.

Decimal128 has the attractive property of being standardized, but adoption is low: even C and C++ have not adopted it into their standard libraries (though it looks like it may be coming in C23).

Different languages ecosystems have different expectations about what a Decimal type would provide. Bridging this gap, while maintaining reasonable efficiency, data integrity, interoperability, and convenience, makes this issue more difficult to solve than it may first appear.

The real world example I demo'd above shows why this is a problem for programmers:
> bool result = ((0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3); // result is false

At my previous job we implemented a fully working gRPC custom data type solution for C#.  The real-world problem this issue causes is that financial computations end up being not equal after transport over a grpc link.  Developers then spend hours or days trying to track down the issue, because unit tests often expect exact results and outside reviewers tend to legitimately worry that errors exist in the financial computations, especially since the computation differences can appear to be signficant.

Perhaps Google could "solve" this problem by providing open source custom gRPC types which allow developers to transport the Decimals types over grpc in a language specific fashion.  Usually the real-world issues involve the same language environment on both sides.  Nobody is expecting transport from C# to a C++ system.  But transport between systems which do support Decimal such as Java and C# would be nice.

My suggestions: just show us a work-around custom type implementation.

> most contributors to this issue have been asking about (`BigDecimal` in Java, `decimal` in Python, `BigDecimal` in Ruby, and `Decimal` in Avro).

To be clear I think it would be worthwhile having a well known type that involves support for native decimal where it exists (and yes the flavour may vary with the various languages) and allows for custom marshalling where it doesn’t. Whether that is something that is feasible is a different question.

If the official position for decimals is DIY then I personally believe that this should be noted explicitly in the docs, with or without sample implementations, rather than people having to find these threads for what is in many domains a required and very standard data type.

> At my previous job we implemented a fully working gRPC custom data type solution for C#. 

I encourage you to open source this, and we can point people to it.

>  Nobody is expecting transport from C# to a C++ system.

With respect, this is something that you don't care about, but if we support it in the core it is something we do have to care about.

> > At my previous job we implemented a fully working gRPC custom data type solution for C#.
> 
> I encourage you to open source this, and we can point people to it.
> 
> > Nobody is expecting transport from C# to a C++ system.
> 
> With respect, this is something that you don't care about, but if we support it in the core it is something we do have to care about.

Unfortunately I no longer have access to that source code.

Yes we would all expect Google to concern itself with transport from C# to C++.  In that case, because C++ does not support a native IEEE 754-2008 type, my suggestion is to coerce the transported 32-bits to a C++ float type.  Obviously this would involve a small loss of precision.

Another example:

Using a native float, five cups of coffee at $4.99 a cup will cost $24.949999, not the expected $24.95.

The advantage of a Google open source implementation is that Google has the resources to build a cross-language custom data type.  Most of us don't have the time or resources to build a complete solution.  Also there are lots of implementation choices and nuances which make any solution non-trivial.

While I personally think that complex type must be part of the specification, and even migrate most of my application to Avro. 

> If the official position for decimals is DIY then I personally believe that this should be noted explicitly in the docs, with or > without sample implementations, rather than people having to find these threads for what is in many domains a required > and very standard data type.

But for everyone who asks about custom complex type - [here is Microsoft .Net example fro C#](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/architecture/grpc-for-wcf-developers/protobuf-data-types#decimals.)
And you can do your own marshaling to any language.

> The advantage of a Google open source implementation is that Google has the resources to build a cross-language custom data type. Most of us don't have the time or resources to build a complete solution. Also there are lots of implementation choices and nuances which make any solution non-trivial.

There's a lot of assumptions built into this statement that we have resources we actually don't have to do anything we want. I think many on this thread should know what it's like to work on software projects for large orgs, especially in open source. We have to be extremely mindful about what we take on as core to the project because of the breadth and depth requirements we have to support, as you've identified.

Also, there's a lot of cost to adding new custom data types that are non-obvious to our customers that we have to balance, aside from supporting it cross-lang. There are also wire format implications that the uninitiated may not anticipate as a hindrance.

This is simply a question of priority.  The cost of doing this work is fairly high and the value of it is not sufficient to justify that cost.  I honestly do not think a team outside of Google will be able to present a business case to us that would lead to a change  in this decision.

As I said above, the desire is not invalid, it is simply the case that we are not actively pursuing it and don't have any medium term plans to.

thanks for responding Matt!
To keep this more positive, as a general question what is required for a community contribution towards creating a new WKT? 
Is an agreed-upon spec sufficient, or is the bar that the PR(s) would have to cover every supported language? The closed #7039 mentions "It's fine for language implementations to provide the bindings independent of other languages (e.g. C# might provide the bindings sooner than some other language)."
Cheers

There are a great many customers of protobuf, many of whom do not care in any direction whatsoever about this feature.  The statement "Everybody wants this" is false.  In fact, not a single team internal to Google has asked for this feature.

While universal support is not a requirement out of the gate, I would want support for C++, java, and upb to be committed to before accepting any part of this.  It would be preferable for other languages to have plans to follow on top of that, but it is not an absolute requirement.

When I say "I honestly do not think a team outside of Google", I am talking about the realities of our business needs and prioritization.  We are a smaller team then you likely guess and so we must pick and choose our engagements so that we can yield the maximum possible impact and reduce our total cost of maintenance.  Within Google we have mechanisms for escalating when one team's choices don't line up with another team's needs.  Externally, the ability to present that business case is greatly reduced.

To be clear, the lack of prioritization of this is intentional.
Thank you Matt for clearly laying out the requirements needed in order for a community PR to be considered for consideration, I appreciate that.
I need it so much.

Please be aware that a key difficulty -- if not *the* key difficulty -- is deciding which decimal representation to use. There are several possibilities, as described here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7039#issuecomment-679083593

This decision has deep performance and interoperability implications. There are many decimal representations in common use, and no clear winner. Making a decision here will require carefully weighing the tradeoffs and deeply analyzing the pros vs. cons of each option. This may require performance experiments so we know the cost of converting each option to other commonly-used representations, as well as analyzing how to handle cases where the conversion cannot be performed without losing precision or accuracy.

> And since this issue can be solved by simply allowing the software architecture used to inject and version the format used

We were evaluating five options, if we consider this one also it will be six. This idea is not a panacea that will solve all problems, it is an alternative that has its own set of pros and cons.

> It really just sounds like the protocol buffer team is refusing to collect data because they are scared of data.

There are 945 open issues on this repo alone. That is just the OSS side, and says nothing of requests we are receiving internally. Please consider that we might be busy working on some of those.

If folks are interested in good-faith exchange on this subject please feel free to ask questions or contribute technical feedback. I will not engage further with this sort of rhetoric.

Seems google have delivered a decimal. https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/type/decimal.proto
If you are using gRPC then it's probably already in your dependency tree

It's a proto type, but does not manage the transformation to a golang specific implementation of a decimal. That still requires implementation to transform the encapsulated string value to a working decimal type.

title: [Proposal] Proto2 support in Google.Protobuf

nodes.body: cc: @jskeet
Thank you for all your work - unfortunately I'm not going to have time to give this the attention it deserves for some time.
@xfxyjwf: Is there any reason for the c++ label here? The implementation would be in C++, but it would only affect C#, right? Just a mouse slip, or have I missed something?
@jskeet Sorry, I think I just clicked the wrong label...

Thanks for you work! Yes we should support proto2 as well. I'd suggest not support group for now because it is deprecated.

Are you happy to split your work into PRs base on each section and assign code review to me?

So one PR for field presence, another one for default values, and another one for extensions?

Also unsure about not supporting groups. I know groups are deprecated in proto3 but by supporting proto2 we'd have to support groups if we want full backwards compatibility, right @anandolee?

Yes, one PR for field presence, another one for default values, and another one for extensions.

Group may need to be supported for full backwards compatibility, but let's implement other parts for proto2 first

That will be very difficult to do since all these features (field presence, default values, extensions, and groups) already exist on the [csharp/proto2](https://github.com/ObsidianMinor/protobuf/tree/csharp/proto2) branch.

So do I just redo all my work for each feature on a new branch or could we consider another option for reviewing all the necessary changes that's easier for everyone. For example, rebasing compiler changes, generated code changes, and library changes each into their own separate commits and making one PR?

Any reason to enforce null check on set? In my opinion, this is very annoying as you have to check for null before calling the set method.
> pb::ProtoPreconditions.CheckNotNull

Also, is there a discussion on "has" vs nullable?
I usually prefer nullable as that clear indicate that the field is optional (can be null), which can potentially reduce the chance of misuse (when null and default scalar type value means different thing).

The enforced null-check is to keep it consistent with the existing proto3 implementation.

"Has" was chosen to keep it consistent with every other language implementation (message.HasField("Foo") in python, has_foo in C++, and hasFoo in Java) as well as the fact that nullable properties are already used for the wrapper types so it might be confusing whether or not a property is for a wrapper type vs an optional value.

Just checked and looks like proto3 c# implementation it checks null for string/bytes when set. I think that is needed as proto3 doesn't differentiated between optional and default value. So it always uses a non-null default value.
In proto2 is different. In other language like java, the compiler generate a clearXXX method, which basically make the field not exists anymore. In c#, I would prefer nullable.

For the wrapper type in proto3 c#, it didn't generate nullable types according to my test. It actually uses a class, e.g. Google.Protobuf.WellKnownTypes.Int32Value, and there is no "has" method.

> For the wrapper type in proto3 c#, it didn't generate nullable types according to my test. 

[This test says otherwise](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf.Test/TestProtos/UnittestWellKnownTypes.cs#L338). You can use a null test as a make-shift "has" method in proto3.

Found my test issue. I did 
> import "wrappers.proto";

 instead of
> import "google/protobuf/wrappers.proto";

which generates different code.

So if we'd like to keep consistent with proto3 c# behavior, we need to generate clearXXX method for proto2.

In my opinion this is not quite fit c# design principal. Imaging you need to set a string member to null, you need to call a clear method, which is not straight forward and may introduce bugs (people accidentally assign it to null and got exception in production).
Any [response](https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/4407#issuecomment-381288501), @anandolee?

@ObsidianMinor Protobuf team don't have resource to work on major C# changes at the moment and it's very unlikely for us to accept large C# PRs before we have a dedicated engineer working on C#. To make progress here I think the only way is to do as @anandolee suggested: break down the proposal into smaller PRs so it's easier to review the change and we can move forward piecemeal. I know it's time-consuming to break down large changes but that's ultimately the right thing to do to ensure the change is appropriately reviewed.
@ObsidianMinor Thank you so much for driving this to the end! I think this can now be closed.

title: integers being returned as string in MessageToJson
body:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/ed4321d1cb33199984118d801956822842771e7e/python/google/protobuf/json_format.py#L284

Is there any reason why integers being returned as a string in the code above?

nodes.body: @skgbanga The JSON format represents int64 fields as a string because otherwise the value might not have an exact representation in JSON. JSON's number type is a double, which can't represent all int64 values.

title: protoc-artifacts Dockerfile: `git clone` fails
body:
The `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/google/protobuf.git` command in `protoc-artifacts/Dockerfile` fails with a pretty generic error message and error code 128. Entering the docker container and running `GIT_CURL_VERBOSE=1 GIT_TRACE=1 git clone ...` shows that the error is caused by a failure in the TLS negotiation. 

I believe this was caused when Github dropped support for TLS1.0 and TLS1.1: https://githubengineering.com/crypto-removal-notice/

The Dockerfile uses CentOS 6.6. It appears that this version of CentOS does not include support for TLS1.2, at least not in the libcurl library used by git: out-of-the-box, `curl` cannot fetch a Github web page. I used yum in update libcurl, and then curl recognized the `--tlsv1.2` flag and was able to get a web page from Github, but doesn't change the failure with git clone.

(FWIW, I tried changing the dockerfile to use CentOS 7, which does support TLS1.2, and encountered an unrelated error with the command in the dockerfile's last line. Using CentOS 6.9 instead, everything built fine, but I'm not sure what reasons went into choosing 6.6 and if 6.9 may have other unwanted side-effects)

title: How to .Unpack( an Any Message in Python
body:
Hi there,

I have some trouble, unpacking an Any message from a protobuf message. Here is a description of what I did:

1. While building my Protobuf message, I generate a message based on my proprietary protocol file as follow:
```
# we generate our proprietary message based on our proprietary proto-file
myMessageExtension = extension_pb2.GeneralContent_Extension()
myMessageExtension.fancyID = 345
myMessageExtension.fancyProjectDescription = "All awesome!"
```

2. I hand-over the proprietary message to my general message, that contains the "extension" defined as Any:
```
# We generate a carrier message to push our proprietary message into the Any-extension of the official spec
some_any = any_pb2.Any()
some_any.Pack(myMessageExtension)
```

3. I attach the extension to my general message:
```
# Fourth, we push our proprietary message to the extension of the official standard
myMessage.extension.CopyFrom(some_any)
```

So far, so good.

But now I want to read the same extension:

4. I generate a local any, copy the content of the already de-serialized protobuf message in there and unpack it:
```
# we now get the extension out of the protobuf
some_any2 = any_pb2.Any()
some_any2.CopyFrom(myMessage_rewrite.extension)
some_any2.Unpack(extension_pb2.GeneralContent_Extension())
```

5. I double-check, if the some_any2 message now reflects the extension definition (very simple message with just the two attributes):
```
print some_any2
print "---"
print myMessage_rewrite.extension
```

6. ISSUE: Both prints are reflecting just the same message (see below). My web-search unveiled, that the "Unpack(" will just return a "TRUE", if it is possible to convert. **But: WHERE DO I FIND THE UNPACKED message itself?**


```
[type.googleapis.com/project.protobuf.extension.data.GeneralContent_Extension] {
  fancyID: 345
  fancyProjectDescription: "All awesome!"
}
---
[type.googleapis.com/project.protobuf.extension.data.GeneralContent_Extension] {
  fancyID: 345
  fancyProjectDescription: "All awesome!"
}
```

title: Issues when cross-compiling for RISC-V
body:
I'm working on a school project where I need to migrate existing C++ code to work on a RISC-V based Linux running on a Zynq FPGA. Because that Linux is not ready yet (built but not running properly on the board), I'm exploring the migration in a docker container environment.

I followed the instruction of the official repo (https://github.com/riscv/riscv-tools) and built the full toolchain as well as the Linux cross-compiler (`riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-gcc` and `riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-g++`). Then I attempted to cross-compile protobuf from source (tag v3.5.1 and v3.5.1.1) following the README, except for the change to the `./compile` call:
```bash
CC=riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-gcc CXX=riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-g++ \
./configure --prefix=$RISCV --target=riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu --host=x86_64-pc-linux-gnu
```
Going down the `make` step though, I ran into this error:
```bash
libtool: link: riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu-g++ -pthread -DHAVE_PTHREAD=1 -Wall -Wno-sign-compare -O2 -g -DNDEBUG -pthread -o protoc google/protobuf/compiler/main.o  ./.libs/libprotobuf.a ./.libs/libprotoc.a /protobuf/src/.libs/libprotobuf.a -lpthread /riscv/riscv64-unknown-linux-gnu/lib/libstdc++.so -pthread

make[1]: *** [all-recursive] Error 1
make[1]: Leaving directory '/protobuf'
Makefile:1465: recipe for target 'all' failed
make: *** [all] Error 2
```
With some searching I found similar issues such as https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3937 . It seems that this error occurred because of lack of implementation for the target platform, and the way to fix it is by submitting a PR with the implementation. Since I'm not a RISC-V developer myself, I'm wondering:

1. Can this be bypassed when building? The existing code we have just builds a protobuf from a JSON file, and we only do this in C++
2. Is this the only module that requires platform-specific implementation? I figured it might just be the first thing I ran into with others yet to come up
3. Of course, I might just have called the commands in a wrong way. Please let me know if this is the case

Thanks in advance!

title: Export cc_library `protobuf` as a .bzl function
body:
Hello Folks,
As mentioned here https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/2365, GzipOutputStream and GzipInputStream needs zlib to build.

This could be achieved by adding the C++ compilation flag -DHAVE_ZLIB to `copts` and a dependency on the external zlib library in the cc_library rule `protobuf`.

The Struct and ListValue of Well Know Types can accept None:

But Struct is a map and ListValue is using repeated field, I am not sure if it what you want. Sample usage:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/internal/well_known_types_test.py

Why do you nee None for bytes field?

Are you using protobuf/python/google/protobuf/json_format.py?

title: eql? and hash key semantics for ruby generated classes
body:
```
syntax = "proto3";
package res_testing;

message OrderCreated {
  string event_id = 1;
  string order_id = 2;
  int32 customer_id = 3;
}
```

```ruby
# Generated by the protocol buffer compiler.  DO NOT EDIT!
# source: events.proto3

require 'google/protobuf'

Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_message "res_testing.OrderCreated" do
    optional :event_id, :string, 1
    optional :order_id, :string, 2
    optional :customer_id, :int32, 3
  end
end

module ResTesting
  OrderCreated = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("res_testing.OrderCreated").msgclass
end
```

```ruby
event1 = ResTesting::OrderCreated.new(
  event_id: "f90b8848-e478-47fe-9b4a-9f2a1d53622b",
  customer_id: 123,
  order_id: "K3THNX9",
)

event2 = ResTesting::OrderCreated.new(
  event_id: "f90b8848-e478-47fe-9b4a-9f2a1d53622b",
  customer_id: 123,
  order_id: "K3THNX9",
)

event1 == event2
=> true

event1.eql?(event2)
=> false

event1.hash == event2.hash
=> true

h = {}
h[event1] = :ok
=> :ok
h[event2]
=> nil
```

I suggest that protobuf generated classes should behave like Struct's in ruby and when all values are equal they should be treated like the same object so:

```
event1.eql?(event2) # should return true
h[event2] # should return :ok
```

Reference:

* https://stackoverflow.com/questions/7156955/whats-the-difference-between-equal-eql-and
* Struct behavior:

```ruby
class OrderCreated < Struct.new(:event_id, :customer_id, :order_id)
end
event1 = OrderCreated.new("f90b8848-e478-47fe-9b4a-9f2a1d53622b", 123, "K3THNX9")
event2 = OrderCreated.new("f90b8848-e478-47fe-9b4a-9f2a1d53622b", 123, "K3THNX9")

event1 == event2
=> true
event1.eql?(event2)
=> true

h[event1] = :ok
=> :ok

h[event2]
=> :ok

event1.hash == event2.hash
=> true
```

nodes.body: I agree that protobuf generated types should behave like `Struct` as much as we reasonably can. Making `eql` and `hash` behave the same sounds like the right solution here.

Cool!

I hope this bubbles up higher in the priority soon! :)

title: [PHP] Serialization error in C Extension on Message::mergeFromJsonString
body:
This is related to #4457 

The special types that are checked for using `GPBUtil::hasSpecialJsonMapping` (and are being checked for [in the native implementation](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/c93174346149f259ebc85fdb46826fcf84abb07d/php/src/Google/Protobuf/Internal/Message.php#L984) are not being checked in the protobuf C extension for `Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message::mergeFromJsonString()`. As a result the following error is thrown if any of these types are included in the response:

```
  [Exception]                                                                                        
  Error occurred during parsing: String specified for bool or submessage field: last_heartbeat_time
```

nodes.body:
This is strange. If you use c extension, this method shouldn’t be called.
On Fri, Mar 30, 2018 at 14:37 Brent Shaffer <notifications@github.com>
wrote:

>
> The special types that are checked for using
> GPBUtil::hasSpecialJsonMapping (and are being checked for in the native
> implementation

> are not being checked in the protobuf C extension for

> following error is thrown if any of these types are included in the
> response:
>
>   [Exception]
>   Error occurred during parsing: String specified for bool or submessage field: last_heartbeat_time
>
> —

Seems to me this is a missing feature for well known types in c extension.

title: Allow skipping path segments during output when mapping package to PHP namespaces
body:
The best example to explain this is with the default Laravel framework project.  The skeleton tells composer to map the `app` dir to the root namespace level `App`.  If I have a `.proto` file that defines the package `app.myDomain`, and I'm `.gitignore`ing the directories created by `protoc` I'll end up with the following directory structure:

```
    app/
        App/
            MyDomain/
```

Whereas I'd rather see:

```
    app/
        MyDomain/
```

Note however that within the file itself, I would still want the namespace to be `App\MyDomain`.  Tricky stuff 😄 

cc. https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/3970

nodes.body: Does this still work with autoload? AFAIK, autoload require namespace to be consistent with file name. You need to change your own composer configuration to do that.

I'm not really asking to change the filename.  Just how much of the path protobuf chooses to take responsibility for creating.

So, instead of protobuf creating the file `App/MyDomain/MyType.php`, I'd like to make `MyDomain/MyType.php` and then I'll point it to the directory `app` as the root for output.  Thus in this specific example, the file would end up being in: `app/MyDomain/MyType.php` (notice that the `app` has a lower-case `a`).

In the case of my example `MyType.php` is unchanged, and the namespace in `MyType.php` still reads as 

```php
<?php

namespace App\MyDomain\MyType;

// ...
```

You can call protoc in ```app``` folder instead of the parent folder of ```app```.
Besides, you need to add ```php_namespace = "App\MyDomain"``` file option to your proto file.

Making me call the tool from a different directory seems like a bit of an inconvenience.  I'm not sure you understand what I'm asking for.

You're also glossing over case sensitivity and some nuances of PSR.  `app` vs. `App`.  Portions of a namespace aren't always going to match the directory structure.  PSR allows for this to be flexible with code organization.

So: Namespace `App\MyDomain\MyType` isn't necessarily going to exist under the directory `App`.  It could be in the directory `src/MyDomain/MyType`, or `app/MyDomain/MyType` or `bicycle/MyDomain/MyType`.
The use case @atrauzzi is definitely a valid one. At the minute I have to move the files manually.

Just tested it. It does look like a cross-compilation bug. Here's what I did:

Within `docker run -it --rm --entrypoint=sh ruby:2.5-alpine`

```
apk add  --update git gcc make cmake libc-dev linux-headers bash wget libc6-compat autoconf automake libtool curl make g++ unzip

# SEGFAULT
gem install google-protobuf
ruby -e 'require "google/protobuf/any_pb"'

# GOOD
git submodule update --init --recursive
./autogen.sh
./configure
make
make check
make install
ldconfig
cd ruby
gem install bundler
bundle
rake
rake clobber_package gem
gem install `ls pkg/google-protobuf-*.gem`
ruby -e 'require "google/protobuf/any_pb"'
```

Let me know if I can help with anything else

I am having a very similar issue:
ruby 2.4.4 alpine 3.7, using google-cloud-pubsub gem
https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/4728

I tested 3.6.x branch. Unfortunately, the linux-x86_64 gem still doesn't work on alpine.
The workaround is to install a native gem which is built on target platform:
```
apk add  --update git gcc make cmake libc-dev linux-headers bash wget libc6-compat autoconf automake libtool curl make g++ unzip
gem install google-protobuf --version=3.5.1.2 --platform=ruby
```
Feel free to reopen this issue if this workaround is unacceptable.

@flipsasser (and others): In this case, the protobuf library is only surfacing a deeper issue, which is the _platform ABI_. The libstdc++ docs include [an explanation of the API/ABI interplay](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/libstdc++/manual/abi.html) which (IMO) is quite clear and well-written, at least relative to the topic, but also a bit C++-centric. The ABI-related issue with Alpine is actually deeper than C++, though: Alpine uses [musl libc](https://musl.libc.org/) instead of glibc . In fact, this is one of the key selling points on [the Alpine linux homepage](https://alpinelinux.org/). However, despite the benefit to the Alpine ecosystem, this also means glibc-based binaries (and libraries) are _generally_ not _drop-in_ compatible with Alpine Linux.

For prebuilt protobuf libraries targeting x86_64 CPUs and the Linux kernel, protobuf prebuilts further use a GNU-based target -- i.e., one where the library named `libc.so` and found by the loader is implemented by glibc. This ABI is commonly denoted as `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` [1], where `-gnu` is notionally the OS, distinct from the kernel `-linux` (and famously so).

Ultimately, for prebuilt binary libraries, we must choose an implementation and version of libc consistent with all other runtime libraries and the running process itself. Unfortunately, this means that protobuf prebuilts targeting glibc are rendered incompatible with Alpine Linux, because they disagree _at a minimum_ on the lowest-level [2] runtime library.

As @TeBoring pointed out, building from source does not tie you to the target OS of our prebuilt binary libraries. The protobuf sources are source-compatible with Musl, and hence Alpine, similar to how they are source-compatible with macOS and Windows targets. (I do, however, appreciate that Docker surfaces the build overhead cost quickly and often.) Alternatively, as @nhattan and @rnnds point out, there are excellent binary compatibility shims you can use to run glibc-targeted binaries under Musl; and as @rnnds also points out, switching away from an Alpine-based image altogether to a Debian-based image also eliminates the issue.

At the risk of droning on, I would also point out that Alpine+Musl's differing ABI is not particularly new, nor is it unique to protobuf, Google Cloud, Ruby, or even C/C++... a [quick web search](https://www.google.com/search?q=%28alpine+OR+musl%29+"abi"+"issue") shows other projects which have tripped over various ABI aspects when targeting Alpine and/or Musl. It is _certainly_ a tricky topic, though, and one of my least favorite parts of Linux build engineering.

[1] The `-unknown` part is a bit misleading... if you want, you can read more about the overall structure, history, and cruft of this name format on the [OSDev wiki](https://wiki.osdev.org/Target_Triplet), the [GNU Autoconf docs](https://www.gnu.org/savannah-checkouts/gnu/autoconf/manual/autoconf-2.70/html_node/Specifying-Target-Triplets.html#Specifying-Names), the [Clang docs](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/CrossCompilation.html), in [Ian Lance Taylor's explanation](https://airs.com/ian/configure/configure_4.html#SEC25), etc.
[2] As a mostly-academic distinction, `libc.so` would _technically_ be the second-lowest level library dependency on a dynamic executable. This is because, under Linux, the dynamic linker is the OS-side, i.e., kernel-external, portion of the program startup implementation. Practically speaking, however, the dynamic linker is also tied to the libc implementation by ABI. This is why the distinction is only _mostly_ academic: glibc and Musl _also_ have their own, separate dynamic linkers: [glibc man page](https://linux.die.net/man/8/ld-linux), [musl conceptual design](https://wiki.musl-libc.org/design-concepts.html).

Thank you for the deeper dive, @dlj-NaN! This is super helpful for understanding the scope of the challenge in distributing protobuf on as many systems as possible. I'll be the first to say that, at a technical level, protobuf is well above my paygrade to criticize, as well as a wonderful and essential piece of engineering. Or rather, I assume it's wonderful; [Clarke's 3rd law](https://www.google.com/search?hl=en&q=clarke%27s%20third%20law) applies for me in this case! 😃

I readily concede that Alpine's choice of musl is causing the headache and that the fault lies there (otherwise we wouldn't have added gcompat to our `apk add` command in the first place). It's also too bad to hear that protobuf is not alone in that complaint against Alpine! In our case, protobuf is the **only** thing that will not play nicely with Alpine, but I wholly admit that we may be an exception. Perhaps more people are struggling with a wider variety of libraries on Alpine than I fully appreciate or grasp. Regardless, I'm grateful for your masterful perspective on the issue, and I totally get that you cannot feasibly account for every possible edge case in distributing your product.

Having considered your perspective on this, I'm hoping you'll be willing to consider mine.

As a level-set, it's worth clarifying that **we do not approach this issue from a purely technical perspective**. My goal is not to argue that "Alpine is right" or "musl is the best." I'm also not attempting to compare it to other serialization technologies like JSON. I don't know enough about C++ or streaming deserialization or whatever API/ABI interplay *even is* to make a big, technical case for doing anything in any way differently.

Instead I ask you to consider that we, as a small, open-source project funded by grants, must contend with a *fiscal reality* in addition to a technical one. From where we stand, we pay (from a limited budget) for the use of GCP, and GCP, in turn, forces the technical decision to use protobuf on us. Our expectation is therefore that protobuf *not* throw a wrench into our process.

We consicously chose Alpine because it is widely used and extremely lightweight, two benefits which reduce costs and speed up build processes. And for most of our project's life, that reasoning has proved sound. In fact, right up until we added a dependency on protobuf (which was well after we cut over to GCP from Heroku), we experienced exactly zero Alpine-specific problems (in fairness, we have since experienced one issue related to timezone data).

We therefore view adopting a different OS (and re-writing and re-testing all of our Docker configuration) to be a non-starter. From our perspective, **we are being asked to invalidate *primary* technical decisions on behalf of a *tertiary* dependency** that we are required to use in exchange for paying Google.

That the technology causing this dissonance solves what *feels, to us,* like a solved problem (in this case serialization) is all the more frustrating. That frustration is compounded by the fact that there are other quick-compiling, light-weight, portable dependencies all over our application. By way of comparison, here are some benchmarks for building fairly high-performance and complicated pieces of software on my 4-year-old iMac:

#### Redis: builds from source in 13 seconds
```
magog:~→ brew reinstall redis --build-from-source
...
==> Summary
🍺  /usr/local/Cellar/redis/6.0.10: 11 files, 3.8MB, built in 13 seconds
```

#### PostgreSQL: builds from source in 2 minutes and 4 seconds
```
magog:~→ brew reinstall postgresql --build-from-source
...
==> Summary
🍺  /usr/local/Cellar/postgresql/13.1: 3,217 files, 42.5MB, built in 2 minutes 4 seconds
```

#### Protobuf: builds from source in 6 minutes and 31 seconds (3x as long as PostgreSQL and 30x as long as Redis)
```
magog:~→ brew reinstall protobuf --build-from-source
...
==> Summary
🍺  /usr/local/Cellar/protobuf/3.14.0: 256 files, 18.2MB, built in 6 minutes 31 seconds
```

Say what you will about the value of comparing benchmarks, this illustrates my point: protobuf appears to take a very long time to build, and (as the ongoing conversation in this Github issue clearly illustrates) still frequently segfaults after it *has* built, on one of the most popular operating systems in the virtualization ecosystem.

**And so, *to your customers*, and regardless of Alpine's C++ std library choices, protobuf feels like a difficult-to-use dependency compounded by frustation at the fact that it feels unnecessary in all but the highest-volume use cases. Paying a vendor, only to be forced into making big technical decisions for the wrong reasons in order to use a serialization technology that feels redundant, overpowered, or both, is a huge, huge, huge bummer.**

Please, please, please do not read this as an attack. I'm confident there are perfectly valid reasons protobuf is written in C++ and takes a very long time to compile, and you've exhaustively convinced me that protobuf and Alpine are not destined to play nicely any time soon, for understandable, fair, and valid reasons.

I am merely trying to illustrate what it feels like being forced to use it, and again, I would never dare offer even comparisons like the above if I weren't paying money to do so.

Ultimately it's our fault for selecting GCP without planning far enough down the road. Had we considered that we'd eventually need a background worker solution, we could have selected a provider who offers such a feature without workarounds involving disparate services like Cloud Tasks and long-running HTTP requests. And we're willing to pay the price for that mistake, but for our money, that price is *not* rebuilding our infrastructure to use a different OS because Google said we should; it's rebuilding our infrastructure with a different hosting provider. And *that is specifically because Google made it too difficult to use theirs and we no longer felt we could trust them not to do it again*.

Thank you for all of your contributions to the cause, and I don't take lightly that protobuf is probably at the core of many of the systems I take for granted on a daily basis. It's simply not a good solution for us. I'd be happy to chat more about this over email or on the phone; my contact information can be found on my website, which is listed in my Github profile.

title: Lots of issues with Timestamp's use of DateTime
body:
Noticing quite a few problematic abstractions around how protobuf's PHP implementation works.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/115199/38178785-c1c67148-35df-11e8-9a3a-c91700fd7b8f.png)

If I use the `DateTime` utility method to set the value of a `Timestamp`, most editors will complain because the docblock hint isn't fully qualified.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/115199/38178811-38053092-35e0-11e8-9020-9e20e6dec35e.png)

Also, because this library performs a naive type check, my instance has to be a `\DateTime` and nothing else:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/115199/38178922-12cb90bc-35e2-11e8-99d5-699da217ad6d.png)

_([`Carbon` subclasses the native `DateTime`](https://github.com/briannesbitt/Carbon/blob/master/src/Carbon/Carbon.php#L55), so it still technically qualifies.)_

I see two possible solutions.  The first - and best - is to add a type hint to the function signature in PHP code.  This would eliminate the need to do the naive check.
The second is to change `DateTime` to `\DateTime` in the docblock so that it's off the root namespace rather than relative to the current namespace.  But that doesn't help with any subclasses of `\DateTime`, so I don't consider it a worthwhile solution.

Also, I'd suggest renaming this method to something like `setFrom`, `setDateTime` or `setFromDateTime` as `fromDateTime` sounds more like a static factory method that would return a new instance, not mutate state.

Which might not be a bad idea to add as well (`Timestamp::fromDateTime`)...

nodes.body:
1) type hint of class is not supported in php5. We can add it after we drop support for php5
2) use instanceof instead of comparing class name?
3) We don't want to change the method name at this point.

1. [Not true.](https://secure.php.net/manual/it/language.oop5.typehinting.php).  It's been supported since `5`.  Moreover, please see the [supported versions page](https://secure.php.net/supported-versions.php). There's no point in supporting anything older than `5.6` at present and anyone who is not using at least `5.6` today is no longer getting security updates.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/115199/38222233-200bf02e-36a9-11e8-81e4-7ac2ae973e2d.png)

2. Given the above, I suggest using the type hint for `DateTime` in the method signature.  This allows the language to naturally handle the type check for you.

3. Fair enough, just understand that it's a really...*really* bad name from a patterns perspective.  What about an alias to the same method?  That way people can start transitioning to a better API and then in the future you can deprecate the old one?  Might be a decent compromise?

We have plan to use type hint through out our code base. Will add type hint later.
Please check #4601

title: PHP - bcmath extension is required, but not typically installed by default
body:
Certain bundles come with the [bcmath extension](http://php.net/manual/en/bc.installation.php), but it is not always included by default. It would be great if we either forced a requirement on this extension in the `composer.json`, or ideally had a fallback for the case where it is not installed.

An error is triggered with calls to [`Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message::mergeFromJsonString()`](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/php/src/Google/Protobuf/Internal/Message.php#L715) (due to [bccomp](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/php/src/Google/Protobuf/Internal/Message.php#L882) calls), and when using the protobuf C extension a segfault is triggered - making tracing the issue extremely difficult.

This was surfaced from a user reported issue at https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/google-cloud-php/issues/950.

title: [docs] Language specification for Syntax is too broad
body:
The documented BNF for syntax is as follows:
```
syntax = "syntax" "=" quote "proto2" quote ";"
quote = "'" | '"'
```

As written, this implies that the following is valid: `syntax = 'proto2"`, where the single and double quote are mismatching.

nodes.body: The spec is not strong enough for automatic tools, and does not cover everything. The goal is only a guide for users.

title: [docs] Language specification for options do not permit aggregates
body:
The syntax for an option is as such:
```
option = "option" optionName  "=" constant ";"
constant = fullIdent | ( [ "-" | "+" ] intLit ) | ( [ "-" | "+" ] floatLit ) | strLit | boolLit
```

Basically, the BNF claims that the option value can only be a `fullIdent`, `intLit`, `floatLit`, `strLit`, or `boolLit`. However, this contradicts the observed behavior of the protoc compiler where:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/e7e6c6b8d1317aa315530024224bfb92e857daa0/src/google/protobuf/compiler/parser.cc#L1439-L1449

Functionally, the enables option values of the following form to be specified:
```
[(path.to.my.option).field = { arg1: "hello", arg2: 100 }]
```

The specification should be updated to cover this case.

title: Add the ability to associate a message with an interface in Java
body:
The most pain I have had using the protobuf Java classes out of the box involved:

1 - not being able to add useful methods to the class (instead using utility classes)
2 - not being able to group related classes together for the purposes of share library usage and such.  This is related to there not be a subclass/superclass relationship, although there are other reasons to want to group a bunch of field and say "any with these is an X" without bundling them together.

Both these problems can be solved as of Java 8 with the ability to optionally add interfaces to the generated code.  I am not certain how it would be represent in the proto code(as far as I can tell you don't have message-level options) but it would be very helpful.  This solved #1 as well in Java 8 now that there are default method definitions for interfaces

Adding interfaces would also be useful in C# and possibly C++.  Even in Ruby and Python, we could get #1 by allowing adding mixins to the class.  

It would be the responsibility of the code writer to ensure that the generated classes actually implement the interface.

nodes.body: I think we intentionally do not want people to customize protobuf generated classes because those customization breaks encapsulation and can cause unforeseen breakages when we change generated code internals.

This is something I've wanted for a very long time, as well.  I don't see how adding an interface to the generated classes would break encapsulation in anway, so it would be nice to hear more on that.  I'd expect the interface to mirror accessor methods, eg. ` interface HasId { public int getId(); }` which could be applied to any message with an `int id` field.  That would give a clean way to pass any message with an id to some method that only needs to use the id from a message.  There'd probably  need to be two options, one to apply an interface with getters to MessageOrBuilder and another that could apply an interface with setters to the message's Builder classes.

Java supports plugin insertion point: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java-generated#plugins. You can insert additional interface at message_implements:TYPENAME and builder_implements:TYPENAME.

I created a change for this and posted to the protobuf mailing list, but never heard back.
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/compare/master...chasebradford:master

I have all of the same concerns with using a custom plugin (brittleness, poor documentation, etc).  Unfortunately, when I actually tried with my change, I quickly realized that older compilers that didn't recognize the option would outright fail instead of ignoring it.

> I created a change for this and posted to the protobuf mailing list, but never heard back.

title: Java DynamicMessage Parsing Sets 0.0 Double Values to NULL

nodes.body:
This is working as intended. In proto3, setting a field to its default value has the same effect as clearing the field. See:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#default

If you call `proto.getAllFields()`, it should return an empty map as well. If it doesn't, that's a bug in the implementation.

I know this is an old, closed issue, but I have exactly the same question so I'm hoping it's ok to extend this discussion here. I'm also interested if the introduction of `optional` into proto3 (which didn't exist in 2018) might change any views on this?

I also view the behaviour described by @westonsankey as a bug, but I suppose it comes down to whether the intent is to:
* Get all values present on the wire
* Get all values semantically conveyed with the message.

The docs for `getAllFields` aren't very clear on this. If I strip the parts of the docs related to required, optional, and repeated fields (none are the case in the posted example), it says the following (emphasis mine):
> Returns a collection of all the fields in this message which are **set** and their corresponding values. The values are exactly what would be returned by calling [MessageOrBuilder.getField(Descriptors.FieldDescriptor)](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java/com/google/protobuf/MessageOrBuilder.html#getField(com.google.protobuf.Descriptors.FieldDescriptor)) for each field.

What is meant by the word **set**? The parser has no way of knowing if the value was set or not if the field doesn't have [explicit field presence](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/docs/field_presence.md#presence-in-proto3-apis). The value could have been set to the default value, but then not encoded on the wire, knowing the semantics are that the parsed message should provide the default value as the value for that field. If this is the meaning of "set" here, it seems impossible to implement.

Alternately, the definition of **set** could be "serialized in the message". If this is the intention, then it seems the existing implementation is correct, but not particularly useful since it doesn't convey the information the sender intended to convey.

What I would propose is **set** in the context of the `getAllFields()` description meant:
* For fields with explicit field presence, all values whose hazzer returns true.
* For fields without explicit field presence, return the default value.

Perhaps to avoid breaking any user relying on the existing interface, there could be a separate (or overloaded) method that used these semantics. Would this make sense?

At this point, we do not wish to change the semantics of the existing method (for the reasons noted by you).  We also don't want to add a new interface with a new semantic because new methods have a surprisingly high cost in terms of the volume of generated code and as a consequence final size for binaries.

title: JSON: 'Any' message should serialize to/from bytes when the message type is not well known.
body:
## Problem
The [Any](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#any) message type specifies that in JSON the properties of the message serialized within an Any message should be serialized as properties.

> The JSON representation of an Any value uses the regular representation of the deserialized, embedded message, with an additional field `@type` which contains the type URL. Example:
>
> 
> ```
> package google.profile;
> message Person {
>   string first_name = 1;
>   string last_name = 2;
> }
> 
> {
>   "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.profile.Person",
>   "firstName": <string>,
>   "lastName": <string>
> }
> ```
> [Reference](
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/google.protobuf#any)

This forces a system that serializes using JSON with unregistered types to either throw an error because it does not know how to parse an unregistered type ([code ref](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/JsonParser.cs#L527)), or to gracefully skip the type and lose information ([pull request #4505](https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/4505)). If the latter is chosen, then when serializing or deserializing the message, information is lost.

## Suggestion
When serializing to and from JSON, messages within an 'Any' message should serialize to and from bytes when the message type is not well known.

_Figure 1: Example of serializing an 'Any' message with not well known type to bytes_
```
{
  "@type": "type.googleapis.com/MyCustomType",
  "value": "eyAiZm9vIjogImJhciIgfQ==" // Base64 encoded bytes
}
```

## Use Case
I have many systems that use common message types, but do not have all message types registered in all systems. They only register the message types that are relevant to them.

If system X requests data from system Y and system Z, system X should not have to know what the message types are in order to pack them into an 'Any'.

## Thoughts
From my limited experience with Protocol Buffers, it seems like all message types have to be registered in the type registry in order to serialize and deserialize fully. This does not seem scalable when an organization shares thousands of message types, and messages are being sent to and from systems that need to modify message types that only they know how to modify, or add message types that only they know about. 

This does not seem to be a problem with binary serialization, as in practice, it uses the `@value` property. However, I don't see the `@value` property documented, so I don't know if this was intentional or not.

_Figure 2: Binary serialization uses the `@value` property when deserializing an unregistered type_
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3875827/38760950-1f09337e-3f4d-11e8-9c7a-9b1f153bfbdc.png)

_Thank you for taking the time to read through this issue._

nodes.body: I found issue https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/658 which is relevant to this topic. I understand that it is valuable to be able to access the properties of types that are unknown. However, this precludes systems who serialize to JSON from being able to modify messages with unknown types.

This issue is affecting a middleware gRPC proxy that translates messages from Proto to JSON. On RPC errors, details commonly contain `Any` and if unable to resolve the type we are forced to either: 1. drop the error and raise a resolver error, or 2. convert the `Any` payload into a message type we understand which then requires the upstream to decode.

Would be great to have support for `Any` to be encoded in JSON as `{"@type": "<url>", "@value": "<bytes>"}`. Then the fallback is well defined and the client can handle it gracefully.

Along the way, we realized we had to prefix enums values with the enum name due to the generated enums, as they are not enum classes.

nodes.body: @gioragutt I think the original reason was that until recently we supported C++98, and enum classes were introduced only in C++11. That's no longer a problem by itself now that we require C++11, but still I suspect it would be difficult to make this change since it would have to be done in a way that doesn't break compatibility with existing code.

The thing is that we try hard to avoid adding new flags, because the work of maintaining them adds up in the long term. If the flag is temporary then that cuts down on the maintenance burden but it's still not ideal to break backward compatibility. Unfortunately I think it's not really worth it to try to make this change at this point.

title: Unit test for string_as_array?
body:
I came across a comment for a utility function, `string_as_array(string*)` (taken from `google3/util/gtl/stl_util.h`) that has an implementation note that only references the unit test:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/da3ce6717156c8b4f8890207895069ce6b102f65/src/google/protobuf/stubs/stl_util.h#L84

I can't find anywhere that the unit test was open-sourced. Could we copy the relevant info into the open-sourced `stl_util.h` (possibly also copying it into the corresponding comment in google3)? Or, failing that, could we copy it to this issue thread?

Some updates to the matter have come along since the function's comment was written:
- `std::string::data()` returns a non-`const` pointer starting in C++17; see http://www.open-std.org/JTC1/SC22/WG21/docs/lwg-defects.html#2391.
- WG21 issue 530 referenced in the comment has moved from "active issue" to "defect report", and so the URL in the comment is no longer valid. The new URL is http://www.open-std.org/JTC1/SC22/WG21/docs/lwg-defects.html#530
- While 2391 is relevant, 530 still should remain referenced. Matt notes vendor conversations and current implementation practice in 530, while 2391 focuses more on the user need for a non-`const` return value.

Found the test here:
https://github.com/flutter/base/blob/master/stl_util_unittest.cc#L256

Apparently we opensource the same piece of code again and again in different projects...

title: Message.toObject() does not respect chosen field name
body:
(Relocated from https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/issues/279)

When generating JS code, given a definition with a repeated field:

```protobuf
message History {
  repeated string paths = 1;
}
```

and the following code:

```js
const history = new History()
history.setPathsList(['/', '/var'])
console.log(history.toObject())
```

I expect the output to be:

```js
{ paths: ["/", "/var"] }
```

Instead, it is:

```js
{ pathsList: ["/", "/var"] }
```

The `(s|g)et*List()` function naming convention is clear and helpful, but failure to honour the specified name when turning it back into JSON creates a lot of work mapping the fields back to what they are intended to be. 

Plus, if `setFromJson` or similar is ever added (https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/4006), that would make roundtripping data through protobufs much more straightforward.

nodes.body: @majelbstoat We don't yet support the JSON format in JS. The `toObject()` method is a bit confusing because it produces output that looks similar to the official JSON format but it is not actually the same.
That makes sense. By 'yet', does that mean it is planned for the future? (Without setting expectations of when it might happen.)
@majelbstoat We do want to eventually support proto3 JSON in JS, but at the moment I think we all have our hands full with other things and so we haven't been able to prioritize it yet.
Curious why this was closed if it's something that's acknowledged as a current deficiency, and future support is planned?

Sorry about the confusion--I agree that proto3 JSON support has not been resolved yet, but I wanted to tidy things up by closing this issue, since most of the discussion around JSON support has already been happening in protocolbuffers/protobuf-javascript#96.

title: Generated code to use std::vector<> instead of RepeatedPtrField<>
body:
It would be nice if protoc could generate code that uses std::vector<> instead of RepeatedPtrField.  This will allow us to swap vectors in/out of the proto message as many programs use std::vector.

To ease backwards compatibility, an option to protoc can be leveraged in order to generate std::vector<> stubs.  I know it seems like a decent amount of work, but I know it will help performance in my use case.

Also, I know there is some discussion regarding c++'11 support and adding the ability to support move semantics, but in my use case leveraging std::vector<> would help in addition to c++'11 support.

nodes.body:
This won't happen because:
1. It requires an API breaking change to protobuf reflection API where repeated fields are exposed as RepeatedField/RepeatedPtrField and won't work if the implementation has been changed to anything else.
2. std::vector or any other type that isn't part of protobuf library won't work with protobuf arena. We explicitly decided to use proto2::Map instead of std::map/unordered_map to implement map fields because of this and we are not going to revert it to std::map/unordered_map. Neither will we replace RepeatedField/RepeatedPtrField with std::vector (or any other std:: container type as long as the type is not under our total control) for the same reason.
3. We hate more options.

Note that the amount of work to implement a feature is usually the least that we are concerned about. Compared to the time/effort required to adapt everyone to a new feature (e.g., update every protobuf reflection based library to be aware of a possible alternative std::vector representation for repeated fields), implementing a feature in protobuf alone takes pretty much no time or effort.

nodes.body: Can you provide a snippet of code or a small demo project showing the leaks?  The semaphore should go away when the messages themselves go away.  You can use the messages from ARC code just fine, the management there will make things work out correctly.

here is the code i use to initiate messages: 
`[[AnyMessageInstance alloc] init]`
I've also tried `+message` and method but still the same

and here is the screenshot of Xcode leaks tool showing one new leak for any new instance:
![screen shot 2018-04-19 at 8 12 13 pm](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/12933186/39081483-120f04c2-4557-11e8-9609-d52e890361d9.png)

Sorry that's not really going to help.  We'll need to see the flow creating and consuming the message.  That screen shot is just how some messages go created, but depending on what variable they went into, it's hard to say what should have triggered their release.

fyi - you don't need to include code from the library, since it is in this repo.  The code calling the library is the interesting parts for this.

You mentioned extensions, but I don't see anything related to extensions in your code you provided, do you use extension some place?

Within your code for `-serializeAndSendData:withMessageCode:flags:andTimeout:STMSupported:withPacketHandler:` you have a call to `-insertUnreceivedPacketAckWithData:messageId:messageCode:flags:andPacketTimeout:isSTMSupport:handler:` and pass the message along.  What does that do?  Does it end up holding on to the message?

I'm assuming all of your code is compiled with ARC enabled?

Any chance you can make a small example program that shows the leak you think you are seeing?

So the `-dispatchOnQueue:` call is passing a block and that block has captured the message (since you are extract data from it).  That means the message is stay alive as long at the block.  So depending on that implementation, that will keep the message alive atleast that long.

title: Support for long in Value.proto

nodes.body: I suspect that the reason Value doesn't contain any integer types is so that it can be compatible with JSON, which only has double-precision float as its number type. So I think we would be reluctant to add another type that would make JSON compatibility more difficult.

I think this is wrong.

It's not possible to store sufficiently-big long values as double.

JSON doesn't dictate "integer" or "double-precision format", JSON grammar dictates "number" as an arbitrary precision arbitrarily big decimal-or-integer number, see https://www.json.org/json-en.html and the grammars.

Right now I can't write in a Struct a big enough number (8484298990673538410) and expect it to keep its value, while in JSON I can.

Struct should support either one single type of Value which can carry all kind of numbers that a JSON can carry without loss of information (which would be backward-incompatible), or additional type(s) of Value(s) which can carry the different kind of numbers that actually can be represented in a JSON.

This decision is forcing people to represent big longs as strings in Structs, whereas in JSON they can be represented with no issue.

Please check: 
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4406
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7039

and please consider reopening this issue.

I think supporting inside Struct the outcome of https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7039 would be probably good enough.

title: [docs] Language specification for ident mismatches implementation
body:
The language specification for identifiers says:
```
ident = letter { letter | decimalDigit | "_" }
```

However, this goes against the documented (and actual) behavior of the protoc parser:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/a21f225824e994ebd35e8447382ea4e0cd165b3c/src/google/protobuf/io/tokenizer.h#L103-L106

Should this be?
```
ident = ( letter | "_" ) { letter | decimalDigit | "_" }
```

Alternatively, "_" can be added to `letter`:
```
letter = "A" … "Z" | "a" … "z" | "_"
```
which matches the implementation:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/a21f225824e994ebd35e8447382ea4e0cd165b3c/src/google/protobuf/io/tokenizer.cc#L137-L139

title: "reserved" grammar is incorrect for field names (should be quoted)
body:
From [spec page](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec#reserved):

```
reserved = "reserved" ( ranges | fieldNames ) ";"
fieldNames = fieldName { "," fieldName }
fieldName = ident
ident = letter { letter | decimalDigit | "_" }
```

And example doesn't match that grammar:

```
reserved "foo", "bar";
```

In grammar reserved field names are not quoted.

nodes.body: This is still wrong in the language reference.
The language reference is now _closer_ to correct. However, it suggests that only valid identifiers are allowed inside the quotes, which is not yet true. Fixing #6335 would also resolve this issue.

On second thought, fixing #6335 isn't _quite_ enough to fix this documentation issue because the grammar currently fails to convey the way adjacent string literals are concatenated by the tokenizer.

So either of the following would be more accurate:

1. ```diff
     reserved = "reserved" ( ranges | strFieldNames ) ";"
     ranges = range { "," range }
     range =  intLit [ "to" ( intLit | "max" ) ]
   - strFieldNames = strFieldName { "," strFieldName }
   - strFieldName = "'" fieldName "'" | '"' fieldName '"'
   + strFieldNames = strLit { "," strLit }
   ```
   With this first approach, we're leveraging the fact that the `strLit` production already includes productions for concatenating adjacent literals. We'd need to include an extra remark that the effective string literal value must match the pattern for `fieldName`.

2. ```diff
     reserved = "reserved" ( ranges | strFieldNames ) ";"
     ranges = range { "," range }
     range =  intLit [ "to" ( intLit | "max" ) ]
     strFieldNames = strFieldName { "," strFieldName }
   - strFieldName = "'" fieldName "'" | '"' fieldName '"'
   + strFieldName = strFieldNameSingle { strFieldNameSingle }
   + strFieldNameSingle = "'" fieldName "'" | '"' fieldName '"'
   ```
   With this approach, instead of re-using `strLit`, we simply re-defined the concatenation behavior in the `strFieldName` production.

title: octEscape grammar doesn't match implementation
body:
[Spec](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec) describes oct escape as:

```
strLit = ( "'" { charValue } "'" ) |  ( '"' { charValue } '"' )
charValue = hexEscape | octEscape | charEscape | /[^\0\n\\]/
octEscape = '\' octalDigit octalDigit octalDigit
```

However, [protobuf unittest contains example](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/a21f225824e994ebd35e8447382ea4e0cd165b3c/src/google/protobuf/unittest_custom_options.proto#L210):

```
 option (bytes_opt) = "Hello\0World";
```

Which doesn't match grammar above, because grammar specifies that there should be exactly three octal digits.

octEscape = '\' octalDigit octalDigit octalDigit

title: Incorrect grammar for option
body:
This is an option from [unittest_custom_options.proto](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/a21f225824e994ebd35e8447382ea4e0cd165b3c/src/google/protobuf/unittest_custom_options.proto#L283):

```
option (.protobuf_unittest.complex_opt1).foo = 42;
```

[The grammar](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec) is:

```
option = "option" optionName  "=" constant ";"
optionName = ( ident | "(" fullIdent ")" ) { "." ident }
fullIdent = ident { "." ident }
ident = letter { letter | decimalDigit | "_" }
```

So according to grammar option name `(.protobuf_unittest.complex_opt1).foo` is incorrect because `fullIdent` cannot start with dot.

Next option:

```
 option (protobuf_unittest.complex_opt1).(.protobuf_unittest.quux) = 324;
```

doesn't seem valid either.

title: Syntax statement specification inconsistency?
body:
The [proto3 language spec](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec#syntax) specifies a syntax statement as being of the form:

```
syntax = "syntax" "=" quote "proto3" quote ";
```

where a [`quote` literal](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec#string_literals) is specified as

```
quote = "'" | '"'
```

This seems like it leaves room for syntax statements of the form

```
syntax = 'proto3";
syntax = "proto3';
```

However, `protoc` rejects either of these forms -- as I would expect it to. This seems like an inconsistency (though a quite minor one) between the specification and the compiler behavior.
