title: Is it possible to reference an inner message from a different package?

nodes.body:
Protobuf follows C++ name resolution rules and every symbol must have a globally unique fully-qualified name. So:
1. "Foo foo1 = 1" is invalid because "Foo" references the package which can't be used as a message type.
2. "Foo.Foo foo2 = 2" and "Foo.Foo.Foo foo3 = 3" are valid and they reference the outer "Foo" message and the inner "Foo" message defined in "foo.proto".
3. You can't have a package and a message both named "Foo.Foo".

If you change the package of "bar.proto" to "Foo" as well:
1. "Foo foo1 = 1" and "Foo.Foo foo2 = 2" are valid and reference the outer "Foo" and inner "Foo" respectively.
2. "Foo.Foo.Foo foo3 = 3" will become invalid because it will resolve to "Foo.Foo.Foo.Foo" according to C++ name resolution rules and that type doesn't exist.

Besides proto language rules, the generated code is also subject to the rules of the programming language it's generated for. In this regard, protoc does not guarantee the generated code to be compilable and I'm pretty sure some programming languages don't allow a "Foo" class nested in a parent class with the same name "Foo".

I believe that the 

> You can't have a package and a message both named "Foo.Foo".

Needs to be in the spec.  It is absolutely not obvious that this is what should happen.  That is, a conforming implementation must not accept such definition.
Closing this issue as I think your question has been answered. Feel free to create an issue requesting for more thorough documentation of the language spec. @anandolee FYI.

title: RepeatedScalarFieldContainer does not implement "index"

[The documentation says "Repeated fields are represented as an object that acts like a Python sequence"](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated#fields), but [the class of that object, RepeatedScalarFieldContainer](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/92898e9e9cb2f1c006fcc5099c9c96eafce63dc8/python/google/protobuf/internal/containers.py#L230-L338), does not implement [the `.index` method](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/datastructures.html#more-on-lists) of [the Sequence type](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Sequence).

title: "extend" is not allowed in proto3 spec, but is used in tests
body:
[Spec 3](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec) doesn't mention `extend` unlike [Spec 2](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto2-spec).

However `extend` with `syntax = "proto3"` is [used in protobuf tests](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/7377d81ca44baf2e505c927a2e25b2f0e3596fed/php/tests/proto/test_import_descriptor_proto.proto).

nodes.body: Only MessageOption, which is internal. Don't use it by yourself.

@TeBoring unfortunately protobuf compiler `protoc` accepts this option. And I'm writing Rust implementation of protobuf, and my implementation should be compatible with `protoc`.

If this option is not meant to be used outside of Google, then public version of `protoc` compiler should probably reject it.
@anandolee, we can still define custom option in proto3, right?

In proto3, custom options are allowed, i.e., users can use "extend" keyword to define their own extensions to proto descriptor options. The spec is missing stuff because it was created after protoc, i.e., it's introduced to describe what protoc does, rather than defining what protoc does. If you are implementing protobuf support in a new language it's better to follow what protoc accepts instead of what the spec doc says.
I know the issue is closed, but can the misleading title (which shows up in searches) be fixed? I believe *now* is supposed to be *not*.
Fixed!  (I hate that typo and am amazed how often I make it)

title: Compatibility in Proto3 for retaining unknown fields

A simple workaround is to use only keys of JSON which are there in proto. But that doesn't look scalable.

nodes.body: There is no way to preserve unknown fields through the JSON-to-proto boundary. If you are doing JSON to proto conversion, make sure you either reject the conversion when unknown fields are present, or make sure your application can tolerate missing unknown fields during the conversion.

```sh
(tmp) ~/tmp 12:53:53 $ tree .
```

The contents of the `.proto` files are as follows:

```sh
(tmp) ~/tmp 12:54:50 $ cat x/pb/tmp/x/pb/x.proto
syntax = "proto3";
package tmp.x.pb;

message Thing {
    string t = 1;
}
(tmp) ~/tmp 12:55:26 $ cat y/pb/tmp/y/pb/y.proto
syntax = "proto3";
package tmp.y.pb;
import "tmp/x/pb/x.proto";

message Thing2 {
    tmp.x.pb.Thing t = 1;
}
(tmp) Ben-Wolfson-Tower ~/tmp 12:55:34 $
```

The reason that `y.proto` imports `x.proto` with the path `"tmp/x/pb/x.proto"` is that when both of these packages are installed, `x_pb2` will be importable as `tmp.x.pb.x_pb2`, and (to my astonishment) the only way to get `protoc` to generate such an import path in python is to import it with that path in the proto file. This means that we generate the `*_pb2.py` files with some `--proto_path` shenanigans:

```sh
(tmp) ~/tmp 12:55:34 $ cd x
(tmp) ~/tmp/x 12:57:54 $ find . -name '*.proto' | xargs protoc --python_out=. --proto_path=.
(tmp) ~/tmp/x 12:58:01 $ cd ../y
(tmp) ~/tmp/y 12:58:04 $ find . -name '*.proto' | xargs protoc --python_out=. --proto_path=$HOME/tmp/x/pb --proto_path=.
```

This works, in the sense that `protoc` doesn't complain about anything, it finds all the necessary files, and it generates Python code. But in another, more accurate, sense, it does not work:

```
(tmp) Ben-Wolfson-Tower ~/tmp/y 12:58:09 $ python
Python 2.7.6 (default, Oct 26 2016, 20:30:19)
[GCC 4.8.4] on linux2
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> import tmp.x.pb.x_pb2
>>> import tmp.y.pb.y_pb2
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/benwolfson/tmp/y/pb/tmp/y/pb/y_pb2.py", line 25, in <module>
    dependencies=[tmp_dot_x_dot_pb_dot_x__pb2.DESCRIPTOR,])
  File "/usr/lib/python2.7/dist-packages/google/protobuf/descriptor.py", line 829, in __new__
    return _message.default_pool.AddSerializedFile(serialized_pb)
TypeError: Couldn't build proto file into descriptor pool!
Invalid proto descriptor for file "pb/tmp/y/pb/y.proto":
  pb/tmp/y/pb/y.proto: Import "tmp/x/pb/x.proto" has not been loaded.
  tmp.y.pb.Thing2.t: "tmp.x.pb.Thing" seems to be defined in "pb/tmp/x/pb/x.proto", which is not imported by "pb/tmp/y/pb/y.proto".  To use it here, please add the necessary import.

>>>
```

That is, even though the protoc compiler made use of the `--proto_path` options in order to find and generate its output, the output it generated is *not* aware of the paths provided: it's precisely *because* `pb/tmp/y/pb/y.proto` doesn't import `pb/tmp/x/pb/x.proto`, but rather simply `tmp/x/pb/x.proto`, that we passed the `--proto_path` option to the compiler!

nodes.body: I think we do not have plan to support relative imports. See #1491 for more discussion

I don't see the connection to relative imports. I have only, and only wish to have, absolute imports; looking at that ticket, it seems like *prima facie* to be a different issue. There isn't a problem with *Python* finding the module I want to import; IMO the problem is with protoc's codegen.

That is, when I run this command:

```sh
(tmp) ~/tmp/y 12:58:04 $ find . -name '*.proto' | xargs protoc --python_out=. --proto_path=$HOME/tmp/x/pb --proto_path=.

```

and `protoc` encounters the line `import "tmp/x/pb/x.proto";`, and it looks for the path `/tmp/x/pb/x.proto` relative to each specified `--proto_path`, it finds it in exactly one, and presumably can know relative to which such path it found the specified import, namely, it was relative to `$HOME/tmp/x/pb`. Nevertheless, it writes out to the generated Python file data that (AFAICT, I'm not an expert on the internals here by any means) seems to suggest/require that `protoc` have found `tmp/x/pb/x.proto` somewhere else.

The failure happens in this instantiation, in `y_pb2.py`:

```python
DESCRIPTOR = _descriptor.FileDescriptor(
  name='pb/tmp/y/pb/y.proto',
```

title: Null pointer dereference in Arena.
body:
If the allocator from the `ArenaOptions` returns `nullptr`, the placement new after that will dereference a null pointer.

https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/b61dd9d9a229c5a82788fdeefa344aa65affae09/src/google/protobuf/arena.cc#L119-L120

I'm currently dealing with this by throwing an exception from my allocator instead of returning `nullptr`, but I'm not really sure if your code is exception safe.

nodes.body: Thanks for reporting this, but I believe it is working as intended because we do not use exceptions in C++, as per the Google C++ style guide (see [here](https://google.github.io/styleguide/cppguide.html#Exceptions)).

I am aware that you aren't using any exceptions at Google, but that doesn't have anything to do with this null pointer dereference.

In `google/protobuf/arena.h` it says:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/b61dd9d9a229c5a82788fdeefa344aa65affae09/src/google/protobuf/arena.h#L130-L135

Given that `malloc` may return `nullptr` if allocation fails, I would expect from that statement, that my custom allocator should do the same.

In any case if a `nullptr` is returned, it is dereferenced when doing the placement new. This has nothing to do with exceptions being enabled/disabled.

You might argue that `malloc` never returns `nullptr` because of overcommit, but:
1. This isn't always the case e.g.:
    * Overcommit could be disabled
    * Some platforms don't do overcommit in the first place.
    * Even with overcommit, `malloc` might still return `nullptr` if the requested size was too large.
2. Given that this pointer can be supplied by any user of the library using `ArenaOptions`, there can be many reasons why a `nullptr` might be returned, that don't relate to how standard `malloc` works.

> I'm currently dealing with this by throwing an exception from my allocator instead of returning nullptr, but I'm not really sure if your code is exception safe.

The above statement was just a way of telling you what my workaround is. And I'm concerned about this workaround being bad, exactly **because** Google doesn't use exceptions. Because this means that Protobuf is written completely without exception safety in mind, making me question if my workaround is safe.

I'm not sure what code clang++/g++ emit for `new` if the allocation fails. I would guess that they call `std::terminate`, because breaking the guarantee that `new` never returns `nullptr` would be really bad!

Assuming that `std::terminate` is called when compiling with `-fno-exceptions` I can see two ways how this library could handle it if `block_alloc` returns `nullptr`:
1. Call `std::terminate`
2. Throw `std::bad_alloc` and rely on the compiler automatically turning it into `std::terminate` if exceptions are disabled at compile time. I would prefer this option because it takes all the users of the library into account, that don't compile their code with exceptions disabled. But this also means that exception safety should be guaranteed in codepaths that lead to `block_alloc` being called.

Ah ok, I see what you're saying. It seems to me like the right solution is to update the comments to clarify that `block_alloc` should never return `nullptr`--really it should behave more like `new` than like `malloc`. We've made no attempt to make the code exception-safe, so I suspect that there's not going be a useful way to attempt to handle a `std::bad_alloc` exception in the context of an Arena. If you don't want to interfere with other code that handles exceptions, it might be best then to call `std::terminate` from within `block_alloc` if for some reason the allocation fails.

I still think that protobuf should check and call `std::terminate`, because it is safer than relying on people to read the comment carefully.

And since this is only used for allocating blocks for the Arena, it won't be called very often, so the additional `nullptr` check isn't likely to cause any performance problems.
@FSMaxB With the current code, wouldn't it cause the program to terminate anyway when block_alloc() returns nullptr?

@xfxyjwf Not necessarily. The placement new in line 120 will call the constructor of `Block` with a `nullptr`.
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/b61dd9d9a229c5a82788fdeefa344aa65affae09/src/google/protobuf/arena.cc#L125-L126

This then tries to write a pointer to `offsetof(Block, next_)`, wherever that might be.

Most systems do have the zero page mapped in such a way that an interrupt is called and the program terminated.

**But** this is not the case on all systems (especially on systems without an MMU, but also if no interrupt is set up). Meaning that the program might keep on running while being in an invalid state. Even worse: After that the memory beginning at `0 + something small` will be used for regular allocations, overwriting everything on it's way.

See the Section *Is there life after jumping to 0x0* in [this article](http://hmarco.org/bugs/CVE-2015-8370-Grub2-authentication-bypass.html) describing a GRUB vulnerability for example (GRUB is running without virtual memory enabled, so no termination on `nullptr` dereference there, even on x86_64).
@xfxyjwf relying on undefined behaviour to cause a segfault and thus terminate is not usually good practice.

title: Multiple problems with repeated binary encoding
body:
# First problem

Repeated fields aren't packed, contrary to what documentation suggests.

Proto definition:

``` protobuf
syntax = "proto3";

message TestSimple {
    repeated sint32 some_ints = 2;
}

message TestMultiple {
    repeated sfixed32 some_fixed = 3;
    repeated string some_strings = 4;
}

message Test {
    repeated TestSimple simple_repeats = 4;
    repeated TestMultiple multiple_repeats = 1;
    oneof either_or {
        TestSimple simple_oneof = 6;
        TestMultiple multiple_oneof = 5;
    }
}
```

Invoking `protoc` with this text encoded message:

```
simple_repeats: {
    some_ints: [1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3]
}
multiple_repeats: [{
    some_fixed: [1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3]
    some_strings: ["foo", "bar", "\x01weird\x10"]
},
{
    some_fixed: [4, -4, 5, -5, 6, -6]
}]
multiple_oneof: {
    some_fixed: [123456789, 987654321]
    some_strings: [""]
}
```

Produces this output (I've labeled it for you):

```
\x0a (field: 1/multiple_repeats of Test, wiretype: 2/lenght-delimited)
-    (length: 45)
\x1a (field: 3/some_fixed of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x18 (length: 24)
\x01\x00\x00\x00 1
\xff\xff\xff\xff -1
\x02\x00\x00\x00 2
\xfe\xff\xff\xff -2
\x03\x00\x00\x00 3
\xfd\xff\xff\xff -3
\x22 (field: 4/some_strings of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x03 (length: 3)
foo
\x22 (field: 4/some_strings of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x03 (length: 3)
bar
\x22 (field: 4/some_strings of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x07 (length: 7)
\x01weird\x10
--- end of (field: 1/multiple_repeats of Test, wiretype: 2/lenght-delimited)

\x0a (field: 1/multiple_repeats of Test, wiretype: 2/lenght-delimited)
\x1a (length: 26)
\x1a (field: 3/some_fixed of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x18 (length: 24)
\x04\x00\x00\x00 4
\xfc\xff\xff\xff -4
\x05\x00\x00\x00 5
\xfb\xff\xff\xff -5
\x06\x00\x00\x00 6
\xfa\xff\xff\xff -6
\x22 (field: 4/some_strings of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x08 (length: 8) --- should be 0.
--- end of (field: 1/multiple_repeats of Test, wiretype: 2/lenght-delimited)

\x12 (filed: 2/some_ints of TestSimple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x06 (length: 6)
\x02 -1
\x01 1
\x04 -2
\x03 2
\x06 -3
\x05 3
--- end of (filed: 2/some_ints of TestSimple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)

* (field: 5 multiple_oneof of Test, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x0c (length: 12)
\x1a (field: 3/some_fixed of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x08 (length: 8)
\x15\xcd[\x07 123456789
\xb1h\xde: 987654321
--- end of (field: 5 multiple_oneof of Test, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)

\x22 (field: 4/some_strings of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x00 (length: 0)
```

# Second problem

See my comment above on incorrectly encoding the length of the string that wasn't specified on input. Its length was set to 8, but, probably the parser ignores this value because it already knows the overall length of the message.

----

Some more general comments:

Encoding repeated fields the way you do in the example above makes parsing messages from stream impossible / meaningless because the parser needs to wait until the entire message is received and processed in order to parse any of it.  This also impairs the parser in that it absolutely must follow your implementation instead of specification. The ability to concatenate message payloads and then parse the result is completely useless (I believe it happened to you by chance that it worked this way, but then you decided to document this bizarre behavior.)  This also prevents alternative implementations from creating more efficient parsers because, except for this part one could assume that a single type specification in parser would map to unique binary representation.  But since this assumption is broken by the fact that you can encode the same value by either repeating field entry multiple times or by writing all field values together, you can no longer use the proto definition as a guide for what to expect from the binary payload.

Bottom line: multiple ways to encode repeated fields is a very bad idea.  Please don't do that.

nodes.body:
I believe everything is actually working as intended here. When you see a field number 4 with a length of 8, that's not the `some_strings` field of `TestMultiple` but instead it's the `simple_repeats` field of `Test`. The empty string doesn't appear until the end, since the serialized output is sorted by field number.

I think your other objection is that once you've read a field, you can't know for sure if it's the real value, because it could be appended or overridden later on. That's true, but at least in practice it would be somewhat rare for this to happen, so you can optimize for the common case of each field being set in one place.

You are right that there is not a unique binary representation for a given message. This is especially for true if you use map fields, because maps are logically unordered and so the order of the serialized entries is arbitrary. In some languages we have APIs for deterministic serialization since some use cases require that, but we only guarantee that the serialization will be deterministic for a given binary (it might still change over time with new protobuf versions).

Your analysis re' `some_strings` vs `simple_repeats` is wrong. Sorry. You can absolutely see that the contents is the strings given on the stdout, and not varints, as would have been, should this actually encode `simple_repeats`.

Re' non-uniqueness of representation: lack of order is acceptable.  If you go further into theoretical properties of the information being generated, you can see that allowing permutations of information is a much weaker kind of inconsistency than allowing two entirely different encodings of atomic information.  This is similar to how we (humans) are normally OK with sums of integers written as `1+2` or `2+1` (and meaning the same thing), but will have problems accepting systems with logical rules like `2=1` and `1=1` (both simultaneously true).

----

So, my other reading of your response is that: you are actually never packing length-delimited repeated fields, so it is safe for alternative implementation to assume that this will be the case for a while (and probably until next major version)?  I think that this is inefficient and creates some useless, and even harmful properties of Protobuf encoding, but if that's how you like it, who am I to tell you otherwise.

Consider this part of your labeled output:
```
\x22 (field: 4/some_strings of TestMultiple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x08 (length: 8) --- should be 0.
--- end of (field: 1/multiple_repeats of Test, wiretype: 2/lenght-delimited)

\x12 (filed: 2/some_ints of TestSimple, wiretype: 2/length-delimited)
\x06 (length: 6)
\x02 -1
\x01 1
\x04 -2
\x03 2
\x06 -3
\x05 3
```

That corresponds to this part of the input:
```
simple_repeats: {
    some_ints: [1, -1, 2, -2, 3, -3]
}
```
If you look carefully this works out perfectly. We have here field number 4 (`simple_repeats`) with a length-delimited payload of size 8. That payload is a `TestSimple` which has a one-byte tag, a one-byte length delimiter, and six one-byte zigzag varints. This is what packed repeated fields are supposed to look like: instead of six separate tag-value pairs, the six varints are concatenated together and put inside a length-delimited payload.

If there is a particular repeated field that you think is not being packed properly, could you point me to which one it is?
This is not the part I'm writing about... the so-called scalar types are the only types that work according to the description in documentation, the length-delimited types are the problem.
The thing is that only repeated fields of primitive numeric types can be packed, so for example, the repeated strings in your example can't be packed.

> The thing is that only repeated fields of primitive numeric types can be packed

What makes you think so?

I see absolutely no problem packing length-delimited fields.  In fact, the first time I wrote the parser, this was exactly the way I did it.  This is the most reasonable and straight-forward implementation: this is how internet protocol stack works for example.

I.e. instead of writing it the way you do it now, you could have done it like this (using ASN):

```
Protobuf ::= BEGIN
  Message ::= SEQUENCE {
    length VARINT
    payload SEQUENCE OF MessageField
  }
  MessageField ::= SEQUENCE {
    fieldNumAndType VARINT
    payload Message | Scalar | Repeated
  }
  Scalar ::= VARINT | FIXED32 | FIXED64
  Repeated ::= SEQUENCE {
    length VARINT
    payload SEQUENCE of (Scalar | Message)
  }
END
```

In other words, you write repeated fields of the type `length-delimited` as individual fields, but I'd expect (and this is what documentation seems to suggest) that these length-delimited fields would be encoded recursively, all into one length-delimited field.

What happens right now is that until the parser reaches the end, it cannot tell how long the repeated field is.  What I'm suggesting is that repeated fields be written continuously as a single length-delimited field, and that the feature of gluing together multiple mentions of the same fields into one continuous field be removed (since it's useless in practice anyways).

I agree that in principle one could pack all types of repeated fields, but this is not something allowed by the current wire format. As the [documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding#packed) says: 'Only repeated fields of primitive numeric types (types which use the varint, 32-bit, or 64-bit wire types) can be declared "packed".' We would be pretty reluctant to make length-delimited fields packable, because existing parsers would be unable to parse messages in the new format. Requiring repeated fields to appear in one continuous field would also break existing parsers.

Allowing multiple mentions of the same repeated field is also not entirely useless. Let's say you want to merge two protos together, and each one happens to have a length-delimited unknown field of the same field number. Those unknown fields might be packed repeated fields, but we have no way of knowing that (they could also be strings or messages for example). That means that when we reserialize the resulting merged proto, it's impossible to pack the unknown fields into your suggested canonical format. The only safe thing to do is serialize them as separate tag-value pairs.

> Let's say you want to merge two protos together

This never happens in practice.  All people I talked to so far about Protobuf are horrified even when they hear that it is possible, in principle, to use two different definitions for the same binary payload: they usually start bursting into flames when they hear such thing.  Merging messages for them makes absolutely no sense.  Most people think about any message format, not necessary Protobuf, as if it was encoding one conceptual message into one binary representation.  Even if there is a possibility to do it differently, nobody would use that.

From a perspective of a user of Protobuf, who is normally a Java / C++ programmer, they just need to put a definition of messages into their source code to make sure that classes on one end of the channel translate into same classes on the other end.  Merging messages in this context would be analogous to be able to merge objects of arbitrary classes, say, `Animal` and `Transaction`.  This just makes one's mind explode :)

People do merge protos in practice: you can search our GitHub issues for examples.

Protocol buffers are designed to make it easy to continuously evolve your schema over time without breaking compatibility. This makes it inevitable that the parser will be somewhat generous in what it accepts, because it never assumes it has the most up-to-date version of the schema.

I think you folks are talking about different things. @acozzette is talking about merging protobuf data (see Message::MergeFrom: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding#optional), whereas @wvxvw misunderstood it to be merging two different proto types.
@wvxvw I am afraid we just can't make breaking changes like that--that would result in all newly serialized protos being unparseable by existing parsers.

Closing as there is nothing we can do here.

@wvxvw If you are creating a new wire format for protobuf, I would suggest make it completely incompatible with the current proto wire format rather than partially compatible. For example, you probably want to use different wire types.

title: The grammar for options is incorrect
body:
`protoc` appears to accept this:

``` protobuf
option (scalapb.options) = {
  package_name: "com.secret.np.api.messages.spb"
  collection_type: "collection.immutable.Seq"
  single_file: true
  flat_package: true
};
```

However, the grammar for option is:

```
constant = fullIdent | ( [ "-" | "+" ] intLit ) | ( [ "-" | "+" ] floatLit ) | strLit | boolLit
option = "option" optionName  "=" constant ";"
optionName = ( ident | "(" fullIdent ")" ) { "." ident }
```

I.e. the improvised hash-table is not a `constant` by any means.

Also, I think I saw `option (foo.bar).baz = ...;` syntax used somewhere, which doesn't match what `fullIdnt` is defined to.

> Protocol Buffers also allows you to define and use your own options. This is an advanced feature which most people don't need. If you do think you need to create your own options, see the Proto2 Language Guide for details. Note that creating custom options uses extensions, which are permitted only for custom options in proto3.

@clearjs Look, this is a simple technical issue. Protobuf language specification, specifically its grammar fails to mention there is a rule to parse `extend`.  That is all there is to it.  Whether this was done intentionally or is an oversight--I don't even want to speculate.

What needs to be done: either grammar needs to include a rule for parsing `extend` or `extend` shouldn't parse. It's that simple.

title: option optimize_for = SPEED; shouldn't parse
body:
If you look at `goolge/protobuf/descriptor.proto`, it contains this:

```
option optimize_for = SPEED;
```

This should **not** parse according to both proto2 and proto3 language spec, but `protoc` accepts this w/o even a warning...

To clarify: my understanding was that identifiers may only be introduced using keywords s.a. `message`, `enum`, `option` etc.  Having and identifier that doesn't identify anything looks wrong.  In this case the intentions seems like it would have been better expressed by having an enumeration with members such as `SPEED`, `CODE_SIZE` and whatever other options are available, and use that instead.

nodes.body: @wvxvw Can you explain your use case? As far as I know the language spec is for documentation purpose only and does not define how protoc actually behaves (i.e., the protoc is not implemented to the spec). If you want to parse .proto files, using protoc is the only way and we do not support parsers in any other language.

My use-case: I'm writing my own implementation of the parser.  I worked under assumption that identifiers must resolve to definitions (this is what normally happens in programming languages, this is the basic difference between an identifier and a keyword), but `SPEED` in the example above doesn't resolve to anything.  It is treated as self-evaluating symbol (eg. like a number or a boolean).

> As far as I know the language spec is for documentation purpose only

This is kind of... frustrating to say the least.  If it's an open-source technology, which is meant for being implementable by multiple independent parties, that's, well, not a good approach.

----

In practical terms, I'd prefer if in the future versions `protoc` disallowed the use of identifiers that haven't been introduced through language mechanisms, or at least warn about such use.  The code above could have easily being a mistake, s.a. typo.

Better yet: disallow the use of identifiers in options definition altogether.  Just use string literals instead.

Protobuf is an opensource technology but there are use cases that we protobuf-team support and there are use cases that we don't support. Implementing your own parser is one use case that we don't support.

body:
Add message-level option `java_classname` that specifies an alternative name for the generated Java class for the message.

The problem of such options is that it adds complexity to both the implementation and the API surface, and it will become a lot worse when multiple options get added and can affect with each other (which is very likely if we are too liberal in adding options). In this case I would suggest you rename the message instead.

title: -std=c++11 flag added on wrong macOS versions
body:
python/setup.py checks the macOS version incorrectly, performing a *floating point* comparison instead of a *version number* comparison:

```
    v, _, _ = platform.mac_ver()
    if v:
      v = float('.'.join(v.split('.')[:2]))
      if v >= 10.12:
        extra_compile_args.append('-std=c++11')
```

So the `-std=c++11` flag will be added for macOS versions with a *floating point* value greater than or equal to 10.12—e.g. 10.12, 10.13, 10.2, 10.3, 10.4, 10.5, 10.6, 10.7, 10.8, 10.9—but not for 10.10 or 10.11. Surely this isn't what was intended. The clang++ compiler in Xcode on macOS only started using libc++ (which supports C++11) as of 10.9, and newer versions of clang++ in newer versions of Xcode on newer versions of macOS support more of the standard. In 10.8 and earlier, the C++ compilers used libstdc++ 4.2.1 or earlier (which doesn't support C++11 at all).

This problem was introduced in the 3.2.x branch in 117f7716414bb0826ad4b78d9b27f30e6f8e2e24 and merged to master as part of 7f3e23707122f31ebfa58b7280bd56cbe77cb44e.

What was the intention? On which macOS versions did you mean to add the flag?

I suspect it is incorrect to add the flag on the basis of a macOS version. You should instead add the flag on the basis of compiler capability. (It is possible to use newer clang++ compilers and libc++ on older versions of macOS and thus give them C++11 capability.)

title: [Java] Merging bool fields
body:
When using the `mergeFrom` method there seem to be an inconsistency between the documentation and the actual behaviour when merging `bool` primitives.

The documentation for `mergeFrom` states:

> * For singular primitive fields, if the field is set in other, then other's value overwrites the value in this message.

While the actual generated code looks like:

```
        if (other.getValue() != false) {
          setValue(other.getValue());
        }
```

Therefore the merge happens only if the other message has a true value.

Probably the documentation should be extended or the generated code should be modified to always merge a boolean.

nodes.body: It seems you are using proto3. In proto3, a bool field is considered set only if its value is true.

title: How can I compile .proto files in PHP?
body:
Hi there,
    In my project, I use protobuf to define the data schema. Before reporting data to the server, users need to submit a .proto file to our web server written in PHP, and web server will validate the .proto file to check if it is compliance with out data specification. I know how to parse the .proto file with C++ importer, but there is no PHP importer, need I write a PHP extension? or is there anyone know other ways?

Is there any way for you to get the serialized descriptor proto info?
On Thu, Jun 7, 2018 at 18:45 gunli <notifications@github.com> wrote:

> @TeBoring <https://github.com/TeBoring>
> Hi TeBoring,
> Importer is a class defined in google/protobuf/compiler/importer.h. In
> C++, we can use this class to compile .proto files without generating
> codes(and this is what I want, 'cause my users will submit a lot of .proto
> files, code generation is not a good idea for me). And then use the
> FileDescriptor to traverse all the messages and use the FieldDescriptor the
> taverse all the fields of a message.
>
> class LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT Importer {
>  public:
>   Importer(SourceTree* source_tree,
>            MultiFileErrorCollector* error_collector);

>
>   // Import the given file and build a FileDescriptor representing it.  If
>   // the file is already in the DescriptorPool, the existing FileDescriptor
>   // will be returned.  The FileDescriptor is property of the DescriptorPool,
>   // and will remain valid until it is destroyed.  If any errors occur, they
>   // will be reported using the error collector and Import() will return NULL.
>   //
>   // A particular Importer object will only report errors for a particular
>   // file once.  All future attempts to import the same file will return NULL
>   // without reporting any errors.  The idea is that you might want to import
>   // a lot of files without seeing the same errors over and over again.  If

>   }

@davenso I fix this by reinstall python package from source code

This error happens when new generated code is being used with an old runtime, That's a configuration we don't support. Upgrade protobuf runtime to newer version later than your protoc version can solve the error.

For compatibility, we support older generated code with newer protobuf runtime.

@rockyzhengwu I noticed that your protoc version and protobuf runtime version are both 3.5.1. Thus this error should not happen. I checked the 3.5.1 protoc, serialized_options was not released in that version. 
Can you double check that your /home/rocky/GitHub/pyemd/test/topic_response_pb2.py file is produced by protoc 3.5.1?

I had the same issue until I realised that checking the pip version with 
`pip show protobuf` 
gives you the python 2 version.
Indeed `pip3 install -U protobuf` did the trick for me.

If protoc is newer than runtime, or if using generated _pb2.py code from other libraries(for example Tensorflow) which is using newer protoc version, it may have this problem. Upgrade the runtime to 3.6.0 or above will solve it

Yes, it works. "serialized_options" matters for :
```
    has_options:  True if the descriptor has non-default options.  Usually it
        is not necessary to read this -- just call GetOptions() which will
        happily return the default instance.  However, it's sometimes useful
        for efficiency, and also useful inside the protobuf implementation to
        avoid some bootstrapping issues.
```

Don't know if ok to delete it.

nodes.body: Does this happen with latest 3.6.0 release?

`require': cannot load such file -- google/gax (LoadError)
Could you provide more detailed steps to reproduce?

Yes, it reproduces with 3.6.0. Here's the full repro:
```
gem install google-gax google-cloud-logging google-protobuf
ruby -e "require 'google/gax'; require 'google/logging/v2/logging_pb'; Google::Protobuf::Any.encode(Google::Logging::V2::WriteLogEntriesPartialErrors.new)"
```

Unlike pack and unpack, Any.encode can only encode Any message. You should do:
```
any = Google::Protobuf::Any.new
any.pack(Google::Logging::V2::WriteLogEntriesPartialErrors.new)
Google::Protobuf::Any.encode(any)
```
However, segmentation fault is not what we want. Instead, exception should be thrown. We will fix that.
Right, I understand that the repro case is contrived. This bug was opened exactly to turn a segfault into some reasonable Ruby-level error or exception.
Fixed in #4885

I've added `gem "google-protobuf", github: "protocolbuffers/protobuf", tag: "v3.7.0"` to my Gemfile, and I'm getting `LoadError: cannot load such file -- google/protobuf/any_pb` when attempting to update to Ruby 2.6.1.

I'm glad that it worked, but unfortunately I've found that my pull request causes something else to break. The problem is that `CUnescape` is also used here to operate on default values for bytes fields, which are not necessarily UTF-8: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/f42d5923f0b6de75611af0a8c8b3354763aece00/python/google/protobuf/descriptor_pool.py#L886

So ultimately I think we need a `CUnescape` function that's capable of unescaping hex and octal escapes for both UTF-8 and raw binary data, and which will work for both Python 2 and 3. I'm afraid I don't have time to work on this now, especially since I don't have a lot of knowledge of Python. But hopefully this summary of the problem will point in the right direction if anyone else wants to give this a try.
Note that my attempted fix caused some failures to pop up in `descriptor_pool_test.py` when run with Python 3, so that is a good place to start looking at the problem further.

I'm working on a fix for this internally.  Testing now.

I too came to this issue via METADATA files as we're updating all sorts of things internally to actually run on Python 3. :)

@kerstin, this issue is fixed on July and marked wait for 3.7.0 release. We haven't release 3.7.0 yet, current valid versions still have the problem

title: Undocumented options syntax

nodes.body:
I share the experience having to deal with option value syntax. I added a lot of logic to my parser (https://github.com/emicklei/proto) in order to deal with many cases found out there. 

Btw, I found your (@wvxvw) example to be parseable with my proto library. See my option_test.go file to discover more unusual cases.
Thanks, I'll sure take a look!

Clues:

The code that does the parsing of options is "ParseOption" here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/parser.cc

These complex option values are put into UninterprettedOption's aggregate_value field: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/parser.cc#L1388

parser.ParseFromString is used to parse the aggregated_value here:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc#L7067

title: Please move from native to Skylark rules for external git/http repositories
body:
Bazel is planning to move away from native rules for external repositories to Skylark rules, mainly because bundling every version control system in bazel does not scale. As part of this effort, we plan to submit https://bazel-review.googlesource.com/c/bazel/+/55932 soon, which will cause bazel by default to insist that the skylark versions the git and http rules for external repositories be used. title: Missing mojo in Method and ServiceDescriptors
body:
I'm spinning up gRPC servers, and have discovered some unpleasant surprises in both MethodDescriptor (across the board) and in the stub classes which the Python protoc generates:

- MethodDescriptor has no information about whether the method is input- or output-streaming! (And from reading the protoc code, it doesn't seem to be stored anywhere in the descriptors)

- Python-specific issue: The generated FooStub and FooServicer classes have no links back to the ServiceDescriptor, nor vice-versa. You can't get to either of these classes from the symbol_database, and if you have these classes, the only way to get the corresponding descriptor is to string-mangle their names and look that up. Likewise, there's no programmatic way to find the `add_FooServiceServicer_to_server` method.

These both feel highly suboptimal for no good reason. I propose the following fixes:

- Cross-language: Add two boolean fields, `input_streaming` and `output_streaming`, to `MethodDescriptor`. (Or if people really prefer, encode this in `MethodOptions`, but that seems unnecessarily opaque given that these parameters are required for interpreting so many things about the method) Populate them in protoc.
- Python only: Extend the Python `SymbolDatabase` to have methods which can return the Stub and Servicer classes given a service name. (These would be populated in `RegisterServiceDescriptor` in much the same way they currently are for message types)
- Python only: In the generated Python Stub and Servicer classes, add an instance method returning the service descriptor. Move the brains of `add_ServiceNameServicer_to_server` to be a class method of the Servicer, and leave the existing function name as a pointer to that for backwards-compatibility.

This would make services and methods lookupable in basically the same way messages are today.

title: using `import` with non-local paths yields unexpected results with C++ code generation.
body:
I'm trying to include a proto file from another directory using `import "foo/bar.proto";`, which results in code generation that somehow incorporates the "foo" directory name in the generated code (but only in references, not actual declared names).
This is entirely unexpected (as well as undocumented as far as I can see), as there also is the "module" spec which is used to wrap declarations into namespaces.

In a nutshell, using `import "foo/bar.proto";` seems entirely unusable, so I'd like to understand a) whether that's intended and b) how to work around it.

nodes.body: @stefanseefeld I think the issue here is that you have to be consistent about how you invoke protoc when you build foo/bar.proto and the other proto file which imports it. If one file imports "foo/bar.proto" then make sure you pass "foo/bar.proto" to `protoc` when you build it (e.g. don't cd to foo/ and then call protoc on bar.proto).

How the protoc currently works is by design. It's a very very common misunderstanding to think that "-I" flag for protoc works the same way as it is for C++ compiler. It isn't and is not designed to work that way. Protoc uses the "-I" option to determine the import path of every .proto file (regardless whether the .proto file is imported or not, it will have a globally unique import path) and generates code that is dependent on that path. For example, that import path is embedded in the generated descriptor data which is later used by DescriptorPool and APIs like DescriptorPool::FindFileByName() relies on that import path as the key to look up descriptors in the entire binary. Ignoring the dirname or not, protoc needs a unique name for every .proto file, and if dirname is ignored, protoc will have to require every .proto file to have a globally unique file name and that's not going to happen.

I agree this is counter-intuitive though. I see too often that users complain about generated code not working because they are not aware of the significance of the import path. Some will even suggest we change the generated code to make it compile (e.g., https://github.com/google/protobuf/issues/1491) but it won't work because of the "unique global import path for every .proto file" requirement. A generated code change will not allow you to do "import ./foo.proto" in one place and "import ../foo.proto" in some other place because the generated code will have embedded descriptor data referencing the same file with different names and that will fail at runtime.

We definitely need better documentation for this. I actually started some documentation for this before but never got the time to finish/publish it...

>
> How the protoc currently works is by design. It's a very very common 
> misunderstanding to think that "-I" flag for protoc works the same way 
> as it is for C++ compiler. It isn't and is not designed to work that way.
>

> will have a globally unique import path) and generates code that is 
> dependent on that path. For example, that import path is embedded in

<speculating>
It could work just the way C/C++ preprocessing works, i.e. it could use 
the import search path strictly for looking up proto files, 
irrespectively of their content. In fact, my surprise stems in part from 
the fact that there also is the "module" spec that generates namespaces 
(in the C++ mapping), and thus could be used to disambiguate.
</speculating>

> I agree this is counter-intuitive though. I see too often that users 
> complain about generated code not working because they are not aware

What I still don't understand is why that requirement exists. Couldn't 
`protoc` simply reuse the established semantics (and idioms) associated 
with C/C++ preprocessing, so a processed file is uniquely identified, no 
matter by what name I include it (which of course also requires some 
form of header guarding (#pragma once could be implicit)).

OK. In any case, despite my complaining, I'm very grateful for the

title: [PHP] Custom default value and JSON serialization
body:
Hello,

We have a proto message that has a float with custom default value (set with `utils.cl_default_float`) of 1.0.

The problem is that `serializeToJsonString` won't serialize a float that has a value of 0.0, because serialization skips all floats with a default 0.0 value,which is done here: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/00d32539c6aa0c4efe9577561a00f443edd9a417/php/src/Google/Protobuf/Internal/Message.php#L1408 

Could it be added to the library that either:
- we can set a custom default field value, so in our case we, at serialization, we skip floats 1.0 but not 0.0,
- default values are JSON serialized in any case, so we'd serialize 1.0 and 0.0.

Is any of these two things already possible? I've checked the code but haven't been able to come up with a solution without modifying the library code.

Thank you 

EDIT:
My current solution works without modifying the library code but is rough one: after protobuf serialization, I parse JSON back to an associative array structure with `json_decode`, recursively iterate it add the default 0.0 values wherever they're missing, and serialize back to JSON using `json_encode`.

nodes.body: This can be done in proto2 support. Unfortunately, I don't have time to implement that.

If you mark fields as `optional`, they will always serialize when you explicitly set them. You can use this to explicitly serialize `0.0` values.  This is a new feature introduced in 3.15.0 (Feb 2021).

There is also a feature currently in review that will allow to you serialize defaults for *all* fields: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9124

title: [Java] Proto generated classes do not shade easily due to shade plugin corrupting internal string constants in generated code
body:
It is a common pattern for the proto package path and the java package to be the same string when generating protobufs. This typically causes issues when shading generated proto classes because shading tools search and replace string constants within classes that match package path strings with the relocated variant.

For example `org.apache.beam.model.pipeline.v1.AccumulationMode.Enum` was changed to `org.apache.beam.repackaged.beam_runners_direct_java.model.pipeline.v1.AccumulationMode.Enum`. This made loading the class fail because the varint field describing the string length was no longer correct causing the descriptor parsing to fail.

See https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/BEAM-4484 for more details.

Please obfuscate string constants within the generated code (such as base64 encoding) to make it easier for users to shade proto generated classes.

nodes.body: CC: @ejona86
CC @garrettjonesgoogle

This seems it would always be a problem when shading protobuf, because either the java package name matches the proto package (which should not be changed during shading) or the `option java_package` value (which may be fine to change, with the exception of length changing problems).

I do wonder whether the shading tool's over-zealousness is widespread. This issue was experienced with Gradle's shadow plugin. It'd be interesting to do a test and see the behavior of jarjar and Maven shade, if for no other reason to better understand the various behaviors.

It turns out its not always a problem because I decompiled the class and looked at what changed and only one of the many package strings were replaced. Since the field is being interpreted as ISO 8859-1 to get access to the raw bytes, I assume the string matching doesn't always get a hit on the descriptor field. You just have to get unlucky like I did.

title: PHP C extension protobuf message class introspection not possible
body:
## Issue
When var_dumping, json_encoding or array casting a generated protobuf message class, an `E_USER_ERROR` `"Cannot access private properties."` is triggered in the [protobuf C extension](https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/php/ext/google/protobuf/message.c#L226).
This behaviour is different from PHPs native behaviour and thus diffierent to the behaviour of the protobuf PHP library.
I found this issue after updating the protobuf extension because the comparison of two protobuf message classes with [PHPUnit's](https://phpunit.de/) `assertEquals` function was failing.

## Expected behaviour
It should follow the PHP native behaviour, that means:
The error should only be triggered if there is a real direct private property access (`$instance->property`).
When json_encoding it should return an empty object. `{}`
When var_dumping it should show the private properties and its values.
Example:
```
object(MyClass)#1 (1) {
  ["my_property":"MyClass":private]=>
  string(9) "someValue"
}
```
When array casting, it should return an array with the keys and values.
Example:
```
array(1) {
  ["MyClassmy_property"]=>
  string(9) "someValue"
}
```

## Additional information
The `E_USER_ERROR` was [introduced with v3.6.0rc1](https://github.com/google/protobuf/compare/v3.5.2...v3.6.0rc1#diff-11d77309bba45672327620da2bf4540d). Curiously, code that would implement the expected behavior was *also* added in that commit, it is just unreachable because of the `zend_error` call.

nodes.body:
We haven't supported assertEquals for message. For now, your test should not depend on that.
For var_dump, could you do that with php implementation only?

Hey @TeBoring, thank you for your quick response!
We already adjusted our assertion to check the properties over the provided getters.
Nevertheless the behaviour of the C extension is not as intended and I would love to see it getting improved.
I don't really understand your last question. Could you maybe explain it again?

In c extension, ```get_properties``` is called when ```var_dump``` or any operations that transform protobuf message object into array (by design we don't allow message object to be transformed into array). Therefore, the only valid use case for ```get_properties``` to be executed is ```var_dump```.
IMO, ```var_dump``` is only used for debug. When you put your code into production server, there is no need to var_dump a protobuf message.

Hi @TeBoring, while I agree that `var_dump` is unlikely to be used in production, that is just one example of a function that can't be used with proto message objects. In my opinion, casting the object to an array or running it through `json_encode` are *definitely* use cases that we should be able to use in production. Would you agree?

In my opinion the main issue is that the C Extension is behaving different than the PHP package.
Things that work with the PHP package are causing an `E_USER_ERROR` in the C Extension.
Also the C Extension is behaving different than plain PHP classes would do.
I guess we all agree that this is not how it should be.
We have now two solutions:

1. Adjust the PHP package to follow the C extension.
This can be done by implementing the functions `__debugInfo` and `__get` and  implementing the `ArrayAccess` interface in the `Message` class to trigger the `E_USER_ERROR` like the C extension is triggering it right now.
2. Adjust the C extension to behave like the PHP package/PHP classes.

I would prefer the second approach since it would be a way more natural behaviour and increase the usability.
I'm hitting this issue also. For now, I'm using `serializeToString()` to do `assertEquals()`, but that's not ideal, obviously.

@tobiasgies, what's your use case for casting the object to an array?
Is ```json_encode``` related to this issue?
@mcos, ```assertEquals``` is a separate issue, right? php implementation also doesn't suppport ```assert Equals```
It mightn't be fully supported, but `assertEquals` with a protobuf message argument works with the composer library.
Oh yes. The unit tests in `google-cloud-php` actually depend on `assertEquals` with protobuf messages and they passed with protobuf extension 3.5.1.1. With 3.6.0, the tests started to fail.
It's welcome to have a PR for this issue.
I am working on a fix: #4946
This issue is very old and covers many different problems. Going to close but please open a specific bug about a feature if you still need it.

title: Python protobuf dynamic decoding
body:
Dear protobuf developer, 
I have a bunch of different .proto file and I have a data stream coming through MQTT messages.

I need to develop a program (using python) that:

1) get the binary data from the MQTT
2) try to identify the "kind" of protobuf message from the .proto file in a folder
3) decode the message and print the data

I have some questions:

1) is possible from the binary data itself to identify the "protobuf type" of a message?
2) is possible with the python  api to read a .proto file at runtime and generate the parsing classes without compiling the proto first? performance is not an issue but the functionality to change the .proto file without relaunching protoc is 

Do you have an example of that?

I've found in the code the reflection api and for example the descriptor pool database that seems to be what I'm searching for 

I've also found this
https://vdna.be/blog/index.php/2016/05/google-protobuf-at-run-time-deserialization-example-in-c/

What I miss is an update example about how to use those API
the documentation about it is pretty laconic

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/pythontutorial#advanced-usage

Thanks
Nick

nodes.body:
To answer your first question, a serialized protocol buffer does not identify its type, so when you parse a message you have to know what kind of type you're expecting. If you want to be able to parse multiple message types, one easy way to accomplish that is to put all the message types inside a `oneof` field in a wrapper message.

For your second question, unfortunately as far as I know there is no good way to have changes to a .proto file take effect automatically without you rebuilding the protos with protoc. In C++ and Java there is a DynamicMessage which allows you to manipulate messages of a type that's only known at runtime, but I don't think this exists in Python. And even with that approach, you end up with messages that you can only access via the reflection API (no generated accessors, etc.), so that doesn't sound like what you are looking for.

Hi @acozzette 
thanks for your response.

I need to explain my problem better.
I have a bunch of .proto files coming from different part of the system.
I need to develop a "viewer" that give the possibility to select a proto file and decode messages for debugging purpose.

eg a developer need to see a particular stream of data and type

proto_decoder -t stream1/data1 -p myprotocol.proto

and see all message in a readable format

  name: "demo.proto"
  package: "demo"
  message {
      name: "n"
      number: 2
      label: "pippo"
      type: TEST_OBJ
    }

in the same manner as the protoc application --decode option.
I cannot use the protoc directly because I have to get the stream of data from a server.

The first part (not needed but cool too have was about the possibility of having in a folder a list of .proto files 
and have the software to try to decode the messages trying those one by one (until it doesn't get an error)

Under Python this seemed more simpe because the protobuf there is generated at runtime!
Here is a generated demo_pb2.py as you see the classes are constructed at runtime with

_reflection.GeneratedProtocolMessageType(

```
# Generated by the protocol buffer compiler.  DO NOT EDIT!
# source: demo.proto

import sys
_b=sys.version_info[0]<3 and (lambda x:x) or (lambda x:x.encode('latin1'))

from google.protobuf import reflection as _reflection
from google.protobuf import symbol_database as _symbol_database
from google.protobuf import descriptor_pb2
# @@protoc_insertion_point(imports)

_sym_db = _symbol_database.Default()

DESCRIPTOR = _descriptor.FileDescriptor(
  name='demo.proto',
  package='demo',
  syntax='proto3',
  serialized_pb=_b('\n\ndemo.proto\x12\x04\x64\x65mo\"\x11\n\x04\x64\x65mo\x12\t\n\x01n\x18\x01 \x03(\x05\x62\x06proto3')
)

_DEMO = _descriptor.Descriptor(
  name='demo',
  full_name='demo.demo',
  filename=None,
  file=DESCRIPTOR,
  containing_type=None,
  fields=[
    _descriptor.FieldDescriptor(
      name='n', full_name='demo.demo.n', index=0,
      number=1, type=5, cpp_type=1, label=3,
      has_default_value=False, default_value=[],
      message_type=None, enum_type=None, containing_type=None,
      is_extension=False, extension_scope=None,
      options=None, file=DESCRIPTOR),
  ],
  extensions=[
  ],
  nested_types=[],
  enum_types=[
  ],
  options=None,
  is_extendable=False,
  syntax='proto3',
  extension_ranges=[],
  oneofs=[
  ],
  serialized_start=20,
  serialized_end=37,
)

DESCRIPTOR.message_types_by_name['demo'] = _DEMO
_sym_db.RegisterFileDescriptor(DESCRIPTOR)

demo = _reflection.GeneratedProtocolMessageType('demo', (_message.Message,), dict(
  DESCRIPTOR = _DEMO,
  __module__ = 'demo_pb2'
  # @@protoc_insertion_point(class_scope:demo.demo)
  ))
_sym_db.RegisterMessage(demo)
```

An interesting class is the descriptor pool class but I don't understand how to populate the FileDescriptor class with a list of file names and the differences between FileDescriptorProto and FileDescriptor...

Ok, I think what you are trying to do should be doable. `reflection.ParseMessage` provides the basic functionality of parsing a message based on a given descriptor: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/d36c0c538a545fac5d9db6ba65c525246d4efa95/python/google/protobuf/reflection.py#L67

I think the best way to get the descriptors you need is to call `protoc` with `--descriptor_set_out=...` to have it generate them for you. I am not too familiar with the Python implementation but I believe `FileDescriptor` is just a nicer in-memory representation of the raw `FileDescriptorProto` message.

Hi @acozzette
thank again for your response I think it's in the right direction.

I've tried to use that function but it require a descriptor class

So to make it work I need a way to generate a Descriptor class from the
descriptor binary representation.

here's what I tried (it doesn't work...)

```
from google.protobuf import reflection as _reflection
from google.protobuf.descriptor_pb2 import FileDescriptorSet

_DESCR_FILE = 'automation.descr'
_BIN_FILE = 'automation.bin'

with open(_DESCR_FILE, 'rb') as f:
    descriptorFile = f.read()

descriptorSetObject = FileDescriptorSet.parseFrom(descriptorFile)

with open(_BIN_FILE, 'rb') as f:
    bin_file = f.read()

_decoded_msg = _reflection.ParseMessage(descriptorSetObject, bin_file)

``` 
Anyone else can help?

Thanks
Nick

I think the problem is that `reflection.ParseMessage` takes a message descriptor but you're passing it a `FileDescriptorSet`. You have to find the `DescriptorProto` for the message you're interested in within the `FileDescriptorSet`, and then call `descriptor.MakeDescriptor(...)` to convert that into a descriptor object which you can then pass to `reflection.ParseMessage`. There's some example code in reflection_test.py here: https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/6a4fec616ec4b20f54d5fb530808b855cb664390/python/google/protobuf/internal/reflection_test.py#L1155
Let me close this just to tidy up my open issues, but feel free to reply here again if you have more questions.

title: [PHP] Segfaults with a wrong autoloader for GPBMetadata

nodes.body: In TextToSpeech/src/V1/ListVoicesResponse.php, line 26, it's referencing class in \GPBMetadata. However, metadata files are put in metadata. My guess is ```php_metadata_namespace``` was added to proto file after the code was initially generated. After  ```php_metadata_namespace``` was added, other generated code were not updated.

Thanks! Here is what I found out so far.

The proto file:
https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/cloud/texttospeech/v1/cloud_tts.proto

It doesn't have `php_metadata_namespace`.

The name resolution in PHP land is done by the autoloader, and the composer.json has the configuration for it:
https://github.com/tmatsuo/google-cloud-php/blob/tts/TextToSpeech/composer.json#L9

```composer.json
            "GPBMetadata\\Google\\Cloud\\TextToSpeech\\": "metadata"
```

and the code is using lower case namespace:

```php
        \GPBMetadata\Google\Cloud\Texttospeech\V1\CloudTts::initOnce();
```

So very likely the right namespace configuration will fix the issue. I'll try that tomorrow.

Yes, the correct path for the autoloader fixed the issue.

I still think the current behavior is not ideal though.
I think the user is supposed to use ```php_metadata_namespace```

title: Allow filenames in _CalledFromGeneratedFile to contain "/pb2/"
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
python (c++ implementation)

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

The company I work with strips the _pb2 suffix from the filenames of the generated python modules. Instead a pb2 python subpackage (e.g. ``companyname.pb2``) is created, which denotes that the modules in this pb2 subpackage are generated by protoc (and postprocessed).

If the c++ implementation of the protobuf bindings is used, importing those generated modules does not work:

```
    652 
    653     def __new__(cls, name, index, number, type=None, options=None):
--> 654       _message.Message._CheckCalledFromGeneratedFile()
    655       # There is no way we can build a complete EnumValueDescriptor with the
    656       # given parameters (the name of the Enum is not known, for example).

TypeError: Descriptors should not be created directly, but only retrieved from their parent.
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Given that a similar bug/feature request was recently fixed (#4262), I would like that _CalledFromGeneratedFile returns true when the filename contains the string "/pb2/".

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

nodes.body:
Do you know why your company strips the _pb2 suffix? 

#4262 is for cython which is a common issue. I don't think it make sense to make a fix if it is only an issue that caused by your company's change.

Yes, I know. It was me who created this `companyname.pb2.xxx` package hierarchy format for our compiled proto-files years ago.

I created this convention because I think that this hierarchy is more pythonic than having modules suffixed with _pb2.

There is a comment in https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/HEAD/python/google/protobuf/pyext/descriptor.cc#L94

suggesting to completely remove the (hacky) `_CalledFromGeneratedFile` function. Are there any updates on this?
@anandolee what do you think about this feature request? Does it make sense if I come up with a PR?

I agree to remove this function, it is a behavior diffs between pure python and c extension as well. 

Add @amauryfa on the TODO-removal, do we still have something to be worried for the removal?

FYI: I've started to work on the removal of _CalledFromGeneratedFile in https://github.com/thisch/protobuf/commit/e0ae30255f1292d8a7e100d012224e603654d671 (there are some python tests that fail with this change: https://travis-ci.org/thisch/protobuf/jobs/428294435)

title: Move protobuf to its own github organization.
body:
Dear Protobuf users,

Since 3.0.0 release, we have brought official support for several new languages into protobuf. Due to that growth, we are considering moving the project to its own github organization. This can help us better manage the project and improve the support we provide to the community.

An organization will allow us to add support for more languages outside the main repo. We can include repos for helpful tools/utilities that are not suitable to bundled with the protobuf core library. Having them all under a single organization can help make them more discoverable.

The github organization we are considering moving to is:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers

After the move, the main protobuf repository will be: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf.

While we believe this move will be seamless for us and the users as everything will be redirected, we want to make sure we have considered all corner cases. Please help us with that by filling up this survey:

https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeH1ckwm6ZrSfmtrOjRwmF3yCSWQbbO5pTPqPb6_rUppgvBqA/viewform

Suggestions on how we should structure the organization are welcome.

- Google Protobuf Team

nodes.body:
> add support for more languages outside the main repo

So will you allow other developers to move their language implementations to the organization like [golang/protobuf](https://github.com/golang/protobuf) or [apple/swift-protobuf](https://github.com/apple/swift-protobuf/) if they desire?

> So will you allow other developers to move their language implementations to the organization like golang/protobuf or apple/swift-protobuf if they desire?

I would hope so, but it's not protobuf-team's call and I'll need to consult the management/legal team about this. I'm not very optimistic about it though.
One thing I would love to see in the future would be the built-in "plugins" (e.g. `--cpp_out`, `--python_out` become separate executables with their own repositories and separate contributors.

Thanks to everyone who has participated in the survey! Here is the overview of the survey result:

![screenshot from 2018-08-17 14-28-00](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8551050/44289606-e25e7480-a229-11e8-91e6-dc243b43e515.png)

A few people have concerns about whether the move will make it harder to find Google official implementations, but we believe this issue be addressed with proper documentations.

Some questions that have been brought up:
1. Can you use the shorter name "protobuf" for the organization? We would very much like to, but unfortunately no. [The "protobuf" github account has been taken by someone else](https://github.com/protobuf), and we cannot convince either github or the owner of that account to transfer it to us. With that option unavailable to us, "protocolbuffers" seems the best one among the alternatives.
2. Are other protobuf projects (e.g., golang/protobuf) also moving to this organization? Maybe. For different languages the best location to host the protobuf repository may differ. If the owners believe moving it to our protocolbuffers organization will help make it more discoverable, we will work with them to coordinate the move. Right now only this protobuf main repository will be moved to the organization.
3. Will you accept unofficial community projects into this organization? We are willing to accept community contributed projects but the exact process hasn't been determined yet. We will announce the process when it's decided.

I'm starting the move for this repo right now.

The repo is now at its new location:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf

Everything should just work as it is before. I will update all references in our code base to the new location.

title: undefined reference to `google::protobuf::internal::SerializeInternal'
body:
Compiling protocolbuffers 3.5.1 for Cortex-M4 processor.

using the following commands:

```
 ./configure  --host=arm-none-eabi --build=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --prefix=/usr --exec-prefix=/usr --sysconfdir=/etc --localstatedir=/var --program-prefix= --disable-gtk-doc --disable-doc --disable-docs --disable-documentation --with-xmlto=no --with-fop=no --disable-dependency-tracking --disable-ipv6 --disable-debug --enable-static --enable-shared --with-protoc=/usr/local/bin/protoc CFLAGS=--specs=rdimon.specs CXXFLAGS=--specs=rdimon.specs CC=/github/arm-none-eabi_gcc_6.3.1/arm-none-eabi/bin/arm-none-eabi-gcc CXX=/github/arm-none-eabi_gcc_6.3.1/arm-none-eabi/bin/arm-none-eabi-g++ --without-thread-safety

cd src/

make CFLAGS=--specs=rdimon.specs CXXFLAGS='--specs=rdimon.specs -DLANG_CX11 -DPROTOBUF_WITHOUT_THREAD_SAFETY  -mthumb -mcpu=cortex-m4 -ffunction-sections  -mlong-calls -mcpu=cortex-m4 -Os' CC=/github/arm-none-eabi_gcc_6.3.1/arm-none-eabi/bin/arm-none-eabi-gcc CXX=/github/arm-none-eabi_gcc_6.3.1/arm-none-eabi/bin/arm-none-eabi-g++ libprotobuf-lite.la 
```

note: you need arm-none-eabi_gcc_6.3.1 

This builds with after minor modifications to the Mutex library (replace the implementation with empty functions)

When linking the created libprotobuf-lite.a with my project, the linker complains about the following:

```
 Error		undefined reference to `google::protobuf::internal::SerializeInternal(unsigned char const*, google::protobuf::internal::FieldMetadata const*, int, google::protobuf::io::CodedOutputStream*)'	XXXX	XXXX\Debug\message_lite.cc	1
 Error		undefined reference to `google::protobuf::internal::SerializeInternalToArray(unsigned char const*, google::protobuf::internal::FieldMetadata const*, int, bool, unsigned char*)'	XXXX	XXXX\Debug\message_lite.cc	1
```

nodes.body: Those two functions are defined in `src/google/protobuf/generated_message_util.cc`, so I'm not sure why they would be missing. Could you check if they were included in `libprotobuf-lite.a`? Another thing to note is that SerializeInternal and SerializeInternalToArray are only used for the experimental table-driven serialization, which is not being used yet. So if you just want a quick fix to get things building, you could probably delete those functions and their call sites without breaking any real functionality.

It seems the function is included in the library (same for SerializeInternalToArray):
```
/github/arm-none-eabi_gcc_6.3.1/arm-none-eabi/arm-none-eabi/bin/readelf -a libprotobuf-lite.a  | ag SerializeInternal
Relocation section '.rel.text._ZN6google8protobuf8internal17SerializeInternalEPKhPKNS1_13FieldMetadataElPNS0_2io17CodedOutputStreamE' at offset 0x62f0 contains 71 entries:
Relocation section '.rel.ARM.exidx.text._ZN6google8protobuf8internal17SerializeInternalEPKhPKNS1_13FieldMetadataElPNS0_2io17CodedOutputStreamE' at offset 0x6528 contains 2 entries:
Unwind table index '.ARM.exidx.text._ZN6google8protobuf8internal17SerializeInternalEPKhPKNS1_13FieldMetadataElPNS0_2io17CodedOutputStreamE' at offset 0x1f74 contains 1 entries:
0x0 <_ZN6google8protobuf8internal17SerializeInternalEPKhPKNS1_13FieldMetadataElPNS0_2io17CodedOutputStreamE>: 0x8034afb0
```

I've found the problem, the declaration and definition of SerializeInternal and SerializeInternalToArray is different:
```
LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT void SerializeInternal(const uint8* base, const FieldMetadata* table,
                       int num_fields, ::google::protobuf::io::CodedOutputStream* output);

void SerializeInternal(const uint8* base,
                       const FieldMetadata* field_metadata_table,
                       int32 num_fields,
                       ::google::protobuf::io::CodedOutputStream* output) {
```
should be
```
LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT void SerializeInternal(const uint8* base, const FieldMetadata* table,
                       int32 num_fields, ::google::protobuf::io::CodedOutputStream* output);
```

When changing int to int32 in the declaration, the linker can find the definition and my program compiles!
Nice, I'm glad to hear you got it working! If you're interested you can send us a pull request with that fix and I'll merge it.

here you go!
https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/4815
Thanks!

title: C# ToString() cannot handle bidirectional references, causing a stack overflow and secure data leakage
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.5.1 (NuGet official)
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
OSX, Windows

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
.NET 4.5 w/ JetBrains Rider IDE

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create two protobufs messages which have a bidirectional reference, i.e.:
```
message ParentMessage {
  ChildMessage child = 1;
}

message ChildMessage {
  ParentMessage parent = 1;
}
```

2. Assign the two messages to reference each other:
```
ParentMessage parent = new ParentMessage();
ChildMessage child = new ChildMessage() { Parent = parent };
parent.Child = child;
```

3. Attempt to print one of the objects:
`Console.WriteLine($"Parent: {parent}");`

Note the stack-overflow and crash. Also note that there is no way around the bug. Sealed partial classes cannot override the `ToString()` implementation. Also note that the `ToString()` implementation may not match with the developer's needs. `ToString()` is often used by debuggers, loggers, etc. and implementing it in a way which cannot be changed deprives developers of an essential feature necessary for use in a business-grade production-safe environment. For example: the protobuf message might include PII (i.e., passwords) which should not be placed into a log file. Libraries relying upon standard introspection features will inevitably end up logging sensitive data, making Protobuf unusable under these sorts of standard security constraints.

**What did you expect to see**
At least some built-in recursion detection. Preferably a pluggable way to replace the built-in serialization methods.

**What did you see instead?**
See above.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
N/A

nodes.body: If you intentionally create cyclic references in the class structure, there isn't nothing the implementation can do. It's just not supported.

@xfxyjwf (1) of course there's something the implementation can do. It's called recursion detection. I've personally implemented it in at least two other projects at large companies. (2) Intentional or unintentional, this has the potential to crash debuggers and entire IDEs. It's simply not a safe bug to have in a Object-level function like `ToString()`, especially when that implementation cannot be changed by the developer.

To be clear: I'm not arguing that protobufs should support bidirectional relationships overall. I understand why this would be undesirable. But the current implementation appears to serve no good purpose. Why does `ToString()` need to serialize into JSON? Isn't the whole point of protobufs to move AWAY from JSON? What if I don't want the serialized version of my messages to print the ENTIRE object?

All I'm saying is that this is not a good implementation of `ToString()`. If it were, say, `Inspect()` or `ToJSON()`, I'd be in support of it.

@zaneclaes As I said, what you are doing is not supported. When you intentionally add cycles into the class structure, the behavior of protobuf runtime should be undefined. If we can catch the error early without adding too much complexity, that's something we should do, but I don't think we want to add complexity or API to let you get around with it.

@zaneclaes Please understand that we are very cautious about API changes. I do not think the problem you are having (code throws exceptions because of incorrect protobuf usage) is worth fixing with an API change. Users facing this problem should just fix their code. If it is causing IDE/inspector to crash, I think it's the IDE/inspector's problem because they should be able to work with any kind of code. If we are to introduce a feature that lets users customize ToString(), it should be for a better use case.
I'm convinced by @xfxyjwf 's last point. IDE/inspectors should be ready to handle any exception from user code.

title: Generated pb2.py files should contain `from __future__ import absolute_import`
body:
I am using protoc 3.5.1 to generate *_pb2.py files.
My Python version is Python 2.7.12 running on Ubuntu 16.04.

I organize my files in a hierarchical structure:

```
my_package
  pb
    my_lib.proto
    sys
      service.proto
```

After generation of pb2.py files and placing `__init__.py` files there, my structure looks like this:

```
my_package
  __init__.py
  pb
    __init__.py
    my_lib_pb2.py
    sys
      __init__.py
      service_pb2.py
``` 

If I now try and import from python:

```
import my_package.pb.my_lib_pb2
```
it fails with the following output:
```
File "/home/my_user/.local/lib/python2.7/site-packages/my_package-py2.7.egg/my_package/pb/my_lib_pb2.py", line 6, in <module>
    _b=sys.version_info[0]<3 and (lambda x:x) or (lambda x:x.encode('latin1'))
AttributeError: 'module' object has no attribute 'version_info'
```

The following pb2.py was generated by protoc:
```
# Generated by the protocol buffer compiler.  DO NOT EDIT!
# source: my_package/pb/my_lib.proto

import sys
_b=sys.version_info[0]<3 and (lambda x:x) or (lambda x:x.encode('latin1'))

...
```

However, using Python 2.7, it now imports the `sys` module inside `my_package\pb` folder instead of the module which comes with Python. Using Python 3.5, everything works as expected, because absolute imports are the default policy in Python > 3.0
If protoc generated a line
```
from __future__ import absolute_import
```
right before the `import sys` statement, the issue would be solved.

I'm not sure if this line could break anything, but since it is the default behaviour for Python > 3.0, I would doubt it.

Python 2 is no longer supported.
