title: How to get position in string when a DecodeError is raised?
body:
### Premise 
I'm attempting to write a simple routine to recover a `string` or `bytes` field from a lossy message however when the field is truncated a `DecodeError` is raised it doesn't describe in what message (type) or position in the buffer the error occurred.

### Question
Is there a way to _hook_ DecodeError to get more fidelity when using `Message:ParseFromString`? 

### Example 
I have an example [in this repo](https://github.com/matutter/protobuf-recovery).

Consider the v3 protobuf here.
```
message MyMessage {
  int32 id = 1;
  string meta = 2;
  string text = 3;
}
```

The field `text` is prone to lossy/truncated transmission. Currently, a `DecodeError` is thrown and the last `MyMessage` is parsed such that `id` and `meta` are recovered but `text` is unset. However, if 1000 bytes of a 1024 byte `text` message is present in the buffer being decoded I lose 97% of a useful message. If I knew the position in the raw-buffer being parsed, I would know the size that `text` should be and could recover it.

Consider the data here.

```
00000110: 38 5B 6D 65 73 73 61 67 65 20 33 3A 57 45 4A 54    8[message.3:WEJT
00000120: 57 44 41 5A 4D 4B 34 30 57 32 4F 47 47 57 37 33    WDAZMK40W2OGGW73
00000130: 46 51 35 43 30 58 4F 30 52 55 4A 34 46 42 47 31    FQ5C0XO0RUJ4FBG1
00000140: 4A 52 51 57 4F 32 59 34 5D                         JRQWO2Y4]
```
Address `0x00000110` has a Int8 value of `56` which is the size the `text` field should be. If i only received a portion of those 56 bytes I could potentially recover it by padding it with `\0` (to make protobuf accept it) and let my application deal with the lossyness of the actual data itself.

If I only had the offset into the buffer where the message being parsed started (`0x00000110`) recovery could be possible.

nodes.body:
Where the parsing ends is entirely up to the parser implementation. In particular our python implementation has a C extension that makes use of C++ parsing code and doesn't return a position at all when parsing fails. It's not possible for the DecodeError to return a position.

I would suggest write a tool to do the padding before feeding it to the proto parser. We actually already have such a library inside Google which does exactly this (recover truncated proto data as much as possible) and it could be a candidate for a new opensource repo.

title: Duplicate custom option names generate compiler error

nodes.body: Your proposal can't be implemented. The name of the extension will be used as the name of the generated extension identifier. For extensions in the same scope their generated extension identifiers will be put inside the same scope in the generated code as well (e.g., in the same C++ namespace, or in the same Java class). If two extensions have the same name, their generated extension identifiers will have the same name and the generated code won't compile. We cannot change this because how and where the extension identifiers are generated is part of protobuf public API.

title: (Minor) Unnecessary integer conversion compilation warning in arena_impl.h
body:
Version: v3.6.0 (present in master as well)

Recreation:
You can see the error when building BVLC's caffe using protobuf with the CUDA nvcc compiler,
although it is easy to understand how this can be seen with other project builds and possibly other
compilers.

The build results in multiple repeated lines of warnings that look like this:
/opt/DL/protobuf/include/google/protobuf/arena_impl.h(55): warning: integer conversion resulted in a change of sign
/opt/DL/protobuf/include/google/protobuf/arena_impl.h(309): warning: integer conversion resulted in a change of sign
/opt/DL/protobuf/include/google/protobuf/arena_impl.h(310): warning: integer conversion resulted in a change of sign

It's a minor issue, but it is a nuisance for the 'caffe' project as the build output is flooded with literally hundreds of repeats of this warning.

Output will vary depending on where the header is installed, of course, but the warning is self-explanatory.  Investigation shows that a negative integer is being used as a mask for an unsigned type of size_t.

It appears this could be avoided via a cast, for example (lines 309-310):
-  static const size_t kBlockHeaderSize = (sizeof(Block) + 7) & -8;
-  static const size_t kSerialArenaSize = (sizeof(SerialArena) + 7) & -8;
+  static const size_t kBlockHeaderSize = (sizeof(Block) + 7) & (size_t)-8;
+  static const size_t kSerialArenaSize = (sizeof(SerialArena) + 7) & (size_t)-8;

nodes.body:
The descriptor for each message (implementation detail) is distinguished by its proto fully qualified name, which is package + message name.
In your example, although you provided different php_namespace, you don't give different package. So in the perspective of protobuf, two ```in``` have the same fully qualified name.
You should define different pacakage in these two proto files.

nodes.body: Looks like you cannot do field.default_value if field.has_default_value == False. Seems reasonable behavior to me.

    _descriptor.FieldDescriptor(

      number=4, type=11, cpp_type=10, label=3,

```

```

```python

title: Option definition allows no value

nodes.body: We probably can't reject it out right because it will be a breaking change. Generating warning for such empty definitions seems appropriate.

I'd suggest a different plan: disallow by default and add extra flag to do the wrong thing.

I don't believe there are that many cases of this in the wild, but when there are, they are genuine bugs: nobody wants an option with no value. This was also the case when I discovered this behavior: a programmer mistakenly commented out the value inside the curly block, but the compiler didn't catch the error.

title: Convert unset StringValue to null when printing to JSON
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Java and proto3

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

When converting a JSON like
```json
{ "a": null }
```
to a protobuf 3 message with definition
```
message example {
    google.protobuf.StringValue a = 1;
}
```
using `JsonFormat.Parser`, the StringValue is unset, which is expected.

**However**, when using `JsonFormat.Printer` on the parsed message to convert it to JSON, we get `{}`. I expect to get `{ "a": null }` since according to the official docs' section on JSON mapping, it mentions `null` is allowed with wrapper types and the comments in the source code of the wrapper types definition mention they all have respective JSON representations.

title: repeated primitives in Java TextFormat
body:
Dear all,

The Java TextFormat implementation doesn't seem to support the 'short form' in the c++ version for repeated primitives. 

It not only creates long-winded results in some cases, but this mismatch between languages also causes headache when try to parse messages authorized in one with another.

Any suggestions are welcome.

Best Regards,
Difu
  
For example,
data: [0, 1] in c++
vesus 
data: 0
data: 1
in java.

nodes.body: We can probably add an option to Java TextFormat to do the same.

sounds like this should simply be done unconditionally (though that risks breaking poorly written golden tests) or not done at all. I don't think an option is needed.

go/textformat-spec

This seems to be already [supported](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/a3c8e2deb05186334b7ee8c1174f44802e38b43d/java/core/src/test/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormatTest.java#L1502-L1508).
Closing the issue as it's not reproducible.

title: [python] in interactive mode, `add()` modifies repeated message field even when there's an error
body:
Not sure if this is a bug in protobuf or in my expectations, but this behavior unpleasantly surprised me.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.0
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
macOS 10.13.5

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.6.5

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Compile this .proto definition:
  ```proto
syntax = "proto3";

message SomeMessage {
	repeated ListElement some_list = 1;
}

message ListElement {
	string value = 1;
}
```
2. Run python3 in interactive mode and run the following:
```python
import some_proto_pb2

some_message = some_proto_pb2.SomeMessage()
some_message.some_list.add("foo")  # whoops, forgot to add value=
some_message.some_list.add(valu="foo") # whoops, spelled value wrong
some_message.some_list.add(value="foo")
print(some_message.some_list)
```

**What did you expect to see**
After running this code, I expected `some_message.some_list` to contain a single element because the first two calls to `add()` produced errors, and I therefore expected them not to modify the collection. I.e., I expected `print(some_message.some_list)` to output:
```python
[value: "foo"
]
```

**What did you see instead?**
Instead, `some_message.some_list` contained two empty elements, followed by the element I expected:
```python
[, , value: "foo"
]
```


Here's a copy & paste from my interpreter:
```python
>>> import some_proto_pb2
>>> 
>>> some_message = some_proto_pb2.SomeMessage()
>>> some_message.some_list.add("foo")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
TypeError: No positional arguments allowed
>>> some_message.some_list.add(valu="foo")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ValueError: Protocol message ListElement has no "valu" field.
>>> some_message.some_list.add(value="foo")
value: "foo"

>>> print(some_message.some_list)
[, , value: "foo"
]
```

nodes.body: Do you know what interactive mode will do after an error is raised: continue with the rest code or stop at the error?  The behavior on your example seems like interactive mode continues with the rest code after error is raised, if it is the feature of interactive mode, then the behavior it correct.
I don't think this is a feature of interactive mode, but I'm not 100% sure. It's hard for me to imagine the interpreter being able to continue execution after an unhandled exception.

What's the behavior if you do in a .py file by try:
```
try:
  some_message.some_list.add("foo") 
except:
  pass
```

In python 3 I don't get an exception (interestingly, with python 2 I get `TypeError: __new__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'serialized_options'`).

I also ran this slightly modified version with python 3:
```py
import some_proto_pb2

some_message = some_proto_pb2.SomeMessage()

print(some_message.some_list)
print(len(some_message.some_list))

try:
  some_message.some_list.add("foo") 
except:
  pass

print(some_message.some_list)
print(len(some_message.some_list))
```
and got this output:
```sh
$ python3 bar.py 
[]
0
[]
1
```

I've tried the following test:
```
  def testAddWrongRepeatedNestedField(self, message_module):
    msg = message_module.TestAllTypes()
    try:
      msg.repeated_nested_message.add("wrong")
    except TypeError:
      pass
    try:
      msg.repeated_nested_message.add(value="wrong")
    except ValueError:
      pass
    self.assertEqual(len(msg.repeated_nested_message), 0)
```

It can pass with pure python in both python2 and python3. Can not pass with python c extension for both python2 and python3 (len is 2 with protobuf python c extension). 


Corresponding code is in AddToAttached, we called AddMessage() first:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/pyext/repeated_composite_container.cc#L142

But do the init check later:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/pyext/repeated_composite_container.cc#L154

Reverse the order could fix the issue. I've created a change for review in our internal code.
Thanks to raise this issue up

title: any_proto weirdness under Bazel 0.15 -c opt vs fastbuild
body:
When I link in the any_proto target and build my executable with -c opt, at startup the program tries to add any.proto to the internal descriptor pool twice and fails. With the default configuration (fastbuild), it does not do this. I can't drop any_proto as a transitive dependency because I have other messages that require the definition of the Any message. What could be going wrong, and why would it differ between build configurations?

I've got an open issue in our project (https://github.com/google/kythe/issues/2834) with more details. The target I'm trying to fix is `//kythe/cxx/common:path_utils_test`

nodes.body: It seems like the any proto is linked into the binary twice? Can you try to add a test in the protobuf code base to reproduce the issue?
Yes, that's what it looks like. Why would this only happen with `-c opt`? It seems to affect any target that depends (transitively) on any_proto.
Fixed by updating to protobuf 3.6.0. Further details in https://github.com/google/kythe/commit/27addcb0b06688d3b080486d57cab0459e9f0f06

title: received SIGSEGV signal when used in Qt gui project
body:
I'm in trouble using protobuf within a Qt gui project.
I'm using ubuntu 16.04 and QT 5.10.
The problem is that, I can compile my project, but cannot run it. It crash because a segmentation error signal. Is it because Qt gui use some library that conflict with protobuf?

nodes.body:
solved by

replace
LIB += -lprotobuf
with
LIBS += /usr/local/lib/libprotobuf.a

Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

I would like to compile the protobuf files related to a specific repository when the CI step is gonna be executed - TravisCI, etc, .. - or when the project is being packaged  - Docker image, etc, .. - to make it ready to be used in production.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like to see how the Python compiler - already shipped with the `protoc` command - is also provided by the Python wheel [1].

So, making the protobuf wheel a requirement of a specific project that uses the protobuf files will allow us to compile the proto files, besides using them.

The compiler might be shipped as an entry point [2] of the setup.py, for example with the name `protoc_python` that would use under the hood the same code as `protoc` but shipped as a library. 

**Additional context**

We, our organization, are considering to ignore the protocol buffer files that are generated from the protobuf files, so not adding them as regular files that are being tracked by the CVS - GIT, etc - system, generating them when they are needed.

Why? Basically, because we do believe that the files generated by the compiler should be none opinionated not being under discussion. Having them as regular CSV files, as other Python files, is a prone error system that can end up with some of the following errors:

- Update the proto files but not generating again the python output file related to that proto files
- Modify the python output files
- etc.

So definitely, we do believe that the python output files that are generated from proto files must be immutables and making them not regular CSV files allow us to get rid of most of the mistakes.

**Aditional advantages**

Also, its worth considers as an additional advantage of compiling the proto files when they are gonna be used as a way of aligning the protobuf version used by the compiler and the runtime library. Right now, this can not be assured.

[1] https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/
[2] https://setuptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/setuptools.html

Protobufs are not guaranteed to store their field data within the footprint of their object. title: C#: Missing Runtime Types for descriptor protos

nodes.body: MessageDescriptor is the runtime type for DescriptorProto. What information do you need but is missing in MessageDescriptor?

I assume DescriptorProto is changed to internal because some proto2 features are not supported.

The access level is change in:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/commit/493e3db98532e99a53cec914d8f4827a556ee408#diff-40a612bde80077a230c176f78b24b669

@jskeet , do you remember why descriptor protos should be private? Are we safe to change it to public or it should wait for proto2 support.

No, we should **not** change them to be public. They're generated as if they were proto3, but only because we know that within Google.Protobuf we don't care about the different semantics. We don't want unrestricted code facing the same issues.

Additionally, we wouldn't want to expose the DescriptorProto instances directly due to mutability.

If we implement proto2, we can make DescriptorProto public, and we could then return clones from the Descriptor class etc.

Fundamentally, this situation is a proto3 file referring to a proto2 file, and that's not supported in C# codegen. It so happens that it's DescriptorProto, but any other proto would fail as well.

So then, should protoc CSharp generation refer to the appropriate run-time representations instead? In other words, should it convert `DescriptorProto` to `MessageDescriptor` much like how the `Int32Value` members get converted to` System.Nullable<int>`?

No, I don't think that would be appropriate either. Basically, using `DescriptorProto` depends on implementing the proto2 features (and then cloning, but that's relatively straightforward). Until that point, I wouldn't expect you to be able to use the message in your first comment.

As proto2 is not supported, we are unable to make them public or provide a run-time representation. @ObsidianMinor is working on proto2 support ( #4642 and more) , we can make DescriptorProto public after that.

Closing this issue for clean up. Feel free to reopen after proto2 is supported or if you have any other questions.

title: Protobuf 3.5.x Fails to Compile on GCC 7+ With -std Less Than C++11
body:
**Version:** v3.5.1
**Language:** C++
**Operating System:** Linux - Debian Testing
**Compiler:** GCC 7.3.0 (Debian GCC 7.3.0-5, specifically)

**Steps to reproduce the behavior:**
1. Compile Protobuf with the -std=gnu++98 flag set

**Expected result:**
Protobuf compiles, as C++98 is still supported on the 3.5.x releases.

**Actual result:**
Protobuf fails to compile with the following error:

```
In file included from ./src/google/protobuf/stubs/common.h:45:0,
                 from ./src/google/protobuf/map.h:45,
                 from ./src/google/protobuf/generated_message_table_driven.h:34,
                 from ./src/google/protobuf/generated_message_table_driven_lite.h:34,
                 from ./src/google/protobuf/generated_message_table_driven_lite.cc:31:
./src/google/protobuf/map_entry_lite.h: In member function ‘bool google::protobuf::internal::MapEntryImpl<Derived, Base, Key, Value, kKeyFieldType, kValueFieldType, default_enum_value>::MergePartialFromCodedStream(google::protobuf::io::CodedInputStream*)’:
./src/google/protobuf/stubs/port.h:247:57: warning: c++11 attributes only available with -std=c++11 or -std=gnu++11
 # define GOOGLE_FALLTHROUGH_INTENDED [[gnu::fallthrough]]
                                                         ^
./src/google/protobuf/map_entry_lite.h:204:11: note: in expansion of macro ‘GOOGLE_FALLTHROUGH_INTENDED’
           GOOGLE_FALLTHROUGH_INTENDED;
           ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

**Investigation:**
The issue is that port.h assumes that `[[gnu::fallthrough]]` is always available on GCC 7+. While the `gnu::fallthrough` annotation is available from 7 on, the C++ annotations feature is *not* available unless the standard in use is C++11 or newer.

This problem exists only on Protobuf 3.5.x releases. Earlier releases did not have this code path. Later releases require C++11 or greater and have removed `GOOGLE_FALLTHROUGH_INTENDED`.

title: C++ aggregate initialization

nodes.body:
I don't have a strong opinion here. But I think we need t o be careful. For one we want the proto compiler to have the ability to reorder fields, while aggregate initialization needs to have to order as specified in the code.

Also removing a field and make it reserved seems a dangerous operation.

Josh any thoughts?

Any kind of order-based initialization seems dangerous, since fields can be added and removed. Also it's unclear whether the order would be based on field number or declaration order in the .proto file.

It seems that aggregate init is not compatible with the primary goals of protobuf. Namely provide a stable back and forwards compatible extensible protocol, both on the wire and as a programming library.
C++20 introduces [designated initializers](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/aggregate_initialization#Designated_initializers). Maybe we can revisit the request?

nodes.body: I think you are missing threading support. Maybe -pthread as an option

I checked your suggestion but -pthread is not missed!

I'm using pkg-config to add the right things to the build command and there is a difference
by 3.6.0! In case of 3.5.1 you can see that there is -lpthread option, but it is missing by 3.6.0!

root@um-deb8-dev:/protobuf/protobuf-3.5.1# protoc --version
libprotoc 3.5.1
root@um-deb8-dev:/protobuf/protobuf-3.5.1# pkg-config --libs --cflags protobuf
-pthread -I/usr/local/include -L/usr/local/lib -lprotobuf -pthread **-lpthread**

root@um-deb8-dev:/protobuf/protobuf-3.6.0# protoc --version
libprotoc 3.6.0
root@um-deb8-dev:/protobuf/protobuf-3.6.0# pkg-config --libs --cflags protobuf
-pthread -I/usr/local/include -L/usr/local/lib -lprotobuf -pthread 

But still you were right!
I realized that this error only happens when I build it as static!

I tried to build the binary by static flags:

g++ -g -std=c++11 -static -static-libstdc++ news.config.pb.cc proto_test_Config.cpp -o proto_test_Config $(pkg-config --libs --cflags protobuf) -lpthread

Not worked!
But it was not enough to add -lpthread to the end of the command!
I have found that linking with -lpthread can cause application crash and other interesting things in static builds! So I had to extend the build command and now works fine:

g++ -g -std=c++11 -static -static-libstdc++ news.config.pb.cc proto_test_Config.cpp -o proto_test_Config $(pkg-config --libs --cflags protobuf) **-Wl,--whole-archive -lpthread -Wl,--no-whole-archive**


So I can close this issue for now!

For example, I'd like to hint that a certain attribute has unique values, like a database has unique keys.

title: Incorrect code generation for nullable types using wrapper types

nodes.body:
If set to ValueOneOfCase.Int32Value for null value, after Serialize and Parse round the data will be changed:
Serialize: Wire format will not seriliaze oneofcase and nothing will be serialized for Value because it is null.
After Parse: ValueOneofCase will be None after Parse


Set null here is what we use as clear oneof field in other languages. However, there's still an issue: we probably need to check if the OneofCase is current field before clear, that's what we do in other languages.

title: Methods ParseFromString and SerializeToString are not generated
body:
Version: v3.6.0
Language: C++

OS: Linux Ubuntu

Compiler: GCC version

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Define my protocol messages as stated in the tutorial
2. Compile files with .proto extension
3. Try to use ParseFromString and SerializeToString methods but they are not generated i.e. there are no definitions in header file

nodes.body:
Solution to this problem is pretty simple.

Methods ParseFromString and SerializeToString are not supposed to have their definitions in a header file. They are rather part of protobuf library which needs to be linked to the project.

If you are using GCC you can link protobuf library by using following flags: -L/usr/local/lib -lprotobuf.
For the first flag I am not sure if it is required at all but you can try with or without it.

Closing my own issue

The resnet34v1.onnx is about 83M.

"pip install protobuf" will install the version with C extension if it's available on your platform. If the C extension is not available, it will fallback to the pure python version which will be much slower. That seems to explain the difference you are seeing.

I just build the protobuf with c++-impl.
`
python setup.py build --cpp_implementation
`
It's faster now.
Thank you.

title: [Ruby] Setting Array/Hash values is inconsistent/buggy
body:
Hi, the behavior in this issue describes has been consistent for all gem releases since 3.0.0.alpha, on all ruby versions, AFAIK. We have worked around it, but I think it can be better, especially as more and more gems are moving to being generated only instead of hand-written, and exposing the protobuf objects directly to users.

The ruby gem provides support for Ruby Array and Hash objects. It will automatically map an Array object to a protobuf RepeatedField object, and a Hash object to a protobuf Map object. Here are some examples using the `TestMessage` protobuf class used in the ruby tests:

```ruby
msg_by_array = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: [1, 2, 3, 4])
msg_by_array.repeated_int64.class #=> Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField
msg_by_array.repeated_int64.to_a #=> [1, 2, 3, 4]

msg_by_hash = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(map_string_string: { 'hello' => 'world' })
msg_by_hash.map_string_string.class #=> Google::Protobuf::Map
msg_by_hash.map_string_string.to_h #=> { 'hello' => 'world' }
```

This is great! Except you can't set a value on an instantiated protobuf object using Array or Hash, because it raises `TypeError`:

```ruby
msg_by_array.repeated_int64 = [1, 2, 3, 4] # TypeError
# TypeError: Expected repeated field array

msg_by_hash.map_string_string = { 'hello' => 'world' } # TypeError
# TypeError: Expected Map instance
```

You also can't set the value in the initializer with a protobuf object, or you get an `ArgumentError`:

```ruby
msg_by_rf = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: msg_by_array.repeated_int64) # ArgumentError
# ArgumentError: Expected array as initializer value for repeated field 'repeated_int64'.

msg_by_map = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(map_string_string: msg_by_hash.map_string_string) # ArgumentError
# ArgumentError: Expected Hash object as initializer value for map field 'map_string_string'.
```

This causes us to perform many workarounds, which for the most part is manageable. But, in general this doesn't seem to be very usable, as it requires users to run into errors more often than they expect.

I've created the following (failing) test file that demonstrates these concepts. It can be dropped into `ruby/test` and should run just fine.

```ruby
#!/usr/bin/ruby

require 'generated_code_pb'
require 'test/unit'

class MismatchedSettersTest < Test::Unit::TestCase

  def test_setting_Array_on_initializer
    m = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: [1, 2, 3, 4])
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField, m.repeated_int64)
    assert_equal([1, 2, 3, 4], m.repeated_int64.to_a)
  end

  def test_setting_RepeatedField_on_initializer
    m1 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: [1, 2, 3, 4])
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField, m1.repeated_int64)
    assert_equal([1, 2, 3, 4], m1.repeated_int64.to_a)

    # This fails with ArgumentError: Expected array as initializer value for repeated field 'repeated_int64'.
    # because it can't take a Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField
    m2 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: m1.repeated_int64)
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField, m2.repeated_int64)
    assert_equal([1, 2, 3, 4], m2.repeated_int64.to_a)
  end

  def test_setting_Array_on_accessor
    m = A::B::C::TestMessage.new
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField, m.repeated_int64)
    assert_not_equal([1, 2, 3, 4], m.repeated_int64.to_a)
    # This fails with TypeError: Expected repeated field array
    # because it expects the value to be Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField
    m.repeated_int64 = [1, 2, 3, 4]
    assert_equal([1, 2, 3, 4], m.repeated_int64.to_a)
  end

  def test_setting_RepeatedField_on_accessor
    m1 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: [1, 2, 3, 4])
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField, m1.repeated_int64)
    assert_equal([1, 2, 3, 4], m1.repeated_int64.to_a)

    m2 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField, m2.repeated_int64)
    assert_not_equal([1, 2, 3, 4], m2.repeated_int64.to_a)
    m2.repeated_int64 = m1.repeated_int64
    assert_equal([1, 2, 3, 4], m2.repeated_int64.to_a)
  end

  def test_setting_Hash_on_initializer
    m = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(map_string_string: { 'hello' => 'world' })
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::Map, m.map_string_string)
    assert_equal({ 'hello' => 'world' }, m.map_string_string.to_h)
  end

  def test_setting_Map_on_initializer
    m1 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(map_string_string: { 'hello' => 'world' })
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::Map, m1.map_string_string)
    assert_equal({ 'hello' => 'world' }, m1.map_string_string.to_h)

    # This fails with ArgumentError: Expected Hash object as initializer value for map field 'map_string_string'.
    # because it can't take a Google::Protobuf::Map
    m2 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(map_string_string: m1.map_string_string)
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::Map, m2.map_string_string)
    assert_equal({ 'hello' => 'world' }, m2.map_string_string.to_h)
  end

  def test_setting_Hash_on_accessor
    m = A::B::C::TestMessage.new
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::Map, m.map_string_string)
    assert_not_equal({ 'hello' => 'world' }, m.map_string_string.to_h)
    # This fails with TypeError: Expected Map instance
    # because it expects the value to be Google::Protobuf::Map
    m.map_string_string = { 'hello' => 'world' }
    assert_equal({ 'hello' => 'world' }, m.map_string_string.to_h)
  end

  def test_setting_Map_on_accessor
    m1 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(map_string_string: { 'hello' => 'world' })
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::Map, m1.map_string_string)
    assert_equal({ 'hello' => 'world' }, m1.map_string_string.to_h)

    m2 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new
    assert_kind_of(Google::Protobuf::Map, m2.map_string_string)
    assert_not_equal({ 'hello' => 'world' }, m2.map_string_string.to_h)
    m2.map_string_string = m1.map_string_string
    assert_equal({ 'hello' => 'world' }, m2.map_string_string.to_h)
  end

end
```

nodes.body: What is this issue looking for? Setting repeated/map fields with ruby array/map?
Or constructor with protobuf object?
Being able to assign an Array or Hash to an attribute, and assign a RepeatedField or Map in an initializer. Basically, make the failing tests pass.

This behavior is the result of some deliberate thinking/design. Basically we try to give predictable behavior, and avoid surprises. And we try to behave like `Struct` generally.

The tricky issue is that, to do proper type checking, we can't just take a reference to the existing array. Consider:

```
arr = [1, 2, 3, 4]
msg_by_array.repeated_int64 = arr

# Whoops, now our repeated int64 field has a string in it.
arr << "Broccoli"
```

Instead we need a separate array-like object, `RepeatedField`, that can enforce that all of the members have the correct type.

It would be possible to make field assignment on a protobuf do the equivalent of:

```
# msg_by_array.repeated_int64 = [1, 2, 3, 4]
msg_by_array.repeated_int64.replace([1, 2, 3, 4])
```

But this is un-Struct like, and would cause surprises if someone wrote:

```
arr = [1, 2, 3, 4]
msg_by_array.repeated_int64 = arr

# Whoops, won't affect msg_by_array.repeated_int64
# even though with Struct it would.
arr << 5 
```

To maintain consistency here, we decided not to allow direct assignment. Both of the following work as alternatives:

```
# Append
msg_by_array.repeated_int64 += [1, 2, 3, 4]

# Replace/assign.
msg_by_array.repeated_int64.replace([1, 2, 3, 4])
```

You could argue that we've already broken this model by allowing the following:

```
msg_by_array = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: [1, 2, 3, 4])
```

But I see that as more akin to how `Array#new` accepts an array parameter which it copies into the new array.

All that said, it's possible our efforts at consistency here are annoying people more than they are saving people from frustrating surprises. We just want to be cautious here, because "copy on assignment" is different than how almost everything else in Ruby works. You would never expect this to be doing any copying:

```
Struct.new("Foo", :a)
foo = Struct::Foo.new

# This will never copy a.
foo.a = a
```

I guess what I'm saying here is that if we can accept an Array in an initializer method, with all the appropriate type checking, then should be able to do the same on an attribute setter method. Similarly, if we can accept a ReleatedField on an attribute setter method, then should be able to accept it in an initializer method. Why is the behavior of initializer methods and attribute setter methods different?

We have seen developers both outside and inside Google bump into this.

> Why is the behavior of initializer methods and attribute setter methods different?

Because `Array#new(arr)` copies `arr` -- that's the prior art we're relying on for allowing it in the constructor. But `foo.a = a` rarely/never copies `a`, which is why we don't (currently) do that either.

On the other hand you're not the first person to ask for this. Here is another:

https://github.com/google/protobuf/pull/4385

Let me poll a few other people and see what they think.

If I were to prioritize, I would place supporting RepeatedField and Map objects in the initializer method above supporting Array and Hash objects on attribute setter methods. I find this behavior the most surprising and don't understand why this is not allowed.

Even though it is the lower priority in my mind, I would still like to see supporting Array and Hash objects on the attribute setter methods. Even with the understanding that the Array/Hash objects are not stored by the method, but mapped to the protobuf types in the class definition. I would offer that this edge case can be adequately explained in the attribute setter documentation so users would not be as confused by the behavior.

To be clear, mapping Array/Hash objects to RepeatedField/Map objects does challenge some ruby semantics. For example, Ruby parses and treats calls methods that end with `=` differently than other methods:

```ruby
class Foo
  def bar
    @bar
  end

  def bar=(new_bar)
    @bar = new_bar.reverse
  end
end

foo = Foo.new
# Chain calls
left_hand_bar = foo.bar = "bar"
# The foo object has the "mapped" value
foo.bar #=> "rab"
# The left-hand object has the original right-hand value
left_hand_bar #=> "bar"
```

That said, I still think the convenience of mapping the values to the correct types is worth the properly documented tweak to Ruby idioms.
@haberman any update?
I agree that there is no reason not to accept RepeatedField/Map in the constructor. Let me write a change to do that part.
Let me know if I can help, but I think #4385 would address this. I can help rebase/test if needed.
Here is another example of a user struggling with the unfriendliness of the current API: googleapis/google-cloud-ruby#2839

> I agree that there is no reason not to accept RepeatedField/Map in the constructor. Let me write a change to do that part.

@haberman Are you still planning on authoring a change to allow this?
Can we help with this? This is a pretty unfriendly API.

I came here from https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-ruby/issues/1477, and still did not find an answer. Why is this so difficult?

How do I create a RepeatedField of a custom type?  Just show me.  Give me an example.

Ugh.  Turns out the answer is just to create your message, and then push new items to that message's RepeatedField.

Here's a janky example:

Your proto is:

```
message InstrumentAttributes {
    ...
    repeated TradingHours trading_schedule = 6;
    ...
}
```

You want to set `trading_schedule` in your message.  Reading [the docs](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/ruby-generated#repeated-fields) might make you think you need to call `RepeatedField.new`, and if you were repeating a simple `string` or `int32`, you could do that.  But you can't, and the docs' example code doesn't demonstrate anything else.

The docs _do_ say that _"The RepeatedField type supports all of the same methods as a regular Ruby Array"_, but I missed it (until revising this comment).  I'm sure I can't be alone in that.

What you really want to do is this:

```
atts = MyNamespace::InstrumentAttributes.new
# atts.trading_hours is currently an empty RepeatedField

trading_hours1 = create_trading_hours() # returns a MyNamespace::TradingHours
trading_hours2 = create_trading_hours()
atts.trading_schedule.push(trading_hours1)
atts.trading_schedule.push(trading_hours2)
```

Now `atts.trading_hours` will be an array of your 2 elements.

I still don't actually know how to _create_ a `RepeatedField` of `MyNamespace::TradingHours`, but I guess I don't need to.

> I came here from [googleapis/google-cloud-ruby#1477](https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-ruby/issues/1477), and still did not find an answer. Why is this so difficult?
> 
> How do I create a RepeatedField of a custom type? Just show me. Give me an example.

You mentioned me there. It was a year ago and I have probably already forgot some details there also the gem has probably been updated a lot. That old code with old gem dependencies "just works" since then for my monitoring needs that did not expand.

As far as I remember, the point of my code was that in the `time_series.points` you have to define only the `time_series` while `points` is being defined automatically and you can just use it immediately to push values into it.

Maybe that snippet is not compatible with current gems -- it has their versions mentioned in comments if you scroll the snippet horizontally. I remember I've spent a day or two greping through libs and specs to come up with it so it's ok to find it to be difficult.

Sorry for the long inactivity on this issue. I agree that we should fix it, in both cases (constructor and assignment).

There is one unresolved question in my mind. Suppose you write:

```ruby
msg1 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: [1, 2, 3, 4])
msg2 = A::B::C::TestMessage.new(repeated_int64: msg1.repeated_int64) # ArgumentError
msg1.repeated_int64 << 5
print(msg2.repeated_int64.size)  # 4 or 5?
```

Should the last line print 4 or 5?

In other words, if you specify an existing `RepeatedField` object in the constructor, should we deep copy it, or point to it by reference?

> In other words, if you specify an existing `RepeatedField` object in the constructor, should we deep copy it, or point to it by reference?

I would expect a deep copy.

We triage inactive PRs and issues in order to make it easier to find active work. If this issue should remain active or becomes active again, please add a comment.

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago.
This continues to be an issue, but I do think this implementation: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/4385 fills the need here?

I think the main things blocking this now are just:

1. Deciding on a consistent set of semantics.
2. Implementing those semantics.
3. Waiting for a breaking change release (if the change ends up being breaking).

Point (1) mainly concerns the question of what is a deep copy vs a reference, ie. what I alluded to above in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4969#issuecomment-1234677460. I think we want to avoid doing deep copies for every kind of assignment, because people frequently want to do things like build a message tree from the leaves up. If every `msg.submsg = submsg` assignment was a deep copy, leaves-up builds would be really unnecessarily expensive.

Probably the simplest resolution would be to allow assignments that are currently rejected, like `msg.repeated_field = ruby_array`, and to only deep copy when performing this kind of implicit type conversion. That could also avoid making this a breaking change, since we wouldn't be changing the semantics of any existing (working) code.

title: contains invalid UTF-8 data when parsing a protocol buffer. Use the 'bytes' type if you intend to send raw bytes.

nodes.body: String fields are only intended for storing UTF-8 data, so if you need to send non-UTF-8 data then it is best to use a `bytes` field instead.

But the data has been changed to type-string on go server, why does the python client cannot parse this data? Maybe the python protobuf should do something to deal with those who contains non-UTF-8 data but defined as string in proto?

I'm not sure how the Go implementation currently handles this, but at least in C++ we validate that strings are UTF-8 during parsing but not during serialization. So if Go does something similar then it is possible to serialize protos with non-UTF-8 strings, which won't be detected later until that proto is parsed again.

If you need to be able to store non-UTF-8 data in that field then you might want to consider just changing it from a string field to a bytes field, which is usually a safe change to make.

title: MessageToJsonString discards extensions

nodes.body: MessageToJsonString only supports proto3 features at the moment. Extension is a proto2-only feature. Currently we don't have a plan to support it in proto3 JSON implementations.

As stated above, we do not implement extensions in C++. I have recently rewritten the C++ JSON codec, which we can hopefully land in a future release externally, which implements extensions, so this will be fixed "soon"; it is just a matter of waiting for our next major release.

./../third_party/googletest/googletest/include/gtest/internal/gtest-internal.h:133:55: warning: converting ‘false’ to pointer type for argument 1 of ‘char testing::internal::IsNullLiteralHelper(testing::internal::Secret*)’ [-Wconversion-null]

                                                       ^

nodes.body: This is more of a gtest issue than a protobuf one.

Well, it's gtest that's emitting the warnings, but wouldn't it be better to do the appropriate casts so that the warnings don't happen?  One of the reasons for such warnings is that comparisons between types that don't match can lead to unexpected equality.  It makes it more clear in the protobuf code that the particular projection in question is intended and safe.

Unfortunately, although cleaning this up is great, early Google style recommended `int` as the type for lengths. Unwinding this bit of tech debt completely would be a somewhat large effort that would be difficult to backstop; I am closing this as "not planned", since we do not have the bandwidth for it.

Note that the proto_path must be an exact prefix of the .proto file names -- protoc is too dumb to figure out when two paths (e.g. absolute and relative) are equivalent (it's harder than you think).

>protoc --csharp_out="A:\Output directory\" --proto_path="a:\proto_dir\" "a:\proto_dir\CNTK.proto"
a:\proto_dir\CNTK.proto: File does not reside within any path specified using --proto_path (or -I).  You must specify a --proto_path which encompasses this file.  Note that the proto_path must be an exact prefix of the .proto file names -- protoc is too dumb to figure out when two paths (e.g. absolute and relative) are equivalent (it's harder than you think).

A:\proto_dir>protoc.exe --csharp_out="A:\Output directory\" --proto_path=. CNTK.proto
Missing input file.

A:\proto_dir>protoc.exe --csharp_out="A:\Output directory\" --proto_path=./ CNTK.proto
Missing input file.

A:\proto_dir>protoc.exe --csharp_out="A:\Output directory\" CNTK.proto
Missing input file.

A:\proto_dir>protoc.exe --csharp_out="A:\" CNTK.proto
Missing input file.
```

nodes.body:
My educated guess is that this is due to the command-line argument parser handling the trailing slash in `--csharp_out="A:\Output directory\"` as "escape the next character" instead of "directory separator". I bet the arguments are being split as

```
a:\proto_dir\CNTK.proto
--csharp_out
A:\Output directory" --proto_path a:\proto_dir\
```

instead of the expected

```
a:\proto_dir\CNTK.proto
--csharp_out
A:\Output directory\
--proto_path
a:\proto_dir\
```

(This is a common problem on Windows.)
This is a duplicate of [#3028](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3028).  I'm not dismissing the underlying problem, but this isn't a bug in our protoc CLI

title: C# - Some types are missing
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.5.1
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
MacOS 10.13.6

**Problem**
I'm trying to generate C# gRPC bindings for the Google Assistant. The command succeeds with no errors/warnings, but types in the `Google.Api` and `Google.Type` namespaces are missing.  Am I doing something wrong or is it a possible bug?

**Script**
```
#!/bin/bash

GRPC_TOOLS_PATH=~/.nuget/packages/grpc.tools/1.14.0/tools/macosx_x64
OUT_PATH=Assistant.Lib

$GRPC_TOOLS_PATH/protoc \
-I ~/dev/github/google/googleapis \
-I ~/dev/github/google/protobuf/src \
--csharp_out $OUT_PATH \
--grpc_out $OUT_PATH ~/dev/github/google/googleapis/google/assistant/embedded/v1alpha2/embedded_assistant.proto \
--plugin=protoc-gen-grpc=$GRPC_TOOLS_PATH/grpc_csharp_plugin
```

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/446036/43635624-f2ea258a-970f-11e8-88c0-7eaf35cf625f.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/446036/43635648-01cdbd14-9710-11e8-9080-ce1616245cc6.png)

nodes.body:
Ok, so i got it working by explicitly specifying the extra proto files. Not sure if that is expected behavior? 

```
#!/bin/bash

GRPC_TOOLS_PATH=~/.nuget/packages/grpc.tools/1.14.0/tools/macosx_x64
PROTO_PATH=~/dev/github/google/googleapis/google
OUT_PATH=Assistant.Lib

$GRPC_TOOLS_PATH/protoc \
-I ~/dev/github/google/googleapis \
-I ~/dev/github/google/protobuf/src \
--csharp_out $OUT_PATH \
--grpc_out $OUT_PATH $PROTO_PATH/assistant/embedded/v1alpha2/embedded_assistant.proto $PROTO_PATH/type/latlng.proto $PROTO_PATH/api/annotations.proto $PROTO_PATH/api/http.proto \
--plugin=protoc-gen-grpc=$GRPC_TOOLS_PATH/grpc_csharp_plugin
```
+Jan, from grpc team

@trydis   I think your fix is correct.  The generated classes for `annotations.proto`, `http.proto` and others need to come from somewhere - so unless you generate them and include the generated code in your project, you'll get an error.

There are some "common" .proto files pregenerated that are bundled in the Google.Protobuf nuget, but those are the only the "well known types" that are defined in the google/protobuf repository (e.g. https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/timestamp.proto).
Google.Api and Google.Type aren't logically part of protobuf - from protobuf's (and grpc's) perspective, they are just another .proto files (for which you need to generate the .cs files).

As a side note, isn't there an official C# client library for Assistant API? Using it would save you the trouble.

Thanks for the explanation.

AFAIK the only official option is the Python library (https://developers.google.com/assistant/sdk/overview#sdk_components).

nodes.body: Hi @skinkie, I think there is a greater chance for this being investigated if you copy-paste in (the relevant parts) from your original issue (in `grpc-java`). This will make the information more easily accessible => lowers the threshold for people to dig deeper into this.

This should only be an issue for the wrapper class. It can be worked around by setting the `java_outer_classname` option to override the class name derived from the file:

```
option java_outer_classname = "MyProtos";
```

I'm not sure how much we want to fix this. There are a lot of file names that are not legal Java class names. Possibly we need a general solution for this problem.
I don't think we're going to change protoc to make this work. The one thing we perhaps should do is error out sooner in protoc itself rather than letting javac find and report the error.
Please set the java_outer_classname to solve this if your filename results in invalid generated names.

title: Add compiler types to C# like CodeGeneratorRequest / CodeGeneratorResponse
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Write a protoc plugin in C#

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Types from plugin.proto made available in a proposed Google.Protobuf.Compiler namespace, specifically CodeGeneratorRequest and CodeGeneratorResponse. Java library includes these types:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java/com/google/protobuf/compiler/PluginProtos.CodeGeneratorRequest.Builder

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Building my own artifact based on protobuf repo. For C# protoc will not build proto2 syntax, which plugin.proto is written in, so this means I'd have to keep a parallel hand-maintained proto3 variant of it.

nodes.body:
I'm actively working on this at the moment. My solution will involve:

- Allowing a set of `FileDescriptor`s to be loaded dynamically
- Potentially including the plugin types within Google.Protobuf (still TBD)

The reason for the latter is that we still won't provide access to `FileDescriptor` itself, which is still proto2. Instead, if we locally modify `CodeGeneratorRequest.proto_file` to be a repeated `bytes` field, then generate the C# code, we can ask the support library to parse each `ByteString` (as we have internal support for `FileDescriptor`).

I already have a working proof of concept of this - I'm turning it into production code, and adding `DynamicMessage` support at the same time (as it's odd to be able to load descriptors dynamically but not support dynamic message handling). No ETA right now, but I'm working on it...

@invidious9000, @jskeet: Exists there a workaround how I can implement plugins in C#? Do I need to convert the plugin.proto to proto3 syntax?

Thanks.

Yes, it's possible to write a plugin in C# now. We have that for the "microgenerator" for Google APIs, which is here: https://github.com/googleapis/gapic-generator-csharp.

That uses a proto3 version of plugin.proto, here: https://github.com/googleapis/gapic-generator-csharp/tree/master/Google.Api.Generator/Google.Protobuf.Compiler

With the proto2 support now available, it's *possible* that you could just use the existing plugin.proto, but I haven't tried that.

I'm afraid I don't know - I haven't been following all the proto2 work in detail. It may be that there's an extra option required; I haven't looked into this. The simplest approach would probably be to use a proto3 version for now.

title: Question: How to set oneof fields in python?

nodes.body:
"Assignment not allowed to field "a" in protocol message object." is not a oneof problem, it is complain about assignment for message field. 

There are two ways you can do:

test.a.CopyFrom(...)
or
test.a.sub_field = ...

For "sub_field", it means a sub scalar field of MessageA. For example:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/internal/message_test.py#L795

Protobuf python does not support assignment for message field, even it is a normal message field instead of oneof, "test.a =" is still not allowed.  "You cannot assign a value to an embedded message field. Instead, assigning a value to any field within the child message implies setting the message field in the parent. " :

title: Add additional behaviour for int64 in JsonFormat

nodes.body: We cannot accept this proposal because including int64 numbers in the output will break interoperability (most proto3 JSON implementations can't parse such output).

I agree, that's why the flag. Adding a flag will not break interoperability. There should be a flexibility of choosing this behaviour and default behaviour should remain same as it is.

Retaining this rigid behaviour will break parsing end system if that system does not use parser with same behaviour. There are some cases where remote parser is not in our hands/control to change.

It's a non-goal for us to maintain compatibility with a parser that isn't JSON conforming (i.e., can't parse valid JSON value) or isn't proto3 JSON conforming (i.e., can't translate JSON values to its original proto values according to proto3 JSON spec). Trying to satisfy some arbitrary parsing behavior that we do not control will make our library bloated with unnecessary complexity. I know your proposed change is very small but I just don't want us to move into that direction at all. If you look at the existing printer flags in JsonFormat, all of them have a strong guarantee that the produced output with/without the flag will both be parsable by a proto3 JSON parser.
Thanks for the effort. Appreciate it.

title: [Docs]: Documentation comments should be language agnostic
body:
The following `.proto` files are well-known and generated in every language:
```
descriptor.proto
any.proto
duration.proto
timestamp.proto
wrappers.proto
empty.proto
field_mask.proto
struct.proto
api.proto
type.proto
source_context.proto
```

However, the comments in each file are often formatted with some syntax that causes the output to be mangled when viewed using some other documentation tool native to the target language. Instead, the comments should be written to make as little assumptions about what documentation tool is used to interpret it.

Example usage of pre-formatted text syntax:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/c9a30c2c279431466e30541ac7c2cd9776c93b9c/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto#L47

Example usage of header syntax:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/c9a30c2c279431466e30541ac7c2cd9776c93b9c/src/google/protobuf/any.proto#L94-L95

Example usage of hyperlink syntax:
https://github.com/google/protobuf/blob/c9a30c2c279431466e30541ac7c2cd9776c93b9c/src/google/protobuf/timestamp.proto#L53

Of all the special syntaxes used, the hyperlink syntax is the most disruptive.

nodes.body: How does the hyperlink look up in Go? I think the comments are written assumed markdown format.

https://godoc.org/github.com/golang/protobuf/ptypes/timestamp#Timestamp

Go's documentation tool, [godoc](https://godoc.org/golang.org/x/tools/cmd/godoc) has very minimal syntax. As such, it doesn't handle the markdown headers nor hyperlinks.

title: Unclear documentation for SerializeWithCachedSizes
body:
The notes on this documentation for the  [SerializeWithCachedSizes](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp/google.protobuf.message_lite#MessageLite.SerializeWithCachedSizes.details) function aren't clear to me.

> The message must not have changed since the last call to ByteSize(), and the value returned by ByteSize must be non-negative. Otherwise the results are undefined.

Are you required to call ByteSize (you can't use [ByteSizeLong](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp/google.protobuf.message_lite#MessageLite.ByteSizeLong.details))? And when would ByteSize return a negative number? what does ByteSizeLong return in that case given that it uses an unsigned integer?

nodes.body:
I think that documentation is just out of date because it predates the existing of `ByteSizeLong`. The problem we used to have is that some people were trying to serialize huge protos, more than 2 GiB in size. That's the scenario where `ByteSize()` could end up returning a negative number, because the true value wouldn't fit in a signed 32-bit int. `ByteSizeLong()` will always return the correct value because it's pretty near impossible to create a message whose size won't fit in a `size_t`.

Just to be safe it's probably best to use `ByteSizeLong`, but in practice I don't think you'll run into any issues unless you're working with huge protos.

title: GetMessage name conflict
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: C++/Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
VC

**What did you do?**
`winuser.h` defines `GetMessage` as `GetMessageA` or `GetMessageW`. `Reflection::GetMessage` is declared in `message.h` and `GeneratedMessageReflection::GetMessage` is declared in `generated_message_reflection.h`.

If you include headers in the order `message.h`, `winuser.h`, `generated_message_reflection.h` you get the following error:

```
error C3668: 'google::protobuf::internal::GeneratedMessageReflection::GetMessageA': method with override specifier 'override' did not override any base class methods
```

This happens a few places when building tensorflow on windows. If `windows.h` is going to be included, make sure it is before anything from protobuf.

Seems like two directions would be to either always include windows.h, or to always undef GetMessage.

title: Add support for printing Javalite to JSON
body:
Affects: javalite

We are encountering a limitation with json formating of proto messages on Android: `JsonFormat` doesn't work with javalite protos.

Our use case is stuffing message objects into an Elastic cluster by transforming the messages into json. This works for our server-side apps(which use normal protos), but not for Android. For example:
```JsonFormat.printer().print(myLiteProto)```
results in a compile error.

We have considered the following work arounds:
1. Sending the proto via grpc to a server which would then do json transformation and stuff it into elastic
1. Using or writing a protoc plugin to generate POJOs with a set of javalite-to-POJO transformers; then using Gson or Jackson to transform the POJO to json
1. Writing a custom gson/jackson plugin to directly translate `GeneratedMessageLite` objects into json
1. Using normal full-protos in Android

Obviously these are not ideal and option 4 seems to be the least-painful. Is javalite-to-json transformation something which could be added?

nodes.body: JSON support in Java lite is something we are considering but haven't decided yet. Protobuf binary format is smaller and more efficient than JSON and that's what we generally recommend. In your case, is it possible to use protobuf binary format on both the client and server?

For normal device-to-server communications (where we own the code on both devices) we already use the binary format with GRPC services.

For this use case (and a few others like it) we want to log the data to an Elastic cluster which works with JSON documents. It is for that reason which we need to have a proto-to-json conversion.
+1 to this. We've a different use case where we need to convert the protobuf into JSON and pass it to a Javascript VM to do some stuff...but we are stuck on the conversion itself.
We are also eager to support the protobuf-lite JSON conversion function, because the full package of this feature, Lite package has no reason not to support. We use it on Android.
Another use-case, we want to store protobufs in postgres but also being able to do some basic querying on it so we want to make use of postgres' JSONB column and store the proto as json there.
Any updates?

<https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d61aede/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/MessageLite.java#L44-L46>

> Use MessageLite instead when you only need the subset of features which it supports -- namely, nothing that uses descriptors or reflection.

`MessageLite`s per se does not have descriptor information, and that doesn't sound very hopeful. Is this still possible given that `MessageLite`s don't have descriptors?
I managed to implement this (very roughly) with reflection, but not really sure about its stability or performance yet.

We are facing the same issue here. We are using protobuf for our analytics - mainly as a spec across platforms (ios, android, front end backend). However, we need to deliver the protos to segments SDK in the ios and Android clients which needs key value pairs. We simply need a reliable way to get field names - all other descriptions are unnecessary. 

I have implemented this using reflection on the builder class (filtering getter methods and reformatting names) but it seems VERY unstable and risky.

We cannot use the full java protobuf as we have a dependency on firebase (which most Android apps would) which uses lite and they are not compatible. Any way to simply get the names of the fields would be hugely appreciated - a converter to JSON would be good enough as from there we could convert to whatever we liked

@ian-ellis I stopped working on my implementation, but what about getting fields metadata from `.proto` file? This might be working without patches to Protobuf libraries. Never tried this myself though.
any update or timeline for this?
IS there any plan to support JSON conversion for MessageLite? 2018->2025?

MessageLite does not contain the names of fields (both for size and to make searching compiled binaries for feature strings harder) .  This is a deliberate choice that we do not wish to undo.  As such, We do not plan to support JSON for MessageLite.

title: C++ JSON parser incorrectly accepts lowercase enum value names.

nodes.body: Apparently C++ JSON parser not only accepts lower-case enum value names, but actually accepts arbitrary casing like "Listings" or "LiStInGs"...

It is intended behavior that case matching is insensitive if requested. That said, support for this in the current parser is a bit broken. I have a new implementation of the JSON codec that will ship in our next major release that fixes this. Closing as "done", since it's simply a matter of waiting for the release for this to be fixed.

title: Proto3 spec is incorrect w/r/t oneofs
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
```
 $ protoc --version
libprotoc 3.3.0
```

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

```
$ uname -a
Linux Ben-Wolfson-Tower 4.2.0-27-generic #32~14.04.1-Ubuntu SMP Fri Jan 22 15:32:26 UTC 2016 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
```

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

whatever apt-get gave me, man

**What did you do?**

Created a message with a grammatically correct oneof field per the grammar given here:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec

**What did you expect to see**

an exit code of 0

**What did you see instead?**

a non-zero exitcode


```
$ cat oneoftest1.proto
syntax = "proto3";
message OneofTest { oneof test { ; } }
$ protoc --cpp_out=. oneoftest1.proto
oneoftest1.proto:2:34: Expected type name.
$ cat oneoftest2.proto
syntax = "proto3";
message OneofTest { oneof test {  } }
$ protoc --cpp_out=. oneoftest2.proto
oneoftest2.proto:2:35: Expected type name.

```

Here are the relevant snippets of the grammar from the proto3 spec:

```
{}  repetition (any number of times)
emptyStatement = ";"
oneof = "oneof" oneofName "{" { oneofField | emptyStatement } "}"
```

This states that it's legal to have, within the curly braces delimiting the fields of a `oneof`, zero or more semicolons. In fact this is quite false! The correct grammar, judging from the behavior of `protoc`, is:

```
oneof = "oneof" oneofName "{"  oneofField { oneofField } "}"
```

i.e., `emptyStatement` is actually not allowed at all, and there must be at least one `oneofField`.

nodes.body: Something similar is true of the grammar for `enum`.

Right now the syntax specification is more or less for information only. It's unlikely that we will make it fully match what protoc does. Barring that, what else can we do to help your use case? Are you using the syntax specification to create a protoc in a different language or something?

Not quite a protoc, but I am writing a parser for `.proto` files. There are some places where the spec is *obviously* off (e.g. according to the spec, `syntax = 'proto3";` should be grammatical) and it's easy enough to fix those up, but others where it's less clear, as here (or as in the treatment of whitespace generally) and one has to go to `protoc` to see what it actually does.

If there's an official grammar other than the `protoc` source, that would be useful! The "spec" can't really be used for information if it is, you know, false.

Having a strict specification is crucial for people implementing protocol buffers in other languages. A specification is supposed to be the authoritative truth on what is correct and what isn't. Unfortunately, often-times people have to turn to the C++ implementation to derive what is "correct".

```
ident = letter { letter | decimalDigit | "_" }
```

Actually, it's valid for an `ident` to begin with a leading underscore.
The incorrect grammar for `ident` is #4554.
I suppose the failure to include any clause at all for `extend` should also be a separate ticket :/.
David, I suspect this doc bug is still real

This has been corrected:
https://protobuf.dev/reference/protobuf/proto3-spec/#oneof_and_oneof_field

title: Search for .bat plugins as well as .exe on windows
body:
The dart protoc plugin is less convenient to invoke on windows (https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dart/issues/74) because the executable is called `protoc-gen-dart.bat` and that is not found on the path.

So this is a feature request to make protoc on windows search for `protoc-gen-x.bat` as well as `protoc-gen-dart.exe`.

Why not just have a protoc-gen-dart.exe:

The dart protoc plugin is implemented in dart.

The way the dart protoc plugin currently is distributed is via pub.
Pub installs an executable to the path that invokes the right dart program.
On unixy systems this executable is a shell script. On windows it is a `.bat` file. (https://github.com/dart-lang/pub/blob/9f00679ef47bc79cadc18e143720ade6c06c0100/lib/src/global_packages.dart#L657)

Creating an exe would require either a change of pub, or a different way of distributing the dart protoc plugin plus a way creating the exe file. Not impossible but quite inconvenient.

https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dart/issues/74#issuecomment-415949609 has some details on how this could possibly be solved.

title: PHP: well known types in C extension do not extend Message class in PHP 7.2
body:
This makes it impossible to reliably use type hints in functions that accept a protobuf message, because passing a well known type to such a function with the protobuf extension enabled will cause a TypeError.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: composer version v3.6.1, c extension version 3.6.1
Language: PHP

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Tested on Ubuntu Travis instance. Details:
Distributor ID:	Ubuntu
Description:	Ubuntu 14.04.5 LTS
Release:	14.04
Codename:	trusty

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
PHP 7.2.4, 5.6.37

**What did you do?**
Run the following script using PHP cli. See below for composer.json file.
```
<?php

use Google\Protobuf\FloatValue;
use Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message;

require __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

$floatValue = new FloatValue();
echo get_parent_class($floatValue) . PHP_EOL;
echo (($floatValue instanceof Message) ? 'True' : 'False') . PHP_EOL;
```

**What did you expect to see**
```
# php test.php
Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message
True
```

**What did you see instead?**
Running under PHP 7.2.4, *without* protobuf c extension:
```
# php test.php
Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message
True
```
Running under PHP 7.2.4, *with* protobuf c extension:
```
# php test.php

False
```
Running under PHP 5.6.37, *without* protobuf c extension:
```
# php test.php
Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message
True
```
Running under PHP 5.6.37, *with* protobuf c extension:
```
# php test.php

True
```


Composer.json file used:
```
{
    "name": "root/test",
    "require": {
        "google/protobuf": "^3.6"
    }
}
```

title: Auto-Generated C# Code has wrong namespace casing that breaks the build
body:
Originally filed as https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/16514, but if confirmed, it's probably an issue in protobuf codebase.

Summary:
on windows, if you define .proto file named `MyProtoFile.proto` (case matters), you can still import it from a different .proto file as `myprotofile.proto`  as on windows the case in file names doesn't matter (and MyProtoFile.proto will be imported).
This can then break the C# generated code  (and possibly in other languages) as references to the imported file will have wrong casing.
(In our example `global::Contracts.Grpc.Alpha.ContractalphaReflection.Descriptor` will be generated, but the referenced class will be named `ContractAlphaReflection` and the build will fail.

nodes.body: This is not generated code breaking the build. It's the incorrect imports breaking the build. If we are to do anything, I would like to update protocol compiler to make the build break even earlier.

title: [PHP] Wrong behavior of GPBUtil::checkUint32 and GPBUtil::checkInt32 ?

nodes.body: GPBUtil is a internal method. I think you should avoid using that.

Hi TeBoring, I am not  using GPBUtil. The reason I wrote the test code is to show the bug of GPBUtil.

The maximum value for UInt32 is 0xFFFFFFFF (or 4294967295 in decimal), but GPBUtil::checkUint32 method turns value  bigger than 2147483647 into a negative number，that's what GPBUtil::checkInt32 should do.
This behavior is actually intentional. This makes the result for both 64-bit and 32-bit machines the same.

My C client send a uint32 value of 2147483648 but my PHP server get a -2147483648, that's weird.

2147483648 is in the range of uint32, but  GPBUtil::checkUint32 make it act as int32.

uint32 in protobuf means 4 bytes unsigned int, right?

Some quick test:

1. php client send uint32 2147483648, C server receive 2147483648
2. php client send fixed32 2147483648, C server reveive 2147483648
3. C client send uint32 2147483648, php server receive -2147483648
4. C client send fixed32 2147483648, php server receive 0

In your tests, only the result for 4 seems incorrect to me. I need to
double check.
On Mon, Sep 3, 2018 at 20:42 Paul Yang <paulyang1211@gmail.com> wrote:

> How php represent uint32 doesn’t affect the data on wire and also doesn’t
> affect what c client receives.
> Besides, each language has the freedom to choose integer representation.
> e.g., Java use signed integer to represent unsigned integer.
> On Mon, Sep 3, 2018 at 19:56 Bruce Lam <notifications@github.com> wrote:
>
>> Another test:
>>
>> syntax = "proto3";
>>
>> message  MyMessage {
>>   uint32 uuid = 1;
>> }
>>
>> $message = new \MyMessage();
>> $message->setUuid(2147483648);
>> var_dump($message->getUuid());
>> $data = $message->serializeToString();
>> $toMessage = new \MyMessage();
>> $toMessage->mergeFromString($data);
>> var_dump($toMessage->getUuid());
>>
>> output:
>>
>> int(-2147483648)
>> int(-2147483648)
>>
>> —
>> You are receiving this because you were assigned.
>>
>>
>> Reply to this email directly, view it on GitHub
>> <https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5101#issuecomment-418226456>,
>> or mute the thread
>> <https://github.com/notifications/unsubscribe-auth/AE9H5XA1Pqs1clK0lz--fW8imCXDl1tgks5uXevTgaJpZM4WU-6l>
>> .
>>
>

It seems the bug still present: checkUint32 doesn't cut off values longer than 4 bytes and works wrong for values greater than 0x0FFFFFFF as described earlier.
Does anyone know about progress on this issue?
Duplicate of https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/10335, progress will be there so closing this.

@acozzette the `3.6.x` branch fails in the same way that the `3.6.1` release tarball does
@acozzette any update on this? Is there some other diagnostic I can perform to gather more information?

Figured I would try the cmake build system (although you market it as only being for building on windows?).

Using the 3.6.1 tarball and the master branch, cmake (and ninja) successfully builds protoc and running `protoc --version` I get the expected `libprotoc 3.6.1` output.

On the 3.6.x branch cmake a small patch is needed to `cmake/protoc.cmake` to allow cmake to finish configuring, but otherwise this branch also compiles and runs successfully.

Why would the cmake build be successful where the autotools build is not?

@Bidski That is interesting and I can't think of why it would work with cmake but not the autotools build. Unfortunately I don't really have time to look into this now but if cmake works then that may be the best workaround. We are considering deprecating the autools build in favor of cmake soon anyway.

The problem `.libs/libprotoc.so: error: undefined reference to 'scc_info_FileDescriptorProto_google_2fprotobuf_2fdescriptor_2eproto'` is caused by this bug in linker GOLD:
https://sourceware.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=24527

Autotools build system uses version scripts (`src/libprotobuf.map`, `src/libprotobuf-lite.map`, `src/libprotoc.map`) which trigger this bug in linker GOLD, but cmake build system does not use them:
```
$ grep -r -- --version-script *
configure.ac:LDFLAGS="$LDFLAGS -Wl,--version-script=conftest.map"
src/Makefile.am:libprotobuf_lite_la_LDFLAGS += -Wl,--version-script=$(srcdir)/libprotobuf-lite.map
src/Makefile.am:libprotobuf_la_LDFLAGS += -Wl,--version-script=$(srcdir)/libprotobuf.map
src/Makefile.am:libprotoc_la_LDFLAGS += -Wl,--version-script=$(srcdir)/libprotoc.map
```

(Issue #6113 for this difference between build systems.)

About the original issue - I've faced the same (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/7114 ). It looks like it happens when pthread is not linked to protoc.

Most probably relates to:
* https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5140
* https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=81517
* https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=55394
I recommend the addition of linux label.
I am facing same issue . Any Updates on this issue??

For cross-compiling, you can specify an protoc binary using
the "--with-protoc" flag. That is:
./configure --with-protoc=/path/to/cygwin/protoc --host=i686-w64-mingw32

this will resolve the issue
Closing out old issues.  Please reopen if this still occurs on recent releases.

body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

OSX 10.13.6

**What did you do?**
Attempt to use a standard (default) optimize_for = SPEED type message in a optimize_for LITE_RUNTIME message, eg the standard "Empty" message from well known types.

Run a .equals comparing the GeneratedMessageLite against another instance.

**What did you expect to see**

Successful comparison returning true or false.

**What did you see instead?**

It compiles successfully, but upon trying to use it in an equality check, it created the following error message:

```console
java.lang.ClassCastException: com.google.protobuf.Empty cannot be cast to com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageLite

	at com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageLite$EqualsVisitor.visitMessage(GeneratedMessageLite.java:1961)

	at com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageLite.visit(GeneratedMessageLite.java:337)
	at com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageLite.equals(GeneratedMessageLite.java:162)
```

The specific line that's failing is: `((GeneratedMessageLite<?, ?>) mine).equals(this, other);`

Ultimately it looks like it assumes all nested messages must be lite messages.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

My project is expected to have a lot of message types, and while I don't need the full runtime most of the time I do occasionally (JSON output) so I'd intended to allow the messages to mix within a single application, optimized depending on if they needed the JSON I/O ability or not.

nodes.body:
Mixing lite and non-lite in a single application is no longer supported. You will either need to use lite everywhere, or non-lite everywhere. The "optimize_for" option will be ignored in a future release. To use lite, you need to follow instructions here:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/lite.md

Generally we recommend server applications to use non-lite and mobile applications to use lite. We are considering adding JSON support to lite as well and that will help if JSON is the only reason you are using non-lite.
