title: cmake .proto with multiple extensions (+patch proposal)
body:
Hello,

I have already reported this issue on cmake's bugtracker and have been asked to report it here.
See https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/issues/18329 for reference.

Here's a summary of the issue.

the following does not work :
```
protobuf_generate_cpp(PROTO_SRCS PROTO_HRDS PROTO_PATH ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR} service.requests.proto)
add_library(proto STATIC ${PROTO_SRCS} ${PROTO_HRDS})
target_include_directories(proto PUBLIC ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR})
target_link_libraries(proto PUBLIC protobuf::libprotobuf)
```
as FindProtobuf.cmake will use
`get_filename_component(FIL_WE ${FIL} NAME_WE)`
to extract the name without extension which in that case will return "service" instead of "service.requests".
protoc will generate files service.requests.pb.cc and service.requests.pb.h while PROTO_SRCS will contain service.pb.cc and PROTO_HRDS will contain service.pb.h
The following patch will resolve the issue
```
$ diff -bup cmake-3.10/Modules/FindProtobuf.cmake.orig cmake-3.10/Modules/FindProtobuf.cmake
--- cmake-3.10/Modules/FindProtobuf.cmake.orig      2018-08-29 09:04:57.119432067 +0100
+++ cmake-3.10/Modules/FindProtobuf.cmake   2018-09-05 10:42:24.054659476 +0100
@@ -168,7 +168,11 @@ function(PROTOBUF_GENERATE_CPP SRCS HDRS
 
   foreach(FIL ${PROTO_FILES})
     get_filename_component(ABS_FIL ${FIL} ABSOLUTE)
-    get_filename_component(FIL_WE ${FIL} NAME_WE)
+    #get_filename_component(FIL_WE ${FIL} NAME_WE)
+    # NAME_WE is longest extension, we want shortest extension, so need to recode it
+    get_filename_component(FIL_NAME ${FIL} NAME)
+    string(REGEX REPLACE "\\.[^.]*$" "" FIL_NAME_WE ${FIL_NAME})
+    set(FIL_WE "${FIL_NAME_WE}")
     if(NOT PROTOBUF_GENERATE_CPP_APPEND_PATH)
       get_filename_component(FIL_DIR ${FIL} DIRECTORY)
       if(FIL_DIR)
```

nodes.body: So cmake get_filename_component considers ".requests.proto" as the extension but protoc thinks ".proto" is the extension. I would agree with protoc in this case. This seems like a bug in get_filename_component and your patch is a workaround for the bug. It looks acceptable to me but maybe the better solution is to avoid multiple "." in the file names?

Well no, get_filename_component has no bug, it's just the way it works. Cmake guys asked me to provide a new component to get_filename_component to extract the longest extension.
As for changing the filename and avoid multiple ".", I cannot do that. I'm porting an existing project from premake to cmake, and although it could be acceptable to rename them, I've been asked to make the lowest number of changes to the source tree.
To me, there is a discrepancy in the way protoc handles file names and how FindProtobuf handles  file names. It is clearly a bug.
@xfxyjwf any news ?

FYI, it looks like cmake added a new get_filename_component here : https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/issues/18329

protobuf's cmake could be fixed easily now

Got it. I think we can do nothing on our side for this issue.
Since it has been fixed in FindProtobuf.cmake, will close for now.
If you still have any questions, feel free to reopen this.

title: Why is map null value rejected on json parsing?
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

About json parser. I'm looking at Java code.

**Question**

`JsonFormat.Parser` throws `InvalidProtocolBufferException` when a map value is null.

What is this for?

Line throwing an exception: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.6.1/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L1542

Test: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.6.1/java/util/src/test/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormatTest.java#L649

This behavior seems to be inconsistent with the ways of handling null for other types.
For repeated fields, [the parser treats it as if the field is not present](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.6.1/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L1510).
For not repeated fields, [it does the same thing](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.6.1/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L1518).

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I'd like to make `JsonFormat.Parser` ignore null values even when they appear in map value.

nodes.body:
Neither repeated field nor map field allows null values:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/util/src/test/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormatTest.java#L435-L442

What's accepted:
```json
{ "singularField": null, "repeataedField": null, "mapField": null}
```

What's not accepted:
```json
{"repeatedField": [null], "mapField": {"key": null}}
```

It's done this way because a null value in repeated/map field can be interpreted in different ways. For example, `{"repeatedField": [null]}` can be interpreted as a repeated field with 0 entries, or a repeated field with 1 entry having a default value. Same applies to map fields. Because of this possibility of misinterpretation and that proto-to-json will never produce such output, we decided to reject such inputs.

Thank you for your explanation. :)
My question was answered.

body: missing PROTOBUF_MIN_PROTOC_VERSION defined

nodes.body: Can you provide more context? What are you doing, what you expect to happen and what happened?

Basically, some .h files are checking PROTOBUF_MIN_PROTOC_VERSION, but this is not defined in other project files.

Regards,

Peizhao Hu

> On Sep 9, 2018, at 1:15 PM, Feng Xiao <notifications@github.com> wrote:
> 
> Can you provide more context? What are you doing, what you expect to happen and what happened?
> 
> —
> You are receiving this because you authored the thread.
> Reply to this email directly, view it on GitHub <https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5129#issuecomment-419730466>, or mute the thread <https://github.com/notifications/unsubscribe-auth/ACsu8Jsd7zQnbg-1MndU34LgfVr7klNZks5uZUyvgaJpZM4WfuX5>.
>

This is a silent error in most cases.

As of version `3.7.0` : 

```
// foo.proto
syntax = "proto3";
message Foo {
}
```

```sh
$ protoc --cpp_out . foo.proto
$ g++ -Werror=undef -c foo.pb.cc
In file included from foo.pb.cc:4:
foo.pb.h:16:15: error: "PROTOBUF_MIN_PROTOC_VERSION" is not defined, evaluates to 0 [-Werror=undef]
 #if 3007000 < PROTOBUF_MIN_PROTOC_VERSION
```

`PROTOBUF_MIN_PROTOC_VERSION` doesn't exist in any protobuf headers. Without `-Werror-undef`, it'll just assume the minimum version is `0`.

There's two probable alternatives: 
- `PROTOBUF_MIN_HEADER_VERSION_FOR_PROTOC` in `google/protobuf/port_def.inc`
- `GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_MIN_PROTOC_VERSION` in `google/protobuf/stubs/common.h`.

I'm guessing an update in the headers wasn't reflected in protoc at some point.

The `Python` module has a deprecated usage pattern for `collections.abc`. Here's the warning I'm getting:

nodes.body:
Have the same problem here
Maybe after 1+ year they will solve it?

This issue is still present:

```
[----------] Global test environment tear-down
[==========] 2110 tests from 195 test suites ran. (79097 ms total)
[  PASSED  ] 2109 tests.
[  FAILED  ] 1 test, listed below:
[  FAILED  ] TextFormatMapTest.DynamicMessage
```

This is due to the line endings when commiting on Windows with `autocrlf = true` settings in Git. The Git will automatically convert the `src/google/protobuf/testdata/map_test_data.txt` to use CRLF line endings. However, in the code the generated data to compare against expected data (read directly from `map_test_data.txt`) uses LF line endings, leading to the error.

Temporary workaround:

1. Create `.gitattributes` in the project root directory with contents below:
```
# Text data.
*.txt text eol=lf
``` 
2. Delete `src/google/protobuf/testdata/map_test_data.txt`
3. Use `git checkout` or `git reset` to re-checkout the repository.

Then, the `map_test_data.txt` will be checked out with LF line endings. You can check it with notepad3 or other tools.

A better solution may be to ignore line endings in the test code.

title: Protobuf uses std::call_once
body:
`std::call_once` is mostly broken and it should not be used. There are some bad interactions among GCC, glibc and pthreads. About the only platform you can count on  `std::call_once` to work as expected is Intel IA-32 platforms.

Another project I work with is C++ and we hit some nasty unexplained crashes on AIX, Aarch64, and Solaris when using it. We did not hit the bug on ppc64-le like reported below, however.

Also see [call_once not C++11-compliant on ppc64le](https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=66146).

(Microsoft is another can of worms with their magic statics, dynamic initialization and call once. Don't believe a damn thing that company publishes. They use MSDN and C++ Feature matrices as marketing bullshit).

nodes.body: We use google::protobuf::internal::call_once which is implemented as std::call_once in once.h. This is on purpose to allow a custom implementation. MSVC is severely bad with global atomics and initialization, that I have no good advice on a good custom implementation.

I am currently experiencing issues with code crashing with Ubuntu 20.04 that seems to be related to the usage of std::call_once. The protobuf version used is 3.6.1.3. The only solution I have found so far is to use the custom implementation that can be found at this URL:
https://github.com/google/sentencepiece/blob/master/python/once.h

This implementation was written for a completely unrelated python project that seemed to experience the exact same kind of crashes.

I understand from previous comments that using atomics may not be a viable option for MSVC. My questions are, is this issue still on the radar and being worked on? Is the above implementation suitable for protobuf? Could these crashes actually be a symptom of other underlying issues that I should look into on my side?

Thanks in advance!

> I understand from previous comments that using atomics may not be a viable option for MSVC. My questions are, is this issue still on the radar and being worked on? 

You don't need to worry it. For people who have concerns on MSVC: std::call_once works perfectly with it. At first, there were some bugs. Later on they were fixed.  Compiler is a software too. Compiler always has bugs. Nobody is perfect. 

(I'm a Microsoft employee)
So it sounds to me that using the custom implementation I linked in my previous comment could be suitable for the protobuf project. Is this being considered?

@mux, I can't answer you question. I'm not a protobuf maintainer. 

There are several ways to implement call once:

1. Use InitOnceExecuteOnce function. It doesn't require a decent C++ compiler since it is C. But it doesn't support Windows XP.
2. Use std::call_once. Read this: https://devblogs.microsoft.com/cppblog/stl-fixes-in-vs-2015-part-2/. But the bug has been fixed many many years ago. 
3. Use magic statics. The constructor of a function local static variable will only be called once. It requires C++11.

For me, they are enough. I don't think there is a need to "roll your own". 

constexpr doesn't mean the variable must be initialized statically. Before C++20, there is no way put such an ask. That's why constinit was added.  Without constinit, all custom implementations are risky.

@snnn, thank you for your advice, but the code I am dealing with doesn't run on Windows at all.

I was asking about the MSVC compatibility because it seemed to be a blocker for having a custom implementation as per @gerben-s's comment. I also cannot switch to other methods since the std::call_once usage comes from Protobuf itself.

The code was using the most efficient, but also the most restrictive TLS model: local-exec. Using initial-exec works fine, and local-dynamic and global-dynamic should be too. title: Add `Serializable` attribute to generated C# classes

**What language does this apply to?**

Just the generated C#.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Generated C# classes should be serializable by default. The official method of implementing this is to use the `Serializable` attribute on class declarations.

The specific use case I have is to make the instances of the generated classes visible in the inspector in Unity3d, which relies on the `Serializable` attribute.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

The C# code generator should add the `[System.Serializable]` attribute before every class declaration. Putting this behavior behind a command-line option is also reasonable, but not necessary.

I considered an automated tool to rewrite the generated `.cs` files to add the attribute.

[Documentation for the Serializable attribute.](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.serializableattribute?view=netcore-2.1)

body:
I posted a request to add `py_proto_library` to `examples/BUILD` in this issue: #5147, which now has been labelled with #documentation and #python. However, I'm making another attempt to integrate `py_proto_library` into our repository myself, aiming to have it look like how `java_proto_library` is shown in the `examples/BUILD` and `examples/WORKSPACE` files.

If I can make it work, I wouldn't mind making a PR to the documentation by extending `examples/..`.

So I thought I'd share what I have here and where I'm stuck. Perhaps someone can help. Please do let me know if I should post this somewhere else, or in a new issue.

So far I've defined the following:

`//dependencies/compilers:dependencies.bzl`:
```
def protobuf_dependencies():

    native.http_archive(
        name = "bazel_skylib",
        sha256 = "bbccf674aa441c266df9894182d80de104cabd19be98be002f6d478aaa31574d",
        strip_prefix = "bazel-skylib-2169ae1c374aab4a09aa90e65efe1a3aad4e279b",
        urls = ["https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel-skylib/archive/2169ae1c374aab4a09aa90e65efe1a3aad4e279b.tar.gz"],
    )

    native.bind(name = "six", actual = "@six_archive//:six")
    native.new_http_archive(
       name = "six_archive",
       build_file = "@com_google_protobuf//:six.BUILD",
       sha256 = "105f8d68616f8248e24bf0e9372ef04d3cc10104f1980f54d57b2ce73a5ad56a",
       urls = ["https://pypi.python.org/packages/source/s/six/six-1.10.0.tar.gz#md5=34eed507548117b2ab523ab14b2f8b55"],
    )

    # This com_google_protobuf repository is required for proto_library rule.
    # It provides the protocol compiler binary (i.e., protoc).
    native.http_archive(
        name = "com_google_protobuf",
        sha256 = "0a4c6d0678eb2f063df332cff1a41647ef692c067b5cfb19e51bca778e79d9e0",
        strip_prefix = "protobuf-3.6.1",
        urls = ["https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/download/v3.6.1/protobuf-all-3.6.1.zip"],
    )
```

`WORKSPACE`:
```
load("//dependencies/compilers:dependencies.bzl", "protobuf_dependencies")
protobuf_dependencies()

load("@bazel_skylib//:lib.bzl", "versions")
versions.check(minimum_bazel_version = "0.5.4")
```

`//client-protocol/BUILD`
```
proto_library(
    name = "client-protocol",
    srcs = glob(["proto/*.proto"]),
    visibility = [
        "//server:__subpackages__",
        "//client-java:__subpackages__",
        "//client-python:__subpackages__",
    ]
)
```

`//client-python/BUILD`
```
load("@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf.bzl", "py_proto_library")

py_proto_library(
    name = "protocol",
    deps = ["//client-protocol:client-protocol"],
    protoc = "@com_google_protobuf//:protoc",
)
```

Everything works fine for `//server:...` and `//client-java:...`. But when I try to `bazel build //client-python:protocol`, I get the following error:
```
ERROR: /Users/haikalpribadi/Workspace/repos/graknlabs/grakn/client-python/BUILD:21:1: in deps attribute of py_library rule //client-python:protocol: '//client-protocol:client-protocol' does not have mandatory providers: 'py'. Since this rule was created by the macro 'py_proto_library', the error might have been caused by the macro implementation in /private/var/tmp/_bazel_haikalpribadi/3cdeaa1301f056ec7b4e7ee46bda5c79/external/com_google_protobuf/protobuf.bzl:382:12
```

I can't find any reference on the internet to the error message shown above, except for this https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/4237

Does anyone have any idea what is the cause of this problem and how to solve it?

nodes.body:
It turns out, I just needed to provide the `.proto` files as `srcs` for the `py_proto_library` rule, instead of providing a `proto_library` rule as `deps`. `py_proto_library` runs its own `proto_gen` and then feeds that into a `py_library`.

i.e. I just needed to add the following to my BUILD file:
```
py_proto_library(
    name = "protocol",
    srcs = glob(["proto/*.proto"]),
    srcs_version = "PY2AND3",
    deps = [
        "@com_google_protobuf_py//:protobuf_python",
    ],

nodes.body:
When you installed protobuf with Python 3.6, it got a prebuilt binary version of protobuf including the C++ implementation. These binary Python packages are called "wheels", and you can see the wheels available for protobuf over at the [PyPI page for protobuf](https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/#files). In particular, that list includes `protobuf-3.6.1-cp36-cp36m-manylinux1_x86_64.whl`, which is the Python 3.6 binary wheel for Linux. (The Linux distribution must satisfy the "manylinux1" spec, which almost all modern Linux installations do so long as you install a few basic packages [listed in the spec](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0513/#id40)).

If you install protobuf and there is no matching binary wheel, then the pure-Python source distribution will be installed instead: `protobuf-3.6.1.tar.gz` in that list. This is the case for Python 3.7, which does not have a binary wheel listed on that page. This explains the difference in behaviour.

If you are determined to use the C++ implementation of protobuf with Python 3.7 then you will have to build it yourself. This requires more than setting an environment variable before running pip. The process is quite involved and I'm not sure it's documented anywhere. At the very least, I believe you need to download and build the overall protobuf library (at least it did when I last did it, but that was over a year ago). It is unlikely to be worth the hassle unless you have specific performance requirements.

Unfortunatelly, the pure python version is unusable for my use-case, not only because it is slow in scaled scenarios, but it also consumes large amount of memory - in one of my scenarios it eats up to 16GB of RAM and i would like to test with even larger scales.

Anyway, thanks, I will keep trying.

Sorry, I didn't notice that you had got a non-C++ implementation for 2.7 too. The only reason I can think of is that there is a mismatch in the [Unicode wideness](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0513/#ucs-2-vs-ucs-4-builds) of the wheel vs the Python distribution, which is a problem that cannot occur as of Python 3.3. But I'm really not sure if it's that or what else it could be.

Any idea when a wheel for python 3.7 on Mac will be available given that 3.7 has been out now for a few months?  I've tried to compile myself but as noted by @JamesOldfield  it is quite involved and not documented.

This question is obsolete; newer versions of protobuf use `PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=upb`. The old backend `PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=cpp` is deprecated/removed: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/main/python#implementation-backends

title: python timestamp objects sort "randomly"
body:
Version: v3.6.0
Language: Python
OS: Mac OS 10.13.6
Runtime: python-2.7 from conda

I have a message with a `google.protobuf.Timestamp` field:

message File {
    google.protobuf.Timestamp time_created = 1;
}

I created a bunch of objects using the corresponding generated Python classes and put them in a python list.  I set the `time_created` field to different values in different objects.  Then I called the python `sorted` function on my list:

  sorted_list = sorted(my_list, key=lambda f: f.time_created)

I expected the resulting list to be sorted in chronological order.  Instead, the list is in "random" (ie. different every time) order.  I assume this is because the Python Timestamp objects don't implement comparison operators, and my list is being sorted by object pointer.

My program worked as expected when I changed my code to this:

  sorted_list = sorted(my_list, key=lambda f: f.time_created.ToDatetime())

I think the Timestamp objects should implement chronological comparison, like the python `datetime` objects.  A similar argument can be made for Duration objects.

body:
Hello,

I am currently working with a protocol which i have control over the client but not the server. Currently we are writing structures to a stream in a specific way. However different sections of the messages store things in completly different ways (e.g. numbers can be stored in seeminly random ways such as a uint64 or bitpacked, same with strings). Is it possible to define exactly how the protocol buffer serializes and deserializes the message to match this existing protocol.

nodes.body: @MaxHayman No, protocol buffers have their own binary wire format and it's not really possible to make them match a different wire format defined somewhere else. If you have to conform to this other wire format then unfortunately protobuf probably won't be of much help.

title: Unspecified/Undefined behavior in enum in wire_format_lite.cc
body: Hello. In file [wire_format_lite.cc](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/wire_format_lite.cc#L101) there is undefined behavior - casting to an unexistent enum value. It's prohibited by C++ standard (before C++17 behavior is unspecified, C++17 and after - undefined) - https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/enum

title: are google.protobuf and google.protobuf.pyext supposed to be namespace packages?
body:
I'm trying to understand why 786f80fe6632902be74f90a577d75e8641494abd added the namespace package stanza to `google/protobuf/__init__.py` and `google/protobuf/pyext/__init__.py`. I see the `google` namespace has a fraught history, but is it actually expected that other packages will put code in `google.protobuf` or `google.protobuf.pyext`? Note also `google/protobuf/__init__.py` technically violates the requirement that a namespace packages's `__init__.py` must not include any other code and data aside from the namespace declaration.

I think either the namespace declaration code should be removed from `google/protobuf/__init__.py` and `google/protobuf/pyext/__init__.py`, or these namespace packages should be declared along with the `google` namespace in `setup.py`.

title: Linking fails on armv6l due to missing libatomic
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.1

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux (NixOS)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
gcc 7.3.0

**What did you do?**
When I attempted to build protobuf for armv6l, I ran into the following linker error:
```
./.libs/libprotobuf.so: undefined reference to `__atomic_fetch_add_8'
```

On armv6l, protobuf needs to be linked to `libatomic` to provide this symbol. Manually adding `-latomic` to `LDFLAGS` fixes the issue.

nodes.body: @lopsided98 Do you want to send us a pull request with the fix?

I actually don't know exactly where in the build system to fix this. Protobuf seems to use both bazel and autotools, so would I have to add it to both?

I used autotools to build it, so I just added the `-latomic` to `LDFLAGS` on the command line.

Updating just the autotools build sounds fine to me, though we are thinking about deprecating it in favor of CMake some time soon so you might want to keep that in mind. By the way, do you have any more details on why we have to explicitly link against `libatomic`? Is that just a quirk of NixOS or armv6l?

I think protobuf uses atomic intrinsics (maybe indirectly though `std::atomic`) that gcc cannot generate directly on armv6l, and instead needs to use a helper function in `libatomic` to implement them. Other architectures have instructions to implement them without `libatomic`.

I think this became a problem when protobuf stopped using its own implementations of atomic operations (`src/google/protobuf/stubs/atomicops_internals_*`) and switched to using `std::atomic` between 3.5 and 3.6.
Ok, that makes sense. I wonder if it's harmless to always link explicitly against libatomic or if we need a way to do that only for certain platforms.

Looks like there's been a regression on this issue somewhere between v3.11.4 and v3.12.2. I'm getting the same link error compiling "@com_google_protobuf//:protoc" v3.12.2 on a Raspberry Pi. v3.11.4 compiles just fine.
I know this is an old issue, but does anyone know _why_ armv6l specifically requires `-latomic`, and other Raspberry Pi platforms don’t seem to need it?

ARMv6 lacks byte and half-word and double word atomic instructions (`LDREXB`, `LDREXH`, `LDREXD`, `STREXB`, `STREXH`, `STREXD`), so they need to be implemented with libatomic instead. See: https://developer.arm.com/documentation/dht0008/a/ch01s02s01

These instructions were actually added to the ARMv6K architecture, which appears to be supported by the ARM1176JZF-S CPU used in the BCM2835, but the compiler is not configured to target this architecture version. See: https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ddi0301/h/summary-of-arm1136jf-s-and-arm1176jzf-s-processor-differences/summary-of-differences/armv6k-extensions-support

title: Allow deferred JSON-decoding of unknown google.protobuf.Any messages
body:
## Abstract

When a JSON object representing a proto3 message is decoded, the generated API for many (most?) languages yields an error when decoding a JSON-encoded `google.protobuf.Any` field whose generated code is not linked in to the program doing the decoding. This is problematic, because an unexpected type for an `Any` field breaks forward-compatibility in JSON encoding, even though it is fine in wire encoding. I propose herewith a modest extension to the rules for decoding `google.protobuf.Any`, that could allow generated code to defer JSON decoding of unknown extensions.

## Background

The `value` field of the `google.protobuf.Any` encodes the wire format of the message. For the JSON decoder, this means the message schema specified by the `type_url` field _must_ be available to decode the JSON value. Most (maybe all) existing per-language JSON decoders will fail with an error if the indicated message schema is not linked. This makes it difficult to use `Any` messages as an extension point with JSON encoding: If a message arrives with a hitherto-unknown `Any` URL attached anywhere, the decoder fails and the message is unusable.

## Proposal

To address the issue described above, I propose that a JSON decoder be allowed to _defer_ decoding of unknown message fields, in the following wise: 

1. Introduce a new well-known message type, `google.protobuf.RawAny` (name for discussion purposes) with the following structure:
    ```
    message RawAny {
       string type_url = 1;  // the type URL of the un-decoded JSON.
       string json = 2;      // the raw JSON (encoded as required, UTF-8).
    }
    ```

2. When a JSON decoder encounters the encoding of a `google.protobuf.Any` message whose structure is unknown, it MAY populate the corresponding field with a `google.protobuf.Any` with the wire-encoding of a `google.protobuf.RawAny` message carrying the un-decoded JSON.

For example, suppose the decoder receives a JSON-encoded `Any` value like:
```
{"@type":"type.googleapis.com/some.unknown.Message","x":"value","y":23}
```
This would be encoded as the following `RawAny` message:
```
type_url: "type.googleapis.com/some.unknown.Message"
json: "{\"@type\":\"type.googleapis.com/some.unknown.Message\",\"x\":\"value\",\"y\":23}"
```
which in turn becomes an `Any` message similar to:
```
type_url: "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.RawAny"
value: "\x28\x0a\x79\x74\x65\x70\x67\x2e\x6f\x6f\x6c\x67\x61\x65\x69\x70\x2e\x73\x6f\x63\x2f\x6d\x6f\x73\x65\x6d\x75\x2e\x6b\x6e\x6f\x6e\x6e\x77\x4d\x2e\x73\x65\x61\x73\x65\x67\x47\x12\x22\x7b\x74\x40\x70\x79\x22\x65\x22\x3a\x79\x74\x65\x70\x67\x2e\x6f\x6f\x6c\x67\x61\x65\x69\x70\x2e\x73\x6f\x63\x2f\x6d\x6f\x73\x65\x6d\x75\x2e\x6b\x6e\x6f\x6e\x6e\x77\x4d\x2e\x73\x65\x61\x73\x65\x67\x2c\x22\x78\x22\x3a\x22\x76\x22\x6c\x61\x65\x75\x2c\x22\x79\x22\x3a\x22\x33\x32\x00\x7d"
```
where the `value` is the wire encoding of the `RawAny` message.

## Discussion

* Deferred decoding does not eliminate the need for the message schema: It will still be needed to re-encode the message to wire format, for example.

* This proposal aims for minimality: It does not require changes to `protoc`. It requires one small new well-known message type (the one described as `google.protobuf.RawAny` above), and some documentation about its intended use for language-API authors.

* Per-language JSON decoding libraries could be updated incrementally: Existing decoders will continue to work as they do now, producing an error for unlinked messages.
  - If the new behaviour is added unconditionally, the only user-visible change is that some decodings that previously failed will now succeed.
  - If the new behaviour is added optionally (default off), there should be no user-visible changes until the caller explicitly requests the new behaviour.

**Context:** This request arose from https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/723. It affects the Kythe project, which makes use of JSON-encoded proto messages in multiple contexts where `Any` extensions are needed.

> Is json a requirement in your case? Can you use binary format?

Yes, JSON is a requirement for us. We get input from tools with poor or absent protobuf support, running in environments where taking a dependency on our proto definitions (or indeed protobuf at all) often isn't desirable or practical. We use protobuf ourselves to define the wrapper, but clients don't necessarily use protobuf.

> [I]f we simply drop the un-parsable Any wrapped value, does it work for your case?

In some instances we could probably reuse the original JSON (pre-decoding), but in others the environment will need to make changes and re-encode (to JSON). That was the motivation for allowing the decoder to preserve the un-decoded field in the above proposal.

Perhaps it will help for me to give more context:

Basically the problem we have is that we have some "generic" plumbing tools that consume JSON-encoded messages from a variety of sources, and dispatch them to other tools. The wrapper messages carry metadata in `Any` extensions. The dispatcher doesn't need to decode the metadata, but does need to pass it along to other tools need them preserved.  (Some tools require protobuf, others operate directly on the JSON; that's an implementation detail for our clients).

Right now anytime anyone adds a new metadata type, we wind up having to build and release new versions of the plumbing. That complicates updates quite a bit.  We use protobuf internally in our indexing infrastructure, so I'm hoping for a solution that allows us to continue doing so. This proposal was motivated by symmetry with field-preservation in the wire-decoding case: Ideally `json-encode(modify(json-decode(X)))` would preserve unknown `Any` values as `wire-encode(modify(wire-decode(X)))` does for unknown field indices.

I hope that helps clarify things, but please let me know if not.
Another potential avenue might be for Any to grow an encoding field/enum `{ WIRE, TEXT, JSON }`

1) Is it possible, in the API you provided, to add a way to let client register the proto type to be wrapped in Any? (e.g., another service to register type, or the API also takes the wrapped type as a parameter). In this way, your service always knows the type of wrapped message.
2) We have struct.proto to dynamically create generic json object: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/struct.proto
If 1) cannot be done, you may think replacing Any field with Struct field.

Re (1): That would be tricky. Inputs often come from an offline process, not necessarily live RPCs. The dispatcher decodes the message in order to discover which analyzer should receive it—so if the analyzer has to advertise its message formats in advance, we're basically in the situation we have now, where we have to re-bake the dispatching-driver for each new message type that exists.

Re (2): We could replace the typed messages with untyped structs. That loses much of the benefit of using protobuf in the first place, though, which was to have static message types in the code that needs them (e.g., the analyzers). It's fine for our purposes to require an _analyzer_ to bake in the message types it cares about; what we're trying to avoid is having to revise the intermediate plumbing (e.g., dispatching driver, storage libraries, etc.). Switching to structs would help the plumbing, but would hurt the analyzers.
Your client can work on normal message which has the type checking. The json encoding of the normal message can be parsed as Struct.

> Your client can work on normal message which has the type checking. The json encoding of the normal message can be parsed as Struct.

I think I must be misunderstanding something about your suggestion, can you be slightly more specific? 

Our wrapper message currently carries fields of type `google.protobuf.Any`, and I think if I understood your suggestion correctly you are proposing we replace those with `google.protobuf.Struct`. Suppose we do that: Decoding JSON into a matching `google.protobuf.Struct` works fine as expected, but then how does one go from that back to a properly-typed message? For example, we have a message schematically like:

```
message M {
  string name = 1;
  string kind = 2;
}
```

If I decode `{"name":"foo","kind":"bar"}` into a `google.protobuf.Struct` I get something like:

```
name: "foo"
kind: "bar"
```

but I'm not sure I see how I go from the `Struct` to an `M`.

```Struct``` is one option. You may also use string field.
For ```Struct``` to ```M```, m.parseFromJson(s.serializeToJson()).
Does that work?

> For Struct to M, m.parseFromJson(s.serializeToJson()).
> Does that work?

Functionally it looks like it should work, but I would describe that as a workaround rather than a solution. To use this, we would have not only to migrate all our existing protos from `Any` to `Struct` but we would also have to (manually) update all the current users of the message to include this decode logic, for each message type they support. As I said above: This makes things better for our plumbing, but worse for our analyzers. That's a poor trade, since the analyzers are often contributed/supported by third parties.

Much of the benefit we get from using protobuf is that the schema defines the layout, and the decoder "just works", whether for wire-format or JSON, and gracefully adapts to forward-compatible changes in the message format. In principle, a new `Any` message _should_ be forward-compatible. Rather than work around the fact that it's currently not for JSON, I think it would be better to provide a deferral mechanism.

It's worth noting that the proposal above also extends to other encoding schemes like textpb, and although our project doesn't rely on textpb, I'm aware of others that do. Having a standard way to express deferred parsing would have very little down-side I can see.

The purpose of ```Any``` is to replace extension in proto2. For extension, you do need to link every related message in order to make it work. I think same requirement for Any seems reasonable. In order to make Any work, you have to link the related messages.

I also feel type checking is also part of the semantic of Any. Any is used for polymorphism for known types not for any random type. And because the type checking is part of the semantic of Any, if a server sends an undeclared Any to client (like in your case), that is considered as a security attack vector. For clients that assumes the type checking semantic of Any, that would be unacceptable.
The other approach I can think of is to provide a way to let client tell sever the type of wrapped message.

> I also feel type checking is also part of the semantic of Any. Any is used for polymorphism for known types not for any random type.

Agreed—but the situation I'm describing isn't one where we want to _discard_ type-checking, only defer it. The end-consumer of the message still has to know the type, and that's appropriate.  The goal is not to allow arbitrary messages, but to allow the channel to inspect known parts of the message structure without forcing a full decode of the unknown parts. This works for wire-format, but not for JSON. Given that the cost to protobuf itself is small (i.e., no functional changes are required to the compiler), I'm not clear on the objection.

> The other approach I can think of is to provide a way to let client tell sever the type of wrapped message.

That doesn't work for our case, because we don't know which client we're talking to until _after_ we've inspected the wrapper message. The dispatcher examines the message, figures out which analyzer to invoke, and does so (note too that this isn't necessarily "client-server" interaction in the Stubby/gRPC sense—in some cases these are pipes or stored files).
"Defer" may mean never. If we allow some decoder to defer parsing unknown Any, how can we guarantee the type checking will be done in the end?

> "Defer" may mean never. If we allow some decoder to defer parsing unknown Any, how can we guarantee the type checking will be done in the end?

The same question applies to unknown fields: Nothing can guarantee that type-checking will be done. Similarly, nothing can guaranteed that for `Any` messages in wire format: The reader can always grab the bytes and do whatever. 

For our case, as in the case you're describing, either (a) we won't use the field at all, or (b) it will be decoded with the proper descriptor.  The question of whether the message is decoded and used is outside the scope of the protobuf language's concern: The language doesn't define how wire-types are mapped to language types, for example. 

This proposal doesn't, as far as I can see, contradict any of the protobuf language goals: A decoder with the descriptor in-harness will still decode the message structure correctly. A decoder without the descriptor in-harness will treat it as an unknown-but-preserved field. Either way, a program in possession of the raw message format _could_ choose to decode and use it some other way—this doesn't make that any easier (or harder).
Actually, for json unknown fields, the default behavior is fail and the optional behavior is discard. So the json Any behavior still seems consistent to me.

> Actually, for json unknown fields, the default behavior is fail and the optional behavior is discard.

Indeed, that is the default, but as the spec says: “Proto3 JSON parser should reject unknown fields by default but may provide an option to ignore unknown fields in parsing.” That option is available for _unknown_ fields, but not (currently) for `Any`. This proposal is one way to allow such an option to exist for `Any`.

Certainly some different proposal could also work: @shahms suggested an alternative above, which I think would also be fine. Even if the default behaviour remains as it is now, I think there should be a standard way for decoders to implement deferred decoding.
The ignoring unknown for json unknown field actually means discard in our implementations, which is not what you want.
For the above Struct solution, could you only update the component which handles the Any parsing to use Struct.

I feel that I am perhaps missing some aspect of your disagreement with this proposal. You've proposed several work-arounds that are functionally actionable but do not address the fundamental issue, viz., that we'd like to use the standard protobuf machinery where it's available, and interoperate cleanly with the JSON encoding rules. I do not disagree that we can hack around the problem, but would like to find a solution that doesn't require hacking. 

Leaving aside the workarounds, is there any particular concern you have about the proposal itself?

For your proposal, 
1) How do I know the format of the value string? is it json or binary?
2) How do I know RawAny is from the client or from some proxy that modifies Any payload?
3) In binary format, we also don't allow unknown type url.
4) In the end, do you need to covert the json data to binary data?

Re (1): The proposal as worded would capture the JSON of the field as written. A similar strategy could be used for textpb—either using a separate message type, or perhaps an enumeration a @shahms suggested.

Re (2): I'm not sure I understand the question. Who is "I" in this example? Generally speaking there is no way to know whether a proxy has modified a protobuf message between the client and the server. This proposal doesn't address that question either way, but maybe I've missed something.

Re (3): Binary format works fine with unknown type URLs. Specifically: You get a raw `google.protobuf.Any` regardless whether the type is known, and only if you explicitly _decode_ the `Any` value does an error result.

Re (4): Both. For our use-case, the dispatcher may read wrappers _either_ in wire format _or_ in JSON format, and passes them along. Wire-format is working fine, only JSON has the deficiency.

2) Suppose there are three components: producer, proxy and consumer. If the consumer get data with RawAny, how does consumer know the RawAny is from the producer or the proxy? Or whether decode the data as RawAny or wrapped message?
4) Could you be more specific about to which path you want to apply your proposal? json-json, binary-json, binary-binary, json-binary?

Re: Proxy vs. producer. The consumer has no way to know, but that's no more or less the case here than with a wire-format message: A proxy _could_ decode a wire-format message and modify the `Any` fields either way. For our use-case this isn't relevant, though: We don't want to _modify_ the contents of unknown `Any` fields, only to preserve them across `encodeJSON(update(decodeJSON(input)))` where `update` may modify the contents of _known_ fields and extensions but will ignore the unknown ones.

Re: Decoding paths. We would like to support a couple of different usage patterns for a given JSON `input` value:

1. On the proxy, the workflow is approximately as follows:
   ```
    let m = decodeJSON(input) in
      let analyze = dispatch(m) in 
         analyze(encodeJSON(update(m)))
   ```
   that is, the proxy decodes JSON, inspects some of its fields to find the analyzer to dispatch to, possibly modifies some of the decoded fields (not the unknowns), then re-encodes the (possibly-modified) message as JSON in a request to the analyzer.

2. An analyzer receives `input` and may either use the raw JSON directly, or may decode it into a generated protobuf type. The latter is preferred where possible. We expect most analyzers to do something like `let m = decodeJSON(input) in analyze(m)`.

Of these, (1) is the focus of this proposal: The analyzer is expected to know the descriptors for the inputs it knows how to handle. The proxy/dispatcher needs only to preserve them.

> A proxy could decode a wire-format message and modify the Any fields either way.

What do you mean by either way? You mean proxy can do whatever it want and hope the consumer can still parse? Doesn't the proxy at least need to follow protobuf's spec?

> For our use-case this isn't relevant

Doesn't the consumer need to know whether the data represent an actual RawAny or an unknown Any converted to RawAny? What if the producer intentionally send RawAny to skip protobuf's type checking?

Use Case1: Previously, you mentioned using Struct will hurt analyzer. But I suggested only using that for dispatcher. And since the analyze happens after encodeJson, I don't see why analyzer is hurt.

Use Case2: Since the analyzer needs to actually analyze the input directly. The analyzer still don't have wrapped message's type information?

> Doesn't the consumer need to know whether the data represent an actual RawAny or an unknown Any converted to RawAny? 

Yes, the consumer does need to know. But the proxy does not.

> Previously, you mentioned using Struct will hurt analyzer. But I suggested only using that for dispatcher. And since the analyze happens after encodeJson, I don't see why analyzer is hurt.

We would have to define separate message types for the proxy and for the consumer, and manually keep them in sync. Presently, the request messages are generated by the producer (in our case, a build process) dispatched, and consumed by analyzers. We could clone the message, replace all the Any fields with Struct, and then keep that up-to-date whenever the original message changes. However, we'd rather not have to maintain that synchronization.

> Since the analyzer needs to actually analyze the input directly. The analyzer still don't have wrapped message's type information?

The wrapper message carries analyzer-specific metadata in Any instances. The producer and the analyzer share knowledge of the Any values, but we want the proxy not to have to. As I mentioned above, the need to do so greatly complicates updates and rollouts to our pipeline plumbing.

> Yes, the consumer does need to know. But the proxy does not.

Then, from the data that proxy produces, there is no information about whether it's actual RawAny or an unknown Any converted to RawAny. How does the consumer figure out?

> However, we'd rather not have to maintain that synchronization.

Can proxy parser the whole json input as Struct? Then there is no need for such sync.

> The wrapper message carries analyzer-specific metadata in Any instances. The producer and the analyzer share knowledge of the Any values, but we want the proxy not to have to. As I mentioned above, the need to do so greatly complicates updates and rollouts to our pipeline plumbing.

Why the analyzer-specific metadata cannot be generalized so that the proxy can also understand it?

> [F]rom the data that proxy produces, there is no information about whether it's actual RawAny or an unknown Any converted to RawAny. How does the consumer figure out?

Why would the consumer care? The consumer doesn't receive a RawAny message in the scenario I've described: The proxy decodes JSON to get a message with some RawAny field values. Encoding that message back to JSON (perhaps with alterations of the known fields) should restore the same JSON that was originally received for those unknown Any types. No information is lost in this proposal, because the original type URL is preserved.

Our programs don't have a dynamic lookup mechanism (we don't have the internal protodb in our open-source project), but a program that does could decode a RawAny by extracting the type URL, fetching the descriptor, and using that descriptor to decode the saved JSON. That aspect of my proposal is intended to allow that workflow without breaking compatibility: Existing decoders without the schema already can't decode those messages and return an error eagerly. Under the proposed option, the decoder would still get an error if it tries to decode the RawAny explicitly, sans descriptor.

> Can proxy parser the whole json input as Struct? Then there is no need for such sync.

It can, but again that loses us the type structure: The proxy doesn't need to know the contents of the Any fields, but _does_ care about the contents of other fields.

> Why the analyzer-specific metadata cannot be generalized so that the proxy can also understand it?

There is no generic metadata format: Each analyzer (potentially) has its own idiosyncratic message type. We could, of course, just convert it to a bag of key/value pairs, i.e., a `Struct` message, but then we lose the format- and type-checks enforced by the decoder.

Revisiting one of your previous points:
> [F]rom the data that proxy produces, there is no information about whether it's actual RawAny or an unknown Any converted to RawAny. How does the consumer figure out?

The intent of the above proposal is that RawAny messages be handled as a well-known type by the encoder and decoder logic. The rules for introducing and eliminating them would be, more or less:

* **Introduction:** When the JSON decoder attempts to decode a JSON object into an `Any` field whose type URL is unresolved, it produces a `RawAny` message instead.
  - Today it cannot do this, because the Any message requires wire-format, and the JSON decoder can't produce wire format without a descriptor.
  - No type information is discarded, so type-checking is still possible for every field, as before.
* **Elimination:** Given an `Any` field carrying a `RawAny` message:
  - If encoding as JSON, the encoder uses the saved JSON value directly.
  - If encoding as wire-format:
    * If the type URL for the saved `RawAny` message is unknown, an error is returned (this is the deferral).
    * Otherwise, the descriptor is used to convert the message to wire format.

Any `RawAny` value can also be explicitly decoded whenever its type descriptor is available, by unpacking the JSON and decoding it in the usual fashion. The only real change is that the error for an _unresolved_ descriptor is delayed until the caller explicitly requests it.

https://github.com/kythe/kythe/pull/3293 updates a tool to process JSON-encoded
proto data. This data contains Any messages that may in turn wrap protos
of unconstrained type. The tool does not need to decode these messages, *but*
it should be able to round-trip them. One possible way this might go is
JSON-encoded Any -> a protobuf Any message with the JSON data base64'd ->
JSON-encoded Any, but the important thing is that the data doesn't get lost.

Despite the tool not needing to decode the Any-encoded data, I still had to
add two dummy protos (https://github.com/kythe/kythe/blob/2be0c1f0d1519d24903572b32c42de593eb80449/kythe/cxx/tools/kindex_tool_main.cc#L237)
to make sure that their types would be linked in. This isn't actually a complete
solution, since we may add other Any-encoded messages in the future, at which
point the tool will break.

We need a way to be able to treat Any messages as opaque when serializing or
deserializing JSON-encoded protos.
Looks like #4511 is related.

https://github.com/i9/bar BetterAnyResolver
minimal code to support unknown Any marshal/unmarshal

title: [PHP] Use After Free Bug: getIterator references $this only weakly
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.1
Language: PHP 7.2.10

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux, macOS

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
PHP 7.2.10, GCC 8.2.0, Apple LLVM 10.0.0

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Checkout this demo project: https://github.com/lhecker/protobuf-issue
2. Run `php test.php`

**What did you expect to see**
Test cases `A)` and `B)` behave the same

**What did you see instead?**
When you run the output you should see either one of these cases to happen:
```
A) This works:
Array
(
    [foo] => bar
)

B) This doesn't:
Array
(
    [] => 1
)
```

Or sometimes, randomly:
```
This works:
Array
(
    [foo] => bar
)

This doesn't:
[1]    16581 segmentation fault  php test.php
```

The difference is that for test case `A)` I'm manually, strongly referencing the `$values` (here: `MapField`) variable and thus keeping it alive while `iterator_to_array()` runs.

In test case `B)` though I'm turning the temporary return value of `makeValues()` right into an iterator, before I stuff it into `iterator_to_array()`.
Since `iterator_to_array()` only strongly references the given argument (the iterator) and not the `MapField` itself, `MapField` is deallocated prematurely.
This leads to either a broken iteration or a segfault.

In case you're using macOS you can reproduce the use after free side of the bug quite easily.
Just run:
```
MallocScribble=1 php test.php
```
instead.

nodes.body: The repo at https://github.com/lhecker/protobuf-issue is no longer available. However I believe this bug is fixed now. MapIterator now contains a zval reference to MapField, which should ensure it is not prematurely freed: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/326ea555ba6677b82c5ec072aab16c7c685dd51c/php/ext/google/protobuf/map.c#L482

body:
Version: v3.6.0.rc1
Language: C++ integrated into a managed C++ CLR project
Using Visual Studio 2017

I have a C++ library using protobufs.
I have enums defined in proto files and use them in my C++ interface
(Say Enums.proto)

I am wrapping my C++ library in a CLR project for access by C#
The CLR based cpp file will need include the Enums.pb.h to use C++ interfaces with enums

The generated Enums.ph.h includes the stubs/common.h

which has this include block:
// TODO(liujisi): Remove the following includes after the include clean-up.
#include <google/protobuf/stubs/logging.h>
#include <google/protobuf/stubs/mutex.h>
#include <google/protobuf/stubs/callback.h>

And stubs/mutex.h includes std [mutex](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.6.0rc1/src/google/protobuf/stubs/mutex.h#L33) (as of 3.6.0.rc1) which is not allowed to be included when building a CLR project.

Error received:

fatal error C1189: #error:  mutex is not supported when compiling with /clr or /clr:pure.

Maybe the include clean-up will fix this if stubs/mutex is not part of common.h
(also once.h includes mutex too)

Maybe a pimpl pattern could be used in WrappedMutex so it does not include std mutex (?)

nodes.body: I just sent out #5260 which should help by removing those includes from stubs/common.h. But are you saying that stubs/once.h is also a problem? We have heard some complaints that `std::once` is not very portable, so we may end up needing to rethink that "once" initialization functionality anyway.

Yes stubs/once.h also [includes mutex](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/stubs/once.h#L81)
 to gain access to std::call_once, to get CLR compatibility, we would need to move those inline functions using std::call_once out of the header

There are still other headers that include stubs/mutex.h (such as descriptor.h)
and stubs/mutex.h still includes the std mutex header.
For CLR compatibility, we would need to take the std mutex include out of stubs/mutex.h 

Those 2 files are the only ones I see including the std mutex header

I will see if I can possibly remove that include from those files and see how things act

On a side note...
 
Your branch has a few oddities I am working out.
For some reason one of my enums in one of my pb.h files is throwing this error when one of my regular cpp files includes it.
(All my other enums are working fine, so I suppose some generated header chain is broken?)

`
 error C2589: '(': illegal token on right side of '::'
 error C2062: type 'unknown-type' unexpected
 error C3805: 'type': unexpected token, expected either '}' or a ','
 warning C4003: not enough arguments for function-like macro invocation 'max'
`

due to this code

`
enum eHeartRhythm {
  NormalSinus = 0,
  Asystole = 1,
  eHeartRhythm_INT_MIN_SENTINEL_DO_NOT_USE_ = std::numeric_limits<::google::protobuf::int32>::min(),
  eHeartRhythm_INT_MAX_SENTINEL_DO_NOT_USE_ = std::numeric_limits<::google::protobuf::int32>::max()
};
`

Here is what I was talking about in making the WrappedMutex use a pimpl pattern so we can remove the std::mutex include in stubs/mutex.h, it works well!

I did this change on master, but the errors I mentioned before happens a lot, so I assume master is not ready for prime time yet. So I created a new branch based on 3.6.x and that works great with my project.

https://github.com/aaron-bray/protobuf/commits/3.6.x-mutex
(Note, I also am trying to remove once.h from where I can)
once.h is pretty embedded in descriptor.h and extension_set.h
I will try to implement the pimpl patter in descriptor classes to see if that helps.
extension_set has an extern'd variable I am not sure what to do with yet...

@aaron-bray I think in some environments `min` and `max` can be defined as macros--maybe that could explain the errors you saw?

Before getting too far into this, I should mention that we will probably not be able to officially support CLR. We can accept pull requests for it, but if we manage to remove `std::mutex` from the necessary headers, there's no guarantee that it won't slip back into those headers over time, so it might require some ongoing fixes if you want to keep it working.

You are right.
I probably need to look into encapsulating the protobuf enum classes for a cleaner interface
They are so convenient to just use as generated though!

The min/max errors I am seeing is also probably an include order/collision for particular file. 
More reason to fully and cleanly encapsulate generated classes

title: FromString abstract method is missing in the google.protobuf.message.Message class
body:
Version: master
Language: Python

Currently `google.protobuf.message.Message` class has several abstract methods, like `MergeFromString` and `SerializeToString`, but `FromString` method is missing.

The only difference I see is that `FromString` is a `staticmethod`, but in Python it is ok to declare abstract static methods: https://docs.python.org/3/library/abc.html#abc.abstractstaticmethod. I'm referencing `abc` module here just for an example.

Was this made intentionally? Is it possible to add this method declaration to the base class? I think this will help slightly improve typing stubs: https://github.com/python/typeshed/pull/2515

nodes.body:
Or why non-abstract `Message.ParseFromString` method exists, but `FromString` method added dynamically to every `Message` subclass and probably with the same content:
```python
def FromString(s):
    message = cls()
    message.MergeFromString(s)
    return message
```
Why not to add this method as a `classmethod` into the `Message` class?
```python
def FromString(cls, s):
    message = cls()
    message.MergeFromString(s)
    return message
```

title: Is there a proto3 version of src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto?
body:
I'm working in a ruby based project, where I'd like to generate ruby classes for my protobuf files.

The ruby protobuf compiler (grpc_tools_ruby_protoc) is not compatible with protobuf2 syntax.

In our project, we are working with existing protobuf files that imports [`src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto) This is because we're working with custom options. Because this file is written in protobuf2 syntax, the ruby compiler fails.

I was wondering if there are plans to update the syntax of this google utility protobuf file, so it can be compatible with the ruby compiler. I'm taking a stab at trying to convert the syntax myself, but there are some complexities with all the extension fields.

Thanks.

nodes.body:
I don't think we would change descriptor.proto. Instead, we will change ruby code generator.
There has been some work done for ruby proto2 supprot: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/4816
Custom option is still missing though.

I was able to get around this by compiling the proto3 file that imports `src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto`, and not compiling the descriptor.proto file directly. It appears that the ruby compiler can handle a proto3 file that imports a proto2 file. So it looks like this is a non-issue on my end. Thanks for the response.
For anyone trying to leverage the `FieldDescriptorProto.Type type` in the `descritor.proto`, I got around the compiler complaining that the Enum is a proto2 type by using `Field.Kind` in `type.proto`

title: google.protobuf not found when installed with pip --prefix='.'
body:
Version: v3.5.1 
Language: Python
Linux: CentOS
Python 2.7.14 :: Anaconda, Inc.

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. pip install protobuf --upgrade --prefix='./' -I 
2. setenv PYTHONPATH`` `pwd`/lib/python2.7/site-packages/``
3. python
4. from google.protobuf import descriptor as _descriptor

I am seeing
```
Python 2.7.14 |Anaconda, Inc.| (default, Dec  7 2017, 17:05:42) 
[GCC 7.2.0] on linux2
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> from google.protobuf import descriptor as _descriptor
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
ImportError: No module named google.protobuf
```

nodes.body:
Found a fix.  Creating empty file in google directory makes it work. (solution given in [issues/6341](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/issues/6341#issuecomment-377804376))
```touch lib/python2.7/site-packages/google/__init__.py```

Note that, when installing using `pip --user`, this issue does not arise. 
Can this be fixed while installing protobuf itself with `pip --prefix=` option?

This is an issue with Python < 3.3. Placing the init file in the google folder will make all other google packages installed somewhere else unusable: http://python-notes.curiousefficiency.org/en/latest/python_concepts/import_traps.html#the-init-py-trap

Solution: Do not place the init file there. Switch to Python >= 3.3 (2.7 will drop out of support by the end of the year)

My request to the maintainers: 

Could you add the ```__init__.py``` file to the python2 package ?  This would mean both versions would work.

**OR**

If you don't want to support python2 anymore:

Don't upload the python2 versions to pypi anymore and delete the old ones with this ```ImportError``` issue ? Because then pip would automatically get the latest version which is still working for python2.


Both of this options would be better(imo) than the current situation:  providing a broken python2 package.

> Could you add the __init__.py file to the python2 package ? This would mean both versions would work.

As I wrote in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5269#issuecomment-546242515 make sure to NOT add that for Python 3.3 and up. I guess this can be easily achieved via the setup call.
I believe we don't support python 2 anymore, closing as obsolete.

- `foo/cpp/bar.pb.h`

nodes.body: I think this is working as intended, though it may initially seem surprising. The idea is that if the path to your proto file is `foo/bar.proto`, then you should be able to include `"foo/bar.pb.h"` to access the header. There is supposed to be a simple correlation between .proto file paths and the generated file paths.

body:

Trying to update my client to latest specs I've been encountering a tricky problem.
As from their Proto message definition [here](http://j.mp/2ysXPNv), I need to define a `DataAtNameQuery` to call `listenForDataAtName`.

After generating the protobuf base, I've found out that it's currently impossible to define a `Par` for the name of `DataAtNameQuery`, because:

```python
In [1]: from rchain_grpc.generated.CasperMessage_pb2 import DataAtNameQuery
   ...: x = DataAtNameQuery()
   ...: x.name.__class__
Out[1]: RhoTypes_pb2.Par

In [2]: from rchain_grpc.generated.RhoTypes_pb2 import Par
   ...: print(Par, x.name.__class__)
   ...: print(Par.__name__, x.name.__class__.__name__)
<class 'RhoTypes_pb2.Par'> <class 'RhoTypes_pb2.Par'>
Par Par

In [3]: isinstance(Par(), x.name.__class__)
Out[3]: False
```

So Python fails on considering the `Par` class for the name as the same one I can import.

Now this difference breaks the current code in:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/internal/python_message.py#L1316

And I get to see:
```
TypeError: Parameter to MergeFrom() must be instance of same class: expected Par got Par. for field DataAtNameQuery.name

Can you give some guidance / suggestions on how should I proceed?

Regards,
Paolo

nodes.body: Are you using cpp extension? Pure python and cpp extension has a behavior difference of the precision: Python does not have C-style float , it only has a C-style double. Thus pure python is using double precision for both float and double field, cpp extension is using float precision for float field.
No, we use pure python, as per the provided sample. We had to change our .proto files to use `double` rather than `float` to work around this precision issue.

```

Note:

title: How to use NDK to build Protobuf to run on Android

nodes.body: Sorry but I'm not very familiar with c++ build on android. Reassigned to Adam.
I don't know for sure but I suspect that there's an ODR violation caused by `libqt_android_protobuf_test` defining some of the same protobuf symbols that are defined in `libprotobuf`.
The same way, there is no problem in windows and linux, I guess the possible compilation of the Android version of protobuf is wrong. I don't know where is wrong.

*After I compile with clang, this problem no longer appears. I suggest you use clang.*

### Using

* Ubuntu 16.04
* Android NDK r16b
* Protobuf v3.5.1
* Language C++
* Qt 5.12.0 on Android

### Build Protobuf with Android NDK

refer to [Android Standalone Toolchains](https://developer.android.com/ndk/guides/standalone_toolchain)

```bash
~/Android/android-ndk-r16b/build/tools/make-standalone-toolchain.sh \
--arch=arm \
--platform=android-26 \
--toolchain=arm-linux-android-clang5.0 \
--install-dir=$HOME/Android/arm-26-toolchain-clang \
--use-llvm \
--stl=libc++
```

#### get protobuf

```bash
git clone https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf.git

cd protobuf

git checkout v3.5.1

./autogen.sh

mkdir build && cd build

vi build-protobuf-android.sh
```

#### build-protobuf-android.sh content

```bash
export PREFIX=$HOME/Android/andrc/protobuf-3.5.1-v7a/
export PATH=$HOME/Android/arm-26-toolchain-clang/bin:$PATH
export SYSROOT=$HOME/Android/arm-26-toolchain-clang/sysroot
export CC="arm-linux-androideabi-clang --sysroot $SYSROOT"
export CXX="arm-linux-androideabi-clang++ --sysroot $SYSROOT"

../configure \
--prefix=$PREFIX \
--host=arm-linux-androideabi \
--with-sysroot="${SYSROOT}" \
--enable-shared \
--enable-cross-compile \
--with-protoc=protoc \
CFLAGS="-march=armv7-a -D__ANDROID_API__=26" \
CXXFLAGS="-frtti -fexceptions -march=armv7-a -D__ANDROID_API__=26" \
LIBS="-llog -lz -lc++_static"

make -j 2

make install
```

#### Build

```bash
bash build-protobuf-android.sh
```

Build Success!

protobuf [has been on pypi for a long time](https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/#history) so that's where the hash comes from - whenever you use `pipenv install` it will resolve versions and generate the lockfile with hashes same as in other platforms like npm.

title: Extend of repeated field does not check types when using compiled version
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: /v3.6.1
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux Mint

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.6.0

**What did you do?**
1. Have a scalar field of in32 type
2. Call `extend(np.array([True], dtype=np.bool))` on it

**What did you expect to see**
Error about type mismatch (bool is not int32) consistently

**What did you see instead?**
No error on Linux with pip-installed versions
Error when using Git-Version (installed with `pip -e`) or on windows.

This came up during a PR for ONNX which uses protobuf (https://github.com/onnx/onnx/pull/1540). The same code causes a failure on Windows, but not on any Linux version tested. I checked out the Github version to be able to debug this and there it errored. Using VSCode I found that the `extend` method is a "native" method when it does not error and a python method when it does.

TLDR: Sometimes the python `RepeatedScalarFieldContainer` is used where the type is checked on append (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/63d2f3bc80a870a09c6aea74025df40aad7dba04/python/google/protobuf/internal/containers.py#L255) and sometimes the native class is used which does not have this type check: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/63d2f3bc80a870a09c6aea74025df40aad7dba04/python/google/protobuf/pyext/repeated_scalar_container.cc#L344

This also has the side effect, that the functions `extend` and `insert` are not provided in the native case.

Question: When/How is decided what to use?   
Bug: Why is the type not checked in the native case and an int32 happily accepts a numpy bool?

nodes.body:
All numbers.Integral are accepted in python protobuf setters for int32 field:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f50a1f843e8c2599a92e9d6bd5324462a5233367/python/google/protobuf/internal/type_checkers.py#L130

I am not sure why windows cause failures on windows, but I'd assume it was not from the set to a protobuf repeated field?

> I am not sure why windows cause failures on windows, but I'd assume it was not from the set to a protobuf repeated field?

A `numpy bool` is not a `numbers.Integral` so the failure is actually the **expected** behaviour. The bug I'm reporting is that it **does not** fail in some circumstances (e.g. on everything *but* windows).

I traced this down to the fact that there are 2 different implementations of the `RepeatedScalarContainer`: 1 in C++ and 1 in Python. The latter does check the type and hence (correctly) fails, but the C++ version does not and hence is wrong.

To reproduce simply download protobuf with pip on linux and assign a numpy bool array to a int32 repeated scalar field. This should work although it is wrong.

Yes we do have pure python and cpp extension. Looks like the issue is not for different platform, it is different protobuf implementations.

For cpp extension, we do have type checks as well:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/46a48e49aa8357bbeee8040819a35e59880e329a/python/google/protobuf/pyext/message.cc#L679

It was surprise me that a Python bools are a subclass of int but numpy bools are not subclass of number type.

My understand is that all types are acceptable if it can be safely convert to the expected type. For example a bool field can accept integral:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/46a48e49aa8357bbeee8040819a35e59880e329a/python/google/protobuf/internal/type_checkers.py#L239

Change the pure python to accept numpy bool make more sense to me

There was a discussion about this: https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/3580

Essentially:

- Python `bool` are integers where `True==1` and `False==0` -> `True+True=2`
- NumPy `bool_` are real bools, but they can be upcast to integer when combined in calculations. But: `bool_(1) + bool_(1) == bool_(1)` (aka `AND` not `PLUS`)

Note that there is also an example posted: `Isinstance(np.int8(0), numbers.Integral) -> False` which does no longer hold (it returns True as it should)

Furthermore: `a=np.bool_(5); b=a+0` -> `a==True` && `b == 1`

Given this I suggest to change the python checker to: `isinstance(t, numbers.Integral) or isinstance(t+0, numbers.Integral)` where an exception should be caught and reported as `False`. This would match the C code: Either it is an Integral or it can be cast/used as one.

title: [Any language] Union with fields of the same name?
body:
I'm trying to create a protobuf that will work for a JSON schema that already exists. 

The schema uses a field called `data` to either be
- a literal string (i.e. `"data": "my string"`)
OR
- a nested JSON object (`"data": { "xyz": 42 } `)

Is there some way I can get protobuf to play nicely with this situation?

Stuff like this:

```protobuf
oneof data_payload {
    string data = 4;
    google.protobuf.Struct data = 5;
}
```

obviously doesn't work, because in each situation the property name (data) is the same.

Is a union of fields with the same name supported, and if so how do I make use of it?

nodes.body:
I will answer my own question here as I missed the obvious answer due to a mistake:

_Don't_ do a union - instead, use `google.protobuf.Value` and both use cases will work

```
import "google/protobuf/struct.proto";
..
google.protobuf.Value data = 4;
```

title: Publish proto3 via IETF or similar industry body
body:
It would be desirable to reference protocol buffers in published specifications. However, it can be seen as "risky" by some to reference a specification that is essentially controlled by one company.

I request that proto3 be published via some industry body to eliminate this risk and to encourage protocol buffer usage in other industry specifications. IETF might be a good venue for this now that protocol buffers are becoming ever mode widely used on the web thanks to gRPC.

title: Full oneof support

nodes.body: Unfortunately I think this would be pretty hard to implement. I'm not sure how we would encode this in a way that is compatible with existing code and serialized messages. The best solution is probably just to use caution when modifying the schema of a `oneof`.

The only difference in the wire format is an extra optional varint field. 

'new' writer -> 'old' reader: This field would end up in the unknown fields. The oneof case value would follow current semantics.
'old' writer -> 'new' reader: No value would be present, so the oneof case value would follow existing semantics.

The 'tough' question is what should happen when the value and the set fields disagree. For example, if an 'old' reader sets a value in the oneof, while also passing on the explicit value set in UnknownFieldSet.

@jgeewax,@wrwg: Curious what you guys think of this idea.

I had another "interesting" idea on how to improve oneof for map and repeated fields.  I believe a 'packed' repeated field can represent an empty list on the wire. Assuming this, it should be possible to:
- Allow packed repeated fields in oneof where "empty but set" would use an empty packed wire representation (a length delimited tag and a zero length)
- Add support for any repeated field to be packed (I believe only numeric types are supported currently, but it should be possible to support all types).

With this any repeated field can be packed, and any packed repeated field (including maps) could be included in a oneof. It also makes skipping past repeated fields in a serialized byte stream much more efficient, as a packed representation includes byte length offset of (ideally) all its values. This doesn't solve the 'none of' problem, but that is definitely the lesser of the two issues.

title: Can reserved be used in oneof?
body:
Is it possible to use "reserved" inside "oneof"?  The proto3 language guide does not specify anything about this.  It seems like something that logically would be supported, but it does not work in the version I'm using (3.1.0) and I don't see anything in the change log that would indicate it has since been added.  

Assuming the answer is "no", is there a reason this support hasn't been or can't be added?

nodes.body: It seems to me that there's not that much value to supporting `reserved` inside a oneof, because you can just as well reserve the same field number outside the oneof (it doesn't really make any difference whether the reserved field appears inside the oneof or not).

That's a fair point.  My thought was that it seemed more intuitive to have the fields reserved inside the oneof, especially if it is deprecating a field that used to be inside the oneof.  Otherwise you have to look elsewhere in the message definition to see what fields numbers and names are no longer allowed.  It's really just a mild aesthetic annoyance more than anything.

If there isn't enough value to add this support, can the proto3 Developer's Guide be updated to note that this isn't supported?  It might save the next person a bit of time.

If deprecate a field that used to be inside the oneof, all the message should avoid the field number not just oneof, put inside oneof will confuse people.

I don't think we want to list all the non support in human words, however we have a spec which shows reserve is not supported in oneof:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec#oneof_and_oneof_field

It's not particularly important to me, but I want to flag that 

> all the message should avoid the field number not just oneof, put inside oneof will confuse people.

Isn't correct, IMO. What confused me is that `reserved` _isn't_ allowed inside a `oneof` field. `oneof` already lists numbers that should be avoided, it's not weird for it to also include reserved ones. It's nice to be able to deprecate fields exactly where they were used.
