title: Add class-scope "FromNanoseconds", "FromMicroseconds", "FromMilliseconds", "FromSeconds", "FromDatetime", and "FromJsonString" methods
body:
**To what language does this apply?** Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Construct a `google.protobuf.timestamp_pb2.Timestamp` from a numeric value of milliseconds in the most-attractive, with-the-best-developer-experience possible.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
`my_timestamp_message = timestamp_pb2.Timestamp.FromMilliseconds(my_numeric_value)`

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
`my_timestamp_message = timestamp_pb2.timestamp_from_milliseconds(my_numeric_value)` would probably be okay.

Protocol Buffers Python currently only supports
```python
my_timestamp_message = timestamp_pb2.Timestamp()
my_timestamp_message.FromMilliseconds(my_numeric_value)
```
. That there is not a single-expression way to construct a populated-from-numerical-value-of-milliseconds `timestamp_pb2.Timestamp` message means that lots of opportunities for attractive code are being missed (and additional temporary variables and helper methods written...).

**Additional context**
Since `FromMilliseconds` is currently an instance-scope method, adding a class-scope method of the same name might require some nicely-encapsulated-and-not-marring-the-public-API hackery like
```python
class Example(object):
    def __init__(self):
        self.FromMilliseconds = self.InstanceScopeFromMilliseconds

    def InstanceScopeFromMilliseconds(self, milliseconds):
        # (some implementation)

    @classmethod
    def FromMilliseconds(cls, milliseconds):
        # (some implementation that returns an instance of the class)
```

Obviously there's nothing special about `FromMilliseconds`; this enhancement should also be done for `FromNanoseconds`, `FromMicroseconds`, `FromSeconds`, `FromDatetime`, and `FromJsonString`.

[Issue 3986](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3986) is something like this in that it asks for something that allows `timestamp_pb2.Timestamp` instantiation on one line, but I don't agree with the one concrete suggestion that it offers (returning `self` from instance-scope `FromMilliseconds`; yuck!).

title: protoc: add way to use internal generators as plugins via CodeGeneratorRequest and CodeGeneratorResponse
body:
One can make use of external generators via plugins, which have to implement the Request/Response message interface defined here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/plugin.proto

This is useful because one can run protobuf code generators in a fairly customised way. There's no need for the input proto files to be on disk, and the generated files don't need to be written to disk either.

We can accomplish half of this with the generators which are part of `protoc` itself. In particular, we can supply the input proto files via `--descriptor_set_in`, and which ones to generate as extra arguments. This is very similar to `CodeGeneratorRequest`, in particular the `proto_file` and `file_to_generate` fields.

It's a bit cumbersome to translate a `CodeGeneratorRequest` to this command-line format, but at least it's possible

However, there's no way to obtain the generated files as a `CodeGeneratorResponse`. The generators will just write the generated files to disk directly. Currently, the only way to accomplish this that comes to mind is to supply a temporary output directory, and walk it to find what files were generated, reading each of them into memory. This is possible in practice, but it's very cumbersome.

I propose that we make it easy to use `protoc`'s native generators as plugins, via the well known `CodeGeneratorRequest` and `CodeGeneratorResponse` interface. We already have a `--plugin` flag to specify what plugin executables to run, so perhaps we could add `--internal_plugin`:

```
protoc --internal_plugin=js < code-generator-request > code-generator-response
```

With this flag, any of the code generators which are part of `protoc` could be accessible as a plugin via standard input and output with just `protoc --internal_plugin=<lang>`.

title: protoc flag to set "-I $PROTOBUF_INSTALL_DIR/include" implicitly
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
`protoc` compiler

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Protobuf installations typically come with the `include` directory that has most of the necessary protobuf files for common types like `google.protobuf.Empty`. 

However, this directory is not included by default, nor is there a simple way to include them during `protoc` invocation.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
- add a new flag `--import-default-includes` to the `protoc` compiler to implicitly add `-I $(which protoc)/../include` (this assumes unzip method, installations via package managers have different structure).
- This will allow users to automatically set the import path to the correct set of supported protobuf files that came with the compiler, by simply doing
```
protoc --import-default-includes -I./path/to/my/other/includes my_file.proto
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
https://github.com/stub42/protobuf-snap/issues/1 <-- proposed setting a global `$PROTOBUF_HOME` during installation via `snap` so that users can do 
```
protoc -I${PROTOBUF_HOME}/include ....
```
but this is not a universal solution as it would only work for `snap`

**Additional context**
`nil`

title: Python3 import issues
body:
## What language does this apply to?
python (3)

## Describe the problem you are trying to solve.
See #1491 

### Structure
```
proto/ <-- git module
    test1.proto
    test2.proto
src/ <-- in PYTHONPATH
    proto_test/
        proto/
            test1_pb2.py
            test2_pb2.py
test_it.py
```

### Files
`test1.proto`:
```
syntax = "proto3";
```

`test2.proto`:
```
syntax = "proto3";
import public "test1.proto"
```

`test_it.py`:
```python3
import "proto_test.proto.test1_pb2"
```

### Run
CMD:
`protoc "--proto_path=$(pwd)/proto" "--python_out=$(pwd)/src/proto_test/proto"`

Run the python file:
```bash
export PYTHONPATH="$(pwd)/src"
python3 test_it.py
```

### Result
`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'student_pb2'`

## Describe the solution you'd like
There are 4 proposed solutions that do not prevent parallelism:
1. Just output them relatively:
    ```
    import public "test1.proto";
    ```
    gets:
    ```python3
    from .test1_pb2 import *
    ```
    ```
    import public "../test1.proto";
    ```
    gets:
    ```python3
    from ..test1_pb2 import *
    ```
    There may be some other cases that need more lookups on how these imports work
2. Use import by file path:
    https://stackoverflow.com/a/67692
    ```
    import public "test1.proto";
    ```
    gets:
    ```python3
    import importlib.util
    from os.path import join, dirname
    test1__pb2_spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("test1_pb2", join(dirname(__file__), "test1_pb2.py"))
    test1__pb2 = importlib.util.module_from_spec(test1__pb2_spec)
    test1__pb2_spec.loader.exec_module(test1__pb2)
    ```
    (could live in a helper function)
3. Implement `python_package` similar to `java_package`
3. Do `python_package` as a CLI flag

Additionally I think for method 1 and 2 it should be optionally triggered by a commandline flag, like `--python3_relative`

## Describe alternatives you've considered
You could do:
```
proto/ <-- git module
    proto_test/
        proto/
            test1.proto
            test2.proto
src/ <-- in PYTHONPATH
    proto_test/
        proto/
            test1_pb2.py
            test2_pb2.py
test_it.py
```
Which would break other things, if you build for multiple languages (which is a core principle of protobuf)

## Additional context
I can create a github repo with an example on request.

title: [go] generated enum mapping to name should use enum type as key
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Go

If it's about generated code change, what programming language?
Go

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
`protoc` provides a maps to convert to/from string/enum value. However the map key are not the enum type but `int32`. This forces users to case the enum to `int32`.

In code:
```go
	dt := pb.DType_TIME

	// name := pb.DType_name[dt] // What's I'd like to have
	name := pb.DType_name[int32(dt)]
	fmt.Println(name)
```
See full example [here](https://github.com/tebeka/protobuf-enum-go)

**Describe the solution you'd like**
The generated maps should be of type `map[<enum>]string` and not `map[int32]string`.

e.g instead of
```go
type DType int32
var DType_name = map[int32]string{
	0: "INTEGER",
	1: "FLOAT",
	2: "STRING",
	3: "TIME",
	4: "BOOLEAN",
}
```

It should be
```go
type DType int32
var DType_name = map[DType]string{
	0: "INTEGER",
	1: "FLOAT",
	2: "STRING",
	3: "TIME",
	4: "BOOLEAN",
}
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
None :)

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

title: Is protobuf serialized data the same when using different language client and protobuf version?
body: I am working for a http server and it accept a http request which contians the protobuf serialized data in the body. In my mind, I want to use redis as a cache server and the redis key is the protobuf serialized data. So when the new request coming, fiststly, I will search the redis using the protobuf serialized data to check whether it existed. So I want to know whether the protobuf serialized data is the same when the request context is same. Of course,  the protobuf serialized data is also same when using different language client and different protobuf version. I hope someone can help me. Thank you!(My english is poor, hope you can understand it!)

nodes.body: @xs233 As far as I know, implementations are fairly consistent between different languages with respect to their serialized output. However, for other reasons I think it would probably not be a good idea to use serialized protos as cache keys. The main one is that map fields are serialized in an arbitrary order, so even with the same language and the same protobuf message, you can get different serialized outputs. Another problem is that unknown fields are serialized at the end (after all the "known" fields), so you can end up with different results depending on whether a particular field is known to the binary serializing it.

OK, if you're going to use a very simple message like that one then it is probably safe to use as a cache key if you're careful. I would recommend writing your own tests to verify that all the implementations you're using are producing consistent output. And the other thing is that you have to be very careful if you ever add or remove any fields, since that could cause problems with unknown fields being serialized differently.
OK. I will do that. Thank you!

title: json format: how should google.protobuf.Any with google.protobuf.Empty payload be rendered?
body:
The [spec](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/google.protobuf#google.protobuf.Any) for `Any` messages states this:

> If the embedded message type is well-known and has a custom JSON representation, that representation will be embedded adding a field value which holds the custom JSON in addition to the @type field.

What is not clear, however, is what does it mean to "have a custom JSON representation"?

I interpret this as having a custom format described in the main [JSON format spec](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json).

That is also how both Java and C/C++ runtimes are implemented for `google.protobuf.Empty`: they do not treat it as having a custom JSON representation and thus would emit the following if encountering an `Any` that has an `Empty` as its payload:

```
{
  "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.Empty"
}
```

However, the [documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/google.protobuf#empty) for well-known types includes this regarding `Empty` messages:

> The JSON representation for Empty is empty JSON object {}.

Does that mean this representation is considered "custom"? The Go runtime assumes yes, and thus renders the message in question as follows:

```
{
  "@type": "type.googleapis.com/google.protobuf.Empty",
  "value": {}
}
```

Admittedly, the value of putting an `Empty` into an `Any` is questionable, but it would be nice if the spec were more clear and if all runtimes behaved the same. As-is, this (admittedly contrived) case reveals an interop problem between runtimes: JSON emitted by one will not be accepted by another.

I originally filed this as a bug against the Go runtime (https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/759), but the response to my bug brought into question the spec itself and the behavior of the Java and C/C++ runtimes.

"The custom JSON representation for Empty is empty JSON object {}."

The word "custom" is used in describing the JSON representation for other well-known types because the description for Any states --

"If the embedded message type is well-known and has a custom JSON representation, that representation will be embedded adding a field value which holds the custom JSON..."

title: Split the compiler from the Bazel rules
body:
Hello protobuf team,

we're experiencing a lot of friction when using Bazel and protobuf, and I think it's caused by the fact that proto rules and the compiler live in the same repository and are always released together. If we could split them, I'd expect these benefits:

1) rules can be released more often (Bazel is moving quite quickly and we expect incompatible changes almost every Bazel release, which is currently every month). Almost every ruleset of the ecosystem depends on protobuf, so not releasing protobuf pretty much blocks everybody.
2) rules can be taught to use system installed version of the protobuf compiler. This is currently something Tensorflow struggles with (https://github.com/perfinion/tensorflow/commit/5e62ff127d07618cb46d1e7919c810f8096937a8).

Maybe there are more, I'm in the brainstorming phase :) Wdyt?

@lberki @dslomov @perfinion @laurentlb @gunan

nodes.body: Are you thinking of having the proto rules released as part of Bazel itself?
Not necessarily (I personally would prefer having fewer rules released with Bazel).

> Are you thinking of having the proto rules released as part of Bazel itself?

Not as part of Bazel itself, but we would like to make sure that protobuf rules can follow released Bazel closely (i.e. follow [Managing breaking changes in Bazel](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Dj5PBLmPVg9ZyApm4GobM3y-mDgY3mVaqpRVttOe-ZQ/)), and protobuf has long release cycles (for a recent problem this has caused, see https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/6675 where the protobuf at head was updated to catch up with incompatible change some time ago, but never released)

Thanks Marcel for opening this!

> Are you thinking of having the proto rules released as part of Bazel itself?

I was thinking the rules should be installed on the system with protoc & libs and similar to how the pkg-config file or FindProtobuf.cmake are installed. 

I was discussing my TF/Bazel issues with Marcel but let me put a summary here for completeness. Basically I've been trying to unbundle all the dependencies from TensorFlow so it can better follow the guidelines for packaging on Linux distros. Unbundling most libraries is fairly easy cuz they only have a library. Protobuf has been comparatively problematic tho. I can point to my system protoc and libprotobuf etc, but I have to duplicate the protobuf.bzl rules into TF itself in order to be able to use those rules which is annoying for maintainability. I *could* download the entire protobuf source tarball but that's a bit extreme considering I only need one single file. I don't mean to pick on protobuf specifically, there are similar problems with other projects too its just that protobuf is so widely used that I've had the most issues with it so I think fixing the issues here would be a good guideline for other projects to follow.

I have opened the PR for unbundling protobuf that works in TF with now things are right now: https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/pull/24004 . I'll definitely be keeping an eye on this and update TF as things change in the future :).

The command-line options to `protoc` change very infrequently, so I don't see any need to couple the protobuf rules (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/protobuf.bzl) with protobuf releases.

On the other hand, the set of files in protobuf itself changes somewhat frequently. The PR referenced above (https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/pull/24004/files) seems to attempt to enumerate all protobuf public headers. I this we should avoid this approach if possible. Perhaps we should ship with protobuf a BUILD file that exposes cc_library() rules for the system-installed protobuf.

This would be similar to how libraries using CMake ship a .cmake file that describes how to use the installed version of a library.

Results of offline chat:

* we can separate the rules from the compiler
* we will include a BUILD file listing all the binaries/libraries/headers with the compiler release.

Josh, can this be left for the protobuf team to take care of?

@dslomov @lberki @gunan Are we all on board with directing Bazel users away from protobuf/protobuf.bzl? Towards native Bazel rules? Towards new rules in bazelbuild org? Do I remember correctly that @dslomov and @haberman discussed this last week? What was the result of the conversation?

Thank you all for participating! It's great to see a will to move forward from the protobuf rules chaos we have right now.
@haberman and I discussed this, and I think the right move would be to steer people towards native Bazel rules (and wrap them in Starlark and eventually migrate)

TF wasnt using the native rules so I kept on not-using them. I will investigate switching things over tho, sounds like thats easiest for everyone. TF also just bumped the minimum bazel version to 0.18 so everyone should be on a new enough version now. :)
@perfinion Did you have time to check if TF can use native rules?

title: Why isn't Java's Any.class an inner class of AnyProto.class?
body:
Inspecting `any.proto`, one can see the following option: 
`option java_outer_classname = "AnyProto";`
Why then isn't `Any.class` an inner class of `AnyProto` in protobuf-java-x.x.x.jar (This is true at least for versions 3.2.0 and 3.6.1)?

Context:
The reason of this question is that I'm using `avro-protobuf` to convert an avro message into Protobuf, and this library looks at the Protobuf schema FileDescriptor to find out the Protobuf class that it needs to instantiate. When looking for Any's file descriptor, this library tries to instantiate com.google.protobuf.AnyProto$Any, because of the java_outer_classname mentioned above. And it looks to me the library is doing the right thing. Here is the code that relies on this metadata to instantiate the class: https://github.com/apache/avro/blob/2bbb99602e9e925058ead86fc8ac4e27055b05d6/lang/java/protobuf/src/main/java/org/apache/avro/protobuf/ProtobufData.java#L225

nodes.body:
Please refer to [the guide](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#options) for **java_multiple_files** option:
> **java_multiple_files** (file option): Causes top-level messages, enums, and services to be defined at the package level, rather than inside an outer class named after the .proto file.

So the **Any** message is just under the package level.

Thanks @BSBandme for the prompt response. 
In this case, what's the point of defining a **java_outer_classname**? If there's no outer class when **java_multiple_files** is used, then probably we shouldn't have **java_outer_classname** if the former is used, right?
Thanks

Sorry that I just saw your comments.

For outer class, we have several other things defined, like descriptor data, file level extensions, etc. So this is needed we you are using descriptor to find a message or get file level extensions.

title: JsonStringToMessage incorrectly rejects lowerCamelCase field names
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.0
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Visual Studio 2017, x86 and x64 toolchains

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a .proto file with an object with PascalCase fields
2. Build .proto file into C++
3. In C++ call JsonStringToMessage with a snippet of JSON which uses lowerCamelCase fields instead of PascalCase
4. Protobuf fails with "Cannot find field" error after failing to match the lowerCamelCase field in the JSON to the pascal case in the type descriptor.

**What did you expect to see**

The JSON mapping section on the protobuf guide [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json) states **"Message field names are mapped to lowerCamelCase and become JSON object keys. ... Parsers accept both the lowerCamelCase name (or the one specified by the json_name option) and the original proto field name."**

**What did you see instead?**

The C++ parser does not accept the lowerCamelCase name in fields as it should.

nodes.body: Its been a long time and looking at the change list it looks like a lot of C++ changes have gone in. Does anyone know if this was fixed at some point?
It has been a couple years and a huge number of major versions and this issue still happens in 3.12.2. Is there some work I can do or that someone can do to push this through? Thanks!

@wd40bomber7 Could you post an example .proto file where you have this problem? We have some tests (e.g. [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/util/json_util_test.cc#L207)) verifying that lowerCamelCase is accepted, so it appears to be working at least in that case.

@acozzette You have only to look at Yury's pull request above to see a test that causes this issue to happen (without his accompanying fix).

See his changes to json_util_test.cc here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/5473/files

If you added that test today it would fail because Protobuf's implementation of casing is not to spec in C++. 

I quoted this in the original issue but I'll quote the passage again here. This is taken directly from the docs: **"Message field names are mapped to lowerCamelCase and become JSON object keys. ... Parsers accept both the lowerCamelCase name (or the one specified by the json_name option) and the original proto field name."** 

The problem is that if your message fields are defined in PascalCase the fields are not correctly mapped to lowerCamelCase and do not correctly deserialize a message with lowerCamelCase message fields.

Please let me know if that's not clear or if I can do anything else to help this along.

Much appreciated!

I think part of the problem here is that we always use `snake_case` field names as per the .proto file style [guide](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/style#message_and_field_names) and therefore don't have any test coverage for how the JSON mapping works with `PascalCase` field names. I talked to some other protobuf team members and learned that using non-`snake_case` field names causes other problems including not working with `FieldMask`. So unfortunately I'm afraid there may be no good solution to this other than to stick with `snake_case` field names.

I don't think that makes sense. I have no idea why a style guide would trump the language spec. Especially since the behavior I'm describing is called out multiple times in the official protobuf 3 documentation.

No where does it mention that you must use snake_case to get correct protobuf behavior. In fact snake case isn't mentioned anywhere. "lowerCamelCase" is mentioned but only to explain that all fields are mapped to lowerCamelCase before serialize/deserialize which isn't true.

Why isn't the right answer just to merge the provided fix? It has some conflicts but they should be easily resolved. **I am willing to do it if the fix will actually be merged in.**

As for the documentation please read these sections from [here.](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3)

Under "JSON Mapping":

> Generates JSON objects. Message field names are mapped to lowerCamelCase and become JSON object keys. If the `json_name` field option is specified, the specified value will be used as the key instead. Parsers accept both the lowerCamelCase name (or the one specified by the `json_name` option) and the original proto field name

Under "JSON Options":

> Use proto field name instead of lowerCamelCase name: By default proto3 JSON printer should convert the field name to lowerCamelCase and use that as the JSON name. An implementation may provide an option to use proto field name as the JSON name instead. Proto3 JSON parsers are required to accept both the converted lowerCamelCase name and the proto field name.

What would it take make this change more palatable? I've been using protobuf (as a part of private industry) with the suggested PR manually merged in to a local protobuf build for a couple years now (needing to update it periodically) and it fixes the only noticeable problem we've ever had with protobuf.

Looking into what you were saying about FieldMask not working and honestly that doesn't seem necessarily related. I'm sure it has uses cases but nothing in the Proto3 documentation specifically mentions them working with all styles (though having a style be mandatory but not automatically enforced/detected/warned against is *insane*) This is very different from the deserialization case which has specifically defined behavior and is mentioned to have that behavior multiple times.

This is a tricky situation because the behavior is determined by the `json_name` option, which is automatically generated by `protoc` if it is not explicitly set. Currently when protoc is given an `UpperCamelCase` field name it will just generate a `json_name` of `UpperCamelCase`. If we changed this behavior then it would affect essentially all implementations at once, since they all rely on `json_name`. But it is hard to know if that would be a safe change. If pretty all much implementations disagree with the spec, then it may make more sense to update the spec than to update every implementation.

The implementations should not rely on json_name alone. 
The spec says:

> By default proto3 JSON printer should convert the field name to lowerCamelCase and use that as the JSON name.

> Proto3 JSON parsers are required to accept **both** the converted lowerCamelCase name and the proto field name.

(Emphasis mine)

So json_name should be the lowerCamelCase of the proto field name, and when mapping a key both the field name and the json_name should be checked. Implementations which aren't checking both are clearly wrong and should be corrected. Do we know what implementations this actually affects?

You said

> If pretty all much implementations disagree with the spec, then it may make more sense to update the spec than to update every implementation.

And honestly I can see that point, if literally every proto implementation does it wrong I can see it might be simpler to fix the spec, but I don't think that's true. All we need to do is check if implementations correctly check both json_name and the protoc field name during deserialize.

I think the problem is that json_name is generated by protoc (unless it's specified explicitly), and the way protoc's logic is written, it works correctly for `snake_case` names but leaves `CamelCase` names unchanged. So protoc will produce these incorrect json_name values and then all implementations will rely on those.

From what I understand, the problem is not that implementations are ignoring `json_name`. They are respecting `json_name` but they're being fed an incorrect value from protoc.

1+ year later and this bug still exists. The official protobuf 3 documentation still has this incorrect line in it:

>  Message field names are mapped to lowerCamelCase and become JSON object keys. If the json_name field option is specified, the specified value will be used as the key instead. Parsers accept both the lowerCamelCase name (or the one specified by the json_name option) and the original proto field name. null is an accepted value for all field types and treated as the default value of the corresponding field type.

This is not true because if your original field is named in PascalCase, the parser will not accept lowerCamelCase. Can we really not accept the PR (after adjustment to the current codebase)?

We ran into this problem on our pubsub push subscriptions after migrating to Google Cloud Run. [Others are having the same issue](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/68490891/google-cloud-platform-push-subscription-sending-duplicate-message-id-fields). I understand not wanting to disrupt existing implementations by changing default behavior, but the solution proposed seems it would help resolve issues like this.

Looking for any update on this topic. Not that I've run into the problem, but I don't want to run into the problem and am currently specifying work to be in a project that utilizes JsonStringToMessage for deserialization of JSON (on disk) to protobuf message (in memory).

I think we are currently using protobuf 3.19.4.

Does anyone have information on this issue in relation to protobuf versions pre-, at, or post- 3.19.4?

title: Inconsistent behaviour when FileDescriptorProto is missing custom extensions dependencies
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.1
Language: Java
**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux jonathan 4.15.0-39-generic 42-Ubuntu SMP Tue Oct 23 15:48:01 UTC 2018 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux

**What did you do?**
We have a tool where we create a [FileDescriptorProto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/704037f23a9ede00ec4fcf40d568712ce6200934/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L61) manually and then pass that to `protoc --python_out=. --descriptor_set_in=/dev/stdin all.proto` via stdin.

When using the google api annotations as custom extensions on the `MethodOptions` which are options for `MethodDescriptorProto`, we were not adding the `google/api/annotations.proto` dependency.

When running the protoc generator for Python, or any language other than Java, protoc succeeds. However, when we run it for the Java generator `--java_out=`, it generates this error:

```
[libprotobuf FATAL ../../../../../src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_file.cc:129] CHECK failed: file_proto_desc: Find unknown fields in FileDescriptorProto when building all.proto. It's likely that those fields are custom options, however, descriptor.proto is not in the transitive dependencies. This normally should not happen. Please report a bug.
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'google::protobuf::FatalException'
  what():  CHECK failed: file_proto_desc: Find unknown fields in FileDescriptorProto when building all.proto. It's likely that those fields are custom options, however, descriptor.proto is not in the transitive dependencies. This normally should not happen. Please report a bug.
```

Then when I add the missing dependency, everything works fine.

I realise that this was an error on our behalf, but there seems to be some inconsistency between Java and the other generators in protoc when it comes to missing dependencies for custom extensions / options. I am just curious as to what the expected behaviour should be; 

1) should protoc error if custom extensions dependencies are missing

title: Latest release broken when building with Bazel at HEAD
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.1.1

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Any

Bazel at HEAD has removed the deprecated `REPOSITORY_NAME` and `PACKAGE_NAME` globals, but v3.6.1.1 still refers to them despite [this change in May (4fcb36c51c1c0355c2a23b1f06ec583f2428cd30)](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/4fcb36c51c1c0355c2a23b1f06ec583f2428cd30#diff-14e64c3c0a0449ceb162062b8291fa19) that migrated to the new APIs. Thus, `protobuf.bzl` fails with an error when trying to import protobuf into a workspace.

Here's an example of a failure this is causing: https://travis-ci.org/bazelbuild/rules_swift/jobs/458163286

Can we please have a new release that includes 4fcb36c51c1c0355c2a23b1f06ec583f2428cd30?

Hey,

My team also recently had a few problems with C# reflections using Unity with il2cpp and enums using the 3.6.1 build. Note I am not the unity dev who dug into this, but this is a list of things we worked through. This sounds like the same issue as this, but maybe it's not?

1. That code accessed only through reflection was stripped because IL2CPP did not know it was needed, and that was solved by link.xml with the contents (DataModelBindings is a .NET lib of all my protoc generated code) 

`<linker>
     <assembly fullname="DataModelBindings" preserve="all"/>
</linker>`

This is probably something that should be mentioned in Protobuf documentation?

Relevant part of Unity documentation: https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/IL2CPP-BytecodeStripping.html


2. Next this error came up:

_Attempting to call method 'Google.Protobuf.Reflection.ReflectionUtil+ReflectionHelper`2[[Cdm.SerializeStateData, DataModelBindings, Version=0.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=null],[Cdm.eSerialization+Types+Type, DataModelBindings, Version=0.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=null]]::.ctor' for which no ahead of time (AOT) code was generated._

(eSerialization is an enum)

The issue appears to be with this file in particular: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/Reflection/ReflectionUtil.cs
GetReflectionHelper() with its call to Activator.CreateInstance() is where things seem to go wrong.

The use of generics through reflection + not letting the IL2CPP compiler know what classes will be needed is what caused the error - code was requested that was not generated, and there was no way to generate it on demand (as it would normally happen with JIT runtimes).
Somewhat relevant part of Unity documentation: https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/ScriptingRestrictions.html ("Ahead-of-time compile" section)

To get past this we ended up replacing the smarts and quickness of the generics via reflection in ReflectionUtils.cs with [pretty simple code that calls invoke instead](https://github.com/aaron-bray/protobuf/commit/d1a323a495042461809e77560b2ec69cc7fda04a).

title: Can not define two same enum name in the same proto file

nodes.body: This behavior is actually expected. The enum values go into the scope enclosing the whole enum definition, so in cases like your example, values in different enums can still conflict with each other. Probably the best way around it is just to put a prefix in front of `UNKNOWN`, like `TEST_ENUM1_UNKNOWN` for example.

@acozzette 
Although this behavior is expected, it's really not friendly to developer. Values in different enums don't  conflict with each other in Java.
The general proto syntax has to taken all supported languages into account.

Isn't it possible to use scoped enums for c++ 11 and implement an option to specify which enums to be used. We mainly use Java and it's seriously utterly stupid that this requires these kinds of hacks.

Same applies in Go where the enum value gets automatically prefixed with the enum name by the code generator.
Manually adding the enum name again as a prefix in the enum value results in stuttering and is very unpleasant to read and use 😢
The design looks odd. Prefixing with the enum name sends me back to the old age of programming.

It is common use case to define UNSPECIFIED/UNKNOWN=0 in enums to avoid undesired defaults, and require explicit values.
Providing syntax to define multiple enum types without isolated scope for their values looks like an incomplete design.
Is there any plans to fix this? Is there any clean workaround for this in 2024? It really doesn't make any sense.

JavaScript projects that use `@grpc/proto-loader` rely on being able to convert enum values into strings and use them as such. The fact that the current solution requires prefixing every enum value with the name of the enum is ridiculous.

Please fix the current design!
For the series: things you won't find in the README.md.

title: C++ Bytes field representation as std::vector instead of std::string
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
C++ (maybe others)
Affects generated code and general APIs (reflection etc.).

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
When working with raw data buffers in C/C++, operating system interfaces or other low level interfaces typically represent those buffers as `void*`, `uint8_t*` or `char*`.
In protocol buffers generated C++ code, `Bytes` fields are represented `as std::string`. This leads to type conversion difficulties:

Unfortunately, std::string does not provide mutable access to its data in `char*` representation. Only non-mutable access is allowed via `const char* data() const noexcept;` ([link](http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/string/string/data/))

This implies, that all low-level code, which creates or modifies buffer contents has to be wrapped using memory copies, for example like this:
```
char * buffer = malloc(size);
lowLevelBufferModifyingFuncationCall(buffer, size);
std::string myString(buffer, size);   // copy happens here
delete buffer;
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
In contrast to std::string, std::vector provides read and write access to the underlying datastructure, as it guarantees, that stored data is consecutively in memory (`&v[0]+n == &v[n]`:
```
      value_type* data() noexcept;
const value_type* data() const noexcept;
```
see [link](http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/vector/vector/data/)

If protocol buffer would expose an interface to access Bytes fields as std::vectors, the above example could be implemented without the seemingly unnecessary copy operation:
```
// initialize the vector to the required size:
// zero initialization is assumed to be faster than copy (see comment below)
std::vector<char> buffer(size); // might also use buffer.resize()
lowLevelBufferModifyingFuncationCall(buffer.data(), size);
// now buffer could directly be used with protocol buffers, no copy necessary
```
Unfortunately `std::vector` does not provide a way to change its size without initializing its contents.
However zero initialization should be faster than a copy, which would still give better performance than the workaround with a temporary buffer.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
The only alternative I currently see is the one described on the problem section. Or derivations of this.

**Additional context**
As far as I know, the main difference of `std::string` vs. `std::vector` is, that `std::vector` guarantees that the data will be allocated as a continuous block of memory. I would be interested in the reasons as to why protocol buffer designers chose `std::string` over `std::vector`.

nodes.body:
Actually if you want to get mutable access to the raw `char*`, I believe you can do that by just taking the address of the first element, e.g. `&s[0]`. According to this StackOverflow [post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/1986966/does-s0-point-to-contiguous-characters-in-a-stdstring), the data was not guaranteed to be contiguous in earlier versions of C++, but starting from C++11 it is guaranteed.

I was reading recently that some people consider it a bad practice to use `std::string` for non-textual binary data. I was surprised by that because we do this quite a bit in the protobuf codebase and haven't had any problems with it. For me this is just the way I am used to doing things. I believe proto1 (the predecessor to proto2 and proto3 which was never open sourced) didn't even make a distinction between `string` and `bytes` fields, so fields were treated the exact same way whether they included UTF-8 text or arbitrary binary data. That may explain part of the reason we ended up following this pattern.

Thanks for your quick answer :+1: 

I did some research. Unfortunately I could not get my hands on the official C++ specification. The closest thing I found was some draft from 2011: [link](www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2011/n3242.pdf)
In section 21.4.1.5, indeed the following is stated:
> The char-like objects in a basic_string object shall be stored contiguously. That is, for any basic_string object s, the identity &*(s.begin() + n) == &*s.begin() + n shall hold for all values of n such that 0 <= n < s.size().

However I still can see two problems:
- This does not give the user the allowance to modify data in this memory region, but merely describes an implementation detail. The API does not expose any method to get a non const accessor to this data region.
- Your proposal about using `&s[0]` does not respect access control of the string class and uses internal knowledge of the std::string class. This sounds to me like a workaround for a const cast. I am certain it will work, but it just looks dirty :hankey:

Maybe this is a bug/missing feature in the C++ API, as it is not (yet) exploiting all aspects of the Specification. Note, that the non-const `.data()` method for `std::vector` was also only added recently with C++11.

So with `std::string` I only have two options:
1. Respect type-safety and make useless copies
2. Drop type-safety by doing const casts or relative addressing starting from the first element

(not sure if type-safety is the correct word here)

Actually I did a little more research just now and found that C++17 adds in a non-const `data()` method for `std::string`, like the one that was added for `std::vector`. So at least starting from C++17 the problem goes away entirely. Still I think the `&s[0]` trick is not really so bad, since it relies only on behavior documented by the standard starting from C++11.

I agree with you. It seems like C++ `std::string` + `std::vector` were primarily designed to be usable within the `std::` ecosystem.
Type-safe interoperability with low-level data-structures only recently seems to get attention. We were just unlucky, that `std::vector` got this attention first :smile:

I am beginning to wonder, what the difference between `std::string` and `std::vector` actually is... Maybe in the future we might get an O(1) conversion between `std::string` and `std::vector` :yum: 

-> closing, as problem seems to be caused by limitations in legacy C++ APIs and does not exist in more recent C++ versions.

Telling people `std::string` is the way-to-go for binary data because it just "works" contradicts why we're using a programming "language" in essence!

Any C++ developer, by reading a code would expect `std::string` to hold null-terminated character sequence, being otherwise makes a lot of confusion!

We write "codes" which we read way more often than we write them, how about spreading them worldwide!

For more reasons, see answers here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/9626914/stdstring-or-stdvectorchar-to-hold-raw-data

Re-opening due to public interest (see comments above).

I recently stumbled on this issue again when inter-operating with other libraries, which expect `std::vector<uint8_t>` as input for work on data buffers.
Modern C++ APIs rarely use raw pointers in favor of containers with `move` or references to containers.
I could still not find a way to cleanly convert `std::string` to `std::vector<uint8_t>` without nasty copy.

While I support the idea that `std::string` is the wrong type to use here, I do want to chime in that likely the reason the original designers of the codebase went with `std::string` may be due to the one small advantage it has: the [short-string optimization](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/10315041/meaning-of-acronym-sso-in-the-context-of-stdstring), which can mean no allocations for short strings (<16 or <20 bytes, depending on implementation).

That being said, using `std::string` in this way to hold binary data blobs is not new to Google codebases -- leveldb also does it.  I think it's a design error because it leads to a certain lack of type safety, but it might not be worth breaking compatibility to redo this anytime soon..

I think it worths to add returning values as `std::string_view` and `std::span<std::uint8_t>` beside `std::string` and `std::vector<std::uint8_t>`, as these will point to the decoded data directly without copying, and the user will know exactly how to handle them.  

Not sure what's needed to add this feature in the library, perhaps decoding without copying the data in essence, where absent data got created on heap and deleted dynamically somehow, or even allowing those return-values dynamically only if present (conditional `if(XX.has_value()`.

There are a great many competing tensions going on here:

- `std::string` is not a great type for binary data (as noted).
- exposing any type as a `const &` constrains the implementation a great deal (as the implementation must then have such a type)
- `std::vector` comes with some significant complexity around how it would interact with protobuf arenas (actually `std::string` already has some of that, but we do some carefully managed encapsulation breaks to work around it)
- Any change to the signature of generated APIs must be embarked on carefully.

The entire motivation behind the new [editions](https://protobuf.dev/editions/overview/) effort is to provide primitives for doing this.

One of the first targets we will use this for is to switch `string` accessors from `const std::string&` to `absl::string_view` parameters.  We can review `bytes` fields at the same time, but there is a lot of value in terms of smooth evolution of user code bases when one can go back and forth between `std::string`.  All this to say, we are thinking about these things, but don't expect any fast motion here.

I think it's better to stick with `std::string_view` for C++17 upwards compilers, as abseil might remove its support.

[As Quoted](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/issues/1122#issuecomment-1060768218):
> 2. Our goal is for Abseil types like string_view to generally disappear when the relevant standard is available. string_view is a C++17 type - by the time there is good compiler support for C++23 we may well be removing Abseil support for string_view.

I understand that protobuf is a very large project, which is loaded with years of backward-compatibility requirements, which naturally slows the pace of introducing new features. Given this, can we expect the no-copy decoding feature to be introduced soon (perhaps within two years)?

For the specific question `std::string_view` vs `absl::string_view`, protobuf is committed to using `absl::string_view` right now.  At the end of 2024, both abseil and protobuf will update their [minimum C++ to 2017](https://github.com/google/oss-policies-info/blob/main/foundational-cxx-support-matrix.md).  Until then we are definitely on `absl::string_view`.  When that happens, the type will dissolve into an alias for `std::string_view`.  After that, we will likely clean our internal spellings to `std::string_view`.  Abseil will probably remove the alias eventually as well, but that is for them to decide.

For the specific case of no-copy decoding, we added support for this via `absl::Cord` in [23.x](https://protobuf.dev/news/2023-04-11/#cord).

Thanks @fowles, got to have a good research before replying here, which concludes that the standard C++ protobuf library seems doesn't fit for an embedded systems regarding binary size, given that adding abseil to use the Cord will increase the size further. As it appears other options as nanopb are more suitable.

I suppose we all agree that `std::string` is a bad abstraction to the bytes buffer data. But what is the most appropriate abstraction so that we can avoid data copy whenever possible?

1. All the bytes buffer can be represented as a pair of `void* data` and `size_t len`.
2. The underlying data can be discontinuous. I believe we should consider such scenario, otherwise the Linux's `iovec ` and `readv`, `writev` would be unnecessary.
3. protobuf message should take the ownership of the buffer.

If we ignore 3, then it's no doubt that a sequence of `std::string_view` or `std::span` is the best. e.g., `std:span<std::span<char>>`. But just forget it. There is no way that we can abandon the ownership.

Let's assume we now have a pair of `void* data` and `size_t len`. We've know how it be allocated and how to release it. Does STL give us a facility to take the ownership of these data without copying memory? I believe the answer is NO.

But we still have a room for refine. We can let each of the protobuf's bytes type hold an instance of `std::pmr::memory_resource`, and replace `std::string` with `std::pmr::string`. Therefore, at least we can construct our buffer on the stack or somewhere where we can customize the behaviour of allocation and deallocation.

---
FYI. I use brpc (https://github.com/apache/brpc) in my corporate project. brpc has a type called `IOBuf` to represent the bytes buffer. If we use brpc to receive the http request, then the http body will be wrapped into an `IOBuf` object. This type enables user to append the user data into the buffer, but without data copy. That is, the buffer can be discontinuous. And we will also pass a deleter object when appending the data, so that when the `IOBuf` destructing, it can release all the data we've appended into it.

Here are some reference of `IOBuf`, hope these stuff can help the evolving of protobuf.

https://brpc.incubator.apache.org/docs/c++-base/iobuf/

https://github.com/apache/brpc/pull/2431 (A PR submitted by myself, change the deleter type from `void(*)(void*)` to `std::function<void(void*)>`.)

https://github.com/apache/brpc/blob/master/src/butil/iobuf.cpp#L1220 (The source codes of `IOBuf`.)

title: proto3 JSON spec breaks backwards compatibility expectations
body:
I'm sorry if this was already discussed. I'm filing as a bug and not a feature request because I believe this behavior breaks sane expectations.

My issue is with the json options specification here: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json_options
```
Ignore unknown fields: Proto3 JSON parser should reject unknown fields by default but may provide an option to ignore unknown fields in parsing.
```

With this specification, updating any protobuf message will break old clients if they use the default json implementation. 

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master/v3.6.0/v3.5.0 etc.
Language: Swift

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
iOS

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
N/A

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create any "Message" protobuf 
```
message CartItem {
    string id = 0;
    string name = 1;
}
```
2. Write code parse the message from json using default options. Ship this code to millions of clients
```
       guard let protobuf = try? CartItem(jsonString: json) else {
            return nil
        }
```

3. Update the message 
```
message CartItem {
    string id = 0;
    string name = 1;
    string description = 2;
    string analytics_id = 3;
}
```

4.  Millions of clients fail to parse cart items with the error
```
▿ JSONDecodingError
  - unknownField : "description"
```

5. Patch clients to use 
```
        var options = JSONDecodingOptions()
        options.ignoreUnknownFields = true
        guard let protobuf = try? CartItem(jsonString: json, options: options) else {
            return nil
        }
```

6. New programmer writes new code that uses the default implementation, and the cycle repeats itself forever.

**What did you expect to see**
I expected that the default implementation wouldn't fail when I updated my Message, and backwards compatibility would be preserved.

**What did you see instead?**
Not what I expected.

nodes.body:
It should be noted that dropping unknown fields means if the message received is sent back out, it has fundamentally changed because those unknown fields are gone.  So enabling the option is dangerous.

The binary format does not have these sorta issues because the binary data can be easily preserved and reflected out.

I believe the intent with JSON was to better deal with these sorta issues, FieldMasks should be used to require the specific data clients want, and also during mutations, include a field mask to say what fields you are specifically changing.  That way the fact that a client/server doesn't know about a field is less of an issue, because it won't be include in the masks it requests/sends, letting the other end know that it is not explicitly removing the field.

That’s a really good point, and a use case that I wasn’t thinking about.

We mostly use binary representation, so mostly this isn’t an issue, but we do use Json for things like embedding data into apns notifications. 

I still think that in my use case, where the server is generating protobufs, and many clients of many different versions are parsing them, this feels very broken.
FieldMask seems the right answer to that. Supporting keeping unknown in json is impossible for us.

I wasn't suggesting keeping unknown in json, just not throwing an exception if an unknown field exists. Thanks for listening, I will file this under "things you just have to know" when working with protobufs.
In several languages, we do allow giving "ignore_unknown" option to json decoding method.

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json
Search "Ignore unknown fields"

Yup! I've added that to every place where we're not using the binary
representation, and will hopefully remember to do so in the future. Thank
you.

title: If a dotnet dependency contains proto files, should extract them and add the extracted dir to --proto_path
body:
Developers using java or go seem to be able to include proto files from referenced assemblies #15.

From my searching, I have not found an equivalent way to do this for dotnet.

I propose that protoc is expanded / or a plugin developed to support specifying a dotnet assembly name as an include argument.

Then protoc could enumerate any proto files in the assembly using something like [this](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.assembly.getfiles?view=netcore-2.0).

body:
**What language does this apply to?**
This issue relates to the C# `Google.Protobuf` package.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Currently there is no way to obtain a `ByteString` from generated code, which represents either a message/proto-file with its dependencies which can be used with `protoc`. The appropriate data structure for this is `FileDescriptorSet`.

In particular I'd like to be able to generate protobuf code for another language given the generated C# protobuf code. We can already get an `IList<FileDescriptor>` of dependencies through the `Dependencies` property on `FileDescriptor`, all that needs to be done is bundling that with the instance of the `FileDescrpitor` and putting that into a `FileDescriptorSet` data structure and serializing.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I'd like to add facility to get the serialized representation of `FileDescriptorSet`, containing all dependencies from either a `FileDescriptor` or a `MessageDescriptor`. This is code I'd be happy to write/test myself.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Ultimately the 2 formats for specifying protobuf messages are:
- .proto files
- `FileDescriptorSet`s
Given the necessary information is already stored in generated code to obtain the `FileDescriptorSet`, and this mechanism allows for easy bundling of dependencies, that seemed like the best way forward.

**Additional context**
The reason I'm looking to generate code for other languages, given the generated code for one (in this case C#), is to facilitate adding Protobuf support to the Pact contract testing framework. I can provide additional context if required.

title: proto4: Add support for nullability / optionality in Java
body:
I think we can all appreciate the importance of having first-class support for nullability / optionality in our programming languages. I think we all recognize there's frequent, legitimate need when programming to distinguish between the default, zero or "zero-like" value of a type, and the complete absence of a value. This is so much the case that many functional programming languages prominently feature some sort of [option type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_type).

Following that, it should be important that the protocol buffers language and accompanying programming language bindings give first-class support for this.

Due to the design of proto3, this isn't currently feasible: e.g., the serialization format cannot distinguish between a default value and an absence of value, Java codegen cannot use Java `Optional`s without requiring everyone to use Java 8, etc. (see #2553).

So right now, we muck around with [wrapper types](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/wrappers.proto) for primitive types, and boxing/unboxing them in our code; checking `com.google.protobuf.MessageOrBuilder#hasFoobar` before calling `com.google.protobuf.MessageOrBuilder#getFoobar`for message types, and checking if a value is `null` (if using a `@Nullable` type) or if `Optional#isPresent` (if using an `Optional` type) before setting anything in a builder; etc. It's a giant mess, and it's no fun.

I would propose that in proto4, we add first-class support for nullable / optional types, both in the serialization format, and the codegen. We can do this in a type safe way that avoids [the pitfalls of `null`](https://github.com/google/guava/wiki/UsingAndAvoidingNullExplained), using modern language support for optional types.

Here's an example of how this could be done in proto4:

- Add back the `optional` keyword to the Protocol Buffers Version 4 Language Specification. This keyword would denote a nullable type. This would require the serialization format to distinguish between a default value and absence of value once again. The default value then of an `optional` field would be none / the empty optional / whatever you want to call it.
- If a field is marked `optional`, then codegen outputs classes whose getters return `java.util.Optional` types, and whose builders' setters accept `java.util.Optional` types. This requires that proto4 require Java 8 and above.

At no point in Java is `null` ever used. Unset `optional` fields do not return `null` when you call its getters, and setters will still throw NPE if you try to pass them `null`. This approach is null safe, while retaining the usability of optionality which so many modern languages already support.

nodes.body: I would even be happy not throwing an NPE on set and returning NULL on get if its not set.
Rather than the `optional` keyword, I look forward to optionality being indicated with the standard `?` after the type.

So if you dont use the `optional` keyword you get the default value transparently?

That leaves you with a small problem. If you *require* a field to be set, you mark it optional, so you can determine whether it was set, and then return an error if it wasn't.

Then you have to live with the irony of having marked a field as 'optional' because it's not.

Suspect you would need a `required` keyword as a *dual* to the optional keyword, otherwise you run into the same kind of semantic nonsense you're trying to avoid

Update: I am aware that leaving this tool out of the toolbox is a deliberate design choice

There is no reason for us to increment any version information and limit this only to a whole new jump in version. The keyword `optional` was already not a valid type, and thus adding it in is unambiguous, which is why a proposal was advanced to add it back into proto3, but keep the default behavior the same: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.12.0/docs/implementing_proto3_presence.md 

There is absolutely no reason to add in `required` again, because it was already fundamentally problematic on many levels. If people want to enforce ensuring a value is set by marking it `optional` and then testing for its presence, then :woman_shrugging: that seems like a whole lot of effort to go through rather than just validating that the value makes sense in the first place.

For instance, a required string field can just as easily be tested for the zero value (which will almost certainly already be an invalid value), as it can for presence. I’ve stumped a whole lot of developers covering validation magic, by pointing out tha `int port [required]` does not guarantee that the value is valid at all. “But a zero value would fail to open up the port.” But, actually, it doesn’t.

There are many good reasons why protobuf should steer clear of any validation of data inputs, even including making a field mandatory or required. Validation of values is a business logic decision, and one that cannot by solved by a data storage/interchange format.

P.S.: Not sure what the purpose of this ticket remaining open should be. We’re already considering the matter through `proto3` changes already, and so wherever that discussion is occurring, this is a duplicate of that issue.

I guess the part that i find weird is that the `optional` keyword has been added in, even though *every* field is optional.

so `optional` doesn't actually mean "you don't have to set this" (which is what you might expect if you weren't familiar with proto3), instead it actually means "I'll be able to tell the difference between you setting it to the default value, and not setting it at all". I've not seen the word `optional` used to describe exactly these semantics in *any other context*.

Can we agree that's just a *little* odd?

As far as I can tell, there are two applications for this:

1. **distinguishing between a default value and an unset value**. There are loads of interfaces for which there's an important semantic difference between a default value and an unset value, or where the default value for a primitive type is valid, but almost certainly undesirable (and we want to be *defensive* about being given this value by accident). It's clear that `0` is *qualitatively* different to `None` (for example. substitute your favourite language) and `optional` allows us to capture that in the general case when we can't or won't use the well-known wrapper types. Fine.
2. **the `optional` keyword can be abused as a way to enforce that a field is set**, as I described above.

It seems clear to me that the first application is the intended one, even if the way 'optional' is being used here is very gently 'off'.

The second application is Bad, and is a great way to generate interfaces which are not backwards compatible (at the application layer). But since it exists, people will use it. Now not only is it a misuse of the functionality, you'll have people using the word `optional` on a  field *specifically because* it is **not** optional.

Now this just the worst kind of issue comment, because i'm not going to offer a solution. I just don't see how you could alter this in a backwards compatible way.

Cap'n'proto has a nice solution- it serialises the same way on the wire, but you can specify your own default values for fields. That means you can choose values that make sense for your application, or set the default value to something absurd so that you can more easily infer that it wasn't set. If you could do *that* then `oneof` wrappers would be sufficiently rare you probably wouldn't mind using them explicitly

:thinking: OK, yeah. I get the point about the name of the keyword.

I think the interest in using the term was because it would restore the `optional` semantics that existed in proto2.

Several existing strongly-typed modern languages
1. provide for an optional field that must be checked at runtime before use (typical syntax: a ? after the type)
2. provide for a required field that must be provided at compile time or provably at object creation time (no ? after the type)
3. require that a field be either optional or required (perhaps with a default value, e.g., 0 or "")
Seems to me that a future proto-n language should satisfy all 3 points. A clean syntax such as ? would be nice. We have to be looking forward, not back, so I would be in favor of an incompatible syntax change.

Just because several “modern languages” support these features, does not mean that protobuf should cater exclusively to them.

There are plenty of languages which are significant users of protobuf, where such features do not exist, and/or make supporting said feature unbearably inefficient.

Very specifically, any sort of builtin requirement that a value _must_ be set or exist before marshalling or after marshalling is going to run head-first into one of the very reasons why there is a `proto3` in the first place: the `requirement` keyword was made with good intentions, but created far more issues than it ever solved.

The proto3 optional keyword satisfies your point 1, and proto3 semantics already satisfy your point 3.

Since [Field Presence](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/implementing_proto3_presence.md) support was added to proto3, would this issue be the right place to track Java support for this feature or is there another issue?
Related: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8012
proto4 is not under development, and it's unlikely this feature will be considered
Isssue #8676 is about essentially the same thing and although it is for kotlin, as I commented there, it could be implemented for java too.

title: Proposal: Allow text format parser to accept unknown fields
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
All languages. There is already an existing issue (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4821) for doing this just in C++, but it's just as useful everywhere else. (My personal interest is primarily in Python right now)

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Handling unknown fields is an important part of the proto deserializer, and occasionally it's useful to apply the same behavior to text-serialized protos. (For example, I have one data store which stored protos as text to aid debuggability, but since certain fields no longer exist, it's no longer possible to parse them at all!)

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add an option to the text-format merge function in each language to ignore unknown fields, which would simply skip those instead of failing with a parse error.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Short of copying and forking all of the text format logic, there's not much else to do. I can't even read the old files, modify them, and write them back easily, since I can't use the proto parser to parse the old files at all.

**Additional context**
I'd be happy to submit a pull request for the Python version of this change, if the API is agreed upon.

nodes.body: (I can't tell from @xfxyjwf 's comment on #4821 whether this already exists in all languages in the internal codebase and just awaits exposure, or if it only exists in C++. But that issue has been idle since June, and the proposed PR to do it in C++ seems to have been abandoned in favor of the internal codebase change at Feng's request. So maybe we can resurrect this issue now?)

@zunger-humu We are a little hesitant to support this kind of feature. The reason is that the text format is primarily intended for storing human-readable and human-editable configuration data, and not so much for transmitting data or storing data for long periods of time. If we allow unknown fields, then there's a risk that you could introduce a tiny typo and accidentally delete an important part of your configuration without any error or warning.

Thus my suggestion that this be an option, rather than default behavior. :)
'allow_unknown_fields' could (and should) have a clear warning on it, but
there are legit reasons to use this for storage. (At least in my case, it's
because I'm working with people who came from a JSON world and are very
leery of having a core config file not be instantly readable from the GCP
UI without tools. Which isn't a terrible thing, really; I've found it handy
in debugging more than once, myself)

title: New zlib dependency breaks protobuf as an external bazel repository
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: Bazel/any

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Ubuntu Linux 18.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
bazel 0.20.0

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
Have the following rule in another repository's WORKSPACE file:

    local_repository(
        name = "com_google_protobuf"
        path = "path/to/protobuf"
    )

...then run `bazel build` on a target that depends upon anything in `com_google_protobuf//...`

**What did you expect to see**
Expected to see it work as it did before the inclusion of the zlib http_archive.

**What did you see instead?**
`ERROR: /home/mumbleskates/.cache/bazel/_bazel_mumbleskates/0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef/external/com_google_protobuf/BUILD:132:1: no such target '//external:zlib': target 'zlib' not declared in package 'external' defined by /home/mumbleskates/repos/projectname/WORKSPACE and referenced by '@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf'`

Essentially, protobuf can no longer be used as an external dep e.g. as a submodule unless we make a fragile copy of the zlib http_archive repo in our own WORKSPACE file.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
This was working at 81c3e0cf, for example, but now that protobuf has an external dependency on another bazel repo, rather than including the dependencies in its own files or cloned into a submodule, this becomes difficult and frustrating.

I feel that a good fix to this issue might be to clone zlib at a desired commit into a submodule and reference it as a package instead of a separate bazel repository. This avoids the requirement that everyone who references _this_ repository needs to know about, and maintain the correct version of in their own rules, every dependency so declared.

nodes.body:
@mumbleskates Thanks for filing this issue. I was wondering if we would run into problems like this when we added the zlib dependency. I can see the rationale for cloning zlib into a submodule, but on the other hand that would make life harder for projects that use protobuf and also independently use zlib. Those projects would then have ODR violations from linking against two copies of zlib.

I have heard that some projects get around these issues by providing a Starlark function that returns all the necessary dependencies. Would it solve your problem if we provided a function like this that you could call?
Yes, that'd probably be an ideal solution, I'd appreciate it!

title: Make RepeatedField's EnsureSize() a public method in C#
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

I need to quickly process a large number of primitives in one array, filter some, and insert them into a repeated field.  I know the size of my output before I begin processing the array.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I would like to preallocate my output RepeatedField, then loop over the large input array only a single time, processing, filtering, and writing out the data to a RepeatedField in a single pass.

_If EnsureSize() were public instead of private, I could accomplish this._

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Adding a RepatedField constructor that takes a capacity parameter, but users don't typically create their own RepeatedFields, and you also couldn't grow the array this way.
- I could process and filter from arrayA to tempArray, then call AddRange(tempArray) on the output RepeatedField, but that would require traversing the large array twice, although it wouldn't be calling EnsureSize() as often.
- I could call Add() for each element.  This would be the most inefficient of all choices.

nodes.body:
Make sense to me. The c++ has this public API as well:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f9d8138376765d229a32635c9209061e4e4aed8c/src/google/protobuf/repeated_field.h#L162

Are you happy to create a PR(including test) and assign to me. I'd prefer to change the naming of EnsureSize() to Reserve() same with C++.

title: Add Support for Cyclic Objects

nodes.body:
I have a proof of concept working and wanted to get your thoughts.  If a user has handle-messages-by-reference option turned on, embedded messages would have 2 forms--pointer form and message form.  The embedded message form would be decided at runtime when traversing the object graph.  While traversing the object graph, objects processed for the first time would be written out in message form.  On the other hand, objects that have already been processed before would be written out in pointer form.  

**Pointer form would look like:** 
  
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5814642/54786607-aea05e80-4bff-11e9-8d39-b716998adb08.png)

**Message form would look like:** 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5814642/54805018-02d13000-4c4c-11e9-8964-71192d8a91ec.png)

This would be a very intrusive change: it would require changing the wire format and all implementations. We have never made a change of this scale, and it would take an enormous benefit to justify the cost. It is very unlikely we would accept a change of this kind, sorry.

I recommend adding ids to your protobuf schema to represent object references if you want to have cyclic object graphs.

Thanks for the response.

Could you explain more on how the following idea would work "I recommend adding ids to your protobuf schema to represent object references if you want to have cyclic object graphs."

For anyone that found this after the fact like me.  Don't forget that C# classes that are created by protocol buffers are `sealed partial class` which means that it cannot be inherited, but you can add to the class with more `partial` classes.  This would help solve any DbContext mapping issues or wanting a `virtual` property.

This was one of the best features of Macromedia's AMF protocol released in 2002 with Flash Player 6.  Once an object of any type was serialized, any future instances seen in the graph were encoded by reference instead of by value.  This was brilliant, and supported very complex object graphs.

title: EnumTypeWrapper objects should be usable according to the enum.Enum interface (or maybe the enum.IntEnum interface)
body:
**To what language does this apply?** Python.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
The Python language (since 3.4) has an `enum` module, but the generated Python classes in `_pb2` files don't behave according to the interfaces of the classes defined in the `enum` module.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I think `EnumTypeWrapper` objects should support being used, as much as possible, as though they were subclasses of `enum.Enum`.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
`enum.IntEnum`, though **disfavored in new code**, exists to allow `int`-based ad hoc "enums" from before Python 3.4 to be upgraded to be usable according to the interface of `enum.Enum`. It _may_ have a role to play.

**Additional context**
This would be really great for type-checking; it would allow authors to describe parameters and return values as of type `my_module_pb2.MyEnum` rather than as of type `int`.

nodes.body: See https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/5234, where I asked whether the EnumTypeWrapper classes can be replaced by enum from the stdlib.

title: C# Reflection methods for google/protobuf/wrappers.proto return inner types
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.1.0
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Mac OS X 10.14.2 (but through Docker)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
C# - .NET Core 2.1

**What did you do?**
For the types in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/wrappers.proto (i.e. `BoolValue`, `StringValue`, etc), it seems that `fieldDescriptor.Accessor.GetValue(msg)` returns a value of the inner type (`bool`, `string`, etc.) rather than the `BoolValue` or `StringValue` type as I would have expected. However if I check `fieldDescriptor.FieldType`, it's a `Message`.

If I say `fieldDescriptor.MessageType.ClrType`, I get a `BoolValue` or `StringValue` as I would expect.

I'm working on a reflection utility to make it easier for us to work with field masks and this is making it a bit tricky to deal with, since the type of the field and the type of the field's value that the accessor returns are different.

I've managed to work around it by checking `fieldDescriptor.MessageType.FullName` and comparing with the wrapper types, however this feels pretty janky, so I'm wondering if I am doing something wrong here or misunderstanding.

Is there a better way to do this? And is there some documentation about whether there are other special types like these?

What I would like or expect is that the type of a field and the type of the _value_ of that field match, or at least some general way to get a value with the same type as the field.

I've seen a few similar issues: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2574 and https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2575 - perhaps this is related?

nodes.body:
Well Known Types(WKT) do have different behaviors/APIs. 
The WKT in C# code:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/WellKnownTypes

Document for WKT:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/google.protobuf

Hey - I think this issue is still valid. In particular, I don't have any way to tell if something is a well known type, which makes it really hard to write reflection routines against them since the type of the field, and the type of the *value* of the field are different.

I think at least we should make `IsWrapperType` - if you agree, I'm happy to make that change. Let me know.
