title: Iterate messages in the order of appearance in file with Python API
body:
I'm writing a plugin for protoc and I'm using Python. I'm having trouble with iterating messages in a file, given a `FileDescriptor` object. The class provides an attribute `message_types_by_name`. When iterating this dictionary, the messages are no longer in the order of their original appearance in the proto file.

Since message definitions have dependencies, being able to iterate them in topological order has certain advantages. Is there any canonical way to do this? I scanned the related APIs but didn't find a nice solution.

nodes.body: I'm not very familiar with python protobuf but I guess there's no public API for that. You may do the topologyical sorting manually by searching all dependency messages.

Based on my research, elements in `message_types_by_name` are actually inserted in order when `FileDescriptor` objects are created and initialized. It's just that Python `dict` does not preserve insertion order. Switching to `collections.OrderedDict` seems an easy enough solution to me, if the team is interested in fixing this. Or the API can provide an additional attribute named `messages` which is a list that preserves this order.

This applies to `enum_types_by_name` too, but as far as I know there are no dependency problems for enums so it's probably not a big deal anyway.

title: Open-source .proto.h codegen that avoids transitive includes
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
c++ code gen

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
We have a couple proto files that include a lot of other proto files (similar to gwslog :-)). This causes a lot of needless recompiling when any of the included proto files change. These files have grown large enough to be problematic.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
This problem can be solved by using forward declarations instead of including the headers of the other proto files. There appears to be an option in the c++ code gen library to do this:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/de9e1a04a68af0c8c5f49121ebd7dd1a2fed37af/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_options.h#L55

However it is not exposed:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/de9e1a04a68af0c8c5f49121ebd7dd1a2fed37af/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_generator.cc#L84

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
We 'hacked' around this by adding proto message option, custom bazel build rules and a protoc plug-in that generates a header file that forward declares all needed messages and defines a wrapper class that owns a pointer to the problematic message, which is also forward declared (it also generates a .cc file that forwards all the accessors to the real accessors on the owned message).

**Additional context**

title: Allow object destruction in C++ Arena but keep the memory for further reuse
body:
Hi,
it seems that the only way to free Arena resources is to call `Arena::Reset()`. 
It seems this function both destructs the objects it owns and releases the memory, i.e. after the call the invariant is that `0 == arena.SpaceAllocated() && 0 == arena.SpaceUsed()`

Does it make sense to provide `DestroyObjects()` function that only destroys the owned objects, s.t.
`SpaceUsed() = 0` but `SpaceAllocated()` stays the same? It could have a positive performance impact when we need to create and destroy series of objects to save malloc/free calls to the upstream allocator.

nodes.body: That is a good point and I have wondered about that in the past as well. For now I think the best alternative is that you can pass an [initial memory block](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/arena.h#L128) to the arena and you can reuse that one memory block in one arena after another.
Thanks, works for me! :+1:

Windows

JDK 8

ByteString.copyFrom(ByteBuffer bytes) should be copying the bytes from 0 to bytes.position()

ByteString.copyFrom(ByteBuffer bytes) is copying the bytes from 0 to bytes.remaining()

title: Option ruby_package causes inconsistent code generation
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.6.1
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
MacOS 10.14

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Ruby 2.4.1

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Compile the following proto: `protoc --proto_path=. --ruby_out=. example.proto`
```
syntax = "proto3";

package google.example;

option java_multiple_files = true;
//option ruby_package = "Google::Example";

service HelloService {
     rpc HiThere (HiRequest) returns (HiResponse);
}

message HiRequest {
    string query = 1;
}

message HiResponse {
    string result = 1;
}
```
2. Repeat step 1 after uncommenting the `ruby_package` line.

**What did you expect to see**
The generated Ruby code should be the same.

**What did you see instead?**
When the `ruby_package` options is specified the generated code is:
```ruby
module Google::Example
  HiRequest = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("google.example.HiRequest").msgclass
  HiResponse = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("google.example.HiResponse").msgclass
end
```

Without the `ruby_package` option it is:
```ruby
module Google
  module Example
    HiRequest = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("google.example.HiRequest").msgclass
    HiResponse = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("google.example.HiResponse").msgclass
  end
end
```

This inconsistency causes issues because the module must already be defined if the `ruby_package` option is used (example: https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-ruby/pull/2782).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body:
Does the title of this issue correctly reflect the problem?
It seems to me the inconsistency is expected. The real issue is if the outer module is not defined. Is that correct?

Why is the inconsistency expected?

The module not being defined is what can cause problems at runtime, but it's not clear to me why it should be different.

title: protoc should not populate `json_name` in descriptor if no `json_name` was specified
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.0
Language: any

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
n/a

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
n/a

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

test.proto:
```proto
syntax = "proto3";

package testing;

message Animal {
  string name = 1;
  bool has_hooves = 2;
  int32 birth_year = 3 [json_name = "year_of_birth"];
}
```

Command:
```shell
protoc -o /dev/stdout test.proto | protoc --decode=google.protobuf.FileDescriptorSet descriptor.proto
```

Output:
```
file {
  name: "test.proto"
  package: "testing"
  message_type {
    name: "Animal"
    field {
      name: "name"
      number: 1
      label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
      type: TYPE_STRING
      json_name: "name"
    }
    field {
      name: "has_hooves"
      number: 2
      label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
      type: TYPE_BOOL
      json_name: "hasHooves"
    }
    field {
      name: "birth_year"
      number: 3
      label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
      type: TYPE_INT32
      json_name: "year_of_birth"
    }
  }
  syntax: "proto3"
}
```

**What did you expect to see**
It should be possible to tell whether `json_name` was specified in the `.proto` file. In particular, there should be a way to distinguish that `json_name` was specified for `birth_year`, and not specified for `has_hooves`.

**What did you see instead?**
It is impossible to tell whether `json_name` was specified in the `.proto` file, because `protoc` invents a `json_name` for each field, regardless.

**Anything else**

1. This makes it impossible to create a json serializer that prefers the vanilla protobuf field names (with underscores, by convention), but lets individual fields be overridden. Instead, the default is the weird java-ish mangled version of field names. I'm fine with that being the default, but other options should be _possible_.  For instance, in Go's `jsonpb`, there is an `OrigName` option. But it's all-or-nothing. If you opt out of the java-ish names, you also opt out of being able to override a name.
2. This bloats the serialized descriptor. The language runtimes can manufacture default json field names just fine.
3. This makes it less possible to recreate something close to the original `.proto` file from the descriptor.

nodes.body:
The one thing this issue fails to address is how this works in a *language neutral* way. If two language runtimes fail to make the same default json field name because of a quirk with one runtime then they can't work together. Sure that might be a bug with the quirked runtime, but the whole issue could just be avoided if the runtime was given the same json name as the other runtimes via protoc. 

On top of that, calculating a json name takes time. It may not be a long time, but it is time and memory. It's not time and memory to calculate it ahead of time and reference it as a constant value (depending on the runtime).

The last point doesn't seem like much of an issue. You should be distributing `.proto` files to anyone that needs them. The only people I know that can't get `.proto` files distributed to them are people writing Steam bots and Pokemon Go bots. Feel free to list any legitimate reasons people should be able to more easily reverse engineer a `.proto` file from a descriptor.

The biggest complaint is that it makes it impossible to tell whether a user specified a `json_name` or not. I suppose it would be possible to add an additional `bool explicit_json_name` field or something.

We have a lot of code still on protobuf 3.0.0, and when we try to upgrade to a newer protobuf release, all the json field names change. We can use the `OrigName` option in `jsonpb`, but that will completely disallow _any_ fieldname customization. What we really need is a `PreferOrigName` option that still allows explicit field renaming. But the fact that `protoc` is synthesizing stuff into the descriptor precludes the possibility of implementing such an option, either in upstream golang/protobuf or even in our own custom serialization code.

As far as the time burden of calculating json names… in compiled runtimes that often happens at generation time (it does in Go, currently), and even in interpreted languages, it's surely highly cacheable. Besides, they all have to have the code/machinery to be able to handle descriptors that lack `json_name` anyway, so it's already there.

It's true that recreating a `.proto` file from the descriptor is uncommon (although they do/can include all kinds of comment and line number information in the `SourceCodeInfo` message, which seems built for that purpose); I guess I was trying to articulate the fact that it “feels wrong” to introduce extra synthetic information into the descriptor.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc#L1972
I think we can have a command line option to decide whether to include json name in the output. @acozzette how do you think?

Yeah, I think a commandline option is perfect. It should always reflect the `json_name` if it was specified in the `.proto` file, but the commandline option could turn off the synthesis of googleCase defaults.
Any updates on this? Would sending a PR help?

Sorry this slipped off my radar. Usually we try to avoid new options but maybe it is justified in this case. I'm guessing if we just removed `json_name` unconditionally then things might break. @haon4 What do you think?

I don't think we should change the current behavior as users are already relying on it. I am also not a fan of adding more command line option, as this doesn't seem like a common feature that other people are asking for, and I really don't like to add more switch for one use-case.

Can this problem be solved at the application level rather than at the protobuf level? Does it really matter if the json_name was explicitly specified or not? If you make the lowerCamelCase transformation on the field name and that matches the json_name option, can you assume that the json_name is not specified? Even if the json_name is explicitly specified in that case, does it matter?

I thought I described why earlier, but no, it is not solvable at an application level, because the way protoc currently populates `json_name` for _all_ fields makes it impossible to tell whether any given field actually had a `json_name` property.

A commandline flag would be perfect.

btw, if y'all don't add a commandline option, we will be forced to fork protoc internally, and add one 😞   Either that or specify a `json_name` on every single existing field that includes underscores (also 😞). I'm happy to rough together a PR adding a commandline option, if that would help 🙂.

Fair enough. If you can put together a PR for this command line option, it may help. Point taken that this can reduce the size bloat on the serialized descriptor, and most languages should already handle the fallback in case `json_name` is not there, so I think that may be something we would want to enable by default in the long term. I see there are still many places that are making the assumption about `json_name` being there though, but having the command line option may enable us to slowly knock them out.

I think removing `json_name` from returned `FileDescriptorSets` is unfortunately a breaking change at this point - external plugins could totally be relying on that to remove the need to compute `json_name` themselves. @jhump 

Another option would be to add a field to `google.protobuf.FieldDescriptorProto` that is something like i.e. `optional bool json_name_explicitly_set = 11;` that `protoc` could populate, and plugins could make decisions based on this. If this was done, the builtin plugins should handle this field as well re: #6175. This seems dirty, but may actually be cleaner than a `protoc` command-line flag, and it is kind of how Protobuf is intended to be used (you can't change the `json_name` field, but you can iterate on your message definition by adding new fields).
Yea, I think having something like `optional bool json_name_explicitly_set = 11;` would be quite nice, actually. I would be happy with that.

> I think it has to be the negative for backwards compatibility reasons

Remember that `descriptor.proto` is proto2 syntax. So it could just use a default value:

```proto
optional bool json_name_configured = 11 [default=true];
```

Good point. One issue though is that makes the definition a tad weird - even if no FileDescriptorSet provider (ie protoc et al) would produce this, what does it mean when json_name == “” && json_name_configured == true?

```proto
string foo = 1 [json_name=""];
```

:P

(Related: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5682)
Lol

I'm fine with `json_name_explicitly_set` with a default of false. If you're in this situation, you can probably just start using a new version of `protoc`. Anything I can help do to push this forward?
I think it needs to be json_name_not_explicitly_set, this does matter for being able to really reason about the value of the field, see above

@elharo Do you know if someone is still working on this? Can we expect this config to be part of future releases?

I am willing to contribute if this is not being worked on.

I don't think anyone is working on this. However, reading through this now I confess I don't see a use case for this feature. That is, why does this matter? Until I can achieve clarity on that I don't think I'd be likely to approve any such PR. Perhaps someone else sees something here I don't.

My thinking (not dispositive) is as follows:

1. Every field has a json_name which is fully determinable by reading the .proto file.
2. When protoc emits a descriptor as JSON, it includes the json_name.
3. The json_name in the .proto can be calculated or explicitly specified, but it doesn't matter which nor should any processing depend on that syntax detail.

I'm not sure about the "fully" in step 1. There are command line options that change this, but that doesn't change my conclusion. This feature simply doesn't seem to be needed, likely encourages bad code and non-interoperable protos, and is unlikely to be worth the added complexity in code.

Metaphorically it's like trying to change the byte code emitted by javac so that we can tell whether it was indented with spaces or tabs.

> Metaphorically it's like trying to change the byte code emitted by javac so that we can tell whether it was indented with spaces or tabs.

@elharo, I think the fact that an artifact of this is that `protoc` itself produces _different_ code based on whether the input is the original source vs. a file descriptor set means this is also a consistency issue. And that's a problem because it means that strategies used by build tools could result in different (non-deterministic) output. That case is described more thoroughly in #6175 (which was closed as a duplicate of this issue).

We have [built parsers](https://github.com/Apicurio/apicurio-registry/tree/master/utils/protobuf-schema-utilities/src/main/java/io/apicurio/registry/utils/protobuf/schema) that can read a file descriptor set and re-create the original `.proto` schema. This feature enables users to  auto-discover schemas during stream processing and register them in the schema registry. Since the file descriptor set generation is different for the same .proto schema, it results in different schemas getting generated. This results in inconsistencies and non-deterministic behavior as called out by @jhump. 

The Protobuf [code base](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/3e1967e10be786062ccd026275866c3aef487eba/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc#L6720) also acknowledges it as a bug and a work around was introduced to deal with it. 

Since this change will be non-backward compatible, I recommend that we add the boolean flag `json_name_explicitly_set` (or a better name) as suggested previously.

**Reference**

[Generating proto schema from FileDescriptor](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8795)

@blacktooth "Since the file descriptor set generation is different for the same .proto schema, it results in different schemas getting generated." What exactly do you mean by *different* here? Are some fields present in one and not the other? Are the fields renumbered? Are the fields reordered? Is the white space changed? Are comments added or removed?

I don't expect the results would be byte-per-byte identical, and some of these changes are more serious than others.
For future reference, relevant code seems to be in protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc void CommandLineInterface::GetTransitiveDependencies
Any progress on this?
I don't think anyone is working on this right now

Sad. #6175 was closed as a dup of this one, but summarizes the problem pretty well:
> protoc: code gen is different between using source files and using descriptor set

We triage inactive PRs and issues in order to make it easier to find active work. If this issue should remain active or becomes active again, please add a comment.

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago.
/keepopen

Coming back to this after a long time. Reading the comments here and on related issues, it seems there is a loose consensus among external tools that if the `json_name` in the protobuf descriptor matches the auto-generated one, then the user/`.proto`-file _probably_ didn't actually specify a `json_name` explicitly.


What if we simply codified that?

Here's my proposal:

If a field in the `.proto` file explicitly specifies a `json_name`, _and that name is the same as the one that would have been auto-generated for the field_, then `protoc` should add the `json_name_explicitly_set` attribute to that field.

This would allow existing tooling to be mostly unchanged, and would provide a solution in the rare cases when the heuristic adopted by external tooling goes wrong: re-generate your proto descriptor with a more recent version of `protoc`, and check for `json_name_explicitly_set`.

title: Protobuf is really missing inheritance
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
proto3 OR proto-future

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Lot's of DRY code in statically typed languages.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I'd like you to add inheritance to current **proto3** or at least the future protobuf versions. An example is:
```
message Parent { }

message ChildA extends Parent { }
message ChildB extends Parent { }
message ChildC extends Parent { }
```

**Alternatives you've considered**
I know about **composition** and it's really not a cure. 

**Additional context**
I know that **protobuf favors composition over inheritance** but it's really not a cure to remove inheritance completely. Statically typed languages like Java or C# suffer from composition only approach. These languages cannot use polymorphism because all the messages have the same parent `GeneratedMessageV3`. If inheritance was available, we could use polymorphism. Instead of having to write:
```
void method(ChildA arg)
void method(ChildB arg)
void method(ChildC arg)
``` 
we could simply write `void method(Parent arg)`. Consequently, the **missing inheritance generates a lot of DRY code is hardly or not at all DRYable**. It leads to wider test suites that take more time to execute. I could go on but I hope I explained myself. (If not, just ask and I'll clarify it.)

nodes.body:
FWIW

To quote the [Protocol Buffers tutorial](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/javatutorial):
"Don't go looking for facilities similar to class inheritance, though – protocol buffers don't do that."

Instead of inheritance, Protocol Buffers tends to favor [composition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Composition_over_inheritance) as a pattern.

@perezd 

GRPC is not doing "favor composition over inheritance" pattern, it's applying **"remove inheritance" pattern**. :D 

There are cases when inheritance is more suitable. Just because it's a good practice to "**favor somehing**", it doesn't mean it should be removed completely (or not implemented at all).  

### Real life example
> Favor public transport over driving a car when going to work

Yes, most of the time we should use public transport because it's better for Earth. On the other hand, you have cases when driving a car is a better option, e.g. if there is no public transport in your surroundings.

For proto3, use Any.
For proto2, user extension.

nodes.body: That is strange. I would actually expect 0 to be the correct value of `ByteSizeLong()` because with proto3 there is no distinction between a field being empty and being set to its default value (which is 0 for numeric types). I can't think of any reason why it would sometimes return 2 then. If you can come up with a full reproducible test case then I could try to debug it.

Hmm, Ok so I was wrong about my assumption about size :) Was my assumptions about size was correct in  proto2? 
As far as the initial issue, I am looking. I did run Valgrind to check for any memory corruptions and I have no leaks. So that is good. title: Does MessageLite::SerializeAsString generate unique string for same proto ?

nodes.body: /cc @diemtvu @qiwzhang

Serialization is not guaranteed to be deterministic, and the usual reason for that is that map fields are serialized in an unspecified order. However, if you need the serialization to be deterministic then you can accomplish that by serializing to a CodedOutputStream after calling [SetSerializationDeterministic(true)](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/8bbabb87a20d28e94a8e2cb778ea25cbd2980a16/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h#L906) on that output stream. But keep in mind that if you do this the serialization is only guaranteed to be deterministic for a given build. It might change over time as you modify your code or if you upgrade your protobuf version. As a result this will only make sense for something like a temporary in-memory map, but will not work well for keys stored in a persistent database.

Thanks @acozzette !  Temporary in-memory map should be good enough for our case, seems envoy already has such [a hash function](https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/88fe0c9310/source/common/protobuf/utility.h#L115), just switched to it and the duplication issue goes away.
Great, I'm glad you were able to find a solution.

title: C#: generated code contains C# 7 features
body:
Release blocker for v3.7.0

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/5183/files has introduced C# features to the generated code:

The `ref` is a C# 7 construct. https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/whats-new/csharp-7#ref-locals-and-returns
```
if (!pb::UnknownFieldSet.MergeFieldFrom(ref _unknownFields, input)) {
        return;
}
```

Protobuf generated code needs to be compatible with older .NET and C# versions (with even older versions that the runtime itself, because the runtime is not built by users), so C# 7 is not acceptable.

The error you get with older C# compiler
```
Math.cs(747,57): error CS1615: Argument 1 may not be passed with the 'ref' keyword [T:\src\github\grpc\workspace_csharp_windows_dbg_native\src\csharp\Grpc.Examples\Grpc.Examples.csproj]
```

nodes.body: @ObsidianMinor Do you think you could help fix this? It looks like this was introduced in 6f73c509365fcb9. I don't really know C# but is this `ref` keyword perhaps just an optimization that we could remove for now?

The issue sounds like the example is using the new compiler with the old library as `ref` parameters have existed since the first version of C# and [CS1615](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/misc/cs1615) is completely unrelated to `ref` locals and `ref` returns.

But I'll remove it anyway. It makes sense that the generated message class knows what its end tag is, right? It was narrow minded of me to make it match the java implementation and it's probably faster to just match on the end tag anyway.

Here's the link to the failure I got when trying to upgrade to the newest version of generated code:

https://source.cloud.google.com/results/invocations/aeae23e1-b6c7-412f-8e58-02ac05cced22/targets/github%2Fgrpc%2Faggregate_tests/tests;group=aggregate_tests;test=run_tests_csharp_linux_opt_native;row=2

I might have spoken too soon because it looks like that the problem here might be just that a new overload of MergeFieldFrom  was added by https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/5183/files#diff-5df82654c5a10e0054aa33823e3d2e74R273
(in my experiment, I regenerated the C# code, but I haven't updated the Google.Protobuf nuget because the 3.7.0.rc2 vesion is not yet available publicly.

@acozzette @TeBoring  can you upload the rc2 nuget so I can re-test?
@ObsidianMinor  what was the original reason for adding a new MergeFieldFrom overload?
CC @anandolee

The original reason the overload was added was that I needed a way to communicate with the class's merge method about whether an end tag was reached. 

Originally I made it so reaching the end tag for the current group would return zero when reading a tag from the input, but after review it was decided I should do it another way and Java's implementation was brought up as an example. The closest thing I had for reference was that Java implementation so I wrote it based on that. 

The overload returns a bool indicating if an end tag was reached and takes the unknown field set as a reference to assign it where originally the generated code would.
I remember we required non-C#-7 in our test setup. Why this still happens?
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/db0a9e0b962084cdb7f51a31d9ed670f54189981#diff-a20d785dbacb8f41a3b7392aa7d03b78

To clarify, the `ref` keyword is not a C# 7 feature (don't confused it with `Ref locals and returns` which is introduced in C# 7). The problem here is not related to `Ref locals and returns`, so force <LangVersion>6</LangVersion> won't detect this issue.
Pending on #5708
Is there anything else needed to close this issue?

title: Is there an easy way to include well-known types in a protoc compilation?

In the Dart [protoc plugin](https://github.com/dart-lang/protobuf) we have been [requested](https://github.com/dart-lang/protobuf/issues/170) to include the well-known types with the plugin.

But depending on how protoc is installed it might be hard to know where the protos for the well-known types are located - forcing the user to duplicate the well-known types to their own repo.
Is there (or should there be) a command-line argument to add the well known types to the include path of a protoc invocation, without knowing where protoc is installed, or even include their path by default?

Reason why this will be good is to get comments (informations) on objects. Yes, this effects compile time, but helps users who reuse generated objects. They can get more info on what some objects do. Maybe a good solution is a flag, where you choose if you want add comments or not.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

All of the wrapper types that correspond to C# value types (`Int32Wrapper`, `DoubleWrapper`, `BoolWrapper` etc) are mapped to `Nullable<T>` where T is the corresponding non-nullable type. For example, a field of type `DoubleValue` results in a C# property of type `Nullable<double>`.

Fields of type `StringWrapper` or `BytesWrapper` result in C# properties of type string and `ByteString` being generated, but with a default value of null, and allowing null to be set as the property value.

String type is compiled as  `Google.Protobuf.WellKnownTypes.StringValue `. I'm expecting `string`.

title: Separate serialization and data types in generated classes

nodes.body: There's no special support for this in protoc, so you could do something like this but you would have to implement it all yourself. I think there are two variations on this. The first is to create your own `Example` class independent of protobuf and copy fields back and forth between that and the generated protobuf class. The second possibility would be to make `Example` just a pure interface, and code can be written against that interface without depending on protobuf. You could then provide an implementation of that interface which is just a thin wrapper around the generated proto.

Nice, I'm glad you found a solution. One thing to consider if you need to add more functionality is that you can let `protoc` do the work of parsing the `.proto` file for you. You can use the `--descriptor_set_out` flag to make `protoc` write a `FileDescriptorSet` proto to a file, and then your Python script can read in that `FileDescriptorSet` to get all the important information from the .proto file.
That's a good idea, I'll look into it. Thanks!

The [logic](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/37581380fbc2a2b683e16de01db628988b72541e/src/google/protobuf/testing/googletest.cc#L89) for finding the top of the directory tree on Windows effectively just cd's upward until it finds `src/google/protobuf`, and with this change it will find the wrong directory because it will see `src/google/protobuf` inside `bazel-bin`. I haven't tested this out because I don't have easy access to a Windows build machine but this makes sense and lines up with @meteorcloudy's observation. I guess the question is, what's the proper way for us to figure out the path to the top of the project source tree? The tests just need to do this so that they can find the path to test data files in `src/google/protobuf/testdata`.
BTW, why didn't it see `src/google/protobuf` inside `bazel-genfiles` before?

@meteorcloudy My guess was that the working directory for test runs must have been inside `bazel-bin/` and not `bazel-genfiles/`.

I just sent out #5927 to fix this. I don't have a good way to test whether the fix works but I think it should. I ended up not using the runfiles library because I realized it would be complicated to have to use a Bazel-specific library when building with Bazel but keep the other logic around for other build systems. Instead I tweaked the existing logic to look for a particular file (descriptor.cc) so that should prevent it from mistakenly using the `bazel-bin/` directory.

title: Sharing a common .proto between multiple python projects.
body:
Hi,

I tried to find a good solution, but I'm stuck.

I have multiple python projects in different repositories, all of them are python libraries installable with pip.
Something like this:
```
Project1/
    foo_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           common.proto
           common_pb2.py
           foo.proto
           foo_pb2.py

Project2/
    bar_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           common.proto
           common_pb2.py
           bar.proto
           bar_pb2.py
```
In Project2 environment Project 1 is installed with pip.
Content of common.proto-s are identical, both foo.proto and bar.proto imports common.proto.

Compiled with `protoc -I{ProjectRoot} --python-out={ProjectRoot} ...`. 
This setup works in isolation, but when I try to import both common_pb2 libraries, it dies:
```
common.UsefulMessage: "common.UsefulMessage" is already defined in file "foo_lib/protobuf/common.proto".
```

I also tried to move out the proto files from the lib's folder like this:
```
Project1/
   protobuf/
       common.proto
       foo.proto
    foo_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           common_pb2.py
           foo_pb2.py

Project2/
   protobuf/
       common.proto
       bar.proto
    bar_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           common_pb2.py
           bar_pb2.py
```
Compiled with `protoc -I{ProjectRoot} --python-out={LibDir} ...`. 
But then even a single import doesn't work, since foo_pb2.py tries to import `protobuf.common_pb2` which is not exsist.

What is the best way to solve this?

nodes.body:
No matter if content of common.proto-s are identical or not, libraries should define different packages to avoid conflict.
For example:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d9ccd0c0e6bbda9bf4476088eeb46b02d7dcd327/src/google/protobuf/api.proto#L33

So something like this?
```
ProjectCommon/
    common_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           common.proto
           common_pb2.py

Project1/
    foo_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           foo.proto
           foo_pb2.py

Project2/
    bar_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           bar.proto
           bar_pb2.py
```

How can I import the `common.proto` from a different library?
Should I have a way to get the path of the installed "common.proto" file and add it to the protoc call with `-I`?

I mean keep folder like this
```
Project1/
    foo_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           common.proto
           common_pb2.py
           foo.proto
           foo_pb2.py

Project2/
    bar_lib/
        __init__.py
       protobuf/
            __init__.py
           common.proto
           common_pb2.py
           bar.proto
           bar_pb2.py
```

Then add package (e.g. 'package project1.foo_lib.protobuf;') in Project1/fool_lib/protobuf/common.proto, and change the usages in Project1/foo_lib/protobuf/foo.proto to avoid conflict

But this would make the contents of the common.proto incompatible, they will have different names (so I can't read the massage saved by one project in the other, especially if I use `Any`), also creates problems when I want to read the messages in a third project (which happens to be in C++).

Just to make it clear, common.proto contains really common stuff, namely serialized NDArrays from numpy. In my projects it is as common as google.protobuf.Any. You don't include Any with different package names in your projects. I want the same for my own stuff.

@takacsd I'm contemplating the same problem.
The same question arises with gRPC protos being consumed by two projects

Although it doesn't seem like an elegant solution, putting all PB's in one project seems like the way to go, as described here:
https://medium.com/namely-labs/how-we-build-grpc-services-at-namely-52a3ae9e7c35

What I don't like in this solution is that you need to `git clone`, and more specifically, clone a repo that contains definitions that are not relevant to the project and maybe protoc build for all languages

If you came up with a better solution I will be happy to hear about it.

title: Java Option for Null

nodes.body:
An alternative to returning null would be to throw an exception in the get if the value is unset.

The main concern my team has is when the value is unset and get is called there is a chance we could get invalid data.  Exceptions would be preferred to data that is invalid.

if I could do the same thing somehow for primitives I would be tickled pink!

I could support primitives with proto2 syntax but proto3 doesn't have enough information

Hello, @efenglu 
In fact in order to support correctly java `null` semantics, it's more ticky than just modifying `get` and `set` behavior. Especially, if your proto object gets serialized, all fields with default value are not sent to wire, thus when you decode the binaries to a protobuf object, you could not tell if a field is missing (thus `null` in java) or it should contain default value.
That being said, without a modification of the wire format (sending default values), it would be difficult to implement properly the `null` semantics.
The ***has\*()*** method is available for nested MessageType's but with primitives we don't even have this option.

Unfortunately I don't think we would want an option that change the semantics of getters / setters. It is too surprising to developers when some Message's getters return default instance while others may return null or throw NPE. We made a decision to return default instance in proto3. While it may not be ideal for many cases, it is consistent everywhere, so developers who are familiar with protos can reliably tell what is going to happen. Whereas if we introduce an option, developer and code reviewer will need to look at the proto file definition to figure out what will happen in case of null. If you chain the getters like entry.getCreationTime().getSeconds(), it is very hard to notice a bug. If you depend on only the .jar file without looking at the actual proto, then you may not even know what will happen.

One not-so-elegant solution for you case would be to add some extra fields to indicate if your fields are set. You can also add some preconditions check to ensure that the data is valid before write to the database. Obviously all of these rely on the developers knowing the behavior for protobuf so they can watch out for it, but it is a one-time learning vs. never knowing what the behavior is.
Proto4?

yes, does the binary format ever get modified.  it would be nice to be able to releasea server that responds with "you need to upgrade your protocol version to talk to this server" Sooooo, that I can at least start using the new binary format that passes default values and empty if null for fields that are nullable.  I personally would want ease of development over wire protocol since most businesses, the developers time in development cost my business way more time, than a very compact protocol.....I mean hell, most use json as it is which is very slow.  Squeezing the protocol seems kind of hard on developers.

ouch, more importantly, how do I do the variations of json then?  json wire format options

   "name": {defaultValue=0 for int} is on the wire
   "name": null
   {name not exist}

These are all used in the wild as different triggers.  If the protobuf binary format can't tell the difference between these 3 things, then it can't truly do json, can it?

FYI, I found a similar request for Dart: google/protobuf.dart#309 while I was looking for this one. [This comment](https://github.com/google/protobuf.dart/issues/309#issuecomment-1173756840) also makes an interesting comparison of the behavior across languages.

title: Insertion points and their future
body:
I've noticed in several other issues (e.g. #3292, #3291, #2684) Protobuf contributors are standing that insertion points should not be used, does this actually mean that in some time custom Protobuf plugins won't be supported at all? 
It's that I'm looking at customizing Protobuf Java output with some extra stuff and e.g. I've noticed an insertion point `@@protoc_insertion_point(message_implements:NAME)` that is actually present in the generated sources but is not documented at the [website](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java-generated#plugins). 

Could you please provide some statement about the insertion points support and usage at all and about `message_implements` insertion point in particular, is it safe to use it?

nodes.body: I'm not sure about the plan for that but I think we're trying to deprecate insertion point and we may break you in the future.

@BSBandme thank you for your attention to the question. Is there any chance to announce any actual "plans" or "dates" if the functionality is gonna be deprecated?
Any plans to discuss this with the community?

I’m also interested in the discussion around this feature. I currently author a library that tags the builder interfaces with a Kotlin specific annotation. It’s purpose is to allow composition of proto message in a type safe dsl like manner, but doesn’t modify the interface in any way. It’s purely meant to provide hints to the ide and compile time safety. 

Is this not an acceptable usage of the insertions api?

@@protoc_insertion_point(message_implements:NAME) is inserted at the following point:
```
public final class Foo extends
    com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageV3 implements
    // @@protoc_insertion_point(message_implements:package.name.Foo)
    FooOrBuilder {
...
}
```

I don't see how this is useful. We may actually want to remove it. Are you trying to use it for something?

We have found that some insertion points are too fine grained and allow developers to get into the way of our implementation details, while others are fine to have. e.g., we have a number of insertion points in C++ for serialize/parse, which isn't something that we would like developers to change. We are reevaluating the values of some of these insertion points to see if they should be removed.

Our stand is not to completely kill _all_ insertion points, but to eliminate certain insertion points that are problematic and likely to cause more harms. Most other insertion points at class scope / builder scope are acceptable to have.

@haon4 we are now using `@@protoc_insertion_point(message_implements:NAME)` and `@@protoc_insertion_point(class_scope:NAME)`.

The first one is very useful when you want to group different message under one particular interface.
Thanks, Yuri. Sounds good to continue using them. We don't have any plan to remove those as far as I can tell.

@yuri-sergiichuk 
Can you please provide an example on how you implemented and used protocol buffer plugins?

title: Messages parsed from a serialized form should know their serialized size
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Java (but the same idea can probably be introduced in all the other languages, too)

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
We're trying to write protobufs to an output as fast as possible and we noticed they're computing their size even though the size should already be known because they were `parseDelimited()`'d from an `InputStream`.

Those protobufs have been read from a socket, filtered and now we're writing them. We expected that protobufs that have been `parseDelimited()` from an `InputStream` would know their size already as there is a size memoizing mechanism.

The problem is that apparently size computation takes around 50% of the writing time as suggested by this profile (heavily censored, sorry): [pump-60s.zip](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/2865616/pump-60s.zip)

![screenshot here](https://i.imgur.com/A10GDnt.png)

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Protobufs read from a serialized form should have their size memoized so that if they're then written elsewhere, the size can be reused. If that's technically unfeasible for whatever reason, the messages read by `parseDelimited()` should know their size for sure.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Honestly, none. ~We can work around all this at the application level by remembering the size ourselves, but that is only that - a workaround~ (no we can't as there's no way to enforce the size on the message and it would be computed anyway).

**Additional context**
The profile above has been taken while using protobuf 2.6.1, but the same behaviour has been observed on 3.6.1, too.

nodes.body: I think this is harder to do than it sounds. There is more than one way to represent a given message, so the size of the proto before it's parsed might be different from the output size after a parse and serialization cycle. For example, singular primitive fields can appear more than once and when you parse them the last one wins. So if you parse a message where a particular primitive field appears more than once, when you re-serialize it the size will get a little bit smaller since the duplicated field will just be serialized once. In your case if you're not modifying the message at all but just filtering out certain messages, is it possible to just hang onto the original serialized message and pass that along without re-serializing it?

CC @ejona86 who knows more about Java performance

I don't really know about the UTF-8 parsers since I don't do much work on Java. About your option 2, I suspect that would be difficult to implement because there are multiple ways for the size to be different from what's expected. A singular field appearing multiple times is one example, but another one would be a non-canonical varint, e.g. a varint that would fit in one byte but happens to appear as two or more bytes on the wire. Varints are variable-length ints that can store small numbers in fewer bytes, but nothing stops you from making them take up more bytes than necessary.

There's a C++ library whose name I've now forgotten which actually takes advantage of non-canonical varints to speed up serialization. It uses 4 bytes for every size-prefix varint. That imposes a size maximum of 256 MiB, but that's plenty for typical use cases. The idea is that it only has to make one pass over the message, because it can set aside 4 bytes for each size prefix and just fill those in later on once the size has been calculated. This way the serialization can happen in one pass without requiring an earlier pass for computing sizes. This is similar to your option 4 but is a valid way of including extra padding.

I know there was also an attempt to implementation serialization in reverse order from back to front, so that by the time we're ready to write the size prefix we will have already calculated it. I'm not sure if this idea went anywhere, though.

These ideas are all kind of interesting to think about, though you may want to be careful about spending too much time on it because this sort of thing is a fairly deep change that will likely be difficult to do. I think it's the kind of thing where if it were easy then someone would have already done it. If serialization is really a bottleneck for your use case, you might want to think about figuring out ways to just do less serialization, or even switch to a  different wire format like FlatBuffers or Cap'n Proto. From what I understand those formats are a little bit harder to use but have the advantage of having almost "free" parsing and serialization, since the wire format and in-memory format are exactly the same.

> I know there was also an attempt to implementation serialization in reverse order from back to front, so that by the time we're ready to write the size prefix we will have already calculated it. I'm not sure if this idea went anywhere, though.

There were some benchmarks and that did show some improvement, although it was hard to make varint itself as fast. But it is blocked on the table-driven parser.

> non-canonical varint

Nasty.

> I think it's the kind of thing where if it were easy then someone would have already done it.

That's exactly the sentiment I had when creating the ticket, and yet I did obviously not see the potential complications.

Thank you for your time and your clarifications. I believe the option 3 outlined above is the only possible implementation of my idea, and yet it is totally not worth it and would mean a solid perf regression for "normal" users.

I think we can close this issue with a clean consciense.

---

For anyone solving the same problem in the future:

We'll try to solve this by implementing our own delegating `Parser` that will reflectively call `setMemoizedSerializedSize()` for trusted sources. The performance of this solution is to be determined, as well as the multi-threaded friendliness. If it doesn't work, we'll memoize the original size outside of the proto object, and then write using

```java
codedOutputStream.writeRawVarint32(origSize);
message.writeTo(codedOutputStream);
```

This only works for proto3 (because `writeTo()` in proto2 calls `getSerializedSize()` internally), but that's alright.

And no, we do not think that the protobuf project should expose any of the machinery required to do this in a cleaner way. It's a potentially unsafe performance hack.

title: Protobuf messages contains Any aren't serialized deterministically even specifying so
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master (currently at 7492b5681231c79f0265793fa57dc780ae2481d6)
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
gcc-7 / clang-7

**What did you do?**
Deterministic serialize a message and calculate hash based on the serialized binary.
Source: https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/master/source/common/protobuf/utility.h#L162

**What did you expect to see**
Same proto generates same serialized binary and hash.

**What did you see instead?**
Same proto generates different serialized binary and hash.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
This is a follow up of #5668, even we use the `CodedOutputStream` with `SetSerializationDeterministic(true)`, the same protobuf message (from JSON debug dump) doesn't produce same binary serialization. My suspect is that the Any in the message has different `value` while they are same. Deterministic serialization should normalize value in Any too.

nodes.body: @liujisi , any ideas? The fix is critical and your help is greatly appreciated.
@acozzette any thoughts?

@lizan This may be a hard problem to solve. The way `Any` was designed, during parsing and serialization we don't treat an `Any` field in a special way and we just treat its payload as an opaque blob. If we want to serialize it deterministically, we would probably need to parse and reserialize the Any payload during serialization. To do that we need to figure out what kind of message the Any is. We could do that by looking up the name in the generated descriptor pool, but that solution is not ideal since it won't work with lite protos (i.e. protos built without reflection support).

If you need a quick short-term fix, I think the best solution would be to have your hash function reflectively examine the proto and normalize all Any fields before doing the deterministic serialization of the full message. That may end up being slow, though. It might also be worthwhile to just avoid Any fields in messages that you want to be able to hash. Do you have a lot of Any fields or just a few?

nodes.body:
Hi, in your script `del foo` is not enough. You should also `del bar` and `del x` to ensure that there is no reference to the data. Or move the iterating steps to another function.

Freed memory is not always returned to the system: at best, only empty pages of 4k can be released. With Python the situation is even worse, because pymalloc will allocate its own large arenas and release them when they are completely empty.
This is not a memory leak: if you retry the operation, memory should not grow again; it should rapidly reach its maximum after a few attempts.

To explain the two levels of memory usage: ParseFromString completely works in C++ land, the message itself takes memory, but there is still a single Python object.
When iterating over the data though, each sub-item will be fetched as a Python object which reference that part of the data. These objects are cached, and not released until the toplevel itself message is freed. This is why the memory usage increases while the code loops over the message.

We could do it differently, and cache these sub-messages in a less aggressive way. This would reduce memory usage, at the cost of more cpu to access fields, because the Python objects need to be rebuilt the second time.

Thanks for your answer @amauryfa.

I was aware of the lazy behavior of the Python API for protobuf [1], what I didn't know is that the scope of the variable of for statement persists after the iteration. This might explain why the memory is not almost all released - without taking into account the internal fragmentation because of the arena or the default allocator.

Though, It's for me unclear why by having only a reference to one of the repeated elements - the last one - most of the memory is unreleased, something that makes me think that the whole repeated element is still referenced. 

am I wrong? Is there any technical decision behind the Python protobuf implementation that proofs this?  

[1] https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/protobuf/7uF1s3BjoH8

So is any opportunities to release memory forcely? We are using protobuf in our project and memory consumption is very sad, because memory only grows.

title: Please publish pre-built Debian packages
body:
Debian stable (stretch) and Ubuntu LTS (18.04, Bionic) both offer very outdated packages of Protobuf, going back to version 3.0.0 released almost 3 years ago.

While newer releases can be built from source and installed, apt does not recognize the manually-built version and will overwrite it with the old release if the `libprotobuf` or `protobuf-compiler` packages are installed (including if one is a dependency of another package you install).

Here is a StackOverflow discussion about that: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54699030/prevent-apt-from-overwriting-a-package-manually-installed

Note that Google already has an official software repository where this could be published so the package can be installed with `apt-get`: https://www.google.com/linuxrepositories/

Otherwise, if you released a package on GitHub, it could be installed with `dpkg -i`.

nodes.body: The newer versions are making their way into Debian testing (e.g., https://packages.debian.org/search?keywords=protobuf-compiler). They have no SLO so we don't know when it will land in stable.

title: Java generated code collision with field named descriptor
body:
Java cannot handle when a field is named `descriptor`, for example:

```
message Foo {
  int64 descriptor = 1;
}
```

Edit: Note that capitalizing `Descriptor` causes this problem, as well as any number of leader or trailing `_`s.

```
Descriptor
 _descriptor
descriptor_
__descriptor
descriptor__
...
```

This will result in bad generated code. The `protoc` compiler should handle this collision.

Note that C++ has a similar problem if a package has `std` as part of it, for example `foo.std.bar`. I could file another bug for this with reproduction steps if it helps.

Fixing this could result in some very big breaking changes. It might be enough for things like this to outlaw certain names. We do this at lint time using our Protobuf linter, but given that the cpp, java, etc plugins are builtin to `protoc`, it feels like these should be outlawed via `protoc`.

title: Dots in .proto file name are removed from C# file names
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.1
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Visual Studio 2017

**What did you do?**
1. Create a .proto file named `foo_bar.baz.proto`
2. Compile that with `--csharp_out`

**What did you expect to see**
FooBar.Baz.cs file. foo_bar and baz getting turned into C# PascalCase identifier separately.

**What did you see instead?**
FooBarBaz.cs file with all of these segments resulting in one pascal cased identifier.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
I'm trying to use the [gRPC MSBuild tasks](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/tree/master/src/csharp/Grpc.Tools/build) for running protoc. These tasks expect no file name mangling. Also in our case, we are splitting our message and service proto files with `Company.messages.proto` and `Company.services.proto` the additional information separated with the dot isn't "C# identifier" and I feel pascal casing it feels wrong.

nodes.body:
The issue seems to result from here:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/e22907f364ee00926a2b6a1fd1c005ffcc69a0e8/src/google/protobuf/compiler/csharp/csharp_helpers.cc#L125-L130

The `UnderscoresToPascalCase` is called _without_ passing the `reserve_period = true` argument.

I would argue that in the case the user has included periods in the original proto file name, they have made a choice to not use underscore, which is the common space character in protobuf names. As such, the period should not be interpreted as if they used the underscore in its place.

(Personally I'd prefer the less surprising "Just change the extension, don't touch the casing at all" approach, which is easier to handle in cross platform build scripts.)

title: Mapping typeUrl of Any message to Java class name
body:
I am looking for a generic way to deserialize an `Any` message in Java. In my use case, the Java app performing the deserialization may receive a variety of message types,  but does not know the exact message name a-priori.  

As is suggested by [this article](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/32613667/protobuf-3-0-any-type-pack-unpack), this is possible through the Java reflection. However, it appears the `typeUrl` is not an exact match to the Java class name -- it corresponds to the descriptor name but does not contain the outer class name.  Ideally, there should be a way for a Java app to derive the exact message class name based on `typeUrl`. 

Is there any plan on supporting looking up Java class name given `typeUrl` (fullname of the message descriptor).  Without such capability, the only mechanism I could think of is load all the subclasses of `google.protobuf.Message` at runtime, and check for equality to a given `typeUrl` one-by-one.   Or, perhaps the Java app could query the outer class name (or .proto file name) from another service, but this adds complexity.

Any suggestion is welcome. Many thanks!

nodes.body: Bump it up.  Note similar support of [DynamicAny](https://godoc.org/github.com/golang/protobuf/ptypes#DynamicAny) available inside GO.

For java, Descriptors are not static loaded, which means we can't load all involved message eagerly like C++ (this is constrained by java class loading), which means we can't automatic build some map like this : descriptor name -> (descriptor or message class).

However you may build the map by hand at the beginning of the your program, you may build a [DescriptorPool by declaring all the proto dependencies](https://cs.corp.google.com/piper///depot/google3/java/com/google/protobuf/Descriptors.java?q=Descriptors.java&dr=C&l=2203), then after get the typeUrl, you may get the descriptor name and find the descriptor from the pool. Then you may either use DynamicMessage or just guess the message class name from the Descriptor's name and Descriptor's file's java related options.

nodes.body: This is just the way protoc works--it will consider the `--proto_path` flags to determine where to look for `.proto` files, but that will not change the `#include`s that it generates. You can still get your code to compile by passing the right `-I` flags to the compiler so that it knows where to search for headers. But probably the best option is to restructure your files so that all your `.proto` files are within a common subdirectory, because otherwise this kind of thing gets confusing quickly.

title: Python Timestamp.ToDatetime() loses precision because of float conversion, fails to round-trip
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.1
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
OS X and Linux, 64-bit

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 2.7.15 and 3.7.2

**What did you do?**
(This is an elaboration on a problem we first noticed in https://groups.google.com/d/topic/protobuf/KEU7CtzAu44/discussion)

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
```
import datetime
from google.protobuf import timestamp_pb2

timestamp = timestamp_pb2.Timestamp()

# This passes:
datetime_1 = datetime.datetime(2019, 2, 22, 1, 2, 3, 456789)
timestamp.FromDatetime(datetime_1)
print(datetime_1 == timestamp.ToDatetime())  # expect True

# This fails:
datetime_2 = datetime.datetime(2555, 2, 22, 1, 2, 3, 456789)
timestamp.FromDatetime(datetime_2)
print(datetime_2 == timestamp.ToDatetime())  # expect True

# This crashes:
datetime_3 = datetime.datetime.max
timestamp.FromDatetime(datetime_3)
print(datetime_3 == timestamp.ToDatetime())  # expect True
```

**What did you expect to see**
Any value that is representable as both a `Timestamp` and a Python `datetime` should be convertible from one to the other with no loss of precision.

**What did you see instead?**
`Timestamp.ToDatetime()` fails to return a `datetime` that matches the `Timestamp`'s value after approx the year 2500, and causes `ValueError: year is out of range` if we try to call `ToDatetime()` with the `Timestamp` set to `datetime.max`.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
In protobuf/internal/well_known_types.py, you implement `Timestamp.ToDatetime()` as:
```
return datetime.utcfromtimestamp(
   self.seconds + self.nanos / float(_NANOS_PER_SECOND))
```
The float division loses precision from the fractional part of `Timestamp`. Furthermore, `utcfromtimestamp()` may not handle timestamps beyond 2038 on 32-bit platforms: https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html#datetime.date.fromtimestamp

Could you please use this implementation instead?
```
_EPOCH_DATETIME = datetime.utcfromtimestamp(0)
...

def ToDatetime(self):
    return _EPOCH_DATETIME + timedelta(
        seconds=self.seconds, 
        microseconds=self.nanos / float(_NANOS_PER_MICROSECOND))
```
Thanks!

Should be fixed

title: Publish symbol package
body:
Symbol packages contain debug files (*.pdb). There is a new snupkg package format and NuGet.org hosts a server for them.

More info:
[docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/library-guidance/nuget#symbol-packages](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/library-guidance/nuget#symbol-packages)

It should involve changing the the arguments to `dotnet pack` so that a snupkg is also output, and then publishing it to NuGet.org.

nodes.body: @jtattermusch , can you help to take a look at this issue?

Sure, I can take a look. I'll discuss offline with Microsoft why the sourcelink integration that's already in place is not sufficient.

I don't think we can publish the symbol packages retroactively (the concern is if we rebuild from the same tag, the newly created pdb might not work well with already-uploaded assemblies), can we?

Source Link adds metadata about the source code repository and the current commit to a package. It allows source code files to be downloaded from GitHub as you debug through a .NET application.

A symbol package is a way of packaging and disturbing symbol files. Symbol files map instructions in a program (create an object, begin a for loop, etc) to specific lines in a source code file.

You need both of them for a good debugging experience.

You could retro-actively publish a source package if you have the same source code and SDK version (I think changes in the compiler could introduce problems).

But I think to be safe you should wait and start publish a symbol package next version. There is no urgency.
I downloaded the Google.Protobuf package and I noticed you're including the pdb file in the primary NuGet package. If you're happy with that approach then you don't need a symbol package.

To be honest, despite including PDBs directly in the nuget package is currently not recommended in the source link documentation (https://github.com/dotnet/sourcelink/#alternative-pdb-distribution), it seems to be the safest and simplest solution at this point. The whole machinery around sourcelink and the new symbol packages seems a bit too complex and it's easy to break things unknowingly (and I can only test the changes manually) - so if things currently work, I'd be leaning towards not changing.
Ok! I agree that each has their own pros and cons.

title: Objective-C builder pattern - syntax change

nodes.body: This library has never had _builders_ for Objective C support.  So it sounds like you were using some other library before and not this one.  So you will need to adapt your code accordingly.

Thanks for clarifying.

I found a plenty of similar libraries, e.g. [minyushov/Protobuf-ObjC](https://github.com/minyushov/Protobuf-ObjC.git) and [booyah/protobuf-objc](https://github.com/booyah/protobuf-objc) which seems to be the base fork for all of those modifications.

Could you please clarify on where do these libraries originate from and how are they related to the Protobuf? I got an impression that it was either an older version of Protobuf or a port of Protobuf to Obj-C before it was available officially. I came to that conclusion since I wasnt able to find Objective-C mentioned in  [official tutorials](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/tutorials).
Sorry for such simple questions, I'm new to using Protobuf in ObjC environment.

I don't have any experience with the other libraries, so I can't really say where they came from.  Internally Google had an objc library, and a few years ago we started including it in the official releases here.

The [reference section](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/overview) has more languages than some other parts of the docs site.  But I don't have much knowledge of the state of docs updates.

Thanks a lot. It seems that the libraries I've mentioned were developed before the release of the internal ObjC library from Google.

The reference section has quite thorough overview, just what I needed.

title: C# Serialization Performance - Part I
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux, Windows

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
MSBUILD 15

bool, double and float should be marked as fixed size. In FieldCodec.cs we create the codecs used by RepeatedField.cs. Having these not be fixed means that on large repeated fields for these fixed length primitives, we will call the size calculator each time, for every single data point (inside CalculatePackedDataSize). I've seen about 40% serialization improvement on repeated fields for these types when they are marked as fixed. 

Straight forward fix is to rename ComputeBoolSize to ComputeFixedBoolSize, ComputeFloatSize to ComputeFixedFloatSize and ComputeDoubleSize to ComputeFixedDoubleSize, then we should change ForBool, ForFloat and ForDouble to send in a dummy value to the computesize functions when creating the codec (we will set the FixedSize attribute to the result).

title: Convert PBArray to NSArray
body:
In newer version of Protobuf the array type changed from `NSArray` to `PBArray` and they have incompatible method signatures.

A lot of code has already been written expecting the `NSArray` type.


Given an instance of `PBArray`, how is it possible to convert it to the standard Objective-C `NSArray`?

nodes.body: This library has never had a PBArray type for Objective C, it sounds like you are using another library instead of this library.  `NSArray`s and boxing aren't used because of the overhead for large arrays.

title: [Protobuf 2.6.1] Objective-C: use NSArray instead of PBArray in generated files
body:
Is it possible to specify `protoc` compiler to use `NSArray` instead of `PBArray` in generated files?

I already have a large codebase expecting `NSArray` and having a `PBArray`(which is not compatible with `NSArray` in method signature) is a huge inconvenience.

Having compiler generate compatible model files will solve the issue for me. Is there any way to achieve it?

nodes.body:
Nope, using `NSArray` for a integers, etc. would require boxing of them and that can use a lot more memory.

Also we try to avoid options like this because you can get into trouble if two things depend on a common proto file and they have tried to use different decisions around what to set an option to (as only one ObjC class can exist with a given name in the runtime at a time).
Clear, I understand the issue with ambiguity of output originating from a single `proto` file but different compiler settings.

title: Enumerate PBArray [Objective-C]
body: What is the correct way to enumerate through an instance of `PBArray` in Objective-C?

nodes.body: This library doesn't have a `PBArray` type, it this is likely a question for another library.  The `GPB*Array` types support a block based enumeration.

title: C# Serialization Performance - Part II
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows, Linux

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
MSBUILD 15

This second issue is to address the function overhead in the current serialization implementation. In, https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet/issues/30 it appears they are considering a redesign. I support this and feel that their is some low hanging fruit in the current design we can leverage while that project is in the works.

I propose that without requiring a complete redesign (in the short-term), we can provide an internal interface to write T[] directly to a CodedOutputStream. A Codec would provide a reader and writer like before, but also an arraywriter.

Inside CodedOutputStream, we can handle the "common case" of the buffer being large enough to handle the entire array. This would allow consumers of CodedOutputStream to set a buffer size large enough to handle an entire array if they knew one was going to be of a predictable length. This means RepeatedField serialization would improve if the array fits within the limit, or it would remain the same speed. I will follow up this issue creation with a pull request which is WIP showing a possible implementation, which yields in my profiling a 100% speedup for repeated fields of fixed size on top of the speedup introduced by pull request #5810

title: [Ruby] `Google::Protobuf::ListValue.new(values: []).to_json` is an empty string
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.7.0
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Any

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

Ruby 2.6.0

**What did you do?**

```
2.6.0 :044 > Google::Protobuf::ListValue.new(values: []).to_json
 => ""
```

This causes calling `to_json` on a Struct with an empty array as a value for some key to output invalid json (e.g. you get `{key:}`)

```
2.6.0 :061 > Google::Protobuf::Struct.new(fields: { 'key' => Google::Protobuf::Value.new(list_value: Google::Protobuf::ListValue.new(values: [])) }).to_json
 => "{\"key\":}"
```

**What did you expect to see**

`{key: []}` (the output of `Google::Protobuf::ListValue.new(values: []).to_json` should be `"[]"`.

e.g. the above should be:

```
2.6.0 :061 > Google::Protobuf::Struct.new(fields: { 'key' => Google::Protobuf::Value.new(list_value: Google::Protobuf::ListValue.new(values: [])) }).to_json
 => "{\"key\":[]}"
```

nodes.body: Fixed in #5857. PTAL

title: Can I re-use object instances to avoid allocations with protobuf-java?
body: I have high volume of message to parse,I found GC becoming very frequently. How to avoid allocations memory? Object pool? How to implement?

nodes.body: We do a lot of memory allocation in Java. One thing you can try is to use an object pool for the Builder, and only pass the Builder around without building it into a Message. That may be able to reduce some memory allocation, but obviously the Builder is mutable and not thread-safe, so use that at your own risk. Other than that I cannot think of any other way to reduce memory allocation in Java.

title: [Ruby] JSON deserialization raises TypeError
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.7.1
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

OS X, but I suspect the behavior is on all platforms.

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

* ruby 2.5.3p105 (2018-10-18 revision 65156) [x86_64-darwin18]
* ruby 2.4.5p335 (2018-10-18 revision 65137) [x86_64-darwin18]
* ruby 2.3.7p456 (2018-03-28 revision 63024) [universal.x86_64-darwin18]

**What did you do?**

Hi, we noticed that the JSON serialization has changed in google-protobuf 3.7.0. We have [updated the google-cloud-ruby project](https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-ruby/pull/2979) to work with the new JSON format, but we had problems deserializing the new JSON format when the JSON includes a deeply nested `Google::Protobuf::ListValue`.

It looks like the JSON that is serialized cannot turn around and be deserialized. Here is an example that demonstrates this:

```ruby
require "google/cloud/spanner/v1"

prs = Google::Spanner::V1::PartialResultSet.new(
  values: [
    { string_value: "hello" },
    { bool_value: true},
    { number_value: 3.14 },
    { list_value: { values: [ { string_value: "1"},
                              { string_value: "2"},
                              { string_value: "3"} ]}}
  ]
)

puts prs.to_json
# 3.7.0 returns the following string:
#=> "{\"values\":[\"hello\",true,3.1400000000000001,[\"1\",\"2\",\"3\"]]}"
# 3.6.1 returns the following string:
#=> "{\"values\":[{\"stringValue\":\"hello\"},{\"boolValue\":true},{\"numberValue\":3.1400000000000001},{\"listValue\":{\"values\":[{\"stringValue\":\"1\"},{\"stringValue\":\"2\"},{\"stringValue\":\"3\"}]}}]}"

prs2 = Google::Spanner::V1::PartialResultSet.decode_json(prs.to_json)
# 3.7.0 raises the following error:
#=> TypeError: wrong argument type false (expected Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField)
# 3.6.1 does not raise an error.
prs2.to_json == prs.to_json #=> true
```

(FWIW, the JSON generated by google-protobuf 3.6.1 cannot be deserialized by google-protobuf 3.7.0, and vice versa. We understand this is intentional.)

title: Conflict when using same proto files in two java libraries
body:
Say I have a proto file, `my_proto_file.proto`.

I create a java "client" library `libClient` based on `my_proto_file.proto`. I create a java "server" library `libServer` based on `my_proto_file.proto`.

That works well, and I can use the resulting `com.package.MyProtoFile` class in both libraries independently. They can communicate with each other because they implement the same protocol.

Now say I decide to write one java app (e.g. and Android app) that will use both `libClient` and `libServer`. Because `com.package.MyProtoFile` is defined in both libraries, it ends up in an error like:

```
Execution failed for task ':app:transformClassesWithMultidexlistForRelease'.
> com.android.build.api.transform.TransformException: Error while generating the main dex list:
  Error while merging dex archives: 
  Learn how to resolve the issue at https://developer.android.com/studio/build/dependencies#duplicate_classes.
  Program type already present: com.package.MyProtoFile$1
```

However, my libraries don't need to expose `MyProtoFile` at all (say the server only needs to be run by the java application).

Is there a way to fix that, e.g. by telling `libServer` to not expose `MyProtoFile`, or by making sure that they end up being the same file in my app?

nodes.body: How did you create the android app? I'm afraid in protobuf layer there's no way to resolve this diamond dependencies issue. Usually you should split `libClient` and `libServer` into `libClient + protoLib` and  `libServer + protoLib`, then depend on all in your android app to solve this kind of issue.
