title: Misleading warning message when specifying a directory as an input file
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: N/A

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Latest protoc build from source using `gcc (GCC) 8.2.1 20181127`

**What did you do?**
I mistakenly passed a directory as an input file to protoc.
For example:
```bash
cd /tmp
mkdir test
protoc -I . ./test --go_out=/tmp/out --java_out=/tmp/out
```

**What did you expect to see**

I'd expect an error message that there are no valid input files.

**What did you see instead?**
protoc outputs a warning about missing syntax version but still generates java and go code (actually happens for all languages) with no message definitions.

The warning message was:
```
[libprotobuf WARNING google/protobuf/compiler/parser.cc:564] No syntax specified for the proto file: test. Please use 'syntax = "proto2";' or 'syntax = "proto3";' to specify a syntax version. (Defaulted to proto2 syntax.)
```
From a quick investigation, the problem is that `OpenDiskFile` [1] does not check if the given input file path is actually a regular file. Since `open(3)` is capable of opening special files (like directories), protoc continues as if it has opened an empty file.


[1] https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/importer.cc#L489

title: protoc marking generated C++ classes final as of 3.7
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.6.1, 3.7
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux, various (Arch Linux, Ubuntu, Debian)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Various; this system uses GCC 8.2.1 20181127

**What did you do?**
Run protoc to generate C++ for a given proto message.

**What did you expect to see**
Prior to version 3.7, classes generated for proto messages were not final. My project has code extending proto messages to add helper functions which index and operate on field values. The code in question builds successfully through protoc 3.6.1. I expected this to continue to be the case.

**What did you see instead?**
The build fails in 3.7 because protoc now tags `final` onto codegen. This change isn't mentioned anywhere that I can find (release notes, documentation) and there doesn't seem to be a flag to control this behavior. To my knowledge, there is also no flag to control the target C++ standard, so we cannot work around this issue by targeting C++03 (before `final` was introduced).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
This issue does not seem specific to any environment.

nodes.body: I think starting from 3.6 we require C++11 (see #2780).

I certainly wouldn't complain about most of the features that came with C++11. But `final` doesn't seem to add anything to the code, and it breaks our project's build (and probably others, who I expect to chime in after a couple more months as 3.7 rolls out).

The documentation [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial#parsing-and-serialization) does officially warn against inheriting from generated message types. However, it's still true that we made this change without giving it much of an announcement at all. It is beneficial because it allows the compiler to take advantage of more optimizations, but maybe we need to introduce a temporary opt-out mechanism to give projects time to refactor.
This is a huge problem for us, would def appreciate an option to disable.

This change also breaks building of Google Mozc project. (Actually now I have a patch.)
An option to avoid `final` (at least per-class) might be nice.

> **What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
> Version: 3.6.1, 3.7
> Language: C++
> 
> **What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
> Linux, various (Arch Linux, Ubuntu, Debian)
> 
> **What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
> Various; this system uses GCC 8.2.1 20181127
> 
> **What did you do?**
> Run protoc to generate C++ for a given proto message.
> 
> **What did you expect to see**
> Prior to version 3.7, classes generated for proto messages were not final. My project has code extending proto messages to add helper functions which index and operate on field values. The code in question builds successfully through protoc 3.6.1. I expected this to continue to be the case.
> 
> **What did you see instead?**
> The build fails in 3.7 because protoc now tags `final` onto codegen. This change isn't mentioned anywhere that I can find (release notes, documentation) and there doesn't seem to be a flag to control this behavior. To my knowledge, there is also no flag to control the target C++ standard, so we cannot work around this issue by targeting C++03 (before `final` was introduced).
> 
> **Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
> This issue does not seem specific to any environment.

I can appreciate compiler optimizations. But this eliminates a solution to another issue with proto that I know has been discussed a lot in the past: adding helper-like accessors. For instance, an `Area()` routine on a `Rectangle` message. Has there been any progress on formalizing that feature request?

I recognize it's no simple request since it must have language-level granularity (ie, the same method can't build for Java and C++ unless we bake an entire language into proto, which seems excessive). Our team would prefer the ability to provide a cut-and-paste block to be moved, verbatim, from the `.proto` source into the `.h` output.

The C++ project that I'm working on also broke because of this. In case anyone still needs it, here's the hack that I've come up with. Add a build step that calls

>`sed --in-place 's \bfinal\b /*final*/ ' <AUTOGENERATED_FILE>`

on files generated by `protoc`.

Using a sed script sounds to me like a good workaround, at least as a temporary solution. For the Rectangle example, I think a standalone function would be the best way to go since that would provide all the necessary functionality without needing to inherit from the generated message.

@acozzette Thanks for the quick reply. Of course my rectangle example was perhaps too simple. My current derived classes have other methods that implement something of a "builder" interface to allow chaining and simple code on the client side, but not always so simple in the derived class. I'm thinking of how to implement something with a set of standalone functions, but it isn't as straightforward as this simple case.

It is not okay to artificially constrain the library by implementing `final`, because it precludes downstream (advanced automation) implementations to specialize. For this reason, Xplicit Computing Inc is internally constrained to version `3.7` for building its code-generated `libxccommon` libraries, which provide `server-client` functionalities. Luckily, my understanding is that customer can still us any Protoc 3 compiler... but we're stuck on this old version that works -- and frankly are starting to assess alternative serialization techniques. Google Protobuf team, please revert this feature back and re-assess such design constraints.
at least give us the option `--no-final`
Bump from the international computational fluid dynamics community...

This change was made quite deliberately and provides a meaningful performance improvement when applied at scale.  The classes themselves have always been documented as not being suitable for derivation.  I would encourage you to consider containment over inheritance as a more efficient paradigm.

Significant investments have been made applying the Protobuf3 infrastructure. A better paradigm as library maintainers would be to not functionally change the spec after it has been deployed... and if so, allow the option for `--no-final`. I will discuss with our meta-programming experts, but as mentioned there are implications of a class being of a type, verses containing or having said type. There may literally not be a computer science opportunity for containment.

From a science and engineering professional perspective, it is generally not acceptable to do what has been done here. This may force us to migrate to Cern::Root sooner than initially planned.
At ICCFD11 two days ago, I just presented protobuf as a viable method for communicating messages between science and engineering teams. Perhaps I was wrong.

For what little it is worth, I agree with you that this should not have been done on a minor release.  We have spent a lot of time over the past year creating and publishing more rigorous policies that we intend to follow going forward.

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#versioning
https://opensource.google/documentation/policies/library-breaking-change
https://opensource.google/documentation/policies/cplusplus-support

Revisiting this particular decision also comes with costs.  Inside Google, that use of `final` provides a significant cost savings in terms of fleet resources and code evolution.  Making it configurable greatly complicates the ability of google to pull in external code that uses protobuffer because of the divergence in semantics exposed by that configuration.

As alluded to, there are workarounds of varying complexity.  The simplest and hackiest being to preprocess the generated sources.  A custom generator that wraps existing protobuf messages in custom APIs could provide you this flexibility and additionally might add significant power that you might find valuable.

Thank you for the info.
I've heard back from our protocol library lead and apparently we were able to sidestep this issue. 
We are now tracking what appears to be a separate issue that appeared in v3.8 but nothing concrete yet. Likely unrelated and probably not your problem

@fowles I am going to use the simplest and hackiest solution you mention, which is process the generated sources. :-(

Using composition isn't particularly feasible. I looked at some of the protobuf generated classes and they have ~100 getter/setter type methods that I would have to replicate so that clients can use all the functionality currently available. I suppose I could just expose the underlying protobuf class, but that and some of the other alternatives seem to violate good software principles as well, e.g. encapsulation. Also, these alternatives also mean changing the APIs I supply to clients, which isn't desirable either.
@emenchen you can sometimes get away with defining an `operator*` and `operator->` that delegate to avoid replicating the methods, but yeah, it can be pretty gross.

title: Consider adding `Interval` as a well known type

nodes.body: Thanks for the suggestions! This sounds reasonable. I'll try to bring this up to the team and see if everyone is okay with this proposal.

Hi Mike. I brought this up to the team. One of the criteria we have for introducing new well known type is check if it is also offered as a basic building block at the language level. While there are many applications for a time interval type, it is not in the standard library for C++, Java, Python, etc. As such, we are unwilling to commit to a "well known" Interval type at the Protobuf level. Thank you for your suggestion, though.

I would humbly ask to reconsider the decision. 
This has recently made it to the "standard Google collection of basic types" (Googlers, see //google/type).
I've been actually bashed for saying it is *not* standard :)

nodes.body:
Without more info, I don't think there is anything we can do to help.

From the limited stack you have provided, it looks like a message was being created from some data, while parsing the data, it was attempt create a submessage for a field, and in creating that the objc class that was needed didn't respond to one of the methods the library provides internally.

So my guesses would be:
- Since you have only seen this happen once, maybe some threading/memory corruption that happened to correct the memory for these objects.  i.e. - other crashes could be the same sorta memory issue, but in this case, it happened to the the protobuf library that failed.
- Some other library is loaded into memory containing a ObjC class with the same name as this message class.  The ObjC runtime only allows one class with a given name to be loaded at runtime, if something attempts to load two classes, the behavior for which one "wins" is undefined.  So if your message class has a common name, there is a chance something like this can happen.  The file level option to add a prefix to the generated objc types can help with this.  Given you say this only happened once, it is possible it is a collision with some private system library that is lazy loaded based on what the user does (i.e. - the System address book support loads some libraries on demand as the public apis are called, so it could be dependent on what the user does in your app before this parse happens), or if this user could have some system wide utility installed that injects into all apps.

When I use the DebugString() function to print a message with an enum type, why is the first element of the enum type not printed, but other elements can?

nodes.body: With proto3 there is no difference between a singular primitive field being empty and being set to its default value (see [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#default)). As a result E1 is not printed out because it is just the default value for that field.
@acozzette Is there any option to print default values?
No, as far as I know there is no option to print default values in text format.

The ability to create a new protobuf resource object by decoding JSON that contains a timestamp.

**What did you see instead?**

A `Google::Protobuf::ParseError` error.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

```ruby
require "time"

time_obj = Time.parse "2019-03-13T15:40:43.729054800Z"
timestamp_obj = Google::Protobuf::Timestamp.new seconds: time_obj.to_i, nanos: time_obj.nsec
```

title: [C++] Generated code compilation error related to name shadowing
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.6.1.3-1, also 3.7.0
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Linux 4.20.12-arch1-1-ARCH #1 SMP PREEMPT Sat Feb 23 15:11:34 UTC 2019 x86_64 GNU/Linux

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

gcc (GCC) 8.2.1 20181127
also: clang: version 7.0.1 (tags/RELEASE_701/final)

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Make a file `Bug.proto`:

```protobuf
syntax = "proto3";

package bug;

message Bug {
    enum Bug {
        UNKNOWN = 0;
    }
    Bug bug = 1;
}
```
2. Generate C++ code:

```bash
protoc -I . --cpp_out=. Bug.proto
```

3. Try to compile C++ code:

```bash
gcc -c Bug.pb.cc
```

4. See error

**What did you expect to see**

Either of below:
A) A proper compilation on step [3.] (no message from gcc).
B) An error during step [2.] (no generated C++ code from protoc, syntax error instead).

**What did you see instead?**

```bash
In file included from Bug.pb.cc:4:
Bug.pb.h:168:19: error: ISO C++ forbids nested type ‘Bug’ with same name as enclosing class [-fpermissive]
   typedef Bug_Bug Bug;
                   ^~~
Bug.pb.h:168:19: error: ‘bug::Bug::Bug’ has the same name as the class in which it is declared
...(OTHER ERRORS RESULTING FROM THE ONE ABOVE)...
```

I am not pasting clang output here because this bug is clearly not compiler-dependent (clang also throws the same kind of error of course).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

When you actually look in the generated file `Bug.pb.h`, it is clear that the `enum Bug` is really a `Bug_Bug`, but then inside `class Bug`, which was generated for `message Bug`, it is typedefed to `Bug`, which causes this error.

The same happens if the nested type is a message (i.e. `message Bug { message Bug { ... } ... }`) instead of an enum.

**Proposed solution**

If name shadowing is valid in protobufs: change protoc to emit proper C++ code (possibly just removing typedef and using full names?)
If it's not: change protoc to emit error when spotting nested declarations with the same names.

title: Why does GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_MIN_LIBRARY_VERSION change for a patch release?
body:
When going from 3.6.0 to 3.6.1 - a patch release - `GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_MIN_LIBRARY_VERSION` was bumped from 3006000 to 3006001 [as seen here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/9e1286b949adc40b450a0097c6ffd4dd491506c0#diff-cbd31ea2a5761cd281396b4277c36887) (and this happens at other patch releases too but I'm interested in 3.6.1).

I think it should have remained at 3.6.0 for a patch release.  Surely binary compatibility was maintained?  Why is it bumped up?

(And bonus question: If I just stomp on that value in `common.h` with `3006000` I'm not going to run into any problems, right?  I'm only interested in a C++/Linux environment, and having checked the [3.6.0->3.6.1 diff](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/compare/v3.6.1...3.6.x) the only things which is problematic to my (inexperienced) eyes are the additional symbol exports from `io/gzip_stream.h` and `repeated_field.h` - but I don't see that the C++ generated code would have changed to reference those symbols...)

(This is causing problems where we're delivering a plugin - compiled against protobuf 3.6.1 - to a product which is compiled against 3.6.0 and thus the protobuf shared library is 3.6.0 and the version check fails.  But any 3.6.x should work.)

nodes.body: I would guess that in this case you could probably safely interoperate 3.6.1 generated code with a 3.6.0 runtime library, but in general we don't really make any attempt to maintain ABI compatibility this way. Usually we require that for C++ the generated code and the runtime library are the exact same version.

title: protobuff 2.4.1 to 2.6.1
body: We are using a very old version of protobuff 2.4.1, a new project requires us to use at least 2.6.1. I want to do some tests on my own to make sure serialize/deserialize works. But want to reach out to see if anyone has done this before. What's the best way to test upgrade and any major changes I should be aware of. Appreciate your help!

nodes.body: I have the same question (maybe?) for the python package `protobuf==3.1` to python package `protobuf=3.6` (on the python side of generated code).  We have different projects that are pointing to different python protobuf package versions that need to interact (I/O wise). Does the compiler version need to match the library version?  Do library versions need to match exactly between projects?  Or is it just 3.x works with whatever 3.y ?  If you could just point me to the relevant documentation I'd much appreciate it.

After 3.0.0 we have compatibility, we guarantee:
generated code can always work with runtime that have never version.  For example 3.1.0 protoc can work with 3.4.0 runtime. But we do not guarantee old runtime with new protoc.

For 2.4.1 and 2.6.1, I am not sure what major changes you should be aware of. But as our wire format never change, serialize and deserialize should work

We do not change our wire format, so the serialization / deserialization should stay the same. As much as possible, we also try to avoid introducing breaking API changes or behavior changes. That said, there have been bug fixes, enhancement, and subtle changes over the years that could potentially affect your project. I do recommend matching the protoc version with the runtime version though to get the best performance.

There are a couple of things that can help ensure that the upgrade is safe:
1) Testing - if you have good test coverage and the tests continue to pass after upgrade, then it is a good sign. It is hard to say that you are 100% safe yet, but at least it is not breaking in any severe way.
2) Gradual rollout - this is easier to do if your project is a server that receive good traffics. You can try to do a gradual rollout (e.g., 10% with the upgraded version) and monitor the traffics to make sure everything is good.

I think these are general strategies that you can apply to any library upgrade.

title: Error detail when parsing length-delimited stream
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
C++ and C#; possibly others

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I have a network stream of protobuf messages, each preceded by a varint length field.  If there is an error parsing the length field then the parser needs to terminate.  However if there is an error parsing the message content then the parser should ignore that message and continue with the next.

There are therefore four possibilities each time the parser receives somes data from the network:

 1. The message is incomplete and the parser needs to wait for more data
 2. Error parsing the length field (i.e. the varint is too long)
 3. Error parsing the message itself
 4. The message is complete and successfully received

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I'd like google::protobuf::util::ParseDelimitedFromCodedStream (C++) and Google.Protobuf.MessageParser<>.ParseDelimitedFrom (C#) to return an error code or throw a typed exception which distinguishes between these cases.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
The C++ ParseDelimitedFromCodedStream outputs success and 'clean EOF' flags but, from what I can tell, the 'clean EOF' flag doesn't help here.  The C# ParseDelimitedFrom either throws an InvalidProtocolBufferException (which doesn't contain any further machine-readable information) or returns successfully.

I've worked around this by reading the varint length directly.  The varint read methods don't distinguish between an unexpected EOF (case 1) and an error parsing the length field (case 2), so I'm detecting this manually by checking the number of bytes available in the stream: anything over 10 bytes is assumed to be an error parsing the length field.  This is not a clean or elegant solution though, as protobuf should be the authority on whether or not there's a parse error.

#4303 is related but doesn't go quite as far.

title: Python: Timestamp.ToDatetime should have an ability to get a timezone-aware datetime object
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

> If it's about generated code change, what programming language?

Python. Well-known-types Timestamp.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

There are many times where it makes a difference between having a timezone-aware and timezone-naive datetime object in Python. For example, you cannot compare equality between a timezone-naive and a timezone-aware datetime object.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I'd *like* for `Timestamp.ToDatetime` to return a timezone-aware datetime with a UTC timezone, but understand this would be a breaking change. Instead, it would probably be preferable to

* Add a `Timestamp.ToUTCDatetime` method to create a timezone-aware datetime.

The answer at https://stackoverflow.com/a/21952077/101923 shows how to create a timezone-aware datetime. Probably the dependency on pytz should be optional. 

https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-python/blob/a6d849912eea6b9260ccb64ffb317d8265b354a6/core/google/cloud/_helpers.py#L630-L633

Shows how to make the dependency on pytz optional.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

* `Timestamp.ToDatetime` to take a `tzinfo` object (though ideally it should always be UTC).
  
  Problematic, because it requires first converting to timezone-aware UTC, then converting to the request timezone for correct behavior.
* `Timestamp.ToDatetime` to take a boolean option to return a timezone-aware datetime.
  
  Problematic, because there isn't really precedent for this in the datetime module that I could find. Also, boolean flags like this are always a bit less clear than having a second method that clearly shows the desired result.

def ToDatetime(self, tzinfo=None):
    """Converts Timestamp to a datetime.
    Args:
      tzinfo: A datetime.tzinfo subclass; defaults to None.
    Returns:
      If tzinfo is None, returns a timezone-naive UTC datetime (with no timezone
      information, i.e. not aware that it's UTC).
      Otherwise, returns a timezone-aware datetime in the input timezone.
    """

nodes.body: If I understand correctly it sounds like TensorFlow bundles its own copy of protobuf, resulting in ODR violations when TensorFlow users try to use both TensorFlow and protobuf. Unfortunately I don't think we can really do anything on the protobuf side to fix this, and the only solution is to avoid linking against two separate copies of protobuf. The static initializers are not the problem, because ultimately ODR violations are undefined behavior no matter what how we do our initialization.

When we want to print the message to a readable string, the Bytes field will be printed as based-64 coding string. Then we need to decode the characters to understand what does it mean. 

like this:
`{
      "UniqueId": "MjkyMTU1Mjg5MzkwNTc2Ng==",
      "VideoId": "aTA4NTBxandmZjI=",
      "Time": "NzE=",

nodes.body:
JsonFormat is designed to round-trip correctly (no data loss with decode(encode(Message))), and it is meant to be transferable to the web browser, so we use base64 encoding on bytes to make sure that all the data can be transferred.

If your fields can be represented as a String, please consider using string fields instead.

--no-as-needed is not supported in clang, any other solution to this. What is the root cause of this issue. Its blocker for me, if anyone can help its appreciated.

Glibc uses a stub implementation of various pthread functions, so that single threaded programs do not have to waste cycles doing things like locking and unlocking mutexes, and yet do not have to link to a different C library. (from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/21092601/is-pthread-in-glibc-so-implemented-by-weak-symbol-to-provide-pthread-stub-functi )

But protobuf need a real one, not the stub. Even protoc is mostly single threaded,  it still need libpthread. 

I believe protobuf has done everything correctly. It added the pthread lib to its linker flags, however, when LTO is enabled, the linker may wrongly think the pthread lib is not needed, and may throw it away. And if it does that,  the final protoc executable won't be usable, it always crashes.  The "--no-as-needed" flag is a workaround for this. 

I would think it is more a bug of the compiler, because it can be solved by upgrading the compiler. The latest one should work fine. If it is not possible for you to make an update on your toolchain,  then please step back from the problem. Is LTO a must? Can you turn it off? 

Another possibility is: protobuf may allow user building it in a purely single threaded way, without all the pthread function calls.  From my experience, it is often needed because not every system supports multiple threading. For example, the symbolic execution engines, trusted execution environments. they prefer to have things as simple as possible.
Thanks for the reply, appreciate it. Seems like i moved away from this after spending too much time on this issue. I will try again after updating the compiler.
I'll close this issue as it is not quite a problem of protobuf,  and solutions are clear.

title: proposal: Comparable structs
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Both proto2 and proto3.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
* Alias for scalar types. Currently, all of my database primary keys are strings. But even though they are of the same type, they have different meanings. A User key cannot be used to look up an Item. So I want to define a type UserKey for User and a ItemKey for Item.
* User-defined scalar types. It might be useful to define 16 bytes as GUID, 12 bytes as ObjectID, a pair of integers as a Point2D, etc. Such types often need comparability. Timestamps and durations may be implemented as structs instead of messages so they can be compared or sorted.
* Comparability. A comparable type can be used as map keys or perform set union/intersection. Currently, messages are usually not comparable and require special handling. I can understand that because there are many edge cases. For example, messages might have unknown fields because we need to be able to add and remove fields from messages. But primitives alone are not useful enough. For example, pairs and triples might be useful.
* A better way to get around the weirdness of proto3 messages. In proto3, the zero value of each primitive is the default value, and it's not possible for a client to distinguish zero values and nonexistent values. In cases when the zero value has a real meaning, it's effectively no versioning at all. The struct drops versioning to make things clearer. It's effectively proto3 messages that consist of primitives only and no fields of message type.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I propose a new type called structs with the following properties:
* Structs consist of multiple fields, and each field must be a scalar type, an enum type or a struct.
* Struct fields do not have a field number. It's determined by the order of the fields.
* Every field must be "required". It might be useful to allow fields to be "repeated" or "optional" too, but how that would be implemented needs more thought, since not every language supports comparable arrays. Oneof is also tricky but it might be possible. For proto3, every field has the zero value as the default value. For proto2 every field has a type-specific default value that can be overridden.
* Structs are fixed and if a struct is changed in any way, by adding/removing fields or reordering them, the new struct and the old struct will no longer be binary compatible with each other.
* Structs cannot be cyclic by traversing "required" fields (such structs don't make any sense).
* Structs can be used like any other primitive in a message and can be encoded/decoded on their own.
* Structs cannot be wrapped in Any.
* For each language, the generated type for the structs should be comparable and can be used as map keys in that language.
* Two structs are equal if and only if each of their corresponding fields are equal.
* Preferably two structs may also be ordered. Struct A is strictly less than struct B if an index i exists such that ith field in struct A is strictly less than ith field in struct B and for index 1..i-1 the field in struct A equals to the corresponding field in struct B.
* The binary representation for a struct is deterministic. Two structs are equal if and only if they marshal to the same sequence of bytes. It might be possible to make their binary representation ordered too.

A dedicated syntax for representing struct values might be necessary so messages can specify default values for struct fields.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I use Go language.  For the first problem, I created a plugin that replaces the field type in generated code with a custom alias. But it doesn't work across languages. Thus I thought about a generalized struct type that might have other uses too.

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

nodes.body: Hi, thank you for proposing this. What you describes sound very similar to FlatBuffers (https://google.github.io/flatbuffers/). Perhaps it is closer to what you want?

title: C#: protoc should update its error and warning messages for the msvs format and include location information

nodes.body: cc @jtattermusch
/cc @kkm000 :)

Doesn't look like there is any authoritative docs on how error codes should be defined and it's left up to the author. That being said, there are a few rules of thumb that may be relevant here:

1. `PROTOC` is a perfect prefix, it's distinct and communicates clearly where the error is coming from. The length is fine, we have `NETSDK` prefix for errors too so the length is okay.
2. The error code should (but not must) be 4 digits long. Generally the thousands digit is used to categorize errors but this is mostly up to the author. You can look to MSB or CS errors for inspiration: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/visualstudio/visual-studio-2008/bb383807(v%3dvs.90) https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/compiler-messages/.

For example, we might want to reseve 0 - 999 for critical or future use and start errors at 1000. We might want to use 1000-4999 for errors and 5000+ for warnings. We might want to categorize argument errors for 1000-1999, syntax errors for 2000-2999, etc.

3. Yes the error codes should be distinct. This would allow better links to references on how to fix the issues for example.

The error produced in descriptor.cc should also call AddError()/AddWarning() in CommandLineInterface:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d0f91c863ae0fbb75b41460c8bbb786ade197a0f/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc#L289

Update: A change has been submitted in internal which can add location error info for import errors (including the two examples above). Expect to see the fix in future release.

Still have some errors in descriptor.cc that do not have location info. I will try to look how many of them can add location info in.
Update: location info are added for all errors in descriptor.cc. Will be included in future release.

for MSVS format, feel free to create a PR and assign to us. Related code:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2350e20cae1a9a1f54147c6e18e1a0da706cca96/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc#L346

title: Split gRPC tools NuGet into Google.Protobuf.Tools and Grpc.Tools
body:
This is first of all a discussion, and also an action item (for me, apparently) if/when agreed to proceed.

Protobuf team, @jtattermusch, what are you thoughts on this?

## What

Split package so each part goes with its own project?

Currently, and intentionally by design, there are two separate parts packaged into one nuget now. One is protoc-only tooling, named Google.Protobuf.Tools. Another is gRPC-only tooling, which can be installed separately (of course, it would depend on Google.Protobuf.Tools). For an example, please see these two subdirectories: https://github.com/grpc/grpc/tree/59ffdd99/src/csharp/Grpc.Tools/build/_protobuf and https://github.com/grpc/grpc/tree/59ffdd99/src/csharp/Grpc.Tools/build/_grpc. The current package control files are only gluing the parts together: 
https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/59ffdd9929667d8d662d4bede6a21d4b3e35a93a/src/csharp/Grpc.Tools/build/Grpc.Tools.props#L7-L10

The C# code and the build DLLs belongs to the Protobuf part entirely; the Grpc.Tools part is only MSBuild scripting. The binaries (executable files) for the compiler and plugins could be packaged each separately. Standard include protos should go with the Protobuf.Tools.

The parts of future separate packages are designed so that the could discover each other, regardless of the order of inclusion. Also, there is a counter, (currently unused, set to 1), indicating the compatibility between packages, like an "API version" exposed by the main, Protobuf part, which allows for some discrepancy between package versions. But this is mainly for 3rd party plugins, I believe.

So, it looks like everything is nearly ready for the surgery.

## When

At this point we have been through multiple GA releases of the Grpc.Tools package. At this point, we have one open issue that I really want to spend some time thinking how to best take care of (namely https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/17672), but I believe we are feature-complete otherwise.

We should not delay this too much, as there are a few packages for protoc tooling exist in the wild. I (humble as I am, of course) believe that our version is superior to these in its dependency tracking. For me, mainly a C++ user, an extra regen of header files results in an [XKCD 303](https://xkcd.com/303/), naturally.

## How

This is the hardest part, or at the least it looks like that from this side of the screen. Apparently, this requires a tight coordination between the two teams (and I am an outsider, so it's not even internal only).

Also, we need to ensure that there is no gap such that user's packages would break for the lack of necessary files. For example, we ship current content of Grpc.Tools, when Protobuf.Tools already carries them too. After a version tick or two, those extra copies in Grpc.Tools may be dropped.

NuGet supports version ranges for dependencies, namely an exact version or version range for packages. I'm sure I could come up with a transition schema such that no users in any combination of current/upgrade version will be broken.

## Other thoughts

Implications on the joint dotnet-grpc project?
/cc @JunTaoLuo

## More information
* https://grpc.io/blog/grpc-dotnet-build
* https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/59ffdd99/src/csharp/BUILD-INTEGRATION.md
----
/cc @jskeet Since he was part of the original discussion.

Supercedes: X-Ref: #1193

nodes.body:
For grpc-dotnet, we'd like to ensure this splitting of the packages is introduced in a backwards-compatible way. For example, project depending on Grpc.Tools right now should still get all the correct assets to build the project when they update the version. Since Grpc.Tools takes a dependency on Google.Protobuf.Tools I think this will be the case so it's fine.

We also need to ensure marking Grpc.Tools with PrivateAssets ensures both its and Google.Protobuf.Tools' assets are build time only and does not flow to the parent project. I believe this should be the case but we'd want to double check when making the change.

@JunTaoLuo yes, there were a lot of issues with NuGet regarding the transitivity of asset restrictions. I vaguely remember some of them were marked fixed some time ago, but we definitely need to check carefully.
Grpc.Cools! What a cool typo I made!

@jtattermusch @jskeet @JamesNK 

I’m revisiting this issue to see if it is still relevant or desirable or needed.

Four years on and `Grpc.Tools` is stable and is now widely used, is a dependency on many NuGet packages (including `Grpc.AspNetCore`), and referenced from Microsoft documentation.

`Grpc.Tools` is a ‘superset’ of what is provided by `Google.Protobuf.Tools` and can be configured to compile _.proto_ files without generating any gRPC code if needed.  There are currently no dependencies between these two packages.

Arguments for splitting `Grpc.Tools` and moving build logic into `Google.Protobuf.Tools` include:

- The _protoc_ binaries belong with the [protocolbuffers/protobuf](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf) project
- The [well-known types](https://protobuf.dev/reference/protobuf/google.protobuf/) belong with the [protocolbuffers/protobuf](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf) project
- `Google.Protobuf.Tools` should integrate with MSBuild to compile _.proto_ files

Counter-arguments are:
- If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it
- The [grpc/grpc](https://github.com/grpc/grpc) project has to build the _protoc_ binaries anyway since it has a dependency on those to build the C# gRPC plugin
- It guarantees the build logic, _protoc_ binaries and plugin binaries are all compatible with each other when changes are made
- The build logic needs to know about the plugins (configuration and know the likely files generated by it)
- Risks in breaking existing projects

I think there is more of an argument for moving `Grpc.Tools` from [grpc/grpc](https://github.com/grpc/grpc) to the [grpc/grpc-dotnet](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet) project since that is now the focus for gRPC C# work. However that is non-trivial since we probably will still want the binaries built by [grpc/grpc](https://github.com/grpc/grpc).

Do we want to still proceed with trying to split `Grpc.Tools` and move things into `Google.Protobuf.Tools`?

Are there any other interested parties that need to be involved in the discussion?

One benefit of moving the build logic into Google.Protobuf.Tools is that when there's a new protobuf release, the new generator becomes available immediately via Google.Protobuf.Tools, rather than having to wait for the release cycle of Grpc.Tools. That's relatively minor, but it's a more practical reason than some of the other "pros". (The compatibility guarantees provided by it being in Grpc.Tools are pretty compelling though...)
I haven't seen people ask for this. But I focus on gRPC rather than independent Protobuf serialization, so that's not surprising.

You can tell `Grpc.Tools` to use other binaries instead of those provided in the package (see [BUILD-INTEGRATION.md](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/src/csharp/BUILD-INTEGRATION.md#using-grpctools-with-unsupported-architectures)), and this nasty hack works if you want to use the _protoc_ from `Google.Protobuf.Tools` by adding this to the _.csproj_ file:
```xml
  <PropertyGroup>
    <Protobuf_ProtocFullPath>$(PkgGoogle_Protobuf_Tools)\tools\windows_x64\protoc.exe</Protobuf_ProtocFullPath>
  </PropertyGroup>
```

Not nice - but possible.

Further notes for myself:

A better way of using binaries in Google.Protobuf.Tools in Grpc.Tools is to add a custom target in the .csproj file:
```xml
  <Target Name="DefineProtocBinary" BeforeTargets="BeforeBuild">
    <PropertyGroup>
       <Protobuf_ProtocFullPath>$(protoc_windows64)</Protobuf_ProtocFullPath>
    </PropertyGroup>
  </Target>
```

The PropertyGroup needs to be in a target rather than at the top level of the project file is because Google.Protobuf.Tools defines its properties in a _.targets_ file instead of a _.props_ file (why?) - the targets file is automatically included _at the end_ of the project file thus the properties are not defined when we want to use them. If they had been in a _.props_ file then they would have been included at the start of the project file.

Thanks for a great pros/cons summary in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5957#issuecomment-1541907341.

A few comments:
- From the perspective of project separation it would be cleaner to rely on the protoc executables produced by the protobuf team (as part of protobuf release), but since gRPC needs to build the protoc plugin binaries anyway, we might as well build protoc binaries while at it (it's really a one line change for us since the dependencies are almost identical). If gRPC builds both protoc binaries and protoc plugins, they'll be guaranteed to be mutually compatible and would have the same range of supported platforms (since they were produced with the same build configuration), which is generally desirable.
- Currently `Google.Protobuf.Tools` is "dumb" in the sense it doesn't have almost any build integration logic, while `Grpc.Tools` is actually quite complex and does a lot. It took us a lot of effort to make `Grpc.Tools` to do everything it does and to test it and fix the bugs (and msbuild is pain to write and test). So while we could argue that some logic from Grpc.Tools logically belongs to `Google.Protobuf.Tools`, it would be a big undertaking to move it there and to test everything to make sure we're not breaking anything. Also, the `Google.Protobuf.Tools` would get much more complex as a result (requiring not only new logic but also some notrivial testing) and since the gRPC team (that has most of expertise and mileage in this area) doesn't own `Google.Protobuf.Tools` it would be tricky transfer the ownership.
- Ad needing to wait for gRPC release to get Grpc.Tools with new protoc binaries: That's a good point but gRPC generally tries to follow a 6weekly release cycle so this is hopefully not that much of an extra wait. We're also trying to get better at upgrading our third_party/protobuf dependency quickly. Also, as @tonydnewell has pointed out, you can override the protoc binaries being used by Grpc.Tools quite easily, so using older Grpc.Tools with the freshly released protoc binaries is possibly.

So IMHO splitting Grpc.Tools logic between Google.Protobuf.Tools and Grpc.Tools wouldn't really be worth the effort and we'll be better off with Grpc.Tools being used for pure-protobuf codegen as well as grpc+protobuf codegen (and investing the resources we have into making Grpc.Tools improvements/fixes rather than in this complex refactoring).

Thanks everyone for their inputs, I will close this issue now.

@tonydnewell  can you please go through the Grpc.Tools sources and find places where we mention splitting the logic (file layout, todos, comments etc.) and perform a cleanup - since we just decided that we're not going to pursue this?

title: Report use of unknown fields
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

C++ (possibly others)

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

We would like to allow unknown fields during proto parsing from wire (and formats such as JSON/YAML), but to report the details for the purposes of logging. Our use case is Envoy (https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy), where configuration with unknown fields can fall into two categories:

1. Intentional delivery of a newer field from a server with a newer API proto than the client. Client should just ignore.

2. Accidental misconfiguration of protos (typically the JSON/YAML representation, but also text proto) by users.

We would be confident enabling unknown fields if we could track their use to support (1) and still detect (2).

**Describe the solution you'd like**

A callback during proto parsing when an unknown field is encountered.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Today, we only allow a binary choice by the user. We encourage them to allow unknown fields if the protos are machine generated and to disallow them if not. This is often too coarse, with a mixture of configuration proto provenance not uncommon.

CC @mattklein123

nodes.body: What are the inputs and return value for the callback you would like to proposal? I think it's some kind of hard to just providing one callback to fully support all users concerns.

It would really depend on what is most idiomatic for protobuf, but the effect that we want is for C++ code calling into functions like `JsonStringToMessage()` or `message.ParseFromString()` to be able to learn which unknown fields were encountered during the parsing operations. Any thoughts?

Also CC @lizan

JsonStringToMessage has an option for ignore_unknown_fields. If you set it to false for (1) and set it to true for (2), would that give you what you need? The parse failure message should inform you approximately where the error occurs in JSON.

We need to programatically obtain a list of unknown fields to use for more detailed logging and stats. We want to accept the unknown fields, but provide an indicator in our own access logs of all accepted unknown fields, and scraping error strings for this seems a bit fragile.

The [converter::ErrorListener](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.7.0/src/google/protobuf/util/internal/error_listener.h#L53) is for this purpose, though it is in internal header so ideally we want to make it as a part of public API.

What kind of information would you like to log? Do you need to know the JSON key that is unknown + the full hierarchy to get there? Do you need to know the line number + column number of that unknown field?

Random idea: if I give you a traverser that can traverse the entire JSON, and for each JSON field that I visit, I'll give invoke your visitor with the JSON key + JSON value + the corresponding FieldDescriptor for that JSON (or absent of FieldDescriptor for unknown field), would that be sufficient for your logging/stats purpose?

I think we just want to know the field names for JSON and the field number for proto, that should be sufficient for logging.

The idea you present would definitely work for JSON, is there a way of also tackling this for proto?
@haon4 ack; in that case, what you suggest in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5967#issuecomment-481056877 sounds great. Do you think this can be added to the protobuf C++ libs?
I had a chat with Yilun about this. We have some ideas, but not enough free cycles :( Once Yilun finishes up his current project he might be able to look designing this.
Great. Meanwhile, we will add support in Envoy for handling the proto3 ingestion path using reflection and then we can consume the JSON support for that path as it becomes available.

title: Undefined behavior in UTF8GenericScanFastAscii
body:
Hello,
On this line https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/stubs/structurally_valid.cc#L507 the computation of

` const uint8* srclimit8 = srclimit - 7;`

may cause a violation of the C++ standard as `srclimit - 7` is not a valid operation when `srclimit` points, for example, to the beginning of a string.
Hope this helps,
Benjamin

Not really helpful because that code is confined to a single repo and cannot be shared easily unless the generated code is shared too, or a special plugin is created. As illustrated, this relationship would also be helpful for the Protobuf codebase because of real covariance. I'm certain that various constructs could be simplified.

title: C++ linker "multiple definition" errors caused by messages with same name in different protobuf packages
body:
Hi, I'm trying to build a C++ linux app which uses protobuf files from two different protobuf packages. The build is failing because of "multiple definition" errors from the linker. These seem to be caused because there is a message with the same name in both packages.

I've put a minimal example in https://github.com/feedhandler/stuff/tree/master/protobuf/clash 
In that example there are two packages, A and B, and there is a message Foo in both packages. The linker errors are like this:
```
multiple definition of `InitDefaults_Foo_2eproto()'
multiple definition of `file_level_metadata_Foo_2eproto'
multiple definition of `TableStruct_Foo_2eproto::offsets'
multiple definition of `assign_descriptors_table_Foo_2eproto'
multiple definition of `AddDescriptors_Foo_2eproto()'
```
Any ideas how I can fix this problem?

(Note: I'm not allowed to edit the *.proto files in my real app, so I can't do things like change the "import" statement in Foo.proto)

Environment:

- protobuf C++ 3.7.1
- g++ 5.4.1
- Ubuntu 16.04 64-bit

Thanks

nodes.body:
I think the problem is your `protoc` commands:
```
protoc --proto_path=A --cpp_out=a Foo.proto Bar.proto
protoc --proto_path=B --cpp_out=b Foo.proto Baz.proto
```

Protoc likes to have its own notion of a unique logical path to each .proto file, and so in this case both versions of Foo.proto have the same path, which causes a conflict (likewise for Bar.proto). If you change your protoc commands to something like this then each file will get a different logical path.
```
protoc --proto_path=. --cpp_out=a A/Foo.proto A/Bar.proto
protoc --proto_path=. --cpp_out=b B/Foo.proto B/Baz.proto
```

That doesn't work because it breaks the `import` statement:
```
dmsdev@dmsdev-VirtualBox> make
pkg-config --cflags protobuf  # fails if protobuf is not installed
-pthread -I/usr/local/include
mkdir -p a b
protoc --proto_path=. --cpp_out=a A/Foo.proto A/Bar.proto
Bar.proto: File not found.
A/Foo.proto: Import "Bar.proto" was not found or had errors.
A/Foo.proto:9:3: "Bar" is not defined.
Makefile:3: recipe for target 'all' failed
make: *** [all] Error 1
dmsdev@dmsdev-VirtualBox>
```
Could you reopen this issue please?
Your import statements need to be updated to reference the full paths, e.g. `A/Foo.proto` instead of just `Foo.proto`.
Unfortunately in the real app I'm not able to edit the *.proto files, so I can't update the import statements

How did the .proto files end up having the same name? That sounds like a strange coincidence. It might be worth asking the upstream maintainers if they could choose more descriptive file names for their .proto files.

The app is intended to be a kind of universal decoder for viewing messages on a message bus. There are many systems using this message bus, and the different systems encode their messages in different ways. The decoder knows what kind of encoding is used in a specific message by looking at the message topic. Some systems encode using protobuf, others use different forms of binary encoding (non-protobuf). And of the protobuf-encoded messages, some use protobuf package "A" and some use protobuf package "B"
In packages A and B there are around 10 to 15 proto files in each package, and it just happens that one of them has the same name in both packages. I guess it's just coincidence that they have the same name. 

It's unlikely that the upstream maintainer would agree to rename the files as there are many systems already using these protobufs without problem, it's only in this app that we are having the problem.

OK, I see. I'm afraid there is no good workaround except to tweak the `.proto` files and build setup so that each `.proto` file has a unique path. Protobuf is just not set up to accommodate multiple `.proto` files with the same path (and by path I mean the logical path to the file, including the file name). For example you can look up the descriptor for a file by calling `DescriptorPool::generated_pool()::FindFileByName("path/to/my/file.proto")`, and this wouldn't make any sense if there were more than one `.proto` file at that logical path.

title: python well_known_type: naming convention
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

proto2/3 - python - well_known_types 

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Most of the python codebase uses the _lowercase_with_underscores_ convention for methods and functions, as it is enforced by linters. The classes defined in _well_known_types.py_ don't follow this convention as they are similar to the definition from other languages. Although it's not an issue, I think we could create aliases for those methods in order to make then more idiomatic. Example from `python/google/protobuf/internal/well_known_types.py:189`

```python

  def ToMicroseconds(self):
    """Converts Timestamp to microseconds since epoch."""
    return (self.seconds * _MICROS_PER_SECOND +
            self.nanos // _NANOS_PER_MICROSECOND)
```

They are fine, but if you put this call in a codebase which follows the lowercase code convention, it's not so good:

```python
if user_profile.created_at.ToNanoseconds() == expected_created_at:
```
Also, it is a little inconsistent since `well_known_types` module uses this convention.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

As python protobuf is widely used, renaming the methods is not a solution. However, I can't see any issues in adding aliases to these methods.

```python

  def ToMicroseconds(self):
    """Converts Timestamp to microseconds since epoch."""
    return (self.seconds * _MICROS_PER_SECOND +
            self.nanos // _NANOS_PER_MICROSECOND)

   to_microseconds = ToMicroseconds
...
```
**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Create an external extension/lib to fix them (I personally dislike it) or keep it as it is.

**References**:

- https://github.com/Azure/azure-cli-extensions/blob/master/pylintrc
- https://www.datacamp.com/community/tutorials/pep8-tutorial-python-code
- https://stackoverflow.com/questions/5220580/change-default-python-coding-style

nodes.body: method_name is suggested but MethodName is also allowed for consistency in google. Most old code in protobuf python are using MethodName for example text_format.py message.py descriptor.py, so well_known_types.py also  use MethodName for consistency

title: n C++, in ReadLittleEndian32FromArray() returning the byte cursor as 'const' makes the idea of a cursor unusable

The underlying data should be const, because we don't need to modify it, but the pointer itself should be mutable because we're incrementing it as we go along.

title: Duplicate Java mergeFrom methods when message contains a from field of its own type
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.7.1
Language: Java

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
macOS Mojave 10.14

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
python version

**What did you do?**
create a_message.proto:
```protobuf
syntax = "proto3";

option java_package = "com.test";

message AMessage {
    AMessage from = 1;
}
```
generate java code:
```bash
protoc --java_out=../java/ a_message.proto
```

**What did you expect to see**
AMessageOuterClass.java will compile successfully.

**What did you see instead?**
AMessageOuterClass.java does not compile due to two methods having the same signature:
```java
public Builder mergeFrom(com.test.AMessageOuterClass.AMessage other) {
```

nodes.body:
Sorry but it can't use `from` as field name since the mergeSomeField method will conflict with mergeFrom method.
@haon4 Do we have any plan for preventing these words that are not java key words appears in protoc?

We do have existing proto messages with 'from' as field name that can compile successfully. The problem here is that 'from' is using the same type as the Message that contains is, causing a signature conflict. We have a couple of options to resolve this:

1. Do nothing - users will just have to update their field name :-/
2. Rename the generated merge method for the field name to something like mergeFrom_. But then we will have mergeFrom(com.test.AMessageOuterClass.AMessage) and mergeFrom_(com.test.AMessageOuterClass.AMessage), which would be super confusing.
3. Return an error when we generate the Java codes with custom error message telling developers to change the field name.

At this point I am leaning toward doing nothing. It is unpleasant, but the work around is quite simple. It is probably better to have the user rename the field than having confusing mergeFrom() and mergeFrom_(). Returning an error earlier would be an ideal long term goal, but requires significantly more investment that we won't be prioritizing yet.

nodes.body: Generally, we only have proto3 json format officially, for proto2 we're still trying to figure out a specification.

Sorry about this, but JSON format is a Proto3 concept, and we didn't specify any behavior for proto2. While it works in happy cases, we can't promise anything about it for proto2. For proto2, we are also discouraging the usage of required fields because it is known to cause issues. If possible, we recommend that you switch to using proto3 if you want to use JSON format. At the minimum, please avoid using required fields.

title: Enum values not defined in enum class
body:
The [documentation for enum](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated#enum) says:

> For example, you can access the values in the three following ways for the following enum in a proto:

```protobuf
enum SomeEnum {
    VALUE_A = 0;
    VALUE_B = 5;
    VALUE_C = 1234;
}
```

```python
value-a = myproto_pb2.SomeEnum.VALUE_A
# or
myproto_pb2.VALUE_A

myproto_pb2.SomeEnum.Value('VALUE_A')

title: Convert bytestream from nanopb to a string that can be parsed in python

nodes.body:
Answering my onwn question:
First I missed the brackets at the end of 
`cmdresponse = my_pb2.ProtoCommandResponse()`

then it asks for bytes rather than for CMessage, which thinking of it makes a lot more sense. Consequently straight foward to solve. In the following confirmed that it is read in correct.

```
mycmd = my_pb2.ProtoCommandResponse()
#fill the message in python
mycmd.command = 123
mycmd.status = False
mycmd.data = 0x123
mystr = mycmd.SerializeToString()
print(mystr)

#the char values from the nanopb
datain = [8, 123, 16, 0]
databytes = bytes(datain) #convert to format SerializeToString() can eat
print(databytes)

#read in the databytes and confirm that serialized is equal
newcmd = mytest_pb2.ProtoCommandResponse()
newcmd.ParseFromString(databytes)
newstr = mycmd.SerializeToString()
print(newstr)
```
Outputs:

```
b'\x08{\x10\x00\x18\xa3\x02'
b'\x08{\x10\x00'
b'\x08{\x10\x00\x18\xa3\x02'
```

Maybe worth noticing that in this c-code line
`proto_command_response_t test_responsemsg = {.command = 123,.data=0x123};`
I missed to init the required field status expecting it to have the default value. Since in C it's jus a structure it take the value I initialized it with and that is for a partly initialized struct just 0 for the uninitialized values.
Additionally since the field 'data' is optional we need to set the has_data flag otherwise the receiver will receive the default value 0 instead of 0x123. With this it is working as intended:
`proto_command_response_t test_responsemsg = {.command = 123, .status = true , .data=0x123, .has_data = true};`
In Python then this is received as:
`[8, 123, 16, 1, 24, 163, 2]`

And then correctly decoded to:
```
123
True
291
```
Thanks, I've made the same mistake - -b
Thx. The same brackets issue confused me for some days

title: Weird string behaviour on MacOS (all string ptrs seem to refer to/modify the same char buffer)

nodes.body: I don't see any obvious reason for why that would happen. Maybe if you step through it with a debugger that could give you some clues to what's happening. I would also be curious to know if `Request->mutable_device_type()` and `Request->mutable_device_id()` are returning the same pointer. If you could run your program under a tool like ASan (AddressSanitizer) that might give some useful information, too.

You might want to double check that the version of `protoc` you're using to generate code exactly matches the `libprotobuf` version you link against and the headers you include. We have some compile-time checks to help enforce that but we got some reports recently making it sound like that enforcement stopped working (I need to look into that more but haven't had a chance yet).

Thank you, acozzette; protoc version was fine, 
but the actual problem traced down to the linkage of PB "default string object".

As it turns out, in our Unreal packaging two different code bodies (transport DLL and main process code) ended up with different values of &::google::protobuf::internal::GetEmptyStringAlreadyInited().
That caused havoc with assigning and releasing all string values in protobuf structures.

Apparent fix is moving all write-access to protobuf messages to one code package;
I wonder, however, what was the original design idea? (for not using flat nullptr value as "default", that absolutely would not depend on linkage mode and/or order of module/object initialization).

Also, maybe it would be a good idea to note this behaviour somewhere in top-level C++ usage 
documentation? (as the side-effects seem to be pretty strange and not immediately understandable :)
Ah OK, that explanation makes sense. That is ultimately just an ODR (one definition rule) violation, so I think the correct fix is to make sure there is only one copy of `libprotobuf`.
Hi, we've run into the same issue occurring in a Linux environment (But not on Windows) with Unreal. Could you share what you mean by your different code bodies, were those modules on Unreal?

title: Choose not to delete messages when Clearing with C++?
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
C++ code change/function addition, no proto3 syntax change.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
When calling CopyFrom at very high rates with most messages having at least 1 sub message there becomes a lot of new and delete calls from the Clear function (or a very large memory leak if using arenas, one test caused 300 GB of ram to be used in 35 mins).

**Describe the solution you'd like**
When generating the cpp code for Clear if the sub message is not nullptr and its not the default instance then call Clear on it. This could be a different function if needed

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
- I have used reflection when clearing messages then calling mergeFrom which causes too much CPU usage to iterate through each field.
- I have tried with an Arena which causes a 300 GB memory leak since the sub message pointer is just set to nullptr.

**Additional context**
The code that could be modified or duplicated if a new function would be required is here.
[cpp_message_field.cc#L355-L358](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_message_field.cc#L355-L358)

Thanks for spending the time to read through this request!

nodes.body:
CC @haberman and @gerben-s 

This seems like an interesting case where the proto3 performance is not as good as proto2. I don't think we can just call `Clear()` on the submessage like you suggest, because we need to keep track of whether the submessage exists or not. We would probably need to reintroduce the bit array indicating whether fields are present (the "hasbits"), at least for submessage fields.

About arenas, the way they work is that everything is freed all at once when the arena is destroyed. I suspect that when you tried arenas you didn't encounter a real memory leak, it's just that it will keep using more memory until you destroy it. Usually arenas work best for servers where you can create an arena just for the duration of one request.

title: Request: protoc should only overwrite files if contents are not identical
body:
If it's straightforward enough I'd be happy to contribute a patch on this.

**What language does this apply to?**
Any language

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I'm implementing Perfetto in Node.js, and Perfetto has quite a large number of generated sources from protobufs. Because these files get overwritten on every build, incremental re-builds are slow. Note that we are using GYP in Node.js which I believe does not assume hermetic builds, so GYP will try to re-build dependents every time the protoc-generated files change.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Something similar to V8's Torque, where [output files are only changed if they are not the same](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/4dd01774c63e9d8a896dcddccb23b964e0c160e0/src/torque/utils.cc#L246).

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
We could wrap protoc in a script that only invokes it if sources are newer.

nodes.body: +1 to this

For future reference, an example script to achieve this in user land:

```bash
#######################################
# Copies a directory without overwriting identical files at the destination.
# Arguments:
#   A source directory, a destination directory.
#######################################
function copy_directory_nondestructively() {
  local SOURCE_DIR="$1"
  local DESTINTAION_DIR="$2"

  for file in $( (cd "${SOURCE_DIR}" && find . -type f) ); do
    local SOURCE_FILE="${SOURCE_DIR}/${file}"
    local DESTINATION_FILE="${DESTINTAION_DIR}/${file}"
    if ! cmp --silent "${SOURCE_FILE}" "${DESTINATION_FILE}"; then
      mkdir -p "$(dirname "${DESTINATION_FILE}")"
      cp -f "${SOURCE_FILE}" "${DESTINATION_FILE}"
    fi
  done
}

readonly PROTO_TMP_OUT_DIR="./protoc_tmp_out"
readonly PROTO_OUT_DIR="./protoc_out"

mkdir -p "${PROTO_TMP_OUT_DIR}"
mkdir -p "${PROTO_OUT_DIR}"

# Initially write the generated code to a temporary directory.
protoc \
    --js_out="import_style=commonjs,binary:${PROTO_TMP_OUT_DIR}" \
    ...

# Copy each generated file into the actual output directory, but do not
# overwrite identical files. 
copy_directory_nondestructively "${PROTO_TMP_OUT_DIR}" "${PROTO_OUT_DIR}"

# Finally delete the temporary protobuf directory.
rm -rf "${PROTO_TMP_OUT_DIR}"
```

This feature would add an extra step of processing the existing generated code and then comparing them.  This is inefficient, so enabling it by default is a no-go.  Making this an opt-in flag doesn't have any technical issues, but it does increase our maintenance burden just to support timestamp-based build systems (which have a number of problems like this).

If you can't migrate to a smarter build system that checks for real changes, I think creating a script similar to what @jul-sh posted would be a good solution.  Protobuf isn't the only library that can update timestamps without making any real changes, so if you set this up it'll likely help you more in the future (instead of having to continue to make this request of all your dependencies).

title: Protobuf message field order in generated classes in PHP is not sorted based on tags as compared to other languages.

nodes.body: I think this is not required. Any reason you need this feature?

Hey @TeBoring, In my company, we rely on Protobuf serializations to work consistently across all languages as we provide our services in different languages. This PHP inconsistency caused some subtle bugs in our PHP solutions, which we discovered recently. 
Our work around was to manually rearrange the fields in ascending order of their tags. We try to write proto files in this way now, but it gets difficult as we grow and remove/add new fields for some reason. It gets difficult for someone new to the technology as well.

I think you are depending on an undefined behavior of protobuf.
Protobuf's field can come in any order. And there will be other inconsistencies in serialization. e.g., each implementation may choose different hash function for map fields.
You will still meet similar problem in the future.
My suggestion is to not depending on protobuf to be encoded consistently.

title: ByteSizeLong() return 0

nodes.body: This behavior may be surprising if you're used to proto2 but it is the expected behavior for proto3. In proto3 there is no distinction between a field being unset and being set to its default value (i.e. 0 for integer fields), so a zero-valued field is not serialized. Since your message just contains zeros, there is nothing to serialize. Note that if you prefer the proto2 behavior you can stick with proto2 by putting `syntax = "proto2";` at the top of your file.

title: Use a reasonable standard for zlib in bazel
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 57b6597f467c2b614a458051f60ba467c5d697ae
Language: Bazel (0.24.1)

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/5389 added support for zlib and made it configurable with the `//external:zlib` label. Unfortunately, this requires all downstream users of protobuf+bazel to need to `bind()` a value for zlib, and given how core proto is, that's a lot of users.

I think there's work that we can do to give this a very reasonable default without requiring any configuration by users.

I think if the default condition [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/1c5e8cbb8fedafbb45f62d28d9d4ff2362168601/BUILD#L145) could be updated to include `@bazel_tools//third_party/zlib`, every regular user will get zlib and msvc users will continue without. We can add another value to the config so that users can specify a custom zlib if they choose to bring their own, bound to `//external:protobuf_zlib` or some other canonical name. (I'm just seeing https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/f313b9ccf7434e04d233ad2f519affc78a9e26a8#diff-7f9ad3c5854d19e307639e89857e646e now, so perhaps @nicmcd you have suggestions about a better way to achieve this. Maybe keep the `@zlib//:zlib` name)

I'm impartial to the solution, so if my suggestion doesn't make sense I'm definitely open to others. My main goal is to be able to depend on proto without any extra configuration that may already be available.

nodes.body:
I think the WORKSPACE style of Bazel forces users to know the dependencies of their dependencies. Without extensive Skylark hacking, in general a user of library A needs to know that library A depends on library B. The user should have library A and library B declared in their WORKSPACE file. I don't see why protobuf should be any different. Do you?

Instead of having zlib declared in the default Bazel configuration, I suggest just making an example bazel project with a BUILD and WORKSPACE file that shows that the user needs to have zilb in their WORKSPACE file.

If there was a necessary dependency that didn't have an alternative, I'd agree with you. But given that Bazel packages a zlib already, it seems reasonable to use it.

You could have the same argument with a build tool like a compiler. Bazel packages a few (`clang`, `javac`, etc). There's nothing stopping you from configuring a different platform, but these are sane defaults that most of the world wants. It would be a significant hurdle if every user had to define their own compiler just to start a new project.
Ok, that makes sense. My biased view is that if the user declares `@zlib//:zlib`, then protobuf should use it. If not, then use the default provided by bazel.

I don't know if there's a way to do that. Open to suggestions.

Is there any benefit of `@zlib//:zlib` over the `@bazel_tools` version? I don't actually know anything about it. Are there in general lots of different implementations that differ greatly? And do those affect proto?

title: Protobuf Python extension module is not ABI compatible with Stackless Python
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: any version, that uses the CPP extension module i.e. 3.7.1
Language: Stackless Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Not relevant

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Not relevant

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Install Stackless Python 3.7.3
2. install protobuf 3.7.1 wheel
   ```$ python -m pip install protobuf```
3. run the following python code (minimal example)
   ```
   from google.protobuf.pyext import _message
   def func():
       _message.Message._CheckCalledFromGeneratedFile()
   func()
   ```
**What did you expect to see**

TypeError: Descriptors should not be created directly, but only retrieved from their parent.

**What did you see instead?**

Segmentation fault (core dumped)

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

The segmentation fault is caused by the following line of code:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/6973c3a5041636c1d8dc5f7f6c8c1f3c15bc63d6/python/google/protobuf/pyext/descriptor.cc#L114

The problem is, that protobuf uses the structure PyFrameObject (`frame->f_code`) which is not part of the C-Python ABI and differs between C-Python and Stackless Python. See https://github.com/stackless-dev/stackless/wiki/Portable-usage-of-PyFrameObject for details.

Merging pull request #5171 would fix the problem.

Another option is compute the offset of the field `f_code` at runtime. Use the macro `PYFRAME_CODE(frame)`  from https://github.com/stackless-dev/stackless/wiki/Portable-usage-of-PyFrameObject.

**Work arounds**

1. Install the pure Python version of protobuf or
2. Compile protobuf using Stackless Python

title: [Java] DynamicMessage needs it's own equals strategy
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: Java

A DynamicMessage equals operator inherits its functionally from the AbstractMessage. The problem of the operator is that it checks the Descriptor on Object equality.

But the purpose of a DynamicMessage is that you can create messages from non-pre compiler descriptors. You can load a descriptor set from file and generate a DynamicMessage from it, but as those Descriptors are created at runtime you can have **semantically equal messages**, but have a _different descriptor reference_.

My proposal is that the DynamicMessage get's it own equal operator, very similar to the AbstractMessage one, but if the Descriptors are non-object-equal it will just check if the **full Message name** is equal and if it is, return **true**.

nodes.body: I'm willing to create a PR for this.

Thanks for filing this issue. I am working on a change to fix this. I think we need to go a little further, check if the full Message name is equal and all the fields + unknown fields are equal. Basically the same as AbstractMessage#equals() but loosening the check for descriptor identity.
Great, that was actually the exact same way I though doing it.

While doing this, I realized that Descriptors may want to have their own equals() method too. Then the question becomes what does it mean to have Descriptor equality. Just the full name (with the underlying proto potentially not being equal)? Or do we expect the full DescriptorProto to be equal (which is expensive as it requires going through all the transitive closure dependency).

For DynamicMessage equality I wouldn't go that far. Reasoning is that equality is **important on the values of the message**, but for the schema it's mostly the intent of defining the message of type "X".

I don't think we can proceed with the proposal as is. Throughout DynamicMessage, we have a lot of verifyContainingType() call, which check that the FieldDescriptor type is the same. If we proceed with this proposal and assert that DynamicMessageA and DynamicMessageA2 are equal because their fullname are equal, we can get into a weird state where you can call dynamicMessageA.getField(fieldDescriptorA) but not dynamicMessageA2.getField(fieldDescriptorA) - which will throw an IllegalArgumentException.

I guess a better way to work around this would be to ensure that we have some sort of mapping that automatically map A2 to A if they have the same name. This seems too risky to put at the core Protobuf level because A and A2 may actually refer to completely two different Descriptors even if they have the same name. It may be more easily solvable at the application level though.
Closing as infeasible :(
