title: using LD_PRELOAD with DSOs using protobuf causes error
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.6.1
Language: C++
OS: Ubuntu 16.04
Compiler: g++-6

I'm building an application with multiple DSOs sharing the same protobuf interface. One of them contains the compiled `.pb.cpp` files, but all of them requiring the `.pb.h`. 

When I link the final executable to all of these DSOs, all is working fine.
However, when I organize my code to preload (via LD_PRELOAD) one of the DSOs, 
I receive the error

```
[libprotobuf ERROR ../../src/google/protobuf/descriptor_database.cc:58] File already exists in database: Digitizer.proto
[libprotobuf FATAL ../../src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc:1401] CHECK failed: generated_database_->Add(encoded_file_descriptor, size): 
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'google::protobuf::FatalException'
  what():  CHECK failed: generated_database_->Add(encoded_file_descriptor, size): 
Aborted (core dumped)
```

It appears as if the loading of a DSO triggers some protobuf initialization, and protobuf isn't prepared to be initialized multiple times.
I found https://stackoverflow.com/questions/37051635/several-shared-object-using-same-proto-leading-the-the-error-file-already-exist which seems to describe the same issue, but `RTLD_GLOBAL` is of no use in my case.

nodes.body:
I find a lot of similar bug reports regarding the "File already exists" problem. However, most of them are closed without comment or "fixed" by using LITE_RUNTIME.

In this thread someone tried to fix this by allowing a duplicate to be added to the db:
https://bugs.debian.org/cgi-bin/bugreport.cgi?bug=721791

For our scenarios this would seem like a good solution...

I would like to understand why this functionality is designed the way it is. Is there any documentation or reference to an issue where this is discussed in detail?

Edit: found a bit more on this here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4126#issuecomment-357333891

Reponse by @xfxyjwf  https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1941#issuecomment-284582895 is unacceptable from upstream, here is an unavoidable example:

* In a python environment where multiple python ```.so``` modules **must** invoke libprotobuf.so library (as shared external), it can happen that ```imports``` (simultaneous) from a top level python (.py) will trigger the issue "already exists in database" and cannot be avoided.

title: Protoc generator for php missing type hint on message getters (yet setters have it)

nodes.body:
I don't think ```Foo[]``` should be added into return type.
We actually always return ```Google\Protobuf\Internal\RepeatedField``` which has similar api as array.

The code already does this for setters, but not for getters. It's an addition to the docblock line, not changing the true return type (which stays as RepeatedField). The PHP client is *extremely* unfriendly to use due to this omission, with IDEs being unable to help with autocompleting off of getters. Again, the setters have this already.

@TeBoring Can you please reread the issue to understand? It's about modifying the `@return` tag in the PHP doc block (`/** ... **/`, not changing the real return type. Again, the generator already does this for the setters... for some reason the getters (which are imo even more useful) were not given the same treatment.

The setter accept both php native array and our internal repeated field.
However, the getter only returns our internal repeated field. If we change
it to php native array, that would be a lie.
Does php have some interface like iterable? Probably we can change both
getter and setter to that.
@haberman, how do you think?

wrote:

I agree with @TeBoring's analysis. The getters are documented to accept `InnerMessage[]` because they do, in fact, accept a  real PHP array of `InnerMessage` instances. The getters are documented to return `RepeatedField` only, because that is the true type of the return value. `RepeatedField` is a type defined by the protobuf library. It behaves like a real PHP array in many ways, but it enforces that all elements are of a single type.

Ideally we could annotate the return type as something like `RepeatedField<InnerMessage>`. Or perhaps as `ArrayAccess<InnerMessage>`, since `RepeatedField` implements the `ArrayAccess` interface. Is such a thing possible?

If not, the question is whether is it acceptable and desirable to write `@return InnerMessage[]|\Google\Protobuf\Internal\RepeatedField` when the function will not actually ever return a PHP array. If writing both return types joined with `|` will solve the IDE problem, it seems harmless enough, as the true return type of `RepeatedField` is still in the list of types.

@bshaffer any thoughts here?
I couldn't agree more with @frickenate. Yes, it's kind of a lie, but that why we always return both with ```@return InnerMessage[]|\Google\Protobuf\Internal\RepeatedField```

I agree it's very important to add the return type of the iterated items, and t's ok to add the union return type for this cause (it's pretty clear what this means). In my testing (PHPStorm), I found the following worked as expected:

```php
    /**
     * @return InnerMessage[]|RepeatedField
     * @return RepeatedField|InnerMessage[]
     */
```

And the following did not work:

```php
    /**
     * @return RepeatedField[InnerMessage]
     * @return RepeatedField<InnerMessage>
     */
```

The first (`InnerMessage[]|RepeatedField`) is my recommended option because PHPStorm suggested the first when it autocompleted the docblock.

Sounds like we have consensus. I'll re-open the issue.

I'd be happy to accept a pull request for this.

Hi all,

I did a little digging here, and it seems as though [generics were supported by PHP storm](https://blog.jetbrains.com/phpstorm/2018/09/phpstorm-2018-3-eap-183-2635-12/) at one point in time while PSR-5 was more active.

As PSR-5 developed, [it looks as though generics support was dropped](https://github.com/phpDocumentor/fig-standards/commit/eb07c50881248dc7219de3f1ff3080362b6e8477#diff-9a10a11696dc38209c125ea9c57a565f) (at least for the time being, based on the verbiage). It looks to me this may be why PHP storm doesn't support generics today - however, [there appears to be an on-going case](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/WI-47158) to get the support back into the IDE (which is recently active).

If it seems like PHP storm may support generics soon, would we be open to using that syntax instead of union? It seems like a more accurate representation of the state of the code and can be supported in the interim with [a metadata file](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/phpstorm/ide-advanced-metadata.html). If the IDE doesn't add support, we can move back to using union instead. WDYT?

Adding generics would help static analysis tools and maybe PhpStorm in the future, but to me it's a bit weird to add tool/ide specific annotations in generated code. That may be my own bias as I didn't use PhpStorm for a long while.

Indeed, `@return RepeatedField<InnerMessage>` would be nice, but:

1. It's not part of the php documentor (phpdoc) standard.

2. PhpStorm will happily auto-complete the type when *defining* `RepeatedField<InnerMessage>`; ie. it doesn't consider the angle brackets an error, and even lets you click on `InnerMessage` to navigate to the class.

3. **However**, PhpStorm does **not** take it into account with code that uses the function/method documented to return that type. So a `foreach()` over such a getter does not offer auto-complete of anything from `InnerMessage`.

Regarding `.phpstorm.meta.php`:

1. Who is going to generate that? I'm not going to manually write those stubs for the hundreds of `Message` sub-classes we are already using.

2. It's PhpStorm-specific, and involves placing the same docblock `@return` statement that can just be added to the existing code generation. Why duplicate the work?

Whereas `RepeatedField|InnerMessage[]` is phpdoc standard, and as such is supported by IDEs other than PhpStorm as well (eg. Eclipse and even Netbeans). It's the only solution that works across the board today, and as I mentioned before is the standard idiomatic workaround.

Fair and reasonable points @pelletiermaxime and @frickenate. I shouldn't have so broadly assumed folks using an IDE nowadays would be on PHP Storm.

> Regarding .phpstorm.meta.php:

> Who is going to generate that? I'm not going to manually write those stubs for the hundreds of Message sub-classes we are already using.

I was thinking it could be scripted, but I haven't proof on concepted that out yet to determine how feasible it is.

>  It's the only solution that works across the board today, and as I mentioned before is the standard idiomatic workaround.

I understand we're between a rock and a hard place here, I'm just bothered by the return block not being truthful - for each case it may help folks there could also be cases where it misleads others. Would you be able to share some examples where this is considered an idiomatic workaround? I'd be open to learning a bit more on the subject.

- [Symfony Example](https://github.com/symfony/symfony/blob/v5.1.2/src/Symfony/Component/Routing/RouteCollection.php#L57)
- [Laravel Example](https://github.com/laravel/framework/blob/v7.20.0/src/Illuminate/Database/Eloquent/Builder.php#L514)
- [Yii2 Example](https://github.com/yiisoft/yii2/blob/master/framework/base/Model.php#L415)
Good data points, thanks. Alright I think I'm convinced this can be a reasonable path forward until (hopefully) generic support lands.

an idea could be to add the generic phpdoc using `@phpstan-return` or `@psalm-return` (keeping the less precise type in `@return`). AFAIK both psalm and phpstan will also attempt to read the annotation of the other tool and convert it to their own if they support the equivalent feature.
this way, tools supporting phpstan or psalm (which include phpstan and psalm of course, but also recent versions of PhpStorm and maybe other IDEs too) could benefit from the more precise types thanks to generics.
It looks like the consensus here is that this can be implemented, but it will not be a priority for the proto team. If you all would like this feature, we would be happy to review and merge a PR!

title: Ruby JSON output incorrectly formats int64/uint64/fixed64 as number
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version:3.7.1/master
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

OS X 10.14.5/Various Linxes

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

Ruby 2.6.0, Ruby 2.4.5

**What did you do?**

Called `to_json` on a message containing int64 fields

**What did you expect to see**

Expected to see int64/uint64/fixed64 serialized as decimal strings, as per spec: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json

**What did you see instead?**

Output was serialized as number

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

Earlier report for the deserialization: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3013
PHP seems to use same serializer, open issue: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5663

**Test case:**

#### `Gemfile`

```
source "https://rubygems.org"

gem "google-protobuf", "3.7.1"
gem "minitest"
```

#### `test.rb`

```
require 'minitest/autorun'
require 'google/protobuf'
require 'json'

class ProtoJSONTest < Minitest::Test
  pool = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.new
  pool.build do
    add_message "JSONTester" do
      optional :int64, :int64, 1
      optional :uint64, :uint64, 2
      optional :fixed64, :fixed64, 3
    end
  end

  JSONTester = pool.lookup("JSONTester").msgclass

  def test_int64_as_string
    jt = JSONTester.new(int64: 1234567890, uint64: 1234567890, fixed64: 1234567890)
    jm = JSON.parse(jt.to_json)

    refute_nil jm["int64"]
    assert_kind_of String, jm["int64"]

    refute_nil jm["uint64"]
    assert_kind_of String, jm["uint64"]

    refute_nil jm["fixed64"]
    assert_kind_of String, jm["fixed64"]
  end
end
```

#### Output:

```
$ bundle exec ruby test.rb 
Run options: --seed 34900

# Running:

F

Finished in 0.001602s, 624.2197 runs/s, 1248.4394 assertions/s.

  1) Failure:
ProtoJSONTest#test_int64_as_string [test.rb:22]:
Expected 1234567890 to be a kind of String, not Integer.

1 runs, 2 assertions, 1 failures, 0 errors, 0 skips
```

title: Reduce the code size of Java Lite
body:
Apologies if this is the wrong place, between [these](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4769#issuecomment-397702062) [two](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5961#issuecomment-481516065) issues, it's not clear 
where Java Lite issues belong

**What language does this apply to?**
proto3, Java, Java Lite

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

We've been using Java Nano since September 2015 with much success.  It
continues to generate the correct wiremodels to interoperate with our backend
service while minimizing the size of our Android runtime (and important thing
for Android development).

Unfortunately, Java Nano support appears to be discontinued starting in the [3.6](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/compare/b5fbb742af122b565925987e65c08957739976a7..449e532b087e43a45ca6d8eae640a6019e547aca#diff-96239ee297e0a92ac6ff96a6bc434ef0L340)
release.  While direction forward for the library as a whole makes sense, there
are concerns which are preventing us from shifting from Java Nano to Java Lite.
Primarily, the size of the code.


Taking a simplistic example:
```
message LocalizedStringSet {
  message LocalizedString {
    string locale = 1;  // IETF language tag (eg "en")
    string text = 2;
  }
  repeated LocalizedString strings = 2;
  string fallback = 1;
}
```

Using the 3.0.2 version to generate Java Nano vs Java Lite produces 271 (in
nano) vs 751 (in lite) Lines of Code after removing whitespace and comments
(obviously the java byte code is smaller).

We also use tools like Proguard to provide dead code elimination that further
reduce this difference (though with some of the calling patterns in the
generated Protos it's been difficult for us to be precise here).  However, it's
still a non-trivial difference and given our heavy adoption of protobuf we're
understandably hesitant to switch.


**Describe the solution you'd like**

Brief inspection of the class seems to indicate that a significant portion of
the size difference is due to the builder patterns adopted in Java Lite.  We
can probably do some work on our end to prevent their usage and eliminating
them, but it would be preferable if there was an option in the Java Lite plugin
to disable builder patterns.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Dead code elimination could also be made more reasonable, in which case we
could simply enforce no-builders in our linting rules.  Having used Proguard (
and tools like it) in the past they can be difficult to make sure that they
produce the expected result in non-trivial cases.  It would seem that modifying
Java Lite to not produce builders is a more simple, and more maintainable,
solution than attempting to redesign the code it generates to be more
accessible to a tool like Proguard.


**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

nodes.body:
There's an [new open sourced version of Java lite](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/lite.md), which doesn't have backwards compatibility with old Java lite. The new one can largely save the binary size after proguard.

If you would like to, you may give a try on that.
Unfortunately, new version of Java lite uses reflection (#6463), so it won't work well with Proguard/R8 now.

nodes.body: I think `if constexpr` only available after c++ 17, and it might not be fixed to that since we need to be compatible with c++ 11

While `if constexpr` is only available starting with C++17 and you may want to remain compatible with C++11, it would be good if this issue could be fixed.
Especially considering that this issue forces users of the library to either globally disable a useful warning or litter the code with 10+ lines of conditional warning disabling around **every inclusion** of problematic protobuf headers.

Preferably by conditionally marking things that can be `constexpr`, something along the lines of
```cpp
#if defined(__cpp_if_constexpr) && __cpp_if_constexpr >= 201606L
#define CEXPR constexpr
#else
#define CEXPR
#endif
```
then using `if CEXPR (sizeof(x) == sizeof(int))` rather than a simple if statement where appropriate.

Alternatively, warnings that you do not care to fix should be disabled in as tight a scope as possible (**without bleeding to the outside**), so that users of the library get to use/enable the warnings they would like to have, rather than the usable warnings being dictated by a third party library.

Your approach sounds like a good idea. If you would like to send a pull request, you could add a `PROTOBUF_IF_CONSTEXPR` macro to `src/google/protobuf_port_def.inc` where we already have similar macros that are defined based on whether compiler support is available for each feature (and undefine it in`port_undef.inc`--we do this to try to keep our macros leaking out into user code). Alternatively, it might be possible to accomplish this with SFINAE without using `if constexpr`.
This file has been removed at head in favor of Abseil's implementation.

title: [Ruby] Message hashes including non-oneof values
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Ruby

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

The Ruby Hash a Message object creates sometimes includes values for fields that are not applicable, specifically fields that are not set as part of the `oneof`.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

The Ruby Hash a Message object creates does not include any field that is set to the default value.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

The Ruby Hash a Message object creates excludes values for `oneof` fields that are not set.

**Additional context**

The Ruby Hash produced by `Message#to_h` sometimes contain fields of a `oneof` that are not currently set, or were reset to their default value. Currently, if a `oneof` value is changed from one field to another, the previous field (with it's default value) will be in the hash along with the new field (and the set value). This makes it difficult to recreate the Message object from the hash. Ideally, the Message should be able to round-trip to/from a Ruby Hash just as it can round-trip to/from a binary proto stream and to/from JSON.

The `ruby/tests/basic_proto2.rb` file has the following test:

```ruby
def test_to_h
  m = TestMessage.new(:optional_bool => true, :optional_double => -10.100001, :optional_string => 'foo', :repeated_string => ['bar1', 'bar2'])
  expected_result = {
    :optional_bool=>true,
    :optional_double=>-10.100001,
    :optional_string=>"foo",
    :repeated_string=>["bar1", "bar2"],
  }
  assert_equal expected_result, m.to_h

  m = OneofMessage.new(:a => "foo")
  expected_result = {:a => "foo"}
  assert_equal expected_result, m.to_h
end
```

This test can be updated with the following code to demonstrate the problematic behavior:

```ruby
# oneof is not set
m = OneofMessage.new
assert_equal "", m.a
assert_equal 0, m.b
assert_nil m.my_oneof
expected_result = {}
assert_equal expected_result, m.to_h

# oneof is updated to a
m.a = "foo"
assert_equal "foo", m.a
assert_equal 0, m.b
assert_equal :a, m.my_oneof
expected_result = {:a => "foo"}
assert_equal expected_result, m.to_h

# oneof is updated to b
m.b = 42
assert_equal "", m.a
assert_equal 42, m.b
assert_equal :b, m.my_oneof
expected_result = {:b => 42}
assert_equal expected_result, m.to_h # actual is {:a=>"", :b=>42}

# create new message object, using incorrect hash
m = OneofMessage.new({:a=>"foo", :b=>0})
assert_equal :a, m.my_oneof # actual is :b
expected_result = {:a => "foo"}
assert_equal expected_result, m.to_h # actual is {:a=>"foo", :b=>0}
```

Additionally, I think it might be a good idea if the Ruby Hash objects simply omitted any field that was set to it's default value. I believe that would correct this issue and the Ruby Hash would be more concise.

nodes.body: Ping.
We just hit this as well.

I agree this should be fixed. My only concern at this point is backward compatibility. There could be code depending on all of the fields being set.

There are two cases I think:
1. For fields with presence (fields in `oneof` and `optional` fields), I think the correct behavior is clearly to emit them only if they are present.
2. For fields without presence (repeated fields and proto3 fields without `optional`), it's less clear to me what the right answer is. We could omit them when they are empty or 0, but that seems more likely to potentially cause breakage.

I suppose we can start by at least fixing (1).

Specifically for the oneof case, we're being dinged by this because we're hitting a Go server. If you have (say) three possible `oneof` values, and you set the first one, Ruby will emit all three values (with the second and third being blank) and Go will read it in as blank. Essentially you can't use the Ruby types at all if you're talking to a Go server and you have a `oneof`.

Wait, how does this affect interop with Go? The issue described in this bug only affects `Message#to_h`, which converts a message into a Ruby `Hash` (data structure). AFAIK it does not affect serialization to any wire format (JSON or binary).

I can play around with it a bit more - we're using `gruf` to send the message and the message itself didn't work, only the hash did, and this bug stopped us from using it. (Sorry for the disjointed info - we were using the hash in one case for a while where there wasn't a \`oneof\`, and then got bitten by this when we tried it in a case where there was.) I'll collect a bit more info early next week.

Yep. Looks like the issue is with `gruf` - it only supports a hash, not a request object for some reason. [https://github.com/bigcommerce/gruf/blob/main/lib/gruf/client.rb#L158](https://github.com/bigcommerce/gruf/blob/main/lib/gruf/client.rb#L158) So either `gruf` is changed to support the direct request objects, or this bug is fixed in order for us to continue :frowning:

At long last, we are able to make a breaking change and fix this behavior: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/15234

One thing we never included in `to_h` output before is extensions. We should figure out what key extensions should use. Probably the most straightforward would be to use: `:"[pkg.ext]"`.

> Ideally, the Message should be able to round-trip to/from a Ruby Hash just as it can round-trip to/from a binary proto stream and to/from JSON.

If we are trying to preserve this invariant, we need to take this into account when deciding how extensions should be represented.

Two options come to mind:

1. Use `:"[pkg.ext]"` as the key for an extension, and accept this when constructing a proto.
2. Use the extension's field descriptor as the key for the extension, and accept this when constructing a proto.

title: protoc: code gen is different between using source files and using descriptor set

nodes.body: cc @pedgeio

I believe the issue is that `json_name` is always populated when it is returned from `--descriptor_set_out`, but when `protoc` calls one of it's builtin plugins internally, it doesn't populate `json_name` unless it is explicitly set (this comment hints at this: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc#L6024). While this seems minor, this is important - I should be able to do a roundtrip with `protoc`, ie generate directly using it, or generate from a pre-computed `FileDescriptorSet`, and have the same result. Possible fixes: - Always populate `json_name` for `FileDescriptorSets` passed to builtin plugins - this immediately fixes everything. - Remove `json_name` when passing `FileDescriptorSets` given with `--descriptor_set_in` before passing them to builtin plugins if the value of `json_name` is the same as the default computed value for `json_name` for that field - this also would fix the builtin plugin issue. As an example example, here's the diff between what is generated by an inputted `FileDescriptorSet` to `protoc`, and `protoc` directly, for `AdImageAsset.java` from https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/ads/googleads/v1/common/ad_asset.proto: ```diff 01c101 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 111c111 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 121c121 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 454c454 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 464c464 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 478c478 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 498c498 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 516c516 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 538c538 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 556c556 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 568c568 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; 583c583 < * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1[json_name = "asset"]; --- > * .google.protobuf.StringValue asset = 1; ```
cc @haon4 (let me know if you don't want cc's for maintainers on issues by the way, if so this will be the only time)

Just for clarification: note in the above example that @jhump provides, regardless of if there is any `json_name` explicitly set on a field or not, this will happen. Ie this https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/ads/googleads/v1/common/ad_asset.proto will produce a diff.
Proposed another fix in #5587 that I personally think is the best of these options

I think this issue's root cause is the same as #5587. 
Close this issue here as this is filed later.

title: Ruby JSON serialize enums as ints
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Ruby proto3

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
The proto3 docs says that a JSON implementation may provide an option to:
> Emit enum values as integers instead of strings: The name of an enum value is used by default in JSON output. An option may be provided to use the numeric value of the enum value instead.

Currently this isn't implemented by the Ruby library. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**

It makes sense to link against one library or the other but not both. Unless you're using `option optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME;` in every .proto file, you probably want to link against only `libprotobuf`.

Second, the windows api has it's own definition of min (in case you are using windows libs), so std::min fails. You have to temporarily change the definition of min (I think also max) whenever you include the protobuf header in your source.

N/A

N/A

nodes.body:
The [protobuf spec for services](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#services) mentions that the core libraries don't generate full impls, some languages generate stubs where you have to provide something for the concrete impl to provide the details.

We haven't bothered with the basic stubs for ObjC because that would require picking some interface for async nature of service requests that might not always match what other implementations would choose on their own (selectors and/or closures, how to model network errors as well the request results, etc.).  So instead the objc generator doesn't generate anything, leaving different service implementation to pick the model they feel is best for them.
Thanks! Makes sense.

title: Produce a complete spec for proto2 and proto3
body:
Last night, I read Ian Lance Taylor's [commentary](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/golang-nuts/6dKNSN0M_kg/EUzcym2FBAAJ) on Golang being Google's language, and it has a very poignant observation:

```
All successful languages have either a single
specification or a single primary implementation.  (Go and C++ are
examples of language based on a specification; Perl, at least before
Perl 6, is an example of a language based on an implementation).
These serve as the definition of what the language is: whatever the
specification says or whatever the implementation does.
```

I've been using various OSS Protobuf parsers for the better part of 18 months now, and this really hit home. Protobuf is an example of the latter, namely that `protoc` that serves as the definition of what the Protobuf language is. This is fine for most cases, but there is a lot of unlocked potential as to what can be built for Protobuf that is held back by this fact. The easiest example is for linters and formatters, but there are many more, and not just in the static analysis realm. The only way to be 100% certain you have a valid parsing of Protobuf is to shell out to `protoc --descriptor_set_out --include_imports --include_source_info ` and use the generated `FileDescriptorSet`, which in itself is unwieldy to use for such a purpose.

As illustrative examples, I've been working in Golang primarily for a while, and there are 10-20 Protobuf parsing libraries on GitHub that attempt to handle Protobuf parsing natively in Golang, however there are only two I've found that come close to actually handling the Protobuf spec.

The first library is [emicklei/proto](https://github.com/emicklei/proto). This is an attempt at doing a parse of Protobuf that does not deal with `FileDescriptorSets`, and is relatively easy to use for static analysis since it produces file:line:column information and parses comments. However, even given the extensive effort of the maintainer (Extensive with a capital "E"), it's not even close. First, `emicklei/proto` [doesn't purport](https://github.com/emicklei/proto/issues/14) to decide whether your files are valid Protobuf, it will produce a parsed result for files that aren't valid, for example missing semicolons. This means that for any actual use of it, you first need to verify that files are valid Protobuf using `protoc`. Second, due to all the various undocumented edge cases, especially around options, it took a [lot of work](https://github.com/emicklei/proto/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aclosed) to identify and fix many parsing failures. I used `emicklei/proto` to build [Prototool's](https://github.com/uber/prototool) linting and formatting functionality, and through Prototool's adoption, Prototool effectively became a massive integration test on `emicklei/proto`, which led us to finding a lot more issues. This trial-and-error method was the only practical way to find all the issues. While most have been found, to this day new things come up. For example, I ran `emicklei/proto` through a test yesterday outside of Prototool against [googleapis](https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis), and just recently a multi-line field declaration was added for the first time, which led to a [new issue](https://github.com/emicklei/proto/issues/111) being filed.

The second library, is [jhump/protoreflect's desc/protoparse package](https://godoc.org/github.com/jhump/protoreflect/desc/protoparse) by @jhump. Josh effectively attempted to [codify the Protobuf specification himself](https://github.com/jhump/protoreflect/blob/master/desc/protoparse/proto.y), I am in awe of how close this comes to `protoc`. `jhump/protoparse` does actually validate whether or not a Protobuf file is valid, and it also generates `FileDescriptorSets` - in fact, Josh wrote [goprotoc](https://github.com/jhump/goprotoc) as a `protoc` replacement in Golang, which comes tantalizingly close to matching `protoc`-generated `FileDescriptorSets` on a **byte-by-byte** level. I've been hitting `jhump/protoreflect` and `jhump/goprotoc` with a tiny-sized battering ram (relative to what we could have, see below) in [pedgeio/goprotoctest](https://github.com/pedgeio/goprotoctest), and it's getting awfully close - it already produces byte-equivalent `FileDescriptorSets` for every directory in `googleapis` when using `--include_imports`. However, through this testing, we still identified [some](https://github.com/jhump/protoreflect/issues/200) [issues](https://github.com/jhump/protoreflect/issues/201) that had to be fixed, and there are [some](https://github.com/jhump/protoreflect/issues/212) [outstanding](https://github.com/jhump/protoreflect/issues/214) [issues](https://github.com/jhump/goprotoc/issues/17) that Josh is working on.

I can't emphasize enough how impressed I've been with this library - I [codified every issue found in emicklei/proto within goprotoctest](https://github.com/pedgeio/goprotoctest/tree/master/internal/goprotoctest/testdata) and it passed with flying colors. However, even given Josh's gargantuan effort here, since there's no official Protobuf spec, we're left to doing trial-and-error against known Protobuf libraries, which doesn't instill a ton of confidence. While I think `goprotoc` is close to matching `protoc`, it's tough when this is the best that can be practically done.

Both of these serve to illustrate the issue with Protobuf being defined by an implementation and not a specification - if you want to do anything that doesn't use the implementation, you're out of luck. There is a [proto2 spec](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto2-spec) and [proto3 spec](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec) posted on developers.google.com, but the dirty secret is that neither of these are fully accurate, which is why developers like @emicklei and @jhump have to do such massive efforts to get this right. Of note, despite the fact that those specs are not accurate, there are a bunch of parsers relying on those specs (search "protobuf parser" on GitHub and look around if you are interested, or I can follow up with examples) that are being used right now.

This is holding the Protobuf community back - if you want to parse Protobuf files and do anything with them, your options are:

- Shell out to `protoc`, which is not great for many reasons, and only produces `FileDescriptorSets` which are not always the best representation for certain kinds of work.
- Build a library that comes close, but still requires trial-and-error, and is subject to small
  edge cases codified in `protoc`.

There are so many things that could be built with Protobuf if this wasn't the case.

**What I'm proposing:**

1. The Protobuf team produces a complete spec for both proto2 and proto3. [Josh's proto.y](https://github.com/jhump/protoreflect/blob/master/desc/protoparse/proto.y) is a decent place to start, although Golang-specific. As part of this, a downloadable EBNF file containing the grammar would be great (I am no compilers expert however, one of the things I regret not learning).
2. (The big one) Optimally, `protoc` uses this spec itself for parsing. The specification needs to be become the definition of the language, not the `protoc` implementation, and optimally this means that `protoc` uses it like any other library would. This is not 100% necessary and could have drawbacks, but given that Protobuf parsing is so quick as it is, it would be great.
3. (Less important but nice to have) Google maintains file-to-FileDescriptorSet libraries when possible - `protoc` already does this since that's the main function of `protoc`, but if a spec were available, having this in i.e. [google.golang.org/protobuf](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-go) should be much easier. This would help eliminate the slight differences in generated `FileDescriptorSets` in other languages.

This is a major task. Actually producing a spec is probably not the biggest issue - even with the options edge cases, this should not be a big blocker. However, moving `protoc` to this is a potentially internet-breaking change if there are bugs. Testing byte-equivalence of `FileDescriptorSets` for a couple repositores like [goprotoctest](https://github.com/pedgeio/goprotoctest) does wouldn't be enough, you'd want to do this integration testing across all of Google's internal Protobuf definitions. There's also the problem of the existing code people may be importing from [src/google/protobuf/compiler](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler) - unless you bump to 4.0 (which I do not think you want to do, I think this should be a backwards-compatible change), you need to keep that code around.

What I'd roughly propose:

- Create the actual specifications for proto2 and proto3.
- Write the replacement parsing library to go from Protobuf files to `FileDescriptorSets` in i.e. `src/google/protobuf/compiler2`, and put it's use behind a flag such as `--experimental_parsing` as part of a release.
- Verify byte-equivalence for `FileDescriptorSets` for every definition at Google you are allowed to get your hands on that will run `protoc --descriptor_set_out` and `protoc --descriptor_set_out --experimental parsing` for the matrix of `--include_imports` and `--include_source_info` on and off. How to do this would be the subject of a lot of debate, some proposals: a massive integration test against the internal monorepo, which will take forever, or rewrite internal Protobuf build rules to call `--descriper_set_out` and `--descriptor_set_out --experimental_parsing` across the `include_imports/include_source_info` matrix for any invocation of `protoc`. If you detect a difference, internally log the path to the files, and the diff. Run this for a few months. This second proposal might not go down very well, as you're going to be logging a lot of internal information you don't want to be, and it will slow down people's builds in theory, although minimally since `protoc` is so quick.

I know this is a big ask, but Protobuf has been getting a lot more adoption over the last few years, and for it to really go to the next level, we need a common agreed-upon spec to build tooling around. Look at Golang's static analysis tool growth as a great example of why this is so useful - a big part of why I like working in Golang is I have so much tooling I can rely on that was produced outside of Google. Beyond static analysis tools, this could eventually lead to a world where Protobuf code generators no longer need to be written as `protoc` plugins that take `FileDescriptorSets` as input, instead working directly from the Protobuf files themselves.

Let me know any thoughts here, this is just a proposal, easier said than done. I appreciate the time you took to read this if you've gotten this far :-)

nodes.body:
I wholeheartedly agree that a published official spec would be _hugely_ valuable to the community.

A spec should be a lot more than just the grammar. The grammar defines the syntax (and is currently available on the developer site, albeit old/wrong), but a spec should also be clear about semantics. Formal language specs usually interleave the two. The Go spec is a relatively simple one and I think a good example: https://golang.org/ref/spec. It is typical in that it describes the type system and other language constraints with prose. (While there are actually formal ways to describe semantics and type systems, but I don't think I've ever seen them used outside of a compilers course.)

The developers site has a lot of information on the semantics. But it would be nice if it were wound up with the syntax in a real language spec. Also, there are some places where documentation is quite light (especially around some of the more complicated aspects, such as how options are validated/interpreted).

I believe it is possible to produce a solid spec _without_ adding an experimental parser. The downside is that they can get out of sync (changes in the parser not properly reflected in the spec and vice versa). But, from what I understand, most significant compilers use hand-written parsers for (1) performance or (2) ability to construct more user-friendly error messages when syntax issues are encountered (or both).

As far as making sure a hand-written parser stays in sync w/ the published grammar, perhaps a fuzzer could handle that job. I'm thinking something that can examine the spec and from it produce all kinds of valid and invalid inputs. It could then feed those through the hand-written parser to make sure it accepts valid programs and rejects invalid ones, per the grammar. (I guess that could very well be a significant effort as well... TBH, I think most languages don't even try to have that sort of validation and instead use careful code review guidelines to make sure the two don't get out of sync...)

Yes, this is a very big ask indeed. It is a problem that we are aware of, and would like to address, but it is not something that we have bandwidth to prioritize at this moment. That said, we have created https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-grammar repo, and would love to get community contribution to it!

@haon4 good news , I also found that repo few days ago but it seems there  is nothing in it 
I'm interested in contributing on it ,  do you have any plan of milestone about that project ?

This as a community project defeats the purpose of creating a definitive grammar/spec that protocolbuffers/protobuf holds itself to - without that component, having a community-written spec is no improvement over the current situation from what I can see, and in fact could create even more fragmentation and confusion, just my two cents.

It's not so much a "community-written spec" that I see as an issue, but that there needs to be a formal statement that the spec is **the authority on correctness**, not the C++ `protoc` implementation, as has been the de-facto pseudo-standard.

In other words, once a spec is written, any divergence from the spec in an implementation should be a considered a bug and the implementation fixed rather than the spec (except for exceptional cases).

For example, in the early days of Go there were two implementations of Go, the original `gc` compiler and the `gccgo` compiler. Divergence in behavior were often deemed a bug and the spec was the authority on defining correct behavior. Sometimes `gc` had to change behavior, sometimes `gccgo` had to change. Rarely was the spec changed to suit either implementation.
I'd like to submit a PR to Google's hiring staff to merge @pedgeio onto the team to work on said spec!! 😄

To be honest, I highly doubt anyone within Google can come up with a spec and say that it correctly matches the `protoc` implementation either. What I am really looking for is this:

1. A draft specification of the protoc parser
2. A set conformance tests to ensure all parser implementations are based on the spec

Once (1) and (2) are done, and we have good confidence that they match what we want, then we can declare that the specification is finalized, and any divergence from the spec should be fixed. If we do need to update the spec in the future, we will need to come up with a process to notify all parser implementations, as well as providing new conformance tests to include the changes in the revision.

If you would like to contribute, please send PRs to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-grammar. We can help review them.

There's now a published spec for text format, which is also used in the `.proto` language for long-form custom option values.

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/text-format-spec

Ok so a couple of points.

1) Using a restriction `~> n` is a bad practice, and does not do anything. You should use `~> n.0`
2) You've just re-iterated what we've said. A small ruby upgrade (Say from 2.1 to 2.3 minimum e.t.c.), does not constitute a breaking change. The fact your plugin doesn't upgrade correctly, doesn't mean this is broken/faulty.
3) As I previously mentioned (Aside from RSpec), *all large* ruby gems will frequently bump their minimum ruby requirement as a minor (Which is what protobuf has done here).

Can you re-read my points and try to understand them. It sounds like your plugin is highly sensitive to protobuf so I would advise a `~> a.b.0` restriction in the gemspec, that way you're less likely to encounter issues.

Actually, ruby 2.3 support has been ended globally: https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2019/03/31/support-of-ruby-2-3-has-ended/

title: memory does not release by clear()

nodes.body: I believe this is actually the expected behavior. title: How do I declare a StringValue in JavaScript?
Proposal: C# RepeatedField.AsSpan() for more efficient access
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

c# protobuf 3

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Efficient lookups and assignments of RepeatedField<> (10s of millions )

It currently performs bounds and null checks inside an indexer method.  Indexing into a span is essentially the same as a ref return and the JIT compiler can optimize that even further to the point it is almost identical to operating on the array itself.  

I haven't yet benchmarked this proposal, but I expect it to perform similarly to ref returns, which are 1.25-10x faster than RepeatedField's current indexer method.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

```
public Span<T> AsSpan(int start, int length) {
    // Bounds check...

    return this.array.AsSpan(start, length);
}

```

Some might say this bypasses the null checks of the indexer method, but the C++ implementation allows you to memcpy entire memory chunks into RepeatedFields from what I understand.  While I feel a good library prevents the developer from using it incorrectly, I also feel it should be possible to squeeze extra performance out of a library if the developer accepts the risks.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Adding a preprocessor variable that exposes a ref readonly indexer to access the array directly, without bounds or null checks.  I saw a 1.25 - 10x speedup in reads and writes.  I don't like this because the developer can no longer simply use the copy of Nuget.  
- I'm using a fork of Protobuf now that exposes the array directly.  

**Additional context**

I'm serving up ~30MB messages that contain millions of integers in RepeatedField<>s.  I need to make it as fast and efficient as possible while still using Protobuf.


Code-wise it's a small addition.  I'm happy to submit a PR if the above looks ok.

nodes.body: One more point to bring up now: Returning a Span will allow the user to potentially write null values to the RepeatedField because it bypasses the null value check.  It's possible to write null values to RepeatedField in C++, too.  This gives such a great boost to performance (1-10x).  I think it is sufficient to add a note to the documentation that the user is responsible for null checks when using this method.
We have a .NET Standard 2.0 target for System.Memory. You should use that.
See the discussion here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/6538#issuecomment-630105124 - we'd need a better design for this than what was proposed in the PR.

 Publish main package to nuget.org and symbols package to symbolsource.org - this can be arrived by one command.

Version 3.6.1 was ok, newer versions (3.7.0 & 3.8.0) are a problem for companies, which take your packages and upload them to validated tools feeds. Then .pdb files will be automatically deleted and signature isn't valid anymore.

title: GPG Signing and Verification of GitHub Release Artifacts
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Any language.

**If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?**

Not applicable.

**If it's about generated code change, what programming language?**

Not applicable.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Ability to verify release artifacts retrieved from GitHub.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

An accompanying `*.asc` file for each platform's `protoc-*.zip` release artifact, containing the `.zip`'s GPG signature. The `*.asc` would be verifiable using `gpg --verify protoc-*.zip.asc protoc-*.zip`, as is commonly done with other projects.

Alternately, a single, intermediate, signed manifest file containing the SHA256 of all the published `protoc-*.zip` release artifacts.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Manually generating a SHA256 for each release, and embedding it wherever necessary (ie, in tools, or CI/CD pipelines). This is an imperfect solution as it is not published by the Protocol Buffers team, and requires manual updating for each release and for each platform variant.

**Additional context**

It would be helpful if the Protocol Buffers team signed release artifacts so future `protobuf` releases can be validated as originating from the Protocol Buffers team in an automated fashion. Other comparable projects published on GitHub make available signed manifests for published release artifacts as part of their release.

The primary use case is to automate downloading and verification of the `protoc` tool from within various continuous integration or deployment pipelines, or wherever verification is needed.

Specifically, the [Gunk](https://github.com/gunk/) team would like to validate the version of the `protoc` release the [`gunk`](https://github.com/gunk/gunk/) tool retrieves from GitHub.

nodes.body:
The AndroidX team would like this too.
It seems to me that in the time since this issue was opened, protobuf is publishing .asc files but that the keys used in those files aren't consistent across releases so it doesn't allow us to validate releases "as originating from the Protocol Buffers team in an automated fashion".

In particular:

```
$ gpg ./3.19.0/protobuf-bom-3.19.0.pom.asc 2>&1 | head -n 4 | tail -n 1
gpg:                using RSA key F1A51E051F527E0C8E24D54D4B1E11D5A4B91E89
$ gpg ./3.11.1/protobuf-bom-3.11.1.pom.asc 2>&1 | head -n 4 | tail -n 1
gpg:                using RSA key 3D11126EA77E4E07FBABB38614A84C976D265B25
```

Any updates here? Pretty much every new release of protobuf is signed with a new key, so far we've seen the following keys used:
- 0x187366a3ffe6bf8f94b9136a9987b20c8f6a3064
- 0x1dbb44e80f61493d6369b5fb95c15058a5eda4f1
- 0x22b79f456b06f4e75b8b579db57bd58ef6d0a713
- 0x3d11126ea77e4e07fbabb38614a84c976d265b25
- 0x4896f7312a5ace4d
- 0x696b6199a2a9d8c29ce78cc0d041cad2e452550f
- 0x95c15058a5eda4f1
- 0xa7764f502a938c99
- 0xae2b18e836c5f30687f37efdcc6346f2ce3872d9
- 0xb57bd58ef6d0a713
- 0xcc6346f2ce3872d9
- 0xd041cad2e452550f
- 0xd75e25b78ebb19e47c0a99bca7764f502a938c99
- 0xf1a51e051f527e0c8e24d54d4b1e11d5a4b91e89

And now when trying to upgrade to `3.21.9`, we just got a new key `f9acd39310b477b691f4e3f9971248996df82053`

This key rotation defeats the purpose of validation of this binary being from the same author as the previous binaries.

We finally got a certificate that we plan to sign our artifacts with, but we still need to put development time into properly using it. We are aiming to use that certificate to make more consistent signing in the next minor release (22.x). I'm sorry it's taken so long.

I'd just like to check - is this effort also tackling MacOS codesigning of binaries, or is it purely focused on GPG signing? 

I ask because #10880 was closed, but unless I'm missing something these look like distinct issues. GPG signatures alone would not be sufficient to satisfy MacOS that the _aarch_64_ (specifically) binaries are safe to execute.

Starting in 23.0 (and newer patches of 22.x), MacOS binaries will be signed! 

We decided to prioritize that work over GPG signing, but I will look into that next.

title: Unnecessary byte array heap allocation which causes GC issues with WriteFloat
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10
**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
MSBuild
**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Write many float values in a second

**What did you expect to see**
No significant GC 

**What did you see instead?**
over MB GC depending on number of float writing


**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

In Google.Protobuf code CodedOutputStream.cs, WriteFloat method uses `byte[] rawBytes = BitConverter.GetBytes(value);`. BitConverter.GetBytes generates a new byte array for every float value writing which will be GC after this method. This generates significant GC burden when a program tries to write a message which contains many float values. 

I forked protobuf and fixed it in our internal PR https://github.com/GravitySketch/protobuf/pull/1/files. Please review and let me know if this PR could be merged into google protobuf.

Thanks

Ke

title: The enumeration of Objective-C will be automatically hump-named！
body:
We use protobuf as the data encoding method for the App and BLE device communication protocol.
In an update, I created an enumeration with "BLE" in messages.proto, and then there was a problem that the communication content could not be resolved in Objective-C. The problem was found to be enumerated naming problem: there is an enumeration named "MKBLEFirmware", using `protoc --proto_path=. --objc_out=./oc messages.proto ` After conversion, the enumeration name becomes "MKBleFirmware".
PS: java does not have this problem, Objective-C class name does not appear this problem, only the Objective-C enumeration will be automatically hump-named.

nodes.body: That is by design.  The generation attempt to remap from the [style guide](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/style) to the Apple conventions to provide names more like what Apple developers will expect.

title: Migrate Ruby to use upb_msg in its C extension
body:
`upb_msg` is a new data structure in upb that provides a language-agnostic message representation.

Once it is ready in upb, we should migrate the Ruby implementation to use it. This will greatly simplify the code, and should also improve performance. Some profiles show GC using 80% of CPU when parsing large messages. In the upb_msg model, Ruby wrapper objects are only created when accessed.

title: Failure to add file descriptor on OSX
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.7.0
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

OSX

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

XCode 5.1

**What did you do?**

For our data driver to connect to and read data from Google BigQuery, we are building gRPC and the BigQuery Storage API into a library which serves as an entry-point for the driver. When we load the driver into iodbctest, the driver loads the library, which throws the below error.

![OSX_Fail](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/50157372/59312049-7b022d00-8c60-11e9-835c-73b9a766e995.png)

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

nodes.body: Drive by - Xcode 5.1 was ~ 2014.  If you are trying to use that and mixing it with things built with newer toolchains, there may be Apple ABI issues coming into play here.

Hi @thomasvl,

Both the data driver and the Storage API wrapper library are compiled and linked with XCode 5.1, and prior to this were running fine with iODBC Test 3.52.8. Is there a known issue with using 5.1 for building gRPC?

Thanks,

Part of the requirements for our drivers is that we support older toolchains like this, so we are locked into supporting 5.1 as a minimum version.

To clarify, this issue is not encountered in our Windows or Linux builds; this problem is only encountered during our OSX workflow.

EDIT: This is also before we explicitly call anything. The object which hosts the Storage API wrapper would not yet be initialized, and so there would be no object the driver creates which sends any sort of buffer.

It looks like there is a failure to parse the serialized descriptors because of invalid UTF-8 data in the `HttpRule.get` field, which must be a custom option somewhere. It would be good to figure out where that custom option is coming from. The simplest explanation is that the `.proto` file might just contain invalid UTF-8 in a custom option.

Hi all,

Apologies for the delay in response; Monday was a holiday.

Would this then be an issue with the BigQuery Storage API part of Google APIs? We aren't using protoc to generate the files in an unusual fashion, we're just using the Makefile included in https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis to generate the files, and then including the relevant BigQuery .h/.cc files in the build for the aforementioned wrapper library. We most recently pulled the repository on May 23rd, from which we generated the files.

Something that's still unclear is why this would be triggered before we actively call any of the Storage API code. Would we be able to pull anybody from the Storage API dev team in on this?

Thanks,
~Jon

I suspect it's not an issue with the Storage API per se but likely a problem with how the storage API protos are getting built or linked.  Generated protobuf messages ordinarily do some pre-main initialization to register themselves in the process-wide descriptor pool, though in this case I assume it's not all happening pre-main because if you're dynamically loading a dylib then it will happen at that time of dynamic loading. That would explain why the crash is occurring before you even call any Storage API code.

The error message is complaining about invalid UTF-8 data but I now suspect that this is a red herring. It seems unlikely that the storage API protos would contain any custom string options with invalid UTF-8, and if they did then that would also affect the Linux and Windows builds.

Instead I would guess that the problem has to do with the dynamic loading.  Within Google we don't really do any dynamic loading of protobuf generated code, so that is an area we don't have much experience with. Is it possible that you have some of the same proto messages represented in multiple dylibs, or the protobuf runtime linked into multiple dylibs? That could cause ODR violations which could potentially explain the crash. If it's at all possible to avoid the dynamic loading then that would also likely simplify things and solve the problem.

On the subject of the necessity of dynamic loading, I'm afraid it is required to dynamically link the wrapper library to the driver. There are conflicts between the gRPC BoringSSL and the OpenSSL we use in the driver, and the only way we were able to get around it was to build the driver and the library separately and link them dynamically. The protobuf runtime is statically linked to the wrapper dylib, and that's the only dylib that has the protobuf runtime linked to it.
OK, I see. Just to make sure I understand, is it correct that the driver dynamically loads the wrapper and the wrapper is a dylib consisting of gRPC + storage API + libprotobuf?

Yes, the wrapper links all of the grpc runtimes and libprotobuf, and the driver loads the wrapper dylib. just as a point of clarity, the Storage API code is compiled into the wrapper dylib, not linked.

Have you tried building gRPC without BoringSSL? I came across this [issue](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/11655#issuecomment-312075733) which seems to say that gRPC can build against OpenSSL. I'm not sure if this is the problem but it's possible that using both BoringSSL and OpenSSL together would cause ODR violations even if BoringSSL is in a separate dylib.

I'll admit that OSX development is similarly not something I've done in any great capacity, so I'm not sure what would make it violate ODR on OSX and not on other platforms. The idea behind the dynamic linking we've been doing was to isolate the symbols and make them accessible from their relevant libraries. The OpenSSL symbols linked to and defined in the driver should not be overridden by those in the wrapper dylib, since the BoringSSL symbols are linked to and defined in the wrapper and not the driver. Why would the BoringSSL symbols linked to an external library conflict with OpenSSL on OSX, but be just fine on Linux?

I think the crux of my confusion here is whether xcode treats ODR differently than gcc when linking. It seems odd that it would differ that severely.

The thing with ODR violations is that they are undefined behavior but aren't guaranteed to cause an observable problem. It could be that the ODR violations exist for all three platforms but only result in a noticeable issue for the OSX build. In principle I believe the dynamic loading could be used to prevent ODR violations but I think you would have to set things up carefully with a linker script so that all the BoringSSL symbols are hidden.

Still I think I would it be worthwhile to try using just OpenSSL and skipping the dynamic loading if that's at all possible because that would simplify everything. Since we almost never do dynamic loading of protobuf code within Google, that use case is not well tested and no one on the protobuf team is very familiar with how to do it properly.

Yes, I think I'll do that. I need to investigate how to specify a location for OpenSSL when building gRPC (we don't use the ones native to the system), and then I'll give it a rebuild on OSX and update this ticket with the results.

title: Debugging help - message_lite.h:108 FATAL CHECK
body:
I am running a C++ program using libprotobuf version 3.7.1, and getting the following FATAL error: 
```
[libprotobuf FATAL /usr/local/include/google/protobuf/message_lite.h:108] CHECK failed: (size) <= (static_cast<size_t>(0x7fffffff)):
```
This, unfortunately, only occurs once or twice a week on a system handling 200 - 2000 message per second.

Can anyone provide advice on how to go about debugging this issue?

Does this error indicate an issue with libprotobuf or is the problem likely an issue with a call into the library from my code?

nodes.body: Protobuf messages have to be less than 2 GB in size. It looks like you are occasionally hitting that limit with some message. To avoid that crash, I would recommend making sure to always call `ByteSizeLong()` instead of `ByteSize()` when you want to determine the serialized size of a message. `ByteSize()` crashes with that assertion because it returns a signed 32-bit int and therefore can't return a correct answer if the size is 2 GB or higher. `ByteSizeLong()` will always return the correct answer. You won't be able to serialize the message if it's 2 GB or higher, but you can at least check for that case and handle it without crashing if you call `ByteSizeLong()`.
Thanks @acozzette. I believe this is the help I needed.

title: Confusing documentation of Python Timestamp.{To|From}Datetime
body:
The [documentation for the Python implementation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated#timestamp) of the Timestamp well-known type mentions that the `ToDatetime()` and `FromDatetime()` methods convert to and from Python datetime objects. However, these functions handle time zones in a surprising way which you can only discover by source-diving. Since interpreting the result wrong causes a numeric error, these can easily slip through and cause trouble.

I propose adding after the example:

"The objects returned from `ToDatetime()` are naive datetime objects in the UTC timezone, like those returned by `datetime.utcnow()`. Likewise, if a naive datetime object is passed to `FromDatetime()`, it will be assumed to be in the UTC time zone."

Separately, we might consider adding an optional tzinfo argument to `Timestamp.ToDatetime()`, which if provided would return an aware timestamp.

nodes.body:
Separately discovered while examining this: The implementation of `Timestamp.GetCurrentTime()` is needlessly complex and expensive. A much faster (but entirely correct) implementation would be

```
def GetCurrentTime(self):
    self.FromSeconds(time.time())
```

This skips the surprising amount of processing and struct conversion and deconversion that using FromDatetime performs.

title: Python install_requires should not include setuptools
body: I believe that including a dependency on `setuptools` can cause installation problems in some cases. Since running `setup.py` already requires `setuptools`, `setuptools` must already be installed on the system, so I don't think there's much benefit in specifying that it must be installed. If the installation process for `protobuf` attempts to replace the already-installed version of `setuptools`, this could cause problems. This reasoning is discussed in https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/522

title: protoc: inconsistent name resolution behavior
body:
Consider the following proto file:
```proto
package foo.bar;
message M {    // declared as .foo.bar.M
    enum E {   // declared as .foo.bar.M.E
        M = 0; // declared as .foo.bar.M.M
    }
    optional M F1 = 1;
    extend M { optional string F2 = 2; }
    extensions 2 to 2;
}
```
There are two relative `M` references:
* `optional M ...`
* `extend M { ... }`

Both relative `M` references occur within the `.foo.bar.M` namespace.

Per the [C++ scoping rules](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/b7a5772caf08d62a20fd1bca258f501fa4db022c/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L186-L191), the following absolute names should be tried in the following order:
* `.foo.bar.M.M`
* `.foo.bar.M`
* `.foo.M`
* `.M`

In our situation, both `.foo.bar.M.M` and `.foo.bar.M` are legal declarations.

However, the way resolution is handled is odd:
* For the case of `optional M ...`,  it first finds `.foo.bar.M.M`, which is an enum value type. Since it's looking for an enum or message type, it ignore this. It continues on to then find `.foo.bar.M`. Since this is a message type, it returns that declaration.
* For the case of `extend M ...`, it first finds `.foo.bar.M.M`, which is an enum value type. Since it's looking for a message type, it throws an error complaining that it found the wrong type.

This is inconsistent. The relative name resolution logic should either:
* always ignore the declaration of the wrong type and keep searching
* always error when finding a declaration of the wrong type

What is the right behavior?

nodes.body:
"always error when finding a declaration of the wrong type" seems like the more desirable behavior. At the minimum, it would highlight that there are some confusing types there, instead of magically resolve to some random type.

If we make it to always error, how many things will break?
FWIW, method input and output names behave the same as extendee -- resolution of these names does not skip over non-type elements as is done for field types.
Same goes for extension name resolution, when resolving option names. Though there is no "ResolveMode" that would work for this (i.e. there is no "LOOKUP_EXTENSIONS" value).
This is sort of related to #9550. Different root cause and symptom, but also about inconsistent behavior when it comes to resolving names from different contexts.

nodes.body:
# My memo on how Kokoro job is setup

- [kokoro/linux/java_jdk7/presubmit.cfg](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/kokoro/linux/java_jdk7/presubmit.cfg) runs [protobuf/kokoro/linux/java_jdk7/build.sh](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/kokoro/linux/java_jdk7/build.sh).
- build.sh runs [kokoro/linux/build_and_run_docker.sh](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/kokoro/linux/build_and_run_docker.sh)
- build_and_run_docker.sh runs $DOCKER_RUN_SCRIPT, which is set to [kokoro/linux/pull_request_in_docker.sh](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/kokoro/linux/pull_request_in_docker.sh) in build.sh
- pull_request_in_docker.sh runs [tests.sh](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/master/tests.sh) with parameter $TEST_SET, which is set to "java_jdk7" in build.sh
- test.sh runs `mvn test` and etc.:

```
# --batch-mode supresses download progress output that spams the logs.
MVN="mvn --batch-mode"

build_java() {
  version=$1
  dir=java_$version
  # Java build needs `protoc`.
  internal_build_cpp
  cp -r java $dir
  cd $dir && $MVN clean && $MVN test
  cd ../..
}

# The conformance tests are hard-coded to work with the $ROOT/java directory.
# So this can't run in parallel with two different sets of tests.
build_java_with_conformance_tests() {
  # Java build needs `protoc`.
  internal_build_cpp
  cd java && $MVN test && $MVN install
  cd util && $MVN package assembly:single
  cd ../..
  cd conformance && make test_java && cd ..
}

build_java_jdk7() {
  use_java jdk7
  build_java_with_conformance_tests
}
build_java_oracle7() {
  use_java oracle7
  build_java oracle7
}
```
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f425b9f059a57dc5f13a6e6a389fff1a6cc06749/tests.sh

nodes.body:
Also, the current behavior goes against the grammar specification, which says that the token should be a `fieldName` which is equivalent to the `ident` token.

Related: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec#reserved
I think validating the reserved field names it a reasonable feature request.  For the related problems, I don't see any unambiguous solution there other than education/documentation.

> For the related problems, I don't see any unambiguous solution there other than education/documentation.

The parser could be updated to allow identifiers:
```protobuf
// unambiguous, omitting the comma is a syntax error
reserved foo, bar;
```
The existing support for string literals could remain, for backwards compatibility. (Though hopefully not forever?)

Given the way that reserved works for field numbers, using it this way with identifiers seems like a clean parallel structure.  It can even be implemented in a way that avoids modifying `descriptor.proto`. title: jsonpb: allow invalid enums to be unmarshalled to zero value int32

nodes.body:
For binary format, unknown enum can be kept using their original value.
However, for json, when it's unknown, we have no way to convert its name to its value. Thus, we cannot properly stored it in memory (memory storage is in favor of binary instead of json).
Your proposal to use default value for unknown enum has some semantic problem. For a round trip, the original sender may end up receive a different value from it sent.
I don't think we want this behavior.

@TeBoring I raised a similar issue in golang/protobuf. In my case, I used protobufs all over -- but need to convert to json for storage in ElasticSearch. When we add a new enum value, currently, we're required to rebuild and deploy all code that reads from ES -- even if they don't care about the new enum value. This seems like a similar situation that caused the existing 'discard unknown' option to be created.

While I agree that keeping the encoding round-trip-safe is an important consideration (and should remain the default), graceful degradation is also a useful attribute.

> For binary format, unknown enum can be kept using their original value. However, for json, when it's unknown, we have no way to convert its name to its value. Thus, we cannot properly stored it in memory (memory storage is in favor of binary instead of json). Your proposal to use default value for unknown enum has some semantic problem. For a round trip, the original sender may end up receive a different value from it sent. I don't think we want this behavior.

We have a problem that protojson does not guarantee the same compatibility as protobuf binary format. I don't know if it should, but this causes a lot of pain.

The original issue causes the nightmare of having to update all clients that consume API when the producer added new Enum value, even if consumers never use the enum.

Any recommended workarounds?

title: protoc: invalid span in source location

nodes.body:
This only happens with `syntax = "proto3"` files, for optional fields. It is trying to emit a source location for the _label_, which is not present (and not allowed for non-repeated fields in proto3).

Since there is no actual label in the source, it attributes the start location to be the start of the field and the end location to be the end of the previous element. The end location calculation incorrectly assumes that the last source location generated would have been the label.
