title: protoc: inconsistent source locations emitted for options
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.5.1
Language: N/A (descriptor output of `protoc`)

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux and OS X

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
N/A

**What did you do?**
Compiled the following to a descriptor w/ source info:

```proto
// p.proto
option go_package = "foo";

message M {
  repeated int32 f = 1 [packed = true];
}
```

Command:
```sh
protoc --include_source_info p.proto -o p.protoset
```

**What did you expect to see/What did you see instead?**

The source locations in the resulting descriptor include a path indicating the file's `options` field: `[8]`. This is _in addition_ to the path for the actual specific option: `[8,11]`. This makes sense per the doc on the `SourceCodeInfo.location` field in `descriptor.proto`: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L759

However, the field option is given no such treatment. It does **not** include a path for the field's `options` field, which would be `[4,0,2,0,8]`. It _does_ of course include the path to the specific option: `[4,0,2,0,8,2]`. This is surprising, not only based on the doc comment linked above, but also because it is inconsistent with the treatment of file options.

(Note that v3.5.1 actually shows all options as uninterpreted options in source info, but I know that is already fixed in newer versions by #4342.)

nodes.body: @jhump Thanks for the bug report. Feel free to send me a pull request if you have a fix.

I think I may have been wrong on this one. I think I misinterpreted some output I was looking at.

It looks like `protoc` intentionally does not emit separate locations for each field option, all with a path that references the `options` field. It instead emits only one for that path, and its span corresponds to all options, from `[` to `]`. So I was expecting it to look like file options, but it doesn't because fields use a compact syntax for defining options.

I'll test a little more and make sure the output makes sense. I'd expect it to have this behavior for enum value and extension range options, too. Whereas all other options (file, message, enum, one of, and service) _can_ be spread around, so should be treated like file options.

title: AttributeError: 'Timestamp' object has no attribute 'seconds' (well_known_types.py, introduced v3.9.0)
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.9.0
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Mac 10.14.5

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

Python 3.7.4

**What did you do?**

This code worked as of protobuf v3.8.0:

```
from datetime import datetime
from google.protobuf.internal.well_known_types import Timestamp

# Datetime str formatter used by google proto Timestamp library
DATETIME_FMT = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%fZ"

def to_protobuf_timestamp_str(date):
    # The Timestamp does specialized padding on the microseconds when
    # serializeing to strings, so use it in order to match test values
    timestamp = Timestamp()
    timestamp.FromJsonString(date.strftime(DATETIME_FMT))
    return timestamp.ToJsonString()

print(to_protobuf_timestamp_str(datetime.now()))
```

**What did you expect to see**

Printed timestamp, ex: `2019-07-17T09:56:56.601774Z`

**What did you see instead?**

```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "<stdin>", line 5, in to_protobuf_timestamp_str
  File "/Users/.../.local/share/virtualenvs/..../lib/python3.7/site-packages/google/protobuf/internal/well_known_types.py", line 190, in FromJsonString
    self.seconds = int(seconds)
AttributeError: 'Timestamp' object has no attribute 'seconds'
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

* After doing some digging it seems like this problem was caused by the introduction for the `__slots__` attribute (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/a1c886834425abb64a966231dd2c9dd84fb289b3#diff-79a29d050e84ff410293a63e1a1551d6R105)
* It seems like I can fix our above code by changing 
  * `from google.protobuf.internal.well_known_types import Timestamp` 
  * to `from google.protobuf.timestamp_pb2 import Timestamp`
* Arguably this is a bug in our code, **however I believe the protobuf bug here is the fact its not at all clear the classes in `well_known_types.py` are actually mixins**, this code worked before and no longer does now, and its not clear what the right thing to do is.
* At a minimum, I suggest: 
  1. Adding comments to these classes to indicate they are mixins and should not be used directly. 
  2. Even better (but possibly more disruptive) would be to explicitly add `Mixin` to their names (eg: `TimestampMixin`) to avoid confusion. Having the mixin classes named exactly the same as the message classes is super confusing.

For those that are curious, it looks like this is the code which does the mixing in: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/744e799bdaad748a6069a1f3fe8a25c708317c25/python/google/protobuf/internal/python_message.py#L144-L150

nodes.body:
Hi Dan, all classes under internal does not intend to be used directly. Users should not import any module under google.protobuf.internal

We have documented how to use the  well known types:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated#wkt

@anandolee Feels like adding these comments is an extremely simple way to help others avoid the pain I went through after updating to the most recent protobuf version. Due to the way python imports work, it was not clear from reading our code which broke we were importing the "wrong" thing. I find it unexpected and not user friendly that a library would have identically named classes and not highlight the fact one is not intended to be used directly.

This problem, and my confusion, was exacerbated by the fact protobuf classes are generated dynamically (an unused pattern in our internal codebases, and a generally uncommon pattern in many popular python libraries). Its entirely unclear when looking at timestamp_pb2.py that additional methods get mixed into the class (particularly when this capability is explicitly unavailable for user generated messages).

title: add SetStringByArray(..., const char *, size_t) method in Reflection
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
cxx and other binding languages such as python's cpp_implenentation

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
the Reflection class in message.h only has `SetString(..., const std::string &value)`interface. in some cases, we just have raw buffer (char * and size), to call the SetString method, we have to construct/memcpy/deconstruct a std::string. But in some time-sensitive case, this consumes much, especially when the the bytes is large enough (eg. 8MB), which will cause large amount of page-faults.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add `SetStringByArray(..., const char *, size_t )` interface, and call it when necessorily.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
even in protobuf, construct 8MB bytes(std::string) will cause large amount of page-fault, this will slow down much. is it possible to setup an allocator for the protobuf. I did not seen such method. 

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

nodes.body: Unfortunately I don't think there's any easy way to do this. Internally messages store `string` and `bytes` fields as `std::string`, so ultimately we have to construct a real `std::string`. However, we could potentially add an overload that takes a `std::string&&` and then we could at least move the string into place without creating another copy.
If the string is passed by value or by rvalue reference then we can eliminate one of the two copies. The user can create the string and then it can be moved directly into place.

Adding an overloaded `SetString(..., std::string&& value)` which utilizes move semantics will avoid using the copy constructor and the std::string object will be moved, not copied which is less costly and will improve performance significantly
copy that. when will this feature be added to the master?
I'm afraid I don't have time to work on it, but if you want to try implementing it yourself then feel free to send me a pull request.

solution:
1. change the Reflection's  prototype from `SetString(..., const std::string&)`   to `SetString(..., std::string)`. 
2. if the caller do not use the created `std::string s` any more , using `SetString(..., std::move(s))`
3. if the caller would like to keep the created `std::string s`, using `SetString(..., s)`
4. in the `SetString`, becuase we get the moved or copied string, we just move it forward

nodes.body: We meet the same problem. Is there any plan to support custom factory?

Does the trick from https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/6401#issuecomment-659395435 really work?
The `_parser` field is readonly as far as I can tell.  Also it's not immediatelly clear that the `static` intitializer beats the generated `_parser` assignment.
If so, I think the trick works, but feels a bit hacky as you're forcibly overwriting a field that intentionally private.

On the other hand, being able to support pooling for messages sounds interesting, if done right.
The problems I see
- you have no easy way to return rented messages to the pool (e.g. there is not Dispose() or Return() method)
- I think a big portion of allocations actually comes from allocating fields like string, ByteString, RepeatedFields, Maps etc., where you can't simply avoid the allocations (and if the pooling only works in very special cases, it's less useful).
CC @JamesNK  as this sounds like an interesting idea. It's a long haul but maybe this could be the start of being able to do high-performance allocation-free gRPC services.

For pooling to be generally useful there needs to be a way to return a hierarchy of messages, and reset all the message properties while you're at it.

I agree with @jtattermusch. I'm not sure how useful it would be. The overhead of renting/resetting/returning a hierarchy of messages is probably more work than GCing them. And usually messages are relatively small compared to the bigger string and byte array allocations.

* I like making CreateTemplate public. With that method being public you can create messages without reflection. I had to use `Activator.CreateInstance` in some [places where I needed to create messages](https://github.com/aspnet/AspLabs/blob/4ca17d158dbd4457b3bbb5744dafa68070963c7b/src/GrpcHttpApi/src/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.HttpApi/UnaryServerCallHandler.cs#L143).
* Is there noticeable perf overhead of using CreateTemplate vs the ctor?
@ ManuelKugelmann Nice work. But I wonder if it's better to provide a way to modify ```_parser``` of all generated messages once for all?

> @JamesNK @jtattermusch
> 
> I have a mostly GC free protobuf running - and as you said, I had to generate/add additional code for instance cleanup and returning them to the pool.
> 
> In my setup I got a large message (full scene desctiption via OpenSimulationInterface) every frame - the messages contain very many nested message fields (e.g. positions vectors). GC was not happy - pooling was definitely faster and produced no GC spikes.

> 
> CreateTemplate was already used in RepeatedFields - I do not believe that it is an performance issue.

It's always best to check - we have a pretty good set of microbenchmarks now, so it would be good if you could run the before and after state and double checked your assertions (please post the results you got on the PR).

> 
> I'll look into cleaning up my Pooling code and posting it here for discussion. An upside to the pooling is, that you get to keep the wrapper objects for e.g. RepeatedFields, Maps, etc...
> 
> @owt5008137 I had the code to replace the parser generated along with the instance cleanup code :)

title: How _should_ source code info look for `default` and `json_name` pseudo-options?
body:
It isn't well-specified exactly how options should look in the source code info for a file.

Prior to #4342, `protoc` emitted fully-structured source code info that mapped back to the AST for uninterpreted options. But interpreted options won't have `path` info that maps to the full AST. In that pull request, it was decided to just emit a single location for the option whose span encompasses the entire option declaration.

However, I've recently discovered that the two pseudo-options for `FieldDescriptorProto` -- `default` and `json_name` -- do not behave this way. Even worse, they are not consistent _with one another_:
* The source code info for `default` emits a span that only encompasses the _actual value_ and omits the `default = ` tokens.
* The source code info for `json_name` emits _two_ locations. The first span encompasses the entire option declaration (including the `json_name = ` tokens). The second span includes only the value.
This is particularly confusing since, for fields, all three of these use the same syntax. So, ideally, they would all be handled consistently.

I'm personally partial to the way options are handled, since I think this best attributes to the path to the span in source code that most logically represents that path. I also believe that would be a trivial patch. And, just from perusing `descriptor.proto`'s doc comments for source code info (which admittedly aren't at all specific for cases like this), I'd sort of guess that this is how it would behave.

However, I can see value in having span information that is only for the value. So I can kind of see why `json_name` is handled the way it is; I just think it's confusing to have two locations with the same path where one span is a sub-span of the other.

I'm happy to contribute a patch to make these consistent. I'd just like some input on what is the _right_ way they should be handled.

nodes.body:
> I'm personally partial to the way options are handled, since I think this best attributes to the path to the span in source code that most logically represents that path.

Sorry, don't understand. Which do you prefer? interpreted option? uninterpreted option?

Also, can you point to me to the context where spanning the whole scope for interpreted option was decided?

> Sorry, don't understand. Which do you prefer? interpreted option? uninterpreted option?

@TeBoring , interpreted options. (Uninterpreted options are nice due to the additional AST and location information, but they are not that helpful since they are referring to elements of the descriptor -- e.g. the 999 uninterpreted option tag -- that are not actually present since the act of interpreting options removes them from the descriptor and replaces them with interpreted option data.)

> Also, can you point to me to the context where spanning the whole scope for interpreted option was decided?

I guess it wasn't really explicit. When I filed the bug and then made the patch, I didn't realize that `default` and `json_name` were handled differently. The only context I can provide is my bug report (#3819) and my patch (#4342).

A downside to only referencing the value, vs. the whole declaration, is that leading and trailing comments are more likely to be for the whole declaration, _not_ just around the value. So I think it's better fidelity and more intuitive to interpret that way, rather than having a span that points only to the value but then comment information that corresponds to more than that (e.g. comments before the `option opt_name =` tokens and those after the `;` token).

> A downside to only referencing the value, vs. the whole declaration, is that leading and trailing comments are more likely to be for the whole declaration, not just around the value. So I think it's better fidelity and more intuitive to interpret that way, rather than having a span that points only to the value but then comment information that corresponds to more than that (e.g. comments before the option opt_name = tokens and those after the ; token).

But you are talking about interpreted options. Those options are usually well defined in our descriptor.proto. I think comments for those options are more for the value.

title: ios  export. M file contains import "XXX /A.h"
body:
Export objc file, export. M file contains import "XXX /A.h", how to deal with?
For example, the two files a.bobjc.h and a.bobjc.m are exported, and within a.bobjc.m there is the import "XXX/ a.bobjc.h"

nodes.body: I'm sorry, I'm not really clear what the issue is.  Can you provide some example `.proto` files that show the issue when generated (and the command line used to generate)?

hi,  @thomasvl How should ios parse data dynamically? For example, if you have an A.proto export file that is A.pbobjc.h and A.pbobjc.m, how can you dynamically know that the pbdata returned by the server is the corresponding data in this A.proto?
pod 'Protobuf', '~> 3.7.0'
What I want to do is get the pbdata returned by the server to which file this pbdata belongs (for example, A.pbobjc.h)?    through the code logic.

The protobuf binary format doesn't actually capture any type information, so you need to know the types of the messages you are receiving from the server to know what specific message type to parse them as.

Protobuf instead defers this sorta information to what ever higher level protocol you are using to send the messages.  gRPC, etc. take case of that layer/wrapping.  But at the raw message later (network or file), it isn't captured.

hi, @thomasvl 
Excuse me, the key with "**_**"(The underline) is defined for key-value, but the property in pbobjc.h you generated is deleted from "**_**"(The underline). For example, if we define a key to be "content_name" and your pbobjc.h file is "contentName", how do we get the value corresponding to "content_name" instead of "contentName"?

And if value is an array, you'll automatically concatenate array after key in.pbobjc.h, for example, if we define an array to be items, you'll automatically concatenate it to itemsArray.
I'm looking at the documentation for you to improve readability,
How can I get an array value from items instead of itemsArray?

I mean not by manually removing the "Array" string from our oc code.

The objc generated attempt to transform the names from the [protobuf styleguide](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/style) into Apple's naming guidelines for ObjC.

So the underscores are removed and things are CamelCased afterwards to create the property names.

As for repeated fields, the older styleguide didn't call for plurals, it recommended singular form; so _Array_ was appended to make it more clear that it was a array of things and not a single item.  The behavior can't be changed because it would change the code generation and break developers existing code; so _Array_ is still appended.

Only the generated ObjC names are changed, this has no impact on the binary format for protobufs.  ObjC fully interoperates just fine with other protobuf implementations.

title: Why the `scratch` argument is here?

nodes.body: In Google's internal version of the codebase we have a couple other ways of storing the string data that we haven't gotten around to open sourcing yet. We can't return those other string formats directly, so we store them in the scratch string and return a reference to that. Sorry about the confusion around this. title: Wrong warning when top-level module name is used in ruby_package option
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.8.0
Language: Ruby

```console
$ protoc --version
libprotoc 3.8.0
```

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
MacOS Mojave 10.14.5

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

```console
$ ruby --version
ruby 2.6.2p47 (2019-03-13 revision 67232) [x86_64-darwin18]
```

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Write a proto file `messages.proto` with `option ruby_package = "MessagesPb";` as below.

```proto
syntax = "proto3";
package my_company.messages;

option ruby_package = "MessagesPb";

message Message {
  string text = 1;
}
```

2. Run `protoc -I./ --ruby_out=./ messages.proto`.

```console
$ protoc -I./ --ruby_out=./ messages.proto
[libprotobuf WARNING ../../src/google/protobuf/compiler/ruby/ruby_generator.cc:417] ruby_package option should be in the form of: 'A::B::C' and not 'A.B.C'
```

3. Then, You will see a warning message `[libprotobuf WARNING ../../src/google/protobuf/compiler/ruby/ruby_generator.cc:417] ruby_package option should be in the form of: 'A::B::C' and not 'A.B.C'` as above.

**What did you expect to see**
Since `MessagesPb` is a valid module name in Ruby, `protoc` should not output warning messages.

**What did you see instead?**
I saw a warning message such as `[libprotobuf WARNING ../../src/google/protobuf/compiler/ruby/ruby_generator.cc:417] ruby_package option should be in the form of: 'A::B::C' and not 'A.B.C'` .

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
This behavior was not seen when I used `protoc v3.7.1`.

```console
$ protoc --version
libprotoc 3.7.1
$ protoc -I./ --ruby_out=./ messages.proto  # No warning
```

I think this behavior was added in [Fix Ruby module name generation when the ruby_package option is used (again) #5794](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/5794).

In ruby_generator.cc, the presence of `::` is checked. This is an invalid behavior, because the top-level module name does not contain `::` in Ruby.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/09745575a923640154bcf307fba8aedff47f240a/src/google/protobuf/compiler/ruby/ruby_generator.cc#L410-L419

nodes.body: This was fixed in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7276.

title: compiling libprotobuf.so with different name to avoid name collison with protobuf2
body:
In my system I have protobuf2 already built, which is named as libprotobuf.so file. While compiling the latest one (version 3.6), it is also generating the libprotobuf.so file and I wanted to use both the old one and the new one. So while compiling the new library I wanted to have the SO file named as libprotobuf3.so. What setting should I change in configure.ac to get libprotobuf3.so (instead of libprotobuf.so)?

Thank you,
Venkata

nodes.body: Unfortunately that will not work. Linking against two copies of libprotobuf.so will result in ODR (one-definition rule) violations and cause problems. Instead I would recommend rebuilding your .proto files with protoc 3.6 and then linking against libprotobuf 3.6 only. For C++ we require the protoc version to match the libprotobuf version.
But I see that there are no symbol collisons in libprotobuf.so file built with protobuf 2 and protobuf 3. So we can compile a binary with both libraries. right?
I would expect there to be symbol collisions for sure. When we bumped the version to 3.0 we didn't make any effort to rename symbols. Why do you want to link against two versions anyway?

I have one question Adam. 
1. If we have messages which are encoded with protobuf2 (libprotobuf.so), and if we try to use protobuf3 in decoder, does it work?
2. Similarly if we encode with protobuf3 and if we decode with protobuf2 in decoder does it work?

There are two completely separate things here: the protobuf version (e.g. 3.6) and the syntax line in the .proto file (i.e. `syntax = "proto2"` or `syntax = "proto3"`. Upgrading to newer protobuf versions is completely safe and wire-compatible and is a good idea because it will include new features, bug fixes, etc. Changing the `syntax` line is more complicated and I wouldn't recommend doing it if you don't need to.

Hi Adam,

you are saying protobuf3 is wire-compatible. Is it both forward and backward compatible? (If we encode in protobuf3, can we decode with protobuf2 libprotobuf.so files)?

Thanks
Venkata

When you upgrade your protobuf version, everything is forward and backward compatible. But don't change from `syntax = "proto2"` to `syntax = "proto3"` unless you know what you're doing, because that is not entirely compatible.

title: Add C# option to generate constructor for messages

nodes.body: Yes but maintaining these constructors will be a pain. Specially if you have a lot of messages.

@pnarimani same here, but proto3 made all fields optional. 

How can you generate a constructor when you can't know which fields are required?
I'm going to close this issue - we have no intention of doing this. Object initializers work well, and generating a constructor would make the code brittle in a number of ways.

title: [C++] MessageToJsonString discards the fields containing 0th enum element in proto3, works fine in proto2..

nodes.body: This is actually the intended behavior. In proto3 there is no distinction between a field being set to its default value (i.e. 0 in this case) and not being set at all. An enum field set to 0 is the same thing as an unset enum field. If you do want to print out zero-valued fields, you can set `always_print_primitive_fields` [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d1eeb852fcbe46b29a3bc47001e997d79358d9f8/src/google/protobuf/util/json_util.h#L75).

title: RuntimeException in MessageSchema on Android with Proguard
body:
Version: v3.9.0
Language: Java/Android
Protoc gradle plugin 0.8.10 for java with option "lite"

When running an proguard obfuscated android app a Runtime Exception is thrown when trying to build a Proto with it's Builder.

```
java.lang.RuntimeException: Field fieldName_ for xxx.yyy.z.b$d not found. Known fields are [private java.lang.String xxx.yyy.z.b$d.h, ...]
        at com.google.e.ck.a(MessageSchema.java:608)
        at com.google.e.ck.a(MessageSchema.java:502)
        at com.google.e.ck.a(MessageSchema.java:221)
        at com.google.e.bz.a(ManifestSchemaFactory.java:85)
        at com.google.e.bz.a(ManifestSchemaFactory.java:71)
        at com.google.e.dc.a(Protobuf.java:93)
        at com.google.e.dc.c(Protobuf.java:107)
        at com.google.e.bh.M(GeneratedMessageLite.java:170)
        at com.google.e.bh$a.ab(GeneratedMessageLite.java:386)
        at com.google.e.bh$a.ac(GeneratedMessageLite.java:394)
        at xxx.yyy.a(XXX)
```
It seems than since 3.8.0 the new Javalite runtime uses reflection for the Schemas. I thought the lite should NOT be using any reflection at all.

nodes.body: Any updates on this? Is this a bug? going forward is javalite runtime always going to use reflection and not work with proguard/r8?

Is there any workaround for this?
I use proguard in my project and I get the same error message. I know this happens because of accessing fields via reflection with hardcoded variable names but shouldn't it possible to tell proguard to just ignore these generated classes? I've already tried many things now in the _proguatd-rules_ files but I'm not able to get it work. Maybe anyone could point me in the right direction?

---

Edit: adding the following line to your _proguard-rules_ file helps to get rid of the error but keep in mind that your protobuf messages will then not be processed by proguard at all.

`-keep class * extends com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageLite { *; }`
I've added a proguard config [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/lite/proguard.pgcfg) as a workaround. Please let me know if it doesn't solve the problem.
Using a proguard exception is a workaround AT MOST, but definitely not a solution! I still think reflection should not be used in lite variant at all.
I think this was needed to remove unused fields from a message. @donaldchai could you please add more context?

MessageSchema is used to avoid generating hashCode/equals/(de)serialization methods since a small schema would be more compact.  Reflection is used to initialize the internal schema data structures the first time.

Removal of unused fields is not directly related.

There is a way: Library should include pro guard rules in `META-INF/proguard` in their jar. It has been used by other open source libraries for years already.

Seems the generator we're using is outputting code which is not designed to be obfuscated, so unless you're up for writing your own generator, disabling obfuscation with proguard rules is the only alternative.

We are having the same issue. The only solution we currently have is using the following rule in ProGuard which seems to work as expected. I believe this should be handled on the protobuf library. Here is the rules that work:

`-keep class * extends com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageLite { *; }`

And here is the rule that generates the problem mentioned here:

title: Document/verify .proto files should have a canonical name
body:
As brought up in https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/19832, `#import`s with .protos and filenames passed to `protoc` should be canonical: a particular file should always be referred to in the same way. When using multiple invocations of protoc it can be possible to change the names of files and cause confusion within the generated descriptors.

Right now there is a weak reference to using a "fully qualified name" at https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#importing-definitions (and the proto2 counterpart): "In general you should set the --proto_path flag to the root of your project and use fully qualified names for all imports." We should probably strengthen that part of the documentation. It's unclear if there are other good places we could mention this canonical rule. It also seems to apply for the filenames passed to `protoc`, even without any imports.

It does not seem feasible to do a check during protoc (except maybe to detect duplicates within a single protoc invocation, which I think is missing today; I seem to remember using a binary descriptor as input detecting such a thing though). However, it could potentially be done during runtime by logging a warning, albeit it would need to be done in multiple languages.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4737 is very similar to this issue, but C++ focused.

CC @acozzette

title: Ruby JSON deserialization fails for Int64Value and UInt64Value
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.9.1
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
OS X

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
ruby 2.5.5p157 (2019-03-15 revision 67260) [x86_64-darwin18]

**What did you do?**
Decode a JSON encoded message with an Int64Value or an UInt64Value field. The canonical JSON encoding for wrapper types is the same as the wrapped primitive, which in the case of int64 and uint64 is a string.
```rb
> MyMessage.decode_json('{"int64value": "123"}')
```

**What did you expect to see**
A decoded protobuf object with the `int64value` field set:
```rb
<MyMessage: int64value: <Google::Protobuf::Int64Value: value: 123>>
```

**What did you see instead?**
```
Google::Protobuf::ParseError: Error occurred during parsing: String specified for bool or submessage field: int64value
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
1. Decoding will work if the JSON value is a number instead of a string. e.g.
```rb
> MyMessage.decode_json('{"int64value": 123}')
```
2. Decoding a JSON string where the wrappers are represented as a nested object instead of a nullable primitive works. (See: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3013) e.g.
```rb
> MyMessage.decode_json('{"int64value": {"value": "123"}}')
```
3. Decoding Int32Value and UInt32Value works because 32bit ints' JSON representations are numbers.

embed SAPI w/ ZTS (pthreads on Linux)

Is anybody still using PHP with threads?

When I researched this a couple years ago, my conclusion was that PHP with threads is deprecated: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/92cdf87f1a276356657ca1b426c115bff0ad2798/php/ext/google/protobuf/protobuf.c#L142-L153

Making an extension thread-safe and thus usable with a thread-safe build of PHP, doesn't have anything to do with whether there's exposure of threading primitives to userland, f.e. by an extension like pthreads or parallel, where btw the latter is the successor to the former. 
https://www.php.net/manual/en/parallel.setup.php

Also, the fact that PHP's configure command renamed the `--enable-maintainer-zts` flag to just `--enable-zts`, doesn't count as an evidence for your conclusion either:
https://www.php.net/manual/en/configure.about.php#configure.enable-zts

This is where too many people get confused about thread-safe PHP development. It's not just about the userspace environment but the PHP virtual machine as well. PHP extensions need to be thread safe so that the virtual machine can be used in threaded server environments.

title: Nit: v3.9.0-rc1 downloads links are "rc-1" not "rc1" breaks automated builder
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

This applies to `protobuf-*` too but I'll use `protoc` as my example.

The [releases](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases) links are generally of the form:

`https://github.com/google/protobuf/releases/download/v${VERS}/protoc-${VERS}-${ARCH}.zip`

The exception to this rule is with `rc1` (both `3.9.0-rc1` and `3.8.0-rc1`) where the first occurrence in the URL is consistent (`v${VERS}`) but the second occurrence is hyphenated `rc-1`.

`.../v3.9.0-rc1/protoc-3.9.0-rc-1-linux-x86_64.zip`
`.../v3.8.0-rc1/protoc-3.8.0-rc-1-linux-x86_64.zip`

Would prefer:

`.../v3.9.0-rc1/protoc-3.9.0-rc1-linux-x86_64.zip`
`.../v3.8.0-rc1/protoc-3.8.0-rc1-linux-x86_64.zip`

I went back to `3.7.0-rc3` and this has a period added on first occurrence and a hyphen on second occurrence:
`.../v3.7.0-rc.3/protoc-3.7.0-rc-3-linux-x86_64.zip`

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Automating container builds of `protoc` and permitting build args for the version and arch.

See the example for Google's Cloud Build community builder for `protoc`:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/cloud-builders-community/blob/master/protoc/Dockerfile

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Reasonable (!) consistency in the release download URL generation of **future** releases such that, for the near-term, release URLs can be determined from the version and arch.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Permitting the builds to fail when release candidate versions are produced.

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

@yzhao1012 Actually I just took a look and I'm not sure if there is a bug here. I suspect that when you're creating a DynamicMessage you're creating a proto2 message, which unlike proto3 defaults to no packing. Can you confirm whether your code is creating a proto2 or proto3 DynamicMessage?

I think this is working as intended actually. `desc_pb` doesn't specify `packed` because it wasn't explicitly set in the proto file. Since it's unset, we rely on the default of false for proto2 and true for proto3. When you call `CreateServiceDescDB`, it looks like you're not setting it to proto3, so it's defaulting to proto2.

> When you call CreateServiceDescDB, it looks like you're not setting it to proto3, so it's defaulting to proto2.

I do not follow.

In my previous message, note the descriptorproto from the c++ message object:
// This prints name: "RepeatedInt32"
field {
name: "ri32s"
number: 1
label: LABEL_REPEATED
type: TYPE_INT32
}

**Note the packed option is not set**
**This seems wrong, as the message clearly behaves in a way that the packed is set**

CreateServiceDescDB is using the DescriptorDatabase API from our protocol runtime, we do not use proto2.

If there is a way to change how packed default work in DescriptorDatabase, please let me know.

This is just how the packed option works. If it's unset, we treat it as true in proto3 but false in proto2. And since it is unset, it is not copied into the `DescriptorProto`. If you want it to be explicitly set to true then you would have to set `packed = true` in the .proto file.

I suspect that in `CreateServiceDescDB` you're using proto2 without realizing it. Unless you explicitly set `FileDescriptorProto.syntax` to "proto3", it will default to proto2.

# Add to_hash to MessageExts, which is included in every message instance.

end

title: RepeatedField uses ArrayPool for improved performance and fewer GCs
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

csharp

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Both when constructing messages to serialize and deserializing messages...

Reduce memory pressure, reduce pauses from Gen 2 GCs (when array > 85kB), increase performance.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Use [ArrayPool](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.buffers.arraypool-1?view=netstandard-2.1) internally to allocate `array`.

It would be nice to allow the user to set the instance of ArrayPool to use so they have further control over how objects are allocated, but I'm not sure where a good place would be.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Allowing the user to pass in the allocated array to use, but that would be terribly messy.  Neither is it realistic because RepeatedField manages the size of `array` and reallocates it as it grows.

**Additional Context**

[A good overview of ArrayPool at Adam Sitnik's blog](https://adamsitnik.com/Array-Pool/)

I am concerned that ArrayPool is slower for arrays less than 1000 bytes, which is why it would be nicer to give the caller control over whether ArrayPool is used.  Perhaps with Google.Protobuf.Options.UseRepeatedFieldArrayPool static... which again feels messy, but I'm not sure where else to put it.

nodes.body: Just a drive-by comment while looking at `RepeatedField`: doesn't this really depend on being able to return the array to the `ArrayPool` when we're done with it? That's fine when we effectively discard an array due to reallocation, but the normal situation of "create a message, populate a repeated field, use the message, then let the garbage collector handle it" doesn't give us anywhere to hook in returning the array to the pool. I don't know how well `ArrayPool` works when arrays are just left for garbage collection.

title: Ruby concurrent map decoding sporadically has empty results
body:
The Ruby unit tests occasionally fail with:

```
Failure: test_concurrent_decoding(BasicTest::MessageContainerTest)
/tmp/protobuf/protobuf/ruby/tests/basic.rb:245:in `block (3 levels) in test_concurrent_decoding'
     242:       thds = 2.times.map do
     243:         Thread.new do
     244:           100000.times do
  => 245:             assert_equal o, Outer.decode(raw)
     246:           end
     247:         end
     248:       end
/tmp/protobuf/protobuf/ruby/tests/basic.rb:244:in `times'
/tmp/protobuf/protobuf/ruby/tests/basic.rb:244:in `block (2 levels) in test_concurrent_decoding'
<<BasicTest::Outer: items: {0=><BasicTest::Inner: >}>> expected but was
<<BasicTest::Outer: items: {}>>
diff:
? <BasicTest::Outer: items: {0=><BasicTest::Inner: >}>
```

Here is a [sample failure in Kokoro](https://source.cloud.google.com/results/invocations/e355b503-6ede-4c49-88d7-dc5bf4450b74/targets/protobuf%2Fgithub%2Fmaster%2Fubuntu%2Fruby23%2Fpresubmit/log).

This was first observed on the PR https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/5866, so is presumed to be related. However the bug is very sporadic and difficult to reproduce, so it's hard to say for sure when it was introduced.

Previously I tried the following strategies to make the bug more reproducible:

- I compiled a custom Ruby that uses 1ms timeslices instead of 100ms
- I've increased the number of map entries to 1,000
- I set GC.stress = 0x01 | 0x04 like gc_test.rb

nodes.body:
I've had the most luck reproducing this on Ruby 2.3, so that's what I've been using.

This doesn't appear to be GC-related. I can reproduce the error even if the test is wrapped in `GC.disable`, `GC.enable`.

I can get this modified version of the test to fail about 1 out of 15 times on the Ruby 2.3 docker image.

```ruby
    def test_concurrent_decoding
      GC.start
      GC.disable
      o = Outer.new
      o.items[0] = Inner.new
      raw = Outer.encode(o)

      thds = 2.times.map do |t|
        Thread.new do
          assert_equal o, Outer.decode(raw), "thread #{t}, raw=#{raw.length}"
        end
      end
      thds.map(&:join)
      GC.enable
    end
```

Run in a loop with:

```bash
while true; do  bundle exec ruby tests/basic.rb -n test_concurrent_decoding ; done
```

But oddly, adding more looping in Ruby itself doesn't help the bug reproduce more often. This suggests that there is some process state in play here, and we only get a chance to trigger the bug in a fresh Ruby process.

Perhaps it has to do with starting threads. Maybe `Thread.new` has to spawn a real pthread the first time, and the bug is triggered only by this initial creating of the thread.

I've narrowed this down to a race condition in the lazy initialization of decoder state in `Outer.decode(raw)`.

Specifically, if I call `Outer.decode(raw)` before spawning any threads, the failure goes away.

It seems that some calls into the Ruby API from C must be capable of releasing the GVL, causing us to re-enter the protobuf C extension from a different thread. I am curious to know more about what operations can do this. Can even a hash table lookup do this (if so, this call is suspect: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/63f324a9937b2fb562ea551f93d1d38740032bc3/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L2220)

@samphippen can you comment? What calls into Ruby can trigger a thread switch and GVL release? Is it any call into Ruby, or just some calls?

To answer my own question, it sounds like anything that triggers a GC, or possibly evaluates some Ruby, has the potential of switching Ruby threads and releasing the GVL.

This is the same issue explained by @tenderlove in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/3560#issuecomment-325781395

I have a fix in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/6541 . Locally it seems to reliably fix the problem.

title: Supporting LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORTS in clang
body:
PROTOBUF_USE_DLLS and LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORTS are currently only [defined/used with MSVC](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/ee4f2492ea4e7ff120f68a792af870ee30435aa5/src/google/protobuf/port_def.inc#L334). Protobuf is used in chrome/chromium where we [patch in this support](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/ac47edd22c481fcfe119769d6b7abf365abea8fa/third_party/protobuf/patches/0004-fix-integer-types-and-shared-library-exports.patch) downstream. However with the new addition of [exporting template instantiations](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/ee4f2492ea4e7ff120f68a792af870ee30435aa5/src/google/protobuf/repeated_field.h#L2658), this requires even more patching thus I thought we should just upstream the changes.

I created this issue to discuss the associated pull request #6535 since it was mentioned in the contributing doc to do so for complex changes (I am not sure if this applies here, but just in case). I would also suggest renaming PROTOBUF_USE_DLLS to something more reflective of the fact that it now also works on non-windows, however I did not do the change since this is something that is visible to third party users of the library rather than just internal macro definitions.

Note: the portion of this cl related to template exporting macros was not written by me but copied from the [chromium repo](https://cs.chromium.org/chromium/src/base/export_template.h) with minor modifications. However it was written by a google engineer and is also covered by the same CLA as this project.

After some investigations I was able to reproduce the exception without gRPC being envolved.

The following code allows to reproduce the issue:

}
```
```python
depth_limit = 34
data = {}
node = data
for _ in range(depth_limit):
    node['a'] = {}
    node = node['a']

payload = ParseDict(data, struct_pb2.Struct())
request = ImportDataRequest(request_data=payload)
request_str = request.SerializeToString()

message = ImportDataRequest()
message.ParseFromString(request_str)
```

This raises exception:
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/alexander.dultsev/Library/Preferences/PyCharm2019.2/scratches/scratch.py", line 17 in <module>
    message.ParseFromString(request_str)
google.protobuf.message.DecodeError: Error parsing message
```

However, if you set ***depth_limit*** to anything less than **34**, it works fine.

**What did you expect to see**
A message created without any exception being raised.

**What did you see instead?**
google.protobuf.message.DecodeError: Error parsing message

nodes.body: any progress on this?

I believe you are using protobuf cpp extension, the cpp extension has a recursive limit 100 as default:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/763c3588740b97e8e80b1b1a1a2dc4f417647133/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.cc#L89

The struct message has map entry, value message which means 34 depth_limit is 34 * 3 = 102 depth in protobuf.

To change this, you can SetAllowOversizeProtos():
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/4e93585e8bb234efeacb7737b8d080968c5ab91e/python/google/protobuf/pyext/message.cc#L1941


I am closing it for clean up. Feel free to reopen if you have more questions

Two questions:
1. Does it mean that it is not possible to serialize any JSON object into a Struct (if you don't know for sure the depth of the nesting)?
2. Could you mention this limitation somewhere in the documentation so other developers don't experience the same issues? I'm happy to open a PR, but struggled to find the place.

title: Issue with python binary wheels when several .proto files have the same name.
body:
## Metadata:
Version: protobuf v3.9.1
Language: Python
Python version: 3.6.8

## Main topic

As for now, if protobuf for python installed via `pip install protobuf`, there is an inconsistent behavior.

If you have several protobuf files with the same file name compiled to python, if you will try to import both, you'll get a following output:


```sh
TypeError: Couldn't build proto file into descriptor pool!
Invalid proto descriptor for file "same_name.proto":
  same_name.proto: A file with this name is already in the pool.
```

**Important note which distinguish this issue from similar ones opened before:**
Both files with the same name have different package name set inside.

## How to reproduce:

```sh
# Create basic folder
mkdir protobuf_issue
cd protobuf_issue

# Create a virtualenv
python3 -m venv protobuf_issue_venv
source protobuf_issue_venv/bin/activate

# Install protobuf
pip install protobuf

# Create folders for proto files and proto files (with the same names) themselves (note that package name differs).
mkdir a_proto b_proto
echo 'syntax = "proto3";\npackage a;\nmessage A { uint64 a = 1; }\n' > a_proto/same_name.proto
echo 'syntax = "proto3";\npackage b;\nmessage B { uint64 b = 1; }\n' > b_proto/same_name.proto

# Create folders for python packages and compile protobuf
mkdir a b
touch a/__init__.py
touch b/__init__.py
protoc --proto_path=a_proto --python_out=a same_name.proto
protoc --proto_path=b_proto --python_out=b same_name.proto

# Run python
python
```

Then inside repl enter the following:

```python
import a.same_name_pb2
import b.same_name_pb2
```

After you'll enter `import b.same_name_pb2`, you'll get an exception:
```sh
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/home/user/protobuf_issue/b/same_name_pb2.py", line 23, in <module>
    serialized_pb=_b('\n\x0fsame_name.proto\x12\x01\x62\"\x0e\n\x01\x42\x12\t\n\x01\x62\x18\x01 \x01(\x04\x62\x06proto3')
  File "/home/user/protobuf_issue/protobuf_issue_venv/lib/python3.6/site-packages/google/protobuf/descriptor.py", line 879, in __new__
    return _message.default_pool.AddSerializedFile(serialized_pb)
TypeError: Couldn't build proto file into descriptor pool!
Invalid proto descriptor for file "same_name.proto":
  same_name.proto: A file with this name is already in the pool.

```

## Workaround

As I found in the Internet, you can get rid of this problem by installing protobuf without binaries:

```sh
pip uninstall protobuf
pip install --no-binary=protobuf protobuf
```

After doing that the example above works as expected, and no errors occur.

## Expected behavior

I see that documentation for protobuf python generated files says:

>The Python code generated by the protocol buffer compiler is completely unaffected by the package name defined in the .proto file. Instead, Python packages  are identified by directory structure.

However, in my case of usage `.proto` files are being received from the remote server and compiled in the runtime.
If I will have to accept those rules, I will have to parse `.proto` files manually to extract the package name from it, then create folder for it, then move this file into this folder. And then compiler will parse this file again, ignoring the that important piece of data. That's not very convenient.

I hope to see some protobuf flag maybe or something else to make python-generated files respect the package name in the `.proto` file.

title: javalite.zip
body:
Our product build (implemented in Bazel) was relying on a javalite.zip with a particular SHA. Sadly, we don't have a local copy that we can find (we thought it would be in our local repository cache, but no....). It seems that the file was just replaced with a newer one, but the newer one breaks our build.

Is there anyway to retrieve the older copy? This is our WORKSPACE snippet:

http_archive(
    name = "com_google_protobuf_javalite",
    strip_prefix = "protobuf-javalite",
    urls = ["https://github.com/google/protobuf/archive/javalite.zip"],
    sha256 = "e1c862a1a32e19e39ef15c7c9fe1aaedd3fee5a76967370a028b786f2a186945",
)

nodes.body: It shouldn't be too hard to figure out which commit it was from. If you look in your repo history to see when that sha256 was last updated, you can then look in the protobuf repo history to see what commit was at the head of the `javalite` branch at that same time. Then update the URL to `https://github.com/google/protobuf/archive/<the Git commit>.zip`.
The URL gets the protobuf version, how can we get the javalite version that goes it? For example, with version 3.6.1.3? Are javalite versions kept as well? @acozzette
Java lite didn't get any releases for a while, because we had to make some ABI-incompatible changes to it. We started publishing lite releases again with 3.8.0, though.
how would I get the 3.8.0 version from the archive? I tried javalite-v3.8.0.zip and javalite-09745575a923640154bcf307fba8aedff47f240a.zip. Is the only way to get javalite.zip is to get the latest?

Yes, sorry for the trouble but I think at the moment the only way to refer to Java lite with Bazel is to specify the Git commit you want, or point to the branch so that you always get the latest. CC @rafi-kamal who might know if there is a better way.

Thanks Adam! With your hints we got a solution. There was this commit two days ago on the javalite branch:

"Prepare for Bazel-incompatible changes"
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/55735abe1ab010f9943c750b507c3ae6b3740437

The commit prior is 0ebb905ff877119d2f0683f968f0a104a54fd0d1. Given that, we converted our Bazel WORKSPACE to use the git_repository rule at that commit instead of http_archive (using latest):

git_repository(
    name = "com_google_protobuf_javalite",
    remote = "https://github.com/google/protobuf",
    commit = "0ebb905ff877119d2f0683f968f0a104a54fd0d1",
)

Boom. Problem solved. Thanks again for the FAST responses.

According to protoc's help:

Fail to printAny with JsonFormat in Java. com.google.protobuf.InvalidProtocolBufferException: Cannot find type for url: type.googleapis.com/api.DataEntity.
Include optional type URL in protobuf wire format
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
Proto3

If it's about generated code change, what programming language?
All languages

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
A serialized protobuf has no type URL.

In certain cases, for example, examining serialized protobufs without knowing its original type, becomes extremely unreliable.

If type URL is embedded in the serialized message, it would be straightforward to figure out the right message type; assuming the .proto files are available, we can then use the right message to interpret the data, either through maintaining runtime type mapping, or reflection.

A noticeable use case of this, is a reflection-based data inspection tool, which can be very powerful for exploratory data analysis. Before building more specific and performant solutions, someone can depend on a commonly-built tool that uses type-url to interpret data, that can be used for ad-hoc query, debugging, etc, which links in the protobuf messages commonly used by a group of engineers.

A somewhat less useful thing is that, a dynamic message, which is produced using protobuf reflection facilities, can optional set a type URL for identification; making it more informative. This case benefits from a type URL in similar manner as the above.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I'd like the serialization format to include an optional type URL field. Its field number can be 0 to distinguish from other fields.

Dynamic message of course would not be able to produce this information. But it could provide an optional API to set its type URL.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
We can include a type url field with field number 1 in the message. But that seems too much work; and it requires manually maintain the code to set the field.

Also, in some cases, it's not reliable. I.e., if I do not know the type information in the first place, I cannot reliably conclude the field number 1 is the type URL. Unless I mandate all protobuf message define a type_url field as the first field, which is not difficult to do, but does incur considerable toil.

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

This option would make our work of dynamically examine customer's protobuf much easier to implement. As we need to deal with the problem of aliasing serialized protobuf messages, i.e., because we do not know who generate the protobuf messages, when we get them, the customer do not want to annotate the messages themselves; they expect us to figure out the right type.

But because some wire types can be parsed as different fields, this makes our detection unreliable.

nodes.body: Thank you for the idea, but I don't think we will be able to implement this change. This kind of change is very difficult to implement because it has to be done in a backward-compatible way and implemented across all 10 or so languages we support. I can see some value in the idea but I just don't think it is enough to justify all the work required. Also, we already have some basic support for this in the google.protobuf.Any type, which includes a type URL and has helper code for populating it.

Just to explore a bit for future reference, such that readers do not find it confusing as to the concrete trade-offs involved for the decision.

> it has to be done in a backward-compatible way and implemented
Naively speaking, if I set the field number for this special type URL field to 0, as protobuf does not allow user specified field number to be smaller than 1, this should be immediately make a few compatibility scenarios easier to handle:

Lets say new message being ones that support embedded type URL.

1. old message parsing a serialized new message: old message recognize a field number 0, and then fail the parsing, as I experimented with this string "\x0A\x03\x64\x65\x66" (field number 0, length prefixed field).
2. new message parse new serialized message: obviously fine
3. new message parse old serialized message: obviously fine

#1 can be resolved set this feature as default disabled, such that new message by default does not produce type URL.

> across all 10 or so languages we support.
This is certainly a killer.

I suppose the work is mostly manual repetition. I am guessing each language will take a few hours of work to code, and a few days for review & land.

title: Python: Issue with json_format
body:
## Metadata:
Version: protobuf v3.9.1
Language: Python
Python version: 3.6.8

## Main topic

Attempt to parse Protobuf Message from json with bytes object doesn't seem to behave right.

If Protobuf Message has a bytes field, and in json it's encoded as a list of bytes (e.g. `[0xDE, 0xAD, 0xBE, 0xEF]`), parsing fails with `ParseError`:

```python
  File "/home/user/workspace/project/project/file.py", line 10, in func
    return json_format.Parse(data_json, protobuf_obj, True).SerializeToString()
  File "/home/user/workspace/project/project_venv/lib/python3.6/site-packages/google/protobuf/json_format.py", line 415, in Parse
    return ParseDict(js, message, ignore_unknown_fields, descriptor_pool)
  File "/home/user/workspace/project/project_venv/lib/python3.6/site-packages/google/protobuf/json_format.py", line 435, in ParseDict
    parser.ConvertMessage(js_dict, message)
  File "/home/user/workspace/project/project_venv/lib/python3.6/site-packages/google/protobuf/json_format.py", line 466, in ConvertMessage
    self._ConvertFieldValuePair(value, message)
  File "/home/user/workspace/project/project_venv/lib/python3.6/site-packages/google/protobuf/json_format.py", line 575, in _ConvertFieldValuePair
    raise ParseError('Failed to parse {0} field: {1}.'.format(name, e))
google.protobuf.json_format.ParseError: Failed to parse pub_key field: Failed to parse data field: argument should be a bytes-like object or ASCII string, not 'list'..
```

The issue here is that json doesn't have `bytes` type, and encoding to `base64` is not what you want to do just to make parser happy.

Fictional reproducing example:
```python
from google.protobuf import json_format

json_data = '{ "data": [12, 34, 56, 78] }'
message = Message()  # .proto for Message is "messasge Message { bytes data = 1 }"
json_format.Parse(json_data, message)

```

## Expected behavior

I think that lists should be attempted to be parsed into bytes in that case, and only if list contains unappropriate values, exception should be rised.

title: If message name has the dash sigbal, it can't compile

nodes.body: Names can't have a dash in them because that would cause problems in many languages--e.g. in C++ `Search-Request` would turn into three separate tokens. The protobuf [style guide](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/style) would recommend `SearchRequest`, though you could in principle also do `searchrequest`.

title: Can ParseFromString() and other parse function fail when parse repeated fields as optional field?

nodes.body: Sorry but we can't change this because that would be a breaking change to the wire format. If a singular field appears more than once, the last one wins. This can actually be a useful feature sometimes because it allows you to change a serialized message by appending onto it.

body:
<!--

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: $ protoc --version  # libprotoc 3.6.1

Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?** Debian stretch

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)** gcc 6.4.0

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Have an enum in an annotation proto message containing a field named `NULL`. 

    https://github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway/blob/3ad0fb96ecfdf73fa2eddb3de116ae98360dbb35/protoc-gen-swagger/options/openapiv2.proto#L218

2. Use `protoc --cpp_out=.......` with the proto file.
3. Attempt to compile the resulting output file `g++ -C -o tmp.o protoc-gen-swagger/options/openapiv2.pb.cc`

**What did you expect to see**
No errors building.

**What did you see instead?**
Due to a conflict with `#define NULL __null` somewhere in the compiler or standard headers, the compiler is not happy:

```
In file included from /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/types/stack_t.h:23:0,
                 from /usr/include/signal.h:303,
                 from /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/sys/param.h:28,
                 from /usr/include/google/protobuf/stubs/port.h:64,
                 from /usr/include/google/protobuf/stubs/common.h:46,
                 from ../../../protoc-gen-swagger/options/openapiv2.pb.h:9,
                 from ../../../protoc-gen-swagger/options/openapiv2.pb.cc:4:
../../../protoc-gen-swagger/options/openapiv2.pb.h:1845:38: error: expected unqualified-id before ‘__null’
   static const JSONSchemaSimpleTypes NULL =
                                      ^
../../../protoc-gen-swagger/options/openapiv2.pb.cc:927:52: error: expected unqualified-id before ‘__null’
 const JSONSchema_JSONSchemaSimpleTypes JSONSchema::NULL;
                                                    ^
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
As enum fields named `NULL` were seemingly broken until now, I propose renaming them just before the code is generated. This does not seem to have been an issue in other languages, and I don't believe this is forbidden by either proto2 or proto3 syntax.

This was reported in https://github.com/grpc-ecosystem/grpc-gateway/issues/1031 -- the annotations there are used in generating OpenAPI v2 ("swagger") JSON description of the `.proto`-defined API. We can perhaps work around this, but this is still an issue in `protoc` generator for C++.

I hit - what appears to be - this when compiling gRPC/protobuf with other code that had macro replacements for MSVC's "__declspec(dllexports)". `port_def.inc` has a comment above the macro definition of `PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_TEST` that says "When [the macros] are not working correctly, a syntax error should occur instead." - and perhaps the wall of errors is the syntax error it speaks of...?

#define PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_TEST_MSVC_HACK_DEFAULT(...) true
```

And that seems to have calmed things down. From the looks of things, these macros have been removed in protobuf 3.12.3, so I imagine this should fix itself (or manifest the underlying problem...?) when moving to that version.

title: Add option to generate C# nullable annotations
body:
**Language** : C#


**Feature Request**

C# 8.0 adds support for [nullability annotations](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/nullable-references).

It would be helpful if the the generated protobuf objects added these annotations. This would provide warnings if people tried to dereference a possibly null value, or for example, tried to assign null to a string property of a protobuf object.

 At first sight it looks like the rules for which types can be nullable and which can't should be quite simple.

I think the first stage would be annotating the Protobuf Nuget Packages.

Of course nullable annotaions are a compile error in earlier versions of C# than c# 8.0. Therefore this has to be off by default, and triggered by a command line option.

It would be helpful if this was added for GRPC as well.

nodes.body:
I'm not generally opposed to having this, but here are the challenges:
1. we would need a clear design - feel free to provide more thoughts here if you want
2. currently this is not a priority so there's no ETA and implementation would need to be contributed by someone from the community (but we'd need a design for this feature first).
3. C# 8 nullable annotations are a brand new C# 8 feature, but we definitely need to maintain the backward compatibility - which probably also means that it's going to take a while before this can actually be used. 

There are two separate areas:
1. annotations in the Google.Protobuf  runtime  (=the nuget) - then concern is backward-compatibility of the APIs (you cannot have an "option" for enabling/disabling this so it would need to work for everyone - and it's going to take a very long time until everyone can use C# 8).
2. annotations in the generated code (you can have a codegen option to enable the default-off feature), the question is how useful these checks would be - it's generated code and most of it is just field accessors, so I'm not sure we'd gain much here (a more detailed design would help).

> annotations in the Google.Protobuf runtime (=the nuget) - then concern is backward-compatibility of the APIs (you cannot have an "option" for enabling/disabling this so it would need to work for everyone - and it's going to take a very long time until everyone can use C# 8).

The annotations are backwards compatible, so I don't think this should be an issue.

> annotations in the generated code (you can have a codegen option to enable the default-off feature), the question is how useful these checks would be - it's generated code and most of it is just field accessors, so I'm not sure we'd gain much here (a more detailed design would help).

A very common mistake I make is to set a string to null. That would be the single most useful gain.

With GRPC specifically, I often by mistake return null from the server implementation. That would be another gain but of course that is for a different repository.

I don't know a huge amount about protoc but my initial design would be:

All string properties are marked non-null.
No change in struct properties.
All collection properties (repeated, or maps) are marked as non-null.
All other properties are marked as nullable.

Parser property marked as non-null.
Descriptor property marked as non-null.

Constructor parameter is non-null
Clone method returns non-null
Equals parameter is nullable
Mergefrom parameter is nullable
MergeFrom(CodedInputStream) parameter is non-null
WriteTo parameter is non-null

Instead of using the normal C# 8 syntax perhaps we could make use of the [code analysis attributes](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.codeanalysis?view=netstandard-2.1), that way the syntax works no matter what version of C# you're using. Of course that'd require that a separate package (like [Microsoft.Bcl.Async](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Microsoft.Bcl.Async/)) for everything under .NET Standard 2.1 but should that ever happen it could probably be done that way.

Were those attributes not specifically added for C# 8? dotnet/corefx#37826 says otherwise. They work with C# 8 flawlessly.

```cs
public string TypeUrl {
  get { return typeUrl_; }
  [global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.DisallowNullAttribute]
  set {
    typeUrl_ = pb::ProtoPreconditions.CheckNotNull(value, "value");
  }
}

// .. somewhere far far away
#nullable enable

any.TypeUrl = null; // Cannot convert null literal to non-nullable reference type
```

All of the cases you mentioned work with these attributes.

String properties => DisallowNullAttribute.
All collection properties (repeated, or maps) => NotNullAttribute.
All other properties => MaybeNullAttribute.

Parser property => NotNullAttribute.
Descriptor property => NotNullAttribute.

Constructor parameter => DisallowNullAttribute
Clone method  => NotNullAttribute
Equals parameter => AllowNullAttribute
MergeFrom parameter => AllowNullAttribute
MergeFrom(CodedInputStream)  => DisallowNullAttribute
WriteTo  => DisallowNullAttribute

@ObsidianMinor

I see I misunderstood which attributes you were referring to. My apologies.

The C# 8 nullable annotations emit attributes themselves. The coreFX attributes are meant for when the behaviour is to complex to be described by these annotations.

In so far as pre C# 8 tooling understands the CoreFX attributes, I would expect it to understand the attributes emitted by the compiler. However I strongly doubt either would work well.

I can probably get a prototype of this working pretty easily but it could only be pulled when and if dotnet/runtime#30801 happens.

Using these annotations would allow us to do this in a backwards compatible way. The behavior of nulls in generated code and the library is too complex to be done with standard `?` and `!` syntax. So rather than doing it using that syntax, we can express what we need using the attributes. This has the included bonus of working on other lang versions. Only downside is this requires the nuget package as shown above.

> Using these annotations would allow us to do this in a backwards compatible way.

Ah you mean to avoid a switch? That sounds like a decent idea.

Alright I wrote a prototype (untested) on my fork on the [csharp/nullability](https://github.com/ObsidianMinor/protobuf/tree/csharp/nullability) branch. As it turns out nullability attributes do not affect code analysis in function bodies as noted in dotnet/roslyn#36039 so depending on whether the attributes affect code analysis in the future we may or may not have to disable warnings on the file level which is a very simple addition. Again, this will only work if a separate nuget package is made for these attributes, it works on the prototype since I manually copy-pasted the attributes into Google.Protobuf.
I don't think we'd want to add another dependency to be able to reference the attributes.

This seems like a fairly decent compromise in reference the the idea of not wishing to add another dependency:
https://www.nuget.org/packages/Nullable/
Essentially does what @ObsidianMinor did where the attributes get compiled into the application without having to copy them into the repo.  Unless the preference is to not have any new dependencies, regardless of if they then cause a dependency downstream to consuming projects.

nodes.body: If you want to get the code size as small as possible, I would recommend statically linking `libprotobuf-lite` into your binary so that you can let the linker remove any unreferenced code. Make sure to compile with `-ffunction-sections` and `-fdata-sections` and link with `-Wl,gc-sections`. Setting `option optimize_for = LITE_RUNTIME;` does also help, but the savings will be roughly proportional to the size of your .proto files. If you have only a small .proto file, then the size of the protobuf runtime (i.e. `libprotobuf` or `libprotobuf-lite`) might dominate over the size of the generated code. I'm not sure offhand how small you can get the code overall, so you might have to experiment with it a bit.

Actually it sounds like you might be using Windows, so I am not sure if the compiler and linker flags I mentioned will work. The important thing is just to enable whichever flags are necessary to allow the most aggressive linker stripping.
If you really need to get the code size down further, you might also want to check out some of the C protobuf implementations such as nanopb, upb, or protobuf-c.

title: How to add any custom metadata for .proto file, protobuf message and protobuf fields
body:
Hi,

May i know if we have a way to add one or more custom metadata for .proto file, protobuf message and fields in protobuf message ? Also is there an API which can be used to get the metadata for each of the scenario ?

Thanks
Jane

nodes.body:
Hi,

Forgot to mention, I would like to know the options available in proto3 and proto2 and any known limitations.

Thanks
Jane

I think the feature you're looking for is [custom options](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#customoptions), which you can use with both proto2 and proto3. It depends on what language you're using but most languages give you a way to read these custom options from the descriptors.

The details of accessing custom options depends on the language. Which language are you using? It sounds like custom options are indeed the right solution if you want to store per-file, per-msg, and per-field metadata.
We are using C++ ...

In that case you just have to get ahold of the descriptor for your message/file/field and do `descriptor->options.GetExtension(...)`. See this [test](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/b9f405ae46036860a4e73e167bee3800dfe53a9e/src/google/protobuf/descriptor_unittest.cc#L2976) for some more examples.

title: Feature Request: Timestamp Wrapper WKT
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
proto3

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Wrapper types are useful in proto3 to represent a nullable field.
As Well Known Types, they are extra-useful because of their concise and easily understood representation when converted to JSON (ie: they allow "null" as the value in json). This is great especially when used with a gRPC-Gateway.
As of right now, there is not a wrapper for the WKT Timestamp.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like to have a Timestamp Wrapper WKT.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
A non-WKT timestamp wrapper (ie: just making my own message with a WKT Timestamp nested in it) would not have the WKT advantages, such as the easily understood JSON conversion.

nodes.body:
I don't think we need a wrapper type for any type that is a message, including Timestamp.

> Wrapper types are useful in proto3 to represent a nullable field.

Any field that is a message is nullable, so the WKT Timestamp is already nullable.

> As Well Known Types, they are extra-useful because of their concise and easily understood representation when converted to JSON (ie: they allow "null" as the value in json). This is great especially when used with a gRPC-Gateway.

Because Timestamp is already a WKT, plugins can take advantage of this and use custom representations for JSON. Adding another WKT that is a wrapper wouldn't change the current situation, which is that it's up to plugin implementers to recognize that it's a WKT and make optimized JSON representations.

> Any field that is a message is nullable, so the WKT Timestamp is already nullable.

That's correct. We won't be adding this, but thank you for the suggestion!

title: TextFormat for C#
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
proto3
C#

Currently C# does not have the functionality of TextFormat, like this:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java/

I've found a version but it's not in .net standard:
https://github.com/jskeet/protobuf-csharp-port/blob/master/src/ProtocolBuffers/TextFormat.cs

nodes.body:
Not supporting text-format in the Google.Protobuf C# implementation is deliberate. 
Google.Protobuf supports canonical mapping to JSON, which should be good enough to satisfy your needs as it provides mostly the same functionality as textFormat. The text format support was more useful before canonical JSON mapping support was added in protobuf 3. (which is also when Google.Protobuf was created and we didn't want to bloat the codebase so we never added test format support for Google.Protobuf).
Btw, "protobuf-csharp-port" is very old, I'd recommend using Google.Protobuf (basically its successor) and the JSON format instead of text format.

The reason we need this feature is because TensorFlow models is using TextFormat to define pipeline, and TensorFlow checkpoint is also using this format. https://github.com/tensorflow/models. 

This issue blocks our work, my team is working on making a .NET binding for TensorFlow. https://github.com/SciSharp/TensorFlow.NET.

Our solution is fork and migrate the old one to protobuf: https://github.com/SciSharp/protobuf/commits/master. Is it possible to merge if we complete this feature?

How much code/complexity would be to add the TextFormat support to the current Google.Protobuf implementation? I think we can accept a contribution assuming it's not overly complex and it's tested accordingly. Ideally I'd like to see a design (what APIs are going to be added) and a list of work needs to be done to make TextFormat support in C# fully functional.

@jtattermusch We have preview version for our own project. we will refactor the code and try to make it more clean before we PR.

https://www.nuget.org/packages/Protobuf.Text/0.1.0

@jtattermusch Yes, the text format support of Protobuf.Text right now just follow the design of current protobuf's JsonFormat implemention with TextTokenizer, TextParser and TextFormatter. And we duplicated test cases from JsonFormat and we are working on making all the test cases work.
Generally, two parsers should only have a few differences, because they just merge document nodes tree to model. But there are more differences between two tokenizers which are used for loading the nodes tree from string. The project Protobuf.Text is an addition for protobuf C# library for now.  But later, we will send a PR to protobuf after we do some sorts of refactoring and the code reaches higher quality level.
BTW, the most of the code of TextFormatter is from protobuf-csharp-port.

@jtattermusch Hello Jan, are you the major contributor of protobuf C# version? We have some progress for the project https://github.com/SciSharp/protobuf.Text. And I am going to has a discussion about design of JsonParser and TextParser with the major contributors.

@kerryjiang    I can review the design but it might take a while because TextFormat support is strictly speaking not a necessity - just a nice to have. Other folks to involve are @anandolee (knowledgeable about implementation in other languages) and @jskeet  (the original author of most of Google.Protobuf code, but most likely won't have cycles to review in detail).
We have seperate package: https://www.nuget.org/packages/Protobuf.Text/

Then if you run this test.py application:

  data = f.read()

fd = FileDescriptorSet.FromString(data)

import test_pb2
fd = FileDescriptorSet.FromString(data)
# This will work and prints out: [MyOption]: "Hello, World!"
print("Options: " + str(fd.file[0].message_type[0].options))
```

**What did you expect to see**
I was expecting to see both print() calls to print out the option.

I would expect that I can load the test.protoset file and be able to read the options set to the MyMessage. However this doesn't seem to be work unless I also import the generated test_pb2.py code.

nodes.body: The test.protoset has embedded "Hello, World!" with extension number 50001 as wire format, to parse it into a known option (named MyOption in your case), the related info should be put into descriptor pool which import test_pb2.py does for protobuf pure python version. Without the import, this will be parsed into unknown fields and you can also see "Hello, Whorld!" but "MyOption" info is missing

body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
