title: min/max namespace collision with Winsock2.h

nodes.body:
Hi @dkonik,

I am new on Google ProtoBuffers and I have the same issue. I found, that in the file `minwindef.h` (in C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Include\<`version`>\shared\) there is a macro definition of `min` and `max` in a **global** scope.
Because of there are member functions `min` and `max` in `std::numeric_limits` too, this causes the fault. Of course the compilation succeeds, if the `*.pb.h` is include **before** including `minwindef.h` (or `WinSock2.h`, which implicitly includes `minwindef.h`).
I think the best choice would be, to change the implementation of ProtoBuffers to do not use min/max from `std::numeric_limits`.

I feel like that's a pretty unreasonable ask. But maybe there is some change that can be made to ensure that they won't collide. FWIW, you can get around this issue by defined NOMINMAX before including winsock2.

I have run into this issue as well, albeit in a more round-about fashion. I have inherited a project that uses both Thrift and Protobuf (don't ask).

Thrift includes Winsock2 so having any transient include chain reference the Thrift file first breaks the protobuffers.

Just wanted to note that this problem can be very tricky to track down when it comes from two different generated sources i.e. not our own code.

Let me close this issue since it has been fixed by some logic in port_def.inc which temporarily undefines these min and max macros: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f57ae5eac31d5322c8fcb350a6cdc13647e5ca53/src/google/protobuf/port_def.inc#L406

add_compile_definitions( NOMINMAX)

title: Provide C# support for garbage free parsing
body:
Language: C#

Problem: Protobuf creates new objects when parsing. As far as I can tell, there is no way to get around this if you have a "nested" type, or something like a `oneof`. It would be great if it supported parsing *into* an already existing object, or somehow taking in a factory that it would use to create objects.

nodes.body:
If you use nested messages at least (so a field of a custom message type) then the generated code does not allocate if the reference is not null. However for oneof it does allocate.

One workaround for oneof is to modify the generated code behind yourself.
Or not use oneof and achieve oneof semantics using your own code.

I acknowledge that being able to parse without needing allocations would be nice and it would be useful for some users (e.g. those who are super performance/latency sensitive), but making that happen would be a big undertaking and would require a lot of design work first.
I think at some point in the future Google.Protobuf might allow allocation free parsing, but there would need to be a clear plan for what needs to be done and how (and how to achieve that without breaking backwards compatibility).
Currently I don't have the bandwidth to work on such (highly complex, as there is a large number of cases that need to be taken into account) design and frankly it seems that the demand for such feature is quite low.
I don't think we are interested in solving this by a half baked approach of randomly adjusting things in different places (e.g. adjusting oneofs) without first investigating whether this whole "allocation free parsing" concept is feasible at all. Without a plan, we will likely make a few smaller changes (that don't really have much performance impact but make our codebase more complex) and then hit the wall after we discover that there's a blocker we didn't think of.

title: Auto-generate interfaces to enforce protocol definition contracts.
body:
**Language:** C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Decoupling the contract defined in the protocol definition from the concrete implementation to facilitate mocking for better testability.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Message declarations currently autogenerate a partial sealed class. The proposed solution is to also auto-generate an interface to explicitly enforce the contract defined in the protocol definition.

For example:
`public sealed partial class Foo : pb::IMessage<Foo>`
becomes
`public sealed partial class Foo : pb::IMessage<Foo>, IFoo`

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Since the auto-generated classes are `partial` it would be possible to manually build a library that defines and enforces these interfaces. However, it would be preferable for the protocol buffer library to provide native support for this capability.

title: Outdated Utf8Decoder for Java?
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**Java 9+**
java.lang.String now internally stores byte[] (i.e. encoded) and a coder directly instead of the char array it used to. Utf8.java has all kinds of decoders that read byte[] or ByteBuffer etc... to convert them to char[]. Then it calls public String(char value[], int offset, int count), which internally converts the char[] array back to a byte[] by encoding it!

**Proposed solution**
For Java 9+, with most common cases of LATIN1 strings, I think the idiomatic java calls to String constructor with byte[] and Charset - public String(byte bytes[], int offset, int length, Charset charset) should suffice. There's no need to decode+encode.

nodes.body:
I also have this problem. 

I often work on different computers, and Windows automatically creates my AzureAD user profile in `C:\Users\MattiasÅslund\`. So far my only workaround is to create a new local user account on each machine, so I get an "acceptable" path. 

If I keep working with gRpc, this will be _really_ annoying.

In case someone else ends up here.

My preferred workaround is [changing where global-packages is located](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/consume-packages/managing-the-global-packages-and-cache-folders).
As described in this issue https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/17995#issuecomment-607159949
The problem is not `protoc` but how windows handles response command files... I also can't find out how to use UTF-8 or unicode in those files.

I also ran into this issue and came here from [grpc/grpc#17995](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/17995).

There is a [PR for Grpc.Tools](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/22916) which implements a work-around for this issue, but it is currently stale as it might introduce other issues. 

It is mentioned [there](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/22916#issuecomment-656593815) that the issue lies in the fact that protoc is ignoring the BOM when reading the response file. The solution suggested there seems relatively simple. Could someone please look into it?

@fowles  this is actually not a problem that's C# specific. Same problem exists for all other languages that use protoc (but C# toolchain happens to use the `@<filename>` commandline argument).

The issue is that when the `@<filename>` cmdline option is used, non-ASCII characters in the input file containing options/arguments are not being processed correctly.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/3f5fc4df1de8e12b2235c3006593e22d6993c3f5/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc#L2096

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/3f5fc4df1de8e12b2235c3006593e22d6993c3f5/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc#L1447

The ExpandArgumentFile function is using `std::ifstream` to read the contents of the argument file and that ends up not working correctly:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/3f5fc4df1de8e12b2235c3006593e22d6993c3f5/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc#L1425

[more details here](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/22916#issuecomment-656593815)
Basically the rootcause of this is https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7474, but I'm not sure if making ExpandArgumentFile support wifstream is feasible.
@joaoportela @jtattermusch I think this can now be closed since https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7474 is fixed.

title: Incorrect double encoding in google-protobuf js module
body:

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.9.2
Language: Javascript

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Any (but I am specifically using macOS 10.14.5).

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Node 10.16.3.

**What did you do?**
I encoded the double `3.9999999999999997` in a protobuf message.

**What did you expect to see**
I expected the field's value to be encoded as `3.9999999999999997` (i.e., `[ 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 15, 64 ]`).

**What did you see instead?**
The field's value was encoded as `7.999999999999999` (i.e., `[ 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 255, 31, 64 ]`)

[Here's some code that demonstrates the issue:](https://runkit.com/srubin/google-protobuf-double-encoding-bug)

```js
const googleProtobuf = require("google-protobuf");
const field = 1;

function testEncodeDecode(value) {
    const writer = new googleProtobuf.BinaryWriter();
    writer.writeDouble(field, value);
    const buf = writer.getResultBuffer();
    
    const reader = new googleProtobuf.BinaryReader(buf, 0, buf.length);
    reader.nextField()
    const decoded = reader.readDouble()
    
    const encoded = new Float64Array(buf.slice(1).buffer);
    
    const target = new Float64Array([value]);
    
    console.log(
        'Value', value, 
        'Target encoded', target[0], 
        'Actual encoded', encoded[0], 
        'Equal?', target[0] === encoded[0], value === decoded
    );
}

testEncodeDecode(3.999999999999999);  // succeeds
testEncodeDecode(3.9999999999999999); // succeeds
testEncodeDecode(3.9999999999999997); // fails
testEncodeDecode(7.999999999999999);  // fails
testEncodeDecode(15.999999999999998); // fails
```

[`splitFloat64`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/763c3588740b97e8e80b1b1a1a2dc4f417647133/js/binary/utils.js#L216) is the culprit here. Regardless of if the bug is fixed within that function, would it make sense to prefer to use TypedArray (`Float64Array`) if it's available? I noticed that [`protobufjs` takes this approach](https://github.com/protobufjs/protobuf.js/blob/e8449c4bf1269a2cc423708db6f0b47a383d33f0/lib/float/index.js#L184).

title: String field processing in getSerializedSize/writeTo looks suspicious
body:
Hey!

Can someone from protobuf team explain to me the rationale behind the Java code for string fields processing produced by protoc?

Protoc generates Java **Object** field for each proto string field and protobuf uses it to store either **ByteString** or **java.util.String** (dunno why).
Also each string field gets two accessor methods: **getXxx** for **String** and **getXxxBytes** for **ByteString.**

The suspicious part begins inside generated methods **getSerializedSize** and **writeTo.**

For both of these methods **getXxxBytes** will be called disregarding the current type of an instance stored in **Object** field which leads to unnecessary **ByteString** allocation when actual type is **java.util.String** (and this is the common case from my perspective).

It looks even more peculiar if we will take into account the fact that in both methods we may see a usage of dual-type-aware **GeneratedMessageV3.writeString**/**GeneratedMessageV3.computeStringSize** literally in the next line after **getXxxBytes** calls.

Is it a bug or an intentional decision?

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.9.2 
Language: Java

**What did you expect to see**
getSerializedSize/writeTo have specialized versions for ByteString/String

**What did you see instead?**
getXxxBytes is always used for isEmpty check

title: Generated C++: Maps with String keys will not compile with 64-bit MSVC with /WX
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.8.0 (gRPC 1.23 submodule)
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows
**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
MSVC x64 (Visual Studio 2019)

**What did you do?**
Generate from a protobuf with a map entry, e.g.
```protobuf
message Msg {
   map<string, Something> Dummy = 1;
}
```
Then, compile with `/WX` (equivalent to `-Werror`)

**What did you expect to see**
Generated C++ code compiles.

**What did you see instead?**
The generated C++ code will fail to compile. In the `ValidateKey` function:

```c++
 static bool ValidateKey(std::string* s) {
    return ::PROTOBUF_NAMESPACE_ID::internal::WireFormatLite::VerifyUtf8String(s->data(), s->size(), ::PROTOBUF_NAMESPACE_ID::internal::WireFormatLite::PARSE, "Dummy.key");
 }
```

The second parameter to `VerifyUtf8String` is an `int`, and MSVC produces the following error: 
`warning C4267: 'argument': conversion from 'size_t' to 'int', possible loss of data`

The solution is probably just to cast to `int` from `s->size()`, although this does technically mean that only strings up to 2 GB are supported.

Conflicting documentation.

For me, this was caused by having the "specific platform" config parameter set to true. For bundler < v2, this was opt-in. In bundler v2 this became the default behavior. You can opt out by adding this to any of the `.bundle/config` files (project, user, global). 

```
BUNDLE_SPECIFIC_PLATFORM: "false"
```
Closing as obsolete.

title: How to use this tool?!
body:
Hello
All I was looking for is a way to generate C# classes from .proto file.
So I installed this tool for C#, and followed all the instructions. There are instructions on Google on how to compile the code, which should give me what I want: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/csharptutorial
`protoc -I=$SRC_DIR --csharp_out=$DST_DIR $SRC_DIR/addressbook.proto`

But, there is no instruction on **where** to call this function from?! I've tried from cmd, I've tried from Package Manager, all telling me this cmdlet is not recognized. There seem to be no further instructions on how I can use this tool now to achieve what I want.
Can you please help.

The instructions on this are very poor :(((

title: Missing Input File
body:
Hello,
Trying to use protoc, but getting "Missing Input File" error message. The file is not missing, because I can navigate to it through Windows Explorer and it finds it. I've tried with "--proto_path" parameter and without like Google suggests, neither of these work.

`protoc -I=D:\myProject\myProject --csharp_out=D:\AnotherProject\AnotherProject --proto_path=D:\myProject\myProject\Common\folder\MyProto.proto`

Also tried
`protoc --proto_path=D:\myProject\myProject\Common\folder\MyProto.proto --csharp_out=D:\AnotherProject\AnotherProject`

How do I call this command?!

nodes.body: The `--proto_path` flag is not for specifying the .proto file to generate code for, instead it's for specifying the top-level directory to search for .proto files. I think in your case the right command should be something like this: `protoc -I D:\myProject\myProject --csharp_out=D:\AnotherProject\AnotherProject Common\folder\MyProto.proto`

I tried, this but it didn't work:
 `File does not reside within any path specified using --proto_path (or -I).  You must specify a --proto_path which encompasses this file.  Note that the proto_path must be an exact prefix of the .proto file names -- protoc is too dumb to figure out when two paths (e.g. absolute and relative) are equivalent (it's harder than you think)`

What I'm actually trying to achieve is to generate C# classes from .proto file. Not other way around.
Cheers

Since this got closed and no one is going to come back to look at this again, I've opened a ticket in Stackoverflow, with much more description:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/58278335/descriptor-proto-file-not-found-protoc-3-10-windows

Hi,
I ran into the same problem. Stackoverflow question is not there anymore. What did you do to fix it?
Best regards

novas1r1 I never managed to solve it unfortunately, after spending hours and hours of researching solution for it, only to see error after error; I communicated it back to my colleagues, it was then decided that priority on it was low enough to ditch it altogether. But yeah, basically now we never ever use it
:( ohoh... hope I can figure it out because I really need it. Thanks for your answer anyway!

I had the same problem and I solved it a little clumsily:

I opened the installation folder of protobuf with binary protoc.exe (C:\protoc-3.19.2-win64\bin) and copied there the .proto file from that I wanted to generate c# classes. Then I opened cmd there and insert this command: 
`protoc --csharp_out=. MyProto.proto`

MyProto.cs was generated in the same folder as MyProto.proto.

I hope that this helps somebody. :)

@ArveSystad: interesting. Too bad only one log has been posted, and it's not quite informative. VS caches a lot of things in this directory. The format also has changed between VS 2017 ans 2019.

There are many variables at play:
 * VS version
 * Package management style: “old”, with the "_solution_/package" directory, or new, when all packages are in the user directory.
 * Project style: classic vs SDK. The thing is that the new NuGet package management can be used with classic project.

In short, it's a mess, and there is no common pattern that could be inferred. But what you did id sensible. Also, with the "new" package management style, the contents of the `obj/` directory (excluding its subdirectories) matters: there are a few files that are not deleted when switching branches. Nobody reported if they are doing that or not. Also, for reasons I do not understand, the NuGet tooling is designed to keep this directory on project cleanup. Again, this applies only to project using the "new" NuGet tooling, with the central package storage (`<PackageReference ...>` items present in the project.

If this is reproducible using MSBuild instead of VS, that would be very helpful. If `msbuild /t:Build  /bl:somename.binlog;ProjectImports=embed` (note the last switch), this binlog file would tell **a whole lot** to me. It will be less chatty if you runt `/t:Clean` separately without it, and only do `/t:Build` with it. It can accidentally a lot of information about your machine, so best of all share it with me privately, if you are ok with that. I'll certainly use it for as short a time as possible, shred it carefully, and I am encrypting all my drives.

If this happens only inside VS, there is also an option to save a .binlog from it, but that one is much more compact, and sometimes does not contain the required info. I'll explain how to get it, id MSBuild command-line build does not repro the issue.

I want to put this issue to rest. It pops up in so many different guises, that I'm not even sure if this is one problem.

---

By the way, switching to the new package management is the right thing to do, even if you want to keep "classic" csproj format. It's much more precise in dependency tracking, and keeps the graph of dependencies as graph, unlike the old, hierarchy-flattening `package.config` format, which is a simple transitive closure of the dependency DAG. The biggest and the most annoying problems it has been designed to solve are
 * if `main.exe` project depends on library A, which in turn depends on B, and A needs package X that depends on W, while B depends on W explicitly, W must be a `<Reference ...` of main.exe project, or it will fail to compile, and listed in its `package.config`. After you remove dependencies, or if packages dependency change with an upgrade, there is no way to tell _why_ W in in main.exe's `packages.config`: does it really use W directly, or is this an artifact of the flattening dependency graph closure into a set?. Finding these becomes a nightmare over time.
 * The modification of `package.config` files is handled by a VSIX extension in VS. `<PackageReference ...>`-style does not, and managed entirely by NuGet MSBuild tasks. You (a) cannot add a dependency without VS with the former, and (b) need to run `nuget restore` to set up packages in the headless build machine, which normally should not have VS, only the
 free Build Tools package. The new style has a `/t:Restore` MSBuild target, and this is even implicitly invoked 
 * The `<Reference>`s updated by the VSIX extension depend on the location of the project within a solution. So if a project is referred from two solutions (E.g., `./main.sln` and `./core/core.sln`, all references are off. This was a huge pain point; we had to run Git filters on the server that rejected PRs with relative paths like `../packages/xxx` or `../../packages/xxx`, and had to modify them to `$(SolutionDir)packages/xxx`, which was gladly reverted into `../(../)+` every time you do anything in the VS package management tool, e.g. upgrade a package.

The rework is manual (remove `package.config`, all <Reference>s to directly packaged be auto-sensed by VS, and manually add `<PackageReference ...>` for **direct** dependencies only. To us, it took time to rework paid off tremendously. An important thing to keep in mind that after checking out different styles of package management it's crucial to delete all `obj/` directories.

title: python: Using python dict to construct message with map to complex type raises an error
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->
Version: libprotoc 3.8.0 from pkg manager 
Language: Python 3.6.8 on Linux

All of the examples, existing code, and documentation for protobuf in Python that I've seen indicates that it's possible to construct instances of complex message types just using built-in lists and dicts. This is really useful since it removes a lot of the constructing-intermediate-objects boilerplate.
I'm running into a scenario where this automatic conversion doesn't work, though. It involves constructing a message with a field that is a map to a message type.

Minimal proto file for the examples below:
```proto
// mollusc.proto
syntax = "proto3";

package mollusc.map.example;

message Mollusc {
  map<string, Cephalopod> cephalopods = 1;
};

message Coleoid {
  Cephalopod cephalopod = 1;
};

message Gastropod {
  map<string, string> gastropods = 1;
};

message Cephalopod {
  string common_name = 1;
};
```

Generating the py library works fine:
```shell
$ protoc mollusc.proto --python_out=.
```

In an interactive python session (and in non-interactive code as well) the following works fine:
```py
import mollusc_pb2

squid = mollusc_pb2.Cephalopod(common_name="squid")
mollusc_pb2.Mollusc(cephalopods={"teuthida":squid})
```
and it generates a proto message with the following representation:

```shell
cephalopods {
  key: "teuthida"
  value {
    common_name: "squid"
  }
}
```

So far so good. The problem occurs when I try to bypass the temporary object by passing in a dict to the higher-level type's keyword param:
```py
mollusc_pb2.Mollusc(cephalopods={"teuthida":{"common_name":"squid"}})
```
generates the following error:
```shell
TypeError: Parameter to MergeFrom() must be instance of same class: expected mollusc.map.example.Cephalopod got dict.
```

Passing in a dictionary as a keyword param works to create a singleton attribute (i.e. constructing a `Coleoid` from a dictionary works fine), and passing in a dictionary works for a message attribute that's a map from a primitive type to a primitive type (i.e. constructing a `Gastropod` from a dictionary also works fine).
The problem seems to be the map construction when the value type is not a primitive.

Is this a known limitation of protobuf in Python? Is there a workaround that means I don't have to construct an intermediate object? I haven't seen anything in the mailing list or issues that seems to match this particular problem.

My particular use case involves auto-generated code that constructs protobuf messages; being forced to use intermediate objects would severely complicate generation due to naming and message type awareness

nodes.body:
It is not limit for message map, this is limit for nested messages, repeated message field and message map field. The correct way to do the construction should give the message instead like:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/internal/reflection_test.py#L165

For map field you can take this test as an example:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/internal/message_test.py#L2278

title: 3.9+ C# lack of backward compatibility with extensions
body:
Version: v3.10
Language: C#
OS: Windows/Linux
Runtime: .NET Core 2.1

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Generate and compile a proto **which has extensions in it** to C# using version 3.8 or earlier, or use Grpc.Tools (which is submoduled to 3.x of this repo).
2. Use the new DLL in a C# project which uses a reference to 3.9 or later of Google.Protobuf. Note again, this can actually be done from the *same* project if you use Grpc.Tools to compile, and Google.Protobuf v3.9+ as a reference.
3. Note exception when running and any code that will trigger the static initializer on the generated class(es).

**What did you expect to see**
No exception

**What did you see instead?**
A static initializer error reading the descriptor.
```
Index was outside the bounds of the array.
   at Google.Protobuf.Reflection.ExtensionCollection.<>c__DisplayClass2_0.<.ctor>b__0(FieldDescriptorProto extension, Int32 i) in T:\src\github\protobuf\csharp\src\Google.Protobuf\Reflection\ExtensionCollection.cs:line 51
   at Google.Protobuf.Reflection.DescriptorUtil.ConvertAndMakeReadOnly[TInput,TOutput](IList`1 input, IndexedConverter`2 converter) in T:\src\github\protobuf\csharp\src\Google.Protobuf\Reflection\DescriptorUtil.cs:line 59
   at Google.Protobuf.Reflection.ExtensionCollection..ctor(FileDescriptor file, Extension[] extensions) in T:\src\github\protobuf\csharp\src\Google.Protobuf\Reflection\ExtensionCollection.cs:line 49
   at Google.Protobuf.Reflection.FileDescriptor..ctor(ByteString descriptorData, FileDescriptorProto proto, IEnumerable`1 dependencies, DescriptorPool pool, Boolean allowUnknownDependencies, GeneratedClrTypeInfo generatedCodeInfo) in T:\src\github\protobuf\csharp\src\Google.Protobuf\Reflection\FileDescriptor.cs:line 87
   at Google.Protobuf.Reflection.FileDescriptor.BuildFrom(ByteString descriptorData, FileDescriptorProto proto, FileDescriptor[] dependencies, Boolean allowUnknownDependencies, GeneratedClrTypeInfo generatedCodeInfo) in T:\src\github\protobuf\csharp\src\Google.Protobuf\Reflection\FileDescriptor.cs:line 344
   at Google.Protobuf.Reflection.FileDescriptor.FromGeneratedCode(Byte[] descriptorData, FileDescriptor[] dependencies, GeneratedClrTypeInfo generatedCodeInfo) in T:\src\github\protobuf\csharp\src\Google.Protobuf\Reflection\FileDescriptor.cs:line 385
   at redacted
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
This comes from here:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/Reflection/ExtensionCollection.cs#L56 where it looks like **closure over `extensions` makes the poor assumption that `message.Proto.Extension` will have the same length**.

v3.9 added extensions into the generated code as seen [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/csharp/csharp_reflection_class.cc#L211).  However older code generated without this GeneratedClrType constructor overload fails at the static initializer reading the Descriptor as it isn't aware of the extensions.

This is also very related to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5957 which seems to indicate that this type of compatibility will be marked by an API version, referenced [here](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/src/csharp/Grpc.Tools/build/_protobuf/Google.Protobuf.Tools.props#L7).

Also opened https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/20557 in the Grpc project to start a discussion about updating the version of protoc submoduled there.

title: to_h generates non-intuitive hash for wrapper types (StringValue, Int32Value, etc)
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Ruby.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

The primitive types in Protobuf are non-intuitive to use because of the wrapping primitive value types. There are two areas of impact:
1) When creating message objects from a hash. The caller has to understand that the primitive types must be assigned `{ value: <value> }` rather than the value itself.
2) When converting message objects to a hash. The downstream users of the hash must understand that every primitive type will have the structure `{ value: <value> }`


For example, consider the following message object
```proto
message Customer {
  google.protobuf.StringValue name = 1;
}
```
It requires a value specification on instantiation: 
```ruby
customer = Customer.new(
  name: { value: "Paul" }
)
```
And requires an understanding of the nested value attribute on `to_h`:
```ruby
customer.to_h # { name: { value: "Paul" } }
```

For these primitive types, the underlying implementation is leaking into the callers of the gem API causing dependent code to be more complex.


**Describe the solution you'd like**

Have these primitive types treated in such a way so that the caller only ever has to deal with the "true" ruby hash structure. No more "{ value: <value> }".

With the example above, it looks like this.
```ruby
customer = Customer.new(
  name: "Paul"
)
customer.to_h # { name: "Paul" }
```

**Benefits**:
- callers don't have to know about the underlying nested value attribute
- the API becomes more intuitive, since the input and output hashes can be structured like normal Ruby hashes.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

None.

cc @TeBoring @thomasvl @acozzette @tobi @sirupsen

nodes.body:
+1. The problem I'm running into is that in our codebase I see people doing a lot of:

```ruby
JSON.load(message.to_json)
```

to get the effect of "convert to a Hash but make strings just be strings, not `{value: "the string"}`"

This is bad for it's own reasons: it means that things like #6251 come into play. Since people aren't using the protobuf-specific JSON decoder, an int64 can turn into a string by round tripping through `JSON.load` (while with `.to_h` it's still a Ruby `Integer` arbitrary-precision object).

I would love to either make `to_hash` flatten messages for which `is_wrapper` is `true` into just the wrapped value itself, or to have a separate method like `to_hash_no_wrapped` (or an optional argument, etc.) that has this behavior.

Wrapper types are now deprecated in favor of true `optional` fields: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1606#issuecomment-618687169 True `optional` fields have the desired behavior.

The behavior change requested in this bug would be a backward-incompatible change now. Since true `optional` fields give the desired behavior, I think we are unlikely to change the behavior of the wrapper types now.

But the problem we are now experiencing is due to the problem of yang and proto3. In the yang file, the dash is allowed to be named, but we will support the data table of yang to support protobuf. module {

The issue with multithreading isn't writing messages on multiple threads, it's writing a message on one thread *while another thread* is mutating it.

For example we have on one thread:
```cs
void ToByteArray(this IMessage message)
{
    var length = message.CalculateSize();
```
but on another thread with the same message passed to `ToByteArray`:
```cs
message.Int32Value = 128; // if this was <127, the size of the message is increased by 1
```
and continuing on the first thread:
```cs
var array = new byte[length]; // the original length before the 2nd thread mutated the message and increased it's size
var output = new CodedOutputStream(array);
message.WriteTo(output);
```

title: C# protoc.exe: Support --csharp_namespace command line option
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Code generator for C# (protoc.exe)

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Today we can define a custom C# namespace for the generated code within the proto file.
```proto
option csharp_namespace = "My.Namespace";
```
I get proto files from another team (C++ technology stack) so this option is not set. I would prefer to take the original proto files without adapting them.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like to pass the option as command line parameter to protoc.exe:
```
protoc.exe --csharp_namespace="My.Namespace"
```

If both variants set the `csharp_namespace` then I would prefer that the command line option wins.

nodes.body: i want this  command line option too,so i dont need to modify the original proto files and add "option csharp_namespace = "My.Namespace"" to every single file ,it is horrible.

I don't think this option is useful. The C++ stack should jut add the `option csharp_namespace = "My.Namespace";` to their .proto files, or (or that's for some reason not possible) you should just patch the .proto files as you import them into your C# project.
Also, the introducing a new option is not a good solution because it cannot accommodate the case when multiple .proto files as being processed by a single `protoc` invocation` (which is quite common). It can also create incompatibilities (different projects could override the cmdline option with different values).

@jtattermusch I would see this as a feature and not an incompatibility:
> It can also create incompatibilities (different projects could override the cmdline option with different values).

Our .proto files provided by the C++ "server" team is used by multiple "client" teams (C#). The client teams are independent of each other. Every client team generates their own C# classes out of the .proto files with different settings (e.g. Namespace) and different Google.Protobuf library version.

---

I still believe that it can be a useful option. I agree that it does not work when a single `protoc` call processes multiple .proto files.

**Alternative solution** would be to specify a base namespace: 
`--csharp_basenamespace="My.Namespace"`

This might be confusing as there is already the [CLI option](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/csharp-generated#compiler_options) `--csharp_opt=base_namespace=Example`.  This creates a directory hierarchy for the generated source code. But it does not change the "base" namespace as some might expect.

I just came across this issue. I thought the `--csharp_opt=base_namespace=Example` did what this request is asking for and wasted a lot of time trying to figure out why it was not working.

I also don't see

> not a good solution because it cannot accommodate the case when multiple .proto files as being processed by a single protoc invocation` 

as a good reason not to do this. Teams that need this option will be making protoc multiple invocations if they need to for the different "batches" of .proto files that may need separate handlinh. 

This feature is even more useful in open source development where the client libraries may be written by groups who wish to namespace different based on their project names.

Missing this option leads to the problem that if you're developing and add tests for a library that generates a grpc client using Internal access level you're generating a ton of warnings when you generate the gRPC message types also for the mocked server.

> Missing this option leads to the problem that if you're developing and add tests for a library that generates a grpc client using Internal access level you're generating a ton of warnings when you generate the gRPC message types also for the mocked server.

This. Lack of that option leads to numerous issues when developing projects, which are testing the main service, and you share .proto files across various projects. As you need to create both client and server types while referencing the main service, you get tons of warnings related to namespace collision and imports must fallback to one of the types.

title: Question: How to parse .proto file into a FileDescriptor in C#
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
C#

After trying for a long time I cannot figure out how to read an existing `.proto` file and get a `FileDescriptor` from it (i.e. I need to process the proto metadata in C#). `FileDescriptor.BuildFromByteStrings` seems to take a different binary format and not the plaintext .proto contents as UTF8 byte array. I think this must be super simple to do but I can't find the API to do so.

nodes.body: There is no API to do so since it's done by `protoc`. Why do you need to parse a `.proto` file in the first place?

Because I want to read .proto files (mainly grpc service description files) into a C# model and then do analysis on it, render a UI (like Swagger UI) etc. 

So if I understand it correctly, if i want to do that in C# I need to write my own .proto file parser?

That *or* you could jump into C++/CLI and use the compiler API from libprotobuf. Then after parsing the files you can serialize them (as FileDescriptor byte strings), send them to C#, and deserialize the byte strings in the normal `FileDescriptor.BuildFromByteStrings` API.
Do you know an article/docs describing how to do that? Or at least show what C++/CLI methods/commands to use?

I’ve decided to use this F# library to parse .proto files in c#:
https://github.com/ctaggart/froto

Seems to be working for my use case but still investigating.

A bit late now, but protobuf-net.Reflection can do this for you (100% managed code - it does *not* wrap `protoc`) - a full example is shown here: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62575156/how-to-parse-proto-file-into-a-filedescriptor-in-c/62579246#62579246

(this is actually the parser that I use on https://protogen.marcgravell.com, which now runs in the browser via Blazor)
seems answered

title: JS: message class should allow all fields to be populated in one statement
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Javascript

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Whenever I need to create and populate a new message, I need to do something like this:

```js
const result = new OperationResult()
result.setOk(true)
result.setStatus(201)
result.setMessage('TODO created successfully')
result.setInfo(todo.getId())
```

This is annoying as it makes code less readable and harder to write.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
There should be a way to populate a new message without having to make each call individually

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
1) Return the instance of the message from `set` methods, allowing chaining like this:

```js
const result = new OperationResult()
  .setOk(true)
  .setStatus(201)
  .setMessage('TODO created successfully')
  .setInfo(todo.getId())
```
2) Have a constructor wich receives the values and populates them into the message like so:
```js
const result = new OperationResult(true, 201, 'TODO created successfully', todo.getId())
```
3) Have a `.populate()` or `.setFields()` method wich receives an object and populates the message as follows:
```js
const result = new OperationResult().populate({
  ok: true,
  status: 201,
  message: 'TODO created successfully',
  info: todo.getId()
})
```

**Additional context**
There's been a short discussion about this kind of thing for generated C++  code on [#562](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/562), but it was closed. I believe the reason for closing that issue does not apply here, since chaining is a very common pattern for Javascript, and, even if it wasn't, there are other ways of solving the problem.

I would love to make a PR for this, but I'd need for someone to point me on the right direction, since I couldn't quite get how stuff work just by reading the code and comments.

nodes.body: `.populate` method would be awesome!

Alternative 1 -- fluent interface -- is a common pattern for builders across languages and should be interesting having it on JS as well.

I'm not in favor of Alternative 2 since it goes against the common sense pattern that we should avoid too many arguments on constructors (or any function for that mater). Also it's terrible for legibility and clarity of code.

But if you combine Alternative 2 with Alternative 3, IMO seems to be a sweet spot for JS:

```js
const result = new OperationResult({
  ok: true,
  status: 201,
  message: 'TODO created successfully',
  info: todo.getId()
})
```

I upgraded to package `3.11.1` today and the ability to chain setters is apparently supported:

```

undefined

{ wrappers_: null,

  arrayIndexOffset_: -1,
  array: [ 'CAD', 'Canadian' ],

>
```

I can confirm this didn't work with `3.9.2` but am not sure if it was added in `3.10`. I don't see anything in the release notes for this feature, but I'm happy none-the-less.

title: use_default_shell_env leads to spurious rebuilds
body:
**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

#2933 introduced a workaround for bazelbuild/bazel#2515. This workaround consists in weakening the hermeticity of the protobuf component of any user's build, by allowing protobuf to depend on `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` and other environment variables set externally to the build. The problem is that this leads to more frequent rebuilds of all of protobuf. Anytime the `PATH` or other environment variable changes (which on some systems can happen very frequently), the build cache is invalidated. Since protobuf is a very common dependency very deep in the dependency tree, rebuilding protobuf will affect many users many times. On my team, protobuf rebuilds have become the one thing Bazel is infamous for.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Revert #2933. I would argue that setting the right environment variables should be a matter for the toolchain configuration, and that toolchains should otherwise be hermetic. This would lead to far fewer cache invalidations anytime the state of the host environment changes.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

An alternative would be to pass through only some variables from the environment, say `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, but not `PATH`. However, this only partially solves the problem above.

title: JavaScript: some float values are serialized into IEEE 754 binary representation incorrectly
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.9.0 (also reproduces on master).
Language: Javascript / Typescript

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10 (1709).

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Typescript 3.6.2, Python 3.7.2 

**What did you do?**
1. Create a message with a float field:
```
message Test
{
  float a = 1;
}
```
2. Generate Javascript code for the message definition.
3. Create an instance of the message, set a value to 0.9999999762949594.
4. Serialize message into buffer - IEEE 754 binary representation of the value will be wrong.

In actual application I experienced this issue as value 0.9999999762949594 was first serialized and then deserialized as 0.5 (!).

**What did you expect to see**
The value is serialized as 0x00, 0x00, 0x80, 0x3F

**What did you see instead?**
The value is serialized as 0x00, 0x00, **0x00**, 0x3F

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
I made investigation of the issue and seems that there is a bug with values close to power of 2.
Function with the bug: [jspb.utils.splitFloat32](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/js/binary/utils.js#L159).
Line of code with the bug: `mant = Math.round(mant * jspb.BinaryConstants.TWO_TO_23) & 0x7FFFFF` [LoC](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/js/binary/utils.js#L204)

Several test cases were added by me into protobuf/js/binary/utils_test.js and tests started failing.
Reason: for some input values mantissa is rounded to a value 0x1000000 and then truncated with a mask 0x7FFFFF => resulting in zero mantissa. In this case we probably have to increase exponent value by 1.

I tried two potential fixes - first is based on the current implementation, second is based on ArrayBuffer/DataView to check my first implementation.

Diff with my tests & suggested fix is attached to this issue: [Fix.zip](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/3847232/Fix.zip)

title: input proto file is not found if --descriptor_set_in is given
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.10.1
Language: any/none

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Ubuntu 16.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
g++ 7.4.0

**What did you do?**

```
$ protoc --descriptor_set_out=base.descriptor base.proto   # works fine
$ protoc --descriptor_set_in=base.descriptor --descriptor_set_out=derived.descriptor derived.proto  # fails: derived.proto: No such file or directory
```

Context:

I have two `.proto` files: `base.proto` and `derived.proto`. `base.proto` is self-contained. `derived.proto` imports `base.proto`. When compiling `derived.proto`, I'm trying to provide `base.proto` as a precompiled `FileDescriptorSet` via `--descriptor_set_in`, but then the source `derived.proto` is not found. I believe this is incorrect? (I'm guessing that if `--descriptor_set_in` is given, all inputs are resolved in the given `FileDescriptorSet`s, which I believe is incorrect)

Note that without `--descriptor_set_in`, the source `derived.proto` is found (as is the dependency `base.proto`, imported from source from current directory).

```
$ protoc --descriptor_set_out=derived.descriptor derived.proto   # works fine
```

**What did you expect to see**

`derived.descriptor` -  the result of compiling `derived.proto` to `FileDescriptorSet` binary proto

**What did you see instead?**

```
derived.proto: No such file or directory
```

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body:
As I understand it, `--descriptor_set_in` must contain a colon delimited list of **all** descriptors for the transitive closure of the proto files you wish to generate, including `derived.proto` in your example.

For your example, I'm guessing that `base.descriptor` doesn't contain the descriptor for `derived.proto`.

Said another way, if you use `--descriptor_set_in`, protoc will only lookup descriptors from the `--descriptor_set_in` flag. protoc will not build descriptors from the target proto files to generate. The target proto, `derived.proto`, is only used to decide which proto files to generate from the set of descriptors.

To fix your example (untested):

    protoc --descriptor_set_in=base.descriptor:derived.descriptor \
        --descriptor_set_out=derived.descriptor \
        derived.proto

title: C++: Built-In JSON Serialization is Extremely Slow
body:
In the system I work on, we weren't aware of the provided protobuf to json facilities (or they didn't exist so many years ago) and so we built our own protobuf to json conversion that is based on protobuf reflection + rapidjson for the json encoding/serialization. It appears that the provided protobuf to json conversion facility is much slower than our approach.

Here are the median numbers in seconds for 10 runs [1] of serializing a large message:

SerializeAsString: 1.99 seconds
MessageToJsonString: 24.24 seconds
To json via our reflection-based approach: 4.33 seconds

So the built-in facility for protobuf message to serialized json takes 460% longer than our approach, which you can find here:

https://github.com/apache/mesos/blob/1.9.0/3rdparty/stout/include/stout/protobuf.hpp#L810-L1042
Which leverages https://github.com/apache/mesos/blob/1.9.0/3rdparty/stout/include/stout/jsonify.hpp

Is this expected? It seems the protobuf built in facility, at least for going from message to serialized json, is extremely slow and can be much faster.

I suppose another technique that would be even faster than our approach would be for the json serialization logic to be generated by the protobuf compiler on a per message basis (much like protobuf serialization is generated), allowing reflection to be avoided entirely.

Would love to hear any thoughts on comments on this topic.

nodes.body:
It looks like 3.11.0 introduced something that really slowed down the JSON parsing in C++
If you use 3.10.1, the performance is great.
I'll add a "me too" to this.  Our JSON parser has gone from about 200ms in 3.10 to 20-odd minutes in 3.11.  Size of JSON is about 15MB.

For JSON parsing in C++ the slowdown appears to be caused by the addition of StringPiece in JsonStreamParser::GetNextTokenType in #6634. HasPrefixString is called three times which takes std::string as arguments causing the StringPiece to allocate new std::string for each call which is slow for large strings and there are a lot of calls to GetNextTokenType. Changing to StringPiece::starts_with instead of HasPrefixString regains almost all of the lost performance and I believe should be the same comparison.
It looks like this issue has been fixed in #7230.
doesnt look like #7230 has fixed the MessageToJsonString.  I compared older and newer version, performance looks same to me.

The JSON codec is not designed to be fast; we do not consider JSON to be the canonical encoding format (you should be using the Protobuf wire format if you need performance, since that's where we focus all of our cycles into).

body:
**What language does this apply to?**
PHP - Non-C extension but may relate to this too.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I am using the [Google Ads PHP API](https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-php) to build a report, the schema for the report is flexible. Currently the only way to pull the relevant data from a request is to use getters on the individual rows.

This is the row I'm describing: https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-php/blob/master/src/Google/Ads/GoogleAds/V2/Services/GoogleAdsRow.php

There are hundreds of properties, which then have sub-propeties as part of the proto, which makes it very challenging to determine which getters contain data, and which are not a part of the request response.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I'd like the ability to run something like this to get a basic keyed array of the data returned:
$message->toArray();

In addition, some values are not appropriately typed, and, for example, Enum's just return the INT value - it is not possible to detect whether a return value (example $googleAdsRow->getCampaign()->getStatus()->getValue()) is an Enum or not.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I considered using Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message::serializeToJsonString() to serialize the row, however the performance is incredibly slow (0.5 seconds for ~400 rows of data, vs. 0.004 seconds when manually using getters).

nodes.body: I don't understand the motivation here. Do you want a compact debug string for manually viewing what is in the row? Or do you want to programmatically iterate over the response, field by field?

I want the data in a PHP array format (or JSON would be fine, if the overhead was reduced) - essentially the full record in a format that can then be used with typical array access methods. Essentially my use case (back in September) was to output the data response from the Google Ads API, for each row to allow for non-defined schema to be output to the end user.

For example, if I create a report in Google Ads, and receive a response there is (was, things may have changed since I wrote this message) currently no (efficient) method to expose that data to the end user without utilising the getters to pull the information - but that requires knowing, in advance, the data that you want to extract - if that makes sense.
I think this request is pretty specific to the use case and can't be solved generally. I would recommend that you look into writing this yourself and reach out if there's any specific help you need.

title: What is the reason for not allow setting null to string field in proto2?
body:
Currently, if a field is string type, the setXXX method doesn't take null.

For C generated code, it has the following check in setXXX(const char* value) method:
`   GOOGLE_DCHECK(value != nullptr);`

For Java, it has 
`         if (value == null) { throw new NullPointerException(); } `

For C#, it has
`         name_ = pb::ProtoPreconditions.CheckNotNull(value, "value");`

This is very annoying, as I need to check if a string is null or not, before assign to protobuf object. Failed to do so will result runtime exception.


C# example to handle this:
` if (name == null) { obj.ClearName(); } else { obj.Name = name; }`

Why don't we just treat it similar to message type, set it to null is the same as calling ClearXX method?
I don't see any downside of this approach. Easier for developer (no need to handle null) and doesn't cause any confusion.

nodes.body: Agree 100%, there is no good reason to throw NullPointerException.  Either get rid of newBuilder() and stop pretending to support the Fluent Builder pattern or implement a simple one line fix.  This issue is a major reason for me not to use Protobufs and go back to using JSON.
Also agree with this! happens in proto 3 as well..
So far I haven't found any reason why this should behave this way, nonsense...

Is there any reason you couldn't use clear_*()?
```
void clear_foo(): Clears the value of the field. After calling this, has_foo() will return false and foo() will return the default value.
```
source: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp-generated#string

If you have more questions, please open a thread at our mailing list. Thanks!

nodes.body: @jtattermusch @ObsidianMinor could you please take a look?

I've came across this one as well. But my understanding is that other language protobuf implementations do not allow adding duplicate extensions for a specific type:

- python: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2228af689f5ff4d929c85079025c49f6945b136a/python/google/protobuf/descriptor_pool.py#L319

- go: https://github.com/golang/protobuf/blob/e91709a02e0e8ff8b86b7aa913fdc9ae9498e825/proto/extensions.go#L549

which means that proto files acceptable in c# will not work in python/go/etc

> I've came across this one as well. But my understanding is that other language protobuf implementations do not allow adding duplicate extensions for a specific type:
> 
> * python: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2228af689f5ff4d929c85079025c49f6945b136a/python/google/protobuf/descriptor_pool.py#L319
> * go: https://github.com/golang/protobuf/blob/e91709a02e0e8ff8b86b7aa913fdc9ae9498e825/proto/extensions.go#L549
> 
> which means that proto files acceptable in c# will not work in python/go/etc

Correct me if I'm wrong but this issue is not about trying to add an extension to the same type twice. It's about adding an extension with the same field number to two different types
(e.g. message1 adds extension with field number 123 and message2 adds extension with field number 123 - which AFAIK is allowed).

title: Protobuf is compiled with -g -O2 despite what configure.ac claims
body:
By default, protobuf is compiled with `-O2 -g`, even though `configure.ac` claims it shouldn't be:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/a9f390f44e3d138e1e94fd17046f865517b3b62d/configure.ac#L39-L44

I'm building latest `master` as follows:

```
./autogen.sh
./configure
make
```

Here's a sample compiler invocation during the build:

```
/Library/Developer/CommandLineTools/usr/bin/clang++ -DHAVE_CONFIG_H -I. -I..
  -pthread -DHAVE_PTHREAD=1 -DHAVE_ZLIB=1 -Wall -Wno-sign-compare
  -O2 -g -std=c++11 -DNDEBUG -MT google/protobuf/generated_enum_util.lo -MD -MP
  -MF google/protobuf/.deps/generated_enum_util.Tpo 
  -c google/protobuf/generated_enum_util.cc 
  -fno-common -DPIC -o google/protobuf/.libs/generated_enum_util.o
```

What would be the best way to compile protobuf without `-g`? This would help a lot with https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs/issues/73919.

nodes.body:
Turns out there is some bit of code which has an opposite intention:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/3be9322e28dfcacdb669f646f76fe833fa274107/configure.ac#L85-L101
I'm not aware of what is considered the best practice for handling debug/release builds in autotools, but it seems like, in the case of protobuf, downstream needs to explicitly set CXXFLAGS to achieve a full release build without "-g" option everywhere and with "-O2" on clang.

MethodDescriptor.CustomOptions no longer works in 3.11.0-rc2 (when old generated code is used)
body:
I want to get custom options off a `MethodDescriptor`. Specifically I want to get `HttpRule` which is from Google.Api.CommonProtos 1.7.0. In Google.Protobuf 3.8.0 I can successfully get this option by doing this:

```cs
const int HttpRuleFieldId = 72295728;
var success = methodDescriptor.CustomOptions.TryGetMessage<HttpRule>(HttpRuleFieldId, out httpRule);
```

With Google.Protobuf 3.9.0 and 3.10.0 `CustomOptions.TryGetMessage<T>` errors, I believe related to this issue: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/6824

When I updated to 3.11.0-rc2 `CustomOptions.TryGetMessage<T>` no longer errors, but it also doesn't return a value. You should fix that for backwards compatibility.

I see that CustomOptions has been made obsolete. How do I use the new API?

```cs
const int HttpRuleFieldId = 72295728;
const uint TagId = 0; // what is this?

var extension = new Extension<Google.Protobuf.Reflection.MethodOptions, HttpRule>(HttpRuleFieldId, FieldCodec.ForMessage<HttpRule>(TagId, HttpRule.Parser));
var httpRule = methodDescriptor.GetOption<HttpRule>(extension); // returns null
```

nodes.body: Actually, wait. Are you loading descriptors dynamically in this case @JamesNK?

Oh I see. In this case you're mixing generated code from different versions. The code from gax-dotnet is using another previous version of code-gen while you're using a future version Google.Protobuf that's expecting you to have extension identifiers generated.
I keep forgetting, is this kind of setup supported @jtattermusch?

Would a solution be to generate code from `annotations.proto` and `http.proto` myself, with the type visibility internal (can you do that? It would avoid type conflicts with anyone who is using Google.Api.CommonProtos) and include that code in my project?
Yes that'd work. All you need is the `internal_access` csharp option when generating code.

Hmm, but it won't work because `Google.Api.AnnotationsReflection.Descriptor` needs to be public because it is referenced as a dependency by the generated service.

And making the types public could easy create conflicts with anyone who is referencing Google.Api.CommonProtos.

You either need to do:
1. Update Google.Api.CommonProtos to have new generated code
2. Make `CustomOptions.TryGetMessage<T>` work again in 3.11.0
3. Support GetOption with mixed generated code versions

Right now I don't see a way for this to work.

I'll probably just fix `CustomOptions` for instances like this, so `GetOption` will only work with code that already has extension identifiers. We can include it in the next patch release with #6938 and #6674 and any other issues that come up in the meantime.
When will the next patch release be?
No idea, you'd have to ask @rafi-kamal.
We are going to do a new release as soon as all the RC2 issues are fixed. I think this one and https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/6936 are the only one that need to be fixed.
What's the state of this issue? I tested the latest package - 3.11.2 - and it is still broken.
Looks like the fix didn't make into the final release. Unfortunately we don't have any ETA for the next release at this moment.

All I need to finish #7005 up is write some sort of tests for it. I'm going to write a quick and easy version using a slightly modified version of `unittest_custom_options_proto3.proto` and later I think I can come back and overhaul tests a bit further to make sure issues like this are caught ahead of time in the future.
#6936 isn't released yet either. (Just taking advantage of it being mentioned in this issue earlier)
Would be any release soon to fix this issue?
HI all.  I have been watching this issue for the past few months as we are rely on the custom options.  Is there any update?

> HI all. I have been watching this issue for the past few months as we are rely on the custom options. Is there any update?

Actually, I think CustomOptions would just work fine for you if you use the latest version or both the generated code and the runtime - AFAIK the problem in this issue was that CustomOptions didn't work if you had a new protobuf runtime, but an old version of the generated code. (The unmerged PR #7005 actually attempts to fix only the scenario where you have old generated code an a new runtime - everything else should work).

Also, you can use the extensions API instead of relying on CustomOptions.

I just closed the long standing PR #7005 which was an attempt to fix this. 
This is only a problem that exhibits itself when a new runtime is used with old generated code (pre 3.11.)
- the 3.11 release is quite old now and there's been several releases since
- in the meantime, there's been significant changes to the generated code (the new Span-based serialization and deserialization), so regenerating the generated code is really recommended regardless of this issue (even though it's strictly speaking not necessary).

With new generated code, there should be an extension identifier named `ProtocommonExtensions.EnumPrettyName`. Using that you can call the new extension API like so:

```cs
var customValue = edv.GetOptions()?.GetExtension(ProtocommonExtensions.EnumPrettyName) ?? default;
```

@ObsidianMinor   Thanks!  Thats a much cleaner way to do it.  Appreciate the help!

Ernie

title: Add GeneratedCodeAttribute to generated classes in C#
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Generated code in C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Code analysis tools use different ways to tell if they need or not to analyse the code. At the moment there is no metadata that would allow such tool to detect that the code is generated instead of user typed. This could lead to auto fixes applied to the generated files.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Tagging the generated classes with [GeneratedCodeAttribute](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.codedom.compiler.generatedcodeattribute?view=netframework-4.8) should help telling VS Code analysis and third party tools to ignore the generated code.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

At first, I considered the attribute [CompilerGeneratedAttribute](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.compilerservices.compilergeneratedattribute?view=netframework-4.8) , but this one is reserved by the .NET compiler as far as I understand.

**Additional context**

[Visual Studio docs](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/code-quality/in-source-suppression-overview?view=vs-2019#generated-code) suggests to use this Attribute for generated code.

title: Allow printing messages to an Appendable in single-line format
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Java.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

I would like to print message objects to a user-supplied `StringBuilder` in the [single-line format](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/e6c5a3b57d20384775950c4f85310e82a4f7a69b/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.java#L727-L729).

Currently only [multi-line format](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/e6c5a3b57d20384775950c4f85310e82a4f7a69b/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.java#L723-L725) is available if I want to supply the `StringBuilder`:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/e6c5a3b57d20384775950c4f85310e82a4f7a69b/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.java#L328-L335

The single-line format is only available in methods that return `String` and use new `StringBuilder`:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/e6c5a3b57d20384775950c4f85310e82a4f7a69b/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.java#L536-L548

I would like to avoid the memory allocations for this internal `StringBuilder`, as well as the returned `String`.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Add `print`-like method(s) to `Printer` that take `Appendable` and use the single-line format, along the lines of:

```
public void printShortDebug(final MessageOrBuilder message, final Appendable output) throws IOException {
  print(message, singleLineOutput(output));
}

public void printShortDebug(final UnknownFieldSet fields, final Appendable output) throws IOException {
  printUnknownFields(fields, singleLineOutput(output));
}
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Printing to `StringBuilder` and replacing newlines/indents achieves the same effect at a performance penalty.

title: Ruby precision wrong in Float fields
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: google-protobuf (3.11.0 universal-darwin, 3.6.1 universal-darwin)
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
MacOS Mojave 10.14.6 (18G103)

**What did you do?**

```ruby
require 'google/protobuf'
  
Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_message "google.test.Float" do
    optional :floating_value, :float, 1
  end
end

Float = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("google.test.Float").msgclass

f = Float.new
f.floating_value = 2.3
p f.floating_value #=> 2.299999952316284
```

I've seen that ruby float precision is a recurring issue of protobuf:
* https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4406
* https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4569
* https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2881

This error renders the `float` type useless in ruby.
We're going to change all the floats to strings. 

Wondering if anyone else had issues with the ruby or any other language implementation.

nodes.body:
This is working as intended.

A `float` field in protobuf is a single-precision floating point value. The Ruby `Float` type uses double-precision floating point. When you convert a double-precision floating point value to single precision, there is going to be some loss of precision.

If you want to preserve the full precision of a Ruby `Float`, use `double` in protobuf, not `float`.

Here are some example calls that I tried:

Even if I chose a wrong path or mistyped plugin name protoc does not show an error.

Exit status of all commands are 0.

But on general protoc given me an error if I miss a parameter in e.x.
```console
$ ▲ Desktop/test/example protoc --plugins=protoc-gen-debug -I proto --php_out=src/ proto/user.proto
Unknown flag: --plugins
$ △ Desktop/test/example echo $?
1
```

What I did wrong?
Thanks for helping.

Below you find more information.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: libprotoc 3.11.0 from Cellar Homebrew [Formula](https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/blob/master/Formula/protobuf.rb)
Language: Any (currently php and go)

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
MacOS Catalina 10.15.1

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
autoconf (GNU Autoconf) 2.69
automake (GNU automake) 1.16.1
Apple clang version 11.0.0 (clang-1100.0.33.12)
Python 3.7.5
Xcode 11.2.1 Build version 11B500

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a simple Plugin "protoc-gen-debug" with execute flag.
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3

import sys
import itertools
import json

from google.protobuf.compiler import plugin_pb2 as plugin
from google.protobuf.descriptor_pb2 import DescriptorProto, EnumDescriptorProto
...
if __name__ == '__main__':
if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.stderr.write('Compiling...')

    f = open('/Users/chrepl/Desktop/test/example/test.json','w+')
    f.write(json.dumps({'whatswrong':'withyou'}))
    f.close()
    
    data = sys.stdin.read()
    request = plugin.CodeGeneratorRequest()
    request.ParseFromString(data)
    response = plugin.CodeGeneratorResponse()
    generate_code(request, response)
    output = response.SerializeToString()
    sys.stdout.write(output)
...
```
2. Call the plugin on the command line more examples you find above:
```console
$ ▲ Desktop/test/example protoc --plugin=protoc-gen-debug -I proto --php_out=src/ proto/user.proto
$ ▲ Desktop/test/example protoc --plugin=protoc-gen-debug -I proto --go_out=src/ proto/user.proto
$ ▲ Desktop/test/example protoc --plugin=protoc-gen-debug.py -I proto --go_out=src/ proto/user.proto
```

**What did you expect to see**
A message "Compiling...." and a file "test.json".

**What did you see instead?**
Nothing.

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).
No errors.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

title: Java Performance regression since 3.8.0
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.8.0-3.11.0
Language: Java

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
protoc and jvm 1.8

Between version 3.7.1 and version 3.8.0, the implementation of `CodedOutputStream.writeInt32NoTag` (and possibly other functions) has changed. The new implementation is 6x slower according to two microbenchmarks:

| Function     | 3.5.1    | 3.7.1    | 3.8.0     | 3.9.2     | 3.10.0      | 3.11.0      |
| :----------- | -------: |-------:  | --------: | --------: | ----------: | ----------: |
| message3     | 15.48 ns | 15.55 ns | 30.91 ns  | 30.81 ns  | 30.95 ns    | 30.97 ns    |
| int32s       | 46.23 ns | 46.32 ns | 298.87 ns | 299.07 ns | 299.27ns    | 299.05 ns   |

The function `message3` calls `toByteArray` on a message with 3 `int32s`. It becomes 2x slower after 3.7.1

The function `int32s`  serializes 100 integers into a CodedOutputStream. It exercises directly the impacted code path and therefore gets ~6.5 times slower after 3.7.1.

Benchmarks project: https://github.com/thesamet/protobuf-issue-6977
Code: https://github.com/thesamet/protobuf-issue-6977/blob/master/src/main/scala/Test.scala

Thanks for the benchmark. We don't use or support Scala. I'm experimenting with reimplementing this in Java so our build system can run it.

The big question here is, as with all optimizations, does it matter? That is, suppose CodedOutputStream.writeInt32NoTag is ten times slower. Does this have any noticeable impact on the performance of anything? E.g. does an app take five seconds longer to start up? Does a batch job complete in a day instead of an hour? Or does a BigQuery cost twice as much to run? Can any significant impact be shown that justifies the effort of improving this? 

Any evidence you have along these lines would be helpful.

title: c# adding an extension to the same type is allowed
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: `3.11.1`
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Ubuntu Linux

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
.net core 3.0

**What did you do?**
Protobuf c# allows adding an extension with the same number to the same type multiple times. Here is an example:

file `a.proto`

```proto
syntax = "proto3";

package pkg1;

import "google/protobuf/descriptor.proto";

extend google.protobuf.FileOptions {
	string version = 50000;
}

option (version) = "1.0.0";

message M1{}
```

file `b.proto`


```proto
syntax = "proto3";

package pkg1;

protobuf implementations do not allow adding duplicate extensions for a specific type:

import "google/protobuf/descriptor.proto";

extend google.protobuf.FileOptions {
	string version = 50000;
}

option (version) = "2.0.0";

message M2{}
```

**What did you expect to see**
I'd expect c# behavior to be consistent with other protobuf implementation and throw some sort of exception on application start or first proto use.

**What did you see instead?**
When building and loading protobuf files in c# apps everything works fine, but trying to consume these proto files in go or python apps leads to errors as those implementation do not allow adding multiple extensions to the same type:

- python: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2228af689f5ff4d929c85079025c49f6945b136a/python/google/protobuf/descriptor_pool.py#L319

- go: https://github.com/golang/protobuf/blob/e91709a02e0e8ff8b86b7aa913fdc9ae9498e825/proto/extensions.go#L549
