title: Instead of using RepeatedField<> use List<> for c#
body:
Hi there,
I have been using protobuf with grpc in c# .net core 3.0 and generating collections as repeatedfield is causing lots of trouble for me, swagger is not generating json because they don't have setters and model binders can't bind to repeated fields. I don't want to create new dto objects, and had trouble creating model binders. Is no one passing these protobuf generated collections to web api controllers. 

If I update to .net core 3.1 model binders bind to RepeatedField if its not readonly. Lack of setter is causing the problems with swagger and model binders. 

Anyone knows the reason why there are no setters?

Thanks.

nodes.body: These fields with no setter make trouble working with GraphQL dotnet.
We (Google) used to have mutable protos. Experience taught us this was a very painful mistake. Immutability is a deliberate feature.

OK, this is C# which I think does use mutable protos for better or worse. I think the issue may be you need to use addFoo rather than setFooList or something like that. Reassigning to @jskeet for triage.

Okay, there are two different requests here:

- The use of `List<T>` instead of `RepeatedField<T>`
- The use of a read-only property instead of having a setter as well

The TL;DR of the above is that I don't think we should change either decision, certainly not in the short term, as both would be breaking changes. We can certainly *consider* changing them in a future version, although I'd be reluctant to do so, personally.

**The use of `RepeatedField<T>`**

By using our own collection type instead of `List<T>`, we are able to put our own validation other other logic in the type. In particular:

- `RepeatedField<T>` does not permit any null elements
- `RepeatedField<T>` overrides `GetHashCode` and `Equals` in specific ways, using specific element equality comparisons

Using just plain `List<T>` would defer all validation to the point of serialization, which I'd prefer not to do - and require the equality/hash checks to be in extension/utility methods - along with all the serialization code which is currently part of `RepeatedField<T>`.

(All of this is also true for `MapField<T>` as well, of course.)

**The property being read-only**

I'll confess I don't remember *all* the reasons I made the property read-only. I do remember that an early prototype that allowed it to be mutable caused problems in all kinds of places... it's possible that some of that may have been related to the later-removed "freezable" feature. 

One *potential* problem with this would be if an instance ever contained any information that had to stay the same beyond just the element type. For example, if in very rare cases we allowed null entries - e.g. a repeated field of a wrapper type. (I believe this was true at one point, but then removed.) With the property being read-only, everything can be certain that the collection itself stays the same, rather than being replaced by a "similar but not quite the same" instance. (The setter could potentially validate this additional state, but that in itself could create some surprising situations, I suspect.)

**Compatibility**

Changing the generated code to use `List<T>` or even an interface would be a breaking change in a fairly obvious way. Code that currently compiles such as:

```csharp
RepeatedField<string> = message.SomeRepeatedStringField;
```

... would be broken by such a change.

Likewise currently code can store a reference to a repeated field from a message object, knowing that any change they make to the collection will still be related to that message object (and only that message object - no other messages will share the same collection). Adding a setter would violate that guarantee, so I'd consider it a breaking change.

**Using protos with JSON**

The challenges of using Swagger and GraphQL aren't *entirely* clear to me, but what I would say is that if you use *any* non-protobuf JSON serializer/parser with protobuf messages, things can easily go wrong. The protobuf JSON code knows exactly what to expect, in terms of the mapping between JSON property names and the C# properties, as well as well-known types such as `Timestamp` and `Duration`.

If you need to integrate with a different JSON framework, I'd strongly recommend building a converter that you can register that basically says "When you need to deserialize a protobuf message, use the protobuf code to do it." It may be somewhat inefficient to do that at the moment in places, but we could talk about that as a very separate issue. But changing the representation of collections to "somewhat" move the needle on other JSON frameworks parsing protobuf JSON *as protobuf message objects* feels like it's just going to lead to further disappointment as soon as you reach something like `Timestamp`.
@erdalsivri: Right, understood. I'll close this as I can't see us changing it - at least not until we're making other major changes - but it *is* good to hear about the impact of various decisions.

Is the option of making other major changes on the table? In particular #9352 (inconsistencies between optional and wrapper types). Between this and that there's some major inconveniences with working with the library, essentially disallowing expressions for constructing protos.

That could be what is mentioned with GraphQL above, I'm not as familiar with that, but I've definitely come across the issue with many things that expect to be able to use expressions to map one type to another. EF being the most inconvenient example. This issue and the other turn a simple `foo.Where(someCondition).Select(x=>new FooProto{...})` into a much more awkward version that has to create intermediate objects simply because protobufs can't safely assign a value to a field.

> Is the option of making other major changes on the table?

*Potentially*, but with a very high bar, basically.
May be worth collecting these with a tag or something rather than closing them outright. Each one individually may not warrant a breaking major version, but enough of them together could.

I agree completely with @Yurunsoft , facing the same weird issue as pointed out by him already in a detailed way via test2.zip

I was also able to reproduce this issue and it was happening for me consistently whenever two similar proto messages with same name and structure belonging to different RPCs get instantiated, in that case the allocation of the latter one fails with out of memory error. This is applicable even when one of the proto message is the subset of other.

Changing the name along with message field names (top to bottom/nested) offered me the workaround for this.
However this is a very tedious workaround and not feasible when this issue is discovered at a later point of time when most of the code might already be live.

Please provide the fix for this, it is an issue with protobuf library.

Looking at the [code](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/php/ext/google/protobuf/php-upb.c#L4661), this issue has to be "fixed" now.
By "fixed" I mean that the test case will now result in "[duplicate symbol](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/php/ext/google/protobuf/php-upb.c#L4607)" error instead of "out of memory", which was definitely not true.

The "duplicate symbol" error is caused by the fact that both grpc1.proto and grpc2.proto from the test.zip above do not have a package defined, so from the point of view of Protocol Buffers both these protocols declare their symbols in global namespace, therefore messages with the same name do indeed clash with each other.

title: Buffer Overflow
body: We have used Protobuf 3.9.0 pod file as per our need. Some VAPT points are mentioned in below picture. Kindly help us asap. **Issue Summary:** The function GPBSetHasIvar() in GPBUtilities.m writes outside the bounds of has_storage on line 320, which could corrupt data, cause the program to crash, or lead to the execution of malicious code.The program writes outside the bounds of allocated memory, which could corrupt data, crash the program, or lead to the execution of malicious code.

nodes.body: GPBSetHasIvar is an internally api to the library, it is only called from places that are taking the input from known structures with valid values, this is why it does't have to do range checking.

The premise also seems to be someone calling that internal api with arbitrary input; if that's the case, then doesn't that already imply the processes has generally be compromised?  So even if the api did some sorta bounds checking, it would be checking against other data structures within the same memory space, and if the space was already compromised, it would be checking against also compromised data, meaning the check would prevent nothing.

If there is a call path where external input (from a file, off the wire, etc.) is directly parsed by the unchanged process space and that causes the issue, then yes, it would need to be addresses.  But I'm not sure there is any way code within an address space can protect itself if that address space is already compromised.

title: Protobuf ignores empty string on encoding [Ruby]
body:
Not sure if this is even a bug or intended behaviour.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.11.2
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
MacOS Mojave

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
mri/Ruby2.6.3

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create protobuf request with empty string value
2. Encode message to protobuf

**What did you expect to see**
Empty string is properly represented in protobuf.

**What did you see instead?**
Empty string is ignored in request encoding.

nodes.body: The default value of a string is an empty string. Default values are not explicitly stored/part of the message, because that's the value you will get if it's not in the binary data.
@albertferras I though it might be the case. So if i want to implement nullify updates i should do it explicitly in a different procedure?

If you want explicit `null` values you can take a look at the wrapper values, which let you differentiate between 'default value' and 'null/not-defined' -> https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/csharp/class/google/protobuf/well-known-types/string-value
It's basically a new 'object' with just one property `value=yourstring`. Makes your code a bit uglier but that's the only solution I've found :/

title: Duplicate symbol issue with bazel and blacklisted_protos
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.10.1
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
macOS 10.14.6 targeting iOS 11.0

**What runtime / compiler are you using**
clang 11.0 (Xcode 11.2.1)

**General description**

When building [envoy-mobile](https://github.com/lyft/envoy-mobile/) we [discovered](https://github.com/lyft/envoy-mobile/issues/617) there's an issue with protobuf where symbols are duplicated in the binary that is produced. This started when we [updated protobuf](https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/commit/4787e0a9b6810ff4cc0dd3f8d78cb8a1d7c2d73a) from v3.9.2 and I narrowed this down to these 2 BUILD file changes:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/7b28278c7d4f4175e70aef2f89d304696eb85ae3
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/a03d332aca5d33c5d4b2cd25037c9e37d57eff02

It appears that when using `proto_library` targets as your `proto_lang_toolchain`'s `blacklisted_protos`s, it does not have the same effect as before (I've filed this bazel bug since I assume this is an issue there https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/10484).

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Checkout a local copy of protobuf at v3.10.1
1. Apply the patch in `envoy-mobile/envoy/bazel/protobuf.patch`
1. In an envoy-mobile clone checked out at d27f0deb854d931f59effb0da6b9e2f8b9a6c4cc run `bazel aquery 'deps(ios_dist)' --override_repository=com_google_protobuf=/path/to/protobuf --output=textproto > /tmp/after.proto`
1. In your checkout of protobuf run `git checkout v3.9.2 -- BUILD` to get the older version of the BUILD file
1. In envoy-mobile run `bazel aquery 'deps(ios_dist)' --override_repository=com_google_protobuf=/path/to/protobuf --output=textproto > /tmp/before.proto`
1. Using [aquery_differ](https://docs.bazel.build/versions/master/aquery.html#diff-tool) in a bazel checkout run `bazel run //tools/aquery_differ -- --before=/tmp/before.proto --after=/tmp/after.proto --input_type=textproto --attrs=inputs --attrs=cmdline | less`
1. Notice that some actions have new inputs of the libraries from the wkt protos such as:

```
+bazel-out/ios-x86_64-min10.0-applebin_ios-ios_x86_64-fastbuild/bin/external/com_google_protobuf/libstruct_proto.a
+bazel-out/ios-x86_64-min10.0-applebin_ios-ios_x86_64-fastbuild/bin/external/com_google_protobuf/libtimestamp_proto.a
+bazel-out/ios-x86_64-min10.0-applebin_ios-ios_x86_64-fastbuild/bin/external/com_google_protobuf/libwrappers_proto.a
```

You can also use this aquery method to see that on the v3.10.1 tag removing `blacklisted_protos` entirely has no effect on the build, which isn't what we would expect. If you do the same test removing `blacklisted_protos` on the v3.9.2 tag you will see there's a similar difference as above where these libraries are included that shouldn't be.

**What did you expect to see**

The libraries such as `libstruct_proto.a` should not be inputs to the build.

**What did you see instead?**

These libraries are included and therefore can lead to duplicate symbols in the produced binary.

**Possible fix**

I believe we should revert the offending commits:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/7b28278c7d4f4175e70aef2f89d304696eb85ae3
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/a03d332aca5d33c5d4b2cd25037c9e37d57eff02

Until there is a clear fix upstream from bazel. Based on their original PRs I do not understand exactly what they were fixing though, so I assume that is not possible. Any other thoughts on how we could resolve this would be appreciated! It's possible we could go back to using a genrule for the `blacklisted_protos` while still keeping the other changes.

title: [PHP] google.protobuf.Empty should be mapped to \Google\Protobuf\GPBEmpty
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

If in the proto file we have a method like this:

```proto
rpc DeleteUser (DeleteUserRequest) returns (google.protobuf.Empty) {
        option (google.api.http) = {
            delete: "/users/{user_id=*}"
        };
    }
```

The (actual) generated php looks like this 
```php
public function DeleteUser(\Proto\User\DeleteUserRequest $argument,
      $metadata = [], $options = []) {
        return $this->_simpleRequest('/api.user.UserService/DeleteUser',
        $argument,
        ['\Google\Protobuf\Empty', 'decode'],
        $metadata, $options);
    }
```

The (expected) generated php looks like this 
```php
public function DeleteUser(\Proto\User\DeleteUserRequest $argument,
      $metadata = [], $options = []) {
        return $this->_simpleRequest('/api.user.UserService/DeleteUser',
        $argument,
        ['\Google\Protobuf\GPBEmpty', 'decode'],
        $metadata, $options);
    }
```

So, in summary, In case the class name is of type `\Google\Protobuf\Empty`, that should be mapped to [\Google\Protobuf\GPBEmpty](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/php/src/Google/Protobuf/GPBEmpty.php) instead. That's due to the fact that there is no "Empty" class in PHP (Empty is a reserved word in PHP), it is called "GPBEmpty". But that's how it is called in other languages like golang.

title: Python: support for optional python_package (or similar) to make import explicit
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Python.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

The Python code generator uses the directory structure of the `.proto` files to generate the generated Python code directory layout and imports (e.g. when Protobuf file A imports Protobuf file B). It doesn't sanitize Python reserved keywords.

This can be problematic in two cases:

1. The directory structure contains a reserved keyword. For example when it contains `as`. In python `import as` fails but also `import as.foo.bar` is invalid.

2. When in case of A depending on B, A will contain an absolute import that might not be on the Python path (e.g. when the generated code is packaged so instead of `import b` it should do `import mypackage.b`). This was mentioned as a fix in the discussions: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1491, but I would consider this a workaround.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

For several languages, there are ways to make the package / module name explicit by defining an `option`, e.g. `option go_package`, `option java_package`, ... (https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#packages). (I believe there is also a `ruby_package` https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/4627).

I believe an optional `option python_package` could solve the above issues as a `as/api.proto` file then could contain an `option python_package = "as_pb.api"` (or `"my_package.as_pb.api"`).

The Protobuf code generator will then take the `python_package` into account when:

* Generating the directory structure for the generated Python code so that it can be imported as `import as_pb.api` (`as_pb/api.py`).
* When defining imports (Protobuf file A depends on B). The generated file A then imports B using the (optional) defined `python_package`.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

My initial approach was to re-define the structure of the original Protobuf files. However, when the Protobuf files are used to generate other languages bindings, this has side-effects (e.g. the Go code now ends up in `as_pb/api`, it should be in `as/api`.

I believe the supported languages should not be leading in how the Protobuf structure looks like.

**Additional context**

> Explicit is better than implicit.

(https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0020/)

:wink: 

See also https://github.com/brocaar/chirpstack-api/issues/5 .

title: Is negative zero a default value for float/double fields?
body:
This question recently came up in discussion of apple/swift-protobuf#935:

> Should proto3 implementations serialize float/double values of `-0.0`?

Proto3 omits any field whose value is the default.  For float and double fields, this means that zero values are not serialized.  Does this apply to both negative and positive zero?  Or should negative zero be serialized in order to ensure that all float and double values can be accurately communicated?

nodes.body: The desired behavior should probably be included in conformance tests for binary, text format, and JSON serializations.
CC @gerben-s who was looking into this problem a couple months ago
While we're at it, I wonder what we do with NaN and Inf?

We ran into this issue while working on a Java-based mutator for Protobuf messages and have to rely on [rather hacky workarounds](https://github.com/CodeIntelligenceTesting/jazzer/blob/7e234b6e73200253eaf2069ad0ad57b7db4e212d/src/test/java/com/code_intelligence/jazzer/mutation/mutator/StressTest.java#L518-L562). Is there a plan to settle this edge case?

> While we're at it, I wonder what we do with NaN and Inf?

NaN and Inf are transferred correctly in all cases already.  There's no problem there.  The problem with `-0.0` is that it tests equal to `+0.0`.  So the question here is really whether a field that has the value `-0.0`:
* **Should** be transferred because it is not the same as the default `+0.0`
* **Should not** be transferred because it is equal to the default `+0.0`

Or put different, is the default `+0.0` or is it "any double value that is equal to `+0.0`"?
While `0.0 == -0.0` in Java, `Double.compare(0.0, -0.0)` returns `1`, not `0`, so this even depends on the kind of equality test.

`Inf`, and `-Inf` are guaranteed to round trip.
`NaN` will remain `NaN` but the exact bit pattern of which `NaN` is not guaranteed.
`-0.0` and `0.0` are treated as equivalent, so an explicitly set `-0.0` will not be serialized in proto3.  If you read wire format that contains a `-0.0`, you may or may not see if from an accessor.

In other words, all `NaN` values form an equivalence class.  Similarly `-0.0` and `0.0` form an equivalence class.  After serialization and deserialization it, which specific value of an equivalence class is observed is unspecified.
Over to @Logofile to work into our official docs

There is an important case in which `-0.0` and `0.0` are _not_ treated as equivalent: When comparing proto message objects, at least in Java. As it stands, two proto message objects with `float32` proto fields, one set to `0.0` and one set to `-0.0`, will not test equal in Java, but will do so after having been written to bytes and parsed back. 

Is this still expected behavior? I would have expected `equals` semantics in Java to be identical to be preserved under a serialization/deserialization roundtrip.
I would have expected that as well.  Honestly, this particular corner of our semantics is likely under covered in tests

Let me add a quick quote from the specs here: https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/encoding/

> ```
> i64        := sfixed64 | fixed64 | double;
>                 encoded as 8-byte little-endian;
>                 memcpy of the equivalent C types (u?int64_t, double)
> ```

If we take this part of the spec at face value **memcpy of the equivalent C types ... double)** than _all_ the behaviors that do not preserve the bit pattern are "wrong".

Edit: However, it would appear that this is orthogonal to the default-values-are-not-serialized rule.

Also, in Dec 2023 [notes have been added to the spec](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protocolbuffers.github.io/blame/b46fe774b7aca4b6f9feb2b040ca0932442ab0d4/content/programming-guides/proto3.md#L522) (ln 522, 539) to clarify the +/- 0.0 behavior: https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/#default :

> ... For float and double types, -0.0 and 0.0 are treated as equivalent
>
> ... Also note that if a scalar message field is set to its default, the value will not be serialized on the wire. If a float or double value is set to -0 or +0, it will not be serialized.

Note that any `repeated double [packed]` fields will have no "default value handling" (even in the unpacked ones I couldn't observe it), and so you **can** transfer a `-0.0` IEEEE double iff you put it into a `repeated` field.

As of [2024-02-13](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protocolbuffers.github.io/commit/025f35021d3d1f3a4d87e150f6727511977f8c6a), this was changed:

> Also note that if a scalar message field **is** set to its default, the value will not be serialized on the wire. If a float or double value is set to +0 it will not be serialized, but -0 is considered distinct and will be serialized.

I cannot tell if or when this has become true in which official protobuf libraries, or if or when this has existed in any part of the conformance tests. There have been [at least some unit tests](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blame/d1cf09abcff7636101fd27e94ea5aa7b9f603f5e/java/core/src/test/java/com/google/protobuf/MessageTest.java#L362-L372) since 2021. it also seems to work in c++ at present...

We triage inactive PRs and issues in order to make it easier to find active work. If this issue should remain active or becomes active again, please add a comment.

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago. This issue will be closed and archived after 14 additional days without activity.

This issue should be closed as "answered"?

There is the commit https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protocolbuffers.github.io/commit/025f35021d3d1f3a4d87e150f6727511977f8c6a from that changed the [current docs](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/#default) to the quote already mentioned above:

> ... for *scalar* message fields, once a message is parsed there’s no way of telling whether a field was explicitly set to the default value ...  If a float or double value is set to `+0` it will not be serialized, but `-0` is considered distinct and will be serialized.

As mentioned, the text "For float and double types, -0.0 and 0.0 are treated as equivalent, and will round-trip" and "[i]f a
float or double value is set to -0 or +0, it will not be serialized" were added to the documentation topic `proto3.md`. If this doesn't fully address the documentation issue, please let me know.

Ummm....  so which is it?

The [current docs](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/#default) say:
>  If a float or double value is set to +0 it will not be serialized, but -0 is considered distinct and will be serialized.

but

@Logofile just above claimed 
> ... "[i]f a float or double value is set to -0 or +0, it will not be serialized"

Apologies: that additional text was removed in a later change. (I was looking at an earlier version of the `proto3.md` file when I added my last comment.) We removed the text "For float and double types, -0.0 and 0.0 are treated as equivalent, and will round-trip" based on guidance from @esrauchg.  

If a float or double value is set to +0 it **will not** be serialized, but -0 **will** be serialized.
Excellent!  I think that's the behavior that most folks on this thread seem to have expected.  Now that we have it documented, we can make that consistent across implementations.

title: js: omitted zero map values (as serialized by protobuf-c) cannot be deserialized
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

Version: 3.11.2
Language: JavaScript
OS: Ubuntu 18.04

**What did you do?**
Take the following .proto definition:
```protobuf
syntax = "proto3";
message MapThing {
	map<string,uint64> values = 1;
}
```
and the message corresponding to the following JSON structure:
```json
{
	"values": {
		"foo": 0
	}
}
```

Depending on the protobuf implementation used, this message may be serialized in two different ways. I also used https://github.com/jmendeth/protobuf-inspector to look at the encoded data.

A) (Golang, C++)
```
0a 07 0a 03 66 6f 6f 10 00
```
```
root:
    1 <chunk> = message(1 <chunk> = "foo", 2 <varint> = 0)
```

B) (protobuf-c)
```
0a 05 0a 03 66 6f 6f
```
```
root:
    1 <chunk> = message(1 <chunk> = "foo")
```

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Take the message B) and deserialize using JS protobuf implementation (google-protobuf):
```js
const {MapThing} = require('./foo_pb');
const data = Uint8Array.from([0x0a, 0x05, 0x0a, 0x03, 0x66, 0x6f, 0x6f])
MapThing.deserializeBinary(data);
```
2. Library will fail with an assertion:

I think the problem comes the fact you are using the `--as-needed` linker option.
Behind the scene, `python setup.py build` will run `protoc` which will not have the NEEDED shared lib dependency onto `libpthread.so.0`.

title: duration.proto missing from protobuf-javalite
body:
Since the fixing of https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1889, `protobuf-javalite` includes the generated code for well-known types. It also includes the `*.proto` files for well-known types *except* for `duration.proto`. This can make the build process difficult for users (see, e.g., https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/issues/6573).

Is there a reason that `duration.proto` was excluded from the `protobuf-javalite` release? I checked the latest version (`3.11.1`) but AFAIK it has not been included in any of the javalite artifacts.

Edit 5/26/2020: It looks like `com.google.protobuf.util.Timestamps` and `com.google.protobuf.util.Durations` are also missing from the javalite artifact.

nodes.body:
I have created  a work around that could hopefully help you. The gist of it is; creating a fatjar using protobuf-javalite , protolite-well-known-types and proto-google-common-protos. Then you can use the output artifact in your gradle dependency inplace of other protobuf artifacts:
 Refer to this git repo:

https://github.com/gitprelimtek/protobuf-javalite-firebase-wellknowntypes.git


> Since the fixing of #1889, `protobuf-javalite` includes the generated code for well-known types. It also includes the `*.proto` files for well-known types _except_ for `duration.proto`. This can make the build process difficult for users (see, e.g., [grpc/grpc-java#6573](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/issues/6573)).
> 
> Is there a reason that `duration.proto` was excluded from the `protobuf-javalite` release? I checked the latest version (`3.11.1`) but AFAIK it has not been included in any of the javalite artifacts.

The workarround doesn't work if you are using protobuf-java for in-app messaging and, for example, Firestore which has nested protobuf-lite dependency.

Is there any way to use protobuf-java:3.11.4 for in-app messaging and firestore:21.4.3?

@ejona86 Not working for me:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5219339/83546935-b901fc00-a516-11ea-9f71-f8285c44da60.png)


I also tried this:
```
            task.addIncludeDir(files("google/api/"))
            task.addIncludeDir(files("google/rpc/"))
```

@Morteza-Rastgoo, it doesn't seem you are impacted by this issue. This issue is concerning javalite containing the generated code for duration.proto, and a few others, but it does not include the .proto itself. It seems you're just wanting to generate code for googleapis. In that case you can use `dependencies { protobuf "com.google.api.grpc:proto-google-common-protos:1.18.0" }`.

Based on the error message, it seems you've modified `annotations.proto` to use `import "http.proto"` instead of `import "google/api/http.proto"`.

`files()` is relative to the project directory, so you'd need to use:
```groovy
            task.addIncludeDir(files("src/main/proto/google/api"))
            // or
            task.addIncludeDir(files("$projectDir/src/main/proto/google/api"))
```

However, that's still very broken, as protobuf-gradle-plugin will run protoc against proto files in src/main/proto; your approach is no better than having `src/main/proto/http.proto`.

Instead, my workaround suggested having a _separate_ folder. For example, you could use `src/main/fix-javalite-proto/google/protobuf/duration.proto` and then have `task.addIncludeDir(files("src/main/fix-javalite-proto"))`.

@Morteza-Rastgoo, that is still not related to this issue. Ignoring the warnings, the error is `field_behavior.proto: File not found.".  I'm not familiar with a "localization.proto" that is doing the import, so it seems likely that is a problem with your own .proto not importing the right path. If there are further issues, I don't expect this issue to be the proper place to discuss them.

@ejona86 I don't think your workaround for protobufing one's own common protos works these days, that was only valid a few years back pre-R8, or when not minifying with R8. Now, when minifying, Android R8 issues errors about duplicate classes from protobuf-javalite, e.g.:

Type com.google.protobuf.ListValueOrBuilder is defined multiple times: /Users/uli/.gradle/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/com.google.protobuf/protobuf-javalite/3.12.0/8d8ca7983eae28ac654f657f6119e85a0bba9402/protobuf-javalite-3.12.0.jar:com/google/protobuf/ListValueOrBuilder.class, /Users/uli/Developer/Android/bugsNtests/protobufr8duplicates/app/build/intermediates/javac/debug/classes/com/google/protobuf/ListValueOrBuilder.class

This behavior was the last straw that led me to create https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/issues/6573 (which in turn led to the creation of this issue), because the experience of building and maintaining an Android grpc project with a few well-known protos and Google common protos is harrowing. The only way to build my pretty simple grpc project on Android is by spending hours and days on finding and applying a bunch of hacks, and then spending more time on maintaining this mess when dependency versions and tools change.

This is not the right place for this discussion, but it appears that the problem did not become apparent from my filing of https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/issues/6573, and the misconception that this works has influenced the handling of other issues like https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/issues/6554.

Or is there another workaround for the duplicate class problem?

I want to confirm that adding Durations and Timestamps to the protobuf-javalite artifact would indeed address part of my issue from https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/issues/6573, so I hope this will happen.

I have a PR to add this file
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7738/files
The PR has been merged

Was this issue rightfully closed? My understanding is that the issue is also about missing `com.google.protobuf.util.Timestamps` and `com.google.protobuf.util.Durations`, which do not seem to have been added by the PR.
Oh, sorry for missing that part. Durations and Timestamps are a different beast!

Hmm... `protobuf-javalite` _shouldn't_ have anything from `com.google.protobuf.util.*`, since that's part of `protobuf-java-util`. I see `com.google.protobuf.Timestamp` and `com.google.protobuf.Duration` in javalite, so the java code looks correct. However, `google/protobuf/duration.proto` was missing which was why this was originally filed. So it seems this is fixed.

I think we should just ignore the `com.google.protobuf.util.*` part, as it is expected and probably just a small mixup when doing the verification.

@ejona86 Having `com.google.protobuf.util.Timestamps` and `com.google.protobuf.util.Durations` in lite version would be very handy to convert Timestamps and Durations to milliseconds, etc and vice-versa. 

Otherwise, adding a protobuf-java-util as a separate dependency in Android causes Duplicate class errors.

@janbolat, I don't disagree. But I don't think that's what this issue was about. It wasn't a feature request. It was a "you can't use lite as a dependency in .protos" bug. It came out of #1889 which was only partially fixed, which actually made things worse in some cases because it broke the workaround.

I'm going to close this. I don't disagree that having utils available to javalite would be nice. But a separate issue should exist for that feature request.

> Otherwise, adding a protobuf-java-util as a separate dependency in Android causes Duplicate class errors.

For that, I think you just exclude the protobuf-java dependency from protobuf-java-util. I'm not saying you won't have any further issues after that, though, since I'm not sure anyone has tested that and to my knowledge it is unsupported.

title: protobuf should support that a integer value is 0 or null (not be set at all)
body:
Currently, protobuf doesn't allow to set a null value. It doesn't give way to generate an integer field as a pointer or without the pointer.

for e.g. protobuf should support that an integer value is 0 or null (not be set at all)
Design decision to not support presence in proto3.  In proto3 there is no "not set" status separate from 0.
https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/1024

<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
GOLang
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
proto3
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?
golang
**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
In proto3 there is no "not set" status separate from 0.
In communication between 2 systems, if we add a new integer field and for some case's it will be set and for others it will be not set. So, the other system receiving values in this new field should able to differentiate between "not set"/nil and 0. i.e. ignore if its nil and consider only if its value present.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Protobuf should support that an integer value is 0 or null (not be set at all)

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.
https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/1024

nodes.body:
You can use Int32Value and Int64Value from the well known types for this - https://godoc.org/github.com/golang/protobuf/ptypes/wrappers

these support being null separate from being 0 (in case of int)

@omjangir [That boat sailed a long time ago and isn't coming back for proto3](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1606).  You can try to make your case for proto4 if / when that happens, but I doubt they will listen.  Too much time, work, and reputations have been sunk into their current approach for them to change now.

protobuf does not directly support the notion of null like JSON does.  Your best hope to get something similar is to infer that absence of a field means null within some context.

For example, if you want to update one field of a resource to be null, then in your update pass a FieldMask that names that specific field, but then have the field be absent in your message, and interpret this situation to mean "set that field to null."

For scalars, like string, sint32, etc., protobuf makes even this approach difficult because default values for scalars will always be absent from the serialization.  So, you won't be able to distinguish between 'absent because we want it to be null' and 'absent because we want it to have the default value.'

To get around that roadblock, you have to wrap all of your nullable scalars in wrapper messages (or use singleton oneofs).  Then you can at least detect whether the wrapper is absent or present.  If the wrapper is absent, then interpret that to mean null in the proper context (e.g. - an accompanying FieldMask specifying it).  If the wrapper is present, then interpret the contained value as normal.

You should probably use [google.protobuf.wrappers.proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/wrappers.proto) for your wrapper types.  These are "Well Known Types" and might get some extra love in the different generated languages than if you used your own.  Unfortunately, there are not wrappers for all the basic scalar types for some reason.
Just serialize the class and pass a string over grpc.  Im sure that removes some of the efficiency, but why jump through hoops just to pass a null?

This should be now possible with new presence api, which is implemented (but still experimental) https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1606#issuecomment-618687169
docs: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/field_presence.md

title: C# : Why generated code throw exception on null values(.e.g string) instead of just setting default value?
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

Why generated code throw exception on null value assignment?
I know in new version of protobuf(v3) you decide to remove optional feature and all field most have value.
But why just don't set default value for some primitive type like string instead of throwing ArgumantNullException? this behavior has conflict with some tools like AutoMapper.
I mean this behavior would affect other part of a program.
if in grpc-area all null value most be replaced with default value so just keep this constraint in grpc-area. throwing a exception for setting null value would cause this constraint flow in other part of program which i think it is not a good practice and it is against cross-cutting concern.

nodes.body: I'm not sure I understand the question. Can you provide an example what is the current behavior of Google.Protobuf (code example) is and how it should be changed?
AIU, your code is generated by grpc, not protobuf.

You can use [StringValue](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/test_messages_proto3.proto#L216) that is mapped to nullable string. Though tests have stuff like [optional string field](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf.Test.TestProtos/TestMessagesProto3.cs#L615), I wonder if string is optional by default.
Yes, But they forward me here. I asked question there at first(https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet/issues/734)

> You can use [StringValue](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/test_messages_proto3.proto#L216) that is mapped to nullable string. Though tests have stuff like [optional string field](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf.Test.TestProtos/TestMessagesProto3.cs#L615), I wonder if string is optional by default.

Actually i'm not looking for a secondary solution. the problem is throwing Exception on assigning null to a string which affect all other part of our code which they got mapped to a protobuff( or grpc) generated class.
I mean with current behavior all models or mappers should do such a thing **`protobuffClass.StringProp = ourModel.StringProp ?? ""`**  for every single string property because if you dont, you will get ArgumantNullException.

Well, yes, if you use the wrapper, you can simply assign the property, see the [generated code](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf.Test.TestProtos/TestMessagesProto3.cs#L1611) - it's simple assignment.

I think the answer is as simple as this behavior would be counterintuitive: in proto3 a string field cannot have a value of null, it can only be an empty string. To allow setting a null to a property, but the value being set to "" in actuality seems confusing and dangerous.
I'm going to close as "working as intended".

> AIU, your code is generated by grpc, not protobuf.

The code for protobuf messages is actually generated by protobuf, but Grpc.Tools bundles the protoc binary to make things simpler (see src/google/protobuf/compiler/csharp in this repository)

> in proto3 a string field cannot have a value of null, it can only be an empty string

That said, the field can be missing altogether, which I would interpret as a null value. Currently the message serialization omits the field when the string is empty, which feels wrong. I'd say nullable C# types should receive null value when the field is missing, non-nullable types like integers should keep default value (they aren't).

As I understand, current design is influenced by repeated fields and dictionaries, where you can't omit a value to express null?
that was (they aren't touched during deserialization when the field is missing)

The protobuf protocol default for an omitted string is an empty string; this is probably influenced by C++ `std::string` not having a null state, only an empty state (albeit that C `char*` does have both).

From this it is reasonable that when you get the property you will get an empty string, not null.  However I do not think that it is correct that (at present) when you set the property it will accept empty string but throw an exception on null.  Even for proto3 it ought to accept null and treat it indistinguishably from empty string.

For proto2, since the underlying wire format supports a null state distinct from empty string (to represent "field not present"), which you can detect by reading the HasX property, setting to null should be equivalent to clearing the value.  This is indeed how it works for message properties, but not for string or bytes properties.

Arguably the generated code should just remove all the HasX properties and instead expose nulls (using the built-in .NET nullable types for scalar types like int etc, and the natural nullability of string, message, and bytestring types).  But that's a bigger change and I'm not arguing for that.  (Though it would be nice if it were an option for the codegen.)

Form the looks of it, proto3 has different representations for null and empty values, it's not different from proto2 in that regard, C# can represent both naturally with nullable string, that would be feature parity with the protocol. It's normal for non-nullable strings to not differentiate between null and empty values, C++ can keep doing what it does now, accidentally business logic usually doesn't care about that distinction either.

The wire format does distinguish these, but the proto3 language, by design, treats the two wire formats as identical (interpreted as empty string).  The proto2 language treats them as separate cases, albeit still as reading an empty string if you read the property directly rather than checking the Has* properties.

My point, however, is that it still doesn't seem sensible to throw an exception on null assignment, in either case.

`null` is an invalid case for proto3 on `string`, as the proto `string` is explicitly non-nullable (as it is with C#8). So I also think it behaves correctly. This special case only occurs because C# was handling string as something between value-type and reference-type, different then all other native types.

In your case, I would also prefer to use `google.protobuf.StringValue` over `string`. This will allow you to assign your property naturally and also say that `null` is a valid value for you. If `null` is not a valid value for your protocol, you naturally have to make the transition from a nullable string to non-nullable string in your code base. And just assuming `null` means `string.Empty` is just that, an assumption, that doesn't hold for everyone using the library.

We in our code base explicitly rely on this feature as expected and correct behavior. And I assume this will become less of a problem if C#8 nullables get a wider adoption, finally cleaning up the mess of not being able to define a non-nullable string.

But when `syntax = "proto2"`, empty string and "absent" are distinguishable, and null string is a natural representation for the latter.  (And it's blocking me from switching from another library, because my existing code expects null == absent, not null == exception.)

HI all, reviving in case someone is looking for a quick solution for this.
I have forked the repo and created a small patch for `csharp` client to use suggested solution by @zeinali0 

also made a docker file that will compile the code on Alpine (which is what we need) 
https://github.com/arthurvaverko-kaltura/protobuf/releases/tag/v1.15.8.1

I understand your point that `string` feels like it‘s meant to be nullable also in proto2. But with the introduction of C# 8 and enabling nullability checks, this would explicitly break since it‘s a `string` and not `string?` and therefore does not allow `null`. So just defining this as default is becoming counter-intuitive.

A better solution would be a helper that get‘s the field you are interested in and the nullable string value, clearing on null and setting on any other value. This makes it a forwards compatible user decision. Another option would be a protoc option so that when compiling, the user can define the behavior explicitly without the writer of the protos having to set this in the files (as it‘s not his intention but the users).

Adding options to protoc is a mess, so I‘m mostly sure that will not be done. So having a helper sounds like the best option here. One option that I can think of is having that defined on the `IFieldAccessor` as `SetOrClearValue`, which could get any nullable (not just `string`). I can write it up as an extension method for you if you like a quick workaround that remains future-proof.

@Falco20019  I agree with C# 8 nullable types this become a very bad implementation.
I like the suggestion of a flag to allow generating null checks or string empty replacement.

This is something I might pick up if you think it can contribute the main repo as a PR .. 
Otherwise ill keep my fork for our internal use and \ or anyone that is getting same issues with C# > 8  versions..

@Falco20019 I think i know how I can add `--csharp_opt` flag .. 
thinkin of `--csharp_opt=allow_null_string=true`, im not happy with the flag name .. so I thought maybe you have other suggestions ?

I would prefer having the helper route over the compiler option, since I personally compile a bunch of files at the same time and this would change all of those in one run. The helper is less intrusive (compile-wise) and can be used a lot more focused, leading to a cleaner API. But that's just my opinion.

If you still want to go with having `null` clear your field, I would not stop at `string` but do it on any nullable and therefore call the option `clear_field_on_null`.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
g++ (Ubuntu 9.2.1-9ubuntu2) 9.2.1 20191008

**What did you do?**
Used a proto file such as the following:
```
syntax = "proto2";

message Message1 {
    required int32 a = 1;
    required int32 b = 2;
}
```
and compiled it with `protoc foo.proto --cpp_out=. && g++ -O3 -Wall foo.pb.cc -c`

**What did you expect to see**
compiles without warnings

**What did you see instead?**
```
In file included from /usr/include/string.h:494,
                 from /usr/include/c++/9/cstring:42,
                 from /usr/local/include/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h:118,
                 from foo.pb.h:23,
                 from foo.pb.cc:4:
In function ‘void* memset(void*, int, size_t)’,
    inlined from ‘void Message1::SharedCtor()’ at foo.pb.cc:111:11,
    inlined from ‘Message1::Message1()’ at foo.pb.cc:96:13,
    inlined from ‘void InitDefaultsscc_info_Message1_foo_2eproto()’ at foo.pb.cc:94:1:
/usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu/bits/string_fortified.h:71:33: warning: ‘void* __builtin_memset(void*, int, long unsigned int)’ offset [29, 32] from the object at ‘_Message1_default_instance_’ is out of the bounds of referenced subobject ‘Message1::a_’ with type ‘int’ at offset 24 [-Warray-bounds]
   71 |   return __builtin___memset_chk (__dest, __ch, __len, __bos0 (__dest));
      |          ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
```

It warns about memset() being called on a field, but writing not just to that field, but also to following fields. See also: https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=90376

The warning doesn't appear when using -O2 instead of -O3, but -O3 is common in CMake release builds (which is how it showed up here).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body:
Hi,

I got the same issue, protobuf 3.11.4 and gcc 9.2.1.
Did you find a fix for that ?

Thanks,
Clement

As work-around we're using `-Wno-array-bounds` when compiling the generated sources now (CMake):
```
set_source_files_properties(${PROTO_SRCS} PROPERTIES COMPILE_FLAGS -Wno-array-bounds)
```
This appears to be the offending memset: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/e667bf6eaaa2fb1ba2987c6538df81f88500d030/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_message.cc#L2605

I think doing the memset (and memcpy above) in terms of the individual field names is undefined behavior.

[This](https://lore.kernel.org/lkml/20190517092502.GA22779@gmail.com/) is how they fixed the problem in the Linux kernel: do the memsets in term of offsets within the parent object.  That requires offsetof, which isn't currently available in the generated pb.cc file (needs `<cstddef>`).

I'm not sure if it's OK to add that dependency.

My security tool finds security vulnerable for *.pb.cc files using memcpy/ memset, and it has security concern that the buffer copy does not check size and will lead to buffer overflow. 
Using memcpy/ memset is unsecure, is there any plan to remove the uses towards something more secure?

Also affected on multiple arm environments: armv7a-unknown-linux-gnuebihf- and armv6j-unknown-linux-ucliceabihf- (both Gentoo) compiling at -O3 (-O2 doesn't issue the warning for me).  Both gcc-9.3.0.
The same warning for gcc (Ubuntu 9.3.0-10ubuntu2) 9.3.0
Should be fixed by #7913.

    add_message "google.ads.googleads.v2.services.CampaignBudgetOperation" do

      end
    end
  end
end

module Google
  module Ads
    module GoogleAds
      module V2
        module Services
          MutateCampaignBudgetsRequest = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("google.ads.googleads.v2.services.MutateCampaignBudgetsRequest").msgclass
          CampaignBudgetOperation = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("google.ads.googleads.v2.services.CampaignBudgetOperation").msgclass
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

include Google::Ads::GoogleAds::V2::Services

def main
  r = MutateCampaignBudgetsRequest.new
  r.operations = [CampaignBudgetOperation.new]
end

if __FILE__ == $0
  main
end
```

currently protobuf gives this error: 
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
	2: from hi.rb:40:in `<main>'
	1: from hi.rb:36:in `main'
hi.rb:36:in `method_missing': Expected repeated field array (Google::Protobuf::TypeError)
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Assigning an array to a repeated field should work if all the values are of the right type

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
N/A
**Additional context**
my ldap pnlpn@ for on-corp discussions.

nodes.body:
I have previously had some reservations about this, mainly because of the following case:

```ruby
def main
  r = MutateCampaignBudgetsRequest.new
  arr = [CampaignBudgetOperation.new]
  r.operations = arr  # This must copy, as RepeatedField cannot alias Array
  arr << CampaignBudgetOperation.new  # Doesn't mutate r.operations!
  assert_eq 1, r.operations.size  # Some people might expect this to be 2!
end
```

However after talking about it more, others have convinced me that the convenience of allowing this outweighs the possible confusion that could arise from the case above.

So we should implement this at some point. It's not currently prioritized, but we would accept a PR.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

macOS 10.15.2

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a new `Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField` with a value in it.
2. Encode it as YAML using `.to_yaml`
3. Decode it using `YAML.load(...)`
4. See that the value that was originally there has been dropped and you are left with an empty `Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField`.

[1] pry(main)> repeated_field = Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField.new(:string) << 'test'

=> Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField
[6] pry(main)> empty_repeated_field.length
=> 0
```

**What did you expect to see**
After doing `YAML.load(...)` we should end up with a `Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField` with the same values as when we encoded it.

**What did you see instead?**
A `Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField` with no values. In my case an easy workaround is to transform the `Google::Protobuf::RepeatedField` to an array before encoding.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

title: Make compiled ruby source use frozen string literals
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?** 
Applies to ruby generated code

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
In ruby, string literals are (unfortunately) mutable. This comes with a memory penalty. There is a magic comment you can use at the top of any ruby file to opt-out of this for the file only:

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

....
```

I think it would be cool if `protoc` output ruby in this manner, albeit _mostly_ because this is a best practice. I'd be shocked if this had any real-world performance gains.

As far as I can tell, the `protoc` compiler never makes use of the theoretical mutability of ruby strings, as it ought not to. Therefore it should not even be an option; all compiled ruby should have mutable strings turned off.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Every ruby compiled source file (`*_pb.rb`) should have the magic comment described above at the top.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
N/A

**Additional context**
I'd be happy to do this if you guys agree :)

title: Question about file name for objective-c code generation
body:
I understand the similar issue had been discussed before: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1372

I would like to ask for some information/advise about generated objective file names as it's currently giving me issues.

we have proto files organised in following structure:

```
common/foo.proto
foo/v1/foo.proto
```

The objc-out will create header files

```
common/Foo.pbobjc.h
foo/v1/Foo.pbobjc.h
```

If `generate_for_named_framework ` is used as option of `protoc`, the import statement for both header files will be same `#import <XFramework/Foo.pbobjc.h>` and Xcode complains about duplicate output as it tries to copy the header files with same name.

I can get away by not using `generate_for_named_framework `, but the generated files are used in an iOS framework project and linked by other projects. Referencing random header files on the disk is not ideal, and if we import the public headers in the umbrella header, the build fails with try to include none-modular header in framework.

I would like to know what's the best option here to address issue like this. Ideally, it would be good to generate the file with the folder structure as part of the name. I do understand the point mentioned in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1372 . I may not aware other alternatives which are better than changing file names.

nodes.body:
First - I'm not sure what the reference to #7106 is for, how do you see it related to the header names?

Frameworks don't generally play great with nested headers.  If you only need your headers to be in one framework, you might be able to no use framework imports style, and instead just let them generate normally, so they should have the paths as part of the generated imports.  Within the framework, I think clang will get things right and see a plain `#include "..."` to also be scoped within the framework.  Code consuming the framework could then do `#import <XFramework/common/Foo.pbobjc.h>`.

If something like that doesn't work, then it sounds like we'd need a way to generate framework imports that keep the paths from the generation. 🙁

@thomasvl thanks for your reply. Sorry I messed up with the link. I've updated the link to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1372 . I think that's somehow related now.

I can make the framework work with plain `#import "..."` (compiler doesn't like the `#include "..."` for objc headers) with header search path set. But that's not ideal to reference headers outside the framework project source. If I add all headers to the framework project, Xcode tries to copy all header files to the same output folder without respecting the path, e.g. "common/Foo.pbobjc.h" and "foo/v1/Foo.pbobjc.h" are all copied to "/usr/include/Foo.pbobjc.h"  which generates build time error.

1372 is just an issue about controlling the `pbobj` part in the generated names.

Are you trying to _install_ the framework?  is that's why you are trying to write into `/usr/include`?  In general, Apple development doesn't really do that.  Apple's been trying to lock down those directories more and more with each OS update.

As far as Xcode flattening things when it copies the files into the Framework - I haven't looked at that in a long time, and I'm not to surprised if it does try to do that; that was some what I was referencing when I mentioned frameworks not always doing well with nested paths.

As far as what to do to try and support this, I'm open to suggestions, the things Xcode imposing is always going to be the gating factor.  The limited support we have at the moment is what some folks needed to get things like CocoaPods working where it constructs the framework projects and wires them together.

Sorry, I was playing around with different build options (framework, static/dynamic library) and got mixed. You are right, framework just copies all headers to the `Headers` folder of output bundle, not `/usr/include` like library.

Currently what I have a work around script which renames the generated files to include the path, e.g. foo_v1_Foo.objc.h and updates all header imports inside the code.

There are a few options I can think of
1. As file options similar to objective c header prefix, e.g. `objc_file_prefix` so the generator takes the value to prefix all the files
1. As a code generation argument similar to `generate_for_named_framework `, which enables the ability to prefix the filename with folder structure, basically what I am doing with the script

I am not too sure how CocoaPods can help here, are you saying each module/package can be grouped by different framework projects in order to avoid the filename conflicts?

I am fine with any solution as long as this one can be solved in a better way than modifying the generated code.

CocoaPods doesn't always use real frameworks, so it seems to make the directory structures itself; like so it can support the `header_mappings_dir` attribute it has to keep structure.

I don't think we'd need this to be an option in the proto files because it doesn't change the generate types.  If there is something needed, it likely can just be a generator option; but I'm still not completely clear what it would end up being.

Looks like someone else did same renaming approach for this issue as well https://github.com/CocoaPods/CocoaPods/issues/1437#issuecomment-111794301 .

May I suggest something like this:

```
--objc_opt=prefix_file_name=path \
```

will output `path/to/path_to_File.pbobjc.h` instead of `path/to/File.pbobjc.h`

```
--objc_opt=prefix_file_name=class_prefix \
```

will output `path/to/XYZFile.pbobjc.h`

Let me know what you think. I can make a PR if you like.

Sorry, still debating the ups/downs of adding this, and if it fully fixes things or if something else is likely to come up.  Once we add it we have to support it, so I'd like to ensure nothing else is going to come up because of it (or in the space it is trying to address).

Quick update - what you call the _path_ case is the one I'm stumbling on. I'm not sure if `path/to/path_to_File.pbobjc.h` makes sense vs. also not recreating the path hierarchy.  For your Framework case, it doesn't matter, but if someone isn't using frameworks, then they don't face the same collisions issues unless for some reason they want a generally _flat_ output directory. So I'm not sure if the option should also impact the creation of the sub directories in general.  Or maybe we have to have two options, one for the prefix (like you mention) and then a second knob to turn off the directory structure part.  But having two options when the usage would seem to be tied also doesn't seem great.

Thanks for the update. Correct me if I am wrong, I cannot see how it will affect non-framework users as this option is opt-in only. If users are not using framework or don't need flat output directory, they won't need to provide any options, and everything should just behave as it is. Only when users run into this situation would need to change the output behaviour by providing this option.

If you are talking about if we should emit the output dir if this option is on. I don't mind either way. My personal preference would be keeping the dir structure even we prefix the file, in case someone wants to exclude certain dirs during build process.

Yes, it is the hierarchy that I'm not sure about.

One thing I've learned over the years is the moment there is an option, some subset of folks will use it for cases you didn't expect; and in this case, having the hierarchy and the name include the transformed hierarchy seems redundant.  I can see someone wanting a flat output directory, so they want the path based filenames to avoid collisions.

title: protoc doesn't allow some field names due to bad json_name logic
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.11.3
Language: none (using `--descriptorset_out`)

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Mac OS X

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
No runtime; just using the `protoc` binary

**What did you do?**
I tried to compile the following proto file:
```proto
// test.proto
syntax = "proto3";
message Foo {
  string abc = 1;
  string abc_def = 2;
  string __a__b__c = 3;
  string _abc_def = 4;
}
```
I used the following command:
```
protoc test.proto -otest.protoset
```

**What did you expect to see**
I expected this to work and to produce a `test.protoset` file.

If I remove the conflicting fields and generate this in isolation, the resulting `json_name` fields in the output descriptors are all different -- so there's no actual conflict. For reference:

* `abc` becomes JSON name of `abc`
* `abc_def` becomes JSON name of `abcDef`
* `__a__b__c` becomes JSON name of `ABC`
* `_abc_def` becomes JSON name of `AbcDef`

**What did you see instead?**
The command fails with the following error:
```
test.proto:6:10: The JSON camel-case name of field "__a__b__c" conflicts with field "abc". This is not allowed in proto3.
test.proto:7:10: The JSON camel-case name of field "_abc_def" conflicts with field "abc_def". This is not allowed in proto3.
```
It appears that it is using a case-insensitive comparison to determine if there is a conflict. But I believe that is wrong for a couple of reasons:
1. Key names in JSON are case-sensitive. So it is fine to have both "abc" and "ABC" in the same output, as well as both "abcDef" and "AbcDef".
2. The error message suggests the conflict is on the camel-case JSON name and doesn't say anything about being case insensitive.

nodes.body:
I think this is related to #5063, at least in the fact that they are both related to how `protoc` tries to check for uniqueness of JSON names.

In fact, adding a `json_name` option does not prevent the above errors. So if we add `json_name = "FOO"` to the `__a__b__c` field in the example above, it still complains with the same message:

```
test.proto:7:10: The JSON camel-case name of field "__a__b__c" conflicts with field "abc". This is not allowed in proto3.
```
FYI, @dsnet, it looks like `protodesc.NewFile` in the new Go runtime has this same issue: it complains about a conflict between two fields with same camel-case, even if one has custom JSON name.

@jhump I think there may be good reason for enforcing that the names are unique without considering custom JSON names. I haven't thought about this in a while but I believe there's a technical reason for why [FieldMasks](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto) can't use custom JSON names and therefore need to use either the original field name or the default JSON name.

If that's really the case then the error message should be improved (since it is talking about JSON names and makes no caveat about why the option is ignored). Further this constraint should be clearly documented. I don't see any documentation for it, but it deserves to be called out in the main [proto3 doc page](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3).

@acozzette, you commented above that protoc may _need_ to require that the _camel-case_ version of each field is unique (not just JSON name). But what about the case described in the issue description? It complains even if the camel-case for one field differs from another by only case. Is that also related to field masks? Or is that possibly a bug?
We are going to shortly release updated json support, that we ought to be able to work in this fix as well

This is still a problem. As far as I can tell from the proto3 language guide, `ab` and `a_b` are different field names. I can trivially convert them to distinct lowerCamelCase (`ab` vs `AB`) or UpperCamelCase (`Ab` vs `AB`) names. All of these would be distinct string keys in JSON objects. These are all distinct identifiers in Go.

And yet you get this nonsensical error

    The JSON camel-case name of field "ab" conflicts with field "a_b". This is not allowed in proto3.

This would only be a valid error for fields like `a1` and `a_1`. These _do_ conflict because "1" is always the same in upper- and lower-case. It seems that it's not actually checking for real camel-case conflicts, rather it is checking for conflicts when all underscores are removed and letter case is ignored, which is a much stronger requirement. I'd expect something in the language guide to point out that while you can put underscores in field names, they are effectively ignored as far as field uniqueness is concerned.

This includes Protobuf objects, especially as these can end up embedded in larger model objects if held onto for a while (rather than copying to a nearly-identical other class).

**Describe the solution you'd like**
The generated classes should implement the standard `INotifyPropertyChanged` pattern.  (Ideally, the [variant](https://stackoverflow.com/a/35582811/43534) that only raises the change when non-equal.)

title: Reflection::GetRepeatedFieldInternal<int> method is not defined for enviroments in which int32_t or int64_t is not a typedef of int
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Custom.

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
gcc 7.5

**What did you do?**
Try to compile the protobuf project on a operating system in which neither  `int32_t` nor `int64_t` are defined as a typedef for `int` (for example, a [ILP32 system](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/types) in which int32_t is defined as `long`).  

**What did you expect to see**
That the library does not have any undefined symbols problems. 

**What did you see instead?**
That the `Reflection::GetRepeatedFieldInternal<int>` method is not defined. 

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
Unfortunately, this problem was reproduced in a private enviroment, and I am not aware of any open OS and toolchain in which it could  be reproduced. However, the issue is quite straightforward. 
The `Reflection::GetRepeatedFieldInternal` methods are defined in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/a104dffcb6b1958a424f5fa6f9e6bdc0ab9b6f9e/src/google/protobuf/generated_message_reflection.cc#L2097 for the types `int32`, `int64`, `uint32`, `uint64`, `float`, `double` and `bool`. Then, the same method is used in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9b0fa3e7fbaf3463c3afa1c9ab111682108eeadb/src/google/protobuf/wire_format.cc#L920 for the type `int`, and everything usually works fine in most systems as `int32` is typically defined as a typedef of `int`, but in my case fails because `int32` is defined as `long`, and `int64` is defined as `long long`, and so the implicit assumption on int fails. Replacing the `int` there with `int32` or `int64` solves the compilation problem, but I do not know what are the effects at runtime on all the supported platforms.

nodes.body:
This thread is open for a year! 
What are security issues might occur? Could you explain with real time example?

Imagine an example, when the blob changes. The security auditor either creates a tool to merge it into a gzip, unzip, and then verify, or they just accidentally accept the change with malicious intent. Stuff like this is best to be in source code and the build engine builds into a zip using a construct like `go:generate`. That is what it is for. `FileDescriptor` is typically something that is meant to store read/write permissions, etc., is not it?

Hi, thanks for sharing your concern and sorry for the late reply.

Protobuf file descriptors describe the types in a proto file. It is itself a proto message of the type `FileDescriptorProto` and it's used for proto reflection. It's usually not used to store read write permissions. You can find the source of it here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto

That being said, I can imagine use cases where security relevant data is stored in this proto, for example using custom options: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#customoptions. Should that be the case, I think checking in the generated code should be avoided. Instead, the build system should be used to generate the code on the fly. 

Generating protocol buffers code on the fly as part of the build system has other advantages, so it's a good idea in general: It reduces the cost for reviewing the code as only the .proto file needs to be reviewed and not the generated code, potentially for different languages and it makes certain that the `.proto` file is always in sync with the generated code.

If you want or need to rely on checked in or pre-generated code, it might be worth considering signing the generated file in a similar   way as other build artifiacts: https://slsa.dev/ is an effort that tries to make that easier, but there are other ways to do that.

Thank you for reiterating on this. I understand your point for this **specific case**.

I still have a concern in **general**. If only the generated file is signed, a malicious build machine can still inject harm into the generated opaque bytes before signing. Build machines are usually dedicated and third parties may ignore differences as versions of golang change **very** often limiting its creditworthiness. It is better not to submit byte code into code repositories but regenerate them every time. The integrity of the build system will be the only factor in this case, and the auditors can do their job properly signing only text and not binary information. The risk is that a second compiler ignores the regeneration seeing the compiled code checked in.

I realized it is better to explain it briefly. Binary data is expected to be signed and tracked. Text and code is designed to be human readable for a reason. I think it is better not to mix to save time and costs.
I agree. I think that's one more advantage of regenerating the generated file on the fly from the `.proto` file and not checking it in.

**What did you do?**

- The documented interface for several of the mapping types inside the `Descriptor` objects is `dict`: https://googleapis.dev/python/protobuf/latest/google/protobuf/descriptor.html#google.protobuf.descriptor.EnumDescriptor

   <class 'DescriptorMapping'>

always the EOL python2 interface

title: Missing wrapper types for scalar types
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

proto3: all languages

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

The most commonly recommended solution for scalar fields where a reader needs to distinguish between 'unspecified' and 'specified but default value' is to use the well known wrapper types in [wrappers.proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/wrappers.proto).  Then presence or absence of the wrapper type can be used to distinguish those two cases.  However, the wrappers defined there are only a subset of the basic scalar types supported by protobuf.  In particular, wrappers for sint32, sint64, fixed32, fixed64, sfixed32, sfixed64 are all missing.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I'd like to see wrapper classes for all of the basic scalar types to be defined and supported.  If protobuf is going to have and support those scalar types, then it seems protobuf should have and support their corresponding wrappers too.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Another alternative is to instead wrap such scalar fields in oneofs.  

However, this is [not the usually recommended approach](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2984#issuecomment-304336313) when someone wants such a scalar -- using the well known wrapper types is.  I have often read that is the main reason why the wrappers are there in the first place.  If oneofs are the preferred approach for such fields, then what is the purpose of the wrapper classes?

It would be great if one way or the other was truly the preferred and recommended way that such fields are used in APIs that use protobuf.  Then people can recognize and understand when that way is being used.

Beyond that, different languages seem to give [significantly different treatment](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2984) to oneof's and scalars they contain.  

Finally, it seems that the well known wrapper types may be given extra love in different languages' generated code or JSON translations to make them easier to use.

title: protobuf-java-util JsonFormat does not allow gson builder override
body:
Until version v3.6.1 of protobuf-java-util, the gson builder was calling `disableHtmlEscaping()`. After this version, it was removed and now the serialisation encodes everything.
This sounds like a breaking change.
Would it be possible to override the default gson builder in the JsonFormat implementation?

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.6.1 -> v3.7.0
Language: Java

**What did you do?**
We used v3.6.1 of protobuf and used to test the JSON serialisation like this:

```protobuf
// with the following proto schema generated
message Address {
    string area_code = 1;
}
```

```Java
  @Test
  public void shouldSerialiseTest() throws InvalidProtocolBufferException {
    String expected = "{\"area_code\":\"my url with an = in the text\"}";

    UserEvent.AddressOrBuilder address = UserEvent.Address.newBuilder()
         .setAreaCode("my url with an = in the text")
         .build();

    String serialised = JsonFormat.printer()
        .omittingInsignificantWhitespace()
        .preservingProtoFieldNames()
        .print(address);

    assertEquals(expected, serialised);
  }
```
**What did you expect to see**
Test was passing in v3.6.1 and was expected to pass in v3.7.0 and the following versions. 


**What did you see instead?**
This error came up:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/8374472/75664277-7f4cfb00-5c72-11ea-9cd2-335fc553e9ec.png)
The equal sign was replaced by a unicode character.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
