I can confirm that neither versions v3.12.2 nor v3.12.3 work with vc142 + "NMake Makefiles", but v3.11.4 **does** work.

I get the same errors compiling the `parse_context.h` file:
```
...parse_context.h(749): error C2491: 'google::protobuf::internal::PackedEnumParser': definition of dllimport function not allowed
...parse_context.h(765): error C2491: 'google::protobuf::internal::PackedEnumParserArg': definition of dllimport function not allowed
```

This can be solved by not exporting the method definitions for `PackedEnumParser` and `PackedEnumParserArg` in `src/google/protobuf/parse_context.h`.
Removing the `PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_DEFINE` attribute in lines 747 and 763 makes them build fine as shared libraries.

Here is a patch:
```diff
Index: src/google/protobuf/parse_context.h
===================================================================
--- src/google/protobuf/parse_context.h
+++ src/google/protobuf/parse_context.h
@@ -744,7 +744,7 @@
     void* object, const char* ptr, ParseContext* ctx);
 
 template <typename T>
-PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_DEFINE
+// PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_DEFINE do not export definition
 PROTOBUF_MUST_USE_RESULT const
     char* PackedEnumParser(void* object, const char* ptr, ParseContext* ctx,
                            bool (*is_valid)(int), InternalMetadata* metadata,
@@ -760,7 +760,7 @@
 }
 
 template <typename T>
-PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_DEFINE
+// PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_DEFINE do not export definition
 PROTOBUF_MUST_USE_RESULT const
     char* PackedEnumParserArg(void* object, const char* ptr, ParseContext* ctx,
                               bool (*is_valid)(const void*, int),
```

title: Java JSON Format includingDefaultValueFields Not Print Empty Field Option
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
Java

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Current Java Util, JsonFormat has option to do `includingDefaultValueFields`. It is usually used as the default value of the Proto field is not printed in converted JSON String. However, those empty fields will also be printed with this option. So could we have an option to not print empty fields? 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Another option to only include default values but do not print empty fields.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I could eliminate those fields on the output of JsonFormat, but it is not easy, and introducing implicit dependency.

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

In the transfer of existing REST service to gRPC, it always has middle stages, when part of the system will using the gRPC but downstream data component requires JSON input. Converting gRPC message to JSON should not happen in the beginning but it is happening. And the problem stated here is common when we want to convert messages to json payload.

title: v3.12 field presence does not support Javascript
body:
The [documentation](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/field_presence.md#javascript-example) for field presence includes a Javascript example, and there are no indications in the [announcement](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1606#issuecomment-618687169) or [release notes](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v3.12.0) that suggest Javascript is not supported.

However, Javascript field presence is not _actually_ supported in v3.12. Since this is blocking for our use of proto3 (see https://github.com/Open-Reaction-Database/ord-schema/pull/176), it would be nice to have an ETA so we can decide whether to downgrade to proto2 instead of waiting.

Unfortunately the only example of this I can find is in Golang, not Java! Can you point me in the right direction? 

Thanks!

Thanks for the report. There is a [completely new C extension](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7614) coming for PHP (intended for the 3.13.0 release) which should significantly improve performance. It would be great to know if the new extension fixes the problem described in this bug.

If you're able to try the new extension with your repro, it would be very helpful. The new C extension is compatible with all existing generated code, so you shouldn't need to regenerate your protos:

```
$ which php
<make sure the correct PHP is on your path>
$ git clone -b php-upb-msg2 https://github.com/haberman/protobuf.git
$ ./protobuf/php/tests/compile_extension.sh
$ ls protobuf/php/ext/google/protobuf2/modules/protobuf.so
```

If you can test with this `protobuf2/modules/protobuf.so` (note the `2`!) that will help me know if the new extension fixes the problem or not.

Note that the command above will give you a *debug* build. If you want a release/optimized build, run `./protobuf/php/tests/compile_extension.sh --release` instead.

title: Error message should be reported after detecting protoc execution failure
body:

After an in-depth investigation, the reason for the build failure is that the library that protoc depends on has not been found or installed in the path where it is located.
And I found that the execution command of protoc is written here:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/1dae8fdd6271d091bbf43c0fd5855603ba533c1d/cmake/protobuf-config.cmake.in#L126

$ make
$ sudo make install
# Update the Shared Libarary Cache:
$ sudo ldconfig

# Varify protoc version
$ protoc --version

```

title: Proto message parsing is ~4x slower in the latest java lite runtime compared to 3.0.1

Android

prebuilt protoc + Java lite runtime v3.12.2

**What did you do?**
We recently noticed an increase in latency in protobuf message parsing using the new/latest lite runtime vs the slightly older, now deprecated lite runtime that used the code-gen plugin (aka v3.0.1). 

The [proto](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/master:android_webview/proto/aw_variations_seed.proto) messages are usually ~8K in size. large increase in latency in proto parsing.

Nothing comes to mind.

title: protoc --descriptor_set_out should include FileDescriptorProto.source_code_info like protoc --XXX_out
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.12.3
Language: n/a

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
n/a

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
n/a

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1) create `comments.proto`:
```proto
syntax = "proto3";
package testing;
message MessageWithComments {
    // Leading field comment.
    string foo = 1;
}
```

2) Write a FileDescriptorSet for it:
```shell
$ protoc --descriptor_set_out temp comments.proto
```

3) Text-format it:
```shell
protoc < temp --decode=google.protobuf.FileDescriptorSet google/protobuf/descriptor.proto
```


**What did you expect to see**

SourceCodeInfo with comments:

```shell
file {
  name: "comments.proto"
  package: "testing"
  message_type {
    name: "MessageWithComments"
    field {
      name: "foo"
      number: 1
      label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
      type: TYPE_STRING
      json_name: "foo"
    }
  }
  source_code_info {
    …
    location {
      path: 4
      path: 0
      path: 2
      path: 0
      span: 4
      span: 4
      span: 19
      leading_comments: " Leading field comment.\n"
    }
    …
  }
  syntax: "proto3"
}
```

**What did you see instead?**

```shell
$ protoc < temp --decode=google.protobuf.FileDescriptorSet google/protobuf/descriptor.proto
file {
  name: "comments.proto"
  package: "testing"
  message_type {
    name: "MessageWithComments"
    field {
      name: "foo"
      number: 1
      label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
      type: TYPE_STRING
      json_name: "foo"
    }
  }
  syntax: "proto3"
}
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

Writing a protoc plugin, wanted to use `--descriptor_set_out` to generate data for unit tests.

nodes.body:
Drive by, from `protoc --help`

```
  --include_source_info       When using --descriptor_set_out, do not strip
                              SourceCodeInfo from the FileDescriptorProto.
                              This results in vastly larger descriptors that
                              include information about the original
                              location of each decl in the source file as
                              well as surrounding comments.
```

Apparently I did not RTFM. 

Thank you for the nudge @thomasvl , much appreciated.

title: Proto3 - PHP assign zeo value

nodes.body:
Normal proto3 fields cannot serialize zero values. However the good news it that `optional` fields are coming to proto3, which will allow you to serialize zero values. For more information see:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/field_presence.md

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v3.12.0

This is not yet implemented for PHP, but will be soon.
Proto3 optional is implemented for PHP. The feature currently requires an experimental flag, but this will be enabled by default in the next release.

title: 3.12.3 release binaries do not include commits present in 3.12.3 Git tag
body:
The commit before the v3.12.3 tagged release is 28cc693f3d05bab5f779b6fc8d514868130e81c1. I would expect to see this commit present in releases tagged for v3.12.3. Unfortunately, it appears as if it is not present; if I download the v3.12.3 release from the Github releases page, and run it, I do not see that "Generated protocol buffer code" message in the generated Python code.

When I install protoc from Homebrew, it checks out the Git tag and compiles, so I do see the message. This is a problem because some of my team members use Linux and some of them use Mac. This means that the generated protobuf file thrashes back and forth when different members of the team generate it.

I can't inspect the binary but I did run strings on it and I did not see the message in the compiled binary. Compare:

```
~/src/github.com/meterup/proto/protoc-3.12.3-linux-x86_64
± (python*) $ strings ./bin/protoc| grep 'Generated protocol'

~/src/github.com/meterup/proto/protoc-3.12.3-linux-x86_64
± (python*) $ strings /usr/local/Cellar/protobuf/3.12.3/lib/libprotoc.23.dylib | grep 'Generated protocol'
"""Generated protocol buffer code."""
```

Could you consider creating a new release that contains exactly the commits described in the release tag? This is the best way to ensure that things are predictable. 

It seems like others have previously reported problems with the Protobuf release process so this may be worth investing some time in. Alternatively, include metadata about the Git commit in the `.zip` file so that it can be compared against the actual Git tag corresponding to the release.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7560 
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7600
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7627

title: JS serializeBinaryToWriter behave different from that in java, python version.
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: Javascript

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?
Linux, MacOS

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Apple clang version 11.0.3 (clang-1103.0.32.59)

**What did you do?**
I have a proto file like:
```
message Code {
        reserved 2;
        reserved 3, 4, 5;
        oneof contract {
            bytes wasm = 1;
            StoredContract stored_code = 7;
            StoredVersionedContract stored_versioned_contract = 9;
        }
        repeated Arg args = 6;
}
```
I want to get serialized byte array by calling code.serializeBinary,  then I find the byte array it generated in JS environment is different from that in Python and Java environment. 

Here is the JS code generated by protoc:
```
proto.io.casperlabs.casper.consensus.Deploy.Code.serializeBinaryToWriter = function(message, writer) {
  var f = undefined;
  f = /** @type {!(string|Uint8Array)} */ (jspb.Message.getField(message, 1));
  if (f != null) {
    writer.writeBytes(
      1,
      f
    );
  }
 f = message.getStoredContract();
  if (f != null) {
    writer.writeMessage(
      7,
      f,
      proto.io.casperlabs.casper.consensus.Deploy.Code.StoredContract.serializeBinaryToWriter
    );
  }
  f = message.getStoredVersionedContract();
  if (f != null) {
    writer.writeMessage(
      9,
      f,
      proto.io.casperlabs.casper.consensus.Deploy.Code.StoredVersionedContract.serializeBinaryToWriter
    );
  }
  f = message.getArgsList();
  if (f.length > 0) {
    writer.writeRepeatedMessage(
      6,
      f,
      proto.io.casperlabs.casper.consensus.Deploy.Arg.serializeBinaryToWriter
    );
  }
};
```

So as you can see, it serializes `stored_code`(index 7) and `stored_version_code`(index 9) before `args`(index 6).  

But in java and python generate code, they would generate one by one by index order, in other words, they would serialize `args` before serializing `stored_code` and `stored_version_code`. 

I think we should keep JS version consistent with other version.

nodes.body:
Sorry, there is no restriction for fields serializing order. Please relax your test to not enforce any field order.
In c++, there is something like deterministic serialization, but that is not feasible in js for performance reason.

According to the documentation https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding#order

> Field numbers may be declared in any order in a `.proto` file. **The order chosen has no effect on how the messages are serialized.**

This implies that this is indeed a bug in the implementation as the order that the fields appears in the `.proto` file does in fact affect the serialization.

nodes.body:
We are working on enforce style guide. Field name like "messageId' does not match our style guide.
For internal google usages, we will raise errors at compile time if the .proto file is not match our style guide. For open source, we raise warnings but may change to raise errors too sometime in future.

The first step for enforce style guide will include:
-Enum names must always be UPPER_CASE
-Field names must always be lower_case
-Message names must always be CamelCase

Hey @anandolee , I'm the owner of this [two year old issue](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5414 ) which also boils down to us not using "snake case" and running into trouble.

I'm just incredibly confused why so many years into the project protobuf would decide to start enforcing a specific style? Even right this very second there are zero mentions of "snake case" [in the proto 3 documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3). How could you think of starting to warn/error on style without even mentioning the recommended style to users?

We have a significant quantity of code that uses protobuf with PascalCase fields and it would be disastrously expensive to rewrite all of it to interact with snake_case fields. Not to mention some of the services we talk to are 3rd party (JSON) and we have no control to enforce that they use snake_case fields. We're going to be stuck with whatever version of protobuf is the last one before snake_case becomes enforced, why not introduce proto 4 and make snake case a breaking change/feature of that language from the start?

Making snake_case mandatory seems misguided to me. It might make sense internal to google where there is a homogeneous style that has been internally enforced this whole time but it makes no sense in the public project where anyone could have done anything for _years_ up to this point.

I would love to discuss this further with stake holders, is there a good place for that?

@anandolee I've added a straightforward test case that highlights the problem here: https://github.com/yuri-sergiichuk/proto-json-same-fields-issue/blob/master/src/test/java/com/github/proto/ProtoDeserializationTest.java

tl;dr snake/camel case distinction is a red herring; the issue is that optional fields must not be specified more than once.

Unfortunately we don't have a public spec for all of JSON (although we are working on fixing it...).

JSON supports parsing either via:
- The name declared in the .proto file.
- The name declated in the `json_name` option, which defaults to the camelcasification of the name declared in the .proto.

However, the issue at hand is not that: it's that you're specifying a name multiple times in JSON. Writing

```json
{
  "my_field": 1,
  "myField": 2,
}
```

is equivalent to

```json
{
  "my_field": 1,
  "my_field": 2,
}
```

which is not valid JSON because a singular field is set multiple times.

title: Any message type throws access violation error in C++

nodes.body:
Debuging server side, here's the error:
```
Unhandled exception thrown: read access violation.
std::_String_alloc<std::_String_base_types<char,std::allocator<char> > >::_Mysize(...) returned 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF.
```

The `set_allocated_` accessors expect to be given a pointer to a heap-allocated message. Since you're passing it a pointer to an `Any` on the stack, it's going to take ownership of it and try to `delete` it, which will cause problems. You could try something like this instead:
`reply->mutable_details()->PackFrom(f);`

nodes.body:
First check the compilation options of your static and dynamic libraries to see if they use different `ABI` related options, such as `-fabi-version`.

For more information about `abi-version` option, see: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/libstdc++/manual/abi.html

> 6. Changes to the default compiler option for -fabi-version.
> It is versioned as follows:
> GCC 3.0: (Error, not versioned)
> GCC 3.1: (Error, not versioned)
> GCC 3.2: -fabi-version=1
> GCC 3.3: -fabi-version=1
> GCC 3.4, GCC 4.x: -fabi-version=2 (Incompatible with previous)
> GCC 5 and higher: -fabi-version=0 (See GCC manual for meaning)

From the two symbols you provide, you may have used a higher version of GCC(>gcc5, default `abi-version=0`), but your dynamic library(`.so` file) is compiled with an old `abi-version`(maybe with `-fabi-version=2`).

**Solution**: 
  If `abi-version` is different, you can solve this problem by compiling both your static and dynamic libraries under the same `abi-version`

title: [MSVC] fails on protostream_objectwriter_test.cc
body:
The file `util/internal/protostream_objectwriter_test.cc` fails to compile with MSVC-2019:
```
protostream_objectwriter_test.cc(107): error C2039: 'tr1': is not a member of 'std'
f:\gv\VC_2019\VC\Tools\MSVC\14.26.28801\include\stack(20): note: see declaration of 'std'
protostream_objectwriter_test.cc(107): error C3083: 'tr1': the symbol to the left of a '::' must be a type
```

Reason seems to be that with `cl -std:c++14`, it does not set the value of `__cplusplus` to a suitable value for:
```c
#if __cplusplus >= 201103L
using std::get;
#else
using std::tr1::get;
#endif
```

But with this, it compiles with any `-std:cxx` value.
```c
#if (__cplusplus >= 201103L) || (_MSVC_LANG >= 201103L)
using std::get;
#else
using std::tr1::get;
#endif
```

nodes.body: @gvanem Thanks for the bug report. We have been requiring C++11 (or newer) starting from protobuf 3.5, so we can just remove this logic that checks for C++11. I made that change to our internal codebase and it should get pushed to GitHub within a few days.

title: Consider change HasFoo to methods instead of  fields in C# when proto2

nodes.body: @jskeet bro, do you think so?

No, these are naturally properties (they're not fields) in my view... and changing them now would be breaking change, too.

I'll leave this open for others to consider, but I'm personally strongly opposed to it.

It is really a breaking change, but now hasn't officially announced it support for proto2 , so I think it's a great opportunity to change it (if want to change it)  
On the contrary, I think only those defined by metadata can be naturally properties, and this is a supplementary and instrumental field, which should not be its naturally properties.
At this point, other language implementations do this(c++,javascript,php)
I have no intention of arguing with you, I just hope you reconsider.
for other one who encountered this, can ref https://stackoverflow.com/questions/12754463/json-net-ignore-property-during-deserialization to ignore all properties start with `Has`

> On the contrary, I think only those defined by metadata can be naturally properties

It's part of the state of the object. It's as naturally a property as (say) `DateTime.Hour` is.

> At this point, other language implementations do this(c++,javascript,php)

Do all those languages *have* properties in the same way? Each language generates idiomatic code, and I can't see why it would be idiomatic for this to be a method. 

In terms of JSON serialization, you shouldn't try to serialize using Json.NET anyway: use the built-in JSON serialization, in order to guarantee compatibility with other languages. There are various ways in which using external JSON serializers will do the wrong thing - not just "Has" properties.

but, the state of the object can be private. all public properties will be serialized, has nothing to do with the serializer. 
btw, JSON.NET is recommended by official documentation, ref: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/jsonpatch?view=aspnetcore-3.1

> but, the state of the object can be private. all public properties will be serialized, has nothing to do with the serializer.

That's got *everything* to do with the serializer. The serializer chooses what it decides to serialize - that's its job. (And that's precisely why you can configure the serializer to ignore certain properties.)

> btw, JSON.NET is recommended by official documentation, ref: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/jsonpatch?view=aspnetcore-3.1

That's not the *protocol buffers* documentation though, is it?

If you serialize protobuf objects using Json.NET, they may well not be deserializable via other protobuf platforms. The naming conventions etc are all specified by protobuf. We would add Json.NET configuration attributes to the generated code, but that would then require a dependency on Json.NET, which we definitely don't want to do.

If you want to serialize something using Json.NET and some of the members are protobuf messages, you should create a Json.NET custom serializer that just uses the `ToString()` method of the protobuf object. (You'd need to configure enums separately.) I suspect that for 99% of the time, you don't really want to mix and match between protobuf and non-protobuf though - so just using the protobuf JSON serializer is fine.

oh I got it , is the `ToString()`

thank you!
Use `Foo.Parse.ParseJson` to parse, and either call `ToString()` or use `JsonFormatter` for formatting.

title: Python modules are generated with incorrect syntax when the folder path contains a folder starting with a number
body:
Protoc version 3.11.2 on Ubuntu 16.04.6

There's probably an easier way to reproduce, but how I found it was to:
1. grab https://github.com/cartographer-project/cartographer
2. Edit https://github.com/cartographer-project/cartographer/blob/master/CMakeLists.txt#L147 and add --python_out ${PROJECT_BINARY_DIR}
3. Build and try to import one of the python files whose path contains a "2d" or "3d" folder.

I think the problem is that the generated python code contains statements like

from whatever.2d.whatever import something as alias

which is apparently a syntax error. I think this is a bug because on this page (https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated) it states  "Note that if the .proto file or its path contains any characters which cannot be used in Python module names (for example, hyphens), they will be replaced with underscores. So, the file foo-bar.proto becomes the Python file foo_bar_pb2.py".

A workaround is to use sed to change all these imports to
alias = __import__('whatever.2d.whatever', fromlist=['something']).something, though I'm not sure if this might cause an issue later.

title: C++ enum_Name functions are now templates, breaking existing code.
body:
I'm upgrading a fairly large codebase to v3.12.3. One change between the versions was that <EnumType>_Name functions are now templates. Here's the list of breakage kinds that I encountered. All examples assume:
```
message X {
  enum E { ... }
}
```

- code that attempts to introduce a short alias for the `_Name` function
  ```
  auto& E_Name = X::E_Name;
  ```
- code that takes the address of the `_Name` function:  
  ```
  void foo(std::function<string(X::E)> bar);
  ...
  foo(&X::E_Name);
  ```
- code that passes a type implicitly convertible to `E`:
  ```
  std::atomic<X::E> e;
  ...
  return X::E_Name(e);
  ```

I realize that reverting the change is not practical at this point, so this is mostly FYI. From the comments on the commits that introduced the change, I got a feeling that the authors weren't sure if this would be a backward-compatible change. It wasn't :)

Version: 3.12.3.
Language: C++

Linux, Ubuntu LTS 16.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

title: What is the rationale of compiling importer.cc and parser.cc into libprotobuf rather than in libprotoc?
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?

**All of the above.**

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

At the time, [compiler/importer.cc](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/importer.cc) and [compiler/parser.cc](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/parser.cc) are linked into `libprotobuf.so` rather than in `libprotoc.so`. See [Makefile.am](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/86b3ccf28ca437330cc42a2b3a75a1314977fcfd/src/Makefile.am#L261), [libprotobuf.cmake](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/86b3ccf28ca437330cc42a2b3a75a1314977fcfd/cmake/libprotobuf.cmake#L5), [BUILD](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/86b3ccf28ca437330cc42a2b3a75a1314977fcfd/BUILD#L215).

These two files, however, implement `.proto` files parsing and thus should be linked into `libprotoc.so`. According to the [statement](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp#google.protobuf.compiler) in C++ API Reference regarding `google::protobuf::compiler` namespace:

> Since this functionality is only useful to those writing custom compilers, it is in a separate library called "libprotoc" which you will have to link against. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Fix the build scripts by moving these two files into corresponding section / library.

nodes.body:
@haberman @acozzette, could you, please, take a look onto this?
Looks like an old and dusty build configuration bug, yet I have no real proofs.

@georgthegreat This does seem like a mistake, but I'm not sure that it is worth fixing at this point. If we moved importer.cc and parser.cc into libprotoc, any code relying on them being present in libprotobuf could break.

Could ABI breakabe happen during next major / minor upgrade?
I could not find any policy describing ABI / API compatibility between protobuf releases. Is there some policy?

Generally, I am fine that you have agreed that this is indeed a bug in configuration. If there is no real option to fix this, I suggest closing this issue.

We don't make any attempt to preserve ABI compatibility, so the ABI breaks on effectively every release and you must rebuild from source when upgrading. In this case it is a bit different, though, because rebuilding wouldn't necessarily be enough, and you might also have to change your build setup to add a dependency on libprotoc.

title: How should PHP report errors?
body:
There appear to be several related but distinct ways of signaling errors in PHP:

1. Zend Exceptions: raise with `zend_throw_exception()`.
2. Zend Errors: raise with `zend_error()`.
3. PHP errors: raise with `php_error_docref()`.

The old extension uses a mix of (1) and (2). I've seem [some info](https://stackoverflow.com/a/52324314) suggesting that PHP extensions should never use (2), only (3). I haven't found a way to unit test for (2) or (3) in a way that works across versions.

What is the right answer here? Can we choose one of these options to use for all errors?

nodes.body:
See [PHP 7 Errors](https://www.php.net/manual/en/language.errors.php7.php) for the main difference. What used to be an uncatchable PHP "error" in PHP 5 is now a catchable `Error` which extends `Throwable` in PHP 7. I do not believe there is a very good argument for throwing errors as opposed to exceptions in the protobuf extension.

You can read more on this [here](https://trowski.com/2015/06/24/throwable-exceptions-and-errors-in-php7/)

Great info, thanks!

Should protobuf define its own exception class, or should we continue to use `Exception` as we do now?

I think it depends. If an [exception exists already](https://www.php.net/manual/en/spl.exceptions.php) which does a good job describing the error (e.g. `InvalidArgumentException` or `RuntimeException`, it's okay to use these. If there's a unique type of exception that doesn't map well to these (say, a `SerializationException`), then defining a protobuf Exception class is preferred so it can be explicitly caught in try/catch blocks.
I'm aligned with @bshaffer

title: Can't call ByteString.CopyFrom(ReadOnlySpan<byte> bytes) on net45
body:
<!--

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.12.3 / v4.0.0-rc1
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10 Pro 2004 (OS build 19041.330)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
.NET 4.7.2

**What did you do?**
```csharp
using System;
using Google.Protobuf;

namespace test1
{
    class Program
    {
        static void Main(string[] args)
        {
            Span<byte> a = new byte[] { 1, 2, 3 };
            var b = ByteString.CopyFrom(a);
        }
    }
}
```

**What did you expect to see**
No exception

**What did you see instead?**
```
Unhandled Exception: System.TypeAccessException: Attempt by security transparent method 'Google.Protobuf.ByteString.CopyFrom(System.ReadOnlySpan`1<Byte>)' to access security critical type 'System.ReadOnlySpan`1<System.Byte>' failed.

Assembly 'Google.Protobuf, Version=3.12.3.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=a7d26565bac4d604' is marked with the AllowPartiallyTrustedCallersAttribute, and uses the level 2 security transparency model.  Level 2 transparency causes all methods in AllowPartiallyTrustedCallers assemblies to become security transparent by default, which may be the cause of this exception.
   at Google.Protobuf.ByteString.CopyFrom(ReadOnlySpan`1 bytes)
   at test1.Program.NewMethod() in D:\Dev\test1\Program.cs:line 11
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
Same issue as "Can't call ByteString.Span on net45 #7139".
Tested putting the [SecuritySafeCritical] on CopyFrom. This solved the problem:
```csharp
#if GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_SUPPORT_SYSTEM_MEMORY
        /// <summary>
        /// Constructs a <see cref="ByteString" /> from a read only span. The contents
        /// are copied, so further modifications to the span will not
        /// be reflected in the returned <see cref="ByteString" />.
        /// </summary>
        [SecuritySafeCritical]
        public static ByteString CopyFrom(ReadOnlySpan<byte> bytes)
        {
            return new ByteString(bytes.ToArray());
        }
#endif
```

title: google::protobuf::util::JsonStringToMessage How to reject a json string when the json string missing a proto3 message field ?
body: Pb3 removed the keyword required and optional, And we want to do the field check when converting from a json string to pb3 message, we find when a field is missing the Jong string, JsonStringToMessage API will automatically set the missing field to the default value, for example empty json string "{}” will set all message fields to default by calling this API, but such json request is obviously illegal. how to do this json field check in pb3?

nodes.body: Proto3 doesn't make a distinction between a primitive field being absent and it being set to its default value (i.e. 0 for numeric types or "" for strings/bytes). Once you have parsed the json into a proto message, there is no way to tell whether or not a particular field was set.

title: Version 4.0
body: The PHP community usually does not consider dropping support for older versions of PHP to be a BC break. If this is the only reason for a 4.0 release, I'd question if it is worth it.

nodes.body: Looking at reflection for [3.2.13](https://git.remirepo.net/cgit/rpms/php/pecl/php-pecl-protobuf.git/plain/REFLECTION) and [4.0.0RC1](https://git.remirepo.net/cgit/rpms/php/pecl/php-pecl-protobuf4.git/plain/REFLECTION) it seems there are lot of changes (54 classes => 14 classes)
How many of those classes where `@internal`?
I believe PHP 5 users will receive an error when compiling Version 4.0, which means it is actually a backwards compatibility break and deserves a major version bump.

Right, but as I said, the PHP community doesn't consider that to be a breaking change. PECL packages and Composer packages drop support for older PHP versions all the time in minor releases, and this is considered to be compatible with semantic versioning.
@GrahamCampbell thank you for weighing in. Can you provide some examples of this?

Of course. The 2nd most popular PECL extension "yaml" dropped PHP 7.0 support in a minor release in April this year. The 3rd most popular PECL extension "xdebug" dropped PHP 5.5, 5.6, 7.0, and 7.1 support all in minor releases, over the last few years. The package manager Composer itself will be dropping PHP 5.3 (and maybe others) in a minor release later this year (https://github.com/composer/composer/issues/8785). The 15th most popular composer package https://packagist.org/packages/doctrine/instantiator with over 200 million downloads dropped PHP 5.3-7.0 in a minor release earlier this year and so did the 16th most popular package https://packagist.org/packages/doctrine/lexer. The list goes on. Even those packages that have not yet done this, have authors that plan to do it in the future, or agree that it is not a BC break.

> Looking at reflection for 3.2.13 and 4.0.0RC1 it seems there are lot of changes (54 classes => 14 classes)

To clarify, many of the classes that appear to have disappeared are still there, but are now implemented with pure PHP that is embedded into the C extension and lazily loaded with `protobuf_internal_loadbundled`:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/php/ext/google/protobuf/protobuf.c#L165-L167
Also, Microsoft dropped PHP 7.0 in version 5.6.0, and PHP 7.1 in version 5.8.0 of their sql server extension: https://github.com/Microsoft/msphpsql.

Regarding #2, the PECL package has already been updated to depend on PHP >= 7.0 in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7730. Composer doesn't need to be updated because the pure-PHP library still supports PHP 5.

Without a major version bump, do we still want to have #7692 (stop referencing legacy class names) in this release?
That change is a API breaking change for very old protobuf php generated code.
My thinking is to include that change, because we have introduced the new class name more than a year ago. Users should have already got enough time to migrate (by just regenerating their generated code.)

> The 2nd most popular PECL extension "yaml" dropped PHP 7.0 support in a minor release in April this year.

It looks like this actually happened in a 2.0 release: https://pecl.php.net/package/yaml/2.0.0

> The 3rd most popular PECL extension "xdebug" dropped PHP 5.5, 5.6, 7.0, and 7.1 support all in minor releases, over the last few years. The package manager Composer itself will be dropping PHP 5.3 (and maybe others) in a minor release later this year (composer/composer#8785).

Xdebug also supplies a nice [wizard](https://xdebug.org/wizard) that helps guide users into which versions are supported. This is one approach, but I think this information can also be signaled to users by using major version bumps when striking changes are applied.

> The 15th most popular composer package https://packagist.org/packages/doctrine/instantiator with over 200 million downloads dropped PHP 5.3-7.0 in a minor release earlier this year and so did the 16th most popular package https://packagist.org/packages/doctrine/lexer. The list goes on. Even those packages that have not yet done this, have authors that plan to do it in the future, or agree that it is not a BC break.

This seems a bit different to me as these are packages installed via composer and not pecl, users can still resolve older versions of the package easily. Also, looking through issues it seems there was a fair amount of confusion brought about by this that may have been avoided by a major version bump.

From what I can tell, this seems to be a fragmented issue with no broad consensus. For each example of teams that don't bump the major version, there are examples of others that do - I think it just comes down to what makes the team comfortable in how they convey this information effectively to users. Personally, I still think a major bump is a nice way to inform folks PHP5 is no longer usable with the extension.
We ultimately decided not to introduce a new major version for dropping PHP 5.x in PECL.

title: PHP extension  4.0 - cast from zend_obj

nodes.body: P.S.  no PR because of damned CLA.

Thanks for taking a look at the new extension!

Did this lead to an actual issue for you (eg. a SIGSEGV) or is this something you just saw from inspecting the code?

I know extensions are supposed to use the pattern above. But we force the property count to zero, which prevents PHP from writing properties after the `zend_object` structure. So in practice it seems to work, at least in the cases I have tried.

To leave a bit more info: in my testing, adding this line prevented PHP from writing to any memory after the `zend_object` member of `struct Message`: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/ffb2b538347d3a1e1f63bf85db8260dc4d514aa9/php/ext/google/protobuf/message.c#L71-L72

This is probably not a totally kosher approach. I could imagine that it might break on a different major version of PHP, like PHP 8. If so, we should implement your fix.

But if not, does it cause any harm to leave in for now?
Also a note that if we do this, we also need to move the `zend_object std` member of the `Message` struct to be at the end instead of at the beginning.

> Did this lead to an actual issue for you (eg. a SIGSEGV) or is this something you just saw from inspecting the code?

From code review, checking for PHP 8 compatibility

> we also need to move the zend_object std member of the Message struct to be at the end instead of at the beginning.

Yes, the zend_object must be first member in 5.x and last in 7.x

Following PHP common practice seems better for code legibility, ad may also help for future version

Ex:
```
+#if PHP_VERSION_ID < 80000
 static zval *Message_read_property(zval *obj, zval *member, int type,
                                    void **cache_slot, zval *rv) {
-  Message* intern = (Message*)Z_OBJ_P(obj);
+  Message* intern = Z_MESSAGE_P(obj);
+#else
+static zval *Message_read_property(zend_object *obj, zend_string *member, int type,
+                                   void **cache_slot, zval *rv) {
+  Message* intern = fetch_message(obj);
+#endif

```

I would rather avoid `#ifdef`.

I'm reluctant to change the current code if it works in practice. But if we do need to change it, I'd rather change it for all PHP versions, rather than use `#ifdef`.
The #if is mandatory, Message_read_property protocol must be different in php 7 (accepting a zval) and php 8 (accepting a zend_object).

In php 8, the writer_property handler needs to return reference to the internal property.
In our new implementation, we don't have a zval property internally. Any suggestion?
@remicollet any idea?
@dstogov could you help here?

I missed @TeBoring's point before. To clarify, in PHP7 the `write_property` function prototype was:

```
void Message_write_property(zval *obj, zval *member, zval *val, void **cache_slot)
```

Whereas in PHP8 it is:

```
zval *Message_write_property(zend_object *object, zend_string *member, zval *value, void **cache_slot);
```

Our message objects do not internally store `zval` values, so we can't return a pointer to our internal storage. But would it work ok if we just returned the `value` parameter?

The change for return value was not in 8.0, but in 7.4 

From UPGRADING.INTERNALS

```
 m. The write_property() object handler now returns the assigned value (after
     possible type coercions) rather than void. For extensions, it should
     usually be sufficient to return whatever was passed as the argument.
```

The `write_property` issue was fixed in #7793.

The cast from `zend_obj` seems to be working fine for now. We can change it if it causes a problem later.

title: Unrecoverable freeze/crash when calling .extend on repeated field with current object
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.12
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
MacOS 10.15.6

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.7.3 (Clang 11.0.3 (clang-1103.0.32.62) on darwin)
protobuf==3.12.2 ('pip install protobuf')
libprotoc 3.12.3 (installed via Homebrew)

**What did you do?**

Using the following .proto file:

```
syntax = "proto3";

message Foo {
    message Bar {
        uint32 dummy = 1;
    }
    repeated Bar bars = 1;
}
```

In a script/interpreter, the following code unrecoverably crashes/freezes (I need to kill my terminal):

```python
>>> import foo_pb2
>>> f = foo_pb2.Foo()
>>> bar = foo_pb2.Foo.Bar()
>>> bar.dummy = 123            
>>> f.bars.append(bar)
>>> f.bars.extend(f.bars)
--- TERMINAL FROZEN - NEEDS TO BE KILLED ---
```

The code below works fine (as I would expect):

```python
>>> import foo_pb2
>>> f1 = foo_pb2.Foo()
>>> bar1 = foo_pb2.Foo.Bar()
>>> bar1.dummy = 123
>>> f1.bars.append(bar1)
>>>
>>> f2 = foo_pb2.Foo()
>>> bar2 = foo_pb2.Foo.Bar()
>>> bar2.dummy = 456
>>> f2.bars.append(bar2)
>>>
>>> f1.bars.extend(f2.bars)
>>>
```

**What did you expect to see**

An error, a success, an exception, anything other than what happened.

**What did you see instead?**

I didn't see anything, but the terminal/python interpreter crashes, and there is no recovery. 

I ran into this problem while writing unit tests for my application and I mis-typed a variable, which led me to debug all my code, and then narrow down on this error and come up with a reproducible use case.

The second example is what I MEANT to do, but I accidentally did the first example - and that led to a large test/terminate cycle.

title: PHP immutable messages

title: MessageToJsonString() serializes integer type map-values as strings
body:
**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Consider a map defined as:

```proto3
 map<string, uint64> RetCodes = 11;
```

`MessageToJsonString()` will output:

```json
{
  "200": "49988"
}
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**

`MessageToJsonString()` will instead output:

```json
{
  "200": 49988
}
```

As the map value is int typed, and can be serialised as such.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Consuming it as is-is possible, but may require extra handling when no schema is used
(e.g. explicitly convert to an int post deserialize)

**Additional context**
https://github.com/envoyproxy/nighthawk/issues/422

nodes.body: I haven't looked closely at this code, but I suspect the motivation might have to do with the fact that JSON numbers are floating-point doubles, so not every uint64 can be represented exactly as JSON, unless it's formatted as a string.

This seems to be the most relevant issue, so I'll leave my comment here. The protobuf JSON serialization behavior of converting `u/int64` values to strings is, in my opinion, a leak of the behavior of 1 particular language that has nontrivial consequences for other protobuf supported languages. I have a [change request](https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/protobuf/+/288353) open to support an `EmitInt64Unquoted` option for the Go library, and I'd like to request for that feature to be standard in JSON serializers across all officially-supported protobuf languages.
Closing this due to Adam's comment above and the comments on the change request in the Go library.

title: Feature Request: Enums as Map Keys

nodes.body: @dlj-NaN I think it was due to Java that we couldn't use enum as key.
Hey, is there any workaround to pass enum as key in map. I have to write .proto file for java files. But enum as key not working in map. Appreciate if we can do this by some workaround.

+1 
I'm using C#. I am interested in creating a map of <enum, string>.

Like @TeBoring mentioned, this is not possible with the core consistency model shared across all target languages.

This is the core issue: if an unrecognized enum value is encountered during deserialization, then there has to be defined behavior for handling it. The problem isn't that we lack an answer, but rather, that we have too many mutually incompatible answers. In other words, whatever functionality is "obvious" in one target language is going to be nonsense in others (at best), or invalidate behavior that is already specified and lead to corruption when dealing with existing serialized values (at worst).

If you want to have a map of strings keyed by enum, the best workaround is to use a `map<int, string>`. The ergonomics of this approach (or lack thereof) exactly mirrors the problem: if the enum type is considered closed, then we (obviously) cannot provide an identity mapping for unknown enum values. However, if the enum type is open, then we have to reject any language niceties that would come from a closed enum type.  Quite simply, the way to use enums as if they are open is to store them as ints.

Unfortunately, I will have to close this FR, because the consistency issues are simply not feasible to address.

Can this issue be reopened? This is just a ridiculous wart, given how core enums are in protobuf. We have many situations where we want to use enums as a key. Being able to specify map<EnumName, .. > is so much better from a documentation standpoint alone.

What about having languages with closed enums have the code generated as if map<int32, ...> was specified, while languages with open enums get properly generated interface with the enum type?
thank you as well for thoughtfully answering my feature request :)

title: lack of specification for serializating NaN and infinity for google.protobuf.Value.number_value
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master/v3.6.0/v3.5.0 etc.
Language: C++/Go (probably other ones too)

I think the following issue https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/1182 is best addressed here first.

The [developers guide](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/google.protobuf#google.protobuf.Value) mentions that the JSON representation for Value.number_value "Represents a double value."  The [guide](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json) also mentions for "float, double" --

"JSON value will be a number or one of the special string values "NaN", "Infinity", and "-Infinity". Either numbers or strings are accepted. Exponent notation is also accepted."

Both the C++ and the Go implementations serialize these values with those special string values.  However, this presents a flaw in round-trip serialization.  Both C++ and Go implementations deserialize the JSON values into google.protobuf.Value.string_value as those are JSON strings.

Given the ambiguity, I think there needs to be better clarification for this and/or treat serialization of these special values as an error for google.protobuf.Value.number_value as proposed by @dsnet .

nodes.body: I think this is unavoidable because "NaN" can also mean a real string. We have no way to tell whether it means a string or a double. Could you use DoubleValue instead?
This issue is not so much about what users can do instead, but what is supposed to be correct serialization behavior.

> I think this is unavoidable because "NaN" can also mean a real string. We have no way to tell whether it means a string or a double.

Precisely, and hence treating NaN and infinity as an error during serialization will ensure that Value.number_value can round-trip properly if it can only contain a real number.
@cybrcodr I think that makes sense. Let me check with my team.

The design document for JSON serialization for protobufs specifies that a `google.protobuf.Value` message without one of the `kind` fields explicitly populated should be rejected in order to ensure proper round-trip preservation of data. Given that proper preservation of data seems to be the intention, it would follow that NaN and Infinity should also be rejected in order to preserve the same property.
Doc has been updated: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json

title: [Java] Add hashCode and equals for Descriptor class

nodes.body: I think that's because the map field doesn't have canonical encoding. @dlj-NaN

Per JDK API docs, " The general contract of hashCode is: Whenever it is invoked on the same object more than once during an execution of a Java application, the hashCode method must consistently return the same integer, provided no information used in equals comparisons on the object is modified. This integer need not remain consistent from one execution of an application to another execution of the same application."

That is, getting a different hash code on a different machine or even the same machine in a new process is not a bug. It's only a bug if two equal objects in the same application have different hash codes. I'm not sure if that can happen here or not.
equals and hashCode are both inherited from java.lang.Object so they're consistent and this behavior is acceptable. It might still be useful to define more value-based equal and hashCode methods.
This seems like an abuse of Java's hashCode and equals which are not meant to be used as stable values across processes. This is primarily prevented by maps having unspecified hash-code behavior.

title: [C#] Google.Protobuf.JsonFormatter: Keep decimal point in all doubles
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What language does this apply to?**
C# / proto3 

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
The Google.Protobuf.JsonFormatter removes the decimal point when serializing double values that do not have digits after the decimal point. So this:

```
[TestMethod]
public void TestSerializeGoogle()
{
     var message = new LargeDoubleTestMessage()
     {
         LargeDouble = 210000000000
     };
     string jsonOutput = Google.Protobuf.JsonFormatter.Default.Format(message);
}
```

produces this json string:

`{ "largeDouble": 210000000000 }`

Unfortunately other serializers might use the decimal point to detect this as a double. So when this json string is exchanged, it might prevent deserialization (too large for an Int32) or it changes the type to Int64, which prevents the JsonFormatter from parsing it back into the original IMessage as a double is expected.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
A solution would be a similar formatting as Newtonsoft Json is using: This:

```
[TestMethod]
public void TestSerializeNewton()
{
    var cls = new LargeDoubleTestClass()
    {
        LargeDouble = 210000000000
    };
    string jsonOutput = Newtonsoft.Json.JsonConvert.SerializeObject(cls);
}
```

produces this json string:

`{"LargeDouble":210000000000.0}`

which makes it exchangeable.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I tried to find settings / flags with which I could influence the formatting behavior of the JsonFormatter, but could not find any. I believe this:

```
else if (value is float || value is double)
{
       string text = ((IFormattable) value).ToString("r", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
```

in JsonFormatter.cs is where a double is written and there is no way for me to change that.

nodes.body:
I would suggest this is fundamentally a problem of "the other serializers". Lots of JSON serializers have their own little variations on what's actually specified - I don't want to go down that route with Google.Protobuf.

(I definitely wouldn't want to do this by default; while we *could* add it as yet another option in `JsonFormatter.Settings`, I'd really prefer not to do so.)

Closing for now - the issue is nearly two years old and hasn't generated any other community enthusiasm. @ConiJB if you feel really strongly about this, please add another comment and I can talk with the main protobuf team about it.

It sounds like the linkage checker may soon help detect this, but FYI, another option is to run Animal Sniffer, as [we do in Guava](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/d8e921fd2df52184708d6eb9516e4869f548d841/pom.xml#L139-L160).

I've heard mixed things about the `--release` flag. It may be simplest to just build with JDK8. But as long as Animal Sniffer or an updated linkage checker is in place, I would assume that anything that works is fine.

If you want to avoid this particular error without changing compiler settings, you may be able to change [the code](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.12.4/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.java#L1686) to upcast the buffer to `Buffer` before calling `flip()`. Maybe I'll put together a fix.

\[edit: [a post with some explanation](https://www.morling.dev/blog/bytebuffer-and-the-dreaded-nosuchmethoderror/)\]

Uh-oh:

- Animal Sniffer detects this, and it _logs_, but it does not report an _error_:
    - https://github.com/mojohaus/animal-sniffer/issues/77
    - https://github.com/mojohaus/animal-sniffer/pull/83
    - https://github.com/mojohaus/animal-sniffer/pull/87
- The signature changes affect _dozens_ of calls in protobuf. So while we _could_ cast to `Buffer` before every call (or maybe change the types of some fields/variables/parameters), it would be a pain, and without an automated check, it would likely regress.

`--release 8` (or just building with JDK 8, which [maven-enforcer-plugin can require](https://maven.apache.org/enforcer/maven-enforcer-plugin/usage.html)) sounds potentially more promising.

(I assume you're building releases with Maven, but I see some (Bazel) BUILD files, too, so it's possible that I'm wrong about that.)

Oh, and I had trouble building _anything_ with Maven with JDK11+ because of a maven-surefire-plugin problem with `SystemUtils.isJavaVersionAtLeast` in recent versions of Java. It's probably fixable by upgrading maven-surefire-plugin and/or some of its libraries.

\[edit: The problem is https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/SUREFIRE-1439, and it's apparently fixable by upgrading to maven-surefire-plugin 2.21.0. I have sent https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7830 to update to the newest version, 3.0.0-M5, but it's stuck because CI uses an old version of Maven.\]

It's possible that `-DskipTests` would at least let you get far enough to see the non-fatal Animal Sniffer messages. If not, another hacky workaround (not to be committed) is to stick this in the parent's pluginManagement:

```xml
        <plugin>
          <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
          <executions>
            <execution>
              <id>default-test</id>
              <phase />
            </execution>
          </executions>
        </plugin>
```

It sounds like the right solution here is to pass `--release` to javac (by setting `<release>` for maven-compiler-plugin).

The pom.xml suggests that you're actually targeting Java _7_, not 8, so that would be `<release>7</release>`, replacing [the existing `<source>` and `<target>`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/7db720e07524f96be558f194ae1ffee4a9d49972/java/pom.xml#L120-L121).

The downside to that is that you need to require that developers who build protobuf themselves build with [JDK 9+ to use `--release`](https://openjdk.java.net/jeps/247). You could hide the `<release>` setting behind a `<profile>` so that you can disable it for JDK 8, but that just means that, when you build with JDK 8, you still won't have a strong guarantee of compatibility with Java 7. (That risk might be tolerable, but it also seems easy enough to avoid.)

Ah, but `--release` prevents usage of `Unsafe`.

I then tried:

`<compilerArgs><arg>--add-exports=java.base/jdk.internal.misc=ALL-UNNAMED</arg></compilerArgs>`

But:

`error: option --add-exports not allowed with target 1.7`

(nor with target 1.8, so (a) you can't just bump to that (even if you wanted to) and (b) this doesn't help us [for Guava](https://github.com/google/guava/issues/3990), either)

The only truly correct solution may be to build with Java 7 \[edit: but I don't know how well supported that is nowadays, including through Maven\] (or at least with Java 8 pointed at a Java 7 bootclasspath). Animal Sniffer can help somewhat, but the fact that it [doesn't actually fail the build](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7827#issuecomment-676563016) is unfortunate. Maybe the best bet is a combination of (a) requiring building with Java 8 and (b) asking Animal Sniffer to look for compatibility with Java 7?

Err, I may have actually seen some evidence that Animal Sniffer's signatures for Java 7 _likewise_ reject usage of `Unsafe`? If so, I was hoping that there was a set of signatures for `java17-sun`, but [it appears not](https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/org/codehaus/mojo/signature/). (Oddly, the `java18` set of signatures that [we use for Guava](https://github.com/google/guava/blob/23be71af402328c19e00c333e370e31357308b4b/pom.xml#L147) _permits_ `Unsafe`.)

So, if you want to use Animal Sniffer, you'll probably have to mark your `Unsafe`-using code with Animal Sniffer's `@IgnoreJRERequirement` annotation (or [a custom annotation you configure to avoid that dependency](https://github.com/google/guava/commit/5f37e53fd73540acdc1d69e33ecc8a91827890a7#diff-600376dffeb79835ede4a0b285078036)).

Supposedly you can generate your own signatures for the JDK or anything else, but that sounds like a pain.

FYI, in Guava, we are adding the upcasts (indirectly, by introducing helper methods): https://github.com/google/guava/pull/3994

- It would prevent us from conditionally using JDK 11 APIs like `VarHandle`.
- It would complicate _testing_ with newer JDKs.

Not necessarily.  It just means that the Protobuf Java developers have to arrange for the `protobuf-java` library to get built in a way that will make it work on all the supported Java versions.  They can do that right now, but they haven't done it yet.  Based on the comments above, it could be done in at least three different ways:

1. Force the calls to methods that got covariant return types in Java 9+ to use the return types as they were before Java 9.  This is what some people are doing when they talk about casting as a solution and is what the Guava developers did but in a way that does not involve casting (i.e., wrapper methods).
2. Build the `protobuf-java` library with JDK 7 or 8. If the Maven Compiler Plugin would work if a JDK 7 boot classpath were specified, then the problem is with how the Protobuf Java developers have configured the build.  However, in their defense, it seems lame that the Maven Compiler Plugin would let you configure a target of Java 7 but that it could still result in a miscompile that won't work on Java 7.  It seems to me that it shouldn't even allow that; I think if the Maven Compiler Plugin is configured with a target Java version, it should require a JDK boot classpath matching the configured target and fail the build if not provided.

title: [C#] Enable pooling of messages with large RepeatedFields
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What language does this apply to?**
C# proto3

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Sending multiple messages, each containing a large `RepeatedField` (all of the same size), without allocating a new backing array for each `RepeatedField`. Effectively, I'd like to be able to pool `RepeatedFields` for reuse.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
One possible solution could be to provide a method similar to `Clear`, which keeps the backing array and only resets the `count` field (see [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/214c77e1b76e63e512bd675d1c300c80438642b6/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/Collections/RepeatedField.cs#L344)).

nodes.body: Reassigning this as I'm not on the protobuf team - but this sort of pooling sounds pretty complicated to achieve.
I agree with Jon, this pooling sounds complicated. We've generally gotten good results from using arenas -- if anything we'd probably be more inclined to go in that direction.

@CodeBlanch: I don't think that's actually what was being requested.

The first comment *explicitly* says:

> Effectively, I'd like to be able to pool RepeatedFields for reuse.

Each message has a separate `RepeatedField` object, and changing that would be a very major change - so changing the implementation of `Clear` wouldn't help that scenario at all.

If the OP was talking about reusing the original message by clearing and re-populating it, that would be different (and certainly more feasible) - but that's not what's been asked for at the moment.

@CodeBlanch @jskeet apologies for the unclear initial issue description. The intention of the issue was pretty much exactly what @CodeBlanch interpreted.

Instead of 

> Effectively, I'd like to be able to pool RepeatedFields for reuse.

Should have written something like

> Effectively, I'd like to be able to reuse messages containing `RepeatedField`s

By now the performance of my use case is good enough for me (through other means), so I personally don't have any need for this change. But @CodeBlanch feel free to hijack this issue :-)

Okay, so the proposed change would *just* be to the `Clear` method, which would keep the existing array, reset it (e.g. with `Array.Clear`) and set the `count` field to 0? That sounds more reasonable, at least. I don't promise to get to this any time soon, but it's good to make sure we're all on the same page.
FWIW, there is prior art for this kind of optimization in C++ protobuf. `Clear()` on C++ protos has traditionally held on to the sub-message objects for re-use.

@jskeet 

> Okay, so the proposed change would just be to the Clear method, which would keep the existing array, reset it (e.g. with Array.Clear) and set the count field to 0? That sounds more reasonable, at least. I don't promise to get to this any time soon, but it's good to make sure we're all on the same page.

That would work for me 👍

Happy to submit a PR if it would be helpful.

title: [Ruby] JRuby - type of oneof is always nil after decoding
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.13.0
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux Ubuntu 16.x and 18.x.

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Ruby 2.6.3 and JRuby 9.2.9.0.
But this bug is already in protobuf for JRuby for a long time...

**What did you do?**
Consider the following Ruby script:
```
require 'google/protobuf'

def assert(lhs, rhs)
  raise Exception, "#{lhs} != #{rhs}" unless lhs == rhs
end

pool = Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.new
pool.build do
  add_message "OneofMessage" do
    oneof :my_oneof do
      optional :a, :string, 1
      optional :b, :int32, 2
      optional :c, :bool, 3
    end
  end
end

OneofMessage = pool.lookup('OneofMessage').msgclass
m1 = OneofMessage.new
m1.b = 666
assert(m1.b, 666)
assert(m1.my_oneof, :b)

bytes = OneofMessage.encode(m1)
m2 = OneofMessage.decode(bytes)

assert(m2.b, 666)
assert(m2.my_oneof, :b)
```
**What did you expect to see**
Under Ruby this script does not report any assertion violations, as expected.

**What did you see instead?**
Under JRuby, the last assert fails as m2.my_oneof is nil instead of :b.
This means that for a receiver of message it is not clear which of the fields of the oneof has been set.

title: Bump Google.Protobuf dependency on System.Memory to version >=4.5.3
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
C#/.NET

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
With version 3.13.0 Google.Protobuf raised dependency on netstandard from >=1.0 to >=1.1 and added dependency on System.Memory 4.0.1.0 (provided by package 4.5.2) - previously this dependency was only present in netstandard2.0 build.

The dependency itself isn't a problem, it's a pretty common package, however the currently used version is a bit old and conflicts with other packages (e.g. Grpc.Core) causing problems upstream, e.g. 
https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/22251 or https://www.gitmemory.com/issue/grpc/grpc/21908/585508325

In my toolset it causes error like this during compilation:
```
error : Can't load types from 'Google.Protobuf, Version=3.13.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=a7d26565bac4d604'. Error: Nie można załadować pliku lub zestawu '
System.Memory, Version=4.0.1.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=cc7b13ffcd2ddd51' lub jednej z jego zależności. Nie można odnaleźć określonego pliku..
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I think matching System.Memory dependency with Grpc by bumping it to 4.0.1.1 (provided by package 4.5.3 or newest 4.5.4) would be desirable. I'm not completely sure about compatibility implications of such change (for netstandard1.1), so a safer plan would be to do this only for netstandard2.0 build, for which version 4.5.2 (currently used) and 4.5.3 of System.Memory do not differ on dependencies:
```
System.Buffers (>= 4.4.0)
System.Numerics.Vectors (>= 4.4.0)
System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe (>= 4.5.2)
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Right now I'm using Google.Protobuf 3.12.4 netstandard1.0 build + Grpc.Core 2.31.0 and they work find together. However trying to upgrade Google.Protobuf to 3.13.0 creates a conflict, downgrading System.Memory to 4.5.2 causes problem with Grpc.Core 

**Additional context**
My .NET compiler for some reason doesn't allow using newer System.Memory assembly with Google.Protobuf 3.13.0, though I think some people got past compilation phase and got a warning at runtime instead, which can be further improved by using binding redirect.

nodes.body:
Adding a `<AutoGenerateBindingRedirects>true</AutoGenerateBindingRedirects>` to your .csproj should help.
http://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/?LinkId=294190

What TFM is your project targeting? Are you using classic .csproj project or the new .NET core .csproj format?

The particular project / compiler that I'm using doesn't support ``AutoGenerateBindingRedirects`` thus I rely on compatible dependencies. I'm targeting net45 here, but whether I pick ``netstandard1.1``, ``netstandard2.0`` or ``net45`` ``Google.Protobuf.dll`` version as dependency I still get the error, since all of them depend on the same 4.0.1.0 ``System.Memory`` that is different than grpc's dependency.
Please upgrade System.Memory to 4.5.3 in Google.Protobuf.dll

I solved it.
Download google protobuf source, enter csharp dir, change `<PackageReference Include="System.Memory" Version="4.5.3" />` from 4.5.2 to 4.5.3, run `dotnet publish -c Release -f net45`, replace Google.Protobuf.dll. Thank you for every contributor, you make the world better!

This will be fixed once #7940 is merged. Alternatively, it can be solved without needing to upgrade anything by adding this line to your .csproj:
https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/9fac907f806c3a9b9b775b15d8e3cb387c4d7048/test/distrib/csharp/DistribTest/DistribTest.csproj#L67

title: Wrong Error Message for fieldname with underscores in them
body:
Working with the protobuf compiler (`protoc`) and noticed that the following error message occurred when there were two fields within the same message named: `phantom` and `_phantom`:

```
The JSON camel-case name of field "phantom" conflicts with field "_phantom". This is not allowed in proto3.
```

This error message is inaccurate, the real reason it failed was because the compiler strips away `_` which results in a naming conflict. 

Fixing this would help developers understand when they have written a protobuf that doesn't compile.

nodes.body: Sorry for the long delay. This is intended behavior and the error message is correct. The reason it fails is because the JSON name of the two are the same since an underscore is appended to `phantom`.

Bob provided me a reproducer script locally (it has some Google-internal details, so it's not attached here). The steps boiled down to this:

1.  Fetch sources from Git for these packages:
    * google-ads-python (internal fork of https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-python, which includes some patches Bob is working on)
    * googleads-python-lib (https://github.com/googleads/googleads-python-lib)
    * protobuf (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf)
2.  Create and activate a new Python venv
3.  Install googleads-python-lib using `pip install .` inside the checkout.
4.  Install the protobuf_distutils package from the protobuf checkout:
    ```
    cd path/to/protobuf
    cd python/protobuf_distutils
    python setup.py build
    python setup.py install
    ```
5.  Install google-ads-python from its checkout:
    ```
    cd path/to/google-ads-python
    python setup.py generate_py_protobufs
    python setup.py build
    python setup.py install
    ```
6.  Pin protobuf==3.13.0 with:
    ```
    python -m pip uninstall -y protobuf
    python -m pip install protobuf==3.13.0
    ```

title: [Question] Autogenerated tag on generated files
body:
As I do not have enough permissions to ask a question in the google group, I'll ask it here anyway. 
Is there a way to add an auto generated tag in the cs files that are generated?
I currently have problems with the rule SA1518: File is required to end with a single newline character
I think the StyleCop Analyzers are ignoring files with those autogenerated tags automatically.
Or is there an other way to work around this?
I tried ignoring it, but then the cs files that need this rule are also ignored.
It looks that the generated file is empty too. Maybe that's the issue. 
I created the same question here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet/issues/1043
and here: https://groups.google.com/g/grpc-io/c/ZdNwCnZNqRk as I don't know who is actually generating the cs files.
I'm pretty new to grpc and protobuf.

Thanks!

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.13.0
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Micosoft Windows 10 Pro - 10.0.19041 Build 19041

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

**What did you do?**
1. Create a project with Stylecop.Analyzers and FxCopAnalyzers, where SA1518 is handled as an error.
2. Add a proto without a service 
3. Rebuild your project

**What did you expect to see**
A cs file with an autogenerated tag on top, even when it's empty.

**What did you see instead?**
A style error, and an empty generated cs file.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/52781305/92564557-a582d180-f279-11ea-8688-9451ea3a31bc.png)

nodes.body: Resolved in another thread: https://groups.google.com/g/grpc-io/c/ZdNwCnZNqRk

> Resolved in another thread: https://groups.google.com/g/grpc-io/c/ZdNwCnZNqRk

@deannagarcia Could you reopen this question. The resolution in the other thread is that the OP just changed the build to not fail with the error. 

NVM, figured out the issue was that a `service` definition was missing, so an empty grpc file was being generated : https://groups.google.com/g/grpc-io/c/l6bZwTLbDb4

> Does your .proto file contain any service definitions (as opposed to just protobuf messages)? If not, no *Grpc.cs file should be generated (as there are no services that gRPC could use).

I think this is the problem isn't it? 

> Does your .proto file contain any service definitions (as opposed to just protobuf messages)? If not, no *Grpc.cs file should be generated (as there are no services that gRPC could use).

Proto files that only contain protobuf message still generate a *Grpc.cs file. And that generated .cs file is completely empty which causes the StyleCop Analyzer to not skip it.

I'm having the exact same problem. SA1518 is complaining about a totally empty file. 4 .cs files are generated and 3 of them are full and have the appropriate `auto-generated` header. But one is totally empty. 
These are generated by two .proto files that I copied into my project from a 3rd party project.

I was able to work around it by creating an .editorconfig file in my obj directory with this content:

```
[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.SA1518.severity = none
```

I then had to add it explicitly to my csproj:

```xml
  <ItemGroup>
    <EditorConfigFiles Include="..\..\obj\.editorconfig" Link=".editorconfig" />
  </ItemGroup>
```

That allowed me to suppress SA1518 only from the generated code but keep the rule turned on for my own user code.

title: C# MergeFrom ReadOnlySpan with no allocations
body:
Hi,

With the latest release of Grpc.Tools, we are now able to execute code that writes the serialized message directly to Span<byte> without incurring allocations. This is based on IBufferMessage. Thank you for that release!

My questions is what is the way to achieve the reverse process? Specifically without allocating a CodedInputStream or any other heap based objects. Is there (or are the plans for) an API that can help us achieve the following:
1. Given an instantiated (new allocated) Message - M,
2. Execute M.MergeFrom(ReadOnlySpan)
3. The above to complete without allocating heap memory (for things like CodedInputStream, etc.)

I have been using a custom solution to achieve the above steps but it involves subclassing **Stream** and a buffer copy to a preallocated buffer. If there were to be a native solution to achieve the equivalent of IMessage.MergeFrom(ReadOnlySpan) without additional allocation then that would help get rid of the workaround code.

nodes.body:
The issue with my solution is that the CodedInputStream eventually hits the state.sizelimit, so i have to allocate a new one every ~2GB of data.

A native solution that does M.MergeFrom(ReadOnlySpan) without allocating any CodedInputStream would be great.

Currently there is 

`YourMessage.Parser.ParseFrom(ReadOnlySequence<byte>)` which allows you to parse without needing a CodedInputStream (and getting a ReadOnlySequence without requiring allocations is relatively easy). 
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/022078d3ee642816688228e9434775f2a137536d/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/MessageParser.cs#L124

There is also a MergeFrom variant of this method, but that one is internal.
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/022078d3ee642816688228e9434775f2a137536d/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/MessageExtensions.cs#L288

Does that satisfy your needs?
@jtattermusch Thank you for that. Unfortunately no it does not as that API allocates the holding proto. My goal is to reuse the proto and also not allocate the CIS.
@MaximGurschi  alright, so you'd basically need a public API for msg.MergeFrom(ReadOnlySequence<byte> data) (something along the lines of the latter internal method I posted), is that correct?
@jtattermusch Precisely :)
Feel free to come up with a PR that proposes the addition of new public method then?

> @jtattermusch it seems like it would still be useful to have overloads that take ReadOnlySpan, as sometimes that's what you're given. For instance, [Confluent.Kafka's IDeserializer](https://github.com/confluentinc/confluent-kafka-dotnet/blob/master/src/Confluent.Kafka/IDeserializer.cs#L42) provides a ReadOnlySpan, which would then have to be copied to the heap to use the ReadOnlySequence overload :/
> 
> `T Deserialize(ReadOnlySpan<byte> data, bool isNull, SerializationContext context);`
> 
> Is there something I'm missing that would allow `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` to `ReadOnlySequence<byte>` conversion without allocations or copying?

Adding overloads that parse directly from `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` is definitely feasible (and it's something you can currently achieve using internal APIs) - it's just we want to add new public APIs carefully, to ensure that the public API has small footprint, doesn't degrade after time and will allow us preserve backwards compatibility.

FTR see
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/70531697bcac53d6d6c6952ee211ceb9374544f7/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/ParseContext.cs#L62
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/70531697bcac53d6d6c6952ee211ceb9374544f7/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/MessageExtensions.cs#L290

Feel free to propose a new public API for parsing from ReadOnlySpan<> and open a pull request (note that there are some other enhancement requests around the newly added APIs - please check the github issues for them first).

slightly related: 
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8036
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7886
