title: Reopening Security Vulnerability issue #8088
body:
Veracode scan found this security vulnerability - integer Overflow or Wraparound in map_entry_lite.h in int GetCachedSize() const override.
The faulty line is
size += has_key() ? static_cast<int>(kTagSize) + KeyTypeHandler::GetCachedSize(key()) : 0;

The explanation provided in issue #8088 was 
GetCachedSize is always called after ByteSizeLong, which ensures the size doesn't exceed 2G.

However, the summation is done inside GetCacheSize(), calling ByteSizeLong before GetCacheSize doesn't guarantee that the sum of kTagSize and KeyTypeHandler::GetCachedSize(key()) is not going to wraparound.

nodes.body:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/bd9a7104e11740e4bcfbde46c190c2d908ef331a/src/google/protobuf/message_lite.cc#L379

The same work of summation should have been done in a ByteSizeLong before calling  the GetCacheSize. Besides, the result of that ByteSizeLong has been checked in the link above. Therefore, the result of GetCacheSize has been pre-checked.

The GetCachedSize for map entry is a little different from other messages'. However, the result is also pre-checked in the way mentioned above.

ByteSizeLong: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/map_entry_lite.h#L258
GetCachedSize: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/map_entry_lite.h#L273

1. Calculation in ByteSizeLong never overflows because of the type is long.
2. The result from ByteSizeLong also doesn't overflow for int32 because of the check in message_lite.cc
3. The thing calculated in ByteSizeLong is strictly larger than the thing calculated in GetCachedSize.

Given those 3, the result (and also each step) in GetCachedSize doesn't overflow for int32.

Could you point out which part of the induction is incorrect?
Feel free to reopen this issue.

> * Calculation in ByteSizeLong never overflows because of the type is long.

But I saw the type is size_t?  So overflow is still possible in 32-bit applications?

I believe 32-bit platforms are still OK, because in that environment it would be impossible to make ByteSizeLong large enough to overflow. If you tried to create a large enough message to do this, you would run out of memory first, since on 32-bit the address space is capped at 4 GiB.

title: `protobuf-java` and `protobuf-javalite` conflict
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.11.4
Language: Java

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Mac OS 10.15.7

**What did you do?**
Including both `protobuf-java` and `protobuf-javalite` causes duplicate class errors on build. The simplest reproduction is to just include both as dependencies:

```
implementation "com.google.protobuf:protobuf-javalite:3.11.0"
implementation "com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.11.4"
```

This will generate these errors on build:

```
Duplicate class com.google.protobuf.AbstractMessageLite found in modules jetified-protobuf-java-3.11.4 (com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.11.4) and jetified-protobuf-javalite-3.11.0 (com.google.protobuf:protobuf-javalite:3.11.0)
Duplicate class com.google.protobuf.AbstractMessageLite$Builder found in modules jetified-protobuf-java-3.11.4 (com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.11.4) and jetified-protobuf-javalite-3.11.0 (com.google.protobuf:protobuf-javalite:3.11.0)
...
```

Even more concerning to me is that you get the same errors even when you just include dependencies on libraries that use these two different libraries. Like firebase:

```
implementation platform('com.google.firebase:firebase-bom:26.1.0')
implementation "com.google.firebase:firebase-firestore"
implementation "com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.11.4"
```

Since we publish a library that has a dependency on `protobuf-java`, this means that our library will always conflict with any library that uses `protobuf-javalite`.

nodes.body: @danwaters-stripe , any luck to resolve this issue?

Sorry for late response, `protobuf-java` and `protobuf-javalite` should never be included in the same project, and here's why:

`protobuf-java` contains both the lite and non-lite runtime inside itself and is primarily targeted for use in JVM server binaries where reflection capabilities are not seriously problematic for performance if the end user choses to use them.

`protobuf-javalite` contains only the essential lite runtime and no support for reflection-based APIs, which is often preferred for size and speed constraints on mobile JVM platforms like Android.

Currently we do *not* make `protobuf-javalite` a dependency of `protobuf-java` and at the moment do not have plans to separate them out this way. *The fact is, the end user should never include both, this is an error* (accidental or otherwise).

Now you might ask yourself, OK, but what if I do end up doing that (or a transitive dependency does)? Well, if you're using Gradle, we recommend an approach like this: https://docs.gradle.org/current/userguide/dependency_downgrade_and_exclude.html#sec:excluding-transitive-deps

Telling the system to exclude `protobuf-javalite` because you explicitly depend on `protobuf-java` is technically OK, but this might have negative side effects to performance or code size on mobile platforms, it also might be totally fine for you, your mileage may vary.

As a good rule of thumb, if you're publishing an Android-targeted library, its recommended you depend on `protobuf-javalite` and the larger ecosystem should be compatible with you. If you run into an unexpected condition, exclusion is probably the best bet.

In this case, @perezd, would it make sense to provide a kotlin-lite version as well? 

Unfortunately, protobuf-kotlin has a dependency on protobuf-java, which causes this duplicate issue.

title: Unexpected behavior of JsonParser
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.14.0.
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
OS: Windows 10.0.17134.885 (1803/April2018Update/Redstone4)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
.Net Core SDK: 3.1.102; 
.NET Core 3.1.2 (CoreCLR 4.700.20.6602, CoreFX 4.700.20.6702), X64 RyuJIT
Build configuration: Release x64

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create .proto file with similar content:
```
message Success {
    int32 Payload = 1;
}
```
2. Compile it in whatever way you prefer (protoc/grpc tools/etc) 
3. Compose JSON like the one below:
```
{ "payload": "56" }
```
4. Try to parse it to C# class produced by compiler:
```
var success = JsonParser.Default.Parse<Success>("{ \"payload\": \"56\" }");
```
5. Observe exception `Google.Protobuf.InvalidProtocolBufferException: 'Unknown field: payload'`

**What did you expect to see**
Properly deserialized C# object. Per [JSON Mapping](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json) section of Protocol Buffers documentation, parser should recognize both `{ "payload": "56" }` and `{ "Payload": "56" }` as valid JSON for the provided class:

> Parsers accept both the lowerCamelCase name (or the one specified by the json_name option) and the original proto field name.

**What did you see instead?**
An exception.

**Additional info**
Looks like the problem is in method `internal static string ToJsonName(string name)` of `JsonFormatter.cs` ([line 257](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/JsonFormatter.cs#L257)). 
What it does, is actually converting `xxx_yyy` to `xxxYyy` leaving input as-is in all other cases, and this works only in certain cases. E.g., if one called a field `xxx_yyy` and passed either `xxx_yyy` or `xxxYyy` field in JSON.
But this does not respect the statement from the documentation. IMO, the `ToJsonName()` method should produce several strings which will match all cases, including case when one doesn't follow naming guidelines. I.e.,:
| Given input | Current Output | Suggested Output |
|--|--|--|
| xxx | xxx | Xxx |
| Xxx | Xxx |  xxx |
| xxxYyy | xxxYyy | XxxYyy |
| XxxYyy | XxxYyy | xxxYyy |
| xxx_yyy | xxxYyy | xxxYyy, XxxYyy |

nodes.body:
This could be documented better, but the behavior you are seeing is intended.

Our definition of lowerCamelCase is:
1. Convert all characters immediately after an underscore “_” to uppercase.
1. Remove all underscores.

This is the algorithm implemented by C# and all other languages's protobuf implementations.

This algorithm converts `Payload` to `Payload`, true. But this field doesn't follow the naming conventions laid out here, which says that fields should be `snake_case`: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/style#message_and_field_names

You can use the `json_name` option in `.proto` files if you want to specify exactly what JSON name will be recognized by the parser.

title: `ShortDebugString()` and `DebugString()` omits booleans that are false
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.14
Language: C++

**What operating system and version?**
Linux -- Ubuntu 18.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
gnu g++ 5.5.0

**What did you do?**
When a message that has a bool as a data member and that data is set false, `ShortDebugString()` and `DebugString()` won't print out the value of that field.  Here's the following example:

Created the following protobuf message:
```
syntax = "proto3";

message MyTest {
    bool a = 1;
    bool b = 2;
    bool c = 3;
}
```
Then wrote the following C++ code using this message:
```
    MyTest first;
    first.set_a(true);
    first.set_b(false);
    first.set_c(true);

    std::cout << "first: < " << first.ShortDebugString() << " >" << std::endl;

    MyTest second;
    second.set_a(false);
    second.set_b(true);
    second.set_c(true);

    std::cout << "second: < " << second.ShortDebugString() << " >" << std::endl;

    MyTest third;
    third.set_a(false);
    third.set_b(false);
    third.set_c(true);

    std::cout << "third: < " << third.ShortDebugString() << " >" << std::endl;
```
**What did you expect to see**
I expected to see the **contents of *all* data members** printed to stdout.

**What did you see instead?**
This is the output I saw when I ran the test code above:
```
first: < a: true c: true >
second: < b: true c: true >
third: < c: true >
```
It only prints the data that was set to true.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
No.  Pretty much covered everything.

nodes.body:
This is how proto3 fields without the `optional` keyword behave. Default values are never printed or serialized. For more information please see: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/field_presence.md

If you want to see fields explicitly set to false, you can use `optional` fields, which are available in proto2 and still experimental in proto3.

title: Wrong initialization of `fixed_address_empty_string` causes `ShutdownProtobufLibrary` to fail
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.14.0, master
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
MSVC 14.27.29110
Platform Toolset v142 (Visual Studio 2019)
Debug Runtime

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
```
#include "addressbook.pb.h"

int main() {
	::google::protobuf::ShutdownProtobufLibrary();
}
```

with `addressbook.proto` (it really doesn't matter at all):
```
syntax = "proto3";

package tutorial;

message AddressBook {
  string name = 1;
}
```

**What did you expect to see**

No exception when execution `ShutdownProtobufLibrary()`. The program should just run-through without any issues.

**What did you see instead?**

The program throws an exception when run in Debug mode on executing `ShutdownProtobufLibrary()`.

It is caused by attempting to destruct a broken `std::string` stored `::google::protobuf::internal::fixed_address_empty_string.value`.
The reason is that the implementation relies on a static initialization of that variable. The variable `fixed_address_empty_string` is default constructed to `dummy` (here https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/bd9a7104e11740e4bcfbde46c190c2d908ef331a/src/google/protobuf/message_lite.h#L158).
However, as the initialization of static global variables is undefined across translation units in C++, it is possible that `InitProtobufDefaultsImpl()` (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/bd9a7104e11740e4bcfbde46c190c2d908ef331a/src/google/protobuf/generated_message_util.cc#L82) is called before the initialization of the `fixed_address_empty_string` (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/bd9a7104e11740e4bcfbde46c190c2d908ef331a/src/google/protobuf/generated_message_util.cc#L77). This causes the allocated `std::string value` to get broken, as the `dummy` value gets initialized "over" the existing `std::string` object.

This happens, for example when including a generated protobuf header file as a call to `AddDescriptors()` is forced there to happen during dynamic initialization time.

The actual exception is thrown by the MSCV STL on destruction as the `std::string` is now malformed.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body: Hello, I see this issue with windows VS2019 16.8.3.61104. is it possible to merge this fix to master please? just updated to latest release and started seeing this issue when shutting down the program with a debug build.

Hi. Unfortunately, none of the above linked commit actually fixes the issue. I was playing around in my fork and it looks like Github already associated these commits here. Not sure how it can be unlinked.

The actual issue cannot be fixed easily, imo. The problem is the `EmptyString` structure that relies on `constinit`, which is not available on MSVC.

The only viable workaround at the moment is to comment-out the `DestroyString` call for the `fixed_address_empty_string` in case of msvc debug builds.
thank you for the update
Seems to be fixed with `v3.15.1`

MacOS 10.14.4

Ruby 2.7

**What did you do?**

Assuming i have a generated Ruby class from Protobuf, called MyMessage

```rb
# raises Google::Protobuf::ParseError (expected)
MyMessage.decode_json("I cannot understand this", ignore_unknown_fields: true)

# returns a MyMessage.new object (expected since number is a valid JSON)
MyMessage.decode_json("1", ignore_unknown_fields: true)

# returns a MyMessage.new object (unexpected? this is a string so I expected it to throw)
MyMessage.decode_json("1 cannot understand this", ignore_unknown_fields: true) 
```

Would this be a known or expected behaviour? 🙇

nodes.body:
The Ruby JSON decoder may not be properly verifying that it is at end-of-file.

There is a major change to the Ruby implementation coming soon. I'll revisit this bug after that is complete, and we can see if the new JSON parser has the same issue.

HI @haberman thank you for the updates and details :)
Looking forward to the new releases 🙇 

would there also be a public roadmap that we can track the progress of this? 🤔

I just tested your examples on https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8184 and all of your examples throw errors now. This is expected since parsing a message from JSON requires a top-level object in `{}`.

Your second example now throws this error: `Error occurred during parsing: Error parsing JSON @1:0: Expected: '{'`

**What language does this apply to?**
Java

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
```

  /**
   * Adds a service implementation to the handler registry.
   *
   * @param service ServerServiceDefinition object
   * @return this
   * @since 1.0.0
   */
  public abstract T addService(ServerServiceDefinition service);

  /**
   * Adds a service implementation to the handler registry. If bindableService implements
   * {@link InternalNotifyOnServerBuild}, the service will receive a reference to the generated
   * server instance upon build().
   *
   * @param bindableService BindableService object
   * @return this
   * @since 1.0.0
   */
  public abstract T addService(BindableService bindableService);

```

could be simplified to 
```
public abstract T addService(CommonSuperInterface service);
```

then the `ServerBuilder` is responsible for interpreting what exactly it is binding.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
```
public abstract T addService(CommonSuperInterface service);
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Example from production code:

```
		CompositeFuture.all(
				Legacy.services(),
				Legacy.unauthenticatedCards(),
				Matchmaking.services(),
				Accounts.unauthenticatedService(),
				Accounts.authenticatedService())

					var builder = VertxServerBuilder.forPort(vertx, grpcPort());

					var list = services.list();
					for (var service : list) {
						if (service instanceof BindableService) {
							builder.addService((BindableService) service);
						} else if (service instanceof ServerServiceDefinition) {
							builder.addService((ServerServiceDefinition) service);
						} else {
							return Future.failedFuture("invalid service");
						}
					}
...
```

**Additional context**
The idea is that the places you get the service from are responsible for binding things like their auth handlers and tracing.

title: Why this program returns segmentation faults?

nodes.body:
The line `l.set_allocated_header(&h)` is a problem because `h` is on the stack but `set_allocated_header` assumes it was allocated on the heap and tries to take ownership of it. Instead of creating the Header on the stack, you can do something like this:
`l.mutable_header()->set_module_name("test");`

title: Allow Custom types in java JsonFormat utility
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

We have a problem where we want to represent a date as an ISO format string in JSON, but we wish to use `google.type.Date` in protobuf. I'm using the `JsonFormat` tool to build the protobuf from the JSON, but this fails since it sees a string in the JSON but the `mergeMessage` method expects it to be a `JsonObject`.

So would you consider a change where people can register custom parsers, so that users can extend the JsonFormat to support any types?


My proposal would involve the following steps:
1, Expose `WellKnownTypeParser` as a public interface.
2. Make `wellKnownTypePrasers` in `ParserImpl` non-static, add constructor params.
3. Add a `usingTypeParser()` method to `Parser`

And analogous steps for `Printer`.

Would this be viable?

nodes.body: My gut is that this won't fly. JsonFormat is designed to supprot a single consistent and reproducible JSON format for protos across languages, not as a general purpose converter between arbitrary JSON formats and protos. I don't think we want to add complexity to the API to support this. However this could be a viable third party library.

title: PHP "float" serialization loses precision

nodes.body: I haven't done the math carefully but this sounds like it could be just caused by the fact that the protobuf `float` type is only 32 bits.  As I understand, PHP always uses double-precision floats and that would explain why the plain PHP implementation doesn't lose precision by itself but only after a serialize and parse. The C extension presumably distinguishes between `float` and `double` and therefore converts immediately to the 32-bit `float`, resulting in the immediate precision loss.
Yes, Adam is correct. The bug here is with pure-PHP, which should truncate this to float precision in the setter.
@haberman So are we saying this is an issue in the Pure-PHP protobuf library, and the way to fix it is to update float setters to truncate to single precision?
I added a fix in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8187 that passes for my test suites
This was fixed in #8187.

However, this still feels like quite a niche requirement - I believe it's better to stick with it being an extension method in libraries that particularly need it, until we see a more widespread requirement for this.

@jskeet I didn't design the original class; was simply looking for a better way to incorporate it into our own bases. However, we can continue with our internal extensions. Fair enough, but that being said, won't know the adoption until it is "there".

Stuff life what? The use of a nullable type for one component of a value? There may well be a reason for *one specific use case* but that doesn't mean it's universally applicable... which is even more reason for different projects with different requirements to use their own extension methods.

title: [csharp] Allow for unsealed message output to be generated
body:
Hello, based on experience working with Google.OrTools, I have a couple of instances where I want to adapt `RoutingModelParameters` and `RoutingSearchParameters` for configuration purposes with a _CSharp_ wrapper framework, and it would be incredibly useful for the message to not be `sealed` when they land opposite the `protoc` invocation. i.e. that is, they land as:

```C#
public sealed class RoutingModelParameters
{
}
```

And:

```C#
public sealed class RoutingSearchParameters
{
}
```

Respectively.

I can workaround the limitation, somewhat; but the effort would be reduced significantly, I think, by perhaps 75-85% with unsealed classes.

Is this an option in the `protoc` compiler as it stands today? Or can it be implemented without much difficulty?

Thank you...

nodes.body:
We try to keep the number of protoc options pretty small - I would definitely prefer not to do this. I would suggest that a practical solution to this would be to post-process the generated classes if you really want to. (It shouldn't be terribly hard to do so; the generated output is very predictable.)

@fowles are you happy for this to be closed, or do you think it should be kept open and considered more internally?
@jskeet Post-process and do what exactly? The point was, I was looking for a way of extending the class in order to do precisely that. Cannot do that when it is `sealed`, right.

@mwpowellhtx: Post-process the source code to remove the `sealed` modifier, and that's all.

I would note that all the classes are *partial* - do you definitely need inheritance, or are you just looking for the ability to add functionality in handwritten code? Because `partial` allows for the latter already, without the tricky aspects of inheritance.

@jskeet Well, that's kind of the point, isn't it? The code is _**GENERATED**_, so best practice suggests you don't want to go mucking around in that code. But if you can extend it, _or even augment it_, i.e. it was `partial`, that might be another thing entirely, correct? Anyway, I let experience be my guide there. I know it is best practice, experientially.

> But if you can extend it, or even augment it, i.e. it was partial, that might be another thing entirely, correct?

It *is* partial. That's my point. You don't need to extend the class in order to augment it.

And yes, I agree that all other things being equal, it's best not to have to modify generated code - but all other things *aren't* equal here, as providing the option to generate unsealed classes introduces not only complexity in terms of more options, but also in terms of working out how inheritance affects every other aspect of protobuf. (When one message contains a field of another message type, how would deserialization know whether to create an instance of the base type or some derived type? If you only ever end up with instances of the base type when you want derived types, that introduces yet more complexity.)

It is `partial`? It's been a bit since I last reviewed the generated code...

Well, in terms of serialization, usually you do that with explicit knowledge of the thing you want to deserialize, i.e. its type; i.e.

```csharp
class A {}
class B : A {}
```

If you serialized `A`, then you want `A` back in response. But if you serialized `B`, then you get `B` back in response; which also happens to be an `A`, but you had the forward type information, i.e.

```csharp
sender.Send<A>(a); // generic type for illustration purposes
// ...
receiver.Get<A>();
```

Now if somehow you are throwing _data shapes_ around without said forward knowledge, that's another thing entirely, i.e. hoping against hope that both sides have a message that agrees with that shape, but I do not know that is the case when we are discussing messaging frameworks such as this one. AFAIK, usually you know the type information of the payload involved at design time. Usually. Either of which is perfectly fine, if that was the dev's intention; neither of which is that offensive or mutually exclusive of one another, i.e. if you wanted `A` or `B`.

What else am I missing here?

Not as far as I can remember, or I would not have posted; i.e. the code I found generated was just that. It seemed a bit strange they were `sealed` and not `partial` as is sometimes the case with generated code like this, like we've discussed. Anyway, good to know, thank you, from a _Protobuf_ perspective.

We've never generated code exactly like that - aside from anything else, all our message types implement `IMessage<T>`. I don't know which generator you were using, but protoc definitely generates partial classes unconditionally. See https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/compiler/csharp/csharp_message.cc#L125

If you think you may have been using a different generator, it's probably worth finding out which - because it could be that *that* generator's maintainers would be willing to support unsealed classes (or may indeed support them now). If you're sure you were using protoc, I'd ask you to have another look at the generated code. If you've really got a way of generating non-partial classes, that's a bug and I'd like to fix it.

Possible? I don't recall hundred percent. It was in the context of _Google.OrTools_, IIRC. In that context, last time I checked they were also leveraging `Protobufs v2`, and not `v3+`, which was a whole other can of worms, to be honest. At the time, I didn't seem to think there was much of any customization of the generators involved, but I could be wrong. Anyway, thanks for the response.

title: Allow custom plugin codegenerators to use imports
body:
**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
At Dropbox, we have a custom code generation plugin which makes use of custom options. For example
```
import "dropbox/api/errors.proto";

message Request {}
message Response {}
service MyService {
  rpc MyRPC(Request) returns (Response) {
    option (api_v2.method_error_type) = "errors.SpecialError";
  }
}
```
Our custom plugin generator currently (and ideally) depends on the import in order to bring in the special error type. However, protoc will warn
```
dropbox/api/my_service.proto:1:1: warning: Import dropbox/api/errors.proto is unused.
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Ideally, there would be a way to suppress this warning in cases where the import is being used by the custom plugin, while still providing in the warning in true cases of unused imports. Perhaps the codegenerator response could include a list of imports that were used by the plugin - for unused import detection.

I could understand if this was an overgeneralization of this problem and I'm open to other ideas.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
We currently ignore unused import warnings for this reason - which is a possibility here, though suboptimal.
Another idea might be to give a fully qualified path in the option string and teach the custom generator to pull in the import separately from protoc. This seems suboptimal as it's reimplementing import logic that protoc has already implemented, but it could work.
Another idea might be to implement support for a warning-suppression comment into protoc eg:
```
import dropbox/api/errors.proto;  // ignore: unused
```
Another idea might be a file-level option for additional imports eg:
```
option (api.custom_generator.additional_imports) = "dropbox/api/my_service.proto";
```

Thanks!

nodes.body: One easy workaround is to replace `import` with `import public`. That feature is intended to facilitate moving definitions from one .proto file to another, but it also has this side effect of disabling warnings about unused imports.

oh that's a neat workaround idea.

It is imperfect in a couple of ways
- It reexports when that's not intended
- If we remove a method with `option (api_v2.method_error_type) = "errors.SpecialError";` - we won't get the "unused import" warning on the removed method.

That being said, this is still probably better than the status quo.
The design sketched out here is good, but we don't have time to pursue it ourselves

title: Better mypy typing for enum values in python
body:
Hi - I'm the maintainer of https://github.com/dropbox/mypy-protobuf - a protoc plugin for autogenerating mypy stubs compatible with the built in python generator.

**What language does this apply to?**
Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Generated enum values are pure ints (per the spec). We prefer type them with a `NewType` wrapper type around int - specific to the enum. See the typeshed stub
https://github.com/python/typeshed/blob/master/third_party/2and3/google/protobuf/internal/enum_type_wrapper.pyi#L9
```python
class _EnumTypeWrapper(Generic[_V]):
    DESCRIPTOR: EnumDescriptor
    def __init__(self, enum_type: EnumDescriptor) -> None: ...
    def Name(self, number: _V) -> str: ...
    def Value(self, name: str) -> _V: ...
    def keys(self) -> List[str]: ...
    def values(self) -> List[_V]: ...
    def items(self) -> List[Tuple[str, _V]]: ...
```

I've been cooking up a strategy inside mypy-protobuf where a proto
```proto
enum MyEnum {
   FOO = 0;
   BAR = 1;
}
```
Autogenerates pyi stubs
```python
class _MyEnum(google.protobuf.internal.enum_type_wrapper.EnumTypeWrapper[OuterEnum.V], builtins.type):
    DESCRIPTOR: google.protobuf.descriptor.EnumDescriptor = ...
    FOO = OuterEnum.V(0)
    BAR = OuterEnum.V(1)

class MyEnum(metaclass=_MyEnum):
    V = typing.NewType('V', builtins.int)
```

This allows callsites to type their code as
```python
x: MyEnum.V = MyEnum.Value("FOO")
```

Unfortunately - because `.V` does not exist at runtime (only in the pyi stubs) - this does not work.
Fortunately, you can work around this with:
```python
x: "MyEnum.V" = MyEnum.Value("FOO")
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I'd like to propose adding `V = int` runtime type alias to the EnumTypeWrapper (in enum_type_wrapper.py) - to avoid the need for this workaround.
```python
class EnumTypeWrapper(object):
  """A utility for finding the names of enum values."""
  # This is a type alias, which mypy typing stubs can type as
  # a genericized parameter constrained to an int, allowing subclasses
  # to be typed with more constraint
  # Eg.
  # def Name(self, number: MyGeneratedEnum.V) -> str
  V = int
  ... [rest of impl omitted]
  ```

This would mean that enum variants named "V" would need to jump through a hoop using getattr to be accessed, but this is already the case with "Name", "Value", "keys", etc - so it seems feasible as an extension. I'm open to other naming ideas for this.

Could do something like this for more clarity - though it does add a dependency on typing module for python <= 3.5
```python
from typing import NewType
V = NewType('V', int)
```

I would also be open to discussing other strategies we could employ across mypy-protobuf, protoc, and typeshed in order to get better mypy typing for enum values (better than just typing as an int) - other than this `V` inner type alias.


**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I've also tried mypy typing V at a sibling scope to `MyEnum` (eg `MyEnumValue = NewType('MyEnumValue', int)`, but this is no improvement - as you still need to play tricks to import it from real code.

Thanks friends! Happy to open discussion.

Another idea we've tried - would be to make `MyEnum` an instance of int. Then we would be typing the enumtypewrapper instance as `MyEnum` as well as the int values as `MyEnum`.

This seems a bit of a departure from reality of the generated code - as those are actually two separate types (instance of EnumTypeWrapper vs instance of int), but it can be made workable. The typing would allow folks to accidentally try and call enumtypewrapper methods on the ints themselves, but it would cut down on this "extra" type.

I'd softly lean toward the `V` solution as it makes clear in the typing that the EnumTypeWrapper and the int values are distinct objects of distinct types.

f(MyEnum.Value("FOO"))

```

@nipunn1313, I stumbled across this issue trying to understand why `MyEnum.FOO` didn't typecheck. I'm reviewing your suggestion and trying to understand how you settled on using `V`? Was it not possible to define a static class that had the enum attributes?

Hi @jaywhy13.
protobuf generates an EnumTypeWrapper (static class) with helper methods, and a raw int for the value type.

Rather than typing as a raw int, mypy-protobuf wanted stronger typing - specific to the enum itself - a pyi file like this:

```python
class MyEnum(EnumTypeWrapper):
  V = NewType('V', int)

  FOO: int
```

I suppose you're wondering why we didn't generate typing stubs more like
```
class MyEnum(EnumTypeWrapper):
   class V(IntEnum):
       FOO: int
```
This could work as well, but still ends up requiring a `V`. May end up being somewhat misleading as the actual generated protobuf code uses an `int` and not an `IntEnum`. NewType around int is truer to the generated protobuf code.

In either case, the base code in `protobuf` itself would still need something like `V = int`

In selecting `V` - chose it to be short for `Value` - but also easy to type (just one letter). Most places in the code would show something like `MyEnum.V` and be clear.

For clarity - I worked on mypy-protobuf and not on protobuf itself, so I don't currently have the flexibility to make changes to both. I'm proposing a minimal change to protobuf to the core protobuf team in #8182  - so that mypy-protobuf can work better.

Pinging some folks who might more actively monitor Github activity: @deannagarcia @TeBoring 
Really would be quite nice to get this one-line change through https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8182

Let me state my summary of this issue, both to check my understanding and to help others who may not be familiar with the Python type-checking ecosystem. Please let me know if I got anything wrong here.

[Mypy](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/index.html) is a static type checking tool for Python. It reads type annotations from the Python source code and spits out errors for any type violations it detects. This type checking is performed without running the code.

A simple example:

```python
# The type annotation here is valid Python 3 syntax, but is ignored
# by the interpreter.
def greeting(name: str) -> str:
    return 'Hello ' + name

# If you run Mypy on this file, it throws an error:
#   Argument 1 to "greeting" has incompatible type "int"; expected "str"
greeting(3)        
```

Mypy is also capable of reading annotations from separate "stub files" with `.pyi` extensions. This gives Mypy type information about modules that are implemented in C, or that don't have type annotations. This is similar to the `.d.ts` ["Declarations Files"](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/declaration-files/introduction.html) in TypeScript:

```python
# test.py
def greeting(name):
    return 'Hello ' + name

# test.pyi
def greeting(name: str) -> str: ...
```

Since protobuf generated code does not currently contain any annotations, a separate project https://github.com/dropbox/mypy-protobuf has implemented its own code generator for protobuf that generates `.pyi` files for each generated module.

This works fine for the generated interfaces themselves. However users writing their own functions have no easy way of accepting strongly-typed protobuf enums:

```python
# In protobuf generated interfaces, enums are ints. We have no way of writing
# a function that only accepts enum values from MyEnum:
def f(enum_val: int):
    print(enum_val)
```

To address this, protobuf-mypy has created a distinct type that is the same as int at runtime, but is treated differently by the static typing framework:

```python
# Doesn't work pre-PEP 563
def f(x: MyEnum.V):
    print(x)
```

However this doesn't work until Python 3.10, or with an explicit import of `from __future__ import annotations`, because it needs PEP 563 to accept this code when `MyEnum.V` is not actually defined by protobuf generated code.

Another edge case is `cast()`, which doesn't work even with PEP 563:

```python
# Doesn't work even with PEP 563
cast(MyEnum.V, x)
```

To solve this problem, and make the code compatible with pre-PEP 563 code (and to make `cast()` work), the proposal is for the actual generated code to include a `V` or `ValueType` alias.

Does that all sound correct?

If that's right, my initial thoughts are:

1. A `ValueType` alias to `int` seems reasonable to enable this use case.
2. We should evaluate our overall plans for static typing in Python, and make sure this overall approach is a good long-term strategy for us.

@haberman This is a great write-up! I hope the team will consider providing types inline with the generated runtime code as part of their long term plans (#2638)! This will improve code editing experience by making jump-to-definition using tools like the [type-aware VSCode Python extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.vscode-pylance) navigate to the actual runtime definition rather than just the stub file.

> Does that all sound correct?
>
> If that's right, my initial thoughts are:
> 
> 1) A ValueType alias to int seems reasonable to enable this use case.
> 2) We should evaluate our overall plans for static typing in Python, and make sure this overall approach is a good long-term strategy for us.

Yep. Fantastic summary. Thanks. I would note one nit
- adding type annotations is now a python3 language feature
- mypy is one of several typecheckers for python using the type annotations (the original one inspiring the language feature). https://github.com/microsoft/pyright is another popular one.

For overall plans - there is some discussion in #2638 - which mostly points people to using mypy-protobuf. Would love a future where either
1) Protobuf itself was able to produce the `.pyi` files.
2) Protobuf Inlined annotations into the generated `_pb2.py`. May be tricky due to the non-explicitness of class types, but it's another option
```
MyMessage = _reflection.GeneratedProtocolMessageType('MyMessage', (_message.Message,), {
...
```

I would personally be happy to have mypy-protobuf integrated into protobuf as a way to implement option 1 if you want to go that route. (adding `--mypy_out` to command line). I suspect a prototype of this might be as easy as adding mypy-protobuf to `install_requires` https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/python/setup.py#L274.

> 1. Protobuf itself was able to produce the .pyi files.

Yes, I'm leaning in this direction, rather than embedding type annotations directly into the generated code.

The reason for this is load-time efficiency. When the schema is large (many `.proto` files, many messages, enums, etc) the time spent parsing and executing the generated code becomes significant. We need to make the generated modules as small and optimized as possible. (We're actually starting on some work right now to shrink the generated code to improve the load time efficiency.)

However, the `.pyi` files would have no such constraint. We could make them as readable and annotated as possible.

My vision is that we drop all pretense of readability for `_pb2.py`, and make them nothing but a serialized descriptor and a builder function:

```python
# foo_pb2.py
from google.protobuf.internal import module_builder
# Embedded in the code as a b'' string or loaded from a
# separate file with pkgutil.get_data().
_serialized_descriptor = "<...>"
module_builder.build(_serialized_descriptor, globals())
```

I like the idea of compensating for the relative loss of readability here with `.pyi` files which document the full interface in a readable way.

We'd need to talk this over as a team and get consensus on it, but I like this direction.

> I would personally be happy to have mypy-protobuf integrated into protobuf as a way to implement option 1 if you want to go that route.

Thanks for this. :)  We'd probably need to make sure this would all work out CLA-wise, and review the design etc, but it's good to know this option is available.

`mypy-protobuf` currently accomodates this by typing enum values as `MyEnum.V` where `V = NewType('V', int)` - a stricter open int. Accepts any integer value, but would need to be written as `m.e = MyEnum.V(12345)` for mypy to be happy. At runtime, `MyEnum.V` is simply `int`. Methods like `Name` and `Value` use `V` as the type for the argument / return value.

Here's an example of generated code: https://github.com/dropbox/mypy-protobuf/blob/main/test/generated/testproto/test_pb2.pyi#L28

Here are the typeshed stubs for `enum_type_wrapper.py` (non-generated)
https://github.com/python/typeshed/blob/master/stubs/protobuf/google/protobuf/internal/enum_type_wrapper.pyi
If you'd like to bring the types for the non-generated types from typeshed into protobuf itself - [PEP 561](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0561/) provides a way with `py.typed`

Let me know how I can help. If you'd like me to be involved in the discussion with the team, I'm happy to help (shoot me an email or lmk here). I've worked on mypy-protobuf for over 4 years, including from the times before we open sourced it at Dropbox. It brought us a *lot* of value over the years. Would be happy to continue maintaining it under the umbrella of `protocolbuffers` and help make typed generated code more standard in whatever way makes sense.

> Accepts any integer value, but would need to be written as `m.e = MyEnum.V(12345)` for mypy to be happy.

That seems like a really nice compromise.

> If you'd like to bring the types for the non-generated types from typeshed into protobuf itself - PEP 561 provides a way with py.typed

Can you spell out in slightly more detail what this would mean?

> I've worked on mypy-protobuf for over 4 years, including from the times before we open sourced it at Dropbox. It brought us a lot of value over the years.

Wow, that is a lot of background and experience! Thanks very kindly for the offer. Let me touch base with some people early next week and get back to you on this.

> > If you'd like to bring the types for the non-generated types from typeshed into protobuf itself - PEP 561 provides a way with py.typed
> 
> Can you spell out in slightly more detail what this would mean?
> 

I think pyright's [docs](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/docs/typed-libraries.md#inlined-type-annotations-and-type-stubs) explain this quite well . My tl;dr is that type annotations for third party python libraries (like protobuf [eg](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/python/google/protobuf/internal/enum_type_wrapper.py)) can be done in a few ways)

1) Inline annotations + a blank `py.typed` file to let typecheckers like mypy know that the inline annotations are correct and complete. Either in the same files, or alongside in `.pyi` stubs.
2) Create your own separate annotation package (eg `pip install protobuf-stubs`)
3) [typeshed](https://github.com/python/typeshed/tree/master/stubs/protobuf/google/protobuf) - which used to ship with mypy, but [recently](https://mypy-lang.blogspot.com/2021/05/the-upcoming-switch-to-modular-typeshed.html) started autogenerating annotation packages like [types-protobuf](https://pypi.org/project/types-protobuf/)).

3 was the original way, especially important in the early days of mypy development, but now that it's more mature, they're encouraging use of 1/2 - so the type annotations are owned by the package developers. PEP 561 is the specification introducing option 1/2. Currently, protobuf uses option 3 - with most of those stubs being contributed to typeshed by the community (much by Dropbox engineers originally).

title: [php] float/double serialization is locale aware and produces invalid json!
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.14.0
Language: PHP 7.3.25 (cli) (built: Nov 24 2020 11:10:55) ( NTS )

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
CentOS Linux release 7.9.2009 (Core)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
libprotoc 3.14.0

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create any message that contains double/float
```
message Demo{
    float floatVal = 1;
    double doubleVal = 2;
}
```

2. Take a look at demo code:
```
setlocale(LC_ALL, "en_US.utf8");
$demo = new Demo();
$demo->setFloatVal(pi());
$demo->setDoubleVal(pi());
$usJson = $demo->serializeToJsonString();
```
and
```
setlocale(LC_ALL, "de_DE.utf8");
$demo = new Demo();
$demo->setFloatVal(pi());
$demo->setDoubleVal(pi());
$deJson = $demo->serializeToJsonString();
```

```
echo 'DE-JSON: ', $deJson, PHP_EOL, ' but expected ', PHP_EOL, 'EN-JSON: ', $usJson, PHP_EOL;
```

3. See output:
```
DE-JSON: {"floatVal":3,14159274,"doubleVal":3,1415926535897931}
 but expected
EN-JSON: {"floatVal":3.14159274,"doubleVal":3.1415926535897931}
```

**What did you expect to see**
Same JSON for all locales!

**What did you see instead?**
Wrong double/float decimal-separators in JSON which produces invalid json.

**Problem hints**
At least in PHP-Version the Problem is located in 
`Google\Protobuf\Internal\GPBJsonWire::182`,
`Google\Protobuf\Internal\GPBJsonWire::194`,
`Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message::1711`,
`Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message::1722`

where the double/float value is formatted with `sprintf('%.8g')`/`sprintf('%.17g')`.

As you can see in [php-documentation for sprintf](https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.sprintf.php), 
the modifier `f` (small f) is locale-aware, while `F` isn't.
Modifier `g` falls back to `e` or `f` (depending on precision) so that it *is* locale-aware in most cases.

`Let P equal the precision if nonzero, 6 if the precision is omitted, or 1 if the precision is zero. Then, if a conversion with style E would have an exponent of X: If P > X ≥ −4, the conversion is with style f and precision P − (X + 1). Otherwise, the conversion is with style e and precision P − 1.`

**Solution**
You could just use `sprintf('%.8F')` or, at least, wait for modifier `H` which will be introduced in PHP 8.

title: Can't instantiate a Map in Ruby

nodes.body:
You need to pass `:message` as the value type, see: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/ruby/tests/common_tests.rb#L514

So something like:

```
my_map = Google::Protobuf::Map.new(:int32, :message, Person)
```

But it's usually easier to just let the map be auto-constructed by referring to a map field in a `Person` message:

```
  p = Person.new
  p.values_by_key[5].values += "abc"
```

```
p.values_by_key = {
        2020 => Person::KeyValueMap.new(values: ["migration"]),
    }
```

```
in `method_missing': Expected Map instance (Google::Protobuf::TypeError)
```

Thanks, adding `:message` to the ctor worked.

Also, maps can be initialized more simply like this:

```
values_by_key: {
            2019 => Person::KeyValueMap.new(values: ["foo"]),
            2018 => Person::KeyValueMap.new(values: ["bar", "baz"])
        }
```
@haberman Please consider including an example for non-primitive types [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/ruby-generated) :)

title: How to pack an arbitrary object as Any?
body:
Using proto3 for Ruby with the [google-protobuf](https://rubygems.org/gems/google-protobuf/versions/3.0.0.alpha.2.0) gem.

[The tests](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/ruby/tests/well_known_types_test.rb#L128-L141) use an existing proto instead of an arbitrary object, which is the whole point of `Any` (to me, at least).

### Proto

```
syntax = "proto3";

import "google/protobuf/any.proto";

package tutorial;

message Person {
   google.protobuf.Any any_blob = 1;
}
```

### Ruby

```
class MyObject
  def initialize(str)
    @str = str
  end
end

person = Person.new(
   any_blob: Google::Protobuf::Any.new.pack(MyObject.new("भारत"))
)
```

### Error on the `pack` line

```
~/.rvm/gems/ruby-2.5.5/gems/google-protobuf-3.14.0-universal-darwin/lib/google/protobuf/well_known_types.rb:52:in `pack': undefined method `descriptor' for MyObject:Class (NoMethodError)
```

### Tried adding a descriptor to the MyObject
```
  def self.descriptor
    Google::Protobuf::Descriptor.new(MyObject.name)
  end
```

```
in `initialize': wrong number of arguments (given 1, expected 3) (ArgumentError)
````

There's no documentation on `Any` [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/ruby-generated) at all. 

Please help, thank you!

nodes.body: @haberman - any insights? :)

I think I figured it out.

```
require 'google/protobuf/well_known_types'

    a_map = {
        "msg": Google::Protobuf::Value.new(string_value: "भारत")
    }
    my_struct = Google::Protobuf::Struct.new(fields: a_map)
    any = Google::Protobuf::Any.pack(my_struct)

    person = Person.new(
        any_blob: any
    )
```

```
    # Unpack Any successfully
    any_blob = json_decoding.any_blob
    puts("Unpacked Any: ", any_blob.unpack(Google::Protobuf::Struct))
```

```
        # Alternative way of initializing Any
        any_blob: Google::Protobuf::Any.pack(
            Google::Protobuf::Struct.new(fields: {
                "msg": Google::Protobuf::Value.new(string_value: "चीन")
            })
```
Sorry I didn't get back to you sooner. Any can only pack proto objects, but as you discovered you can use `Struct` to store arbitrary JSON data.

}

    repeated ObjectType workingField = 1;
    repeated int32 nonworkingField = 2;
}
PS> protoc --java_out=. .\test.proto
```

**What did you expect to see**

The following methods (among others) generated in `MyMessage.Builder` (as described [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java-generated#repeated-fields)):

```java
public Builder addWorkingField(Test.ObjectType value)
public Builder addWorkingField(int index, Test.ObjectType value)
public Builder addNonworkingFiled(int value)
public Builder addNonworkingField(int index, int value)
```

**What did you see instead?**

```java
public Builder addNonworkingField(int index, int value)
```

nodes.body: `public Builder addWorkingField(int index, Test.ObjectType value)` should be `public Builder setWorkingField(int index, Test.ObjectType value)`. That's the mistake here. There should be a `setNonworkingField(int index, int value)`
Need to investigate further but we might have to won't fix this one, valid as it is, for reasons of backwards compatibility.

This is working as documented and expected. I can't personally explain why it's addFoo(int index, int value) for message types and setFoo(int index, int value) for primitive types, but that's the way it is.

title: [C++] Set byte count in CodedOutputStream
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
C++

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
According to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3254, the way to flush a `CodedOutputStream` is to destruct and create a new one.  But the byte count is lost during this process.  Is there a way to set the byte count same as the old instance?

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Provide a `CodedOutputStream::ByteCount(int)` method to set the byte count.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Adding `CodedOutputStream::Flush()` so that we do not need to create a new instance to implement the flush.

title: Update Ruby gem with arm64 binaries (Apple M1 support)
body:
The Ruby gem is shipped with compiled extensions (via https://github.com/rake-compiler/rake-compiler), but it is missing arm64 binaries.

This results in errors like the following when installing the gem and requiring:

    $ gem install google-protobuf

    $ ruby -e 'require "google/protobuf"'
    Traceback (most recent call last):
    	2: from -e:1:in `<main>'
    	1: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:92:in `require'
    <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:92:in `require': cannot load such file -- google/protobuf (LoadError)
    	6: from -e:1:in `<main>'
    	5: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:156:in `require'
    	4: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:168:in `rescue in require'
    	3: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:168:in `require'
    	2: from <snip>/gems/google-protobuf-3.14.0-universal-darwin/lib/google/protobuf.rb:49:in `<top (required)>'
    	1: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:92:in `require'
    <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:92:in `require': dlopen(<snip>/gems/google-protobuf-3.14.0-universal-darwin/lib/google/2.7/protobuf_c.bundle, 9): no suitable image found.  Did find: (LoadError)
    	<snip>/gems/google-protobuf-3.14.0-universal-darwin/lib/google/2.7/protobuf_c.bundle: mach-o, but wrong architecture
    	<snip>/gems/google-protobuf-3.14.0-universal-darwin/lib/google/2.7/protobuf_c.bundle: mach-o, but wrong architecture - <snip>/gems/google-protobuf-3.14.0-universal-darwin/lib/google/2.7/protobuf_c.bundle
    	7: from -e:1:in `<main>'
    	6: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:156:in `require'
    	5: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:168:in `rescue in require'
    	4: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:168:in `require'
    	3: from <snip>/gems/google-protobuf-3.14.0-universal-darwin/lib/google/protobuf.rb:48:in `<top (required)>'
    	2: from <snip>/gems/google-protobuf-3.14.0-universal-darwin/lib/google/protobuf.rb:51:in `rescue in <top (required)>'
    	1: from <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:92:in `require'
    <snip>/rubygems/core_ext/kernel_require.rb:92:in `require': cannot load such file -- google/protobuf_c (LoadError)

A workaround is to force compilation of native extensions on install which works perfectly:

    $ gem install google-protobuf --platform=ruby

or globally via this bundler setting:

    $ bundle config set force_ruby_platform true

Related to #8062

# HACK(bouk): Overwrite Bundler's platform matcher to ignore universal CPU

  def match_platform(p)
    return false if ::Gem::Platform === platform && platform.cpu == "universal"

  end
end

title: Provides richer exception information when processing messages and json conversion fails due to the Any type
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

target ：JAVA ， proto3

**Now, when `JsonFormat.printer().print(message)` is executed, if there is a Descriptor pointed to by the Any node that has not been added to the printer, an InvalidProtocolBufferException will be thrown. `JsonFormat.parser()` also faces the same problem when it works. This exception in the scenario has very limited help at runtime.**

**Provide a more specific exception that is different from InvalidProtocolBufferException to describe the TypeUrl/Descriptor required for the missing Any type to read and write, so that the program can take some other remedial measures**

**If an if (type == null) occurs when an IOException is thrown during the execution of `printAny (MessageOrBuilder message)`, then the current processing scheme: `throw new InvalidProtocolBufferException("Cannot find the type of URL:" + typeUrl);` Modify it to: `throw new InvalidAnyProtocolBufferException( "Cannot find the type of url):" + typeUrl, typeUrl);`**

**Additional context**

Now I have a serialization tool, but it relies on InvalidProtocolBufferException.getMessage(), which is very fragile

```
ProtobufSerializer.java:
public class ProtobufSerializer {

    private static final AtomicReference<JsonFormat.Printer> jsonPrinter = new AtomicReference<>(JsonFormat.printer());
    private static final AtomicReference<JsonFormat.Parser> jsonParser = new AtomicReference<>(JsonFormat.parser());

    private static final Set<Descriptors.Descriptor> descriptors = new CopyOnWriteArraySet<>();
    private static final Map<String, Boolean> loadTag = Collections.synchronizedMap(new WeakHashMap<>());

    public static Optional<? extends GeneratedMessageV3> unpackAny(Any pack) {
        return ProtobufTypeCache.findClass(pack.getTypeUrl()).filter(pack::is)
                .map(ThrowingFun.unchecked(pack::unpack));
    }

    public static String toJson(GeneratedMessageV3 messageV3) throws InvalidProtocolBufferException {
        JsonFormat.Printer printer = jsonPrinter.get();
        if (printer == null) throw new RuntimeException("printer not found");
        try {
            return printer.print(messageV3);
        } catch (InvalidProtocolBufferException e) {
            String message = e.getMessage();
            String noPrefixTypeUrl;
            // Fragile code
            if (message.startsWith("Cannot find type for url: type.googleapis.com/")
                    && !loadTag.containsKey(noPrefixTypeUrl = ProtobufUtils.removeGooglePrefix(message))) {
                updateDescriptors(noPrefixTypeUrl);
                return toJson(messageV3);
            } else throw e;
        }
    }

    public static Message fromJson(String json, com.google.protobuf.Message.Builder builder) throws InvalidProtocolBufferException {
        JsonFormat.Parser parser = jsonParser.get();
        if (parser == null) throw new RuntimeException("parser not found");
        try {
            parser.merge(json, builder);
            return builder.build();
        } catch (InvalidProtocolBufferException e) {
            String message = e.getMessage();
            String noPrefixTypeUrl;
            // Fragile code
            if (message.startsWith("Cannot resolve type: type.googleapis.com/")
                    && !loadTag.containsKey(noPrefixTypeUrl = ProtobufUtils.removeGooglePrefix(message))) {
                updateDescriptors(noPrefixTypeUrl);
                return fromJson(json, builder);
            } else throw e;
        }
    }

    private static void updateDescriptors(String nextType) {
        Optional<Descriptors.Descriptor> descOpt = ProtobufTypeCache.findDescriptor(nextType);
        loadTag.put(nextType, descOpt.isPresent());

        Descriptors.Descriptor descriptor = descOpt.orElseThrow(() -> new RuntimeException("no descriptor by " + nextType));
        descriptors.add(descriptor);
        while (!jsonParser.compareAndSet(jsonParser.get(),
                JsonFormat.parser().usingTypeRegistry(JsonFormat.TypeRegistry.newBuilder().add(descriptors).build()))) {
            Thread.yield();
        }
        while (!jsonPrinter.compareAndSet(jsonPrinter.get(),
                JsonFormat.printer().usingTypeRegistry(JsonFormat.TypeRegistry.newBuilder().add(descriptors).build()))) {
            Thread.yield();
        }
    }
}
```

**Hope**

```
public class InvalidAnyProtocolBufferException extends InvalidProtocolBufferException {
    public final String typeUrl;
    public InvalidAnyProtocolBufferException(String desc, String targetType) {
        super(desc);
        this.typeUrl = targetType;
    }
}
```

title: allow to pass file level options as parameters to protoc
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
If it's about generated code change, what programming language? all languages

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
In a proto file I can specify file level options like `java_package`, `go_package` or `optimize_for`. These are all options that are about the code generation but not about the actual data that is being generate later on. When a project publishes an API as a proto file they currently have to make implementation choices for multiple languages, included those that have nothing to do with the project that published the proto file. This breaks the separation of concern and can cause problems for the user of an API if the producer is not adding the settings for the clients language. The other other option is to make a copy of the proto file and add the options in there, which also doesn't feel right.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like to be able to pass in file level options and have those override the option in case it was also set in the proto file.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
See above, basically make a copy of the proto file and add the options that I need in my private copy.

I think this feature is beneficial upstream so all languages and plugins can utilize it.

I expected the compilation to fail since optional is historically disallowed in syntax "proto3" for extensions. And it does not make sense to allow it as "proto3 optional" since that implies that the field goes into a oneof, which is not supported for extensions.

**What did you see instead?**
The compile succeeded.

I inspected the descriptor with this command:
```
protoc --decode google.protobuf.FileDescriptorSet google/protobuf/descriptor.proto < test.protoset 
```

This showed the following output from the compiler:
```
file {
  name: "test.proto"
  dependency: "google/protobuf/descriptor.proto"
  extension {
    name: "foo"
    extendee: ".google.protobuf.MessageOptions"
    number: 50001
    label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
    type: TYPE_STRING
    json_name: "foo"
    proto3_optional: true
  }
  syntax: "proto3"
}
```

Not only did compilation succeed, but `protoc` even marked the extension with `proto3_optional: true`, which must be a bug since a proto3 optional will implicitly exist in a single-field oneof (which this extension clearly does not and, in fact, cannot).

nodes.body: Great catch. Extensions should be effectively always `optional`, and we should definitely not be putting extensions into a synthetic oneof.

Oh my, that will be unfortunate.

I thought proto3 optional is just a matter of field presence and internal usefulness when proto reflect would give explicit presence information instead of defaulting to empty values.

Without synthetic oneof there will be no way of understanding which field options were set (especially when I do want to set it to the default value).

> Extensions should be effectively always optional, and we should definitely not be putting extensions into a synthetic oneof.

@haberman Oh, wait. Does that mean proto reflect will give correct information about the presence of the extension?

I can't speak to proto reflect. In protobuf extensions inherently have presence, eg. you can always call `msg.HasExtension(foo_extension)` and get a meaningful answer, even if the extension was defined in a proto3 file.

> and that the proto3_optional element on the field descriptor should always be false

I agree with all of your analysis up to here. But it's not clear to me that this point follows from the rest.

In an ideal world, we would have required that all extensions defined in a proto3 file explicitly specify `optional` or `repeated`, because as you note, the proto3 "singular field" semantic does not exist for proto2 messages or their extensions.

However that did not happen, and it would be a breaking change to enforce it now. So we have to live with extensions in proto3 files that are declared without any label, and know that they behave as if `optional` had been written.

Now that `optional` is supported in proto3, it seems we should allow it in extensions, because otherwise extensions in proto3 would be inconsistent with everything else (this is from a pure language level, not considering the descriptor). The true semantics of extensions in proto3 are `optional`, so we should let users write the keyword there in a way that matches proto2 and other proto3 optional fields.

When it comes to the descriptor, it can be useful to know if the `.proto` file did actually contain the `optional` keyword. And there is a method on `FieldDescriptor` for checking this: [FileDescriptor::has_optional_keyword()](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/a530dbe50c8295bf7b19e245b9be8525e235e6cb/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.h#L704-L706). Ideally this method will work even for extensions in a proto3 file, otherwise the semantic of that method becomes more complicated. The method could be useful for eg. implementing a linter that suggests that an explicit `optional` be added to bare extensions in a proto3 file.

For these reasons, I would advocate that:

1. We allow, but do not require, the `optional` keyword on extensions declared in a proto3 file.
2. We set the `FieldDescriptorProto.proto3_optional` field for extensions with an explicit `optional` keyword in proto3. This gives a signal that [FileDescriptor::has_optional_keyword()](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/a530dbe50c8295bf7b19e245b9be8525e235e6cb/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.h#L704-L706) can use to return the right answer.
3. We clarify the documentation to specify that synthetic oneofs are are only required when `proto3_optional` appears on a regular field, *not* for extensions. In practice this is the behavior that is already implemented.

(1) and (2) are the behavior that is already implemented. So I think this may end up being a documentation change only.

@haberman if you mean to suggest that extensions _should_ allow the `optional` keyword in proto3 (now, thanks to proto3 optional support) and that the generated descriptor _should_ have the `proto3_optional` flag set to true, then I guess there is nothing to be done here... except perhaps document the expectations more clearly? The doc I had read lead me to believe that `proto3_optional` means the field will have a synthetic oneof, which clearly isn't the case with an extension.

Maybe we should close this issue?
@haberman is there more to do here?
I think this bug requires no further action.

title: Any plans to use MemoryPool when deserializing ByteString?
body:
This is a question in regards to .NET implementation of protocol buffers.
I started using protobuf together with gRPC, so sorry, if I'm missing the bigger picture or don't take other use cases into account.

Considering the big number of guides & tutorials (including MSDN) recommending to use ArrayPool or MemoryPool to minimize memory allocations and improve performance, I was wondering why ByteString doesn't use the memory from MemoryPool?

I saw that recently there was a PR that changed ByteString to use memory and added unsafe create without copy.
This allows to rent the memory from pool, create ByteString, send it, and release the memory.
This should be beneficial for client side, but on server side, it's the protobuf's code that does the allocation, and it currently creates an array for the whole field.

So back to the question: are there any plans to rent the memory from the pool for ByteStrings, and let the users dispose of it once they are done? Or is there a reason why it's a bad idea? Or will the benefits actually be so small, that it's not worth the effort?

nodes.body:
The fundamental problem is that currently ByteString (or any other objects for representing protobuf fields / messages) doesn't provide an API for disposing the underlying values, which makes the scenario of renting memory from a pool a returning it non-intuitive and it's easy to get things wrong and either leak memory or erroneously read from memory that was already returned to the pool.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7645 was mostly introduced for advanced and "use at your own risk" scenarios, not as a general purpose API that everyone should use. Using the new API you can achieve renting the byteStrings for some scenarios when you really need to (and after you've measured it's worth it), but as was pointed out in that PR's thread already, using it in your day-to-day usage of protobufs is not recommended (because there's no way of controlling the lifecycle of the rented memory).

title: Option to disable the generation of deprecated classes for PHP
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
PHP

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

The generated code for nested types is currently done in 2 ways for the PHP code:
- namespaced classes, which will be there for Protobuf 4
- `_`-separated names, marked as deprecated, for compatibility with older Protobuf 3.x versions

When starting a new project using protobuf-php, there is no need for the compat classes, as these classes are not used anywhere in consumer code (as that's a new project so none of the classes are used yet). These deprecated compat classes are creating useless noise in the project.
If the generated code is exposed as a public project (instead of staying purely internal), things become even worse because these classes are then part of the API of your package, which means that removing them requires a major version of the package.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

For such case, I'd like a way to opt-in for generating only the new code (i.e. namespaced classes for nested types).
Ideally, this opt-in should be available through an option controlled when running `protoc` rather than something set inside the `proto3` file itself, as that's a setting that makes sense to be controlled by the maintainer of the PHP package (which is the one running `protoc`), not by the author of the `proto3` file (and someone else might have started using the same `proto3` file to generate PHP code for their own project earlier and so benefits from the compat layer).

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

I could post-process the generated code to remove the BC layer after running `protoc`. But this does not only involve removing files for the old names. The new files also contain some `class_alias` logic. So this complicates things and it might be fragile if the code generator changes things in its output.

**Additional context**
I discovered this when working with the sass/embedded-protocol definitions, in which we have 34 nested types among the total of 39 types, so the generated code current contains 73 classes, with 34 (46%) being for the compat layer that's irrelevant for my use case.

nodes.body:
These options have been marked deprecated with `@trigger_error` since [Protobuf 3.6.0](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v3.6.0), released in June 2018 (committed in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/4536).

I'm inclined to think we should just remove the legacy names at this point.

From a semver point of view, this might require releasing Protobuf 4.0 though.

But anyway, I'm fine either way (personally, I don't care as I don't have a legacy project relying on old class names)

Open to PRs
Closing, please re-open to help raise priority

title: Add merge option for protojson.Unmarshal

nodes.body:
If we were to add this, we would want it to behave the same way as `Merge` in [`proto.UnmarshalOptions`](https://pkg.go.dev/google.golang.org/protobuf@v1.27.1/proto#UnmarshalOptions). Which has an equivalent behavior in [`proto.Merge`](https://kotlinlang.org/docs/data-classes.html). IIUC, this means that

```
var m proto.Message
_ := proto.Unmarshal(ba, m)
_ := proto.UnmarshalOptions{Merge: true}.Unmarshal(bb, m)
```

is equivalent to

```
var m, tmp proto.Message
_ := proto.Unmarshal(ba, m)
_ := proto.Unmarshal(bb, tmp)
proto.Merge(m, tmp)
```

You mention that this doesn't work for you though, so I am wondering if the behavior you're looking for really is merging. Could you elaborate a bit on what you want to achieve?

The problem is when using the following 2 JSON examples (using the types from the initial msg):
```
{"PropA": "value"}  != {"PropA": "value", "PropB": ""}
```
When first unmarshalling either of those 2 JSON objects we end up with the same proto message though:
```
{
   "PropA": "value",
   "PropB": "",
}
````

When I now use `proto.Merge` I end up with `PropB` not being overwritten, no matter which JSON was used.
From looking at `proto.Merge` the doc reads:
```
Populated scalar fields in src are copied to dst
```
So no matter if `PropB` is populated in JSON or not, once converted to proto this information is lost.

Comparing this `merge` functionality with UnmarshalString, I'd end up with either (assuming PropB was set to "X"):
```
{
   "PropA": "value",
   "PropB": "X",
}
````
and 
```
{
   "PropA": "value",
   "PropB": "",
}
```
So the 'new' Unmarshal' first resets the object, which wipes out my `PropB / X` and by using Merge we lost the notion of `ProbB` existing in the JSON or not.
It's a 'shortcoming' in the language as the absence of a primitive is not distinguishable from the default value. 

Another alternative would be to convert all types to use proto.wrapper values, unfortunately we don't have control over all types being used and it'd be inconvenient.

jsonpb offers UnmarshalString, which merges only available properties and doesn't overwrite missing props.
We'd either need UnmarshalString in `protojson` or the `Merge` option to avoid calling `Reset` on the proto message.
Sorry for the long delay. This repository does not maintain go protos, you should file a bug in [their repository](https://github.com/golang/protobuf) for help.

Version: 3.14.0, 3.15.8
Language: C++
The protobuf library has been compiled with the following command line:
```
cmake -G "Visual Studio 15 2017 Win64" -Dprotobuf_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON ..
```


**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10 64bit

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2017 15.9.24

**What did you do?**
With the following proto definition (my_message.proto):

```
syntax = "proto3";

message MyMessage {
}
```

and the following test program:

```
#include "my_message.pb.h"
#include <google/protobuf/arena.h>
#include <google/protobuf/message.h>
#include <google/protobuf/any.pb.h>
#include <iostream>

std::uint64_t leak()
{
  google::protobuf::Arena arena;

  google::protobuf::Any* any_msg = google::protobuf::Arena::CreateMessage<google::protobuf::Any>(&arena);
  MyMessage my_msg;

  any_msg->PackFrom(my_msg);    //  <--  this causes the memory leak

  return arena.SpaceUsed();   // [1]
}

int main()
{
  std::uint64_t max_size = 0;
  std::uint16_t n = 0;

  while (true) {
    const std::uint64_t size = leak();

    max_size = std::max(size, max_size);
    ++n;
               
    if (n == 0) {
      std::cout << "max = " << max_size << std::endl;
    }
  }

  return 0;
}
```

Memory usage of the program grows indefinitely (observed with Process Explorer and Visual Studio diagnostic tool).  When however the Any object in leak() is allocated without an arena (i.e just with plain `google::protobuf::Any any_msg;`) the memory usage stays constant. 
It makes no difference whether the MyMessage object "my_msg" is arena-allocated or not.

[1] arena.SpaceUsed() always returns the same value, even when the memory usage shown in the diagnostic tool is growing.
