title: MessageToDict converts uint64 to string in python

nodes.body: Hey guys. I just wanted to check up on this issue.

Looking at the source code, int64 is explicitly converted to string, which seems odd to do without any valid reason. Searching a bit further, this seems to be done because Javascript's implementation of `Number`. 

From https://www.w3schools.com/js/js_numbers.asp:
**This format stores numbers in 64 bits, where the number (the fraction) is stored in bits 0 to 51, the exponent in bits 52 to 62, and the sign in bit 63:**

Comparing `2 ** 58` as example for python and javascript gives different results:
```python
# Python
$ 2 ** 58
288230376151711744
```
Which gives
```javascript
// Javascript
$ 2 ** 58
288230376151711740
```

So I would guess this string conversion happens because of JavaScript, which is understandable but somewhat annoying to work with if JavaScript isn't even part of the mix.

The behavior is correct according to our json mapping:

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json

title: Python: Implementation agnostic way to determine type of the elements of an empty repeated field
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Python generated code

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

There is no public method to determine the type of entries in an empty repeated field.

The [`proto-plus`](https://pypi.org/project/proto-plus/) package wraps protobuf messages for many of the Python Google Cloud Client Libraries. 
When a repeated field has no entries the proto-plus implementation [deep-copies the whole message](https://github.com/googleapis/proto-plus-python/blob/c6c4c52ac9ec9fdbb75f6bf644162d8a2f0fe9e3/proto/marshal/collections/repeated.py#L98-L111), adds an entry, and fetches the type of the field from that copy. The deep copying results in a performance hit.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

An implementation agnostic (works with both C++ and Python implementation types) way to determine type of the elements of an empty repeated field.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

To try these examples, `pip install googleapis-common-protos` to get the built `google.api.quota_pb2` proto. Proto file is [here](https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/api/quota.proto).

**1. Add an entry to determine the type**

This is what we're currently doing but would prefer not to, since we have to copy the whole message first.

```py
>>> from google.api import quota_pb2
>>> q = quota_pb2.Quota()
>>> limit = q.limits.add()
>>> type(limit)
<class 'google.api.quota_pb2.QuotaLimit'>
```

**2. Use `_message_descriptor._concrete_class`**

This only works in the **Python** implementation and relies on private attributes.

```py
>>> from google.api import quota_pb2
>>> q = quota_pb2.Quota()
>>> q.limits._message_descriptor._concrete_class
<class 'google.api.quota_pb2.QuotaLimit'>
```

In the C++ implementation the code above results in an error:

```
>>> q.limits._message_descriptor._concrete_class
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
AttributeError: 'google.protobuf.pyext._message.RepeatedCompositeCo' object has no attribute '_message_descriptor'
```

**Additional context**

 See https://github.com/googleapis/proto-plus-python/pull/226 for additional context.

nodes.body:
We are facing the same problem where we have to disable the warnings as errors or edit the file, non of the options are good enough for CICD pipelines. 


Any good reason to not fix this?
I think it should be fine to change those `if`s to `ifdef`s. If you want to send a pull request and tag me on it I would be happy to merge it.

Why not just turn off the warnings?

Ever since ANSI C back in 1989/1990, the C and C++ standard preprocessors
have very well-defined behavior when it comes to an undefined identifier in
a #if directive: it is treated as though it were zero.

That way, rather than having to write
#ifdef MACRO
#if MACRO
// stuff
#endif
#endif

You can just write

#if MACRO
// stuff
#endif

If a warning prevents you from taking advantage of this time-saving
behavior, then by all means you should turn off that warning.

-- Jorg

title: ${PROTOBUF_INCLUDE_DIR} should *not* point to <prefix>/usr/include
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.15.8
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Ubuntu 21.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
`armv7at2hf-neon-fslc-linux-gnueabi`

**What did you do?**
Add following code to `CMakeLists.txt`
```
find_package(Protobuf REQUIRED)
include_directories(SYSTEM ${PROTOBUF_INCLUDE_DIR})
```
aka adding protobuf includes as `SYSTEM` includes. The variable is filled with `<prefix>/usr/include`.

**What did you expect to see**
Compilation should work just fine.

**What did you see instead?**

Can't compile because `stdlib.h` not found.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

This is the case, because it adds `-isystem<prefix>/usr/include` to the compilation flags which conflicts with `#include_next <stdlib.h>` within `cstdlib`.
More details in: https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=70129

nodes.body: Would you be able to send a PR for this?
After reading over the details again, I think there is nothing which protobuf can do to fix the issue. There are multiple approaches listed in the linked GCC bug though.

title: Define field mask path for non-last repeated fields
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**

proto3 I guess since [google/protobuf/field_mask.proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto) seems to be proto3 only.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Given,

```protobuf
syntax = "proto3";
package example;

message M {
  repeated N ns = 1;
}

message N {
  string a = 1;
  string b = 2;
}
```

Why does [google/protobuf/field_mask.proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/5e84a6169cf0f9716c9285c95c860bcb355dbdc1/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto#L85-L86) say,

> A repeated field is not allowed except at the last position of a paths string.

This makes the official field masks incredibly crippled for any message which uses repeated fields and it seems reasonable to want to be able to say I only want `ns.a` or `ns.b` just as if the field were not repeated.  Obviously one could be concerned about filtering/indexing like how JSONPath uses `[0]`/`[*]` but it seems like allowing `ns.a` would not preclude something more complex being added later.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I would like to be able to specify a field mask path with a repeated field in a non-last position.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Forking or using something besides field masks.
- Having to specify additional field masks for each repeated field.

**Additional context**

A recent change in the Go implementation of Field Masks, https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/1179, broke us.  It is just trying to comply with a constraint from here,

> [field_mask.proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9b0fa3e7fbaf3463c3afa1c9ab111682108eeadb/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto) mentions that ...
> 
> ```protobuf
> // Field masks are used to specify a subset of fields that should be
> // returned by a get operation or modified by an update operation.
> 
> ...
> 
> // # Field Masks in Projections
> // ...
> // A repeated field is not allowed except at the last position of a
> // paths string.
> 
> ...
> 
> // # Field Masks in Update Operations
> // ...
> // Note that a repeated field is only allowed in the last position of a `paths` string.
> ```
> 
> Given those statements, I think FieldMask.IsValid should return false if a path contains a repeated field that is not in the last position.

I also found this question asked, [How do I create a field mask for a field of a repeated field?](https://groups.google.com/g/protobuf/c/vfOKR5Hq0Mk/m/jx-dGpFPBwAJ), but the response was from two years ago,

> This is not supported at the moment, i.e., you can't use 'cats.name' in the FieldMask because 'cats' is a repeated field.

nodes.body:
A coworker noticed [AIP-161: Field masks: Wildcards](https://google.aip.dev/161) is accepted as of March and satisfies this issue.  What is the process it will take to get from AIP to defined here?

For convenience/reference here are some excerpts:

-  [AIP-161: Field masks: Map fields](https://google.aip.dev/161#map-fields) says,

    > Field masks may permit the specification of specific fields in a map, if and only if the map's keys are either strings or integers, using the . character for traversal.

    ```protobuf
    // Valid field masks: reviews, reviews.smith, reviews.`John Smith`
    map<string, string> reviews = 2
    ```

- [AIP-161: Field masks: Wildcards](https://google.aip.dev/161#wildcards) says,

    > Field masks may permit the use of the * character on a repeated field or map to indicate the specification of particular sub-fields in the collection

    ```protobuf
    // Valid field masks: authors, authors.*.given_name, authors.*.family_name
    // Invalid field masks: authors.0, authors.0.given_name
    repeated Author authors = 2;
    ```
What language? I think C++ has this and Java is under way.

@elharo Go.  Go made a change, https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/1179, based on the language in [field_mask.proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9b0fa3e7fbaf3463c3afa1c9ab111682108eeadb/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto#L85-L86),

> // A repeated field is not allowed except at the last position of a
> // paths string.

And `field_mask.proto` does not make any mention of the wildcards or map features I cited above.

The change broke us and we created an issue there, https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/1315, but they are [deferring to this repo](https://github.com/golang/protobuf/issues/1315#issuecomment-896125608),

title: Support a way to statically represent a field as a int64 id
body:
Assume I need to represent a field - `Table::Column::DataType::FieldA`  and I need to pass this field to some function, which is suppose to visit on a proto message of `Table` type and it's supposed to do something on all fields of Table (recursively)  excluding `FieldA`. How do I pass `FieldA` without passing the `"Table::Column::DataType::FieldA"` string ? I need a int64_t representation for performance reasons.

I know that I can do this with:

1. Member function pointer - `DataType::has_FieldA`, and cast it to int64_t, because this function pointer is guaranteed to be unique as long as `has_FieldA` is not inline and it's is defined in `table.pb.cc`. But it's not guaranteed that future version of protobuf will not break this requirement.

2. I can use Pair(const Descriptor*, int field_number)... where Descriptor is for the parent `Message` (DataType in this case) and `field_number` is calculated using `DataType::k{Field}FieldNumber`... This is kind of ok but has require 16 bytes to store and not seamless to use.

How about creating a method: 
`static int64_t DataType::FieldA_Id();` ?

This Id is going to be unique for FieldA. One way to create this id is  - `combined_hash(int64 casted Descriptor*, field_number)`....

This cannot be solved by adding a wrapper on top of generated C++ code. It has to be incorporated in the generation layer itself.

**What language does this apply to?**
C++14

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Described above.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Described above.
Here is another solution : Generate a type for each field.. 
Currently it's generated for each Message field but we need to generate it for primitive types as well.
For example - Generate an opaque type `struct fieldA_t { };`  for each field in a message. I could use typeinfo or other things to generate a unique id for a unique id. In fact there are lot other benefits of a unique type for each field.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Described above.

**Additional context**
N/A

nodes.body:
If your performance requirements necessitate some custom codegen for this, I'd recommend implementing your own code generator. It's reasonably easy to do this with the code generator framework (see https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp/google.protobuf.compiler.plugin) and it would give you full freedom to implement whatever extra code you need.

I think your use case is specialized enough that it probably wouldn't make sense to add this to the main C++ code generator.
Ok. Thanks.

title: [Ruby] Exception inspecting a message on Windows (3.15 regression)
body:
/attn: @haberman

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.15.8
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows Server 2019 (10.0.17763), via the "windows-latest" platform on GitHub Actions.

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
n/a (using the binary gem release)

**What did you do?**

```ruby
require "google/protobuf"

Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_file("windoze.proto", :syntax => :proto3) do
    add_message "windoze.SimpleTest" do
      # Note: No fields necessary
    end
  end
end
module Windoze
  SimpleTest = ::Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("windoze.SimpleTest").msgclass
end

message = Windoze::SimpleTest.new
puts message.inspect
```

**What did you expect to see**

I expect a string representation of an empty message to be displayed.

**What did you see instead?**

A `TypeError` is raised with the following message: ```in `inspect': wrong argument type nil (expected Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool)```.

The stack trace identifies the final line in the provided Ruby code (`puts message.inspect`) but no further information is given. (I believe the `inspect` method is [implemented in C](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/38e1b592581983548eb8012e45a3a1da64b6504f/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L748).)

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

* This appears to be a 3.15 regression. It does not reproduce on 3.14, but does reproduce on various patchlevels of 3.15. (I tried 3.15.8, 3.15.6, and 3.15.2.)
* This appears to be Windows-specific. I can get it to reproduce on a Windows machine (via GitHub Actions), but not on MacOS or Linux.
* I can reproduce it by installing the `x64-mingw32` build of the gem, and by forcing the platform to `ruby` and building the gem from source on install.
* The error appears regardless of whether there are fields present in the proto description or not.
* There are different ways of reproducing the error. The sample code above is the simplest, but I'm also able to reproduce it under certain circumstances when fetching fields in a nested message structure. I can provide additional repro examples if needed.

nodes.body:
It's been difficult for me to get a real stack trace since I don't actually have a Windows machine to test or build on, but based on an analysis of what kind of code will trigger the exception and what won't, I believe the exception is coming from the following call stack. (Links are from the 3.15.8 tag.)

* ~`ruby_to_Descriptor()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c` line 401](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L401))~
* `Descriptor_DefToClass()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c` line 2486](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L2486))
* `Message_PrintMessage()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c` line 141](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L141))
* `Message_inspect()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c` line 752](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L752))

~If I'm reading this right, `Qnil` is being passed to `ruby_to_Descriptor()`. Tracing this back out, the only way I can account for that is if the `msgdef` field is`NULL`, and gets passed in [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L2485) and runs afoul of [this code](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L2441-L2443). I think the only place that `msgdef` gets set is [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L83). Is there a way that a class's Descriptor could be uninitialized?~

No, that's not it. The descriptor seems fine. I can retrieve it from the class and call methods that reference the `msgdef`. And looking again at the exception I'm getting, it's actually the DescriptorPool that's nil:

* `ruby_to_DescriptorPool()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c` line 273](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L273))
* `get_def_obj()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c` line 2435](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L2435))
* `get_msgdef_obj()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c` line 2456](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L2456))
* `Descriptor_DefToClass()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c` line 2485](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/defs.c#L2485))
* `Message_PrintMessage()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c` line 141](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L141))
* `Message_inspect()` ([`ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c` line 752](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L752))

The DescriptorPool is coming from the ObjectCache. I'll see if I can confirm whether that indeed is coming back as nil...

Wow excellent debugging work.

What version of Ruby is this on? Ruby <2.7 has big differences with Ruby >=2.7 in the object cache.
I've tried it on both 2.7 and 3.0. Same behavior.
oh but I haven't tried 2.6. Lemme try that.

Good to know. Ruby 2.7 is using the simpler ObjectCache code, so that somewhat narrows down where the bug could be.

I'm worried we're running into weirdness with `ObjectSpace::WeakMap` itself, which could be hard to work around. :/
Does not reproduce on 2.6!!

I have a theory. If you're able to modify the source, could you add the following line here, before the return: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/protobuf.c#L347

```
  if (!RB_FIXNUM_P(ret)) rb_raise(rb_eRuntimeError, "Key must be fixed!");
```
Ah sorry, I mean right before `#if USE_SECONDARY_MAP`

I am not sure if I can come up with a way to modify the source, but I'll try.

(Note: if I understand where you're going with this, it suggests something else I've seen but haven't gotten a chance to report yet, might be related. Sometimes, calculating the hash of a message on Windows, results in Ruby asserting internally saying the value is not a legal fixnum.)

After a bit more investigation, I'm having more confidence in my theory.

The theory is that on Windows, pointer values when converted to an integer are too big to fit in a Ruby `Fixnum`. I think this is true because [Ruby uses `LONG_MAX` to decide what will fit in a `Fixnum`](https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/b85fd1d690b65efaa126cf9c24da73f31eee7a4e/include/ruby/internal/arithmetic/fixnum.h#L41-L42), but [on 64-bit Windows `long` is 32 bits](https://stackoverflow.com/a/59852878/77070).

The object cache uses `ObjectSpace::WeakMap`, which will collect and erase any entries where the key *or* value is collectible. We were counting on the keys not being collectible because they are `Fixnum`, but on Windows this assumption doesn't hold, causing object cache entries to get evicted prematurely.

The workaround code from Ruby 2.6 and earlier helps because it create a secondary map that is not weak to store WeakMap keys. Since the WeakMap keys are referenced from the secondary map, and because the value (the DescriptorPool) is presumably referenced from somewhere else, the entries don't get collected and the object cache lookup succeeds.
And I can confirm that the key is not a fixnum.

I actually wonder if this is a bug in Ruby. The [comment here](https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/b85fd1d690b65efaa126cf9c24da73f31eee7a4e/include/ruby/internal/arithmetic/fixnum.h#L32-L34) says:

```c
 /* FIXABLE can be applied to anything, from double to intmax_t.  The problem is
 * double.   On a  64bit system  RUBY_FIXNUM_MAX is  4,611,686,018,427,387,903,
 * which is not representable by a double.
```

But this is not true on Windows 64-bit systems.

In any case, we'll clearly need a workaround for this to accommodate existing Ruby deployments on Windows.

If Ruby is wanting 64-bit max on 64-bit systems, I think `INTPTR_MAX` would do the trick. That requires C99, if Ruby is trying to be C89 compatible they could try `SIZE_MAX`, though that is unsigned.

More info here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64-bit_computing#64-bit_data_models

Do you have any Ruby contacts you could ask to clarify about this?

Yeah, I can confirm the behavior.

```c
sprintf(infostr,
  "key=%p ret=%llx ptrsiz=%d valsiz=%d fixmaxsiz=%d fixmin=%lx fixmax=%lx lonmin=%lx lonmax=%lx",
  key, ret, sizeof(key), sizeof(ret), sizeof(RUBY_FIXNUM_MIN),
  RUBY_FIXNUM_MIN, RUBY_FIXNUM_MAX, LONG_MIN, LONG_MAX);
```

(where `key` is the incoming pointer, and `ret` is a VALUE, the result of running `LL2NUM((intptr_t)key >> 2)`)

A typical run for 64-bit windows:

```
key=0000020db8d824c0 ret=20db8eedbb8 ptrsiz=8 valsiz=8 fixmaxsiz=4
fixmin=c0000000 fixmax=3fffffff lonmin=80000000 lonmax=7fffffff
```

Note that `ret` is clearly a different pointer. Ruby has allocated a new object. And sizeof(long) is 4, so the 64-bit pointer is outside the range.

A typical run for 64-bit Linux (or MacOS):

```
key=0x5570071017f0 ret=2ab803880bf9 ptrsiz=8 valsiz=8 fixmaxsiz=8
fixmin=c000000000000000 fixmax=3fffffffffffffff lonmin=8000000000000000 lonmax=7fffffffffffffff
```

In this case, `ret` is the expected `((key >> 2) << 1) + 1` for a Fixnum.

I can try to reach out to Aaron; he'd at least know who to talk to. It may be that they agree that it's an error to assume `sizeof(long) == sizeof(ptr)`. However, that said, it's also possible the intent actually is to ensure that fixnums always fit in a `long`, independent of the size of a pointer. I think we should consider retaining the secondary map (or otherwise creating some other workaround) for platforms where the size is indeed different.

In fact, looking at more of the Ruby headers, there's a lot of code that just assumes `long` for representing fixnums. For example, Fixnum creation funnels into [`RB_INT2FIX`](https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/b85fd1d690b65efaa126cf9c24da73f31eee7a4e/include/ruby/internal/arithmetic/long.h#L82-L96), which uses `long`, and there is no `long long` equivalent. I suspect that's the intent (for now), and we're just going to have to adjust our assumptions on the protobuf side.

Thanks for the confirmation!

I agree that fixing Ruby on Windows to use 64-bit fixnum would be a bigger fix that would involve replacing `long` with `intptr_t` or similar in a lot of places. Changing the constant alone would not be enough.

It would surprise me if it's truly the intent that 64-bit Windows systems behave differently than 64-bit Linux/Mac. But maybe there's some history there that I'm not aware of.

I agree we'll need a workaround for now regardless. It should be a simple matter to change the `#ifdef` so that the secondary map is used unconditionally on Windows. It's a bit of a bummer because it's some complex code and it has a measurable performance impact. But it's our only option at this point I think.

It may have been an oversight originally, but at this point it may very well be a backward compatibility issue, if there are a lot of C extensions that assume fixnums can fit in a long.

In any case, I confirmed that turning on `USE_SECONDARY_MAP` fixes the original issue on Ruby 2.7.3 and 3.0.1 on Windows, so I think we can call that a fix for now.

Ah yes I could see that.

I found this: https://bugs.ruby-lang.org/issues/14378  The main rationale given there is that it would be a big change to the source code.

Glad that the workaround works. Feel free to send a PR for that!

And BTW, it looks like this is indeed related to the other issue I was seeing. Calling `Message#hash` on Windows results in a C assertion. I suspect the reason is, again, `Message_Hash()` is returning `uint64_t` and then `Message_hash()` is trying to call `INT2FIX` on that.

Thanks for this excellent information!

Looking at the code in question, it is relatively straightforward and there is not a lot of room for a bug to live. It seems likely that the bug is not in this code per se, but that the proto was somehow corrupted before reaching this point.

Is there any chance the bug would reproduce under Valgrind? That could give some extra information to validate the status of the memory that the encoder is trying to read.

Unfortunately, I don't have a concrete reproduction step yet to use Valgrind. Right now I can only retry our build process, which takes an hour to finish.

Will compiling this Ruby extension with AddressSanitizer via `-fsanitize=address` help? Let me find out.

I think `-fsanitize=address` could help, but you might have to build Ruby with this flag also to make it work. I generally have had trouble getting ASAN to work for Ruby extensions.

I'll brainstorm some more the best way to debug this, I don't want to send you on too many wild goose chases.

Does the issue repro fairly quickly once the process has started, or is it more intermittent?

> Does the issue repro fairly quickly once the process has started, or is it more intermittent?

It's intermittent but annoying enough that happens a few times a day. It definitely happened with the upgrade to v3.15.8. We reverted to v3.14.0 and never hit the error. We had to upgrade to v3.15.8 a few weeks after the revert, and now we see the issue again. We just retry the build whenever it happens.

I'm not sure if it ever happens in production, though. I'll have to look for that.

Ah I see, if it's that intermittent then debug printf might not be the best way to tackle this one.

Yes it totally makes sense that 3.15 would have been the point where this was introduced. There was a major change in 3.15, a rewrite of the data layer basically (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8184), which improved performance and simplified the code a lot. But like all new code, it's had some bugs to work through. Thanks for your patience while we figure them out.

Can you give a summary of how this message (the one that is crashing in `#encode`) is built? Is it built from scratch, or was it originally parsed from a different payload? Is there anything particularly interesting about the way that it is built? In particular, how are the values in this repeated bytes field (`repeated bytes paths`) populated?

The message is built from scratch: https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/ffed5fe4139bb4a49cf1b262dfabff16b7dd38fc/lib/gitlab/gitaly_client/commit_service.rb#L331-351

Line 349 is where the repeated call happens. In the test that hit this effort above, I think the value of `options[:path]` should just be `README.md` or some other filename.

The `encode_binary` just forces a Ruby string to a binary encoding: https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/blob/ffed5fe4139bb4a49cf1b262dfabff16b7dd38fc/lib/gitlab/encoding_helper.rb#L89-91

Thank you for the code reference; that was enough of a lead that I was able to find the bug!

See the attached PR, which I am confident will fix the crashes you are seeing. I was able to reproduce the issue under Valgrind and verify that my fix removes the Valgrind error.

This fix should be released in 3.17.1, which I expect will be released on Monday or Tuesday.
@haberman Awesome, thank you very much!

@stanhu You're welcome!

Small update: this will be in 3.17.2, not 3.17.1. The 3.17.1 release was already in progress when I submitted this. But 3.17.2. should still be released in the next day or two.

@haberman I think 3.17.1 has this fix. 😄 

```
commit 367e4691d2bc97de28b422d7461e4135d556d301 (tag: v3.17.1, origin/3.17.x)
Author: Joshua Haberman <jhaberman@gmail.com>
Date:   Fri May 21 23:04:09 2021 -0700

    Fixed memory bug: properly root repeated/map field when assigning. (#8639)

    * Fixed memory bug: properly root repeated/map field when assigning.

    Previously the protobuf extension would not properly root
    memory from a repeated field or map when assigning to a
    message field (see the attached test case).  This could cause
    crashes if the repeated field is subsequently accessed.

    * Add accidentally-deleted Ruby test.
```
Excellent, even better. :)
Now I wonder how long it takes for this release to land in Rubygems. https://rubygems.org/gems/google-protobuf
I think it is up now: https://rubygems.org/gems/google-protobuf/versions/3.17.1-x86_64-linux
Just to follow up here, I have not see a seg fault since we upgraded to v3.17.1, so thanks for all the work here. I should have remembered that funny things can happen during garbage collection.

title: [Ruby] Message#hash crashes with a C assertion on Windows
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.15.8
Language: Ruby 2.7.3, 3.0.1

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows Server 2019 (10.0.17763), via the "windows-latest" platform on GitHub Actions.

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
n/a (using the binary gem release)

**What did you do?**

```ruby
require "google/protobuf"

Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_file("windoze.proto", :syntax => :proto3) do
    add_message "windoze.SimpleTest" do
      # Note: No fields necessary
    end
  end
end
module Windoze
  SimpleTest = ::Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup("windoze.SimpleTest").msgclass
end

message = Windoze::SimpleTest.new
puts message.hash
```

**What did you expect to see**
An integer hash value displayed

**What did you see instead?**
The Ruby VM terminates with the following assertion coming from C code:
```
[BUG] Unnormalized Fixnum value 0xbb5cc1f7724449a5
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

I found this while investigating #8554. The assertion is coming from [here](https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/b85fd1d690b65efaa126cf9c24da73f31eee7a4e/numeric.c#L3545) and seems to happen if the value claims to be a Fixnum but doesn't fall within the range of the `long` type. Thus, it could trigger on 64-bit Windows where longs are 32 bits, if the Fixnum is set from a 64-bit value. This is indeed the case in `Message_hash`, which takes a [64-bit integer from wyhash](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L720), and [crams it directly into `INT2FIX`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/436bd7880e458532901c58f4d9d1ea23fa7edd52/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L737).

This does not seem to trigger on Linux or MacOS, which is unsurprising because `long` is 64-bit on those platforms.

title: Protobufs creation is slow when using nested objects compared to using bytes
body:
I would like to serialize a small tensor, but I've experienced different performance outcomes. The scenario is: I want to send a tensor over the network, for which I have a protobuf implementation <torch_tensor_proto>.I have multiple proto messages in my use case, the best approach being to use an  `oneof`. The two methods that I have considered are:
* serialize the tensor to bytes and then store the bytes in the oneof protobuf (I considered this slower)
* include the torch tensor message in the oneof message

A minimal snippet of code is here

```
from syft import serialize
from syft.proto.syft_message_pb2 import SyftNative
import boltons.gcutils
import torch

# message Syft Native{
#   oneof {
#       bytes data = 1;
#       <torch_tensor_proto> data_tensorproto_57 = 2;
#   }
# }



def serialize_to_bytes(proto):
    torch_bytes = proto.SerializeToString() # 14
    proto_wrapper_object =  SyftNative(data=torch_bytes) # 15
    wire_bytes = proto_wrapper_object.SerializeToString() # 16
    return wire_bytes

def wrap_in_proto(proto):
    proto_wrapper_object = SyftNative(data_tensorproto_57=proto) # 20
    wire_bytes = proto_wrapper_object.SerializeToString() # 21
    return wire_bytes


#disable GC
with boltons.gcutils.toggle_gc:
    obj = torch.randn((100, 100))
    # <torch_tensor_proto>
    proto = serialize(obj, to_proto=True)

    while True:
        serialize_to_bytes(proto)
        wrap_in_proto(proto)

```


The problem is that the solution where I store directly the bytes is fine in terms of speed, while the other one is really slow. Benchmarks of this using `py-spy` gave me:

```
 89.00%  89.00%   56.55s    56.55s   wrap_in_proto (bench.py:20)
  3.00%   3.00%    2.06s     2.06s   wrap_in_proto (bench.py:21)
  3.00%   3.00%    1.45s     1.45s   serialize_to_bytes (bench.py:14)
  2.00%   2.00%   0.610s    0.610s   serialize_to_bytes (bench.py:15)
  2.00%   2.00%   0.530s    0.530s   serialize_to_bytes (bench.py:16)
```

I've annotated the lines that are present in the benchmark. The constructor of SyftNative with another protobuf object passed in it Python is very slow.


**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
libprotoc 3.15.8

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
DISTRIB_DESCRIPTION="Ubuntu 20.04.1 LTS"

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
python 3.7 with a c++  compiled backend for protobuf as described here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/master/python


**What did you expect to see**
Using a protobuf message in the constructor instead of copying bytes to be faster.

**What did you see instead?**
Using bytes is way faster than passing another probuf message in the constructor. You can see that line 21 according to the posted benchmark is eating up most of the cpu time. Why?


**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
The inner message that I am transforming to bytes/wrapping:
https://github.com/OpenMined/PySyft/blob/dev/proto/lib/torch/tensor.proto

title: Make JsonFormat.parser().mergeAny build com.google.protobuf.Any when type is missing from type registry

nodes.body:
This is unfortunately infeasible.

`google.protobuf.Any` requires that the data is represented as a protobuf binary string. But there is no way for us to convert JSON to a protobuf binary string unless we have the type information for the message in the `Any`.

I am surprised this worked in your debugger. I don't know the Java code that well, but it appears that your change will cause it to construct a message of type `google.protobuf.Any`. But that message only has two fields: `type_url` and `value`. If your JSON has other fields for your unknown message, say `foo`, then the JSON parser should fail to set the `foo` field on the `Any` message.

title: Use of alignas(64) on struct ThreadCache (arena_impl.h) causes link problems on 32 bit platform esp32
body:
Version: 3.15.8
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
esp-idf v4.2 

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
xtensa gcc 8.4.0

**What did you do?**
created a custom cmake file to compile protobuf lite for this architecture

**What did you expect to see**
**What did you see instead?**
The binary image for this chip / architecture has a specific address requirement for certain headers. The use of alignas(64) on struct ThreadCache causes some sort of alignment offset to be introduced that shifts these headers by 32 bytes, resulting in an invalid binary. Changing to alignas(32) addresses the issue. Recommend the following change to address this:

#if GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_ARCH_64_BIT
  struct alignas(64) ThreadCache {
#else
  struct alignas(32) ThreadCache {
#endif

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-idf/en/v4.2/esp32/index.html

title: Change representation of bytes in text format to something like Base64
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
This is a change to the text encoding of protobuf, not the IDL.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
The protobuf text format produces output which is hard to read and process for binary data (bytes data type).
Example (I omitted all non-bytes fields):
```prototxt
session {
  session_hash: "N\201\310\345\314\261\364!\310I\200\346\311\376\256|\360\241\365\2508^1`\230\252\265\314\355Nmn"
  nonce: "\203\022@\302\302\264\363|\237H\005Y7\273=\347"
  user_session {
  # ....
    id: "V^]\362\237\3507r>5\026\267\274ea\254"
  }
}
```
Representing arbitrary binary data as ASCII text with escape sequences is IMO unintuitive and very verbose. For example the `session_hash` is 97 characters wide in the standard protobuf text encoding while plain Base64 would take 43 characters which is less than half. The used escape sequences also only work on a small subset of programming languages (for example Go and Rust don't like binary data in strings) and tools, whereas something like Base64 works pretty much everywhere.
Depending on how the new representation is going to look it will also make it possible to easily distinguish between strings and binary data in the protobuf text encoding.
**Describe the solution you'd like**
Something along the lines of
```prototxt
session {
  session_hash: ToHI5cyx9CHISYDmyf6ufPCh9ag4XjFgmKq1zO1ObW4
  nonce: gxJAwsK083yfSAVZN7s95w
  user_session {
  # ....
    id: Vl5d8p/oN3I+NRa3vGVhrA
  }
}
```
I'm not married to that format, but it would have the advantage of being backwards-compatible (note the missing quotes) and is very compact. The only disadvantage this has is it is possible to construct base64 strings which look entirely like integers which might be confusing if you don't have the IDL files handy. It might be preferable to have some form of marker character to signify a binary value, but I haven't found a good one yet.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Another encoding could be used, but hexadecimal is verbose and Ascii85 hard to parse as it uses a lot of characters used as delimiters in normal prototext for a very moderate gain in efficiency.

nodes.body: Doubtful we can change the textproto encoding given the need for old software to process new messages

title: brackets messed up in src/google/protobuf/stubs/port.h in version 3.17.0
body:
I'm on Windows using MSYS2 shell and GCC MinGW-w64.
When I build versions 3.17.0 there are a bunch of errors in src/google/protobuf/stubs/port.h in the definition of `static inline uint64 bswap_64(uint64 x)` all related to missing/mismatched brackets/parentheses.
The code looks like:
```
static inline uint64 bswap_64(uint64 x) {
  return (((x & uint64_t{0xFFu)) << 56) |
          ((x & uint64_t{0xFF00u)) << 40) |
          ((x & uint64_t{0xFF0000u)) << 24) |
          ((x & uint64_t{0xFF000000u)) << 8) |
          ((x & uint64_t{0xFF00000000u)) >> 8) |
          ((x & uint64_t{0xFF0000000000u)) >> 24) |
          ((x & uint64_t{0xFF000000000000u)) >> 40) |
          ((x & uint64_t{0xFF00000000000000u)) >> 56));
}
```
When I change it to:
```
static inline uint64 bswap_64(uint64 x) {
  return (((x & (uint64_t)0xFFu) << 56) |
          ((x & (uint64_t)0xFF00u) << 40) |
          ((x & (uint64_t)0xFF0000u) << 24) |
          ((x & (uint64_t)0xFF000000u) << 8) |
          ((x & (uint64_t)0xFF00000000u) >> 8) |
          ((x & (uint64_t)0xFF0000000000u) >> 24) |
          ((x & (uint64_t)0xFF000000000000u) >> 40) |
          ((x & (uint64_t)0xFF00000000000000u) >> 56));
}
```
it builds fine.

title: Is it safe to cast different versions of protobuf pointers in C++?
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
proto3

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I have two different versions of task.proto, say v1 and v2, and I compiled them into two C++ classes, namespace1::V1 and namespace::V2. If I change the pointer of the new type to the old type, like (V1*)(&V2). Is this safe? Is there a difference between with using V1.ParseFromString(V2.SerializeToString())?

**Describe the solution you'd like**
At the moment my program works fine, but I don't know if it's safe. like (V1*)(&V2)

Can you give me some advice?

nodes.body: Casting is not safe since V1 and V2 are different C++ classes, but you can safely convert between them by serializing one and parsing it into the other as you mentioned.

title: Repeated of message which wraps "oneof" filed is not packed.

nodes.body: The first suggestion (omitting `val`) is not going to work as the parser won't know whether the repeated blocks refer to `val` or `shape`.  The second suggestion (omitting both `val` and `val_d`) suffers from the larger problem of synthesizing the name for `data` and `data_type` that is not ambiguous in a larger context.
If you are wed to that format, I would recommend custom parsing and serialization
It is cool if I can have customized serialization format to achieve that. (hopefully, proto text parser is also able to deserialize to object). How can I start from it ? Could you give an example?
I suggest you start with one of the many json parsers that are available and then write a wrapper function that takes json and fills in a protobuf that corresponds to what you want.
reasonable, ok

title: Kotlin library cause duplicate classes error
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.17.0
Language: Kotlin

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Android

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

target sdk version 30

**What did you do?**
1. `implementation 'com.google.protobuf:protobuf-kotlin:3.17.0'`
2. See a lot of duplicate class error and build failed

```
Duplicate class com.google.protobuf.AbstractMessage found in modules jetified-protobuf-java-3.17.0 (com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.17.0) and jetified-protobuf-kotlin-3.17.0 (com.google.protobuf:protobuf-kotlin:3.17.0)
...
```

It seems that `protobuf-kotlin` will implement `protobuf-java` also, but they have a lot of duplicate classes. Code below will solve the problem:

```
implementation ('com.google.protobuf:protobuf-kotlin:3.17.0') {
    exclude group: "com.google.protobuf", module: "protobuf-java"
}
```

nodes.body: Thanks for this report! I will look into how to fix this on our side to stop the errors, but I think this should be fixable on the user's side in the meantime by only using `protobuf-kotlin` and not `protobuf-java`.
Can you provide more information about your build system and how we could reproduce this error?

When you look into `protobuf-kotlin` 's [pom.xml](https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/google/protobuf/protobuf-kotlin/3.17.0/protobuf-kotlin-3.17.0.pom), you can see that `protobuf-kotlin` will import `protobuf-java` as dependency.

title: No documentation on the text representation format
body:
There is no (that I can find) documentation on the syntax of the text protobuf format on the developer site (https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers). As working with text files is one of the main ways in which end users will interact with them when protobufs are being used for, e.g, configuration files, it'd be good to go into some detail about this; I'd expect there to be a document similar to https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto2-spec describing the precise syntax. A more human-readable reference describing things like comment characters, continuation characters, string escapes etc would also be nice.

See also https://stackoverflow.com/questions/18873924/what-does-the-protobuf-text-format-look-like.

nodes.body: You are sadly correct that this is missing a formal specification.

@fowles what about go/textformat-spec? I'm not at G anymore, but I assume it or a derivative still exists (I was the original author). Can it be released? 

Not only is text format useful on its own, it's also a subset of the .proto language in the form of custom options. People working on .proto tooling are often unaware of the full scope of these options (e.g., https://github.com/devkanro/intellij-protobuf-plugin/issues/25)

I would also love to have this documented officially.

The benefit of the text format is it's 1:1 correspondence with the wire-format - whereas JSON has quite a few implicit conversions the user needs to know about (for instance timestamp.proto).

For my open source project [protocurl](https://github.com/qaware/protocurl), I made a [bare minimum documentation](https://github.com/qaware/protocurl#protobuf-text-format), as otherwise users could not use the simpler text format there. From my own user experience with it, the text format does offer some level of easier usage in contrast to JSON.

Is there need or a wish for support here, since there was no progress in the past year on this?
David is working on this.  It turns out that our documentation needed a lot of love and this is part of the overall effort he is leading to improve it.
We now have a text format spec here: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/text-format-spec It may not be perfect but should be fairly close.

**What did you see instead?**
```
[----------] Global test environment tear-down
[==========] 2263 tests from 200 test suites ran. (19714 ms total)
[  PASSED  ] 2262 tests.
[  FAILED  ] 1 test, listed below:
[  FAILED  ] MapImplTest.RandomOrdering

 1 FAILED TEST

```
The full log is attached.
[log.txt](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/6529615/log.txt)

nodes.body:
I regularly observe this failure on windows in our conda-forge infrastructure. Perhaps every 1-in-3 or 1-in-4 runs. Looks like:
```
[ RUN      ] MapImplTest.RandomOrdering
D:\bld\libprotobuf-split_1708422242031\work\src\google/protobuf/map_test.inc(1350): error: Value of: MapOrderingIsRandom(i, j)
  Actual: false
Expected: true
Map with keys 1 and 9 has deterministic ordering

[  FAILED  ] MapImplTest.RandomOrdering (0 ms)
[ RUN      ] MapImplTest.TransparentLookupForString
```

Edit: of course, now that I guesstimate a frequency, I get it 4 out of 4 times in a row... 🤦

It sounds like the test for whether nondeterministic ordering is observed might be failing in environments where the goal is to have a deterministic build and *prevent* nondeterministic behavior. The clock in particular might be stubbed out.

The fix might be to make [the seed function](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9c0d130168936120b4ed1953d041db86d7f362de/src/google/protobuf/map.h#L707-L732) rely on something other than the clock and the object address hash? Maybe the C random number API?

There should be [50 different addresses being used in the test](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9f52d5e380e98d588926c54f01f016d4431c51d5/src/google/protobuf/map_test.inc#L1335-L1337), and they shouldn't all roll the same bit as to how to order the keys, though. So maybe something is wrong with the pointer hash function from Abseil?

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: libprotoc 3.17.0
Language: Kotlin

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Mac OS X 11.3.1

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. cd into `analyticsproto/proto` folder
2.  `~/protoc/bin/protoc  `find . -name '*.proto'` --kotlin_out=../output`
3. Check the `output` folder

Files can be found here:
[analyticsproto.zip](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/6535110/analyticsproto.zip)

**What did you expect to see**
No outer classes generated

**What did you see instead?**
Empty outer classes generated, that also don't compile

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

Potentially related to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8629

nodes.body: Hi! The reason there isn't an outer class is because we have set Kotlin to automatically use the `java_multiple_files = true` option and we don't need any outer class methods yet for Kotlin. When you run protoc to compile kotlin protos you also need to use `--java_out` as well as `--kotlin_out` because the generated Kotlin files rely on the generated Java files. If you change that, will the code compile?

Oh I see, the [docs](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/kotlintutorial) make it seem like `--kotlin_out` is the only parameter needed.
![Screen Shot 2021-05-26 at 11 37 51 AM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/863461/119713698-d6f6f980-be16-11eb-92c1-a446d9c7f128.png)

 I ran `--java-out` with the same output folder and it builds now!

In a related vein, does the team plan to move to a purely Kotlin-based implementation eventually? If yes, will the Kotlin models generated now be roughly the same syntactically?
Moving to Kotlin-only is a long-term goal, but we are not willing to break source compatibility.  Any future changes will remain fully compatible, not just "roughly the same syntactically."
And I will update the docs, thanks for pointing out the documentation problem!

title: Kotlin: Why not use kotlinx serialization?
body: The code will looks more clean and simple.

nodes.body: https://github.com/Kotlin/kotlinx.serialization/blob/master/docs/formats.md#protobuf-experimental

It's not an unreasonable choice to use kotlinx.serialization, but we believe continuing to use .proto files to generate message types adds significant value.

- Cross-language support, especially with Java interop.
- proto3 support
- A variety of issues associated with message evolution, including:
  - Adding a field to Kotlin protos can never break code.
  - Field numbers can be marked reserved after deletion.
  - Message extensions are supported.
- Existing proto infrastructure is heavily optimized.

title: Kotlin: `getFieldorNull` in addition to get `getField`
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?
Kotlin

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
When trying to extract fields from the protobuf, I have to add an extra check to see if the field exists or not. 
For example, this is fairly verbose:
```
    val buttons = mutableListOf<Common.ButtonContent>().apply {
      if (buttonList.hasButtonOne()) {
        add(buttonList.buttonOne)
      }
      if (buttonList.hasButtonTwo()) {
        add(buttonList.buttonTwo)
      }
      if (buttonList.hasButtonThree()) {
        add(buttonList.buttonThree)
      }
    }
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
A non-breaking API change would be to add a `fieldorNull` method. This code becomes much cleaner and easier to read.
```
val buttons = listOfNotNull(
      buttonList.buttonOneOrNull,

)

+1

1. Would it make sense to define it at the java level instead of kotlin? Kotlin would then autoconvert the `getFieldOrNull` to a property.

2. In my project I've also implemented (through now-dead kroto-plus) and used the analogic function on builders to set a value - `setFieldNullable(value: T?)` which only added the value if it was not null.
Such a function standalone could maybe be viewed as not bringing enough value. But here, because `fieldOrNull` would become a property in kotlin, it would be imo very handy to implement it as a setter of this property (on builders only ofc). This would look like:
```kotlin
var fooOrNull: String?
   get() = if(hasFoo()) foo else null
   set(value) {
        if(value != null) setFoo(value) else clearFoo() // not sure about the else branch - maybe just don't touch the value on null?
   }
```

title: vs2019 update 16.10 : illegal initialization of `constinit` entity with a non-constant expression
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

Version: `2021-04-07 version 3.15.8`
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Windows.

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

Visual Studio 2019 msvc **Update 19.10** . Latest version that just recently added support for `constinit` on May 25th - [announcement here](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/releases/2019/release-notes#summary-of-whats-new-in-this-release-of-visual-studio-2019-version-16100).

**What did you do?**

Nothing horribly bad.. Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Make sure the language set to C++20, `-std:c++latest`, e.g. for CMake that'd be `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)` .
2. Try to compile some code that uses generated protobufs that include `port_def.inc` header .

**What did you expect to see**

Code compiles.

**What did you see instead?**

Code fails to compile with errors:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/34072974/120559291-a59da100-c3b5-11eb-8342-d282acb55ed4.png)

**Patch Proposal**

The most trivial hacky patch would be to apply the same logic as applied for `__GNUC__` , the issue described in #8310 .

Adding `!defined(_MSC_VER)` check - "resolves" the issue. And so `constinit` is not used:

```cpp
// Our use of constinit does not yet work with GCC:
// https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8310
// Our use of constinit does not yet work with Visual Studio 2019 Update 16.10:
// https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/TBD
#if defined(__cpp_constinit) && !defined(__GNUC__) && !defined(_MSC_VER)
#define PROTOBUF_CONSTINIT constinit
```

And the code works great after that even with latest Visual Studio 2019 compiler. This could be used as an interim patch to unblock customers using the latest compiler.

title: Backward incompatible change in 3.8.0:
body:
protobuf 3.8.0 introduced the following changelog entry:

```
* Always declare enums to be int-sized
```

In practice, this results in a generated code change for 
```
enum Foo { 
    ONE = 1,
    TWO = 2
}
```

Due to this change the generated C++ code was changed from
```
enum Foo {
    ONE = 1,
    TWO = 2
}
```
to 
```
enum Foo : int{
    ONE = 1,
    TWO = 2
}
```

This resulted in a migration problem for the following case:
```
enum Foo { ... };
message Bar {
    optional uint32 foobar = 1; // for possible values @see Foo
}
```

This technique was used to workaround enum expansion problem: foobar field was always valid and it was comparable with any enum values. As all enums are inherited from int, an attempt to compare signed and unsigned integers will trigger `-Wsign-compare` warning.

Could you, please, elaborate a bit? Why int was chosen? Have you considered an option to allow alternative basic types?

nodes.body:
The original motivation for the enum base was to make it possible to forward-declare enums, which we rely on in an internal-only feature. I'm not sure how much thought went into the signedness of the type; I think we were probably more concerned with just making sure it was large enough to store any enum value. Proto3 allows unknown enum values to be set directly via the getters and setters, so in principle they need to be able to handle values that are larger than any of the values explicitly defined in the .proto file.

We generally try hard to avoid adding any new options if we can avoid it, so I don't think we would want to add one in this case unfortunately. One thing you could try would be to just change your `foobar` field to be of type `int32`, which would be a compatible change.

Thanks for the clarification.

I will consider both options (that is, changing enum to proto3 and convering field types into signed ints) and will try to work something out.

Just to clarify one thing, I didn't mean to suggest changing the enum to proto3 and I don't think that would make a difference. I just meant to say that proto3's handling of unknown enums is another motivation for explicitly specifying the enum base, since the type has to be large enough to be able to handle any possible value, even if the value is larger than any enum values defined in the proto file.

title: Kotlin library cause duplicate file error
body: **What version of protobuf and what language are you using?** Version: v3.17.2 Language: Kotlin **What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?** OSX 11.4 **What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)** Protoc version 3.17.2 Gradle version 7.0.2 Android Studio 4.2.1 **What did you do?** Steps to reproduce the behavior: 1. Create a new Android studio project 2. Add dependency on `com.google.protobuf:protobuf-kotlin:3.17.2` 3. Build project 4. See error **What did you expect to see** Project builds successfully **What did you see instead?** Gradle outputs the following error: ``` FAILURE: Build failed with an exception. * What went wrong: Execution failed for task ':app:mergeDebugJavaResource'. > A failure occurred while executing com.android.build.gradle.internal.tasks.MergeJavaResWorkAction > 2 files found with path 'google/protobuf/field_mask.proto' from inputs: - /Users/jmols/.gradle/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/com.google.protobuf/protobuf-kotlin/3.17.2/3edd99a5479d55c364eb75027d925ece524e77d5/protobuf-kotlin-3.17.2.jar - /Users/jmols/.gradle/caches/modules-2/files-2.1/com.google.protobuf/protobuf-java/3.17.2/d7eec2ad499b605f24d07f49bdcb41c801aafbfc/protobuf-java-3.17.2.jar Adding a packagingOptions block may help, please refer to https://google.github.io/android-gradle-dsl/current/com.android.build.gradle.internal.dsl.PackagingOptions.html for more information ``` As the error suggests, this is caused because both `protobuf-kotlin` and `protobuf-java` include the same `*.proto` files. Hence this would require all our customers to add this to their `build.gradle` file, which increases the integration effort or our SDK. > Note: this issue is very similar to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8631, though now the conflict arrises from duplicate `.proto` files instead of source files. **Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

title: Improve Kotlin Builder DSL

nodes.body:
This was deliberately left out of the API.  Here's why: imagine those three protos were defined in three separate .proto files in three separate projects/compilation units/BUILD targets, whatever.  So `parent.proto` depends on `child.proto` and `car.proto`.

What happens if `car.proto` does not have a Kotlin DSL generated for it?  The compilation of `parent.proto` can't even necessarily _tell_ that `car.proto` doesn't have a Kotlin DSL.  Maybe `Car` is defined in a Java-only dependency library that `Parent` is using.  We specifically want to support that use case, where not all your proto dependencies have opted into Kotlin code generation.

We could maybe support this feature if the messages _are_ defined in the same proto file, but that seems likely to lead to chaos if there's a later refactoring.  At least with `option java_multiple_files = true`, pulling a proto message out to its own file is currently a safe change, and this would make that no longer a safe change.

2. Include a `generated_message_table_driven.h` via a generated `pb.h`

Workaround available by adding 5054 to MSVC warnings list in `port_def.inc`.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/37b18c5f1205038c848a199060d84989ca5e51a0/src/google/protobuf/generated_message_table_driven.h#L100-L108

nodes.body:
Hello There, 

Here is suggestion to fix this warning. Is to use `kSpecial = static_cast<datatype> kNumTypes * static_cast<datatype> kNumTypeClasses`

Thanks

Maybe better to use the newer stuff

#if defined(__cpp_lib_to_underlying)
kSpecial = std::to_underlying(kNumTypes ) * std::to_underlying( kNumTypeClasses)  
#else
kSpecial = kNumTypes * kNumTypeClasses  
#endif  

std::to_underlying is already avaialble in at least VS 17.1
Unfortunately protobuf does not support C++ 20 at this time. Since this is only a warning, the fix will need to wait until protobuf officially decides to support C++ 20.

 {mac_address:BVU=}

message data{

@xhochy @OgreTransporter Hey guys, I have solved this problem. 
Firstly, i clone the source code, then use the following code to download the submodule.
```
git submodule update --init --recursive
```
The problem with the above statement may cause the downloaded submodule to not correspond to the protobuf version.

Finally, I downloaded the compressed package of release and successfully compiled protobuf.
The [release zip](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases)

The compile environment is win10 + vs2019 + cmake 3.21

@a2824256 Yes, the release works. But the bug must be fixed in the master branch, otherwise future releases will not work. The point is not to find a working version, but that the code works in the future.
This code is in the process of getting a pretty big overhaul.  We should have a fix soon

title: com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java-util 3.17.3 has a dependency convergence problem
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.17.3
Language: Java

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Just use com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java-util 3.17.3 and run maven-enforcer-plugin

**What did you expect to see**
No dependency convergence problem

**What did you see instead?**

maven-enforcer-plugin fails because protobuf-java-util 3.17.3 depends transitively on 2 different versions of com.google.errorprone:error_prone_annotations

```
[INFO] --- maven-enforcer-plugin:3.0.0-M3:enforce (enforce-maven) @ contract ---
Dependency convergence error for com.google.errorprone:error_prone_annotations:2.5.1 paths to dependency are:
+-dev.knative.eventing.kafka.broker:contract:1.0-SNAPSHOT
  +-com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java-util:3.17.3
    +-com.google.guava:guava:30.1.1-android
      +-com.google.errorprone:error_prone_annotations:2.5.1
and
+-dev.knative.eventing.kafka.broker:contract:1.0-SNAPSHOT
  +-com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java-util:3.17.3
    +-com.google.errorprone:error_prone_annotations:2.3.4 
```

You can see the problem is on master too: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/util/pom.xml#L28 & https://github.com/google/guava/blob/v30.1.1/android/pom.xml#L286

title: Including Timestamp Field In proto File Causes Compile Error in Generated *.pb.cc File
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.15.2.0
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10 x64

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Visual Studio 2019 VC142 C++ 17 profile.

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Compile the following with Protoc.
```
syntax = "proto3";

import "google/protobuf/Timestamp.proto";

option csharp_namespace = "Test";

package Test;

message SettingsManagerTransitionLog
{
   google.protobuf.Timestamp Timestamp = 2;
}
```
2. Compile the resulting Test.pb.cc in a Visual Studio vcxproj project using VC142 as the compiler version.

**What did you expect to see**
File compiles with no errors.

**What did you see instead?**
2 compile errors as follows:
```
error C2039: 'descriptor_table_google_2fprotobuf_2fTimestamp_2eproto': is not a member of '`global namespace''
error C2065: 'descriptor_table_google_2fprotobuf_2fTimestamp_2eproto': undeclared identifier
```
seems to be complaining about this line:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/45209147/121543308-b75bf580-ca00-11eb-8658-84c37ffa4efc.png)

The project is also using the gRPC plugin as well, but this seems to be entirely located in the ProtoBuf specific files.

It feels like I'm missing something obvious. I found 1 reference to these errors on stackoverflow but that writer had directed their include directories incorrectly. My includes follow what they corrected to. Otherwise I've not been able to find any other reference to these errors.

title: Benchmarks are using an old version of tcmalloc
body:
The benchmarks are using tcmalloc from gperftools, which is old.
The benchmarks should be using this version of tcmalloc: https://github.com/google/tcmalloc (which is much newer).

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d1ef6d98261f874714bac0b3ef50f10227c5fe34/kokoro/linux/benchmark/run.sh#L13

The challenge is that google/tcmalloc has a different build system and currently only supports bazel (which might make it tricky to integrate it with benchmarks since the current approach of enabling tcmalloc uses make and libtcmalloc.so pre-loading).

title: LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT missing visibility("default") on linux systems
body:
Hello, we upgraded from some old version protobuf to new and noticed that in the new protobuf the port.h contains a section as following:
```
#if defined(_MSC_VER) && defined(PROTOBUF_USE_DLLS)
  #ifdef LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORTS
    #define LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT __declspec(dllexport)
  #else
    #define LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT __declspec(dllimport)
  #endif
  #ifdef LIBPROTOC_EXPORTS
    #define LIBPROTOC_EXPORT   __declspec(dllexport)
  #else
    #define LIBPROTOC_EXPORT   __declspec(dllimport)
  #endif
#else
  #define LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT
  #define LIBPROTOC_EXPORT
#endif
```

However I am missing the 
`#define LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT __attribute__((visibility("default")))`
section. We are having one module that compiles all protobuf messages and has them availabile for other modules. These modules have by default visibility hidden. So the question is is this the new way to go that we need visibilty default in all our projects? Or how can we export protobufs from one .so

Thanks

nodes.body: Sorry I realized that we are not using the library default but using run with =dllexport_decl=LIBPROTOBUF_EXPORT .... Closing
