title: SourceCodeInfo in Java generated code descriptor
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Java, but maybe it could be applied also to others.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
We are using gRPC and [Reflection](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/doc/server-reflection.md), for example with [grpcurl](https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcurl) and [grpcui](https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcurl) tools, and more. Unfortunately, if we get descriptors from the Reflection endpoint exposed by a Java gRPC service, the returned descriptors don't contain _source code info_ (we would like to read comments).

Also, see [this issue](https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcui/issues/50) that there is another use-case that requires having the _source code info_ included in the descriptors.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
There is a new `include_source_code_info` (intentionally the same name as existing `protoc` switch) `opt` for `java` plugin. Default value is `false`. If set to `true`, the generated code contains _source code info_ in the `descriptorData` field (as generated [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_shared_code_generator.cc#L136)).
Consider a similar solution for other built-in plugins.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
[scalapb](https://scalapb.github.io/docs/customizations) offers `retain_source_code_info` that works like a charm. We are able to get also comments from the Reflection endpoint exposed by a ScalaPB-base application. But this is not usable for pure Java projects.

**Additional context**
The `descriptorData` field is printed [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_shared_code_generator.cc#L136). Hopefully, it could be as easy as the current code for exporting protosets with _source code info_, see [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/command_line_interface.cc#L2500). So just `file_->CopySourceCodeInfoTo(&file_proto);`

For Python, exactly the same change would be required [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/python/python_generator.cc#L336).

nodes.body: If you turn this flag on when calling protoc directly do you get what you'd expect from Java generated code? I'm having a hard time discerning if this is a grpc-java issue or a java proto generator issue.
cc'ing @ejona86 for their opinion here as well.

> If you turn this flag on when calling protoc directly do you get what you'd expect from Java generated code? I'm having a hard time discerning if this is a grpc-java issue or a java proto generator issue.

Yes, I tried to enable that flag but the serialized descriptor in Java generated code still didn't contain comments. The descriptor exported to a new file did contain the comments. 
That is exactly what I expected after I read the source code.

The change is definitely required in the Java generator but you're right that maybe it requires the same change also in the gRPC Java generator. I expected that it just reuse the descriptors from Java generated code so I didn't check it.

I think this is mostly a protobuf issue as grpc-java just dumps whatever Descriptors protobuf has available.

I guess dsc files already contain the comments, since that is needed by code generators already. I'm normally strongly against codegen options because they "fork" the ecosystem. _Maybe_ this could be okay, but it isn't clear. Protos owned by the project using them are mostly okay, but I do think there would be tension for projects pulled in transitively to 1) be small and 2) include comments, which are contradictory. It might also cause trouble if you want comments to manage your backends but you ship a (non-mobile) fat client to customers and you _don't_ want comments included; there's no real way to manage that. Really, for _any_ client this would just be "code bloat."

Yeah, I'm inclined to agree with @ejona86 here, I don't think this is something that we'd generally want to provide/endorse, this is already accessible through `--descriptor_set_out` and `--include_source_info` at compile time, and baking this into generated code would rarely be a good practice.

> I think this is mostly a protobuf issue as grpc-java just dumps whatever Descriptors protobuf has available.

Can confirm this, the `descriptorData` field is in the code produced by Java Protobuf plugin only. The gRPC plugin generated code just _ships_ it via Reflection API.

> I guess dsc files already contain the comments, since that is needed by code generators already.

Yes, if you use `--descriptor_set_out` and also `--include_source_info` switches then the _exported_ descriptors contain the comments. And the _source code info_ is IMHO sent to all the plugins (for example plugins for documentation generating rely on this).

> I'm normally strongly against codegen options because they "fork" the ecosystem. _Maybe_ this could be okay, but it isn't clear. Protos owned by the project using them are mostly okay, but I do think there would be tension for projects pulled in transitively to 1) be small and 2) include comments, which are contradictory. It might also cause trouble if you want comments to manage your backends but you ship a (non-mobile) fat client to customers and you _don't_ want comments included; there's no real way to manage that. Really, for _any_ client this would just be "code bloat."

I absolutely agree that codegen-specific options could "fork" the ecosystem but it seems that it could be trivial to add support for this option to all the built-in generators, or even introduce it as a new `protoc` switch.

Speaking about fat clients. My idea was that I would use the new option only when generating code for server implementation. When building a fat client to distribute, I wouldn't enable that option, because the generated code already contains the comments.

Thank you all for your feedback and time! 🙏 

I feel that I didn't explain the motivation and potential use-cases thoroughly. Generally speaking, I see the Reflection API as a **machine-readable live documentation of the service**. This is the main reason why I think it makes sense to have comments included in this API, and the only missing piece to make it happen is to **allow** not to strip source code info from the descriptors in the generated code.

It would enable the following use-cases:
* [grpcui](https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcui) (or other [UIs](https://github.com/grpc-ecosystem/awesome-grpc#gui) using Reflection API) could render the comments. This would be very useful when exploring a new API.
* Reflection API is sufficient for on-fly proxies (without seeing the original proto files). With the comments included, we would be able to generate also full-featured documentation on-fly. Now, as the comments are available in the protos only, the server implementor is responsible for documentation generating. So each consumer could generate the documentation how they want, not relying on the server implementor.

So I believe this feature could be vital for the gRPC community 🙏

> I absolutely agree that codegen-specific options could "fork" the ecosystem but it seems that it could be trivial to add support for this option to all the built-in generators, or even introduce it as a new protoc switch.

I'm not concerned about "forking" the codegen options. I'm concerned about forking _which options are used_ between different usages. In many languages you _must not_ include the generated code for a proto twice in your binary, otherwise you get runtime failures. The only manageable solution to that is to have "canonical" generated code for each proto. The moment you have two pieces of generated code for the same proto you now put a rift in the ecosystem as you must ensure that both copies are not both present _anywhere_ in the dependency tree.

> Speaking about fat clients. My idea was that I would use the new option only when generating code for server implementation. When building a fat client to distribute, I wouldn't enable that option, because the generated code already contains the comments.

That can mostly work for 1st party protos. But it fails horribly for protobuf-using libraries. You can say, "oh, we don't care about that case," but should protobuf itself use the include_source_code_info option for well-known protos?

> It would enable the following use-cases:

I see the value in grpcui and other human-poking-at-running-server usages. I do think it would be really neat, so the problem isn't "is it useful?" The problem is, "how can the person generating the code make a decision about including the docs, since the same generated code is used for multiple contrary purposes?"

Passing options to plugins used to be much more common, but then we learned the hard way that it produces untold pain. We then swapped to including options in the .proto itself as it guarantees the generated code is built consistently. But this documentation use-case doesn't fit well into the options-in-the-proto framework, as some users want it and some don't. We've certainly seen cases like that before, but we either 1) killed the feature, 2) turned it on for everyone, or 3) figured out an alternative. The solution was not "use a protoc plugin option."

One option I am considering is to create a separate, custom plugin that _only_ emits the source info, in a way that is linked into the target library (similar to how the primary plugins link in the descriptors). My concrete case is Go, but the approach described below could be extended to other languages.

With this feature _not_ existing in the core runtimes, it means I will have to write a separate runtime API to re-hydrate the descriptors. This API will be used to load the source info, registered by generated code from this other plugin, and merge it into the descriptor defined by the generated code from the primary language plugin.

An approach like this allows the source code info to be a separate artifact (with its own canonical location: class name, package, file name, whatever, all derived from the location of the main artifact). This could be managed as a separate dependency.

If this feature were part of the core protobuf project, the various language runtime libraries could provide the source info in this fashion for the well-known protos, publish in a separate module/package/artifact. Only users that care about the source info would link it in.

Having it be part of the core runtimes also means that it can be automatically incorporated into the gRPC reflection service: the reflection service implementation could look for source info (in presumably the same way it discovers the descriptors) and fallback to just excluding that if the source info dependencies are not linked in. (With my approach, an external plugin and library, I will have to fork or wrap the existing gRPC reflection service in order to augment the descriptors with the source info.)

Anyhow, I understand this idea might not be super-compelling as an innate feature in protobuf and gRPC, but I certainly wish it were. Even if it never makes it as a first-class feature, the approach can serve as a pattern that 3rd-party developers can use to provide this capability via a bolt-on library.

title: Optimize varint deserialization
body:
We find a hot spot that deserialize varint64 when we deserialize PB disk files to memory data.
Current deserialization logic：
1. Find out the length of the data by judging highest bit of every 8 bits.
2. Splice the lower 7bit of each 8bit.

We can optimize deserialization by SIMD/AVX
for 1: we can find highest 1 bit by batch compare 0x80.
for 2: we can batch right shift data.

my optimize use 64bit in SIMD/AVX, I think we can merge 1,2 to to improve the performance of SIMD/AVX processing data.

My test:18% increase in deserialization process. 
Ps:my data is **hash64**, and I think SIMD/AVX does not significantly improve short data, but improves long data.

I am happy to contribute my code

nodes.body: We have looked at this a bit in the past.  We explicitly do not wish to use AVX instructions as those can cause the processor to down clock and have antagonistic behavior for other programs sharing that core.  Early instructions like SSE are potential options.  That said, the vast vast majority of these are actually 1 byte versions in a real world setting.

One thing to consider is that if you're storing a hash then it's probably best to use a `fixed64` instead of `int64`. Hash values will almost always be large enough to require the maximum number of bytes, so the variable-length format of varints won't help there. This would not be a wire-compatible change, though, so you would need to migrate carefully (e.g. create a new `fixed64` field with a fresh field number, migrate to that field, and then delete the old field).

https://dev.to/martinhaeusler/is-your-kotlin-compiler-slow-here-s-a-potential-fix-4if4 looks like it has something that is worth trying

Hi, we're facing an issue with the same combination: Kotlin + Protobuf, not with large but a lot of .proto files. In my computer setting XMX for kotlinc worked but it didn't when tried to do the same using a Docker gradle container.

according to Kotlin this has been repro'd on their end: https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/KT-47270 

Any additional solutions are blocked on whatever they end up doing.
We are looking into this issue more, but for now the best workaround is to configure a higher memory limit.

The root of the issue is that the representation of Java source files is quite ineffective in Kotlin compiler, so when we read huge generated 18 MBs HelloWorld.java it leads to high memory footprint.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/863207/168957597-0a530ac8-039b-4159-9e6b-244ae6b69d9d.png)

Potentially, more than 68% of the heap is allocated for the pieces of that file.
To be honest, I don't think it's possible to replace the representation soon, so I'd suggested as a workaround if it's possible to compile HelloWorld.java before running kotlinc and then supply it in a form of a class-file.
But unfortunately, I'm not sure there is a possibility to have such a workaround via gradle/protobuf infrastructure.

BTW, there is another workaround, namely putting this to build.gradle:
```
compileKotlin {
    kotlinOptions.freeCompilerArgs += ['-Xuse-javac']
}
```

But this compiler flag (enabling a different internal representation for Java) is still very experimental and unfortunately we can't give any guarantees it would work correctly in every environment.
Closing this since it's being tracked with jetbrains.

Conan recipe (hosted in Conan centre)

We need to cross compile and our systems use the Conan package manager. Currently our recipes require dependencies:

- protobuf/3.9.1@bincrafters/stable
- protoc_installer/3.9.1@bincrafters/stable

These work no problem, but are deprecated. We attempted to move to the Conan centre, switching to protobuf/3.17.1, but experienced cross compilation issues. Resulting in error: `/bin/sh: 1: /root/.conan/data/protobuf/3.17.1/_/_/package/1ea143163c6ae43b7dcd78006f69dc4ed2cc53db/bin/protoc: Exec format error
`

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Not sure the reason why the libraries got combined back into a single Conan recipe. Maybe we are missing something? Some additional options perhaps?

But essentially we would like either additional options exposed in the recipe for cross compilation or the libraries to be split again and function in a similar manner to how they were at version 3.9.1.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
We hacked a local copy of the recipe to point to an already pre-existing x86-64 Linux build of the protobuf library (containing the protoc tool). However, we do not want to modify/maintain our own custom version of the recipe. title: Didn't find any option for csharp_outer_classname in protocol buffers with C#. Is there any other way I can setup outer classname in proto file?
body:
Hi,
Is there any option for csharp_outer_classname in protocol buffers with C#? I am using "option java_outer_classname" for java based setup. But I didn't find this kind of outer class declaration for the C#.

My protobuf file name starts with digits such as 180myfile.proto and option csharp_namespace = "com.180myfile.Proto"; and when I am building an auto-generated file in C# it's not liking namespace and class name which is starting with a digit and throwing error. 

Can anyone help me to get any other solution to work around it?

Thanks!

nodes.body:
No, there's no option for this. The C# namespace you've specified isn't a valid C# namespace, but that part is very easily under your control - just change your option. (I'd also suggest making it a namespace that follows C# conventions, which the one you've specified at the moment doesn't.)

For the class name, there's no option to control this - but I'd strongly recommend that you just rename the proto file. I suspect this won't be the only issue you face by naming the file using a digit to start with. I suspect it'll save a lot of time if you face that now and just rename the file.

You *could* rename the file just temporarily, as part of your build, then name it back after generating the C#, if you absolutely *must* keep it named that for some other reason.

Hi Jon,

Thanks for providing the simplest solution. Yes, I am aware of renaming the protobuf file name and remove the numbers from the starting, it is working well. My concern is only if we can tweak it or change the class name any other way. I have rigid things from my side to maintain the file name starting with numbers. 

I also checked GRPC tools settings to make changes in the class name but they don't have anything like that.

title: Support generating original .proto file from FileDescriptor in Java
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
Java

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

I am implementing a schema registry for Protobuf schema definitions and looking for a functionality to obtain the original `.proto` file content from a `Message` object. It is possible to fetch the `FileDescriptor` from a `Message` object and get it's proto content by using following code. However, the generated proto content is not in `.proto` format. It would be helpful if `FileDescriptorProto` can preserve the original `.proto` content or a new `getSource` method is added to generate the text in `.proto`.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

```
message.getDescriptorForType().getFile().toProto().toString()
```

**Current format**

```
name: "Phone.proto"
package: "com.foo.bar"
message_type {
  name: "Phone"
  field {
    name: "model"
    number: 1
    label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
    type: TYPE_STRING
  }
  field {
    name: "name"
    number: 2
    label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
    type: TYPE_STRING
  }
  field {
    name: "serial"
    number: 3
    label: LABEL_OPTIONAL
    type: TYPE_INT32
  }
}
options {
  java_package: "com.foo.bar"
  java_outer_classname: "Contact"
}
syntax: "proto3"
```

**Proposed format**

```
message.getDescriptorForType().getFile().toProto().getSource()
```

```
syntax = "proto3";

package com.foo.bar;

option java_outer_classname = "Contact";
option java_package = "com.foo.bar";
message Phone {
    string model = 1;
    string name = 2;
    int32 serial = 3;
}
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

The alternative now is to generate it manually by either parsing above text or using other helper methods. It would be helpful is this functionality is provided natively within the library.

nodes.body: I think the FileDescriptor contains all the information. Why the original format is required?

It's helpful in schema registry like use-cases used with streaming services like Kafka, Kinesis etc. When producers produce data, they need to validate if the schema they are using is valid and accepted by consumers. They do it by querying a central service over HTTP with the original `.proto` text. If schema is valid, the service returns a UUID corresponding to the schema. The producers embed the schema UUID into messages that they produce. When the messages are de-serialized by consumers, they query the central service to verify the schema UUID is valid and get corresponding schema (`.proto` file) to read the message. 
The process of converting `FileDescriptor` to `.proto` file is tedious and can be error prone if developers implement their own versions. It would be great if the original reference is retained or Protobuf library provides a standard implementation of it.

Sorry but this isn't something we'll be doing. Generally if you need this, its advised to provide it through a sidechannel adjacent to the Protos themselves, this can lead to significant jarfile bloat that most users don't need.

I agree JAR size is a big concern. Alternatively, is it possible to provide a method that can generate it at runtime? In case of separate implementation, it's hard to keep it consistent with changes in Protobuf. With growing use-cases for schema registry with protobuf, we believe this will be useful.

When you say changes in protobuf, do you mean the protobuf library itself? Or your own .proto files? There are tools out there such as https://github.com/perezd/protopoet (shameless plug) that you could use to generate these yourself, but we're not likely to support this directly in the protobuf library itself. This sort of thing we like to leave to customers to design externally as there are so many way people want to approach this.

FWIW, free design review opinion: Whatever your needs are, if you're basing it on the source code and not the descriptor, this is probably more brittle than you mean for it to be. The DescriptorProto API is really the source of truth in all cases internally and externally.

> When you say changes in protobuf, do you mean the protobuf library itself?

I meant the protobuf library. 

> The DescriptorProto API is really the source of truth in all cases internally and externally.

Can a serialized form of the DescriptorProto be used to uniquely identify a Proto definition? Thanks for the information on this!

> Can a serialized form of the DescriptorProto be used to uniquely identify a Proto definition? 

Yes it should be, now how are you going to encode/represent that? That is up to you! I'd suggest a deterministic hashing process.

>Yes it should be, now how are you going to encode/represent that? 

SHA256 hash the `FileDescriptor.toByteString`. Is it guaranteed to be same with future Protobuf library upgrades?

I'd check the code and double check that deserialization ordering keeps that deterministic, I am not positive that anything guarantees that and it may need to be externally guaranteed by your code in a more explicit way.

body:
**What did you do?**

Generate

package p;

>>> from p_pb2 import E

  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "p_pb2.py", line 419, in <module>
    DESCRIPTOR.message_types_by_name['E'] = _E

Either protoc should failfast, or the generated code should work in some capacity.

nodes.body:
for some detail, what's happening here is that the module level descriptor for `p` (`p.DESCRIPTOR`) is getting overwritten with a global enum variable `DESCRIPTOR = 2`, hence the error above.

I can think of a couple options

- Make it illegal to define a field named DESCRIPTOR, since it seems like it would break generated code across several languages. Not sure how practical this is.
- Produce a warning when generating python code with DESCRIPTOR, and suppress generation of `DESCRIPTOR = 2` line.

title: Ability to reuse existing memory for RepeatedField
body:
My particular use case in C++, where the data for a RepeatedField is constructed elsewhere via more advanced computation on std::vector, Eigen matrices, etc, which would not be possible with the RepeatedField data structure. As these outside data structures are already contiguous memory blocks, I'd like to just reuse their underlying memory for RepeatedField. Right now, it seems the only way to convert to a RepeatedField is copying all the elements over (constructor or Add w/ iterator uses std::copy internally). As it is just using an Elements* buffer internally, seems we could do a zero-copy reuse.

I have a couple suggestions for how we could add that API:

- Have a `set_allocated(Elements* data, int current_size, int total_size)` method for RepeatedField. Internally `data` would get wrapped in a `Rep` struct with arena being null. Could have a second signature where user provides a `Rep` struct or `Arena`.  Looking at source code for `Reserve`, it doesn't look like you realloc the `Elements*` memory block, instead just creating a new one. So I believe this should work out of the box with all other class methods.
- Have another class `ConstRepeatedField`, which only implements the getter methods (e.g. elements cannot be modified). We'd still have a method `set_allocated(Elements* data, int current_size, int total_size, bool own)` (possibly with overload for additional `Arena`/`Rep`). There is an additional `own` flag, which functions like the `release_foo` API for Message; when false, the class destructor will not try to deallocate `data`.

nodes.body: Experience with borrow/steal APIs like this for strings have not been good.  It turns out that these things leak implementation details pretty heavily.  It is unlikely we will add something like this in the near term.

The API already exposes the pointer to `Elements*`, so I don't see that we'd be leaking any implementation details that aren't already. We'd just be adding that `set_allocated` method. I think it would be a very quick pull request... work out of the box. If we're concerned with the `delete` that would happen in `Reserve` method, I personally would be fine having a `ConstRepeatedField` instead, which does not have setter methods, only `set_allocated` and getters.

Did you have any specific concerns regarding the API I changes I suggested, specifically? Perhaps you could explain further what implementation details would get leaked.

To start with RepeatField only backs primitives, not Message or strings, so there is RepeatedPtrField as well whose underlying buffer is a T**.  Next issue is that to extract the values from a vector you need some way to steal the underlying buffer from that vector (or you can lie about actual ownership, which has a bag of worms).

As you go down this path, you will discover that `set_allocate`/`release` behave differently when arenas are involved and that the fixes you are suggesting end up increasing the volume of allocations and copies.  Then you start to play games with `unsafe_arena_set_allocated`/`unsafe_arena_release`.  There is a really large space of complexity here that we have found the hard way.  We are not going to broach this particular bag of worms lightly and do not have time to go into the detailed designs required right now.

PHP

nodes.body: We have learned (through painful experience) that insertion points are a very fragile extension mechanism.  They expose all of our internals in a way that makes future evolution very difficult.  As such, we have avoided adding them to newer language bindings.

I opened this ticket because what I'm really looking for is for PHP to support custom options by adding API support for it, however the [existing issue for this](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3065) has been open for ~4 years now with no resolution, so I figured instead I'd look into the feasibility of emulating this functionality via a custom plugin. I think this should still be possible even without insertion points, but am still trying to flesh out the details.

I added an update to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3065. Sorry it's been such a long wait.

I'll plan to close this bug because we don't want to add insertion points. But hopefully we will have true custom option support in PHP before too long.

I had the same problem and discovered it was because required shared libraries are missing from the `-py2.py3-none-any.whl` pure python wheel that gets pulled in automatically. 

I was able to solve it by building the protobuf wheel from source:
```bash
brew install protobuf
export CFLAGS="-I$(brew --prefix protobuf)/include"
export LDFLAGS="-L$(brew --prefix protobuf)/lib"
# In my virtual environment: 
pip install protobuf=="$(brew list --version protobuf | awk '{print $2}')" --install-option="--cpp_implementation"
# If the pure python protobuf wheel is already installed, run this instead:
# pip install protobuf=="$(brew list --version protobuf | awk '{print $2}')" --force-reinstall --no-deps --install-option="--cpp_implementation"

```

Hope this helps!


### Edit (2021/11/09): 
- Note that this installs the version of the protobuf Python library that matches the version of the pre-compiled protoc binary that was installed via brew (`brew install protobuf`). 
- If you need a newer version than what brew provides, you're going to have to build protoc from source. Assuming you already have the pure Python protobuf wheel installed, this would look something like:

```bash
# Download and unpack protobuf compiler source code
PROTOBUF_RELEASES_URL="https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/download"
TARGET_PROTOBUF_VERSION=$(pip show protobuf | grep Version | sed -r 's/Version: (.*)/\1/') # get the version of the (broken) protobuf wheel currently installed
PROTOC_SRC_ARCHIVE="protobuf-cpp-${TARGET_PROTOBUF_VERSION}.tar.gz"
curl -sSL "${PROTOBUF_RELEASES_URL}/v${TARGET_PROTOBUF_VERSION}/${PROTOC_SRC_ARCHIVE}" | tar -C /tmp -xzf -

# Build protobuf compiler from source (this will take a while)
#   see: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/README.md
PROTOC_SRC_PATH="/tmp/protobuf-${TARGET_PROTOBUF_VERSION}" && \
pushd "${PROTOC_SRC_PATH}" && \
./configure && \
make -j8 && \
make check && \
sudo make install && \
popd && \
rm -rf "${PROTOC_SRC_PATH}" # Clean src/build files 
```

```bash
# In your virtual environment:
INSTALL_PREFIX_PATH="/usr/local" && \
export CFLAGS="-I${INSTALL_PREFIX_PATH}/include" && \
export LDFLAGS="-L${INSTALL_PREFIX_PATH}/lib" && \
pip install protobuf=="${TARGET_PROTOBUF_VERSION}" --force-reinstall --no-deps --install-option="--cpp_implementation" 
```
This solved my problem. Thanks!

title: how to generate message NOT order by field number in C# ?

nodes.body: @jskeet help pls

No, there is no way to do this and I wouldn't expect there to be. No guarantee is made as to serialization order, but IIRC there are internal documents *recommending* that field number order is used, which is what we do for C#. (I believe Java also uses this approach, or at least did when we first implemented the C# plugin.)

The [documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding#order) states:

> Field numbers may be used in any order in a .proto file. The order chosen has no effect on how the messages are serialized.

That suggests that the C# implementation is doing the right thing here - the second sentence suggests that reordering the fields shouldn't make a difference to serialization, whereas you're asserting that it *does* make a difference in Go and Node.

Note that parsers should be able to parse values in any order anyway.

macOS, 11.2.3

Kotlin 1.5.21

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Write a proto and specify `option java_package = "in.some.path";`
2. User protoc to generate the code `protoc --java_out=... --kotlin_out=... *.proto`
3. Check the generated java file, the package name is `package in.some.path` which is expacted
4. Check the generated kotlin file, the package name is same `package in.some.path` which throw an error because `in` is a reserved word in kotlin.

**What did you expect to see**
In Kotlin file the reserved word should be escaped automatically: ``package `in`.some.path``. 
I use Android Studio. The IDE does the escape for me when I use `in` in the package name. I think protoc should do the same, to escape any reserved word in the package name.

**What did you see instead?**
`package in.some.path`

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body: Hello, thanks for this report! I don't think we want to allow for the package name in Java and Kotlin to be different (where one is escaped and one is not) as that makes the imports look different. We currently don't error check package names in either Java or Kotlin and I think it makes sense to keep it that way since this can be fixed by changing the java package name to either be escaped already or to have a different name that isn't a Kotlin keyword.
Thanks for explaining this case, it's helpful to understand why this is a problem. I will look into fixing it and keep you updated when I have a fix.
This issue should be resolved with https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/cc696d4babf8c4faf59984c596033701ed479ef6

Thanks for the very useful report. It's especially helpful that the C stack trace has function/line info, how did you get that? [Other reports](https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-ruby/issues/339#issuecomment-889835412) don't have symbol information, since I believe the gem gets its symbols stripped during release (which I would like to fix, but I'm not sure how to get the Ruby toolchain not to do this).

It appears that this crash is in the DSL. This is a bit surprising as the DSL has not changed very much since https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/5866 in 2019. I took a look and could not find an obvious explanation for this crash.

Since getting a root cause could be difficult, I thought an easier fix would be to port the DSL from C to Ruby. I've wanted to do this for a while anyway, since there's no reason for the DSL to be implemented in C anymore. If the code is in Ruby, it can't cause SEGV bugs (there could still be SEGV bugs elsewhere in the library, but at the very least this will narrow down where the bug could be).

title: ReferenceError: exports is not defined
Support explicit API mode in Kotlin
body:
Kotlin compiler supports a "strict" mode called [explicit API mode](https://github.com/Kotlin/KEEP/blob/master/proposals/explicit-api-mode.md). The mode enforces explicit visibility modifiers and type declarations in public API.

Right now, if the mode is enabled and Kotlin is generated from Protobuf, Kotlin compiler fails with an error because the generated code does not comply with the explicit mode.

There could be two possible scenarios:
 1. Allow users to specify whether or not we want to generate code with explicit visibility modifiers.
 2. Generate all the code this way. Disabling this compiler mode would not break the more explicit code.

nodes.body: Seems like (2) is the better choice.  Generate the strictest thing we can and let others opt in.  What do you think?
If you ask me, (2) seems preferable indeed, as it implies less effort and less code to maintain in the future.
Approach (2) was submitted in #8968, so the generated code should be explicit API mode compatible now. Please reopen if you encounter any issues with this!

Thanks for the rapid response and the effort.

Seems like this change hasn't made it to production yet. Yesterday I checked with the compiler of versions `3.18.0` and `3.18.1` with no luck.

Is there any ETA for this?
I believe 3.18.1 was already in the works when this was added. This should make it into the 3.19.0 release which is in the works right now and should be released soon, tentatively today.

title: Bazel Rule Support for Kotlin
body:
To support generating Kotlin protos via Bazel, we need some support for the classes which the generated Kotlin protos use:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/master/java/kotlin

Can be inspired by: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/core/BUILD

This will be used by new rules which will have examples:
https://github.com/grpc/grpc-kotlin/pull/266

Please assign to: @deannagarcia

nodes.body: This has been resolved in the grpc-kotlin repository here: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-kotlin/pull/290
Shouldn't this ultimately belong to this repo? It feels weird having rules for protobuf, which shouldn't require gRPC, in the gRPC repo.
This is a temporary solution to unblock the gRPC team to use kotlin proto examples, a long term solution will be coming later that will ultimately belong to this repo.

I think this should stay open, as what's in grpc-kotlin is a workaround. Note that this issue isn't for Kotlin protobuf Bazel rules themselves, but rather the fact that such rules depend on protobuf-kotlin. Currently, the way to get this dependency is as a pre-built Maven artifact (`com.google.protobuf:protobuf-kotlin`), whereas it would be cleaner for Bazel projects to be able to build this artifact from source.

title: System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe
body:
hello, 

I am using Visual Studio 2019, Windows 10, .Net Framework 4.8, in C#.

I have my proto `model.proto` that compiles into `Model.pb.cs`, and I use it in my program. 

The program in question simply fills the data model and saves it to file.

```
using PMOD = MyProtobuf.Model;

using NLog;
using NetMQ;
using NetMQ.Sockets;
using System;
using System.Text;
using System.IO;

var req = PMOD.MyDataModel();
// fill up req with all data ...
using (var file_output = File.Create("path/to/save/PB/file/into")) {
   using (var stream_output = new Google.Protobuf.CodedOutputStream(file_output)) {
      req.WriteTo(stream_output); <---- this one gives errors
   }
}
```

the relative `.csproj` is something like that
```
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net48</TargetFramework>
    <PlatformTarget>x64</PlatformTarget>
    <OutputType>Library</OutputType>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
      <Protobuf Include="../../protobuf/model.proto" Link="model.proto" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="coverlet.msbuild" Version="3.0.3">
      <IncludeAssets>runtime; build; native; contentfiles; analyzers; buildtransitive</IncludeAssets>
      <PrivateAssets>all</PrivateAssets>
    </PackageReference>
    <PackageReference Include="Google.Protobuf" Version="3.15.6" />
    <PackageReference Include="Grpc" Version="2.36.4" />
    <PackageReference Include="MathNet.Numerics" Version="4.15.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="MathNet.Spatial" Version="0.6.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="NetMQ" Version="4.0.1.6" />
    <PackageReference Include="NLog" Version="4.7.9" />
    <PackageReference Include="System.Text.Json" Version="5.0.2" />
  </ItemGroup>

  etc etc ... with files to compile
```


this is the error
```
Could not load file or assembly 'System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe, Version=4.0.4.1, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b03f5f7f11d50a3a' or one of its dependencies. The system cannot find the file specified.
```

It looks like `Google.Protobuf` needs System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe >= 4.5, and  `System.Text.Json`  needs >= 5.0. So I added it from **NuGet** :
```
<PackageReference Include="System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe" Version="5.0.0" />
```

--> I still get the same error. 


later I checked [this post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/62764744/could-not-load-file-or-assembly-system-runtime-compilerservices-unsafe) and tried to apply the same solution doing either `gacutil /i System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.dll` or saving the config into the `app.config` (that wasn't needed before). 

--> I still get the same error. 


What should I do ?

nodes.body:
Apparently it is due to incorrect versioning done at System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.

The System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.dll from nuget package for  4.5.2  shows version  4:0:4:1 in manifest.

And when Google.protobuff compiles with System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe 4.5.2   it is reflected in its manifest.

.assembly extern System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe
{
  .publickeytoken = (B0 3F 5F 7F 11 D5 0A 3A )                         // .?_....:
  .ver 4:0:4:1
}

title: C++ generated code missing global scope operator
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master/v3.12.4 master/v.3.17.3
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux, Debian Testing

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
N/A

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a protobuf file with one of the fields being of type ".google.protobuf.Any". Have the package be "com.google.*"
1. Compile to c++ (e.g. "protoc --cpp_out=. minimal_with_any.proto" with the attached file)
2. Inspect output ("minimal_with_any.pb.h")

**What did you expect to see**

I expected all references to `Any` be "::PROTOBUF_NAMESPACE_ID::Any" (because I used a leading '.' in the protobuf file)

**What did you see instead?**

The message class implementation used "PROTOBUF_NAMESPACE_ID::Any"

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

Because the package is "com.google.*", this will cause a compilation failure because the compiler will search in the local namespace (looking for "::com::google::protobuf::Any") and not the global namespace ("::google::protobuf::Any").

See attached example.
[minimal_with_any.proto.txt](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/6970685/minimal_with_any.proto.txt)

Sorry, I need to compiler proto2 to ruby, but got the error:

```
# protoc -I ./def --ruby_out ./lib def/foo/wwdocument.proto
--ruby_out: foo/wwdocument.proto: Can only generate Ruby code for proto3 .proto files.

In PHP, on designing or extending an API, we often require responses in JSON format, but this language does not have `JsonFormat` to convert Protobuf object to JSON string, whereas other languages like Java does have this functionality in the `util` folder. This force as to manually create the JSON from the Protobuf object. **Describe the solution you'd like**

$json = $message->serializeToJsonString();
$message = $message->mergeFromJsonString($json);

//`JsonFormat` library is missing in PHP, but is available in
//other languages. I am expecting something like below. This
//will print JSON string.
print( JsonFormat.parse( $message ) );
```

Right now, it is impossible to print Protobuf object or convert it to JSON. We have to manually create the JSON in PHP, which is not the best way.

nodes.body:
I don't understand what you are asking for.

In https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8846 I mentioned that these two lines work right now:

```php
$json = $message->serializeToJsonString();  // Serialize to JSON
$message = $message->mergeFromJsonString($json);  // Parse from JSON
```

So I am confused when you say:

> Right now, it is impossible to print Protobuf object or convert it to JSON.

The first line quoted above will do exactly that. What is wrong with this solution?

If you want it in a separate function, you can implement that manually:

```php
function JsonFormatParse($message) {
  return $message->serializeToJsonString();
}
```

@haberman Correct me if I am wrong, in my point of view serialised JSON string would not always be human readable(I mean the key/value inside the JSON). There could be encoded content in it. So, in order to get the original content, we have to either deserialise it or use a method like `JsonFormatParse`.

title: How to force a cleanup of memory allocated by the constant initialized variables
body:
Version: >= 3.15.0
Language: C++
Windows 10,  MSVC 14.28.29910

Starting with 3.15.0 version, the global message instances are constant initialized (see https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.15.0/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_message.h#L129) which seems to upset some memory detection tools (e.g. AppVerifier) when protobuf is statically linked in a DLL which gets unloaded at runtime (by FreeLibrary). 

Backtraces are usually pointing to stuff like:

`operator new+0x0000000000000013 [vctools\crt\vcstartup\src\heap\new_scalar.cpp @ 35]
 std::_Default_allocate_traits::_Allocate+0x0000000000000028
 std::_Allocate<16,std::_Default_allocate_traits,0>+0x0000000000000047
 std::allocator<std::_Container_proxy>::allocate+0x0000000000000035
 std::_Container_base12::_Alloc_proxy<std::allocator<std::_Container_proxy>
 std::basic_string<char,std::char_traits<char>,std::allocator<char>>::basic_string<char,std::char_traits<char>,std::allocator<char>>

 google::protobuf::internal::ExplicitlyConstructed<std::basic_string<char,std::char_traits<char>,std::allocator<char>> >::DefaultConstruct
 google::protobuf::internal::SerializeInternalToArray
 google::protobuf::internal::InitProtobufDefaultsSlow
 rtps::"dynamic atexit destructor for '_MyMessage_default_instance_'"
`

In the past I've encountered similar issues with protobuf and global memory but it was possible to force a cleanup (right before unloading the DLL) by calling **google::protobuf::ShutdownProtobufLibrary**. However, for those constants this doesn't seem to be working.

Thus, the question is if there's a way to either cleanup the memory allocated by the global constants initialization OR to turn off the constant initialization of the global message instances?

nodes.body:
Hi, could you provide a full instruction to reproduce this issue?
1) the OS
2) code
3) how to compile
4) how to run

(Late) Update: I was wrong about the initial statement - the **google::protobuf::ShutdownProtobufLibrary** method is indeed freeing the memory hold by the constant initializers.

However, it seems there is a difference in behavior starting with **protobuf 3.15**: prior that version the protobuf globals were allocated at the 1st usage while with 3.15+ they're created at "load" time. In my case, I have protobuf statically linked into a shared library which means that a **LoadLibrary** followed by **FreeLibrary** leaks with **3.15+**.

@TeBoring I have created a small POC for the above part, see the attached archive. The idea of the test is to have a shared library (that statically links against protobuf) which is then dynamically loaded, used and unloaded by an executable that is monitored by appverifier. The dependencies of the POC are: Windows 10 (it should work with other versions too), cmake >= 3.13, appverifier and a compatible MSVC compiler. 

**Compile and run the POC**
[proto_load_unload_leak.zip](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/7661823/proto_load_unload_leak.zip)


Unpack the zip archive. For every protobuf versions to test against (used **3.14.0** and **3.19.1** in my local tests), do the following:

- Generate the build tree for the version **X**. E.g. `cmake -GNinja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DPROTOBUF_VERSION=3.14.0 -B build-with-proto3.14.0 proto_load_unload_leak`
- Build the POC. E.g. `cmake --build build-with-proto3.14.0`. This will create an executable (**testapp.exe**) and a shared library (**testlib.dll**)
- From an administrator console (because it's starting _appverif_) `cd build-with-proto3.14.0 && ctest -V`. In this step, the **testapp.exe** will be attached to **appverif** and then 2 runs will be performed - 1st will explicitly cleanup the protobuf resources from the **testlib.dll** before unloading it while the 2nd test will only load (aka LoadLibrary) and unload (aka FreeLibrary) the **testlib.dll** library.

**Test results of the POC**

The above tests pass if the **PROTOBUF_VERSION** is <= 3.14.0 and they fail at the **run-testapp-load-only** case with **PROTOBUF_VERSION** 3.15+

**Possible Solutions**

I'm not sure if there will be a lot of real-life scenarios to reach into this sort of setup. However, if that happens (like in my case) it would be nice to have a good (to be read as `compliant`) solution for it.
In general, I considered 2 possible ideas:

- Export a symbol from the shared library which must be called by the user to explicitly free up the memory. That's a bit nasty because if one only does LoadLibrary and FreeLibrary (due to whatever reason), it will have to load and call an extra symbol in order not to leak.
- Automatically cleanup the protobuf resources when the library is unloaded. This can be implemented using yet another static/global C++ object (at dll "level") whose destructor calls protobuf' cleanup. I have implemented an example in the POC, which "activates" the code under the `-DPROTO_AUTO_CLEANUP=ON` cmake variable. E.g. `cmake -DPROTO_AUTO_CLEANUP=ON <rest of params>`. I know there might be other solutions, like special hooks which are called when the library is loaded/unloaded (e.g. defining/overwriting `DllMain` on Windows, the deprecated `.init/.fini` or the "new" `__attribute__((constructor))/((destructor))` on unix) but the global object seemed the most straightforward fix.

Therefore as a conclusion, I'll shift the original question to asking for your suggestion(s) regarding what would be the most compliant solution to (preferably automatically) cleanup protobuf resources in the above described use-case? Could there be any pitfalls in using the global C++ object method? Thank you!

nodes.body: Obviously we cannot promise timelines, but this is something we have an active project for right now
Awesome!  I'm excited to hear more!
Any rough guess on timelines?  No promises.  We added more latency logging and python protobuf latency is a significant portion of our latency.

We're aiming to have something in prerelease in the next few months.

If you're feeling adventurous, you can try it out from my development branch now. It is not 100% complete, but most APIs are implemented and passing tests. The performance should give you a rough ballpark of what to expect.

To try it out:

1. install the Python protobuf package from the master branch of [protobuf/python](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/master/python).
2. compile your Python protos with a `protoc` built from the master branch of [protobuf](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf). You'll know you did this correctly if your `_pb2.py` files contain the string `AddSerializedFile`.
3. Build the C extension from my development branch using Bazel:

```shell
$ git clone --branch python https://github.com/haberman/upb.git
$ cd upb
$ bazel build -c opt python:message_ext python:api_implementation_ext
$ ls bazel-bin/python/google/protobuf/**/*.so
bazel-bin/python/google/protobuf/internal/_api_implementation.cpython-39-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
bazel-bin/python/google/protobuf/pyext/_message.cpython-39-x86_64-linux-gnu.so
```

Copy these `.so`'s to your PYTHONPATH, such that they can be loaded as `google.protobuf.internal._api_implementation` and `google.protobuf.pyext._message`, respectively.

If you have any feedback it could be useful in helping to gauge the performance improvement vs. the existing C++ extension. It could also help point to any places where we still need to optimize further.

title: How to best add metadata to protobuf messages?
body:
What's the best way to add metadata to a protobuf meesage after the message has been created?

We have a large number of protobuf messages in our ecosystem and they are being used for pub/sub and streaming. When the event producer creates a protobuf message and hands it to the library that calls the pub/sub API, we want to be able to add metadata to the message before publishing it.

Likewise, when the event is forwarded from, say, the pub/sub platform to streaming, we want to add additional metadata on top of what's already there.

2. bazel run //:main

No duplicate resources.

**What did you see instead?**
Multiple copies of the same class in in `@com_google_protobuf//java/core:core-project`, `@com_google_protobuf//java/core:lite_runtime_only` and `@com_google_protobuf//:timestamp_proto`.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body:
TLDR: I've done some diffing and comparison and I think this diff is causing this behavior for you, but I'm pretty sure this is intended behavior (I'll explain further):
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/89a9f459e9b6996c36051f59c99b6c40650ad25b

Maven users of protobuf-java have always had an extra folder "google/protobuf/..." in the runtime jar which contains the .proto source files for all of our well known types. Here's an example of it in 3.17.3:
![Screen Shot 2021-08-30 at 2 48 19 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/20598/131410220-13215dc9-4a53-40d3-a8b5-266770f027fc.png)

These are not compiled class files, these are just the source of the complied class files found in the analogous com.google.protobuf.* package.

Having said that, I see you're using protobuf directly through bazel, bypassing maven entirely. Historically, we discovered that the java_library targets that provide the runtimes were inconsistent with what maven was doing RE: these source file resources, and so the commit above fixed it by adding them.
Here's a screenshot of the jars from your reproducer in both 3.17.3 and 3.18.0-rc1 built from bazel: 
![Screen Shot 2021-08-30 at 2 50 53 PM](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/20598/131410460-bd6a65bc-ea06-4a84-833e-d112d86360e0.png)

As you can see, this results in the addtion of the new google/protobuf/... folder, which I think your ClassGraph scanner is accidentally interpreting as a duplicate .class file. _To be clear, I was unable to detect any duplicate classfiles._

The problem with you analysis is that you use the merged `_deploy.jar` target, which chooses just one of the duplicates. Of course there can't be duplicate resources there.

This is also obvious when you run
```
java -jar "$(bazel info bazel-bin)/src/main/java/com/example/main_deploy.jar"
```
The duplicates are gone.

Also, AFAICT I'm using the official Bazel rules here.

When you do `bazel query "kind('java.*library' , deps(//:main))"`, you'll get
```
//src/main/proto/example/v1:examplev1_java_proto
@rules_jvm_external//private/tools/java/rules/jvm/external:byte-streams
@com_google_protobuf//java/core:core-lib
@com_google_protobuf//java/core:lite_runtime_only
```

Then `bazel build @com_google_protobuf//java/core:core-lib`
```
...
  bazel-bin/external/com_google_protobuf/java/core/libcore-lib.jar
```
and for `bazel build @com_google_protobuf//java/core:lite_runtime_only`
```
...
  bazel-bin/external/com_google_protobuf/java/core/liblite_runtime_only.jar
```

`bazel build //src/main/proto/example/v1:examplev1_java_proto`
```
...
  bazel-bin/external/com_google_protobuf/libtimestamp_proto-speed.jar
  bazel-bin/src/main/proto/example/v1/libexamplev1_proto-speed.jar
  bazel-bin/src/main/proto/example/v1/examplev1_proto-speed-src.jar
```

So in 3.17 `bazel-bin/external/com_google_protobuf/java/core/libcore-lib.jar`, `bazel-bin/external/com_google_protobuf/java/core/liblite_runtime_only.jar` and `bazel-bin/external/com_google_protobuf/libtimestamp_proto-speed.jar` were on the class path when you run `bazel run //:main`. This is also relevant because it is included in `java_image` container images.

In 3.17 you had only this:

- `jar tf $(bazel info bazel-bin)/external/com_google_protobuf/java/core/libcore-lib.jar`:
```
...
com/google/protobuf/Timestamp$1.class
com/google/protobuf/Timestamp$Builder.class
com/google/protobuf/Timestamp.class
com/google/protobuf/TimestampOrBuilder.class
com/google/protobuf/TimestampProto.class
....
```

- `jar tf $(bazel info bazel-bin)/external/com_google_protobuf/libtimestamp_proto-speed.jar`
```
...
com/google/protobuf/Timestamp$1.class
com/google/protobuf/Timestamp$Builder.class
com/google/protobuf/Timestamp.class
com/google/protobuf/TimestampOrBuilder.class
com/google/protobuf/TimestampProto.class
```

In v3.18.0-rc1 the class path has changed, see `bazel query "kind('maven_project_jar' , deps(//:main))"`, and `bazel build @com_google_protobuf//java/core:core-project`:
```
...
  bazel-bin/external/com_google_protobuf/java/core/core-project.jar
```

So, in v3.18.0-rc1 the dependency to `libcore-lib.jar` is replaced with `core-project.jar`, the relevant content being:

OK chatting, w/ a teammate, I think that the reason for dupes on timestamp comes from the fact that proto_library deps timestamp_proto, and gets converted automatically to a java proto transitively through the java_proto_library target you define, which makes sense. 

The challenge here is that Bazel cannot see that this well known type can be reused because we also compile an identical copy into the srcs of ":core" and ":lite" java_library targets. I'm going to see if I can generate those targets atomically and treat them as deps for core/lite, and see if this goes away as a result.

Naively attempting to create java_proto_library targets for the well known types and then treating them as deps for the core runtime results in a circular dependency w/ bazel toolchains:

```
 //src/main/java/com/example:main
 //src/main/proto/example/v1:examplev1_java_proto
 //src/main/proto/example/v1:examplev1_proto with aspect BazelJavaProtoAspect
.-> @com_google_protobuf//:java_toolchain
|   @com_google_protobuf//java/core:toolchain
|   @com_google_protobuf//java/core:core
|   @com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_java_proto
|   @com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_proto with aspect BazelJavaProtoAspect
`-- @com_google_protobuf//:java_toolchain
```

This is the core reason for the dupes. You'll find that if you depend on "@com_google_protobuf//:descriptor_proto" in a proto_library you'll get dupes of that too, it's any proto we provide that you might use that the runtime also depends on that'll end up like this unfortunately.

OK I think I've almost got all the dupes erased, we're stuck on one blocker here:
https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/13928

OK, lite proto support for `blacklisted_protos` attribute is now checked into bazel, so it won't do much until the next cut of bazel but it will eventually eliminate the duplicate classes. I'll go ahead and send the PR for it now.

title: Optional Field Presence Check for Python in Protobuf3 (_pb2.py)
body:
There's no way to tell the difference between a field being explicitly set to its default value vs. not having been set at all using the auto generated .pb2 files from the protobuf. (version 3.17.3)
I followed the recommended solution to include optional support(that by default not been supported) for proto3 that seems to only work for C++. (https://newbedev.com/how-to-define-an-optional-field-in-protobuf-3)

Details:

`import "google/protobuf/wrappers.proto";`

When `wrappers.proto` included to .proto file, protobuf compiler gives me the `has_value` method for each optional fields in protobuf messages only in the generated code for **C++** (.h .cc) but not for a **python** (_pb2.py). 

Is there any way to provide _optional field presence support_ to protobuf3  for Python?

Thanks
Sezer

Thanks

title: Ruby repeated uint64 values error out with "wrong argument type Hash"

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: `3.18.0.rc.1`, tried `master` too
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

Ruby 2.7.4

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Checkout https://github.com/pganalyze/pg_query
1. Bump `google-protobuf` version to `3.18.0.rc.1`.
1. Run `bundle exec rake`.

We see:

```
An error occurred while loading ./spec/lib/truncate_spec.rb.
Failure/Error: repeated :notnulls, :uint64, 11, json_name: "notnulls"

TypeError:
  wrong argument type Hash (expected String)
# ./lib/pg_query/pg_query_pb.rb:295:in `repeated'
# ./lib/pg_query/pg_query_pb.rb:295:in `block (3 levels) in <top (required)>'

# ./lib/pg_query/pg_query_pb.rb:6:in `instance_eval'
# ./lib/pg_query/pg_query_pb.rb:6:in `build'
# ./lib/pg_query/pg_query_pb.rb:6:in `<top (required)>'
# ./lib/pg_query.rb:4:in `require'
# ./lib/pg_query.rb:4:in `<top (required)>'
# ./spec/spec_helper.rb:1:in `require'
# ./spec/spec_helper.rb:1:in `<top (required)>'
# ./spec/lib/truncate_spec.rb:1:in `require'
# ./spec/lib/truncate_spec.rb:1:in `<top (required)>'
No examples found.
```

The `notnulls` definition is here (https://github.com/pganalyze/libpg_query/blob/802caf25b78ddeb8ade13cd4804d772b6d986eb3/protobuf/pg_query.proto#L307-L322):
 
```proto
message TableFunc
{
  repeated Node ns_uris = 1 [json_name="ns_uris"];
  repeated Node ns_names = 2 [json_name="ns_names"];
  Node docexpr = 3 [json_name="docexpr"];
  Node rowexpr = 4 [json_name="rowexpr"];
  repeated Node colnames = 5 [json_name="colnames"];
  repeated Node coltypes = 6 [json_name="coltypes"];
  repeated Node coltypmods = 7 [json_name="coltypmods"];
  repeated Node colcollations = 8 [json_name="colcollations"];
  repeated Node colexprs = 9 [json_name="colexprs"];
  repeated Node coldefexprs = 10 [json_name="coldefexprs"];
  repeated uint64 notnulls = 11 [json_name="notnulls"];
  int32 ordinalitycol = 12 [json_name="ordinalitycol"];
  int32 location = 13 [json_name="location"];
}
```

**What did you expect to see**

No errors.

**What did you see instead?**

```
  wrong argument type Hash (expected String)
```

The Ruby-compiled `.proto` yields:

```ruby
      optional :ordinalitycol, :int32, 12, json_name: "ordinalitycol"
```

@haberman It seems `options` is no longer a parameter:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/66d749188ff2a2e30e932110222d58da7c6a8d49/ruby/lib/google/protobuf/descriptor_dsl.rb#L304-L306

nodes.body: Thanks for the quick fix! It looks like https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8936 fixes this.

### Problem

Hi. it's unclear to me whether this is fixed. I assume the `pg_query` code used to work, and then stopped working when updating to this version. So presumably the last 2 arguments could be missing, or either one or the other of them could be passed. Thus, passing `options` without `type_class` will cause the `options` to be set into the `type_class` arg.

### Potential solution:

This will probably work, assuming that this lib doesn't need to work with really old Rubies (🤔 also, if the options can be non-symbols, then you might need to do some testing, I think that in the early incarnations of keyword args, the `**` wouldn't collect non-symbolic keys)

```ruby
def repeated(name, type, number, type_class = nil, **options)
  internal_add_field(:LABEL_REPEATED, name, type, number, type_class, options)
end
```

🤔 that said, I have no idea how this lib gets built. Those invocations don't seem to directly call this code, I assume they call some compiled C code based on this code. That piece of wiring is completely mystifying to me, so my evidence comes from changing the arguments rather than the parameters, and thus may not be valid.

> Those invocations don't seem to directly call this code, I assume they call some compiled C code based on this code.

Prior to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8850, the DSL was implemented in C. If you are seeing the DSL call straight into C, rather than `descriptor_dsl.rb`, then I suspect that you are loading a version of the C extension prior to 3.18.

It's loading version 4.0.0.rc.2:

```sh

/Users/josh/.gem/ruby/3.0.1/gems/google-protobuf-4.0.0.rc.2/lib/google/protobuf/repeated_field.rb
/Users/josh/.gem/ruby/3.0.1/gems/google-protobuf-4.0.0.rc.2/lib/google/protobuf.rb
```

Ah, that would explain it. 4.0.0-rc2 was from around the time of 3.13. We thought we were going to increase the major version number, but ended up not doing it, and 4.0.0 was never released.

That version should be yanked from Ruby gems if it's not already.

Hmm. I unfortunately can't check to see what happens in version 3 (it tries to `dlopen` protobuf_c.bundle, which wasn't built for the Apple M1), but we can compare the args to the params without needing to load up the libraries. And when we call a fn with the new signature, using the invocation from `pg_query`, we can see the options are set into the wrong variable.

```ruby
RUBY_VERSION # => "3.0.2"

# https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8936/files#diff-9c33a618a9c7713c83d727ffa7fb2072a2afd1a8a29a41efd13dffa195216007R304
def repeated(name, type, number, type_class = nil, options=nil)
  name       # => :notnulls
  type       # => :uint64
  number     # => 11
  type_class # => {:json_name=>"notnulls"}
  options    # => nil
end

# https://github.com/pganalyze/pg_query/blob/e66b01cc85120dba3edc461af6e8883b326b292a/lib/pg_query/pg_query_pb.rb#L295
repeated :notnulls, :uint64, 11, json_name: "notnulls"
```

🤔 if it's not failing for anyone else, then perhaps the underlying `internal_add_field` rearranges its arguments? 

Ahh, yeah, that's what happens, lol: [descriptor_dsl.rb#L364-L367](https://github.com/haberman/protobuf/blob/6d8b05bfd47db6d217ec4a7c9f4795e69fa900f4/ruby/lib/google/protobuf/descriptor_dsl.rb#L364-L367).

Disregard me, it is probably working on version 3.18 🤷

Define an interface (IParseableMessage) that allows custom parsing of a message from JSON
body:
Language: C#
Proposal: Add an IParseableMessage interface to allow messages to parse their own JSON

I understand there is no built-in decimal type. That's fine, I guess. However, for compatibility reasons, I want to be able to load and save the JSON for my custom type as a straight decimal value, not an object.

Right now, a DecimalValue of 12345.6789 would be serialized like so (example from <https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/grpc/protobuf?view=aspnetcore-5.0>):
`myValue: { units = 12345, nanos = 678900000 }`
and therefore the JSON deserializer expects that object format.

I would like to serialize and deserialize this object instead as `myValue: 12345.6789`

The well-known types can do something similar because they are special-cased in JsonParser.cs. How do we extend to support custom types?

The JsonFormatter seems to allow marking a message class as IFormattable, which would allow me to output the desired value. What we're missing is an equivalent interface in the Parser that would allow arbitrary strings to be parsed into messages.

Adding an interface like IParseableMessage would be a very maintainable addition. JsonParser would use the interface to parse the JSON token and merge the fields. And JsonFormatter just continues to call IFormatter. Maybe even the well-known types would use the interface instead of being hardcoded in the parser.

FYI, as an attempted workaround, I created custom converters for System.Text.Json. Loading the object was successful, but it turns out using the system JSON parser doesn't work for `repeated` proto fields because they cannot be directly assigned to. `Add` or `AddRange` must be called. So all my arrays were empty, and this was not acceptable for my use case.

nodes.body:
On even further consideration, i realized that full control over the JSON is unnecessary to solve the problem. I just need a single value.

So instead, I propose IStringValueSerializer and INumericValueSerializer interfaces. These will address the core need.

I'm experimenting on a branch now
The goal for the formats is interoperability, not customizability. It is an explicit non-goal to enable custom serializations.

I think this is an interoperability issue. Timestamp and Duration have custom JSON serializations because it makes sense. If protobuf implemented IEEE 754-2008 decimals, you would probably implement the same serialization I'm trying to accomplish.

I'm only making this proposal because there is no other way I've found to read in a typically formatted decimal from JSON.

title: proto defined enums conflicts with globally defined variables using protoc cpp
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master/v3.11.1 proto3 syntax.
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10 Enterprise (v1909)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
vs2019 (v142), SDK 10.0.18362
**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Using globally defined names in enums in proto files conflicts with each other resulting in build errors. Here is an example:
Using the following enum type:
```
enum AlarmSeverityProto {
  SEVERITY_INFO = 0;
  SEVERITY_WARNING = 1;
  SEVERITY_ERROR = 2;
}
```
conflicts with a globally defined variable (SEVERITY_ERROR) defined in winerror.h which is included in one of the following header files:
```
#include <grpc/grpc.h>
#include <grpcpp/grpcpp.h>
#include <grpcpp/channel.h>
#include <grpcpp/client_context.h>
```

Investigating the proto ph.h header file generated:
```
...
PROTOBUF_NAMESPACE_CLOSE
namespace NOV {
namespace Valhall {
namespace AlarmHandling {

enum AlarmSeverityProto : int {
  SEVERITY_INFO = 0,
  SEVERITY_WARNING = 1,
  SEVERITY_ERROR = 2,
  AlarmSeverityProto_INT_MIN_SENTINEL_DO_NOT_USE_ = std::numeric_limits<::PROTOBUF_NAMESPACE_ID::int32>::min(),
  AlarmSeverityProto_INT_MAX_SENTINEL_DO_NOT_USE_ = std::numeric_limits<::PROTOBUF_NAMESPACE_ID::int32>::max()
};
bool AlarmSeverityProto_IsValid(int value);
constexpr AlarmSeverityProto AlarmSeverityProto_MIN = SEVERITY_INFO;
constexpr AlarmSeverityProto AlarmSeverityProto_MAX = SEVERITY_ERROR;
...
}}}
```
I can see that in the line `constexpr AlarmSeverityProto AlarmSeverityProto_MAX = SEVERITY_ERROR;`, SEVERITY_ERROR gets resolved to the global defined variable in winerror.h. I think this is weird behaviour as I would think the compiler would instead use the one defined in the namespace 🤷 

Currently I have found 2 workarounds for this bug:

1. Do a `#undef SEVERITY_ERROR` before including the grpc/proto core header files mentioned above.
2. Insert the namespace of the enum in line `constexpr AlarmSeverityProto AlarmSeverityProto_MAX = SEVERITY_ERROR;` as the following `constexpr AlarmSeverityProto AlarmSeverityProto_MAX = AlarmSeverityProto::SEVERITY_ERROR;`

**What did you expect to see**

Expected it to use its own namespace defined enum instead of the global one.

**What did you see instead?**

It uses the global defined one. 

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
Here is the error message I receive:
[protolib_build_error.txt](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/7104685/protolib_build_error.txt)

nodes.body: This can be fixed with an appropriate update to `port_def.inc` and `port_undef.inc` for which we would accept patches

If I am understanding correctly, your proposed flags would make the C++ library compile with `-fvisibility=hidden` under CMake.

Have you tested with this configuration? Can you verify that the test suite and your own programs work under this flag?

I ask because `-fvisibility=hidden` will require that all symbols intended to be exported are properly marked as `PROTOBUF_EXPORT ` (which will do `__attribute__((visibility("default")))`).

We should *probably* be in good shape here, since Windows depends on proper `PROTOBUF_EXPORT` annotations for DLL support. But it would be good to have confirmation that this is working properly.

I can confirm that Mixxx builds and runs with this configuration. 
Unfortunately I cannot do more testing, because I have no access to a MacOs machine. 
Do you expect issues at runtime or should be all issue be evealed at link time?
I have been using local builds of Mixxx with this protobuf configuration on macOS as well as builds from GitHub Actions. I have not identified any problems from this.

https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg/pull/19908
Is the alternative solution in the vcpkg domain to work around the issue. Do you recommend to merge that, or will we have a solution upstream anytime soon?

I would support adding `-DCMAKE_C_VISIBILITY_PRESET=hidden`, `-DCMAKE_CXX_VISIBILITY_PRESET=hidden`, etc. to CMake.

If/when we are supporting a build of `libprotobuf.so` from Bazel, I would favor adding it there too.

> I would support adding `-DCMAKE_C_VISIBILITY_PRESET=hidden`, `-DCMAKE_CXX_VISIBILITY_PRESET=hidden`, etc. to CMake.

@haberman Can you confirm that vcpkg should merge the PR indicated above then? We want to avoid merging changes in the 'exposed interface' of a thing without the nominal owners of the thing OKing wherever possible:

> [microsoft/vcpkg#19908](https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg/pull/19908) Is the alternative solution in the vcpkg domain to work around the issue. Do you recommend to merge that, or will we have a solution upstream anytime soon?

We can of course back that out if/when a change is adopted in protocol buffers' own CMakeLists.txt.
@haberman Please have a look at the question above. This let us make progress in the vcpkg repro. Thanks.

I would prefer to make this change in our own CMake files, so it's tested in our CI.

If we patch `-DCMAKE_C_VISIBILITY_PRESET=hidden` via vcpkg, then we have no visibility in our own CI of whether it is working, or if one of our changes is breaking it.
This bug is open since 8 Sep 2021, will you take care about it?

We rely on users to contribute fixes to system-specific problems like this.

We have many users across many different systems. We don't have the bandwidth or the background to drive fixes to a problem like this that so far has only surfaced with one package manager.

Please feel free to send a PR to add this flag to our CMakeLists.txt.

body:
**What language does this apply to?**
python
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
It seems that I cannot control `protoc` `python_output` arg in `py_proto_library` genrule
**Describe the solution you'd like**
I want to control `protoc` `python_output` args in `py_proto_library` genrule
**Describe alternatives you've considered**

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.
I want to use `setuptools` in edit/developer mode e.g. `pip install -e .` in a git checkout.
The problem is that I need to import the generated python files from source dir without creating too much problem in the version control so I need that the source dir with `.proto` and the generated python file with `bazel build` will  have a different names. In this way I can a create symbolic link on the generated python files back in the source without name conflicts.

See https://github.com/keras-team/tf-keras/issues/86

nodes.body: If I'm interpreting this correctly, you want to check generated files into version control? That's a little known antipattern. Do you still need this if you're not checking generated files into version control?

Not exactly, this is why I want to control the output directory like `python_output` `protoc` arg.

In the specific case in the source code we have `keras/portobuf` subfolder with only `.proto` fiiles.
If we cannot control the `python_output` arg in `bazel-bin/` we  will have the generated file under `keras/protobuf`.
So I cannot create e.g. a symbolic link between `bazel-bin/protobuf` and source `keras/protobuf` as the directory has the same name.
Instead If rename `keras/protobuf` as `keras/protobuf_defs` and control the `python_output` name as `keras/protobuf` then I can create a symbolic link  between `bazel-bin/protobuf` and source `keras/protobuf` and put `keras/protobuf` under `.gitignore` as we have still the source available under version control in `keras/protobuf_defs`.

It seems that I don't have any other plausible workaround as playing with `PYTHONPATH=bazel-bin/` will be ignored for the conflict with the `keras/protobuf` parent namespace between the source and the compiled one.
In `setuptools` [develompent/edit mode](https://setuptools.readthedocs.io/en/latest/userguide/development_mode.html) we work in source tree directly.

Sorry for the long delay.

This seems like more of a problem in how you generate the protos. Are you still using a bazel genrule? If so, you can use that to copy the file to the place you want it to go. In general, it is dangerous to use generated files in version control because if something in the proto files change you will have an error that is hard to track down.
It Is not related to the Bazel genrule as It is realated to the mentioned development/edit mode in python setuptools
