title: A plea in favor of resurrecting "group" encoding, for sub-messages, for serializer performance
body:
## Problem statement

Currently, sub-messages are always encoded with the length-delimited wire type, which means that in the scenario

``` proto
message A {
    B b = 1;
    // other things
}
message B {
    // other things
}
```

we write this as:

- field header: field 1, wire-type 2 (2=length prefixed)
- varint of the serialized byte-length of `b`
- that same number of raw bytes representing the payload of `b`

This is effective, but it has the problem that before we can start writing `b`, we need to know the *length* of `b`; this has problems; in particular, it requires us to *either*:

1. buffer the entire payload in-memory; write the buffer length as varint; copy the buffer out
2. serialize twice, once to a nul output
3. already know the length (see †)

This starts to get particularly gnarly for deep models, where A->B->C->D->E (or whatever, perhaps recursive, perhaps lists) - forcing multiple buffer operations or computations.

† In some API implementations, this may be simple because the lengths are computed while building the data model, but this is not universal between platforms and libraries.

When handling nested deep/recursive models there *are* some internal optimizations that can be done here so that the length of E isn't computed multiple times, but: fundamentally, this is a design that is not hugely compatible with zero-copy low latency output streaming.

## Proposal

Historically, there was another encoding variant available, that was used by the "groups" metaphor in the proto DSL. The "groups" metaphor has been removed from proto3 - which is fine, and I **do not** propose that we look at that. However, the *raw encoding* used by groups may still have utility.

Let's consider we had an opt-in mechanism in the .proto schema to enable this mode, which means that the serializer would use the group *encoding* (but still talking about a message in all ways):

we write this as:

- field header: field 1, wire-type 3 (3=start group, already exists, disavowed)
- payload of `b`
- field header: field 1, wire-type 4 (4=end group, already exists, disavowed)

Here, the "start group" and "end group" tokens are used as sentinels around the payload. This means we can now write in a purely forwards-way, with zero buffering and zero payload length pre-calculations, and true zero-copy writes in suitable scenarios. In terms of implementation impact, this comes down to:

### serialization

1. a different wire-type gets gets written in the field header
2. we *do not* compute or write the length before the message
3. we stomp the end-group sentinel *after* the message

### deserialization

1. when deserializing a group-encoded sub-message, we store or pass-onwards the expected "end group" field-header/field-number
2. after reading a field-header, in the "unexpected field" branch, we check whether it is an end-group that matches the number we stored in 1. immediately above; if so, we exit out as though we had reached the end of the length
3. assertions that we *have* correctly exited out from the group, i.e. we didn't EOF mid-group

The code for all of this should already exist in all implementations, precisely because it existed for groups historically.

It is my view that this should significantly help serialization performance, especially for large/deep models. Even when an overall payload length is required (for example, as an http content-length header), this should still help, by simplifying the work required in that operation, and limiting us to only *one* event of "write to a buffer, write the buffer length, copy the buffer" or "write to a nul stream and count what we would have written, write the length, write to the real stream" (depending on the implementation). We no longer have the problem of deep/recursive/repeated models forcing multiple length computations.

Emphasis I do not propose to resurrect the groups concept in terms of the object model; purely the encoding. This would also be strictly opt-in, presumably as a custom option or new DSL feature. Note that it is also perfectly possible for a deserializer to permit either encoding, if desired (similar to how a primitive list/array deserializer may allow packed and non-packed).

A minor payload size difference exists in that since the field number now gets written twice, large magnitude field numbers on sub-messages are marginally more expensive. A counterpoint to that is that large *payload size* sub-messages used to add a few extra bytes for the length prefix, which no longer applies. In the best case (small field number and small payload size) they are identical, each taking 2 bytes cumulatively.

One complication is that it makes the "skip unexpected field" a little more expensive than just jumping a number of bytes (as it requires parsing the sub-headers until the end-group), but not hugely so; and this code should already exist in all implementations *anyway*, since groups undeniably exist. Perhaps with that in mind, this is effectively "optimize for read" (default) vs "optimize for write" (opt-in).

I welcome thoughts.

nodes.body: Changes to the wire format have an incredibly high bar for happening because of the potential for data loss and long term risks associated with this kind of evolution.  We are currently focused on other optimization opportunities and won't be pursuing this for several years at the soonest.
@fowles that's the beauty: there is zero wire format change above (in terms of new protocol features, at least); everything discussed already exists, it just isn't used

@fowles perhaps another way of phrasing this: what would the bar need to be? Hypothetically, if I spiked this as a personal experiment, what would the improvement in performance need to be to make it at least interesting enough to be discussed further?

What about using a heuristic instead? One idea I had when I wrote a code generator for protobuf serialization in C# was to estimate the object size either statically or using runtime statistics. Then you could allocate the space in the pipe buffer for that varint and then serialize "forward only" to a pipe writer. Once the subobjects are serialized and you know the size you write it out and advance the pipe.
Some twists to this could be in how to handle too small estimation of length of varint. Reserialize or move all data forward x bytes in pipe buffer.
The idea of course requires pipelines instead of streams. And buffer pool must handle full messages, but I guess that is inherent in protobuf.
It would also be possible to calculate max possible length of types, and serialize a "bad" varint which is bigger than needed.
Disclaimer, none of the above was ever tried :) My object graph depth was so low that it was no issue to Calc the size (using generated optimized code with many just being constants folded compile time).

There's actually an implementation called ProtoZero that already does this [trick](https://perfetto.dev/docs/design-docs/protozero#deferred-patching) of setting aside space for a larger-than-needed varint.

@acozzette I use the same trick in some scenarios in protobuf-net, but you still need to keep a live buffer so you can backfill the length when known, which has limitations for zero-copy scenarios where you don't necessarily control the final buffers, so can't guarantee the lifetime unless you lease your own and do a separate copy. It still isn't as ideal as just: not needing the length.

@acozzette nice, then maybe I will try it some day. Now that we have code generators in C# we can do all sorts of optimizations, since we don't need one big dll that does it all. For example we could att hint attributes on types for calculating reasonable max lengths and throw if user don't follow those hints. The maybe we could have a perfect varint for each type calculated at compile time.

@maloo as long as you only ever err on the side of over-estimate, you can combine that with what @acozzette said above, but you still have the problems with external buffers in zero copy scenarios, and you still have the problem that the cost of even an estimate increases significantly for deep models; ultimately, to get even close with an estimate, you end up doing *basically* the same work as writing to a nul stream (consider utf-8 costs, for example)
@mgravell do you have some scenarios in mind that could be shown in benchmark.net? if so, people could look at it and try out different ideas... or maybe some unit tests in protobuf-net

The scenario in general applies to deep models in most cases. I'm not specifically thinking in terms of protobuf-net, but: if you're familiar with "pipelines" (which is available and used in the .NET gRPC implementations): that's a great example of an external buffers scenario, where you can't just hold onto the existing target buffer and backfill sizes, unless you create an extra buffer copy yourself. But it applies similarly to large data payloads on regular streams; I'm aware of the recommended sizes from protobuf, but I regularly see people with many orders of magnitude larger models, and having to buffer that kind of thing just to put a size in at the end: really expensive.

I've not used pipelines to the extent you have, but what prevents you from holding on to pooled memory while serializing sub messages? As long as you don't call Advance on the pipewriter... but that has to come after the length has been filled in.

@maloo That's simply not how pipelines works. You can lease a buffer with a size-hint, but pipelines decides what to give you; it could be massive, it could be just big enough; if you ask for too much, it might not meet your request; that buffer is only guaranteed well-defined until you call Advance, and you only have one leased outstanding buffer at a time. You can't hold onto an old buffer past Advance, as it could well have been written to the underlying device and recycled to service a completely independent operation - and you'd a: be too late for your change to be useful, and b: be writing into someone else's memory. And since the slice you get isn't guaranteed to be "big" (it could be a 1k slice, for example), even a modest message could exceed the leased buffer.

But I feel we're missing the point by focusing on specifics here. I'd rather focus on the bigger picture. There aren't many scenarios I can think of where *needing* to provide a length can compete with: not needing that.

Smaller picture:
I asked about calling multiple GetMemory() without calling Advance(). I understand why you can't hold on to a pooled buffer once released. But that is not the case here. I expect the client to get as much memory it needs to serialize the object, then update the sizes and finally release it with Advance(). If you can allocate twice the amount and copy it, allocating it once should be fine.

Bigger picture:
I guess protobuf is not only used by terminal endpoints, but also proxies that want the size to be able to forward a blob of memory without having to parse it. Even terminal endpoints might want to send a sub message directly to storage without passing, so length is nice.
I have no issues with an option without length if it give obvious perf improvements. But backfilling size should not force you to do multiple serialization or copies as shown above. If you have to it seems to indicate client library limitations rather than protocol limitations.

Sorry, but that understanding of pipelines is incomplete and won't work. That is not the intended usage.

Calculating a length is always more expensive than: not doing that. Maybe I should just do a spike so we can talk more concretely.

Initial benchmark using the Google C# implementation:

``` txt
generated tree of 1525538 length-prefixed nodes; 278911835 bytes
generated tree of 1525538 grouped nodes; 277804287 bytes
```

|                 Method |      Mean |    Error |   StdDev |     Gen 0 | Gen 1 | Gen 2 |  Allocated |
|----------------------- |----------:|---------:|---------:|----------:|------:|------:|-----------:|
| ComputeLength_Prefixed |  82.44 ms | 0.782 ms | 0.693 ms |         - |     - |     - |       35 B |
|  ComputeLength_Grouped |  77.89 ms | 0.362 ms | 0.321 ms |         - |     - |     - |          - |
|     Serialize_Prefixed | 856.84 ms | 9.443 ms | 8.371 ms | 1000.0000 |     - |     - | 16691008 B |
|      Serialize_Grouped | 224.62 ms | 1.740 ms | 1.628 ms | 1000.0000 |     - |     - | 16697792 B |

So that's almost a 4x speedup for deep models! I'm not saying that's huge, but: that's huge. For reference, the main reason this happens is the multiplication of the number of times the length of leaf nodes get evaluated

[Code is here](https://github.com/mgravell/protobuf/commit/1db7e40bcb5ff8a52a5696058188bad587309d35); in a rookie moment I forgot to branch my fork - if I get a moment, I'll fix that and update the link. For simplicity, there's two versions of the generated code; one is the original from protoc, and one has been hacked; changes are marked `// ****`, but come down to

``` c#
private static readonly pb::FieldCodec<global::ForwardsOnlyBenchmark.Grouped.Node> _repeated_children_codec_grouped
            = pb::FieldCodec.ForGroup((ChildrenFieldNumber << 3) | (int)pb.WireFormat.WireType.StartGroup, (ChildrenFieldNumber << 3) | (int)pb.WireFormat.WireType.EndGroup, global::ForwardsOnlyBenchmark.Grouped.Node.Parser); // ***** ForGroup
```

and

``` c#
children_.WriteTo(output, _repeated_children_codec_grouped);
```

and (note: not tested by this benchmark)

``` c#
                    case ((ChildrenFieldNumber << 3) | (int)pb.WireFormat.WireType.StartGroup): // ***** tag value
                        {
                            children_.AddEntriesFrom(input, _repeated_children_codec_grouped);
                            break;
                        }
```

all with zero library changes, and retaining the ability to deserialize from either grouped or prefixed notation!

@mgravell We already know the performance opportunity is there.  The things needed to make this happen are around time and evolution.  We need all existing parsers to be able to handle both formats for messages, which implies a pretty long time before serializers can produce it.  We need parameters to control which format is used by writers.  There is a bunch of work going on at the moment to enable us to have these sorts of long term flexibility, but we simply aren't there right now and we predict the prerequisites will take us several years.
@fowles Have you looked at @mgravell 's change in detail?

(well yes bot, I'd absolutely love to keep this on the radar...)

It isn't exactly what you are asking for but it might serve your purpose.  Editions allows for explicitly specifying encoding on specific fields (or all fields in a file).  It does not support saying "this message is always encoded with groups".

https://protobuf.dev/editions/features/#message_encoding

Cheers!
That... actually might be perfect, thanks @fowles ; I need to catch up on the status of "editions"

Nice! @fowles is there a way to generate parsing code for both delimited & length-prefixed cases?

That'd allow migrating existing fields without breaking backwards compatibility with existing serializers and binary data. The tags are different, so it would be possible to migrate similarly to how the `packed = true` flag worked for repeated fields.
@ennerf if it on our internal roadmap and plan, but likely won't get done until late 2024.
Thanks. Great to know that this is on the roadmap.

So I think there's 3 questions here, all of which we have concrete plans for:

1) **Group encoding for submessages** - edition 2023 removes the group syntax and allows you to specify DELIMITED encoding on any message field.  This is already released under an `--experimental_editions` flag, and we plan to ship it in all of our supported languages for the 27.0 release in a few months

2) **Allow parsing of both group delimited and length prefixed encoding for the same field**.  This will provide a migration path and a way for us to eventually remove length prefixed encoding.  We plan to implement this in 2024, and flip the default encoding to DELIMITED for edition 2024.  Actual removal of length-prefixed encoding will likely take many years while we wait for those changes to roll out everywhere

3) **Prototiller** - this is just a tool for programmatically modifying proto files.  It is orthogonal to protoc atm, but we might want to unify those at some point in the future.  We hope to release prototiller this year, and it can be used to help migrate your protos to editions.  It's won't be doing any special magic though, and you could also migrate them by hand fairly easily

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.17
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10, Mac Catalina

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
gcc version

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

protoc an enum with a plural enum name and singular prefix. Simplified example:

```proto
enum Attributes {
  ATTRIBUTE_INVALID = 0;
  ATTRIBUTE_SIZE = 1;
  ATTRIBUTE_DISPOSITION = 2;
}
```

**What did you expect to see**

```csharp
  public enum Attributes {
    [pbr::OriginalName("ATTRIBUTE_INVALID")] AttributeInvalid = 0,
    [pbr::OriginalName("ATTRIBUTE_SIZE")] AttributeSize = 1,
    [pbr::OriginalName("ATTRIBUTE_DISPOSITION")] AttributeDisposition = 2,
  }
```

**What did you see instead?**

Note `Size` was truncated as `Ize` because [TryRemovePrefix ](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/3f5fc4df1de8e12b2235c3006593e22d6993c3f5/src/google/protobuf/compiler/csharp/csharp_helpers.cc#L227) matches `ATTRIBUTE_S` to the enum name `Attributes`.

```csharp
  public enum Attributes {
    [pbr::OriginalName("ATTRIBUTE_INVALID")] AttributeInvalid = 0,
    [pbr::OriginalName("ATTRIBUTE_SIZE")] Ize = 1,
    [pbr::OriginalName("ATTRIBUTE_DISPOSITION")] AttributeDisposition = 2,
  }
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

I realize that it's hard to change this. Can the prefix matching logic require that there be a trailing `_` after the match to avoid splitting words?

nodes.body: @astarche Any reason of why is this issue still open if PR is merged.

I worked around this in my code because I was able to rename the enums in our `proto` files so that the prefix exactly matched the enum name. So it doesn't affect me now and I will know how to avoid the issue in the future. The issue in the C# protoc plugin still exists (I assume).

I'm OK with the issue being rejected if it's not considered worth fixing. It's not clear to me if fixing this is even allowed in `protoc`. The current behavior is "wrong" but fixing it could break client code.

Fixing this would definitely be a breaking change. It's definitely *unpleasant* behavior... I'm not sure what the "right" fix would be even if we were willing to change it though. (This is one of those features which is really helpful when it does the right thing, and pretty awful when it doesn't.)

One way of fixing it in a non-breaking way would be to add a C#-specific option for either an enum as a whole ("don't perform prefix-removal") or a specific enum value (either suppression, or "use this name instead"). But given that this *appears* to rarely be a problem (this is the first time I've encountered it) I think it's probably best to close the issue with no further action for now.

title: commonjs no longer works in Node.js
body:
As a result of #8864, the generated commonjs `*_pb.js` files no longer work in a Node.js environment, because it [references `window`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.19.0/src/google/protobuf/compiler/js/js_generator.cc#L3637), which is undefined in Node.js.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.19.0
Language: JavaScript

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Node.js 14.18.1

**What did you do?**

1. Run protoc: `protoc --js_out=import_style=commonjs,binary:path/to/out/dir --proto_path=. *.proto`
2. Try to import and use the generated `*_pb.js` files.

**What did you expect to see**

Import and use without errors (just as prior to 3.19.0)

**What did you see instead?**

```
    ReferenceError: window is not defined

      14 | var jspb = require('google-protobuf');
      15 | var goog = jspb;
    > 16 | var global = (function() { return this || window || global || self || Function('return this')(); }).call(null);
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

N/A

@nottmey when I do this I have errors such as `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'Event')`, any idea where this might come from?

@maelp sorry, no idea. Our generated files don't even contain any access on `Event` so I suspect it's an error that was previously hidden from you. (My fix also only applies to a Node.js environment. You don't wan't to do this where any code actually needs `window` or `self`.)
@nottmey I'm using it in a Nodejs environment, but I guess there's another package which is fiddling with globalThis and expects perhaps to find something there then?
@maelp yes that could be the case

I was also forced to downgrade, but I was able to work around this issue by using `commonjs_strict` instead of `commonjs`:

```
protoc --js_out=import_style=commonjs_strict:. my_proto_file.proto
```

The generated code doesn't access `window`, allowing it work in strict mode.

body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.17.3
Language: Java

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Android

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
NDK r21d clang

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Build a Message instance of a certain type.
2. Serialize the built message to `ByteString` using the `toByteString` method.
3. Use the `parseFrom` method of another message type to parse the message from the serialized bytes.

**What did you expect to see**
An `InvalidProtocolBufferException` being thrown after the call to the `parseFrom` method.

**What did you see instead?**
No exception has been thrown and received a partially parsed message.

**Code Example**
```
MyMessage message = MyMessage.newBuilder()
        .setStringValue("hello, world")
        .build();

AnotherMessage another = AnotherMessage.parseFrom(message.toByteString());
System.out.println("Another uint32Value: " + another.getUint32Value());
```

The code output is: `Another uint32Value: 0`

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body: Can you tell me if there are any fields present if you call `getUnknownFields()` on the `another` instance? Curious if they are sitting in there.
Message.parseFrom appears to simply delegate to Parser.parseFrom

@perezd Thanks!
I ran `getUnknownFields` on the `another` instance and received the a set that includes the string value. But when I ran it with two messages with integer fields of different sizes (`uint32`, `uint64`) I received an empty set.

@elharo Thank you for your response.
Does `Parser.parseFrom` throw an exception when invoked with a message of the wrong type?

In general, no. Protobuf messages are not self-describing so it's not possible for a MessageParser to tell which type of message it's reading. I think (need to do some more reading on this myself) it simply tries to match the tags it finds in the streams to the proto definition it's configured with, fills in defaults if any are missing, and stuffs anything extra into unknown fields.
@elharo Got it, thank you **so** much :)

title: Better document exception in MessageLite.Builder
body:
There's been some user confusion over when and why IOException and InvalidProtocolBufferException are thrown from `mergeFrom` and similar methods. E.g. in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9157 

Add the necessary `@throws` clauses to clarify. Briefly:

1. IOException thrown due to an underlying error reading from the stream
2. InvalidProtocolBufferException thrown when the stream bytes are read but found to be syntactically incorrect

title: Comparison of protobufs with objects of other types is broken (e.g., mock.ANY)
body:
```
from unittest import mock
# Suppose msg is some protobuf message
# This assertion passes, as expected
self.assertEqual(mock.ANY, msg)
# I was hoping that this assertion will pass as well, but it doesn't
self.assertEqual(msg, mock.ANY)
```
Presumably this is due to incorrectly returning `False` from `__eq__` in [here](https://github.com/malthe/google-protobuf/blob/ca3abfb7340b1c5dddf1ab18482b668bb409be59/python/google/protobuf/internal/python_message.py#L685), but I haven't verified this. If so, it would be a similar issue to https://github.com/googleapis/google-cloud-python/issues/3455. 

In general, `return False` instead of `return NotImplemented` when rhs is of a different type is a common error, and there many instances of that in the google-protobuf. Which of them are worth fixing (and whether it's safe to do so) is unknown to me.

nodes.body: Funny, I'd expect both of these to fail.

I think that this is expected behavior. Mock.Any will always return true. But Any does not have the matching type nor features of a protobuf message. Even if you decide to try to make this true you would be stuck adding in a hack to check if the type is Mock.Any and just pass it. A fix you can try is to create a mock object that inherits from or is very similar to a protobuf message so that all of the attributes are the same and the type is masked as a PB message.
Equality *should* be symmetric for logical reasons. If that's not true, then something is broken here, perhaps deeply. The issue might not be in protobuf though.

title: protoc allows invalid UTF-8 in source and in option values whose type is string
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
The latest:
```
> protoc --version
libprotoc 3.19.1
```
**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

OS X 11.6.1

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

N/A

**What did you do?**

I compiled a file with invalid binary data in it. While the specs don't say that the source should be UTF-8 encoded, this issue in GitHub states it to be true: #1418. (Note: the docs should really be updated to explicitly state this, for clarity.)

In order for the source to be valid compilable source, I put it in a string literal for an option whose type is `string`. I actually created two files that are semantically equivalent:

```proto
// tmp.proto
syntax = "proto3";

package foo;

option java_outer_classname= "my?value";
```

The question mark above is actually binary value `0xbc`. To play with the binary data of this example file, you can use `xxd -r` with this:
```xxd
00000000: 7379 6e74 6178 203d 2022 7072 6f74 6f33  syntax = "proto3
00000010: 223b 0a0a 7061 636b 6167 6520 666f 6f3b  ";..package foo;
00000020: 0a0a 6f70 7469 6f6e 206a 6176 615f 6f75  ..option java_ou
00000030: 7465 725f 636c 6173 736e 616d 653d 2022  ter_classname= "
00000040: 6d79 bc76 616c 7565 223b 0a              my.value";.
```

The second file uses an escape sequence:
```proto
// tmp2.proto
syntax = "proto3";

package foo;

option java_outer_classname= "my\xbcvalue";
```

So `tmp.proto` includes invalid UTF8 input in the source. And `tmp2.proto` contains valid UTF8 in the source, but it defines a string constant that has invalid UTF8 data.

I compiled the files just to descriptor sets:
```
protoc -o tmp.protoset tmp.proto
protoc -o tmp2.protoset tmp2.proto
```

**What did you expect to see**

I expected `protoc` to:
1. _Either_ replace the invalid data with the UTF replacement char � (U+FFFD)
2. _Or_ complain that the input was malformed UTF-8.

For the first file, it should complain about the input in the source program itself.

For the second file, it should complain about the value for a string option not being valid input (since strings are expected to be UTF-8 or 7-bit ASCII according to [the](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#scalar) [docs](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#scalar)).

**What did you see instead?**

Compilation succeeds just fine with both files. Other than the file name, they produce identical descriptors:

```
> protoc --decode google.protobuf.FileDescriptorSet google/protobuf/descriptor.proto < tmp.protoset
file {
  name: "tmp.proto"
  package: "foo"
  options {
    java_outer_classname: "my\274value"
  }
  syntax: "proto3"
}
```

The `\274` is an escaped byte, not unicode point `0xbc`. This is not valid UTF8, but the `java_outer_classname` option is defined as type `string`.

nodes.body: I suspect the invalid UTF-8 values for string options might be allowed due to #7364. But maybe it could also be due to the odd way that options are interpreted (they are first interpreted directly into "unknown bytes" and then an attempt is made to unmarshal them into the options message).
@googleberg, Hi! I see this was assigned about a month ago. Is this something that you expect will be fixed? If I looked into it, would you review and potentially accept a pull request for it?
I can answer on his behalf: Yes! We'd love to review if you'd be willing to take a stab.
My apologies for the delay. Absolutely!

@perezd, @googleberg, cool, I'm looking at it now.

There are really two parts to this issue:
1. File input is valid UTF8
2. String constants contain valid UTF8

For the first part, I was going to add a flag to the tokenizer for enabling UTF8 verification. For now, only the parser will set it. I was worried that otherwise the "blast radius" might be too large. (This same class is also used for parsing the text format -- which probably should also require UTF8 input, but that also seems like a bigger risk with regards to backwards compatibility.) There is some subtlety, like if a multi-byte code point crosses the boundary of the tokenizer's buffer, which isn't so tricky to implement right as it is to verify in a test. But this first part is the easier part I think.

The second part looks more complicated. The check itself is easy (there's already a function to do it in the `google/protobuf/stubs` folder), and I think there are only two places to invoke it -- when processing/type-checking a field's default value and the code that interprets all other options. However, there is a lot of stuff already in the codebase around whether to check if strings are UTF8. That code looks to be referencing file and field options that don't actually exist in `descriptor.proto` (maybe part of a Google-internal migration)? It defers the UTF8 checks to the various runtimes -- so the C++ runtime can implement its own check as can the Java runtime. So addressing the second part seems less clear as to how to proceed (and maybe higher risk?). I'm not sure if there is an easy way to enable the check in `protoc` yet still easily allow it to be disabled, such as via an environment variable or maybe a pre-processor definition to turn it off at compile time.

Do you have any advice?

> enforce_utf8 is documented as deprecated

@googleberg, like I mentioned, though the code refers to such an option, it does not actually exist in the open-source version. Take a look:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L539

I think you may be looking at an internal version of `descriptor.proto`. Many comments related to enforcing UTF8 suggest it was for an internal migration (perhaps migrating to actually enforcing UTF8?).

The documentation (for both [proto2](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#scalar) and [proto3](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#scalar)) states that strings must always be valid UTF8.

I looked into this and found that the problem most likely has nothing to do with my PR https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8280 (which only affects the build or aarch64 wheels and it doesn't change anything for the x86_64 wheels).

@haberman  is correct that there was a sudden switch from `manylinux1` to `manylinux2014` for x86_64 (so for systems older than what manylinux2014 supports, only the pure python version of protobuf python will be available - thus no cpp support, which explains the behavior reported in this issue).

It seems that the unintended switch from manylinux1 to manylinux2014 wasn't actually caused by a change in this repository, but by a change in https://github.com/matthew-brett/multibuild.
To build python wheels, we are using the multibuild scripts and we always clone the HEAD of that repository so any changes in that repository will be automatically picked up in the protobuf wheel build.
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/47e05427e3341c9b18fff047e7d9f79af0dafe9b/kokoro/release/python/linux/build_artifacts.sh#L28

On Aug 21, matthew-brett/multibuild has switched the default manylinux image from `1` to `2014` (see PR https://github.com/multi-build/multibuild/pull/423/files).

Some extra evidence:
- the 3.18.0-rc1 release (from Aug 20) still has the manylinux1 wheels: https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/3.18.0rc1/#files
- the 3.18.0-rc2 release (from Aug 31) only has manylinux2014 wheels for x86_64: https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/3.18.0rc2/#files  (and so the change from Aug 21 has almost certainly caused the regression).

The solution is relatively simple:
- make sure we explicitly set `MB_ML_VER=1` for the x86_64 wheels
- pin the clone of  matthew-brett/multibuild to a specific version to avoid unexpected changes like this in the future.
- it should also be possible to retroactively generate the missing manylinux1 wheels for older releases if needed.

title: with clang, [[nodiscard]] is emitted also for -std=c++11
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.19.1
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

OpenBSD -current

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

clang 11.1.0

**What did you do?**

Build protobuf 3.19.1, then try to build protozero 1.7.0.

**What did you expect to see**

protozero 1.7.0 builds

**What did you see instead?**

The build failed because protozero builds with `-pedantic -std=c++11 -Werror`. On the one hand, this is enough to have `PROTOBUF_NODISCARD` defined as `[[nodiscard]]`. On the other hand, this then trips over `-Werror` due to `-Wc++17-extensions`:

```
[79/90] /tmp/pobj/protozero-1.7.0/bin/c++  -I/tmp/pobj/protozero-1.7.0/protozero-1.7.0/include -I/tmp/pobj/protozero-1.7.0/protozero-1.7.0/test/include -isystem /tmp/pobj/protozero-1.7.0/protozero-1.7.0/test/catch -isystem /usr/local/include -isystem test -O2 -pipe  -std=c++17 -DNDEBUG   -std=c++11 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wsign-compare -Wunused-parameter -Wno-float-equal -Wno-covered-switch-default -Werror -pthread -MD -MT test/CMakeFiles/writer_tests.dir/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc.o -MF test/CMakeFiles/writer_tests.dir/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc.o.d -o test/CMakeFiles/writer_tests.dir/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc.o -c test/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc
FAILED: test/CMakeFiles/writer_tests.dir/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc.o /tmp/pobj/protozero-1.7.0/bin/c++  -I/tmp/pobj/protozero-1.7.0/protozero-1.7.0/include -I/tmp/pobj/protozero-1.7.0/protozero-1.7.0/test/include -isystem /tmp/pobj/protozero-1.7.0/protozero-1.7.0/test/catch -isystem /usr/local/include -isystem test -O2 -pipe  -std=c++17 -DNDEBUG   -std=c++11 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wsign-compare -Wunused-parameter -Wno-float-equal -Wno-covered-switch-default -Werror -pthread -MD -MT test/CMakeFiles/writer_tests.dir/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc.o -MF test/CMakeFiles/writer_tests.dir/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc.o.d -o test/CMakeFiles/writer_tests.dir/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc.o -c test/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc
In file included from test/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.cc:4:
test/t/bytes/bytes_testcase.pb.h:190:3: error: use of the 'nodiscard' attribute is a C++17 extension [-Werror,-Wc++17-extensions]
  PROTOBUF_NODISCARD std::string* release_s();
  ^
/usr/local/include/google/protobuf/port_def.inc:463:30: note: expanded from macro 'PROTOBUF_NODISCARD'
#define PROTOBUF_NODISCARD [[nodiscard]]
                             ^
1 error generated.
ninja: build stopped: subcommand failed.
```


**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

It seems `#if __has_cpp_attribute(nodiscard)` is insufficient to determine whether `[[nodiscard]]` is actually allowed. A similar issue was also reported here: https://github.com/nlohmann/json/issues/1535

This could be avoided if PROTOBUF_NODISCARD were only defined to `[[nodiscard]]` with

```c++
#if __has_cpp_attribute(nodiscard) && PROTOBUF_CPLUSPLUS_MIN(201703L)
#define PROTOBUF_NODISCARD [[nodiscard]]
#elif
...
```

or similar.

The `import weak` syntax only exists to support weak fields, so we have been assuming that it's never used outside of Google. Apparently Gogoprotobuf relies on this syntax, though, and makes use of it [here](https://github.com/gogo/protobuf/blob/226206f39bd7276e88ec684ea0028c18ec2c91ae/protoc-gen-gogo/generator/generator.go#L1382).

Hey @stanguturi -- Like Adam said, weak imports are a feature that only happened to be exposed in our Github repo while we (internally, at Google) worked towards removing its use. The intent was not for options, but something else entirely.

It looks like the containerd changes have been around since 2017 or so in containerd/containerd@50532f231a29f0c04f7ee62696b78d322a84cf33 ... this seems like a pretty bad situation, since it means they cannot build for C++ (as you now see). Based on Github's search results, it looks like containerd may be the only project that actually relies on weak imports. Most of the other hits are either tests or internal to Go protobufs.

Without getting too far into the details, I don't think this is something we can address in the very near term, although it's an interesting use case. (Very short version: this would violate some correctness preconditions that guard against built-in schema corruption... the error you got was not directly related to this issue.)

I do see that you are working with system-installed protos (under `/usr/share/`). You can always work around this issue by modifying the files to remove the `weak` syntax, and use the modified versions to build for C++.

title: Building static protobuf on Windows forces linking to static MSVC runtime.
body:
When protobuf is built as a static library on Windows using CMake, it is linked to the static MSVC runtime. This is not compatible with an application that links to the dynamic MSVC runtime, since all objects linked into the application must use the same runtime. This issue is present when using CMake >=3.15 due to the [logic in CMakeLists](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/7ccf4d8f67878a6ceb2184df279478cb3314372b/cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L184). The `protobuf_MSVC_STATIC_RUNTIME` option is not respected when using CMake >=3.15. I am forced to patch CMakeLists for my application. It would be great if the logic was fixed to respect this option.

One way to do this is to change
```

title: protoc: emptyStatement is not allowed in extend
body:
`protoc` errors on emptyStatement (a single ";") in an extend definition.

The proto2 spec defines extend as:

```
extend = "extend" messageType "{" {field | group | emptyStatement} "}"
```

Based on that I think an extra ";" should be valid.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.19.1
Language: N/A

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
macOS 11.6

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
N/A

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a.proto with this content:
```protobuf
syntax = "proto2";
package a;
import "google/protobuf/descriptor.proto";

extend google.protobuf.FileOptions {
  optional bool foo = 1000;;
}
```
2. Run `protoc -o ./protodump a.proto`

**What did you expect to see**

File descriptor written to protodump and exit 0.

**What did you see instead?**

exit code: 1
stderr:
```
a.proto:6:28: Expected "required", "optional", or "repeated".
a.proto:6:28: Expected type name.
```

nodes.body: Sorry for the delayed response. Based on the spec I don't see why an empty line with just a semicolon should be valid. Why do you want to be able to add the extra semicolon?

When I created this issue I was using protoc as an oracle while fuzz testing another program that parses proto files. Testing revealed a discrepancy when there is a second semicolon at the end of a line in an extend. The inclusion of emptyStatement in proto2 specification indicates that it should be allowed because it is defined as `emptyStatement = "'"`. 

To answer your question of why I want to add the extra semicolon, I don't. I just created the issue because I thought the maintainers would be interested to know that protoc is divergent from the published spec.

protoc's actual behavior would be better describe by 
```
extend = "extend" messageType "{" (field | group) {field | group} "}"
```
because emptyStatement isn't allowed and at least one field or group is required.

I am not currently working with protoc or protocol buffers, so I don't have a stake in the outcome of this issue. Feel free to close it or keep it open based on the needs of the project.
FYI, this is closely related to #5075

title: NPE issue with setter on the generated class
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
Java

If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
proto3

If it's about generated code change, what programming language?
Java

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
For the message below, 
```
message Position {
    string portfolio =1;
}
```

The generated setter would be something like this
```
      public Builder setPortfolio(
          java.lang.String value) {
        if (value == null) {
         throw new NullPointerException();
        }
  
        portfolio_ = value;
        onChanged();
        return this;
      }
```

There is a throw NPE within the method. 

I think this is really an opinioned approach, which instead should leave to developers to decide whether to handle it or throw NPE.
There could be a position message, for example, with many known optional field which could be null. Developers should be in a better position on how those fields should be set.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

The generated class should take the value to be set as it is. Something like
```
      public Builder setPortfolio(
          java.lang.String value) {
//        if (value == null) {
//         throw new NullPointerException();
//        }
  
        portfolio_ = value;
        onChanged();
        return this;
      }
```


**Describe alternatives you've considered**

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

I guess the current "opinioned" approach probably could be due to a constraint from the protobuf format, where an int was used to determine the length-delimited value's length. If no, I think by introducing a negative int (**-1**) could tell whether the following value is really empty (**0**) or null (**-1**).

nodes.body: Opinionated but deliberate. Proto3 does not support nullable fields. This isn't just an issue for Java but for the wire format and interoperability across languages. The NullPointerException here is a result of that, not a decision in itself.

title: Error in CMakeLists.txt in 3.19.1: Runtime Library for Visual Studio
body:
CMakeLists.txt in 3.19.1 includes the following block which is meant to set if we should use the dll or the static version of the C runtime. The lower block only switches to static runtime if the CMake option protobuf_MSVC_STATIC_RUNTIME is set. In the upper block which is used when a more recent cmake is available, the option protobuf_MSVC_STATIC_RUNTIME is ignored. I propose to change this to allow users of modern cmake versions to specify if they want static or dynamic runtime.

Old code:

```
if (protobuf_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS)
  set(protobuf_SHARED_OR_STATIC "SHARED")
else (protobuf_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS)
  set(protobuf_SHARED_OR_STATIC "STATIC")
  # The CMAKE_<LANG>_FLAGS(_<BUILD_TYPE>)? is meant to be user controlled.
  # Prior to CMake 3.15, the MSVC runtime library was pushed into the same flags
  # making programmatic control difficult.  Prefer the functionality in newer
  # CMake versions when available.
  if(CMAKE_VERSION VERSION_GREATER 3.15 OR CMAKE_VERSION VERSION_EQUAL 3.15)
    set(CMAKE_MSVC_RUNTIME_LIBRARY MultiThreaded$<$<CONFIG:Debug>:Debug>)
  else()
    # In case we are building static libraries, link also the runtime library statically
    # so that MSVCR*.DLL is not required at runtime.
    # https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/2kzt1wy3.aspx
    # This is achieved by replacing msvc option /MD with /MT and /MDd with /MTd
    # http://www.cmake.org/Wiki/CMake_FAQ#How_can_I_build_my_MSVC_application_with_a_static_runtime.3F
    if (MSVC AND protobuf_MSVC_STATIC_RUNTIME)
      foreach(flag_var
          CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE
          CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_MINSIZEREL CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS_RELWITHDEBINFO)
        if(${flag_var} MATCHES "/MD")
          string(REGEX REPLACE "/MD" "/MT" ${flag_var} "${${flag_var}}")
        endif(${flag_var} MATCHES "/MD")
      endforeach(flag_var)
    endif (MSVC AND protobuf_MSVC_STATIC_RUNTIME)
  endif()
endif (protobuf_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS)
```

Change could be this:

```
  if(CMAKE_VERSION VERSION_GREATER 3.15 OR CMAKE_VERSION VERSION_EQUAL 3.15 AND protobuf_MSVC_STATIC_RUNTIME)
```

title: Two-way map/conversion between two proto messages
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
A proto syntax addition (can apply to both proto2 or proto3, but for proto2 it's better).

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

I'm trying to have a cross-platform way to automate conversions between two proto messages.
Very useful for refactorings, API changes, etc. When you want to create a better proto message without breaking existing APIs.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Using proto annotations (like [protoc-gen-validate](https://github.com/envoyproxy/protoc-gen-validate)) to map between an old field to a new field (using full field paths, possibly enabling some general conversion methods, like int->string, or string->enum, etc.)

Each language would need to implement its usage separately.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Creating a conversion per-language separately. There are libraries I found that do it for Java. But that's not cross-language, and wouldn't work for API-clients using another language.

**Additional context**

***Requirements:***

1. The two messages could have a completely different structure (e.g., sub messages, field renames, different enum types)
2. I'd want the conversion to be automatically created for all languages (e.g., by a build rule). If it's not possible, support for both Java and C++ is mandatory.


***Example:***
Conversion between A and B:

```
message A {
  optional string name = 1;
  optional Enum type = 2;
  enum Enum {
    TYPE1 = 1,
    TYPE2 = 2,
  }
}

message B {
  message Metadata {
      optional string name = 1;
  }
  optional Metadata metadata = 1;

  message SemanticData {
      optional SimilarEnum type = 1;
      enum SimilarEnum {
        TYPE_RENAMED1 = 1,
        TYPE_RENAMED_REVALUED2 = 5,
      }
  }
  optional SemanticData value = 2;  
}
```

nodes.body: This would make a nice third party utility. It doesn't seem like it's something that needs to be in core.
Is there a way to suggest/request something like this as a third party utility?
I doubt the core team has the resources to prioritize or create such a thing right now. However this could be done by anybody with the interest. Not every good idea needs to b done in this repo.

While the proto team won't be able to support this effort directly right now, I'm going to reopen the issue and tag it with help wanted in order to preserve this idea and hopefully get some help implementing from contributors.
If this is implemented would this belong in this repo or a separate project? That is, would it need to be in core?
Hi, @Your-Eye I am having a similar requirement as stated above by you. Wanted to know how you were able to achieve it ? Thanks.

> Hi, @Your-Eye I am having a similar requirement as stated above by you. Wanted to know how you were able to achieve it ? Thanks.

Unfortunately, I didn't. This issue is still open. For now, the only solutions I'm familiar with are solutions for a specific language rather at the protobuf level.

Where I work, we have a `@AutoConverter` for Java (like `@AutoValue`) to automatically convert messages by fields' names. But I don't think it's externally available.
> @Your-Eye Hi.. If you know any utility specific to C++, kindly let me know. Either way, appreciate you replying. Thanks !!

I think this is better off outside the core of protobuf.  If I were designing a thing like this, I would probably use custom options to define the interfaces and then publish a spec for how each language must interpret those options.  Then you can handle them on a per language basis either with a code generator plugin or with reflection.
@fowles So what is the correct location to request this? How can the idea be preserved so a third party can implement this as @deannagarcia suggested?
I don't know that there is a good clearing house for ideas for OSS projects that people wish existed.

title: JsonFormatter omits null when Message type
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.19.1
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
.NET 6

**What did you do?**
I updated some code that were previously referencing Google.Protobuf 3.9.1 and noticed some changes with regards to formatting JSON. 

Steps to reproduce:

Use following proto:
```proto
syntax = "proto3";

message Foo
{
  message Bar {
    string baz = 1;
  }

  string baz = 1;
  Bar bar = 2;
}
```

Serialize to JSON and print (add `formatDefaultValues: true`):
```csharp
using Google.Protobuf;

var json = new JsonFormatter(
                new JsonFormatter.Settings(formatDefaultValues: true))
                .Format(new Foo());

Console.WriteLine(json);
```

**What did you expect to see**

```
{ "baz": "", "bar": null }
```

as with Google.Protobuf 3.9.1

**What did you see instead?**

```
{ "baz": "" }
```

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

I'm pretty sure this change changed the behavior.
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/7487

Not sure if it was intentional or not. But I'd think when explicitly adding `formatDefaultValues: true`, then message type fields with default value should be serialized as `null`.

nodes.body:
Firstly, apologies that it's taken so long to respond to this.

Yes, I believe you're right that that PR changed the behavior - and yes, it was a breaking change, which we should have spotted as such. (I noted that it would be a breaking change in a comment, but I suspect there was an internal discussion which isn't included in that comment.) However:

- This is now conformant with an internal specification, which states that the "format default values" switch should only affect fields which don't support presence. That's actually the documented behavior as well (now): "This option only affects fields which don't support "presence" (e.g. singular non-optional proto3 primitive fields).". Message fields *always* support presence as you can tell the difference between `null` and a non-null reference.
- Changing it back now would be *another* breaking change. If we'd only just released the breaking change, it might be worth doing, but even when this issue was first raised, the new behavior had been out for over a year.

I'm going to close this as it's working as intended (and should be consistent with other languages), even though I completely agree it was a breaking change when it was first made.
@jskeet Have you considered adding a new option on the printer to include null values. I do understand your argument of presence, but our customers don't...

nodes.body: What file is the error found in? Do you have the complete source code of that file handy?
Can you confirm you're using the newest runtime when compiling the source code produced by that version of protoc? I think we've seen a similar issue in the past.

I've experienced a similar issue will trying to use the latest version of protoc, protbuf-java and grpc-java to being able to compile the protos in a Mac M1 trough the protobuf maven plugin.

com.google.protobuf.protoc = 3.19.1
protoc-gen-grpc-java.plugin = 1.42.1 (has an internal dependency on protobuf-java = 3.17.2) (does not contain `com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageV3.isStringEmpty`)
protobuf-java = 3.19.1
protobuf-java-util = 3.19.1

The problem is that the latest protoc generates code that depends on function (`com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageV3.isStringEmpty`) that are available from 3.17.3+.

So, as @perezd said, probably your compiling agains an older version of protobuf-java.

So a workaround would be using protoc 3.17.3 as I've mentioned https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8062#issuecomment-977716425 and https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/issues/8724 (where if also asked to upgrade to the latest protobuf 3.19.1 release)

```xml

    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.google.protobuf</groupId>
            <artifactId>protobuf-java</artifactId>
            <version>3.19.1</version> 
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.xolstice.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>protobuf-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>0.5.0</version>
                <extensions>true</extensions>
                <configuration>
                    <protoSourceRoot>${project.basedir}/proto</protoSourceRoot>
                    <outputDirectory>${project.build.sourceDirectory}</outputDirectory>
                    <clearOutputDirectory>true</clearOutputDirectory>
                    <temporaryProtoFileDirectory>
                        ${project.build.directory}/protoc-temp
                    </temporaryProtoFileDirectory>
                    <protocExecutable>
                        D:/arch/myexe/protoc/bin/protoc.exe <!-- libprotoc 3.19.1 -->
                    </protocExecutable>
                </configuration>
                <executions>
                    <execution>
                        <goals>
                            <goal>compile</goal>
                            <goal>test-compile</goal>
                        </goals>
                    </execution>
                </executions>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>


```

**implementation 'com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.19.1'**

title: Generated descriptor set reserved field range end off by one
body:
If I generate a descriptor (with `--descriptor_set_out`) for the following:

```protobuf
message Foo {
  reserved 1, 5 to 6;
}
```

I get the following (formatted as JSON for readability):

```json
{
  "name": "Foo",
  "reserved_range": [
    { "start": 1, "end": 2 },
    { "start": 5, "end": 7 },
  ]
}
```

What I expect to get is this:

```json
{
  "name": "Foo",
  "reserved_range": [
    { "start": 1, "end": 1 },
    { "start": 5, "end": 6 },
  ]
}
```

For enum reserved ranges, I do get the expected output, this is only for message reserved ranges.

protoc version:

```
$ protoc --version
libprotoc 3.19.1
```

nodes.body: Just a guess but it looks to me like the ranges are half-open: that is start is inclusive but end is  exclusive. This pattern has always confused me to, but it is common in programming for reasons I've never really followed. E.g. in Java String indices.

If that's the case, then there is a bug in the ranges for enums, because as I stated above, it's the opposite, the range is inclusive. One of them has to have a bug, they can't both have conflicting behaviour and be right. Which one will you accept? Should I raise another bug for enums?

That certainly sounds confusing and less than ideal. I'm not sure it's a bug though. They are two different things and could perhaps have been implemented at different times by different programmers who didn't realize they were being inconsistent with each other. Is one of them contrary to the specification? Or can you show a failing test that demonstrates a bug?

If there isn't a specification for the output of the file descriptors, that's a doc bug we should fix. 

And yes, I am saying that it is not a bug if enums and messages define the reserved ranges differently. It's not good that they do, and if anyone had noticed this way back when this was first created it certainly wouldn't have been done this way. However it's not wrong, just surprising and confusing. I doubt we could change the behavior now without breaking backwards compatibility.
I'm going to mark this closed since it appears to have been fixed. There are comments in descriptor.proto indicating which fields are meant to be inclusive and which are exclusive.

title: min/max namespace collision on Windows
body:
Hi,

I am using Windows 10, protobuf in C++.
When I updated to 3.19.1, my code does not compile anymore.

```
\protobuf-src\include\google/protobuf/stubs/stl_util.h(60,21): error C2589: '(': illegal token on right side of '::' 
\protobuf-src\include\google/protobuf/stubs/stl_util.h(60): error C2144: syntax error: 'unknown-type' should be preceded by ')' 
```

This is caused by the line
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v3.19.1/src/google/protobuf/stubs/stl_util.h#L60

And a classical min/max problem on Windows
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/13416418/define-nominmax-using-stdmin-max

A solution for me would be to `undef max` before including `protobuf`, I tested, it works, but it's quite hackish.
I think protobuf should protect itself from such uses and should not break existing builds when the users update to a newer version. 

Thank you

nodes.body: The way we usually work around this is to include `<google/protobuf/port_def.inc>` as the last include at the top of the file and then include `<google/protobuf/port_undef.inc>` at the end of the file. `port_def.inc` will `undef` the `max` macro and then `port_undef.inc` restores it. If you send me a pull request to do this in `stl_util.h` then I would be happy to merge it.

- Golang environment
  - go1.16.2 darwin/amd64
  - google.golang.org/protobuf v1.27.1
  - github.com/gogo/protobuf v1.3.2

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Write `prototest.proto` for a proto3 message including int64 type.
```proto
syntax = "proto3";
package tmp
option go_package = "my_project_path/tmp";

message Int64Msg {
  int64 i64 = 1;
}
```

2. Generate go source code
`protoc --go_out=$(GOPATH)/src -I./proto/ prototest.proto`

3. Run the following code in go.    

```go
func TestInt64(t *testing.T) {
	st := &Int64Msg{}
	st.I64 = 1638243612614987000

	bz, err := proto.Marshal(st)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	fmt.Printf("%x\n", bz0))
}
```

**Output is `08f899e0cbacbc8dde16`**

4. Generate javascript source code
`protoc --js_out=import_style=commonjs,binary:./proto -I./proto/ prototest.proto`

5. Run the following code in javascript.      

```js
import Proto from '../proto/prototest_pb.cjs';

let st = new Proto.Int64Msg();
st.setI64(1638243612614987000);
let bz = st.serializeBinary();
console.debug(Buffer.from(bz).toString('hex'));
```

**Output is `08809ae0cbacbc8dde16`**

6. golang's output (`08f899e0cbacbc8dde16`) is not equal to Javascript's output(`08809ae0cbacbc8dde16`)

**What did you expect to see**

The result of serializing the same data should be the same in both javascript and golang.


**What did you see instead?**

As mentioned,   
**golang's output (`08f899e0cbacbc8dde16`) is not equal to Javascript's output(`08809ae0cbacbc8dde16`)**

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body: Generally proto serialization is not deterministic at the byte level, not even within the same language binding, much less between languages. As long as the protos decode the same given the same schema, there's no bug here.

@elharo 

When the serialized in javascript is deserialized in golang, I think that the original value should be recovered. 
But it is not true.
In my case, 
when the `08809ae0cbacbc8dde16`(js serialization result)  is deserialized, the result is not `1638243612614987000` (original value) but `1638243612614987008`.

isn't it a bug?

If it is not a bug, why use the protobuf for serializing data?
Is the protobuf only for standalone application?

And the my problem is not the byte level. The 'int64' is scalar value type.

OK, that makes a little more sense. That said I think there's something inobvious happening here that has nothing to do with protos. What happens when you go JavaScript to JavaScript? JavaScript (not protos but JavaScript itself) represents all numbers as IEEE 754 doubles which do not have as much precision in the integer part as a true int64 or long. I suspect your long value is rounded because JavaScript cannot precisely represent 1638243612614987000.

See https://stackoverflow.com/questions/5353388/javascript-parsing-int64

@elharo 

Thank you!!!

I have one more question.

Why `jspb.BinaryConstants.TWO_TO_63` is `0x7fffffffffffffff`, which is larger than `2^53-1`
In the protobuf lib for javascript ("google-protobuf": "^3.18.0-rc.2"), 
the function writeInt64() allows integer less than this value to be serialized.

title: Code quality: use __attribute__((format)) with StringPrintf-family functions
body:
# What language does this apply to?

N/A, protobuf code quality/cleanup

# Describe the problem you are trying to solve.

Functions in the `StringPrintf` family accept a format string and forward it to `vsnprintf`, which make them textbook candidates for `__attribute__((format))`, a GNU extension that allows the compiler to check at compile-time that format specifiers used in a format string match the arguments that are passed. ([GCC documentation](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-3.2/gcc/Function-Attributes.html); no anchor available)

`__attribute__((format))` has been documented in gcc since version 2.95 released >20 years ago, and has been available in Clang at least since version 2.6 released >10 years ago, the first release to be included in LLVM. In both cases, the attribute has possibly been available for even longer. Both also support a `-Wformat=2` warning flag that request the compiler to warn aggressively about format string issues, including format specifier mismatches and format strings that cannot be verified to be static at compile-time.

While MSVC can type-check the variadic arguments of functions in the `printf` family, it does not appear to be possible at this time to direct this capability at user-defined functions.

Although the upstream version of protobuf dutifully uses the right format specifiers for all of its format strings, using `__attribute__((format))` when the compiler supports it would offer modest (but desirable) ecosystem services at a similarly modest cost by preventing issues in protobuf and its forks going forward.

Without this change, building protobuf with `-Wformat=2` will not allow the compiler to type-check `StringPrintf` invocations, and it will flag each `StringPrintf` function for using `vsnprintf` with a format string that hasn't been found to be valid somewhere else.

# Describe the solution you'd like

I am facing corporate obstacles securing the approval to sign the Google CLA. However, the solution I would like is fairly simple:

* Add a `PROTOBUF_` macro for the `__format__(printf, FMTIDX, VAARGIDX)` attribute (where FMTIDX is the one-based index of the function's format parameter, and VAARGIDX is the one-based index of the position of the ellipsis in the function prototype). This macro can be guarded by `PROTBUF_GNUC_MIN(2, 95)` or `__has_attribute(format)`, and be defined to nothing otherwise.
* Apply this macro to the declarations of `StringPrintf`, `SStringPrintf`, `StringAppendF` and `StringAppendV`.
* Enable `-Wformat=2` warning when building with Clang or GCC.
* Use [warning control pragmas](https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Diagnostic-Pragmas.html) to suppress `-Wformat` warnings around `StringPrintf` in `StringPrintfVector`, which cannot be verified (and, incidentally, is not used anywhere by the official protobuf).

I am also able and happy to answer questions regarding these attributes, although none of this should be considered a contribution.

body:

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: Java

**What did you do?**
I called `DynamicMessage.setField(FieldDescriptor field, Object value)` with a default value on a FieldDescriptor with explicit presence and expected it to be set.


**What did you see instead?**

The default value was not set due to this code:
```
      } else if (field.getFile().getSyntax() == Descriptors.FileDescriptor.Syntax.PROTO3) {
        if (!field.isRepeated()
            && field.getJavaType() != FieldDescriptor.JavaType.MESSAGE
            && value.equals(field.getDefaultValue())) {
          // In proto3, setting a field to its default value is equivalent to clearing the field.
          fields.clearField(field);
          return this;
        }
      }
```

Perhaps there needs to be a check of `field.getProto().isProto3Optional()` before calling `clearField()`

nodes.body:
I'm not 100% sure but I think this is working as intended. "Note that for scalar message fields, once a message is parsed there's no way of telling whether a field was explicitly set to the default value (for example whether a boolean was set to false) or just not set at all: you should bear this in mind when defining your message types. For example, don't have a boolean that switches on some behaviour when set to false if you don't want that behaviour to also happen by default. Also note that if a scalar message field is set to its default, the value will not be serialized on the wire."

Can you point to language in the spec that suggests the code shouldn't be behaving as you observe? Or produce a test case that gives clearly wrong output? I don't think there's a setField method in DynamicMessage

This sounds like a real bug to me. I think the key thing is that this field is explicitly marked `optional`, so it should not behave the same as usual proto3 singular fields: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/field_presence.md

Yes, I believe this is a real bug that is blocking our use of the `optional` keyword that was added back to Protobuf v3 in release 3.15.   Here is the language indicating that this is a bug:

```
- Explicit presence discipline:
   -  Explicitly set values are always serialized, including default values.
```
from https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/field_presence.md
This is not a bug after all.  The optional FieldDescriptor that I had created by hand was not in a synthetic oneof.

title: Wrong relative path in protobuf_generate
body:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/88384c99ec9621c0054e24bc80cab7709f550357/cmake/protobuf-config.cmake.in#L111
Under Windows, the command `file(RELATIVE_PATH _rel_dir ${DIR} ${_abs_dir})` returns an absolute path when the include path and the file path are on different drives.
Sample: called with $DIR=C:/include_path and _abs_dir = D:/current_repository/, the command returns an absolute path without any `..` in it.
The `_is_in_parent_folder` is set to false and therefore a wrong directory is accepted as relative path.
The result is that `_rel_dir` points to an absolute path which generates bad pathnames line 126

Tested with cmake 3.21

nodes.body: Thanks. What's the impact of this? What fails?

If you translate a file `D:/current_repository/package/proto_file.proto` with an include path of `[ C:/include_path, D:/current_repository ]`, the relative path should be `package`. But it is `D:/current_repository/package`

The generated cmake file contains a path "D:/current_repository/out_dir/D:/current_repository/package/proto_file.pb.h".
The inner `D:/current_repository/package` should only be `package`. In effect I'm unable to build the project.

As workaround, the order in the `IMPORT_DIRS` can be changed. If the "good" directory is the first entry in the list, the loop breaks in line 114 with the correct `package` and everything works fine.

Is this problem have some improve?

```cmake
find_package(Protobuf REQUIRED)
set(PROTO_GEN_DIR "${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}/pb")

protobuf_generate(
        PROTOS "${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}/../../pb/test.proto"
        TARGET Test
        IMPORT_DIRS "${PROJECT_SOURCE_DIR}/../../pb/"
        PROTOC_OUT_DIR "${PROTO_GEN_DIR}")

include_directories("${PROTO_GEN_DIR}")
target_link_libraries(Test PUBLIC protobuf::libprotobuf)
```

The Test target will include bad test.pb.cc path which in "../../pb/" but not "pb" directory.

I've encountered this issue today as well and was able to fix the behavior with a [simple check](https://github.com/cgudrian/protobuf/commit/668f6dc900870756f0ad17cfed0441cb128d84f5) in protobuf-generate.cmake. I have not yet tested whether this still works on non-Windows systems.

Here's the output of
```cmake
file(RELATIVE_PATH rel_dir ${base_dir} ${abs_dir})
```
for some combinations of `base_dir` and `abs_dir`:

|     base_dir      |           abs_dir           |           rel_dir           |
| ----------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `c:/Users/Me`     | `c:/Users/Me/test.cmake`    | `test.cmake`                |
| `c:/Users/Me`     | `c:/Users/You/test.cmake`   | `../You/test.cmake`         |
| **`c:/Users/Me`** | **`d:/project/test.cmake`** | **`d:/project/test.cmake`** |
| `/Users/Me`       | `/Users/Me/test.cmake`      | `test.cmake`                |
| `/Users/Me`       | `/Users/You/test.cmake`     | `../You/test.cmake`         |
| `/Users/Me`       | `/project/test.cmake`       | `../../project/test.cmake`  |

The bold combination is the one that makes path composition fail in Windows as this leads to the final composed path
```
c:/Users/Me/d:/project/test.cmake
```
which obviously won't work.

Looking at the other results (especially those using POSIX paths) I think that my quick workaround (see previous comment) should work on all systems (not only Windows). That workaround detects the problematic case (where CMake returns `abs_dir` unaltered) and skips to the next entry in the loop.

I'll open a pull request for this change.

title: Auto-generated Enum_ARRAYSIZE is incorrect if enum has negative values
body:
What version of protobuf and what language are you using?
Version: latest (haven't tested, just inspected code. originally discovered in the protobuf version that shipped with grpc v1.41.1)

What did you do?
Try making an enum that has a negative value. Then size will be wrong.

Summary:
The array size for an enum is computed [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/cpp_enum.cc#L151) as the `max + 1`. The `max` is hard-coded to be the largest value in the enum, just as the `min` is defined to be the minimum value (which can be negative). Therefore, I believe the length should actually be `(max - min) + 1` (assuming values are continuous).

Without fixing this, the `Enum_ARRAYSIZE` will be too small (one short for every negative enum there is).

@dazuma FYI

Sounds like it might be time to drop Ruby 2.4 support. Pinning to irb 1.1 was solely for the benefit of Ruby 2.4. But per https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/downloads/branches/, Ruby 2.4 has been eol since March 2020 (creeping up on two years ago).

I'd be supportive of dropping 2.4 at this time. Our cadence on the client library side has generally been to try to support versions for 10-11 months after the EOL date (i.e. until we're able to support the next new version after that EOL date). So client libraries officially dropped 2.4 early this year as soon as we got 3.0 support stable, and we expect to drop 2.5 support around the same time next year once 3.1 support is stable.
