title: Custom scalar type with own serializer
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
It could be a feature for all languages, but I need it mainly in C#.  C++ and node in addition.
I would need it only for proto3, but I think it is independent from them.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Currently I started developing a API with GRPC where the server is implemented in C# and clients can be at the end in any language, but in first step I have C#, Node and C++ in focus.
Defining the interface in IDL and generating code (service base class, client stub, request & response messages) is exactly what we need, because we don't want to spend lot of time in maintaining all the different clients.
So far no problem.
But have one problem where the usage is not nice and it could have performance impacts to the solution at all.

At some point of interface design you need to define the datatype of a request/response message field.
I know that it is possible to define sub-messages which can be used here. In the common interface definition (proto file) this is also fine, because it is now programming language independent.

In our API we have some message types I would call "scalar data types". They are definitions on top of basic types (string, int, ..) or structs which gives them a specific semantic.
Some examples for better understanding:
```
message BitField32
{
    uint32 value = 1;
}
```
The `BitField32` gives an 32 bit integer value the semantic of a field of bits with a length of 32 bits. In the implementation it provides methods which allows easy manipulating the bits.
```
message ObjectIdentifier {
  uint32 systemId = 1;
  uint32 objectId = 2;
  uint32 elementId = 3;
  uint32 attributeId = 4;
}
```
The second example is a implementation of a struct which combines several integer values to one object which gives them the semantic of addressing our solution objects by ID.

I know that the generated code can be easy extended by use of partial class, but this does not work for me for several reasons: 
The structs and classes are not defined by me, they are defined in a lower level of our application and it is not possible to bring a reference to protobuf to this assembly.
The objects are already delivered and used by customers and therefore I must consider also compatibility.
The objects are used by other solutions which are independent from our GRPC solution.

The only possible solution right now is to do it similar like the WellKnownTypes like `timestamp`.
In this case we need in our workflow always an additional conversion step from the proto type to the real type or vice versa.
This solution works and is also what we would implement in first step, but this additional conversion step is hard to understand by or customers, who will use the API. Furthermore this extra conversion step will sure not increase the performance.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

From a basic perspective I want like to archive that the generated code for common request/response messages uses instead of the generated proto types the already existing self implemented types, when there is such a type existing. If not than it generates the type like now.
But as the protoc compiler can't know how the memory model of the self implemented type is, it cant generate the seralizer code for it. This means this part must be implemented by my own.

I took a look at the code which is generated by the protoc compiler for C#.
I think the output can be logically split into following parts:
- Descriptor: Holding the reflection information about the types which are defined in IDL
- Message implementation: Properties for defined fields, some convenient like `Equals()`
- Serializer: Writer and parser logic for the defined message properties/fields

The descriptor logic is already most of it in a own class independent from the generated message type. I think this could stay almost as it is.
The message implementation is not needed, because it is self implemented.
The serializer is still needed but must be implemented partly manually.

The basic solution idea:
The protoc compiler generates for such messages just a abstract base class which is representing the serializer (writer + parser) and defines some virtual methods which needs to be implemented in concrete self-implemented class.
This base class has also properties and fields (e.g. index number, Parser, Descriptor, ...) which are currently available at generated message class.
I think in the protoc plugin this makes no big difference.

Important for me is also that the solution work with immutable structs.
I think this is only possible if there is a own interface definition for the serializer, because the current interface implies that the parser updates the current object, which is not possible for such structs. Here we would need the result as reference parameter so that it is the decision of implementation if it updates current object or creates new one.

Open question is: How does the protoc compiler plugin know which messages has there own serializer?
- The easiest way is to define a option at the message type. But this has the disadvantage that interface definition defines how it is implemented.
- Therefore I think it would be better to define it as command argument at protoc compiler.
- Or in a configuration file beside the other files which is given to the protoc compiler. This could be also a proto file.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

There is beside [Grpc.Core](https://github.com/grpc/grpc) and [Grpc-DotNet](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet) based on ASP.NET core also a third implementation [protobuf-net.Grpc](https://github.com/protobuf-net/protobuf-net.Grpc) for C#.
There it is possible to do also a code-first which maybe solve the problem. But this solution uses its own ecosystem (inclusive code generator) and is therefore incompatible to Grpc-DotNet. And I think it is less maintained, less documented and not so feature-rich (at least my impression). 
This are the main reasons why it is not a option for us.

title: Better Java8 support for repeated fields in builders
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?: Both
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?: Java

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Manipulating `Proto.Builder` objects doesn't often play nice with Java 8 constructs like streams and lambdas.
For example, it is pretty common to use a stream to fill up a builder:

```java
Foo foo =
    Foo.newBuilder()
      .addAllBar(
        bars.stream()
         .filter(Bars::isValid)
         .map(Bars::someTransform)
         .collect(toImmutableList())
    .build())
```

Note that we have to collect to an ImmutableList to feed the `bar`s to `addAllBars`, because that method only takes `Iterable`s, not streams. It's just a detail to keep the compiler happy; it does not capture programmer intention at all. Programmers also don't know if it is the most efficient intermediate structure; that seems like something the proto library would be more aware of.

It is also pretty common to want to modify repeated fields in builders. A `Foo.Builder` can give you a List of immutable `Bar`s, but the only way to get a mutable `Bar.Builder` is by index. So, you have to do this:

```java
for(int i = 0; i < foo.getBarCount(); i++) {
  fooBuilder.getBarBuilder(i).setQux(0);
}
```

Again, this iteration over indices is trivial here, but obfuscates programmer intent.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Would be great if `addAll` accepted `Stream`s directly:

```
Foo foo =
    Foo.newBuilder()
        .addAllBar(bars.stream().filter(Bars::isValid).map(Bars::someTransform))
        .build();
```

This could be implemented internally by simply collecting to a list, but presumably the maintainers of the proto library would know what was best.

It would also be nice to have some way to functionally manipulate repeated fields. Perhaps `Foo.Builder` could have a method that accepted a `Consumer<Bar.Builder>` like so:

```java
fooBuilder
  .updateBars(barBuilder->barBuilder.setQux(0))
  .build();
```

or, for more advance use, an updater that accepted a `Function<List<Bar>,<Stream<Bar>>>`:

```java
fooBuilder
  .updateBars(bars->
    bars.stream().map(...).filter(...)
  )
  .build();
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

I'm sure there is some way of using reflection to extract the `getBarCount` and `getBarBuilder` methods from a `Foo.Builder` instance in a generic way, and to use that to write a generic helper method to update any type of builder. But I couldn't write one, and it would hurt the fluency of the builder code- so I think it really does belong in the `Builder` class itself.

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

nodes.body: This is not an bad request; however, it has a risk of significantly increasing the size of built code for java mobile.  As such, we would have to take a great deal of care to test this, but it simply isn't a high priority right now.

title: Add std::optional support to generated C++ proto code.
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**

C++

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Transparently preserve presence information between proto and C++'s std::optional type.

Consider the code:

```proto
package my.proto;

message MyProto {
  optional double my_optional_field = 1;
}
```

```c++
struct MyStruct {
  explicit MyStruct(const MyProto& input)
      : my_optional_field(input.my_optional_field()) {}
  std::optional<double> my_optional_field;
};

int main() {
  MyProto my_proto;
  MyStruct my_struct(my_proto);
  return !(my_proto.has_my_optional_field() == my_strict.my_optional_field.has_value());
}
```

The program will return a nonzero (failure) exit code, but it should return success. That is, the presence data in the std::optional field should convey the presence data in the proto for the corresponding optional field. I only discovered that this occurs while tracking down how an unpopulated optional field was manifesting as a populated-but-invalid value in my program.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

The generated code should include casting operators for std::optional<typename> for optional fields of that type, wherein the returned `std::optional` object does or does not have a value depending on whether or not the field in the proto is or is not populated.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

My code for MyStruct at present must look like:

```c++
struct MyStruct {
  explicit MyStruct(const MyProto& input) {
    if(input.has_my_optional_field()) {
      my_optional_field = input.my_optional_field();
    }
  }
  std::optional<double> my_optional_field;
};
```

This is ungainly, especially when there is a mixture of optional and non-optional fields.

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

nodes.body: We have looked into this option, but have decided not to support it for a few reasons. First, it is in the best interest of the proto team to have pretty similar APIs across languages and having this specific ability in C++ but not in other languages could be problematic. Additionally, this would cause a large change in the design of Protocol Buffers since unset fields currently return a default value which users likely depend on.

title: PHP Package and PHP extension has different behavior when passing null message property which expects string
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: all version
Language: PHP

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
All Version
**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
All runtimes
**What did you do?**
When passing null to message property which expect string get error invalid value passed but when using package there are no such error.

For example 
```
message TestProtobuf{
      string random_property = 1; 
}
```

With package 
```
$test = new TestProtobuf();
$test->setRandomProperty(null);
```
no errors but with extensions
```
$test = new TestProtobuf();
$test->setRandomProperty(null);
```
exception.

I managed to track to [part](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/01e84b129361913e5613464c857734fcfe095367/php/ext/google/protobuf/convert.c#L339) it looks like it doesn't have case for `NULL`

nodes.body:
The C extension and the pure-PHP library should have the same behavior. Cases where the behavior differs should be fixed.

In this case, we would have to decide whether we should allow `NULL` or not.  I would lean towards not allowing it here.
if we don't allow NULL how should we handle when not all message property are set? IMO we should allow NULL

> if we don't allow NULL how should we handle when not all message property are set? 

I don't follow.

1. You can always write `$test->setRandomProperty("")`.
2. We could consider supporting `$test->clearRandomProperty()`, which we will definitely want if we support proto2.
Closing due to no response, feel free to reopen with more details if you're still seeing this.

Hi! Sorry for opening this again, but the error still happens. The problem is that if you come from using the package, switching to the php extension may break your application, because you might be setting some property to null (because the package allowed it)  and it will work but then you switch to using the extension and it  will throw an error.

For example:

Given this message:
```
message TestProtobuf{
      string random_property = 1; 
}
```

And given this piece of code:

```
$test = new TestProtobuf();
$test->setRandomProperty(null);
```

**With the package**

This will result in `$test->random_property` being set to `''` (empty string) due to `GPBUtil::checkString` function casting its value to the [string default value](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/01e84b129361913e5613464c857734fcfe095367/php/src/Google/Protobuf/Internal/GPBUtil.php#L98C9-L100C10)
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c98947fa-b0bc-4d2e-bdeb-63289a490bbb)


**Now with the extension**

The same piece of code will result in an error because of [this](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/01e84b129361913e5613464c857734fcfe095367/php/ext/google/protobuf/convert.c#L50C3-L51C70)
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6de8bede-8b37-4d4e-8102-67fda3e09b52)

title: [C-Sharp] Inconsistent generated code for wrapper primitive types and new proto3 `optional` keyword

nodes.body:
CC @jskeet @haberman @moserware

@jskeet  and @haberman  will probably know more about why we chose the approach we did for proto3 optional.

> If for some reason we need to avoid the breaking change for the default behavior

... which we do, to avoid breaking everyone who already uses it, including the Google Cloud client libraries. Note that support for optional in proto3 isn't really "very new" - it's been in the protoc for C# since April 2020.

It's worth noting that in the current design, adding `optional` to a field is not a breaking change in terms of the generated code. It adds the ability to detect whether or not something was explicitly set, but that's all. Using nullable types instead changes that completely. While it's been a long time since I implemented the C# support, I expect that was my reasoning for the design at the time... as well as it following what Java does, as the most similar language.

I would be strongly against changing the default behavior. I would be moderately against introducing a plugin option for this, as I expect it will make the plugin code significantly more complex, and have repercussions on the library support as well.

As I'm not on the protobuf team it's not my decision though.

I agree with @jskeet on all points. I would add that a primary goal of protobuf is to have consistent semantics across languages.  One of those semantics is that `optional` fields return a default value when unset, not `null`.

For protos with `syntax="proto2";` [you can even set an explicit default value in the `.proto` file](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#optional). If we returned `null` instead of the specified default, this would create an even larger behavior difference between languages.

A lot of users request `nullable` semantics, and many languages have types that represent this (eg. `std::optional` in C++, `Option` in Rust, etc). To bring this to protobuf, it would need to be a larger effort that targets all languages, not just some, in order to keep the semantics consistent across languages.

>> To bring this to protobuf, it would need to be a larger effort that targets all languages, not just some, in order to keep the semantics consistent across languages.

So why was the `optional` keyword brought back into Proto3 and [Google recommending using it in place of nullable types](https://cloud.google.com/apis/design/design_patterns.md#optional-primitive-fields) if it wasn't to do exactly what you're saying, i.e. a larger effort to target all languages to represent nulls consistently?

And yes agree there is a difference in the on the wire representation of the wrapper object vs the nullable field, but technically making a field go from nullable to not nullable or visa versa IS a breaking change or at least should be considered that from the point of view of your code base. I would want it if I changed that field that everywhere it used to compile would now need review with a compiler warning which is exactly what would happen in C# if you did that and the field actually became a nullable field.   It doesn't break your code, but it will warn you that there might be an issue now.

However because you don't change anything about the property when you change it from non-optional, to optional in the current implementation, you negate that whole benefit.

You also argued my case in the last point. 
>> A lot of users request nullable semantics, and many languages have types that represent this

The C# implementation of Protobuf DOES use nullable semantics because C# is a language that supports it. I'm just saying that the intent of an "optional" field is exactly that, a nullable type. So C# should use nullable types there. You're already doing it for the wrapper types!  While I might agree that this could be considered a breaking change and should be gated behind some option, it should still be available.  It's logically the correct answer even if it does cause differentiation between the proto2 and proto3 representations.  There is already differences between them.  If google recommends you don't use the well known wrapper types any more in exchange for using the new "optional" keyword, then if I convert my proto files from using wrapper types to optional keywords, they should generally function similarly in the generated code.

> I would add that a primary goal of protobuf is to have consistent semantics across languages.

Unfortunately that ship has long sailed. 

Protobuf.js for instance went with `optional` returning `null`: https://github.com/protobufjs/protobuf.js/pull/1584, as did several other libraries. It's not surprising when google's docs literally say:

> Protocol Buffers v3 (proto3) supports optional primitive fields, which are semantically equivalent to nullable types in many programming languages. 

This is the page where google recommends getting rid of wrapper types, and when it says that most libraries can't even tell the difference, it's clear that factors into their motivation for their recommendation.

The fact that C# can tell the difference makes it unusual, but worse C# doesn't allow migrating from one to the other. If your API is using wrappers and you want to switch to optional, you not only have to worry about serialization changes (which are to be expected and can be handled by renaming proto fields) but you have to worry about rewriting all your code, removing any situation where you use an expression to create a protobuf.

It's incredibly odd to see the library massively changed it's mind on how to handle semantically equivalent things, especially when they new way is more awkward to use, doesn't play well with core language ideas, and comes at a time where the downsides of using `null` are massively decreased within C#.

I understand not wanting to introduce breaking changes, but that happened when `optional` support was added. Worse it's not a compile-time error in the case of `optional string`, it's a runtime error. You'll change wrapper values to optional, as google says you "must" do, and everything will seem to work until the day you start getting exceptions on production and discover the change in nullable semantics. Introducing a change here will be a breaking change for those of us who've already been burned by this, but it makes it so anyone who hasn't migrated yet will no longer come across this silent major change.  And I think those of us who have already migrated our protos are willing to accept another breaking change when it means such a huge improvement in both type safety and ease of use.

nodes.body:
The cycle is:

  - `protobuf.rb` -> `descriptor_dsl.rb`
  - `descriptor_dsl.rb` -> `descriptor_pb.rb`
  - `descriptor_pb.rb` -> `protobuf.rb`

Simplest fix would be to split out [this fragment from `protobuf.rb`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/b48ba578dd01adfebeb4fac0887db1eeb163e00f/ruby/lib/google/protobuf.rb#L44-L54) into its own file, say `protobuf/_extension.rb`

Then the generated code (eg. `descriptor_pb.rb`) could require only `google/protobuf/_extension`.
Warning was removed in the attached PR.
Great, thanks @ntkme and @haberman!

title: Revisit upb_msg_next() and extension behavior
body:
The upb_msg_next() function currently returns extensions iff the `ext_pool` parameter is provided.

This may not be necessary; the `upb_symtab` can be derived from the `upb_msgdef`. Do we know of any cases where we would want a different extension pool?

Also should there be a more explicit way of including/excluding extensions.

title: C++ Python implementation handles bytes/strings differently from pure python impl
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

Compile
```

Consistent behavior. I actually think the pure-python behavior is more correct, but any consistent behavior would be ok.

Today I started updating our apps and noticed that `google-protobuf` is not compatible with Ruby 3.1 yet.

Cheers and Happy New Year.

body:

Ubuntu 20.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
GCC11 and Clang13

**What did you do?**
Generated a simple message and tried to compile it with our toolchain and default warnings.

**What did you expect to see**
No warning / no error.

**What did you see instead?**
Member ZeroFieldsBase::_cached_size_ is shadowed in derived classes.

For example: src/google/protobuf/empty.pb.h defines class Empty, extending ZeroFieldsBase and defining _cached_size_ yet again.

The field in the base class is defined as 

     mutable internal::CachedSize _cached_size_;

while the field in the derived classes is defined as:

      mutable ::PROTOBUF_NAMESPACE_ID::internal::CachedSize _cached_size_;


Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

Is this shadowing intentional? Can the field in the ZeroFieldsBase be renamed to avoid it?

title: protoc: imports and descriptors resolver plugin support
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

protoc, just the compiler itself.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

At the moment, protoc loads imports and descriptors from local files only. All dependencies have to be either vendored, causing redundancy and risk getting out of sync, or complex build tools like Bazel have to be used to specify repos to map a source to an include path. And there's still a risk that import paths are ambiguous: a too generic path like `"service/options.proto"` might come from more than one source.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

It would be great if protoc allows specifying an imports and descriptors resolver plugin via flag, similar to how output plugins are supported. The default resolver looks for local files. A custom resolver could fetch and make available external imports, like `import "github.com/owner/repo/path/file.proto@v1.2.3";` (similar to Go module resolution) or Bazel like labels: `import "@repo//package:path/file.proto";`.

Additionally and to safeguard backwards compatibility, the `remote` qualifier keyword for imports would trigger non-local resolution. That should prevent any surprises, but requires change to the syntax.

`import remote "github.com/owner/repo/path/file.proto@v1.2.3";`

(Can be combined with `public`.)

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

A syntactical change to proto files in form of a new directive or a file option to specify the source location(s).

nodes.body: #8067 is related. That case could be handled by the above proposal by allowing remote files like `github.com/owner/repo/path/file.proto@latest` to be specified on the command line and the resolver would do the same as for imports.
Maybe an ExternalResolverSourceTree implementation would be a good start. It runs the executable resolver plugin in the background and relays mapping requests via stdin/stdout.

Inside google this problem is completely solved by the source repository. .proto files are source code and can be shared just like .java files, .xml files, .py files or anything else. This doesn't seem like a feature that belongs in the layer of the proto library itself.

Yes, I know how it works inside Google, spent over eight years there. The outside world is a lot less homogenous, source code is much more distributed, not everyone can use blaze/bazel. And I wasn't suggesting to turn the protoc compiler into a package manager, just to add a hook that would allow external tools to handle import-path translations.

title: php: Not possible to emit unpopulated fields in JSON encoding
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?** 
PHP

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
With `google.golang.org/protobuf/encoding/protojson`, there's an [option](https://pkg.go.dev/google.golang.org/protobuf/encoding/protojson#MarshalOptions) to emit unpopulated fields:

```go
	// EmitUnpopulated specifies whether to emit unpopulated fields. It does not
	// emit unpopulated oneof fields or unpopulated extension fields.
	// The JSON value emitted for unpopulated fields are as follows:
	//  ╔═══════╤════════════════════════════╗
	//  ║ JSON  │ Protobuf field             ║
	//  ╠═══════╪════════════════════════════╣
	//  ║ false │ proto3 boolean fields      ║
	//  ║ 0     │ proto3 numeric fields      ║
	//  ║ ""    │ proto3 string/bytes fields ║
	//  ║ null  │ proto2 scalar fields       ║
	//  ║ null  │ message fields             ║
	//  ║ []    │ list fields                ║
	//  ║ {}    │ map fields                 ║
	//  ╚═══════╧════════════════════════════╝
	EmitUnpopulated bool

```

In the PHP extension, I [see](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/66d749188ff2a2e30e932110222d58da7c6a8d49/php/ext/google/protobuf/php-upb.h#L4802) `UPB_JSONENC_EMITDEFAULTS`, which looks like what we're looking for, but no way to set it in `serializeToJsonString` on the message itself.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/a1d8f8f96900468f09ced2ce9d23dea5a1bc070c/php/ext/google/protobuf/message.c#L773-L812

I also took a glance through the pure PHP protobuf library and didn't see any reference to this functionality.

My organization uses PHP (w/ protobuf C extension) to serialize messages to JSON for consumption by non-protobuf-enabled clients, so an absent field is functionally different than one with its default value.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Parity with Golang protobuf JSON encoding: the ability to emit unpopulated fields.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
🤷‍♂️ 

**Additional context**
N/A

Yes this is missing functionality in PHP that would make sense to add.

The only tricky part is API. Currently there is a single optional `bool` parameter for `preserve_proto_fieldnames`. We would want to change this into a keyword arguments array, so a user could specify either one of these options by name.

I don't remember exactly how arguments arrays work in PHP, but feel free to send a PR for this.

title: Disable check for Objective C compiler (AC_PROG_OBJC) on non-macOS systems
body:
Autotools build system currently unconditionally checks for Objective C compiler:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/0ac74b8126b76498075f43c37603d67a15d8d205/configure.ac#L83

However later there is:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/0ac74b8126b76498075f43c37603d67a15d8d205/configure.ac#L217-L224

`OBJC_CONFORMANCE_TEST` is used in `conformance/Makefile.am`.
The only usage of Objective C compiler is for compiling source files which are used only when `OBJC_CONFORMANCE_TEST` is true.

This means that aforementioned check for Objective C compiler is unnecessary on non-macOS systems (when `$target_os` != `darwin*`).

Fix:
```
--- configure.ac
+++ configure.ac
@@ -80,7 +80,7 @@
 ACX_USE_SYSTEM_EXTENSIONS
 m4_ifdef([AM_PROG_AR], [AM_PROG_AR])
 AM_CONDITIONAL(GCC, test "$GCC" = yes)   # let the Makefile know if we're gcc
-AC_PROG_OBJC
+AS_CASE([$target_os], [darwin*], [AC_PROG_OBJC], [AM_CONDITIONAL([am__fastdepOBJC], [false])])
 
 # test_util.cc takes forever to compile with GCC and optimization turned on.
 AC_MSG_CHECKING([C++ compiler flags...])
```

nodes.body: Does this break anything?
We have downstream report of user ("targeting Gentoo Linux and Chromium OS") complaining about check for Objective-C compiler selection: https://bugs.gentoo.org/830584
cc @10ne1

For context, we are interested in building packages only with LLVM tools/Clang and OBJC defaults to gcc. We intentionally block GCC/binutils, but we still need to keep it around for glibc and a very small handful of other packages which can't be built with LLVM/Clang (yet! it will happen eventually heh).

Again this is only a minor annoyance because we can explicitly set OBJC to Clang, but it would be nice to not have to do so. Thanks again!
I'm not likely to get the to look at this in the near future, if someone wants to submit a patch, great.

`https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/6113` (also important for ABI compatibility) and possibly other bugs still remain.

title: Proto3 docs refer to "optional" proto2 field rule?
body:
["Updating a message type" in "Language Guide (proto3)"](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#updating) has the following
> For `string`, `bytes`, and message fields, `optional` is compatible with `repeated`. Given serialized data of a repeated field as input, clients that expect this field to be `optional` will take the last input value if it's a primitive type field or merge all input elements if it's a message type field. Note that this is not generally safe for numeric types, including bools and enums. Repeated fields of numeric types can be serialized in the packed format, which will not be parsed correctly when an `optional` field is expected.

If I have understood right, `optional` is a field rule only in proto2, more or less matching proto3 default, singular? ("Specifying Field Rules" in ["Language Guide (proto2)"](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#specifying_field_rules) vs in ["Language Guide (proto3)"](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#specifying_field_rules))

Thus verifying: Does the above excerpt apply for proto3 singular and if yes, could it be updated? Thanks!

title: Specify that varints should be encoded shortest possible way
body:
Encoding spec at https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding is underspecified. It doesn't say whether non-canonical varint serializations are allowed (i. e. whether it is okey to serialize number "5" as two bytes). I propose to explicitly forbid such serializations. I. e. to require reader to fail when reading such serialization. This will ensure (at least for simple schemas) that equal values serialize to equal binary strings.

This bug is also present in other binary formats, which explicitly refer to "protobuf varint", for example, Avro ( https://avro.apache.org/docs/current/spec.html ), this page contains link to https://code.google.com/apis/protocolbuffers/docs/encoding.html#types . So, I propose using very careful wording, which will refer not only to protobuf, but to varint itself. I. e. use wording, which implies you are defining meaning of "varint", not meaning of "protobuf". I. e. write "non-canonical byte strings are not valid varints" instead of "non-canonical byte strings are not allowed in protobuf". The former wording defines term "varint", not term "protobuf" and thus "fixes" not only protobuf, but also all specs explicitly referring to protobuf varint, such as Avro.

It would be even better to explicitly write "In all other specs for various binary formats non-canonical varint encodings are forbidden unless explicitly stated otherwise in that spec"

nodes.body: I think we actually want to allow non-canonical varints. Our implementations always make them as short as possible, but sometimes it's useful to make them larger than necessary so that you have a consistent size. There's an implementation called [ProtoZero](https://perfetto.dev/docs/design-docs/protozero#deferred-patching) that does this for example.
@acozzette , if you really want to support non-canonical varints, then please write in spec explicitly that they are allowed

Everything not forbidden is permitted.

Might be worth clarifying this point, but the spec is not incomplete as written, nor could we add an additional requirement like this at this time without breaking backwards compatibility. On a related note, it might be worth auditing our code to make sure it behaves correctly in the face of longer than required varints.

title: Utf8.decodeUtf8: Simplify and optimize for ascii strings
body:
`Utf8.decodeUtf8` can be replaced with a call to `String(byte[] bytes, int offset, int length, Charset charset)` and then a search for the replacement string `'\uFFFD'` in order to decide whether to throw `InvalidProtocolBufferException`.

If this idea is not ruled out, I can provide benchmark results that compare different strings (ascii / non ascii). Spoiler: for ascii strings of 50 characters this method is ~30% faster than the current implementation on modern JVMs.

I created a PR that makes this idea concrete.

nodes.body: What do benchmarks show for non-ASCII strings?

Tested out the following strings:
"The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" (ascii)
"Quizdeltagerne spiste jordbær med fløde, mens cirkusklovnen" (German, ISO-8859-1 code points, requiring a single byte per codepoint in Java 9)
"𠜎𠜱𠝹𠱓𠱸𠲖𠳏𠳕𠴕𠵼𠵿𠸎𠸏𠹷𠺝𠺢" (Chinese)

The comparison was between current `Utf8.decodeUtf8` with `UnsafeProcessor` and the suggested version of `decodeUtf8`.

I ran the tests with Java 8/11/17 on my Mac.

Regarding the terrible performance of Java 11/17 for German, this baffled me so after consulting with HotSpot folks, it will get resolved in [this](https://github.com/openjdk/jdk/pull/7034) PR.

Summarizing the results for Java 11/17:
ascii is 30% faster.
German is 100% slower but the allocation rate is 25% lower.
Chinese is 12 - 20% slower

body:
In the [encoding documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding), I read:

`If you use int32 or int64 as the type for a negative number, the resulting varint is always ten bytes long`

Shouldn't this be 5 bytes for int32? Since a varint can store 7 bits per byte, with 5 bytes we can store 5 * 7 = 35 bits, which is enough for any 32 bit value.

nodes.body: The docs are correct as written. Negative int32's occupy ten bytes. I whipped up a quick test to verify this, and if you dig around in CodedOutputStream.java you'll see how.

Okay, thanks for clearing this up.

I guess they made it this way so int32 and int64 are compatible.

title: Compile error with clang for x86 Windows in debug mode
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.19.3 / master

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux / Windows

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
clang 13.0.0 / trunk

**What did you do?**
Try to compile the `generated_message_tctable_lite.cc` file with Clang to x86 Windows target without optimizations.
Example command for this (paths to windows sysroot must be changed):
```sh
cd src
clang++ -I. -target i386-windows -Xclang -internal-isystem -Xclang path_to_win_sysroot/msvc/include -Xclang -internal-isystem -Xclang path_to_win_sysroot/winsdk/include/ucrt -Xclang -internal-isystem -Xclang path_to_win_sysroot/winsdk/include/shared -Xclang -internal-isystem -Xclang path_to_win_sysroot/winsdk/include/um -std=c++20 -c google/protobuf/generated_message_tctable_lite.cc
```

**What did you expect to see**
Compile succeeds

**What did you see instead?**
Clang crashes with `fatal error: error in backend: failed to perform tail call elimination on a call site marked musttail` error
The bug is in LLVM, I've reported it there as well with a minimized reproduction case: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/issues/53271

**Proposed solution**
This happens because the `[[clang::musttail]]` attribute is not properly working on Windows x86. In https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/41e22cde8d8a44c35127a26c19e08b180e0b30a4/src/google/protobuf/port_def.inc#L233 there is already some architectures listed where this attribute is disabled, add x86 windows to that list. I'll open a PR with this approach.

nodes.body: https://blog.reverberate.org/2021/04/21/musttail-efficient-interpreters.html

This applies to mips64 too, so protobuf with clang13 (on openbsd 7.2 for instance) fails unless something like this is added:
```
 #endif
-#if __has_cpp_attribute(clang::musttail) && !defined(__arm__) && \
+#if __has_cpp_attribute(clang::musttail) && !defined(__arm__) && !defined(__mips64__) && \
     !defined(_ARCH_PPC) && !defined(__wasm__) &&                 \
     !(defined(_MSC_VER) && defined(_M_IX86)) &&                  \
     !(defined(__NDK_MAJOR__) && __NDK_MAJOR <= 24)
```

I took a look at this (including all of the comments posted at https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab/-/issues/350296).

I am not too familiar with the tracepoint functionality of the Ruby interpreter. The fact that the protobuf C extension is not on the C stack when this crash occurs leads me to believe that the protobuf C extension is not the culprit. If we were failing to properly GC-root any of our objects, I would expect a much more obvious failure that is easier to reproduce.

Any chance you can reproduce this under Valgrind? It could help determine whether there are any other memory errors occurring prior to the actual SEGV.
I'm wondering if the problem might be resolved by https://github.com/ruby/ruby/pull/5470. I'm going to merge this into our CI and see.

Thank you both for looking into this, appreciate it!

> Any chance you can reproduce this under Valgrind?

Not yet; I will spend some time on this today again. I had tried to reproduce it by isolating out the code in question and artificially applying GC pressure, hoping it would lead to a crash earlier or more frequently, but it hasn't crashed on me once even after thousands of iterations.
I've run it through `Memcheck` several times now, but it hasn't come back with anything.

Without any Valgrind errors, and without protobuf code in the stack trace, it's hard to see how this would be a bug in protobuf.

I'm going to close this for now, please re-open if you get any more specific evidence that protobuf is at fault here.
Agree, will do, thanks!

title: Improve FileDescriptor.BuildFromByteStrings in C#
body:
Hello!

**What language does this apply to?**

C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

The following API `FileDescriptor.BuildFromByteStrings` is relatively impractical to use directly:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/41e22cde8d8a44c35127a26c19e08b180e0b30a4/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/Reflection/FileDescriptor.cs#L486-L521

The underlying code forces the input byte strings to be ordered. In order to order them, you need to load them in proto class instead, re-order them by their dependencies and re-serialize back to ByteString. This is quite inefficient.

I had to workaround this while developing [grpc-curl](https://github.com/xoofx/grpc-curl):

https://github.com/xoofx/grpc-curl/blob/f7bbe35af79713f278150b96ce51817807a06581/src/DynamicGrpc/DynamicFileDescriptorSet.cs#L139-L163

**Describe the solution you'd like**

* This API should handle the re-order. We are already loading the proto from the loop. We can resolve them in the same go to properly order them before initializing the `FileDescriptor`.
* A new API could be added to also allow to load from `FileDescriptorProto` directly.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

The workaround is described above and is inefficient.

**Additional context**
none

nodes.body: I ran into this recently as well, and it is indeed a pain. It doesn't help that the [C# service implementation](https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet/blob/38738af700a3180e87054f922f953e67d9cdd82b/src/Grpc.Reflection/ReflectionServiceImpl.cs#L141) also doesn't return things in dependency order since it uses a HashSet internally. Fixing that would help alleviate the need for this improvement, but it would only help when communicating with services implemented in C#. I'm not sure what other language implementations typically do here, but to be safe, the dependency order checking is probably still needed. If nothing else, have the server return things in the proper order would at least prevent worst case search performance in the work around code linked above.

title: Make some internals of FieldCodec<T> public
body:
Hello,

**What language does this apply to?**

C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

In [grpc-curl](https://github.com/xoofx/grpc-curl), I have to serialize/deserialize message directly from existing user structures (e.g `List<double>`). 

The current API forces to copy existing structures to e.g `RepeatedField<double>` in order to serialize/deserialize back:

```c#
  case FieldType.Double:
      {
          var repeated = new RepeatedField<double>();
          // TODO: inefficient copy here!
          foreach(var item in values) repeated.Add(Convert.ToDouble(item));
          repeated.WriteTo(ref output, FieldCodec.ForDouble(tag));
      }
      break;
```

It makes it also difficult to build e.g an efficient protocol dispatcher that can dispatch early while decoding.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Make many fields in FieldCodec more public:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/41e22cde8d8a44c35127a26c19e08b180e0b30a4/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/FieldCodec.cs#L684-L742

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

The copy performed above, but very inefficient. 

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

nodes.body:
(Apologies that it's taken so long to get to this.)

Could you use `CodedOutputStream.WriteTag` and `CodedOutputStream.WriteDouble` (etc)?

I'm personally reluctant to make more of the API public if we can possibly avoid it - because it limits future changes. For example, the current `ValueWriter<T>` delegate was only introduced in 2020 - if we'd made everything about FieldCodec public before, we probably wouldn't have been able to introduce that and migrate FieldCodec to it, at least without keeping all of the old behavior as well. (The `ValueWriter` property used to be an `Action<CodedOutputStream, T>`.)

I do feel your pain here, but I'd really prefer to keep the flexibility of keeping this internal.
It has been a long time since I looked at that code, I think I tried to use other APIs back in the days but it was not possible, but maybe I missed something. I'll try to double check later tonight.

nodes.body:
David Seifert (@SoapGentoo) analysed the [bug](https://bugs.gentoo.org/831728#c1) on our Bugzilla:
>on my Ryzen:
>alignof(std::mutex):      8
>alignof(pthread_mutex_t): 8
>alignof(max_align_t):     16
>
>on a HP C8000:
>alignof(std::mutex):      16
>alignof(pthread_mutex_t): 16
>alignof(max_align_t):     8
>
>That is, on HPPA any struct/class that includes a std::mutex as member automatically becomes an over-aligned type. Over-aligned types have a history of being hard to deal with in C and C++, because std::malloc only guarantees the alignment of >its returned pointer to alignof(std::max_align_t). As such, up to and including C++14, such types could not be used in >standard containers like std::vector, as they lacked the mechanisms to request correctly aligned memory for such types >(C++17 has fixed this).
>
>The alignment to 16 bytes is not a bug, this is due to PA-RISC's requirement for 16 byte aligned words and doublewords for memory locking (https://parisc.wiki.kernel.org/images-parisc/7/73/Parisc2.0.pdf, p106 last paragraph).
>
>I have tried protobuf by just sed'ing out the offending static_assert on a C8000, and the code compiled fine for me. I haven't done any in-depth tests to check whether the code works fine.

It looks like Debian have needed to use a similar workaround for e.g. [MySQL](https://www.mail-archive.com/debian-bugs-dist@lists.debian.org/msg1793133.html). Note that the contributor of that patch is one of the maintainers of the HPPA GCC port, so with the above analysis, I'm reasonably sure that we need to just `#ifdef` this for HPPA for the time being until C++17.

I'll try running the test suite on 3.17 (which builds for me) and on 3.19.1 with the workaround applied and compare.
Test suite passes with the assert removed on HPPA.
This code no longer exists at head. Please confirm if this is still an issue.

So, disabling opcache is a simple quick fix.

If this only occurs on 8.1, and only with opcache enabled, it seems like something changed on the PHP side.

It seems like perhaps the message is being destroyed between Message_create() and zim_Message___construct(). Or perhaps it's being constructed without being created first.

That is correct, there has been no movement on this issue.

We have not received a repro for this issue, and the fact that the issue only occurs with opcache enabled suggests to me that something has changed on the PHP side -- either a bug or an intended semantic change that breaks protobuf somehow.

Unless PHP 8.1 has introduced a known/documented change in the C API semantics, I'm inclined to think this is a bug on the PHP side.

The only somewhat unusual thing we are doing (that I know of) is this. If the PHP 8.1 opcache breaks this behavior somehow, perhaps we need to stop doing this: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/10df21ed5e06df20385f1ee8ca01ecd22e0e4087/php/ext/google/protobuf/message.c#L63-L76

@remicollet may have ideas here.

>   // This also allows us to put our zend_object member at the beginning of our

zend_object should be the last entry since 7.0, and minimal supported version is 7.0... (according to package.xml)

If we think that this SEGV might possibly be related to the `zend_object` thing, I'm happy to change it.

In the past, putting `zend_object` first has helped us detect and disable cases where PHP was adding unnecessary and unwanted storage into our objects, eg. property storage that we do not need or want.

My team cannot update to 8.1 until this issue has been fixed. It's now over 6 months since the release of 8.1. What progress has been made, should we expect an update soon?

We will migrate off protobuf if there is no plans to resolve the issue. Deactivating OPCache is not feasible.

Thank you. @haberman @remicollet

To date we have still not received a repro. Without a repro, the best we can do is guess. The best way to help accelerate a fix is to provide us with a self-contained repro.

We can try making the change I outlined in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9446#issuecomment-1079255619, but that idea is based on guesswork. If it does not fix the problem, we are back to square one.

I will work on implementing the idea in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9446#issuecomment-1079255619 and hope it helps. Hopefully we can get it into the release that will be going out in the next week or two.

After starting the implementation of this, I feel some more confidence that this theory is correct, and that the idea mentioned above will fix these SEGVs.

On the downside, the simple fix will also increase memory usage, because we will be allocating storage for message fields at both the PHP and the C levels. This is a side effect of the fact that we use the same generated code for both pure-PHP and C-accelerated PHP, so the generated classes always have PHP-level properties for all message fields.

Previously we were suppressing the PHP-level properties when using the C extension, but this hack appears to be incompatible with OPCache. So we will have to allocate memory for the PHP properties even when using the C extension, which will increase memory usage until we can change the generated code.

I have implemented the change I described above in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9930

Can anybody who is experiencing this problem try this out to verify whether it fixes the SEGVs? Unfortunately it will probably have some CPU/memory overhead also, so it could cause regressions if deployed to prod. But if there is a test cluster that reliably reproduces the behavior, a test there would be very helpful.

If this indeed addresses the root cause of the issue, we should rework the generated code so that we get the fix without the overhead.

I have managed to reproduce this locally!

Thanks everyone for your help in reaching this point. This will make it much easier to get to a root cause.

A few early results that rule out possible causes:

* Crash occurs even with `opcache.optimization_level=0`, so we can rule out opcache optimizations as a root cause.
* Crash occurs even with `opcache.jit=disable`, so we can rule out the opcache JIT as a root cause.
* Crash occurs regardless of whether `opcache.preferred_memory_model` is set to `mmap`, `shm`, or `posix`.

The crashes appear to be specific to the shared memory operation under concurrency:

* Crash does *not* occur with `opcache.file_cache_only=1`, so it requires that shared memory is activated.
* Crash does *not* occur unless we make concurrent requests

I have a fix that appears to work for me: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9995

If anyone can confirm the fix, that would be very helpful to ensure that this fixes the bug for others.

title: Java: TextFormat.unescapeBytes unable to decode a valid UTF8 escape
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: `com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.17.3`
Language: `Java/Kotlin`

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

macOS 12.1

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

`kotlin` @ `1.4.20`

```
...
    kotlinOptions.jvmTarget = "11
....
```

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

```
TextFormat.unescapeBytes("\\U000358da")
```

Happy to set up the full file if needed.

**What did you expect to see**

String with unescaped sequences.

**What did you see instead?**

```
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException
        at com.google.protobuf.TextFormat.unescapeBytes(TextFormat.java:2432)
```

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

Using `org.apache.commons.lang3.StringEscapeUtils` I was able to unescape this sequence and get a character that got properly converted to bytes.

nodes.body: \u was introduced in C++ 11. I'm not sure we support that format, though the docs should be clearer on this point.

"Escapes bytes in the format used in protocol buffer text format, which is the same as the format used for C string literals. All bytes that are not printable 7-bit ASCII characters are escaped, as well as backslash, single-quote, and double-quote characters. Characters for which no defined short-hand escape sequence is defined will be escaped using 3-digit octal sequences."
See TextFormatTest. \U000358da is not a valid escape sequence for this method.

@elharo 

> See TextFormatTest. \U000358da is not a valid escape sequence for this method.

Could you please clarify that? I definitely see tests for unicode escapes:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/core/src/test/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormatTest.java#L916

Looking at the implementation, it's 8 bytes as expected. So it's definitely being handled.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.java#L2409

I see an example of invalid code point handling 

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/java/core/src/test/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormatTest.java#L1008

However, the case I've specified here doesn't seem to be handled.

I'd also like to clarify that this is the output I got via `cbt`, so I'm assuming the string was escaped used this library.
I have an open bugs to clarify the docs on this behavior.
I can repro this. Still not sure exactly what's happening.

Looks like this is returning null:

                Character.UnicodeBlock unicodeBlock = Character.UnicodeBlock.of(codepoint);
Fixed in google3 and will arrive in this repo with next sync.
Amazing, thank you! 🙏

title: Why is there a Java 4.0.0-rc-2 release?
body:
I have been searching and cannot find any explanation for the existence of the 4.0.0-rc-2 version of Protocol Buffers [listed](https://mvnrepository.com/artifact/com.google.protobuf/protobuf-java-util/4.0.0-rc-2) in the Maven repository.

It’s old (Jul 21, 2020) and it’s been stuck at that futuristic release-candidate version while the apparently real releases have been progressing from 3.12.14 to 3.19.3.

It sure seems odd.  An explanation would be welcome, published somewhere.

nodes.body: Because Maven central doesn't allow us to delete anything since published, and prioritize later unstable versions over smaller stable version numbers or more recently published artifacts with lower version numbers. I am sorry this shows up as the first release. It shouldn't.  That effort is no longer in progress, and if there ever is a 4.0.0 for Java it will not be derived from that.
Perhaps you could annotate the release on Maven Central so people would know?
How might one do that? If there are instructions somewhere, I can take a look. My understanding is that Maven Central is very close to a write-once repo.

title: Crash using `FieldMask.MergeMessage` and deserialized messages
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

Version: 3.19.4
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Linux, I think 


**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

Python 3.9

**What did you do?**

Consider this proto file:

```proto
syntax = "proto3";

package repro.crash;

message Thing {
    string name = 1;
    map<string, string> labels = 2;
}
```

This code works:

```py
def works():
    print("This works")
    target = test_pb2.Thing(name="original", labels={"k0": "label0", "k1": "label1"})
    changes = test_pb2.Thing(name="changed", labels={"k0": "label0", "k1": "label1"})
    mask = field_mask_pb2.FieldMask(paths=["name", "labels"])
    mask.MergeMessage(changes, target)
```

While this code, which only serializes and deserializes the `changes` proto crashes:

```py
def crashes():
    print("This crashes")
    target = test_pb2.Thing(name="original", labels={"k0": "label0", "k1": "label1"})
    changes = test_pb2.Thing(name="changed", labels={"k0": "label0", "k1": "label1"})
    serialized = changes.SerializeToString()
    changes = test_pb2.Thing()
    changes.ParseFromString(serialized)

    mask = field_mask_pb2.FieldMask(paths=["name", "labels"])
    mask.MergeMessage(changes, target)
```

The error message I get is:

```
[libprotobuf FATAL google/protobuf/map_field.cc:357] CHECK failed: IsMapValid() && other.IsMapValid(): 
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'google::protobuf::FatalException'
  what():  CHECK failed: IsMapValid() && other.IsMapValid(): 
Aborted (core dumped)
```

**What did you expect to see**

I expected both functions to work and produce the same results.

**What did you see instead?**

A crash, see above.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

I am a Googler, ping me directly if you have additional questions.   I have attached a tarball that reproduces the problem, the instructions on how to use it are in the Dockerfile.

body:

For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master/3.19/3.14, seems to affect all recent versions
Language: C++/Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Linux

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

Not really applicable

**What did you do?**

Trying to compile a python extension using pybind11_protobuf, the Header proto_api.h, which is inside the python package in this repo is not found.

It seems this header is not included when installing the python package, e.g. in wheels or the arch linux python-protobuf package.

**What did you expect to see**

Header is included.

**What did you see instead?**

See above.

nodes.body:
`proto_api.h` will be going away soon, as we will be releasing a [new implementation of the Python Protobuf library](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/tree/main/python) that is based on https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb instead of C++ protos.

The new Python Proto library cannot support the existing `proto_api.h` interface, as Python objects will not have a `proto2::Message*` inside of them. Instead they will have a `upb_Message*`.

We will likely expose a new/different capsule eventually to allow pybind11 users to access the upb proto object. But this will not be in the first version.

What implications does this have for creating python bindings to a C++ library using the C++ protobuf library and not upb?

It sounds like it will require serialization/deseralization to transform c++ message instances into python upb instances.

That would be very unfortunate for  us and would bring us back to the current state, which we had hoped to improve by using `pybind11_protobuf`
I believe the pybind11_protobuf build should be fixed by: https://github.com/pybind/pybind11_protobuf/pull/165

We cannot support `-fpack-struct`, this is an ABI-impacting flag that will make our library ABI-incompatible with anything else that was not compiled with `-fpack-struct` (for example libc or libc++).

My suspicion is that the decode calls leave many garbage-collectible Ruby objects that don't take up much room in the Ruby heap while referencing to a large amount of upb memory, and Ruby sees no need to run GC.  The forced GC calls worked in this test, but in my actual application it was only good for slowing down the memory growth, and even at that level the growth was much too fast whereas with 3.14.0 the memory usage remained nearly flat.

There was another [recently report issue](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9384) that sounded similar.  It was closed due to lack of action after a suggestion to run GC, but I feel forcing GC is not an acceptable solution  It doesn't contain the issue well enough as I observed in my application, and besides it should not be necessary to force or tune GC just to use the protobuf gem.

I can see a few different ways to resolve this:

1. Find a way to fix the leaky behavior and keep memory usage low and stable, like with 3.14.0.  This is the ideal solution.
2. Reintroduce the non-upb allocation strategy as an option.  But this will understandably add maintenance burden, as @haberman explained in [this comment](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8337#issuecomment-785456828).
3. Commit to backporting security fixes and some key features (such as Apple silicon support) to 3.14.x.  This would work well for users who value stability over improved performance. (myself included)

Option 3 is easy to attain, and it would be great to make it happen while the proper fix (option 1) is investigated.

nodes.body:
Hi, thanks for the detailed report. The clear numbers and simple repro will make it easy to investigate further.

Your analysis clearly shows memory differences in 3.15.0 on, and these warrant further investigation to see how we can mitigate them. But as a matter of terminology, this is not a memory leak: if it truly was a leak, the memory usage would grow *even with* manual GC calls.

I say this partly to clarify what the proper remedy will be. If this was a true leak, we would need to be searching for places where we are somehow allocating memory without freeing it, or holding onto references improperly from some global object. But this is not the case: your tests show that manual GC calls cause us to reach a clear steady state. This means that all memory is accounted for and will be freed eventually, the issue is just that is it not freed soon enough.

Going back to 3.14.x is not an option. Far too many fixes have happened since then. We need to find a way to push forward.

As a random thought, some GC systems a manual GC call pushes harder on weak references than an automatic one.  In effect some GCs have concepts like partial collection vs full collection and the explicit calls trigger a full collection.
Yes, agreed this is not a memory leak per se.  A leak-like behavior, if you will, but I couldn't think of a better way to describe it in the title.  Feel free to update it as you see fit.

It turns out that Ruby does have a mechanism by which [extensions can report](https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/master/doc/extension.rdoc#c-struct-to-ruby-object-) how much memory a given object is taking!

> dsize calculates memory consumption in bytes by the struct. Its parameter is a pointer to your struct. You can pass 0 as dsize if it is hard to implement such a function. But it is still recommended to avoid 0.

If we implement this function on our `Arena` object, hopefully it will convince Ruby to run the GC more often.
We have what looks like a very effective fix for this in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9586
This should be fixed by https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9586.

title: [Objective-C] Add ability to pass `objc_class_prefix` as an argument vs file option
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
Objective-C

If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
N/A

If it's about generated code change, what programming language?
Objective-C

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
While the `objc_class_prefix` file option works for most cases and for a single iOS app, it does not scale well when multiple iOS apps want consume the same `.proto` file but use a different class prefix throughout their codebase.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
It would be nice if the `objc_class_prefix` can be passed as an `--objc_opt` argument, similar to `use_package_as_prefix`. This would allow iOS apps to invoke `protoc` and pass a different prefix to use. Example invocation:

```
protoc --objc_out=my_proto.proto --objc_opt=objc_class_prefix=SMPL
```

This would allow different iOS apps to consume the same `.proto` file and avoid having to `sed` or somehow edit the `.proto` file to update the `objc_class_prefix` prior to `protoc` invocation.

This option should be honored _after_ the file option but _before_ the `use_package_as_prefix` option and documentation should state that. We could also error out if both options are passed.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Not many right now, as mentioned above, the current workaround is to edit the `.proto` file right before the `protoc` invocation to workaround this issue.

**Additional context**
N/A

title: Serialize and Parse google::protobuf::Any directly to and from JSON

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
People can build their own AAR files though they may not recognise what the appropriate build flags to use are and anyone who does so will have to figure out the process on their own.

**Additional context**
I just put up a [repo with code that will generate an AAR for protobuf based on running a single python script](https://github.com/ReenigneCA/make_prefab_aar/blob/main/make_protobuf-aar.py). I decided to create a feature request rather than issue a pull request for 2 reasons 

1. To figure out if its something the protobuf project is interested in (perhaps ndkports would be a preferred solution?) and 
2. I prefer to keep my original copy under a BSD license just so I can be lax about modifying the script for other libraries I decide I want to build so I'm guessing the papertrail so to say would be better if I state here I'm happy with this project incorporating a copy under this project's license as a dual license situation where my original copy stays under the 3 clause BSD license.

Whether the script is something this project is interested in or not I'd appreciate any comments on it, particularly if there are any improvements I should make to the configure flags.

title: Additional Units for `Duration`
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Python (potentially other langs)

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
It would be nice if `google.protobuf.duration_pb2.Duration` offered more units - preferably `days`, `hours`, and `minutes`. This would help with readability.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like if `Duration` added support for days, hours, and minutes. This can look like:
```python
Duration(
    days=30
)
```

rather than:
```python
Duration(
    seconds=2592000  # 30 days
)
```

Internally, `days`, `hours`, and `minutes` can convert to `seconds` if it helps with the implementation.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
The only alternative I can see is using `seconds` and adding a comment to describe.

**Additional context**
Using this library via https://github.com/googleapis/python-storage-transfer.
Here's a sample where it is used: https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/python-docs-samples/blob/8aac63759f64b97800a82c180c43d826bb78908d/storagetransfer/nearline_request.py#L52-L81

Possibly related to: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3986

nodes.body: Days are not actually a unit of time.  They are a unit of *civil time*.  One cannot convert days to seconds without knowing when and where you are.  1 day is only 24 hours 363 days of the year in most time zones.  Even then it can be different because of leap seconds.  We do not want to be in the position of providing a full set of time libraries in all of our target libraries, as they are *very* complex.  See https://github.com/google/cctz or JodaTime for good libraries in C++ and Java respectively.

title: Generated Python code is unidiomatic
body:
It's been pointed out in many tickets that the generated Python code is unidiomatic, and not IDE-friendly.

I think it's best summed up in the [better-proto](https://github.com/danielgtaylor/python-betterproto) README (which i'm paraphrasing here)

- No typing support or code completion/intelligence (requires additional mypy plugin)
- No `__init__.py` module files get generated
- Output is not importable
    - Import paths break in Python 3 unless you mess with sys.path
- Bugs when names clash (e.g. codecs package)
- Generated code is not idiomatic
   - Completely unreadable runtime code-generation
   - Much code looks like C++ or Java ported 1:1 to Python
   - Capitalized function names like HasField() and SerializeToString()
   - Uses SerializeToString() rather than the built-in __bytes__()
   - Special wrapped types don't use Python's None
   - Timestamp/duration types don't use Python's built-in datetime module

**I think most of this has been pointed out in various ways and in various tickets. What I haven't seen is whether there's any plan or roadmap to address this?**

nodes.body:
the type hints in master helps quite a bit - https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2638#issuecomment-1034471949

it doesn't go any way to preventing the code from singing my eyeballs, but it does mean you get type hints in an IDE

Hi @danieleades,

Our overall strategy here is:

1. Provide IDE completion with `.pyi` files.
2. Potentially add native support for the [proto plus](https://github.com/googleapis/proto-plus-python) API, with a few extra enhancements.

Going through your list:

> - No typing support or code completion/intelligence (requires additional mypy plugin)

This should be addressed by our `.pyi` generator.

> - No `__init__.py` module files get generated

This is unfortunately [fundamentally incompatible](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1491#issuecomment-883735797) with parallel compilation. If two different projects use the same protobuf package and run `protoc` separately, it will break.

> - Output is not importable
>  - - Import paths break in Python 3 unless you mess with sys.path

I wrote up a solution for this in [the related bug](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1491#issuecomment-1022571406). I know some folks are still unsatisfied with this.

@sbrother has [a great idea for making `setup.py` do the right thing](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1491#issuecomment-1022757287), so that dependent protos can be installed with `pip install`. This should avoid the need to change `PYTHONPATH`.

> - Bugs when names clash (e.g. codecs package)

I don't know what this means.

> - Generated code is not idiomatic
> - Much code looks like C++ or Java ported 1:1 to Python
> - Capitalized function names like HasField() and SerializeToString()

These issues should all be addressed if/when we adopt [proto plus](https://github.com/googleapis/proto-plus-python).

> - Completely unreadable runtime code-generation

Going forward, our intention is:

1. The `_pb2.py` files are primarily optimized for fast loading speed. They offer no pretense of readability, they are designed only to import as fast as possible, which can matter if you have hundreds or thousands of protos you are importing (as can happen if your protos have lots of imports).
2. The `_pb2.pyi` files offer full typing hints, to show exactly the effective API of each generated type, and provide full code completion for IDEs.

> - Timestamp/duration types don't use Python's built-in datetime module

We will endeavor to offer very easy conversion between `Timestamp`/`Duration` and Python's types. But we can't use the Python types directly as the native storage, because the Python types only offer microsecond precision and our types need nanosecond.

> - Uses SerializeToString() rather than the built-in `__bytes__()`
> - Special wrapped types don't use Python's None

I like both of these; we should be able to do these with [proto plus](https://github.com/googleapis/proto-plus-python).

> @sbrother has a great idea for making setup.py do the right thing, so that dependent protos can be installed with pip install. This should avoid the need to change PYTHONPATH.

I’m making great progress on this, it’s actually gotten easier and nicer with the ecosystem improvements to Python packaging. I’ll share here soon.

thanks for the detailed response @haberman, I really appreciate it.

proto plus looks interesting, i wasn't aware of this.

@sbrother i'll keep an eye out!

to be honest the `*.pyi` files go a *long* way towards solving this for me. Looking forward to that being released

I just commented this in the linked centithread, copying it here too:

> OK, I just made a [custom setuptools command](https://github.com/sbrother/protobuf-custom-build) and an example protobuf repository that implements it: https://github.com/sbrother/python-protobuf-repo-example. This solves the use case I've run into most frequently where I want to have a separate, shared schema module with protobuf definitions, which I then want to compile into generated code in several different services.

> The idea is that you can just include these python packaging artifacts (pyproject.toml, setup.py, setup.cfg) that call out to the custom rule, and then moving forward you can install working Python generated library with `pip install /path/to/your/protobuf/repo` (it will also work hosted on GitHub or a PyPI server). It uses the awesome protoletariat library @cpcloud mentioned above to do the heavy lifting; so thanks again for that!

title: Improve IDE support for Ruby
body:
The generated Ruby code is not very IDE-friendly, and could be improved to support things like auto-completion. For Python, we're going in the direction of making the main generated code small and efficient but not human-readable, and generating separate `.pyi` files that are more human-readable and IDE-friendly. We need to figure out a plan for Ruby, though.

#7593 suggests one solution, which would be to embed code in `if false` blocks so that it's visible to the IDE and to human readers without changing behavior. @haberman also suggesting doing something like this:
```
Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.add_serialized_descriptor(
  "<serialized_descriptor>"
)

# Google::Protobuf::Message defines #inherited to hook in the correct behaviors.
# This fails if #add_serialized_descriptor has not been called for "Foo."
class Foo < Google::Protobuf::Message
  # The base class overrides attr_accessor to do the right thing (maybe even
  # define it as a no-op if #inherited is handling the hard part.
  attr_accessor :foo
end
```

nodes.body:
I think RBS is a promising direction here: https://blog.appsignal.com/2021/01/27/rbs-the-new-ruby-3-typing-language-in-action.html

We could make the main generated code `foo_pb.rb` nothing but a serialized descriptor. Then we could have a separate `foo_pb.rbs` file that contains full static typing information, for IDE-friendliness.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.19.4
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Macos 12.0.1

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

Ruby 3.1.0

**What did you do?**

When calling `to_json` on a Hash or Array that contains a protobuf message an `ArgumentError` is raised (`Expected hash arguments. (ArgumentError)`).

I've created this minimal reproducable example:

``` ruby
require 'bundler/inline'

gemfile do
  source 'https://rubygems.org'
  gem 'google-protobuf', '= 3.19.4'
end

require 'json'

Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_file('msg.proto', syntax: :proto3) do
    add_message 'Msg' do
      optional :some_field, :string, 1, json_name: 'some_field'
    end
  end
end

Msg = ::Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.lookup('Msg').msgclass
msg = Msg.new(some_field: 'some_value')

puts msg.to_json
puts({ msg: msg }.to_json)
```

**What did you expect to see**

```
{"some_field":"some_value"}
{"msg": {"some_field": "some_value"}}
```

**What did you see instead?**

```
{"some_field":"some_value"}
/Users/luka/.asdf/installs/ruby/3.1.0/lib/ruby/gems/3.1.0/gems/google-protobuf-3.19.4/lib/google/protobuf/message_exts.rb:44:in `encode_json': Expected hash arguments. (ArgumentError)
	from /Users/luka/.asdf/installs/ruby/3.1.0/lib/ruby/gems/3.1.0/gems/google-protobuf-3.19.4/lib/google/protobuf/message_exts.rb:44:in `to_json'
	from bug.rb:24:in `to_json'
	from bug.rb:24:in `<main>'
```

nodes.body:
After some digging I found out that the options being passed to [`#to_json`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/8bfa7d00839a31e898a496ef4472b7ce211d543a/ruby/lib/google/protobuf/message_exts.rb#L43-L45) are a `json::Ext::Generator::State` object. This class implements [`#to_h`](https://apidock.com/ruby/JSON/Ext/Generator/State/to_h) and can be used as Hash arguments instead of raising.

Not sure if this is the right way. Would love to get some feedback on my PR #9513 and possibly get this issue resolved.
