nodes.body: There isn't much to go on here.  We don't have other reports of issues around description, but from the little bit you have, it does sound like a common problem in developer code - the classes generated for Messages are not safe to access from multiple threads if you are mutating them - i.e. - mutations must be done with exclusive access to the message and all messages reference in sub fields.  My guess is your NSURLSession delegate is acting on the message, but something in that message graph is still being used/mutated by another thread, and that causes the thread trying to create the description to crash as the objects are changing underneath it.

That code is just building up the `NSMutableRequest`.  The problem is going to be in your code that acts on the Message (`parameters` in that snippet); odds are it is being used from multiple threads while that request is being sent and the `NSURLSession` delegate is gets completion/status.

title: Ruby Protobuf Map `#Merge` inconsistent with Hash behaviour
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

Version: v3.14.0
Language: Ruby

**What operating system and version?**

Debian GNU/Linux 10 (buster)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

ruby 2.7.1p83 (2020-03-31 revision a0c7c23c9c) [x86_64-linux]

**What did you do?**

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Attempt to merge two `::Google::Protobuf::Map`'s with a provided block and duplicate keys
2. See map returned with field overriden and block not called

Minimal reproduction of the issue:

```ruby
hash1 = {
  "a": "First element", 
  "b": "Second element"
}
hash2 = {
  "a": "Different first element"
}
# Raises the exception "collision found a"
hash1.merge(hash2) { |key, _, _| raise "collision found #{key} "}

map1 = ::Google::Protobuf::Map.new(:string, :string, hash1)
map2 = ::Google::Protobuf::Map.new(:string, :string, hash2)

# Does not raise exception, returns the following (written as a hash):
# {
#   "a": "Different first element",
#   "b": "Second element"
# }
map1.merge(map2)  { |key, _, _| raise "collision found #{key} "}
```

**What did you expect to see**

As per the [ruby generated code guidelines](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/ruby-generated#map-fields) which state "Map fields are represented using a special class that acts like a Ruby Hash", it was expected that `#Merge` would behave the same for `::Google::Protobuf::Map` as it does for a `Hash`. That is, if a block is provided then the block is executed whenever there is a key collision. 

In the above example it is expected for `map1.merge(map2)...` to raise the exception `collision found a`.

**What did you see instead?**

The block was not executed for the duplicate keys and the original value was overwritten.

nodes.body:
The `merge` operation has a special meaning for protobuf, and `Map#merge` implements the protobuf semantics for merge.

While we could support a callback for collisions, the callback would have extra limitations, for example the type of the returned element would need to match the value of the map.

Given how easy this is to implement manually, I am inclined to keep `#merge` the way it is, which is to just implement the standard protobuf semantics.

title: Message FieldNameEntry not allowed as map value type for field_name
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: stable 3.19.4
Language: N/A

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

macOS 11.6.4

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

N/A, happens before language-specifc code generation

**What did you do?**

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Attempt to use a message with a name of `FieldNameEntry` as a map value in field `field_name`

2. See `protoc` return the error: `map_entry should not be set explicitly. Use map<KeyType, ValueType> instead.`

Minimal declaration:

```protobuf
syntax = "proto3"; // also happens on proto2

message AEntry {}

message Container {
    map<uint32, AEntry> a = 1;
}
```

**What did you expect to see**

I expected the declaration above to compile cleanly and with no errors.

**What did you see instead?**

The compiler emits `map_entry should not be set explicitly. Use map<KeyType, ValueType> instead.` before reaching any language-specific generator.

It took me a bit to realize this has to do with [backwards compatibility between maps and repeated values](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#backwards_compatibility), but the error message did not make sense to me at first, and I did not expect `protoc` to forbid this usage.

If this is an expected error, perhaps it should be documented (apologies if it is already, and I didn't see it)

nodes.body: Interesting. Do you have a complete reproducible test case, ideally as a failing PR here? I don't immediately see how the code corresponds to the report.

The relevant checks happen here:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2f91da585e96a7efe43505f714f03c7716a94ecb/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc#L6905-L6906
Thanks for the additional info. Spec say, "The value_type can be any type except another map." so this should be OK. Assuming I can reproduce this, it's probably a bug.

The naming convention reserves *Entry for internal usage: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2f91da585e96a7efe43505f714f03c7716a94ecb/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc#L6917
Closing this as this is WAD

It appears that `*Entry` is a reserved field name. In the interim I'll add workaround in my local code to rename the field to `*Entry_` . Please could we re-open this issue?  It would be great to have a more elegant solution.
I agree. This isn't documented in the spec and protoc should generate name mangling as needed to make this work.
At some point, we need to have a much more systematic review of how we handle keywords and conflicting names.  This is another piece of that much larger puzzle
I assume we want a documentation bandaid in the meantime? I can add something to the proto and proto3 topics.
Yeah

The problem here is that protoc is generating a message named FooEntry for the map field foo and that conflicts with your user-defined message FooEntry.  protoc is not adding the map_entry option to your type based on the name.

Name mangling needs to be applied to the generated map entry type to allow a nested FooEntry type and a map<> foo to coexist.

> the example given by @elharo (which has no namespacing workaround).

@googleberg, were you referring to this example? https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9520#issuecomment-1175080496

While that is a little annoying, at least the error message is comprehensible. I think the more egregious issue with the original example is that the error message is confusing and misleading (incorrect even).

Name mangling, like as is done with synthetic oneofs for proto3 optional, would indeed help. However, it isn't perfect since it would still be _possible_ to name a user-defined type the same thing as the mangled name (even if highly unlikely). A more robust fix would be to alter the symbol resolution logic (when resolving relative references) to _ignore_ synthetic map entry messages. A possible solution might be to use a mangled name with characters not otherwise allowed in an identifier. But this will mostly likely cause issues with runtimes that validate descriptors during initialization: when the embedded descriptors are initialized (such as to create "rich" descriptors around embedded descriptor proto data), they could choke on a name that appears to be invalid.
I have encountered the same error. As a workaround, change `MappingEntry` to something like `MappingE` etc.

title: Big numbers (uint64, fixed64) bug in PHP
body: Hi! Generated setters for fixed64 or uint64 are using `intval($var)` in case of `PHP_INT_SIZE == 8` (any 64x system). But max value of uint64 is greater than PHP_INT_MAX: `2^64-1` vs. `2^63-1`. I have written tests: https://github.com/zlodes/protobuf-bugs-demo There are results: https://github.com/zlodes/protobuf-bugs-demo/runs/5235953996?check_suite_focus=true Code fragment from tests: ```php $foo = new Foo(); /** * Max uint64 value: 2^64-1 * @see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integer_(computer_science)#Long_integer */ $value = '18446744073709551615'; // max uint64 value: 2^64-1 $foo->setFixed64($value); self::assertEquals( $value, $foo->getFixed64() // It returns 9223372036854775807 (PHP_INT_MAX) ); ``` ... and from generated class: ```php /** * Generated from protobuf field fixed64 fixed64 = 1; * @return int|string */ public function getFixed64() { return $this->fixed64; } /** * Generated from protobuf field fixed64 fixed64 = 1; * @param int|string $var * @return $this */ public function setFixed64($var) { GPBUtil::checkUint64($var); $this->fixed64 = $var; return $this; } ``` More you can find here: https://github.com/zlodes/protobuf-bugs-demo ## Environment: ### PHP: ``` ❯ php -v PHP 8.1.3 (cli) (built: Feb 16 2022 14:36:17) (NTS) Copyright (c) The PHP Group Zend Engine v4.1.3, Copyright (c) Zend Technologies with Xdebug v3.1.3, Copyright (c) 2002-2022, by Derick Rethans with Zend OPcache v8.1.3, Copyright (c), by Zend Technologies ``` ### Protoc ``` ❯ protoc --version libprotoc 3.19.4 ``` ### google/protobuf package ``` ❯ composer info google/protobuf name : google/protobuf descrip. : proto library for PHP keywords : proto versions : * v3.19.4 ... ```

nodes.body:
PHP doesn't support `uint64`:

> PHP does not support unsigned ints. int size can be determined using the constant PHP_INT_SIZE, maximum value using the constant PHP_INT_MAX, and minimum value using the constant PHP_INT_MIN.

In that case, what is your suggestion to fix that? The only way to return `'18446744073709551615'` is using string, which will have a performance penalty and you should use `bcmath` library to manipulate it anyway. Returning strings and numbers, mixed, will break any `===`. 

It's possible a duplicate of https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/5216

@inkeliz 
> The only way to return '18446744073709551615' is using string

Yes. And it would be correct. 
And then the developer may use `bcmath` or another way to operate with big number.

Now it looks like that method will return `int|string` (original PHPDoc reference) and method was written to return `int` if the number fits to `int` and `string` otherwise. But there is a mistake and it doesn't work properly.

And now to fix this mistake I should to remove `GPBUtil::checkUint64($var);` from generated code to make it works.
This is a known issue that we are working to prioritize
Is there an update on this issue? I am also running into it.
Just opened PR to fix that. I've waited for more than a year and decided to fix it by myself 😄

title: Proposal: Generics/template syntax
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
proto3 syntax change

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I am working with "delta" types which basically store modifications on the field of an object.

For example if my object is the following:
```go
type User struct {
    Subscriptions        []string
    NotificationsEnabled bool
}
```

I will then have the following delta object:
```go
type UserDelta struct {
    Subscriptions        *delta.List[string]
    NotificationsEnabled *delta.Value[bool]
}
```

Using that I can then send the following delta:
```json
{
    "Subscriptions": {
        "Operation": "ADD",
        "Value": ["hello", "world"]
    }
}
```

Which will add those values to the `Subscriptions` list, or:
```json
{
    "NotificationsEnabled":  {
        "Operation": "SET",
        "Value": true
    }
}
```

Which will set `NotificationsEnabled` to true.

> This is very very simplified here

I would like to change my json API to a protobuf one.
In my `UserDelta` object I would like to use similar types such as `*delta.Value[bool]` or with any other subtype.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

```proto
message DeltaList<type T> {
  oneof input {
    T add = 1;
    T remove = 2;
  }  
}

message DeltaValue<type T> {
  T set = 1;
}

message UserDelta {
  DeltaList<string> subscriptions = 1;
  DeltaValue<bool> notifications_enabled = 2;
}
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

I have two other solutions, each with massive drawbacks:

1. Use `any` which loses the type information:
```proto
message DeltaList {
  oneof input {
    any add = 1;
    any remove = 2;
  }  
}

message DeltaValue {
  any set = 1;
}

message UserDelta {
  DeltaList subscriptions = 1;
  DeltaValue notifications_enabled = 2;
}
```

I will definitely not use that as it loses a lot of the benefits of protobuf.

2. Define a specialized type for each variant:
```proto
message DeltaListString {
  oneof input {
    string add = 1;
    string remove = 2;
  }  
}

message DeltaValueBool {
  bool set = 1;
}

message UserDelta {
  DeltaListString subscriptions = 1;
  DeltaValueBool notifications_enabled = 2;
}
```

This would be acceptable in that scenario, however in my case I have many more specializations to do which would be extra-cumbersome.

**Additional context**
The second alternative could simply be the processed result of the generic syntax I proposed.

The parser's and compiler's job is much simpler than in the case of a regular programmation language as we only need to generate the types that were explicitely instanciated.

Each language could implement it as a "hardcoded" type such as `DeltaValueBool` or if the language supports generics/templating it could be implemented as such for readability.

I feel like this could simplify the job of many people without adding too much complexity:
- There is no metaprogramming in any way (I'm particularly thinking of C++)
- There is no type inference needed
- It's almost like a glorified `Find and Replace`

nodes.body:
Generics like this are very complex and will impact every language we target (many of which have their own generic systems we will want to interact with).  Given that it took multiple years of design to add generics to a language like Go, I expect this would be a similarly sized effort.

Even reviewing an external design would require a huge volume of effort.  We have no plans to start this exploration nor would we be likely to accept an external design for it.

I understand your point of view tho I disagree on the size of the effort.

With imperative languages such as Go or C++ there are many complexities added: type inference, casting, constraints, type erasure, ...

Protobuf is a declarative language, here there is no need for all of those "features". Everything is static, everything is explicit.

It doesn't have to correlate to generics in the output language, every message can be defined as a static type.

I understand that the idea of generics seems a bit spooky, particularly after the example of implementing them in Go, but with a declarative language it's basically syntactic sugar.

I'll totally understand if you are still against it as even that effort might not be worth the benefits, but I just hope it can make it look less like that giant spaghetti monster and more like a yummy spaghetti plate :)

While I appreciate the aspects that make this simpler than a full language, I think there is way more here than you give credit for.

* can languages refer to messages without fully in there generics or must they be fully specialized.  If they must be fully specialized I can tell you what one of the earliest feature requests we would receive is. If you can refer to the generic without instantiation in host languages, what is the API for that and how does it interact with that languages generic system?
* what does reflection for these types look like?  Presumably we will need to do something to augment the APIs for reflection in all most all of the languages.
* descriptor.proto will need enhancements so folks can import these things and then instantiate them after import, those will require design
* do generics allow primitives or only Messages? if the former there is a big bag of worms, if the latter I know what your second bevy of feature requests will be
* how do generics show up in serialized format for Any?  
* How do generics interact with extensions?  Should they allow injection of an extension number?  This one doesn't seem to have a "no" alternative, but is going to provide a fair amount of complexity that we have not broached yet.

So yeah, I am going to stick with my initial assessment.

That's a lot of good points, would probably be easier to start everything from scratch.

Thanks for the very detailed answer!

title: Ruby Arena object should use xrealloc/xfree so Ruby is aware of allocated memory
body:
Once the upb arena can report the number of bytes allocated (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/issues/528) we should make the Ruby `Arena` object report bytes allocated via the [`dfree`](https://github.com/ruby/ruby/blob/master/doc/extension.rdoc#c-struct-to-ruby-object-) member of [`Arena_type`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/6a77c9bab4bd3c8e10096694469b203bc211246f/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/protobuf.c#L190-L194).

This will hopefully convince Ruby to run the GC more often and prevent the growing memory usage we have seen reported in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9467.

nodes.body: We can test this theory simply by lying to it and reporting large numbers and seeing what happens

After trying Matt's suggestion to report arbitrary large number (also adding print statement to sanity check) showed that implementing dsize (note: initial issue has typo `dfree` -> `dsize`) doesn't help since dsize never gets called by GC.

However, Josh found this lead which seems much more promising: https://github.com/ffi/ffi/issues/753
Adding a ruby-specific `upb_alloc` using  xmalloc/xrealloc/xfree in place of `upb_global_alloc` for `Arena_alloc`  (by using upb_Arena_Init instead of upb_Arena_New) should allow Ruby to be aware of the memory being allocated.
Fixed by: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9586

title: protoc: strange inconsistency in message literals in custom options for when a colon is needed

nodes.body:
I expect to find this in the EBNF but I don't:

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec

If we follow that spec, none of this is allowed. We probably need to update that spec.

Yeah, it does not go into the format for message literals. The implementation actually relies on the `libprotoc` implementation of the text format -- so it just provides everything between the `{` and `}` to the text format parser.

Also relevant:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-grammar/pull/2
https://github.com/jhump/protocompile/tree/master/grammar
Realistically, this language blemish is something we have to live with. Fixing this is a significant breaking change that we're unlikely to have staffing to drive.

While I understand that changing the _text format_ could be a significant effort, I think it might be simpler to just patch `protoc`. Also, it would not be a breaking change as it would make `protoc` strictly _more_ permissive, not less (i.e. programs that omit a colon that are rejected today would suddenly be accepted by the compiler).

As far as this only effecting `protoc`, not the text format, this could be achieved by letting the descriptor database or options interpreter (whichever class parses the data when interpreting options) be a "friend" class to the C++ text format implementation. The text format could then have a private method that allows toggling off the requirement that list literals be preceded by a colon, and only the option interpretation step of the compiler actually uses it.

This alternate way to address might be small enough for a contributor to look into a pull request, instead of marshaling the resources of Google's protobuf team.

**What language does this apply to?**
Github release process

Linux distro's like Ubuntu don't include `unzip` by default. The releases already include `tar.gz`. Why would the linux binary builds not use `tar.gz`? Might make sense for Windows, but not Linux.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Archive with `tar.gz` instead of `zip`

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Installing `unzip` which is an unnecessary step if the archive was not `zip`.

nodes.body: I don't see us replacing the existing zips, as we have to be mindful of people's existing dependencies on our release artifacts. If anything, it's possible we'd _add_ tar.gz variants, but this is overall low value work (hard for us to prioritize it in the near term), and there's a reasonable workaround.

title: Python ServiceDescriptor.FindMethodByName raises exception (inconsistent behavior between C extension and native Python + documentation)
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: master
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Ubuntu 20

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.8.10

**What did you do?**
```
service_desc = desc_pool.FindServiceByName(service_name)
service_desc.FindMethodByName(_INVALID_SYMBOL_NAME)
```

This raises a KeyError exception.
However, the [documentation](https://googleapis.dev/python/protobuf/latest/google/protobuf/descriptor.html#google.protobuf.descriptor.ServiceDescriptor.FindMethodByName) says:

> Returns: the descriptor for the requested method, if found.
> Return type: [MethodDescriptor](https://googleapis.dev/python/protobuf/latest/google/protobuf/descriptor.html#google.protobuf.descriptor.MethodDescriptor) or [None](https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html#None)

More specifically, the [native Python](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/349d74d92e8268c41fbb726b0a8292d588c63e20/python/google/protobuf/descriptor.py#L867) implementation & documentation is:

```Python
  def FindMethodByName(self, name):
    """Searches for the specified method, and returns its descriptor.
    Args:
      name (str): Name of the method.
    Returns:
      MethodDescriptor or None: the descriptor for the requested method, if
      found.
    """
    return self.methods_by_name.get(name, None)
```

While the [C-extension](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/349d74d92e8268c41fbb726b0a8292d588c63e20/python/google/protobuf/pyext/descriptor.cc#L1736) implementation is:

```CPP
static PyObject* FindMethodByName(PyBaseDescriptor *self, PyObject* arg) {
  Py_ssize_t name_size;
  char* name;
  if (PyString_AsStringAndSize(arg, &name, &name_size) < 0) {
    return nullptr;
  }

  const MethodDescriptor* method_descriptor =
      _GetDescriptor(self)->FindMethodByName(StringParam(name, name_size));
  if (method_descriptor == nullptr) {
    PyErr_Format(PyExc_KeyError, "Couldn't find method %.200s", name);
    return nullptr;
  }

  return PyMethodDescriptor_FromDescriptor(method_descriptor);
}
```

Note the `PyExc_KeyError` part in this code.

**What did you expect to see**
Consistency between Python and C-extension implementation (and the documentation).

**What did you see instead?**
They are not consistent.

Despite the title, I tend to think that the exception is the more correct behavior, based on these aspects:
* It feels more Pythonic.
* DescriptorPool.FindMethodByName raises a KeyError in this case. There are also tests for this behavior `python/google/protobuf/internal/descriptor_pool_test.py`, while there are no corresponding tests for `ServiceDescriptor.FindMethodByName`.
* Fixing this inconsistency will be a breaking change for either the C-extension or Python users, depending on the fix. I assume that most environments are using the C-extension version, so changing to an exception will be less harmful.

I can try to submit a patch, but I want to check first that this is the correct direction, i.e. change the native Python code to raise an exception, update the documentation accordingly, and add an appropriate test.

I'm willing to do the legwork to fix this, but I want to check first that this is the right direction.
Thanks.

title: [PHP] option exclude backwards compatible proto files
body:
For PHP all nested messages generate two classes, the current namespaced class and a file to support backwards compatibility with the previous non-namespaced files. There's also a `class_alias` call at the bottom of every nested message. See [this PR from almost 4 years ago](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/4536). 

As been almost 4 years, these files are now more of a nuisance. I see three potential options here, ranked from least to most risky:

 - Add a flag to tell `protoc` to not generate these files for PHP (opt-out, most conservative)
 - Add a flag to tell `protoc` to generate these files for PHP (opt-in, could potentially break some very slow to upgrade users)
 - Remove the backwards compatibility logic all together (as it's been throwing deprecation errors for almost four years, I feel comfortable with this solution)

I'm happy to give a PR a try any of these options are possible!

nodes.body:
I think removing the backward compat logic is the way to go at this point.

Four years with deprecation warnings seems sufficient.

The only issue I can think of is for libraries like `google-cloud-php`, we wouldn't want to _remove_ the `class_alias` code from proto files which currently have it. Not because we think it's needed, but because it would constitute a backwards-compatibility change. So what we _could_ do is:

1. Only remove the old alias file (e.g. `Nested_Message.php`) but keep the class alias (e.g. the call to `class_alias` at the bottom of `Nested\Message.php`) for now
2. Add a flag (once again) for removing or adding the call to `class_alias`
3. Not care at all and we can handle it on our end :)

since the latest release still outputs deprecated files...

grep 'is deprecated and will be removed in the next major release' -R path/to/proto -l | xargs rm'

nodes.body:
This is an interesting idea. Unfortunately, we probably won't have time to look at it any time soon, so I'm going to remove myself as assignee.

We could consider patches, but since this is a change to the JSON spec, it would need to be applied to all languages (and not just C++... that label seems to have been applied by mistake).
This is a duplicate of #4328

FWIW, there is a possible work-around using existing language features: add `option allow_alias = true` to the enum and create an alias for each numeric value with the desired JSON name.

This is admittedly an imperfect work-around for a few reasons:
1. I think most (maybe all?) runtimes will use the first declared name when marshaling. So you end up having to use the desired JSON name as the first name and declare other names as aliases. (Ideally, this would be reversed, where the "canonical" name and thus first value can differ from the JSON name.)
2. Because enum value names are scoped like C++ enums (e.g. the values are in the enclosing lexical scope), some names cannot be used because they may conflict with other names in the enclosing scope.
Closing in favor of https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4328.

title: Ruby: int64 type using decond_json always get even number even if its original value is odd number.

nodes.body: How does ruby represent int64? This feels like a loss of precision on large numbers. goods_id perhaps should be a string if you're not doing arithmetic with it.

> How does ruby represent int64? This feels like a loss of precision on large numbers. goods_id perhaps should be a string if you're not doing arithmetic with it.

We use ruby 2.7.5.  Since ruby 2.4, Integer can represent any large number.

irb(main):009:0> m
=> 554490979814473729
irb(main):010:0> m.class
=> Integer
irb(main):012:0> z=m*10338133830491
=> 5732401957122113052510058670939
irb(main):013:0> z.class
=> Integer

```ruby

irb(main):014:0> json_str
=> "{\"source\":1,\"scid\":10,\"name\":\"iPhone x\",\"sku\":\"00112233\",\"main_pic_url\":\"http://xxx.xxx.xxx01\",\"goods_id\":554490979814473729,\"type_flag\":8,\"origin_price\":6999.9,\"current_price\":5999.8,\"stock_num\":211,\"has_discount\":true,\"opt_price_days\":31}"
irb(main):015:0> hash=JSON.parse(json_str)
=> {"source"=>1, "scid"=>10, "name"=>"iPhone x", "sku"=>"00112233", "main_pic_url"=>"http://xxx.xxx.xxx01", "goods_id"=>55449...
irb(main):016:0> m=hash["goods_id"]
=> 554490979814473729
irb(main):017:0> z=m*10338133834091
=> 5732401959118280579842164095339
irb(main):018:0> z.class
=> Integer
irb(main):019:0> m.class
=> Integer

```

To get full precision for an int64 in JSON, you need to quote the number.

Instead of:

```
\"goods_id\":554490979814473729
```

you should use:

```
\"goods_id\":\"554490979814473729\"
```

This is documented in the JSON mapping, which shows int64 integers as quoted values: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#json

Like most JSON parsers, the Ruby protobuf JSON parser will parse any unquoted number into a `double`, which will lose precision for large int64 values.

Thanks. We add some tranfer to it. It passed.

In javascript,  we just avoid use max int64,  because it use double to present it.
But in Ruby, the json parser can parse big number than 2**52 without losing precision. 
So I think there is confused for ruby programmer.

```ruby
irb(main):001:0> require 'json'
=> true
irb(main):002:0> data = { :begin_timestamp => 0, :count => 2, :goods_id => 577848671777849345 }

irb(main):004:0> hash_data=JSON.parse(json_data)
=> {"begin_timestamp"=>0, "count"=>2, "goods_id"=>577848671777849345}
irb(main):005:0> hash_data["goods_id"] == 577848671777849345
=> true
irb(main):006:0> 
```

There's not much else we can do on this repo, as this is just Unity moving away from .NET standards, which will continue to follow.
As per my last comment, I'll close this issue now, but do feel free to leave a comment if you belive we could help further.

Forgive me for commenting on an old thread Maintainers, but I wanted to leave an extra breadcrumb for the next person.  The recommendation of bringing over the missing DLL worked for me.  My Unity is currently using .NET 2.1, so I downloaded the binaries from Microsoft.  Unfortunately, the .Net 2.1 binaries download did not have the necessary file.  I tried .Net 8 (specifically .8 SDK 8.0.300-win-x86) hoping that this file hasn't changed much and everything successfully compiled.  Haven't tried using the protobufs yet, but compiling is a good sign and I'll edit this post if it turns out it didn't work. When you download the zip the file will be in `shared/Microsoft.NETCore.App/8.0.5/System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.dll`. Good luck!

**EDIT:**

While that DLL version did compile and allowed for most of the functionality of the Protobuf library to work, I could not use the IMessage.WriteTo function.  You will need the DLL in [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe 4.5.3](https://www.nuget.org/packages/System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe/4.5.3). Just download the package, open it with WinRAR or 7Zip, and then the file I used is `lib/netcoreapp2.0/System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.dll`.

import project_b.base_pb2 as B

nodes.body:
How are you running `protoc`?

When you run `protoc` avoid using `-Iproject_a` or `-Iproject_b`. You need to let protoc see the full path of the proto (eg `project_a/base.proto` and `project_b/base.proto`) so that it does not appear to be a duplicate filename.

title: [C#] MethodOptions.GetExtension cast exception
body:
I get a cast exception from `GetExtension` when trying to get `HttpRule`.

Imagine we have two projects:

Project 1 has a gRPC service that uses http extension. It passes http.proto to protoc: 

```xml
<Protobuf Include="..\Proto\greet.proto" GrpcServices="Server"  ProtoRoot="..\Proto\" Link="greet.proto"/>
<Protobuf Include="..\Proto\google\api\annotations.proto" GrpcServices="Server"  ProtoRoot="..\Proto\" Link="google\api\annotations.proto"/>
<Protobuf Include="..\Proto\google\api\http.proto" GrpcServices="Server"  ProtoRoot="..\Proto\" Link="google\api\http.proto"/>
```

Project 2 tries to get `HttpRule` from gRPC service in Project 1. Project 1 references the `Google.Api.CommonProtos` package which contains a different copy of `HttpRule`:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Google.Api.CommonProtos" Version="2.2.0" />
```

Code:

```cs
var options = methodDescriptor.GetOptions();
var http = options?.GetExtension(AnnotationsExtensions.Http);
```

Error message:

> [A]Google.Protobuf.ExtensionValue1[Google.Api.HttpRule] cannot be cast to [B]Google.Protobuf.ExtensionValue1[Google.Api.HttpRule].
> Type A originates from 'Google.Protobuf, Version=3.18.1.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=a7d26565bac4d604' in the context 'Default' at location 'C:\Development\Temp\GrpcHttpApiIssueSample\Service_Api_Reference\bin\Debug\net6.0\Google.Protobuf.dll'.
> Type B originates from 'Google.Protobuf, Version=3.18.1.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=a7d26565bac4d604' in the context 'Default' at location 'C:\Development\Temp\GrpcHttpApiIssueSample\Service_Api_Reference\bin\Debug\net6.0\Google.Protobuf.dll'.

I understand why this happens. There are two copies of `AnnotationsExtensions.Http` and the copy being used to get `HttpRule` in Project 2 isn't the one that the gRPC service was compiled with in Project 1.

And a fix is for Project 1 to not compile its own copy of http.proto and instead reference the `Google.Api.CommonProtos` package.

What I'd like is to make this problem disappear so people don't need to worry. When Project 2 attempts to get the extension:
* GetExtension recognizes this situation and parses the proto data with the different copy of the type
* Or there is an API that exposes raw bytes that lets the caller do this

cc @jtattermusch @jskeet

nodes.body: Will look at this tomorrow.

FYI this is the real world example of this problem: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet/issues/167#issuecomment-1065268763

(the library in this case was using the old `descriptor.CustomOptions.TryGetMessage` which silently returns null. When I updated the code to use `descriptor.GetOptions().GetExtension` then I saw the new error).

I wonder if a non-generic way to get the extension message would be a solution?

e.g. a GetExtension method that returns `IMessage`. If the extension type isn't expected then the caller could convert the message into a byte array and then reparse the bytes using the known type.

FYI: this is still definitely on my plate, but I didn't get to it today. It's really unfortunate that the error message looks non-sensical due to the difference being in the type argument (`Google.Api.HttpRule`) rather than in the `ProtobufExtensionValue<>`.

Thanks for the link to the repro - that should make it easier for me to understand. I'm afraid my brain always takes a while to get back into extensions.

A method that returns `IMessage` *might* be feasible - for message-based extensions, of course. (It would have to fail for string-based ones.) Will prototype a bunch of options.

At the very least I'd like to detect the problem and provide a more descriptive error message :)

> A method that returns `IMessage` _might_ be feasible - for message-based extensions, of course. (It would have to fail for string-based ones.) Will prototype a bunch of options.

I didn't know there are string extensions. A method returning object is also fine. Testing the value is `IMessage` isn't a burden.

To save anyone else reading this from issue-hopping, @JamesNK has now provided a nicely-minimal repro here: https://github.com/JamesNK/ProtobufExtensionBug

One thing to note before I really delve into what's possible: this isn't so different from how the rest of .NET behaves. If I were to define my own `HttpClient` class and then try to use `IServiceProvider.GetService<HttpClient>()` after calling `services.AddHttpClient()`, then it wouldn't find that, either... and I wouldn't expect the ASP.NET Core DI folks to try to find something with "the same type name but in a different assembly".

This isn't to say I don't think we should do anything - just that "two types with the same name but in different assemblies aren't interchangeable" has been a fact of life since the beginning of .NET. Protobuf just brings an extra dimension of "same proto compiled into different assemblies" - much as you could have the same C# source compiled into different assemblies. We'll need to think carefully about how we resolve this.

(Returning `object` would allow the caller to get a bit further, for sure - but then if they tried to cast it to their expected type, it would still have a problem. And I'd be worried about trying *too* hard to assume that two proto-based types were actually identical, based on the FQN - they could easily be different versions of the same original proto.)

Much to ponder.

That looks like it solves my immediate problem. However, does it matter that the new method isn't on `IExtendableMessage<T>`? I'm not using that interface at all so I don't really know.

The existing generic methods should probably have some type checking so they can provide a better error message. That can be a separate piece of work.

> However, does it matter that the new method isn't on IExtendableMessage<T>? I'm not using that interface at all so I don't really know.

Hmm... that's slightly irritating. We can't add to `IExtendableMessage<T>` as adding a method to an interface is a breaking change (and we can't use default methods due to targets). Given that this is already very much a corner case, I think even if we *do* go ahead, we could probably not worry about putting it into the interface, at least to start with.

> The existing generic methods should probably have some type checking so they can provide a better error message. That can be a separate piece of work.

I'd definitely be happy to do that, regardless of whether we take any other actions. Mind you, it probably needs to stay as the same exception *type* to make it less of a breaking change. It'll probably be more about changing just the message rather than anything else.

Your changes made me think about how `GetExtension` works. Here is a hacky idea that allows the caller to declare their own `Extension` that returns object: https://github.com/JamesNK/protobuf/pull/3

The pro is no new public API. Con is it is a hack and is an extremely non-obvious workaround to this issue.

I'm not sure that it's a problem for it to be non-obvious if it's a *massively* corner case which hardly anyone will ever see - which is still my expectation. To put it another way: if you hadn't run into this with the gRPC/REST transcoding example which can be fixed with a documentation change (which makes the instructions simpler rather than more complicated, if I've understood correctly), would you expect to see this problem anywhere else?

(But I do quite like the hack as a workaround for this... we could potentially have a static method in `Extension` for "create read-only extension that can be used to access an extension without knowing about the type".)

nodes.body:
Compiling on Linux I see

```
$ protoc --java_out=/tmp  test_conflict_message3.proto
[libprotobuf WARNING google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_file.cc:232] test_conflict_message3.proto:
The file's outer class name, "TestConflictMessage3", matches the name of one of the types declared 
inside it when case is ignored. This can cause compilation issues on Windows / MacOS. Please 
either rename the type or use the java_outer_classname option to specify a different outer class 
name for the .proto file to be safe.
```

That suggests this is a known issue, but perhaps we should emit a better error message on Mac/Windows?
I'm using protoc 3.18.0 on the MacBook and 3.19.4 on Linux. This could explain the difference in comments, but why the difference in the capitalization of the class name?
Upgraded my MacBook to 3.19.4 but that didn't change anything. Perhaps gLinux was built from head and not 3.19.4?
Problem looks like it wants to create both testConflictMessage3 and TestConflictMessage3.java but can only create one.

I understand what's going on now. Since java_multiple_files is true, protoc generates two .java files:

1. The wrapper class whose name is formed from the file name (since there's no java_outer_classname option). This is TestConflictEnum3.java
2. The message class formed from the message element in the .proto file. This is testConflictEnum3.java

In this example these differ only in the case of the first letter. This works on Linux (though I don't recommend it) but on a non-case-sensitive system like Mac or Windows the second one generated overwrites the first.

I don't think we can plausibly support this case. However, perhaps we can (and perhaps should) fail the build. At least we can make the warning a little clearer. 

I haven't dug into the enum example but I assume it's basically the same problem.
I suppose we could sidestep this by compiling straight to jar files without materializing the .java files on disk, but I seriously doubt that's worth the effort.

I suspected it was due to case-sensitive quirks. In other scenarios protobuf's way to handle name conflicts with types is to append [OuterClass](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2d69d44cc18beaa0a3a62d353f80aead669abb5c/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_name_resolver.cc#L49) to the top level file/typename. Does it make sense to handle this case in the same way? If that was the case the generated type names would be the same between `java_multiple_files = true` (top level file, first char lower case, class matches file name) but just be located in a different spot as `java_multiple_files = false` (embedded in the top level type that doesn't have any name conflicts and doesn't need `OuterClass` suffix).
That would likely be incompatible with how it works presently on Linux. The real disconnect here is in Java, which believes that test.java and Test.java are two different files.

This is working as intended. The generated class name is transformed with `UnderscoresToCamelCase` [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2d69d44cc18beaa0a3a62d353f80aead669abb5c/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_name_resolver.cc#L154). That function is defined [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2d69d44cc18beaa0a3a62d353f80aead669abb5c/src/google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_helpers.cc#L207) to capitalize every letter that is preceded by a non-alpha character. This follows protobuf's general enforcement of camel case for fields as well.

JLS specifies that top level type name and file name should match [1], which is what the compile errors [2] refers to. The bug is that the generation is not consistently camel casing the file name and type name for top level types.

[1] https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se7/html/jls-7.html#jls-7.6
> If and only if packages are stored in a file system ([§7.2](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/specs/jls/se7/html/jls-7.html#jls-7.2)), the host system may choose to enforce the restriction that it is a compile-time error if a type is not found in a file under a name composed of the type name plus an extension (such as .java or .jav) if either of the following is true:
> The type is referred to by code in other compilation units of the package in which the type is declared.
> The type is declared public (and therefore is potentially accessible from code in other packages).

[2] `error: class testConflictMessage3 is public, should be declared in a file named testConflictMessage3.java`
@andyfurnival I don't think what you're describing is the same problem, though the symptoms look similar. Please open a new issue to track this, though it might indeed be working as intended.

Sorry I see my comment didn't address the original issue. Making messages (and enums) lower camel case is against the [style guide](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/style#message_and_field_names).

There are 2 easy workarounds:
- Specify an outer class name
- Rename your message to conform to the style guide

I agree the error message could be clearer, but this behavior is working as intended.

title: How to support package option for a custom CLI?
body:
We have implemented a custom CLI to generate relevant [Ballerina language](https://ballerina.io/) stubs from a given protobuf file. Now, we need to support a protobuf package option in our CLI. Something like Java and Go packages;

```proto
option go_package = "example.com/messages1";
```
```proto
option java_package = "com.example.tutorial.protos";
```

Our idea is to have something like,
```proto
option ballerina_package = "example.com/messages1";
```

As far as we understood, to address that, we can either:
- contribute to the [descriptor.proto]( https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto#L341) OR
- introduce a custom file option

We want to know, what would be the standard procedure to introduce such an option from the protobuf perspective?. What is your opinion on this requirement?.

nodes.body: A custom file option is the way to go. You can send us a pull request to update docs/options.md to allocate an extension number for this.

title: `separators` for json_format.MessageToJson
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
This is concerning the python `google.protobuf.json_format`

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I'm trying to compress the JSON string that is resulting from json_format.MessageToJson, I've done something like:

```python
json_format.MessageToJson(message, indent=None)
```

However there are still some insignificant whitespaces. The code given above give a string like:

```json
{"id": 42, "isSimple": true, "name": "My name", "sampleLists": [3, 4, 5]}
```

what I want is:

```json
{"id":42,"isSimple":true,"name":"My name","sampleLists":[3,4,5]}
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
In order to stay consistent with the Go `google.golang.org/protobuf/encoding/protojson` and the Java `com.google.protobuf.util.JsonFormat`, it would be great if we can add the named parameter called separators to MessageToJson and pass that to the `json.dumps` function in the `_Printer.ToJsonString`. We could also add the have a default value of:

```python
separators=(', ', ': ')
```

So that it is directly backward compatible.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
The alternatives I considered would be:
- to trim the whitespaces manually, which is not really necessary since `json.dumps` already support that.
- change the `indent` interpretation, but that would make the behavior non consistent with `json.dump` (which I think is important, to keep)

**Additional context**

I would like to get an approval to work on this as a Pull Request, I read [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#pull-request-guidelines) that it would be better to discuss about it here first.

nodes.body:
The question here is whether the benefit outweighs the extra complexity and support burden in the API. Is there a reason you need to remove the whitespace in the output? It makes the output less readable for a trivial space savings. Since we already have this in other languages, I suppose it might be OK. 

I don't think a list of separators is the way to go though. This should be a simple boolean consistent with the other languages.

Thanks for the feedback, the reason I want that is because on a large JSON the space saving is not trivial. I just gave a small example to explain what I was trying to do.

Then I thought about the separator list just to be consistent with the `json.dumps` function, the `ToJsonString` already use parameters that are similarly named and typed. But I guess a Boolean would also be fine.

I kind of like the Java way of doing that (`omittingInsignificantWhitespace`), but I guess a more pythonic way of doing that would be to add a parameter like `trim_spaces` or `trim_whitespaces`. Any feedback on that is welcome
How much savings do you estimate? How does that compare to simply gzipping the file?

You are probably right for the gzip part, did a little experiment on a 196K JSON and I got the following:

ls -l output:
```
201097  default.json
177251  default_half_compressed.json
36351   default_half_compressed.json.gzip
153412  default_compressed.json
35805   default_compressed.json.gzip
```

where the gzip + 'half compressed' (understand with insignificant spaces) and gzip + compressed are finally both at 35K. There is still a small improvement but the benefit might be outweighing the extra complexity.

JSON format is not at all optimized for size. If size is a concern, binary format is a much better choice.

If you are size-conscious, why not just use binary format?

@haberman I'm totally aware of that. But I see 2 potential reasons why I would use JSON. Here they are:

- Debugging. This would be feasible for small size JSON and it wouldn't clutter my terminal. However I agree that pretty printed would be OK too.

- Compatibility with older apps. If my/others older code is only accepting JSON and I do not have time to change that or I do not have control over the project, I would like to have a payload as small as possible.

I agree that compressing the original JSON covers most of the payload size problem. We could still go further and remove the unnecessary spaces. But I also understand the problem in terms of maintaining the project.

Yes, we generally try to keep roughly the same set of options between languages, so adding it to Python would imply adding it to other languages as well. For this reason we try to keep to the set of options with the biggest impact.

One option would be to parse and re-serialize the JSON if you want it to be in a specific format. That's probably not an entirely satisfying answer, as it will have some performance cost, but it's something you can do today.

title: Fix generated Python imports
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.12.4
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Debian 11

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
protoc

**What did you do?**
Proto structure:
```
pkg1
  pkg2
    file.proto
```
with
```protobuf
// file.proto
message MyType {
  uint64 my_field = 1;
}
```

Run protobuf python compiler:
```sh
protoc --python_out=. --proto_path=.
```

**What did you expect to see**
```python
# file pkg1/pkg2/__init__.py
from .file_pb2 import *
```

Such that I can use it like
```python3
import pkg1.pkg2.MyType
```

**What did you see instead?**
I need to import
```python3
import pkg1.pkg2.file_pb2.MyType
```

**Workaround**
I am running the additional method on the generated files:
```python3
def create_init_py_recursive(package_dir):
    package_files = []
    for package_node in package_dir.iterdir():
        if package_node.is_dir():
            subpackage_files = create_init_py_recursive(package_node)
            init = package_node / "__init__.py"
            with open(init, "w") as f:
                for subpackage_file in subpackage_files:
                    if subpackage_file.name == '__init__.py':
                        continue
                    f.write(f"from .{subpackage_file.stem} import *\n")
        elif package_node.is_file() and package_node.suffix == '.py':
            package_files.append(package_node)
    return package_files
```

**Additional references**
All other programming language bindings hide the name of the proto file from the user and only take package names into account as described in the [documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#packages).

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.20.0-rc-1
Language: Java

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
macOS 12.3

using `com.google.protobuf:protoc:3.20.0-rc-1:exe:osx-x86_64` compiler artifact
invoked via `org.xolstice.maven.plugins:protobuf-maven-plugin:0.6.1`

```
% java -version
openjdk version "18" 2022-03-22
OpenJDK Runtime Environment (build 18+36-2087)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (build 18+36-2087, mixed mode, sharing)
```

**What did you do?**
Compile the code generated from the following proto definition:

`example.proto`
```
syntax = "proto3";

package test;

option java_package = "org.example.test";
option java_outer_classname = "TestProto";
option java_multiple_files = true;

message KeyValuePair {
  string key = 1;
  string value = 2;
}
```

**What did you expect to see**

No compiler warnings when compiling the generated Java source code.

**What did you see instead?**

As part of https://bugs.openjdk.java.net/browse/JDK-8274336 https://bugs.openjdk.java.net/browse/JDK-8274335 Java 18 added additional linter checks.

Java 18 reports the following warning for generated source files, and fails compilation if `-Werror` is specified:

```
KeyValuePair.java:[19,4] [serial] non-transient instance field of a serializable class declared with a non-serializable type
```

See [KeyValuePair.java.txt](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/8344770/KeyValuePair.java.txt) for the generated source

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

Today possible workarounds are to either:
a) not pass -Werror to the Java compiler
b) mangle the source code generated by protoc using something like the maven-replacer-plugin, to add the necessary `@SuppressWarnings` annotations, which is rather ugly and brittle
e.g.
```
    <plugin>
        <groupId>com.google.code.maven-replacer-plugin</groupId>
        <artifactId>maven-replacer-plugin</artifactId>
        <executions>
          <execution>
            <phase>generate-sources</phase>
            <goals>
              <goal>replace</goal>
            </goals>
          </execution>
        </executions>
        <configuration>
          <includes>
            <include>target/generated-sources/**/*.java</include>
          </includes>
          <regex>true</regex>
          <regexFlags>
            <regexFlag>MULTILINE</regexFlag>
          </regexFlags>
          <replacements>
             <replacement> 
               <token>public final class</token> 
               <value>@SuppressWarnings("serial") public final class</value> 
             </replacement> 
          </replacements>
        </configuration>
      </plugin>
```

nodes.body: We don't promise a warning free build, and do not yet support Java 18.

key and value are declared like this as Object since they can be either a String or a ByteString:

```
  private volatile java.lang.Object key_;
```

There's a custom serialized form so these objects are serializable, warnings aside.
I suppose protoc could generate `@SupressWarnings` annotations in the source code.

@elharo if those warnings are false-positives, then I it probably makes sense for protoc to generate additional `@SupressWarnings` annotations. I see protoc already generates a bunch of those in other places in the code.
If you want to send a PR to add the `@SupressWarnings` annotations, that would be great! I don't think this will be prioritized in our work since we don't officially support Java 18.

I need this

@AqlaSolutions: Well, we're not proposing to implement it - there are *many* aspects which are really challenging here. If you genuinely believe you need this, then as I said back in October, I'd suggest you fork.

@jskeet Is there a way to have this triaged and put on the backlog if there is enough interest? I have a feeling with the increasing amount of gRPC usage in .NET code that people really might want this feature to reduce allocations for high-traffic services. Is a revamp as you mention the possibility of to support record types as well on the radar? CC: @davidfowl @JamesNK

@stebet: There's no specific backlog that I'd put it on. But I really don't anticipate having the time to devote to considering all the many, many implications of this any time in the near future I'm afraid. It's just a *huge* change - and one that I can't justify spending large amounts of time on.

Our ProtoActor-based trading server already has >50% cpu time spent in 0-1 generation collections. The allocations are mostly protobuf messages, byte arrays and Tasks. So struct support would really help.
@AqlaSolutions: I'm not saying it wouldn't be potentially worthwhile. I'm saying that it's a huge amount of work, and not something I have capacity for at the moment, or in the foreseeable future.

> @stebet: There's no specific backlog that I'd put it on. But I really don't anticipate having the time to devote to considering all the many, many implications of this any time in the near future I'm afraid. It's just a *huge* change - and one that I can't justify spending large amounts of time on.

I think that this feature is a great fit for the upcoming .NET 9. Since it’s a short term servicing release, it’s more suitable for making infra changes; struct generation could have matured by the time .NET 10 arrives. Needless to say that all close competitors of C# (Rust, Go, Swift, etc) support struct generation. Given the performance-focused mission of .NET Core, one would expect this feature to be there since day 1. Anyway, I suggest that we reopen this issue to be handled this year.

> Since it’s a short term servicing release, it’s more suitable for making infra changes

The .NET release cycle isn't the Protobuf release cycle. Protocol Buffers is not a .NET project that decides when to make breaking changes based on the .NET support dates.

> Anyway, I suggest that we reopen this issue to be handled this year.

title: Docs on the necessity of --experimental_allow_proto3_optional are outdated
body:
Doc [protobuf/docs/implementing_proto3_presence.md](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/implementing_proto3_presence.md) mentioned using option `--experimental_allow_proto3_optional` to enable [the feature of explicit `optional` label in proto3](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/master/docs/field_presence.md). However, protoc 3.19.4 is able to compile a `syntax = "proto3"` protocol file that uses the feature without needing this option on the command line.

Therefore, it seems the two docs linked above are outdated. Could you add a notice on those docs that the feature is no longer behind an experimental flag & since which version? Thanks.

body:
<!--

For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:

Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.20.0
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
GNU/Linux (Debian Buster, dockerized)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.10.3

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Build the `test_py` target in the minimal example given below (`$ bazel build :test_py`)

**What did you expect to see**
A successful build.

**What did you see instead?**
```
ERROR: /home/epertoso/test/BUILD:3:17: Label '@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf_python' is duplicated in the 'deps' attribute of rule 'test_py'
ERROR: error loading package '': Package '' contains errors
INFO: Elapsed time: 0.038s
INFO: 0 processes.
FAILED: Build did NOT complete successfully (0 packages loaded)
```

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
We depend on gRPC, which in turns depend on [protoc-gen-validate](https://github.com/envoyproxy/protoc-gen-validate). We saw the error after updating protobuf to v3.20, the failing target is [validate_py](https://github.com/envoyproxy/protoc-gen-validate/blob/dfcdc5ea103dda467963fb7079e4df28debcfd28/validate/BUILD#L28).

The error was introduced by this PR: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9187, as the test https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/bc799d78f81115940eec953e2937245c70e3e6e4/protobuf.bzl#L549 fails because `py_libs` and `deps` contain strings, and not `Label`s.

**Minimal example**

`WORKSPACE`
```
workspace(name = "test")

load("@bazel_tools//tools/build_defs/repo:http.bzl", "http_archive")

http_archive(
    name = "com_google_protobuf",
    sha256 = "b07772d38ab07e55eca4d50f4b53da2d998bb221575c60a4f81100242d4b4889",
    strip_prefix = "protobuf-3.20.0",
    urls = ["https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/archive/refs/tags/v3.20.0.tar.gz"],
)

load("@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf_deps.bzl", "protobuf_deps")

protobuf_deps()
```

`BUILD`

```
load("@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf.bzl", "py_proto_library")

py_proto_library(
    name = "test_py",
    srcs = ["test.proto"],
    deps = ["@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf_python"],
)
```

`test.proto`
```
syntax = "proto2";
package test;

message Foo { optional int32 bar = 1; }
```

nodes.body: This is a very tricky problem and indeed one I did not foresee. We can't do 1 since the strings passed in are not "absolute" labels, and unfortunately `str(some_label_object)` isn't always "absolute" either (cue years of tech debt). We can't do 2 as you said, but we should do some variant of it: we'd need some way to convert strings to labels but using the current package's context, essentially restoring a deprecated API that was removed (`Label(..., relative_to_caller_repository=True)`).

> restoring a deprecated API that was removed

https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/commit/b859571804f2095caaf018b172b59c90f185fd51 claims to be exactly that.

title: [Question] Use protobuf C++ within Matlab S-function Builder?
body:
Is there a way to use C++ protobuf within a [Matlab S-function Builder](https://de.mathworks.com/help/simulink/sfg/s-function-builder-dialog-box.html) (C++)?
More precisely: I have a Matlab Simulink model which includes a [Matlab S-function Builder](https://de.mathworks.com/help/simulink/sfg/s-function-builder-dialog-box.html) block. Within this block I want so serialize some data and send it via udp.

Using a windows machine I already tried the following steps:
1. installed protobuf via vcpkg: [`vcpkg install protobuf protobuf:x64-windows`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/README.md#c-installation---windows)
2. created `addressbook.proto` as shown in the [example](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial) (here I used `syntax="proto3"` to match the current protobuf version)
3. created `addressbook.pb.h` and  `addressbook.pb.cc` using `protoc` as shown in the [example](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial)
4. placed the folder `<protobuf_folder>/include/google` in `<matlab_simulink_model_folder>/include` which is used as include folder for my Matlab Simulink Model
5. placed `<protobuf_folder>/lib/libprotobuf.lib` in  `<matlab_simulink_model_folder>/include`
6. placed `addressbook.pb.h` and  `addressbook.pb.cc` in  `<matlab_simulink_model_folder>/include`
7. In Matlab S-function Builder window -> Libraries: add path and entry of `addressbook.pb.h`  and `libprotobuf.lib` as descripted in section ["Use the Libraries Table to Specify External Code and Paths"](https://de.mathworks.com/help/simulink/sfg/s-function-builder-dialog-box.html) (for section scroll down)
8. Adding the header file `#include "addressbook.pb.h"`
9. Adding `GOOGLE_PROTOBUF_VERIFY_VERSION;` to the code

The error:
Compiling this fails with a lot of linker errors. Basically I can find the `addressbook.pb.h` but not the basic class `google::protobuf::Message` and it's methods.

What I checked:
I checked for the correct library for my architecture (it's x64)

Is this perhaps caused by different compile options (debug-flags, runtime library, etc.) of S-function and libprotobuf.lib? (I'm not very familiar with compiler stuff). 

Does anyone have any ideas on how to make it work?

Thanks in advance!

title: [Question] Using the Java library, how to convert from protoText file to protoBinary ?
body:
Hello,

I have a protoText file and I'd like to convert it to a binary format so i can be used by the library to parse incoming messages. Is there a way to do this using the library ? I'd hate to have to write the code to implement https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding :) 

Thank you !

nodes.body:
Something like:

```
TextFormat.parse(protoTextString, YourProto.class).toByteArray();
```

Would convert the text string into a serialized message as bytes.
More docs:
https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.html#parse-java.lang.CharSequence-java.lang.Class-

title: JSON serialization produces invalid results for certain unicode values
body:
*Version:* v3.19.4
*Language:* C++
*O/S:* Linux (5.15.15-1rodete2-amd64 #1 SMP Debian 5.15.15-1rodete2 (2022-02-23) x86_64 GNU/Linux)
*Compiler:* clang 13.0.1-3

**What did you do?**

Using Protobufs as a JSON string serializer, and differentially test/fuzz against other string serializer operations. There are several ranges of valid UTF-8 sequences where protobuf serialization produces incorrect values. In some cases protobuf serialization prints an error message and returns an empty string. In other cases it takes a valid 4-byte UTF-8 sequence and produces two unicode escapes, which is incorrect. It would be correct for it to return a single unicode escape or leave the UTF-8 sequence as is.

The code in question that behaves incorrectly is in a PR in the Envoy codebase, in a PR where we are trying to switch to a faster serializer but want to test and fuzz against protobuf behavior. We are working around this now by generating a list of unicodes where the protobuf serialization does not work as expected. 

The 3-byte UTF-8 sequences where protobuf serialization fails are discovered here: https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/0fd80eef63bc9770186c4f4aa345ee63e464cab3/test/common/json/gen_excluded_unicodes.cc#L81

and the 4-byte ones are discovered here: https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/blob/0fd80eef63bc9770186c4f4aa345ee63e464cab3/test/common/json/gen_excluded_unicodes.cc#L109

The code in question ultimately calls `Protobuf::util::MessageToJsonString`.

The unicode ranges where the bad behavior occurs are:
```
    // Range of unicodes from 3-byte UTF8 sequences where protobuf serialization spews an error message
    // and returns an empty string
    [0xd800, 0xe000) from utf8 \355\240\200 ... \355\277\277

    // Unicode ranges generated from 4-byte utf-8 where protobuf serialization generates two small Unicode
    // values instead of the correct one.
    [0x1d173, 0x1d17b)  utf8  \360\235\205\263 ... \360\235\205\272
    [0xe0001, 0xe0002)  utf8  \363\240\200\201
    [0xe0020, 0xe0080)  utf8  \363\240\200\240 ... \363\240\201\277
```
 I will add the utf-8 sequences that get you to those unicodes.

**What did you expect to see**: valid hex unicode escapes, or pass-through the valid UTF-8

**What did you see instead?**: two incorrect unicode escapes, or an empty string.

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body: The PR with the repro has now merged so I updated the description to reference the Envoy main branch rather than a PR.

You said the problems are generated inside of `Protobuf::util::MessageToJsonString`.

What is the message that you are serializing?  Specifically, I assume you can repro this with a simple proto that just has a single field which is a string.  What are all the bytes of that string?

You mentioned these ranges as being problematic:

    [0xd800, 0xe000) 3-byte utf8 => these correspond to Unicode surrogates...
    [0x1d173, 0x1d17b)  4-byte utf8  => these correspond to musical symbols
    [0xe0001, 0xe0002)  4-byte utf8  => these correspond to tags
    [0xe0020, 0xe0080)  4-byte utf8  => these are also tags

For the first range, you said that the code "spews an error message".  Can you say what the error message is?  Your example cites D800 and DFFF but those are both undefined in unicode, so an error message would appear to be called for.

For the tag space, e0000 through e001f are either unallocated or deprecated.  e0020 through e007f are now emoji modifiers.  So again, it would seem these are potentially invalid, depending on context.

RE repro with a simple string: correct. I put the byte-sequence being serialized in the Issue description. Range is \355\240\200 ... \355\277\277.  but I can enumerate them more completely if you like.

RE error message: `[libprotobuf ERROR external/com_google_protobuf/src/google/protobuf/wire_format_lite.cc:581] String field 'google.protobuf.Value.string_value' contains invalid UTF-8 data when serializing a protocol buffer. Use the 'bytes' type if you intend to send raw bytes. `

I think it's OK to return an error code if the input sequence generates a unicode that's not considered valid. However I think the inputs are all valid utf-8 based on the wikipedia definition of utf-8.

In any case I think it'd be better not to send bytes to stderr when that happens. If we could get that info back as a StatusOr instead that would be a little bit nicer :)

But I do think generating two small unicode values from what looks (based on wikipedia's utf-8 definition) to be a valid 4-byte utf-8 sequence seems broken.

Note -- this was not discovered using "normal" use-cases in production -- these corner-cases were found by exhaustive differential testing and fuzzing against the nlohman json library, so it's not surprising this finds the dark corners of the spec :)

The unicode characters you're talking about may be valid, or not, depending on the context of the full utf-8 string that they are in.  That's why I'm asking for entire contents of the string field of the proto message that you are passing to MessageToJsonString.  because it appears that the routine `IsStructurallyValidUTF8` from src/google/protobuf/stubs/structurally_valid.cc is returning false on the string in question, and absent any more context, that appears to be correct.

These are entirely synthetic benchmarks so the entire sequence being tested is what's in the Issue description -- just the 3 or 4 byte utf-8 sequence; no other context.

I'm not a unicode expert and I don't know why a unicode character would be valid or not depending on other bytes in the sequence. Also I think it's OK for the protobuf serialization to declare "this is bogus I'm not translating that". But I think it's behavior in the presence of invalid sequences is not convenient:
 * in the 3-byte cases it writes messages directly to stderr which can't be trapped
 * in the 4-byte cases it looks to me like it make incorrect translations.

classes' definitions are now dynamic created in internal/builder.py.

That why pylint falls.

Protoc is able to generate python stubs (.pyi) with --pyi_out, you can use this for type check.

title: IMessage<T> interface includes static interface parse method.
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
Not applicable.
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?
C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I have an inheritance data structure where the base type contains a byte array (any) and a discriminator field.
I then parse network data as the base packet and then dynamically switch on the discriminator to determine what the byte array needs to be parsed as.

Packet.proto:
```
syntax = "proto3";

import "google/protobuf/any.proto";
import "PacketType.proto";

message Packet
{
    PacketType PacketType = 1;
    google.protobuf.Any Payload = 2;
}
```

```
Packet.proto (base type)
Implementation1.proto <- Packet.proto
Implementation2.proto <- Packet.proto
...
```

Right now, the `IMessage<T>` interface only has instance members and the code generation for protobuf includes the parser on the type as a static member. This means that there is no dynamic way to parse / deserialize data.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
With the introduction of static interface members in C# 8, I would like to expose / add the field:
```cs
public static pb::MessageParser<T> Parser { get { return _parser; } } 
```
to the `IMessage<T>` interface so that I can leverage generics to parse payloads.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Generating another type that will take in a type to deserialize to, and a `byte[]` similar to other serialization frameworks i.e
```cs
var instance = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<T>(byte[] ...);
```

title: PHP: The mirror repository used to host protobuf for packagist has not been synced
body:
This is causing an issue with installations via composer, [as it is allowing PHP 5.5/5.6](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-php/blob/master/composer.json#L9) to install versions such as v3.20.0 which [actually require PHP >=7.0](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/php/composer.json#L9).

For example, due to the inclusion of return type hinting:
```
PHP Parse error:  syntax error, unexpected ':', expecting ';' or '{' in /tmpfs/src/github/google-cloud-php/vendor/google/protobuf/src/Google/Protobuf/Internal/RepeatedField.php on line 240
```

nodes.body:
cc @haberman 
Unfortunately this one is breaking anyone using protobuf on < PHP 7.0. This is because the [latest versions](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-php/blob/v3.20.1RC1/composer.json#L9) say they support PHP 5.5 but they're actually only compatible with PHP 7+.

We need to fix `composer.json` to be correct and then remove those tags (because composer will _always_ pull them in for PHP 5.5 / 5.6 even after we fix `composer.json` because they will be seen as the latest compatible versions of this library for those PHP versions).

Until we do that, protobuf will be completely broken for anyone on PHP 5.5 and 5.6
@haberman is this something that we missed as part of a release step?
I am submitting https://github.com/googleapis/gax-php/pull/382 to exclude the broken version of protobuf until we can get this resolved
We are also looking at [php/release.sh](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/php/release.sh), because this doesn't seem to be getting called

I think the underlying problem was fixed in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9832 (with a related fix in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9819).

Separately, we need to yank the 3.20.0 release since it advertises compatibility with PHP 5.5 but is not actually compatible.

title: [JRuby] RepeatedField#[] inconsistencies with negative ranges
body:
This is a follow-up to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9722#issuecomment-1088937852.

The `RubyRepeatedField#index` implementation assumes that ranges have a positive size:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d54cafb7c8dffab9cb54d23ed3997207760773dc/ruby/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/jruby/RubyRepeatedField.java#L145-L147

However that doesn't always hold for ranges involving negative indexes:

```rb
a = [1,2,3]
a[0..-1] # => [1, 2, 3]
(0..-1).size # => 0
```

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/compare/main...lucthev:range-access shows some failing cases (the first one, `0..5`, works fine, but the others fail). There's a lot of odd edge-cases here, and it might not be worth supporting them all.
