title: PHP: string form of enum contains "PB" prefix used to differentiate the constant from reserved words
body:
In #3612 the step was taken to protect generated PHP code for Enums from use of PHP reserved words that would cause interpretation exceptions. e.g. an Enum value named `CLASS = 1` would be generated as `PBCLASS` in PHP. This did the job.

However, as part of #5342, the string value that the PHP constant maps to _also_ includes the `PB` prefix (which was prepended to the constant identifier to disambiguate it). Use of the `name` helper to map from Enum value to the string form retrieves a name that doesn't represent the proto. The same example as above would result in `"PBCLASS"` as the name, while the name for the value in the proto is `CLASS`. Here is a specific [example in Google Ads](https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-php/blob/5d8c5837ccbb9284b42182e1260376609ba2e6f3/src/Google/Ads/GoogleAds/V10/Enums/ConversionActionCategoryEnum/ConversionActionCategory.php#L168).

Is this ideal? In my opinion it seems like a misrepresentation of the enum value names.

Could the `PB` prefix be excluded from the generated string form? I could see this being perceived as a breaking change if users were depending on the emergent behavior of names including the prefix.

I believe this is only really a concern for users of the generated `name` helper in enum classes. The JSON serialization code uses the proper string form I believe. 

cc: @fiboknacky @bshaffer @dwsupplee

nodes.body:
> I don't see how that would have been used successfully up to this point (since the API would reject it).

I _think_ you are right. If the user encodes their payload/params themselves (e.g. instead of using `serializeToJsonString` for a JSON payload), uses `name()` to get `'PBCLASS'`, I believe a backend could see this as an issue - unless it was expecting such a name and decodes it into `CLASS` properly (this is what I mean by users depending on the emergent behavior). Or the backend might be using `value` which would successfully decode it (because the backend _also_ has a `PBCLASS` constant). 

Personally, I don't think a breaking change WRT the `value` helper (even to fix an actual bug) is warranted here. But it still remains that the string `'PBCLASS'`, for example, might still be in use in user code so if `name` starts returning `'CLASS'` their logic may break...I'm torn.

I consider a change like this an acceptable breakage, as anyone writing code reliant on a bug would hopefully consider the bug might get fixed. Also it's quite an edge case. But we can leave that decision up to the maintainers.
Agree with all points, especially the acceptable breakage. It's pretty clear from the link that Noah provided, but please let me know if you need any more input.
Ok I will take a shot at the code changes starting with the backwards incompatible approach.
@fiboknacky the fix referencing this issue will be in the x.21.0 release early next month per https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9780#issuecomment-1101845213
Cool! Thanks for the update.
@noahdietz Could you tell approximately when this will be released? Thanks.
It will be in the x.21.0 release early next month per https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9780#issuecomment-1101845213

title: Clarification: Field presence for message
body:
The field presence docs show a [table](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/docs/field_presence.md#presence-in-proto3-apis) indicating that "explicit presence" applies to message-typed fields _regardless of the optional keyword_.

**Does the optional keyword have any effect on message-typed fields?**

The reason I am asking, and the feature that I am looking for, in the context of update requests, is distinguishing between (A) "please null out this field for me" versus (B) "I do not know or do not want to change this field, so please keep its existing value".

As such, I'm wondering if the optional keyword on a message-typed field can be used to distinguish between a _deliberately assigned_ null/default value versus "no value was set".

nodes.body:
> Does the optional keyword have any effect on message-typed fields?

It does not have any semantic effect. It doesn't change the generated API or the semantic behavior of the field in any way.

> As such, I'm wondering if the optional keyword on a message-typed field can be used to distinguish between a deliberately assigned null/default value versus "no value was set".

Yes, for a message-typed field you can distinguish between a deliberately assigned default value versus "no value was set."

However, this is always true, regardless of whether or not `optional` is specified. Even for a field *without* optional, you can still tell whether the field was set or not, as long as the field is a message.
@haberman Thank you for your quick response! For clarification, could you show a quick example, on a message-typed field, of an "is not set" check versus a "null value" check?
Message fields are bi-state: either set or unset. They are not tri-state (set, not set, null value).

> Message fields are bi-state: either set or unset. They are not tri-state (set, not set, null value).

This is the essence of my question.

Say we are performing an update of our personal details, which includes (among other things) a complex Address field. What is the recommended way that we address the tri-state nature of updates?

1. "Set my address to this set of fields"
2. "Set my address to null" (say, because [GDPR](https://gdpr-info.eu/))
3. "Do not touch my address, since I am only updating _other_ components with this call" (say, because the client is on a version that does not _know_ about the new Address field)

I'd like to emphasize how important such distinctions are to contract versioning. For example, imagine the server introducing the Address field in v2, and a client on v1 omitting this field it does not even know about. It'd be a shame if the server went and nulled out everybody's address as a result.

@haberman Apologies for my delayed reply.

I appreciate your efforts at a solution, but I do not believe that we have a foolproof one yet. For example:

- If the object happens to be a set of three integers, then there is no difference between an "empty" object and an object containing three `0`s. (Correct me if am wrong.)
- If the object contains nullable properties, then we cannot always distinguish between "unset the address property" vs. "update the address property to these fields, and I just happen to want to set all of them to null".

These things create confusion, in my experience. Protocols rely on utter clarity, and we are talking about a fairly common occurrence for updates.

I realize that I could create a separate tombstone property, but that seems to defeat the purpose and applicability of the optional keyword. Is there a cleaner way to achieve what I'm talking about?

target_link_libraries(try_protobuf ${Protobuf_LIBRARIES})

title: Fail 同
Undocumented breaking change in 3.20.0 for Python - numpy singleton arrays
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.20.0
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Ubuntu 20.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
libprotoc 3.19.4, installed from https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/download/v3.19.4/protoc-3.19.4-linux-x86_64.zip
Python 3.8.10
numpy 1.19.5


**What did you do?**

In version 3.19.4, it was valid to assign a numpy ndarray of shape `(1,)` to a scalar field, such as `float`:

```python
In [1]: from google.protobuf.wrappers_pb2 import FloatValue

In [2]: import numpy as np

In [3]: m = FloatValue(value=np.array([1.0]))

In [4]: m
Out[4]: value: 1.0
```

In version 3.20.0, this is now a `TypeError`:

```python

In [4]: import numpy as np

In [5]: m = FloatValue(value=np.array([1.0]))

Successful build

**What did you see instead?**
```
/pobj/protobuf-3.20.0/protobuf-3.20.0/src/google/protobuf/arenastring.cc:67:1: error: static_assert failed due to requirement '(kStringAlign > kNewAlign ? kStringAlign : kNewAlign) >= 8' ""

^             ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
1 error generated.
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
kNewAlign is set in the #ifdef'd lines above; in this case it is 4 bytes and comes from `__STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__`. alignof(::max_align_t) and alignof(std::max_align_t)  are 8 bytes.

nodes.body:
This was fixed in OpenBSD's LLVM by adjusting the target info to take our malloc alignment into account, which effectively changes `__STDCPP_DEFAULT_NEW_ALIGNMENT__` to be 16 on i386:

https://github.com/openbsd/src/commit/dc1895c3dde03d61ceaa07854da438264dccc5d6

Maybe FreeBSD will want a similar fix @sunpoet ?

Seeing a whole bunch of [build failures](http://autobuild.buildroot.net/?reason=protobuf-3.20.1) related to this with [buildroot's](https://buildroot.org/)(linux cross compilation toolkit) autobuilders on a few different architectures.

See also this: https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1785285#c12

Per that discussion, this just looks like a buggy expectation in protobuf's source code.  Not knowing the protobuf source, I do not yet have a suggested fix.  It would be appreciated if someone who does could weigh in.

I believe this is already fixed at head.
Can you confirm?

> I believe this is already fixed at head. Can you confirm?

I believe that head has a change to address one of the alignment problems - specifically the one mentioned by the OP regarding kStringAlign.

As another similar alignment problem example, however, the build for FreeBSD/i386 (32-bit x86 which has `alignof(uint64_t) = 4`) still fails with the recent 21.5 release:

    In file included from ./google/protobuf/arena.h:52:
     ./google/protobuf/arena_impl.h:643:10: error: requested alignment is less than minimum alignment of 8 for type 'google::protobuf::internal::ThreadSafeArena::CacheAlignedLifecycleIdGenerator'
      struct alignas(kCacheAlignment) CacheAlignedLifecycleIdGenerator {
             ^
    1 error generated.



This is not exactly the same error as the one described by the OP, but it is closely related.  It is another case where requiring alignment of 8 bytes causes build errors on certain platforms.

`CacheAlignedLifecycleIdGenerator` no longer exists at head.
Please verify if this problem persist on some other code.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: main
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
gLinux

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Debian clang version 13.0.1-3

Also reproducible with Chromium's clang

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
```
git clone https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf.git
cd protobuf
git submodule update --init --recursive
./autogen.sh
./configure CXX=clang++ CXXFLAGS="-Werror -Winvalid-noreturn"
make -j20
```

**What did you expect to see**
The build passes

**What did you see instead?**
The build fails with:
```
In file included from google/protobuf/generated_message_tctable_lite.cc:36:
./google/protobuf/generated_message_tctable_impl.h:256:1: error: function declared 'noreturn' should not return [-Werror,-Winvalid-noreturn]
}
^
google/protobuf/generated_message_tctable_lite.cc:57:15: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'google::protobuf::internal::AlignFail<4UL>' requested here
template void AlignFail<4>(uintptr_t);
              ^
In file included from google/protobuf/generated_message_tctable_lite.cc:36:
./google/protobuf/generated_message_tctable_impl.h:256:1: error: function declared 'noreturn' should not return [-Werror,-Winvalid-noreturn]
}
^
google/protobuf/generated_message_tctable_lite.cc:58:15: note: in instantiation of function template specialization 'google::protobuf::internal::AlignFail<8UL>' requested here
template void AlignFail<8>(uintptr_t);
```

The issue seems to be that AlignFail calls `GOOGLE_LOG(FATAL)`, but `GOOGLE_LOG(FATAL)` is not obviously a `[[noreturn]]` function. The abort is deep inside `LogFinisher::operator=` -> `LogMessage::Finish` -> a check on `level_`. Instead, I think the macro needs to do the token concatenation trick so that it can call a different function marked `[[noreturn]]`. For instance, move the abort to `LogFinisher::operator=` and then use a different `FatalLogFinisher` type whose `operator=` is marked `[[noreturn]]`.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
This impacts the update to Chromium's copy of protobuf, since this is one of the warnings we enable.

Curiously the one compiler that appears to be fine with this construct being `noreturn` is also the one compiler that does not get that function declared `noreturn`.

https://godbolt.org/z/13n59aM8s

title: extreme performance degradation on M1 with python
body:
Hi, I'm not a protobuf user directly, but ran into this using pulumi.

On a Mac M1 Max, python3.9 arm64 build, trying to serialize roughly 8k of yaml from a Struct, takes a very, very long time. I give up after 10 minutes or so, not sure if it ever completes. The exact same code on Linux (running in an arm64 VM on the Mac) completes instantly. 

```python
# !pip install protobuf==3.19.4 pyyaml

import time
import yaml
from google.protobuf.struct_pb2 import Struct
import urllib.request

k8s_yaml = urllib.request.urlopen('https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.8.0/cert-manager.crds.yaml')

y = list(yaml.load_all(k8s_yaml, Loader=yaml.Loader))[2]

x = Struct()
x.update(y)

# uncomment to complete script in < 1s
# x['spec']['versions'][0]['schema']['openAPIV3Schema']['properties']['spec']['properties']['solver']['properties'].Clear()

t = time.time()

# this line is very, very, slow.
x.SerializeToString()

print(f'serialize={time.time() - t:.4f}')
```

nodes.body:
You are probably getting the pure-Python implementation on the Mac, instead of the C++ accelerated version you are seeing on Linux.

I do not believe we are publishing aarch64 binaries for Mac at the moment. You can compile one yourself using the instructions posted here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8820#issuecomment-961552604

ok, that was the reason. I did do a local build of the grpcio package, but that clearly didn't build the protobuf extension as well. Thank you. Two questions, if I may. When is the M1 support coming? And shouldn't the pure python version still work in a reasonable fashion? How is it possible that it is so non-functional, at least in my use case? Thanks again.

> When is the M1 support coming?

The next release of Python will have a completely rewritten C extension. This should ship sometime next month, and I expect that it will ship with aarch64 binaries.

> And shouldn't the pure python version still work in a reasonable fashion?

The pure-Python implementation is very slow, just due to the performance limitations of Python as a language. Still, 10 minutes for an 8k payload seems excessive.

What do you get if you do `print(x.ByteSize())` with the C extension?

> What do you get if you do print(x.ByteSize()) with the C extension?

58225

> The pure-Python implementation is very slow

Python can be slow, but not this slow. There must be either a bug in the pure python code, or something O(n2) going on.

Another data point. Disabling the extension in Linux also causes the above test code to never finish:

```bash
$ PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=python python test.py
```

> Disabling the extension in Linux also causes the above test code to never finish:

It is expected that the pure-Python implementation on Linux and Mac would give similar results.

> Python can be slow, but not this slow. There must be either a bug in the pure python code, or something O(n2) going on.

I agree this is an extreme result. We probably won't be able to prioritize a diagnosis and fix of this anytime soon, because performance-wise we focus on the C/C++ extensions. We would welcome PRs for this though.

nodes.body:
It only happens when package is empty. 

The .proto file starts with a package declaration, which helps to prevent naming conflicts between different projects. In Python, packages are normally determined by directory structure, so the package you define in your .proto file will have no effect on the generated code. However, you should still declare package to avoid name collisions in the Protocol Buffers name space as well as in non-Python languages.
Closing this since the similar issue is fixed: https://github.com/googleapis/python-api-core/issues/372

title: Python: Version compatibility guarantees
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Currently there are no documented guarantee that a minor version bump of the protobuf Python library is backward-compatible.

There are some python libraries that depend on Protobuf, but are depending on a strict range of minor versions because there are no guarantee that `<4` versions would work if the library now works with `3.20` for example. See https://github.com/mitmproxy/mitmproxy/issues/5160 as an example.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Based on previous changes to this library, I assume the intention is to keep backward compatibility between minor versions, so I propose documenting this guarantee.

nodes.body:
It is indeed our intention to keep backward compatibility between minor versions.

We are doing a major version bump for Python this week. This link speaks to that and mentions our intention to rev the major version number whenever there is a breaking change: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#versioning

nodes.body: On Windows we say some programs are ANSI programs, some programs are Unicode programs. Unicode programs only use wide char(UTF-16) strings. If every sting is unicode, then the same code works for all languages that Windows can support.  Otherwise it would be less ideal. If you need to run any ANSI program with localized language support, you should set your system's display language and system locale  to the language. Here I saw your UI is english, but you want to use Chinese. It is fine for Unicode programs, but it is not good for ANSI program.

title: Python: using native namespace packages
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/python/google/__init__.py
Python package is using pkg_resources style namespace by default, which is not compatible with PEP420

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Delete the `google/__init__.py`
From https://github.com/pypa/packaging.python.org/blob/main/source/guides/packaging-namespace-packages.rst

> It is extremely important that every distribution that uses the namespace package omits the :file:`__init__.py` or uses a pkgutil-style :file:`__init__.py`. If any distribution does not, it will cause the namespace logic to fail and the other sub-packages will not be importable.
 
And also:

> Some older recommendations advise the following in the namespace package :file:`__init__.py`:
> ```
> try:
>     __import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(__name__)
> except ImportError:
>     __path__ = __import__('pkgutil').extend_path(__path__, __name__)
> ```
> The idea behind this was that in the rare case that setuptools isn't available packages would fall-back to the pkgutil-style packages. This isn't advisable because pkgutil and pkg_resources-style namespace packages are not cross-compatible. If the presence of setuptools is a concern then the package should just explicitly depend on setuptools via install_requires.

Is there any use cases that require using legacy style pacakge namespace?

nodes.body:
@fancl20 : If you install the package with pip (and not `setup.py install`), the `__init__.py` files will not be installed. That will maintain the native namespace package for `google`. You can install to an isolated venv, or to your user-level library, to avoid conflicting with system packages.

(Sadly, the `__init__.py` file is still around in the repo for various reasons, none of which are good reasons. However, this should not be an issue as long as you use pip for the final installation step.)

title: Python ParseFromString gets "error: Error parsing message" when reading Serialiezed String from file.
body:
I have the following codes in my project:
```
message Log {
  string id = 1;
  string code = 2;
  string message = 3;
}
```
and I am serialize the data into string and write it with other information (e.g. timestamp) into files. (each line contains a serialized message)
```
msg = logs_pb.Log(id = "id", code = "code", message = "message")
logfd = os.open(file_path, os.O_APPEND | os.O_RDWR | os.O_CREAT)
gevent_file_obj = gevent.fileobject.FileObject(logfd, 'w')
gevent_file_obj.write('{} | {}\n'.format(time.time(), serialized_msg.strip('\n').strip('\t')))
```
then when reading the file, I get the serialized data by
```
logfd = os.open(file_path, os.O_RDONLY)
gevent_file_obj = gevent.fileobject.FileObject(logfd, 'r')
data = gevent_file_obj.readline()
msg = data.split('|')[1].strip()
```
The errors `error: Error parsing message` occurs when I tried to deserialize the string using
```
parse_data = logs_pb.Log()
parse_data.ParseFromString(msg)
```

I understand writing the serialized data into string in files might cause some problem
`gevent_file_obj.write('{} | {}\n'.format(time.time(), serialized_msg.strip('\n').strip('\t')))`
as the serialized string might have some special characters like `\t`.

Then if there any recommendation if I would like to write the serialized data with other strings in files and let it be read and parsed later? What's the proper way to store the data and read it later?

nodes.body: I would recommend storing the serialized proto in a file by itself. This would simplify things quite a bit since then you wouldn't be mixing text and binary in the same file. If you need to include the current time, you can always just make that a field in the proto. Otherwise if you really need to have free-form text along with your proto, you could base64-encode your serialized proto so that it's represented in plain text.

Could you help me understand and elaborate more on "free-form text along with your proto"? Are you recommending `import base64` and something like `base64.b64encode(the_byte_message)`, so the encoded bytes will not contain those special characters and could be parsed as normal string?

title: .NET 3.5 support is now infeasible for C# - remove references to it
body:
The [C# README](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/csharp/README.md) suggests that .NET 3.5 is supported, and indeed there's quite a lot of code that is conditional on .NET 3.5.

However, since all of the serialization changes to use `Span<T>` in the middle of 2020, it's basically infeasible to make the current codebase work with .NET 3.5 without an entirely separate path just for that platform.

IMO we should remove all mention of .NET 3.5 in both the README and the code.

cc @jtattermusch

title: Using cpp generated pb within python
body:
## 🐞 Issue

As can be seen from the [benchmarks](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/docs/performance.md), `python pb` show an immense performance boost while using the option with `c++` generated code. I tried searching for docs on how to use it but found none except a [thread](https://groups.google.com/g/protobuf/c/z7E80KYJscc?pli=1) dating back to 2010. I then tried the [solution](https://groups.google.com/g/protobuf/c/z7E80KYJscc/m/ysCjHHmoraUJ) but no significant change in performance occurred.

## Details

In more details what I did was to (follow the solution):

1. Create an empty `my_module.cc` module that imports `Python.h` as can be seen from the solution.
1. Generate `cpp` code from the `protobuf` definitions and move it to the same directory as `my_module.c`.
1. Import the generated `cpp` code header from within `my_module.cc`.
1. Add an extension to the `setup.py` file and build a shared object for `my_module`.
1. Import `my_module` within the `python` code before importing any other modules.
1. Benchmark the parsing performance of the code and observe no significant changes.

## ❓ Questions

1. Is the option is still relevant and viable?
1. Is there any proper guide on how to implement it? (not just some long forgotten thread)
1. Is there a way to check if I'm actually using the option, i.e. whether the message creation process is delegated to the `cpp DescriptorPool/MessageFactory`?

Thank you in advance.

---
PS - This is different from using only the recommended option with the `c` extension of `protobuf`. As I understand it when using `cpp` generated code the `c` extension should switch to directly using the `cpp` code instead of reflections of `python` code.

title: Python bindings should coerce pathlib objects to strings when serializing
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?

generate Python bindings

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

as we migrate our codebase from `str` for paths to `pathlib.Path` (with our APIs usually accepting `Union[str, os.PathLike]` akin to Python stdlibs), we find ourselves having to coerce Path's into strings when generating messages.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

generate protobuf bindings should accept `Path` for `string` types and coerce them into strings for us

nodes.body:
Discussed with some other team members and we think we do not want accept Path for string field.

Any class can define `__str__` for string representation. If we did `str(val)` without a type check then we would accept any kind of object and convert it to string. But we want stronger type checking than that.
that's why you'd type check against `pathlib.PurePath`, not just see if the class has `__str__` (since, afaik, every class does)

title: FromJsonString timezone_offset set to wrong character
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: protobuf==3.19.1
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Mac 

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.8.5

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Define a proto definition with the google timestamp type `google.protobuf.Timestamp time`
2. Generate the python message stubs
3. Convert a json string with that value mapping to the protobuf python type using `json_format` 
```
from google.protobuf import json_format
```
Example time string:  `2022-05-02T16:18:58.925142` which matches the documented expected format:
```Example of accepted format: '1972-01-01T10:00:20.021-05:00'```
from the source code [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/python/google/protobuf/internal/well_known_types.py#L135)
**What did you expect to see**
Successful mapping
**What did you see instead?**
```
google.protobuf.json_format.ParseError: ... time data '2022-05' does not match format '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S'...
```
No error occurs if I replace the `T` with a `Z` to match the code but that doesn't match the expected format. 
Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body: The `Z` character isn't meant to match the `T` in the middle, but rather matches information given about the timezone (hence the name `timezone_offset`). The format of this time requires a time zone specified. You can see in the example of accepted format the `-05:00` suffix denotes the timezone. If you don't want to specify a timezone, you can append the character `Z` to specify a UTC offset of `00:00`. You can read more about this format [here](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3339).

title: Bug: Big endian assumed on little endian QNX targets
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

Version: v3.15 and later
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

QNX SDP 7.0 for aarch64 (little endian)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

gcc 5.4 (supplied with QNX SDP 7.0)

**What did you do?**

Compile protobuf for a little endian aarch64 QNX SDP 7.0 target.

**What did you expect to see**

`PROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN` should be defined.

**What did you see instead?**

`PROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN` is not defined.  We have root-caused this to be why we have observed byte-swapped `fixed64` fields (!!).

The method to determine the endianess of the target changed in v3.15.  Prior to this, the header `sys/param.h` was used.  It was replaced by a method that includes `endian.h` for several different platforms.  A later change (bd9d47db41) skipped over the inclusion of `endian.h` for QNX targets, since the file does not exist on the QNX platform.  However, this leaves neither `sys/param.h` nor `endian.h` included for QNX targets, resulting in `PROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN` _not_ being defined on little endian QNX targets.

We suggest small change like this could be applied to `src/google/protobuf/stubs/port.h` and `src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h`
```
 #include <sys/endian.h>  // __BYTE_ORDER
+#elif defined(__QNX__)
+#include <sys/param.h>  // __BYTE_ORDER
 #else
```

nodes.body: @glenn-elliott If you want to send a pull request with that change then I would be happy to merge it.

title: 'string' is no longer a member of 'google::protobuf'
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.20.0
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 11

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Visual Studio - MSVC 14.29

**What did you do?**
I updated from protobuf version 3.19.4 to 3.20.1 for my project and started seeing a build error:
`error C2039: 'string': is not a member of 'google::protobuf'`

**What did you expect to see**
I expected to see no build errors since this is just a minor version change.

**What did you see instead?**
I'm seeing build errors like this:
`error C2039: 'string': is not a member of 'google::protobuf'`

**Details**
I compared the headers between version 3.19.4 and 3.20.0 and noticed an important difference in the file src/google/protobuf/stubs/common.h. Specifically, the following lines were removed:
```c++
// This is at the end of the file instead of the beginning to work around a bug
// in some versions of MSVC.
using std::string;
```

This means that code can no longer use `google::protobuf::string`. This seems like an unintended breaking change. @acozzette - This seems to have happened between [Jan 27](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/22d0e265de7d2b3d2e9a00d071313502e7d4cccf/src/google/protobuf/stubs/common.h) and [Jan 28](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/18521f60556b48be8beb6623dc6cb0c0ed80a79b/src/google/protobuf/stubs/common.h) for the `common.h` header file. Was the intention to move the `using` statement to the beginning of the file?

Thanks for looking into this issue!

nodes.body: Thank you for the bug report, but this was actually an intentional change. We used to have `using namespace std;` in this file to allow us to refer to anything in `std::` with a shorter name, but we cleaned that up a while ago enough so that the only symbol we referred to in this way was `std::string`. And then more recently we finally cleaned that up as well, and deleted the `using std::string` line. Is it possible to update your code to refer to `std::string` instead of `google::protobuf::string`?
Thanks for the quick clarification @acozzette! Yes, it's definitely possible to update code to use `std::string` instead. I wanted to be sure it was an intentional change before I made that move :)

title: ABI may depend on NDEBUG

nodes.body:
For the record, my current workaround is to build both release and debug and in my app's CMakeLists.txt I have to do:

if (NOT WIN32) ## this is a workaround for https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9947
    set(Protobuf_LIBRARY optimized ${myproject_SOURCE_DIR}/3rdparty/lib/libprotobuf.a
                         debug ${myproject_SOURCE_DIR}/3rdparty/lib/libprotobufd.a
    )
endif(NOT WIN32)
Supporting mixed compilation modes is not something we intend to do, as avoiding ODR violations under this kind of a context comes with significant performance costs that we are unwilling to pay.

As I'm used to compiling under windows where you almost always have to compile things twice (1 debug, 1 release), I'm not shocked. The only nice thing that would help is then if FindProtobuf would find both release and debug libs on its own.

I understand the desire not to support situations which are _stricto sensu_ undefined behaviour.

It also makes protobuf more difficult to use in situations where pre-built release binaries are available (e.g. Debian/Ubuntu packages), but no debug ones.

Adding my voice here: I think it is a deviation from common practice to change the ABI based on whether `NDEBUG` is defined or not.  Or put another way: it is common practice on Linux to install a library using the system package manager, and then use this library (which naturally was compiled in release mode) to compile your *application* in debug mode [*]


[*] I am sure it is also common practice to install different libraries for debug and release. Both practices can be "common" at the same time.

> Supporting mixed compilation modes is not something we intend to do, as avoiding ODR violations under this kind of a context comes with significant performance costs that we are unwilling to pay.

Where can we see the performance metrics this decision seems to be based on?

@fowles

As @cwharris wonders, I don't think fixing this without ODR violation costs such significant performance costs either. Modern processors with sophisticated memory hierarchy and branch predictors should be able to handle the branch depending on the debug switch in a few cycles, which is much cheaper than the core deallocation logic. Is there really no chance such costs can be tolerated?

@cwharris the performance measurements we are using are only available inside google.  They are essentially websearch performance tests.  Even a half a percent of websearches overall performance foot print turns out to be a very large number.
@coryan that is only one of quite a few things that have ABI dependencies
It's the only problem that seems to be breaking third-party downstream projects, though, so probably worth tackling?
If someone has the cycles to create a PR, I can review it
Re-opening since we would be willing to review a PR, but we cannot commit to fixing this in the near term (we are too busy with other commitments).

title: Allow invoking the plugin of `protoc --plugin` with arguments
body:
Currently the `protoc --help` says this:

```
  --plugin=EXECUTABLE         Specifies a plugin executable to use.
                              Normally, protoc searches the PATH for
                              plugins, but you may specify additional
                              executables not in the path using this flag.
                              Additionally, EXECUTABLE may be of the form
                              NAME=PATH, in which case the given plugin name
                              is mapped to the given executable even if
                              the executable's own name differs.
```

And EXECUTABLE is limited to name an executable.

I suggest that EXECUTABLE be replaced with a full command (including arguments)


Context:
This is coming from dart-specific view-point, but I think the solution has more general applicability:

Currently the [suggested](https://github.com/google/protobuf.dart/tree/master/protoc_plugin#how-to-build) way to use the dart protoc_plugin is to do `dart pub global acticivate protoc_plugin` because that will create a "binstub"  (a small executable script that invokes the dart vm with protoc_plugin.dart`) on the PATH.

**Ideally** we'd like to be able to install protoc_plugin as a local dependency in your project, and run it from there. But that will not give you a single executable to run.

 and then invoke 

`protoc --plugin='dart=dart run protoc_plugin' --dart_out=...`

Currently this can be done by making one's own shell/batch script that invokes `dart run protoc_plugin` but that is somewhat cumbersome.

nodes.body: Unfortunately this is the only way to use plugins and we will probably not be prioritizing this work soon, since there is a simple workaround.

nodes.body:
> `_message.Message._CheckCalledFromGeneratedFile()`

This error indicates that you are using old generated code. The file `error_details_pb2.py` must have been generated by a protoc prior to 3.19.0.

Per the update at https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#python-updates, protobuf 4.21.0 requires that the `_pb2.py` files are generated from protoc >= 3.19.0

If you regenerate the `_pb2.py` files it should fix the problem.

> The strange thing is that installing grpcio-tools solved the issue, however removing grpcio-tools did not bring the issue back.

My hunch is that installing grpcio-tools downgraded protobuf to 3.x.

@haberman - since it looks like 4.21.0 final is not yet released, could the protobuf team please consider improving the error message that users get in this case to make it clearer what's broken, prior to the final release?

For example, maybe `google._upb._message.Message` could be populated with some shim that emits an error message pointing users to https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#python-updates or some other indication that the `protobuf` dep is too new for the generated code to work?

The context is that my team also got a report of this issue: https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorboard/issues/5703  Older releases of our pip package that have generated Python proto files don't have an upper bound on their `protobuf` runtime dep, which historically hadn't been a problem, but I'm concerned it will become a significant breakage as soon as 4.21.0 is released, and it would help a lot of if the error message was a bit more self-explanatory that downgrading the protobuf dep to the 3.x major version series would at least temporarily resolve the problem.

Edited to add that this will also break a lot of existing released TensorFlow pip packages with the same unclear failure mode, as I think you've seen: https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/issues/56077#issuecomment-1125724970

I am not on the TF team but FWIW, my understanding is that they are blocked on upgrading protoc due to https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/issues/53234 which is very unlikely to be something that can be resolved in a few days, and TF's release cadence almost certainly wouldn't allow rushing out a patch release in that time frame either, so a fix on the TF side seems very challenging given the relatively short notice.

> could the protobuf team please consider improving the error message that users get in this case to make it clearer what's broken, prior to the final release?

Yes I think that is a good idea. I had been thinking a similar thing.
@haberman Thanks for considering, that would be much appreciated 👍

title: PHP: `ReflectionProperty` returns default values for `optional` fields

nodes.body:
The properties of our generated class are `protected` and are therefore an implementation detail. No contract is made about what these properties will contain if you access them directly.

The correct way to do this with protobuf would be to use protobuf reflection. However the protobuf library does not currently support reflection in PHP. Feel free to file a feature request for this.

Another option would be to call the generated accessor by string name. However you would have to camel-case the name yourself, eg.

```php
$name = 'getValue2';
var_dump($payload->{$name}());
```

> My impression was that native extension is the drop-in performance boost.

The native extension is a drop-in performance boost as -- long as you use the public API only.

For example, a call like `$payload->getValue2()` will behave the same whether you have the native extension or not.

Accessing protected properties of the generated class using `ReflectionProperty` is not supported, and therefore the results are not guaranteed to be the same.

> What's the difference between `$payload->getValue2()` and `$payload->{$name}()`?

If `$name == 'getValue2` then those two should be identical -- they are both calling `$payload->getValue2()`.

I see, then extension would also return the default value, not accounting for the optional null.

Would changing getters’ behaviour to return nulls for optional be a non-starter? This values are not passed into the serialized payload, so not sure why do they have to carry defaults.

Protobuf semantics are always to return a default value for primitive types like strings/numbers. When implementations deviate from this, it tends to cause problems.

For example, for `syntax="proto2";` files (which PHP doesn't currently support, but should someday) [users can specify explicit defaults](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#optional). If we returned null for unset values, any user-specified default value would be ignored.

title: Failed to parse the serialized value with gcc -O2

nodes.body:
This line:

```
*(char *)&a = 0xff; 
```

is Undefined Behavior in C++.

Under C++ rules, once Undefined Behavior is exercised, the behavior of the entire program is undefined: the compiler is free to optimize and rearrange code while assuming well-defined behavior, so anything depending on a `bool` variable actually being 1 bit may no longer function correctly.

Unfortunately, per C++ language rules, if your code has undefined behavior, there is not much that protobufs can do to make sense of it.

Hi @dlj-NaN

Thanks for your reply.
My question is why serialization can succeed, but deserialization fails? When serializing, it can save 0xff to bool value, and when deserializing, it should be able to parse out from 0xff to bool value.

body:
**What language does this apply to?**

This applied to Kotlin generated code

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

In the java generated code we are able to build from another Message or Builder by doing:

```newBuilder(messageOrBuilder)```

this will populate the existing fields to the new Builder.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I think we simply need to generate an overload function of the Message Builder and add a parameter to it before the Builder lambda.

**Additional context**

nodes.body: Sounds reasonable. It would require a Tier 2 review.
I don't think I fully understand what you are proposing. Can you provide an example of what you have to do now to workaround this and what you would like the syntax to look like?

Right. Sorry for not being clear. Let's say I have the following message:

```
message SearchRequest {
  string query = 1;
  uint32 page = 2;
  uint32 page_size = 3;
}
```
and let's say that I already such a request but I need to create a new one and change the page_size. With the Kotlin DSL when creating such a request I need to do:

```
searchRequest {
    this.query = that.query
    this.page = that.page
    this.page_size = newPageSize
}
```

in Java though I could do the following:

```
SearchRequest.newBuilder(that).setPageSize(newPageSize).build()
```

I'm not reassigning all the fields.

So I hope we can generate something like:

```
public inline fun searchRequest(from: SearchRequest, block: SearchRequestKt.Dsl.() -> kotlin.Unit): SearchRequest
```

and that instead of using the `newBuilder` in the `_create` function, we use the `from.toBuilder()`. This would then assign all the already existing fields to the instance and we could only change the necessary ones.

This would make the syntax much clearer and shorter:

```
searchRequest(from = that) { pageSize = newPageSize }
```

Hope that's clearer

Thanks for the example!

Kotlin protos are based on Java protos so you also have access to all Java protobuf methods, including the `newBuilder` that you want to use. So currently the easiest way to do what you are asking for is:
```
SearchRequest.newBuilder(that).apply {
    pageSize = newPageSize
}.build()
```

While this is better than the Kotlin DSL example you gave, I agree that the syntax you suggested is shorter, clearer, and more idiomatic. 

Given that we already have an implementation (even though it isn't optimal), I'm hesitant to prioritize the work. That being said, if you are still interested in contributing I can move forward with the team to see if we can get this proposal approved and ready to work on.

title: PHP version of protobuf has hardcoded total_byte_limit equal to 32MB
body:
Protobuf v3.x, PHP all versions, all systems and evironments.

There is a hardcoded limit which prevents reading ONNX files which are typically very large (hundreds of MBs):
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/07303d6f54e4768700925119a003493aacdb70ff/php/src/Google/Protobuf/Internal/CodedInputStream.php#L53

Raeching the limit starts chain of failures that finally throws Exception with misleading name and description:
> Fatal error: Uncaught Google\Protobuf\Internal\GPBDecodeException: Error occurred during parsing: Unexpected EOF inside bytes field.

For other languages this limit is not only much, much higher (like, 2GB for C++ instead of 32MB for PHP):
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/07303d6f54e4768700925119a003493aacdb70ff/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h#L623

...but also there are methods to change it programatically.:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/07303d6f54e4768700925119a003493aacdb70ff/src/google/protobuf/io/coded_stream.h#L367-L384

Either add a method to raise the limit or increase the hardcoded value. And make some better exception message for this.

nodes.body: My pull request with proposed setTotalBytesLimit() method (analogous to C++ one): https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/9992
Interesting that it's only 32 MB, though that is still much larger than protobufs were designed for. Data formats that are in the 100+ megabytes really shouldn't be using protobufs.
Duplicate of https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9521, follow along there for progress.

title: 21.0-rc2: Extra 3 in release assets.
body:
The language-specific release tarballs and zips for [21.0-rc2][1] have an extra `3` version digit at the beginning when compared with [21.0-rc1][2].

For example, [protobuf-cpp-3.3.21.0-rc-2.tar.gz](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/download/v21.0-rc2/protobuf-cpp-3.3.21.0-rc-2.tar.gz) used to be [protobuf-cpp-3.21.0-rc-1.tar.gz](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/download/v21.0-rc1/protobuf-cpp-3.21.0-rc-1.tar.gz). The same is true for all other languages.

This isn't special to this release, but is also a bit confusing: the tag is `v21.0-rc2` while the assets have an additional hyphen in their name `21.0-rc-2`. It would be great if only one spelling of `rcN` could be used throughout.

[1]: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v21.0-rc2
[2]: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v21.0-rc1

nodes.body:
Thanks for pointing this out! I will make sure in the final 21.0 release doesn't have the extra number.

I agree the discrepancy between `-rc2` and `-rc-2` is confusing. Right now we are trying to keep the naming consistent with previous releases, but we will be looking in the future toward renaming/rethinking these source artifacts.

While rethinking the source distributions it would be helpful to understand how users are using them. Would you mind explaining what you use these tar files for?

Thanks!

We use  the C++ and Python language runtime for packaging in OpenBSD. The C++ runtime has been used since  Protobuf 2.3.0 and has a sizable number of consumers (about 150-160 packages, mostly via Qt). The Python bindings were added much later (in 2018). Python originally used PyPi, but this never had release candidates and always had a bit of a delay, so it was switched to using the release assets directly.

I am aware of a number of people using both C++ and Python runtime for their development. There has never been a need for the other language bindings, and switching to using `protobuf-all` always seemed more trouble than it's worth, so we stuck with what is known to work.

I notice the discrepancies in the version numbers in my workflow while testing before committing the actual release, because the naive bumping of version numbers in the build infrastructure then fails.

nodes.body:
Per spec, "mergeFrom(Message other): (builder only) merges the contents of other into this message, overwriting singular scalar fields, merging composite fields, and concatenating repeated fields" so it does seem that the repeated payloads fields should be concatenated instead of replaced. 

I'm not sure what to do about this, or if it's possible to change this. We might decide to bless the current behavior.

> 

I think it probably make better sense to even just throw a `"Not Implemented"` than providing a `random` implementation. 

For my case, I have several messages each with around 1 million repeated fields (the `payload`). While the front tier (a graphql) return the combined result (expecting several million of records back), however, always return 1 million fields. It took me quite a while to troubleshoot till surprisingly found out the protobuf implementation is totally different from what the API (`mergeFrom`) sounds like, make me almost feel like it's a prank.
To get the behavior you want you'd need to take the bytes out of value, deserialize it as a PositionGroup, and then merge.

> 



> To get the behavior you want you'd need to take the bytes out of value, deserialize it as a PositionGroup, and then merge.

Yes, that's how I did as a workaround as well. 
However, I think the `mergeFrom` in `Any` could be fixed. I guess instead of swapping the value/bytes, it should have for example trim the ending bytes of PositionGroup1, and trim the beginning bytes of PositionGroup2, and concatenate them.

Ideally, as the spec says, `Any` should operate generically, without worrying about whether it has wrapped is a `PositionGroup` or `OrderGroup`. And a `swapValue` implementation should either not be there for a `mergeFrom` or at least warn the developers.

I'm not sure how that would work. An Any proto does not know what's inside of it.

Semantically an Any proto is just a URL and a BLOB. It knows nothing about the contents of the BLOB.

> 



> I'm not sure how that would work. An Any proto does not know what's inside of it.
> 
> Semantically an Any proto is just a URL and a BLOB. It knows nothing about the contents of the BLOB.

Alternatively, I think the type URL should be fixed. At the moment, the URL only contains the Simple name, something like `com.googleapi/PositionGroup`, this could provide the fully qualified name instead. With such, then `Any` could call out the right class for the actions for example `mergeFrom`.

Either way, `Any` could be more helpful in acting towards as a generic type.
That would be a backwards incompatible change in Any and in mergeFrom.

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

For a message like this
```
messages Orders {
  repeated Order payloads = 1;
}
message Order {
  ...
}
```
Actually this can be any message with size above ~2GB.
With a `toByte` call, it would result in `CodeOutputStream was writing to a flat byte array and ran out of space`.

sample code:
```
  Any.pack(orders).toByteArray();
```

This is actually an issue with the size variable being an `int`. Hence, the `message.getSerializedSize()` would give a wrong value (smaller than its real size). Hence, when the `CodeOutputStream` was trying to write the bytes, eventually it write more than the `limit` which is from `message.getSerializedSize()`.

nodes.body: With messages that large the standard libraries indeed do not work. You need to write your own custom own code for managing such large protobufs based on the wire format spec.

For protobuf this was a planned breaking change, which is why we rev'd the major version number. Please see the error message for possible workarounds that you can use until the other projects have regenerated their files:

> For protobuf this was a planned breaking change, which is why we rev'd the major version number.

You bumped the minor version number, not the major version number. According to [semver](https://semver.org/), you should bump the major version number for forward-incompatible changes. Of course, it's up to you how closely you want to follow semver (Python is removing distutils without bumping the major version), but at a minimum I think a deprecation warning for a couple of minor releases would avoid a lot of headaches.

> You bumped the minor version number, not the major version number. 

It was both, interestingly -- as far as non-RC package versions on PyPI, protobuf went from 3.20.1 to 4.21.0.  Fortunately for the moment 4.21.0 has been yanked from PyPI, but we have as yet no indicator of whether another breaking-change version will appear presently, so the instant reaction among many packages I'm seeing has been to pin our dependencies to protobuf<4.  This is unfortunate in numerous respects for the ecosystem; I hope a proper fallback path can be implemented so that we're not forever held to older versions.

Ah gotcha, didn't notice the major AND minor bump. I think a deprecation warning would still be appreciated, but you are following semver, so then I think the blame falls on packagers for not using `protobuf~=3.X` and assuming that a new major version will also work.

We do plan to roll forward w/ 4.21.0, We've discovered python cloud libraries were not adequately testing against our RCs and they discovered this late, despite our communications both [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06) and [here](https://groups.google.com/g/protobuf/c/qBgEzyvtvoY).

This will be a breaking change, and folks will need to either pin to 3.20.x, or simply update your usages to be compatible, that's a great option. :)

There are many great performance benefits to this new release, and we hope folks are able to take advantage of it.

@perezd - Respectfully, a relnote from two weeks ago and a forum post with < 50 views are arguably not enough notice for the whole ecosystem to react.  It's normal for packages not to look at RCs of their countless transitive dependencies; they won't even get installed unless you explicitly request `pip install --pre`.  Over a dozen engineers just within my group have had to scramble today to deal with fallout here from the many packages we depend on (only some of which we control).

What would you suggest we do differently? I'm open to suggestions. We bumped major version here, I guess your teams need to re-evaluate their adoption of major versions?

> It's normal for packages not to look at RCs of their countless transitive dependencies

That's completely the decision/culture of our customers to decide. We've followed best practices w/ semver, and if mission critical systems are negatively impacted by their loose dependency definitions, I'm struggling to understand how we could have been more accommodating here?

My advice would be to set up a CI system that verifies things are working as expected w/ `pip install --pre` as a canary.

>  and if mission critical systems are negatively impacted by their loose dependency definitions,

Well, this includes for example TensorFlow, which had its dependency specification as only `>=` until 6 days ago: https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/commit/60d5bfbf0241e00267884b0dc1723bbdfee1806a

I'm not saying this is great practice, but it's also incredibly common among Python packages (see the rest of that TensorFlow setup.py for example), which can and do bump major versions all the time without necessarily being indicative of breaking changes.  There's not much way for consumers of Python packages to know whether semver is or isn't going to be followed.

My suggestion would have been to give a deprecation period as @adamjstewart said, and better still to provide a fallback path to the 3.x-ish behavior wherever possible.

FWIW, TensorFlow identified this regression and worked with us during the RC phase, I'd call that working as intended.

> My suggestion would have been to give a deprecation period as @adamjstewart said, and better still to provide a fallback path to the 3.x-ish behavior wherever possible.

You're not required to upgrade to 4.21.x, we do follow semver for mitigating breaking changes, and the fallback is to accurately pin your dependencies.

We're here to support community engagements and follow best practices, and I believe our team has done that here.

As much as I would love to see a deprecation period, I can sympathize with the protobuf developers here. It can difficult with large refactors to have periods where both the old and new behavior is supported. I agree with @perezd that libraries that depend on protobuf really should be using `~=3.X` or `>=3.X,<4` until they've verified that their code works with 4.X. Once it works with 4.X, they should bump that to `>=3.X,<5`.

We did provide a deprecation period of sorts: 4.21.0 is compatible with generated code from protoc >= 3.19.0, which was released Oct 20, 2021. It would follow that anyone who was broken by 4.21.0 was using generated code that is at least seven months old.

For the deprecation window to really be effective though, users need to be made aware that some action is required on their part. We didn't make this clear back in October. However it's not clear how we could have done that. The communications channels we tried earlier this month (the [news page](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06), the [post to protobuf@googlegroups.com](https://groups.google.com/g/protobuf/c/qBgEzyvtvoY?pli=1), and the release candidates) clearly did not reach all of the interested parties.

I suppose we could have made the protobuf library log a warning starting back in October that users should update their generated code (and that the warning will soon become an error). I think this would have been the right way to go. The [Python stdlib `warnings` module](https://docs.python.org/3/library/warnings.html) is probably the best way to communicate such future changes in a way that downstream developers will see (or should, in their test-suite), but that doesn't immediately break end-user code.

> However, if it has to happen, I would also expect end users to pin the runtime to the exact version they generated said code with.

It has been pointed out to me that this would be infeasible because Python resolves dependencies across a whole project, so different protobuf-using libraries cannot pin to different specific versions of protobuf.

I agree that the blast-radius from this change was worsened by widespread use of `>= 3.x` in place of `~= 3.x` but using the major version of the Python package version in SemVer-style is only a good idea (a recommendation at strongest) in Python packages, not a requirement unlike some other languages, so `~=` is not the habitiual default for a lot of Python users, sadly.

I would go so far as to not label this "too subtle" but wrong in the context of understanding how these things are deployed and used.

The comment above about not checking in generated source, and thinking that semver fixes anything in a python/system wide installation reveals the bias that the authors are not actually using this in the same way their users are and seem to be running on a largely theoretical understanding of the python deployment ecosystem (I'll just be blunt about this versus dancing around it because it is a common bias in Google oss).

Concrete critiques:

* This isn't about checking in generated code. This is about pypi being full of (now read only) packages which include generated code from your code generator which you just decided it was fine to break on an arbitrary day in may, 2022. Some of these are "classic" versions of things that are years old and pinned to various lts release schedules. Not making a value judgment on that state, just saying how it is. A seven month, single version hard break like this would have been exceptionally user unfriendly no matter how you messaged it.
* It is true that there should be more diligence in downstream version specs with respect to allowable ranges, however I am not aware of anyone, without a good reason, who would defensively pin all of their deps with a complicated expression guarding against theoretical major version incompatibility for a project like this. You have to consider that you've effectively signaled a compatibility policy of forward compatibility for basically the life of the project and then just changed this in one step. Most of the people hitting this aren't protobuf users but users of users of the ecosystem you've built. When Tensorflow didn't change their version spec at head to a major version constraint until ~8 days before, you should have taken that as a strong signal and not just hid behind semver. If this had been my project, I would have seriously considered yanking the release based on this bug if I hadn't had the foresight.
* Versions need to be satisfied system wide. For a common "basement level" dep like this to introduce a hard break and advise that people start actively adding constraints on major version ranges... This will create a ripple effect over the coming months of people failing to be able to install any version that matches all constraints.
* As mentioned above, you have a fallback. It is common courtesy in python land to not require system level hacks (ie. An env var) for things to just work.
* A "basement level" dep like this, which has signaled a defacto lts/forward compatibility state on the order of many years probably needs O(years) notice and diligence to introduce a hard break. I know it's hard to be a code generator and deal with the various horizons but that's kind of the job of a library like this... It needs to bias towards a pragmatic, user sensitive compromise when worse comes to worse and things have to change in unsupportable ways. Semver is definitely a tool, but it is not a hammer for hitting users with, imo... And it doesn't actually solve the things you think it does in practice.

Feel free to take or leave my feedback. You asked, so I attempted to answer directly. In response to "strict adherence to semver guidelines", I would say -- put your users at least on equal footing as your beliefs on this front and reach for pragmatism and care with respect to how you pursue that end. Things break... That is life. But if I have a choice as a user, I avoid deps for basic things like this where the authors apply these kind of theoretical calculations.

title: PyPi repository for 4.21.0 doesn't specify required Python version
body:
Because the 4.21.0 release of protobuf on PyPi (https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/4.21.0) doesn't specify the required Python version, this leads to the installation of the library via `pip install protobuf` to fail when using Python versions smaller than 3.7 (leading to `protobuf requires Python '>=3.7' but the running Python is 3.6.9` for example). This also leads to other libraries such as `ortools` to fail installation.

How to replicate (the commands were ran from an Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS machine):

1. `python3.6 -m venv venv`
2. `. venv/bin/activate`
3. `pip install protobuf`

UNKNOWN

title: [java] Rename of java_names.h -> names.h causes downstream breakages
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.21.0
Language: Java

`google/protobuf/compiler/java/java_names.h` was renamed to `names.h` in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/40db3dabf0fe72b572e89c1e176318b04d3e2408. Ideally there'd be some forwarding header to ease this transition.

See discussion about grpc-java at https://github.com/grpc/grpc-java/pull/9218

Edited by ejona86: Fixed the commit link to reference protobuf instead of grpc PR commit

nodes.body: Changing the name is fine from our perspective; we don't need the old header long-term. But it would have been good if the first release that included the new name didn't also delete the old one. That is a flag-day that is guaranteed to cause breakages and prevent upgrades.

I'm sorry this breaking change was unannounced and no transitions were available. The protobuf team is working harder to ensure that breaking changes are intentional and well publicized, and will now follow [this policy](https://opensource.google/documentation/policies/library-breaking-change). 

Would forwarding headers still be helpful or has this issue been resolved?

gRPC Java has preprocessor logic to fix the build starting in 1.47.0. Most people don't build the grpc java protoc plugin from source, so they aren't impacted either way. I expect this mainly impacted Bazel users. To upgrade to newer Protobuf, those Bazel users would also need to upgrade to newer gRPC.

At this point forwarding includes wouldn't hurt, but I don't know if it'd actually benefit someone.
Ok I will go ahead and close this bug since I think it's likely people already did the necessary migrations.

An update on this since I ran into this issue while integrating the new Protobuf version with gRPC. The issue seems to be that `AddSerializedFile` will return `None` on subsequent invocations for the same file and same symbol DB. When `None` gets passed to `BuildMessageAndEnumDescriptors`, it has this error.

Since the symbol DB is a process-level singleton, this means that the module-level code of a `_pb2.py` file is executed multiple times within a single process, you'll encounter this error. Normally, this should be fine since modules are cached and subsequent imports of the same `_pb2` will not result in its module-level code being imported.

The issue in _our_ repo was that there was a latent bug in our test runner that imported each _pb2 multiple times under _different names_. By ensuring that each `_pb2` was only imported once under a single module name, this problem was avoided entirely.

```
grpcio==1.47.0
grpcio-tools==1.47.0
```

Installing _just_ `grpcio==1.47.0` caused a separate `free()` on a null pointer, which pointed me to this solution: https://github.com/googleapis/python-pubsub/issues/414

I wanted to understand what had happened, so I dug into the code. In my case, I was running on an M1 Mac. All of our builds were running perfectly fine under our x86-based infra which was the first clue. Looking into the code on version 1.37.1:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/909a0f36a10075c4b4bc70fdee2c7e32dd612a72/python/google/protobuf/descriptor.py#L60-L74
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/909a0f36a10075c4b4bc70fdee2c7e32dd612a72/python/google/protobuf/descriptor.py#L966-L985

Note that it attempts to load in extensions. If they aren't present (which they aren't by default under ARM64), you end up with a completely different metaclass for the descriptor.

In our case, we were calling `AddSerializedFile`. In the pure python implementation, there's no `return` which led to our `NoneType` error. https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/909a0f36a10075c4b4bc70fdee2c7e32dd612a72/python/google/protobuf/descriptor_pool.py#L204-L216

title: If a submessage created from Arena was moved to another object(no arena object),  is this Arena still hold the submessage?
body:
like this code:

`MyMessage* my_msg = google::protobuf::Arena::CreateMessage<MyMessage>(arena);`
`... set my_msg attributes`
`MyMessage my_msg_obj = std::move(*my_msg);`

if I delete arena object, is `my_msg_obj`  still can get these attributes`s value?

nodes.body:
**When I deteled the `arena` object, I found I still can get the values of these attributes from `my_msg_obj `.**

But this submessage and its attributes/values should be allocated in arena memory chuck, and the behavior of `std::move` not change its place in arena memory chuck. So I think this attributes/values should be null as the arena object is deleted.

It's not possible to efficiently move a message between arenas or between an arena and the stack/heap.  When you attempt to do this, it will actually just do a deep copy and leave the old message intact.

So this line:
`MyMessage my_msg_obj = std::move(*my_msg);`
will allocate a new MyMessage on the stack, and deep copy my_msg into it.  It's 100% equivalent to:
`MyMessage my_msg_obj = *my_msg`

Since the second object is purely owned by the stack, deleting the arena has no affect on it

I ran into this too.
The Unsafe class that Unity provides is internal rather than public. 
It looks like [Unity has purposely removed the Unsafe package from the .NET version they provide](https://forum.unity.com/threads/bug-1214643-2019-3-0f5-system-runtime-compilerservices-unsafe-clashes-with-imported-dll.816426/), as that package seems to be updated faster than they release, and their version quickly gets out of date and clashes with other assets providing/requiring a more up-to-date version of the dll. 

I believe Unity is expecting you to provide the Unsafe DLL version that works for you
You can find this dll in your MSVC install location (ex. C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2019\Community\MSBuild\Current\Bin) (other versions are also provided if you need a specific target platform)
Just drop it in your Managed Plugins folder

Since this is all managed code, unity should be able to extract all the appropriate code out of this dll when building your project when using il2cpp (you may need to create a link.xml file to prevent il2cpp from stripping out code from the Google.Protobuf.dll)

Hi, is there any update on this? We are also seeing this problem and are in a bit of a bind as our system is unable to scale to any reasonable capacity due to memory leaking rapidly on high volume use causing crashes and restarts.

> Hi, is there any update on this? We are also seeing this problem and are in a bit of a bind as our system is unable to scale to any reasonable capacity due to memory leaking rapidly on high volume use causing crashes and restarts.

@lurk26:

You could use the Python implementation by setting the environment variable:
PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=python 

Though it might be too slow for your system, but it doesn't have this memory issue.

After much debugging, I've gotten to a root cause for this.

The problem is that the glibc `free()` function doesn't actually return memory to the OS.  It returns it to the heap, for possible use by another `malloc()` call, but it doesn't give it back to the OS with `munmap()` or `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)`.

The [pymalloc allocator](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/memory.html#the-pymalloc-allocator) on the other hand returns memory to the OS as quickly as possible, using `munmap()`.

When you use the pure-Python protobuf library, all of the proto objects are allocated using pymalloc, so when they are collected pymalloc immediately returns the memory to the OS. But when you use an extension module, the proto objects are allocated at the C layer using `malloc()` and `free()`. Even though the extension module is properly freeing all of the memory it allocates, the RSS does not go down because of glibc's behavior.

There are two possible solutions to this problem. I have verified that both of these solutions successfully make the RSS go down in the test case attached to this issue:

1. Make the native extension allocate message data using the [Python memory allocation functions](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/memory.html#memory-interface) `PyMem_Malloc()`, `PyMem_Realloc()`, and `PyMem_Free()`. This will make the extension module use the same allocator as regular Python objects, causing the memory to be returned to the OS eagerly.
2. Add explicit calls to the [glibc function `malloc_trim()`](https://sourceware.org/git/?p=glibc.git;a=blob;f=malloc/malloc.c;h=b8c0f4f5802c73a1770e3f1c0f22bcf8a83b5977;hb=5e8d1b0328a850c229146f40e18848728b104583#l703) so that glibc will return memory to the OS.

There are pros and cons to both of these. It's not immediately clear which one is better. (1) has the benefit of being more portable, since it only relies on Python APIs that will always be available, whereas (2) introduces a conditional dependency on a glibc-specific function. On the other hand, the pymalloc functions for (1) require that the GIL is held, and it may be difficult to guarantee that if we are sharing messages between Python and another language.

For example, if you want to call a C or C++ API that takes a proto, you may want to pass the Python proto to C or C++ without a copy. At the point it may be difficult to ensure that C or C++ will not hold a reference that is freed at an unpredictable time. But maybe this is not a concern, as it could be unsafe anyway for C or C++ to hold a reference, since Python message objects are mutable and this could introduce data races.

There is also the question of performance of pymalloc vs glibc malloc. It is worth benchmarking which one of these is faster in a microbenchmark, just to see if there is a significant difference.

title: Remove const from function return type if returning const value
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
c++ codebase

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
It is better to avoid the `const` qualifier on function return type if the function returns by value. The `const` qualifier may prevent move semantics if the type is movable. https://quuxplusone.github.io/blog/2022/01/23/dont-const-all-the-things/#return-types-never-const

From [Scott Meyer](https://www.aristeia.com/BookErrata/ec++3e-errata.html):
> Declaring by-value function return values const will prevent their being bound to [rvalue references in C++0x](http://www.artima.com/cppsource/rvalue.html). Because rvalue references are designed to help improve the efficiency of C++ code, it's important to take into account the interaction of const return values and the initialization of rvalue references when specifying function signatures.



**Describe the solution you'd like**
Remove `const` from function return type if returning const value.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Leave it as it is if the `const` qualifiers are there for some reasons.

**Additional context**
I would like to merge [this commit](https://github.com/nglee/protobuf/commit/ab5a485c2959aef027881972d21fd1e6f1b13763) if accepted.
