title: python: pylint no-name-in-module
body:
Since v3.20.0 generated protobuf files trigger pylint `no-name-in-module` when importing the message types. Compiling `foo.proto` (see below) on two different protobuf versions obviously different results, however the old (3.19.x) can be pylinted successfully, but the new (3.20.x) result cannot be pylinted. Compilation command: `python3 -m grpc_tools.protoc -I . --python_out=. foo.proto` ```proto syntax = "proto3"; package foo; // Foo service service Foo { // Say Foo rpc SayFoo(SayFooRequest) returns (SayFooResponse) {} } // Say Foo Request message SayFooRequest {} // Say Foo Response message SayFooResponse {} ```
libprotoc 3.19.4 output 
$ python3 -m grpc_tools.protoc --version
libprotoc 3.19.4
```py # -*- coding: utf-8 -*- # Generated by the protocol buffer compiler. DO NOT EDIT! # source: foo.proto """Generated protocol buffer code.""" from google.protobuf import descriptor as _descriptor from google.protobuf import descriptor_pool as _descriptor_pool from google.protobuf import message as _message from google.protobuf import reflection as _reflection from google.protobuf import symbol_database as _symbol_database # @@protoc_insertion_point(imports) _sym_db = _symbol_database.Default() DESCRIPTOR = _descriptor_pool.Default().AddSerializedFile(b'\n\tfoo.proto\x12\x03\x66oo\"\x0f\n\rSayFooRequest\"\x10\n\x0eSayFooResponse2:\n\x03\x46oo\x12\x33\n\x06SayFoo\x12\x12.foo.SayFooRequest\x1a\x13.foo.SayFooResponse\"\x00\x62\x06proto3') _SAYFOOREQUEST = DESCRIPTOR.message_types_by_name['SayFooRequest'] _SAYFOORESPONSE = DESCRIPTOR.message_types_by_name['SayFooResponse'] SayFooRequest = _reflection.GeneratedProtocolMessageType('SayFooRequest', (_message.Message,), { 'DESCRIPTOR' : _SAYFOOREQUEST, '__module__' : 'foo_pb2' # @@protoc_insertion_point(class_scope:foo.SayFooRequest) }) _sym_db.RegisterMessage(SayFooRequest) SayFooResponse = _reflection.GeneratedProtocolMessageType('SayFooResponse', (_message.Message,), { 'DESCRIPTOR' : _SAYFOORESPONSE, '__module__' : 'foo_pb2' # @@protoc_insertion_point(class_scope:foo.SayFooResponse) }) _sym_db.RegisterMessage(SayFooResponse) _FOO = DESCRIPTOR.services_by_name['Foo'] if _descriptor._USE_C_DESCRIPTORS == False: DESCRIPTOR._options = None _SAYFOOREQUEST._serialized_start=18 _SAYFOOREQUEST._serialized_end=33 _SAYFOORESPONSE._serialized_start=35 _SAYFOORESPONSE._serialized_end=51 _FOO._serialized_start=53 _FOO._serialized_end=111 # @@protoc_insertion_point(module_scope) ```
libprotoc 3.20.1 output 
$ python3 -m grpc_tools.protoc --version
libprotoc 3.20.1
```py # -*- coding: utf-8 -*- # Generated by the protocol buffer compiler. DO NOT EDIT! # source: foo.proto """Generated protocol buffer code.""" from google.protobuf.internal import builder as _builder from google.protobuf import descriptor as _descriptor from google.protobuf import descriptor_pool as _descriptor_pool from google.protobuf import symbol_database as _symbol_database # @@protoc_insertion_point(imports) _sym_db = _symbol_database.Default() DESCRIPTOR = _descriptor_pool.Default().AddSerializedFile(b'\n\tfoo.proto\x12\x03\x66oo\"\x0f\n\rSayFooRequest\"\x10\n\x0eSayFooResponse2:\n\x03\x46oo\x12\x33\n\x06SayFoo\x12\x12.foo.SayFooRequest\x1a\x13.foo.SayFooResponse\"\x00\x62\x06proto3') _builder.BuildMessageAndEnumDescriptors(DESCRIPTOR, globals()) _builder.BuildTopDescriptorsAndMessages(DESCRIPTOR, 'foo_pb2', globals()) if _descriptor._USE_C_DESCRIPTORS == False: DESCRIPTOR._options = None _SAYFOOREQUEST._serialized_start=18 _SAYFOOREQUEST._serialized_end=33 _SAYFOORESPONSE._serialized_start=35 _SAYFOORESPONSE._serialized_end=51 _FOO._serialized_start=53 _FOO._serialized_end=111 # @@protoc_insertion_point(module_scope) ```
Test file (`test.py`) ```py from foo_pb2 import SayFooRequest, SayFooResponse ``` Running `pylint --disable=all --enable=no-name-in-module test.py` With 3.19.x generated code 
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Your code has been rated at 10.00/10 (previous run: 0.00/10, +10.00)
With 3.20.x generated code 
************* Module test
test.py:1:0: E0611: No name 'SayFooRequest' in module 'foo_pb2' (no-name-in-module)
test.py:1:0: E0611: No name 'SayFooResponse' in module 'foo_pb2' (no-name-in-module)

----------------------------------------------------------------------
Your code has been rated at -90.00/10 (previous run: -90.00/10, +0.00)
Clearly this is due to the abuse of `globals()` when using the builder to inject the descriptors into the module context. However, this is dynamically generated code, why does it have to be so _clever_ (c.f.: obfuscated) that industry standard tooling can't ensure that your code is integrating with the library code properly?

title: [PHP] Reference documentation for classes in PHP package
body:
We'd like to have reference documentation for [the protobuf classes](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-php/tree/master/src/Google/Protobuf) in PHP's `google/protobuf` package. The idea is to link to them from our own reference documentation on [cloud.google.com](http://cloud.google.com/). Some examples are 
`Google\Protobuf\Internal\Message` and `Google\Protobuf\Internal\RepeatedField`, which show up in our public API quite often (despite `Internal` being in the class name).

The [existing "reference" documentation](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/php-generated) is more of a tutorial, and does not contain the class reference docs for the methods / return types / etc that we're looking for. Some of the other languages (Dart, Go, Java, Python) have a section for "API" which contains these reference docs.

We could generate the docs and have them hosted at developers.google.com like the other language reference docs (see below) using Doctum like we do with [google/gax](https://googleapis.github.io/gax-php/1.15.0/) and [google/common-protos-php](https://googleapis.github.io/common-protos-php/3.1.0/)

Other language references:
 - C# API: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/csharp
 - C++ API: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp
 - Python API: https://googleapis.dev/python/protobuf/latest/
 - Kotlin API: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/kotlin
 - Java API: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/java
 - Go API: https://pkg.go.dev/google.golang.org/protobuf/proto
 - Dart API: https://pub.dev/documentation/protobuf/latest/

title: [Objective-C] NSObject property with the same name will skip message forwarding and cause Getter to fail
body:
We encountered some problems with the iOS file generated by the PB script. When executing description, the value of valueType is 1, but when calling the getter method, it gets 4.
![screenshot-20220809-210727](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/5634288/183654645-5ea64684-3342-4ec8-8cd8-3d2e1a85d292.png)
During the investigation, **it was found that there is a valueType property with the same name in NSObject**. Since NSObject is the base class of the PB class, the call of NSObject is directly triggered when the Getter method of valueType is executed, rather than resolveInstanceMethod.
Is there any way to avoid this problem?

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Language: Objective-C

nodes.body:
Extending the diff into the `.swift` test files also seems to show things working:

```diff
diff --git a/objectivec/Tests/GPBSwiftTests.swift b/objectivec/Tests/GPBSwiftTests.swift
index 03d751068..0117d82db 100644
--- a/objectivec/Tests/GPBSwiftTests.swift
+++ b/objectivec/Tests/GPBSwiftTests.swift
@@ -35,6 +35,15 @@ import XCTest
 
 class GPBBridgeTests: XCTestCase {
 
+  func testValueType() {
+    let msg = TestingIssue()
+    XCTAssertEqual(msg.valueType, 0)
+    msg.valueType = 1000
+    XCTAssertEqual(msg.valueType, 1000)
+    let desc = msg.description
+    XCTAssert(desc.contains("value_type: 1000"))
+  }
+
```

Ugh, yea, there's not anything the library can do for that, if you are using other libraries that are clamming selectors on NSObject it's going to have issues like this.

For our own projects, we tend to only allow categories that put prefixes on the selectors they add for just this sorta reason, they can end up conflicting with newer Apple SDK apis, as well as getting into issues like this.
All right.It seems that it can only be solved from the category specification,thank you again.

title: Serveral problem of cmake users(output name, including path and installation config)
body:
Hi, I'm a cmake user and I tried to use `cmake/make_cmakelists.py` to generate `CMakeLists.txt` and integrate upb into my project and find some problems.

1. The generated dependency of `utf8_range` is invalid because it has a `/third_party/` prefix.
2. CMake CONFIG files and is missing and also nothing to install when I try to create a prebuilt package.
3. Should all exported header be under `upb/` ? The `third_party/utf8_range/utf8_range.h` is a different path from others.
4. Could all output name of libraries in upb startswith `upb` ? There are a lot of targets (`extension_registry`, `mini_table`, `fastdecode` and etc) now , and if we install them into any path, we can not tell which files are belong to upb.

Could we have a disscuss these topics and can I create a PR for them?

nodes.body: Quick question about 4.  Do you mean C level symbols or file paths or something else?

> Quick question about 4. Do you mean C level symbols or file paths or something else?

I mean file path, the `OUTPUT_NAME` of cmake target property only affect file path.

It is intended that `CMakeLists.txt` will be available in the repo (either on the `main` branch or a separate branch) without users having to generate it first. Unfortunately the setup for doing this is currently broken.

The right way to generate the `CMakeLists.txt` is to use the Bazel commands:

```
$ bazel test cmake:test_generated_files
$ bazel-bin/cmake/test_generated_files --fix
```

It is also possible to test the CMake build through Bazel:

```
bazel test cmake:cmake_build
```

> CMake CONFIG files and is missing and also nothing to install when I try to create a prebuilt package.

Can you say more about your use case? What are you trying to create a prebuilt package for?

upb's API and ABI are both unstable. It is not intended to have prebuilt packages available in package repositories.

> Should all exported header be under upb/ ? The third_party/utf8_range/utf8_range.h is a different path from others.

upb uses the UTF-8 decoder from this project: https://github.com/cyb70289/utf8. To truly CMake-ify upb, we would probably want to give that project its own `CMakeLists.txt` and depend on it from upb.

Within the upb repo, we need to keep it in a separate `third_party` directory since it is not Google-owned code.

> Could all output name of libraries in upb startswith upb ?

I think it would be fine to add a `upb_` prefix to all upb CMake targets.

@haberman 
I want to use upb and lua binding in my project. With installation of cmake CONFIG files, we can just link the exported target, let cmake to include the dependency header path and link the necessary libraries automatically, just like it does in bazel.
Also we use grpc in our project which also depend upb, and it just link the upb runtime library, we want use both upb libraries, protoc-gen-upb, protoc-gen-lua and etc, I have to build the same version of upb, but without cmake CONFIG files I have to read the bazel scripts to know the relations between the libraries and executables in upb and then get which directory I should include, which libraries I should link.

I have written a patch file for my usage at https://github.com/atframework/cmake-toolset/blob/main/ports/grpc/upb-e4635f223e7d36dfbea3b722a4ca4807a7e882e2.patch . It's simular to the upb port in vcpkg(https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg/blob/master/ports/upb/0001-make-cmakelists-py.patch), but I think it's very hard to follow the changes in the future.So I wondering if it can be done in this repo?

I'm not sure whether bazel can add a prefix for headers of some exported libraries.In my cmake patch file, I copy the header of utf8_range to a temporary path starts with  `upb/third_party/utf8-range` . Or if it's a standalone library, maybe just removing `third_party` prefix is a better way?

title: Lua binding compatibility for lua 5.3+
body:
1. `luaL_checkint` is replaced by `luaL_checkinteger` and is removed from lua 5.3
2. `lua_isinteger` is already defined in lua 5.3+
3. `else if (isprint(ch))` in `upb/bindings/lua/upbc.cc` is UB when ch is negative, and will crash when compiled by MSVC.

title: Compiler error in wire_format_lite.cc with clang trunk
body:
Hi,

I'm getting the following compile error in Clang trunk:

```
src/google/protobuf/wire_format_lite.cc:102:9: error: integer value -1 is outside the valid range of values [0, 7] for this enumeration type [-Wenum-constexpr-conversion]
        static_cast<WireFormatLite::WireType>(-1),  // invalid
        ^
```

Casting an integer outside of the range of an unscoped enum without underlying type is Undefined Behavior, which the compiler is required to diagnose on constant expressions.

title: coverity: resource leaks in metadata_lite.h
body:
Coverity reports two resource leaks in `metadata_lite.h`

Are these are legitimate issues or false positives?

```
191  template <typename T>
192  void DoSwap(T* other) {

   1. alloc_fn: Storage is returned from allocation function mutable_unknown_fields.
   2. noescape: Resource this->mutable_unknown_fields() is not freed or pointed-to in Swap
   3. leaked_storage: Failing to save or free storage allocated by this->mutable_unknown_fields() leaks it.

193    mutable_unknown_fields<T>()->Swap(other);
194  }

title: protoc allows option that incorrectly indicates multiple values for the same map key

nodes.body:
This is correct behavior. We don't enforce order or uniqueness here, as per the wire format, it's possible for you to merge/overload/override any field value and only the "last" value remains present in the resulting output.

Options are encoded as wire format, and so that behavior applies here. You should not rely on the compiler to detect this sort of condition if it's relevant to your needs.

For more context, this is outlined in some detail within the scope of this larger article:
https://carlmastrangelo.com/blog/why-does-grpc-insist-on-trailers

@perezd, I am quite familiar that this is valid on the wire. However, contrary to what you suggest is "expected behavior", `protoc` already:
1) Prevents you from setting the same field more than once with options.
2) Prevents you from trying to set more than one field inside a oneof.

Why are the above worthy of validation but the constraints for map keys not? This is a consistency issue.

nodes.body:
Hey Joshua,

I think the big issue here is that you tried to run *all* our tests via Bazel.  A lot of these are still a work in progress and require some very specific flags or environments (see our kokoro tests for some examples).  I plan to do a pass over everything so that `bazel test //...` only runs tests that are compatible, but we're not there today.  To run C++, Python, or Java tests you should scope the command to the relevant directories (e.g. `bazel test //src/...`)

@mkruskal-google, that's fair regarding all of the dependencies (so you'd only install the ones you need based on which tests you are trying to run). But the the toolchain stuff still looks to be broken for Mac OS.

I tried to run everything just to make sure I had a functioning install/build. (I was about to make a pull reuest, and was doing some prep to make sure I'd be able to run tests... didn't yet know what tests I'd be running.)

Yea the toolchain stuff is *completely* broken outside of our internal test environment!  It wasn't designed to ever be used externally, and the only reason you're trying to run those tests is because of the `...` wildcard.  I think marking some of these broken targets with a `manual` tag to prevent wildcard expansion would be reasonable.  I already made an attempt to mark `compatible_with` where appropriate, but as you've noticed I missed a lot.

Long-term, I'd like to write a test that just runs *everything* under `//...`, to keep that in a good state.  But we have a lot more work to do towards Bazelification, so that may be a while.  Until then, I would stick to top-level directories only and relying on our PR presubmits.  Ruby and C# require some awkward configuration for bazel tests, and Objective-c only runs on Mac.  But the following command should be pretty good for qualification:

`bazel test //src/... //python/... //java/...`

And maybe throw in `//objectivec/...` on mac.

title: Q: How to configure/remove Abseil?
body:
I'm trying to build protobuf for a very popular platform (under NDA), and as such, one cannot always rely on where certain headers are, if they're complete or what defines are used by the ocmpiler.

E.g. the define FreeBSD happens to be set, but the header isn't available:
```
#if defined(__APPLE__) || defined(__FreeBSD__)
#include <sys/sysctl.h>
#endif
```
(and the list goes on ofc...)

In particular, I cannot opt out of the Abseil situation, and it doesn't seem to be configurable. at all?

How do you propose I make this work with Abseil?
Is there an option to use protobuf now without it?

Or am I forced to use an older version of protobuf?
v21.5 seems to be without Abseil, but it is also stuck at C++ 11, and my compiler requires C++14+.

Please advise.

nodes.body:
The dependency on Abseil is not conditional and the 22.x release line will have it.  This is a very important change for removing literal decades of tech debt from protobuf.

In the short term, you can say on the 21.x release line which does not have an abseil dep (and won't).  In the medium term, you can contribute patches to abseil and protobuf to make them work on your system.

Both protobuf and abseil publish their supported platform criteria at https://opensource.google/documentation/policies/cplusplus-support.  If your platform is not officially supported it would fall under "best effort" and would likely require contributions to ensure continued compatibility.

Thanks for the info!
Yeah, I was thinking of doing contributions, but wasn't sure of if they're welcome or not.
For the time being, I dodged the immedate issue by disabling one of our unit tests, and simply modifying some headers.

I had to make three changes, one is fairly straightfroward:
E.g I detect the define `GOOGLE_USE_PROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN`, which then sets `PROTOBUF_LITTLE_ENDIAN`.
This way I can sidestep the entire "endian.h" bonanza.

I'll make some PR's when I'm back from Gamescom in a week or so.

title: protobuf CMake dependency management using add_subdirectory
body:
I'm having a similar issue to this one reported on gRPC a while back:
https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/29608

Namely: I have a C++ project (https://github.com/google/binexport), that already includes Abseil and uses protobuf via CMake's `add_subdirectory()`. \
We don't use the LTS version of Abseil and therefore have no "install" of it (so no `absl-config.cmake`, etc.).

Now, Protobuf only has two modes for using Abseil: "module" (Git submodule) or "package" (system-wide install). Neither works out of the box or without resorting to workaround/hacks.

I suggest a similar solution to the one chosen by the gRPC team: Check if there exists an `absl::strings` target in the project. If there is one, skip any/all special handling for Abseil, as it is already there. If not, continue with `protobug_ABSL_PROVIDER`.

nodes.body:
Note: for PR #10436 to work on a non-LTS Abseil, one needs to set `protobuf_INSTALL` to false before including protobuf.
These are the settings that I just confirmed working:
```CMake
set(protobuf_ABSL_PROVIDER "package" CACHE STRING "" FORCE)
set(protobuf_INSTALL OFF CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)

# Download/check out into `_deps`. This ultimately calls `add_subdirectory()`
FetchContent_MakeAvailable(protobuf)
# Protobuf targets available starting here

# Make protobuf_generate_cpp available by providing necessary info to find_package()
set(Protobuf_INCLUDE_DIR "${protobuf_SOURCE_DIR}/src" CACHE INTERNAL "")
set(Protobuf_LIBRARIES protobuf::libprotobuf CACHE INTERNAL "")
find_package(Protobuf 3.21 REQUIRED)
```
Thanks for the fix Christian!

title: Import Error: cannot import name '_message' M1 macOS
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.17.3
Language: Python - 3.9.11 and 3.9.7

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
macOS Monterey 12.5.1, AppleM1 Pro

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.9.11 and Python 3.9.7
**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Create virtual environment
          pyenv virtualenv 3.9.11 'env-name'
          pyenv local 'env-name'
          pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install wheel
          export PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION="cpp"
          export PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION_VERSION="2"
          pip install protobuf==3.17.3


2. pip install --upgrade --force-reinstall protobuf==3.17.3
```
Collecting protobuf==3.17.3
   Using cached protobuf-3.17.3-py2.py3-none-any.whl (173 kB)
 Collecting six>=1.9
   Using cached six-1.16.0-py2.py3-none-any.whl (11 kB)
```

**What did you expect to see**
I am expecting to run without errors

**What did you see instead?**
When I try to run I get the following error:
```
from google.protobuf.pyext import _message
ImportError: cannot import name '_message' from 'google.protobuf.pyext'
```
Also '_message.py' file is missing from /google/protobuf/pyext.

I tried the same steps on macOS Big Sur 11.6.8 Intel Core/protobuf 3.17.3/python 3.9.7 and the package installs and there are no errors.

nodes.body: Same issue for me.
Please upgrade to a newer version. Our setup for cross-compiling the binary wheels has been completely rewritten in 4.21.0 and M1 should work properly now.

Strange it was working for me in 3.20.1 and no more for 3.20.2. Maybe it was just an install issue. I fixed the version for now.

Can't upgrade to newer version as grpcio-tools require <4

Ah, sorry I didn't realize this represented a regression from 3.20.1.

An issue has been discovered this morning where none of the binary wheels were released. This is being addressed now.

cc @deannagarcia

My bad I didn't give any more details as the issue was still open. 
Perfect ! Many thanks.
I believe this should be resolved now. Please re-open if it occurs again.

        if(!is_null($user) && !is_null($shop)){

            $provider = new Google([
                'authorizationUri' => 'https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth',

                'clientId' => 'MY_CLIENT_ID',

                'redirectUri' => 'MY_REDIRECT_URI',
                'accessType' => 'offline',
                'approval_prompt' => 'force',
                'scopes' => ['https://www.googleapis.com/auth/adwords'],
            ]);
            if (!isset($_GET['code'])) {
                    $authUrl = $provider->getAuthorizationUrl();
                    $_SESSION['oauth2state'] = $provider->getState();
                    $_SESSION['shop'] = $request->get('shop');
                    header('Location: ' . $authUrl);
                    exit;
            }elseif (empty($_GET['state']) || ($_GET['state'] !== $_SESSION['oauth2state'])) {
                      unset($_SESSION['oauth2state']);
                      exit('Invalid state.');
            } else {
                // Try to get an access token (using the authorization code grant)
                $token = $provider->getAccessToken('authorization_code', [
                    'code' => $_GET['code']
                ]);

                // Optional: Now you have a token you can look up a users profile data
                try {
                    $shop = $_SESSION['shop'];
                    // We got an access token, let's now get the owner details
                    $ownerDetails = $provider->getResourceOwner($token);
                    $ownerDetails = $ownerDetails->toArray();
                    // Use these details to create a new profile
                    $user = User::create([
                            'access_token' => $token->getToken(),
                            'refresh_token' => $token->getRefreshToken(),
                            'name' => $ownerDetails['name'],
                            'email' => $ownerDetails['email'],
                            'store_name' => $shop,
                        ]);
                   
                    $user->save();
                    return redirect()->route('list-access-customer', ['shop' => $shop])->with(['shop' => $shop]);
                } catch (Exception $e) {
                    // Failed to get user details
                    exit('Something went wrong: ' . $e->getMessage());
                }
             }
        }
    }

title: Is optional field officially supported in proto3?
body:
Hello,

After going through documentation and little bit of source code, I cannot come to a conclusion whether "optional" keyword is officially supported or not. Release notes of 3.15 shows, 

```
2021-02-05 version 3.15.0 (C++/Java/Python/PHP/Objective-C/C#/Ruby/JavaScript)

  Protocol Compiler
  * Optional fields for proto3 are enabled by default, and no longer require
    the --experimental_allow_proto3_optional flag.

```

Does this mean that its promoted to officially supported feature from experimental from 3.15 onwards ?

But latest code shows this, which is little confusing ( especially the comments part)

```
 uint64_t GetSupportedFeatures() const override {                                                                      
    // **We don't fully support this yet**, but this is needed to unblock the tests,                                        
    // and we will have full support before the experimental flag is removed.                                           
    return FEATURE_PROTO3_OPTIONAL;                                                                                     
  }
```

nodes.body: What language bindings did you find that comment in?

cpp code,
src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/generator.h:91
It is officially supported, this is probably just a typo, asking @haberman to confirm.
We officially support proto3 optional in C++;  this is a documentation bug.

In the Proto3 language guide, all descriptions and documentation of keyword 'optional' have been removed and. all examples of 'optional' are in the context of Proto2 if any indication is given (that I can find). 

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3

- There is no documentation that `optional` is a valid keyword in **Proto3**
- There is no documentation for the behavior of `optional` in **Proto3** that I can find. Additionally, is it the same as **Proto2**? How is it different?
- There is no clear documentation on if the keyword was removed from Proto3, or removed from certain versions and added back in others. 
- There is no guidance on when or if I should use `optional`, or if it is discouraged, or if there is a recommended alternative method to solve the same problem. 
 - There are a few ancillary mentions; suggesting to me that `optional` might have existed and these instances should have been removed from the documentation but were missed, but aren't enough to clarify this is a language feature I can use.

Oddly, I feel like there was more documentation on 'optional' a few months ago, discussing how it changed from Proto2 to Proto3, and the alternatives to use instead,. I remember reading about it, and now I can't find what I read. I thought it was in the context of "how to tell if a field has been explicitly set or if was default initialized". 

Could the documentation please be updated?

### Is this how Proto3 'optional' works?
Going a step beyond "is it supported", I've surmised in Proto3 all values are implicitly "optional". If no value is set, then it is default-initialized in all cases. This leaves the question _"is this `int score` really exactly `0`? Or was no score given?"_, _"is this `bool` really `false`, or was no value set at all?"_, which could be a very different thing.

Based on a few references, my guess is that the entire purpose of `optional` in Proto3 is to tell ProtoC to generate the `has_()` method for a particular value, thereby allowing one to know if it was explicitly set by the program, or ignored and default-initialized. 

According to C++ Reference [Singular Embedded Message Fields](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/cpp-generated#embeddedmessage) this happens (the `has_()` methods are generated) automatically in the case of a Singular Embedded Message (aka. a value of a user defined type), but not in any other case (except for `oneof`). Presumably `optional` gets you the `has_foo()` method for all scalars and any other cases. _Whether any of this is true, and the details of it are exactly what I was hoping to find on the_ [Language Guide (proto3)](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3) _page_ (in addition to the bullet points in my prior comment)!

Somewhat ironically, reading the Proto**2**  [Optional Fields And Default Values](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto#optional ) the implication is that using `optional` _creates_ this ambiguity problem with no solution given, and no mention of the `has_()` methods. Yet in Proto3 my understanding is that `optional` _solves_ the ambiguity problem rather than creating it. Hopefully this can be discussed on the Proto**3** page in the `optional` section when it is updated.

---
Additional references:  StackOverflow [How to define an optional field in protobuf 3](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/42622015/how-to-define-an-optional-field-in-protobuf-3)
There is now proper documentation for `optional` in proto3: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#specifying_field_rules
Now that optional is officially supported, is it fair to say that the wrapper messages (such as `StringValue` and `Int32Value`) are now obsolete?

Yes, I think it is accurate to say that wrappers are now obsolete. The only reasons to use wrappers today would be:

1. Wire compatibility with messages that already use them.
2. If you want to put a scalar value into an `Any` message.

But in most cases, there are better options:

1. For new messages, it's better to use regular explicit-presence fields (`optional` in proto2/proto3, regular field in edition >= 2023).
2. Extensions are generally a better option than `Any`.

title: Lexical syntax spec is not in sync with the implementation
body:
In the spec, lexical syntax for identifiers start with a "letter", where "letter" is defined as `letter = "A" … "Z" | "a" … "z"` (https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto2-spec#letters_and_digits, https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec#letters_and_digits)

In particular, underscore character (`_`) is not a letter, so an identifier cannot start with a `_`.

In the implementation, underscore is considered a letter: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/8d3a7327606b115dda871be54c8b8cb66d41ff90/src/google/protobuf/io/tokenizer.cc#L138-L139

As a result, a single underscore is not a valid identifier according to the spec, but the implementation allows it.

This causes friction when implementing a protobuf compiler as a protoc plugin, because protoc accepts `_` as a valid identifier, but if you implement your plugin by following the spec then you don't expect to see `_` as an identifier.

Rejecting `_` in protoc will not be feasible, so we should update the spec to reflect the implementation.

(Context: https://github.com/google/protobuf.dart/issues/736)

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3? proto3
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Suppose you pass around configurations as protobuf messages. You want to be able to parse configurations from JSON using `util::JsonStringToMessage` and override a configuration with another one using `MergeFrom` (so that all fields in the first one which are present in the second one are overwritten). This works fine, as long as all your fields are optional and singular. But then you want to be able to override `repeated` fields; in particular, you want to be able to override a non-empty list of values with an empty one. To date, this is not possible, as the representations of JSONs with `"a": []` for a repeated field `a` are indistinguishable from representations of those where the field is not present.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Support `optional repeated`

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Wrap all `repeated` fields in something like
```proto
message MyMessage {}

message MyMessageList {
  repeated MyMessage values = 1;
}
```

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

title: Ruby should embed a serialized descriptor into generated code instead of using the DSL
body:
Currently our generated code for Ruby uses a DSL to specify protos, eg:

```ruby
Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.build do
  add_file("google/protobuf/timestamp.proto", :syntax => :proto3) do
    add_message "google.protobuf.Timestamp" do
      optional :seconds, :int64, 1
      optional :nanos, :int32, 2
    end
  end
end
```

This provides some readability, but has a high cost: any options that have not been specifically implemented in the DSL are dropped. This includes both built-in options like `packed=true` (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2294) as well as all custom options(https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1198).

To solve these problems, the generated code should embed a serialized descriptor. This will naturally preserve all options, and is easy to implement. eg.

```ruby
descriptor_data = File.binread(__FILE__).split("\n__END__\n", 2)[1]
Google::Protobuf::DescriptorPool.generated_pool.add_serialized_file(descriptor_data)

__END__

 google/protobuf/descriptor.proto^R^Ogoogle.protobuf"G
^QFileDescriptorSet^R2
^Dfile^X^A ^C(^K2$.google.protobuf.FileDescriptorProto"ì^C
^SFileDescriptorProto^R^L
^Dname^X^A ^A(>-^R^O
^Gpackage^X^B ^A(>------^R^R
<snip>
```

This does make the generated code less readable though. So we should not do this until we are generating `.rbs` files: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9495

Then we will have a world where:

1. `_pb.rbs` provides a *readable* description of the protobuf interface
2. `_pb.rb` provides a *compact*, *efficient* description of the message, optimized for completeness and fast runtime loading.

nodes.body: Blocked by: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/9495

Is it worth unblocking this by ignoring the rbs piece of this problem?

- Who is currently reading the generated code and expecting it to be readable?
  - They need to understand how the DSL generates ruby classes
  - Whereas if they just read the proto directly, they need to understand how it maps to ruby
  - In either case, you need to understand some (very simple) mapping.
    - Seems like the proto -> ruby should be the default here. People interacting with the protos need to know proto anyway... 

Could RBS be considered orthogonal? Fixing the generated code now, while backsliding on readability (but, per above, is that actually negative?), provides real benefits (like being able to use get proto options, which has been an ask for 6.5 years...).

Readability can then be "fixed" later with RBS. 

---

Edit: Also, fwiw, the DSL also describes / is much closer to the _proto_ itself, not the _ruby_ classes, where as RBS would describe _ruby_. So the difference between the proto and DSL is super minimal today (imo), meaning I'm not sure there is a readability backslide at all... reading the DSL today is basically reading the proto...

Fixed in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/bd52d0483987f1a5186fc3daa261d1d76a787bcf

Announced in: https://protobuf.dev/news/2023-04-20/

title: Use a different naming pattern for "major-less" tags
body:
Hi!

I help package protobuf for the conda-forge ecosystem, and to be able to integrate over a whole ecosystem, we rely on automated scraping of upstream repos for new tags, and more specifically, tags that follow the pattern specified in the recipe, e.g.
`v{{ version }}` or `packagename-{{ version }}`.

Whenever the bot encounters a new tag of that pattern, it will raise a PR to update the respective packaging repo to the newest available version. This works really well in general, but now that protobuf is [publishing](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tags) both (e.g.) `v3.21.5` & `v21.5` as pointing to the same commit, the bot picks up "21.5" because it is higher.

TBH I've no seen any other project publish `minor.patch` tags, and so working around this would require some protobuf-specific & fragile hacks in our infrastructure.

So I wanted to ask: Would it be possible to use a different naming pattern between the major-full & major-less tags (i.e. not both using `v[\d\.]+`)?

title: JSON parsing of large 32-bit floating point values fails.
body:
The proto3 JSON spec doesn't give very much guidance on *exactly* how floating point values are represented.

The maximal finite 32-bit floating point value is precisely 340282346638528859811704183484516925440. Both .NET and (I believe) Go format this as 3.4028235e+38.

Unfortunately that fails to round-trip in .NET, because of the way we handle JSON parsing of 32-bit floating point numbers:

- Parse as a 64-bit float
- Compare with the maximal 32-bit float - if it's less than or equal, proceed, otherwise throw an exception

There are 64-bit floating point values closer to 3.4028235e+38 than the max 32-bit value, so we end up throwing an exception.
We should, instead, try casting to `float` and see whether the result is infinite.

nodes.body: @mcy: This feels like something that could usefully be in the JSON conformance test suite. (I'm adding unit tests to the C# code of course.)

The conformance tests already have a "max float" case, but they are testing for `3.402823e+38` rather than `3.4028235e+38`: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f8be28167c151846a911a6b33ea35d8ea8e3990b/conformance/binary_json_conformance_suite.cc#L2085-L2088

Also it appears the min float case has a copy-and-paste bug, where it's accidentally checking the max float value again: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f8be28167c151846a911a6b33ea35d8ea8e3990b/conformance/binary_json_conformance_suite.cc#L2089-L2092

title: MessageToJson indent param not documented or typed as Optional
body:
The [docstring](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/4efbcc44605731dc31507b94f0b81d2bd5ec169b/python/google/protobuf/json_format.py#L111-L112) for `MessageToJson` (and hence the [API reference](https://googleapis.dev/python/protobuf/latest/google/protobuf/json_format.html#google.protobuf.json_format.MessageToJson)) as well as the [type stubs](https://github.com/python/typeshed/blob/ff3c3b8373c6f67c2b1f79bf543e1f4e7f655e95/stubs/protobuf/google/protobuf/json_format.pyi#L16) only mention integral values for `indent`. However, the `indent` parameter is directly [passed into](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/4efbcc44605731dc31507b94f0b81d2bd5ec169b/python/google/protobuf/json_format.py#L198-L199) `json.dumps()`, where `indent` is optional and the default of `None` gives a standard single-line JSON string. 

Given the support in other languages to create a JSON string without newlines, and the fact that this has worked for years with `None`, I believe it's safe to expand the documentation & type here to "officially" support `indent=None`.

title: ######why are negative numbers of type int32 encoded using 64-bit varints? Instead of using 32-bit varint encoding
body: Why are negative numbers of type int32 encoded using 64-bit varints? Instead of using 32-bit varint encoding

nodes.body: Can you add a bit more detail here? What language/architecture are you using? Can you provide an example/something reproducible so we can run it?

> Why are negative numbers of type int32 encoded using 64-bit varints? Instead of using 32-bit varint encoding

The designers wanted the 32-bit varints to be forward compatible with their 64-bit counterparts.

From https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/proto3#updating

> int32, uint32, int64, uint64, and bool are all compatible – this means you can change a field from one of these types to another without breaking forwards- or backwards-compatibility. If a number is parsed from the wire which doesn't fit in the corresponding type, you will get the same effect as if you had cast the number to that type in C++ (for example, if a 64-bit number is read as an int32, it will be truncated to 32 bits).

and

> sint32 and sint64 are compatible with each other but are not compatible with the other integer types.
thank

title: Question: why are package names limited to <512 bytes?
body:
In reference to this check:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc#L4980

I see there is also a [nesting depth limit of 32](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc#L3695), but there doesn't appear to be any length limit on the name of a message. So, even with the limits that _are_ in place, the total length of a fully-qualified name is unbounded. Intentional?

nodes.body: Probably not intentional, but I guarantee that there exist protos with names long enough that they would break if we changed the limit.  So without a clear reason will just let this continue as is.

@deannagarcia @alexander-yevsyukov let me add my observations on the subject.

After some investigation, I have found that the changes made within this PR are indeed present in the `protobuf/main` branch. And they were present in every changeset since this PR was merged.

title: [PHP] Wrong "latest version" published on PECL
body:
When we install the protobuf PHP extension, we usually install the latest version.
This is done by fetching the tarball available at https://pecl.php.net/get/protobuf (or at https://pecl.php.net/get/protobuf/stable)

The problem is that the protobuf versions published on the PECL archive have wrong dates (see https://pecl.php.net/package/protobuf):

![immagine](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/928116/190968896-068b0042-cfba-498a-a4d1-6618e90d6819.png)

So, PECL thinks that the latest version is 3.18.3 instead of 3.21.6, and it serves that version.

nodes.body: I think that PECL is using strict "release date" and not actually looking at version numbers.  This might be fixed by simply re-pushing 3.21.6

I absolutely don't know how PECL works, but sure, I agree that the first guess would be to fix the release dates

(and I'd do it for all the versions with wrong dates, that is the ones that *seems* to have been published on 2022-09-13 and on 2022-09-14)

I agree with Matt here that the problem is that PECL is just sorting by release date and nothing else.

In our experience, PECL is extremely picky with how dates work. I believe this is a PECL issue and not a protobuf issue and would recommend you file a bug there with how versions are being dealt with. We will continue to have this issue with any patch release. 

Reuploading the package in PECL requires code changes and with it new tags, which I think will cause even more confusion.
Maybe @cmb69 can give you a tip, @deannagarcia

I don't think that the PECL Website even sorts by release date; instead, it looks like it shows releases in the order they have been published (might just sort by fmtime/fctime)). That works well for extensions with a "linear" release cycle, but not for extensions which do also support older branches with revisions. A work-around would be to publish in the desired order (e.g. 3.18.3, 3.19.5, 3.20.2, 3.21.6). A more sophisticated approach might be reasonable. Maybe someone wants to provide a PR to https://github.com/php/web-pecl. Maybe discussion on the pecl-dev mailing list would also be appropriate/useful.

I'm closing this issue since it's related to PEAR/PECL in general, and not specifically to the protobuf PHP extension.

PS: I [wrote to the pecl-dev mailing list](https://marc.info/?m=168137915918907) about this problem.

> I [wrote to the pecl-dev mailing list](https://marc.info/?m=168137915918907) about this problem.

Just an update: nobody replied to that message of mine in the pecl-dev mailing list, so [I suggested a fix](https://github.com/php/web-pecl/pull/92) directly in the repository of the pecl website.
This issue has been resolved: see https://github.com/php/web-pecl/pull/92

title: C# .NET deserialization of message that contains self-defined message type field and empty value field, decodes incorrectly
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v3.5.1
Language:C++/C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Win10

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
msvc

**What did you do?**
Hi, jskeet~
The problem performed like this: i use language C++ to serialize a message to a file named 'a.label', however, when i deserialize 'a.label' to a message in language C#, i get a incorrect result, details are as follows:
the .proto file contents is:
```
syntax = "proto3";
import "google/protobuf/any.proto";

message Rect2f {
    float w= 1; 
    float h= 2;
}
message Shape{
    enum ExampleType{
        Type1= 0;
        Type2= 1;
    }

    ExampleType data_type = 1;
    Rect2f rect_size = 2;

    google.protobuf.Any origin = 3;
}
```
I serialize or deserialize Shape message in C++, the result is:
```
 {"data_type":"Type1","rect_size":{"w":300,"h":400}, "origin":{}}
```
but when i serialize Shape message in C++ and deserialize it in C#, i get this: 
```
{ "dataType": "Type1", "rectSize": { "w": 300, "h": 400 }, "origin": { "@type": "", "@value": "" }}
```
it looks like some key fields are changed: data_type-->dataType, rect_size-->rectSize, empty value field is changed: "origin":{}-->"origin": { "@type": "", "@value": "" }.
By the way, theye are many blank spaces appearing in result, i wonder the essential reason.

**What did you expect to see**
```
 {"data_type":"Type1","rect_size":{"w":300,"h":400}, "origin":{}}
```

**What did you see instead?**
```
{ "dataType": "Type1", "rectSize": { "w": 300, "h": 400 }, "origin": { "@type": "", "@value": "" }}
```

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

- use function SerializeToArray(...) to serialize message in C++;
- write the file as "std::ofstream::binary" in C++;
- use function Parser.ParseFrom(data_bytes) to deserialize message in C#, the type of parameter data_bytes is byte array.

Looking forward to the reply, thank you.

nodes.body: It would really help if you could provide a sample file for me to try to parse from C#.
Of course, moments need to wait, cause there is only complete .label file for my own project, i will show you a sample .label file soon.

I'm sorry for the late uploading, sample file named "1.log" is provided. By the way, i saved this file with '.log' suffix due to github file type support.
[1.log](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/files/9642457/1.log)

Unfortunately that link gives me a 404. Are you able to upload and share a file on Google Drive?

Looking again at your question, I think this *may* just be a matter of how an `Any` is represented in JSON in C#. I don't think it's actually *decoding* the `Any` incorrectly - it just isn't showing what you'd expect in JSON.

We can look at that (encoding an `Any` without a type URL as just `{}` rather than exposing the blank type and value) but I strongly suspect that's the problem rather than the *decoding* side being wrong. That means you should be able to work with the data in C# without any problems, *other* than when you encode it as JSON (if you even need to do that).

Here's a simpler repro of it, in C#:

```csharp
using Google.Protobuf.WellKnownTypes;

var any = new Any();
Console.WriteLine(any);
```

That prints `{ "@type": "", "@value": "" }` where it sounds like you'd expect it to print `{}`.

An alternative way of addressing this is not to populate the field *at all* in the C++ code unless you have a valid value to "pack" into the `Any`. This is effectively an invalid `Any` value, given that it doesn't have a type URL or any serialized data.

I'm going to close this, as internal discussions have suggested that we should really be failing to serialize an "empty" Any value to JSON entirely... so both the C++ and C# behavior here would be viewed as "wrong". That will be fixed as part of a larger JSON consistency drive.

The solution is just to not populate a field with an Any unless you have a *real* Any value.

title: parser: weird formatting in a trailing comment causes all comments for next element to be ignored
body:
Here's an example source:
```protobuf
message Foo {
  optional string s = 1; /* is this a trailer
                            comment? */ // is this detached?

  // this is clearly a detached comment
  
  // and this is clearly a leading comment
  optional int32 i = 2;
}
```

Because the trailer comment above does not have a newline between it and the subsequent "is this detached?" comment, the parser gets confused and gives up on all of the rest of the comments from there to the next element.

So the above source code results in _no_ comments in source code info in the resulting descriptor.

The issue is that it gets confused [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v21.6/src/google/protobuf/io/tokenizer.cc#L868), thinking that the next _token_ is on the same line (even though the next "token" is actually another comment).

If it were actually a non-comment token, the behavior makes sense: it is not clear whether the comment should be attributed as a trailing comment for `s` or a leading comment for the next element, so it gets dropped.

But since the next thing is actually another comment, I'd suggest that the correct interpretation is:
* `s` trailing comment `"is this a trailer\ncomment?"`
* `i` detached comments
   *  `"is this detached?"`
   * `"this is clearly a detached comment"`
* `i` leading comment `"and this is clearly a leading comment"` 

I could see an argument that the first two comments are weird and might be dropped, instead resulting in the following:
* `s` has no trailing comment
* `i` detached comment `"this is clearly a detached comment"`
* `i` leading comment `"and this is clearly a leading comment"` 

But I think the current behavior, where it fails to attribute any detached or leading comments to `i` is clearly wrong.

FWIW, I think the first interpretation above is the easier one to implement (and seems useful to preserve more comments).

nodes.body: I agree with your assessment and we would be happy to accept a PR that implements your first suggestion.
FWIW, the PR I just pushed proceeds with the handling in the previous comment. But it's trivial to adapt to drop the less clear attributions. Just let me know what you think.

title: Allow Value to support an int64 value

nodes.body:
I believe this type was developed for JSON that allows interop with JavaScript and as such limits the numeric type to the IEEE 754 double.

This seems in line with https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7159

We're unlikely to update this type with int64 support since that would break interoperability.

As a workaround, you could use a string to carry larger integers and convert them in the application layer.

> Can you confirm if this issue reproduces in 3.19.5, 3.20.2, or 21.6? 3.18.x has technically fallen out of our support window, so actually moving to a newer version (ideally 21.x) would be better anyways.

Python Protobuf 3.19.5, 3.19.6, 3.20.2, 3.20.3, 4.21.6 all work well from my Mac. Only Python Protobuf 3.18.3 will bump into a seg fault crash issue.

> If you use our pre-built protoc (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v3.18.3) instead of pip install, do you still hit the same issue?

I tried protoc 3.18.3 from your link and it will still bump into issue if the environment has Python Protobuf 3.18.3. Other Python Protobuf version work fine.

> If you can provide a repro for this issue using protobuf directly without onnx, this will make it easier for us to dig into this.

Yes, but it's quite hard for me to decouple a small piece from the original onnx build. I will try, but meanwhile I am happy to help you resolve onnx build issue if any.

> "Protobuf compiler version doesn't match library version 3.18.3" (though my protoc --version is indeed 3.18.3).

Have you `git clean -xdf` under onnx directory? Or, a quick workaround might be finding a clean Mac environment with single installed protoc. Protoc version shouldn't matter here so you can have any version >=3.16. As long as onnx can find your protoc and you use Python Protobuf 3.18.3, you should be able to repro this crash. Feel free to let me know if you see other onnx build issue. Thank you for your time.

Is there any reason why onnx using 3.18.3? 3.18.x is no longer in our support window (we've already stopped doing patch releases for other major fixes on this branch) so we're unlikely to get to this. Onnx should ideally move to 4.21.x or 3.20.x.

Typically ONNX ecosystem does not frequently bump dependency version (Protobuf, NumPy, and etc.) because ONNX downstream tools might need lower version for different kinds of reasons. Therefore, ideally I would like to keep required Protobuf version for ONNX as flexible as possible.

3.18.3 is a fresh patch release very recently (a month ago) and this is the only version seems broken with some use cases on Mac. According to the experiments, there might be something needs to be further fixed in the patch updates (commits from 3.18.2 to 3.18.3) for Mac. Although Python Protobuf 3.18.0-3.18.2 are fine, going forward we cannot really use them due to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/security/advisories/GHSA-8gq9-2x98-w8hf. I was just worried other users might also see similar issues on Mac with Python Protobuf 3.18.3 if they also need this new patch release.

title: Java: `getFieldOptional` for optional message fields
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
If it's about generated code change, what programming language?
**Java** 

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Currently if I want to create an `Optional<MyField>`, I usually have to do something like
```
Optional<MyField> maybeField = myMessage.hasMyField() ? Optional.of(myMessage.getMyField()) : Optional.empty();
```
which is pretty verbose.

Another, less important issue, is that it would be nice to be able to set an `Optional<Message>` for optional fields in the builder. Currently I have to do something like,

```
Optional<MyField> maybeField = ...;
MyMessage.Builder builder = MyMessage.newBuilder();
maybeField.ifPresent(builder::setMyField);
```

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add a `getFieldOptional` that returns an optional with the value if provided and `Optional.empty()` otherwise. Then the above would become:

```
Optional<MyField> maybeField = myMessage.getMyFieldOptional();
```

To solve the builder issue, we could generate an overload of `setField(MyField field)` that is `setField(Optional<MyField> field)` that sets the field if the optional is non-empty, and unsets the field if the optional is empty. 

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

Instead of using Java optionals, we could also just do something like `getFieldOrNull` as there is currently in Kotlin and have the caller wrap with `Optional.ofNullable`, but it feels preferable to me to force the user to explicitly handle the empty case by returning an `Optional`. 

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

This seems similar to `getFieldOrNull` recently implemented for Kotlin: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/8676.

This also should be a backwards compatible change.

nodes.body:
While I understand the desire, this idea has been considered in the past and we have made a deliberate decision not to do it.  The major points in this decision are:

- Adding new methods per field has a significant cost in terms of the size of generated code.  Size of generated code is an important property for Android .apk size and thus android app start-up time.
- optional causes a double indirection since it is functionally boxing the pointers in java.  The performance negatives are not good.

Kotlin avoids the second point by having nullability in its type system.  The first point is mitigated (but not fully resolved) through tree shaking, unused method stripping, and inlining.

@fowles thanks for the response! 

Just for my own curiosity, what's the reason we can't mitigate the first issue in Java using the same methods that Kotlin uses? I'm not familiar enough to know if there is some language specific feature that allows us to trim down the size of unused methods in Kotlin that is not available in Java.
Kotlin has "inline" methods which forcibly inline into callers and don't really exist at the JVM level.

title: Inconsistent versioning (3.21.7 vs 21.7)
body: Latest version seem to have dropped major component (e.g. 21.7 instead of 3.21.7) https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v21.7, however some files protobuf-cpp etc. still use old version (3.21.7). Please keep versioning consistent (by sticking with the one and only scheme everywhere - tag and release names, download file names, changelog, build system), otherwise it introduces mess and makes downstream package maintainership harder.

nodes.body:
This is actually WAI. In release 21.0, we switched to per-language major versions. Thus, the release is now "v21.7" with "3.21.7" or "4.21.7" referring to the major versions used for each specific language. For example, cpp is on 3.21.7 but python is on 4.21.7.

Note, we still have add tags for each language's major versions (v21.7, v3.21.7, v4.21.7) for now.

See https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#versioning

Is it really a good idea to spawn a bunch of different versions from a single codebase? It complicates packaging (for instance, when all language counterparts are created from a single source package, versioned after "main" version, they'll have "main" version too), automaked new release notifications and checking against vulnerability databases.

> Is it really a good idea to spawn a bunch of different versions from a single codebase?

Not with the exact same tag-pattern, but unfortunately, it was [rejected](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/10497) to change this.

title: [java] ByteString needs a serialVersionUID
body:
Version: latest (3.21.7 in particular, but it's in git)
Langauge: java

ByteString.java does not currently specify a serialVersionUID. This is wreaking havoc on countless places that include byte strings in their serialization format. For example, the google-cloud-datastore `Entity` class is serializable and frequently serialized into memcache-like services, but it composes ByteString so serialization breaks with different versions of the protobuf jar.

Some of the subclasses specify serialVersionUID which is great, but the base class needs to as well. Looks like an oversight.

title: Protoc Plugin support should allow custom parameters before other parameters
body:
This applies only to the protoc CLI.

With some code generator toolchains (such as dotnet nuget), local tools get installed in a way that requires a call to a framework binary with the tool as the first parameter. For example, `dotnet protoc-gen-fsharp`. However, you currently cannot tell protoc to put a custom argument before the others. It would be nice to be able to call such a command with leading arguments directly as the plugin input to protoc.

For dotnet nuget, we can install the tool globally which removes the need for `dotnet` at the beginning, which is undesirable but the currently recommended solution. We could also deliver shell scripts, but that locks you into a specific shell dependency on the client. We could also deliver the plugin as a full fat executable, but that would involve shipping every possible runtime that people might use, greatly increasing the size of the package.

libprotobuf-lite.a            libprotobuf.so                libprotoc.so
libprotobuf-lite.so           libprotobuf.so.32             libprotoc.so.32
libprotobuf-lite.so.32        libprotobuf.so.3.21.4.0       libprotoc.so.3.21.4.0
```
which look correct (I have 3.21.4 installed).  We've recently revamped our versioning scheme, and hopefully this will be smoother now :)

thank u! That would be much more life saving!

BTW, may I ask a further question?

1. From which version start the protoc --version is same as version str as lib?
2. if you have 3.21.4, but protoc is 3.21.2 or 3.21.1, will they still claim `your protoc version is older than lib` even just minor version mismatch?

So there are two different versioning schemes today.  For protoc, we have no major version numbers (e.g. 21.7, 22.1) and for the language runtimes we have major+minor versions (e.g. 3.21.7, 4.22.1).  The major version numbers indicate breaking changes to the runtimes, and the minor versions indicate changes to protoc.  The third patch number represents backwards-compatible bug fixes.

In general we recommend that you use matching versions of both the runtime libraries and the compiler.  In many cases mismatched patch numbers will be compatible though, and we have internal logic for checking this (e.g. see https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/stubs/common.h)

title: protoc: doesn't accept capital X in hex escapes in string literals
body:
In the [specs on the developer site](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/proto3-spec#string_literals), string literals can use `\X` (capital X) to initiate a hexadecimal byte literal:
```
hexEscape = '\' ( "x" | "X" ) hexDigit hexDigit
```

However, attempting to do so results in a syntax error:
```protobuf
// test.proto
syntax = "proto2";

message Foo {
  optional bytes bar = 1 [default = "\XBC"];
}
```
```
$ protoc test.proto -o /dev/null
test.proto:5:39: Invalid escape sequence in string literal.
```
Changing the string literal to `"\xBC"` (lower-case X) fixes the problem.

This appears to be a bug in the tokenizer, not in the documentation. I say this for a couple of reasons:
1. Both lower-case and capital X are accepted for hexadecimal integer literals.
2. Decoding the contents of `default_value` for a bytes field accepts hex escapes that use capital X.

To test the latter, I modified a file descriptor set so it included `"\\X74"` in a default value:
```
protoc test.proto -o /dev/stdout | xxd > test.protoset.txt
```
```
# edit the output of xxd (see third line, third word) to use capital X escape
00000000: 0a2b 0a0a 7465 7374 2e70 726f 746f 221d  .+..test.proto".
00000010: 0a03 466f 6f12 160a 0362 6172 1801 2001  ..Foo....bar.. .
00000020: 280c 3a04 5c58 3734 5203 6261 72         (.:.\X74R.bar
```
It turns out that `protoc` happily accepts this, even though it would complain about the escape if it appeared in a proto source file.
```
$ xxd -r < test.protoset.txt | protoc --descriptor_set_in /dev/stdin -o /dev/stdout test.proto | xxd
00000000: 0a28 0a0a 7465 7374 2e70 726f 746f 221a  .(..test.proto".
00000010: 0a03 466f 6f12 130a 0362 6172 1801 2001  ..Foo....bar.. .
00000020: 280c 3a01 7452 0362 6172                 (.:.tR.bar
```
As can be seen above, the `\X74` escape was accepted and translated to `t`.

nodes.body: Agreed that this is a tokenizer bug.  Feel free to send a fix if you have one ready!

title: Serialization & Deserialization not working for unititialized bool
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.19.4.0
Language: C++


**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux Ubuntu 20.04


**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
- g++ 10.2.0
- I've also tried g++ 9.4.0 giving me the same result


**What did you do?**

I tried to serialize a protobuf message as a string and then and deserialize back to the original message. All my files compile and link correctly.

I have the following proto file (named `fancy_messages.proto`):
``` 
syntax = "proto3";

message MainMessage {
    uint64 num = 1;
    SubMessage sub_message = 2;
}

message SubMessage {
    bool my_bool = 3;
}
```

My Cpp file looks as follows:

```
#include <fancy_messages.pb.h>
#include <iostream>

int main(int argc, char const* argv[])
{
    class Test
    {
      public:
        bool m_isGood;
    };

    MainMessage message;
    message.set_allocated_sub_message(new SubMessage);

    Test* array = new Test[100];

    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++)
    {
        std::string serialized;

        // Set data and serialize to string
        message.set_num(20);
        message.mutable_sub_message()->set_my_bool(array[i].m_isGood);

        message.SerializeToString(&serialized);

        MainMessage reparsedMessage;

        std::cout << "m_isGood: " << array[i].m_isGood << std::endl;

        // Try to deserialize into new message
        if (!reparsedMessage.ParseFromString(serialized))
        {
            std::cout << "Failed to reparse message" << std::endl;
            break;
        }
    }
    delete[] array;

    return 0;
}
```


**What did you expect to see**

I expected to not see the "Failed to reparse message" when reparsing the message, and successfully serialize and reserialize the message.

**What did you see instead?**

I saw the error message and the deserialization failed to parse the string back into a `MainMessage`. 

I noticed that when I print the value of `m_isGood` and its below 128 then I don't get the error and the serialization works. It looks like the encoding for bools in protobuf (set to anything above 127) doesn't play nice when set to some uninitialized value, causing the serialization to fail and hence the deserialization. I also noticed that if I have the `Test` instance on the stack then it works fine (im guessing because `m_isGood` is intialized).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

I compile with CMake for release with optimizations. When I compile for debug I dont have the issue. My guess is that the evaluation of the input is optimized away causing the uninitialized value to be written directly instead of being evaluated.

title: Change extension of C# generated source code in Google.Protobuf
body:
We have a fair amount of generated code in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/main/csharp/src
It can be useful to differentiate this code based purely on the extension, and .NET typically uses .g.cs as a file extension.

We should change our [generation script](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/csharp/generate_protos.sh) to explicitly specify .g.cs as the extension while building (using `--csharp_opt=file_extension=.g.cs`) and delete the old code.

Maybe I'm missing something but starting from 4.21.0 release pypi doesn't seem to contain various kinds of wheels it used to contain for versions 3.x. Simply compare https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/4.21.7/#files to https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/3.20.3/#files 
During the installation it does use protobuf-4.21.7-cp37-abi3-manylinux2014_x86_64.whl for Linux and protobuf-4.21.7-cp37-abi3-macosx_10_9_universal2.whl for MacOS respectively (which might be a valid behavior), but they do not contain any binaries in google/protobuf/pyext folder.
And it's not like it can be explained by API change because this import I'm trying to make is still [present](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/0cb8c1353bfbc6ba6c992c9c1c22ef1845be79e5/python/google/protobuf/descriptor.py#L51) in the latest code.

nodes.body:
The native module in the pre-packaged wheels of `protubuf>=4` was changed from one based on the c++ implementation of protobuf to the new upb library (a lightweight C implementation). This is what prompted the bump in major version of the Python package to 4.x and the new v21 nomenclature for this GitHub repo. 

https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06

While it's not something you would normally import directly, you can check the _upb based extension is installed correctly:
```
import google._upb._message
```

This should be used by default unless you explicitly set `PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION` to something other than `upb`.

You can still build the old C++ implementation manually [from the current code base](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/main/python) and set an environment variable to use it:
```
export PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=cpp
Closing for now, since this seems to be answered by @ajasmin (thanks!) but @yigor please feel free to reopen if this is not resolved yet.

@ajasmin thank you so much for your explaination! I wish different python implementations were documented more thoroughly [here](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated) for example.

title: The numbers of bytes needed when float and int32 type serialized to string are different.

nodes.body:
3.14.0 is very old, it is recommended that you upgrade to our latest versions 3.21.x or 3.20.x.

[SerializeToString serializes to binary format](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/cpptutorial#parsing-and-serialization) but float and int32 are encoded differently in [Protobuf's wire format encoding](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/encoding) so a difference in the encoding length is not surprising. 

int32 is encoded using wire type VARINT (1 byte in your example) and float is encoded using I32 (4 bytes).

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: main/v3.6.0/v3.5.0 etc. (NOTE: please try updating to the latest version of protoc/runtime possible beforehand to attempt to resolve your problem) protobuf = 4.21.6/4.21.8

Language: Python 3.9

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?** MacOs

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)** Python 3.9

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. t = element of Point class
2. assert isinstance(t, GeneratedProtocolMessageType)
E           AssertionError: assert False
E            +  where False = isinstance(<class 'Point'>, GeneratedProtocolMessageType)
3. It used to pass till 15 Oct.

**What did you expect to see** Assertion passes

**What did you see instead?** Assertion failed

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body:
What version did you move to 4.21.6/4.21.8 from? If it was 3.20.x or below the major version bump moving python to use upb is likely what broke you.

You can check your python api implementation via the following:

```
from google.protobuf.internal import api_implementation
print(api_implementation.Type())
```

In 4.21.0 we changed python implementation to use upb ([announce](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#python-updates)) which likely changed the classes. Setting the [PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/python-generated#sharing-messages) can override the default api implementation to verify this.

GeneratedProtocolMessageType is used by pure python and cpp extension, but upb might use a different class. You can use [mro](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#class.mro) to find the type to check against.

We have tracked the issue down to a recent libc call to `strdup` which was introduced between the two versions you've identified:
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/fa5a9e1035fcf42fbe5035ae14e442c67c3b53b6#diff-59207bba65826c3573d4ee8e8daa23fbfbf7daa0764dc67bc73b07ad403fc617

Our native .so file is built using [ManyLinux](https://github.com/pypa/manylinux/issues/37) which is not compatible/friendly with Musl-based environments like Alpine (which both of the reproductions are using).

To be clear, we do not explicitly test or support Musl-based libc currently so these kinds of regressions could happen again without notice. We'll continue to be best effort compatible based on these sorts of reports.

[This PR](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/10811) removes our use of libc's `strdup` (and replaces it with our own version), restoring musl compatibility _for now_. In the near future, we'll be moving to source gems that can compile at time of use which will prevent this sort of compatibility issue altogether.

We'll be doing a release shortly (3.21.9) which will include this fix.

title: Decode "bytes" fields as hexadecimal when printing to standard out
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
N/A - decoding protobuf into text by running "protoc --decode" from the command line

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Trying to decode and read a "bytes" type field is very tedious.  Instead of the output being shown as a string of hexadecimal bytes, the output is a combination of octal and ASCII characters.  Then a user must manually convert that to hexadecimal bytes, which is presumably the most human-readable option that users would prefer when using a data type of "bytes".  This makes troubleshooting issues time-consuming and often confusing to those who are less familiar with the output format.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I'd argue that the default behavior should be to use hexadecimal for bytes, but alternatively there could be an option passed in when using --decode that would force the protoc executable to output all "bytes" fields in a hexadecimal format, rather than the current default.


**Additional context**
Current output of a bytes field:  
`value: "\001\nu%J\320"`

Desired output of that same bytes field:
`value: "\x01\x0A\x75\x25\x4A\xD0"`

nodes.body: Depending on what you are trying to do, you might find https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protoscope to be a better tool.  Text format has a lot of usage already so we are unlikely to change it lightly.

I'll look into protoscope to see if it's feasible for us, but I'd still argue that adding this support to the text format is a valid and reasonable request.  Using hexadecimal in strings is already supported when encoding text files into protobuf; I don't understand why we wouldn't want to allow an option for the decoding logic to produce the same output, especially for something that seems to make a lot more sense than the default behavior.
Command line flags on protoc itself have a fairly high cost.  I would argue that the tool should probably not have a `--decode` flag at all, but that ship has clearly sailed.

body:
