-->


**What language does this apply to?**
C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

I would like to generate c# code where the generated classes are internal, not public. Is such a thing possible?

**Describe the solution you'd like**

I understand I would need a compiler flag or a proto option to tell the compiler to replace "public" by "internal"

**Motivation**

The classes generated by proto are to be used for serialization/deserialization and not as part of a public API

On more complex scenarios, I have a proto that is shared across multiple messages in multiple libraries/projects; Because the classes are public, I am forced to generate the code in its own library, and that library is shared between the projects that require these messages.

If classes would be allowed to be internal, I could generate the classes directly into the projects that require it. Yes, the classes would be duplicated on each project that uses it, but since the classes would be internal there would be no type collisions.

nodes.body:
This is already implemented - pass `--csharp_opt=internal_access` to protoc.

Looks like we need to document this on https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/reference/csharp-generated#compiler_options though.
(We should document the `serializable` option as well.)
Documentation updated internally; it'll appear when the site is next published. I'll close this issue now as there's no further work to do.

title: Python wheel's macOS deployment target is incorrect
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 4.21.8
Language: Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
macOS 12.6 with M1 chip

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.9.9

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
```bash
# Download the latest protobuf wheel and unpack it 
$ pip download --no-deps protobuf
$ unzip protobuf-4.21.8-cp37-abi3-macosx_10_9_universal2.whl
# Check the deployment target of the x86_64 slice of the one compiled file it contains
$ otool -mcpu=x86_64 -l google/_upb/_message.abi3.so | grep minos 
    minos 11.3
    minos 11.3
```

**What did you expect to see**

The macOS deployment target (a.k.a. the minimum supported version of macOS that this library supports - `-mmacosx-version-min` parameter to clang) of the compiled extension module should match that which the `.whl` file's filename declares.

**What did you see instead?**

The wheel declares support for macOS >= 10.9 but `google/_upb/_message.abi3.so` is compiled only for macOS >= 11.3. This means that for any macOS user with macOS version >=10.9 and <11.3  who runs `pip install protobuf`, pip will happily install this wheel thinking that it's compatible when it might not be, potentially leading to messy symbol load errors or crashes at runtime.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

Nope.

title: Python generated code is no longer compatible with Cython since 3.20
body:
Version: 4.21.8
Language: Python

Before the 3.20 update, the generated code was statically defining all the messages, and could be given to cython without issues.
Since the 3.20 update, those messages are dynamically generated, leading to a cython error.

For example, given this proto file

```proto
syntax = "proto3";

message Foo {
    bool a = 1;
}
```

The codegen gives this:

`$ protoc --python_out=gen proto/a.proto`

```py
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
# Generated by the protocol buffer compiler.  DO NOT EDIT!
# source: proto/a.proto
"""Generated protocol buffer code."""
from google.protobuf.internal import builder as _builder
from google.protobuf import descriptor as _descriptor
from google.protobuf import descriptor_pool as _descriptor_pool
from google.protobuf import symbol_database as _symbol_database
# @@protoc_insertion_point(imports)

_sym_db = _symbol_database.Default()




DESCRIPTOR = _descriptor_pool.Default().AddSerializedFile(b'\n\rproto/a.proto\"\x10\n\x03\x46oo\x12\t\n\x01\x61\x18\x01 \x01(\x08\x62\x06proto3')

_builder.BuildMessageAndEnumDescriptors(DESCRIPTOR, globals())
_builder.BuildTopDescriptorsAndMessages(DESCRIPTOR, 'proto.a_pb2', globals())
if _descriptor._USE_C_DESCRIPTORS == False:

  DESCRIPTOR._options = None
  _FOO._serialized_start=17
  _FOO._serialized_end=33
# @@protoc_insertion_point(module_scope)
```

This can no longer be compiled by cython:

```sh
$ cython gen/proto/a_pb2.py
Error compiling Cython file:
------------------------------------------------------------
...
_builder.BuildMessageAndEnumDescriptors(DESCRIPTOR, globals())
_builder.BuildTopDescriptorsAndMessages(DESCRIPTOR, 'proto.a_pb2', globals())
if _descriptor._USE_C_DESCRIPTORS == False:

  DESCRIPTOR._options = None
  _FOO._serialized_start=17
 ^
------------------------------------------------------------

gen/proto/a_pb2.py:23:2: undeclared name not builtin: _FOO
```

Cython does not dynamically check variables from modifications of `globals()`, and thinks the variable is not set.

This isn't really a regression since I suppose you do not support Cython. However, a small change could make this work with native python and cython:

Instead of generating this:

`_FOO._serialized_start=17`

generating this would fix the issue:

`globals()["_FOO"]._serialized_start=17`

This is not an easy fix to do with some post processing of the generated files with regexes and seds and stuff like this, but shouldn't be too hard to do in the code generator I suppose.

Would you be OK with such a change? That would be really useful for cython users. I can try to make this change if needed.

nodes.body: What is the use case for this? What is the expected behavior if you let Cython compile the generated code?

The expected behavior is to have the exact same behavior as without the Cython pass. Cython is usually used to improve performances, but it can also be used for obfuscation and protecting the source code.

I see. That seems reasonable. We reference `globals()` several times, I could see rewriting this to:

```python
_globals = globals()
_builder.BuildMessageAndEnumDescriptors(DESCRIPTOR, _globals)
_builder.BuildTopDescriptorsAndMessages(DESCRIPTOR, 'proto.a_pb2', _globals)

if _descriptor._USE_C_DESCRIPTORS == False:

  DESCRIPTOR._options = None
  _globals["_FOO"]._serialized_start=17
```

We could use `_globals` for any case where we are referencing a variable we did not directly assign.

I would worry some about the performance, except that `_descriptor._USE_C_DESCRIPTORS` will always be true unless we are using the pure-Python library, which is slow anyway. So I think we are ok there.
Yes that would work well!
Are you working on this @haberman ? I can try to make a PR for it otherwise
I am not working on this currently. PRs welcome.

nodes.body: I believe the problem here is that you're not linking in `Protobuf_LIBRARY`.  The protoc library (libprotoc) uses the C++ runtime (libprotobuf) as a private dependency, and exposes some headers.  You need to link against the C++ runtime to get the definitions though.
What is the difference between `${Protobuf_LIBRARIES}` and `${Protobuf_LIBRARY}`? OP was already linking against the former. In my build both variables contain the same string.
May be unrelated but my issue was that I never actually was building the message cc file into an object for compilation. Adding it as a source resolved the issue

body:

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.21.6
Language: C++/C#/Javascript

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows10

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Visual Studio 2019

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Set post-build options on Visual Studio 2019:
2. \\\\shald062\Code\vcpkg\installed\x64-windows\tools\protobuf\protoc.exe --proto_path="\\\\shald062\Code\vcpkg\installed\x64-windows\include" --proto_path="./protos" --cpp_out="./generated" ./protos/*.proto
3. Build the project
4. See error: \\\\shald062\Code\vcpkg\installed\x64-windows\include : warning : directory does not exist.

**What did you expect to see**
Build successful

**What did you see instead?**
Build failed

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
I also tried the command in Powershell. Fail too.
When I use a local path, both VS and command line success.

nodes.body: I don't think protoc supports network drive paths right now, and I don't think we necessarily have plans to add this. What's your use-case for wanting this, and if this is something we would be willing to help support/review, would you be interested in contributing this yourself?

@zhangskz  Thanks a lot for replying. My use-case is: I exported the c++ package of protobuf from vcpkg and stored it on a network drive, so all team members can build projects using the same source library. Once I need to use the types supplied by protobuf (like 'any'), I have to set the --proto_path as the network drive, the the problem occurs. Surely I can also add the "Include/google" folder into our repository, but I don't think it's the best way. Do you have any suggestion for my use-case?
Note that UNC (network) path should be recognized as normal file paths by the windows API and standard C/C++ functions on Windows. I'm not sure what the problem is here but it may be an easy fix.

title: If Protobuf is statically linked into a binary, but also dynamically loaded as a transitive dependency of a shared library, reflection breaks
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.12.4 (as shipped in Ubuntu 22.04)
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux, Ubuntu 22.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
g++ (Ubuntu 11.2.0-19ubuntu1) 11.2.0

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Run these commands:
```bash
cat >thingy.proto <<EOF
syntax = "proto3";
package ex;
message Thingy {
    string text = 1;
}
EOF
protoc thingy.proto --cpp_out=.
cat >library.hpp <<EOF
#include "thingy.pb.h"
ex::Thingy make_thingy();
EOF
cat >library.cpp <<EOF
#include "library.hpp"
ex::Thingy make_thingy() {
    ex::Thingy made;
    made.set_text("Hello world");
    return made;
}
EOF
g++ -fPIC -c thingy.pb.cc -o thingy.pb.o
g++ -fPIC -c library.cpp -o library.o
g++ -shared library.o thingy.pb.o -o liblibrary.so
cat >executable.cpp <<EOF
#include "library.hpp"
#include <iostream>
#include <google/protobuf/descriptor.h>
int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    std::cerr << "Checking for Protobuf descriptor pool..." << std::endl;
    const google::protobuf::DescriptorPool* pool =  google::protobuf::DescriptorPool::generated_pool();
    if (pool == nullptr) {
        throw std::runtime_error("Cound not find Protobuf descriptor pool: is libvgio working?");
    }
    std::cerr << "Found descriptor pool at " << pool << std::endl;
    ex::Thingy thingy = make_thingy();
    std::cout << thingy.text() << std::endl;
    return 0;
}
EOF
g++ -fPIC executable.cpp -llibrary -lprotobuf -o executable # One copy, dynamic
./executable # Works
g++ -fPIC executable.cpp -llibrary -Wl,-Bstatic -lprotobuf -Wl,-Bdynamic -o executable # One copy, static
./executable # Works

g++ -shared library.o thingy.pb.o -lprotobuf -o liblibrary-protodep.so # Two dependencies on dynamic libprotobuf (so one copy)
g++ -fPIC executable.cpp -llibrary-protodep -lprotobuf -o executable
./executable # Works
g++ -fPIC executable.cpp -llibrary-protodep -Wl,-Bstatic -lprotobuf -Wl,-Bdynamic -o executable # Static direct dependency and dynamic transitive dependency
./executable # Fails
```

**What did you expect to see**

In version 3.6.1 of Protobuf, I didn't see any problems arise from linking Protobuf statically into the binary and also dynamically as a transitive dependency of a dynamic library dependency. At least as long as the same version/build of Protobuf was used in both cases. (Though my reproduction above throws `system_error` from inside Protobuf on library load on 20.04, even when I link only one copy, my actual project is different somehow and works.)

I'm not sure if linking "the same" library multiple times in multiple ways is supposed to be allowed or not.

I would like to be able to statically link Protobuf without having to worry about whether Protobuf is a transitive dependency of any of my dynamically-linked library dependencies. For example, if `libcurl` someday starts to depend on Protobuf, and I dynamically link `libcurl` and statically link Protobuf, I don't want my application to break when built against the new Protobuf-using `libcurl`.

**What did you see instead?**

```
Checking for Protobuf descriptor pool...

Hello world

Hello world

Hello world

terminate called after throwing an instance of 'google::protobuf::FatalException'
  what():  CHECK failed: file != nullptr: 
Aborted (core dumped)
```

nodes.body:
Hi Adam, long time no see! I think you can accomplish what you're trying to do, but it requires two important things:
- Keep all protobuf symbols hidden so that they're not visible across dynamic library boundaries. This will prevent ODR violations.
- Treat the main binary and each protobuf-using dynamic library as its own private protobuf universe. So each one will have its own descriptor pool and other global data structures, and don't try to pass protos from one to another. (If you really need to do this, you can serialize the message on one side, send it over as raw bytes, and then parse it on the other side.)

Hey Adam! Nice to see you again too; thanks for working on this extremely useful thing!

Unfortunately in my application what I actually want is one Protobuf universe between the library and the rest of the code, since my library interface involves Protobuf types. But luckily I control the library and the application, so I can make sure that the whole tree uses exactly one of `libprotobuf.so` and `libprotobuf.a`.

I'm reluctant to blame the C++ ODR for why using both versions of the library doesn't work, because I can't find a version of the ODR from the standard that says anything about static or dynamic linking or even `.o` files. The circa C++20 version is [here](https://timsong-cpp.github.io/cppwp/n4868/basic.def.odr), and it only talks about "translation units", which the standard [seems to define](https://timsong-cpp.github.io/cppwp/n4868/lex.separate#def:translation_unit) as something like output strings of the preprocessor.

I would say that all the .o files that go into `libprotobuf.a` are the same "translation units" as the ones that go into `libprotobuf.so`, as long as the set of defines isn't being changed inside the Protobuf build process, because the same preprocessor output is being used to build each of them.

But `ld` doesn't seem to agree with me; it won't even work properly if I feed it the same compiled translation unit twice on one command line:

```
cat >library.hpp <<EOF
int do_thing();
EOF
cat >library.cpp <<EOF
#include "library.hpp"
int do_thing() {
    return 5;
}
EOF
g++ -c library.cpp -o library.o
cat >executable.cpp <<EOF
#include "library.hpp"
int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    return do_thing();
}
EOF
g++ -c executable.cpp -o executable.o
# This will fail
g++ -o executable executable.o library.o library.o
```

The linker seems to think that multiple visits to the output of translating the same translation unit are actually multiple distinct translation units:
```
/usr/bin/ld: library.o: in function `do_thing()':
library.cpp:(.text+0x0): multiple definition of `do_thing()'; library.o:library.cpp:(.text+0x0): first defined here
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
```

I don't see why `ld.so` would handle this any better. But I also don't see where in the standard it is pulling from when it decides this, so this might *really* be a linker limitation rather than something the standard says I shouldn't be allowed to do.

Either way, I don't think Protobuf is going to be able to do much to avoid it. And the workaround of hiding all the Protobuf symbols from the application's linker is going to work perfectly for the hypothetical Protobuf-enabled `libcurl` that I was talking about.

title: Disabling protobuf's TLS callbacks on Windows
body:
Platform: Windows
Version: protobuf:x64-static-windows=3.21.4 (vcpkg)

Protobuf is generating TLS callbacks.

Just by including any .cc files (generated by protobuf) in the project, protobuf causes the final executable to have TLS callbacks present inside of it.

1- What's the purpose of these TLS callbacks?
2- How would one disable this behavior?

`option optimize_for` does not change anything about this.

nodes.body: Assuming "TLS" means "thread local storage", protobuf uses thread locals for some concurrency optimizations.  Assuming you mean "transport layer security", I am quite stumped.

> transport layer security

I've never heard of transport layer security **callbacks** before 😅

Is it possible to omit these "concurrency optimizations" and manage them myself?

The compiler flag /Zc:threadSafeInit- (with the hyphen) allows for exactly this.

I'm not sure how to apply it for an external library such as protobuf or even better, if this was probably a built-in option?

Please don't tell me "compiling protobuf myself is the only option" because it was so painful and didn't even work in the end.

I also tried using vcpkg's triplets as follows:

set(VCPKG_CXX_FLAGS "/Zc:threadSafeInit-")
set(VCPKG_CXX_FLAGS_DEBUG "/Zc:threadSafeInit-")
set(VCPKG_CXX_FLAGS_RELEASE "/Zc:threadSafeInit-")
set(VCPKG_C_FLAGS "/Zc:threadSafeInit-")
set(VCPKG_C_FLAGS_DEBUG "/Zc:threadSafeInit-")
set(VCPKG_C_FLAGS_RELEASE "/Zc:threadSafeInit-")

The TLS callbacks were still present.

Is protobuf maybe using some other external libraries that are using TLS callbacks? Isn't there a recursive way or some built in feature? I've been struggling with this for a while now.
@Ou7law007 did you by any chance happen to find a solution for this?

I still think it would be worth mentioning in the actual documentation, however.

title: Protoc finds "oneof" where it isn't present

nodes.body:
Okay, as far as I can see this is how field presence is implemented in proto3 (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/docs/field_presence.md)

This leads us to some questions:

- Is there a way to differentiate the "optional" field from the explicitly added "oneof"? 
   It is essential for us as we use the Descriptor to implement various checks against proto-files
   and for transformations
- Is adding an "optional" label incompatible change?

- I'm not sure about other languages, but in C++ you can call `FieldDescriptor::real_containing_oneof()`, which will return the `OneofDescriptor` only if it's a real oneof and otherwise return `nullptr`. `OneofDescriptor::is_synthetic()` will also tell you if the oneof is a "synthetic" one (i.e. created internally as part of an `optional` field).
- Adding `optional` to an existing singular proto3 field is fine, but just keep in mind that binaries using the old definition will of course not know about it, so for example they might think a 0-valued `optional` field is unset and drop it.

**What language does this apply to?**
Generated C/C++ code and the specific cmake target.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
When I link to the generated cmake target and set the BUILD_SHARED_LIBS variable globally I get linker errors because the protobuf created code is not relocateable.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
In my user code I use something like the following:

~~~~~~
# ensure relocateable code
if (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS)
  set_property(TARGET ${PROTO_TARGET} PROPERTY POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE TRUE)

I tried this on my laptop and was able to reproduce the error. When I run `nm -C -D libprotobuf.so.3.21.4.0`, I see that the `google::protobuf::RepeatedPtrField<std::__cxx11::basic_string...` symbols are not being exported. It's strange that they do appear when I try this on my workstation, though.

Ok, I think I've figured out what's going on. I suspect it's a behavior difference between Clang and GCC, because on my laptop with GCC I can run `objdump -Ct ./CMakeFiles/libprotobuf.dir/src/google/protobuf/repeated_field.cc.o` and see the symbols listed as `hidden`, whereas on my workstation with Clang they show up without `hidden`.

The Clang behavior is surprising to me, because it's treating the symbols as visible even though we're building with `-fvisibility=hidden`. We do set the visibility to public [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/2880fef06cb7443ba24dc1264ba9f02115407f2c/src/google/protobuf/repeated_ptr_field.h#L2024), but the compiler currently doesn't have access to that declaration when it's building repeated_field.cc.

So I think the fix is just to make sure the `PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_DECLARE` declaration from repeated_ptr_field.h is visible before we instantiate the template with `template class PROTOBUF_EXPORT_TEMPLATE_DEFINE RepeatedPtrField<std::string>;`. As long as the compiler sees that declaration (which includes `__attribute__ ((visibility ("default")))`) then it should generate code that correctly marks the symbol as public.

Let me send out a change to fix this.

title: Using `m` as a package name leads to invalid code
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

Language: Java

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux

OpenJDK 11

**What did you do?**

The following proto leads to a Java code that doesn't compile:
```
syntax = "proto2";

package m;

message Foo {}

message Msg {
    repeated Foo foo = 1;
}
```

Error:
```
[error] Test.java:862:1: cannot find symbol
[error]   symbol:   variable Test
[error]   location: variable m of type m.Test.Foo
```

The breakage appears to have been introduced in this change: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/10667/files#diff-1f7aa0e2fe4f343ea4da9e797d4e55c69af1ee6a7778ea5aafc2f0a35195a646R1310-R1316 - where the variable used is `m` rather than `$name_` which was meant to resolve name clashes. I know a package named name `m` is quite contrived, but maybe there are additional scenarios where this change could lead to name clashes. This issue was discovered by ScalaPB's test framework which generates random protocol buffers.

nodes.body: Yeah. We have a number of these kinds of problems with generated names. We need a better strategy for making naming collisions less likely.

title: How to accomadate max `uInt32` value in the java `CodedOutputStream`?
body:
For `uInt32`, the maximum value possible is 4,294,967,295. But the maximum value of java `int` is 2,147,483,647.
In the apis exposed in `CodedOutputStream` like `writeUInt32`, `computeUInt32Size` only accepts an `int` value for the argument. How can I provide a max `uInt32` value for this?

nodes.body:
I found that I can use https://guava.dev/releases/snapshot/api/docs/com/google/common/primitives/UnsignedInts.html to pass unsigned `int`s here.
`UnsignedInts.checkedCast(4294967295l)`

And also I think a workaround would be `Integer.parseUnsignedInt("4294967295l")`.

Not to segment fault.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3048602/198870342-896a4c85-ea07-4aef-8d84-c63d6716db4c.png)

body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: main
Language: C++

Debian GNU/Linux rodete

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
bazel 5.3.2

**What did you do?**
Attempt to depend on `@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf` from another cc_library target.

**What did you expect to see**
A successful build and import of that target.

**What did you see instead?**
```
Error in glob: glob pattern 'src/**/*.h' didn't match anything, but allow_empty is set to False (the default value of allow_empty can be set with --incompatible_disallow_empty_glob).
```
Using `--noincompatible_disallow_empty_glob` yields an `#include` error on some of the headers which would've been found by the glob if it didn't cross a package boundary.
Depending on both `@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf` and `@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf_headers` appears to work (but is ugly).

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

It's particularly obstinate if you've enabled `layering_check` in bazel.

nodes.body:
Note the work-around with `:protobuf_headers` only works for *some* things, it's still missing headers from at least the visibility-restricted targets:
`@com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf/util:json_util`
`@com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf/util:type_resolver_util`
`@com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf/util:delimited_message_util`
`@com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf/util:differencer`

It's also missing a lot of headers from `@com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf/io` but that target is public, so easier/better to use directly anyway :-)
Thank you for the bug report. I guess we should probably start listing the headers explicitly since recursive globs are discouraged anyway as I understand.

Hey Shahms,

Bazel doesn't actually enforce that you directly depend on the headers you include (like Blaze does).  So the simplest solution here is just to delete the useless globs and keep everything else the same.  Is there another reason you need a direct dependency on the headers?  I could try to fix protobuf_headers while I'm at it, but if we're not actually fixing a reproducible bug it's almost guaranteed to regress in the future

Bazel's default C++ toolchain supports `layering_check`, just not `parse_headers` (yet?).  We generally prefer to have `layering_check` enabled when possible (even if it is less effective w/o `parse_headers`) as it's generally helpful, particularly with imports.

Completely understand if that's low priority, though :-)

Following up, `package(features = ["layering_check"])` will enable layering checks.  We should do this for our repo, even though an open bug about `parse_headers` will prevent it from actually fixing this problem.

Note that this affects release v22.2 as well

(Not the glob issue, so much as the layering_check).
We now comply with the layering_check as of last week with https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/a7b0421c78412baa48704d727601a17ac0f451d1.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
A more type safe approach to handling Protobuf `oneOf`

**Describe the solution you'd like**
To have `oneOf` fields from Protobuf represented as `sealed interface`s in Kotlin

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
In theory, for the simplest cases, `enum class`es is a possible solution, but we should probably reserve those for Protobuf `enum`s. `sealed interface`s (or `sealed class`es) are a more appropriate solution here.

**Additional context**
For instance, we have a `oneOf` message like:
```proto
message Identifier {
  oneof identifier {
    string map_id = 1;
    string common_id = 2;
    string person_id = 3;
  }
}
```

In our system, we had to manually create:
```kotlin
sealed interface Identifier {
    fun asProtobuf(): UserPrivacyControlProtos.Identifier
}
data class CommonId(val value: String) : Identifier {
    override fun asProtobuf() = identifier { commonId = this@CommonId.value}
}
data class MapId(val value: String) : Identifier {
    override fun asProtobuf() = identifier { mapId = this@MapId.value}
}
data class PersonId(val value: String) : Identifier {
    override fun asProtobuf() = identifier { personId = this@PersonId.value}
}
```

And to convert from the current generated Protobuf class:
```kotlin
fun UserPrivacyControlProtos.Identifier.asSealedData(): Identifier? =
    when (this.identifierCase) {
        IdentifierCase.COMMON_ID -> CommonId(this.commonId)
        IdentifierCase.MAP_ID -> MapId(this.mapId)
        IdentifierCase.PERSON_ID -> PersonId(this.personId)
        IdentifierCase.IDENTIFIER_NOT_SET, null -> null
    }
```

It would be nice if this can be automated by the Protobuf Kotlin code generator.

nodes.body:
We absolutely considered this in our original design for the Kotlin proto APIs.  There are a few problems with it that made it difficult, or at least made us want to delay until we could come up with a better design.

First, we cannot break code when a new field is added to a oneof.  This means that we cannot seal the type.  (We _could_ have an abstract class with an internal constructor, though; we'd force users to have an `else`  case -- but that's the point, really.)

The other half of this is the performance implications of allocating an object every time someone accesses a oneof -- which are tolerable in many environments, but intolerable to our Android apps, where we are very careful to minimize allocations.  We could potentially just remove this feature in the [lite runtime](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/java/lite.md), but that's not an ideal solution.

Compare, for example, the `kotlin.Result` type, which is effectively a sealed union -- but not implemented as a sealed type, and not supporting the `when is` approach, for performance reasons.  Instead, it offers visitor-style methods.  It's not clear to us if that approach would be preferable to the status quo of oneofs in Kotlin today (even if it were possible, which it may not be if e.g. two oneof options share a type).

The way @jackgene has suggested this feature be implemented, you would only pay the cost of allocating an object when the `asSealedData` function is called. In performance constrained environments, the traditional strategy could be used avoiding that allocation cost.

I think that getting a compilation failure when a new field is added is the feature @jackgene is really looking for. The advantage of a sealed class/interface is that the compiler can let us know when a case is missed. As with the performance considerations, if a user does not want code that could fail to compile when a new cases is added, they can opt out of this feature by simply not calling the `asSealedData` function.

Historically, the protobuf project as a whole has been unwilling to add APIs that you should use only in some cases that can be footguns in others.  Compare, for example, the complete omission of `required` fields from proto3 -- a very comparable decision, actually, a choice to omit up-front checking of some constraints that could be footguns.  Relatedly, this also affects API constraints for protos you don't own -- this introduces new risks for a team evolving a proto and breaking code that depends on that proto.  (In particular, this _forces_ you to change the proto and all its consumers atomically if you want to keep the build green, which is very concerning.)

That said, as I think about it, it may _already_ be the case that the exhaustive when on enums breaks when a new oneof field is offered.  This is quite unfortunate -- and actually adds a little motivation to add the class representation just so we have an option that _isn't_ sealed.

title: libatomic mis-detected as required with strict compiler flags
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: main
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
macOS, but the problem is more general

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Apple clang version 14.0.0 (clang-1400.0.29.202)
Target: arm64-apple-darwin22.1.0

**What did you do?**
I am including protobuf via CMake into a larger project (https://github.com/shaka-project/shaka-packager).  In that context, the entire project is built with very strict compiler flags and -Werror.

What I see is that this test:

```
  check_cxx_source_compiles("
    #include <atomic>
    int main() {
      return std::atomic<int64_t>{};
    }
  " protobuf_HAVE_BUILTIN_ATOMICS)
```

fails with an error about integer truncation from int64_t to int, even though 64-bit atomics are available without a library.  But this error occurs on macOS, which doesn't have libatomic, leading later to a link error.

I found that a simple solution is to add a static cast to the test, so that it produces the correct results even in a very strict environment:

```
  check_cxx_source_compiles("
    #include <atomic>
    int main() {
      return static_cast<int>(std::atomic<int64_t>{});
    }
  " protobuf_HAVE_BUILTIN_ATOMICS)
```

I'll send a PR, in the hopes that this is an acceptable solution.

title: Java's getSerialized size implies serialization?
body:
Language: Java

I'm a little confused about [streaming](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/techniques) in protobuf. I know we need to set the message size before the actual message, but the question is can we actual calculate the serialized size without serializing the message itself?

I'm checking java's implementation and based on my understanding, the library indeed calculates the serialized size without serializing the message first. Even in `writeDelimitedTo()` it calls first: `final int serialized = getSerializedSize();` .

The only trick to it is that `getSerializedSize();` is generated by the compiler plugin each time.

title: Optimized Python NumPy Bindings for Repeated Fields
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Fast Protobuf to numpy array conversions

**Describe the solution you'd like**
We have an internal design proposal approved for implementing  ` __array__` for fast protobuf -> NumPy conversion. This was also requested in https://groups.google.com/g/protobuf/c/P7-5iqUZa5s.

Filing this for tracking of status/timeline, since we've received several requests related to this from open-source customers.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
This was requested in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8047 via implementing buffer protocol in repeated primitive fields. However, we don't want to implement the buffer protocol because it exposes more of our internal implementation, and may cause problems if the underlying repeated field is modified while a view to it exists.

nodes.body: @zhangskz - Any updates on this issue? Did the approved internal design ever move towards implementation?
@zhangskz - I'm also interested in knowing if there have been any updates on this issue.

The original proposer had an implementation in progress, but I believe progress here stalled. We haven't implemented this further on our side yet, but will see what we can do to get this prioritized given the demand.

For unrelated reasons, I happened to find my way to https://docs.python.org/3.12/whatsnew/3.12.html#pep-688-making-the-buffer-protocol-accessible-in-python which is new in the upcoming Python 12. I wonder if it might play a role in solving this problem.

Thanks for sharing!  We had previously considered `_buffer_()`` in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8047#issuecomment-1032920157 but buffer protocol exposes more of our internal implementation and may cause problems if the underlying repeated field is modified while a view to it exists.

Sure, I definitely understand about not wanting to leak implementation details, and can't really speak to how that might be mitigated. On the second part though, I'd say that's a risk worth taking, or perhaps better phrased as a risk worth permitting the user to take. In the case where you really need zero-copy behavior into numpy, that's unavoidably going to imply view semantics one way or another, and by opting in the user agrees to play by more subtle (though hopefully well documented) rules. Just my thoughts on the issue - I'll be interested to see any future solution. I think it is an important one.

title: Proto2 protobuf cannot handle enums with value higher than 31 during serialization in Python
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: protoc 3.21.9
Language: Python - protobuf 4.21.9

OS: Windows 11

Interpreter: Python 3.11.0

**What did you do?**
1. Create proto2 protobuf that contains Enum with values larger than 31
2. Compile using protoc
3. Instantiate the protobuf in code and set the enum field to value larger than 31
4. Serialize the protobuf to string
5. Deserialize the protobuf

**What did you expect to see**
The deserialized protobuf has the enum field set to the value larger than 31

**What did you see instead?**
The deserialized protobuf has the field clear (the serialized form does not contain the value at all).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
I can provide minimal reproduction example if desired, but it was pretty simple to reproduce. The issue was also reproduceable on protobuf lib versions as low as 4.21.3 and with grpcio-tools as low as 1.49.1. Lastly, switching the syntax to proto3 does fix the issue, however it is currently not viable for us.

nodes.body: Thank you for the bug report. This sounds like a potentially serious bug. Would you mind providing the reproducible example?

This must be a Windows-specific bug. When I try your repro on Linux, I get:

```
a TaskType: ad
Name: "Name1"

---
b TaskType: ad
Name: "Name1"

---
a TaskType: ac
Name: "Name2"

---
b TaskType: ac
Name: "Name2"
```

I suspect this is related to `long` being only 32-bits on Windows. I will investigate further.
I also cannot reproduce the bug on (64-bit) Linux.
I can also confirm that I cannot reproduce it inside WSL. It does indeed seem to be Windows specific (both machines I tried this on were either Windows 11 or Windows 10).

Can you print out `len(serialized)`? I suspect it will be non-zero, but want to verify.

(I don't have quick access to a Windows machine to verify).

len(serialized): 9
len(serialized2): 9
serialized in base64: 'CCASBU5hbWUx'
serialized2 in base64: 'CB8SBU5hbWUy'

Great, thanks. It appears to be serializing correctly. When we parse it though, the decoder thinks the value (32) is not in the enum for some reason.  In proto2, when you parse an unrecognized enum value, it goes into the unknown field set, which is what appears to be happening here.

The only question now is why the decoder thinks that 32 is an unknown value for this enum.

This is the code performing the check. The bug is *likely* here or nearby, but I can't see it: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/blob/f45eeec625a1b5b4514683aba4b38d1864f0e211/upb/decode.c#L410-L440

In particular, this check looks correct to me. We cast `1ULL` to `unsigned long long`, so it should be 64-bit even on Windows, which has 32-bit longs: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/blob/f45eeec625a1b5b4514683aba4b38d1864f0e211/upb/decode.c#L437
Another helpful thing I can point out is that this is an regression introduced in 4.21.x. Protobuf 3.20.3 deserializes the message correctly.

> Another helpful thing I can point out is that this is an regression introduced in 4.21.x.

That makes perfect sense, as 4.21.x introduced a completely rewritten native extension. More info here: https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#python-updates
I would be mildly surprised if the bug turned out to be in decode.c since that code has not changed much at all. I'm wondering whether this may be related to the mini descriptors.

It's true that decode.c has not changed much, but we also have much less usage on Windows than other platforms.

Keep in mind that we're releasing from the 21.x branch, which has not gotten any of the recent changes around MiniDescriptors: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/tree/21.x/upb

I have a root cause and a fix for the bug. The problem was in the `UPB_LIKELY()` macro, which uses `__builtin_expect()`. The arguments to `__buitin_expect()` are `long`, so on Windows this truncates the arguments to 32 bits.

The fix is to cast the argument to `bool`:

```patch
--- a/upb/port_def.inc
+++ b/upb/port_def.inc
@@ -96,8 +96,8 @@
 
 /* Hints to the compiler about likely/unlikely branches. */
 #if defined (__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__)
-#define UPB_LIKELY(x) __builtin_expect((x),1)
-#define UPB_UNLIKELY(x) __builtin_expect((x),0)
+#define UPB_LIKELY(x) __builtin_expect((bool)(x),1)
+#define UPB_UNLIKELY(x) __builtin_expect((bool)(x),0)
 #else
 #define UPB_LIKELY(x) (x)
 #define UPB_UNLIKELY(x) (x)
```
A fix for this has just been pushed so I am closing.

title: int128, uint128, int256, uint256
body:
int128/uint128
protobuf types

Someone marked completed,
but quite clear it has not been implemented
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/2180

There's a clear reason why many hesitate usage of
__uint_128_t in c => it differs in implementation
at the tail end of os distributions (how to pad?)
There's logical inconsistencies in the heterogenous approach
of RTOS/OS/etc/etc.

There's not a clear reason why protobuf can't
handle uint128_t for the c/c++ language
w/ a custom type.
There's logical consistency in the homogenous approach
of protobuf wrt ints.

That is, every non-fixed integer in core protobuf
library modeled precisely as a varint. A set of contiguous
bytes with only a bound in size. This way, for the super majority
of ints small in size utilized (most signifiant bit) vs size available (4/8/16/32/etc),
it's automatically "compressed"

We propose implementing int128/uint128 in c/c++ under
the same premise =>  varint, set of bytes, with a custom type,
that handles comparison operators.

There are multiple examples in the ecosystem of addons/extensions.
They are useless without a standard in this library.
Let's start & finish the spec for how to achieve int128/uint128 :)

nodes.body: This seems like a useful feature, but I just doubt that we will get to this any time soon, since we are currently busy with higher-priority projects. Adding a new type like this is a pretty large amount of work since it needs to be done separately for every language we support.

@acozzette 
what's higher-priority?
happy to jump in.
we need this :)

If we achieve future-proof/consistent design,
will be quite easy to jumpstart c/c++

I would propose:
var int (series of bytes),
never support fixed int.
If we can achieve consensus on that, 
becomes significantly simpler to scale
into other languages.
Any reason this is closed @vitruvvius ? I've seen other issues where others would like it. I'm working with Rust and the lack of 128 bit support in the protobuf is challenging
no response in < 3 days to comment above

> Any reason this is closed @vitruvvius ? I've seen other issues where others would like it. I'm working with Rust and the lack of 128 bit support in the protobuf is challenging

^+1
I'm on the same page as @dado0583, working with Rust without 128 bit primitive support in protobuf is indeed very chanllenging

definitely agree to the Rust comment - altogether, the process for integrating a net new type into protobuf quite long & tedious. u128/u256/u512 all quite common given pervasiveness of sha + crc. best path forward to fork repository & work off intra company variant
Need this badly aswell! 128/256 are highly needed

Came up ^^^ in the context of C# / .NET

However, compatibility is a huge issue, since

1. any solution needs to be at least usable (even if not native) on a wide range of platforms,
2. any solution needs to at least be ignorable by older library versions that don't know about it

I think the second bullet rules out:

> We propose implementing int128/uint128 in c/c++ under the same premise => varint, set of bytes, with a custom type, that handles comparison operators.

since some of the existing implementations report errors after the 10th varint byte. A custom wire type is out for similar reasons. Personally, I suspect the best option would be to use the "bytes" encoding, i.e. length prefixed, but trimmed to the bytes below the first non-zero byte (and declaring an endianness) - so: the value 1 would be sent as "length 1, payload { 0x01 }", but "length 12, payload { x12 }": also fine. IMO it also makes sense to allow "sint128", using the same approach, just: after applying zig/zag to the value.

The "bytes" approach is marginally larger for low values, and marginally smaller for high values, than varint; since we expect large values, this seems a good compromise, but: the real point of the above is: compatibility.

The first bullet may demand custom hacks (for example an encapsulated pair of 64-bit integers) on platforms that lack a native int128
Just curious -- what's best practice for performant 128-bit integers right now? bytes? any Proto3 branches? ASN? etc?
It is a pity that no progress has been made in this work

> Just curious -- what's best practice for performant 128-bit integers right now? bytes? any Proto3 branches? ASN? etc?

if you're after high perf, and most of the ser/des workload has tiny values, then crafting a varint for i128/u128 with bytes.
https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/encoding/

title: Any reason why protobuf doesn't use the last version of bazel skybuild?

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

`libprotoc 3.21.6`

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

**What did you do?**

I defined a Bazel workspace from scratch, such as:

```bazel
workspace(name = "my_workspace")

    name = "rules_proto",

rules_proto_toolchains()

then, I have an empty BUILD file in my root and the following BUILD file in the proto directory:

```bazel
load("@rules_cc//cc:defs.bzl", "cc_library")
load("@rules_proto//proto:defs.bzl", "proto_library")

    name = "account_cc_proto",
    deps = [":account_proto"],
)

    name = "account_proto",

```

**What did you expect to see**

I expected it to create my library.

**What did you see instead?**

if I run `bazel build //proto:account_cc_proto`, I have the following error:

```
ERROR: /private/var/tmp/_bazel_clement/117db2068dbf3b2a936098c10c02808c/external/com_google_protobuf/BUILD:85:10: error loading package '@com_github_protocolbuffers_protobuf//': cannot load '@bazel_skylib//rules:common_settings.bzl': no such file and referenced by '@com_google_protobuf//:cc_toolchain'
```

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

After finding [this issue comment](https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_go/issues/2530#issuecomment-639647805), I added:

```bazel
http_archive(

title: crash when write file for iOS

nodes.body: @thomasvl Do you have any ideas what could be going wrong?

There's not much to go on here, but since the quoted crash is on _Thread 6_, odds are you are running into a general threading issue.  Protobuf Messages are not thread safe for **mutation**, you can read them from multiple threads, but if you are going to mutate then only one thread can be accessing the message.  My guess is you are using a background thread to write out your message, but you also use that message to collect the global logging information, so some other thread was modifying the message at the same time it was writing to write out, so the initial calculations about size didn't match what and hence the error was throw.  I'd suggest checking your code to ensure when you go to write out the message, you hand off the message and no one else keeps a reference so you can't get into this state.

@thomasvl  ,thank you for your reply. first we process the log message to a GPB model  in a serial dispatch queue, and new a model to receive a log message.then put the allocated model to a NSArray. every ten log messages would trigger a coded output stream to flush the messages to write to file. namely we called the flush function to write file for every ten log messages. all those operations happened in another serial dispatch queue. briefly speaking we construct GPBMessage Model in one serial dispatch queue A then pass another serial dispatch queue B to handle the write file thing.in B we write file every ten log messages.
and about the mutation condition I checked earlier but found nothing. above is our handling process for GPBMessge to save to file. and you can point out something wrong for it?

It's hard to tell from the description since I don't know what your messages are, etc.

- what's actually in your messages in the array?  Do they have sub objects?  Are they exclusive to the model or does someone else keep a reference to them?
- when you say you flush the array every ten, is that thread safe?  Do you hand off the array and start collecting into a new array or do both operations share the same NSArray so there could be a race there?
- How are you actually flushing out the 10 message since there isn't an api to directly write out an NSArray of messages?  Does that logic have some issue.

If you can make a small example that shows what you are doing, then someone might be able to see the problem (or it might become clear as you make the example), but otherwise, in the abstract, there's isn't really much guidance anyone can give except to suggest you audit the codepaths to ensure you aren't mutating the same objects that are being written out by another thread.

There are potentially a lot of details in the things being called that aren't included.  Posing a complete example that someone can try out is the best way to ask for help others someone is just making guessing on partial details.

A fair amount of initialization is left out, so I'd suggest you maybe double check those things (what type of queue is `writeLogToFileQueue`), also you seem to use some "globals" (like `mLogMetaData`), are those only used in a thread safe way?

@thomasvl ,I fix the question by try catch. but I don't get the root point about why it crashes. one condition is there is no space left to write. the other conditions is not caught by debugger so I don't know why it write file failure.

I believe the root is still going to be you have one thread mutating some of the same protobuf objects that another thread is trying to write out. The objects are not thread safe for writing operations.

body:

-->

**What language does this apply to?**
Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Since upb library was added in python protobuf in 4.21.0, I would expect `upb` to be the default back-end as long as it's accessible. However, the lines 55-59 in `api_implementation.py` ([link](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v21.9/python/google/protobuf/internal/api_implementation.py#L50-L59)) prefers the `cpp` back-end as long as `api_implementation.cc` file is compiled.

It works good with the packages from pypi, but it causes issue with custom builds or conda builds. The `protobuf` builds provided by conda-forge does not include the `upb` back-end. I would expect a user could simply copy the `google/_upb` folder or build a `upb` package to enable the `upb` back-end.

I know we can use the `PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION` environment variable to choose the preferred back-end. But the use case here is always choose `upb` as default as long as `upb` is accessible and `PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION` is not set.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Can we remove the lines 55-59, and have it relies on lines 73-76 ([link](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v21.9/python/google/protobuf/internal/api_implementation.py#L73-L79)) to pick up the backend?

title: Java: expose specialized primitive collections (IntList) to avoid auto-boxing
body:
[fastutil](https://fastutil.di.unimi.it/docs/index.html) offers data structures for primitive Java types that are smaller in size and faster for reading and mutating. If protoc used e.g. `IntArrayList` rather than `ArrayList<Integer>` and provided `getInt()` then boxing and unboxing could be avoided.


**What language does this apply to?**
generated Java code

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
improve read/write performance and size of proto messages

**Describe the solution you'd like**
utilize data structures provided in fastutil (or another package providing similar benefits) and provide the richer `get` API so client code can work with unboxed primitives as much as possible.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
For smaller collections the difference is negligible, for larger ones we convert them from the source proto object so the penalty of using the regular `ArrayList<Integer>` is minimized

nodes.body: Are you able to perform the experiment and share the details of your finding at this time?

One example I found of intSet performance vs. HashSet<Integer>:

https://www.baeldung.com/fastutil#1-performance

https://github.com/Krumpet/protobuf-performance

```

Then, users who care about this performance gain can use the `IntList` and avoid auto-boxing.

title: python 3.11 support

nodes.body:
> but setup.py and tox.ini do not mention python 3.11

That is true, we should update setup.py to be more clear about supporting Python 3.11.

> when I tried building 21.9 with python 3.11.0 (from pkgsrc), I see

It looks like you are trying to build the old extension. The code in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/main/python/google/protobuf/pyext is deprecated in OSS and is no longer used in our official releases.

If you install binary wheels from our PyPI packages, it should support 3.11 without you needing to compile anything. That said, we should make it easier to build from source when necessary. Our source packages appear to contain the old extension code. We should update that to contain the new extension from https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/tree/main/python instead.

> If you install binary wheels from our PyPI packages, it should support 3.11 without you needing to compile anything. 

Hi!
I can install protobuf on from pypi on macos, just mentioning that `protobuf-4.21.9-cp310-abi3-win_amd64.whl` exists but 
`protobuf-4.21.9-cp311-abi3-win_amd64.whl` is not. Isn't it needed to install on Python 3.11 on win64?
https://pypi.org/project/protobuf/4.21.9/#files

> Isn't it needed to install on Python 3.11 on win64?

No, protobuf uses the [Python Limited API](https://docs.python.org/3/c-api/stable.html#stable-application-binary-interface) where possible. Any packages that have `abi3` in the name are compatible with that version of Python *or higher*.

So `protobuf-4.21.9-cp310-abi3-win_amd64.whl` is compatible with Python 3.10 *or higher*. We will never need to build a Python 3.11-specific package.

Ideally we would have used `abi3` for all our packages. But for Python 3.7, 3.8, and 3.9 on Windows there was one function we need that is not in the limited API. But in Python 3.10 it was added, so now the Python 3.10 `abi3` packages will work on all future versions of Python (well, maybe until Python4, if that ever happens).

> If you install binary wheels from our PyPI packages, it should support 3.11 without you needing to compile anything. That said, we should make it easier to build from source when necessary. title: protoc has complicated and unnecessary check for pseudo-uniqueness for enum value names
body:
When compiling protos, `protoc` rejects enums that have values where names are unique but, after a complex transformation, may not be unique.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/v21.9/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.cc#L5913

At first glance, this seems similar to the check of field names relating to JSON names -- they both undergo a transformation and case-insensitive check. Also, they are only enforced for files with syntax "proto3", which was when a specification for the JSON format was published.

There is a comment in the code that suggests that this is to allow code generators to safely transform the name without risking conflicts. However this explanation does not really pass muster:
1. Code generators do some level of transformation for _many_ symbols in the file (including message, field, service, and method names). This is to make the generated code use idiomatic naming conventions for the target language. Yet these other elements have no similar transformation and validation. It is generally up to the code generator to ensure it is not producing conflicting names when it makes these transformations.
2. It is only enforced in proto3, not proto2. That means that code generators realistically may _not_ transform the name or else they may still produce problems when generating code for "proto2" syntax files.

Given the direction of field name and JSON name checks that appears to be happening ([link](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TsKvK9uU7q42-kVyVPzCTSEpJKpQ74rkrQz0UHCibiY/edit?resourcekey=0-XkzVi_BpzVsOCelkscBbpQ#heading=h.f4bilzmezze2)), perhaps for consistency it also makes sense to relax these checks for enum value names?

cc @mkruskal-google

title: memory leak by google::protobuf::internal::ArenaStringPtr::NewString
body:
My protobuf response message is: 

> message FileAck { string filename = 1; ... }

I have a stream of request messages to be processed by a writer. When grpc::ClientWriter::Finish() is called by a client writer instance, one of the side effects is to (per grpc::ClientWriter doc)

> Attempts to fill in the response parameter passed to the constructor of this instance with the response message from the server

So what happened during the filling of the response parameter _filename_ is that 

> google::protobuf::internal::ArenaStringPtr::NewString 

is called which again calls 

> operator new(unsigned long)

which caused direct memory leak of 32 bytes and indirect 31 bytes in my case. The details are here:

Any idea? Thanks a ton.

nodes.body:
Odds are extremely strong that you are doing one of 

* leaking a protobuf instance
* leaking a protobuf arena
* using an unsafe API incorrectly

Without all of the code we are unlikely to be able to determine which.
`*(fileAck.release_filename())` is a memory leak.  You are releasing the string but not freeing the memory associated with it.  You wanted your code to simply be `fileAck.filename()` there.
Bingo! You are the hero. I thought release_ would transfer ownership of the string to the caller, hence no need for freeing memory. There is a nuance to release_.
`release_` does transfer ownership to the caller and hence requires the caller to free it (as you do in approach 3)

title: Compatibility of generated Python code with protoc >= 3.19.0
body:
I have some questions regarding the compatibility guarantees of generated code with individual language APIs, specifically Python. According to https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#python-updates:

> each language has its own major version that can be incremented independently of other languages, as covered later in this topic with the Python release. [...] The first instance of this new versioning scheme is the new version of the Python API, 4.21.0

As everyone is aware from https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/10051

> Python upb requires generated code that has been generated from protoc 3.19.0 or newer.

That makes sense going forward when trying to use upb with protobuf 4.x. Some questions:

1. Will code generated with protoc >= 3.19.0 continue to work with Python protobuf 3.x? When will protoc stop being compatible with protobuf 3.x?
2. Now that individual language API major versions are incremented independently, how are users expected to know which protoc version generates code compatible with which individual language API version? Right now, the latest protoc version is 3.21.10 which "targets" python 4.x afaict. The mismatch of major versions here is confusing.

I found https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/4945 referencing compatibility tests, but they were deleted in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/8570. Apologies if this Is this documented somewhere and I missed it.

## Additional context

https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python/issues/2880#issuecomment-1334556835

nodes.body: Historically protobuf has been very bad about providing a crisp definition here.  The good news is that I have something in progress that should define this more carefully and I will try to publish it in the next month or so (holidays may interfere)

The code generated by 4.21.x happens to be backwards compatible with 3.20.x and (I think) 3.19.x.  The eventual criteria we are aiming for will not guarantee that code generated from a newer compiler supports an older runtime.

> The code generated by 4.21.x happens to be backwards compatible with 3.20.x and (I think) 3.19.x.

Anecdotally, protoc 3.19.4 works with `opentelemetry-proto >= 3.19` and gives the upb benefits for 4.x. protoc 3.20 did not work with protobuf 3.19.x.

I have to say I am truly puzzled. How is a Python project using protobuf supposed to _cleanly_ manage its dependency?

I would really appreciate any documentation, best practices, or at least sanctioned reference projects.

Our thoughts were this:
- Compiled `_pb2.py` files don't belong under version control because they are compiled.
- Therefore we have to detect and use `protoc` during `setup.py`
- Since `protoc` doesn't come from pypi (except for [unofficial short-term packages](https://pypi.org/project/protoc-wheel/#description) - we have to use the `protoc` from the developer or build environment
- However, we cannot make too strict assumptions on the `protoc` version due since they come from different sources
- So we have to support multiple `protoc` versions
- But we have had incompatibilities between `protobuf` and the generated `_pb2.py` files if the `protoc` and `protobuf` versions don't match
- So we need to set a dependency to the specific `protobuf` version based on the `protc` version during compilation
- Previous to the [2022 versioning change](https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers/docs/news/2022-05-06#versioning) we basically depend on `protobuf=m.n.*` based on `m.n.p` from `protoc --version` (which felt already pretty unclean)
- But now, on the one hand, to keep ensuring `protoc`/`protobuf` compatibility we'd have to depend on `protobuf=*.n.*` - which to my knowledge is not possible to formulate as requirement
- And of course this raises the question of compatibility between our code and the `protobuf` library due to major version changes in `protobuf`.
- But how does one retain compatibility to a range of `protoc` versions while also specifying compatibility to `protobuf`?

What we came up with is to sort of hardcode a minor->major map in our `setup.py`, so the build works sort of like this

- Get `m.n.p` from `protoc`
- `m' = 3 if n < 21 else 4`
- Depend on `protobuf>=m'.n,<m'n+1`

But this means hardcoding these major version jumps.

Also when a major jump happens, let's say to 5.25.0 and we want to support the latest `protoc` 3.25.0 on development environments, we need to 1) check/hope that the major version is compatible with 5. and 2) add this to the hardcoded list because there will never be a 4.25.0 - right?

> The code generated by 4.21.x happens to be backwards compatible with 3.20.x and (I think) 3.19.x. The eventual criteria we are aiming for will not guarantee that code generated from a newer compiler supports an older runtime.

Would it be possible to include the compiler version as a comment in the generated code?
E.g. for python this could look like this:
```
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
# Generated by the protocol buffer compiler.  DO NOT EDIT!
# compiler: protoc 3.19.4
# requires: protobuf >= 3.19.4, == 3.* ; python_version < "2.7"
# source: some_file.proto
"""Generated protocol buffer code."""
```

While this won't help for "ancient" code, where the compatibility issues hurt the most, it could at least help future generations to put the puzzle pieces together.
We have work under way to add explicit compatibility checks to our various codegen targets.

maybe-uninitialized is not a perfect diagnostic, and you really shouldn't be using it in a warnings-are-errors situation.  This comes up from to time, for example here -> <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51093415/why-does-this-code-trigger-gccs-maybe-uninitialized-warning>

title: Expose container types in public API
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
We do have a library that automatically decodes some common protobuf types to native Python structures. E.g. `ScalarMap` is decoded to `dict`. The problem is that with arrival of `protobuf==4.*`, protobuf no longer creates instance of `google.protobuf.internal.containers.ScalarMap`, but instance of `google._upb._message.ScalarMapContainer` instead. I don't particularly like importing this class from something that looks like a private module that may break at any time. Also, I don't really understand why protobuf has two classes that are very similar, but one is not inherited from the other. It's confusing.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I'd like you to publish `MessageMap`, `RepeatedCompositeFieldContainer`, `RepeatedScalarFieldContainer`, `ScalarMap` as a public API that will only break in major versions. Of course, protobuf should create instances of these public classes so we can test them with `isinstance` call.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
I can conditionally import from private module. This may be quite fragile.

If you do have any other suggestion how I might recognize `ScalarMap` (and other types mentioned above) instead of testing them with `isinstance` and without the need to import from private module, I'd appreciate that.

nodes.body:
All of the internal implementation classes inherit from `MutableMapping`, for example: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9e0e7d5f59ecd2501ae638eeb1b65ccf361f008a/python/google/protobuf/internal/containers.py#L366

The public API for testing `isinstance()` would be `isinstance(container, MutableMapping)`.

Will that work for you?

Hi @haberman, thanks for the reply. I didn't get to this in a while. I'm afraid this works in Python protobuf `3.*`, but not in `4.*`. Example:

```proto
# proto/example.proto
message DictMessage
{
    map<string, string> values = 1;
}
message ListMessage
{
    repeated string values = 1;
}
```

```python
# test.py
from proto.example_pb2 import DictMessage, ListMessage

d = DictMessage()
print(type(d.values).__mro__)
# outputs: (<class 'google._upb._message.ScalarMapContainer'>, <class 'collections.abc.MutableMapping'>, <class 'collections.abc.Mapping'>, <class 'collections.abc.Collection'>, <class 'collections.abc.Sized'>, <class 'collections.abc.Iterable'>, <class 'collections.abc.Container'>, <class 'object'>)

l = ListMessage()
print(type(l.values).__mro__)
# outputs: (<class 'google._upb._message.RepeatedScalarContainer'>, <class 'object'>)
```
So, the solution works for `ScalarMapContainer` which is instance of `MutableMapping`, but not for `RepeatedScalarContainer`, which is not instance of `MutableSequence`.

We have unit tests that verify that our sequences are instances of `MutableSequence`: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/b9eb6bf759cf6edf449291215bd4ee2c572845d2/python/google/protobuf/internal/message_test.py#L706-L710

I tried your example and got similar results, however when I tried printing `isinstance(l.values, MutableSequence)` it returned true.

So perhaps this is not reflected in `__mro__` for some reason, but `isinstance()` is behaving as expected.

Ahh, that's interesting. `isinstance(l.values, MutableSequence)` returns `True` although `MutableSequence` is not listed in `mro`. Now I'm confused. Why does `MutableSequence` not show up in `mro`?

I actually do have gRPC decoder which needs to recognize these types and uses `mro` to discover decoding function for type that is closest to the type of object submitted to decoder. `isinstance` won't tell me anything about the distance. I guess I could make some kind of fallback for this, but it would be kind of ugly.

It looks like we call `MutableSequence.register(RepeatedScalarContainer)` instead of deriving from `MutableSequence`: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/blob/main/python/repeated.c#L807-L810

This is documented here: https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#module-collections.abc

title: Java generation: allow non-final generation for classes
body:
<!--

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?

Java.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I am trying to write unit tests for the generated classes, but because they are not final I can't mock it.
I have to use mock-maker-inlined, however, I do not want to have an extra overload and affect performance, I am keen to have not final classes (open/interfaces) to mock it properly.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
An option to disable "public final class"

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

**Additional context**

```
public  final class MyResponse extends
``` 
where final can not be mocked

nodes.body: Is there a particular end state or goal you're aiming for which you would need to mock the generated classes?

Protobufs should not ever be mocked. We have extensive experience with this at large scale internally at Google and can emphatically and definitively say this is not the right approach to testing that involves Protobuf messages.

If you want to write unit tests to assert the functionality of generated classes, test the actual code, not what your mocks say is the actual code. This gives you a false sense of security if/when we change things on you. Who would know to update the mocks?

100% disagree about mocking.  Please learn how mocks and pure white-box unit tests work.

Whatever you guys did wrong in learning that lesson, please look at it again.  The entire rest of the world, outside of google, in my experience, seems to get it.

Here is the key problem with that argument:

> test the actual code, not what your mocks say is the actual code.

We are NOT testing GRPC's generated code in those tests.  We ARE testing our own code, that uses GRPC.  Hence the mock.  That's a pure whitebox test.  We use pure black-box tests to validate third-party code.

@fowles was just reminded of this thread, so hope the late response is welcome.

On (1) you are right that we don't want to mock model objects (as long as they are clean model objects without any logic in them).  I did not intend to suggest that we want to mock model objects.  However, there is a lot of generated code with logic/functionality and using those - without mocking - requires sockets, so very bad for a pure unit test.  So I understand why you think I might have been conflating issues, but I don't believe that was the case.

On (2) you are right - my response saying "please learn" and more - was too much.  I apologize.  I lost my patience.  At the same time, there should be a response to the comments from @perezd.  Making such strong assertions that clearly indicate a lack of interest to work with the OP is stonewalling, and certainly does not show any consideration of the position of the users of the protobuf tools.

Lastly, would love to have an actual conversation on the merits of unit testing and mocks, and how protobuf (and perhaps other google projects) participate and enable good development practices for the users of those libraries / tools.

@artnaseef  I am genuinely confused.  Where do the sockets come into this?  I will admit to way more familiarity with C++ protobuf than Java protobuf, but I am pretty sure the generated objects don't have any dependency on sockets or any networking anything.  Can you point me towards what you are referring to?
Yup, that is definitely in the gRPC side of things.
OK, so the OP really needed to be pointed over there.  Simple mistake.  Too bad it wasn't caught earlier.

hi @rovo79 ,
did you solved your problem?
I have same issue when use the google analytic: "google/analytics-data": "^0.8.4" with Acquia hosting and still not find out way to fix it.
@flashvnn I have not found a solution. Ended up stepping back from google analytics as our solution.

I am having a similar issue with a PHP site using this library and have determined the source of the problem is the data passed to protobuf from `analytics-data/metadata/V1Beta/Data.php`. In short, during the build process this file gets altered so that some of the bytes get trimmed, which results in `protobuf/src/Google/Protobuf/Internal/CodedInputStream::pushLimit()` throwing an exception because this test fails:
`$byte_limit <= $this->current_limit - $current_position`

This might be something outside the scope of this library. @rovo79 do you know how your code gets pushed up to the cloud? It seems that this is actually being altered in GitLab before it gets to our cloud environment, so I am wondering if there is a similar cause for your case.

I think the point of protobuf is to generate the code on your server. 

I've abandoned pursuing google cloud data for my project.

I have been working with others on this problem and have found a work around - you can find my [Drupal specific solution here](https://www.drupal.org/project/google_analytics_reports/issues/3323218#comment-15002334). 

The summary is that this and other Google PHP packages have compiled PHP code in a file with a PHP file extension. Look at [this file for instance](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-php/blob/master/src/GPBMetadata/Google/Protobuf/Api.php#L21). The Special characters in text files can cause problems when committing te library with Git.

Not all users of PHP libraries deploy them directly, the platform I work with takes a composer.json file and , builds the code base for the website and commits it to a Git repository, then checks out that commit on the servers. Committing the files to Git is what causes the problem as we get this warning when adding the files to the repository
> warning: CRLF will be replaced by LF in vendor/google/analytics-data/metadata/V1Beta/Data.php.
This changing of the CRLF to LF characters in compiled code is what causes the problem, changing the file and making the file stop working as expected.

We ended up adding a vendor/google/.gitattributes file with
> vendor/google/** -text diff
to the build script to prevent Git from trying to change the file names.

Drupal specifically comes with a [.gitattributes file](https://git.drupalcode.org/project/drupal/-/blob/10.0.1/.gitattributes) listing PHP files as text
> *.php     text eol=lf whitespace=blank-at-eol,-blank-at-eof,-space-before-tab,tab-in-indent,tabwidth=2 diff=php linguist-language=php
unfortunately as there are several packages provided by Google which contain these *.php files with compiled code the solution was to tell Git in the .gitattributes file to treat all files provided by Google (in vendor/google) as non-text (binary).
In my case I removed vendor and node_module and then I reinstalled it.

Solution from @jiulongw doesn't work for me for the Drupal site. 
The platform I work with has `vendor` folder  in `.gitignore `list. Pipeline builds the composer packages and deploys to Acquia hosting.

> Solution from @jiulongw doesn't work for me for the Drupal site. The platform I work with has `vendor` folder in `.gitignore `list. Pipeline builds the composer packages and deploys to Acquia hosting.

I'm not sure who you are referring to in your edited comment. I do see in the emails generated on each edit of your comment that you mentioned @jrglasgow and I will state that the solution he stated is working for our site.

To better clarify his fix:
1. In your composer.json, you need to allow and configure the drupal/core-composer-scaffold plugin
2. In the composer's "scripts" entry you will need to have a "post-drupal-scaffold-cmd" entry and add this script to create the .gitattributes file:
`"echo '** -text diff' >> vendor/google/.gitattributes"`

As an example, your composer should have something like this:
```
  "scripts": {
      "post-drupal-scaffold-cmd": [
          "echo '** -text diff' >> vendor/google/.gitattributes"
      ]
  }
```
Thanks @wantell for sharing the detailed steps but looks like in my case i need to fix other dependent packages as well.
Should a simple .gitattributes file be added to https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf-php to fix this for all the people checking the vendor folder into their git repos?

FYI on pantheon all of these echo scripts append `*.php -text diff` to `vendor/google/.gitattributes` during each composer build making the .gitattributes file grow indefinitely within the artifact repository lol.

See #16572 for possible solution?

> I also have `open-telemetry/gen-otlp-protobuf` package as dependency which contains similar compiled PHP code. Adding `.gitattributes` file to both packages solves the problem for me.
> 
> ```
>     "scripts": {
>         "post-drupal-scaffold-cmd": [
>           "echo '*.php -text diff' >> vendor/google/.gitattributes",
>           "echo '*.php -text diff' >> vendor/open-telemetry/.gitattributes"
>         ]
>     }
> ```

Replace `>>` by `>` to avoid appending new lines during each build.

```
    "scripts": {
        "post-drupal-scaffold-cmd": [
          "echo '*.php -text diff' > vendor/google/.gitattributes",
          "echo '*.php -text diff' > vendor/open-telemetry/.gitattributes"
        ]
    }
```
