Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10 

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
.NET 7.0.102

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Clone https://github.com/daniel-eichinger-bl/protobuf-example (includes simple protobuf file with a message named `Descriptor`)

2. Run `dotnet build`

3. See error: `C:\dev\protobuf-example\obj\Debug\net7.0\proto\Example.cs(50,40): error CS0542: 'Descriptor': member names cannot be the same as their enclosing type [C:\dev\protobuf-example\protobuf-example.csproj]`

**What did you expect to see**
Build should succeed and the protoc compiler should handle this collision.

**What did you see instead?**
.NET error `CS0542` informing about name clash.

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

nodes.body: That's interesting - I'd *expect* this to already be handled by [the collision list](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f128ced675364ec4b57c4db776c4615fe5aeb1d6/src/google/protobuf/compiler/csharp/csharp_helpers.cc#L277). Will investigate.

Ah, no, that's for *fields* named `descriptor`. In this case we'd need to rename the class itself to `Descriptor_` or similar.
Shouldn't be *too* hard to do - although we'll probably need to be careful to avoid collisions between the class name provider and the property name provider...

Hmm. I've been looking at this again, and it's more complex than I'd anticipated, for a few reasons:

- We don't want to break backward compatibility. Therefore any class or enum name which already compiles shouldn't be changed.
- As an implementation matter, we generate the class name in two places: once in a fully-qualified way for referencing it, and once as just the simple-name to declare it. Ideally we don't want to put the logic in two places...
- Enums need some care as well, but possibly *only* if they're nested. You can't currently declare a nested enum called "Types", but you can declare a top-level enum called Types. Nested enums which conflict with inherited members (GetHashCode etc) currently generate a warning, but do compile... so although it would be nice to "escape" them, it would be a breaking change. Sigh.

I'm still working on it, but it'll take longer than expected.

Okay, proposed changes:

**Message types**

All of the names below must be "escaped" - by using a suffix of `__`. Note that just a single `_` would be insufficient, as that's added if there's a *field* with that name. (Imagine a `Descriptor` message with a `descriptor` field - we should generate `class Descriptor__` with a property called `Descriptor_`.)

- Types
- Descriptor
- Equals
- ToString
- GetHashCode
- WriteTo
- Clone
- CalculateSize
- MergeFrom
- OnConstruction
- Parser

Note that `Types` must be "escaped" even for a top-level message, in order to permit it to have nested messages/enums (which would be generated under `Types__.Types`)

**Enums**

Enum names can currently cause *warnings* when nested, but we won't try to fix those. The only change should be when an enum called `Types` is nested in a message, in which case it should be renamed to `Types__`.

**General**

The change needs to be applied to both the message/enum declaration *and* references to it (e.g. property types and in the reflection descriptor).

**Tests**

We should at least have test protos with:

- Top-level messages with all of the above names
- Nested messages with all of the above names
- Top-level enums with all of the above names
- A nested enum called `Types`
- *Possibly* nested enums with other names - with the downside that that will cause warnings

Version: v22.2
Language: C++

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

**What did you do?**
1. Build and install protobuf from source code, and install it into the prefix of gcc.
2. Write the following cmake project containing 3 files: `CMakeLists.txt`, `test.proto` and `main.cpp`. They are located in same dir.
  
```cmake
#CMakeLists.txt
find_package(protobuf REQUIRED)

protobuf_generate_cpp(pb_src pb_hdr test.proto)

add_library(test_pb_lib ${pb_hdr} ${pb_src})
target_include_directories(test_pb_lib INTERFACE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR})
target_link_libraries(test_pb_lib PUBLIC protobuf::libprotobuf)

add_executable(test_pb main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(test_pb PRIVATE test_pb_lib)
```

```protobuf
// test.proto
syntax = "proto3";

message test {
  int32 msg = 1;
}
```

```cpp
// main.cpp
#include <iostream>

#include <test.pb.h>

int main(int, char **) {

  ::test test_msg;

  std::cout << "Hello, world!\n";
}
```

```bash
cmake.EXE -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE:STRING=Debug -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER:FILEPATH=D:/ProgramFilesU/gcc-compilers/mingw-gcc12/bin/gcc.exe -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER:FILEPATH=D:/ProgramFilesU/gcc-compilers/mingw-gcc12/bin/g++.exe -SD:/Git/learnProtobuf -Bd:/Git/build-learnProtobuf-win -G Ninja
```
6. Build the project

```bash
cmake --build .
```

My code is compiled with no error.

You can pass `-DCMAKE_FIND_PACKAGE_PREFER_CONFIG` to cmake and it will use "Config" first.

Otherwise use the following so it's compatible with older versions of Protobuf too.
```
find_package(Protobuf CONFIG)
if(NOT Protobuf_FOUND)
  find_package(Protobuf REQUIRED)
endif()
```

```
if(NOT protobuf_PROTOC_EXE)

endif()

Got that, but given that gRPC's upgrade to protobuf 22.x has been dragging on for quite a while now and there are still several other issues to resolve with the upgrade, IMHO fixing this one warning would make our lives much easier.
gRPC actually enables the unused-parameter warning in quite a few builds and the draft PR to upgrade us to protobuf 22.x is already way too complex and makes many other necessary adjustment.

So if we fix this warning (seems trivial to fix) and backport it to 22.x branch, it would help us prevent bloating the upgrade PR even more and allow us to focus on real problems with the upgrade instead. WDYT?
We will accept a patch and cherry pix for this, but it can break again without any notice.

What do we mean by "fix" here? I think the fix the protobuf team wants is for this warning to be explicitly excluded in this file: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/port_def.inc. Would that work for grpc?

```

I think this is still too grpc-specific for us to help debug, especially with the custom server and bazel rules. Do you ever see the odr violation anywhere else? Can you point us to a proto rule that is making either of these files?

@jtattermusch can you help me understand what these virtual imports are needed for? I don't really understand why this is an issue on our side? Can you help me understand the need for all this? I am seeing this `protobuf.bzl` file is the grpc repo not ours.

Ok, I looked at the situation more in depths are here are my findings:

- One of the targets that ultimately ends up depending on two different copies of `wrappers.pb.cc` is `//src/proto/grpc/channelz:channelz_proto` (see https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/47ea5062cb0f5167ae7f36438750888aea63a9fe/src/proto/grpc/channelz/BUILD#L25)
- By analyzing the dependencies, I found out that it depends both on `@com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf:wkt_cc_proto` and  `@com_google_protobuf//:wrappers_proto`

AFAICT, the `@com_google_protobuf//:wrappers_proto` is necessary since without it, compilation fails with `src/proto/grpc/channelz/channelz.proto:29:1: Import "google/protobuf/wrappers.proto" was not found or had errors.`

Is seems that the @com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf:wkt_cc_proto dependency comes the dependency chain `@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf ->  @com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf:protobuf -> @com_google_protobuf//src/google/protobuf:wkt_cc_proto` and AFAICT there's nothing wrong with depending on `@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf` (I'd expect that exactly what one would depend on?)

The wkt_cc_proto target was added here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/10576/files
(and seems new in 22.x+)


Questions:
Is adding a dependency on `@com_google_protobuf//:wrappers_proto` the correct approach to allow a  `*_proto_library`  target to reference the wrapper WKT? (It worked for us until now and is done automatically by `grpc_proto_library` if the `well_known_protos = True`.

Should grpc_proto_library not depend on `@com_google_protobuf//:protobuf`? (and what should it depend on?) I think we're in fact not adding that dependency ourselves, but we're getting it through the native.cc_proto_library:
https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/451b2303588965f7110526e4ae57f88ca4abfce7/bazel/cc_grpc_library.bzl#L87

I see the issue, and the `wkt_cc_proto` target you link was our attempt to fix that in our repository. We added a `//src/google/protobuf:protobuf_nowkt` to use instead of `//:protobuf`. I'm confused why you are just seeing this issue now, given that the `.pb.cc` files for wkt were in that target before.

I think the easiest workaround is for you to use [proto_lang_toolchain](https://bazel.build/reference/be/protocol-buffer#proto_lang_toolchain) like we were using [before](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/10576/files#diff-7fc57714ef13c3325ce2a1130202edced92fcccc0c6db34a72f7b57f60d552a3L297). You can blacklist the wkt protos to stop the extra definition from being pulled in.

We are taking over these rules from bazel long term, so this is an issue we can hopefully look to resolve in the future.
Update: this was fixed in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/12419.

title: Generate mutable_foo() for numeric and enum fields
body:
### What language does this apply to?
C++ generated code for proto3

### Describe the problem you are trying to solve
Currently, filling or modifying a protobuf message requires writing quite a bit of boilerplate code that is difficult to abstract away because the generated API is inconsistent between field types.
For example, string fields provide `mutable_foo()` access that allows one to operate directly on the field, pass it to other functions to modify, etc. while the numeric/enum fields do not.

### Describe the solution you'd like
Generate a `T* mutable_foo()` function for numeric and enum fields similarly to string fields.

### Examples
**A trivial example: incrementing**
`message.set_my_int(message.my_int() + 1)`
becomes `++message.mutable_my_int()`

**Another trivial example: encoding the result of a C function that returns values by pointer**
```
int temp;
message.set_frac(frexp(arg, &temp));
message_set_exp(temp);
```
becomes `*message.mutable_frac() = frexp(arg, message.mutable_exp());`

**A real-world example:**
Many modern C++ libraries contain functions that either return or operate on tuples.
A use-case we have recently encountered is issuing a DB query that returns many columns, and sending it as a protobuf message to another component for further processing.
An ideal implementation would be to use `std::tie` to create a heterogenous tuple of references to the mutable fields in the message, and directly save the results into it.  This has the added advantage of failing to compile if the tuple size differs from the number of returned columns.
Whereas today we need to store the results in a temporary and copy them field-by-field into the message, which is inefficient, error prone (e.g., forgetting to copy a new field after the query changed, or getting the query and the message out of sync), tedious, and ugly; especially if you have dozens (or hundreds) of different queries to maintain. 

### Describe alternatives you've considered
Writing lots of ugly and error-prone boilerplate code.

### Additional context
The proposed change is non-breaking since all existing functionality will be preserved.

nodes.body:
> A use-case we have recently encountered is issuing a DB query that returns many columns, and sending it as a protobuf message to another component for further processing. ... especially if you have dozens (or hundreds) of different queries to maintain.

If you have hundreds of database queries putting their results in protobuf messages, then manually mapping the columns to protobuf fields is more boilerplate than I would be comfortable with. That's still true even if your request were accepted and you were using `std::tie`. Not that I have anything against your request as such; it just doesn't seem to be addressing your core problem.

Instead, I suggest that the column names in the query match the field names in the protobuf (you can rename the columns with `AS` in the SQL, if necessary). Then use protobuf reflection to put the right columns into the right fields. The code would be a bit fiddly, but you only need to write it once for all your queries. I suggest caching the mapping from column name/index to `FieldDescriptor` between rows (or even between runs of the query) because I've found doing the string matching repeatedly for every row is too slow.

In fact I did this in a rather more complex situaton where I was joining multiple tables together putting the rows into complex nested messages. (I put message types and field names into the SQL column names, like `MessageType0field_name`.) That was definitely simpler than writing that code out separately for each message type.

In my case, it would have been much better if I could have just put the messages directly in the database (e.g. in [JSON format columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-json.html)) but unfortunately I didn't control the database schema. Maybe that could also be an option for you, even if your tables are mapping directly to flat messages.

> Instead, I suggest that the column names in the query match the field names in the protobuf (you can rename the columns with AS in the SQL, if necessary).

Not always possible when multiple teams are working on a big project.
As well as reflection being a drag on performance.

This is not an API that we wish to add.  In fact we would prefer to wean ourselves off of  `mutable_` methods altogether.  Mutable methods force the exposure of types in a way that makes internal optimizations more difficult.

@fowles are you suggesting that setting values using `mutable_` methods is not the most efficient way? Can you provide an example of how it should be done? Even the main documentation uses `mutable_` to set string values.
`mutable_` methods prevent changing the underlying representation to more compact forms (for example storing fields in some kind of packed representation that is only materialized on demand).

title: Support WASM as a build target
body:
It'd be very useful if this codebase compiled to WASM:

* WASM is easier to distribute, sandbox, and execute than a binary, so this makes Python, C++, etc. code gen more accessible.
* It'd make `protoc` is easier to run in browsers (and possibly other environments too).

Currently, building WASM requires a variety of small patches, especially for the Bazel build definitions. We'd like to upstream our patches so that building WASM is part of this repository's CI.

From talking to @fowles, it sounds like this aligns well with Google's plans. My intention is to have the @bufbuild team link PRs back to this ticket so it's easy to identify them as part of this effort.

@fowles, does this sound right to you?

body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: protobuf==3.20.3
Language: Python 3.11

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Linux, reproduce is in docker image python:3.11 from https://hub.docker.com/_/python

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Python 3.11

**What did you do?**

Install protobuf 3.20.3 (latest package from 3.x branch) from PyPI in Python 3.11, observe that 'python' protobuf backend is used.

```
~$ sudo docker run -ti --rm python:3.11 /bin/bash

root@492034476e29:/# python3 -m pip install protobuf==3.20.3                                                                                                                                                      
Collecting protobuf==3.20.3

     ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 162.1/162.1 kB 1.9 MB/s eta 0:00:00

python
root@492034476e29:/# ls /usr/local/lib/python3.11/site-packages/google/protobuf/pyext/
__init__.py  __pycache__  cpp_message.py
```

**What did you expect to see**
'cpp' protobuf backend being used and C++ _message.cpython-311-x86_64-linux-gnu.so library to be present in google/protobuf/pyext.

**What did you see instead?**
'python' protobuf backend is used. This is observed as huge performance degradation from python 3.10 -> 3.11 upgrade (provided that protobuf package version is fixed to 3.x), that is not so easy to debug if you are not familiar with the protobuf internals. This issue is not present in protobuf 4.x branch.

I'm wondering whether it is intended or is a bug, and also want to document this behaviour for others to know, even if it is not going to be fixed. Of course, 3.x protobuf branch is now obsolete with the release of 4.x and upb backend, however, some users may have considerations to stick to 3.x branch.

**Note**
In python3.10 and below, 'cpp' backend is correctly used, and the shared library with Python/C++ extensions is present.
```

...
root@959cbd650c05:/# python3 -c "import google.protobuf.internal.api_implementation; print(google.protobuf.internal.api_implementation.Type())"
cpp

__init__.py  __pycache__  _message.cpython-310-x86_64-linux-gnu.so  cpp_message.py
..

nodes.body: It is a known issue but we can not change the released version's default backend.  We would ask users to use newest version instead of stick to 3.X

title: upb cmake libraries have names that conflict with absl libraries.
body:
cmake targets `base`, `hash` (and possibly some others) have the same name as targets from absl cmake build.
So if one includes both upb and absl in a single cmake project via `add_subdirectory`, you'll get the error listed below.

gRPC depends on both upb and absl, so if we were using upb's cmake build, we would run into this problem.
For now gRPC uses a custom build for upb (for team internal reasons), but we want to switch to using the official upb's CMakeLists.txt soon and this issue prevents it.

The error:
```
CMake Error at third_party/upb/cmake/CMakeLists.txt:96 (add_library):

  same name already exists.  The existing target is a static library created

  "/usr/local/google/home/jtattermusch/github/grpc/third_party/abseil-cpp/absl/base".
  See documentation for policy CMP0002 for more details.


CMake Error at third_party/upb/cmake/CMakeLists.txt:102 (target_link_libraries):

  the target "base".  All uses of target_link_libraries with a target must be
  either all-keyword or all-plain.

  The uses of the keyword signature are here:

   * third_party/abseil-cpp/CMake/AbseilHelpers.cmake:255 (target_link_libraries)



CMake Error at third_party/upb/cmake/CMakeLists.txt:299 (add_library):

  same name already exists.  The existing target is a static library created
  in source directory
  "/usr/local/google/home/jtattermusch/github/grpc/third_party/abseil-cpp/absl/hash".
  See documentation for policy CMP0002 for more details.


CMake Error at third_party/upb/cmake/CMakeLists.txt:304 (target_link_libraries):
  The keyword signature for target_link_libraries has already been used with
  the target "hash".  All uses of target_link_libraries with a target must be

   * third_party/abseil-cpp/CMake/AbseilHelpers.cmake:255 (target_link_libraries)

nodes.body: CC @haberman
CC @veblush this might be important for the followup after breakages in https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/34199#issuecomment-1698670932

> if we were using upb's cmake build

upb's current CMake build isn't really used by anybody right now. I agree we want to get to a point where gRPC would be using a upb CMake build, but to get there I think we should probably start from scratch. I don't think incremental evolution of the existing CMake files is the way to go, especially since they use a Bazel -> CMake translator that we need to re-evaluate.

It would help to get a set of requirements from gRPC about what parts of the library you use. I think we'd want to keep our set of exposed targets relatively small, rather than translate every cc_library() into a public CMake target like we do now.
Wait, what? The library names need to be globally unique? The full pathnames don't disambiguate them? How broken is that.

Oh this looks to be caused by how gRPC pulls in dependencies. gRPC has two ways of doing this; i) `add_subdirectory` and ii) `find_package`. `find_package` doesn't have this limit where two different libraries cannot have targets with the same name but `add_subdirectory` does.

- https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/-/issues/22687
- https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/29608

So gRPC may need to revisit this issue of dropping `add_subdirectory` option for its dependencies.

> Oh this looks to be caused by how gRPC pulls in dependencies. gRPC has two ways of doing this; i) `add_subdirectory` and ii) `find_package`. `find_package` doesn't have this limit where two different libraries cannot have targets with the same name but `add_subdirectory` does.
> 
> * https://gitlab.kitware.com/cmake/cmake/-/issues/22687
> * [gRPC Cmake dependency management using add_subdirectory grpc/grpc#29608](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/issues/29608)
> 
> So gRPC may need to revisit this issue of dropping `add_subdirectory` option for its dependencies.

So this make sense from some perspective, but generally CMake's `add_subdirectory` (or FetchContent, which under the hood does add_subdirectory anyway AFAIK) is quite a common way to add dependencies in the cmake world (especially if you are using a "developer" build, not a final installation by the end user), so using it doesn't really strike me as wrong.

Ad @ericsalo 's comment: yes, in a sense library names need to be globally unique (or it's a big advantage at least) - for example, look at library names in linux distributions, you can't have two libraries of the same name.  I think for upb's cmake build, this can be achieved by combination of two approaches:
- add a "upb_" prefix to all the libraries exposed by cmake (= the ones other projects are supposed to depend on) - this greatly reduces the chance that other projects will choose to name their libraries with the same name
- reduce the number for libraries exposed by upb's cmake (e.g. by amalgamating internal upb libraries into "public" targets and not exposing them in the CMakeLists.txt directly). Fundamentally, cmake is a different build system than bazel and it has different needs. While in bazel it makes a lot of sense to have a large number of very granular library targets with possibly complex dependency trees, in cmake you should only publicly expose libraries that are supposed to be visible public libraries in e.g. the linux/unix style - i.e. they need to be installable into e.g. /usr/lib, which requires them to have "globally" unique nam. Since such libraries are often packaged separately (dpkg, vcpkg etc)., there's high overhead on having many publicly exposed libraries.

When compiling I got a warning (which we treat as errors) that `PROTOBUF_RTTI` is used in port.h before it is defined:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f7a2f4acea7c981108f75210185ecdee8c13ea82/src/google/protobuf/port.h#L46-L56

From what I can tell, the `#include "google/protobuf/port_def.inc"` at line 56 defines `PROTOBUF_RTTI`, so the macro is undefined when used at line 46. Everything compiled fine if I moved lines 46-48 after line 56.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body: Thank you for the bug report, I think you are right that we're trying to access `PROTOBUF_RTTI` before it is defined. I will send out a change to fix this.

title: protobuf.pc pkgconfig file generated by protobuf's cmake build doesn't declare absl and utf8_range dependencies.
body:
Starting from 22.x, protobuf now depends on absl and utf8_range, but the protobuf.pc pkgconfig file doesn't properly declare those dependencies.
As a result, the build is broken if someone installs protobuf and then wants to include it via pkgconfig (since they'd be missing absl and utf8_validity symbols when trying to link).

See https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f11079b01f075bc7c5b3286d85a8feca798c09e9/cmake/protobuf.pc.cmake

This issue breaks grpc's build-and-install "distribtest" that tries to build helloworld example with grpc and protobuf:
https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/24d83cda9bb1caaff9c03ace6f418e946e88c49d/examples/cpp/helloworld/Makefile#L28
(which runs pkgconfig to get a list of libraries to link against when building a project that depends on grpc++ and protobuf).

title: C# - Resizing RepeatedField with RepeatedField<T>.Capacity does not allow this[index] = value set indexer
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.22.1
Language: C#

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a new .proto file containing a `repeated` field.
2. Generate the C# source for it
3. Create a new instance of that object
4. Call `.Capacity = 1` on the `RepeatedField` property
5. Call `this[0] = something` on the `RepeatedFieldProperty
6. See error: `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`

**What did you expect to see**
The set indexer should succeed

**What did you see instead?**
```
System.ArgumentOutOfRangeException: Specified argument was out of the range of valid values. (Parameter 'index')
   at Google.Protobuf.Collections.RepeatedField`1.set_Item(Int32 index, T value)
```

---

The set indexer checks for the `count` field in the `RepeatedField` class, not the capacity, I think this is a bug and not intentional.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f11079b01f075bc7c5b3286d85a8feca798c09e9/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/Collections/RepeatedField.cs#L624-L627

nodes.body:
> The set indexer checks for the count field in the RepeatedField class, not the capacity, I think this is a bug and not intentional.

No, it's absolutely intentional. It's the same as the `List<T>` indexer.

The capacity is effectively an implementation detail to allow users to avoid repeated re-allocation of the internal array. But it's *not* intended to affect whether an indexer operation succeeds or not.
You are correct actually.

body:
Recent release notes keep mentioning [Protobuf News](https://protobuf.dev/news/) as a source of important news. But how are we supposed to learn there are new news items? It seems it is just a bunch of bullets on a page.

In the HTML, Hugo is including alternate reference to an RSS feed, but [the feed has no entries](https://protobuf.dev/news/index.xml). Is that a bug? Or is there an alternate expected form of notification?

Without any way to receive news notifications, News is not a method of announcement. That's a real shame because it is clear effort is being put into them.

Right now they feel more like a notice "on display in the bottom of a locked filing cabinet stuck in a disused lavatory."
I swear that I've spent several hours trying to fix this! But your wonderful humor has inspired me to give it another go. Wish me luck!

The [default RSS template](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/master/tpl/tplimpl/embedded/templates/_default/rss.xml) finds the news items. But the [docsy RSS template](https://github.com/google/docsy/blob/main/layouts/_default/list.rss.xml) doesn't use `.Pages` or `.RegularPages` _when the parent of the section is Home_ and instead loops over the entire site's pages and filters by type: `where $.Site.RegularPages "Type" $.Section`. Unclear why it does that, but it seems it would generally be fine.

But that doesn't work because the news items all have `type = "docs"`. Which... seems strange. It really seems like there should be `news/chrony/` and `news/release/` sections, and add `date` to news items to sort them. Since no date is set, removing `type = "docs"` is not enough, because the pages are in a random order and thus you can't show "the 50 most recent news items."

Backfilling dates is annoying but simple. But I don't know whether y'all would prefer making a new RSS template that uses `.Pages` (least invasive approach) or removing `type = "docs"` (probably best long-term, but unclear why that was done originally).

Tarball should contain all necessary components. Git modules can't work from the tarball.

Version: 22.2
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
FreeBSD 13.1

nodes.body: Confirmed
Confirmed
IMO you should make a new release with the fix.

We purposefully don't put abseil files in our distribution tarball. Please download directly from https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp. This keeps our distribution tarball a reasonable size and also ensures files aren't duplicated if users were already using abseil.

@deannagarcia 
Why don't you/is there a way to use externally installed abseil-cpp?

Our README was updated to include the command you need to use externally installed abseil-cpp: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/cmake/README.md. Specifically, you'll need to add these flags: `-Dprotobuf_ABSL_PROVIDER=package` and  `-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/tmp/absl  # Path to where I installed Abseil`

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

**What did you expect to see**

**What did you see instead?**
When protoc is running on addressbook.proto you get the output: cpp_out: No such file or directory and off course building add_preson.cc fails because addressbook.pb.h is not available.

nodes.body: Thanks for looking into this! Would you be willing to send us a PR with this fix?

I believe the problem is actually the variable `protobuf_PROTOC_EXEC` not being set when running `add_custom_command`. Hence the command becomes `cpp_out` which is of course not recognized.

For what it is worth, I made it work for myself by
 - running cmake with the flag `protobuf_MODULE_COMPATIBLE` set, which ensures that `Protobuf_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE` contains the path to the protobuf compiler
 - in `protobuf-generate.cmake`, replacing the occurences of `protobuf_PROTOC_EXEC` by the variable mentioned above
This allowed me to compile the examples and my own projects.

I have not investigated further to understand why the protobuf compiler variable was not set, as I am not extremely competent on cmake. But I thought this might help someone.
This should be fixed in b30259722de17626b64fc46d3eae6af003858729.

Windows 10, 64-bit

- Installed protobuf from vcpkg as per [these instructions](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/README.md#c-protobuf---windows) (vcpkg install protobuf protobuf:x64-windows)
- Installed latest LLVM toolchain from their [releases](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/releases) (LLVM-16.0.1-win64.exe)
- Installed Visual Studio 2022 (cl.exe version is 19.35.32215)

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Save [this proto structure](https://protobuf.dev/getting-started/cpptutorial/#protocol-format) as addressbook.proto
2. Run `C:\vcpkg\packages\protobuf_x64-windows\tools\protobuf\protoc.exe --cpp_out=. addressbook.proto`
3. Save [this code](https://protobuf.dev/getting-started/cpptutorial/#writing-a-message) as writer.cpp
4. Run `C:\Program Files\LLVM\bin\clang-cl.exe /std:c++20 '/IC:\vcpkg\packages\protobuf_x64-windows\include' -EHsc .\writer.cpp /MD /link '/LIBPATH:C:\vcpkg\packages\protobuf_x64-windows\lib'`

**What did you expect to see**
Successful compilation

**What did you see instead?**
A compiler error in the `protoc`-generated C++ code using `offsetof` in a `constexpr` statement. The MSVC-provided `offsetof` macro uses `reinterpret_cast`.

```
In file included from .\writer.cpp:4:

      'kRepHeaderSize' must be initialized by a constant expression
  static constexpr size_t kRepHeaderSize = offsetof(Rep, elements);
                          ^                ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
C:\vcpkg\packages\protobuf_x64-windows\include\google/protobuf/repeated_ptr_field.h(645,44): note: cast that performs
      the conversions of a reinterpret_cast is not allowed in a constant expression
  static constexpr size_t kRepHeaderSize = offsetof(Rep, elements);
                                           ^
C:\Program Files (x86)\Windows Kits\10\Include\10.0.19041.0\ucrt\stddef.h(47,32): note: expanded from macro 'offsetof'
        #define offsetof(s,m) ((::size_t)&reinterpret_cast<char const volatile&>((((s*)0)->m)))
```

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body:
That standard library used does not follow the requirements for `offsetof`. It is required that it evaluates to an integer constant expression.
How old is this standard library? You might want to upgrade to a newer one.

title: Missing release assets in 22.3?
body:
The [v22.3 release](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v22.3) does not include many of the archives included in previous releases (22.12 release has 26 assets, while 22.3 has just 12 assets).

Is this deliberate, or an oversight?

nodes.body: This is deliberate, and all v22.x releases have the same number of assets. We announced [here](https://protobuf.dev/news/2022-08-03/#lang-specific-distros) that starting with 22.0 we will no longer publish language specific distributions, just a single tar/zip file for the whole repository.

Protobuf has not yet tested or advertised compatibility with Bazel 6. So it is not too surprising that there could be incompatibilities with Bazel 6.

@haberman Sorry, to give a bit of context, we are from the Bazel team. Since protobuf is a pretty important dependency, we maintain a build for protobuf on Bazel CI, the CI config is [here](https://github.com/bazelbuild/continuous-integration/blob/master/pipelines/protobuf.yml), and the pipeline is https://buildkite.com/bazel/protobuf/builds/4515. > Are you saying that https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/5d3d9aa372de7a83f3916d8336c75d8a8653255e is the commit that broke Bazel 6 compatibility?

No, that commit is basically the last green protobuf commit on Bazel CI, the breaking commit should happen between (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/5d3d9aa372de7a83f3916d8336c75d8a8653255e, https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/e56cf5d8d41ca339d94c8941141a9fcfcae1743b ]

@haberman BTW, what would be the minimal targets you would recommend we should specify in [protobuf.yml](https://github.com/bazelbuild/continuous-integration/blob/master/pipelines/protobuf.yml) to verify the basic functionalities of protobuf?

The references to Bazel 4 seem unrelated. We have compatibility tests that exercise Bazel 4, but these are not causing the problem. The problem is just that we aren't compatible with Bazel 6 yet.

body:

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

WSL2-Ubuntu 22.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

clang: clang-16.0.0
Python: 3.9.0 (this should be irrelevant though)

**What did you do?**

`bazel build @com_google_protobuf//python:all`


**What did you expect to see**

Everything is built properly without error.

**What did you see instead?**
```text
 %  bazel build @com_google_protobuf//python:all
ERROR: /home/zhongmingqu/.cache/bazel/_bazel_zhongmingqu/33d097c4393d1ec801bb3e6d74ed212d/external/com_google_protobuf/python/BUILD.bazel:191:20: in internal_copy_files_impl rule @com_google_protobuf//python:copied_test_messages_proto2_files:

        File "/home/zhongmingqu/.cache/bazel/_bazel_zhongmingqu/33d097c4393d1ec801bb3e6d74ed212d/external/com_google_protobuf/python/internal.bzl", line 11, column 17, in _internal_copy_files_impl
                fail("Source does not start with %s: %s" %
Error in fail: Source does not start with src/: ../com_google_protobuf/src/google/protobuf/test_messages_proto2.proto
```

**Other information that might be relevant**

bazel version: 7.0.0-pre.20230405.2

This error could be avoided by checking `ctx.workspace_name`, which would be non-empty if protobuf is built as an external bazel repository.

I did an initial triage like the following:

```diff
 % git diff
     for src in ctx.files.srcs:
-        if src.short_path[:len(strip_prefix)] != strip_prefix:
-            fail("Source does not start with %s: %s" %
-                 (strip_prefix, src.short_path))
-        dest = ctx.actions.declare_file(src.short_path[len(strip_prefix):])

title: FieldMask JSON serialization improvement proposal
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->

**What language does this apply to?**
This feature request concerns FieldMask JSON serialization.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
We are using FieldMasks as described in [https://google.aip.dev/161](https://google.aip.dev/161). We understand that the semantics described in AIP are slightly different than the original semantics described in the [field_mask.proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/983dac24c34f07a278d45fdfd30348775d95d12a/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto#L43). Some differences were discussed in https://github.com/aip-dev/google.aip.dev/issues/673 and https://github.com/aip-dev/google.aip.dev/issues/1013.

The differences in semantics are not ideal, but also not a deal-breaker since each implementation can decide on the specifics or give config options.

The wall that we hit is with [https://google.aip.dev/161#map-fields](https://google.aip.dev/161#map-fields) in REST JSON services. The current protobuf FieldMask JSON serialization tries to `camelCase` all fields in the mask and fails if uppercase letter is encountered, for example:
* [FieldMaskUtil.java](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/983dac24c34f07a278d45fdfd30348775d95d12a/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/FieldMaskUtil.java#L176)
* [field_mask.py](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/983dac24c34f07a278d45fdfd30348775d95d12a/python/google/protobuf/internal/field_mask.py#L41)

This means that it's not possible to implement [https://google.aip.dev/161#map-fields](https://google.aip.dev/161#map-fields) that extends `FieldMask` semantics to traverse into map keys. For map keys that contain an uppercase letters or special characters, we get an exception during JSON serialization of `google.protobuf.FieldMask`.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
The mentioned AIP suggests a solution:
> Field masks should support string keys that contain characters that are problematic for the field mask syntax, using the backtick character.

We could extend JSON ser/de of FieldMasks to enable backtick quotation. For quoted fields, we wouldn't attempt camelCase/snake_case conversion. I found [one implementation that implements this](https://pkg.go.dev/go.chromium.org/luci/common/proto/mask).

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Workarounds that we considered are:
* use binary serialization
* since we don't use protobuf field mask utils, we don't need to use `google.protobuf.FieldMask` but a custom similar message

**Additional context**
If you agree with the approach, I can start by sending a PR that adds a recommended conformance test which asks JSON ser/de of FieldMask not to fail on quoted fields with special characters.

nodes.body: Hmm... will give this some thought tomorrow (UK time). My main concern will be compatibility. Definitely happy to see a conformance test to start with, as a good way of documenting the proposed changes.

Thanks, I'll look carefully through the PR. It's likely that I'll need to write an internal proposal doc for changes and evaluate the impact... basically this could take quite a while, I'm afraid. But hopefully we'll get there.

This bit surprises me though:

> In the process of doing so I observed that map keys containing a . character are a problem for binary serialization as well. A reader can't unambiguously read "map_field.anton.grbin".

Could you clarify exactly what you mean by this? Binary serialization of a FieldMask should just be "normal protobuf binary serialization" - there's no special-casing here; a FieldMask just contains a list of strings, which should be serialized and deserialized (in binary) just like any other list of strings. How that's *interpreted* is a different matter.

Right - but that doesn't indicate "a problem for binary serialization" to me - it indicates a concern around the *semantics* of field masks.

Fundamentally, if I can serialize the FieldMask and deserialize it again, and get the same value that I started with, then the *serialization* part works. And that's what I'd expect to always be the case for binary serialization, because there's no custom code.

If the concern is "FieldMask semantics for map fields need work" then I'm completely on-board.
Got it! I agree that there is nothing wrong with the binary serialization of FieldMasks!

Starting to write a doc on this now. Please could you clarify this statement:

> The current protobuf FieldMask JSON serialization tries to camelCase all fields in the mask and fails if uppercase letter is encountered, for example

Does serialization throw an exception, or does it produce an inappropriate result?

I looked into 3 implementations:
* Python, serialization raises an exception if uppercase letter is encountered [code pointer](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/983dac24c34f07a278d45fdfd30348775d95d12a/python/google/protobuf/internal/field_mask.py#L148)
* C++, serialization returns false (gives up) if uppercase is encountered [code pointer](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/983dac24c34f07a278d45fdfd30348775d95d12a/src/google/protobuf/util/field_mask_util.cc#L77)
* Java, serialization produces inappropriate result - [tested here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/12566/files)

Hope this helps!
Definitely, thanks. I strongly suspect this is going to be annoying in all kinds of ways, but we'll see what we can do...

Just as a heads-up after a while, I'm coming back to FieldMask stuff at the moment. There's a lot to do, and I'm trying to put together a plan for what's required before executing on any of it. This will take quite a while, I'm afraid - but hopefully we'll get to a better place in the end.

Thank you for the heads up and thank you for working on this!

For transparency, I can share how my team mitigated the problem in the meantime. We went with the minimal change over https://google.aip.dev/161#map-fields where we add a constraint that map keys must **always** be quoted with backticks. We implemented FieldMask ser/de (for now only in Kotlin) which doesn't transform between snake and camel for quoted path elements.

Having said this, I would be interested to learn early if your plan ends up diverging from https://google.aip.dev/161#map-fields significantly. For example there might be an alternative where we use `[]` syntax to access map keys.

I'm using VS2022 17.4.4 and it gets the same compile error. lines 102, 145 and 159
as a workaround I changed -align to (-(long long)align) for my x64 build

My work-around is to add "bookends" around any protobuf includes:

#pragma warning(push)
#pragma warning( disable : 4146 )

... include any protobuf headers ... 

#pragma warning(pop)

We have a few pragmas before and after protbuf includes (e.g.: #undef min, #undef max, #undef new).

One of my collogues just added include files so that we can bracket our protobuf includs with:

#include "BeforeProtosIncludes.h"
... include any protobuf headers ...
#include "AfterProtosIncludes"

There is probably a way to tell the protobuf compiler inject the code automagically, but I'm not enough of a protobuf ninja to make it happen (or know if it is really possible).

Since I think there are a few people out there using MSVC++ I submitted the issue since I think it would be easy to change the sources to eliminate the error.

you can send a patch to [port_def.inc](https://cs.github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9bbea4aa65bdaf5fc6c2583e045c07ff37ffb0e7/src/google/protobuf/port_def.inc?q=port_def.inc+repo%3Aprotocolbuffers%2Fprotobuf#L1033-L1046)

To expand on that a bit, this is a warning not an error.  You *could* just ignore it, but we will accept changes to this list of disabled warnings: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/port_def.inc#L1035
I think this was fixed with https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/12697 which has been cherry picked to 23.x and 22.x and will be released shortly.

title: Make `AbstractMessage` public in Ruby
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
> If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3?
> If it's about generated code change, what programming language?

Ruby

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

[In this change](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/10281) the `AbstractMessage` parent class was added for Ruby code. The motivation was to be a pure performance win, exploiting how classes and objects are laid out in the Ruby code.

But as it happens, having a common base class that has all these methods defined is particularly convenient. When using an optional static type checker in a Ruby project, it's very easy if you can write `Google::Protobuf::AbstractMessage` in a type signature, and know that it has [all these methods](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/message.c#L1396-L1421). For example, using Sorbet, it would be possible to write a signature like

```ruby
sig do
  params(
    proto_class: T.class_of(Google::Protobuf::AbstractMessage),
    bytes: String
  )
  .returns(Google::Protobuf::AbstractMessage)
end
def decode_and_log(proto_class, bytes)
  puts("Decoding with class: #{proto_class.descriptor.name}")
  proto_class.decode(bytes)
end
```

Right now it's annoying to write signatures for these methods, because methods like `descriptor` and `decode` aren't actually defined on the only other common type in the inheritance hierarchy, `MessageExts::ClassMethods`:

```
[dev] main:0> Google::Protobuf::MessageExts::ClassMethods.instance_methods
=> []
```

So there's not a convenient type you can write—but there would be if `AbstractMessage` were not a private constant.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Can we remove `private_constant :AbstractMessage`?

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/5233990ad79b4dc4a484bbb3fafaa7c8a715dfac/ruby/lib/google/protobuf/message_exts.rb#L56

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

An alternative would be to actually define the methods on `MessageExts::ClassMethods`.

In the Sorbet type system this is slightly less ergonomic to use, `MessageExts` and `MessageExts::ClassMethods` look like completely orthogonal modules to the type system. (For example, it doesn't know that `MessageExts::ClassMethods` has all the methods that a normal class would have, like `.name` or `.ancestors`.) That means you have to go around writing things like `T.all(Google::Protobuf::MessageExts, Class)` which is confusing.

It's a lot easier to just mention the exact superclass you want in your type annotation, which in this case is `AbstractMessage`.

**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.

nodes.body:
@haberman thanks for the quick response, really appreciate it!

> If we followed the common expectation of base classes, then once AbstractMessage is a public base class, people could start sending us PRs to add any number of convenient methods to it.

Seems feasible to make it clear where the line is drawn on contributions there, both with a comment in the code and with code review.

> But this is asking for conflicts, because the generated class will have accessors for every field defined in the `.proto` file.

Doesn’t this problem exist regardless of whether you define methods like decode and descriptor on AbstractMessage or you pretend they’re only accessible on each concrete message class?

The PR that came before this already introduced AbstractMessage. If someone defines a proto message with fields whose names collide with names already used by AbstractMessage, they _will_ override them, regardless of whether AbstractMessage is public or private.

Also, correct me if I'm wrong, but this only applies to instance methods, right? I'm not sure that `optional int32 to_json` (or any other name) will ever collide with singleton class methods on `AbstractMessage`. So maybe in your example you meant to use something like `optional int32 to_s` or `optional int32 dup`.

In the case of having field names collide with method names, there's even **more** reason to want to expose `AbstractMessage`:

```ruby
bad_for_ruby = # ... create BadForRuby message
Google::Protobuf::AbstractMessage.instance_method(:to_s).bind(bad_for_ruby).call
```

This `.bind(...).call` pattern allows calling the **real** `to_s` method directly, avoiding problematic overrides. This pattern is used all over the place in Ruby code that has to be defensive against people overriding built-in functionality (for example, in a gem I maintain, we have [a whole module full](https://github.com/sorbet/sorbet/blob/master/gems/sorbet/lib/real_stdlib.rb#L4) of this pattern).

So my argument is:

- the colliding names problem is not made worse by making `AbstractMessage` public
- in fact, it's actually made better, because it empowers people to work around it as they see fit

I wish there was a way of writing this more like:

```ruby
sig do
  params(
    proto_class: Google::Protobuf::MessageClass,
    bytes: String
  )
  .returns(T.instance_of)
end
def decode_and_log(proto_class, bytes)
  puts("Decoding with class: #{proto_class.descriptor.name}")
  proto_class.decode(bytes)
end
```

It's really the singleton methods you are interested in here, which are like instance methods on the class. The fact that the proto has a base class isn't interesting or important, except in what it says about what singleton methods are available.

On the other hand, I notice that `Struct.new()` in Ruby returns classes that have `Struct` as a base class, which is a pretty close match for what we are doing here. So maybe a public base class makes sense.

> I'm not sure that optional int32 to_json (or any other name) will ever collide with singleton class methods on AbstractMessage.

I think `to_json` and `to_proto` are defined on `AbstractMessage`, as non-singleton methods https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/ruby/lib/google/protobuf/message_exts.rb#L43-L49

Tested here: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/ruby/tests/basic.rb#L110

> I think to_json and to_proto are defined on AbstractMessage, as non-singleton methods

ah thanks, I had only checked the C defined methods 

> Google::Protobuf::MessageClass

is this a class that already exists? If not, could you say more about how you thought this would be defined?

also, in your example what does T.instance_of mean?

Again, I’m pretty sure that the relevant Sorbet machinery exists to write a sig, as long as the methods are defined on some class or module that already exists.  

If the singleton class methods were defined on Google::Protobuf::MessageExts::ClassMethods, that would good, but AbstractMessage would still be better.

Basically: any solution that involves defining the methods that are common to all messages on a common ancestor of all messages is what unblocks better types. That could be a parent class, or a module, but it has to be some class/module that actually is visible at runtime and actually has the methods defined on it.

Writing the type annotations is easier and involves less boilerplate when it’s a class like AbstractMessage, but if the instance methods were on MessageExts and the singleton class methods on MessageExts::ClassMethods, sorbet would be able to write types for that too (again, this approach would just add verbosity to users, but at least this is tolerable).

> It's really the singleton methods you are interested in here, which are like instance methods on the class.

So I’m also interested in the instance methods, to a lesser degree. We have 120 MB of proto-generated Ruby code in our codebase, which adds about 120 + 120*4 MB to the memory used when parsing and type checking. If these methods were defined on a parent class, we could define them once and not have to make seemingly-identical definitions for all the instance and singleton class methods. This would cut down on the size of generated files, making type checking faster and use less memory.

Sorry for not bringing up this point in the original post, as I only realized it yesterday afternoon.

> Basically: any solution that involves defining the methods that are common to all messages on a common ancestor of all messages is what unblocks better types.

Right, and my concern is that I don't want messages to have common methods. As much as possible, I want message instances to have accessors for the fields defined in a `.proto` file, and nothing more.

We do have common methods on message *classes* (ie. class-level methods). That's why I would favor a solution that can somehow represent that protobuf classes have common class-level methods, but not object methods.

`MessageClass` doesn't exist currently. I was thinking that if a class derived from `T`, then `T.instance_of` would be an instance of that class.

> Right, and my concern is that I don't want messages to have common methods.

... but there already are common methods, right?

If a message defines a field named `hash` or `to_s` or `to_proto`, those common methods will already be shadowed by the corresponding message field. So if you did

```ruby
my_message.hash
```

you would be calling the accessor for the proto field named `hash`, not calling the hash function defined by the `Message_hash` C function in this gem.

**But** if `AbstractMessage` were public, anyone who is already aware of this pre-existing problem with methods getting shadowed would instead be able to write

```ruby
Google::Protobuf::AbstractMessage.instance_method(:hash).bind_call(my_message)
```

which lets the user forcibly call the real `Message_hash` function. So making `AbstractMessage` public is a way to let the shadowed methods be called even though they have already been shadowed.

The gem as written today, where `AbstractMessage` is private, does not actually prevent people from making the mistake that calling `to_h` or `hash` or `to_json` on a message class might actually access a proto field with those names. Another example: the following code is already valid—the Ruby runtime will not prevent the call to `to_h` simply because `to_h` is defined on the parent class, and the parent class is private
```ruby
def count_fields(message)
  as_hash.to_h.size
  #       ^^^ expected to call `to_h` in parent, but might actually access a field
end
```

The user will only find out that it misbehaves the first time they happen to import a proto file with an uncommon name—whether `AbstractMessage` is public or private doesn't actually change this problem.

> We do have common methods on message classes (ie. class-level methods). That's why I would favor a solution that can somehow represent that protobuf classes have common class-level methods, but not object methods.

Given what I've said above, I'm confused how to satisfy these criteria. The way I read this request suggests that you're nearly asking for the changes in #10281 to be reverted, which started to define common instance methods on all messages via a superclass. I am not suggesting that we add more common methods to all messages, but merely that the existing parent class be made public.

> MessageClass doesn't exist currently. I was thinking that if a class derived from T, then T.instance_of would be an instance of that class.

Without getting into a full discussion of how most type systems for Ruby work (including Sorbet's type system), suffice it to say that as long as some constant like `SomeClass` exists, you can write `T.class_of(SomeClass)[T.type_parameter(:U)]` to represent "any singleton class which is equal to or a subclass of `SomeClass`", and then use `T.type_parameter(:U)` to represent "whatever an instance of that class is."

So the feature you're describing already exists, although it has different syntax from the syntax you propose.

But that syntax requires that `SomeClass` be a public class, otherwise you can't write the class's name in a type annotation.

It sounds like this bug was caused by a Bazel commit (https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/commit/4853dfd02ac7440a04caada830b7b61b6081bdfe). How do we know that the bug is in upb, and not in Bazel itself?

We use proto_common, and I believe that we propagate linking contexts as we are supposed to: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/blob/b399576ccdb97ed37afc045327852b298e32eff3/bazel/upb_proto_library.bzl#L110-L169

I think that we are propagating CcInfo as we are supposed to also. If we did not do that, this would fail at the compile step, not the link.
@keith Can you give some advice here since you fixed similar breakages mentioned in https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/commit/4853dfd02ac7440a04caada830b7b61b6081bdfe#commitcomment-96449986
the fix has been here for a while https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/pull/1180

Sorry for not reviewing https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/pull/1180 sooner.

The fix in that PR does not seem right to me. The proposed fix would have us change the upb project from:

```bazel
    (linking_context, linking_outputs) = cc_common.create_linking_context_from_compilation_outputs(
        actions = ctx.actions,
        name = name,
        feature_configuration = feature_configuration,
        cc_toolchain = toolchain,
        compilation_outputs = compilation_outputs,
        linking_contexts = linking_contexts,
        disallow_dynamic_library = cc_common.is_enabled(
            feature_configuration = feature_configuration,
            feature_name = "targets_windows"
        ),
        **blaze_only_args
    )
```

to:

```bazel
    (linking_context, linking_outputs) = cc_common.create_linking_context_from_compilation_outputs(
        actions = ctx.actions,
        name = name,
        feature_configuration = feature_configuration,
        cc_toolchain = toolchain,
        compilation_outputs = compilation_outputs,
        linking_contexts = linking_contexts,
        disallow_dynamic_library = cc_common.is_enabled(
            feature_configuration = feature_configuration,
            feature_name = "targets_windows"
        ) or not cc_common.is_enabled(
            feature_configuration = feature_configuration,
            feature_name = "supports_dynamic_linker"
        ),
        **blaze_only_args
    )
```

It seems like the fix should go in `create_linking_context_from_compilation_outputs()` instead. We are already passing the `feature_configuration` parameter, so the function could perform this logic internally instead of making every project copy and paste this code.

It seems like we should be able to remove even the existing value of `disallow_dynamic_library`. This logic isn't specific to upb.
Yea maybe someone from the bazel side can comment on that but in general that is true when you're using the cc_library etc rules directly, but when using this underlying API that's not the case.

@meteorcloudy can you comment?

Given that `supports_dynamic_linker` is a [well-known feature](https://bazel.build/docs/cc-toolchain-config-reference#wellknown-features), it seems like cc_common should handle checking it.
/cc @oquenchil is our C++ expert who should answer this.

I can't remember which internal target was the reason for me needing to do this https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/commit/00b57b17adcf9a76bd92d4ed0fd948bb6392d0b0 but I do remember something breaking.

I also can't remember which combination of features was failing for that target. It could be that I didn't think of checking for `supports_dynamic_linker`. It seems that the original condition also created the dynamic library as long as win_def_file was passed.

You can send a PR to Bazel changing `create_linking_context_from_compilation_outputs` and in the worst case it will be rolled back.

title: [Protoc - Java] Is there a way to override hashCode() and equals() methods for a proto message?
body:
Hello,

we were using protobuf-java library version 2.3.0 at our enterprise software,
until recently several security vulnerabilities were found in this version and we have to upgrade it at some point.

Protoc compiler version 2.3.0 didn't generate _hashCode()_ and _equals()_ methods,
so we inserted the corresponding custom code explicitly into generated Java files using the _protoc_insertion_point_.

A newer version of protoc (e.g. 3.16.3) generates the implementation of _hashCode()_ and _equals()_ by default.
And I have not found a way how to control it.
E.g. disable completely in order to insert my own code or somehow mark the fields at a proto file to generate _hashCode()_ and _equals()_ methods with custom set of the fields by protoc).

Is there a way to control/override this?

body:

For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 3.22.3
Language: Ruby

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Arch Linux; Debian 10/11

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Ruby 3.x

**What did you do?**

`a.sh`:

```sh
v=ruby:2.7.8-slim-bullseye
v=ruby:3.0.0-slim-buster
v=ruby:3.2.2-slim-bullseye
docker run --rm -it "$v" sh -euc '
    mkdir app
    cd app
    cat > Gemfile <<EOF
        source "https://rubygems.org"
        gem "anycable", "1.3.0"
        gem "google-protobuf", "3.22.3"
EOF
    cat > a.rb <<EOF
        require "anycable/protos/rpc_pb"
        m = AnyCable::ConnectionRequest.new(env: {"headers" => {"A" => "a"}})
        encoded = AnyCable::ConnectionRequest.encode m
        p encoded
        decoded = AnyCable::ConnectionRequest.decode encoded
        p decoded
        p decoded.env.headers
        decoded.env.headers.delete("A")
        puts "done"
EOF

'
```

```
$ sh -eu a.sh
...
"\x1A\b\x12\x06\n\x01A\x12\x01a"
<AnyCable::ConnectionRequest: env: <AnyCable::Env: url: "", headers: {"A"=>"a"}, cstate: {}, istate: {}>>
{"A"=>"a"}
a.rb: failed to allocate memory (NoMemoryError)
```

The issue manifests itself at least on Ruby 3.0.0..3.2.2. Without `-it` it somehow succeeds. I believe it can be reproduced not only in a `docker` container.

**UPD** Actually not only after decoding, this fails too:

```
m = AnyCable::ConnectionRequest.new(env: {"headers" => {"A" => "a"}})
m.env.headers.delete("A")
```

The [protobuf][a] [files][b].

**What did you expect to see**
No error and the program finishes correctly.

**What did you see instead?**
The error and the program terminated.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
Affects `google-protobuf-3.22.0..3.23.2` (but not under any conditions, i.e. under some conditions it might work).

[a]: https://github.com/anycable/anycable/blob/v1.3.0/protos/rpc.proto

nodes.body:
I'm still investigating, and I have a more standalone case:

```sh
v=ruby:3.2.2-slim-bullseye
docker run --rm -it "$v" sh -euc '
    apt-get update
    apt-get install -y protobuf-compiler
    mkdir app
    cd app
    cat > Gemfile <<EOF
        source "https://rubygems.org"
        gem "google-protobuf", "3.22.3"
EOF
    cat > a.proto <<EOF
        syntax = "proto3";
        message MyMessage {
            map<string,string> my_map = 1;
        }
EOF
    mkdir out
    protoc a.proto --ruby_out out
    cat > a.rb <<EOF
        require "./out/a_pb"
        m = MyMessage.new(my_map: {"a" => "b"})
        m.my_map.delete("a")
        puts "done"
EOF
    bundle
    bundle exec ruby a.rb
'
```

Decided not to change what's already triaged.

With `python` expectedly it works:

```sh
v=python:3.11.3-slim-bullseye
docker run --rm -it "$v" sh -euc '
    apt-get update
    # apt-get install -y protobuf-compiler
    cat > a.proto <<EOF
        syntax = "proto3";
        message MyMessage {
            map<string,string> my_map = 1;
        }
EOF
    pip install protoc-exe
    protoc a.proto --python_out .
    pip install protobuf
    cat > a.py <<EOF
import a_pb2
m = a_pb2.MyMessage(my_map={"a": "b"})
del m.my_map["a"]
print("done")
EOF
    python a.py
'
```

Incredible repro, thanks for that.

I can confirm that the repro triggers `NoMemoryError`.

> Incredible repro, thanks for that.

@haberman I just like filing bug reports :D

Long story short, you broke it in 3.22.0 when you were doing the 4-step change (adding the value parameter to `upb_Map_Delete()`).

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/commit/3f173c4b810dd36c1ed24f4ffc82c1b2fb3eb60c \
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/b598b2dd1f00510dd7ebf0a075d55ef38c895172 \
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/commit/0c6b72dbf891eafc91050ad60733ea3022fac2b3 \
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/b7d54ace5ea769a86da03cb65d3f97aa0580f71c

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/482156c0f96dd670b9f1ba4f946e66edeb04535f/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/ruby-upb.c#L507-L512

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/482156c0f96dd670b9f1ba4f946e66edeb04535f/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/map.c#L464-L473

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/482156c0f96dd670b9f1ba4f946e66edeb04535f/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/ruby-upb.h#L994-L996

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/482156c0f96dd670b9f1ba4f946e66edeb04535f/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/ruby-upb.h#L474-L486

In `upb_Map_Delete()` you change only the first 8 bytes of `upb_MessageValue`. Particularly, when `self->value_type_info` is `kUpb_CType_String`, `upb_MessageValue` contains `upb_StringView`:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/482156c0f96dd670b9f1ba4f946e66edeb04535f/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/ruby-upb.h#L422-L425

Which means `size` is left uninitialized (usually a very big number), and when it tries to convert it to a `VALUE`, it fails (I don't have so much RAM!!!:)):

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/482156c0f96dd670b9f1ba4f946e66edeb04535f/ruby/ext/google/protobuf_c/convert.c#L266-L270

Affects only `ruby`.
This was fixed in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/pull/1341 and the fix will be released this week.

title: Expose `transitive_pb_h` option or comparable to not generate `dependency.pb.h` includes
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
proto3 generating C++

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
We are using protoc to generate `pb.cc` and `pb.h` files for our messages we transfer through a custom protocol via wire. 
Due to some missing features in terms of customizing the generated C++ code (e.g. pre compiled header or custom headers) we are doing the following: 

* We let protoc generate the files to a "temp" directory. 
* We have custom C++ Header and Source files where we respectively import the Headers and sources from protoc after our custom includes and defines. 

This now causes some weird conflits in our case when we have protobufs across library boundaries due to declspecs and include orders being twisted.  

**Describe the solution you'd like**
We would like to disable that if you `include "proto1.proto"` in a `proto2.h` that there is a `#include "proto1.pb.h` in the `proto1.h`. We want to fully take care of correct includes (order and relative paths) ourselves. 

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
We are trying to currently get things at least compiling by adding the individual include paths, add everywhere manually the right includes. 

**Additional context**
There is already an option `transitive_pb_h` in the C++ generation code which decides on whether include statements of dependencies are generated. But there is no way to specfiy this option from outside within the proto file or via command line. 

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f6c7fdf88cdba6a8c7e2215f72578b0b50d2c4ca/src/google/protobuf/compiler/cpp/file.cc#L340-L342

nodes.body: Unfortunately we can't currently prioritize this work in the short/medium term but it is an idea we have thought about and could potentially work on longer term.

Hi fowles, thanks for your reply and I took a close look at Kythe which is a language-agnostic protocols and data formats describing source code as well as a series of tools/utilities. 

However, we don't have a monolithic giant code repository like Google and we just built and packaged Java sources generated from protobuf, then released into a repository for downstream data applications in various of teams and repositories some of which we even don't know or have access. 

In other words, source code relationship/dependency is loose in our case and I'm trying to find possible ways to collect ```getXxx``` field usage at **runtime** given the common jar in repository is fully controlled by us, the maintainer of the ```Log```.

If you want to do *dynamic* collection of data (which it sounds like you do), I don't really have good answers.  I would look into using existing java dynamic code coverage tooling and try to reverse the mangling `protoc` uses.

insertion points expose too many internal details and are extremely fragile, so we do not wish to add them to other languages.  You may be able to do something equivalent using bytecode weaving.  But we don't have any plans to add a feature like this to java protobuf.

title: Generating a getter for an optional float field
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
PHP

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

In the Google Ads API PHP client library, the generator creates a getter for optional float field by providing an initial value when the value is `null` like this:

```php
public function getBidModifier()
{
    return isset($this->bid_modifier) ? $this->bid_modifier : 0.0;
}
```

Ref: https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-php/blob/main/src/Google/Ads/GoogleAds/V13/Resources/CampaignCriterion.php#L314

This looks convenient to some users, but for Ads users, we need to distinguish between unset value and set value.
I know we can use a [hasser](https://github.com/googleads/google-ads-php/blob/main/src/Google/Ads/GoogleAds/V13/Resources/CampaignCriterion.php#L319) to check the availability of the value first, but does setting initial value (e.g., `0.0`) benefit any users in general?

With the current style, Ads user cannot pass around the value right away without calling a hasser, which is more verbose.

nodes.body: Setting initial values should help unless you have many nested messages to deal with
In Google Ads API, it actually doesn't help because we need to distinguish between `null` and the real `0` like I mentioned.

title: CMake issues when linking against Protobuf v22.3 with Abseil dependency
body:
Hello!

I encountered issues when using Protobuf v22.3 with CMake due to its Abseil dependency. I have documented the steps I took and the issues I faced below.

I built and installed Protobuf v22.3 from source with the following commands:

```
$ cmake -Dprotobuf_BUILD_TESTS=OFF -DABSL_PROPAGATE_CXX_STD=ON -Dprotobuf_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=/usr/local ..
$ cmake --build . -j 10
$ sudo cmake --install .
```

Then, in my project's CMakeLists.txt, I added:

`find_package(Protobuf REQUIRED)`

and linked the Protobuf libraries to my target:

`target_link_libraries(${TARGET_NAME} PRIVATE protobuf::libprotobuf protobuf::libprotoc)`

However, when building my project, I faced multiple unresolved symbols related to `utf8-range` and `Abseil`. To resolve these issues, I tried the following:

1. Manually `find_package(utf8_range)` and added `utf8_range::utf8_validity utf8_range::utf8_range` to my target (resolving some errors).
2. Manually added `find_package(absl)` and  and linked multiple `absl::*` targets (the [same ones as in the cmake protobuf build script](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/482156c0f96dd670b9f1ba4f946e66edeb04535f/cmake/abseil-cpp.cmake#L46-L81)), but still had missing symbols
3. Built Protobuf as a static library and linked against it, but still faced unresolved symbols related to Abseil.

Eventually, I reverted to Protobuf v3.21.12, which has no Abseil dependency while still supporting CMake. With this version, I could build and run my project without any issues using `find_package(Protobuf REQUIRED)`, `target_link_libraries` as before and nothing else.

I believe there should be a more straightforward way to handle the Abseil dependencies when using Protobuf v22.3 with CMake. Also, I still don't understand why a static build of protobuf would require additional imports. Any guidance or improvements in this area would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you!

This should be getting generated in both the binary directory (during a build with `EXPORT(TARGETS`), and in the install directory (through `INSTALL(EXPORT`). Generally you do something like `sudo apt install protobuf-dev` and it will install headers, pkg-config files, an the cmake files.

That's how it *should* be, but Linux distros don't ship `protobuf-config.cmake`[^1], so `find_package(Protobuf CONFIG REQUIRED)` is a CMake error when building against system libs.

This Works For Me™:
- Keep using the CMake module. Backwards-compatible and avoids having to port to `protobuf_generate`.
- On Protobuf >=22, ask `pkg-config` for the version found by CMake and link that to get `abseil` & friends.

```cmake
# No changes here, keep using CMake module + protobuf_generate_*
find_package(Protobuf REQUIRED)
protobuf_generate_cpp(PROTO_SRCS PROTO_HDRS foo.proto bar.proto)

...

# Make it link with recent Protobuf
string(REGEX REPLACE "^[0-9]+\.([0-9]+\.[0-9]+)$" "\\1.0" proto_libver "${Protobuf_VERSION}")
if(proto_libver VERSION_GREATER_EQUAL "22")
    find_package(PkgConfig REQUIRED)
    pkg_check_modules(protobuf REQUIRED IMPORTED_TARGET protobuf=${proto_libver})
    target_link_libraries(myapp PRIVATE PkgConfig::protobuf)
else()
    target_link_libraries(myapp PRIVATE protobuf::libprotobuf)
endif()
```

The regex converts the Protobuf version from the headers (e.g., `4.24.1`) to the library version (e.g., `24.1.0`, [context](https://protobuf.dev/news/2022-05-06/#versioning)).[^2] Linking against the imported targets ensures header/defs/libs consistency, even if CMake and `pkg-config` somehow manage to find different installations. Make sure to not also use `${Protobuf_INCLUDE_DIRS}`/`${Protobuf_LIBRARIES}` to avoid possible issues.

[^1]: Arch is the only exception I found.
[^2]: This doesn't build with pre-releases of Protobuf since their library versions don't end in `.0`.

title: Automatic-Module-Name entry missing since release 3.21.12
body:
**Issue**
Any newer release of protobuf-java after 3.21.12 is missing the Automatic-Module-Name entry in the META-INF/MANIFEST.MF file. This prevents using the protobuf module with a stable name instead. Instead, we are forced to the bad practice of using a filename-inferred module name.

Please restore the Automatic-Module-Name entry in the manifest or (alternatively) provide a proper module-info.class in the library.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Versions containing the issue are 3.22.0, 3.22.1, 3.22.2, 3.22.3 and 3.23.0-RC2
Last version to be correct: 3.21.12
Language: Java

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Irrelevant as issue pertains to the Java Platform Module System.

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Java 17

**What did you do?**
1. Add "requires transitive com.google.protobuf;" to the module-info.java of a project using protobuf-java.
2. Find compilation error due to "com.google.protobuf" cannot be resolved to a module.
3. Find that the protobuf manifest contains no Automatic-Module-Name  since version 3.21.12

**What did you expect to see**
I expected an Automatic-Module-Name entry in META-INF/MANIFEST.MF. This was last seen in version 3.21.12.

**What did you see instead?**
I found no Automatic-Module-Name entry in META-INF/MANIFEST.MF.

**Note**
I reported this before in #12175, which was closed because it was suggested the fix for #12017 would also restore the Automatic-Module-Name entry. However with #12017 fixed the OSGi entries are restored but the Automatic-Module-Name entry is still missing from the manifest.

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/d580fde63aa8ea5c6f4619396e68aaf017fc9d61#diff-580cdf6ec10b074d78ecc4a185c2f5ca053ae488c7ec41cd957f6dab0d9cf9e8 should have been released in 26.x which should add back `Automatic-Module-Name` to manifest.

Please reopen if this is still not working with 26.x+. Note that 26.x was a breaking release for Java, so we may backport this back to 25.x.

Another issue should be filed to track request to add add `module-info.java`, though I'm not sure we have capacity to do this right now and our support is for Java 8+ per https://cloud.google.com/java/docs/supported-java-versions

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

2. Try to extract the enum value options

No segfault

Segfault

```
syntax = "proto3";

```

TEST_F(UserTest, Experiment1) {

// Successful

        val = userid::UserId_descriptor()->value(user)->options().GetExtension(userid::custom_val);
    }
