nodes.body: It looks like the protobuf version you're using is pretty old and is no longer supported. Can you upgrade to the newest version (23.2) and see if you still see the issue?

I ran into the same issue trying to upgrade to 23.x and here's my diagnosis:

MSVC cl.exe has a limitation (https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/clexe-compiler-driver-cannot-handle-long-file-path/975889) on filename lengths of 260 characters (MAX_PATH). There appears to be no workaround using UNC paths.

Within Protobuf there are a number of source files organized like this:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/BUILD.bazel

with rules like (abbreviated):

```
cc_library(
    name = "objectivec",
    srcs = [ ... ],
    hdrs = [
        ...
        "text_format_decode_data.h",
    ],
    include_prefix = "google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec",
)
```

When bazel encounters rules like this it constructs include paths to provide the  `include_prefix` mapping similar to this:

`<bazel_output_base>/<hash>/execroot/<root workspace>/bazel-out/x64_windows-<config>/bin/external/com_google_protobuf/src/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/_virtual_includes/objectivec/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/text_format_decode_data.h`

Counting the hash, using `fastbuild` for the config, but not counting `<bazel_outout_base>` & `<root workspace>`, this filename is already at 215 characters. 

That leaves a maximum of 40 characters for the other parts.

It's pretty easy to run out of that. The default output base for my username is >30 characters.

One option to fix this is to reorganize the src/google/protobuf/compiler files to remove the nesting.

One workaround which I am using now is to set a bazel startup option to gain that 30 characters back: `--output_base=C:\O`, but that's probably not a great long-term solution.

See related bazel issues:

https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/15961
https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/4149
https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/18683

I tried to rename my dependency from `com_google_protobuf` to `protobuf`. There are two things which encumber that.

1. The built-in repository `@bazel_tools` references `@com_google_protobuf://protoc`. There does not appear to be a way to override the `repo_mapping` for this repository to make it reference something else. There is a repository https://github.com/bazelbuild/rules_proto which maybe bazel is using to externalize proto rules, but it doesn't seem very active. I'm not sure of the state of that.

2. grpc binds 'protobuf' already. This may not be the place to lament the style of the grpc bazel rules, but their extensive use of bind complicates my attempt to get a hermetic environment where my repository controls all the dependencies and does not allow dependencies to load third-party repositories.

So it turns out that it's a bit challenging to save characters simply by renaming the repository.
@meteorcloudy could you recommend the best solution for us?

Using a shorter output base / output user root is the only direct workaround I can think of as recommended at https://bazel.build/configure/windows#long-path-issues

@oquenchil Is it possible to create the `virtual_includes` dir under some path that the length is `O(1)` instead of `O(package path length)`?
CC @jskeet, would it be an option to not use `include_prefix` in the C# BUILD files at all?

@hlopko: I'm afraid I'm really not the person to ask about this - my understanding of both C++ and Bazel is pretty low. I have no objection to it being changed, but it's not something I'd have confidence either doing or reviewing.
I guess we can at least try and see if it breaks any tests? ;)

> @oquenchil Is it possible to create the virtual_includes dir under some path that the length is O(1) instead of O(package path length)?

I don't think so. 
- Assuming source code cannot be changed the directory structure must be as listed on the include directive
- The symlink must be in a folder belonging to the package of the target creating the symlink

That doesn't leave out anything that can be shortened using a hash like we do for shared libraries on Windows.

I can't think of anything except what's already been mentioned: not using `include_prefix` or shorter output base.

> The symlink must be in **a folder** belonging to the package of the target creating the symlink

This is currently also a package path right? Can we replace it with a hash? 

Essentially 
```
<bazel_output_base>/<hash>/execroot/<root workspace>/bazel-out/x64_windows-<config>/bin/external/com_google_protobuf/src/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/_virtual_includes/objectivec/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/text_format_decode_data.h
```
becomes
```
<bazel_output_base>/<hash>/execroot/<root workspace>/bazel-out/x64_windows-<config>/bin/_virtual_includes/<hash of package path>/objectivec/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/text_format_decode_data.h
```

I think that this would require a bazel change; basically bazel would need to be able to hand out such a directory with a shorter prefix. I don't know what that would entail.

I filed a feature request for that: https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/18683

It was recategorized to c++ rules, which may not be a great category.

Looking around, it seems that the reason to have all the 73 instances if include_prefix in the repo is easier compatibility with the Google internal clone of this repository. One solution here would be to fix header include paths in all C++ sources so we don't need include_prefix at all.

> `<bazel_output_base>/<hash>/execroot/<root workspace>/bazel-out/x64_windows-<config>/bin/external/com_google_protobuf/src/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/_virtual_includes/objectivec/google/protobuf/compiler/objectivec/text_format_decode_data.h`
> 
> Counting the hash, using `fastbuild` for the config, but not counting `<bazel_outout_base>` & `<root workspace>`, this filename is already at 215 characters.
> 
> That leaves a maximum of 40 characters for the other parts.
> 
> It's pretty easy to run out of that. The default output base for my username is >30 characters.
> 
> One option to fix this is to reorganize the src/google/protobuf/compiler files to remove the nesting.
> 
> One workaround which I am using now is to set a bazel startup option to gain that 30 characters back: `--output_base=C:\O`, but that's probably not a great long-term solution.
> 
> See related bazel issues:
> 
> [bazelbuild/bazel#15961](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/15961) [bazelbuild/bazel#4149](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/4149) [bazelbuild/bazel#18683](https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/18683)

title: Add built-in proto files that support HTTPAPI
body: **What language does this apply to?** Proto3、C#/NET7 **Describe the problem you are trying to solve.** In NET7, the GRPC server can support both GRPC and `JSON Web API` requests based on `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger` packets But it is necessary to ``` import "google/api/annotations.proto"; import "http.proto"; ``` in each proto file These two files are not built-in, which makes it very troublesome to connect them in the development environment **Describe the solution you'd like** Build the aforementioned proto files into the protobuf project, just like `google/protobuf/descriptor.proto` **Additional context** [annotations.proto](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/src/Grpc/JsonTranscoding/test/testassets/Sandbox/google/api/annotations.proto) [http.proto](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/8b601c3a73ba66de4e6ca35530b5d32a48c76c5b/src/Grpc/JsonTranscoding/test/testassets/Sandbox/google/api/http.proto) https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-cn/aspnet/core/grpc/json-transcoding?view=aspnetcore-7.0

nodes.body: No, these are fundamentally not part of protobuf. Microsoft may well be able to add to the gRPC tooling to make the API-oriented protos easier to consume, but they really don't belong in this project I'm afraid.

What I mean is to embed two proto files into the protobuf project
According to the [google.api](https://cloud.google.com/service-infrastructure/docs/service-management/reference/rpc/google.api#http) document
The above two files are required during the implementation of `gRPC/REST` mapping process

But those are protos that simply don't belong in the protobuf project. Protobuf and gRPC are entirely distinct - indeed, even gRPC doesn't fundamentally depend on protobuf, even though it's by far the most common payload type.

title: No way to disable protoc builds for java, csharp etc when using CMake
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
C++/CMake subproject

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I build protobuf as a submodule. I only use C/C++ in my project, so I don't need all the java and csharp protoc bits compiling.
It is apparently possible to disable these with bazel, but I use protobuf via CMake and I won't be switching build systems anytime soon. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add flags to disable compilation of certain languages. 

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Suffer the compile time penalty. 

**Additional context**
This has been tried before at:
- #1448 
- #1446

nodes.body:
You can try these definitions:
```
protobuf_BUILD_LIBPROTOC=OFF
protobuf_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF
protobuf_BUILD_PROTOC_BINARIES=OFF
```
Is that fine to do if the dev happens to have a different protobuf version than the one we build?

In both bazel and CMake it is impossible to only compile the protoc compiler for a single language, because all the compilers are registered [in the same file](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/compiler/main.cc).

In the future we could look to add flags to disable that, but unfortunately that won't be highly prioritized by the team because:
1. Our protoc compile times aren't too long (If your compile times are really long, let me know)
2. We provide a compiled binary in our [releases](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases/tag/v23.2) so compilation isn't strictly necessary.

title: java util's json printer always quotes 64 bit integers
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 23.2 or main
Language: Java

**What did you do?**

I noticed that uint64s in protobufs were serialized as quoted numbers when using `JsonFormat.printer().print(MessageOrBuilder)`.

For example,

**What did you expect to see**

```json
{ "unit64" : 12345 }
```

**What did you see instead?**

```json
{ "unit64" : "12345" }
```

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/java/util/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/util/JsonFormat.java#L1228

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body: Fixed by https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/12993.

That behavior matches the [JSON mapping](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/#json). JSON numbers are often [parsed as doubles](https://stackoverflow.com/a/39681707/3574093) and limited to `2^53`, so `int64/uint64` could overflow / lose precision.

![image](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/assets/5491587/8e16fdcf-29b7-41a0-b099-1e050437bf29)
That's fine. I'm not changing that behavior. I'm making it an option to make 64 bit ints not quoted. That is how the protobuf 2 version of this worked.

```
This starts to eat into `ARG_MAX`, and makes it very difficult to read my build output log, because almost all of it is repeated compiler options.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

I think the problem is that Protobuf depends on over 30 separate Abseil sub-libraries, each of which has a separate pkg-config file which specifies a copy of the repeated options. pkg-config [hasn't been able to remove duplicate options for 10 years](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/pkg-config/pkg-config/-/commit/9adfd9ebfcb8a9656999116307c15061364bf7df), and doesn't seem to be designed to work with 30 different libraries all of which have identical options.

The right place to fix this might really be in Abseil and how it explains its large number of substantially identical libraries to pkg-config.

title: SemVers broken on protobuf-config.cmake
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 23.3
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Ubuntu 22.04

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Shipped gcc-11

[This Article](https://protobuf.dev/support/version-support/) tells, that protobuf is using [SemVer](https://semver.org/).
This versioning defines which kind of changes are reflected to the version. An breaking API change will always bump major version.

As far as I understood is the major version coupled with the language, which allows API changes in that language to take place without impact to other languages. In case of `protobuf-config.cmake` - which ships with the cmake-install - this major version is not visible. Moreover, the minor-version became the major and the patch became the minor. The original major is missing at all.

**Consequences:**

- Every call like `find_package(protobuf 4.99.2)` will succeed. Since the `protobuf-config.cmake` reports `23.3.0`.
- If I tied `find_package` to search for all within `3.21.0...3.99.3` cmake complains that `23.3.0` is not within range.

```
find_package(protobuf 3.21.0...3.99.3 REQUIRED CONFIG)
```
```
[cmake]   Could not find a configuration file for package "protobuf" that is
[cmake]   compatible with requested version range "3.21.0...3.99.3".
[cmake] 
[cmake]   The following configuration files were considered but not accepted:
[cmake] 
[cmake]     /usr/local/lib/cmake/protobuf/protobuf-config.cmake, version: 23.3.0
```

Since protobuf > 3.21. brings some changes in cmake scripts it is mandatory to check for an installation with at least that version **or higher** which is not possible so far.

**Expectation:**

If protobuf 3.23.3 is installed, I expect `protobuf-config.cmake` to report version `3.23.3`, not `23.3.0`

nodes.body:
There's a bit of an ambiguity here because our cmake configs are for *both* protoc and the C++ runtime.  Right now we're setup to use the protoc versioning scheme, in which *every* release is a potentially breaking change (you should always regenerate your proto files for the runtime version you're on).  If we switched to the C++ runtime version numbers, it would then imply that protoc version bumps are safe even when they're not (notably if you're using protoc to generate code for a non-C++ language that had a major version bump).

We could potentially ship *two* cmake packages with different versioning semantics, but that's a major breaking change to all our users.  Could you just check for `>= 21.0`?  We do guarantee that our minor version numbers are strictly increasing (to match the fact that they're protoc major version numbers)

I understand your point regarding protoc. But as an library user, protoc is shipped with the library, so it is tight coupled. The issue an library user faces is not protoc to lib. It is user code to lib.
My code must be api compatible with the protobuf lib. For this protobuf claims to use SemVers.
And as I wrote before:
The issue is, that __you report the minor version as a major version__ doing this __violates SemVers__ and __lead CMake to reject V22.x if >V21.x is requested.__
this has nothing to do with your internal tooling. By the way, the config script is complaining about miss match in the versioning to protoc (regarding same versioning transformation) but this will be another issue,

I'm not talking about anything internal here.  If someone uses cmake to generate code for non-C++ languages via protoc, the version of the C++ runtime would be completely incorrect.  I think the root problem is that:
1) we ship both protoc and the C++ runtime under the same cmake package
2) protoc and the C++ runtime have different version schemes
3) there is an additional constraint on any project using runtime version x.y.z that they also be using generating code with protoc version `y.*`

I think the proper solution here is to ship multiple cmake packages, one for protoc and one for each runtime.  We could then declare 3) as a `find_package` constraint.  But like I said, this seems like it would be a major breaking change for all cmake users.  We might want to consider bundling this in with our upcoming cmake cleanup though (@coryan FYI)

@martijnvels I looked into my failure a little more and it seems that ASAN is specifically complaining about overrunning the source pointer in the `memcpy` (aka `pold`) when copying from old to new inside `GrowNoAnnotate`. Specifically https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/215154eb2c1b92c1eb55fb4cc08e0e0a20b13385/src/google/protobuf/repeated_field.h#L975

~That caused me to look closer at the sanitizer annotations, and I see something that looks suspicious - see https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/215154eb2c1b92c1eb55fb4cc08e0e0a20b13385/src/google/protobuf/repeated_field.h#L1000 :~

~The 2nd call to `AnnotateSize` doesn't seem right to me - `GrowNoAnnotate` has just allocated new memory and so `current_size` is the _old_ current size, but is passed into the `new_size` parameter of `AnnotateSize`. It looks to me that this would cause the sanitizer to think the usable portion of the array is smaller than it actually is, which would explain why later it complains when trying to read the source pointer in the `memcpy`.~

~Apologies if I'm wasting your time here, as I'm not terribly familiar with how these explicit sanitizer annotations work.~

Actually - sorry I did in fact misunderstand how the annotations work, so nevermind that, but hopefully pointing toward the problem being with the source array is helpful.

Following up on my issue - I was able to catch it in a debugger and the annotations provided for the `elements()` of the `RepeatedField` are clearly wrong. It seems like some of the annotations calls are being skipped, and the debugger agrees with me as setting breakpoints on the annotations calls shows that they are not always called as expected.

After looking at our build process, it seems that our `asan` build config was only building our application with `-fsanitize=address`, and not building `libproto` with it. Adjusting this to also build `libproto` with the sanitizer made the problem go away for me. I then found https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/AddressSanitizerContainerOverflow#false-positives which pretty much says the same thing.

I wonder if this is what others are running into as well?

That's an excellent point, and can well explain discrepancies. 

@phallot, can you verify if this applies? If the library is not build with the same sanitizer (and other) flags, then you will experience likely a mix of inlined code with sanitizer hitting out of line code without, etc.

title: Blank name when toString() on Java enum with value = 0
body:
When applying `toString()` to a Java object generated by _protoc_, the enum names are replaced by blank if the value defined in the .proto file is zero.

In the [sample code](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7745) it's the case for the name `RED`.

It's annoying because when avoiding zero value we get the message
> First enum value must be 0 in proto3

_Originally posted by @ThomasCollignon in https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/7745#issuecomment-1602121988_

nodes.body: The problem also happens with `int32` when the variable value is zero (whatever the name value in the .proto file).
This is the expected behavior for proto3.  Proto3 values have a zero default and when explicitly set to zero are omitted in serialized representations.

title: Add option to generate lightweight Model inner class (or constant static field map) for swagger
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**Java, and maybe others**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3? **add an option** of code generation
If it's about generated code change, what programming language? **Java**

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Recently I've been working with GRPC backend servers and the flutter front end.
The front sends rest requests to the backend, while the backend servers communicate with protobuf between them.
When implementing a swagger for the front developers, I see using the protobuf generated Java class as schema in leads to unresponsive swagger whenever I try to see the definition of a given API (probably too many definitions with all the parents classes)

For example: 
@PostMapping("/edit")
public String edit(@RequestBody @Schema(implementation = **ProtoMessage**.class) String json)

With maven dependency 
springdoc-openapi-ui 1.6.1
And spring-boot 2.7.0
The generated swagger will become unresponsive when I click on the API /edit

**Describe the solution you'd like**
I would like that when protobuf is generating classes, it can generate a lightweight Model inner class, or a lightweight json model static field (for languages like python)
So when trying to use it on swagger, I can simply do as below

@PostMapping("/edit")
public String edit(@RequestBody @Schema(implementation = ProtoMessage.**Model**.class) String json)

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
What I've been using, is to automatically copy the generated *OrBuilder.java files, and do some regex so it becomes *Model.java files, which contains only the necessary getter of the real fields for given class, then use them in code

For example 
@PostMapping("/edit")
public String edit(@RequestBody @Schema(implementation = **ProtoMessageModel**.class) String json)

**Additional context**
I can work on adding the feature if someone is willing to guide me

nodes.body:
My actual process of generation in pom.xml (using Maven) 

            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-antrun-plugin</artifactId>
                <executions>
                    <execution>
                        <phase>generate-sources</phase>
                        <goals>
                            <goal>run</goal>
                        </goals>
                        <id>java</id>
                        <configuration>
                            <target name="Generate Java Models for Swagger">
                                <copy todir="${basedir}/src/generated/java/example/model">
                                    <fileset dir="${basedir}/src/generated/java/example/proto">
                                        <include name="**/*OrBuilder.java"/>
                                    </fileset>
                                    <globmapper from="*OrBuilder.java" to="*Model.java"/>
                                    <filterchain>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="example\.proto" replace="example.model"/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern=".*get.*OrBuilder\(\)\;" replace=""/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="OrBuilder extends" replace="Model"/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="com.google.protobuf.MessageOrBuilder" replace=""/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="Message " replace="MessageModel "/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="Message\>" replace="MessageModel>"/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern=".*OrBuilder.*" replace=""/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="      int index\)\;" replace=""/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern=".*ByteString.*" replace=""/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern=".*get.*Bytes\(.*" replace=""/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="int.*get.*Value\(.*" replace=""/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="Generated by the protocol buffer compiler." replace="Generated by the protocol buffer compiler. Modified by antrun plugin."/>
                                        <replaceregex pattern="example\.model\.ExempleEnum" replace="example.proto.ExempleEnum"/>
                                    </filterchain>
                                </copy>
                            </target>
                        </configuration>
                    </execution>
                </executions>
            </plugin>

I don't think this is something we would have the bandwidth to guide you through or even a desire to accept were it offered in the short term.

My suggestion is to refactor your `.proto` files a bit to not use nested messages.  Then you can have client and server views for the same files some of which do not have fields as needed.

Keeping the fields in sync is slightly awkward at the moment, but we have plans to release a tool called Prototiller to help with this in the future.

nodes.body:
Judging by the bazel rule it looks like there are still supposed to be included. Im not very familiar with bazel but if I had to guess, I think the issue may have been introduced from either:
* The switch from `java_export` to `protobuf_java_export`
* The switch from `//:built_in_runtime_protos` to `//src/google/protobuf:descriptor_proto_srcs`

### Before 22.0
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/f0dc78d7e6e331b8c6bb2d5283e06aa26883ca7c/java/core/BUILD.bazel#L189-L199

### After
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d97c8ed86025a855058b20ed484b59a69284d1c6/java/core/BUILD.bazel#L228-L238

I may be able to contribute a fix for this if I'm able to get some guidance on what needs to be looked at and how I can package the jars so I can debug. Just looking for any way I can be of assistance here since this is blocking roll out of an upgrade to multiple applications and automation systems.

So what likely changed here is the adoption of these bazel rules for our release process. I believe we had previously used Maven for these source jars prior to 22.x.

Based on https://bazel.build/reference/be/java#java_library and https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/8457, it seems `resources` (which is where the missing well known types and `descriptor.proto` are included) has *never* been included in the outputted source jars and these bazel targets actually work as intended. This seems to be true for 21.x as well.

Can you help us understand your use-case for these protos, and if/why this currently causes problems for your systems? Arguably, these protos probably shouldn't have been included in our source jars in the first place and they can still be accessed instead via the non-source jars. Would this work for your use case?

Note that for the above changes:
* the switch from `java_export` to `protobuf_java_export` was trivial and simply wrapped `java_export` to set flags to support java8
* the switch from `//:built_in_runtime_protos` to `//src/google/protobuf:descriptor_proto_srcs` shouldn't affect this either

> they can still be accessed instead via the non-source jars. Would this work for your use case?

I didn't realize that was the case. It should work for our purposes. There may have been something IDE specifc (intellisense / inspection realted) that caused us to originally rely on the sources jar. Not sure if this would affect other users that have the same dependency. 

I did notice the compiler protos are missing. Would there be another jar that contains the compiler protos or was the intention to completely omit them? We have and edge case with some tooling that depends on referencing the types in those protos.

For context, in some scenarios we use jars for proto publication, distribution and consumption since they are natively handled by the [protobuf gradle plugin](https://github.com/google/protobuf-gradle-plugin).

By compiler protos do you mean `google/protobuf/compiler/plugin.proto`? This change seems to stem from the switch from `//:built_in_runtime_protos` to `//src/google/protobuf:descriptor_proto_srcs` which no longer includes this proto.

Is the tooling you mentioned that depends on referencing these the protobuf gradle plugin as well, or is that something separate?

body:

Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create the following file in path `net/example/v1/example.proto`:
```proto
syntax = "proto3";

message Sample {
  string net = 1;

```
2. Generate the code with:
```
$ mkdir -p src/main/{java,kotlin}
$ protoc --java_out src/main/java --kotlin_out src/main/kotlin net/example/v1/example.proto
```
3. Compile the code with Maven/Gradle/etc. Here's the pom.xml I used: https://gist.github.com/pkwarren/ea8315f579dc0b2b5ebd362ea46e75d7

**What did you expect to see**
No error compiling generated code.

**What did you see instead?**
```
$ ./mvnw compile
...
[ERROR] Failed to execute goal org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-maven-plugin:1.8.22:compile (compile) on project example: Compilation failure: Compilation failure: 
[ERROR] /example/src/main/kotlin/net/example/v1/SampleKt.kt:[50,7] Unresolved reference: example
[ERROR] /example/src/main/kotlin/net/example/v1/SampleKt.kt:[50,65] Can't inline 'block' here: it may contain non-local returns. Add 'crossinline' modifier to parameter declaration 'block'

The following change to the generated code appears to resolve the issue - I'm guessing the Kotlin compiler needs to be updated to use backticks for fully qualifying package names:

diff --git a/src/main/kotlin/net/example/v1/SampleKt.kt b/src/main/kotlin/net/example/v1/SampleKt.kt
index f1f9dd4..f703d05 100644
--- a/src/main/kotlin/net/example/v1/SampleKt.kt
+++ b/src/main/kotlin/net/example/v1/SampleKt.kt
@@ -47,5 +47,5 @@ public object SampleKt {

body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
Python

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Use generated enums for type hints and similarly to normal python enums. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**
When generating a python enum, it might be more logical to generate them as [python enums](https://docs.python.org/3/library/enum.html) rather than as a combination of inheriting from `int` and the `google.protobuf.internal.enum_type_wrapper` metaclass. 

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Could be generated as a separate and differently named class, to avoid loosing backwards compatibility, or some additional flag or similar can be set to generate a python enum rather than an `int` wrapper. Could possibly add some methods to generate a python enum implementation during runtime. 

**Additional context**
I guess this might've been considered earlier, and dropped for some reason? Maybe to ensure that the serialized message is an integer? Python enum seems to be from python 3.4, while protobuf requires python 3.7.

nodes.body:
Language level enums are a poor choice for protobuf enums because of questions around open and closed behavior.  https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/enum/ has a pretty extensive explainer on this.  In particular, the ways that Java has very unfortunate behavior because of using language level enums is illuminating.

In short, Language level enums are inherently "closed".  The program has a finite set of options that it can see.  Protobuf enums are inherently "open", new values could come from a newer server/client.  As such, we do not want to make this change.

title: Avoid library SONAME/install name changes on patch releases
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
C++ (libprotobuf/libprotoc)

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
The past two patch releases (23.4 and 23.3), and possibly earlier ones, change the SONAMEs/install names of `libprotobuf` and `libprotoc`.

This mandates recompilation of dependent software, but this is often disruptive and rather wasteful of compute resources.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Avoid ABI-breaking changes on patch releases so that the libraries can be versioned according to the minor version (23). This ship has probably already sailed for v23.x, but perhaps it could be adopted for v24+.

It looks like this was already the case for the [update from 23.3 to 23.4](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/compare/v23.3...v23.4) (i.e. the SONAME bump was not needed here), but I'll admit to not having taken a careful look.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Recompile linked software with every version bump.

**Additional context**
This is primarily motivated by our experience at Homebrew, where we've found the need to recompile dependent software for the last two Protobuf version bumps:
- https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/pull/133818
- https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/pull/135993

This was not our experience for the v21.x series, where we found that new patch releases were drop-in replacements for the previous version. See, for example:
- https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/pull/112013
- https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/pull/113448
- https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/pull/114310
- https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/pull/117355
- https://github.com/Homebrew/homebrew-core/pull/118228

Of course, it's possible that the apparent ABI stability of the 21.x series was just a happy accident, but I imagine your downstream consumers would probably appreciate it if that happy accident continued.

title: Evaluate Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO)
body:
Hi!

Recently I checked Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO) improvements on multiple projects. The results are [here](https://github.com/zamazan4ik/awesome-pgo/).

Since PGO showed measurable improvements in compiler-like loads (Clang, Clangd, clang-format, GCC, Rustc, etc.) I think it could be useful to check PGO on Protobuf compiler (protoc) as well.

We need to perform PGO benchmarks on `protoc`. And if it shows improvements - add a note about possible improvements `protoc` performance with PGO. Providing an easier way (e.g. a build option) to build scripts with PGO can be useful for the end-users too. Improving `protoc` performance can help with faster Protobuf compilation time (and that's nice to have e.g. on CI).

I suspect this is probably working as intended. Protos can take up much more space in their in-memory format than they do in the wire format, mostly because unused fields still take up space in the memory layout.

If you're using arenas then that could be another reason for the high memory usage. An arena's memory is not freed until it is destroyed, and so for example as you grow the `notification` repeated field, whenever the array length is doubled the old array will not be freed immediately. You might get better results by reserving the full length of the repeated field in advance with something like `protoResp->mutable_notification()->Reserve(notif_count);`.

Hi @acozzette, 

Can you please share a reference that guides us on how to utilize the proposed "Reserve" keyword in our code and which protobuf version supports it.

There's a `reserve` keyword in the .proto file language, but I'm just referring to the `Reserve()` method on `RepeatedField` and `RepeatedPtrField`. It works the same way as [std::vector::reserve](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/reserve) and lets you pre-allocate the array in advance. I'm not sure when exactly we added it but I think it's been around for a long time.

I still think this code is probably working as intended. The thing is that fields in the in-memory representation take up space even if they're unset. Each time you create a new submessage you're allocating space for all fields even if you don't set all of them. You might find it useful to experiment with the `SpaceUsedLong()` method on messages to get an estimate of how much space is used.

title: Feature Request: Add client_streaming and server_streaming attributes to MethodDescriptor in python
body:
## Description

This is related to [a very old issue](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/3168) in core `protobuf`: When inspecting a `MethodDescriptor` python object, it's not possible to determine the values of `client_streaming` and `server_streaming` without serializing the in-memory python object back to its proto representation with `CopyToProto`. The request here is to add these as instance attributes of the in-memory python object.

## Details

In [py-to-proto](https://github.com/IBM/py-to-proto/blob/main/py_to_proto/descriptor_to_file.py#L200) we perform a reverse serialization from in-memory descriptor objects to a `.proto` file and we need to know whether the given method supports streaming on either the input or output side in order to properly write the `proto` syntax. We've worked around this for now by using `CopyToProto` to extract the information, but it would be cleaner to have those values available on the in-memory python object.

## Investigation

From what I can tell, adding this feature would primarily consist of replicating [the code that extracts these fields when serializing to proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/blob/main/upb/util/def_to_proto.c#L471) over to [the collection of exposed getters on MethodDescriptor](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/blob/main/python/descriptor.c#L1334). If there's architectural interest in this feature, I'd be happy to work on it as an initial contribution.

Protobuf 3.24.x is dropping support for CRuby <2.7: https://protobuf.dev/news/2023-07-06/#dropping-python-37-support

Unfortunately we were not able to update our gemspec to `s.required_ruby_version >= 2.7`, because that broke compatibility with JRuby 9.2, which we still support. So currently we still list `s.required_ruby_version >= 2.5`.

Hey!

I work with Marco and noticed that since you already have a `if RUBY_PLATFORM == "java"`, you should be able to move the required_ruby_version inside it, e.g. something like:

```ruby
Gem::Specification.new do |s|
  s.name        = "google-protobuf"
  s.version     = "3.23.0"
  git_tag       = "v#{s.version.to_s.sub('.rc.', '-rc')}" # Converts X.Y.Z.rc.N to vX.Y.Z-rcN, used for the git tag
  s.licenses    = ["BSD-3-Clause"]
  s.summary     = "Protocol Buffers"
  s.description = "Protocol Buffers are Google's data interchange format."
  s.homepage    = "https://developers.google.com/protocol-buffers"
  s.authors     = ["Protobuf Authors"]
  s.email       = "protobuf@googlegroups.com"
  s.metadata    = { "source_code_uri" => "https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/#{git_tag}/ruby" }
  s.require_paths = ["lib"]
  s.files       = Dir.glob('lib/**/*.rb')
  if RUBY_PLATFORM == "java"
    s.platform  = "java"
    s.files     += ["lib/google/protobuf_java.jar"]
    s.required_ruby_version = '>= 2.5'
  else
    s.files     += Dir.glob('ext/**/*')
    s.extensions= ["ext/google/protobuf_c/extconf.rb"]
    s.add_development_dependency "rake-compiler-dock", "= 1.2.1"
    s.required_ruby_version = '>= 2.7'
  end
  s.add_development_dependency "rake-compiler", "~> 1.1.0"
  s.add_development_dependency "test-unit", '~> 3.0', '>= 3.0.9'
end
```

Code in the gemfile gets evaluated at packaging time, and its output is distributed inside the `.gem` file.

We ended up opting to drop support for JRuby 9.2 and 9.3 in 24.x release, after adding tests for JRuby 9.4 support. This means we can now consistently enforce >=2.7 as our required ruby version, which should resolve this issue.

This will be released in 24.0-rc2 which we are planning to release this week.

This decision was made based on the support window for the corresponding Ruby version per https://cloud.google.com/ruby/getting-started/supported-ruby-versions.

That works great for us as well!

As a follow up, would you mind yanking the `3.24.0.rc.1` version with the incorrect metadata ([this one](https://rubygems.org/gems/google-protobuf/versions/3.24.0.rc.1)) once rc2 is out?

> We've yanked all 3.24.0.rc.1 artifacts for Ruby, and 3.24.rc.2 has been released with the updated required ruby version number. Please let us know if you still have any trouble, and thanks for catching this in our -RC!

> It does seem surprising to us that our -RC version would get picked up automatically given these are release candidates that are expected to be somewhat unstable. How is this being picked up on your side?

That's a very very good question. My understanding matches yours -- rubygems/bundler should not automatically pick up rc releases unless you ask it to.

And yet, that's what we saw in our CI (and I could reproduce it locally as well): https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/DataDog/dd-trace-rb/10871/workflows/90c509f6-a12a-441a-8e1d-ad0b1567efed/jobs/405709 .

Our Ruby 2.6 image used for testing doesn't appear to be particularly fancy [(link 1)](https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-rb/blob/master/integration/images/ruby/2.6/Dockerfile) and the Gemfile excludes a few other versions of `google-protobuf` (for compatibility with even older Rubies), but nothing seems to jump out at me either [(link 2)](https://github.com/DataDog/dd-trace-rb/blob/master/integration/apps/rack/Gemfile).

but it cannot be automatically decoded in PHP, and an exception will be reported.

import "google/protobuf/any.proto";

echo $response->serializeToJsonString();
```
`Exception: Error occurred during JSON serialization: Couldn't find Any type:reatang.rpc.SomeDetail`

In code: [php-upb.c#L5162](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/php/ext/google/protobuf/php-upb.c#L5162)

Is it possible to open the function of `type_url` mapping to the corresponding class in the php extension.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

This issue is labeled `inactive` because the last activity was over 90 days ago.

> Is it possible to open the function of type_url mapping to the corresponding class in the php extension.

Can you be more specific? How would you like this to work in code?

> > Is it possible to open the function of type_url mapping to the corresponding class in the php extension.
> 
> Can you be more specific? How would you like this to work in code?

For example, open a function to register the association between type_url and class

```php
<?php

namespace Grpc;

function register_any_type($type_url, $class_name) ;

```

```php

use Reatang\Rpc\SomeDetail;

register_any_type("type.googleapis.com/reatang.rpc.SomeDetail", SomeDetail::class);

```

The `type_url` registered using this function can automatically identify the `Any` type by `serializeToJsonString`.

It shouldn't generally be necessary to do that. Any message that you `use` should get registered into the pool that is used to look up types by name.

You can see some examples in the unit tests: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/5c7b41a76974bf1af0b605090fed27ce63fcd36b/php/tests/EncodeDecodeTest.php#L1518-L1535

I am not sure why that didn't work in your case.  Did you have `use Reatang\Rpc\SomeDetail;` in the code where you called `serializeToJsonString()`?

title: 浮点数压缩VarFloat
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3? 
proto2 and proto3, or just proto3


**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
double using fixed64 encoding has a lot of wasted space.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Expect to add new floating-point number types sfloat and sdouble to support the use of compression algorithms.
增加新的浮点数类型:  sfloat 和 sdouble，新的浮点数类型可使用压缩算法


**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the feature request here.
---
我在设计Dson二进制流的时候，使用了protobuf的 CodedInputStream和CodedOutputStream，varint、uint、sint、fixed是非常有用的算法，不过ProtocolBuf并没有现成的float和double的压缩方案。我查看了 IEEE754 浮点的表示法，发现一些特点：

1. **数据集中在指数位附近**，即内存的高位，这是由浮点数的求值方式决定的  。
2. **前两个字节无压缩意义**，因为规格数的指数1开始，因此规格数前两个字节一定有1。
3. 一个不能被二进制精确表达的数，其浮点数的有效位将被用尽以达到更近似的值，因此是无法压缩的。
4. 而一个能被二进制精确表达的数，有效位只使用到其需要的精度的位置，后面就全部为0，因此是可以压缩的。
5. 整数总是能精确表示的，因此能压缩；而小数大多不能被精确表示，因而很难压缩。

由以上的特征，可以得到压缩算法：

1. 获取浮点数的原始bits，统计后导0占用的字节数（Float只统计后2个字节，Double只统计后6个字节），在编码时跳过这些字节。
2. 在编码时，以字节为单位进行逻辑右移，将所有的非0字节编码 -- 仍然表现为小端编码。
3. 在解码时，以字节为单位进行左移，或上新读取的字节即可。

关于压缩收益  
实际的压缩收益是难以直接确定的，与我们使用的值的分布有关，但我们可以按下面这样分析：

1. 对于float，共23个有效位，而前7个有效位已随着指数位序列化，因此：
    1. 2字节占比 7/23
    2. 3字节占比 8/23
    3. 4字节占比 8/23
    4. 因此平均的字节数：3.04，节省的字节数为 0.96，占比 24%
    6. 也就是说，如果我们使用的数都是可精确表达的，能节省1/4的开销。

2. 对于double，共52个有效位，而前4个有效位已随着指数位序列化，因此：
    1. 2字节占比 4/52
    2. 3、4、5、6、7、8字节分别占比 8/52
    3. 因此平均的字节数：5.23，节省的字节数为 2.77，占比：34.6%
    4. 也就是说，如果我们使用的数都是可精确表达的，能节省1/3的开销。
    6. 另外，4字节的double有20个有效位，只比float少3个，因此涵盖了float的大量数据，压缩double可降低用户从float迁移到double的成本。

### Dson
在Dson中，`tag = dsonType <<3 |  wireType` ，对于int32和int64以外的数据类型，wireType的bits用于存储其它信息，因此对于float和double，我用它存储后导0占用的字节数。

```
    /**
     * 浮点数的前16位固定写入，因此只统计后48位
     * wireType表示后导0对应的字节数
     */
    public static int wireTypeOfDouble(double value) {
        long rawBits = Double.doubleToRawLongBits(value);
        for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) {
            byte v = (byte) rawBits;
            if (v != 0) {
                return i;
            }
            rawBits = rawBits >>> 8;
        }
        return 6;
    }

    public static void writeDouble(DsonOutput output, double value, int wireType) {
        long rawBits = Double.doubleToRawLongBits(value);
        for (int i = 0; i < wireType; i++) {
            rawBits = rawBits >>> 8;
        }
        for (int i = wireType; i < 8; i++) {
            output.writeRawByte((byte) rawBits);
            rawBits = rawBits >>> 8;
        }
    }

    public static double readDouble(DsonInput input, int wireType) {
        long rawBits = 0;
        for (int i = wireType; i < 8; i++) {
            rawBits |= (input.readRawByte() & 0XFFL) << (8 * i);
        }
        return Double.longBitsToDouble(rawBits);
    }
```

### protobuf
在protobuf中 `tag = fieldNumber <<3 | wireType`，因此没有额外的空间来存储float和double丢弃的字节信息，protobuf有两种可选方案。

首先，需要定义新的数据类型 sfloat 和 sdouble，才能启用压缩算法，一个测试消息如下：
```
    message  Test {
        sfloat fv= 1; 
        sdouble dv= 2;
    }
```

#### 增加两种WireType： Fixed24 和 Fixed 48
这也可以通过替换 startGroup 和 endGroup 来实现；以 **sdouble** 的序列化为例，在编码时需要先求得其WireType，然后才能进行编码，求wireType的代码如下：
```
    public static int wireTypeOfDouble(double value) {
        long rawBits = Double.doubleToRawLongBits(value);
        if ((rawBits & 0xFF_FFL) != 0) {
            return WIRETYPE_FIXED64;
        }
        if ((rawBits & 0xFF_FF_00_00L) != 0) {
            return WIRETYPE_FIXED48;
        }
        if ((rawBits & 0xFF_00_00_00_00L) != 0) {
            return WIRETYPE_FIXED32;
        }
        return WIRETYPE_FIXED24;
    }
```
这种方案可同时用于float和double。

#### 仅优化double
增加两种WireType和DataType可能有较大的工作量，而且可能达不到满意的效果，因此一个简单的方案是只优化double：当double的后32位全为0时，序列化为Fixed32。
这种方案较为简单，也能起到一定的压缩作用。

```
    public static int wireTypeOfDouble(double value) {
        long rawBits = Double.doubleToRawLongBits(value);
        if ((rawBits & 0xFF_FF_FF_FFL) != 0) {
             return WIRETYPE_FIXED64;
        }
        return WIRETYPE_FIXED32;
    }
```

---
我关闭了这个问题，因为算法的实际收益很小。
在提交issue之后的数个小时里，我一直在思考压缩算法的收益问题，也进行了测试，发现一些现象：
1. 在我们实际传输的float中，能被压缩的float只占15%~20%，远低于50%，因而压缩的整体收益低于4%
2. double的传输占比 < 1% ，而int32的传输占比 >80% ... 因此仅优化double的收益几乎为0。

关于能压缩的数与不能压缩的数之间的比例，我之前期望能有1:1，但明显我的猜测有误，这个值可能更接近于 4:1 或 5:1，我还没有想的太明白。

title: experimental-codegen=enabled does not work with --rust_out
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
libprotoc 23.4
Language: Rust

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
protoc

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Use `--rust_out=experimental-codegen=enabled` to generate experimental rust files

**What did you expect to see**
Generated rust files

**What did you see instead?**
```
--rust_out: test.proto: The Rust codegen is highly experimental. Future versions will break existing code. Use at your own risk. You can opt-in by passing 'experimental-codegen=enabled' to '--rust_out'.
```

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**
Freshly downloaded copy of protoc from the github release page

Full command:
```
protoc -I[proto path] test.proto --rust_out=experimental-codegen=enabled
```

nodes.body: Turns out I just needed to add `,kernel=cpp:.` to the end of the command (`--rust_out=experimental-codegen=enabled,kernel=cpp:.`) for it to generate code, as pointed out by a friend of mine.

To debug an issue like this, we need a repro.

Does simply importing pg_query in an empty app trigger the crash?

If not, how much of your app can you delete and still get the crash? I recommend trying this on a branch. Try deleting things until you have the smallest amount of code that still triggers the crash.
Yeah, I guess. Actually, there is no code using the gem in the app, just the gem in the Gemfile.

On my M1 mac, I tried the following:

```
$ /opt/homebrew/opt/ruby/bin/gem install pg_query
$ /opt/homebrew/opt/ruby/bin/ruby -e "require 'pg_query'"
$ /opt/homebrew/opt/ruby/bin/gem list google-protobuf

*** LOCAL GEMS ***

google-protobuf (3.24.0.rc.2 arm64-darwin)
```

This did not reproduce the crash. So it appears that merely importing pg_query is not enough to reproduce this issue.

So we still need a repro before we can debug this.
I'm running it in Docker (Alpine 3.16) which probably results in using different architecture (`aarch64-linux`), can it be different?

> I'm running it in Docker (Alpine 3.16) which probably results in using different architecture (aarch64-linux), can it be different?

It could be that, or it could be a hundred other things about your setup. The only way to find out is to reduce the crash until you have a minimal repro.

There are some tips for creating a minimal repro here: https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example

Actually, now that you mention it, I don't think our binary gems are compatible with Alpine, see: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/12904#issuecomment-1589718935

That comment also contains workarounds for this.
I see. Thanks, I missed that issue.

title: Conan package 3.17.1 (or newer) CMake build issue "The filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect."
body:
Issue:
When compiling C++ project with CMake and Visual Studio 17 generator, error pops out:

```
Running cpp protocol buffer compiler on C:/Users/user.name/cppTest/proto/ecu_state.proto
  The filename, directory name, or volume label syntax is incorrect.
```

I have created demo project to easily reproduce the issue.

Steps to reproduce:

- git clone https://github.com/ibosnic00/demo_cmake_conan.git
- cd demo_cmake_conan
- start build_and_compile.bat script

Note: 
In conanfile.py, line 22 make sure the version of protobuf is 3.17.1 or newer `self.requires("protobuf/3.17.1")`


It looks like 3.17.1 and newer packages are not adding protoc to PATH (when added manually, build passes), while 3.16.0 package does it okay.

title: CodedOutputStream: Option to throw an exception for unpaired surrogates
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Java library class `CodedOutputStream`.

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

Currently, when using [`CodedOutputStream`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d4f2d48101b1aba771b3ac4c09b3a38c3591e0bd/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/CodedOutputStream.java#L59C1-L59C1) and writing strings that contain unpaired surrogates, they are replaced by `?` characters and a warning is logged, see [`inefficientWriteStringNoTag`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d4f2d48101b1aba771b3ac4c09b3a38c3591e0bd/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/CodedOutputStream.java#L982C33-L982C33) method.

If a user wants to avoid that, they currently have to manually check all strings before using `CodedOutputStream`, adding some performance overhead.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

It would be very useful if the `CodedOutputStream` could throw an exception in that case instead. Note that there's even a TODO in the code for that:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/d4f2d48101b1aba771b3ac4c09b3a38c3591e0bd/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/CodedOutputStream.java#L1478-L1483

The existing behavior can't be changed because of compatibility, but a setting could be added that turns on the new behavior (there is precedence for this with the `useDeterministicSerialization` setting).

So the changes to `CodedOutputStream` would be:

1. Add a `private boolean throwOnUnpairedSurrogates;` field (defaulting to `false`) and a setter/getter method
2. In `writeStringNoTag` methods (or `inefficientWriteStringNoTag`), when encountering unpaired surrogates, check the field and if it's true, throw an `IOException` instead. Otherwise, keep the existing behavior.

I'm happy to create a PR with those changes if that sounds good.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

I initially thought I could extend `CodedOutputStream` until I saw that the constructor is private :). As mentioned above, the only alternatives I can think of is to build a wrapper around it and check all strings before passing them to `writeStringNoTag`, which adds a performance overhead.

nodes.body:
Thanks for the request! In the long run, we would like to move towards stricter UTF8 validation behavior in general which should include validating unpaired surrogates on serialization.

Our hope is to eventually address this via [Editions](https://protobuf.dev/editions/overview/) features to move towards stricter behavior here rather than introducing additional configuration points within individual classes/methods. This probably wouldn't make it in our first edition, but is on our radar.
Thanks, that makes sense!

Someone can add  PROTOC_OUT_DIR  argument to  `protobuf_generate_cpp`  argument list ?

Like this :

```
function(PROTOBUF_GENERATE_CPP SRCS HDRS   OUT_DIR )  // --> see OUT_DIR

....

  protobuf_generate(${_append_arg} LANGUAGE cpp EXPORT_MACRO ${protobuf_generate_cpp_EXPORT_MACRO} 
OUT_VAR _outvar ${_import_arg} PROTOS ${_proto_files} PROTOC_OUT_DIR ${OUT_DIR})  // --> SEE PROTOC_OUT_DIR

```

title: `FieldDescriptor::has_presence` does not behave exactly like `FieldDescriptor::has_optional_keyword`

nodes.body:
This is WAI. `has_optional_keyword()` is deprecated and to be replaced by `has_presence()` in preparation for [Editions](https://protobuf.dev/editions/overview/) which will make the `optional` keyword obsolete and instead use features to control presence.

`has_presence()` is not exactly the same as `has_optional_keyword()` since it checks for presence rather than the keyword itself. Some types (messages, oneofs) always have presence regardless of whether the optional keyword was set, hence the discrepancy on `optional_message_field`.

Most users using `has_optional_keyword()` intend to check for presence e.g. for access to hassers. Depending on your use-case, you may want to add additional checks to consider the field type as well. If you do in fact need to check for the optional keyword itself (e.g. to output a .proto file), it is ok to still use `has_optional_keyword()` for now.

nodes.body:
Unfortunately we cannot upload missing artifacts to Maven after-the-fact for an existing release -- typically we would need to create a new patch release. 

I believe we were still in the process of introducing these artifacts when releasing the `20.x` line so these artifacts may not have been built/named correctly yet, until officially released/supported in `21.x`. Apologies for the confusion!

`20.x` is also long out of support window per https://protobuf.dev/support/version-support/ -- we recommend upgrading to a current protobuf version (e.g. `23.x`)  which should also include the missing artifacts.
Sounds good. I appreciate the response! Thank you.

changing 2.0 to 2.1 results in correct behavior

nodes.body: Can you reproduce when constructing and serialize `ApiMessage` in C++ with test=2.0 before parsing instead of trying to pass the transformed byte string?

> Could it be the string is getting truncated bc of the null charecters?

That would be my guess, yes. You don't appear to be passing in a C++ std::string (which contains a length), but instead a C (char*) - which is null-terminated.

> so would you say this is not a bug in the library but the fact that the const char * is getting truncated when converting to a std::string?

Yes. The library is correctly parsing the truncated string that it is being given.

title: Officially support reproducible (hermetic) builds with CMake
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

C++ built with CMake

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

My C++ project has reproducible builds: running build from a specific commit always produces the same binary. (This requirement should be familiar to you, because that's also a requirement for google3 projects.)

The protobuf library is currently breaking reproducible builds, because it cannot be built as a CMake subproject from the equivalent of third_party (vendored). (At least not in any way I could find.) Instead, the assumption is that the library is installed somewhere in /usr/ for all users of the system.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

absl has the ideal support here - you can simply add_subdirectory(third_party/absl) and everything works. That may not be achievable with protobuf, because it is so complex and assumes it's the top-level CMake project.

There are other ways to achieve this goal - **my feature request is that you pick one, then endorse and document it.**

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

- Using Docker to achieve reproducible builds "one layer up"
- I could use CMake's ExternalProject, but this really seems the road less traveled, missing generated targets, etc.

**Additional context**

I believe reproducible builds are a supply chain security issue for Google and your security team will corroborate this.

title: Communication of Deep Learning models with Protobuf and grpc: analysing the overhead
body:
Hi everyone. This is not an issue, but is like a discussion. Sorry if the section is not correct.

Suppose you have two different Deep Learning models, such as ResNet-18 and MobileNet-V3 small. Below you can see the number of parameters, the total size in megabytes and the number of layers of both models:
| Model                          | Parameters | Size (MB) | Layers |
| --------------------- | ---------- | --------- | ------ |
| ResNet-18                   | 11.175.370 |   42.67   |   68   |
| MobileNet-V3 Small   | 1.527.818  |    5.88   |  210   |

The DL framework considered is PyTorch.
Now, considering that the MB size of ResNet is about 6 times bigger than the size of MobileNet, and the total number of trainable parameters of ResNet is 9 times the number of those of MobileNet, I think that when I have to send this model through one machine to another one, then the communication time of ResNet will be greater than the time required to send MobileNet.
However, my empirical considerations show that the time necessary to send MobileNet (20 seconds) is more or less double the one to send ResNet (10 seconds). 
The framework that I adopted uses Protobuf, grpc and TLS to serialize and communicate. I have zero knowledge of both of these technologies. The only thing that I noted is bigger in MobileNet is the number of layers. Indeed MobileNet has around 3 times the number of layers of ResNet (210 vs 68).  However, a lot of these layers are ReLU and AvgPool, so they do not contain trainable parameters.
Can the number of layers influence so much the time requested to serialize a deep learning model?

Because the `return_immediately` option has been deprecated some time ago, this produces a deprecation log on every pull request:

title: protoc: reserved names should be identifiers in the grammar, not strings
body:
As a follow on from #6335, the grammar for reserved names should be updated to support identifiers as values, not just strings:

```diff
- reserved = "reserved" ( ranges | strFieldNames ) ";"
+ reserved = "reserved" ( ranges | strFieldNames | fieldNames ) ";"
  ranges = range { "," range }
  range =  intLit [ "to" ( intLit | "max" ) ]
  strFieldNames = strFieldName { "," strFieldName }
  strFieldName = "'" fieldName "'" | '"' fieldName '"'
+ fieldNames = fieldName { "," fieldName }
```

Bare identifiers aren't as error-prone since there's no risk of forgetting a comma causing the parser to concatenate adjacent tokens into an unintended reserved name.

Eventually, it would be nice to deprecate or remove support for using string values, but removal would be a backwards-incompatible change.

nodes.body: @Logofile for the doc part of this

@fowles, @Logofile, just to be clear, this isn't a doc bug for the grammar, but a proposal to change the actual parser to accept identifiers (instead of string literals).

This was discussed in a tier 1 review on October 7th, 2022. IIUC, this part of the proposal (the grammar/parser change) was to be delayed until "edition zero". I opened this issue since it looks like "edition zero" is getting close and also for posterity, so this proposal is documented in GitHub.
Ah! That's the piece I was missing. I will add this to the list of things that need to be documented for Editions.

title: protoc: explicit map_entry option is sometimes allowed
body:
In the following example source file, `protoc` correctly produces an error:
```protobuf
// test.proto
message Foo { option map_entry = true; reserved 10 to 1; }
message Bar { optional Foo foo = 1; }
```
```
> protoc test.proto -o /dev/null
test.proto:3:24: map_entry should not be set explicitly. Use map<KeyType, ValueType> instead.
```
Interestingly, the reported position in the error message is where the message is _used_, not where it is defined.

**However**, if the file does not actually refer to the offending message type (`Foo`), the compiler _accepts_ the invalid input:
```protobuf
// test.proto
message Foo { option map_entry = true; reserved 10 to 1; }
```
With the above, running `protoc test.proto -o /dev/null` produces no error.

This is inconsistent, but it also leads to "errors at a distance". If I define a file elsewhere that uses this message, I get an error in that other compile operation, instead of in the original:
```protobuf
// test2.proto
import "test.proto";
message Bar { optional Foo foo = 1; }
```
```
> protoc test2.proto -o /dev/null
test2.proto:3:24: map_entry should not be set explicitly. Use map<KeyType, ValueType> instead.
```

nodes.body: Also a bug, feel free to send a PR.

title: protoc: message reserved tags allowed to be out of order
body:
The following file successfully compiles, even though the start and end tags for the reserved declaration are backwards:
```protobuf
// test.proto
message Foo { reserved 10 to 1; }
```
Running `protoc test.proto -o /dev/null` succeeds.

If I try to generate code, some plugins complain about this when processing the descriptors in the code generation request.
```
> protoc test.proto --go_out ./tmpgen --go_opt Mtest.proto=foo.bar/baz
protoc-gen-go: invalid FileDescriptorProto "test.proto": proto: message "Foo" reserved ranges has invalid range: 10 to 1
--go_out: protoc-gen-go: Plugin failed with status code 1.
```

Note that it is only reserved tags for messaged that exhibit this issue. If I do the same thing (swap start and end) in reserved numbers for enums _or_ in extension ranges, the compiler correctly complains:
```protobuf
// test.proto
message Foo { reserved 10 to 1; }
message Bar { extensions 10 to 1; }
enum Baz { BUZZ = 0; reserved 10 to 1; }
```
```
> protoc test.proto -o /dev/null
test.proto:3:26: Extension range end number must be greater than start number.
test.proto: Reserved range end number must be greater than start number.
```
(Interestingly, there is no line and column reported for that second error, which suggests the error is happening when the descriptor is added to the compiler's pool instead of during parse. Whereas the error for the extension range does include line and column details.)

title: Python weakref support for upb protobuf implementation.
body:
Weakref support was dropped in the upb-backed  implementation of protobuf for python.

This is a regression as you can imagine, since any application depending on weakref to cache shared proto objects cannot work with the upb implementation. See for instance this issue: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/11834

The pre-existing python and cpp message implementations have support for weakref: support in the python implementation is trivial as objects defined in python are weakrefable by default, except for a few cases. For the cpp implementation it seems that the weakref protocol was appropriately implemented using the CPython APIs.

If there are no design considerations as to why upb should not have weakref support then I propose we add them similarly to what we have for the cpp implementation.


I have opened the following two PRs to address this issue:
1. https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/13464 this adds tests to the protobuf repository to expose the weakref regression (note that the tests would not fail in the protobuf repo as they are exercised only against the python and cpp implementations.
2. https://github.com/protocolbuffers/upb/pull/1458 this adds weakref support to the upb impelementation. Prior to this changeset, linking the upb python package against the protobuf repo @ https://github.com/bostikforever/protobuf/tree/weakref-tests should cause these new test failures:
   * See https://github.com/bostikforever/upb/tree/weak-ref-tests-fail pointing to https://github.com/bostikforever/protobuf/tree/weakref-tests where the weakref tests fail without the weakref support added, and
   * https://github.com/bostikforever/upb/tree/weakref-support-test where the weakref tests pass as we have weakref support on this branch. 

The changes themselves are quite trivial, I am open to modifying to suit style, etc. Please give feedback regarding objections as to why weakref support might not be suitable for upb.

nodes.body: Please could you post your specific .proto file? (It's not clear what you mean by "namespace" here - protobuf package, or csharp_namespace option. If you want a specific C# namespace, the simple fix would be to specify it explicitly.)

Hello,

i mean package in proto file, e.g.:

package my.scope._3

in C#:

namespace my.scope.3

the underscore gets removed which does not work in C#.
The bugfix i linked seem to only preserve the underscore before numbers at the beginning, but the routine has to check and preserve the underscore before numbers on every part of the package/namespace string separated by dots.

Right. I'd expect that to actually be modified to `My.Scope.3`.

option csharp_namespace = "my.scope._3";

title: [Ruby] Warnings due to unused variable in Ruby files generated by protoc >=23
body:
In Ruby files `*_pb.rb` generated by version 23.x of the protoc toolchain, there is an unused local variable name that results in warnings (when Ruby is run with warnings turned on). These warnings look like:

```
/usr/local/google/home/dazuma/opt/asdf/installs/ruby/3.2.2/lib/ruby/gems/3.2.0/gems/google-protobuf-3.23.4-x86_64-linux/lib/google/protobuf/any_pb.rb:15: warning: assigned but unused variable - e
```

and appear once for each Ruby file loaded. The issue is in this part of the file:

```ruby
begin
  pool.add_serialized_file(descriptor_data)
rescue TypeError => e  # <-- This variable "e" is not used in the rescue block
  require 'google/protobuf/descriptor_pb'
  # ...
```

This should be a trivial fix to the Ruby generator: just remove ` => e` from the line.

title: Add API to prevent boxing of `Enumerator`s

nodes.body:
While I acknowledge the small performance benefit available, I would really rather not address this. I would be really surprised to see this make a significant difference in any real application code, and the additional code has complexity just due to being "additional code".

If you have evidence that this is causing a problem in *real* code instead of microbenchmarks, I'm happy to reconsider - but I don't like micro-optimizing just because there's an opportunity to do so.

I came across this when profiling a real world application. The application has some hot loops where the boxing causes enough garbage to put pressure on the garbage collector. Caching the enumerator also isn't really an option, as the collection may be modified.

The `for` loop workaround is fine for the `RepeatedField`, but I could find no such workaround for the `MapField`. If you have any suggestions as to how I might prevent boxing the `MapField` enumerator too often, I'm all ears.

I have to say this surprises me... I'd expect that in almost all real world applications, what you *do* with the content of the collection is likely to be more significant than fetching the iterator. The one obvious exception to this is when the field is empty, of course - where creating the iterator is basically all there is to it. That's one area where `MapField` enumeration code (in a hot path) could have an optimization: if the count is 0, don't iterate.

Would that have helped in your use case, or were you actually iterating over non-empty fields but doing very little on each iteration?

(To set expectations: I'm still skeptical that this is worth doing in terms of the maintenance cost vs the benefit it provides to users - even if that benefit happens to be significant for you. I'm aware that `List<>` and `Dictionary<,>` do this, but the bar for micro-optimization in the BCL is significantly lower than it is for protobuf, due to such wide usage.)

I was iterating over non-empty fields, during which I collect some values. These values are used later on. Which values are collected depends on some input arguments, which is why the lookup has to happen quite often. Changing this is not feasible, and because modifications are possible caching is also quite hard.

I do get your point about the benefits potentially not outweighing the maintenance cost, so if you decide not to add this, I understand. There are other areas where the application can be improved performance wise, but as these boxed enumerators showed up as a significant part of the allocations I thought it would be worth asking at least :).

Okay, thanks for the conversation. I'll mull on it... 

For the map iterator type, I'd definitely want us to have our own custom struct rather than building the implementation detail of `LinkedList<KeyValuePair<TKey,TValue>>.Enumerator` being exposed in the API. But I suspect that could be an implementation which just delegates all calls. It's a shame we can't do that for the `RepeatedField` iterator as well (which we could if we used `List<T>` behind the scenes).

Will discuss it with colleagues and see. (Even if we end up doing it, it won't be for a while - just to set expectations.)
I feel like that's a fine trade-off, I don't mind having to use a slightly more inconvenient API to get more performance.

@KnapSac: My suggestion is that having a method returning an enumerable rather than an enumerator would be *more* convenient than your original proposal. I agree with your analysis that it would be a breaking change to simply change the type of the existing method. (That's something we could do in a new major version, if that ever happens, of course.)

If you think `CreateNonBoxingEnumerator()` (or whatever) would be preferable go `CreateNonBoxingEnumerable()`, please let me know your reasoning. I may have missed something.
I don't see a problem with `CreateNonBoxingEnumerable()` at first glance, as long as it's possible to prevent boxing the enumerator it should be an improvement.
@jskeet so would you be open to a PR adding `CreateNonBoxingEnumerable()`?

@KnapSac: I still need to discuss it with colleagues. The fact that it's entirely separate from the "normal" flow at least reduces the risk - if we get something wrong in the optimized flow, it won't affect anyone else.

I'm happy for you to create a PR for it should you wish, but without any guarantees that we'll take it in the end. It's *probably* simplest for you to just sit tight - I don't expect the code to take me long if we decide to do it.
Alright, I'll wait and see.

Okay, I've discussed this with a colleague, and given that it's purely opt-in (so there's no risk of breaking existing users) we're happy to go ahead. Now we get to bike-shed on the names :) I'd suggest nested struct names of "Enumerable" and "Enumerator"... so we just need the name of the method to create the enumerable. Thoughts welcome :)

How about `EnumerateNonBoxing`? I feel like that captures the intent of the method pretty well, while also providing a reason for its existence in addition to the regular `IEnumerable` implementation.

Hmmm... arguably it doesn't *start* enumerating - it just provides what you need to do so.

How about `AsNonBoxingEnumerable()`? The "As" gives the appropriate impression of "this returns something which is a view over the original data"... it's a bit long-winded though.
(I'm expecting this to go back and forth a lot - and we might end up coming back to EnumerateNonBoxing at the end. Hope it's not too frustrating.)

Haha, no problem!

I like the `As` part, especially because this is quite a common pattern in C#. What would be a more concise way of saying non-boxing? Perhaps `AsStructEnumerable` might be an option, but I don't really like that more than `AsNonBoxingEnumerable`.
@KnapSac: Please could you look at #14284 and see if this looks okay to you in terms of the code? If it does, I'll write up the docs, which will probably take longer than the code...

In debugging mode, the following error occurs when the map data structure is used. The key value type of the map is string. It works properly in v23.4.

F0000 00:00:1692071300.022799 1933594 map.h:1078] Check failed: BucketNumberFromHash(hash_function()(k)) == VariantBucketNumber(RealKeyToVariantKey<Key>{}(k)) (5 vs. 4) 

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v24.0
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

nodes.body: can you include the `.proto` file you are using and the payload you are parsing it from as well as any other steps you need to reproduce?

Can you include more information about how this was built and linked?
I suspect there might be an ODR violation where there is more than once copy of Abseil being used.
`absl::Hash` has seeding that would make having multiple copies of it in a single binary an issue as they will not agree on the results.

This means that the call to `absl::Hash` from the inlined function in `map.h` might give a different result than the call from the out-of-line function in `map.cc`.
After I recompiled and installed the absl library, the problem was solved, thank you very much.
