title: Enable debug_redact for Java Logging
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

Java and Proto version -> libprotoc 23.4

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

There are many ways that protocol buffers might be stringified into logs and then printed into stack traces or service/application logs, etc. The built-in behavior stringifies the entire protocol buffer (protobuf) recursively, including all field data.

So for example, assuming that ```Person``` is a protobuf generated class (so it extends ```com.google.protobuf.GeneratedMessageV3```) and there is an instance of it "```person```" then `System.out.print(person);` will print all the fields and values.


I can see a two conversations going on around redacting sensitive information from protocol buffers when they are stringified. Those discussions can be found at:
- https://groups.google.com/g/protobuf/c/uENdMwYSgmo?pli=1
- https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1160

It seems like ```debug_redact``` has been added into [descriptor.proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/descriptor.proto) and generate the code, I can see that the generated Java files can have access to it. However, when I try to stringfy the object, the values for ```debug_redact```enabled fields are still being printed into the logs. I believe that happens because there is no check in ```toString()``` method for this field in Java.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

It seems like currently ```toString()``` method uses private ```printFieldValue()``` method while stringifyinh values - and it does not check whether the descriptor is being used or not - or whether ```debug_redact``` set to ```true``` or not. Maybe we can add a check at the beginning of that method, so that if the ```debug_redact```  is set to ```true``` then the value will not be printed. The following might be added before line 546 (in this [method](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/71a9ae22326d4a9b9fc6c4c87265c2967d4497ab/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.java#L543-L607)), where the ```switch``` statement is:
```
......
    private void printFieldValue(
        final FieldDescriptor field, final Object value, final TextGenerator generator)
        throws IOException {
      if (field.getOptions().hasDebugRedact() && field.getOptions().getDebugRedact()) {
        break;  // do not print anything
     }
      switch (field.getType()) {
        case INT32:
        case SINT32:
        case SFIXED32:
......
}
```

There are other ways to achieve this goal as well but this is a straigtforward solution I believe. 

Dear @acozzette, I kindly wanted to ping you as well since you have some background information and idea about this issues. And it seems like you also recently made some changes into ```TextFormat.java``` class. 

Additional context

- Seems like a possible way is already present in Go: https://github.com/bufbuild/prototransform/blame/main/filter.go


https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/71a9ae22326d4a9b9fc6c4c87265c2967d4497ab/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/TextFormat.java#L543-L607

This will likely be in ~early 2024.

I assume the C++ version will take care of Ruby, etc. Are y'all planning on making the same change in Go?

(Redaction of fields marked with the `squareup.redacted` option is basically the main remaining reason for our internal protobuf forks, and I would _love_ to unfork and just use upstream…)

Hello! Just wanted to kindly ping about this issue.
@zhangskz bump 🙏

I am one of the internal contributors working on this feature.

We are working on making Protobuf `Message.toString` output a redacted format right now (which will, for example, respect `debug_redact` annotation). Currently it looks like we open source that **no earlier** than 2026 as there are a lot of work left and Protobuf rolls out breaking changes once a year.

For now, you can use [`DebugFormat`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9dc5aaa1e99f16065e25be4b9aab0a19bfb65ea2/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/DebugFormat.java#L9) to create a redacted debug format of a message. For situations where we want to log the `toString()` output of a non-proto object that may contain protos, [`ProtobufToStringOutput`](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/9dc5aaa1e99f16065e25be4b9aab0a19bfb65ea2/java/core/src/main/java/com/google/protobuf/ProtobufToStringOutput.java#L9) may help.

**Please note that the debug format (the redacted output format of `DebugFormat` and `ProtobufToStringOutput`) are unstable and will be changed in the future.** For example, we will introduce a randomized prefix so that the debug format is always not parseable regardless of whether the original proto contains fields annotated with `debug_redact` or not.

title: Add annotations for exporting generated functions from a Windows DLL
body:
I'm currently engaged in some work with gRPC aiming at merging a PR which permits gRPC to be built as a dynamic library under Windows (i.e. a DLL). [here](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/pull/34103). gRPC makes use of μpb and needs to expose symbols generated by it from a DLL. That requires that the functions marked as extern be annotated with '__declspec(dllexport)' when compiled and '__declspec(dllimport)' when consumed.

For the protoc compiler, this is achieved by prefixing the file output location on the command line with [dllexport_decl=MY_EXPORT_MACRO](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/64449006/generate-a-dll-which-uses-protocol-buffers), and then defining MY_EXPORT_MACRO as either __declspec(dllimport) or __declspec(dllexport); or empty string, as appropriate, but this feature doesn't appear to be available in μpb.

Can something similar be added?

title: Python: global constants are annotated with ClassVar for extends blocks.
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version:  libprotoc 23.4
Language:  Python

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Archlinux


**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

python 3.11.3

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Create a protbuf file like the following:
```protobuf
syntax  = "proto3";

package test;

import "google/protobuf/descriptor.proto";

extend google.protobuf.MessageOptions {
  optional string version_msg = 50000;
}

```

then run `protoc --pyil_out=. test.proto`

This results in the following code:

```python
from google.protobuf import descriptor_pb2 as _descriptor_pb2
from google.protobuf import descriptor as _descriptor
from typing import ClassVar as _ClassVar

DESCRIPTOR: _descriptor.FileDescriptor
MY_VERSION_FIELD_NUMBER: _ClassVar[int]
my_version: _descriptor.FieldDescriptor
```




**What did you expect to see**

`MY_VERSION_FIELD_NUMBER` should be typed as `int`

**What did you see instead?**

`MY_VERSION_FIELD_NUMBER` is typed as `ClassVar[int]` python type checkers such as `mypy` and `pyright` complain about `ClassVar` being used outside of a class.

body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

C++ with protobuf 24.2, installed via Homebrew


**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

macOS  13.4.1

```
$ clang --version
Apple clang version 14.0.3 (clang-1403.0.22.14.1)
```

**What did you do?**

Code that previously compiled with `-Wall` is now failing with:

```
/Users/danpat/test/example.pb.h:677:33: error: extra ';' inside a struct [-Werror,-Wextra-semi]
    PROTOBUF_TSAN_DECLARE_MEMBER;
```

It looks like the change was introduced with this commit:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/33b8c451a6a584ccfa52317eb5be6fc90bbbee17

When `PROTOBUF_TSAN` is not defined, `PROTOBUF_TSAN_DECLARE_MEMBER` is defined as empty, which leaves a standalone `;` in the generated headers.  This triggers a warning/error on Apple clang via the `-Wextra-semi` option, which is enabled as part of `-Wall`.  I believe it would also trigger on newer GCC which also supports `-Wextra-semi`, but I'm not currently using any newer GCC versions and don't have a setup to test it.

**What did you expect to see**

My code still compiled after updating protobuf

title: DescriptorProtos' `leading_comment` (etc) should keep indentation
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
I am using both proto2 and proto3, and my plugin is written using the Python library

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
During writing my own `protoc` plugin in Python, I noticed that when accessing `leading_comment` (or any of the other comment properties), that any indentation is stripped and all lines in a multi-line comment appear to be equally indented.
This is a bit of a challenge, because we include certain formatting in our `.proto` file comments that we would like to pass on to custom output classes.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Ideally all indentation is passed on to the `leading_comment` (and other) function, and the user can then normalize indentation on their side, e.g., by using `inspect.cleandoc` in Python or other means.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Another alternative might be to convert indentations to special characters (e.g., "@" for each `tab`) in the `proto` file so they are being retained, but that is going to make writing and understanding comments in the `.proto` files cumbersome.

nodes.body: The change you mention has been rolled back already, could you try to reproduce with the latest protobuf version?

Hi, this was rolled back in v24.4 and v25.x releases per https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/2a55706f9d36afd1742c97fd0d611ea8af0ac3f8#r128350688 and https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/14245 since this behavior change was known but unintentionally broke compatibility with old gencode. title: Optionally annotate extern symbols with __declspec(dllimport)/__declspec(dllexport) so they are exported from a Windows DLL
body:
I'm currently working with developers on grpc/grpc to make it possible to build gRPC libraries as shared libraries (DLLs) under Windows. One sticking point is that µpb-generated code can't expose its symbols from a DLL because there is no mechanism for annotating functions with the __declspec(dllexport) and __declspec(dllimport) decorations - which is a requirement for doing so.

It is possible to do that with protoc, for example.

I'd like to propose a change that would facilitate this. So for example we might support command line parameters which nominate macro names that can be declared by the code building the DLL or the code consuming the DLL (or not declared at all for static builds)

So, running (as before):
protoc-gen-upbc < my_proto.proto

...will emit code like:
extern const upb_MiniTable envoy_admin_v3_SimpleMetric_msg_init;

Whereas:
protoc-gen-upbc MY_PROTO_DLL < my_proto.proto

...would instead emit:
extern const MY_PROTO_DLL upb_MiniTable envoy_admin_v3_SimpleMetric_msg_init;

This is similar to what happens with protoc's --cpp_out=dllexport_decl=MY_PROTO_DLL:... 

I can do this work, with your agreement

title: Support using c++ standard library module rather then #include
body:
Currently the generated c++ and C++ headers like `arena.h` use `#include` of the standard library so `#include <vector>`
This is a request to allow consumers to use `import std` instead.
I created a PR for catch2 to do this a while back see https://github.com/catchorg/Catch2/issues/2575 which documents some of the issues.
One things that gets raised a lot is that the standard says that you should be able to mix old style #include and import. However MSVC does not support this and my understanding is that Clang probably won't either, at least in the short/medium term. This means a user can use `import std;` in there code and include any ProtoBuf headers, generated or not.

Note this is NOT a request to create a C++ module of the ProtoBuf code base, I'm sure others will request that. I suspect doing that will be a bigger task.

nodes.body:
It sounds like you're requesting the ability to use the import statement for the C++ standard library in your ProtoBuf code instead of the traditional #include statements, similar to what you attempted in the Catch2 project. While the C++20 standard introduced module support to C++, the adoption and support for modules vary among different compilers. As of my last knowledge update in September 2021, not all C++ compilers fully support modules.

The use of import std to include the C++ standard library is more in line with module support. However, it's important to consider that C++ module support may not be universally available across different compilers and build environments, as you mentioned, and it's possible that the situation hasn't changed significantly since then.

Here are a few points to consider:

Compiler Support: As of my last knowledge update, MSVC was working on C++20 module support but had some limitations. Clang might also have limitations. It's essential to check the latest compiler documentation and support status for the features you want to use.

Project Specifics: The ability to use import for the standard library might depend on the specific build system and configuration for your project. Some projects and build environments might not support modules.

Compatibility: Mixing traditional #include and import statements can be problematic, as not all compilers may support this, as you've mentioned. It's important to consider the impact on users who might have different compiler setups.

Community and Maintenance: Be prepared for potential maintenance challenges. If you enable this feature, you may need to provide compatibility and support for users with different compilers and configurations.

Future-Proofing: While C++ modules are the future, their full adoption might take time. Consider whether enabling import for the standard library aligns with the long-term goals of your project.

It's great to see efforts to modernize C++ codebases, but it's essential to balance this with practical considerations based on the current state of compiler support and the needs of your project's user base. Always stay updated with the latest compiler developments and standards to make informed decisions.

The protobuf project supports a large number of compiler and language variants.  https://github.com/google/oss-policies-info/blob/main/foundational-cxx-support-matrix.md

As of right now, we can't make this change without a fairly large burden to make opt out for various configurations and compilers.  So unfortunately, I don't expect that we will make this change for quite a few years.

OK that's fair enough, I suspect that you will see a faster adoption of `import std;` than many people expect. Particularly now that the major compilers have agreed to back port the std module support to C++20 mode. So I suspect over the next year or so there will be an increasing pressure to support this.
I have linked this issue to https://arewemodulesyet.org/ so we can track modules support in the c++ eco system.

title: Exception on checking extension equality in python
body:
Version: 3.15.7
Language: Python

I'm trying to compare two instances of protobuf message of the same type (say, MyMessage) via ==. MyMessage has extensions. Comparison operation fails with the exception:

```
google\protobuf\internal\extension_dict.py:127: in __eq__
    my_fields = [field for field in my_fields if field.is_extension]

.0 = <list_iterator object at 0x000001E9179E3940>

>   my_fields = [field for field in my_fields if field.is_extension]
E   AttributeError: 'tuple' object has no attribute 'is_extension'
```

I believe the reason is that when `_ExtensionDict.__eq__` method calls `ListFields()` on MyMessage it gets back collection of fields. Each `field` is a `tuple` like
`(<google.protobuf.descriptor.FieldDescriptor object at 0x000001B44FCEC310>, 1)`
So changing condition `field.is_extension` -> `field[0].is_extension` seems to fix the problem.

body:
I am using filed mask on the same proto structure as mentioned in https://google.aip.dev/161. I am doing this in kotlin. The dependencies being used are :
- com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java:3.23.2
- com.google.protobuf:protobuf-java-util:3.23.2
- com.google.protobuf:protobuf-kotlin:3.23.2

The issue i face is that when validating if it is a correct field mask for the example given in 161 it always gives false:
  require(FieldMaskUtil.isValid(Book::class.java, request.mask)) { "Invalid Field mask" }
  values i have tried are: "book.reviews.smith", "reviews.smith", "reviews.`smith`", "reviews.*.smith" etc
  i have tried all possible combinations.
  Can you guide me is this supported in protobuf current version and am i missing anything ?

nodes.body: @jskeet

I'm travelling at the moment, but will answer properly next week. The TL;Dr is - yup, the protobuf libraries and AIP-161 are unfortunately in conflict at the moment. I have a longstanding task to try to at least document and ideally improve this, but it's not likely to be soon. More detail next week.

Right, now I'm back...

Basically there are *multiple* discrepancies between how field masks are described in [fieldmask.proto](src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto) and how they're described in AIP-161.

#12524 describes how some field masks described in AIP-161 don't have a valid JSON representation. In addition, there are various utility classes in protobuf runtimes which either prohibit the additional features of AIP-161 entirely, or implement them partially and inconsistently. `FieldMaskUtil.isValid` is just part of this.

This has been on my plate for a while, in terms of trying to improve things as much as I can *without breaking anything* - that last part being absolutely the most important. (There will always be *some* risk to changes, even safe-sounding ones like expanding JSON serialization/deserialization, but it'll be a trade-off.) As a sort of "side-project" it's frankly hard to find time for this - but I'm *trying* to do so.

body:
Version: 3.24.x
Language: Java

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/commit/2a55706f9d36afd1742c97fd0d611ea8af0ac3f8 is a breaking change for oneofs for gencode before 3.15.x.

This technically violates https://protobuf.dev/support/cross-version-runtime-guarantee/ since we currently guarantee compatibility with old gencode and new runtimes within same major version. 

This should be rolled back and reintroduced in the next release that bumps the Java major version.

title: C#:  preserve directory structure in generated code
body:
**What language does this apply to?**

C#

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**

We have a tool that generates a package with a potentially large number of .proto files with a specific directory structure.  The file _paths_ are of course unique, but file _names_ are based on user input and aren't guaranteed to be unique.  When there's a collision, this means that generating C# code fails, because the C# code generator generates a flat directory of `.cs` files with filenames matching the input filenames.

This problem does not exist in C++, Go (with `paths=source_relative`), or Swift; these all preserve the directory structure.  It also doesn't existing with Java/Kotlin, where the output is in a flat directory but the filenames are based on message names or the `java_outer_classname` option.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

A protoc plugin option to generate code with a directory structure matching that of the input.  This is the same behavior exhibited by C++, Swift, and (with `paths=source_relative`) Go.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**

* Modifying the generator to guarantee unique filenames (but this uglifies our output)
* Forking the C# protoc plugin

nodes.body:
While there isn't an option to preserve the directory structure of the *source* protos, there's an option to create a directory structure based on *namespace*. Specify the `base_namespace` option (which can be empty):

```sh
protoc --csharp_out=. --csharp_opt=base_namespace= p1/test.proto p2/test.proto
```

The files will then be generated base on the C# namespace for each file (based on the proto package or the `csharp_namespace` option in the file). Hopefully that matches the structure of the files anyway - and is more in-keeping with typical C# practices for source control.

If you specify a non-empty base namespace, then that prefix is effectively removed - so if you generated code in a C# namespace of "A.B.C.D" and specified `base_namespace` as `A.B` then it would create a file under a directory of `C/D`.

Does that solve your problem? I'd personally rather not add a completely separate option for folder structure to the generator.

(Note that if you've got multiple protos with the same name generating code in the same namespace, that will cause problems at compilation time anyway - unless your plan is to only compile some of them at a time.)

I tried that option, and it doesn't (in isolation) solve my problem.  Let's assume I generate a directory structure like (forced toy example):

* resources/
  * check.proto
  * receipt.proto
* custom_methods/
  * receipt/
    * check_receipt.proto

(Whether that last file is `check_receipt.proto` or `check.proto`, I have a filename collision.)

I _could_ generate different C# namespaces for these files, e.g. `resources/receipt.proto` and `custom_methods/receipt/check_receipt.proto` are both about the `Receipt` resource and so could have a `My.Api.V1.Receipt` namespace.  This comes at a (small, admittedly) developer experience cost for the API implementor, and it also adds a bit of complexity to the generator (right now it doesn't specify `csharp_namespace` at all).

I recognize that changing the C# protoc plugin is a heavier lift that my changing our API contract generator.  But I thought it was worth asking, given that this isn't an issue with any of the several other languages I checked, and given that someone else could easily run into this problem as well.  Having unique filenames seems like an idiosyncratic requirement.

I may be missing something, but I'd expect your toy example to work, generating Check.cs, Receipt.cs and CheckReceipt.cs.

One thing that's really important to note is that the reflection class within the file (CheckReflection etc) is based on the filename as well... so even if we *did* generate source files in the same directory structure, they still wouldn't be able to be compiled together afterwards. Are you expecting to be able to compile all the generated code together in one assembly? If so, the fully-qualified name really will need to be unique.

Also note that you don't have to specify csharp_namespace in particular - the namespace is derived from the protobuf package if you don't specify the csharp_namespace option. I don't think forcing "package + filename" to be a unique combination is particularly strange, personally.

Hmm, yes, I somehow confused myself while (re)writing that example and messed it up.  There should have been a third file called resources/check_receipt.proto...but of course that's a less realistic resource name, which undermines the example a bit. :/  I can try to think of a more realistic example if that would help.  (Right now I haven't run into a real one, just noticed that a filename collision is possible.  This came up because the current version of our generator actually uses `custom_methods/receipt/check.proto`, which _does_ cause a collision today, because we have two different resources with a custom method named `:increment`.  Changing to e.g. custom_methods/receipt/check_receipt.proto addresses the kind of collision we had, but while I'm at it I'd want to make all filename collisions impossible, if that's what we need to do.)

> I don't think forcing "package + filename" to be a unique combination is particularly strange, personally.

It seems to be a uniquely C# requirement when it comes to protobuf, and it is a stricter constraint than filesystems impose (which is of course that file _paths_ must be unique, but not file _names_).

Anyway, it all seems irrelevant given your point about generated reflection classes, since changing how that works seems infeasible.  Thanks for the info and the quick responses!

body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**

Version:

libprotoc 24.4
```
Language: Java

macOS 13.5.2

N/A

**What did you do?**
1. Compile `test.proto` with:
```bash

```
`test.proto`:

```proto
syntax = "proto3";
package test;
service test {
  rpc test(TestIn) returns (TestOut);
}
message TestIn {};
message TestOut {};
```

2. Load the file using Java API (ver. 3.19.6):

```scala
val inputStream = Files.newInputStream("test.desc")
val proto = FileDescriptorProto.parseFrom(inputStream)
val descriptor = FileDescriptor.buildFrom(proto, Array.empty)
println(descriptor.getName)
```

**What did you expect to see**

I expected a valid descriptor object containing Test service and Test method.
`println` should result in `test.proto`.

**What did you see instead?**

Resulting `descriptor` object is malformed. It contains no services and no methods.
`println` displayed:

```


test.prototest" 
TestIn"	
TestOut2+
test#
test .test.TestIn
.test.TestOutbproto3
```

Opened compiled descriptor in hex editor and found extra bytes at the beginning of the file, which corrupt descriptor object:

![Screenshot 2023-10-10 at 11 38 15](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/assets/45422152/3d3fb3ff-c0f4-476f-a144-bae986cc17e0)

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

 `test.proto` bytes:

![Screenshot 2023-10-10 at 13 14 23](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/assets/45422152/2fc5d143-b0e1-48ca-9d13-e41bbb780b16)

Compiled `test.proto` also with libprotoc 3.20.3, same issue. Is there anything I am doing wrong? Many thanks for looking into this.

nodes.body: @PeterFras The output from the compile with --descriptor_set_out is a FileDescriptorSet proto message, not a single FileDescriptorProto message. The extra bytes are the field tag and length prefix for the repeated `file` field.

title: Value.Builder support in Struct.Builder APIs.
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for feature requests (including cleanup requests) only. For questions or troubleshooting, please see the protobuf mailing list: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf

-->


**What language does this apply to?**  Java
If it's a proto syntax change, is it for proto2 or proto3? Possibly?
If it's about generated code change, what programming language? Java 

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
Right now, the Struct.Builder APIs don't support Value.Builder as inputs, only Value. It requires deferred computation for the struct if the value is not set on the Value.Builder ahead of type.  


**Describe the solution you'd like**
If Struct.Builder APIs (primarily, putFields API) can accept a builder as input, the reference back to the Value.Builder.build() could be called from Struct.Builder.build() and deferrred computation would not be needed.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Deferred computation with lambdas has already been considered. However, the order of build calls needs to be maintained and this limits opportunities to execute logic in parallel. For instance, if I build a recursive Struct structure like a tree, I must build from leaf to root. So, if traversing a tree structure from root to leaf, a second traversal is required to build.

N/A

nodes.body:
Check Protobuf Installation: Make sure you have Protobuf (protobuf compiler) correctly installed on your system. You should be able to download pre-compiled binaries suitable for macOS. You can download it from the official Protobuf GitHub releases page: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases 
Verify Installation: After downloading, extract the binaries if necessary and verify that the protoc executable is present. You can check this by running the following command in your terminal:
protoc --version
If you see the version information, that means Protobuf is correctly installed.

Update Your PATH: Ensure that the directory containing the protoc executable is added to your system's PATH environment variable. You can do this by adding the following line to your shell configuration file (e.g., ~/.bashrc, ~/.zshrc, or ~/.profile):
export PATH=/path/to/protoc:$PATH

Replace /path/to/protoc with the actual path to the directory containing the protoc executable. After adding this line, save the file, and either restart your terminal or run source ~/.bashrc (or the appropriate file) to apply the changes.
Quarkus Configuration: If you're using Quarkus for your project, make sure that the Quarkus protobuf extension is correctly configured in your project's pom.xml or configuration file. Ensure that the plugin is using the protoc compiler from your PATH.

Environment Variables: Double-check that your Java environment variables are correctly set, especially if you've updated your PATH variable. Environment variables can affect the behavior of your build tools.

  key: "Length of this key increases the leak"
  value:"No observable impact on the leak"
}
"""

```

> import dill # Leak doesn't happen without this import.

Leak correlates with this line: https://github.com/uqfoundation/dill/blob/f66ed3b602d6e9b942542491614dfd18622583d7/dill/_dill.py#L72C32-L72C32

Here is a repro that doesn't use dill:

```
import __main__ as _main_module # Leak doesn't happen without this import.
import sys
from google.protobuf import text_format

proto_def="""
syntax = "proto3";

message MessageWithAMap {
  map<string, string> some_map = 1;
}
"""

with open("repro.proto", "w") as f:
  f.write(proto_def)

from grpc_tools import protoc
args = [
    sys.executable, # unused
    "repro.proto",
    "--proto_path", ".", "--python_out", "."]
protoc.main(args)

from repro_pb2 import MessageWithAMap

proto="""
some_map {
  key: "Length of this key increases the leak"
  value:"No observable impact on the leak"
}
"""

message = MessageWithAMap()
text_format.Parse(proto, message)

key = list(message.some_map)[0]
for _ in range(500000):
  unused_values = message.some_map[key] # memory leaks here
```
Leak doesn't happen with protobuf==3.20.3 or with `PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=python`.

I think I see the root cause. In map lookup, we use the message's arena to convert the Python `key` object to raw C data that we can use to perform the lookup in upb. But this data will never be freed until the message is freed: https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/022d223488c0807e11d1c2509123901f5cc6b0b6/python/map.c#L203-L205

We should use a temporary arena to perform the conversion. Only at the point where we are allocating non-temporary data should we use the message's arena.

That explains why `import __main__ as _main_module ` has an effect. Leak is still happening without this statement, but this statement makes it easier to register the leak with the profiler as references to `message` persist longer.
Indeed, in `top` memory keeps growing without `import __main__ as _main_module` and memray also registers the leak when used without `--leak` flag.
`PyUpb_MapContainer_Get`  also has this leak https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/022d223488c0807e11d1c2509123901f5cc6b0b6/python/map.c#L259-L261`
And probably several other places in `map.c` where `PyUpb_PyToUpb` is used.

This is still happening, and the PR was closed by inactivity. This is sad :/

There seem to be two complications here:

1) no_standard_descriptor_accessor - this option is supported and will fix this problem, but it needs to be set on the message.  Since we support fields named `descriptor` in java today with this option, this proposed change is breaking

2) java lite - java lite shares the same code as java full for forbidden keywords, but doesn't have any conflict for `descriptor`.  That means this proposal would be a breaking change for java lite.  We have a similar issue with internal variants of java that aren't open-sourced.

I don't see how to fix this without it breaking someone else (we could work around 2, but 1 is a deal-breaker).  We could try to schedule it for our next breaking release though, and maybe try to turn down `no_standard_descriptor_accessor` at the same time.

Edit: I suppose we could fix this by only modifying the field name when `no_standard_descriptor_accessor` is unset in java full.  That would prevent this from being a breaking change, but it would also require a ton of ad-hoc code outside of our forbidden name infra just for this one field name.  I'd be very worried about missing a case where field name consistency is required

@mkruskal-google I'm okay with scheduling it for a future, breaking release (we can work it around for now, but it would be much better for all people involved if we used the standard solution as it is supposed to).

Unfortunately our next Java breaking change won't be until January 2026.  I agree this is a real bug we should fix tho.  I think the non-breaking approach is an option before then, it's just a question of prioritization.

If anyone wants to send us a PR for the non-breaking change I think we could accept that.  We would basically need to decouple java and java-lite forbidden names, and make it so that in java only we modify the name when `no_standard_descriptor_accessor` is unset (e.g. the case that's broken today only)

title: oneof fields when creating c# class
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!forum/protobuf 
Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: Protocol Buffers v24.4
Language: C#

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10 Enterprise

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

gcc version

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a simple proto contract with oneOf fields:

```
syntax = "proto3";

// The options 'java_package' and 'java_outer_classname' may be changed.
// Version 3
option java_package = "de.suu.proto";
option java_outer_classname = "UploadVxProtoMEB";
option csharp_namespace = "CCG.SUU.ProtobufV3";

// COMMUNICATION CONTROL BETWEEN VEHICLE AND BACKEND
message Response {
 string id = 1; // Timestamp when it was created
 // The message payload
 oneof data {
  Class1 class1 = 2;
  Class2 class2=3;
  Class3 clas3=4;
 }
}

message Class1{ 
 double number=1; 
 string name=2;
}

message Class2{ 
 double number=1; //micro degrees to degrees (*10^-6)
 string type=2;
}

message Class3{ 
 double number=1;
 string description=2;
}
```

2. Generate a c# class

`./protoc.exe ./myProto.proto --csharp_out=./`

3. The new generated will have the properties with getter and setter inside:

```
/// <summary>Field number for the "class1" field.</summary>
    public const int Class1FieldNumber = 2;
    [global::System.Diagnostics.DebuggerNonUserCodeAttribute]
    [global::System.CodeDom.Compiler.GeneratedCode("protoc", null)]
    public global::CCG.SUU.ProtobufV3.Class1 Class1 {
      get { return dataCase_ == DataOneofCase.Class1 ? (global::CCG.SUU.ProtobufV3.Class1) data_ : null; }
      set {
        data_ = value;
        dataCase_ = value == null ? DataOneofCase.None : DataOneofCase.Class1;
      }
    }
```

4. The problem is that data_ (the object that contains one of the fields) will be overwritten by the latest field from the oneof block, because the setter does not check if the data_ is already set, or not. so if only Class1 have value, we will end up with null value for it because the last one who enters the setter, Class3, will set data_ to null.

if we receive something like:
{
...
    "class1": {
    ...
    }
    "class2": null,
    "class3": null,
...
}

**What did you expect to see**

```
/// <summary>Field number for the "class1" field.</summary>
    public const int Class1FieldNumber = 2;
    [global::System.Diagnostics.DebuggerNonUserCodeAttribute]
    [global::System.CodeDom.Compiler.GeneratedCode("protoc", null)]
    public global::CCG.SUU.ProtobufV3.Class1 Class1 {
      get { return dataCase_ == DataOneofCase.Class1 ? (global::CCG.SUU.ProtobufV3.Class1) data_ : null; }
      set {
        data_ = value == null ? data_ : value;
        dataCase_ = value == null ? dataCase_ : DataOneofCase.Class1;
      }
    }
```

I would expect to check if the value is null, and if so, just let the value that was already set in the oneof fields. Also dataCase_ should maintain the value.

**What did you see instead?**

As I wrote above

Make sure you include information that can help us debug (full error message, exception listing, stack trace, logs).

I've inserted the .proto file in the step 1.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

nodes.body:
This is how oneof fields have worked in all languages that I'm aware of.
I don't believe we'd want to make any change for just C#.

Indeed, it's described in the [documentation](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/proto3/#oneof-features):

> Setting a oneof field will automatically clear all other members of the oneof. So if you set several oneof fields, only the last field you set will still have a value.

As such, this is working as intended - if you want to propose a completely different model for oneofs, that wouldn't be done just for C#.

Yes: the behavior listed is deliberate. Besides the quote jskeet wrote see also the sentence further above in the same documentation:

> Note that if multiple values are set, the last set value as determined by the order in the proto will overwrite all previous ones.

Especially in the explicit setters api, if we had the 'first write sticks' it would likely be even more confusing because it would mean silently discarding the second write.

Apologies for any confusion on this case!

title: Valid UTF-8 character of £ makes gRPC request fail
body:
<!--

NOTE: this form is for bug reports only.
For questions or troubleshooting, please post on the protobuf mailing list:

Stack Overflow is also a useful if unofficial resource https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/protocol-buffers
-->

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v24.3
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 10

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
Visual Studio 2022

**What did you do?**
I'm seeing an issue when sending a valid UTF-8 character from a gRPC client to server, using protobuf as the wire format. The issue can be easily re-produced by updating [this line](https://github.com/grpc/grpc/blob/master/examples/cpp/helloworld/greeter_client.cc#L89) from `std::string user("world");` to `std::string user("£");`. For some reason when using the `£` character, the request fails with this error:
```
wire_format_lite.cc:626] String field 'helloworld.HelloRequest.name' contains invalid UTF-8 data when parsing a protocol buffer. Use the 'bytes' type if you intend to send raw bytes.
```

However, unless I'm missing something, this doesn't seem right as `£` is a valid UTF-8 character. Changing the proto definition to `bytes` does fix it, but I'm trying understand why simply using `string` is causing an issue.

**What did you expect to see**
Request to work as expected.

**What did you see instead?**
Request fails with mentioned error above.

nodes.body:
This should work; I suspect this issue still potentially relates to the string being represented as something other than utf-8 in your configuration. An std::string is agnostic to encoding and can contain to any byte sequence, but gRPC requires it be represented in utf8 representation.

To confirm if this is the root cause of your issue, if you look at the string it will need to be equal to the utf8 representation, which for £ is "\xC2\xA3" (the std::string should have length=2 and contain those two bytes). It may be that the representation of your .cc / .cpp file is UTF16 and the string literal is following that representation.

If your string already is those 2 bytes and you are still getting the error let us know. Thanks!

Thanks @esrauchg .

I'll double check that. I have just realised one thing, the character set on the project (within Visual Studio) is `Use Multi-Byte Character Set`. Could that be the source of the issue?

@esrauchg here's a screenshot showing the values of the string being sent in the gRPC request.
![protobufutf](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/assets/24831976/3386b5f8-f0d6-4007-9af6-ca16f4b8aace)

Is it possible to look into this please? It's easily reproducible with the hello world example from gRPC. We'd like to address it soon as it's going to become a blocker for our upcoming release.

We can change all string types to bytes, but I don't know what the consequence of that is.

Thanks.

I think all evidence still suggests you are simply passing something that
is not utf8 encoded in: the debug UI shows it is the std::string it shows
length=1, but the £ character as an std::string in utf8 should take 2 bytes
( .length() on the std string only counts bytes not characters/codepoints).
If its a 1 bytes £ that seems like it's only possible in Latin-1 string
encoding which is not supported by gRPC strings.

I believe your issue is still with your C++ project configuration and not
any issue with protobuf/gRPC itself.

You can choose to use "bytes" for the type on your message and pass strings
any encoding you want, but it will simply defer your problem to the
receiving side of the rpc to turn that back into a usable string. In that
sense you can use a bytes field with Latin-1 encoded strings and then it's
up to you to coordinate that on all of your other endpoints (and most
Unicode characters won't be representable at all in Latin-1). If you use
string type then you do need to use utf8 encoding, but then gRPC will do
the right thing to expose it as the language's string type in other
languages (only in C++ does the bytes and string protobuf type use the same
type in the language bindings).

On Thu, Nov 2, 2023, 5:55 PM Ali Alamiri ***@***.***> wrote:

> @esrauchg <https://github.com/esrauchg> here's a screenshot showing the
> values of the string being sent in the gRPC request.

What I'm trying to say is that it's not just my own project that is exhibiting the issue, it's also the example project from gRPC repo itself.

Unfortunately I don't think we are scoped to assist you in debugging issues with the broader C++ development environment: the spec behavior of protobuf/gRPC is that if you use string type you must provide it with utf8 encoded string.

Your screenshot reflects that you have constructed an std::string which is not in utf8 encoding and so it being rejected by the library is working as intended behavior. C++ doesn't proscribe an encoding of unicode characters and also doesn't even carry the signal of what the encoding is, so it wouldn't be possible for gRPC to 'know' that it is actually a Latin-1 string and handle it correspondingly. Really all it can do is mandate utf8 encoding and leave it up to the application developer to ensure they have strings in that encoding; it may be that the _file_ itself in windows needs to be set to another encoding (not the visual studio _project_) or some other configuration which is specific to your machine that makes it so the string literal is being treated as utf8 encoded when the compiler runs.

If your C++ service received a utf8 encoded string at runtime (from another service, or read from a file) and you passed that string in it would work, so the issue is narrowly in the construction of a string literal in your C++ file. If you can't figure out how to get a C++ string literal to be utf8 encoded under your C++ development environment, you can always fall back to spelling out the characters through explicitly writing out the escaped byte sequence, which would be "\xC2\xA3" in the case of the £ symbol in utf8 encoding. Or, if you are confident that you do reliably have a Latin-1 encoded string literal, you could use a function that will explicitly convert from Latin-1 to utf8 like boost::locale::conv::to_utf (but in this specific case this may be brittle, if the behavior is related to your machine configuration then explicitly converting it would break on another machine).

Apologies that we aren't scoped to assist you further in debugging the general C++ dev environment, but I think given your screenshot reflects that the behavior of gRPC+Protobuf is matching the intended spec I'm going to close out this issue. If you do find evidence that there is actually a bug in Protobuf please reopen the issue. Thanks!

> Unfortunately I don't think we are scoped to assist you in debugging issues with the broader C++ development environment

I completely disagree with this. Protobuf/gRPC support C++ environments, and if gRPC's own source code (the helloworld example) exhibits an issue when built using a supported environment, as per the documentation from BUILDING.md, then to me that's a bug.

Not sure what more evidence I can provide as I've already provided the exact steps to reproduce the problem **_using gRPC's own source code, and build steps_**.

Also there is still not much clarity on what consequences using `bytes` would have? Both the client and server are done in C++ using the same environment, but nothing seems to explain what exactly is the difference between `string` and `bytes` in C++ protobuf. I keep reading there is no difference, but clearly there is when UTF-8 characters are involved.

> if gRPC's own source code (the helloworld example) exhibits an issue when built using a supported environment

I understand that its frustrating but I believe the relevant behavior has nothing to do with the gRPC code, or the project or specific compiler but your own individual Windows / file configuration. You may have luck reaching out to Visual Studio support forums for how to configure your specific computer so that string literals will be UTF-8 encoded strings. I did some preliminary searches for you for some related questions on this topic:

https://developercommunity.visualstudio.com/t/hangul-character-encoding-in-cp949-when-using-a-fi/120458
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/688760/how-to-create-a-utf-8-string-literal-in-visual-c-2008

I think in general there is no C++ standard way to write "£" as a constant literal in a source file. If you want the "definitely correct on all machines" way to do it the answer would be to write std::string POUND_SIGN = "\xC2\xA3"; if gRPC had to provide single guidance about unicode literals that works in Visual Studio on all machines that would be the answer.

>  I keep reading there is no difference, but clearly there is when UTF-8 characters are involved.

The difference is:
- string in every language uses the native languages string type, encoded on the wire as utf8. When used on C++ the application developer needs to make sure their std::string is using utf8 encoding, and it is validated to be utf-8

- bytes accept any arbitrary sequence of bytes,  usually used for binary content. It is exposed in all platforms through the idiomatic "sequence of arbitrary bytes" language native type. C++ is unusual in that this type happens to also be std::string (since in C++ std::string is the same type for both "text shown to user" as well as "binary data you may read from a file"). When you use bytes type any arbitrary byte sequence is allowed; there's no extra validation.

So if you use gRPC solely with C++ then really the only difference between bytes and string is that string mandates utf8. If you use any other languages the difference will be bigger.

But the validation may be helping you catch an issue that you didn't realize here: if you write message.set_bytes_field("£") it'll be 1 byte on your machine but verbatim the same C++ code / project / compiler on another configuration that may compile to be a 2 byte string. When you use gRPC with a bytes field it'll verbatim pass through whatever you gave it, so the receiver of the message would see either the 1 or 2 byte encoding exactly as it was set on the caller side in this case and need to handle it appropriately.

Hope that clarifies things!

So just to be extra clear, if bytes type is used, and both the client and server are built using the same environment/c++ configuration, will the server receive the same bytes that the client sends? I'm confused by this statement:

> When you use gRPC with a bytes field it'll verbatim pass through whatever you gave it, so the receiver of the message would see either the 1 or 2 byte encoding exactly as it was set on the caller side in this case and need to handle it appropriately.

Why would the receiver see either 1 or 2 bytes if the bytes type is used? What does "handle it appropriately" mean exactly, how would the receiver handle it?

Our set up is that the client and server are both built in C++, using the same VS configuration, targeting the same platform (Windows), so I'm still a bit unclear on if the bytes type will introduce problems or not.

Thanks.

The situation of Unicode in C++ is complicated and not great.

If you write a single C++ project and compile it, and it reads from a file,
from the terminal, from a GUI input, from another RPC, each of those
std::strings could have any different byte representation of the same
conceptual text. If you typed the £ character in each of those places, run
a single binary locally, they may all show up as != strings.

When you have a string variable and go to use it for any case that can
display text (write to file, write to terminal, show in GUI, send to an
rpc), each of those will have the encoding that they require and if you
give it a string which happens to have text with a different encoding than
that the result is usually Mojibake:
https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mojibake

The behavior you are reproducing is that this specific file on this
specific machine is set up such that the string literal that you typed it
is using Latin-1 representation. That unfortunately doesn't actually mean
your overall C++ project has coherently decided strings will be Latin-1:
even on your exact machine in this same file at this exact moment any other
strings which aren't this string literal can be some different text
encoding. Any libraries which handle text to show to the user, it will be
broken if you pass it a string with an encoding other than what that
library requires.

If you use the bytes type then any std::string value will be passed through
by gRPC, but that will probably just defer your problem of not having a
firm grasp of the encoding that the unicode string is. On the receiving end
of the RPC your C++ code will want to do something with that string, if you
allow the sender to write utf8 or Latin-1 it probably won't be able to
handle both cases carefully.

It is an option to use bytes type and just "know" that you will only write
Latin-1 encoded text in, and then you may need to convert that to utf8 or
wchar strings or similar before it can be used with whatever other library
you're using it with. Note that this is already the case with your current
string literal: at this moment you currently know that variable is Latin-1
and if you wanted to display that string to the user it would probably need
to be converted depending on the expectations of whatever you're using to
display it.



On Sat, Nov 4, 2023, 7:37 AM Ali Alamiri ***@***.***> wrote:

> So just to be extra clear, if bytes type is used, and both the client and
> server are built using the same environment/c++ configuration, will the
> server receive the same bytes that the client sends? I'm confused by this
> statement:
>
> When you use gRPC with a bytes field it'll verbatim pass through whatever
> you gave it, so the receiver of the message would see either the 1 or 2
> byte encoding exactly as it was set on the caller side in this case and
> need to handle it appropriately.
>
> Why would the receiver see either 1 or 2 bytes if the bytes type is used?
> What does "handle it appropriately" mean exactly, how would the receiver
> handle it?
>
> Our set up is that the client and server are both built in C++, using the
> same VS configuration, targeting the same platform (Windows), so I'm still
> a bit unclear on if the bytes type will introduce problems or not.

> Thanks.

> <https://github.com/notifications/unsubscribe-auth/BBPPJWKRXKRMBGTN6EBF46LYCYSGFAVCNFSM6AAAAAA6CWQZX6VHI2DSMVQWIX3LMV43OSLTON2WKQ3PNVWWK3TUHMYTOOJTGQYTSNJVHA>
> .
> You are receiving this because you modified the open/close state.Message
> ID: ***@***.***>
>

So essentially if I use bytes, then the same exact string content from the client will be received by the server? In other words, if I pass "£#@-+&\0", those exact same bytes will be received by the server, including the null terminator? The main thing is that the bytes stream is represented as a string in c++ rather than bytes array like C# for example? Also in this case, is the string size going to include the null terminator?

> those exact same bytes will be received by the server, including the null terminator

This is really getting at C++'s string semantics.

If you write const char* c = "x\0\0"; thats a char[4]: 'x' followed by 2 \0 bytes that were typed, followed by another \0 byte as the implicit null terminator. If you do strlen(c) it will give back 1 because the way C's strlen works is that it just counts characters until it sees a \0 char.

The way std::string works is that it has a .length, it holds that number of chars as data, and it also stores that with a \0 byte immediately after (for some amount of backwards compatibility with C functions). When you write std::string s = "somestring";  the right hand side is a C string and it it gets converted into a C++ string approximately like {.chars=s, .length=strlen(s)}

If you write std::string s = "x\0";  per above that literal is a char[3] with 'x' and 2 '\0'. Assigning that to an std::string will take strlen() and construct a C++ string with length=1. If you use that string with gRPC the 1 bytes would be sent on the wire regardless of your protobuf type is string or bytes. When you read the 1 bytes string on the other side it will be placed back into an std::string which stores that 1 byte of data and always separately puts a '\0' char one-past-the-end.

But std::string can have null bytes, you just can't construct one from simple implicit conversion from a C string. If you  instead write std::string s("x\0", 2) it will construct a std::string of length 2, where the contents of the string will be an 'x' followed by one '\0'. This string's held data will be 2 bytes, 2 bytes would be sent over the wire, when a server receives it and puts it into an std::string that will hold the 2 bytes of data (and it will put that data in memory with another '\0' one-past-the-end of the data).

> if I pass "£#@-+&\0",

If you write:
  std::string s = "\A3" "x\0";    You'll have a constructed a length=2 std::string which, if those bytes were interpreted as Latin-1 would conceptually be "£x". gRPC will reject this on a string-type field because it is not valid utf-8.

  std::string s("\A3" "x\0", 3); You'll have constructed a length=3 std::string which has a \0 byte in it. Again Latin-1, meanig it would only be usable with 'bytes'.

  std::string s("\xC2\A3" "x\0") ; You'll have constructed a length=3 std::string, if those bytes are interpreted as utf-8 would be "£x". gRPC would accept this for either bytes or string field.

  std::string s("£x");  This is basically ambiguous source code and so "what happens when I type this into my .cpp file" won't have any single answer. In reality you as the developer have constructed a string and 'choose' either case 1 or 3 above, but when you're looking at your source in the editor you literally can't "see" what choice that is because it depends on hidden state like the encoding of the .cc's file itself. When handling Unicode in C++ it is the reality that the developer must simply "know" the encoding of any of their strings, and also know the encoding required by any libraries they send the string to and handle conversions if they don't match. Since the literal in a .cpp file is obscure in what encoding it is, if you type the literal that way it will likely be difficult for you to long term handle correctness of your code.

title: Protobuf/Gradle Case Sensitivity Issue on macOS - class x is public should be declared in a file named x.java
body:
I encountered an issue with Protobuf and Gradle on macOS, which I believe may be related to case sensitivity of file names. When using two Protobuf message types, ChecklistItemMsg and CheckListItemMsg, where the only difference is the letter 'L' case, the Gradle build process fails on macOS but works fine on Linux.

```
message ChecklistItemMsg {
}
```

```
message CheckListItemMsg {
}
```

**error:** class ChecklistItemMsg is public, should be declared in a file named ChecklistItemMsg.java
public final class ChecklistItemMsg extends
             ^

Expected Behavior:
I expected that the Gradle build process would generate two Java files, one for each of the .proto files. Specifically, it should generate ChecklistItemMsg.java and CheckListItemMsg.java.

Actual Behavior:
However, on macOS, the build process only generates one of the expected files (e.g., CheckListItemMsg.java), while the other file (ChecklistItemMsg.java) is missing. This results in a build error because the missing file is referenced in the code.


**Platform Information:**

- Laptop: Macbook Pro with M2 chip
- Operating System: macOS [Version]
- Development Environment: IntelliJ IDEA 2023.2.4
- Java Version: OpenJDK 17
- Protobuf Version: 3.x
- Gradle: Embedded with the IDE


**Additional Information:**

- I've verified that the issue is specific to macOS as the build process works as expected on a Linux system.
- I had to change the name of one of the messages to resolve the issue, which is not an ideal solution.
- It appears that the issue is related to the case sensitivity of file names in the macOS file system.

nodes.body:
Looks like you can tweak the case sensitivity for mac per: https://support.apple.com/guide/disk-utility/file-system-formats-dsku19ed921c/mac

I would probably recommend renaming these messages anyways. I'm assuming this is with `option java_multiple_files = true;` to get the per-message files? I think you would also avoid this problem if setting that to false. 

FYI, Protobuf gradle is also not owned by us -- you may want to file a ticket to https://github.com/google/protobuf-gradle-plugin for anything gradle specific though this seems like it probably isn't.

title: [bazel] Automate publishing releases to Bazel's central registry
body:
Currently https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/releases has many releases beyond what currently appears on https://registry.bazel.build/modules/protobuf, which is currently 10mo old.

We could attempt to keep this updated manually, but like many processes that live in OSS, it will be easy for Googler maintainers to miss this.

Fortunately the Bazel community already created a GitHub app, https://github.com/bazel-contrib/publish-to-bcr/ . With a bit of configuration in this repo, and after "installing" that app to the repo, then every release will be automatically published as a pull request to https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel-central-registry/pulls

I'm happy to take on this work, just filing the issue first to have a place for discussion. Note that we may need a couple of extra releases when we "launch" in case of mistakes in the automation which are hard to test ahead of time.
FYI @comius @thesayyn

title: Fork of rules_ruby
body:
Every Bazel user of this repo depends on ruby, due to an eager `load` statement evaluated during Bazel's loading phase
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/30f157529d660bdb36ec3ed5abeaa50cec2d4e5f/protobuf.bzl#L5

However, this doesn't depend on a canonical rules_ruby which could be placed in the Bazel Central Registry, rather it's a protocolbuffers-team specific fork:

https://github.com/protocolbuffers/rules_ruby

which all bazel users are getting in their workspace due to
https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/30f157529d660bdb36ec3ed5abeaa50cec2d4e5f/protobuf_deps.bzl#L115

This seems like a pretty major tech debt in this repo, and inhibits the task of providing protocol buffers on Bazel's registry, as I don't think we want your fork to be registered as the canonical rules_ruby, since you probably aren't offering to take the maintenance burden.

Note that the current entry https://registry.bazel.build/modules/protobuf/21.7 doesn't have this problem since the rules_ruby load statement didn't appear until later, introduced by https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/10525

I'll try cutting this load by moving everything ruby-related under the //ruby package.  It still means bzlmod users won't be able to use the ruby well-known-types, but at least it makes the dependency graph satisfiable.

nodes.body: @mkruskal-google maybe you could give some more context about the decision to fork rules_ruby and whether you had any long-term plans for getting off that fork, or finding a maintainer for it?

The reason we forked this is because we couldn't find any canonical rules_ruby.  IIRC at the time there was some issue with bazelruby's.  I vaguely recall it being deprecated/unmaintained?  or maybe it wasn't endorsed by Bazel?

Anyway, if there is a canonical rules_ruby now we'd be happy to switch to it (and maybe upstream our changes), although it would likely take some time (@zhangskz FYI).  Would renaming this to something more clearly internal unblock this for now?

I don't think the situation has improved that there's a single canonical rules_ruby. I just learned that the selenium team has Yet Another One https://github.com/p0deje/rules_ruby

Renaming is only slightly helpful to disambiguate "this is the rules_ruby maintained by the protocolbuffers team". The problem will remain that yours will be the only rules_ruby on the Bazel Central Registry, which will appear to users to be the canonical one. Then you have a really big gap between the level of investment and maintenance that users will expect, vs. what you intend to provide (you call it "clearly internal" but it's not internal at all since all protobuf users depend on it)

I think the ideal answer is for the protobuf repo to have fewer language-ruleset dependencies. I'd like to explore the design space of how we could have no `rules_ruby` here at all, yet still generate `.rb` files and expose them with generic targets such that it's still **possible** (though maybe less ergonomic) for a rules_ruby user to use them in their `ruby_library`.

Do you have any "downstream" project that consumes the ruby WKT where I could verify whether some protobuf change can still work for users?

I don't know of any downstream projects using ruby (and I would expect most don't use Bazel), but our CI is heavily dependent on rules_ruby to actually test it.  We do generate the `.rb` sources too [here](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/protobuf.bzl#L524), although I'm not sure that helps much here
I think the best answer here would be for Bazel folks to converge on a canonical rules_ruby, and then have people migrate to it.  Having none of them in the central registry seems like a big problem

See the linked issue for that convergence. Maybe it can be funded by the rules authors SIG.

As a short term answer, if you really only need a rules_ruby in order to test with CI, then I think we should do a refactoring so that it's a "dev dependency" and not exposed to protobuf's users. Something like https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/pull/14570
I'd be more than happy to move bazelruby/rules_ruby to the main org.
I have been working on rules_ruby for the last week, I'm disappointed no one from the protobuf team replied here to indicate you had a different solution in mind.

I had no idea there were so many forks.

Honestly when I started this project I was hoping Yugui would be my partner
in crime :)

But she ended up living in Japan and is very busy with something completely
not Bazel :)

title: C# documentation differs from actual FieldMask proto
body:
The [C# protobuf.dev documentation](https://protobuf.dev/reference/csharp/api-docs/class/google/protobuf/well-known-types/field-mask.html#class_google_1_1_protobuf_1_1_well_known_types_1_1_field_mask) states:
`If a repeated field is specified for an update operation, the existing repeated values in the target resource will be overwritten by the new values.`
whereas the [FieldMask proto](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/field_mask.proto) states:
`If a repeated field is specified for an update operation, new values will
be appended to the existing repeated field in the target resource.`

The C# documentation also says:
`If a sub-message is specified in the last position of the field mask for an update operation, then the existing sub-message in the target resource is overwritten.`
whereas the FieldMask documentation says:
`If a sub-message is specified in the last position of the field mask for an
update operation, then new value will be merged into the existing sub-message
in the target resource.`

Is this difference in documentation intentional, or should the C# docs match the protobuf ones?

nodes.body:
It looks like protobuf.dev does not have the latest documentation. If you look at the [C# actual code](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/csharp/src/Google.Protobuf/WellKnownTypes/FieldMask.pb.cs) it's up-to-date.

I know a while ago there was a problem regenerating the documentation for the web site - I don't know whether that's still the case. I'll find the relevant person and check with them.
@Logofile Are you the right person to check what the status is here?
Generating docs is still a work in progress. Yes, I'm the right person to assign this bug to.

title: Correctly pick up & use `Protobuf_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE` in cross-compilation
body:
It seems that when using `find_package(Protobuf CONFIG)`, any eventual setting of `Protobuf_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE` is ignored.

This makes it hard for us in conda-forge, because `find_package(Protobuf CONFIG)` is necessary to avoid picking up CMake's own implementation of finding protobuf (and prefer an up-to-date `protobuf-config.cmake`; which is necessary for correctly linking abseil for example).

On the other hand, we simply _must_ cross-compile on several architectures (e.g. no osx-arm64 runners at scale), and so if `Protobuf_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE` gets ignored (which carefully points to the build environment that matches the arch or the agent, and not the target environment for the final binary) we run into `Bad CPU type in executable` when it calls the wrong `protoc`.

The work-around we have come up with (and keep reinventing) in several places boils down to (courtesy @traversaro):
```diff
 find_package(Protobuf CONFIG)
 if(Protobuf_FOUND)
     message(STATUS "Found protobuf via cmake config")
+    if(Protobuf_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE)
+      set_target_properties(protobuf::protoc PROPERTIES
+        IMPORTED_LOCATION_RELEASE "${Protobuf_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE}"
+      )
+    endif()
 else()
     message(WARNING "Falling back to cmake FindProtobuf as Protobuf was not found via CONFIG")
     find_package(Protobuf REQUIRED)
 endif()
```

However, not everyone encountering this issue might be able to investigate and come up with this solution, so we keep running into it. I don't see why this shouldn't be supported out of the box, hence this issue.

**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: 4.24.3
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**

linux/osx

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**

**What did you do?**
Cross-compile a package that requires protoc, pass `-DProtobuf_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE=...` to CMake invocation

**What did you expect to see**

Correct `protoc` (corresponding to `Protobuf_PROTOC_EXECUTABLE`) gets used.

**What did you see instead?**

Wrong `protoc` gets picked up.

**Anything else we should know about your project / environment**

Some examples from conda-forge:
* https://github.com/conda-forge/opencv-feedstock/commit/bbe46049a19e30c96cadbdf07affcaf0b8c6230d
* https://github.com/conda-forge/protozfits-feedstock/commit/e752d336d2aee5a7626330d06f12084c42d94b2b

title: allow to specify underlying type of enum, e.g. uint64
body:
**What language does this apply to?**
It targets the proto3 syntax itself, subsequent it would affect all generated code. 

**Describe the problem you are trying to solve.**
I'd like to have enums with larger numbers than just the implicit 32bit.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
something like the following (anotherthing would be nice to have as well)
```cpp
enum Foo : uint64
{
  none = 0,
  something = 0x8000000000000000,
  anotherthing = 1<<42
};
```

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Instead of setting the bits themself I could encode the bit position and then execute something like `(1<<Foo::something)` but that might look odd in some circumstances and is cumbersome, e.g. `obj.set_foo((1<<Foo::something) | (1<<Foo::otherthing));` Moreover when specifying the bit position the default enum value (mostly `none = 0,`) would actually be a valid thing instead of indicating `void` / nothing.

title: v25.0 regression: `C2370` compile error from `map_field.h` when compiling with `cl.exe` and `/permissive-` option
body:
**What version of protobuf and what language are you using?**
Version: v25.0. Looks like a regression in 95d57237b3059548a98da12cdf28807ffcacad5b.
Language: C++

**What operating system (Linux, Windows, ...) and version?**
Windows 11 ver 22H2 (OS Build 22621.2428)

**What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g., python version or gcc version)**
* Microsoft Visual Studio Community 2022 (64-bit) Version 17.7.0
  * Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.37.32822 for x64
  * cmake version 3.26.4-msvc4

**What did you do?**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
```
"C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\2022\Community\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvarsall.bat" amd64_x86
git clone -b v25.0 https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf.git --recursive
cd protobuf
cmake . -DCMAKE_CXX_STANDARD=20 -Dprotobuf_ABSL_PROVIDER=module
cmake --build . -j
```

**What did you expect to see**
Build succeeds.

**What did you see instead?**
Build fails with the following error.

Hi @chadlwilson. Thanks for reporting the issue.

The addition of the `ffi` and `ffi-compiler` gems to the [dependencies](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/ruby/google-protobuf.gemspec#L22-L23) was intentional, but only for JRuby. They both have first class support for Windows as the host OS. However, there are no test configurations in our CI that exercise the combination of Ruby Protobuf + Windows, so this is the first that we're aware of the problem.

Can you provide additional details about:
* Do both the `ffi` or`ffi-compiler` gems install on your system without issue?
* What compiler is on your system? From the logs, I see `No such file or directory - cc`, but I can't tell if that's a path problem or if a different compiler is installed.

Hiya @JasonLunn 👋

> * Do both the `ffi` or`ffi-compiler` gems install on your system without issue?

Both of these gems seem to have installed OK.

> * What compiler is on your system? From the logs, I see `No such file or directory - cc`, but I can't tell if that's a path problem or if a different compiler is installed.

Well that's kind of the issue. 😅 I don't have a compiler installed on our Windows build machines, deliberately. I also didn't expect a native compiler stack to be on the critical path for a feature documented as optional.

On my side this is a Java and Ruby project. Im trying to compile some sass stylesheets with sass-embedded (needs grpc, protobuf) and every other Ruby gem has proper native gems, pure Java/Ruby variants, or Java variants which download a platform appropriate pre-compiled binary at extension install time.

If this change in behaviour is all deliberate, perhaps this ticket is a won't fix, but I'd suggest at the very least docs need updating as it's a breaking change to the expectation of the build environment given the current logic fails if it can't compile for use of functionality that is supposed to be opt-in?

The feature is optional, but the intention is that JRuby installations would compile the FFI version at installation time, as is the norm for Ruby gems with native extensions. Long term this is the way we see JRuby support in Protobuf going, because it will let us unify on single implementation across CRubies, JRuby, TruffleRuby, and whatver Rubies get popular in the future.

Are you able to install a compiler on your Windows build machines, and let us know if the FFI compiler module works as expected?

> The feature is optional, but the intention is that JRuby installations would compile the FFI version at installation time, as is the norm for Ruby gems with native extensions.

It may be the norm for Ruby gems with native extensions, but this still sounds not great for Java. Perhaps I misunderstand how the gems currently work but it sounds like it's turning the current cross-platform Ruby/Java variant into something architecture dependent which poses other challenges for packaging.

> Are you able to install a compiler on your Windows build machines, and let us know if the FFI compiler module works as expected?

Which compiler/toolchain has been validated for Windows? I previously avoided depending on anything on Windows because it's a pain, _especially_ from JRuby.

> > The feature is optional, but the intention is that JRuby installations would compile the FFI version at installation time, as is the norm for Ruby gems with native extensions.
> 
> It may be the norm for Ruby gems with native extensions, but this still sounds not great for Java. Perhaps I misunderstand how the gems currently work but it sounds like it's turning the current cross-platform Ruby/Java variant into something architecture dependent which poses other challenges for packaging.

The intention is keep the protobuf gem for JRuby (the one with the platform set to `java`) platform independent, and work long term towards making the gem interpreter independent.

Today protobuf releases platform specific gems targeting `java`,`arm64-darwin`, `x64-mingw32`, `x86_64-linux`, `aarch64-linux`, `x64-mingw-ucrt`, `x86-linux`, `x86_64-darwin` and `mingw32`, plus a source only gem used by any other architecture. All of our users on other architectures already have to have a compiler available at installation time to build the native extension part of the gem when they install the from the source gem.

The `java` gem is already about an order of magnitude larger (5M) than the other platform specific gems  (~500K-700K) by download size due to having to embed the protobuf Java implementation's JAR into it. Ruby does not have a mechanism to further differentiate `java`-based interpreters based on their native architecture when it comes to packaging, i.e. there's no such thing as a `java-x64-mingw32` platform so far as gem's are concerned.

My understanding is that while it is technically possible to for us to pre-compile the FFI implementation for *every* architecture we support with binary distributions today and add them all to the gem we package for `java`, this would make our most bloated gem even worse.

We understand that asking users to bring a C compiler is a non-trivial tradeoffs, but there are outstanding upsides in return. The path we're pursuing for JRuby has the potential to simplify our packaging, by allowing all JRuby users to be able to install from the source gem. It has the potential to improve performance by giving JRuby users an implementation backed by the C implementation of upb. As maintainers, we'd be able to remove the entire Java src tree under the ruby directory, and as a result users would enjoy feature parity between CRuby and JRuby for free going forward.
 
> > Are you able to install a compiler on your Windows build machines, and let us know if the FFI compiler module works as expected?
> 
> Which compiler/toolchain has been validated for Windows? I previously avoided depending on anything on Windows because it's a pain, _especially_ from JRuby.

We haven't been testing our Ruby implementation on Windows to date, though this issue has started discussions about what it would take to improve that. In theory, any compiler that FFI supports will do. We can see from looking at their [GitHub Actions](https://github.com/ffi/ffi/actions/runs/6803405742/job/18539459632) that they do some testing with Windows + JRuby.
